Editor: Lakṣmaṇa Śāstrī;

*Śrī-Śrītantrarāja-tantra*.
Initiated and supervised by Śrī Ārthāra Avalana;
edited by Mahāmahopādhyāya Śrī Lakṣmaṇa Śāstrī; in the city of Kalikātā.
It was printed at the Mahāmāyāyantra press by the venerable Siddheśvara Caturdhurīṇa,
for Lujāk Eṇḍa Kāṅ, in the capital city of London.
Published.
Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa.
Now begins the King of Tantras,
together with the commentary *Manoramā*.
Chapter One.
Victorious is Kāla-Vināyaka, who is without beginning or end, independent, the master of the three worlds, eternally pervasive throughout the universe. || 1 ||
The *Manoramā-Ṭīkā* begins. Homage to Śrī Gaṇeśa!
With the first verse, a praise of Vināyaka is performed, which contains within it the meaning of the entire work. Therein:

He is without beginning or end because he is devoid of the beginning and end of time; he is independent, being free from the impulsion of others; he has the three worlds under his own control, meaning the three worlds consisting of the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge are subject to him;
"he triumphs" means he is superior to the universe; and he is unceasing because time flows on continuously.
"Pervading the universe" because he is unconditioned by either space or form. "Time" is the name of the qualifier.

"Vināyaka" means the Lord of Obstacles (*vighneśvara*), or "one whose leader has departed" (*vigatanāyaka*). This is what is meant: Vināyaka, who is thus described as having the nature of time, becomes the most excellent of all; such is he.

The venerable teachers teach that it is indicated here as the meaning of the entire composition’s statement that time, being free from destruction, is the most excellent of all things; thus, the fact that Lalitānityā—who is the ultimate reality in the form of time—is identical with the universe, as well as the practitioner's identity with her, are suggested herein. || 1 ||
O Blessed One! All the tantras were previously spoken by you to me—the sixteen Nityās and the nine tantras in their entirety. (2)
Due to their mutual dependence upon one another, a confusion of understanding arises among them;
therefore, O Lord, tell me that independent system of theirs.
Listen to the Kādimata Tantra, complete and independent of others;
it must be guarded with every effort, for concealment is enjoined by the Tantra.
O Maheśvara, tell me how that system is known by the name Kādimata;
for previously, I understood those two powers to be Kādi and Kālī within that doctrine.
The tantra known by the name Kādikālīmata has been proclaimed by him;
listen now to that which is the king of all tantras and the bestower of all accomplishments. (6)
That power, whose nature is "bhavat" and which begins with the letter "ka," exists for the sake of all accomplishment;
it fashioned the Tantra as I have described it, along with the nine lords of the worlds.
Through her and through them, the Tantra unfolds in every world, age after age;
at the conclusion of the kalpas, she shall go to me along with them.
Now, with seven verses beginning with "O Blessed One" (*atha bhagavan*) and ending with "he should go to me" (*vrajecca mām*),

[the author] teaches the sequence of the introduction to the Tantras. In this context, "all Tantras" refers to the sixty-four Tantras, such as the *Rudrayāmala* and others, as mentioned in the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*.

The nine tantras are known as the *Sundarīhṛdaya*, the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*, the *Candrajñāna*, the *Mātṛkātantra*, the *Saṃmohanatantra*, the *Vāmakeśvara*, the *Bahurūpāṣṭaka*, the *Prastārācintāmaṇi*, and the *Meruprastāra*.

Thus [it is said]. Because of mutual dependence, this is stated by way of accepting the worship of the deities as taught in other tantras. "Vibhrama" means delusion. Regarding those sixteen Nityās: because the instruction is given without depending on others—that is, without adopting the worship of the deities as taught in other tantras—it is said that "concealment is enjoined by the tantra."
The meaning is: "by means of the method of convention (saṅketa) stated in fifty-six verses in the thirty-fifth chapter.

With the nine lords (navanātha), whose essential natures were explained in the second chapter; "he fashioned" means he extended [them]. By that power (śakti) beginning with *ka*; by those nine lords; she should go together with them to me.
At the conclusion of the eons, in the first [period] there is the introduction of the Tantra and so forth; in the second, the maṇḍala of the Lord;
in the third, there shall be the eternal extraction; and in those two [periods], the worship of Lalitā.
In the sixth [day], there shall be occasional (naimittika) and optional (kāmya) worship;
Kāmeśvarī is in the seventh, and thereafter Bhagamālinī.
Nityaklinnā is remembered in the ninth, Bheruṇḍā in the tenth;
Vahnivāsinī is in the eleventh, and Vajreśvarī is considered [the next].
In the thirteenth [day] there shall be Dūtī; in the fourteenth she is Tvaritā.
From Kulasundarī onwards, in the other [days], Nityānityā is in the sixteenth.
Then there should be Nīlapatākā; Vijayā is in the eighteenth [position], and after that, the one named Sarvamaṅgalanityā and Jvālāmālinī. (13)
In the twenty-first [chapter] is Citrā; immediately following that is Kurukullā;
in the twenty-third is Vārāhī, and the meditations follow immediately after that.
In the twenty-fifth [chapter] is the attainment of the Mātṛkās; in the twenty-sixth, the majesty of the mantras;
in the twenty-seventh, the forms of the breaths; and in the twenty-eighth, however, the state of the worlds.
Immediately following this, the preparation of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the ritual of oblation (*homa*) take place thereafter.
The meaning is that the power of the letters beginning with *ka* (the *kādi-śakti*), together with the nine lords (*nava-nātha*) and the Tantra, remains dissolved within me.
With ten verses beginning with "ādya" and ending with "saṅgraha," he teaches those chapters and their meanings: in two places, namely the fourth and fifth; subsequently in the eighth;
and then in the twelfth.
(On page 4: In the thirty-first [chapter], and beyond that, there are the highly efficacious fire-oblations (homas) for the fulfillment of specific desires. || 16 ||
In the thirty-third chapter, however, are the diagrams according to their different results;
in the thirty-fourth, the names; and in the thirty-fifth, the underlying rationale for them.

In the thirty-sixth [chapter], there is the description of one's own self; these chapters consist of the essential forms [of reality]. There shall be one hundred verses for each chapter; such is the compendium of the Tantra. (18)
Handsome, pleasant-faced, pure, easy to approach, and a knower of many tantras; free from doubt, a cutter of doubts, and without expectations—such a one is considered a guru. (19)
Beauty is faultlessness; furthermore, in physical form it is amiability, speaking with a smile first, clarity, and straightforward conduct. (20)
It is easily accessible, free from pride, characterized by contentment and manifoldness;
it is free from doubt regarding the awakening to reality because it brings about the realization of that power. (21)
Freedom from expectations, lack of greed, gravity, and speaking what is beneficial—one should know such a person as a true guru; any other brings suffering to the disciple. (22)

Endowed with the first four [qualities], one who possesses faith and a very firm resolve [attains the result] in the fifteenth [moment]; then in the seventeenth; in the next, the nineteenth; from there, in the twentieth;
in the immediately following, the twenty-second; in the one after that, the twenty-fourth; and in the next, the twenty-ninth.

Above that, in the thirtieth; above that, in the thirty-second. Of this [practice], such as worship and so forth. Their essential forms (tattva-vigrahas) are characterized by the number thirty-six. || 9 || 10 || 11 || 12 || 13 || 14 ||

With these four verses beginning with "sundara" and ending with "duḥkhada," he teaches the characteristics of a teacher (*deśika*). In this context, "contentment" (*santoṣa*) is fullness, arising from the exposition of reality (*tattva*). "The other" is a teacher who lacks the aforementioned characteristics; such a person brings suffering to the disciple.
The meaning is: by means of the theft of wealth, physical suffering, delusion of the intellect, and so forth. || 19 || 20 || 21 || 22 ||
Free from greed, with steady limbs, acting with circumspection, and having conquered the senses. || 23 ||
A disciple should be one who possesses faith and firm devotion toward the guru, the mantra, and the deity;
such a person is a true disciple, whereas any other causes suffering to the guru.
When the guru speaks, one should always utter these words with respect: "Be gracious, O Lord! O God! and likewise, "So be it. (25)

Having prostrated, he should sit at the side; likewise, he should depart only with permission. He should serve while looking toward the [teacher's] face and perform whatever is commanded with reverence.
One should not speak untruth in his presence, nor should one engage in excessive chatter;
likewise, one should avoid lust, anger, greed, pride, laughter, and flattery. (27)
Fickleness, crookedness, jests, lamentation, the giving of debts, as well as the non-giving [of what is due], and the buying and selling of goods; || 28 ||
A disciple who desires prosperity should never act in opposition to the guru;
since the guru is Śiva himself in visible form, one should worship him by praising and prostrating before him. (29)
"Just as [it is] with the deity, so it is with the mantra; just as it is with the mantra, so it is with the guru.
With these two verses beginning with "by four" and ending with "of the guru," he teaches the characteristics of the disciple.
In that regard, [the disciple] is endowed with the first four [qualities], which are stated as the characteristics of the guru.

He is endowed with the four qualifiers beginning with "beauty" (sundaratva). The other [type of teacher], being devoid of the aforementioned qualities, causes suffering through such things as bringing dishonor upon the guru, causing misfortune, and inflicting mental and physical distress. || 22 || 23 || 24 ||

With these five verses beginning with "gurūcyamāna" and ending with "bhajet," he teaches the sequence of conduct for a disciple. In that regard, "stuti" refers to praise of oneself and others; "jihmāni" means crooked things; "paridevanam" means lamentation or idle chatter; "bhūṣṇuḥ" means desiring to live; and "bhajet" means one should serve or attend upon. || 25 || 26 ||

O Dear One! Through these ten verses beginning with "Just as [toward] the God" and ending with "endowed with devotion," Pūjyapāda has taught that the sequence of devotion toward one's own self is exactly the same as that toward the Guru. (30)
On the birthday of the Guru, one should perform a festival with devotion,
including special worship, feeding the yogis, and honoring his feet.
When [the deity] has pervaded and gone afar, one should worship the venerable one among the elder brothers and others;
when he is at a distance, constant service is performed in a single location according to the sequence of *yojanas*.
Starting from one [yojana] and increasing by seasons, at a distance of six yojanas within a year, service consists of not going too far from there and the fulfillment of his commands. (33)
One should worship his seat, bed, garment, ornament, sandals, as well as his shadow, his wife, and whatever else is dear to him. (34)
In a single village, one should not perform a separate worship without permission.
When the object of worship arrives during the course of the worship, one should bow and announce one's presence.
When told, "Perform the remainder," he should do so; if not, then by his command, he too should perform that remainder with an unwavering mind. (36)
If, during the midst of worship, the Guru, the object of worship, or others should arrive, this is the prescribed course of action: one should not observe silence in their presence.

One should not perceive the Guru as a mortal; for if one were to so perceive him, [the text] teaches the procedure for his dismissal (*pāstikrama*). In that regard, when he has departed to another world through his pervasive power (*vyāpti*), or when he has gone far away—having traveled to a region at a distance characterized by a number of *yojanas* greater than the six *yojanas* to be mentioned hereafter.

By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), he indicates those [relations] to be mentioned later, such as "the elder brother of the guru" and so forth, in relation to the elder brothers and others. Regarding the case where the teacher and the disciple reside in a single location— such as a village, city, district, hamlet, small town, or port— and so on.

The syntactical connection is that [the deity] is situated at a distance measured in *yojanas*. "In a single village" is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the previously mentioned cities and so forth. "Separate worship" refers to [worship] of others excluding the Guru.
Success will never be attained through mantras or through the worship of deities. (38)
One should perform his worship with the mantra exactly as prescribed;
having understood that [worship] thoroughly from its respective chapter, one should do so endowed with devotion. (39)
For those who are eternal and belong to the three cities (Tripura), the [astrological] divisions such as the *aṃśaka* and so forth are not to be considered;
nevertheless, something is stated here for the sake of accomplishing rites such as *abhicāra* (sorcery).
In the constellations beginning with Aśvinī, one should join the first four letters, excluding the *bindu* and the *visarga*; however, the *bindu* and *visarga* are present in all of them.
One should count by means of that syllable of the mantra and the first letter of the name,
wherever the sixth, eighth, or twelfth [syllable] occurs.
The first letter of the enemy's mantra and so forth would be [the same as] his own; by that, harm would come to him.
This applies when [the planets] occupy the seventh, fifth, or third positions from the zodiac signs and asterisms other than those [of the enemy]. || 43 ||

One should know that even for those seeking spiritual goals (*sādhya*), such as the *aṃśaka* and so forth, or for the sake of bestowing grace upon deities, one should not perform the worship oneself; rather, it should be performed by another who is worthy of worship, or by someone else who has acquired the knowledge in his presence, and so forth—in any one of these cases mentioned in the second chapter of that [same] chapter. (29–33)

With twenty-two verses beginning with "Of the eternal ones" (*nityānām*) and ending with "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*), he teaches the divisions of the *aṃśakas* and so forth for the mantras. In that context, in the phrase "the *aṃśakas* and so forth" (*aṃśakādayaḥ*), the word *aṃśaka* denotes the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and the like; by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the calculation of the *siddha*-wheel and the rest, as well as [the status of] debt (*ṛṇa*)—
The term "ṛṇi" and so forth are explained as follows: it means within the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī and within the zodiac signs beginning with Aries.

"Excluding the bindu and visarga" means devoid of the nasal dot (bindu), the visarga, and the letter 'kṣa'. "Caturaḥ" is the masculine accusative plural. The remaining word is "the letters beginning with 'a'."

The *bindu* and the emission (*sarga*), however, are all-pervasive; because the *bindu* and the emission are the nature of Śiva and Śakti, they possess the state of being the self of all. Therefore, by means of the sequence of syllables joined within the groups (*rāśi*), this is what is meant: for every single syllable, thirty-three *ghaṭikās* consisting of three quarters arise, and by those [units].
One should know the portion belonging to the goal and the means (p.
8), for they have been urged [to act] because they are devoid of the knowledge of reality. || 44 ||
By the application of five lines running east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east, sixteen squares are formed here; in these, one should write the syllables in their proper sequence.
One should indeed arrange those [mandalas] in sequence by dividing each into four parts;
the first [mandala] is in the first of the first [sections], and likewise the second in the first of the second.
One should arrange a second [syllable] from another source, and likewise imagine yet another;
one should write each respective fifth syllable within those various squares.
"In this way, one should draw [the diagram] up to the stage of *kṣānti* within the four squares.
Thus, one should calculate, beginning from the numerical value of the first letter of the enemy's name and ending with the numerical value of the first letter of the mantra.

The meaning is that one should perform rites such as *abhicāra* (sorcery) against an enemy using mantras beginning with the letters situated in the sixth, eighth, and twelfth signs (*rāśi*). The phrase "as stated regarding the signs" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Regarding the asterisms (*ṛkṣa*), namely Aśvinī and so forth;
regarding the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), [one should act] as before with those situated in the seventh, fifth, and third [houses].

The meaning is that, having calculated from the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) corresponding to the first letter of the enemy's name up to the lunar mansion corresponding to the final letter of the mantra, one should perform rites such as *abhicāra* against him using mantras consisting of the initial letters found in the third, fifth, or seventh lunar mansions from that point. "Of the targets" (*sādhyānām*), and so forth.

The meaning is that among the three types of practitioners to be described later—namely, the *sādhya*, the *sādhaka*, and the *siddha*—the first [the *sādhya*] lacks the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*); therefore, one must attend to the previously mentioned [methods], such as the *aṃśaka* and others, for the sake of his grace. || 40 || 41 || 42 || 43 ||
Regarding the instruction "one should write the letters in sequence," the meaning of the word *krama* (sequence) is demonstrated here:

having designated sixteen squares by dividing them into groups of four in a clockwise direction, one should assign them to the four classes of *sādhya*, *siddha*, *susiddha*, and *ari* which are to be described; [beginning] with the first of the first [groups].

One should write the first syllable in the first square of the first group of four. In the first [square] of the second [group], that is, in the first square of the second group of four according to the sequence previously stated— meaning one should act here exactly as was done for the first square of the preceding four groups— one writes the second [syllable], which is the letter *ā*.

One should write. And in the first cell of the third group of four, as previously described, one should write another, namely the third vowel *i*. In the same manner, one should arrange the others as well, just as in the three preceding groups of four. "Another" refers to the fourth group of four. The word "api" (also) is used in the sense of inclusion (*samuccaya*). One should arrange them, that is, write them.
The fourth *ī* is that which is seen in the square where the first letter of its own name is stated to be among the four groups of four [vowels] previously mentioned. (48)
One should count from the *siddha* [category] onwards until the first syllable of the mantra is reached.
Through recitation, the *siddhasiddha* becomes accomplished; the *siddhasādhya* becomes accomplished through double that amount. (49)

The meaning is that one should write it in the very first square. "In those respective squares" refers to the second squares of each of the four sets of four mentioned. "Those respective fifth [letters]" refers to the fifth letters among the syllables written in the first, first, second, and third squares.
The meaning is that one should write [them]. Thus, as before, one should write the fifth letters of the second group of cells into the third group of cells;
and one should write the fifth letters of the third group of cells into the fourth group of cells. In each of the aforementioned sets of four, [one should proceed likewise].
Furthermore, by repeatedly writing the fifth vowel in each cell, one should write [the sequence] up to the letter *kṣa* in all four sets of four cells. When it has been written in this manner,
there are the four letters *a*, *ka*, *tha*, and *ha* in the first cell of the first set of four.
In its second square are the three syllables *uṃ apa*; in its third square are the three syllables *ḷ jha ma*;

in its fourth square are the three syllables *o ḍa va*. In the first square of the second group of four are the four syllables *ā kha da la*; in its second square are the three syllables *u ca pha*; and in its third square are the three *ḷ*s.
Thus, three [syllables] in the first cell of the third group of four; "oḍhaśa"—three [syllables] in its fourth cell;

"igadhakṣa"—four [syllables] in the first cell of the second group of four; "ṛcchava"—three [syllables] in its second cell; "eṭara"—three [syllables] in its third cell; "aṃṇaṣa"—three [syllables] in its fourth cell; [and] in the first cell of the fourth group of four...
In the first [square], "idhana" consists of three [syllables]. In the second square, "ṛjabha" consists of three [syllables]. In the third square, "aiṭhala" consists of three [syllables].
In the fourth square, "aḥ tasa" consists of three [syllables]. When written in this manner, these are the syllables situated above the syllables of the first group of four squares.
They are seen in the squares of the second group of four in their respective order.

The meaning of the term "the previously mentioned order" is that the fifty-one letters, beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, are seen within those sixteen squares in a disordered sequence. || 46 || 47 ||

With six verses beginning with *siddhasiddha* and ending with *suniścitam*, he teaches the results of those sixteen syllables of the grid. In that context, "other than this" (*ato'nyathā*) means other than *susiddha-sādhya*; the meaning is that which follows immediately after is *susiddha*.
In the case of an abhicāra rite against an enemy, if it leads to one's own ruin— meaning that at the time of performing the abhicāra against the enemy,
if the abhicāra mantra is *susiddha* or *susiddhatara*, it results in the death of that very performer of the abhicāra.
In the yogas beginning with *ṛṇasiddha*, and especially in the bestowing of mantras: (p.
10) when *siddha* is attained, *susiddha* brings success; *siddhāri* destroys those born of one’s own lineage;
through great affliction, *sādhya-siddha* [brings results]; and *sādhyasādhya* causes extreme suffering. (50)
A *sādhya* [mantra] that is well-mastered (*susiddha*) bestows prosperity through worship, while a *sādhya* that is an enemy (*sādhyāri*) takes away one's own fortune.
A *susiddha-siddha* [mantra], moreover, grants the desired fruit through mere study. (51)
One who is "well-accomplished" (susiddha) becomes "to be accomplished" (sādhya) through recitation and other means for the sake of success; otherwise, it would be different.
But one who is "well-accomplished" (susiddha) is already established [in success], having exerted effort in previous births.
Therefore, one who would recite the mantra for the sake of accomplishing all siddhis,
or likewise for the malevolent rites against an enemy, should do so only if it does not lead to his own ruin.
One who is well-accomplished (susiddha) will certainly destroy his own family without exception;
one accomplished by an enemy (arisiddha) will kill his son, and one to be accomplished by an enemy (arisādhya) will kill his own wife.
An *ari* (enemy) mantra, even if well-perfected, gradually brings about the destruction of one's lineage;
an *aryari* (enemy-of-an-enemy) mantra, however, certainly destroys one’s own self as soon as it is attained. (55)

Starting from the first letter of the name up to the final letter of the mantra, one should divide [the sequence] into three parts and split them with the vowels; the other [method] is the reverse of that.
One should utter the well-known name by which she awakens when she is fast asleep.

With these six verses beginning with "The first syllable of the name" and ending with "from all sides," [the author] teaches the relationship between the practitioner and the mantra as creditor and debtor, as well as their respective fruits. In that regard:

The meaning is that one should count the letters of the mantra and so forth in the order of the *mātṛkā* alphabet, beginning from the first letter of one's own name up to the first letter of the mantra. Having divided that number into three parts, one should multiply it by three. By the word "vowels" (*svaraiḥ*), the numbers sixteen, seven, and three are expressed. Among these—

The number seven is accepted according to tradition. One should divide [the sequence] by that number and extract the remainder. Other than that, one should take the letters of the Mātṛkā starting from the first letter of the mantra up to the first letter of one's own name. This is the reverse order with respect to the seven.

The meaning is that one should bring [the result] by increasing [the count] by three. This is what is being said: the method for knowing the creditor-debtor relationship (*uttamarṇādhamarṇatva*) between all *vidyās* and *mantras*, as well as all those to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth, begins from the first letter of one's own name according to the order of the recitation of the *mātṛkā* letters.
Having performed [the rite] for the intended object, one should be known as a debtor; if one is already a debtor, one should employ the supreme mantra.
If one is oneself a debtor, one should abandon that mantra, because one was previously a debtor. (57)
Tell me, how is there a state of indebtedness for the mantras and for the practitioners?
When there is practice performed in a previous birth, why does sin cause the failure to obtain the fruit? (58)
When evil is destroyed, there is the attainment of fruit; through the dissolution of the body in due time, one becomes free from debt.
Merely by its reception, the previously [received] mantra leads to success.
That man who, having received the mantra from his perfected guru, became a possessor of supernatural powers, disregarded the pride of wealth and obtained enjoyment through the mantra. (60)
One should be known as a debtor to the six mantras; devotion to them is the prerequisite.
Therefore, the purification of that debt must be performed by everyone, in every way. (61)
Also with rudrākṣas called padma, with putrajīva, with kucandana, with crystal, with coral, with pearls, and with those made of gold.
Having counted the syllables preceding the first syllable [of the mantra] and multiplied that number by three,

one should divide it by seven and ascertain the remainder; likewise, having counted from the first syllable of the mantra up to the first syllable of one's own name and increased that number by seven.
"Having brought [the total] by three, one should know what remains. By the words "having done so" (*kṛtvā*) and so forth, this is what is meant:

the debtor (*adhamarṇa*) is the one possessing the higher number among the remaining numbers mentioned in the preceding verse, while the creditor (*uttamarṇa*) is the one possessing the lower number. In that case, if the mantra belongs to the debtor...

Since there is an abundance of fruit when one is a debtor [to the mantra], whereas it is fruitless when one is a creditor, one should therefore abandon mantras and *vidyās* that act as creditors and accept only those that act as debtors. This applies to all practitioners (*sādhakas*) and all objects of practice (*sādhayas*).
"From all" means among all mantras and *vidyās*. 56–62.
With these four verses beginning with "rudrākṣaiḥ" and ending with "japam," he instructs on the rosary and other implements; therein, "kucandanaiḥ" means with red sandalwood. 63 || 64 ||
A rosary made of silver yields progressively greater results for the Guru as one proceeds from the beginning to the end;
indeed, the rosary is constituted by the letters from *a* to *kṣa* according to their true significance. (63)
One should recite the Mātṛkā with the letters interspersed, both in forward and reverse order.
Thus, one becomes endowed with all virtues and a possessor of all accomplishments.
One should perform the act of recitation with the tips of the fingers, excluding the index fingers;
or one may count the recitation by touching the joints of the fingers.

If an act is performed quickly, whether prescribed or forbidden, without prior conscious intent, one should recite the Vidyā a hundred times; by that means, one is certainly liberated from that sin. (66)
To pacify the faults arising from the transgression of obligatory rites, one should recite the Vidyā one hundred times;
in the case of transgressing occasional rites, one should then recite it one thousand times.
With a pure body and face, wearing white garments and remaining clean,
he should turn his face away from censuring others and from gazing upon deities.
Free from desire for the suffering of others' wives or the land, endowed with compassion for all people, discerning, and free from longing. || 69 ||
He who is a believer, devoted to his guru, and constantly endowed with self-restraint,
being possessed of all virtues, shall attain the perfection of knowledge.
For one who possesses knowledge but conducts themselves otherwise for a long time, there will be no success anywhere, at any time, or in any way. (71)
With the two verses beginning with *abuddhi* and ending with *tadā*, he teaches the expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

With the four verses beginning with *viśuddha* and ending with *kathañcana*, he teaches the conduct of the practitioner (*sādhaka*). In that regard, [it concerns] the visions of the deity (*devatā-darśana*) and within the deities themselves.
Averse to censures; [and] regarding philosophical systems such as the Vaidika, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and so forth. (69–72)

(13) At the beginning there is *yoga*, and at the end there is *pallava*; *sampuṭa* occurs when these two are joined. *Grathana* consists of alternating [the two], while *vidarbha* is formed by doubling [each] with an interval.
Having recognized the defects of a mantra, the Guru should eliminate them instantly;
otherwise, that Guru will certainly destroy the disciple before long. (73)

With the verse beginning "In the beginning, yoga... and so forth, he teaches the method for applying the rites to be accomplished (*sādhya-karma*) within the mantras. In this regard, what is being stated is that the term "yoga" refers to the application of the practitioner's goals and the rites to be accomplished at the very beginning of both mantras and vidyās.
At the end of the mantra and the vidyā, due to the previously mentioned conjunction, it is designated as "pallava" (sprout).
At the beginning and end of both the mantra and the vidyā, due to the previously mentioned conjunction, it is designated as "saṃpuṭa" (enclosure).
[This occurs] through the mutual blending of each individual syllable of the mantra, the vidyā, and those previously mentioned.

"Grathana" (interlacing) is the technical term. "Vidarbha" (piercing) is the term for the mutual joining of pairs of syllables between the mantra and the *vidyā* and those previously mentioned; that [vidarbha] is of three kinds:
one method is to insert each single syllable of the *sādhya* (the object of the rite) between two syllables of the mantra.
Between every two syllables of the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), one should join a single syllable from the mantra and so forth;

this is the other [method]. Between every two syllables of the mantra and so forth, one should join two syllables each from the name of the one to be accomplished and so forth; this is yet another. Thus, there are three varieties. || 73 ||

With these nine verses beginning with "The defects of mantras" and ending with "the guru," he teaches the defects of mantras and so forth. In that context, in the phrase "he is the guru," the word "he" (sa) refers to the mantra;
for it reaches both ears simultaneously through being recited by two people other than oneself, due to excessive repetition.
From the recitation of mantras for minor deities together with mantras for superior deities, there arises fear for the minor deity;

it becomes arrogant and does not face the practitioner. "Obtained without the ritual" means acquired without the rites of initiation (*dīkṣā*) and so forth. "Residing in the compartments of enmity" refers to those residing in the four compartments belonging to the previously mentioned group of enemies.

"Vanquished" means defeated. "Due to the abundance of karma" means due to the abundance of the practitioner's evil deeds in previous lives. "Lacking *ha*" means devoid of the letters *ha* and *sa*. "Devoid of essence" means lacking strength. "Incomplete in form" means having deficient syllables in what is to be expressed. "Severed."
Because they occupy a single part of the great whole (mahāvayavin). They are "stilled" (stambhitāḥ) regarding the granting of what is desired by the practitioner.

They are "nasalized" (sānunāsikāḥ), consisting mostly of the final syllables within the groups of stops (sparśavarga). By "inappropriate application" (akālaviniyoga), there is the application of the mantra at times when it should be asleep, such as during [the periods of] recitation and so forth. [This applies] to mantras.
The characteristics of sleep and awakening are now stated:
mantras consisting primarily of the syllables *praṇava* (oṃ), *kṣa*, *ra*, and *ha* are fiery (*āgneya*).
Mantras consisting primarily of lunar (*indu*) syllables are gentle (*saumya*). Regarding the practitioner’s breath in the right nostril...
When [the breath] flows fully in the fire-channel (āgneya), O Goddess, listen with a concentrated mind to its remedy;
I shall explain the method of that remedy according to the principles of the yogas. (74)

A mantra that reaches six ears is burnt; it becomes terrified by excessive recitation; it is arrogant when obtained through improper rites; and those that reside in the "enemies" and "enmity" syllables are its adversaries.
The young are characterized by short syllables, while the old are endowed with long syllables;
those who have been overcome by the abundance of karma are devoid of strength and lack vitality.
This is the time of awakening for the *saumya* (lunar) mantras and others; for the others, the *āgneya* (fiery) mantras and so forth, it is precisely the time of sleep.
When the breath flows through the left nostril, it is the time of awakening for the *saumya* mantras and others, and at that same time, it is the time of sleep for the other *āgneya* mantras.

The meaning is that a practitioner who employs mantras for desired tasks without understanding all of this becomes one who causes their [the mantras'] fainting and affliction; "fainted" means rendered inactive— that is, rendered incapable of activity in accomplishing the practitioner's intended goal.

The rivers flow toward the practitioners as if they were asleep; this is because, from the day the mantra was received from the Guru, they have not accepted the practice according to the sequence prescribed by him. Here, the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) is inconceivable due to its divine nature. The mantras become intoxicated for one whose habit is correct worship.

The meaning is that they accomplish both the goals and the misfortunes of the practitioner equally. "From reciting on leaves" means that, without having acquired [the knowledge] from the mouth of a guru according to the prescribed rule, one sees the mantras and so forth on some random leaves and performs recitation (*japa*) by reciting them there. "By other letters" means [letters] other than the syllables of the mantra.

By those external [syllables]. Their occurrence there may happen either through the practitioner's lack of attention or through misreading; they are "impaled" (kīlitāḥ), just as a stake called "Time" (kālākhya) takes on various forms when driven into trees, walls, and so forth, so too by the syllables produced through the similarity of names and the practitioner's lack of attention.

The meaning is "pinned down" (kīlitāḥ). The meaning is "obstructed," "restrained," or "warded off" (ruddhāḥ niruddhāḥ nivāritāḥ). "With broken joints" (visandhikāḥ) means having lost their euphonic combinations (vigatasandhikāḥ), that is, those for whom euphonic combination has not been performed despite the occasion for applying rules such as *guṇa*, *vṛddhi*, or the substitution of *yaṇ*. "Attaining suffering" (prāptaduḥkhāḥ) means attaining affliction (*kleśa*). "Endowed with enemies" (vairisamanvitāḥ) means by means of enemy mantras and the like.

The mutual enmity among the limbs of the mantras has already been served; it will not be discussed here because it will be explained later in the chapter on latent impressions (*vāsanā*). "Fragmented" means having broken forms.
"Due to reciting a portion" means due to reciting only a single part of the mantras and *vidyās*. "Devoid of limbs" [means lacking their constituent parts].

They are devoid of the mantras for the ritual placement on the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*). They are unrestrained and unprotected; through protection there is dignity, whereas through public disclosure there is fruitlessness.
(p. 15) They may be incomplete in form, severed, paralyzed, or nasalized.
Awakening from sleep occurs through recitation at an improper time.

Those who are intoxicated, those whose mantras are read upon leaves, those pinned down by other syllables, those who are obstructed, those with broken joints, those who have encountered suffering, and those accompanied by enemies—[these are the types of mantras]. || 78 ||
Those who have become fragmented, those lacking limbs such as hands and feet, those who are unrestrained, and those taught by one who is incomplete—these are considered to be of deficient vigor. (79)

Through constant practice, there is dullness; through excessive delay, there is affliction; through muttering while ill, there is faltering; and through mixing with other mantras, there is confusion. (80)
Due to recitation performed with a state of indifference, these defects arise from irregularity and contempt; the teacher should pacify those twenty-five faults that have been pointed out.
And this is stated everywhere regarding all mantra-deities: [it concerns] one who has acted without completion in the rite of grace—

that is, one who has proceeded without the command of the guru, such as the *pūrṇābhiṣeka*— and who is of low vigor and diminished strength because he was initiated by one whose power had not been generated due to his failure to perform what was prescribed, with respect to this disciple.

The meaning is that they fail to perform their functions and cause harm. "Dulling" (*kuṇṭhatva*) means the failure to perform one's function. Even mantras and the like, though well-established, become dull—that is, devoid of sharpness—toward the practitioner at all times, like a sharp weapon [that has lost its edge]. This is the state of being afflicted (*kliṣṭatā*).

"Afflicted by afflictions" (*kleśārditatva*) is due to excessive delay; that is, by delaying longer than the prescribed time while reciting the syllables of the mantra and so forth. "The sick" (*rugṇāḥ*) means those who are tormented. "By muttering through chatter" (*pralapanairjjāpāt*) means by muttering after repeatedly conversing with those who are unfit for conversation. "By other mantras" (*anyamantraiḥ*) means by [reciting] mantras other than the one intended to be recited.

"Agitated" means confused; when one mantra is being recited while another mantra is being recited in the midst of it, both mantras become agitated. The meaning is that their fruitlessness, misfortune, and other such evils arise. "Neglect" means abandonment. [This occurs] because of reciting with instability.

The meaning is: having set aside any one of the paths taught by the Guru, the Kalpas, or those conceived by oneself, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) according to the sequence as it has been prescribed. "Due to disparity" means due to the disparity among the mantras and deities in their recitation, worship, fire-offerings (*homa*), and so forth; "due to a state of inequality" means because of deficiency or excess.
"Insulted" means treated with contempt; "the Guru should pacify them" means by the method that will be described. (74, p.

16) The binding [of the disciple] through the *yonimudrā* and the application of the potency (*vīrya*) of the mantras—making the disciple understand both of these, the self-possessed Guru should protect him. (82)
The characteristic of the Guru is this much: he should make known the first and the last [letters].
For letters devoid of the first and the last would be like autumn clouds.
Therefore, from the very beginning, he who possesses that respective sense of ego should act;
for by the realization of that ego, a man becomes equal to me.
Know that to be the attainment of identity, established through the beginningless sequence and the union of the beginning and end of the *mātṛkā*, which embodies the meaning of all mantras. (85)
The purificatory rite for the twice-born has been proclaimed as that which is declared in the Vedas;
regarding them, one should perform the ritual according to the specific knowledge required in each respective case.
He should perform the recollection of the vidyā and the ritual action prescribed for every occasion;
by that, the accomplishment of identity with that [vidyā] certainly occurs everywhere. (87)

With these four verses beginning with "bandhanam" and ending with "vigrahām," he teaches what must be performed by the teacher. In this context, "bandhana" means "anusandhāna" (concentration). Regarding the *yonimudrā*, [the procedure] will be explained later in the chapter on fire-offerings (*homapaṭala*) as the connection between the vital breath and the mind from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*.

The *yonimudrā* consists of the movement back and forth through the interior of the *suṣumṇā*; the meaning of "binding the *yonimudrā*" is the contemplation (*anusandhāna*) thereof. "Joining the potency" (*vīryayojana*) means the joining of the potency of the mantra—with which it was previously described in the chapter on latent impressions (*vāsanāpaṭala*)—with the mantra itself and with the practitioner; this is the meaning of "joining the potency of the mantra."
This should be understood more clearly from the mouth of the venerable teacher.

"The first and the last" refers to the beginning and the end. "Devoid of the first and the last" means devoid of the connection with the knowledge of the beginning and the end. The phonemes (*varṇa*) are merely the embodiments of syllables.
The meaning is "mantras. That specific performance [of the rite] consists of the two syllables—the first and the last—of the Mātṛkā. 83 || 84 || 85 || 86 ||
By this verse beginning with "beginningless" (anādi), the following is stated:
from the conjunction of the first and last phonemes— *a* and *ha*— of the *mātṛkā*, which is the aggregate form of phonemes established in a beginningless sequence, the word *ahaṃ* is produced.

And for that purpose, according to the principle of withdrawing from beginning to end, one should realize one's own self as being of the nature of the Mātṛkā, or rather, as being of the nature of all the deities who are the forms expressed by her. || 87 ||
One should also perform the rites for other castes with the Vidyā-mantra.
At the conclusion, there is cremation with the Vidyā; one should perform all other [rites] with the Vidyā. (88)
Having worshipped him, one should feed either a single person or many according to one's capacity—the yogi who is perfected through the Vidyā and has been invited beforehand. (89)

Having worshipped and bowed to Him with rings, garments, and other offerings, the practitioner of mantra should dismiss Him with the Vidyā for the sake of attaining success in his own Vidyā, O Śivā! (90)
The birthday of the Guru, the day one received the sacred knowledge, one's own birthday, and the day of the Lord’s pervasive manifestation—these indeed [are the auspicious occasions]. (91)
The day of the conjunction of the three syllables, as well as the full-moon day, these six parvans are distinguished; together with the new-moon day, they constitute the seven parvans.
One should perform worship of these [deities] either monthly or annually;
however, as long as the Guru is alive and constantly present, one should perform it for his sons and so forth.
One should worship him as equal to that [deity] and attend upon him with prostrations and other services;
in his absence, one should worship someone of his lineage or a devotee of his.

With these five verses beginning with "dvijātīnām" and ending with "śive," he teaches the duties of the Master (*nātha*). Among them, "dvijātīnām" refers to the twice-born—the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas. "Saṃskāram" refers to the purificatory rites such as the birth-ceremony (*jātakarma*) and so forth. "Anyeṣām" [refers to] others...
[This applies] to the castes (*varṇa*), the Śūdras, and those of mixed origin (*saṅkara*) produced through *anuloma* and *pratiloma* unions.

(Verses 86, 87, 88) With these five verses beginning with "of the guru" and ending with "should be," [the author] teaches the lunar days (*parvan*) and so forth. Among these, the day of the conjunction of the three syllables will be explained later in the *Mātṛkāpaṭala*.

Among the days consisting of syllables to be described hereafter, that day on which three syllables—the two syllables of a *varga* and the one syllable of a *ghaṭikā*—coincide is called a "day of the conjunction of the three syllables" (*akṣaratrayasaṃpātadina*).
Since the method for this will be explained more clearly in that very place, it is not elaborated upon here. || 91 ||
One should constantly praise [Him] with these five verses for the sake of all accomplishments.
By reciting them at the time of awakening in the morning, one's day shall become auspicious. (95)
Salutations to you, O Lord! O Blessed One! To Śiva, who is the very form of auspiciousness;
to you who have assumed manifold forms for the sake of successfully bringing about the descent of knowledge! || 96 ||
Salutations to you, who are ever-new and of ever-new form, whose singular nature is the ultimate reality,
the sun that shatters the darkness of all ignorance, and the mass of pure consciousness.

Salutations to the one who is independent, whose form is fashioned out of compassion, whose nature is auspiciousness; to the one who is dependent upon his devotees, appearing in an auspicious form for those who are destined for liberation. || 98 ||
To the one who provides discernment for the discerning, reflection for those who reflect, illumination for the luminous, and who is the very form of knowledge for the wise. 99.
In front, on both sides, behind, above,
and below— always, in the form of my very mind, grant me your seat.
"The pervasion consisting of the reality of the planes" has been correctly explained.

With five verses beginning with "Obeisance" (*namaḥ*) and ending with "the seat" (*āsana*), he teaches the hymn to the Lord (*nāthastotra*). Therein, [it is addressed] to the New One (*navāya*), who is always...
To the one who is desirable because of His state of being ever-new; to the one whose form is ever-new, distinguished by the number nine;
to the one whose sole form is the ultimate reality—meaning, to the one whose singular form is Śiva.
The meaning is the knowledge of the true nature of discernment (*viveka*) and reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), that is, of "this-ness" (*idantā*) and "I-ness" (*ahantā*). Of the manifestations...
Of those whose nature is truth. || 96 || 97 || 98 || 99 || 100 ||
By the verse beginning with "purastāt" (before), this is what is meant:
"O Creator, grant that I may possess identity with You through space, time, and form. May there be auspiciousness. || 101 ||
By the thorough churning of this [consciousness], that very reality is made one's own within the mind. (101)
Thus ends the first chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, a tantra of the sixteen *nityās*. 1.

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, upon the complete tantra known as the *Śrīkādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The first chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the introduction to the Tantra and so forth, has been fully examined.
[End of] the count of verses.
In the first [section], there shall be one yantra; the number of verses is stated to be sixty-three, exceeding a hundred, based on a thorough examination of the commentary.
Now begins the second chapter.
Next, I shall proclaim the Lords, whose forms are identical to mine and who possess eternal bodies;
they are the stairways for the descent of the Vidyā, as well as their worship.
Furthermore, "Luminosity," "Reflection," and "Bliss" are other [names];
thus, by means of these different names, I manifest in the world in a divine form. (2)
From them three were born, and they are indeed the three Siddhas;
Jñāna, Satya, and Pūrṇa—thus they are proclaimed from the mouths of the Śrīs.
The divine ones dwell constantly in my presence, and the Siddhas likewise reside here upon this earth;
from them, moreover, the three [classes] have arisen.
Svābhāva, Pratibha, and likewise Subhaga—by these names they are known;
imbued with my own nature, they dwell eternally upon this very earth. (5)
Thus, by those nine [sages], the Tantra of established majesty was propagated in the world; for in the Kṛta Yuga, the power beginning with ‘Ka’ (Kādi-Śakti) was non-different from you.

These [deities] have two eyes and two arms, endowed with graceful forms; they possess serene faces, are smiling, and are equipped with hands displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
The Second Chapter.
Having taught in the preceding first chapter the introduction to the Tantra and so forth, [the author now teaches] the nine [deities] who introduce the Tantras and illuminate all human goals.
[The text] teaches the true nature of the Lords (nātha), their specific modes of worship, and so forth (p.

21): "Such [Lords] are indeed to be worshipped in their respective maṇḍalas and other [spheres] during worship; however, the Goddesses residing within the Śrīcakra assume the forms of the Goddesses by their command. (8)
Addressed with pleasing words, they are all endowed with bliss;
O Goddess, in their respective mandalas they end with the Lord (Nātha), and in the [central] mandala they end with Śakti.
Likewise, Māyā, Lakṣmī, and the others, as well as those known as the nine syllables (Navārṇā),
should be employed in the worship of the nine Śaktis and their respective deities.
O Goddess! One should worship with that seven-syllabled vidyā which brings satisfaction to all and bestows all accomplishments, preceded by [the deity's] name. (11)
"Tell me that vidyā which brings about all that is dear;
listen, O Goddess! It is the bringer of great siddhi and the maker of everything beloved. (12)
Then, by means of the second chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, O Lord" (*atha nātha*) and ending with "therefore" (*tadyata*),

[the following is taught]. Therein, by means of the eleven verses beginning with "Now, O Lord" and ending with "preceded by names," the generation stage (*utpattikrama*) of the nine lords and its function [are explained].

Through them, he propagates the Vidyā and instructs its mantras. In that context, by the statement "those whose forms are mine," their possession of an eternal form (*nityavigrahatva*) is indicated. The word "likewise" (*tathā*) is used in a conjunctive sense. They are "glorious-faced" (*śrīmukhāḥ*), meaning they possess names beginning with the word "Śrī.
They are "of my own nature" (*madātmakāḥ*), meaning they have the form of Śiva. These are the uncommon [deities] whose names consist of three syllables.

The nine designations consisting of three syllables are common to all; the meaning is that they are to be understood as divine, accomplished, and human, respectively, according to the sequence of three. By means of explaining the meaning of the uncommon three-syllable names of these nine lords, [one realizes] Śiva, whose form is indivisible.

The state of formlessness (a-rūpatva) is to be understood from the very mouth of Ārādhya. Regarding the phrase "in their respective maṇḍalas and so forth," he will describe the maṇḍalas later on. The word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to their own heads and other parts.
"Endowed with bliss" (ānandasaṃyutāḥ) means having names associated with the word "bliss" (ānanda). [This applies] to the nine.
The word "of the protectors" (*nāthānām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Preceded by their respective names" means preceded by those specific names [in each case].
With these five verses beginning with *tān me* and ending with *namasāsthitih*, he teaches the seven-syllable mantra common to all the *Śaktitantras*. In that regard, the one which...

The seven-syllable mantra is as follows: the syllable *pa* is swift; *marut* is swift and joined with *marut*; *gotrā* is conjoined with *dharā*. Furthermore, *prāṇa* joined with *marut* shall be the third, which is *nabhaḥ*. (13)
Again, *ja* is swift and endowed with earth (*kṣmā*); *vā* is joined with the bowstring (*jyā*) and the wind (*vāta*).
The sixth syllable is the sky pervaded by the friend of the wind (*marutsakha*, i.e., fire); the seventh syllable is fire (*agni*). (14)
Thus has the seven-syllabled mantra been proclaimed in the Śakti-tantras as bestowing success; it may be formed with the names of all the Śaktis and deities. (15)
That [mantra] should be joined with the name at the beginning for the sake of accomplishment; likewise, it is common [to all].
In tantras other than the Śaktitantras, the form remains with "namaḥ. (16)
The nine names of the nine [deities] each consist of nine syllables;
through their conjunction with the seven-syllable [mantra], each becomes sixteen syllables long.
Those sixteen eternal forms should be known in their proper sequence;
O Dear One, the names of those nine [forms] and the formation of the mandala shall now be told.
"Tradition" (pāramparya) is said to be the attainment [of knowledge] in the continuity of the lineage of learning;
through that purity, there is purity in the knowledge, otherwise it is otherwise. (19)

The letter *ā* is from *ākāra*. *Gotrā* is the letter *da*; by *dharā*, it is the letter *u*. *Prāṇa* is the letter *ka*; by *marut*, as before. *Nabhaḥ* is the letter *ma*, meaning the *bindu*; the third syllable is the remainder. *Javī* is as before; by *kṣmā*, it is the letter *u*. *Jyā* is the letter *ja*; *vāta* is the letter *a*. It is pervaded.
The letter *ya*. *Marut* is the vowel *ā* as before. *Nabhaḥ* is as before. *Agni* is the vowel *ī*.
The mention of "of the deities" refers to the masculine gender. 12, 13, 14, 15, 16.
With the three-quarter verse beginning with "of the nine" (navānām) and ending with "names" (nāmāni), he teaches the sixteen-syllable names of those nine Lords who consist of the sixteen Nityās.
In this context, the word "name" (nāma) is to be understood as "a name consisting of sixteen syllables. (17–18)

With the verse beginning with "maṇḍalīkaraṇam" and ending with "anyathā," he teaches the uninterrupted nature of the lineage through the word "pāda" and so forth. In that context, *maṇḍalīkaraṇa* refers to the connection between the beginning and the end; *āpti* means authoritative validity (*prāmāṇya*); and *anvaya* means continuity (*santati*). || 19 ||
The names of the practitioners, or alternatively, those corresponding to the days, as well as the letters of the days, are likewise Amāya and Anantya. (20)
O practitioner! these three names—namely, "attained through synonyms," "attained at the [proper] time," and "that which is well-known from the outside"—are established. (21)
Therefore, the practitioner who has attained knowledge should perform the worship, verses, and praises with these three, for the sake of establishing the lineage.
One should perform the worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru on the seven festival days;
on the full moon day, having written the sixteen-syllable names, one should worship them.
But on other occasions during the six parvas, one should write only the nine syllables;
there too, O Śivā, one should worship while reciting the seven-syllabled mantra.
In all worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru, nine services are prescribed;
therefore, one should worship with them—listen to those as well. (25)

With these three verses beginning with "sādhakānām" and ending with "prasiddhaye," he teaches the three names to be heard by mortals. Therein, the word "vā" signifies a conjunction; thus, the meaning is that there are two names. [These are] the letters of the day.

These will be explained in the twenty-fifth chapter. Likewise, they are of two kinds: *amāyaḥ* (without *m* or *y*) and *avisarjanīyaḥ* (without the *visarga*). *Anantyaḥ* means devoid of the final letter, *kṣa*; the word *prakāraḥ* (the letters) is to be understood as the remainder.
This is what is meant: among the *ghaṭikā*-letters that will be described below...

By accepting one of the two—the visarga or the letter *kṣa*—and discarding the other, there are fifty syllables. This is obtained through alternation; it is obtained through another name of one's own guru.
It is obtained according to time, spanning nine [days] starting from the first day of the *yuga* until the day the *vidyā* is attained.

When the days of the yuga are divided by the number nine, the name obtained by the remaining number of days is established externally as that given by one’s mother and father. By these three names— this being the ellipsis—
it means that in the maṇḍalas and other rites, one should perform worship, verses of praise, and hymns using only the name obtained in its respective order.
One should perform [it]. || 20 || 21 || 22 ||

With these four verses beginning with "gurumaṇḍalapūjām" and ending with "samīritā," he teaches the sequence for writing the syllables of the names within the worship maṇḍala and so forth. In that regard, there are seven joints as stated in the first chapter; and in each of those cases as well—
Fragrance, flowers, incense, lamps, as well as food offerings, betel, prostration, and hymns of praise—these are declared to be performed by means of one's own self. (26)
O Maheśvarī! One should perform the construction of the maṇḍala of the Guru upon a pedestal, on a wooden plank, or even on a ground that is perfectly pure, level, and stable.
O Goddess of the Gods! One should lay down ten threads extending east, west, south, and north, with intervals of five finger-breadths; from that, [the grid] is produced. || 28 ||
The mandala is square and consists of eighty-one squares;
the first [square] is in the very center, while the second is in front.
To its left, one should draw that third [line] within each of the nine squares;
thus, the mandala is endowed with nine times nine [squares] across the seven sections.
Having divided the ninefold [grid] into nine parts by laying down two threads across the center,
one should write the nine syllables of the name within them and worship them in sequence.
Having placed three sets of three threads in the center of that [mandala] on the full-moon day (pūrṇā),
the meaning is that one should worship with the names joined by the seven-syllable mantra in the mandalas to be described hereafter,
because of the offering of oneself by means of one's own self. || 23 || 24 || 25 || 26 ||

With these five verses beginning with "gurumaṇḍala" and ending with "kramāt," he instructs on the drawing and worship of the guru-maṇḍala to be honored during the six festival days (*parva*). In that context, it says: "One should draw [the maṇḍala] in nine groups of nine; within those nine [sections], one should draw the nine groups of nine Lords."
This is what is meant: starting from the central group of nine within the eighty-one squares,

and proceeding clockwise through the other groups of nine situated in the east and other directions, the respective lords of those [groups] are to be placed in their corresponding central squares in due order.
One should understand that the remaining [syllables] are situated around [the center] according to the sequence already stated;
the meaning is that one should write the nine letters of the name, beginning from the center and proceeding clockwise starting from the east. || 27 || 28 || 29 || 30 || 31 ||

With these five verses beginning with "pūrṇā" and ending with "siddhaye," [the author] teaches the specific details regarding the circle of gurus (gurumaṇḍala) to be worshipped during the *pūrṇā* offerings.
(p. 25) Having thus prepared the sixteen [vessels], one should indeed write those names upon them as follows: || 32 ||
In this way, while the Guru is living, these honors are indeed offered;
or, when he has passed away, having formed a maṇḍala of these places, it is held that [the worship] should be performed there by means of a painting.
Thus, O Śivā, he who worships the Lords with focused attention becomes an excellent teacher and an adept; from that, the highest attainment of knowledge is achieved. (34)
Otherwise, the attainment of either [of these two] is certainly for one's own misfortune:
either suffering from disease, weapons, and the like, or mental delusion, or death in water. (35)
Thus, one encounters calamities such as these, and death may come from the king or from lightning;
therefore, for the sake of accomplishing all goals, one should act precisely according to the stated sequence.
Having observed the suitability [of candidates] for one, two, three, four, or five years,
as well as their devotion and qualities, according to the order of the castes and the mixed castes (saṅkara).

One should recite the Vidyā with undistracted mind according to the sequence just described; otherwise, if one should recite it differently, the teacher, along with his disciple, shall meet with destruction.

Regarding the phrase "there, one should write among those [cells] in this manner," the word "in this manner" means that one should write according to the sequence of the tradition as received through oral transmission (*pāramparya*). For example, starting from the cell situated at the bottom-left of the central group of four,
one proceeds clockwise through the central group of four according to the aforementioned order.
One should likewise proceed externally. "Having approached me, the Liberated One" means having drawn a circular figure by encircling [the space].
Otherwise, the meaning is that they would be devoid of the worship of the Guru-maṇḍala. In the phrase "and so forth," the word "etc.
(ādi) is an elliptical indicator (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the removal of all misfortunes and other such matters. || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 || 35 || 36 ||

With these two verses beginning with *eka-dvi-try-ādinā* and ending with *gurur āpnuyāt*, he teaches the time for the examination of the disciple and so forth, according to the [number of] syllables. In this context, "fitness" (*yogyatā*) refers to being pure in the aforementioned conduct and so on. (37) (38)
(26) Thus, the threefold installation is said to be performed upon the wheel, the goddess, and likewise the disciple;
that [installation] must be carried out by one who knows the reality and follows the tradition. (39)
The wise man should have it constructed during a firm, favorable moment endowed with auspicious planets and virtuous qualities, or on a full moon day when there is a rising of a benefic planet.
On the day of the conjunction of the three syllables, during the three days of the full moon, on the five other [specified] days, or always when an auspicious rising occurs. || 41 ||
One who has attained self-realization (siddhātmā) should perform the consecration, and no other who is arrogant of his knowledge;
for if one performs it out of delusion or greed without the permission of the Guru, [he incurs sin]. || 42 ||
One who meets his death while accompanied by sons and wife shall go to hell;
therefore, one should practice [the rites] only after having received permission through the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka).
With honey, clarified butter, and milk first, and then with coconut water;

[the author] teaches the threefold nature of the installation and so forth through these five verses beginning with "In the wheel" (*cakre*) and ending with "one should perform" (*samācaret*). Therein, "in the wheel" (*cakre*) refers to the wheel for the worship of Lalitā; "in the Goddess" (*devyām*)...

In the image of the Goddess: [it should be performed] by one who follows the tradition, who knows the reality, and who is devoted to the daily and occasional worship; "in a stable zodiacal sign" is the ellipsis. "Favorable" refers to the time of day and so forth. "Endowed with qualities" is an epithet of the specific *muhūrta*. Alternatively, this is said in the event that those [other conditions] are not established.

Or [the word] "eva" (only) serves as a restriction. One should perform [the rite] specifically when the breath is full and auspiciousness arises; the meaning is that one should not look at anything other than that. On the day of the conjunction of the three syllables, according to the sequence of syllables mentioned in the twenty-fifth chapter, among the syllables of the *ghaṭikā* of the daily *nityā*, [one should focus on] a single syllable.
The meaning is: on whichever day the vision of the three locations occurs;

that is, during the three full-moon days—the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth lunar days—or during the five other aforementioned auspicious occasions (*parvan*), excluding the two specific occasions mentioned here, on the remaining five.

One alternative view is that, whether at all times or specifically when auspiciousness arises, one should act only when there is the arising of auspiciousness for one's own breath—without regard for everything prescribed regarding lunar days (*tithi*), weekdays (*vāra*), yogas, asterisms (*nakṣatra*), full moons, and so forth; this is the position concerning those who have attained perfection. One who has attained perfection is a knower of reality (*tattvavid*). Delusion (*moha*) is ignorance (*ajñāna*).
Greed is the desire for wealth. Niraya is a place of suffering. 39 || 40 || 41 || 42 || 43 ||
With these eight verses beginning with *kṣaudra* and ending with *bhaviṣyati*, he teaches the installation of the Śrīcakra and other rites. (p.
27) Then, having consecrated [it] with water boiled with medicinal herbs containing the two syllables (*akṣara*), || 44 ||
Having invoked and worshipped them at that moment, one should establish them upon the wheel and worship them;
having worshipped them in sequence with the vidyās arising from the time of attaining the eternal principles (tattvas).

One should recite the mantra while touching the Śrīcakra with the tips of the fingers, and one may also worship it. Having performed this for three days, one should thereafter engage in the daily ritual sequence.
For three nights, one should worship the Goddess together with yoginīs and yogis, using perfumes, flowers, fresh incense, lamps, food offerings, and libations. (47)
Thus, in the consecration of a goddess, this is the sequence that brings about her presence;
one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Guru, who is Śiva himself manifest before one's eyes.
Or he may give his entire property, or half of that, or half of that, according to his command; otherwise, how will there be the transmission of his power? (49)
Elephants, horses, female buffaloes, rams, cattle, female slaves, land, gold, ornaments, clothing, a residence, or whatever else is desired. (50)

Therein, [one should perform the rite] with the fifty medicinal herbs for the eyes mentioned in the thirty-fifth chapter, boiled together; and with the Vidyā arising at the time of attaining the Nityā-tattva, which is the Vidyā of the specific daily Nityā obtained at that time as declared in the twenty-fifth chapter; these [should be applied] in sequence.

The *nityā* mantras mentioned in that chapter number twenty-one thousand seven hundred and thirty-six. The particle *api* is used out of its usual order; it means "or else, touching [the mantra], one should recite. This is what is intended: immediately after the invocation, one should recite with the *nityā* mantra of that specific day, using the third section of the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*).

Having worshipped each [deity] three times with the root-vidyā, one should worship them with those [mantras] after the sequential service (*kramasaparyā*). Alternatively, having touched the Śrīcakra, one should mutter the aforementioned number of *Kālanityās*. With libations (*tarpaṇa*) consisting of pleasing nectars, [one worships] thus, O Goddess.

The phrase "according to the previously mentioned sequence" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "By his command" means by the will of the Guru. In the expression "or a dwelling," the word *vā* (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "According to one's own power" means according to one's available wealth. The meaning is that being dependent upon him, one should perform all of one's activities only with his permission. || 44 || 45 || 46 || 47 || 48 || 49 || 50 ||

One should give according to one's own capacity with devotion; however, if one is entirely incapable, then [the deity] will always remain dependent on that person, and through that, accomplishment (siddhi) will come to pass.
By worshipping Vāmeśā as well, one shall obtain the respective fruits;
this should be performed during the various yogas, or even during other intermediate periods.
One should worship the deities mentioned in the mantras associated with the day of the week, the asterism, and the lunar date, arranged in their respective directions: Agni, Rakṣas, Vāk, and Īśa.
One shall obtain the fruits of the endeavor to pacify disease;
thus have been declared the deities of the lunar days and constellations with the thought that they are like arrows.
O Supreme Lord, tell me the sequence of the lunar days (tithis) and their corresponding asterisms (ṛkṣas):
Fire, the two Aśvins, Water, Moon, Vighna, Serpent, the Six-faced One, and the Sun.
The Mothers, as well as Durgā, the Quarters, Yakṣeśvara, Hari, Yama,
Hara, and Śaśin— these are proclaimed as the lords of the lunar days (tithīśas).
Listen also to the deities of the lunar mansions, which I shall declare according to the rule:
the two Aśvins, Yama, Vahni, Dhātṛ, Candra, Śiva, and Aditi.
The Gurusarpas, the Pitṛs, Aryaman, Bhaga,
Dinakṛt, Tvaṣṭṛ, as well as the Maruts, Indra, Agni, and Mitra.
Indra, Nirṛti, the Viśvedevas, and likewise the oblation;
the Vasus, Varuṇa, and behind them Aja Ekapāt.
Ahirbudhnya and Pūṣan are likewise declared to be the deities of the lunar mansions;
and Kāraskara, Āmalaka, Udumbara, and Jambuka are also [deities].
Khadira, two types of black bamboo (kṛṣṇavaṃśa), two types of Pippala, Nāgara and Rohiṇa, Palāśa, Plakṣa, Kāmboja, Bilva, Arjuna, and Vikaṅkata.
The *varala*, *sarala*, *sarja*, *bakula*, and likewise the *panasa*;
the *arka*, *śamī*, *kadamba*, as well as the *nimba* and the *atima* tree were there.
And Madhuka—these are declared to be the sequence of trees;
[the substances are] horse, elephant-ichor, goat, snake, female serpent, and female cat.
Akṣamā, Akṣarīmukhā, Mūṣakī, Vṛṣamāhiṣī,
Vyāghra, Mahiṣa, Vyāghrī, Mṛgī, Mṛgaśunī, and Kapi.
When there is affliction from the pain of disease and other such misfortunes, it is preceded by my sons seeing a cow, a piece of sugar-cane, a monkey, a woman, a mare, a mountain, or elephants.
By means of the number of muhūrtas, there shall be peace; by double that, wisdom.
There are five cakras in the Ādhāra and four in the Svādhiṣṭhāna.
One should meditate upon those [five] in the Maṇipūraka for as long as they were described;
thereafter, one should thoroughly contemplate the five yantras in the Anāhata.
In the [cycle] called Viśuddhi, however, one should meditate upon the auspicious Ṣoḍaśī in this sequence: four, five, and then nine, on the respective lunar days.
One should worship the Goddess residing in each respective wheel for the sake of all prosperity;
one should contemplate the wheels within the *ādhāra* and other centers through the yoga of meditation.
Indeed, nowhere at any time do all [the limbs] exist in their manifest state;
for those who are incapable of such contemplation, they likewise exist externally through their respective yantras.
Having established the previously described foundation lotuses, one should perform the ritual there;
thus, on the various days and weekdays, one should worship Śivā as she resides within the wheel.
Having worshipped the Goddess, one shall obtain desired objects within the days prescribed;
and on those very days, one should offer oblations according to the ritual injunctions.
Fifty pairs are proclaimed here for the wheel at midnight;
likewise, at midday and during the two twilights, the Mistress of those situated in the wheels [is present].
(30) O Sovereign Lady, the wheels of power (*śakticakra*) for those who move by means of the wheels of mantra have been clearly declared as the forms of the mantras consisting of the *kūṭas*.
At those various times, one should offer oblations to them with the subsequent [mantras];
however, for the Goddess, the offering of food (naivedya) is said to be an act of grace, consisting of a large morsel of rice-cake.
Having placed [the vessel] in the center and having lit a lamp soaked in ghee,
one should place [the couples] there with their respective mantras in successive order.
Through each of the goddesses, success shall be attained.
[He should initiate] a disciple endowed with the aforementioned characteristics, adorned by right conduct, and purified for many days by means of the two vidyās consisting of five and six kūṭas. (52)
Having quickly consecrated [the disciple] with water-pots and having seated him within the Śrīcakra,
one should contemplate the wheel in the center, at the base, the heart, and the head.
Having invoked [the deity] from his own heart, established her, worshipped her along with the ritual placement (nyāsa),
and being one whose mind is full, the teacher— whose self is the Goddess— should whisper the thirty-fold Vidyā into the ear.
One should contemplate with the intellect the oneness of the deity, the guru, the mantra, and one's own self;
standing before it, one should recite the mantra a hundred times and reside nearby for three days.

With these six verses beginning with "uktā" and ending with "dhanādibhiḥ," he teaches the sequence of instruction for a good disciple and the duties of the disciple following that instruction. Therein,
[the disciple] has been purified over many days for the sake of attaining stability in faith, devotion, and worship, as well as knowledge.

The purification for many days is performed with nine, four, or one water-pots. From the center—that is, from the middle of the three Śrīcakras—and from the heart of the preceptor, that is, from his own self. Here, there is a certain subsidiary matter which, because it is obtained at the time of the Ācāryābhiṣeka from the mouth of the preceptor himself, is not mentioned here.

Having contemplated one's own self as the Goddess with a full mind, and having realized one's own nature as the form of the Goddess and bound oneself as being identical with Her— this is what is meant: that one who is solely of the form of the Deity should teach by means of a compassionate mind that is independent of anything else and manifests in the form of the universe.

The unity of the deity, the guru, the mantra, and one’s own self (*devatā-guru-mantra-ātma-tattva-aikya*)—meaning the essential identity of the deity, the guru, and the mantra with one's own self—in the manner described in the verse at the conclusion of the fourth chapter. (p. 31) "Otherwise, the mobile power (*saṃcāriṇī śakti*) undoubtedly enters the guru."
Therefore, one should perform acts such as worship and the preparation of the place of offering in his presence. || 56 ||
Since he has attained identity with the Guru who is the essence of the mantra,
from that time forward, his wealth and other possessions are dependent upon him.
Then, having obtained the two kinds of consecration by his command, one should perform acts of grace and so forth for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, it will not come to pass.
Having fashioned a wheel and placed a jar in its center upon a yoni,
one should fill it with decoction water, consecrate [the disciple] with these [waters], and recite the mantra.

For one who is devoted to the traditional conduct passed down through lineage and who possesses spiritual power, one should perform the second consecration for the sake of attaining the self-perfection of the Goddess. 60.
Having fashioned a large wheel with sixteen spokes according to their respective origins,
and having constructed triangles therein, one should place a jar in the center.
*Cañcalā*. According to the method stated at the conclusion of the fourth chapter regarding the mantra-self (*mantrātman*), [one should worship her].
Regarding the phrase "with wealth and so forth" (*dhanādibhiḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to houses, fields, and the like. || 52 || 53 || 54 || 55 || 56 ||

Now, with fifteen verses beginning with "Then, initiation is twofold" and ending with "one should perform [it]," he teaches the two kinds of initiation for practitioners, as well as their methods and so forth. In that context, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "for the sake of favor and so forth" (*anugrahādī*), [he refers to] ritual applications (*prayoga*).

It is said: having prepared the wheel—the worship mandala described in the thirty-third chapter—with decoction waters, that is, with the cooled decoctions of the medicinal herbs for the eyes to be mentioned later; "the sequence" refers to the daily sequence; "the second" refers to the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*); and "the extensive wheel" is that which was previously mentioned.

The meaning is that one should fashion the *lalitāpūjācakra* with the dimensions suitable for the placement of the pitcher (*kumbha*) which will be described later; we shall state those dimensions in that very place. Furthermore, having placed sixteen triangles upon each *yoni*, [one should proceed] with each triangle according to what will be described in the thirty-third chapter.
One should draw nine horizontal lines according to the measurement and tradition;
by this, sixteen triangles are formed.
[The mandala may be made] of gold, silver, copper, glass, or even clay.
It was filled with a khārī-measure of boiled water containing medicinal herbs that improve the eyesight.
Having placed the nine gems and various kinds of grain,
as well as gold and copper, one should wrap them with two cloths.
