With red sandalwood, sprouts of the mango, jackfruit, and holy fig tree, bound with the *śatakratu* creeper and provided with *mātuluṅga* fruits; || 64 ||
Having prepared other jars, one should place them individually within others;
they are said to be in sequence in the numbers five, thirty-six, and one thousand and five hundred.
Having placed the elements beginning with water within the wheels in the center, and having invoked and worshipped them,
one should recite the mantras of the Kālātmanityās on the preceding day.

This is what is meant: one should draw sixteen triangles containing smaller triangles within them at the locations of the deities on the petals of the lotus and at the locations of the weapons within the Śrīcakra;
"in the center" means in the very middle of all. (With *khārī* water—that is, with water measuring one *khārī*; and a *khārī* is [equal to] *pala*...)

And it has been said: "A *palā*, a *kuḍava*, a *prastha*, an *āḍhaka*, and a *droṇa* are to be understood as measures for grain and the like. A *droṇī* consists of sixteen [droṇas], a *khārī* consists of twenty [droṇas], and a *kumbha* is likewise to be made [of that measure]. The nine gems will be described below."
The [eight] gems known as ruby, pearl, coral, lapis lazuli, topaz, diamond, sapphire, and emerald;

the grains such as rice, sesame, mung bean, black gram, barley, wheat, and so forth; the arrangement of sprouts by means of the perfuming with branches of the celestial tree (*suradruma*); and by the mention of the *mātuluṅga* fruit.

This indicates coconuts and the like. Furthermore, the local (deśī) designations for things such as creepers and sprouts apply to their actual forms (*svarūpa*) and to matters concerning oral tradition (*mukhāgama*). This number—thirty-six thousand five hundred—is the count of the ninety-five various [treatises].

Because each of the power-deities (*śakti*) residing in the *śrīcakra* possesses sixteen forms, just like the root deity (*mūladevatā*), there are fifteen hundred and twenty varieties resulting from the sixteenfold division of the ninety-five powers.

The root deity has sixteen divisions. Thus, there are fifteen hundred and thirty-six Śaktis; consequently, there are exactly that many jars, produced according to the previously mentioned method by way of the sequence of the fivefold number of jars. This is what is meant.
Because weapons are of two kinds, [the mandalas] consist of eight or sixteen triangles containing a womb,
facing one another in the form of a thunderbolt (vajra). On one's birth star (janmarkṣa), having risen in the morning, one should worship one’s own Nityā there.
Afterwards, one should recite it a thousand times and perform an oblation on all sides.
With the sounds of horns, cymbals, conchs, and other instruments, accompanied by singing and dancing,
each one was attended by joyful throngs of yoginīs who were embodiments of the deities.
The Guru himself should perform the consecration together with those who have been honored for their conduct;
from that time forward, he too should explain his own tradition to him.
If that [mantra] should fail, one should perform it in an uninterrupted sequence;
one should recite the vidyā a thousand times, accompanied by an ablution.
Alternatively, one should place ninety-six jars there;
having invoked the Śaktis into them and worshipped them, one should perform the consecration.
Or, having prepared a single water-pot on one's birthday, one should perform the consecration;
in this manner, one should constantly perform the occasional rite without interruption.

Having drawn [the figure] and, within the three corners of the central triangle, having formed three triangles containing sixteen triangles by means of three horizontal lines, and having drawn a circle in the space between them,
[one should place] within that [circle] sixteen yonis containing triangles.

"One should draw them facing each other in the form of a vajra" refers to the mantras of the Kālātmanityās which will be taught in the twenty-fifth chapter, as well as the mantras of the Nityās for that specific day. This means that in all consecrations, on the preceding day—

One should perform the consecration (abhiṣeka) on another day after first performing the preliminary rite of propitiation (adhivāsana); or else, one may perform the propitiation immediately. The meaning is that one should perform the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka) on the birth asterism or the birthday of the disciple.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the sequence prescribed for the daily oblation; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. On all sides...
The connection [of this] follows above. "With the *vṛttas*" means with those previously consecrated as being of the nature of the deity.
"One's own sequence" refers to the sequence of syllables. By the word "uninterrupted succession," thirty-six days are expressed. This is what is meant: without the command of the Guru...
In the case of an interruption in the sequence, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) consisting of one thousand [recitations] along with the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) has been prescribed.

For each of the days that were interrupted, there is a recitation (*japa*) of the three junctions (*sandhyā*), the sixty *ghaṭikās*, the Lords (*nāthas*), the Principles (*tattvas*), the Nityās, and the Kālanityā Vidyā. (p. 34)
In the foundation, in the heart, in the head, in fire, in the sun, and in the moon. || 73 ||
Meditating during the three junctions of the day, one should recite the entire alphabet of consonants and vowels;
and one should perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the locations of the Mātṛkā for the sake of attaining perfection of that body. 74.

One should perform the consecration even during the adverse transits of the planets, during an eclipse of both [the sun and the moon], at the occurrence of the new moon (kuhū), or when there is affliction from enemies. || 75 ||
By the power of that, defects—whether petty, cruel deeds, or magical spells devised by enemies—never touch him at any time. (76)

Having performed the expiation one hundred times, one should worship from that day forward. In this context, "there" refers exclusively to the Śrīcakra. The alternative view that it may be "one [time]" pertains to the domain of optional rites (kāmya). 58–64.

With these two verses beginning with "By the Nāthas" and ending with "the accomplishments," he teaches the worship during the three junctions (*sandhyā*) as well as a specific *kāmyanyāsa*. In this regard, the following is stated:
since the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*) begins with the Nāthas, by them the morning junction of the universe [is presided over].
Because it abides as the nature of the thirty-six principles, it is the midday *sandhyā*;

because it is fulfilled through the reflective awareness of the nature of eternal *avidyā*, the evening *sandhyā* is performed. This is the meaning of the phrase "the sound of the ointment that emits all worlds."
Since it will be explained in the twenty-fifth chapter, it is not elaborated upon here. One should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) in the locations of the *mātṛkā*— that is,

in all the locations for the *mātṛkā*-placement that will be described in the fifteenth chapter— along with the respective syllables transmitted through the lineage, together with the daily *nityā* deity for that particular day.
There is also a tradition that one should perform the placement (nyāsa) of Śrīvidyā; thus says Upavarṣa. || 73 || 74 ||

With these five verses beginning with "Of the planets" (*grahāṇām*) and ending with "the consecration" (*abhiṣecanam*), he teaches the specific time for the consecration and its efficacy. "During the eclipse of the two," namely the moon and the sun. "Minor [rites]" refers to those such as inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*) and expulsion (*uccāṭana*). "Afflictions" (*kleśāḥ*).

[These are] the internal, the divine, and the elemental. The affliction of suffering is the total pain of all sufferings; the affliction of suffering is the pain arising from the contraction of the mind. || 75 || 76 || 77 || 78 || 79 ||
O Supreme Lord! Tell me how that power of consecration comes to be;
tell me that power by which the afflictions are destroyed without remainder. (77)
By the mere touch of water that takes the form of the moon, sun, and fire, all defects are destroyed without remainder; therefore, there is indeed nothing equal to this sprinkling.
The nature of water as being composed of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni has been proclaimed;
therefore, for the sake of pacifying the affliction of all suffering, there should be an ablution [with it]. (79)
One should respectfully perform worship of the Guru with a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) on the seven auspicious occasions mentioned in the Sūtras, or on other meritorious days, or indeed every year.
When the aforementioned portents have occurred, one should worship with golden flowers;
having been consecrated according to the rite, one should then bestow a sacrificial fee upon the preceptor.
One should likewise [bow] to the Guru who has attained knowledge in his presence, as well as to his younger brother;
and to the Guru’s Guru and his [Guru’s] Guru, from one who has obtained knowledge in their presence.
One should please [the deity] through acts of worship such as prostration, ritual offerings, hymns of praise, and service;
otherwise, one's own power will pass away to him.
One should prepare the guru’s maṇḍala everywhere using pastes composed of camphor, sandalwood, saffron, and light musk.
With these four verses beginning with *saptasu* and ending with *bhavet*, he teaches the worship of the Guru and so forth.

In that context, in the phrase *pratyabdameva vā*, the particle *eva* indicates the necessity of performing [the rite], while the word *vā* suggests an inferior alternative. Worship performed every month with wealth and other means is considered middling.

The secondary alternative (*pakṣa*) is as follows: worship with wealth and other offerings on the seven festival days (*parvan*) and on other auspicious occasions is the superior alternative. [This applies] during the occurrence of portents (*utpāta*), consisting of the threefold categories of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial phenomena, and during specific types of disturbances. [In such times,] one should perform ritual attendance (*upāsana*).
Conformity with the mind; one's own [mind] as it pertains to the disciple; that which goes toward him, which goes toward the guru. 80, 81, 82, 83.

With these two verses beginning with *candre* and ending with *parameśvarī*, he teaches the materials and other requirements for the construction of the circle of gurus (*gurumaṇḍala*). In this context, *candra* refers to camphor;
*laghu* refers to agallochum (*aguru*). With the words beginning with *bhāla*, he explains that [the mark] must necessarily be worn. In every respect...
It succeeds everywhere. || 84 || 85 ||

At the conclusion of the worship, having performed the ritual cleansing, one should apply the *sarvato-lakṣmī* [mark] upon his forehead, chest, and shoulders; thus the Supreme Goddess becomes present within the essence. (85)
In all those locations within the previously mentioned maṇḍalas that were specified for worship, one should visualize lotuses.
Then, at the beginning and at the end of the worship and other rites, one should recite five verses;
having attained the state of being the Self of the Goddess through the Guru, one should then recite the twelve verses.

I bow to the Goddess who is Mātṛkā, consisting of mantra, whose form is the zodiac signs, and who embodies Gaṇeśa, the planets, the lunar mansions, and the Yoginīs, as well as the sacred seats (pīṭhas). || 88 ||
I bow to the Great Goddess, the Mother, the Supreme Sovereign,
who brings an end to the turbulent agitation of the surging waves of Time.
With the verse beginning with "pūrva" (the east), he teaches the specific procedure for the previously mentioned guru-maṇḍala.

This is what is meant: having constructed an eight-petaled lotus together with a pericarp according to the rules using nine-by-nine squares, one should write the syllables of the names therein in the order of the rows.
We shall explain that measurement and the method of its construction very clearly in the chapter on mechanical diagrams (yantra-paṭala).

With the verse beginning "In worship and so forth" (pūjādau), he teaches the time for the recitation of the two hymns for the Lord (nātha) and the deity; therein, it is the Lord himself who appears in the form of the deity.
The meaning is: "having realized the ultimate truth. || 87 ||

Beyond this, since the twelve verses of the *Devīstotra* have already been commented upon by the great Kashmiri masters in the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*, that very commentary on those twelve verses is written here. [Regarding the verse beginning with] "Gaṇeśa": Gaṇeśa...

Vināyaka; he is said to be the form of Time (Kāla). The planets (graha) are those beginning with the Sun. The lunar mansions (nakṣatra) are those beginning with Aśvinī. Their mantras and so forth, as well as their names, will be explained further on. The Yoginīs are those beginning with Vaśinī. The zodiac signs (rāśi) are those beginning with Aries (Meṣa). [She is called] Rūpiṇī because she is the cause of these. Thus, "the Goddess."

This is the statement of worship. She consists of mantra because she is composed of syllables (*akṣara*). "I bow" (*naumi*) expresses an identity (*tādātmya*). "Mātṛkā" means like a mother; she is Mātṛkā, the progenitor of the universe. "In the form of the sacred seats" (*pīṭharūpiṇīm*) means she is the form of the support of all in the manner described. This is what is meant: of the mass of sounds (*śabdarāśi*), of Time...

And the stability of contemplation upon [the Self] as one's own nature is *jīvanmukti*. "I bow"—[to her] who has brought to rest the turbulent agitation of time. When even a single syllable of that [mantra] is mastered, a man rivals Time itself. (p. 37)
By the Sun, Tārkṣya, the Moon, Kandarpa, Śaṅkara, Anala, and Viṣṇu. || 90 ||
I bow to the Goddess Mahāśrīsiddhamātṛkā, the Sovereign of All, by whose syllables the three worlds are adorned with the moonlight of the digits of the moon. 91.
I bow to that Siddhamātṛkā, upon which these three worlds—from the cosmic egg down to its outer shell—are strung like beads on the great thread of the Imperishable. 92.

Because of that seed-syllable arising from the three corners, which is the eleventh support, the universe is seen even today, from the cosmic egg (Brahmāṇḍa) down to the shell of the universe (Āṭāha). || 93 ||
The *hallohalo* is the momentum; the *ullolakalanā* is the connection between what precedes and what follows. This is what is meant:
when there is perfection in the previously mentioned meditation and mantra, no affliction arises due to the tyranny of time.
Regarding the phrase "that which is in the syllable," the meaning of "consisting of a single measure" (*ekamātra*) is to be understood from the mouth of the venerable teacher (*ārādhyapāda*).
When it has been perfected according to the method taught by the venerable teachers, it rivals the sun by means of its illumination and so forth;

Tārkṣya by means of its wheel and its removal of poison and so forth; the moon by means of its nectar-like nature and so forth; Kandarpa by means of its beauty and so forth; Śaṅkara by means of its blissful nature and so forth; and Anala as well.
[He is] "conquered by majesty" (pratāpāditaḥ). And [he is] "by Viṣṇu" because of being the self of the universe (viśvātmatvāt). This is what is meant:
when even a single syllable of the Mātṛkā is mastered, that [goal] is accomplished accordingly. || 88 || 89 || 90 ||
Regarding the phrase "yadakṣara": because the moon (*śaśin*) consists of nectar (*amṛta*), it signifies the light (*jyotsnā*) which is the nature of illumination.
"Adorned" (*maṇḍita*) means connected with that. The "three worlds" (*bhuvanatraya*) consist of the nature of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
"The perfected *mātṛkā*" is so called because the comprehension of meaning from all words arises from it. This is what is being said:
The pervasion of the Self over both word and meaning is established without exception. Regarding the phrase "that which is in the syllable":

it is "great" because it is beginningless, and it is a "sūtra" because it indicates specific meanings; it is "strung upon" (prota) in the sense of having a fixed relationship. "This" refers to its perceptibility.

From the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) to the shell of the universe (kaṭāha), "the cosmic egg" signifies the ultimate extent of greatness, while "the shell" signifies the lowest limit of subtlety. What is meant is this:
when, as previously stated, there is a complete pervasion of both word and meaning, [then the state of being Śiva is attained].
Having taught that there is a specific intermediate relationship [between the letters], the identity of the Self with that [relationship] is established.

Regarding the verse beginning with "yadekā" (91): *ādhāra* means the substratum (*adhikaraṇa*). *Bīja* means the cause. Having stated that the eleven syllables take on the form of three corners (*koṇa*), their arising from those [corners] is described as "born from the three corners."
The meaning is that it is seen as established through the direct perception of the world; this demonstrates the direct perception of the previously mentioned phenomenal expansion (*prapañca*).

What is being said is this: having taught that even a single syllable of the *mātṛkā* possesses the status of being the cause of the universe, it follows that one's own identity with that [syllable] is thereby established. || 93 ||
[She is] adorned with the letters *a*, *ka*, *ca*, and so forth, as well as *iṭ*, *ta*, *na*, *ddha*, *pa*, *ya*, *sa*, *kṣa*, *ra*, *va*, *gi*, and *ṇī*;
she dwells in the head, the limbs, the arms, the heart, the back, the hips, and the feet. (94)
I bow to that Great Goddess, who is extracted from the syllable *tām*, who is the essence of essences, higher than the highest, and whose nature is supreme bliss. (95)
Even today, the gods do not know even slightly regarding her—who she is, from where she comes, or by whom she was created—whether she possesses form or is formless. (96)
I bow to that supreme, auspicious Goddess, who is the form of the imperishable letters of the Mother-grammar, and who shines forth amidst the surging waves of the Kula lineage. 97.

He says "akaca" etc. [She is] manifest as the totality of the eight powers, Vaśinī and so forth, which will be described hereafter; and as the individual letters of the Mātṛkā, appearing everywhere as her very body in their separate forms. This is what is meant: of the Mātṛkā...

Having taught that embodied beings possess embodiment through the form of both the aggregate and its individual parts, it follows as a remainder that one's own identity with that [reality] is established. The extraction (*uddhāra*) consists of the form of the script; she herself is the essence of essences.
She demonstrates the object of the term "essence of both" by saying "beyond the supreme" (*parātparām*); she is of the nature of supreme bliss.

Regarding the letter *i*, which consists of the *bindu* and the *visarga*: because it is the nature of the essential identity (*sāmarasya*) of Śiva and Śakti, this is what is meant: when one meditates upon the letter *i*—which is the form of the unity of the *bindu* and the *visarga-jīva* (the cause of the *mātṛkā*)—as one's own self, as will be described in the passage beginning with "the conceptualization of the *bindu*."
"The experience of supreme bliss. || 94 || 95 ||
"Even now" praises the secret previously mentioned. "Deities" refers to the sense organs (*indriya*).
What is this [deity] in its essential nature (*svarūpa*)? For what reason? In what place? By what means? [The answer is:
by the cultivation of form (*sarūpabhāvanā*) and the cultivation of formlessness (*amarūpabhāvanā*). This is what is meant.

Pierced by the side-glances of those who lack a guide, they do not yet—up to this very moment and at all times—know even slightly, in the slightest degree, what the nature of the six sense organs is, for what reason they exist, in what location they reside, or by what means [they function]; nor do they know the cultivation of form (*sarūpa-bhāvanā*) or the cultivation of the formless (*arūpa-bhāvanā*). Regarding this:
The four questions are to be understood from the mouth of the venerable teacher; they have not been disclosed here because of their extreme secrecy. || 96 ||

"I bow" means: I, the Self in the form of the Mātṛkā, through the contraction of the beginning and the end; [I bow] to the Imperishable One, who is born between the letters *a* and *kṣa*, whose nature is the syllables of the Mātṛkā, and who is reached by the path revealed in the seventh Sūtra.

I praise her, the Mistress of the eight great siddhis arising from the eight groups (aṣṭavarga), in whom eight measures (mātrā) are established through the sequential order of the consonant classes. 98.
I bow to the illustrious Tripurā, who dwells within the Śrīpīṭha beginning with the letter Ja that fulfills all desires, and who is the treasury of the four commands. 99.
Thus, this hymn consisting of twelve verses brings about all accomplishments;
for it is a hymn to you, O Goddess, who are of indivisible form.
The *kula* (the body) shines forth, surging with waves of creative power (*kala*), because it dissolves into the earth;

*kalā* here means a portion. It shines intensely, rising higher and higher, as the supreme *vaikharī* speech, possessing an inconceivable majesty of nature. For one who contemplates this, the following is said: its form is unmanifest.
And by directing one's attention toward the form of Mātṛkā, which is manifest in form, the identity of one's own self with that [Mātṛkā] is accomplished.

He arranges [them] by means of the sequential application taught in the seventh sūtra. That group of eight *mātṛkās* is also mentioned therein [as]: "the Mistress of the Eight Great Siddhis arising from the eight groups," and "the Mistress of the Eight Siddhis beginning with *aṇimā* arising from each individual group. This is what is meant: regarding the *mātṛkā*...

There are eight groups, and their presiding deities are the eight Mothers; for each of them, there are the eight supernatural powers beginning with *aṇimā*. These together constitute sixty-four. The collective power (*samaṣṭi-śakti*) which is the cause of those individual powers (*vyaṣṭi-śakti*) is established as one's own Self (*svātman*). Herein also lies a secret.
That should be understood from the mouth of one whose feet have been propitiated. || 98 ||
Regarding "kāma": that seat whose initial letter is *ja* is the "jakārādya," namely the Jālandhara-pīṭha. The Śrī-pīṭha is the Oḍḍiyāna-pīṭha because it is the abode of the Goddess.
She dwells everywhere in the form of space within this quartet of seats consisting of earth, water, fire, and air.
The Command (ājñā), which is the treasury of the fourfold Command—the ancient tradition and so forth—is a treasury because it is the cause of all things. Tripurā is the Mātṛkā;
she is elevated by means of the Mātṛkās, which consist of the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge, and are known as the reality of the nature of the Self.
"It fills" means this:

by means of the eleven aforementioned sūtras, the Power (śakti) whose nature is the manifold universe (viśvaprapañca) is established as one's own self (svātmatva) through its pervasion of the specific locations of the Mātṛkā taught therein, as well as the specific principles (tattva).
From here onwards is our own commentary. 99.
With this verse beginning with "iti," he teaches the fruit of reciting the hymn (*stotra*).
In that regard, [the fruit arises] from the identity with *mātṛkā*, which is of an undivided nature and unconditioned by space or form. Thus, all is auspicious (*śivam*). 100.

The pervasion consisting of the reality of water has been correctly demonstrated. Through the thorough churning of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is assimilated into one's own self. (101)
Thus ends the second chapter in the Śrīkādimata among the sixteen Nityātantras. || 2 ||
Thus, in the *Manoramā* commentary composed by Subhagānandanātha, titled *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete *Tantra* known as the *Śrīkādimata* among the *Śrīṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
The second chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the worship, the names, and other aspects of the majesty of the nine lords (Navanātha), has been fully examined and completed. || 2 ||
Now begins the third chapter.
Now, the sixteen vidyās of the sixteen nityās shall be taught in order:
those of Vārāhī, Kurukullā, and of one's own [mantra] consisting of eight syllables. (1)
O beloved! Listen now to the mantras for the elements and the powers in their proper order, as they are proclaimed through the conventions of the scripts previously described by the virtuous. || 2 ||
She is described as being playful through the heart, prāṇa, ilā, haṃsa, dāha, and vahni;
she is threefold according to the distinctions of the haṃsa. Listen to these [three] in their proper order.
Now begins the third chapter.
Having taught in the preceding second chapter the procedures for the worship and the majesty of the nine lords (*navanātha*), [the author] next...

He teaches twenty-five mantras in total: the sixteen mantras of the sixteen Nityās and nine ancillary mantras (aṅgamantras). This is done by means of the third chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "atha ṣoḍaśa" and ending with "balermanuḥ. Therein, [the section] beginning with "atha ṣoḍaśa"...

With these two verses ending with "prāgudīritaiḥ," he teaches the summary of the chapter's subject matter and so forth. In that context, "by means of conventions" refers to the names used according to the convention; "previously mentioned" means those declared in the thirty-fifth chapter of the previous tantra. || 1 || 2 ||

With these three verses beginning with "hṛt" and ending with "samīritā," he teaches the essential nature of the primary Lalitā-vidyā—the principal Nityā—as well as its divisions and so forth. In this context: *hṛt* (heart) is the letter *sa*;
*prāṇa* (vital breath) is the letter *ka*; *ilā* (earth) is the letter *la*; *haṃsa* is the letter *ha*; *dāha* (burning) is the letter *ra*; and *vahni* (fire) is...
The letter *ī*; its own *bindu*. By the passage beginning with "haṃsa" and ending with "svam," *hṛllekhā* is expressed as *hrīṃ*.
The remainder is that she is Lalitā, who is Vidyā. [She is so called] by the differentiation of the *haṃsa*, that is, by the differentiation of the application of the letter *ha*.
(3) [She is] by that which begins with *haṃsa*, i.e., by that which begins with the letter *ha*. Lalitā.
The first [mudrā] is by means of the *haṃsa* and so forth; the middle one is by means of the *haṃsa* situated at the beginning and the middle;
that same third is the *prakṛti*; and the fourth is by means of those [elements] together with the final *māyā*.
Among these, the fourth leads to liberation, while the other three lead to prosperity;
thus has the Vidyā of Tripurasundarī been correctly proclaimed.
The first [syllable] is *suciḥ* joined with its own [vowel]; the second would be *lalitā*.
Then there is *śūnya* joined with fire (*agni*), followed by *rayaḥ* joined with *vyāpta*. (6)
The vital breath (prāṇa), joined with the fire of essence (rasāgni) and the pair of voids (śūnyayugma) accompanied by the mobile (cara);
then this [vital breath] is again conjoined with the sky (nabhaḥ), the earth (gotrā), and burning (dāha). || 7 ||
The water (ambu) should be joined with the mobile (cara), and the heart (hṛt) should be joined with the forest-power (vana-śakti);

"by the Vidyā" is the remainder [of the sense]. In the phrase "with the haṃsa situated at the beginning and middle," the word "middle" refers to the position above the letter *ka*. That very one is Lalitā; that very Vidyā. The fourth is the *turyā*. By those, together with the final *māyā*, by them...

By means of the syllables belonging to the three peaks (*kūṭa*), with the final *māyā*— that is, the *hṛllekhā* situated within— the following is what is meant: by the syllables of the aforementioned three peaks arranged in the stated order, [the first and second peaks] being devoid of the *hṛllekhā* situated at their ends, and [the third peak] being [devoid of the *hṛllekhā*] situated at its end...
Together with the Hṛllekhā, they are called the "entirety," which is the fourth Vidyā. Regarding these four Vidyās: || 5 ||

With these three verses beginning with "śuciḥ" and ending with "ekādaśākṣarī," [the author] teaches the eleven-syllable mantra of the second deity, Kāmeśvarī-nityā. In this context, "śuciḥ" refers to the vowel *ai*. "Joined with its own" (*svena yutaḥ*) means joined with its own *bindu* (nasal dot); thus it becomes *ai*. The phrase "the first letter" is the understood remainder.

*Lalitā* is the *vidyā* previously mentioned. *Śūnya* is the letter *na*. *Agni-yuta* means joined with *agni*, which is the letter *i*; thus it is *ni*. *Rayaḥ* is the letter *ta*. *Vyāptena saṃyutaḥ* means joined with *vyāpta*, which is the letter *ya*; thus it is *tya*. (6) *Prāṇaḥ* is the letter *ka*. *Rasāgnisahitaḥ* means joined with *rasa* and *agni*; *rasa* is the letter *la*.
The syllable *kli* is formed by the letter *ka* together with fire (*ra*) and water (*i*). The pair of voids is the two *na*s.
Joined with movement (*cara*), which is the letter *e*, it becomes *nne*. The sky is the letter *ma*.
This is the eternal Kāmeśvarī, the sole bestower of desires, consisting of eleven syllables. (8)
Kāmeśvarī and others constitute the beginning; then there is Rasa and Sthirā;
then Rasa joined with Dharā and Carā; thereafter Sthirā; and finally Rasa is recorded.

When *sthirā* is joined with *agni* in the void (*śūnya*), it becomes *rasa*; immediately after that, *sthirā* combined with *bhūḥ* is *gotrā*, and when *sadāha* is joined with *agni*, it is *rasa*, followed by *sthirā*. (10)
The sky (*nabhas*) joined with the wind (*marut*); the sap (*rasa*) accompanied by movement (*cara*).

"Gotrā" refers to the letter *da*. Again, this [is] the letter *da*; joined with burning (*dāha*), where burning is the letter *ra*, it is joined with that inseparably. (7) Water (*ambu*) is the letter *va*; joined with movement (*cara*), where movement is the letter *e*.
"Accompanied by *ve*": *vana* joined with power (*śakti*) means the vowel *au*; "power" is the visarga. Accompanied by these two, it is *sauḥ*, where *hṛt* is the letter *sa*.
Thus, in the manner described, the meaning is that it consists of eleven syllables. || 8 ||

With twenty-three verses beginning with "Kāmeśvarī" and ending with "Mohinī," he teaches the three-hundred-and-fifty-syllable Vidyā of the third Nityā, Bhagamālinī. Therein, the first [syllable] is the letter *ai* accompanied by the *bindu*, namely *aiḥ*. *Rasaḥ* [is the second].

The letter *bha* is the "taste" (*rasa*). The letter *ga* is the "stable" (*sthira*). The earth (*dharā*) is the letter *u*; joined with that, it becomes *bhu*. The "mobile" (*sacara*) is joined with the number one (*ekāra*), making *e*. The "stable" is the letter *ga*, thus *ge*. The "taste" is the letter *bha*.
(9) The "stable" and the "void" (*śūnya*) are the letters *ga* and *na*. Each is joined with the fire (*agni*), which is the letter *i*.

"Gini" means: *rasa* is the letter *bha*; *sthira* is the letter *ga*. "Accompanied by *bhū*" (*bhūḥ-sahitā*) means accompanied by *bhū*, which is the vowel *ū*. The expression "accompanied by *bhū*" (*bhūḥ-sahitā*) is used here as a technical term (*saṃjñā-śabda*); its meaning is "by means of the syllable endowed with the name *bhū*. Thus, it should be understood everywhere else in this section as well.
Nirvāha: *go* is the syllable *ga*; *gotrā* is the letter *da*; *sadāha* is the letter *ra* together with the *repha* (visarga); *agni* is the letter *i*; *ri* is the letter *ra*;

*rasa* is the letter *bha*; *sthirā* is the letter *ga*. (10) *nabhaḥ* is the letter *ma*; joined with *marut*, that is, joined with the letter *ā* from *marut*, it becomes *mā*; *rasā* is the letter *la*; it is endowed with *cara*.
Then the *rasa* [fluid] is stabilized, and subsequently joined with the vital air (*marut*). || 11 ||
Ambu (water), haṃsa (swan), and sacara (mobile); then rasa (taste) joined with sthira (fixed).
Sthira is endowed with dharā (earth), and haṃsa is joined with both vyāpta (pervasive) and cara (mobile). 12.
Rasa, Sthirā, then Vyāptam, Bhūyutam, Śūnyam, Agniyuk; Rasa, Sthirā, then Sāgni, Śūnyam, Javiyuta, Marut. (13)
The letter *ra* with *śūnya*, joined with fire (*r*), heart-burning (*ṛ*); thereafter, with water (*ṝ*);
then *rasa* (*l*), *sthirā* (*l̥*), water (*v*), and space (*ū*) joined with itself (*ū*), as well as *prāṇa* (*ai*). || 14 ||

"Dāha" is the syllable *ya*; therefore, "sthirā" (the earth) conjoined with "dāha" is *yasthi*. Together with the letter *e*, it becomes *leyasthi*. "Rasa" is the letter *bha*. "Sthirā" is the letter *ga*. Conjoined with "marut" (wind), and joined separately with the vowel *ā*, it becomes *gā*. (11) "Ambu" is the letter *va*. "Haṃsa" is the letter *ha*.

The letter *ha* is accompanied by *acara*, which is *e*. "Rasa" is the letter *bha*. "Sthirā" is the letter *ga*. "Dharānvitā" means accompanied by *u*, thus *gu*. "Haṃsa" is the letter *ha*. With "vyāpta," which is the letter *ya*, and "cara," which is *e*—joined with those two, it becomes *hye*. (12) "Rasa" is the letter *bha*. "Sthirā" is the letter *ga*. "Vyāpta" [is the letter *ya*].
The letter *ya*. Joined with *bhū* and accompanied by *o*, it is *yo*. *Śūnya* is the letter *na*.
Joined with fire (*agni*) and accompanied by *i*, it is *ni*. *Rasa* is the letter *bha*. *Sthira* is the letter *ga*.
Together with fire (*agni*), it is accompanied by *i*. *Śūnya* is the letter *na*. This designation, "together with fire," is intended as a qualifier for the thing named (*saṃjñin*).

The meaning is that the phoneme called *śūnya* (the letter *kṣa*) should be accompanied by the vowel *i*. In this entire treatise, it should be understood that there is a rule regarding the indication of gender for qualifiers, based on the fact that the reference is primarily to the name (*saṃjñā*) and the named (*saṃjñin*). In that regard, the rule for the indication of gender with respect to the named is threefold, depending on whether it refers to the word "phoneme" (*varṇa*).

With respect to the word *akṣara* and with respect to the word *lipi*, [it is as follows]: by that, *ni*. Joined with *javi* (the letter *ja*), it is accompanied by the letter *pa*; *marut* is the vowel *ā*, thus *pā*. (13) Now, *rayaḥ* is the letter *ta*. *Śūnya* is the letter *na*. Joined with fire (*agni*), meaning accompanied by the vowel *i*, this qualifies *śūnya* itself; thus *ni*. *Hṛt* is the letter *sa*.

"Burning" (dāha) is the letter *ra*. Together with "water" (*ambu*, *va*), it becomes *rva*. "Taste" (*rasa*) is the letter *bha*. "Firm" (*sthira*) is the letter *ga*. "Water" (*ambu*) is the letter *va*. "Ether" (*viyat*) is the letter *sa*. Joined with itself, that is, accompanied by the nasal drop (*bindu*), it is *saṃ*. "Vital breath" (*prāṇa*) is the letter *ka*. (14) "Burning" (*dāha*) is the letter *ra*. Joined with "fire" (*agni*, *i*), it is *ri*.
The letter *bha* is *rasa*; the letter *ga* is *sthira*; the letter *ū* is *kṣmā*. (p.
45) Together with *sacara* and *javī*, they follow in sequence from the third syllable of the aforementioned *vidyā*. 15.
Then there is a group of four vowels, followed by the sixth [vowel] (rasa), and then the stable one (sthirā) joined with the heart (hṛt) and water (ambu);
then burning (dāha) with earth (kṣmā), which is mobile (sacara) and swift (javī), and the heart (hṛt). 16.
The burning element (tejas), joined with water and wind; then space (ākāśa) with fire and taste (rasa);
the stable earth (pṛthivī) also joined with wind; and the void (śūnya) with fire and the two moving elements (wind and space). 17.
The swan (haṃsa) is joined with the pervasive wind (marut); from that, the void (śūnya) and water (ambu) are pervasive;
burning (dāha) is joined with the mountain (gotrā) and speed (raya), and likewise there is burning and speed. (18)
The heart (ha) together with the earth (la), followed by fire (ra) and water (va);
then water (va) and the firm one (sthirā = ma), then breath (pra) together with water (va) and fire (ra). || 19 ||

"Joined with *dāha*": *dāha* is the letter *ra*; "joined with that" means accompanied by *ra*, namely *rū*. "With *cara*" means accompanied by the letter *e*. "The swift one" is the letter *pa*, namely *pe*. "From the third of the previous vidyā" means, in sequence, the four letters beginning with the third letter [of the previous vidyā]. This is the meaning.
This is what is meant:
the four syllables—the third, fourth, fifth, and sixth—of the *Kāmeśvarīnityā* mantra (following "na pe"), namely "ni-tya-kli-nne," are to be known as these secret [mantras]. 15. Raso.

The letter *bha*; the stable one is *ga*; the heart is *sa*; water is *va*. Joined with *kṣmā*, that is, with the vowel *ū*, it becomes *bu*. Burning is *ra*, as in *rū*. The swift one is *pa*; joined with *cara*, that is, with the vowel *e*, it becomes *pe*. The heart is *sa*. (16) Burning is joined with water and wind.
"Joined with the letters *va* and *ā*, [it is] *dāha*; by that, [the phrase] 'all these' [is formed]. *Vyoma* is the letter *ṇa*.

With fire (*agni*), it is accompanied by the vowel *i*, thus *ṇi*. *Rasa* is the letter *bha*. *Sthira* is the letter *ga*. In this context, the word *sarva* (all) also implies conjunction. Joined with *marut* and joined with the vowel *ā*, it is *gā*. *Śūnya*..."

The letter *na* is *ni*, being accompanied by the letter *i*. "Moving in the sky" (*nabhaścarau*) means the letter *ma* (sky) and the letter *e* (moving); that is to say, the letter *ma* accompanied by the letter *e*. (17) *Haṃsa* is the letter *ha*.
"Joined with the pervasive wind" (*vyāptamarudyuktaḥ*) means joined with those two: the letter *ya* (pervasive) and the letter *ā* (wind).

"Hyā" means: the letter *na* is "void" (*śūnya*). The letter *ya* is "pervaded" (*vyāpta*). "Beyond this" is the remainder [of the phrase]. "Water" (*ambu*) is the letter *va*. "Burning" (*dāha*) is the letter *ra*. "Mountain" (*gotrā*) is the letter *da*. "Joined with *cara*" means accompanied by the letter *e*; thus, *de*. Likewise, "burning" (*dāha*) is the letter *ra* accompanied by the letter *e*; thus, *re*. Similarly, "speed" (*raya*) is the letter *ta* accompanied by the letter *e*.

This is the meaning of "te" (verse 18). "Hṛt" is the letter *sa*. "Dharāsahitam" means accompanied by *u*, thus forming "su". "Dāharayau" refers to the letters *ra* and *ta*. "Carasamanvitau" means joined with *e*; that is, the letters *ra* and *ta* are each accompanied by the vowel *e*, thus forming "rete". "Rasaḥ" is the letter *bha*. "Sthirā" is the letter *ga*.

A pair of zeros joined with the letter *ca* (c), then the same as before; thereafter a pair of zeros and *go* (g), followed by *trā* (tr) joined with fire (*da*) and water (*ba*), and the letter *ca* (c). (20)
Prāṇa is joined with Rasācarī; beyond that, it is pervaded by Gotrā.
Gotrā is joined with the Dāha wind; therefore, it becomes pervaded by water.
Vāta and Nabhas are conjoined with Bhū; Vāścara is endowed with [the same].
Rasa is joined with Sthira, Ambu, and Agni; Vāyu-yugma is accompanied by Cara. (22)

Subsequently, the *rasa* (sixth) joined with *grāsodharā* (the fifth vowel), conjoined with *śakti* (the nasal *m*), and the *grāsa* (the letter *bh*) accompanied by *bhūḥ* (the letter *l*), O Goddess; thereafter, the *rasa* (*ṣ*) pervades the heart. (23)
After that, O auspicious lady, there is burning, then water, then speed accompanied by water and wind,
then the void alone, and finally the taste, including all moving and stationary beings.

The letter *ka* is *prāṇa*. Accompanied by *rasa* and *agni*: *rasa* is the letter *la*, and *agni* is the letter *i*; together they form *kli*. (19) The pair of voids is the two *na*s; joined with *cara* and accompanied by *ekāra*, it is *nne*. Following that, from the previous [syllable], hereafter is this syllable.

The meaning is that the preceding syllable is itself the succeeding syllable. *Kli* refers to the pair of voids, which is the double *na*, i.e., *nna*. *Gotrā* is the letter *da* accompanied by *dāha* (*ra*), thus *dra*. It is joined with *ambu*, the letter *va*; *cara* is the letter *e*. (20) *Prāṇa* is the letter *ka*; *rasā* is the letter *la*; *cara*...

The letter *e* joined with those two is *kle*. *Gotrā* is the letter *da*. *Vyāpta* is the letter *ya*. *Gotrā* is the letter *da*. Joined with *dāha* and *marut*, [it is] *drā*; *dāha* is the letter *ra*, and *marut* is the letter *ā*, thus *drā*. *Ambu* is the letter *va*. *Vyāpta* is the letter *ya*. *Vāta* is the letter *a*. *Nabha* is the letter *ma*.

"Accompanied by earth" means joined with the letter *ū*, thus *mo*. "Water" is the letter *gha*. "Endowed with movement" means accompanied by the letter *e*, thus *ghe*. "Taste" is the letter *bha*. "Firm" is the letter *ga*. "Water" is the letter *va*.
"Joined with fire" means joined with the letter *i*, thus *vi*. "A pair of winds" refers to two *ca* letters. "Endowed with movement" [means joined with the letter *e*].
"Accompanied by the eleventh" (ekārasahitam) means: the "swallower" (grāsaḥ) is the letter *kṣa*; joined with "earth" (*dharā*), that is, joined with the vowel *u*, it becomes *kṣu*.

"Taste" (*rasaḥ*) is the letter *bha*; endowed with "power" (*śakti*), that is, accompanied by the visarga, it becomes *bhaḥ*. The "swallower" is the letter *kṣa*. "Joined with earth" (*bhūḥ sahitaḥ*), that is, joined with the vowel *o*—in this case as well, [it is] "joined with earth."
The inclusion of the nature of the name and the word means "accompanied by the name *bhū*";
*kṣo* is the vocative "O Goddess. *Rasa* is the letter *bha*; *vyāpta* is the letter *ya*; *hṛt* is the letter *sa*. || 23 ||
"With *dāha* and *repha*" means accompanied by [the syllable] *ra*; "water" (*ambu*) is the letter *va*, thus *rva*. "Heart" (*hṛt*) is the letter *sa*.
"Speed" (*rayaḥ*) is the letter *ta*. "Endowed with water and wind" (*ambumarudanvitaḥ*) means water is *va* and wind is *ā*, thus *tvā*. "Void" (*śūnya*) is the letter *na*.
(47) Space joined with water is *dāha*; fire joined with itself is *śuci*.
Earth, taste, and earth joined with themselves are the five [elements] situated at intervals of one. || 25 ||

The five elements, beginning with the seed-syllables (bījas) situated within those [vowels], are indeed conjoined with their own [consonants]: they are, in order, the bowstring (jyā), the moving one (sacara), the sap (rasa), the earth (bhū), and that joined with the sky (nabhas). (26)
The *haṃsa* (ha) is joined with the *cara* (ya) twice; then the *prāṇa* (ra) is joined with *rasa* (6) and *agni* (3).
Then there is a pair of *śūnya*s (00) joined with *cara* (ya); then *hṛd-dāha* (ha) and *ambu* (va) joined with *marut* (ya). (27)
Then, O Dear One, one should place the sky (L) together with fire (R), and the taste (V) made stable by the wind (Y); then one should place the void (H) with fire (R), accompanied by the mobile (C).

And "kevalam" is simply *n* without a vowel. "Bhadre" is the address to the Goddess, not separated by a mantra. "Rasaḥ" is the letter *bha*. That, together with "cara," which is the letter *e*, becomes *be*; "sthirā" is the letter *ga*, thus *ge*. (24) "Viyat" is the letter *sa*. Joined with "amba," which is the letter *va*, it becomes *sva*. "Dāha" is the letter *ra*, joined with "agni," which is the letter *i*.

*Sahita* is *ri*. It is joined with its own *bindu*, becoming *r̥*. *Śuci* is the letter *e*, forming *ai*. *Bhūmi* is the letter *ba*. Joined with *rasa*, *akṣmā*, and *sva*: *rasa* is the letter *la*; *kṣmā* is the letter *u*; and *sva* is the *bindu*. Combined with these, it becomes *blū*. These five letters are situated at intervals of one; this is the *kūṭākṣara* (cryptic syllable) *blū*.

The meaning is that this [mantra] and the others, with one syllable intervening between each, should be employed five times. Those seed-syllables (bījas) separated by those [intervening syllables], conjoined with their respective [vowels], are indeed five; these five seed-syllables, situated above in the intervals of the previously mentioned seed-syllable *blū*, are [to be applied] in sequence, together with the nasal bindu (*m*).
The word "I shall tell" is the ellipsis. *Jyā* is the letter *ja*, i.e., *jaṃ*. *Sacara* means accompanied by *eka* (the number one);

*rasa* is the letter *bha*, i.e., *bhe*. *Bhūḥ* is the syllable *oṃ*. *Nabho-yutā* means joined with *nabhaḥ* (the sky), which is the letter *ma*; thus, *mā*. || 26 || *Haṃsaḥ* is the letter *ha*. *Carayutaḥ* means accompanied by *cara* (the number one); thus, *he*. *Blūm* is [the seed-syllable].

The meaning is that at the end of the fifth seed-syllable (bīja) previously mentioned, the seed-syllable *hem* should occur twice. For example: *blū ja blū mo vlū he blū he*. In this manner: *prāṇa* is the letter *ka*; *rasāgni-yuk* means joined with *rasa*, which is the letter *la*, and *agni*, which is the letter *ri*; it is accompanied by those two.

*Kli* means the pair of voids (*śūnyayugma*), which is the two *na*s. Joined with *cara*, meaning accompanied by *e*, it is *nne*. *Hṛt* is the letter *sa*. *Dāha* is the letter *ra*. *Ambu* joined with *marut*: *ambu* is *va*, and *marut* is *ā*; together they form *vā*. (27) *Vyoma* is the letter *ṇa*. Accompanied by fire (*agni*), it is *ṇi*. *Rasa*...

The syllable *bha*; the remainder is that it is joined with the letter *ā* of Marut (i.e., *bhā*). The firm one is the letter *ga*, i.e., *gā*. The void is the letter *na*. That which is with fire is joined with the letter *i*, i.e., *ni*. The sky is the letter *ma*.
That which is with movement is joined with the letter *e*, i.e., *me*.
After water comes space; from that arises the sky joined with wind, which is both void and pervasive, endowed with the heart and with its own fires of speed and heat. (29)

The syllable *haṃsa* is joined with "burning" (*sadāha*), "water" (*ambu*), "taste" (*rasa*), and "movement" (*acara*). It is declared that the final [syllable] is joined with "burning" (*dāha*), "fire" (*vahni*), and "steadiness" (*svaira*). (30)
O Supreme Goddess! This Nityā Bhagamālinī, which consists of three hundred and thirty-five syllables, has been described as the enchantress of women.
The *haṃsa* [mantra], joined with the fire of burning (*dāhavahni*), is said first;
it shall consist of the eight syllables beginning with the third letter of *Kāmeśvarī*. (32)
The heart-mantra joined with the wind (ha), and the *haṃsa* joined with the wind (sa)—
this eleven-syllable mantra is proclaimed as the eternal Nityaklinnā.
"O Beloved" (*priye*) is the address to the Goddess. (28) "Water" (*ambu*) is the syllable *va*. "Sky" (*viyat*) is the syllable *sa*. "Ether" (*nabhas*) is the syllable *ma*.
The word "but" (*tu*) is used for conjunction. "Endowed with wind" (*marudanvitam*) means together with the letter *ā*, forming *mā*.
"Void" (*śūnyam*) is the syllable *na*. "Pervaded" (*vyāptam*) is the syllable *ya*. "Heart" (*hṛt*) is the syllable *sa*. It is "joined" (*yuktam*).

*Raya* is the letter *takāra*; *dāha* is the letter *repha*; *sva* is the *bindu*; and *vahni* is the letter *ikāra*. Joined with these, it is *strīṃ*. (29) *Haṃsa* is the letter *hakāra*; *sadāha* means accompanied by the letter *repha*.
It is conjoined with *ambu*, *rasā*, *cara*, and *sva*: *ambu* is the letter *vakāra*; *rasā* is the letter *lakāra*; *cara* is the letter *ekāra*; and *sva* is the *bindu*.

The *bindu* is conjoined with these. This is what is meant: one *kūṭa* consists of the letters *ha*, *ra*, *va*, *la*, *e*, and the *bindu*; thus, *hvlū*. *Haṃsa* is the letter *ha*. "Conjoined with *dāha*, *vahni*, and *sva*": *dāha* is *ra*; *vahni* is *i*; *sva* is the *bindu*. It is conjoined with these.

The word "final" refers to the seed-syllable; that is to say, the syllable *hrīṃ*. The word "Vidyā" refers to the Nityā Bhagamālinī; this is the sense. "O Supreme Sovereign" (*parameśānī*) is an address to the Goddess. || 30 || 31 ||

With these three verses beginning with "haṃsa" and ending with "sundarī," [the author] teaches the eleven-syllable mantra of the fourth Nityā, Nityaklinnā, as well as the fruit resulting from its recitation and other practices. In this context, "haṃsa" refers to the letter *ha*; "joined with the fire of burning" means the letter *ra* (dāha) and the letter *va* (vahni).

The letter *i* with its own bindu; joined with these, it means "hṛllekhā. The remainder is that *hrīṃ* is the first seed-syllable (*bīja*). There is a group of eight letters beginning from the third letter of Kāmeśvarī;
this is the *vidyā* of the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī, starting from the third syllable.
Up to the tenth syllable, there are eight syllables beginning from the second syllable here; thus, nine syllables are produced. *Hṛt* is the letter *sa*. *Ambu* joined with *marut* (p.
49) is the fire (*agni*) that melts the women and the butter through recitation (*japa*) and other means.
The practitioner constantly becomes more beautiful than even Kandarpa. || 34 ||
First, *bhūḥ* is joined with its own [seed-syllable]; then *prāṇa* is joined with that by means of burning;
then *rasa* is joined with that by means of burning; then *prāṇa* is joined with its own [seed-syllable] by means of burning and vanishing.
The syllable *kaṃ* joined with *dāha*, the *prabhā* joined with *dāha*, and the bowstring (*jyā*) joined with *dāha*; finally, the two [syllables] *nityaklinna*. (36)
This nine-syllabled Nityā Bheruṇḍā bestows all accomplishments;
by the mere remembrance of her, the three kinds of poison are destroyed in an instant.

The syllable *va* is water (*ambu*). The syllable *ā* is wind (*marut*). Joined with these two is *svā*. The syllable *ha* is the swan (*haṃsa*). Joined with the wind, the syllable *ā*, it means *hrīṃ*. Fire is the "melter" (*drāvaka*) of women and butter. This is what is meant: by the mere sight of this one who has attained mastery over the vidyā...
Women become submissive and provide assistance in matters of wealth, life, and other such needs. || 32 || 33 || 34 ||
With three verses beginning with *bhūḥ svena* and ending with *kṣaṇāt*, [the author] teaches the nine-syllable mantra of the fifth deity, Bheruṇḍā-nityā. Therein, *bhūḥ* is the syllable *o*;
"joined with its own" means accompanied by the *bindu*, thus *om*. The phrase "the first seed-syllable" is the understood remainder. *Prāṇaḥ*...

The letter *ka* [is joined] with *dāha*, which is the letter *ra*; the meaning is that the syllable *ka* conjoined with *oṃ* is *krau*. *Rasa* is the letter *bha*; [it is joined] with *dāha*, which is the letter *ra*; the meaning is that the syllable *bha* conjoined with *oṃ* is *bhro*. *Prāṇa* is the letter *ka*.

"Dāha," "vana," and "sva": *dāha* is the letter *repha* (ṛ); *vana* is the vowel *o*; *sva* is the *bindu*. Joined with these, it is *kro*. (35) *Kaṃ* is the letter *jha*. With *dāha*, which is *repha*, meaning the syllable *jhakāra* joined with that and joined with the vowel *oṃ*, it is *jhro*. *Prabhā* is the letter *cha*. With *dāha*, which is *repha*...
"Joined with that" means joined with the syllable *oṃ*, [resulting in] *cchro*. "Jyā" means the letter *ja*.

"By burning" means by the letter *ra*. "Joined with that" means joined with the syllable *oṃ*, [resulting in] the letter *ja*, [i.e.,] *jro*. "Nityaklinnā at the end" means [the mantra of] Nityaklinnā is at the end of the Vidyā.
The meaning of the two syllables is "svāhā. Nityā Bheruṇḍā is the Nityā Vidya; this is the sense.

Poison (*garala*) is threefold, distinguished as stationary (*sthāvara*), mobile (*jaṅgama*), and artificial (*kṛtrima*). Among these, the stationary consists of *kāraskara*, *karavīra*, and so forth; the mobile consists of [poisons from] snakes, scorpions, and so forth; the artificial—
Likuca, rasaka, karpūra, and so forth. || 37 ||

(50) Here, the first [group] shall be Bheruṇḍā and so forth; after Nityaklinnā and so forth, there is water joined with the void and the swan-fire (haṃsāgni), and then water joined with wind (marut). 38.

The heart [HŪṂ] joined with fire [RA], the void [ŚŪNYA] joined with the pervasive [VYĀPTA] and the pure [ŚUCI], and the void [ŚŪNYA] joined with the power of space [NABHAḤŚAKTI]; this is declared to be the nine-syllabled mantra. (39)
Eternal, the bestower of all aims, dwelling in fire, the devourer of the universe—by the mere remembrance of whom the three worlds become submissive. (40)
The second [syllable] belongs to Vahnivāsinī, Nityaklinnā is the fourth;
the fifth begins with Bhagamālā, and the second [syllable] belongs to Bheruṇḍā. || 41 ||

With these three verses beginning with "bheruṇḍādyam" and ending with "trayam," he teaches the nine-syllable mantra of the sixth Nityā, Vahnivāsinī. Therein, "bheruṇḍādyam" refers to the first syllable of the Bheruṇḍā-nityā mantra.

The meaning is that the first syllable of the *Nityavidyā* of Vahnivāsinī occurs; by this, "Oṃ" is established. Immediately after [the mantra of] Nityaklinnā, the first syllable of the *Nityavidyā* of Nityaklinnā is the syllable *hrīṃ*; the meaning is that this is its second syllable. Then, immediately after that, "ambu" refers to the letter *va*.

"Śūnya" is the letter *na*. "Joined with Haṃsa and Agni" means accompanied by the letters *ha* and *i*; that is, the word *vahni* (fire). "Ambu" is the letter *va*. "Joined with Marut" means joined with the vowel *ā*. [This forms *vā*. || 38 || "Hṛt" is the letter *sa*. "Joined with Agni" means accompanied by the letter *i*, thus forming *si*. "Śūnya" is the letter *na*. [It is] pervaded (*vyāptena*).

By the letter *ya*, and by the letter *e* which is pure (*śuci*), it is joined (*yukta*)—meaning conjoined with these two—as *nyai*. The letter *na* is "void" (*śūnya*). The letter *ma* is "sky" (*nabhaḥ*). Conjoined with power (*śakti*), that is, accompanied by the visarga, it is *maḥ*. || 39 || She is the devourer of the universe (*viśvaghasmarā*), the one who swallows the entire world at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*). || 40 ||

With these three verses beginning with "the second" and ending with "Tāriṇī," he teaches the twelve-syllable mantra of the seventh [deity], Mahāvajreśvarīnityā. In that context, "the second" refers to the second syllable of Vahnivāsinī, that is, of the Vahnivāsinīnityā mantra.

The first syllable is *hrīṃ*. "Nityaklinnā" refers to the fourth and fifth [syllables], meaning *ni* and *tya*. The first of Bhagamālā is the vowel *ai*. The second of Bheruṇḍā is the syllable *kroṃ*. [Then] the second and third [syllables] of Nityaklinnā are the two syllables *ni* and *tya*.

The sixth and seventh [syllables] are of that very [seed-syllable], meaning "mada. The eighth and ninth are subsequently of that very same [seed-syllable], meaning they should be the eighth and ninth syllables, respectively, meaning "drave.
"Etadādyaṃ" means the first [syllable] of this Mahāvajreśvarī, meaning the syllable *hrīṃ*.
The meaning is that she is the one who enables the crossing over the mass of suffering and the crossing over through lack of discernment. || 43 ||
The second [is] *nityaklinnā*, the third and the sixth and seventh, the eighth and the ninth, and thereafter this first one—thus it has been declared. (42)
The eternal Mahāvajreśvarī is proclaimed as having twelve syllables;
she is the one who carries one across the multitude of cruel sufferings of wildernesses and oceans.

The last [letter] of Vajreśvarī should be joined with the first; then there is ether (viyat) conjoined with fire (agni). Then there is water (ambu) conjoined with wind (marut), and then the earth (gotrā) conjoined with earth (kṣmā). || 44 ||
Immediately after that, there should be the letter *ra* joined with the pervasive (*vyāpaka*) and the pure (*śuci*).
The two final letters [are joined] with Vahnivāsinī; this is declared to be the Nityā Dūtī. (45)
The seven-syllabled [mantra] removes all transgressions, delights the universe,
brings about prosperity, effects the attainment of the state of Śiva, and bestows all perfections.
The first [syllable] belongs to Vahnivāsinī; after that is the messenger (dūtī) and so forth; then the Haṃsa joined with the sister of the Earth (Dharā), accompanied by Tejaścara.

With the three verses beginning with "Vajreśvarī" and ending with "Siddhide," he teaches the seven-syllable mantra of the eighth Nityā, Dūtī. In that regard, "the last [syllable] of Vajreśvarī shall be the first": the final syllable of Vajreśvarīnityā becomes the first syllable of this [mantra].

In the *Dūtīnityā*, the first syllable is "hrīṃ"—this is the meaning. "Viyat" (space) joined with "agni" (fire): "viyat" is the letter *śa*; "joined with fire" means accompanied by the vowel *i*. Thus, the second [syllable] is "śi". "Ambu" (water) joined with "marut" (wind): "ambu" is the letter *va*; "joined with wind" means accompanied by the vowel *ā*, thus [the third syllable is] "vā".

The third syllable is *gotrā* joined with *kṣmā*. Here, *gotrā* is the letter *da*, and it is joined with *kṣmā*, which is the letter *ū*; thus, *dū* is the fourth syllable. Immediately after that, *rayaḥ* should be joined with *vyāpta* and *śuci*.
Here, *rayaḥ* is the letter *ta*, and it is joined with *vyāpta*, which is the letter *ya*, and *śuci*, which is the letter *ai*. Thus, *tai* is the fifth syllable.
"Joined with 'tyai'": the meaning is that the two final syllables [of the mantra] are for Vahnivāsinī, namely "namaḥ". || 45 ||
She is the remover of all transgressions and the destroyer of that which has arisen from a lack of discernment. || 46 ||

With these four verses beginning with "The first" (*ādyam*) and ending with "the performer" (*kāriṇī*), he teaches the twelve-syllable mantra of the ninth *Nityā*, Tvaritā. Therein, "the first" refers to the syllable *oṃ* of Vahni-vāsinī; "the messenger" (*dūtī*) and so forth refers to the syllable *hrīṃ* immediately following that.
The second seed-syllable is *haṃ*. "Haṃsa" refers to the letter *ha*; "dharā" is the letter *u*;

and "sva" is the bindu (*m*). Joined with these two, it becomes the third seed-syllable, *hūṃ*. Fire, wind, and light, joined with movement, together with the "swallowing" (*grāsa*) and endowed with power (*śakti*).
O Dear One! With the heart, the speed, and the burning, one becomes fire; this is the eighth [letter], O Beloved! || 48 ||
The *haṃsa* joined with *kṣmā* is the *grāsa*; joined with *cara*, it is the second. *Dyuti* joined with *nāda* is the eternal *tvaritā* consisting of twelve syllables. (49)
It brings about the attainment of fortune, beauty, fame, knowledge, wealth, health, and long life;
it pacifies poison and suffering, and fulfills all desired wishes. || 50 ||
The first [syllable] is Śuci joined with itself; the second is Rasa accompanied by Vahni; the third is Prāṇa joined with itself, followed by Vanahṛt and Śakti. || 51 ||
Thus described, this three-syllabled Nityā is Kulasundarī;
by the mere remembrance of whom, omniscience is produced.

The letter *kha* is joined with *tejas*; joined with the moving letter *e*, it is *khe*, the fourth [syllable]. The letter *ca* is *vāyu*. The letter *cha* is the radiance (*prabhā*) of the [word] *pada*. Joined with *cara* and joined with *e*, it is *che*, the sixth [syllable]. *Grāsa* conjoined with *śakti*—*grāsa* being the letter *kṣa*—[conjoined] with *śakti*, which is the visarga.

"Endowed with *kṣa*," thus is the seventh [seed-syllable]. With the heart [syllable], with speed (*raya*), with burning (*dāha*), the fire-god (*vahni*)—that is, the letters *sa*, *ta*, *ra*, and *i*—[forming] "strī," thus is the eighth seed-syllable. "O Dear One! (*priye*) is the vocative address to the Goddess. || 48 ||

The *haṃsa* (the letter *ha*) joined with the earth (*kṣmā*, the letter *la*) and the vowel *u* is *hū*; this is the ninth [syllable]. The *grāsa* (the letter *ga*) joined with the moving one (*cara*, the letter *ra*) is *gre*; this is the tenth. The second [syllable] of this very [mantra] is its second seed-syllable, *hrī*; this is the eleventh. *Dyuti* (light) joined with *nāda* (sound):
*dyuti* is the letter *pha*, and *nāda* is the letter *ṭa*. Joined with that, it is *phaṭ*; this is the twelfth seed-syllable. || 49 ||
It is the pacifier of poison and suffering; it destroys both poison arising from snakes and the like, as well as suffering arising from poverty and the like. || 50 ||

With the two verses beginning with *śuciḥ* and ending with *jāyate*, he teaches the three-syllabled Vidyā of the tenth deity, Kulasundarī Nityā. Therein, *śuciḥ* joined with itself and accompanied by the Bindu is the vowel *ai*; thus, *ai* is the first seed-syllable (*bīja*). [The second is] *rasā* conjoined with *vahni*. *Rasā*...

The letter *la*, fire which is the vowel *ī*—endowed with these two is *li*. The vital breath is the letter *ka*; joined with itself and endowed with the bindu, it is *klī*: this is the second [seed-syllable]. Beyond the forest, the heart, and power (*vana-hṛc-chaktibhiḥ*) is *sauḥ*: this is the third seed-syllable.
51 || By the mere remembrance of her—meaning, even by the deficiency in recitation, worship, and so forth—52 ||

The *haṃsa* (the vital breath), conjoined with the heart, the life-force, and the [subtle] fluids that perform the act of burning, is united with the *vidyā* Kulasundarī according to the oral tradition. (53)
The eternal [Vidyā] is eternal, consisting of three syllables and joined with six peak-syllables;
it is multiplied by the seventy-two forms, such as those in reverse order and so forth.
By worshipping her, a man becomes a perfected being who moves through the sky and is happy; furthermore, his power of restraint and grace arises at will and incessantly. (55)
The first [syllable] shall be the penultimate [of the preceding], followed by *dyuti* (the letter *d*), joined with *dāha* (the letter *r*) and *cara* (the letter *s*) and its own [vowel];
then *hṛt* (the letter *h*), joined with *dāha* (the letter *r*), *kṣmā* (the letter *s*), and its own [vowel]; and after that, the fifth is *vajreśī*. || 56 ||

With these three verses beginning with "haṃsa" and ending with "aniśam," [the author] teaches the three-syllabled mantra of the eternal Ekādaśī as well as the number of its variations. In that context, "haṃsa" refers to the letter *ha*; it is accompanied by "hṛt" (heart), "prāṇa" (vital breath), and "rasādāhakuḥ" (the burning of the essence). "Hṛt" [is the first syllable].
The letter *sa* is the vital breath (*prāṇa*); the letter *ka* is the essence (*rasa*); the letter *la* is burning (*dāha*); the letter *ra* is the earth (*ku*);
and the letter *ha*, known as *haṃsa*, is accompanied by these five. What is meant is that [the mantra] consists of these six syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *u*.
Thus, by joining the beginning and end in forward order for each individual [syllable], there are six distinct variations; subsequently,
by joining the beginning and end in reverse order for each individual [syllable] starting from *ukāra* and ending with *hakāra*, it is likewise.

Through the application of the *saṅketavidyā*—which consists of six distinct varieties and serves as the source (*prakṛti*) for the *nityāvidyā*—in accordance with tradition, seventy-two varieties of *nityāvidyā* arise; among these, this [present one] is the foremost and primary. || 53 ||

By the verse beginning with "nityānitya," the mention of seventy-two divisions out of the one hundred and twenty divisions of ignorance (*avidyā*) that will be explained later is for the purpose of showing the predominance of their application among those divisions of manifestation (*vibhava*) that follow in sequence. [End of verse 54. Of which...
With the verse beginning with "bhajanataḥ," he describes the power of one who has attained *vidyā*-siddhi.

In this context, "by his own will" means that, through the power of yoga, he exercises the subjugation (*nigraha*) and grace (*anugraha*) mentioned in the chapter on the *Nityānityā* [Tantra]. || 55 ||

With these five verses beginning with "Tvaritā" and ending with "Kāmadoditā," he teaches the seventeen-syllable vidyā of the twelfth [deity], Nīlapatākānityā; therein, the penultimate [syllables] are: śha 1, sha 2, lk 3, and lvaha 4.

*Lva-sṭra* (5), *ḍl-spha* (6)—thus, in the order of direct sequence (*anuloma*), Marut joined with its own [consonant] is remembered as being at the beginning of the middle [group] from the tenth [vowel], in due order.
*Bhūmī*, *rasa*, *akṣmā* joined with their own [consonants] are *Vajreśī* from the sixth [vowel], in sequence. (57)
The six syllables are Tvaritā; immediately after that is the third [syllable].
Due to its nature of burning and moving, the first [syllable] of this [mantra] follows immediately thereafter.
The eternal mantra named Nīlapatākā, consisting of seventeen syllables, has been described;
it bestows victory in battle and grants the supernatural powers of the sword, the sandals, and the collyrium.
She is the one who provides the means for Vetālas, birds, servants, Piśācas, and others;
she is the provider of the enjoyments of hidden treasures and perfected foods, and she is manifested as the granter of all desires.

There are six permutations: iṃ 1, dra 2, lu 3, klu 4, svlu 5, sku 6. Thus, there are six permutations in reverse order. In this way, from the application of the sixfold symbolic vidyā within the twelve permutations, seventy-two permutations arise: ai ī oṃ 1; ī ai oṃ 2; ī oṃ ai 3; ai oṃ i 4; oṃ ī ai 5; o... [and so forth].
Ī ĀI 6. These are the sixfold divisions of the Root-Symbol-Vidyā (mūla-saṅketa-vidyā), which is directly Brahman. "Hṛllekhā" refers to *hrīṃ*;

this is the first seed-syllable (*bīja*). The second is *phreṃ*, joined with the letters *pha*, *ra*, *e*, and the bindu, along with light (*dyuti*), burning (*dāha*), and the earth (*cara*) [which is *la*]. "Hṛt" (the heart) joined with burning (*dāha*), the earth (*kṣmā*), and itself [is the third].

The third [syllable] is *srū*, joined with the letter *sa*, the letter *ra*, the letter *ū*, and the nasal dot (*bindu*). Then follows *vajreśī*, which means the fifth [syllable] is the letter *oṃ* as the fourth. Then follows the letter *ā* joined with the wind (*ma*) and accompanied by the nasal dot; thus *ā* is the fifth. These are remembered in sequence from the middle and the beginning of the tenth [verse].
The first two seed-syllables (*bīja*) from the middle of the tenth [deity], Kulasundarīnityā, are *klī* and *aiṃ*;
the meaning is that these constitute her sixth and seventh syllables.
The letter *va*, joined with the earth (the letter *la*), the essence (the letter *ra*), the earth (the letter *la*), and the sun (the letter *u*), along with the *bindu*, becomes *vlū*. Thus.
The eighth seed-syllable is Vajreśī, following the sequence from the sixth.

"Those six syllables are always in a state of flowing ecstasy. Thus, by these [syllables], fourteen syllables of the mantra are accounted for. Following that, the third [syllable] is *tvaritā*, and immediately after that, *huṃ* is the fifteenth seed-syllable (*bīja*).
The second [seed-syllable] of this [mantra] is the letter *pha*, joined with *ra*, *e*, and the nasal drop (*bindu*), due to its nature of burning and moving.
The sixteenth syllable is *kūṭaṃ phreṃ*. The meaning is that immediately following this, the seventeenth is the syllable *hrīṃ*. (58)
Taste, space, burning, and the earth preceded by the forest—when these are joined with their own [corresponding elements], they are considered the eternal one-syllable *vijayā*. (61)
By her mere remembrance, Vijayā, the sovereign glory of the universe, bestows constant victory in debates, in difficult battles, and in legal proceedings. 62.
When joined with the heart-lotus, she herself becomes the eternal Sarvamaṅgalā;
one who has mastered this single-syllable mantra becomes a sky-walker (khecara) in an instant.
Earth with the void and ether; earth and water, then stable earth and water;
speed joined with fire; the bowstring (jyā) as water joined with air; and water joined with air. (64)
The sky, joined with the wind, [is situated] in the space devoid of taste and conjoined with fire;
[the items] such as the sword and sandals, which will be clearly explained later in the chapters on the ritual procedures for the Nīlapatākā-nityā, are introduced here. || 59 || 60 ||
With these two verses beginning with *rasa* and ending with *vaibhava*,
he teaches the one-syllable mantra (*ekākṣarī vidyā*) of the thirteenth Nityā, Vijayā, as well as her power; therein, *rasa* is the letter *bha*,
*nabhaḥ* is the letter *ma*, *dāha* is the letter *ra*, *vyāptam* is the letter *ya*, and *kṣmā*...

The syllable *u*. Preceded by *va*, joined with the vowel *au*, and conjoined with its own [inherent] bindu. This is what is meant: the single-syllabled *vidyā* is of the form of a *kūṭa* (cryptic seed-syllable) consisting of the letters *bha*, *ma*, *ra*, *ya*, *au*, and the bindu—namely, *bhmyrauḥ*. This is the *kūṭa*. || 61 || In battle, in difficulty, in war, and in that which is difficult to conquer. || 62 ||

With the verse beginning with "hṛdambu," he teaches the one-syllable mantra (ekākṣarī-vidyā) of the fourteenth Nityā, Sarvamaṅgalā, as well as its power. Therein, the single syllable is "svauṃ," which is the peak-syllable (kūṭa) consisting of the letters *sa*, *va*, *au*, and the nasal bindu, joined together. 63.
With these eight verses beginning with *bhūḥ śūnye* and ending with *bhavet*, [the text] teaches the sixty-three-syllable Vidyā of Jvālāmālinī Nityā, who is the Fifteenth [Kalā].
In this context, *bhūḥ* is the syllable *o*; *śūnye* consists of two *na*s, as in *nnēti*; and *nabhasā* is *bhūḥ*.

The syllable *mo* consists of the vowel *o* joined with the letter *ma*. *Rasa* is the letter *bha*. *Sthirā* is the letter *ga*. *Ambu* is the letter *va*. *Raya* is the letter *ta*. Joined with fire (*agni*) means accompanied by the vowel *i*, thus *ti*. *Jyā* is the letter *ja*.
Joined with water and wind (*ambu-marut*) means joined with the letters *va* and *a*, thus *jvā*. *Rasāmarut* is *lā*. 64.
The sky is the letter *ma*; joined with the wind (*marut*) by means of the letter *ā*, it becomes *mā*. In the void of taste (*rasa*), there are the letters *la* and *na*.
(p. 56) The mountain (*gotrā*) together with the movement (*cara*) is likewise the syllable preceded by water (*ambu*). || 65 ||
Ambu and Agni, residing in the heart, cause burning; Ambu, joined with Rasa, Kṣmā, and Ravi, resides in the heart.
Haṃsa is joined with Marut and causes burning, and Prāṇa is likewise joined with Marut. (66)
"Burning" (dāha) with fire (agni) is the *prāṇa* [syllable]; the bowstring (jyā) accompanied by the Maruts is "speed" (rayaḥ).
Water (ambu) is formed by adding the "movable" (cara); the "cow-pen" (gotrā) with fire (agni) and the bowstring (jyā), joined with its own essence (rasa), is "water" (ambu). (67)
Then, the fire, the earth, the water, and the taste—these two [fire and water] are swift;
thereafter, by this burning, there would be a "haṃsa" twice, joined with the fire and the wind.
The *haṃsa* [fire] consists of its own burning fires (*dāhavahnīn*) plus ten earths (*kṣmā*);
thus there are seven burnings for this [element], while the eight and subsequent ones are indeed five.

"Joined with fire" means combined with the letter *i*; "lini" refers to the syllable *de*. "Gotrā" is the letter *da*. "Accompanied by *cara*" means accompanied by the letter *e*, thus forming *de*. "Ambu" is the letter *va*. "The preceding syllable likewise" means the preceding syllable is *de*, [forming] *deva*. || 65 ||

Water and fire: *ambu* is the letter *va*, and fire is the letter *i*; thus, *vi*. Heart is the letter *sa*. Burning water: the letters *ra* and *va*; thus, *rva*. Taste and earth: *rasa* is the letter *bha*, and earth is the letter *ū*; thus, *bhū*. Speed is the letter *ta*. Heart is the letter *sa*. Joined with itself: joined with the bindu. "Joined with itself" refers specifically to the letter *sa*.

The qualifier is *saṃ*. The connection is "the *haṃsa* joined with the wind," which is *hā*. The burning is the letter *ra*, thus *ra*. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) joined with the wind is *kā*. (66) The burning is together with fire, thus the letter *ra* accompanied by the vowel *ī* is *ri*. The vessel of the vital breath is *ke*. The bowstring (*jyā*) together with the wind is *jā*. Speed (*rayaḥ*).

The letter *ta* with *cara* (the vowel *e*) is *ve*; *gotrā* (the vowel *ā*) is the letter *da*. *Hṛt* (the letter *sa*) with fire (*agni*, the vowel *i*) is *si*. *Jyā* (the letter *j*) with water (*ambu*, the vowel *u*) is *jva*. *Rasā* (the letter *la*) joined with itself is *laṃ*. *Rayaḥ* (the letter *ya*) accompanied by fire (*agni*, the vowel *i*) is *ti*. *Jyā* (the letter *j*) with water (*ambu*, the vowel *u*) is *jva*. *Rasā* (the letter *la*). Again, these aforementioned groups of syllables shall occur once more as *jvala*.
Thus: the letter *pa* joined with the burning [letter] (*ja*) and the letter *ra* becomes *pra*. By this, "those" (*te*) should be doubled;

by this syllable-by-syllable repetition, the two previously mentioned syllables "those" (*te*) are doubled. The meaning is that one should utter the three syllables "jvala jvala" and "prajvala" twice. The syntactical connection is that this occurs "above" the word "syāt."

The meaning of *hrīṃ* is that one should join [the syllable] with the wind (*marut*) of the flaming swan (*haṃsa*). The meaning of *hrīṃ* is also that the swan (*haṃsa*) is joined with its own flames of fire (*dāhavanhi*). And "that [syllable] joined with the earth (*kṣmā*) of the burner (*dāha*)" refers to *haṃsa*;
the letter *ha* itself is *hū*. The "seven burnings" (*saptadāha*) means *ra*; thus, it should be uttered seven times. Then—

Immediately following: the word "of this vidyā" is to be understood as the ellipsis. The term "syuḥ" (they would be) applies to both the preceding and the following [clauses] according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣigolakanyāya*). Furthermore, the five beginning with the eighth belong to this vidyā.
(57) That which stands below the penultimate [letter] immediately after the blue banner (nīlapatākā), as well as the final letter of Tvaritā, Bheruṇḍā, the eighth, and likewise the ninth. || 70 ||
This goddess Jvālāmālinī Nityā is proclaimed to consist of sixty-three syllables; she brings about piercing, attraction, heating, subjugation, and possession.

That two-syllable mantra, variegated by the elements of air (vāyu), vital breath (prāṇa), and forest-wealth (vanaspati), serves to attain supernatural powers (siddhi), wealth, grain, and the discovery of one's own hidden treasure. 72.

Then, by its own [element], the earth becomes pure and empty; the solid [earth] is filled by space (nabhas). Subsequently, water [is formed]; then mountains together with fire; likewise, wind, water, and mountains. (73)
The fire conjoined with *ilā* (earth), then water conjoined with *marut* (wind), burning by means of the wind, and the *haṃsa* which is fire—these three again [form the sequence]. (74)
The meaning is that the five syllables beginning with the eighth and ending with the twelfth are the Jvālāmālinī. [The syllable] situated below the penultimate [syllable] of Nīlapatākā— that is,
the syllable preceding the final syllable of the Nityā-vidyā of Nīlapatākā— [is to be taken].

The meaning is "the syllable situated at the beginning," which is *huṃ*. "The final [syllable] of Tvaritā" means the last syllable of the Tvaritā-vidyā, which is *phaṭ*. "Bheruṇḍā, the eighth and likewise the ninth" refers to the two syllables, the eighth and ninth, of the Bheruṇḍā-vidyā, which is *svāhā*.
This is the meaning. || 70 ||
With the verse beginning with "Jvālāmālinī," he teaches her numerical value of syllables and five uncommon fruits. || 71 ||

With the verse beginning with "vāyu," he teaches the two-syllabled mantra of the sixteenth deity, Citrānityā, as well as the fruit of its accomplishment. In this context, "by means of vāyu, prāṇa, and vanasva" means by means of the letter *ca*, the letter *ka*, the vowel *au*, and the bindu (*m*). Among these, the letter *ca* is the first syllable.
The attainment of self is the knowledge of one's own true nature. || 72 ||

With sixteen verses beginning with "Śuci" and ending with "akhileṣṭada," [the text] teaches the hundred-and-ten-syllable Vidyā of Vārāhī, as well as her names and so forth. In that context, "Śuci" is [the seed-syllable] *e* by its own nature. "Śūnya" is the letter *na*. "Nabhasā bhūḥ" is *mo*. "Rasa" is the letter *bha*. "Sthirā" [is...]

The letter *ga* is [the first part]; *ambu* (water) is the letter *va*; *rayaḥ* (velocity) with fire (*agni*) is *ti*. *Marut* (wind) with *ambu* (water) is *vā*. In *rayau* (dual of velocity), there are two *ta*s. Likewise, *marut* accompanied by [the suffix] is *ttā*. (73) *Ilā* (earth) joined with *agni* (fire):
*ilā* is the letter *la*; *agni* is the letter *i*; thus it is *li*. These three syllables have been stated again.

The meaning is that one should utter [the syllables] once again. (p. 58) Water, the burning of the cloud joined with wind, the *haṃsa* (the letter *ha*) together with the earth (*la*), then the sky (*kṣa*);
fire with fire (*ra*), then the five [vowels], and the wind (*ya*) conjoined with itself (*ya*). || 75 ||
First, water with *careṇa*; then water joined with fire (*agni*);
then the void (*śūnya*) with the pervasive (*vyāpta*) and the pure (*śuci*); and the void joined with space (*nabhas*) by means of power (*śakti*). (76)
Dāha, udhara, sva, and sahita, along with toya and carasamanvita—these four mentioned previously [are to be placed] below this; hereafter [follows the next].
The bowstring is conjoined with its own [nature], as is the moving sap; this is the first part.
The sap is spoken of again by Agni; from the group of four, three [remain] at the end.
The sky [is joined] with the earth, and the swan [is joined] with the mobile;
the swan [is joined] with fire—this is the first triad, the heart joined with its own [essence]. (79)
"Or *marudyutam* (joined with the wind)"; *dāha* (burning) joined with the wind is *rā*; *haṃsa* (the swan) joined with fire is *hi*.

The meaning of "these three again" is that one should utter these three syllables once more. *Ambu* is the letter *va*; *dāha* joined with the wind is *rā*; *haṃsa* is the letter *ha*; [and] with *dhara* (the earth), which is the letter *u*.

Sky is the letter *ma*, namely *mu*. Fire is joined with fire; fire is the letter *kha*, namely *khi*. Again, the five syllables of Vārāhamukhī are declared for her once more: Wind is joined with itself; wind is the letter *a*, namely *oṃ*. Water is joined with the moving one; water is the letter *dha*, namely *dhe*.
