The remainder [of the phrase] is "that which precedes it is the syllable. *Aṃ* is water joined with fire (*dhī*). Above that is the void, the letter *na*. It is joined with the pervasive and the pure; the remainder is *nyai*. The void is the letter *na*. Joined with power and space: power is the visarga, meaning *maḥ*. [This is] burning. || 76 || Burning.

"Accompanied by Dharā and Svasā is *rūṃ*; accompanied by *tmyaṃ* and *cara* is *dhe*. The meaning is that this [syllable] is preceded by *rūṃ*. Beyond the four previously mentioned [syllables], one should join the four syllables *dhinyai namaḥ*, which were situated before *ruṃ dhe*, above this"—this is the meaning. || 77 || Jyā.

The letter *ja* joined with its own [vowel] and joined with the *bindu* is *jaṃ*. "Rasa" together with movement is *bhe*. The meaning of "its predecessor" is the letter preceding the aforementioned syllable, namely *jaṃ*. "Rasa joined with fire" is the remainder, which is *bhi*. Again, from the previously mentioned group of four, take three at the end; [this refers to] the group of four beginning with "Obeisance to Dhinyai" as stated before.
The meaning is that one should join the three syllables "nyai namaḥ" above [the previous mantra], excluding the first letter.

The phrase "nabho bhuvā yutam" (joined with the earth of the sky) is the remainder; this refers to "mo". By means of the "care" [suffix], there is also "haṃsaḥ"; the word "api" is used for conjunction; and "he" is [the vocative].

(59) O Dear One! [The mantra consists of: *rasa* (ṣa), preceded by *cara* (ca) and joined with *agni* (ra); then *rasa* (ṣa) joined with *yuta* (ya); then the three [syllables] joined together; and finally *nabhaḥ* (ha), joined with the lower part of *vāta* (va). || 80 ||

Subsequently, the vital breath (prāṇa) is joined with its own [essence]; thereafter, the heart is joined with its own essence, and the rasa; finally, these three are pervaded by the fire of the heart combined with water. 81.

The *gotra* (nasal) joined with *dharā* (earth), *sparśa* (touch) joined with *nāda* (sound), and *java* (speed) joined with *dāha* (burning); each preceding one is joined with the preceding one, and each preceding one is joined with *marut* (wind). 82.
The void [element], accompanied by wind and with the burning of the heart, moves through water;
touch, accompanied by wind and with the burning of the heart, is conjoined with water. (83)
The fire (Ra) joined with its own vowel (A) becomes Haṃsa; likewise, water (Va) together with wind (Ya), joined with its own heart (A), and rasa (Sa) joined with itself (A). || 84 ||
The two [elements] beginning with *prāṇa* (fire) are joined with *dharā* (earth); again, those two are joined with *vahninā* (fire), and *viyat* (ether).
*Vār* (water) is joined with *dāha* (fire) and becomes water; *viyat* (ether) is pervaded by itself and conjoined with itself. (85)

The meaning of "etasya pūrvakaṃ he" is that which precedes "ha," namely "mo. "Haṃsa" is [accompanied] by fire, thus "hi. The triad mentioned previously is the three syllables "nyainamaḥ. The heart is conjoined with its own [seed], thus "staṃ. "Rasa" is with the moving one, thus "bhe"; that which precedes it is this very "bhe."

The first syllable is *staṃ*. *Ca* (the letter *ca*) is joined with fire (*ra*), and *bhi* is used for conjunction. Then, the triad mentioned previously—namely the three beginning with *nyai namaḥ*—is applied. *Vātaḥ* is the letter *a*. *Nabhaḥ* (the sky) is joined with *dharā* (the earth), resulting in *yu*. "O Dear One" (*priye*) is an address to the Goddess. *Prāṇaḥ* (the vital breath) is joined with itself, resulting in *kaṃ*. || 80 ||
The Heart is *svayutam* (joined with *sva*), which is *staṃ*. The Essence (*rasa*) is the letter *bha*. The Pervaded (*vyāpta*) is the letter *ya*.
These three, which were previously mentioned, followed by the three syllables *staṃbhaya*, should occur once again. The Heart is the letter *sa*.
Joined with the Burning (*dāha*) and the Water (*ambu*), it is *rva*. The Earth (*gotrā*) is the letter *da*. Endowed with the Support (*dharā*), it is *du*.

The touch-consonant joined with the sound is the letter *ṣ*; the sound is the letter *ṭ*, thus forming *ṣṭa*. The swift one joined with burning is the letter *p* joined with the letter *r*, thus forming *pra*. Prior to the syllable *pra*, the preceding syllable of that prior syllable is *du*. And prior to that, by Marut...
In this context, the word "pūrva" (prior) refers to the preceding syllable of the word "du," meaning that it is placed before it.

82 || *Śūnya* (the letter *ha*) joined with its own [vowel] and *marut* (the letter *sa*) is *nāṃ*; *sakāraḥ* (the letter *sa*) is the heart. *Caraḥ* (the letter *ca*) joined with *dāha* (the letter *ra*) and *ambu* (the letter *va*) is *rve*. *Sparśa* (the letter *pa*) joined with *marut* (the letter *sa*) and its own [vowel] is *ṣāṃ*. *Sakāraḥ* (the letter *sa*) is the heart. Joined with *dāha* (the letter *ra*) and *ambu* (the letter *va*), it is *va*. || 83 || *Jyā* (the letter *ja*) joined with *agni* (the letter *ra*) and its own [vowel] is *ji*. Likewise, *haṃsaḥ* (the letter *ha*) joined with *ambu* (the letter *va*) and *marut* (the letter *sa*) is *tathā*. || 83 ||

In this entire section, the term *hvā* signifies conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, *staṃ* is joined with its own heart (*hṛdaya*), and *bhaṃ* is likewise joined with its own essence (*rasa*). (84) Furthermore, there are the two previously mentioned syllables preceded by *prāṇa*, as well as *śuci* joined with itself.
The stable tastes are from the forest; the two fires are Haṃsa and Dharāsvayu. 86.
Dyuti, Nādavatī, followed by Hṛd, Ambu, and Marut;
then Haṃsa and Marut—this is the Vidyā consisting of one hundred and ten syllables. (87)
Vārāhī is the fifth, Viśvavijayā, Bhadrakaumudī, and Vārtālī;
she is thus renowned as the bestower of all desired aims, such as the rites of immobilization (stambhana) and others. 88.

The two [syllables] *prāṇa* (pra) and *dāha* (da), joined with *dharā* (bhū); then again the first [syllable], and *marut* (ra) in the *rasa* (sixth) position; pervaded by *marut* (ra) joined with *śakti* (ī), and then *bhūḥ* (bhu) joined with itself—then these three. (89)
At the beginning of this [mantra], however, there is a pair of *rasas* (the letters *sa* and *va*) joined with *cara* (*ya*);
then follows *haṃsa* conjoined with *dāha* (*ra*), *vahni* (*ra*), and *śakti* (*ī*). (90)

"Sky" (nabhaḥ) is *śa*; "twice heart-burning-water" (*dvir-hṛt-sadāha-ambu*) means *jya* twice; "void" (*śūnyam*) joined with "sound" (*svana*) is *ha*; "two burnings" (*dāhau*) joined with "earth" (*dharā*)—the remainder being that these are to be applied individually—is *ra*; "do it again, do it again"—these are the syllables. "By fire" (*vahninā*) [is] "sky" (*viyat*), which is *śī*. "Water" (*vāḥ*) joined with "burning" (*dāha*) is "water" (*vāḥ*), which is the letter *gha*, namely *ghra*. "Water" (*ambu*)...

The letter *va*. [The phrase] "the sky (*viyat*) pervaded by itself joined" is *śyaṃ*. (85) Starting from the syllable *vaśyaṃ*, which consists of two previously mentioned letters, the meaning is that one should place [the next element] before the preceding group of four syllables. "Pure (*śuciḥ*) joined with itself" is *aiṃ*. "Stable (*sthirā*) joined with *rasāva* and itself"—this is the remainder—[is] *ṭhalauṃ*.
The two *ṭhaka* syllables are "ṭha ṭha. The *haṃsa* is "huṃ," conjoined with the earth (*dharā*) and the self (*sva*). || 86 ||
After *dyuti* comes *nādavatī*, followed immediately by *phaṭ*. "The heart-water joined with wind" means *svā*;
and "the *haṃsa* joined with wind"—this is the remainder—means *hā*. (87)
With the verse beginning with "Vārāhī," he states the five names of the Goddess. || 88 ||

With these five verses beginning with *prāṇa* and ending with *kramāt*, he teaches the twenty-five-syllable, seven-syllable, and thirteen-syllable mantras of Kurukullā. In that context, the remainder is that the syllables *pra* and *āṇa*, joined with *dā* and *ha*, and *dha* and *rā*, are each [to be combined] as "Kuru."

Again, the first; again, the first of those two is *ku*. In *rasa* (the sixth vowel), there are two *la*s (*lla*). *Marut* (the second consonant) joined with *ākāra* (the long *ā*) is *llā*. Pervaded and joined with *marucchakti* (the power of the wind, *y*) is *yāḥ*. *Bhūḥ* joined with itself is *oṃ*. Then, the triad.

89. At the beginning of this [mantra], above the syllable *oṃ*, there should be the three syllables *kuru ku*, which constitute the commencement of this mantra; such is the meaning. Joined with the pair of tastes (*rasa*) and the moving one (*cara*), it becomes *lle*.
Then follows *haṃsa* conjoined with burning (*dāha*) and the two fire-powers (*vahni-śakti*), which is *hrīḥ*. 90. *Nabhaḥ* (the sky) twice.
The word "might be" (*syāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Mine" (*mama*).
O Dear One! Water is subsequently joined with space, but space is joined with wind. (91)
The void (ha) and the pervader (la), the *haṃsa* (ha-ka-sa), and the first and last [letters] of the three mantras;
from the five letters beginning with the sixth of this [group], the last two are said to be the first [of the next]. (92)
The last two [mantras] consist of eleven syllables; the second is said to have [the syllable] *smu*;
the third consists of twenty-five syllables; thus the mantras are declared in sequence. (93)
The syllable *bhūḥ* with its own [seed-syllable] is *haṃsa*; joined with its own [seed-syllable], it is *haṃsaka*.
With *hṛt*, *māyā*, and *bhūḥ*, it becomes *hṛt*; joined with its own [seed-syllable], it is *haṃsa*. (94)

The final two syllables of Kurukullā constitute the eight-syllable mantra of the Self; it is remembered as a wish-fulfilling tree easily accessible for the complete attainment of all desired aims. (95)
By means of ten syllables uttered according to the convention, each [group] by ten:

*hṛt* is the letter *sa*; *sadāhāmbu* means water (*ma*) accompanied by burning (*dāha*), that is, with *ra*; *jyā* is the letter *ja*; *śūnyaṃ svena yutaṃ* is *na*; *ambu* afterwards, immediately following, is the letter *va*; *viyat*...

The letter *sa* [is joined with] *marut* (wind), meaning it is joined with *ya*; thus, up to *mā*, it means "O beloved," which is an address to the Goddess. The letter *na* is *śūnya* (void). The letter *ya* is *vyāpta* (pervaded). With *bhuva* (earth), the remainder is *haṃsa*, namely *ho*. The first and last letters of the fifth *vidyā* are the final two syllables of the mantra.

The meaning is "svāhā. There may be three mantras; the meaning is that this very mantra becomes three mantras through the sequential application of the division of its syllables. Of this [mantra], the last two [syllables] beginning with the sixth are the fifth group of five syllables; the first is said to be the initial [group]. This is what is meant: of this...

Having uttered the sixth syllable through to the tenth syllable of the twenty-five-syllable mantra, one should thereafter say "svāhā. By that, the first seven-syllable vidyā is formed. The second [seven-syllable vidyā] is declared to consist of the last two [syllables] starting from the eleventh syllable.

This is what is meant: having uttered the first eleven syllables of this very twenty-five-syllable mantra, beginning from the first syllable, one then joins the final two syllables, *tat* and *svāhā*, which belong to the last element; thus, the thirteen-syllable vidyā is formed. This is the third [method].

The twenty-five-syllable mantra, which was already mentioned previously as the basis for the first and second [mantras], is the third mantra consisting of thirty-seven syllables; this is the meaning. || 93 ||

With the two verses beginning with *bhūḥ svena* and ending with *suradrumaḥ*, he teaches the eight-syllable mantra of the Self (*ātma-aṣṭākṣarī*), which is the science of the ritual sacrifice (*prapañcayāga-vidyā*). In that context: *bhūḥ svena oṃ*. *Haṃsaḥ* is the syllable *hrīṃ* by virtue of being the fire of combustion; *haṃsakaḥ* is *haṃ* by virtue of being the self.

The word "he" (sa) implies that he is joined with the *māyā* [the letter *ī*] in the heart; thus, with the earth [the letter *la*], the heart becomes *so*. With his own [the letter *ha*], it is endowed with *haṃsa*, becoming *haṃ*. And the two final letters of Kuru-kullā are *svāhā*; this is the meaning. || 95 ||

With the two verses beginning with *saṅketena* and ending with *carācaram*, [the author explains] how each of the five elements is associated individually with one of the branches—prāṇa, fire, wind, water, and earth—conjoined with the seven syllables of the Śakti-mantra. (p. 62) 96.

The five elemental mantras have been fully described; they bestow the accomplishment of all aims, and through their illumination, the entire universe, including the moving and the unmoving, exists. 97.

The first two of the preceding [group], that which precedes them, the fourteenth, and the last of those; fire with water, water with fire, that [same] with zero, breath joined with the speed of water. (98)
He teaches the mantras consisting of twenty syllables. Regarding the phrase "by means of the letters uttered according to the convention," this is what is meant:
by means of the names uttered for the letters of the *mātṛkā* as they are distributed among the elements in the thirty-five verses stated in the [fifth] chapter, beginning with "vāta" and "marut."

The four [mantras] consisting of Prāṇa, Agni, Ilā, and Ambā, each endowed with ten syllables and ending with their respective names, the Śakti-mantra, and the seven-syllabled Śabda-mantra— thus each being twenty-one syllables long— are together with the twenty-syllabled Vyoma-mantra.

Thus are the five mantras; they belong to the five elements according to the stated sequence. As for those [mantras], although the nature of even those five mantras was not written out here in the sequence of the *Lalitānityā-pūjā-vidhi*, their nature [is as follows]: [The mantras follow: 1. *Oṃ hrīṃ āṃ hūṃ haṃ kṣaṃ pṛthivyai namaḥ* 2. *Oṃ hrīṃ iṃ hūṃ haṃ kṣaṃ apyai namaḥ* 3. *Oṃ hrīṃ uṃ hūṃ haṃ kṣaṃ tejase namaḥ* 4. *Oṃ hrīṃ ṝṃ hūṃ haṃ kṣaṃ vāyave namaḥ* 5. *Oṃ hrīṃ ḷṃ hūṃ haṃ kṣaṃ ākāśāya namaḥ* [End of mantras]
First, it is clearly revealed: having drawn eleven lines— six vertical and five horizontal—
with equal intervals running east, west, south, and north, one should place the five short vowels *a, i, u, ṛ, ḷ* in order from top to bottom within the five rows consisting of ten squares each.

Having written [the letters] in the first row, one should write the five long vowels— ā, ī, ū, ṝ, and ḹ— in sequence in the second row; having written the five syllables e, ai, o, au, and aṃ in the third row,
one should proceed in the fourth and subsequent rows according to the stated order.

Having written the six groups of consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *śa*, five in each row, and having written the five syllables *ṣa-kṣa-la-sa-ha* in the very last row, one should contemplate them.
The ten syllables in the uppermost row are of the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Below that—

The ten syllables situated in the ten squares of the second row located there are of the nature of fire (*agni*). The ten syllables situated in the ten squares of the third row located below that are of the nature of earth (*ilā*).
The ten syllables situated in the ten squares of the fourth row located below that are of the nature of water (*ap*). Below that...
The ten syllables situated in the ten squares of the fifth row are composed of the element *kha*.

At the end of those ten, one should join the two-syllable name of each [deity], the single syllable of *vyoman*, and everywhere the two-syllable word "Śakti," followed above that by the seven-syllable mantra. When this has been done—

The mantras of the five elements consist of twenty-one syllables each and ten syllables [respectively]; this means that by virtue of their light and power, they continue to exist even today, meaning they are still being practiced. || 97 ||
With these three verses beginning with "pūrva" and ending with "manuḥ," he teaches the sixteen-syllable *bali* mantra common to the sixteen *Nityās*. In this context,
the first two [syllables] are the syllables of the *praṇava* and *hṛllekhā*, which constitute the beginning of the previously mentioned eight-syllable *ātman* mantra.

The meaning is that the first and second syllables should be [as follows]. That *parvan* consists of the fourteenth and its final [letters]; it should be joined with *rasa* (the sixth vowel), *vyāpta* (the letter *ya*), and *māyā* (the letter *ī*). Its third and fourth [syllables] are *rasa* (the sixth vowel) joined with *kṣmā* (the letter *la*) and *raya* (the letter *ra*), followed by *cara* (the letter *ca*), O Parameśvarī! (99)
The *rasa* (sixth) joined with the *vyāptabhūmi* (the letter *ha*), then the *haṃsa* (letter *sa*) followed by the earth (*la*) and ten thousand (*kṣma*),
and finally the first and last letters— thus is declared the sixteen-syllable mantra of Bala.

"The pervasion consisting of the fire-element (vahni-tattva) has been correctly and thoroughly contemplated; by withdrawing this [pervasion] from the mind, that very element is assimilated into one's own self. (101)
Thus ends the third chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
Regarding the *Kurukullā-vidyā*, which precedes the eight-syllable mantra of the Self (*ātma-aṣṭākṣara-mantra*),
the two syllables "sa" and "rva" constitute its third and fourth syllables respectively.
The meaning is "they should be. The word "ambu" (water) is not joined with "agni" (fire); this is the sense of "vi. "Vāḥ" (water) is accompanied by "sa" and "śūnya" (zero), thus "ghra.
"Prāṇa" (vital breath) is endowed with "jala" (water) and "raya" (speed), and is joined with the letters "ka," "ṛ," and "ta," thus "kṛt. || 98 ||

"Rasa would be [formed] by the two, Vyāptā and Māyā; 'bhya'. In this Tantra, the word *māyā* and the word *śakti* are each designators for one of the two *hṛllekhās* (the letter *hrīṃ*) and the *visarjanīya* (the visarga).
This being the case, the meaning is that the application of either one [of these two terms] is due to the force of the oral tradition (*sampradāya*). This is its third [part].

The fourth [syllable] is *sarva*, consisting of the ninth and tenth letters. "Rasa" is joined with "kṣmaya"—this is the remainder; "bhū" is the eleventh letter. "Raya" is joined with "careṇa te"—this is the twelfth. "Parameśvarī" is the vocative case. (99) "Rasa" is joined with the two pervasive "bhūs"—"bhyo" is the thirteenth. "Haṃsaḥ" [is the fourteenth].

The syllable *kṣmā* followed by its own [seed-syllable] and then *hūṃ* is the fourteenth syllable. The first and last letters of the previous [mantra], along with the self and the eight-syllable mantra, followed by *svāhā*, constitute the fifteenth. Thus, the sixteen-syllable mantra of Bala is said to consist of sixteen syllables; in this way, [it applies] to all [of them].
The meaning is that the *bali* mantra for the sixteen *Nityās* has thus been stated. || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named Manoramā, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa, upon the complete Tantra known as the venerable Kādimata among the venerable Ṣoḍaśanityātantras.
The third chapter, which is devoted to revealing the nature of eternal ignorance, has been fully examined.
The number of verses in the third [chapter] is stated to be two hundred and ninety-seven and a half, including one diagram and its commentary.
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Now, O Dear One, I shall describe in due order the worship of the first among the sixteen Nityās, which, when performed daily, bestows the accomplishment of all goals.
Now listen to the occasional (naimittika) and the optional (kāmya) rites through three chapters,
by which even one joined with great sin certainly attains perfection.
The mantras for the three types of nyāsa, the four mantras for the seats, then the mantra for invocation, and likewise the mantra for the complete worship.

The seed-syllables of the hand-gestures (mudrā) and weapons, the mental impression for forming the gestures, the meditation on [the goddess] together with her retinue, and the sequence of the ritual for daily worship. (4)
The names of the nine obscuring powers (navāvaraṇa-śakti), as well as the sequence of worship,
the yoga consisting of mantra, the ritual services for worship, and the procedure for recitation (japa).
The first [syllable] is Vāta joined with its own [consonant]; the second is Marut with its own [vowel];
the third is joined with Hṛdvan; and this first [syllable] belongs to her (Prakṛti).
Now begins the fourth chapter.
Having taught the sixteen Nityā-vidyās and so forth in the preceding third chapter, [the author now teaches] the primary Aṅginī Nityā immediately thereafter.

The Lalitā-vidyā teaches the sequence of worship through both regular (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites. This is done via three chapters, each consisting of one hundred verses, beginning with "Now, the sixteen nityās... and ending with "...one shall become identical with That. Among these, [the first chapter] begins with "Now, the sixteen nityās... and ends with "...the sequence."

With five verses, he indicates the subject matter of the fourth, fifth, and sixth chapters. Therein, "constant worship" is the meaning; "occasional" and "optional worship" are qualifiers of that [worship]. [He refers to one who is] "even though joined with great sin and hostile to discernment. [This is explained] by the passage beginning with "of the threefold placement," and so forth.

With the verse ending in "bījāni" and consisting of twenty-two lines plus one quarter-verse, the enumeration of the mantras is completed. Regarding this, the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) holds that the mention of the "threefold placement" (*nyāsatraya*), although it deviates from the order of enumeration, is for the sake of the convenience of the verse. [The mantra] for the worship of the whole is the form of the two seed-syllables (*bīja*). || 5 ||
With the half-verse beginning with *vāta* and ending with *mārjanāt*,

he teaches the *karaśuddhi-vidyā* (the mantra for purifying the hands) and the method of purification. In that context, *vāta* joined with its own [seed] refers to the first seed-syllable *oṃ*, by virtue of being the wind (*marut*).
One should perform the purification of these two hands by wiping them against each other.
[Then one performs] the six-limbed rite: the heart, the head, the crest, the armor, the eye, and the weapon. (7)
She who is eternal and the beauty of the Kula is to be known as the second;
she alone is the third, the primordial Śakti, by whom this throne of the Goddess's self is constituted.
The Cakrāsana is proclaimed through the conjunction of the three with the Haṃsa;
likewise, the fifth is formed by the Haṃsa and the Heart-mantra, and it is the seat for all mantras.

The second is *āṃ*, thus the second. By this same method, the third is *sauḥ*, thus the third. "But this first is indeed *vidyā*" is the remainder [of the verse]. Regarding "purification" (*śuddhim*):
purification is the making of the articles for worship fit to be touched, through their mutual cleansing.
The phrase "of the palms of the left and right hands" is to be understood as the ellipsis.

With the two half-verses beginning with *hṛt* and ending with *sundarī*, he teaches the six-limbed [mantra] and the vidyā for the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). Among those, by means of the second [verse], [he teaches] from among the thirty-two [mantras] previously mentioned...
The phrase "by the second knowledge" is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 7 ||

With the second half-verse beginning with "the third" and ending with "by this," he teaches the Goddess’s own seat-mantra (*āsanavidyā*). Therein, "the third" refers to that very Kulasundarī mantra taught for the six-limbed ritual application (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). "Beginning with Śakti": here, "Śakti" is Hṛllekhā.

The word *triṣu* (in the three), which occurs at the beginning of the subsequent verse, governs everything up to the end of the *āvāhana-vidyā* (invocation mantra). By this it is meant that one should make each of the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) preceded by *hṛllekhā*. [Thus: *hrīḥ aiḥ hrīḥ klīḥ hrīḥ sauḥ*. This is the seat of the Goddess's own self (*devyātmāsana*) for those whose forms are limited, yet who possess the nature of the Goddess.

The meaning is that it is the seat (*āsana*) of all powers— that is, the locus of their manifestation— and the locus of manifestation for all deities. Here, the sequence of the enumeration is set aside in favor of explaining the fourfold knowledge of the seats (*āsanavidyācatuṣṭaya*) because they are connected to the second vidyā, for the sake of ease.
The sequence of enumeration as "the third" is for the sake of ease. || 8 ||

With the first half of the verse beginning with "in the three," he teaches the *cakrāsana-vidyā*. In that context, due to its conjunction with the *haṃsa*, the pronunciation of the syllable *ha* at the beginning of each of the three seed-syllables of Bālā—namely *haiḥ*, *hklīṃ*, and *hsauḥ*—constitutes the fourth *cakrāsana-vidyā*. This is the meaning.
Regarding "the wheel-throne" (*cakrāsana*): it is the throne, that is, the locus of attainment, for all the *yantras* whose nature consists of the deities of mantra.
With the latter half of the verse beginning with "haṃsa," he teaches the *vidyā* which is the throne for all mantras. In that regard:
The phrase "joined with *haṃsa* and *hṛd*" is the ellipsis. As before, because each of the three seed-syllables is pronounced beginning with the letters *ha* and *sa*, [the result is] *hsai*.
Then there is *ambu* (water), joined with *rasa* (taste) and accompanied by *cara* (movement).
That which stands between that [Śiva] and Śakti is proclaimed as the sixth.
One should bestow the Sādhyasiddhāsana by means of that [mantra] through the worship of the Goddess;
one should perform the invocation on the seventh day with the "namas" mantra and the Trikhaṇḍā.

Hsklī/ Hsauḥ. The fifth is the Vidyā that is the seat of all mantras. "The seat of all mantras" is a designation for the Śrīcakra; since it will be explained later that the lines of the triangle consist of the Mātṛkās beginning with 'A', 'Ka', and 'Tha', the meaning is that it is the locus where all mantras are found. (9)

With the one and a half verses beginning with *tataḥ* and ending with *samarcanāt*, he teaches the mantra for the seat of accomplishment (*sādhyasiddhāsanavidyā*). In that context, *tataḥ* [refers to] "water" (*ambu*) joined with "flavor" (*rasa*), and that water is the letter *va*. The word *ca* is used for conjunction; "flavor" (*rasa*) is the letter *la*. "Moving" (*cara*)...
The letter *e*; *svam* is the *bindu*, joined with those two; the letter *ca* is for the purpose of conjunction (*samuccaye*); the word *tat* refers to that specific form. This is what is meant:
when joined with the letters *va*, *la*, and the *bindu*, it becomes the cryptic syllable (*kūṭākṣara*) *vle*. And of that, [and] of the Power (*śakti*).

That which is situated in the middle is declared to be the sixth of that aforementioned syllable *vleṃ*. [It belongs to] the power (*śakti*) known as Hṛllekhā. "Situated in the middle" means situated between these two. This is what is meant:
the three seed-syllables (*bīja*) of that Bālā [mantra] begin with the syllable *hrīṃ*, namely *vleṃ*.
And there should be garments of silk (kārāva). Hrīḥ, Aiḥ, Hrīḥ, Klīḥ, Sauḥ, Vleḥ—such is that young woman;

she would be the *sādhyasiddhāsana-vidyā*. Regarding "the seat of the accomplishment of what is to be accomplished" (*sādhyasiddhāsana*): it is the locus for the attainment of all desired accomplishments (*siddhi*).

The meaning is: "because of the accomplishment of the reflective awareness (vimarśa) of the nature of the indivisible Self. Here, the phrase "due to the worship of the Goddess" applies to each of the four seats as well. The method for joining the mantras to these four seats will be explained in the fifth chapter.

With the first half-verse beginning with "saptamyā" and ending with "samīritaḥ," he teaches the seventh mantra, the *āvāhana-vidyā* (invocation mantra). In this context, the words "by the seventh mantra" are to be supplied as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
The phrase "joined with *namaḥ*" is also to be supplied; the meaning is that it ends with the word *namaḥ*. It is [to be recited] with the aforementioned three-part division (*trikhaṇḍā*).

The word "mudrā" is to be supplied [as the subject]. He states everywhere that even what is to be explained later has already been said. "That very [mantra] joined with the burning of the heart of the Haṃsa should be considered the seventh"—this is what is meant:
the Kulasundarī-vidyā is joined with each of the three syllables *ha*, *sa*, and *ra* within the three seed-syllables.
This means it is the *āvāhana-vidyā* (invocation mantra). Regarding the "burning conjunction" (*dāhayoga*) at the end of the consonant in the middle [mantra]:

the meaning is that one should join the letters *ha* and *sa* before the middle seed-syllable, and then join the letter *ra* at the end of the letter *la*. Thus, [the sequence is] *ha*, *sa*, *ka*, *la*, and *ra*.

The middle seed-syllable ends with *māyā* (the letter *ī*) and the *bindu*. In the other [seed-syllable], however, that same [syllable] is considered the seventh when joined with *haṃsa*, *hṛd* (the letter *ha*), and *dāha* (the letter *ra*). Furthermore, the conjunction with *dāha* (*ra*) at the end of the consonant is taught for the middle [seed-syllable]. (12)
Space, Being, Fire, and one's own power—these should be [visualized] as being self-existent.
One should then mutter the names of all the powers beginning with those, which reside within the wheel.
The seed-syllable of Vaśinī is said to consist of the letters for fire (ra), earth (la), water (va), and space (ha).
The great syllable of Kāmeśvarī is joined with the vital breath (sa), water (va), and the power (i). (14)
The mantra of Mohinī consists of the void (ha), water (va), fire (ra), and its own conjunction (i);
it is said that the seed-syllable of Vimalā is pervaded by taste (ra), earth (la), and its own union (i).
The mantra becomes *aruṇā* through its own conjunctions with the bowstring (*jyā*), the sky (*nabhas*), fire (*vahni*), and burning (*dāha*).

The meaning is that one should join the letter *ra* between the vowel *sa* (the letter *sakāra*) and the vowel *u*. Thus, with the two letters *ha* and *sa*, the letter *ra*, the diphthong *au*, and the visarga, the final seed-syllable ending in *māyā* is *hsau*; [and similarly] *hsklṛī* and *hssrau*: *ḥ namaḥ*.

With the verse beginning with "viyat" (the sky), he teaches the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) that constitute the *praṇava* for the worship, names, forms, and mantras of the powers (*śakti*) residing within the Śrīcakra of Lalitā. In this context, "viyat" refers to the letter *sa*. "Sadāhavahnisvam" refers to the letter *ra* together with the vowel *ī* and the bindu, forming the syllable *śrīṃ*.

"Beginning with Śakti" means beginning with Hṛllekhā. This is what is meant: one should worship all the Śaktis with the mantras for the names of the deities, preceded by Hṛllekhā and the Śrī-bīja. || 13 ||

With the verse beginning "dāhabhūmi," he teaches the *vidyā* consisting of the syllables of the *kūṭa* of Vaśinī and the *vidyā* consisting of the syllables of the *kūṭa* of Kāmeśvarī. [The mantra] is *vlū*, formed by the letters *repha* (r), *vakāra* (v), *lakāra* (l), *ūkāra* (ū), and *bindu* (ṃ). Prāṇa is conjoined with the power of Rasa.
Prāṇa is the letter *ka*; rasa is the letter *la*; Śakti is Hṛllekhā. Joined with these—the letter *ka*, the letter *la*, and Hṛllekhā—the seed-syllable (*kūṭa*) is *klhrīṃ*. || 14 ||
With the verse beginning with "śūnyam" (the void), he teaches the two *kūṭākṣara* mantras of Mohinī and Vimalā. Therein, "śūnya" is the letter *na*.
"Through its union with ambu, rasa, and vahni" means through the union of the letters *va*, *la*, and *ī* with the bindu; thus, [the mantra is] *vlī*.
The letter *ya* pervades [the first syllable]. The letter *la*, conjoined with *rasa* (6), *akṣmā* (1), and *sva* (3), and accompanied by the vowel *u* and the bindu, becomes *ylūṃ*.
With the first half of the verse beginning with "jyā nabhaḥ," he teaches the Aruṇākūṭākṣarī-vidyā.
The *haṃsa* (the letter *ha*) together with the essence-water (*sa*), joined with the pervasive earth (*la*) and stability (*ra*), constitutes the mantra. (16)
It is declared that for one who seeks victory, this [mantra] bestows victory everywhere—in debates, in legal disputes, and in battles—this is certain. (17)
The mantra "Kaṃ nabho dāha sahitaṃ vyāptakṣmā svayutaṃ" is proclaimed as that of Sarveśvarī; it always bestows all spiritual accomplishments.
The *grāsa* mantra is joined with the fire that burns the sky; this is the *kaulinī* mantra.
With these eight mantras, conjoined with the [eight] groups of letters (*varga*), they become the Śaktis. (19)

The ritual placement (nyāsa) should be performed with the names ending in "Vāgdevatā," by which even a mortal becomes identical with the Goddess and is worshipped at all times and in all places by all the gods.

In that regard, *jyā* [is formed] from the sky (*ja*), fire (*ra*), and its own union (*ya*), through the mutual application of the sequence of release of the letters *ja*, *ma*, *ra*, *ī*, and the bindu; thus: *jmrī*. || 16 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *haṃsa* and ending with *niścitaṃ*, he teaches the victorious *kūṭākṣara-vidyā* (the secret syllable-mantra) and its power. In that context, *haṃsa* refers to the letter *ha*.
*Sahṛdrasāmbu* means accompanied by the letters *sa*, *la*, *va*, and *ka*. *Vyāptakṣmāsvairyutaḥ* refers to the letter *ya*.
"And joined with the letter *ū* and the bindu. This is what is meant:
the letters *ha*, *sa*, *la*, *va*, *ya*, *ū*, and the bindu form the *kūṭa* [mantra] *hslyū*.
[This is explained] by the first half-verse beginning with *kam* and ending with *sadā*.

He teaches the science of the seed-syllable (kūṭākṣara) of Sarveśvarī and its power: *kaṃ* is the letter *la*; "accompanied by the burning of the sky" means accompanied by the letters *ma* and *ra*; "joined with the earth-pervader" means the letter *ya* joined with the vowel *ū* and the nasal bindu. This is what is meant: [the syllables] *la*, *ma*, *ra*, and *ya*.
With the letter Ū and the bindus, [the syllables] lmryū are formed. || 18 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with "grāsa," he teaches the Kaulinī-kūṭākṣara-vidyā; therein, "grāsa" is the letter *kṣa*.
With the [letters] "nabhas" (space), "dāha" (fire), and "vahnisva" (fire-self)—that is, with the *m*, *r*, *ī*, and the bindu—one obtains *kṣmrī*. Thus it is said.

With this first half-verse beginning with "by these" (*etaiḥ*) and ending with "always" (*sarvadā*), he teaches the sequence of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of Vaśinī and the others, as well as its fruit. In that context, the phrase "with the mantras" implies "with the eight aforementioned syllables of the *kūṭa*"; [the word] "with the powers" (*śaktibhiḥ*) [is also understood].

One should place [the seed-syllables] in the aperture, on the forehead, as well as in the *ājñā* [cakra], the throat, and the heart; likewise in the navel, the *ādhāra*, and both feet, from the base up to the tip. (21)
From the *gotra* [of the letters], the first [type] arises from the vowels (*amarutsvaiḥ*); the other [the second] is from the reverse order (*vyatyayāt*).
The third would arise from the vowels (*a*), the wind (*marut*), fire (*vahni*), the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the essence (*rasa*), fire (*vahni*), and the vowels (*svaiḥ*). 22.
The fourth [syllable] is *bhū* (earth), followed by *rasa* (taste), *akṣi* (eye), and *asva* (horse); then the fifth is *śakti* (power) and *hṛt* (heart).
Next is *prāṇa* (vital breath), then *dāha* (burning), *bhū* (earth), and *svena* (by oneself); and again, the seventh is *anantara* (immediate).
The Haṃsa [mantra] is characterized by the heart, splendor, and radiance, joined with the nature of burning and movement;
the eighth is proclaimed as being endowed with the heart, the Haṃsa, the forest, and one's own possessions.
Likewise, the ninth is proclaimed as being pure when joined with its own [seed-syllable].
O Maheśvarī, these are single-syllabled mantras in the form of mudrās.

The remainder [of the phrase] is: "joined with the eight powers (śaktis) beginning with Vaśinī as previously described. "Combined with the groups" means with each of the syllables beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa* and ending with the deities of speech (*vāgdevatā*). Regarding "the deity of speech":
by means of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) using names consisting of four syllables. [He becomes] "of the nature of the Goddess," meaning his body is that of the God, [and] of the Goddess.
The meaning is that [the deity] possesses a body composed of syllables themselves. This is what is being said:

having uttered the sixteen vowels from *a* to the visarga (*ḥ*) together with the bindu (*m*), and having uttered the "peak-syllable" (*kūṭākṣara*) *klṛ* above them, one should perform the placement while reciting: "Oblation to Vaśinī, the goddess of speech (*vāgdevatā*)."

In this manner, one should install the other seven mantras along with the seed-syllables (*bīja*), names, and the goddesses of speech (*vāgdevatā*) ending with *namaḥ* and *oṃ*; the meaning is that one should effect the aforementioned embodiments (*vigraha*). Here, the addition of the word *namaḥ* is because its application is prescribed later for the worship, following the introduction of the term *namaḥ*. || 20 ||

With the verse beginning with "randhra," he teaches the locations for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantras of the eight powers, Vaśinī and the rest. Therein, "randhra" refers to the *brahmarandhra*; "ājñā" refers to the space between the eyebrows; and "mūlāgrakāvadhi" [refers to] up to the tip of the root.

The meaning is that one should touch [the body] with both palms, starting from the base of the feet up to the tips [of the toes], while reciting the mantra. Immediately thereafter, one should touch from the head down to the heart with the first section of the root-vidyā, and from the heart down to the tips of the toes with the second section.

One should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) three times: with the third section [of the hand] from the forepart of the feet to the heart, and with both hands in the manner of joined palms (*añjali*) according to the procedure shown by the teacher. The underlying rationale (*vāsanā*) for this must be understood from the mouth of the guru alone. || 21 ||
With these four verses beginning with *gotrā* and ending with *maheśvarī*, he teaches the nine seed-mantras of the nine mudrās in sequence. In that context, *gotrā* is the letter *da*;
[the mantra for] *dāha* is formed by the letters *ra*, *a*, and the bindu (*m*).
(70) O Goddess of gods! Listen indeed to the syllables of the arrow (bāṇa), which bestow good fortune:
*dāha* pervaded by *rasa*, followed by *ambu*, and then *hṛt* joined with *marut* individually. (26)
The five syllables of the mudrās at the beginning are the "arrows" (bāṇas) that cause universal expansion;
they are to be known as Śākta and Śaiva, and are proclaimed to be five each.
In the Śikhitoṣa [Tantra], it is said: "The two bows, joined with their own [seeds], are all-deluding;

*drāḥ*. Another, the second [mantra], is *drīḥ*, formed by the transposition of the wind (*vāyu*) and fire (*agni*) elements. This is what is meant: one should apply the vowel *ī* in place of the vowel *ā* in the first seed-syllable.

The syllable *klī* is formed by the letters *ka*, *la*, *ī*, and the nasal bindu, representing breath (*prāṇa*), taste (*rasa*), fire (*agni*), and the self (*sva*). (22) The letter *va* represents the earth (*bhūmi*). The letter *lū* is formed by the letter *la* joined with the vowel *ū* and the nasal bindu, representing taste (*rasa*), the earth (*akṣmā*), and the self (*sva*). The "Power" (*śakti*) is the letter *sa* together with the heart (*hṛt*) and the visarga; this is the meaning. The "Supreme" (*para*) is the fifth [vowel], which is *s*. [This is] by means of the breath (*prāṇa*).

With the letter *ka*, which has the nature of burning, [is joined] the letter *ra* together with the vowel *au* and the bindu; immediately following is the sixth [vowel], *ū*, thus forming *krau*. The *haṃsa* is joined with the *hṛt*, the *tejas*, and the *dyuti*, along with the nature of burning and movement. Here, *haṃsa* refers to the letter *ha*; *hṛt* refers to the letter *sa*; *tejas* refers to the letter *kha*; and it is understood that it is joined with *dyuti*, which is the letter *pha*.

The letter *repha* (the letter *r*) joined with *dāha* (the letter *h*), *cara* (the letter *kh*), *sva* (the letter *ph*), and joined with the letter *e* and the *bindu*—this is what is meant: the seventh mantra shall consist of the form of a *kūṭākṣara*, namely the letter *ha* joined with the letters *sa*, *kha*, *pha*, *e*, and the *bindu*. Thus: *Hskhphreṃ*. The eighth is *Haṃsa*.

The remainder is "mantra," [referring to] those who have obtained the forest wealth of the heart. Joined with the letters *ha*, *sa*, the vowel *au*, and the bindu, the eighth [syllable] is *hsau*. [The syllable] *ai* is the pure one joined with itself.
These are the forms of the mudrās, consisting of the threefold knowledge (*traividya*) according to their gross, subtle, and supreme levels.
For it has been stated that [the levels of speech] are: the gross (sthūlā), consisting of syllables; the subtle (sūkṣmā), consisting of latent impressions (vāsanā); and the supreme (parā). || 25 ||

With these two verses beginning with *bāṇa* and ending with *samīritāḥ*, he teaches the two types of external syllables and their tenfold variety. Therein, [the syllable] *ya* is pervaded; *dāha* (fire) is *ra*; *rasa* (taste) is *va*; *ambu* (water) is *la*; and *hṛt* (heart) is *ha*. These are joined separately with *marut* (wind), which is *sa*, and with itself. Thus, *yakāra* and *repha* [are established].

The five syllables *la*, *va*, *sa*, *ra*, and *lā*—each joined with the vowel *ā* and the nasal bindu—are the nine arrow-syllables of Śakti: *yā*, *rā*, *lā*, *vā*, *sā*. These are the five mudrā-syllables.
Following these five previously mentioned mudrā-syllables, there are the first five: *drā*, *drī*, *klī*, *vlū*, *saḥ*.

There are five syllables. They are the expansions of Śiva, whose nature is desire, and they bring all women of desire under control. The threefold nature of the arrows—according to their gross, subtle, and supreme forms—he will explain in the fifth chapter. || 26 || 27 ||
With the first half of the verse beginning with "Śikhī" (the Peacock), he teaches two syllables of the bow (*cāpa*). In that regard:
"By Śikhī, Toya, Haṃsa, Gaira, Dāha, Vahni, Sva, and likewise by Marut. (28)
The two nooses (pāśa) of those two are taught to bring all under control;
the one that causes the paralysis of all is the sixth mudrā, the goad (aṅkuśa), belonging to those two.
Invocation, installation, confinement, veiling, that which is known as the bringing into presence, the weapon-mudrā, and salutation. (30)
Agitation, driving away, attracting, subjugation, intoxication, the great goad, the sky-farer, that which is called the seed-source, and the raising up of the power (śakti). || 31 ||
Twenty mudrās have been taught; hear now their formation, by which, when properly formed, mantras are accomplished with effort. (32)
Having formed the hands in the *kṛtāñjali* gesture, one should cross the two ring fingers;
when the nails of those [ring fingers] are grasped by the index fingers, this is the *trikhaṇḍā*, which brings about grace.

The two bow-syllables of Śiva and Śivā are *thaṃ* and *dhaṃ*, respectively, formed by the letters *tha* and *dha* joined with their own inherent conjunctions and the *bindu*. The threefold nature of these two bows will be explained in the fifth chapter.
[This is stated] by means of the two verses beginning with "haṃsa" and ending with "vaśaṅkarau."

By means of the latter half and the former half of the verse, he teaches two syllables for the two *pāśas*. Therein, with *haṃsa-ga-irdāha-vahni-svaiḥ*, it is *hrīṃ*; with *sasvena-marutā*, it is *āṃ*. These two syllables of the *pāśas* are thus indicated; as before, these are the *pāśa*-syllables for both.
With the second half of the verse beginning with *sarvastambha*, one syllable of the goad (*aṅkuśa*) common to both is stated; therein, the sixth *mudrā* is the syllable *krauṃ*. (28–29)

With these three verses beginning with "āvāhanam" and ending with "ayatnataḥ," he teaches the names of the twenty mudrās to be fashioned; therein, "sannidhāpana" means the mudrā known by the name "sannidhāpana. By the word "heti"—
The arrow, bow, noose, and goad are mentioned; by these, four mudrās are formed. || 30 || 31 || 32 ||

With the verse beginning with *kṛta*, he teaches the method of forming the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā for the purpose of invocation (*āvāhana*). It is called *lalitāvahā* because it has a three-part form (*trikhaṇḍākāra*)— consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge— and because it shatters the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*).

"Āhvānakarī" (The Invoker). Here, the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) holds that the invocation of Lalitā, who is the soul of the universe, consists of discerning and observing her. The rest is easy to understand. || 33 ||
With both hands joined face down and the fingers extended, one should form the *sthāpanī* mudrā; this is considered to be the *saṃsthāpanī* for all [deities]. (34)
The two hands, with the nails of the thumbs joined to the middle joints of the little fingers and the fists clenched,
with the fingernails closely touching— this is the Sannirodhinī mudrā.

With both hands, the fingers straightened and the fists clenched, one should place them at the sides; then, having crossed them and moved them toward the opposite shoulders, one should settle them in their initial positions.
This is the Avaguṇṭhanī mudrā, which brings about the presence [of the deity];
furthermore, the añjali mudrā should be known as being either open or in the form of a bud.
The mudrā of the arrow and bow consists of a fist with the thumb held straight;
the mudrā of the noose, however, is formed by that same hand through the joining of the index finger and the thumb.
With the thumbs placed on the backs of the little and ring fingers, and the index finger curved while the middle finger remains straight—this is the mudrā known as the *aṅkuśā*. (39)

With the two verses beginning with *adhomukhau* and ending with *sannirodhinī*, he teaches the sequence for forming the two mudrās— the common placement and the subsequent restraint— of all the deities. Therein:
"Sannirodhana" (complete restraint) means the prayer for single-minded devotion to the deity. || 34 || 35 ||

With the two verses beginning with *ṛju* and ending with *mukulāpi vā*, he teaches the sequence for forming the *avaguṇṭhana-mudrā* (the veiling mudrā) and the sequence for forming the *sannidhāpana-mudrā* (the invocation mudrā). Therein, at the outset:

The meaning is that when the right hand begins its movement, there is the resting of the left hand; and when the left hand begins its movement, there is the resting of the right hand. "Veiling" (*avaguṇṭhana*) means making [the deity] an object inaccessible to unworthy vision. "Bringing near" (*sannidhāpana*)...
This is intended as a prayer for the acceptance of the practice through the direct orientation toward the Name. || 36 || 37 ||

With the verse beginning with "bāṇa," he teaches the procedure for forming the Bāṇamudrā and the procedure for forming the Pāśamudrā. In that context, "from the union of the index finger and the thumb" means from the joining of the tips of the index finger and the thumb. || 38 ||

With the verse beginning with "the little finger" (*kaniṣṭhā*), he teaches the procedure for forming the *aṅkuśa* (hook) mudrā; therein, "joined with the middle finger in a straight form" is the meaning. These four weapon-mudrās (*hetimudrā*) are for the purpose of realizing the essential nature of the deity.

(73) When the two index fingers are straightened and joined together at the middle of the back of the hands of the Khecarī mudrā which is about to be described, this is said to be the mudrā for salutation.
Having joined the little fingers, the ring fingers, and the middle fingers with their nails together,
one should place the two thumbs upon the little fingers and keep the index fingers straight.
This is the Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī mudrā, which causes agitation throughout the three worlds.
O Goddess, when its two middle fingers are made like the index fingers [of the hands], [it is so formed]. || 42 ||

One should contemplate those respective weapons in their respective places on the hands. These [deities] are to be fashioned in their respective locations precisely as the nature of one’s own deity. Regarding the fashioning with mantras, the traditional teaching (sampradāya) is that one should fashion them accompanied by their respective mantras. || 39 ||
With the verse beginning with "khecaryā," he teaches the sequence for forming the mudrā of salutation (*namaskāramudrā*).

In that context, what is called "salutation" is the demonstration of a gesture (*abhinaya*) by means of making oneself appear distinct from the body of the one worthy of worship. This is the "extreme secret."
This is the traditional teaching (*sampradāyārtha*). By that very [means], prostration everywhere brings about grace (*prasāda*).
The tradition holds that one should perform the display of the five mudrās—ending with the *sthāpana* and *namaskāra*—using the third section of the *mūlavidyā*. || 40 ||

With the half-verse beginning with *kaniṣṭhā* and ending with *kāriṇī*, he teaches the sequence for forming the *saṃkṣobhaṇī-mudrā*. In this context, *tarjanī* means "the two index fingers. She is the one who causes the agitation of the three worlds and brings about bliss for all the deities.
The meaning is that from the sight of this, the hearts of all women experience a surge of joy. || 41 ||

With the half-verse beginning with "etasyāḥ" and ending with "yoṣitām," he teaches the procedure for forming the *sarvavidrāvaṇī* mudrā. In this context, "etasyāḥ" refers to this *saṃkṣobhaṇī* mudrā; the word "aṅgulī" (fingers) is to be supplied after "madhye" (in the middle); and "devī" is a vocative address.

The meaning is that they should be made straight like the *tarjanī* [finger]. When this has been done, the word "being" (*sati*) is to be supplied. (42) It is "the dispeller of all" because it brings all deities under control and because it causes the dispersal of the wombs of all women.
The *sarvavidrāvaṇī* (all-dispelling) mudrā belongs to all women as well;
when joined with those two [mudrās] that have the form of a goad (*aṅkuśa*), it is considered the *ākarṣaṇī* (attracting). (43)
Having turned the fingers around so that the nails touch the palms,
with the thumbs joined to the index fingers by their nails, this is the *āveśakāriṇī* [mudrā].
Having extended the fingertips and crossed the two little fingers, one should bend the middle fingers by joining their tips, while the ring fingers remain straight. (45)
When the two index fingers rest upon those nails, with the thumbs placed above the middle fingers—this is the Unmādinī mudrā, which causes the infatuation of all. (46)
When the ring fingers of this [mudrā] are bent and the two index fingers are shaped like hooks, this is the Mahāṅkuśā mudrā, which effects immobilization and attraction. (47)
One should properly cross the left and right hands over the elbows and bind the palms together at the wrists with the backs of the hands facing each other.
With the second half of the verse beginning with "tābhyām" (by those two), he teaches the procedure for forming the *ākarṣaṇī-mudrā* (the summoning mudrā). In that context,
"by those two" refers to the two [hands] which have the form of a hook (*aṅkuśa*), joined in the form of a hook as previously described.
The middle and index fingers are joined together, as is understood from the phrase "of the two ring fingers.
What is meant is this: the previously mentioned Drāviṇī-mudrā itself becomes the Ākarṣaṇī-mudrā through the joining of the middle and index fingers in the shape of a hook upon the two ring fingers.
"Attraction" (ākarṣaḥ) means bringing near. The meaning is that having arrived, there is stability in the fulfillment of one's own desire. || 43 ||

With the verse beginning with "parivṛtta," he teaches the sequence for forming the mudrā of possession (*āveśana*). In that context, "with fingers turned back" means with the fingers interlaced; "causing possession" means causing the awakening of the state of the deity. (44)

With the two verses beginning with *karāgre* and ending with *kāriṇī*, he teaches the procedure for forming the *unmādinī-mudrā*. In that context, *sarvonmādakāriṇī* means "that which causes universal intoxication," i.e., that which causes all women to become intoxicated and brings about their arousal. || 46 ||
With this verse beginning with "asyā," he teaches the procedure for forming the Mahāṅkuśa mudrā.
In that context, "asyāḥ" refers to this Unmādinī mudrā; [it is formed] by bending [the fingers] through the contact of the tips of the thumbs. (47)

With these three verses beginning with "savya" and ending with "devatā," he teaches the procedure for forming the khecarī mudrā. In this context, "madhyapṛṣṭhayoḥ" means on the backs of the two middle fingers. Khecarī is that which brings about the accomplishment of the state of being a sky-walker (khecaratva). Here—
No commentary is written for the texts that explain the formation of mudrās, as they are easy to understand. (48, p.
75) Having bent the two index fingers, one should make the two thumbs straight; one should place the little and ring fingers on opposite sides of the back of the hand. (49)
This is that Khecarī Mudrā, which brings delight to Lalitā;
by its very performance, all the deities are accomplished.
The middle fingers are placed at the middle sides and below; the little fingers are reversed at their tips; the ring fingers are crossed below; and the index fingers are shaped like hooks.
The others [are formed] at the tips of those nails; this is declared to be the seed-mudrā (bījamudrā).
The joining of the little finger and the thumb is the triple-sectioned great yoni (mahāyoni-trikhaṇḍikā).
The little finger, ring finger, and middle finger are placed in reverse order behind [the palms],
while the two hands, with the index fingers straightened, are turned upward by means of a twisting motion.

With the two verses beginning with "madhyamā" and ending with "trikhaṇḍikā," he teaches the sequence for forming the seed-mudrā (*bījamudrā*) and the sequence for forming the great yoni-mudrā (*mahāyonimudrā*). In that context, "by way of reversal" (*viparyayāt*) means that they should be [performed] in the opposite manner. The seed-mudrā is so called because it is the cause of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).

With these two verses beginning with "the little finger" (*kaniṣṭhā*) and ending with "is proclaimed" (*samīritam*), he teaches the sequence for forming the mudrā that raises up the Śakti. In this context, *samādhi* means that which is properly placed (*sam-ā-dhīyate*); the meaning is the state of identity (*ahaṃbhāva*) with the deity within one's own self.
The meaning of "mūrtīkaraṇa" (the act of embodiment) is the conceptualization of one's own body as the form of the deity. || 54 ||

With these five verses beginning with "mudrā" and ending with "śiva," [the author] teaches the threefold nature of the mudrās, their latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the etymological derivation of the word "mudrā," and the logical justification thereof. In this context, *tattva* means "thatness," "being-ness," or "reality. From the thumb...

In sequence, beginning from the thumb and following the order from space down to earth: *māyā* is that which conceals the knowledge of one's own self as the phenomenal world (*prapañca*). By your grace, through the realization of your own nature, it "gives" (the fruit); this is derived from the verbal root *rādā* meaning "to give," thus signifying that it bestows [liberation].

Regarding the statement "anger and joy [arise] from a slight difference": when there is uniformity in the fist during both striking and prostration, a slight curvature or straightness at the wrist is called a "slight difference. This means that joy is the opposite of anger, and anger is the opposite of joy.

Regarding the striking and the directing [of a gesture], when a single fist— whether curved or straight— expresses both anger and favor, the fist that conveys favor is designated as a *mudrā*, while the fist that conveys anger is simply a fist. || 59 ||
(76) This is the *śaktutthāpana-mudrā* for recitation, worship, and meditative absorption;
its formation is declared to be the act of making [the deity] manifest in bodily form.
O Goddess! Mudrās are of three kinds according to their form, mantra, and reality (tattva).
They are known as gross, subtle, and supreme; O Beloved, hear now about these three types.
The nature of the *racanā* and the *mantra* has now been explained to you;
the fingers are the forms of the *tattvas*, [beginning] from the thumb (*aṅguṣṭha*) in successive order.
However, by observing the arrangement of those various reversals, it is said:
"Through your grace, may I become 'I-ness' (ahantva) that has transcended your māyā. (57)
It is called a *mudrā* because it bestows joy (*mudaṃ rāti*); indeed, it is simply a fist formed by joining [the hands].
Because of its slight variations, it generates anger or joy in living beings. (58)
By that very [means], the mudrās of all the gods are considered to be bestowers of joy;
O Śivā, those mudrās should always be displayed at the time of worship. (59)

With the two verses beginning with *triloha* and ending with *śiva*, he teaches the fivefold arghya vessel, the method for preparing the arghya, and so forth. In that context, by the word *triloha*, gold, silver, and copper are meant; [the vessel may be made] from one or another of these.
Having prepared the *arghya* water according to the method to be described in the fifth chapter, one should display the *dhenu* and *yoni* mudrās over it. As for the binding of the *dhenu* mudrā:
having formed the *añjali* with the fingers crossed in order, one should [join] the two index fingers of the left and right hands.
Joining the right and left middle fingers together like a staff,
likewise join the two little fingers of the left and right hands to the right and left nostrils respectively like a staff.
One should join the right and left ring fingers together like a staff; this is the Surabhi-mudrā.
One should learn the manner of displaying it from the mouth of the Guru. Immediately after displaying it, one should recite each of the six-limbed Nityātārtīya mantras ten times.

The meaning is that one should perform either the recitation (*japa*) or the worship (*samarcana*) of the mantras of the Six-limbed Nityās once, and the third section of the Root-Vidyā ten times. Thereafter, one should worship three times with the Root-Vidyā in its form of three sections, which is the Nityā-vidyā for that particular day.
"One should recite" refers to that which is heard from tradition (the Veda). "In the form of the Vidyā according to the prescribed sequence" is an adjective for this water of *arghya*;
it means by means of the Lalitā-vidyā and the *trikhaṇḍa*. By means of sprinkling (*abhyukṣaṇa*), one brings about the state of being identical with the Vidyā. || 60 || 61 ||
(77) The preparation of the *arghya* offering is performed in one vessel made of the three metals, glass, or clay;
each [vessel] is consecrated ten times with the six-limbed *Nityātārtīya* mantras.
O Śivā! One should sprinkle all the implements for one's own worship without exception with the water of the arghya offering, using the mantra in the form of the vidyā while reciting it.
One should meditate upon her, red in hue and graceful, holding in her hands an arrow, a bow, a noose, and a goad, while she joyfully embraces the King of Desire (Kāmarāja) in her lap.
Endowed with the form described in the *Kāmyadhyāna* and surrounded by her powers (*śaktis*),
she is prescribed for all daily rites (*nityārcana*) as well as for occasional rites (*naimittikārcana*).
Because the central principal goddess is of the nature of supreme radiance,
the meditation on the powers of the nine enclosures should be performed as one with the goddess.
O Supreme Goddess! Except for the ornaments, colors, weapons, and so forth associated with the Kāmāṅka yantra, everything else pertaining to the locations of the cakras is entirely the same. 65.

With the two verses beginning with "aṇimā laghimā" and ending with "arcanam," he teaches the visualization for the daily and occasional rites of Lalitā. In that regard, [she holds] the arrow, the bow, the noose, and the goad in her hands...

The placement of the weapons in the four arms follows the stated sequence, proceeding counter-clockwise from the right lower arm to the right upper arm. The meaning of the term *yantritām* (restrained) is to be understood solely from the mouth of the Guru. She is *muditām* (joyful) because her very form consists of hundreds of blisses.

"In the form described in the *Kāmyadhyāna* means possessing the appearance endowed with anklets, hero-bands, bracelets, the arrangement of garments, the svastika-marked necklace, neck-ornaments, armlets, bangles, rings, ear-ornaments, crowns, and so forth."
The meaning is that she is to be meditated upon during both the regular (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) worship. || 62 || 63 ||

With the two verses beginning with *madhye* and ending with *aśeṣataḥ*, he teaches the meditation on the host of powers (*śakti*) that constitute the retinue. In that context, [it is said] "because of its nature as a radiant manifestation," referring to the Goddess’s exertion according to the thought: "May I become many; may I be born forth."
The esoteric meaning of the phrase "other than from the mechanical device of the limbs of desire" (kāmāṅkayantrāt) is to be understood solely from the mouth of the Guru.
With these five verses beginning with "aṇimā" and ending with "in the first enclosure," [the author describes] the square in the first enclosure.
Likewise, there is lordship, mastery, and the power of irresistible will, conjoined with enjoyment. (66)
All desires joined with the *icchā-rasa* (the flavor of will) become the ten *siddhis*.
[The mantras] beginning with the two seed-syllables and ending with *siddhi*, when conjoined with the seven-syllabled [mantra], [attain success]. (67)
Brāhmī, Māheśvarī, followed by Kaumārī and Vaiṣṇavī;
likewise Vārāhī, Indrāṇī, and immediately after that Cāmuṇḍā. (68)
The powers (śaktis) residing in the square are said to be Mahālakṣmī and so forth;
these eight [powers] proceed in order from those two [beginning with] "tat" up to the end of the seven-syllable mantra.
Seated at the doors, corners, and cardinal directions, and situated both below and above—
one should worship all of them in the first enclosure (āvṛti) in a clockwise direction.
Desire, intellect, ego, sound, and after that touch;
likewise form, taste, and smell, as well as mind, fortitude, and memory. (72)
The name, the seed-syllable, likewise the self (ātman), the nectar together with the body,
the vowels beginning with the seed-syllable, and those ending with the attractor (ākarṣiṇī) follow in sequence.

He teaches the mantras of the eighteen powers (*śakti*) and the sequence of their worship. Since those verses are easy to understand, we shall demonstrate one of those mantras and state that the others should be applied in the same manner. For example: *hrīḥ śrīḥ aṇimāsiddhipādukām*.
"I worship," and so forth. At the eastern and western gates; the corners are the intermediate directions;
the two directions are the south and north; the conceptualization of "below" and "above" pertains to the vicinity of the eastern and western gates.
In the first enclosure, which is square. (Verses 66–71)

With these three verses beginning with *kāmam* and ending with *sundari*, he teaches the mantras for the worship of the sixteen Śaktis and the sequence of their worship in the second enclosure on the sixteen petals. In this context, *ātmā* means "the self," and *saśarīrakaṃ* means "with the body."

In this case as well, because the hidden meanings are easy to understand, we state that after demonstrating the nature of one mantra, others should be understood in the same way; we do not elaborate further for fear of making the text too voluminous.
"The petal" refers to the foremost petal of the Goddess. Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Akāmākarṣiṇī Nityā.
I worship Kalāpādukā. In this manner, the other fifteen mantras should also be inferred [and applied]. || 72 ||
Then, O beautiful one, one should worship in sequence with the seven-syllable mantra "nityā kalā" starting from the petal and proceeding counter-clockwise. (74)
Kusumā, Mekhalā, and after her Madanā, who is afflicted by passion;
then Rekhā, Veginī, Aṅkuśā, and Mālinī. || 75 ||
All [the goddesses], beginning with Dvayāṅgā and ending with Saptākṣarī,
are to be worshipped in a clockwise direction in the eastern and other cardinal directions, as well as in the corners beginning with the southeast.
And on all eight petals, situated in the third enclosure, starting from the western spoke of the fourteen-spoked [mandala] and proceeding counter-clockwise: || 77 ||
The first is Saṃkṣobhaṇī (the Agitator), followed immediately by Vidrāviṇī (the Melter); then Ākarṣiṇī (the Attractor), Āhlādanikā (the Gladdener), and Sammohinī (the Bewilderer).
Stambhinī, Jambhinī, then Vaśaṅkarī and Rañjanī; Unmādinī is to be known after that, and thereafter Arthasādhanī. (79)

With one and a half verses beginning with *kusuma* and ending with *sthitāḥ*, he teaches the mantras of the eight powers (*śakti*) on the eight petals in the third enclosure (*āvaraṇa*), as well as the sequence for their worship.
Therein, by demonstrating a single mantra, the other seven mantras are to be applied: *hrīḥ*, *śrīḥ*.
"I worship Anaṅgakusumāpādukā," and so forth. || 75 || 76 ||

With three and a half verses beginning with *antarityādi* and ending with *anvarthasaṃjñikā*, he teaches, within the fourth enclosure on the fourteen-spoked [mandala], the fourteen mantra-śaktis and the sequence for the worship of the two ten-syllable śaktis. Therein:

Regarding the phrase "in the fourteen-syllable [mantra] and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) indicates that in both the ten-syllable mantras as well, one should worship the Goddess starting from the top and proceeding counter-clockwise; this means "O Vaśaṅkarī, O Vaśaṅkarī. The term "preceded by 'sarva' and the two" means that the word *sarva* is placed above the two previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*).

One should join [the mantra] at the beginning of the fourteen [syllables]. Regarding the term "the seven-syllabled Śakti," the tradition holds that only the two syllables "Śakti" are taken, and not the *visarga* and the *hrīṃ* syllable.
"In sequence" means in the order previously specified. "To each Śakti" means in every corner.

The meaning is that one should perform worship beginning from the front corner of the Goddess. "Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, I worship the sandals of the power Sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇī. In this manner, one should apply the other thirteen mantras. (77) (78) (79)
(80) She who fulfills all attainments, who consists of mantra, and who brings about the destruction of duality;
she who is the source of both the dual and the non-dual, and all others—all these are joined with the seven-syllabled Śakti. || 79 ||
Thus, one of the lines [reads]: "O Queen of the Gods! all these [goddesses] are to be worshipped in sequence according to their etymological names;
within the pair of inner ten-spoked [lotuses], however, is the Goddess whose nature consists of seven syllables. (80)
The third [vow] bestows the perfection of spiritual attainments and is thereafter called Priyaṅkarī;
the fourth is declared to be Śakti, and likewise Maṅgalakāriṇī.
She is the bestower of desires, the liberator from suffering hereafter, the pacifier of death, and likewise the warder-off of obstacles. (82)
Aṅgasundarikā and Saubhāgyadāyinī;
these ten Śaktis, beginning with Dvaya and Sarva, are to be worshipped in sequence. || 83 ||
The power of knowledge (jñāna-śakti) is likewise considered to consist of wisdom and bestows sovereignty;
she is declared to be the fifth power, as well as the destroyer of diseases. (84)
Another is declared to be the nature of the support (adhāra), and another is the remover of sin;
thus it is said to be composed of bliss (ānandamayī) and likewise to have the nature of protection (rakṣā).

With the three and a half verses beginning with *antardaśāra* and ending with *kramāt*, he teaches the mantras of the ten powers (*śakti*) to be worshipped in the fifth enclosure (*pañcamāvaraṇa*). Therein, the goddess consists of seven syllables: the two syllables *devī*, followed by the seven-syllable mantra [to be repeated] ten times.

One should apply [these] to the mantras, and to the ten-syllable mantra within the group of ten. [The names are: "Bestower of the wealth of accomplishments" (siddhisampatpradā), "Bestower of all accomplishments" (sarvasiddhipradā), "Bestower of wealth" (sampatpradā), and "Liberator from suffering" (duḥkhavimocinī)—the meaning being that she liberates one from suffering beyond [all else]. The rest is easy to understand. [She is called] Aṅgasundarikā.

The meaning is "one whose limbs are beautiful. Regarding the [mantras] beginning with *dvaya*, *sarva*, and so forth: one should place the word *sarva* after the two previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bīja*) at the beginning of these ten-spoked power-mantras (*śakti-mantra*). [For example: *hrīḥ śrīḥ sarvasiddhipradādevīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. In the same way, the other nine mantras are also formed.
These are to be applied accordingly. || 83 ||
With these three verses beginning with *jñāna* and ending with *yajet*, [the author] teaches the ten mantras of the powers to be worshipped in the second ten-spoked wheel of the sixth enclosure. (p.
81) "The tenth power, when arisen, shall bestow the desired fruit."
One should worship these [deities], beginning with Dvaya and Sarva, as the sixth, residing within the enclosure.
Likewise, in the intermediate directions and also from the west,
one should worship Vaśinī and the others counter-clockwise as before, using the seven-syllable mantra with the word "namaḥ" at the end.
One should worship the central triangle on all sides, as well as arrows and a bow;
and this quartet consisting of a noose and a goad should be worshipped near its arms. 88.
O Maheśvarī! The seed-syllables and names ending with "namaḥ" have been declared;
and the Lords are behind the Goddess, between Jayinī and Vimalā. (89)

In this context, *jñā* means "omniscient" (*sarvajñā*). As before: *hrīḥ śrīḥ*, "I worship the sandals of the omniscient goddess. In the same way, one should apply the other nine mantras as well. || 84 || 85 || 86 ||

With the verse beginning with *antarityā*, he teaches the mantras of the eight powers to be worshipped in the eight-spoked [cakra] of the seventh enclosure, as well as the sequence for their worship. In that context, "starting from the west" means beginning from the front (the western spoke), and "as before" refers to the application of the seed-syllables of the [vowel] groups; the remainder is that this is to be done together with the seven-syllable mantra.

The meaning is that one should remove the word "namaḥ" as prescribed in the sequence of placement (*nyāsakrama*) from the "pada," and in its place, apply the seven-syllable mantra within the eight mantras. *Hrīḥ Śrīḥ A Ā I Ī U Ū Ṛ Ṝ Ḷ Ḹ E AI O AU A AḤ VLŪ*. I worship the sandals of Vaśinī, the goddess of speech.

In this way, other mantras are also to be applied accordingly. Here too, the application of the two seed-syllables occurs everywhere because they are prescribed in the first rule and subsequently followed elsewhere. 87.

With this one and a half verses beginning with *madhya* and ending with *maheśvarī*, he teaches the worship mantras and the sequence of worship for the weapons. In that context, it is said: "surrounding the central triangle. [This refers to] the principal deity.

One should worship the various weapons, beginning with the arrow and ending with the goad, in their respective positions on the arms around the central triangle of the garment. As for the stated seed-syllables (bījas), this is what is meant:
at the end of the two previously mentioned seeds, *hrīḥ* and *śrīḥ*, [one should place] *yā*, *rā*, *lā*, *vā*, *śā*, *drā*, *drī*, *klī*, *vlū*, and *saḥ*.

The mantra for the arrows is: *namaḥ sarvajambhanebhyo bāṇebhyaḥ*. Then follows the mantra for the bow: at the end of the two previously mentioned seed-syllables *hrīḥ* and *śrīḥ*, [one recites] *tha dha sarvamohanāya dhanuṣe namaḥ*.
Thereafter, at the end of the two previously mentioned seed-syllables *hrīḥ* and *śrīḥ*...
The goddess in the center is indeed one alone, yet she abides in sixteen forms;
therefore, one should worship the other fifteen within her body. (90)
In the corners of the central triangle, starting from the west and proceeding clockwise,
[one should worship] Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśī, and likewise Bhagamālinī.
Then the first two [syllables], followed by the Vidyā, and then each name of a Pīṭha;
then the names of the Śaktis joined with the seven-syllabled Devī-mantra. 92.
Thereafter, he should worship them with those [offerings], and likewise worship the Goddess in the center;
both together, along with the entire Vidyā, accompanied by the name of the Pīṭha Goddess.
Thus has been described your worship, accompanied by the seven-syllable mantra of the Goddess;
and in each wheel, one should worship the deity situated in the center with the Vidyā and the nine names.

*Hrīḥ āḥ, obeisance to the noose for the sake of subjugating all*—this is the mantra of the noose (*pāśa*). Furthermore, after the two seed-syllables *Śrīḥ* and *Hrīḥ* have been uttered, [the mantra] *obeisance to the goad for the sake of paralyzing all* (*sarvastambhanāya aṅkuśāya namaḥ*) is the mantra of the goad (*aṅkuśa*). Here too, the application of the two seed-syllables is as before.
With the second half of the verse beginning with "nāthānityādi," he teaches the place of worship for the nine Nāthas. || 88 ||

With the verse beginning with "madhyastha" and ending with "samarcayet," along with the six additional syllables beginning with "madhyatrikoṇa," he teaches that the Goddess consists of the nature of the sixteen Nityās, and by means of that, the worship of the other fifteen Tithi-Nityās within her form.
With two verses, he teaches the three Śaktis to be worshipped in the three corners of the central triangle in the eighth enclosure, their mantras, and the sequence of their worship. Therein,
beginning from the corner opposite the Goddess in the west, one by one of the sections of the Vidyā—
The meaning is "of each individual power. The *pīṭhas* are the three known as Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, and Jālandhara; the names of the powers are the three:
Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī. [The mantra] is joined with the seven-syllable name of the Goddess. The Goddess...

"Beyond these two syllables, one should join the seven-syllable mantra preceded by *Śrī*. [The mantra is: *Śrī* / *Hrī* / [Root Mantra] First Section: I worship the *Śrīpādukā* of Goddess Kāmeśvarī at the sacred seat (pīṭha) of Kāmarūpa. In this same manner, the other two mantras should also be joined. Herein:
The employment of the word "Śrī" is due to traditional usage.
One should worship and likewise honor [the deity] together with the seven-syllable mantra. These two are declared to be the *guṇas* and also the *yoginīs*. (95)

Regarding the covering of the Abhidhā [mantra], worship is said to be performed according to the sequence: "May they accept" (gṛhṇantu) for the [male] deity, and "May she accept" (gṛhṇatu) for the Goddess; therein lies a threefold distinction—listen, O beloved! (96)

With the two half-verses beginning with "paścāt" and ending with "pūjanam," he teaches the worship of the gross form of the Goddess in the very center of the ninth enclosure by means of the ten-syllable mantra and others. Therein, "the entire vidyā" refers to the previously mentioned fourth vidyā.

It consists of the name of the *pīṭha* joined with the name of the goddess; that is, the name of the *pīṭha* and the name of the goddess. Therein, the name of the *pīṭha* is "Oḍyānapīṭhe," and the name of the goddess is "Śrīmahātripurasundarī. Having uttered the two syllables "Devī" as before, one should then utter [the name] preceded by "Śrī," joined with the seven syllables of the Goddess.

The meaning is that one should utter the seven-syllable mantra: *hrīḥ śrīḥ*. [One should say: "I worship the sandals of the Goddess Śrī Mahātripurasundarī at the sacred seat of Oḍyāna-pīṭha," together with the entire root-vidyā.
Here too, the employment of the two words *śrī* is according to the tradition, as previously explained. || 93 ||

With the half-verse beginning with *praticakram* and ending with *bhavet*, followed by one full verse ending with the third quarter, he teaches the nine names for the Goddess's worship in each of the nine enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), as well as the nine mantras for that worship and the nine mantras for the offering of that worship.
The meaning is that there, in the fifth chapter, one should worship with the nine names beginning with "Tripurā" as stated in verses fourteen and fifteen,
and with the mantras according to the methods of application explained therein. In that regard, the application is as follows:

The method is as follows: "I worship the *pāduka* of the Root-Vidyā Tripurā-Nityā. In this manner, one should apply the other eight [mantras] in sequence. Regarding these nine mantras, the tradition holds that the addition of the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) should not occur; however, in the ninth [mantra], there should be the employment of the word "Śrī" twice.
According to the tradition: "that and that" refers to the two-fold worship; "the pair" refers to the two seed-syllables (*bīja*).

"Qualities" refers to [the qualities] beginning with *Prakaṭā*. "The qualities known as Śrī and Śakti"—these too have been taught in the fifth chapter by the twelfth and thirteenth verses. They are called "Yoginīs."
Thus it connects here. It is said [to be] "divine" because of its transcendental nature.

The names such as Trailokyamohana and others belong to the nine *āvaraṇa-cakras* (enclosure wheels) of the primary manifestation (*abhidhā-māvṛti*). These have been declared in the fifth chapter by means of the ninth and tenth [verses]. They...
