"Just as Hrī and Śrī—may these manifest Yoginīs accept worship in the Trailokyamohana Cakra. In this way, one should likewise [worship] the other eight [Yoginīs].
[One should worship them] grossly by their collective names, and subtly as the body of mantra.
But for Śivā, worship is known through the offering of one's own form as that of another. 97.
O Goddess, the Vidyā consists of the three seed-syllables topped by the fourth vowel;
that very form of the fourth vowel is said to be like three points (bindus). || 98 ||

O wise one, listen now to that auspicious meditation which brings about great exaltation—the realization of identity with the Goddess that arises for both the Goddess herself and the practitioner. (99)

One should apply the mantras. In that regard, the final one is: *hrīḥ śrīḥ*, "May this most secret Yoginī accept the fruit of the great worship in the Great Wheel of Universal Bliss. Here too, the employment of the word "great" (*mahā*) is according to the tradition. 94–95.

With the passage beginning with "Its threefold nature" and ending with "in Śiva," consisting of one and a quarter quarters, he teaches the threefold form of the Goddess situated in the center as gross, subtle, and supreme; therein, the gross form is that which was described [previously] starting with "the red," and so forth, by means of the entire Vidyā, the fourth Vidyā.

The meaning is that one should worship. By means of "name-and-name"—that is, by means of the knowledge consisting of names and forms—one should worship the subtle form; this means [worship] the mantra-body, which is the embodiment of syllables.
This connects with the phrase "this subtle form" regarding the Goddess.

"Subtle form" means consisting of syllables (akṣara). "Supreme form" is that which is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth. "By offering," meaning by the presentation of worship—the word "should worship" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. The meaning is that one should worship the supreme form of the Goddess with the mantra for the presentation of worship. [The following refers to] auspicious things.

Everything must indeed be offered to the Goddess. For this very reason, by the principle that "that which is most auspicious [should be offered]," her worship and that very thing itself must be offered; the meaning is that everywhere, both the deity and her worship must be offered.
The words "it becomes known" and "worshipped" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. Having known [this]...

The meaning is that one should worship. What is intended is this: having realized, "I worship the gross form of the Goddess with the Vidyā called Samastā, the subtle form consisting of syllables with the Vidyā called Nāmarūpā, and the supreme form with the Arpaṇa Vidyā."
One should worship [them]. In this same way, it should be understood for the other eight as well. || 96 || 97 ||

With these three verses beginning with "vidyā" and ending with "bhāvayet," he teaches the meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) of the yoga of the identity between the Guru, the Mantra, the Deity, and one's own Self.
Because this subject matter is extremely secret, it is not to be disclosed; nevertheless, by the command of the Nātha, it is explained in detail. [The first verse begins: "Vidyā..."
The "three seeds" are the three sections of the root-vidyā; "crowned by the fourth vowel" means ending with the fourth vowel, that is, ending with the letter *ī*.
Above is the wheel consisting of the *bindu*, and below is that which consists of two *bindus*.
And one should meditate on the ugly form with the remaining [parts], and the remaining limbs with the rest. || 100 ||

The pervasion consisting of the wind-principle (vāyutattva) has been correctly explained; by the thorough refinement of this within the mind, that very principle is assimilated into one's own self. 101.
Thus ends the fourth chapter, titled "The Worship of Lalitā," in the *Kādimata*, within the *Śrīṣoḍaśanityātantra*.
The phrase "the nature of that fourth" (tatturīyasvarūpam) means the nature of that syllable *ī*, which is the fourth.

By "nature," the written form is meant; it is described as possessing three dots (*bindu*s). In all scripts, the fourth nature indeed exists as the essence of the three dots; therefore, it possesses this very character.

It bestows [the fruit] upon the teacher, the deity, and the practitioner; it brings about great exaltation through the cultivation of that [state], which is the cultivation of identity with it, because of the attainment of the nature of the indivisible Self. || 99 ||

With the verse beginning with "Above" (*ūrdhva*), he teaches the sequence of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanākrama*) of yoga which effects the realization of the identity of the Guru, the Mantra, and the Deity as one's own self. In that context, "above, consisting of the Bindu": this means that [the same applies] even to the three sections of the Root-Vidyā.

Because it ends with the fourth vowel *e* and because its essential nature consists of three *bindus*, there is a face above by means of the [upper] *bindu*, two breasts below by means of the two [lower] *bindus*,
and the complete limbs of that Goddess by means of the remaining line of that syllable. Thus...

The identity of the deity and the mantra is established by that [means]; therefore, meditating upon the Guru and one's own self as abiding in that very nature, one should recite this Vidyā. Through the attainment of identity with it, the aforementioned fruits are indeed accomplished. That the Guru is of the nature of the mantra is to be understood from his own mouth. || 101 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, upon the complete *Tantra* known as the venerable *Kādimatā* among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*, [the section on] Lalitā—
The fourth chapter, dedicated to elucidating the sequence of the worship of the eternal and the non-eternal, has been fully examined.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
By means of that very cultivation, one who is concentrated on the vidyā should recite;
union with the essence of the mantra is certainly accomplished, there is no doubt. || 1 ||
With the third section of the Vidyā, one should perform the services of worship:
water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, bathing, garments, and ornaments.
Fragrant flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, water for sipping, betel, worship, hymns of praise, libations, and prostrations— (3).
Regarding the number of verses: in the fourth chapter there is no yantra;
the number of verses belonging to the commentary shall be two hundred and seventy-eight.
Now begins the fifth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding fourth chapter the practice of the yoga of the identity of the Guru, Mantra, Deity, and Self for the Lalitānityā-vidyā, as well as its daily worship, [the author] next—

In the fifth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "bhāvanā" and ending with "tathā," he teaches the remaining rites starting from the daily worship of that Goddess Lalitā up to the division of the *kūrma* diagram; therein, by means of the verse beginning with "bhāvanena," he explains the method of mantra recitation (*japa*).
And he teaches the non-deviation from accomplishment (*siddhi*). In that regard,
"by that very cultivation" means by the yoga of cultivating the identity-form of the guru, the mantra, the deity, and oneself at the conclusion of the previous chapter.
Sāyujya is identity. || 1 ||

With the first half of the verse beginning with "vidyā," he teaches the mantra for the offering of worship to the deity. Although it was stated there that "by the third section," it means that one should perform those [offerings] with that [section] together with the daily [mantra] of that day; thus, it must be done according to the command of the Lord (Nātha).
The tradition. || 2 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *pādya* and ending with *namaskriyām*, he teaches the sixteen services (*upacāra*) common to all Tantras. Among these, because it is a subordinate part of the food offering (*naivedya*), the second *ācamana* (water for sipping) is not counted as a separate service. [The term used is] *tarpaṇa*.

The offering of the arghya water is said to consist of honey, milk, coconut water, fruit juices, or whatever is available. One should perform the prostrations and the mudrās as prescribed by the samaya; such is the connection [of the verse], that one should thus perform sixteen types of ritual services (pūjopacāra). || 3 ||

Having thus performed worship, one should recite [the mantra] a thousand times, or a hundred times, or for that day's duration, endowed with the previously mentioned yoga, in front [of the deity]. || 4 ||
Then, by the grace of the Goddess, one should contemplate oneself as equal to her;
having performed the threefold ritual placement (nyāsa), one may then wander at ease, being the very self of the Goddess.
Thus, for that person who is devoted to the Guru and performs the daily ritual sequence,
no affliction whatsoever shall ever arise from any source at any time.
Whoever should practice inauspiciousness, affliction, or even indifference toward her, for him those [consequences] shall come through our grace; for that indeed is the sign.
Listen now to the names of the nine enclosures as well as the names of their respective Śaktis, by worshipping them in their respective circles one attains incomparable Siddhi.
The external [mudrā] is the Deluder of the Three Worlds, the Fulfilled of All Hopes, the Agitator of All, and the Bestower of All Good Fortune. || 9 ||

With the two verses beginning with *evam* and ending with *sukhī*, he teaches the concluding rites of the worship. Therein, *purataḥ* means in front of the Goddess; *taddinajam* means belonging to that day of worship; *vā* is used in the sense of restriction (*avadhāraṇe*); and *prātaḥsandhyoktam* refers to what was stated regarding the morning twilight ritual, namely nine times.

The meaning is that one should recite [the mantra] one hundred and twenty-one times: thirty-six times as prescribed for the midday *saṃdhyā*, sixteen times as prescribed for the evening *saṃdhyā*, and sixty times according to the number of *ghaṭikās* in that day; thus, by grace.
By the power of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of identity bestowed by the divine state;
the meaning is that immediately after the absorption (*āsana*) into the self of the Goddess, one should always move about endowed with the sense of "I am the deity" (*devatā-ahambhāva*).
[This is explained] by the two verses beginning with *evam* and ending with *tat*.

He teaches the power of one who practices the perpetual rite (*nityakrama*). In that regard, "devoted to the guru" means one whose every activity is dependent upon him. The word "characteristic" (*lakṣaṇa*) refers to the practitioner of the perpetual rite; this is the implied meaning.
What is being said is that for the practitioner of the perpetual rite, there is favor, opposition, or indifference.

In the sequence of the nine coverings (*navāvaraṇanityakrama*), equanimity (*upekṣā*) occurs through decrease and increase; it arises through the grace produced by our favorable equanimity and by means of praise. || 7 ||
With this verse beginning with "nava," he introduces the names of the nine coverings (*āvaraṇa*) and the names of their respective powers (*śakti*).
Among these, by which names [the following are designated]... (8)
It accomplishes all aims, removes every disease, provides all protection, and bestows all spiritual attainments beyond this. (10)
The central point of the bindu consists of all-bliss and is of the nature of Śiva;
thus, O Pārvatī, are these nine names associated with their respective qualities.
Then there are the manifest traditions that move externally, and those that are secret; then there are those even more secret, situated within them—the Kula, Kaula, and Nigarbhika traditions.
Those ending with "tad" are the secret ones (rahasya), while those ending with "parāpara" are the very secret ones (parāpararahasya).
Those ending with "atipūrva," however, are the most secret ones (atipūrvarahasya); they stand in the middle and possess gross forms.
Tripurā, Tripureśī, Sundarī, Suravāsinī, Śrīmālinī, Siddhāmbā, and Mahātripurasundarī. (14)
With these three verses beginning with "trailokya" and ending with "pārvatī," he teaches the nine meaningful names of the nine enclosure-circles (*navāvaraṇacakra*). Among them,
*sarvasaṃkṣobhaṇa* means that which thoroughly agitates all and brings about complete renown.

The meaning is "that which brings about renown. In the word *paridāyakam*, the prefix *pari-* is for the purpose of completing the meter; the meaning is "that which bestows all prosperity. [Verse 9] Regarding *sarvarogaharam*: one should apply the word *hara* after the word *sarvaroga*; thus, the meaning is "the remover of all diseases."

Because it consists of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhi*), it bestows all accomplishments; "it bestows all accomplishments" and "it consists of all accomplishments"—this is the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*). The "place of the *bindu*" (*bindusthāna*) refers to the central place of the *bindu*.
The grammatical connection is: "consisting of all bliss, having Śiva as its essence. The place of the *bindu* is like Brahman.
The meaning is "in the midst of all. [The names] are descriptive of their qualities (*anvarthāni*). "O Pārvatī" is the vocative case. || 11 ||

With the two verses beginning with *prakaṭā* and ending with *vigrahāḥ*, he teaches the nine names of the powers of the nine enclosures (*navāvaraṇa-śakti*) according to their etymological meaning. In this regard, the tradition holds that their qualifying attributes are their unconditioned (*nirupādhika*) natures. Among these:

The names for the qualities of the third and final veils are reversed; for example, "the most secret Yoginīs" and so forth, and "the extremely secret Yoginī. However, all other names for the qualities are as follows: "the secret Yoginīs" and so forth. Both [categories] are also designated as "Kulakaulas" and "those who have transcended Kula."

"Possessing the tradition" (sampradāyavat) means that they are to be practiced according to the command of the Master (nātha). "Nigarbhikās" means those which are "nigarbhas" (innermost secrets). "Parāpararahasyakās" means those which are "parāpararahasyas" (secrets of the supreme and the non-supreme). "Atipūrvarahasyās" means those which are "ati-śabda-pūrva-rahasyas" (secrets preceded by the word 'ati'), meaning "extremely secret" (atirahasya).
"Those situated in the middle" means those with gross forms; "those situated in the middle with form" means they are extremely secret.
Here, the gross form is the veil of the subtle mantra-form, while the supreme form is [beyond] space, time, and shape.
In the middle hexagon, however, one should worship with these [syllables] joined in the middle of the seven-syllable Vidyā, preceded by the word "Tripura. (15)
The sequence of worship, its specific details, the ritual for accomplishing the vidyā, the observance of the practitioner's vow, and these very signs of accomplishment; || 16 ||

One should meditate upon the Self as identical with Tripurā, situated at the aperture in the crown of the head in the form of light; and those whose bodies have been consecrated by the placement [of mantras] should contemplate the form of the Lord’s feet.
Women of various colors, bearing diverse weapons, forms, vehicles, and ornaments,
who are omnipresent and grant all perfections at all times, [are attained] through the offering of oblations.

The traditional meaning (*sampradāyārtha*) is as follows: although the gross and subtle forms lead one to the supreme form, they appear as if they were obscuring it due to their limited nature; thus, they are called "obscuration" (*āvaraṇa*). This is the secret teaching (*upahvara*). || 13 ||

With the two verses beginning with *tripurā* and ending with *arcayet*, [the author] teaches the nine specific names for each of the goddess’s nine enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), as well as the sequence for applying the mantras for worship in those respective locations. Among these, [the first two names are] *Tripureśī* and *Tripureśvarī*.

This is the meaning. Regarding the six names in the middle hexad, beginning with Sundarī and ending with Ambā: there, in the name "Puravāsinī," the meaning is "Tripuravāsinī. It is the established tradition that one should indeed join the word "tri" [to each]. "Vidyā" refers to Śrīvidyā. The method for joining the *manus* (the seed-syllables) has been explained previously.
This has been stated by us in the [relevant] chapter. || 14 || 15 ||

With the verse beginning "The sequence of worship" (pūjākrama), he then poses five questions; therein, "its specific features" refers to those in the form of the process of contraction (saṅkocakrama), and "the signs of accomplishment" refers to the signs of accomplishment in the Vidyā. || 16 ||

With the two verses beginning with *tripurātmānam* and ending with *dānataḥ*, [the author] instructs the practitioner on what must be performed at the time of awakening in the morning. Therein, at the time of rising,
after the meditation upon the crown of the head (*mūrdhin*), immediately thereafter follows the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the self as Tripurā.

The meaning is that one should contemplate the nature of the Goddess as being identical to one's own nature, preceded by a continuous connection with the [ritual] procedures to be described hereafter. From the offering of the *bali*, it should be understood that this is done with the sixteen-syllable mantra.
The *bali* is accompanied by flowers and various condiments (*vyañjana*); through the offering of that, they shall become bestowers of all accomplishments (*siddhi*).
The remainder [of the instruction]: having meditated thus for the sake of all accomplishments, one should offer the *bali* in the morning; this is the remainder.
(17–18) Clad in red garments and perfumes, wearing garlands, adorned with red ornaments and the like, with a serene mind, and having his body scented with camphor. (19)
Seated in the lotus posture, facing east, and having restrained his breath with self-control,
he should offer an oblation with the sixteen-syllable mantra and worship the gurus.

Thereafter, by his command, one should perform worship upon the head according to the prescribed rite, having meditated upon the Lord as having become one with that [deity] and oneself as being of that same nature. (21)
One should worship the island consisting of nine jewels, adorned with its nine divisions, by means of the Mātṛkās beginning with the first letter of its name and ending with the word "namaḥ."

With these three verses beginning with "raktā" and ending with "tadātmakam," he teaches the sequence for commencing the worship. In that regard, the lotus posture (*padmāsana*) is not mentioned here because it will be described later; [one should perform] breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) after restraining the vital breaths.

Having performed [this], I shall briefly explain here the breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) which will be described further below: having expelled the breath, the vital air (*māruta*), through the right nostril while blocking the left nostril according to one's capacity, immediately thereafter, by blocking the right nostril...

Having drawn in the breath through the left nostril according to one's strength, and having again performed exhalation and inhalation in this same manner, one should hold it within according to one's strength and then release it very slowly. This is the regulated sequence for *prāṇāyāma* in all cases.

With all external and internal organs withdrawn from other objects, one should offer the *bali* with the sixteen-syllable mantra whose nature was taught at the conclusion of the third chapter, and worship as before. The meaning is that one should worship the Gurus situated in the crown of the head (*brahmarandhra*) according to the tradition. "Of him" refers to this.
The domain of one's own Lord (*svanāthaviṣaya*). "According to rule" means in the manner that will be described hereafter.
And "having realized the Lord as having become identical with that" means having understood that the Lord himself exists in the form of the Goddess.
|| 19 || 20 || 21 || [This is explained] by the eight verses beginning with *navaratna* and ending with *mātaraḥ*.
In these verses, he teaches the sequence for the worship of the Goddess’s abodes and their respective mantras.

Regarding the phrase "beginning with Mātṛkā": one should utter the fifty-one letters from *a* to *kṣ*, each accompanied by the nasal bindu (*m*), preceded by two seed-syllables; above those, one should place her name, followed by the word *namaḥ*.

The meaning is that one should join [them] together. For example: hrīḥ, śrīḥ, a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, ṛ, ̐ṝ, ḷ, ̐ḹ, e, ai, o, au, a, aḥ, ka, kha, ga, gha, ṅa, ca, cha, ja, jha, ña, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ḍha, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, na, pa, pha, ba, bha, ma, ya, ra, la, va, śa, ṣa, sa, ha, la, kṣa, [and] *navaratnadvīpāya* (to the island of the nine jewels).
With the word "namas" [one offers]:
blue flowers, lapis lazuli, coral, pearl, as well as emerald, diamond, go-meda, and ruby. (23)
One should also worship the seasons with the mantras of the Kalpa-gardens;
there, one should worship the senses in the form of horses from the western side.
One should first worship the elephants, which are the objects of the senses, by their respective names; then, from west to the center, one should worship the nine jewels in reverse order.
Time, the Mudrā, the Mātṛkā, the Jewel, the Place, the Guru, as well as the Principle (tattva), the Planets, the Form, and that which is named the Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśvarī). || 26 ||
In this context, one should worship each [deity] by its respective name, ending with "namaḥ," preceded by the sense organ and the object. || 22 ||

With the verse beginning with "puṣpam," he teaches the names of the nine gems; therein, the statement "emerald from the northeast" (īśānmarakatam) indicates the clockwise sequence, because it will be stated in the Kurukullā chapter that the western [gem] is the topaz (puṣparāga), starting from the northeast (īśāt). "From the northeast" means in the northeastern direction.

This is the meaning. || 23 || Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, obeisance to Kalpakodyāna. Right here on this Jewel Island, Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, obeisance to the Seasons (Ṛtus). The ten sense faculties are: hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell, speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals.
To the west, in front of the Goddess’s pavilion, [one should offer] *hrīḥ* and *śrīḥ*: "Obeisance to the senses and the horses.
[One should worship] the sense-objects—namely sound, touch, form, taste, smell, speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure—in their respective order.
Ten [offerings]. To the west of the rear part of the Goddess’s pavilion, one should worship the Nine Jewels with the mantra: *hrīḥ śrīḥ indriyārthagajebhyo namaḥ*. || 24 || 25 ||

With the verse beginning "Time, Mudrā," and so forth, he teaches the worship mantras for each of the nine segments (*khaṇḍas*), which consist of the nine jewels such as Time and the rest, and which are each of the nature of the Nine Lords (*navanātha*). Here, "Lord" (*nātha*) means the Guru. In that regard, the ninefold nature of Time is as follows:

The ninefold nature of the *ghaṭikā* (hour) consists of the forms of day and night, the days of the week, lunar dates, fortnights, months, seasons, and years. The ninefold nature of the *mudrā* arises from the previously mentioned [states] such as *saṃkṣobhaṇa*. The ninefold nature of the *mātṛkā* arises from the sequence of the groups (*varga*) to be described below. The ninefold nature of the *ratna* (jewel) is according to the form already explained.

The land has nine realms (*dhātu*), like the ninefold realm of jewels. The Lords have nine realms according to the stated sequence. The principles (*tattva*) have nine realms through the process of quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) of the triad consisting of the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge. This is due to the acceptance of their eternality. [Likewise for] the planets...

The state of having nine constituents (*navadhātva*) is indeed very clear. As for the ninefold nature of the forms, they consist of skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, *ojas*, and breath (*prāṇa*);
their names end with the title "Mistress of the Wheel" (*cakreśvarī*). || 26 ||

O Dear One! Having worshipped the respective Mistress of the Wheel (cakreśvarī) according to the stated sequence, [one should worship] the pavilion of central rubies, which has a moat of the waters of compassion. (27)
One should worship the place, the time, as well as the form and the sound in the corners;
then [one should worship] the Yoginīs of the musical performance together with the Rūpiṇī Śakti.
One should worship all the Mothers, who are endowed with the entire assembly of secret and manifest Siddhayoginīs and joined with the wheels, and who are accompanied by the seven syllables.

One should place the *arghya* water, mixed with yellow pigment (*rocanā*), camphor, saffron, and small quantities of musk, in a vessel made of gold or other precious materials that has a stand, using pure water.
O Supreme Goddess! One should meditate upon the elements as fire, sun, and moon;
one should recite the mantra ten times and thereby satisfy the Yoginīs with that [recitation].

The meaning is that these nine Cakreśvarīs have been described in sequence; one should worship them by uttering the word "Cakreśvarī" at the end of each respective name preceded by the word "Śakti. For example: *Hrīḥ Śrīḥ Kālacakreśvarī-śakti-pādukāṃ pūjayāmi*. Thus, the word "Śakti" is used here.

"Obtained through tradition. The plural number is used because each of the nine [deities] possesses a ninefold nature. "O Dear One" (*priye*) is an address to the Goddess. "A moat of the waters of compassion" (*karuṇātoyaparikhām*) means a ruby pavilion surrounded by a moat filled with the waters consisting of the Goddess's compassion.
Hrīḥ Śrīḥ! Salutation to the moat filled with the waters of compassion; Hrīḥ Śrīḥ! Salutation to the pavilion of rubies.
Here too, the application of the word "salutation" (namaḥ) follows the traditional practice. || 27 ||

With the words beginning with "deśam," he teaches the powers that effect contraction. Therein: *hrīṃ śrīṃ, I worship the sandal of the power whose form is Deśa (Space)*. In the same way, there are three other mantras; likewise, they proceed in reverse order starting from Nirṛti. Here, the words *deśa*, *kāla*, and *ākāra* are each mentioned twice.

In accordance with the correspondence between cause and effect, that which is of the nature of the effect is first, consisting of ninefold forms, and that which is of the nature of the cause is second. I worship the Saṃgatayoginīs—the Śaktis who provide diversion through dance, song, and instrumental music—the sandals of the Saṃgatayoginī-Śakti, Hrīṃ Śrīṃ. Here too—
The application of the word "power" (śakti) and the plural number are as before. || 28 ||

The meaning is that the form of the mantra consists of the first half of the verse beginning with *samastagupta*, excluding its final syllable. In this context, *yogini* means *yoginī*. [The mantra is: *hrīḥ śrīḥ samastaguptaprakaṭasiddhiyoginīcakra*.
One should contemplate the three sections of Vidyā within the cavity of the heart, the locus;
they are red, and by the penetration of their radiance, one's own body becomes red as well. (32)
Then, having performed breath control (prāṇāyāma) and having carried out the purification of the hands as prescribed,
one should likewise perform the ritual posture (āsana) with the first [verse] and with those beginning from the third up to the sixth.
I worship the Śrī-pādukās. Here too, as before, the plural number and the use of the word "Śrī" are employed because of their multiplicity; "all Mothers" means all the Śaktis.
This application of the seven-syllable mantra is common to each of those respective Śaktis. By these eight [mantras]...

This is what is stated by these verses: the Goddess is to be understood as the manifestation of her own nature, which is fashioned from the sounds arising from her own form consisting of body and senses. || 29 ||

With the two verses beginning with "Hema" and ending with "yoginīḥ," he teaches the method of preparing the *arghya* offering for the worship of the deity and its application; therein, "candram" means camphor, and "laghu" means *aguru*. || 30 ||

"O Supreme Goddess" (*parameśvarī*) is an address to the Goddess. One should mutter that third section of the Vidyā, "tat-tat," ten times; with that water for the *arghya* offering, he addresses the "Yoginīs"—the powers (*śaktis*) who constitute the retinue of the Goddess. This is what is meant: [he should offer it] into the water of the supporting cup (*ādhāra-caṣaka*).

Having understood that [the Śrīcakra] consists of the three sections of Vidyā, whose nature is Fire, Sun, and Moon, one should contemplate the five substances placed within it as being sequentially composed of the five elements beginning with Earth; then,
having displayed the Dhenu and Yoni mudrās according to the previously stated sequence, one should likewise contemplate the Śrīcakra in the midst of the water.
Having meditated there, according to the sequence of the external [offerings] and so forth to be described in the *Nityaklinna-paṭala*,
one should perform the worship once with the six-limbed mantras (*ṣaḍaṅga-mantra*), once with the sixteen *Nityā* mantras,
ten times with the third section of the Vidyā, and [ten times] with the Root Vidyā and the two *Dinanityās*.
Having worshipped and recited [the mantra] three times each, one should perform the prescribed rites with the water for the guest-offering (arghya). || 31 ||

With the verse beginning with "the support" (ādhāra) and ending with "then having performed" (vidhāya atha), he teaches in this additional quarter-verse what is to be meditated upon during the time of breath control (prāṇāyāma). In that context, "in the aperture" (randhre) means in the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra).
"By the piercing of their radiance" (tatprabhāvedhāt) means by the piercing of their radiance. Piercing (vedha) is the state of becoming one with that.
The two splendors of the first and final segments— consisting of fire and moon respectively, located in the *ādhāra* and the *brahmarandhra*— spread sequentially with their faces upward and downward;
meanwhile, the splendor of the middle segment, consisting of the sun and located in the heart, spreads both upward and downward.

By those two, it becomes united; this is what is meant: the radiance of the solar energy of the second part located in the heart, which is inlaid with the fire-energy of the first part situated in the *mūlādhāra*, is joined with that [fire].

One should meditate internally and externally upon the radiance of the third crescent moon situated at the *brahmarandhra* and the threefold radiance [of the sun, fire, and moon] as having a unified form merged into an undivided appearance. The breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) is as before,
followed by the recitation (*japa*) and worship of the *Lalitā-vidyā*.
One should worship [the deity] joined with the names of those of humble mind and those who are neutral;
then, one should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) as prescribed by the second [verse]. || 34 ||
The heart is indicated by the palm of the hand with the fingers extended;
the head likewise; the crest-lock (śikhā) by the fist with the thumb properly pointing downward.
With such hands, [the fingers] beginning from the shoulder armor and reaching up to the navel—the index, middle, and ring fingers—are prescribed for the three eyes in sequence. (36)
When the palms are extended, it is declared to be the three-fold clapping (tālatraya);
when joined with the index and middle fingers while making a sound, it is declared to be the weapon mudrā (astramudrā).
Likewise, one who removes obstacles [should do so] in the cardinal directions, the intermediate directions, above, below, and in the center;
then, having performed the Nyāsa of Vaśinī and the others according to the previously mentioned yoga.

In the meditative absorptions (samādhis), one should contemplate the threefold fire in the form of the three sections of knowledge as being precisely the breath-control (prāṇāyāma). Elsewhere, one should contemplate the threefold fire alone as residing within the three supports.

With five verses beginning with *kṛtvā* and ending with *yogataḥ*, comprising three and a quarter stanzas, he teaches the three types of ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth; therein, by means of the first [verse], which was previously stated in the preceding chapter as "*vātaḥ svasaṃyutaḥ*" and so on.

The meaning is that one should worship the four seats with the four mantras beginning with the third and ending with the sixth. This is joined with the names situated between the seed-syllable (*bīja*) and the salutation (*namaḥ*). Above each of the aforementioned syllables of the *vidyā*-kūṭas, the name of the respective seat [should be placed].

The meaning is that one should utter [the seed-syllables] ending in the dative case and then join them with the word *namaḥ*. *Hrīḥ aiḥ hrīḥ klīḥ hrīḥ sauḥ devyātmāsanāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the seat of the Self of the Goddess). *Hraiḥ hsklīḥ hsauḥ cakrāsanāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the seat of the wheel).
*Hsaiḥ hsklīḥ hsauḥ sarvamantrāsanāya namaḥ* (Salutation to the seat of all mantras). *Hrīḥ aiḥ klīḥ sauḥ vlūḥ*

Regarding the four mantras for the seats beginning with "sādhyasiddhāya namaḥ," according to the tradition, the two seed-syllables are not joined at the beginning. [The first mantra is formed] by the second [mantra] using the Kulasundarī-vidyā taught in the previous chapter under the heading "hṛcchira" (heart and head): *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ hṛdayāya namaḥ* and *aiṃ klīṃ sauḥ śirase*.
Svāhā ai/ klī/ sauḥ to the crest (śikhā), Vaṣaṭ ai/ klī/ sauḥ to the armor (kavaca), Hum ai/ klī/ sauḥ to the three eyes (netratraya), Vauṣaṭ ai/ klī/ sauḥ to the weapon (astra) Phaṭ. || 33 || 34 ||

With three and a half verses beginning with *prasāritatala* and ending with *hṛdi*, he teaches the method for the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). In this context, "three claps" refers to striking the palms together three times with sound. The phrase "with the Kulasundarī-vidyā recited three times" is the understood remainder [of the verse].
On the seventh [day], one should perform the invocation with the *trikhaṇḍā* vidyā;
having placed her within the center of the *yoni* situated in the middle wheel at the front. (39)
Having meditated upon her in such a manner, together with her veil, one should display the mudrās;
thus the seventeen [mudrās] have been declared, and then one should worship her with the ritual services (upacāras).
One should worship the nine Lords three times each in the center of Jayinī and Vimalā; then, because they are the very forms of the Goddess herself, one should also worship all fifteen Nityās.
One should mutter the respective vidyās in the image of the Goddess, becoming absorbed in them in sequence;
then, beginning from the right branch of the western door, one should perform worship.

Likewise, one should worship the eight [deities] beginning with Brāhmī in the first enclosure, as they are proclaimed in the eight directions around [the central deity], as well as above and below. (43)

In all three types of *nyāsa*, there is no occurrence of the two seed-syllables at the beginning; this is due to the previously mentioned yoga, that is, the yoga with the *varṇa-kūṭākṣara* and so forth as established in the preceding chapter. (35–38)

With twenty-five verses beginning with "The invocation is by the seventh" and ending with "may [the Goddess] be happy," he teaches the daily worship of the Goddess, the procedure for the daily fire-sacrifice (*homa*), and the conclusion of the worship;
therein, the connection is with the "seventh vidyā. This refers to what was stated in the preceding chapter, beginning with "the heart of the *haṃsa*," and so forth.

The phrase "with the three-part mudrā" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. One should display such mudrās as have their forms described in the previous chapter in the verse beginning with "the red one," and so forth. The seventeen [rites] mentioned—beginning with installation (*sthāpana*) and ending with the four starting with *heti*—are those taught in the previous chapter.

The meaning is that one should display the mudrās. [This is done] with either sixteen or five services (upacāras); the five services, however, consist of perfume, flowers, incense, lamps, and food offerings. || 93 || 94 ||

Three times three—meaning nine—divine, siddha, and human [beings] are seated in three rows from the goddess’s left side to her right side, gazing at the goddess. The meaning is that she herself abides as those very forms; thus, in sequence.

By the sequence of increasing by one [digit] at a time, [one should worship] Dakṣa and Śāśvatī on the right and left branches of the Goddess's door. (41–42) Regarding the word "on both sides" (*abhitaḥ*): here, first in the cardinal directions, then in the intermediate directions;
and in each of those places as well, on the right side of the Goddess, just like Aṇimā and the others.
Therein, on the right side of each respective goddess, one should worship [the goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī, together with the root-vidyā, using their stated names in the center;
and in the nine enclosures, one should worship them in sequence with the nine mantras that have been taught. (44)
One should present that worship and perform the mudrās nine times each;
likewise on the sixteen-spoked [wheel], the eight-petaled [lotus], and its fourfold enclosure.
One should perform the worship according to the prescribed sequence with the aforementioned Śaktis;
one should worship at the tip and the base of the central yoni, as well as on its sides and outside.
O Īśvarī! [He] places five arrows, as well as a bow, a noose, and a goad, situated all around from the exterior to the northeast (Īśāna) in a counter-clockwise direction.
Arrows are said to be of three kinds, according to their gross, subtle, and supreme natures:
the gross are made of flowers, while the subtle are declared to be of the nature of mantra. (48)
Furthermore, the subtle latent impressions (vāsanās) have been described; now hear, O beloved, about the gross ones:
the lotus, the white water-lily, the red lotus, the kahlāra, and likewise the indīvara. (49)
O Īśvarī, these five flowers born of the *sahakāra* tree have been described;
through the performance of worship and fire-offerings (*homa*), they generate the agitation of passion. (50)
By the names previously mentioned, beginning with "Tripurā" and so forth,
and by the offering-mantras (arpaṇa-mantra) previously stated by us according to the sequence already described [in verses 43 and 44]. That worship consists of both gross and subtle forms.
The worship is that previously described; "each one by one" is the remainder [of the sentence], referring to each successive enclosure (āvāraṇa). || 45 ||

The phrase "according to the stated sequence" and so forth was already explained by us previously; it means on the outside of the top, the root, and the sides—that is, on the exterior of the central *yoni*. The meaning is that this is the vacant space situated in the middle of the eight squares of the *Vaśinī* group. The word "red" (*rakta*) is an adjective qualifying the *kairava* (white water-lily).
49 || "The flower born of the *sahakāra* tree" is the remainder [of the phrase]. "Pertaining to Love" (*mānmatha*) means relating to Kāma;

it is that which generates agitation and draws the minds of both men and women toward one another. "By means of the procedure for worship and *homa*" means by performing the rites of worship and so forth with the aforementioned five flowers.

The meaning is that it causes agitation. "By the five mantras" means by those connected with the Śiva-arrows (śaiva-bāṇa). The meaning is that in all cases, one should perform recitation, worship, and so forth, using the five Śiva-arrow mantras. Such [a state] exists through the distinction of gross and subtle.

The grammatical connection is: "and the bow made from the stalks of red sugarcane. According to the tradition, the gross form of the noose and the goad is made of gold; their subtle and supreme forms are as previously described. By the aforementioned sequence—that is, by the sequence mentioned before and the sequence previously stated—there are four.
Through the recitation of mantras and ritual applications, and by means of the five perfected mantras, that bow becomes of such a nature—gross, and made from the stalks of the Puṇḍra sugarcane. (51)

One should worship the powers beginning with Kāmeśvarī according to the stated sequence, numbering the middle, the womb, the tip, the corner, and so forth; likewise, one should worship Śivā in the center.
Then, having displayed the nine mudrās and the four [mudrās] in succession,
one should perform the ritual services (upacāras) endowed with the prescribed yoga.
Having recited [the mantra] ten times, one should remember oneself as having the body of the deity;
one should worship those fifteen Nityās within one's own self.
Then, having worshipped with devotion by means of the five mantras of the elemental selves (bhūtātman),
and having performed worship with the eight-syllable mantra of the Self (ātma-aṣṭākṣara-mantra), one should then perform the recitation (japa).
One should perform a thousand [recitations] before the Goddess, or a hundred, or that which is produced on that day;
or the three junctions (sandhyās) may be performed sixty times, according to the stated form.

Thus [ends] the fourfold mudrās. "In sequence" means in the order previously stated. "The services" refers to those mentioned earlier. "In sequence" means that one should perform the sixteen services by means of the Vidyātātī and Khaṇḍadinnityā-vidyās; this is the meaning. "Endowed with the aforementioned yoga" refers to what was taught at the conclusion of the previous chapter. 52

The statement that there are fifteen [deities] is for the purpose of establishing that one's own self is essentially the sixteen-fold Lalitā-vidyā. [54] By means of the elemental selves (bhūtātman) taught in the third chapter, and also by means of the eight-syllable mantra of the Self (ātma-aṣṭākṣara-mantra).
Its form is as taught in the third chapter. For the mantras of the elements and the self-mantra, there is the addition of two seed-syllables at the beginning;
however, according to the tradition, there is no application of the seven-syllable mantra for the self-mantra.

With the verse beginning with "A thousand," he teaches the primary and secondary alternatives for the recitation (*japa*). In that context, the mention of "a hundred" pertains to both alternatives because it constitutes a form of expiation (*prāyaścitta*). The statement "it has been said" refers to the aforementioned form; [the word] "five"— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly.]
Then, having made an offering of a handful of flowers and worshipped with the root mantra, one should perform the fire oblation (homa).

Having sprinkled [the site] with the water of the *arghya* offering using *kuśa* grass, [one acts] either in the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) or in the middle of the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*). (57)
One should draw four lines, oriented toward the east and the north;
then, having placed the fire in the center, one should discard the portion belonging to the flesh-eaters (kravyāda).
Having sprinkled [water] around and strewn [grass] around, one should manifest the power of the fire;
one should offer nine oblations of clarified butter for each of the seven tongues of flame.
Then, having offered oblations sixteen times according to the sequence of worship with the root mantra,
one should contemplate her as dissolved into the abode of the Bindu.

Then, one should offer the bali-oblation before [the deity], reciting the Kurukullā-mantra three times, by means of the offering of food, side-dishes, flowers, and water, according to the prescribed form.

Because the meaning taught in the twenty chapters always abides in the heart; the word "vā" (or) has the sense of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). This is what is meant: by the aforementioned ritual procedure, one should [visualize] the number of the three junctions (*sandhyā*) produced on that day and the number of sixty *ghaṭikās* in this manner.
One should recite the number exactly as it was stated collectively. (56) "Then" means after the recitation.

"With the root" means with the root-vidyā. "Having worshipped, one should establish [the fire] in the hearth" means in a hearth whose nature is described in the twenty-ninth chapter, or in the middle of a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*); "sacrificial mound" refers to that very place.

He describes a particular type of sacrificial mound (*dhiṣṇya*) in the shape of a square, measuring one cubit in length and breadth, with a height of one finger-breadth, and constructed from sand. [Verse 57] "In the middle" refers to the central square among the nine squares drawn with *kuśa* grass. In all cases here, when no mantra is explicitly mentioned, [the standard mantra is to be understood].
The remaining portion [of the sentence] is that the two mantras of the daily *nityā-vidyā* belonging to the third section of the *Vidyā* [cycle] are to be known.

One should discard the "flesh-eating" (*kravyāda*) portion; the meaning is that one should cast the fragment of charcoal toward the southern direction with the words, "Obeisance to the flesh-eaters" (*kravyādebhyo namaḥ*). Having performed the sprinkling (*pariṣecana*), [one should sprinkle].

"By way of circumambulation" means with *kuśa* or *darbha* grasses—this is the ellipsis. "In the seven tongues" refers to those named Hiraṇyā and so forth, which will be described in the twenty-ninth chapter. Having first recollected each respective tongue, one should offer oblations with the *Vidyā* and the *Tṛtīyakhaṇḍa-dinanityā*.

"One should perform [this]," such is the tradition (*sampradāya*). Elsewhere, in all cases, [one should do so] with the names of those respective tongues. "From the root" means by means of the *mūla-mantra*. At the end of the fire-oblation (*homa*), one should recite the number of oblations offered; this is the tradition for all cases. "In the abode of the drop" means in the middle of the two eyebrows. "In front of the deity" [is said] because of the three mantras.

One should offer the *bali* to Kurukullā with three mantras. Having worshipped the Goddess residing in the wheel according to the described nature— that is, according to the nature taught by the Guru— and likewise having become one with her own form, [one should proceed].
With his own mudrā, he should unite the wheel of energies (śakticakra) with himself by means of the Khecarī [mudrā]. || 62 ||
Then, having performed the three types of nyāsa preceded by prāṇāyāma,
and having recited the pair of hymns, one whose self is the Goddess may move about happily.
O Goddess of gods! Listen to the specific modes of worship that are proclaimed for daily practice in their proper sequence;
however, they are recommended for those who are incapable of elaborate rites as well as for times of adversity. (64)
Otherwise, the worship of the Goddess with contracted [limbs] would be fruitless;
the first [part] should be with the weapons in the center and so forth, while the second is within the nine yonis.
The fourth [mantra] is said to be from the middle of the fourteen spokes according to the previously described form;
the fifth destroys all suffering and affliction and bestows one's desires.
By means of the mudrā; and that [mudrā] consists of two fists formed by both hands, with the two index fingers extended after three strikes with the palms,
positioned one above and one below the deity.

She is described as one whose supreme form consists in the vision of the sacrificial materials offered as oblations (61). Through her, he becomes possessed of that form—the deity who has attained the grace of expansive likeness (sārūpya). By means of his own mudrā, which consists of the three portions of the Vidyā visualized at the mūlādhāra, the heart, and the brahmarandhra;

By means of the Mahātripuramudrā described previously, one [unites] the circle of Śaktis—that is, the multitude of powers—by means of the Khecarīmudrā, whose formation was taught earlier. This is accompanied by the recollection of the respective mantras. The method of unification within oneself is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. (62) [One should recite] the pair of hymns dedicated to the Lord and the Goddess.
The self of the Goddess is [the subject], because all duties have been rendered easy through the threefold nyāsa and so forth. || 63 ||

With these four verses beginning with "pūjā" and ending with "siddhidā," he teaches the fivefold ritual procedure of worship (saparyāprakriyā) in its contracted and expanded forms. Among these, [the first is for] those who are incapable, such as royal women and others; [the second is for] times of distress, such as fire, falling [into calamity], fever, and so forth. || 64 ||

Otherwise, for one capable of extensive worship, a worship performed with arbitrary contraction would be fruitless; "fruitless" means that it results in misfortune due to such independence [of whim]. Regarding the phrase "with weapons": the worship of the four central deities should be accompanied by the worship of the four weapons, beginning with the middle one.

The first is that which consists of contracted desire and so forth. The second means the worship within the nine *yonis*, beginning with the nine *yonis* and ending with the central one. The third means the ritual service (*saparyā*) extending from the fourteen-spoked [wheel] up to the center of the fourteen-spoked [wheel]. The fourth...
"O Goddess of gods! Listen now to its specific varieties in the worship of Kurukullā.
Thus, the fivefold worship has been described, which bestows the accomplishment of all aims. (57)

The means for accomplishing the vidyā, its perfection, the vow pertaining to it, as well as what is to be avoided, the signs of its manifestation, and the obstacles arising from past actions—all these [are explained]. (68)
Listen in due order, O Goddess of gods! [to that which] always causes delight, by which even a mortal may attain perfection, becoming liberated while living and identical with Me. (69)
Having bathed in fragrant waters and assumed the form prescribed for the preliminary worship,
one should satisfy the Guru with wealth and then practice the Krama in a red chamber.
Reciting [the mantra] a thousand times while observing silence throughout the three junctions of the day,
one should offer milk-porridge (pāyasa) mixed with plantains, jaggery, and sugar.
The meaning is that the fourth [stage] of worship consists of the forms already described, beginning with the square and ending with the center.

"The fifth worship" is the remainder of the sentence. Regarding "its method": the procedure for the fifth service will be explained in the twenty-second chapter on Kurukullā; the meaning is, "listen to that very [method] therein."

With the two verses beginning with "vidyāyāḥ" and ending with "bhavanmayaḥ," he teaches the introduction to the six topics and the fruit of accomplishment (*siddhi*). In that context, "of the *vidyā*" refers to its practice; "accomplishment" refers to the accomplishment resulting from the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*); and "that vow" [refers to the observance thereof].
The vow of the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) for the mantra (*vidyā*). This is to be avoided at the time of accomplishing the mantra and at all other times as well.

"Signs of facing toward" refers to the signs of the mantra facing toward [the practitioner], while "obstacles to facing toward" refers to the obstacles [that prevent it]. These arise from past [karma] and so forth, due to the excessive attachment to negative latent impressions (*durvāsanā*). In which [cases]...

"Listen to those [teachings] which bring joy to those for whom the contemplation of one's own Self becomes the very form of the fruit—by means of which fruit the body of the Goddess consists of existence. (69)

With seven and a half verses beginning with "snāta" and ending with "kramam," [the author] teaches the method of accomplishing the knowledge (*vidyā*) and the attainment of its preparatory practice (*puraścaraṇa*). In that regard,
one who possesses the form previously described for worship, having the body as taught for the daily worship, and having gratified [the deity] with wealth and so forth;
Only when instructed by a satisfied guru should one perform the rite; that is, the daily rite (nityakrama). || 70 ||

"A thousand" at each junction of the day means a thousand [offerings]. "Mocā" refers to the fruit of the plantain tree. "Sitāḥ" refers to white sugar. "Arpayet" means one should present; the word "at each junction of the day" is to be understood as the remainder of the sentence. || 71 ||
One should also perform the *nīrājana* rite with camphor during those very twilight periods;
one should perform the fire-oblation (*homa*) one-tenth the size [of the mantra-repetition], and the libation (*tarpaṇa*) with water mixed with camphor. (72)
One should perform the recitation of the "Svānityā" mantra two thousand times every day; by that means, O Īśvarī, the full one hundred thousand (lakṣa) will be completed at the end of the period.
Thus, three hundred thousand [years] are declared for the first Kṛta Yuga;
likewise, it is twice that in Tretā and remembered as three times that in Dvāpara.
In the Kali age, it is said that the number of syllables is fourfold;
that third [set] consists of seven, and thus by that calculation, the total becomes twenty-one.

The tenth part of the number of recitations (*japa*) [should be performed] with water containing camphor. And there is also the *tarpaṇa* (libation). By the word "and" (*ca*), the phrase "in the tenth part" is drawn over from the previous verse. After one's own daily practice (*svanitya*), the number of recitations for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) is the total number of recitations required for the three daily junctures (*sandhyā*) as prescribed for one's own daily practice, multiplied by sixty *ghaṭikās*.
The meaning is "those which are separate. By the statement "a *lakṣa* is the full end," the meaning is that one should recite three thousand three hundred and thirty-four [mantras] every day.
This is what is being said: one who desires to perform the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*) [should honor] a guru according to his own capacity.

Having propitiated [the deity] with wealth and being permitted by him, he— remaining within the sacrificial pavilion for the worship beginning with "Lohitam," free from idle chatter, restricted in diet, avoiding contact with women,
with an undisturbed mind, bathed with fragrant waters, and adorned with garments, ointments, garlands, and ornaments of the color of the highest number (parārddha)— [should proceed].

At each juncture of the day, immediately following one's own daily obligatory rites (*svanityakrama*), having performed the sequential worship (*kramapūjā*) in the form previously described, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) one hundred and twelve times or one thousand times, and offer libations (*tarpaṇa*) with the same number of parts— that is, one-tenth of the recitation— using *palāśa* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
Having performed the fire-oblation (homa) with safflower or white water-lilies (kahlāra) according to the ten-part sequence,
one should perform worship and recitation (japa) with that same number of reddish flowers or fragrant blossoms,
completing the full count up to one hundred thousand as prescribed, beginning with the final oblation (pūrṇāhuti).

"One should recite everywhere" (verse 73). "Thus, three hundred thousand times" means this: for all the seed-mantras of the *piṇḍas* and *kartarīs*, one should recite three hundred thousand repetitions for each non-repeated syllable during the Kṛta Yuga; [and during] the three [subsequent ages], the Tretā, Dvāpara, and Kali Yugas.
Due to the reduction of one-quarter, one-half, or three-quarters, the previously stated number of recitations becomes double, triple, or quadruple. For mantras consisting of one to nine syllables—
whether designated as *piṇḍa*, *kartarī*, or *bīja*— the count is reached by means of one hundred thousand repetitions of non-repeated syllables.

Japa is performed according to the increase in the sequence of the proclaimed Yugas. For mantras consisting of ten to twenty syllables, the japa is one hundred thousand repetitions per syllable, as previously stated, in accordance with the respective Yuga.
For mantras consisting of twenty-one to one hundred syllables, [the japa is]...
Therefore, in other ages, an increase in the number [of repetitions] is prescribed;
provided that no obstacle arises from the agitation caused by women or from sensual enjoyments. (76)
When those numbers are complete, having made the request, one should follow the sequence;
O Goddess of Gods! hear now what things are to be avoided on those days and always.
Conversing with atheists, sexual intercourse condemned by others, sleep, grief, idle chatter, and wandering through foreign lands—(these should be avoided). 78.
O Śāṅkarī! Other things to be avoided at those gates have been declared;
listen now to those which are destructive to everyone everywhere and at all times. (79)
One should not harbor a desire for another’s field, house, or wife, nor should one engage in their censure; one should not direct anger toward women, nor strike them, even if they are wicked. (80)

The recitation (*japa*) consists of exactly one hundred thousand repetitions; for mantras consisting of syllables exceeding that number, the recitation is ten thousand. This is what is stated in the *Mantratantraprakāśikā*.
This applies to all tantras.
When no specific number for the recitation during the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa) has been stated, it should be understood as being accepted [as ten thousand]. || 74 ||

That number seven is for the third part of the Vidyā, because of the non-return [of the practitioner] through its seven syllables. "Twenty-one lakhs" is the remainder; the meaning is that the total number of recitations (japa) in the first age, the Kṛtayuga, is twenty-one lakhs. By that—

Gradually; in other ages such as the Tretā and so forth; from enjoyment that causes agitation for women—that is, from enjoyment permitted by young women; [the completion] of the number of recitations for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) as prescribed, free from the obstacles of enjoyment with young women; *sampūrtiḥ* means accomplishment; one’s own sequence.
This is declared as the perpetual practice.

With the second half of the verse beginning with "varjyāni" (those to be avoided), he introduces the things to be avoided by those intent on the practice of *vidyā*. In that context, "on that day" refers to the day of the preparatory rite (*puraścaraṇa*), and "at all times" means at every moment. || 77 ||

With these three verses beginning with "nāstikaiḥ" and ending with "yojayet," he teaches those things to be avoided both at the time of the *puraścaraṇa* and at all other times. Among them, on those days—the days of the *puraścaraṇa* and so forth—there are others; these are the things to be avoided at all times. These include [those things] that involve censuring him.
Reproaches directed at others, even when they are wicked or even when they are disobedient. || 80 ||
The signs of accomplishment have been described by me in the discourse on latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
Now listen to the signs of favorability for one who is practicing [the path]. (81)
In dreams at night, there is a meeting with groups of women on boats, wandering upon the peaks of elephants, mountains, and palaces, and the sight of kings. (82)
Beholding elephants and women, witnessing dance and song, attending festivals, as well as seeing and touching liquor and meat. (83)
O Goddess of the gods! Listen to the censurable [omens] which cause obstacles and misfortune:
being struck by black-clad soldiers in a dream, and the smearing of oil. (84)
Sexual intercourse with the wives of others, as well as the loss of sensory control, disturbances in the kingdom, fear of fire, wind, and water, and the destruction of kinsmen. (85)

Neglect toward the guru, lack of success with ritual materials, affliction by disease, faith in the worship of other mantras, and constant obstacles during the daily worship—[these are the impediments]. (86)
And that which occurs for men through the performance of difficult merits over many lifetimes—namely, steadfastness in faith and the daily worship established by tradition. (87)

With these three verses beginning with *siddha* and ending with *tathā*, he teaches the primary signs of the deity for the practitioner. In that regard, concerning the description of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) in the thirty-fifth chapter:
"for one who accomplishes," meaning for one intent on the practice; "then," meaning at all times previously mentioned. (81)
The construction is "the sight of dance and song"; likewise, "the touching of those two" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 82 || 83 ||

With these three verses beginning with "nindyāni" and ending with "aniśam," he teaches the signs that obstruct one's orientation toward the deity due to the abundance of prior sins. Among those, "vighnānarthakarāṇi" refers to those things which are both obstacles and causes of misfortune.
The syntactical connection is: "the non-acquisition of the [necessary] things. This is what is meant:

here, the black-colored soldier, the oil massage, the observation of the emission of the senses, the neglect of the Guru, and devotion to another mantra—these five are causes of misfortune; the others are causes of obstacles. || 84 ||
With the verse beginning with "narāṇām" (of men), he teaches the cause for attaining steadfastness in true devotion, the tradition, and constant worship. (p.
104) Without knowing the posture of the tortoise (*kūrma-sthiti*), one remains fixed in the rules of recitation (*japa*) and so forth.
He does not obtain the aforementioned fruits; otherwise, he meets with destruction. || 88 ||
Therefore, having understood the entire division of the tortoise, one should perform [the rite] in its entirety.
That [division] is fourfold in this world; listen to its modes, O beloved! (89)
The first is the supreme tortoise, then that which pertains to a region, as well as that which pertains to a village, a cow-pen, or a house; such is its fourfold classification. (90)
Then, one should divide the country, village, or dwelling into nine parts;
from east to west, one should assign the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*.
One should place four identical syllables on the two outer [sides] of the Lord; then, one should assign the vowels in the middle, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise.

"Over many births for a long time. Regarding the establishment of the tradition (*sampradāya*), here is the statement of an authority on the etymological derivation of the word *sampradāya*: "The prefix *sam* denotes correctness (*samyaktva*), while from *pra* comes excellence, and from *dā* comes bestowing."
Because it is a real entity (vastu), that supreme knowledge is transmitted from one who is not non-existent (astunah).

This is what is meant: the knowledge obtained from a true guru through the lineage (sampradāya) is that which brings about the attainment of one's desired goal; thus it possesses a true lineage. || 87 ||
With these eleven verses beginning with *kūrma* and ending with *sadā*,

[the author] teaches the division of the universal *kūrma-sthiti* common to all systems (*sarvatantra-sādhāraṇa*), the fruit of knowing it, and the transgression incurred by not accepting it. The aforementioned practices such as the worship of deities have been described.

Thus they have been declared. Otherwise, not only will the aforementioned results not be attained, but the entire undertaking—including the layout of houses, villages, cities, ports, market towns, and hamlets—will fail. (88) That is the tortoise;
its manner refers to the manner of the tortoise's placement. (89) This is the supreme tortoise.
The tortoise is the stable supporter of the earth, which is fifty crores of yojanas in extent;
"then, the second" refers to the manner already described. Its establishment is the establishment of the tortoise. || 90 ||
"One should divide into nine parts"—this is what is meant: by means of four lines drawn with equal intervals running east-west and north-south, there arise nine squares.
Among them, starting from the square in the eastern row and proceeding to the end of the square in the middle of the western row...
Having written the letters from *ka* to *ma* in groups of five, five by five in each of the five compartments in clockwise order,
one should thereafter write four letters each, from *ya* to *ha*, in the two directions starting from the north (the left) and ending at the northwest (the wind direction).

p. 105) At the end of the *īśa* [syllables], one should subsequently place them in pairs; from whichever syllable the name begins, that becomes the face, and then the two sides, the two hands, the two flanks, and the two feet, each in their respective order. (93)
One [line] at the tail, then one in the middle, and likewise one on the back—thus it possesses six limbs.
Success in all aims occurs when it is in the mouth; when it is on the two hands, it brings about only minor success.
In the belly and thighs there is constant fruitlessness; in the feet, it causes all suffering; in the tail, death is certain; but on the back, it bestows all desired objects.
Therefore, having thoroughly understood that, one should perform everything as prescribed:
the consonants should be in the Deśakūrma, and likewise the vowels in the Gṛhakūrma. (96)
In the village-tortoise there is a pair, but in the supreme tortoise those three do not exist;
because he is eternally facing the east, his accomplishment is thus proclaimed.
Having written [the letters] in the two corner cells, one should write the remaining two syllables,

"lakṣa," in the northeast cell. In the central cell, one should write the sixteen vowels, from *a* to the visarga (*ḥ*), two at a time in each of the eight directions starting from the east and ending in the northeast, proceeding clockwise.

One should draw two [lines]. When this has been done, whichever square in the aforementioned diagram contains the first letter of the name of the house and so forth previously mentioned, that square should be known as the mouth of that tortoise; the two squares situated on either side of that square [are its ears].
Following that, the pair of hands of that tortoise, then the two cavities, and his belly. || 93 ||
Immediately following that, one square is its tail; the very center, endowed with the vowels and consonants, is its back—the ninth square.
Thus, that tortoise possesses six limbs known as the mouth, hands, belly, feet, tail, and back.

The essential nature [of this] is as follows: everywhere, beginning from the grid of the letters of the name, one should conceive of the mouth and other parts of that tortoise. (94) The phrase "worship" is to be understood as "bestowing all desired objects. (95) The phrase "all has been declared" is to be understood as "through the practice of worship. The consonant is situated within the letters of the name.
The vowels are those situated at the beginning of the names [of the regions]. (96) There are two types of syllables: vowel-syllables and consonant-syllables.
This is what is meant: in the aforementioned wheel of the regional tortoise (*deśakūrma*), whichever square in which the consonant-syllable at the beginning of a name is seen, that is its mouth.
The vowel-syllable that is seen in the square of whichever house-tortoise (gṛhakūrma) has a name beginning with a particular letter belongs to that very [person].
Thus, this fourfold division of the tortoise has been described;
by means of it, the accomplishment of all mantras will then occur in every respect. (98)
Having increased the length by one and divided the width by eight, one should determine the remainder;
from among those [remainders], one should designate the first as the name. (99)
In the case of dwellings whose forms are unknown, they may be known by their names;
yet in those respective locations, there is invariably misfortune as well as emptiness.
Pervasion consisting of the principle of space (vyomatattva) has been correctly described;
by the thorough churning of this within the mind, that very principle is assimilated into one's own self.

The "mouth" of villages and other entities is that square in which the first letter of the name—whether a vowel or a consonant—is seen; one should perform the stated rites on the limb corresponding to that mouth. If the two [the name-letter and the house-letter] do not correspond to each other, one should act according to one's preference on whichever limb corresponds to either of them.

One should perform [the rite]. If the first syllable of the name of the regional tortoise (*deśakūrma*) consists solely of a vowel, one should designate the outer square located in the direction of that particular square as its mouth; the remaining part of the sentence implies that the practitioner faces east toward the supreme tortoise (*parakūrma*). Because it is thus fixed in its position, its accomplishment is proclaimed.
It depends on the state of the arrangement of its parts; by which [knowledge] one knows the divisions of the tortoise.

With the two verses beginning with *samvardhya* and ending with *tathā*, he teaches the method for assigning names to the planets and so forth, whose specific names among the aforementioned types of sites (*vāstu*) are unknown. In that context, *āyāmena* means by the measure of length; [the site] by eight...

By means of eight numbers; "from the remainder" means from the remainder of the invocation. One [syllable] from the group—that is, one syllable from among those group-syllables—is the first syllable. (99) Regarding those whose forms are unknown and whose names are unknown—this is what is meant: for one whose name is unknown but who is desired by oneself...
Having increased the length by the width of the site and multiplied that number by eight,

one should determine whichever consonant-group (varga)— namely ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, or śa— corresponds to the remaining number; then, among the letters born of that group, [one should take] the first letter from the beginning or the end.
"One should imagine the name" means: [one should do so] with respect to well-known names, that is, among houses whose names are already established; this is the sense.
By means of that, one should imagine the limbs of the tortoise in their respective places—namely, the positions of the feet, the tail, and the belly.
Emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is fruitlessness (*niṣphalatā*). || 100 ||
(p. 107) Thus, the fifth chapter of the venerable *Kādimata*, among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*, has been fully examined.
Thus [ends] the venerable *Kādimata*, known as the *Paripūrṇa* (Complete) Tantra, among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.

Thus concludes the fifth chapter, dedicated to elucidating the ritual procedure for the daily worship of Lalitā Nityā, within the commentary titled *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the name *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*.
[This has been] examined.
Regarding the number of verses: there shall be one yantra in the fifth [chapter], which pertains to the commentary on the text.
Two hundred and sixty-five is thus observed.
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Now, O beautiful one, listen as I shall describe the occasional (naimittika) and the optional (kāmya) rites for those whose souls are devoted to the daily worship of the sixteen Nityās.

The obligatory (nitya), the occasional (naimittika), and the optional (kāmya) [worship] depend upon one another in their sequence; if one performs worship otherwise while desiring [results], one brings about a succession of calamities.
Those perfected ones (siddhas) who are devoted to daily worship must perform occasional worship (naimittikārcana).
Therefore, I shall describe its procedure, beginning with Caitra and ending with Phālguna.

In the month of Caitra, on the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight, one should prepare [the offering] with *damanaka* plants— either with their roots or in clusters— and having established it at night with the mantra, || 4 ||
Now begins the sixth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding chapter the procedure for the daily worship of Lalitā, [the author] next [teaches] that which is common to all the Nityās for those devoted to her.

He teaches the sequence of occasional and optional worship by means of the sixth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, the sixteen daily [rites]" and ending with "one should become identical with That. Therein, by means of the verses beginning with "Now,
the sixteen," in those...
With thirty-two verses ending with the word *pīti*, he teaches the sequence of occasional worship (*naimittikārcana*).

Therein, by means of two verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "the succession of calamities" (*āpatparamparām*), he indicates the transgression incurred by performing the occasional and optional rites out of their proper order, as established by the summary of the chapter's subject matter.

He teaches [this]. In that context, the remaining portion refers to occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) worship. This is said to be mutually dependent: those who are devoted solely to daily worship (*nityārcā*) are qualified for occasional worship, while those devoted to both types of worship are qualified for optional worship.
Otherwise, "cultivation" refers to cultivation in a sequence contrary to what has been stated; this applies to all [the stages] in common. || 2 ||

With the verse beginning "nityārcane" (in the daily worship), he introduces the prescription of the qualities and the method for the performance of all occasional (naimittika) modes of worship. || 3 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with "In Caitra" and ending with "worship," he teaches the procedure for worship with *damanaka* flowers; the phrase "with *damanaka*s" implies "together with their roots. "With clusters" means with their branches—this is the secondary option. "Having established [the deity] by means of the Vidyā"—this is what is stated.

In all ritual ceremonies for specific purposes, the prescribed materials for worship should be placed on a pure vessel the night before, which has been consecrated with the *vidyā*; then, using the daily *vidyā* of that day, one should perform worship with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, food offerings, and prostrations.
On the following day, at the conclusion of the daily worship, one should perform worship with these [mantras].
And on the full moon day of this month, one should perform the worship for the Spring Festival (Vasantotsava).
One should perform a brilliant worship as before, using flowers produced at that time, along with moon-fragrance (candracandana), saugandhika lotuses, and saffron (kāśmīra).
On the full moon day of the month of Vaiśākha, one should worship with golden lotuses,
or else with camphor, musk, sandalwood, and cool water.
And on the full moon day of the month of Jyeṣṭha, one should worship the Goddess with fruits produced from plantain, jackfruit, and mango trees, as before, for the sake of attaining all perfections.
On the full moon day of the month of Āṣāḍha, one should worship Śivā with sandalwood paste mixed with saffron, along with cardamom, kakkola, and jasmine.
On the full moon day of the month of Śrāvaṇa, one should worship Śivā with sacred threads (pavitra). O auspicious lady! Listen to this procedure for it, which bestows good fortune.

Having worshipped [the deity] with the fivefold salutations and the five types of offerings, and having placed [the image] in a certain place of worship, on the following day at the conclusion of one's own daily ritual sequence of worship, one should perform a special worship with those [offerings] according to one's means, as well as the worship of the Guru. || 5 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with "In this" (*asmin*) and ending with "radiant" (*ujjvalam*), he teaches the worship for the spring festival (*vasantotsava*). "In this month" means in the month of Caitra.
"With sandalwood, camphor, and fragrant flowers," along with all kinds of garlands and saffron—that is, those combined with *kuṅkuma*.
As before, preceded by the previously mentioned consecration (adhivāsa). || 6 ||

With the verse beginning with "vaiśākha," he teaches the worship for the month of Vaiśākha. In that context, the phrase "with snow-lotuses" (himapuṣkaraiḥ) implies "even with snow-water" (himajalaiḥ), which is an alternative option intended for those who are incapable [of the primary practice].

[The flowers should be] "scented" (vāsitaiḥ) with camphor, musk, and sandalwood; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. Here too, it should be preceded by the preliminary rite of consecration (adhivāsa).
It must be performed. || 7 ||
With the verse beginning with "jyeṣṭha," he teaches the worship of the month of Jyeṣṭha; in each case, the preliminary consecration (sādhivāsa) is to be performed as before. // 7 //
With the verse beginning with "Āṣāḍha," he teaches the worship of Āṣāḍha; here too, one should perform the worship accompanied by the ritual perfuming (adhivāsa). || 9 ||

With these ten verses beginning with *śrāvaṇe* and ending with *vinaśyati*, he teaches the procedure for the festival and worship of the offering of the sacred thread (*pavitrāropaṇa*) in the month of Śrāvaṇa. (p.
110) [One should use] threads made of gold, silver, or even those produced from silk cloth.
With auspicious red threads made from cotton, multiplied ninefold. || 11 ||
One should prepare a purifying thread (pavitra) for all the Śaktis measuring sixteen finger-breadths,
or nine finger-breadths, or that same number [of fingers], provided with knots and other such features.
Alternatively, having assigned the respective number of finger-breadths and so forth to the functions and powers,
one should worship them in their proper order after first performing the preliminary consecration (adhivāsa).

At home, the pavitraka should consist of a single-strand knot; its measure should be one span, and it should be made with one hundred and eight threads, or according to one's capacity, using a single strand.
One should suspend the worship [offerings] from the canopy with a cord, as one does for the primary Śakti, in the case of the Śaktis such as Vārāhī and Kurukullā. || 15 ||
