In this context, "with the purifiers" refers to those that will be described hereafter, which consist of the principles (tattvas); "their procedure" refers to the procedure for the purifier (pavitravidhāna).
Or, in the alternative case, with "red" [flowers], meaning those dyed with saffron, sandalwood, and other such substances. || 11 ||

The grammatical construction is "with threads nine finger-breadths [in length]. Alternatively (vā), in another case, one should make it endowed with that same number of strands and knots; in the case where the length is sixteen finger-breadths, one should make it with sixteen strands and sixteen knots, and in the case where the length is nine finger-breadths.
One should make it nine-fold and with nine knots. Here, the word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to the subject of dyeing;
the meaning is that one should apply dye to each knot. "Alternatively" (athavā) indicates another option. Its measurement is in finger-breadths and so forth;
here, the word "etcetera" refers to the number of strands, the knots, and so on. This is what has been stated.
One view is that one should prepare a *pavitra* (purifying ring) joined with as many knots as there are numbers of powers (*śakti*) in whichever particular obscuration (*āvaraṇa*) exists;
according to this view, for the *hetu* [obscuration], the *pavitra* is eight finger-breadths in length and possesses eight knots.

For the nine lords, it should be nine finger-breadths in length with nine-fold knots; for the three [goddesses] beginning with Kāmeśvarī, it should be three finger-breadths in length with three-fold knots;
and for the principal one situated in the middle, because she consists of the sixteen Nityās.

One should prepare a purifying thread (*pavitra*) for the other fifteen *Nityās*, who are the limbs of Lalitā, measuring fifteen finger-breadths in length and having fifteen knots; it should have sixteen strands. The word "having prepared" (*kṛtvā*) connects with what follows below.

"Preceded by acceptance," as before; "with those purifiers" (pavitra). || 13 || "That measurement" refers to the length that was agreed upon for the three fortnights; "with those one hundred and eight" [strands], the remainder being that they are joined with knots (*saragranthi*).
|| 14 || "Of the powers (*śakti*) such as Vārāhī and Kurukullā"—by the word "etc. (*ādi*), the fifteen *Nityās* are included.

It is said: One should fashion the purifier (*pavitra*) for the principal deity according to its own measure and with the number of strands prescribed, just as for the Root Power (*mūlaśakti*). For disciples who know the sequence of the tradition, it is declared that [the purifier] should be made according to their own measure, as for oneself. (16)
For other yogic powers, it is not at the single-knot center, nor by the measurement of the surrounding cloth, but rather from the single thread of the pavilion. || 17 ||
Having fashioned three purifiers (pavitra) joined with ninety-six finger-joints, one should offer them to the Goddess.
Among the three stated measures, one should accept whichever is appropriate from all of them;
one should not create a confusion of measures, for if one does so, one perishes.
Then, in the month of Bhādrapada, on the full moon day, one should worship the Goddess with ketaka flowers, according to the previously mentioned procedure.

In the month of Āśvayuja, however, there is a special rule: beginning from the first day (pratipad) following the new moon (darśānta), one should worship the Goddess with perfumes, flowers, and offerings.

At home, one should offer a hundred oblations and so forth; when that has increased until it is complete, one should daily perform a thousand oblations and likewise carry out the recitation of mantras.
Just as one of the three positions previously mentioned has been accepted, so too for the Aṅga-nityās:

[the worship] of the fourteen *saras* and so forth belongs to the one situated in the middle, while that of the fifteen *saras* and so forth belongs to the others. (15) The sequence refers to the sequence of syllables (*akṣarakrama*). The tradition (*āgama*) refers to the *Kādimata* and other such systems. (16)
According to the measurement of the circumference of the hips, which is the standard for Śakti-yoginīs. || 17 ||
The position stated beginning with "saragranthī" concerns those who are incapable of practicing the three previously mentioned positions.
Regarding the intermingling of mental [worship] among the three stated positions,
the verse beginning with "atha bhādrapada" teaches the worship for the month of Bhādrapada.
Therein, it is accompanied by the previously mentioned procedure, preceded by the rite of consecration (adhivāsa). || 20 ||

With these four verses beginning with "In the month of Āśvayuja" and ending with "worship," he teaches the sequence of worship for the month of Āśvayuja. In that context, "the new moon day" (darśānta-pratipad-tithi) refers to the first lunar day immediately following the new moon; "offering" (upahāra) refers to the food to be presented. || 31 ||

"By an increase of one hundred and so forth" means by an increase of one hundred for each hundred; thus, when the *pūrṇāhuti* is completed, having invoked the Goddess into the girl and worshipped her with devotion, [one offers] six hundred [oblations]. (p. 112)
Having given ornaments, garments, and so forth, one should also bestow a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). || 23 ||
In this way, O Dear One, one should worship until the end of the full cycle by increasing [the offerings] by one each time;
by that, the wise man becomes a perfected Siddha and makes even a king his devotee.
On the full moon day of the month of Kārtika, one should worship with saffron;
at night, one should perform offerings with lamps and oblations enriched with ghee.
One should place sixteen lamps before the Goddess in sequence with the Vidyā;
one for each of the Śaktis, however, should be placed in front of each respective one.
Alternatively, having placed one [flower] in the center of the vessel and nine around it,
he should offer them along with flowers while reciting the root mantra.
And on the full moon day of Mārgaśīrṣa, O Moon-joined one!
having offered coconut water and worshipped according to the prescribed rite with cakes made of mung-bean flour, one should present them. || 28 ||

The meaning is that one should offer oblations with the root-vidyā. And likewise for the recitation: the meaning is that one should perform the recitation by increasing it from a hundred [repetitions] onwards. Having worshipped according to the sequence prescribed for the daily rite. || 23 ||

In this manner, with an increase of one and so forth, when [the number] is complete, one should worship sixteen maidens. By that sacrifice, what is meant is this: after the worship of the remains of the Goddess (devīśeṣa) and the fire-oblation (homa), one should perform the worship of the maidens. || 24 ||

With these three verses beginning with "Kārttika" and ending with "prasūnakam," he teaches the sequence for the worship during the Kārttika festival of lamps; therein, one should perform the *homa* with the mantra prescribed for daily rites. "By the Vidyā" means by the Śrīvidyā. "Of the Śaktis" refers to Vārāhī, Kurukullā, and the others.
The phrase "with their respective mantras" is to be understood as referring to the powers of the retinue (*parivāra-śaktīnām*).

According to this view, it is the tradition that one should place fifteen lamps during the separate worship of the fifteen *Nityās*, using their respective *vidyās*. For Vārāhī and Kurullā, it is as for the Goddess [Bhuvaneśvarī]. Alternatively:
This alternative position is a figurative one. || 27 ||

With the verse beginning "Mārgaśīrṣa," he teaches the worship of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa. In that context, "joined with the moon" means joined with camphor (*karpūra*). Having offered coconut water along with that *arghya* offering, one should worship with cakes made of mung-bean flour; this is the meaning. This should be done according to the rules, preceded by the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsa*). || 28 ||
And on the full moon day of the month of Puṣya, one should worship with sugar or jaggery for the attainment of desired goals, and should offer cow's milk as an oblation. (29)
And on the full moon day of the month of Māgha, one should always worship with white and other kinds of sesame seeds, along with milk offerings, white cakes, and the like.

On the full moon day of the month of Phālguna, one should worship with golden and silver lotuses, as well as with mango blossoms, fragrant flowers, and madhūka flowers, for the attainment of one's desires.
One should perform special worship on the equinoxes, solstices, new moon days, the beginnings of the Yugas, and on those other meritorious occasions mentioned in the Agamas. (32)
For those of restrained mind who are devoted to the daily and occasional rites of worship,
the six types of ritual actions (ṣaṭkarmāṇi) intended for specific desires are proclaimed through these modes of worship.

Desired rites have been declared [to be accomplished] through the application of mechanical devices, fire-oblations, ritual actions, meditation, yoga, libations, and worship; one should perform other [rites] according to their specific application.

With the verse beginning "In the month of Puṣya," he teaches the worship of the month of Puṣya, either in that context or as an alternative. "Gavya" means relating to a cow. The use of the term "gavya" is for the purpose of excluding the milk of goats, buffaloes, and so forth. || 29 ||

With the verse beginning "In the month of Māgha," he teaches the worship for the month of Māgha; therein, "pure" means white, and "others" means black. "Likewise" (tathā) refers to the other fortnight. "Sitā" means sugar.
The word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to fruits and the like. "Always" (sadā) means during all daily acts of worship. || 30 ||
With the verse beginning "In the month of Phālguna," he teaches the worship of the month of Phālguna; therein, the words "with flowers" imply "with flowers made of gold and silver. || 31 ||
With the verse beginning with "viṣuve" and so forth, he teaches specific forms of worship on auspicious days.

In that context, "on the beginnings of the ages" refers to the lunar dates (tithis) mentioned in the [sections on] the months of Vaiśākha and so on, which are designated as the "beginnings of the ages.
"Special" refers to the twofold sequence of worship: both the regular daily worship and the occasional worship.
On the days of the birth of one's guru and other such occasions mentioned in the scriptures. || 32 ||
Immediately thereafter, with sixty-eight verses beginning with "nitya" (1.27),

he teaches the procedure for optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*). Among these, with two verses beginning with "nitya" and ending with "samarcanāt," [he teaches] those who are fit to perform optional worship and the attainment of desires through worship alone.

He instructs as follows: therein, for those self-controlled and discerning ones, the forms of desire are to be sacrificed—that is, they are intended [as objects of worship]. By means of "adorations," which refers to modifications such as ritual diagrams (*yantra*) and fire-offerings (*homa*). "Action" refers to piercing with thorns and so forth upon effigies.
Protection, pacification, victory, acquisition, suppression, and likewise destruction—these are the six rites; because others are subordinate to them, they do not exist separately. (35)

O Pārvatī! These [rites] from the beginning of Caitra to the end of Caitra, along with the lunar days and weekdays, are properly described in sequence according to the materials for worship, the locations, and the times.
One should worship in the *bhūpura* for protection, in the water-mandala for peace, in the fire-house for victory, and in the wind-mandala for gain. (37)

In the remaining [four] houses of her [zodiacal sign] situated in the sky, one should worship the day and the night by dividing them into six parts, respectively, using yellow, white, reddish, and black substances. || 38 ||
These segments are declared to be the seasons beginning with Caitra;
they are to be worshipped during the ritual of worship with those nine names of the Goddess that have been proclaimed. (39)

With these [mantras] beginning with "Lalitā," "Kāmadā," and "Kāmā," one should perform offerings and worship in those [months] according to their names, starting with Caitra, in sequence for twelve months. (40)

Dhyāna is the recollection of the time of the emergence of the element; yoga is the contemplation of the identity between the object to be accomplished and one's own self. (33) In the ritual application, it is other than worship. This is what is meant: among the seven [methods] taught as means for attaining their respective desired goals, [it is distinct] from the last one.
Other than the seventh worship, that which follows will be explained later; here, the attainment of one's desired object is taught solely through the specific method of the seventh worship. || 34 ||

With the verse beginning with "rakṣa," he teaches the nature of the six rites (*ṣatkarma*), among which are others such as subjugation (*vaśya*), attraction (*ākarṣaṇa*), and causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). (35)

With the verse beginning with "tāni" (those), he teaches the manner of explaining the sequence for the performance of optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*). In that context, "those" refers to the six rites (*ṣaṭkarmāṇi*).
Regarding the phrase "by place and time," the word "time" (*kāla*) denotes the auspicious moments (*muhūrta*) and so forth. || 36 ||
With fifteen verses beginning with *rakṣa* and ending with *samaśnute*,

he teaches the specific fruits resulting from worship within the circles of the elements (*bhūtamaṇḍala*) and worship on specific seasons, months, lunar days, and weekdays using particular substances. Therein, [he describes] the square [enclosure] of the *bhūpura*, which is provided with eight spikes at the ends of its lines.
In the water-mandala, which is semicircular in shape and endowed with two peaks and a lotus;
in the fire-house, which is triangular and endowed with a svastika in each corner;
and in the wind-mandala, which is circular and joined by six dots arranged inside and outside at single intervals—[these are for] the remaining two.
In the case of subjugation and destruction, one attains all desired goals through the accomplishments of strength, passion, and so forth, when situated alone in the house of space (the tenth house),
provided with rice, mung beans, barley, honey, ghee, oil, milk, and clothing. || 41 ||
One should give gold, gems, sesame seeds, and mung beans— these substances in sequence—
to one who knows the Vidyā, and worship him while uttering the prescribed sounds during the months beginning with Caitra.
Śleṣmāntaka, karañja, akṣa, nimba, aśvattha, kadambaka, bilva, and vaṭa are declared to be the trees for the Mothers. (43)

Candana, dvaya, karpūra, and cūta are located in the pīṭhas in reverse order; by worshipping them during the months beginning with Caitra, one's attainment of the Command (ājñāsiddhi) shall become firm.
One should constantly worship with flowers produced in the seasons beginning with Caitra;
one eternally enjoys longevity, beauty, prosperity, land, and victory. (45)
Starting from the first lunar day (pratipad), increasing by one each day,
he should also offer coconuts, jaggery, and coconuts until the full-moon day (pūrṇā) in the fire sacrifice.
Then, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipadā), one should perform it one day at a time in sequence;
on the new moon day (darśa), however, there should be one [additional day], and by doing so, one shall become a king endowed with prosperity.

In the *Vṛtti*: "With yellow, white, reddish, and black [colors], and with the colors of wind, ether, water, and earth; these substances are for the worship of the maṇḍala of the elements (*bhūtamaṇḍala*) alone. Having divided the day into six parts by means of five *ghaṭikās* each, and having likewise divided the night according to the stated sequence... [The word] *khaṇḍāni* [refers to these divisions].

Regarding the *ghaṭikās*: having divided day and night into six parts by means of five *ghaṭikās* each within the five domains (*viṣaya*), one should perform their protection and so forth in sequence during those six seasonal periods (*ṛtu*) by means of the nine names beginning with "Tripurā" (verse 39). In sequence.

The ellipsis is "have been stated. (40) The ellipsis is "together with the *siddhis*. *Payaḥ* means milk. (41) The word division is *hema*. The ellipsis is "one should worship him. (42) [This refers to] the Mothers, such as Vaśinī and the others, who are the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). (43) Regarding the phrase "those situated in the inverted *pīṭhas*," this is what is meant:

[The seats] are known as Cūta, Karpūra, Raktacandana, Candana, Kāmarūpa, Pūrṇagiri, Jālandhara, and Oḍyāna. In those twelve seats (viṣṭara), [one should perform] the daily rite (nitya-karman). One should offer oblations with the Vidyā at the conclusion of the daily fire-sacrifice (nitya-homa).
One should perform the oblation with the prescribed number of substances. Then, from the full-moon day onwards; when this is done, the king shall become Lakṣmī—this is the syntactical connection.
On Sunday, with red lotuses; on Monday, with night-lilies (kumuda);
on Tuesday, with red water-lilies (raktotpala); and on Wednesday, with substances derived from *tagara*. (48)
One should worship with devotion for a year: with white water-lilies on Thursdays, with white lotuses on Fridays, and with blue lotuses on Saturdays.
One should offer these in sequence during those seven days beginning with Sunday: milk-rice on Sunday, milk on Monday, plantains on Tuesday, fresh butter on Wednesday, and ghee on Thursday.
Having thus propitiated the Goddess for a year in due order with perfumes and other offerings,
one quickly overcomes the affliction of the planets and attains their favorable countenances.
Beginning from a square, nine wheels are arranged in succession;
from the center upward, each wheel should be progressively higher, resulting in the destruction of poverty and the attainment of wealth.
That which is elevated by three or three steps brings about good progeny and prosperity;
an elevation of one, two, or six steps conduces to fortune and fame.
For the sake of accomplishing all desired aims, [one should fashion] new,
well-proportioned [images] in gemstone, gold, silver, copper, and stone, respectively.

With *tagara* and *sambhava* flowers, or with special aquatic flowers such as the *nandyāvarta*; [this applies] to a white mound or a figure made of sand. Regarding the phrase "with perfumes and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to other modes of ritual service (*upacāra*).
By means of these six verses beginning with "caturasram" and ending with "sarvathā," [the text describes] the specific nature of the construction of the Śrīcakra,
the specific distinctions of the fruits and accomplishments, and the specific materials to be employed.
He teaches that there are prohibited locations based on specific results, and that committing [the act] in those places leads to transgression.

Therein, from the center up to the middle of the triangle where the deities reside, death occurs; after the acquisition of wealth, death occurs. [Death occurs] elevated by a progression of three triplets.
From the form of two four-cornered lotuses, the fourteen-spoked and ten-spoked wheels rise;
from that, the nine triangles. That is the Śrīcakra—this is the remainder [of the meaning]. The elevation follows the sequence of one, two, and six:
from the four-cornered [lotus], the two lotuses rise; from that, the fourteen-spoked and so forth rise. || 53 ||

Having performed the construction of the Śrīcakra according to the "Navāni" [method] (p. 117), one should install and worship it for the attainment of prosperity, beauty, fame, sons, wealth, health, and other such goals. || 55 ||
Furthermore, in the case of lead, bronze, and similar materials, the opposite of what was previously stated applies;
one should never place [the image] upon a wooden plank, a cloth, or a wall.
If, out of greed, delusion, or even ignorance, one has established [a claim], it utterly destroys one's lineage, wealth, and offspring in every way. (57)
One should worship the Goddess on a mountain peak at night with *palāśa* flowers and perfected substances; within seven days, union with the *khecarīs* will occur.
In the forest, at the foot of a banyan tree, or in a mountain grove,
one should worship Śivā with *kadamba* and *jātī* flowers and with perfected substances (*siddhadravya*).
In one month, the Yakṣiṇīs become perfected, appearing visibly to grant all desires;
and with Ketakī flowers, the Ceṭakas are perfected on the shore of the ocean.
By his will, he may constantly bestow upon him the desired command, women, illusions of great wonder, riches, garlands, ornaments, and so forth.

"Divine" means "not [perceptible by ordinary senses]"; "of equal form" means "nine wheels of identical shape"; "on level ground. "In a gem" means in any one of the sixteen gems; "on a stone" means on a slab. These substrates are common to all permanent daily worship and ritual expansions. One should "establish," meaning one should perform the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).

55. By the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "lead, bell-metal, etc.," he includes tin and iron. The meaning is that what is done contrary to what was stated previously brings about misfortune (*alakṣmī*) and so forth. 56. "Out of greed" means through a desire for wealth;
"out of delusion" means through lack of discernment; "out of ignorance" means through ignorance of the prohibition. 57.

With fifteen verses beginning with "on the mountain peak" (*parvatāgre*) and ending with "possessing diversion" (*vinodavān*), he teaches the means for the sevenfold accomplishment (*saptavidhasiddhi*). Among these, the accomplishment-substances (*siddhadravya*) and the accomplishment-substance itself are to be obtained only from the mouth of the Guru. The union with the *khecarī* [goddesses] and the union with the *apsarases* [are taught]. [Verse 58: In the bower...

In the *Kandarā* [chapter] (59), there are the thirty-six forms of the Yakṣiṇīs which will be described in the *Nīlapatākāpaṭala*. The *Ceṭakas* are the deities named Ceṭakas, who have sixty-four forms and will be described in their own chapter (60). [The term] *māyām* refers to those things subject to one's will.
Having constructed a pedestal with *makṣa* trees, one who possesses the power to manifest artificial forms should worship the Goddess there at night for a month,
using *śālmalī* flowers and consecrated substances, remaining fearless. (62)
O Goddess of the gods! In a cremation ground, the Piśācikās grant him success;
for a long time, his enemies are slain by him through the falling of stones, blows, and other such means. 63.
In a solitary forest at night, for the duration of one month, he should fearlessly worship the Goddess situated within the wheel, provided with the substances of accomplishment.
By means of *mālatī*, *jāti*, *punnāga*, *ketakī*, and *manu* flowers respectively, the *vetālas* are accomplished; having mounted them, one may move about at will. (65)
In a cremation ground, in the temple of Caṇḍikā, or even in a solitary forest,
one should worship the Goddess at midnight, adorned with black garments and ornaments.
One should recite that [mantra] which is extremely black within the black wheel, with a mind full of intense wrath;
then, one should offer and present an oblation (bali) before the womb of the victim (sādhya).
Endowed with accomplished substances, for one month [the practitioner performs the rite] from that eye on his forehead;
terrifying *kṛtyās* are born from them, and he should present the object to be accomplished to them.
Satisfied with the destruction of the universe, they depart again by their own will;
through the prayer of the Goddess, those who possess the eye on the forehead become invisible.
One should give [it], with the understanding that "one by one" is the implied sense. Being fearless means having a mind untroubled by the sight of piśācas and other such beings.
62 || The Piśācikās are certain deities named Piśācikās who possess terrifying forms. 63 ||

The meaning is that one should worship her who resides in the wheel within the wheel described for constant worship (*nityasaparyā*), according to the method stated therein, by means of the seven aforementioned methods for attaining supernatural powers (*siddhi*). For other [deities] as well, there is occasional (*naimittika*) and optional (*kāmya*) worship in their respective wheels of constant worship. (64) The *vetālas* are those who are deformed and of terrifying appearance.
Certain deities are beyond numbering. (65) [He is] adorned with black garments and so forth;

by the word "and so forth" (ādi), perfumes, garlands, ointments, and the like are meant. (66) In the Kṛtyacakra, fashioned from liquid collyrium and a paste of aguru, [one should place] the womb of the sādhya in the north.

Having meditated upon the goddess whose birth-star is the one to be described as the object of accomplishment, one should worship her in a secluded garden, his body adorned with red ornaments, garments, unguents, and garlands. (70)
Through white water-lilies, campaka flowers, aśoka, pāṭala, and śatapatra flowers,
combined with the substances of the perfected ones, magical powers (māyās) are accomplished within a month.
By obtaining the grace of whom a man may become one who assumes forms at will;
by whom he becomes composed of the universe, moving through the universe, and possessing universal delight. (72)
Having meditated upon the wheel in the center of the lotus of the six supports, one should worship it with moon, sandalwood, musk, and deer-urine, which bring great prosperity.
One who knows the three times should contemplate the Goddess within them correctly;
when the realization is complete, auspicious results arise, while it is said that when it is incomplete, they are inauspicious.
One should meditate upon the Goddess together with her discus within the water held in the hollowed palms;
having repeated the Vidyā three times along with the Mātṛkās, one should contemplate it as being of the nature of nectar.
Meditating on the Sarasvatī-nāḍī, the tongue, in the form of a lamp, one should drink [the nectar];
within a year, the fourfold scholarship arises for him upon this earth. (76)
The formal analysis (*vigraha*) will be explained below [in verse 67]. [Verse 68: "By means of entreaty":
"Through your favor, our desired goal has been accomplished; go back the way you came"—this is by means of entreaty. [Verse 69: 68–69.

The practitioner (sādhaka), whose body is adorned with garlands—this is the remaining [part of the] sense. (70) With all [flowers] beginning with the white water-lily (kalhāra), or with any one of them; thus it is in every case. (71) Possessing universal diversion through the display of magic illusions (indrajāla) and so forth. (72)

With the two verses beginning with "In the six seats" (*ṣaḍādhāra*) and ending with "is proclaimed" (*īrita*), he teaches the means for the direct perception of future and present objects. Among those, he will explain the six seats, the lotuses, and so forth later on; one should contemplate the wheel within any one of them.

The great prosperity is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. (73) [One should worship] the goddess Lalitā "properly," that is, according to the form prescribed for the daily worship. When there is full realization—that is, when the accomplishment of the meditation on the described form is achieved—auspicious blessings are attained; this is the ellipsis. In the case of an incomplete [practice], however...
If there is a throbbing that indicates a deficiency in the color, form, or parts of one's weapons, it is inauspicious and ill-omened. || 74 ||

By means of these three verses beginning with "The Goddess" and ending with "the knower of the Self," [it is taught that] one who possesses a purified mind should thus perform [this practice] at the time of dawn as a means for attaining the fourfold scholarship and so forth.
(p. 120) Thus, he who performs it daily at the time of dawn with a pure mind...
That yogi is a knower of the science of Brahman, a Śiva-yogi, and likewise a knower of the Self.
One should worship the Goddess, who abides in the wheel of speech of grace and is surrounded by those [attendants];
from the month [of practice] with *campaka* and blue lotuses, health arises. (78)
Fever, possession by spirits or planets, insanity, shivering, jaundice, eye pain, toothache, earache, fever, headache, abdominal tumors, and ailments arising from the belly; || 79 ||

O Supreme Goddess! all other diseases born of the three humors—such as ulcers, urinary disorders, vomiting, hemorrhoids, and chronic dysentery—all come to an end together with that [disease] through worship. || 80 ||
Regarding the material for the construction of the wheel, saffron from Kashmir is prescribed;
alternatively, vermilion, red ochre, lac, cinnabar, or sandalwood may be used. (81)
One should draw a wheel joined with sixteen triangles at the entrance of the pit;
with vermilion, one should worship the Supreme Goddess situated in its center.
He instructs [thus]. In this context, the remainder is that the water consists of the nature of nectar (amṛta). Regarding the tongue:

what is meant is this—one should visualize the tongue as having the form of the Sarasvatī channel and as having the form of one's own self-luminous splendor, and then drink that nectar within that splendor with the mental conception of it being an oblation (homa). This is the fourfold scholarship.
[The qualities] consist of being a musician, a poet, an eloquent speaker, and an expounder. (76) "Constantly" means for as long as one lives.

Although the fivefold [classification] described in the passage beginning with "one who possesses yoga" is of a single nature, this description of various forms is intended to accord with common worldly usage. (77)

With these three verses beginning with *anugrahoktā* and ending with *parameśvarī*, he teaches the worship for the removal of all diseases. In that context, "situated in the wheel of grace" (*anugrahoktacakra*) means situated in the wheel of grace as described in the chapter on Nityānityā; [the worship] is performed with those [mantras].

There, one should worship with the forty-eight Śaktis, beginning with the Ḍākinīs, as previously mentioned; the phrase "according to the prescribed procedure" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. With *indīvaras*, that is, blue lotuses (*nīlotpala*). The mention of the sixteen types of diseases, beginning with fever (*jvara*), is for the purpose of indicating all diseases in general.

In that context, in the term *dantakarṇajvara*, the word *jvara* signifies affliction (*pīḍā*). *Śiraḥśūla* means headache or disease of the head. *Tridoṣajāḥ* refers to diseases produced by the combination of each of the individual disorders of wind (*vāta*), bile (*pitta*), and phlegm (*śleṣman*);
the remainder [of the meaning] is "all diseases" (*sarvarogāḥ*). || 79 || 80 ||

With this verse beginning with "dravyam," he teaches the seven substances for constructing the Śrīcakra during the consecrations and other rites; therein, "candana" refers to cool red sandalwood. (81)
Together with those powers, with perfected substances, and with fragrant flowers, you two shall meet the daughters of the Nāgas within a single month. (82)
In the worlds such as Pātāla, the wives of the Yakṣas, Rākṣasas, Gandharvas, Siddhas, and Vidyādharas delight their beloveds for a long time.
O beloved! Piśācas, Guhyakas, Vīras, Kinnaras, and Uragas attain success there through worship at the time prescribed for that purpose. || 84 ||

With *kiṃśuka* flowers for the attainment of ornaments, with *pāṭala* flowers for the mastery of elephants, with red lotuses for the mastery of horses, and with white water-lilies for the mastery of donkeys. (85)
With blue lotuses, one achieves success with camels; with *tagara* flowers, success with cattle;
with citron fruits, the acquisition of buffaloes; and with *lakuca* fruits, success with goats. (86)

With pomegranates for the attainment of treasures, with madhuka flowers for the attainment of nāgas, with bakula flowers for the attainment of women, and with kalhāra flowers for the attainment of sons. || 87 ||
With *śatapatra* flowers for the attainment of victory, or with *ketaka* flowers for the acquisition of a vehicle, and with fragrant blossoms for the constant accomplishment of good fortune. (88)

With these four verses beginning with "biladvāre" and ending with "kālataḥ," he teaches the means for achieving the eleven accomplishments, such as that of the Naga maidens. Therein, "at the entrance of the cave" (biladvāre) means in the vicinity of the gateway to the path for entering the subterranean realm (pātāla). It is joined with sixteen triangles.

According to the procedure taught for the *pūrṇābhiṣeka* (full initiation), by means of those [mantras] numbering ninety-six, and by those powers (*śaktis*) numbering one thousand four hundred and forty-four—this worship of the wheel belongs to Lalitānityā alone, and not to others. That practitioner... [82]
Yakṣas and so forth are specific types of deities. Among them, the heroes (vīras) have the form of human siddhas.

With these four verses beginning with "kiṃśukaiḥ" and ending with "saubhāgyasiddhaye," he teaches that by worshipping with fifteen kinds of flowers, one attains the fulfillment of fifteen kinds of desired objects. Among those, "raktotpalaiḥ" refers to red lotuses, and "raktakusumaiḥ" refers to red flowers.
With *tagara* flowers as before; with *jambīra* and *nāraṅga* fruits. For the attainment of vehicles—that is, for the accomplishment of chariots, palanquins, and so forth. || 85 || 86 || 87 || 88 ||
One should worship for at least one month, or twice that, or thrice that, or until the attainment of the fruit, using milk, sugar, ghee, and milk-rice porridge. (89)

One should satisfy that goddess, who is accompanied by her wheel-retinue and situated in the midst of the waters, with flowers and respectful offerings (arghya) for the sake of pacifying all calamities. 90.
With ghee, for the perfection of full lifespan; with honey, for the perfection of good fortune;
with milk, for the attainment of health; and with all three, for the perfection of sovereignty. || 91 ||
One should sprinkle Maheśvarī with coconut water for the sake of affection, with cold water for the attainment of kingship, and with [other] waters for the accomplishment of all goals. 92.

One should worship the Goddess day and night with the substances of accomplishment (siddhadravya) in a betel-nut grove; dwelling there and offering those flowers, one becomes like a second god of love.
On full-moon days, one should certainly worship the Goddess in a young girl;
the spells (kṛtyās) sent by enemies and the mantras that have turned away will surely devour them.

With the verse beginning "One should worship" (pūjayet), [the author] teaches the times for obtaining desired fruits and the substances to be offered as oblations (naivedya) in all cases. Among these, the meaning is that the four substances, milk and so forth, are the naivedyas for all [deities]. || 89 ||
With the verse beginning with "sacakre," he teaches the ritual of gradual libation (*kramatarpaṇa*) and so forth for the pacification of all calamities. In this regard, the following is stated:

in cases such as royal wrath, the three kinds of portents, affliction by enemies, disturbances caused by planetary spirits (*graha*), or suffering from disease, [one should perform the rite] at a body of water.

Having bathed, wearing clean garments, seated upon a lotus-seat, performed the ritual placement (nyāsa), and completed the worship, he should, by the command of the Lord, visualize the Śrīcakra upon the water; then, having visualized the Goddess situated in its center, he should offer the water for the guest-offering (arghya) from a vessel made of gold, silver, or copper, filled with water.
One should offer [the oblation] for each śakti in that sequence with fragrant flowers such as camphor, using the mantras of the daily worship; by this, all calamities are pacified. || 90 ||

With these two verses beginning with *ghṛtaiḥ* and ending with *maheśvarīm*, he teaches the sevenfold consecration of the Goddess by means of six substances for consecration, as well as their fruits. Among those, [the first] three are as stated [in verse 91]; [the others are] for the sake of pleasure and for one's own fulfillment [in verse 92].
With these six verses beginning with "pūga" and ending with "ghoratarairapi," [the author] describes,
in each verse and by means of a single mode,
the Goddess residing within the three *liṅgas* together with her own powers (*śakti*) situated within the wheels (*cakra*).
By worshipping [it], one obtains everything desired, both in this world and in the next. || 95 ||
By worshipping with golden flowers weighing a hundred mānas, which are perfumed with fragrance, one is liberated from the sins of previous births within just one month.
Likewise, one should worship her month by month with nine jewels;
thus, liberated from the flood of all sins, one beholds her with the eye.
One should worship the Goddess for a full month with fragrant garments;
one is then liberated even from the most terrible sufferings arising from sinful deeds and the like. 98.

Meditating upon his own self as the form of the Goddess, the wheel, and the powers (śaktis) all around, and worshipping them with the flowers of the sense-objects, he shall become absorbed in that. || 99 ||
He teaches the sixfold mode of worship. In that regard, "with those flowers" means with betel-nut blossoms. 93–94.
[She is] situated within the three genders—that is, residing in self-manifested (svayambhu), Bāṇa, and other types of lingas;
and she resides in the mūlādhāra, the heart, and the brahmarandhra. [She is] with those [powers] such as aṇimā and so forth, which reside in the cakras.
"Here" refers to the sphere of objectivity (idantā); "elsewhere" refers to the sphere of supreme subjectivity (parāhantā). This is what is meant:

Having visualized [the Goddess] residing in one of the centers (cakras) described for daily worship—located in the *mūlādhāra*, the heart, or the *brahmarandhra*—and surrounded by the powers (*śaktis*) such as *aṇimā* situated therein, one who worships her shall obtain the desired fruit. (95) [This applies even to those affected] by the sins of previous births or by long-standing, evil latent impressions (*durvāsanās*). (96) Month after month...

For each jewel, one month [is spent] amidst the floods of evil and states of contraction. By the mention of "with the eye," he speaks of what is established through mental experience. Through the sufferings of sinful deeds and the like, through sins, through one's own [lack of] discernment, and through the sufferings of hostile acts arising from improper application.

The meaning is: by those [means], such as magical spells (*kṛtyā*) and so forth—the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) referring to mechanical devices, powders, medicinal herbs, and deposits—and by the sufferings produced by them. || 98 ||

With the verse beginning "The form of the Goddess" (*devīrūpam*), he teaches the complete fruit consisting of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*), which arises from the contemplation of the Deity as the indivisible form of the universe. In this context, the "wheel" (*cakra*) is the Śrīcakra, which serves as the abode for all deities; [and] the "powers" (*śaktīḥ*).

The infinite number of one's own powers, consisting of the power of obscuration (āvaraṇa-śakti) and so forth, [should be dissolved] by means of objects in the form of sound and the rest. "Becoming identical with that" means that one should dissolve one's own ego (svāhaṅkāra) into that [universal] ego (tadahaṅkāre). || 99 ||
Visualizing one's own self as the form of the Goddess, the Cakra, and the Śaktis all around, and worshipping them with the objects of the senses as flowers, one becomes absorbed in that. (100)
The pervasion consisting of the reality of smell has been correctly described;
by the thorough realization of this within the mind, that very reality is assimilated into one's own self. (101)
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the *Kādimata*, among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
Thus [ends this work] by Subhagānandanātha, known as Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa, within the venerable *Kādimata* among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
Thus, in the commentary named Manoramā, the sixth chapter, which elucidates the methods for the daily, occasional, and optional worship of the sixteen Nityās, is fully concluded and examined. || 6 ||
The number of verses in the sixth chapter is one hundred; there are seven diagrams, and the commentary extends beyond one hundred verses.
It has been correctly stated that it consists of sixty-three and three-quarters [verses].
Now begins the seventh chapter.
Now, among the sixteen Nityās, that which is proclaimed as the second is called Kāmeśvarī; listen to how she and all [the others] grant every desire according to reality.
The placement of the principles (tattvanyāsa), the various types of meditation, their powers, their worship, the methods of their yoga, and their yantras which bestow desired objects. || 2 ||
O Goddess, the form of the Vidyā has already been clearly explained to you previously;
one should thus perform the six limbs in sequence using the very syllables of the root-vidyā.
With one [syllable] the heart, with that many (two) the head, and then with two the non-dual;
likewise, with four the eye, and with one the weapon is enjoined.
Now begins the seventh chapter, concerning first the daily worship of the principal deity Nityā Lalitā, and the sequence for the common obligatory, occasional, and optional rites of all the Nityās.

Having taught [the first nityā] by means of the fourth, fifth, and sixth chapters, he next teaches the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) for the second nityā, Kāmeśvarī, by means of the seventh chapter consisting of one hundred verses, beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "somewhere" (*kvacit*). Therein, [the section] beginning with "Now, sixteen" provides the meanings.
With these two verses ending with "ca," he teaches the subject matter of the chapter. In that context, "tatvataḥ" means "as it truly is. || 1 ||
"Those powers" means those powers which constitute its veil. || 2 ||

With these four verses beginning with "vidyārūpam" and ending with "krameṇa vai," he teaches the sequence of the placement of the Vidyā (vidyānyāsakrama). [The mantra is: "aiḥ sklīḥ nityaklinne madadrave sauḥ.
Regarding this, it was already stated in the third chapter: "By one [syllable], the heart. By that much—by just one—this is what is meant.
The heart [mantra] is formed with the first syllable of the root-vidyā of Kāmeśvarī; the head with the second;
the topknot (śikhā) with the third and fourth; the armor (kavaca) with the fifth and sixth;
the eye with the four syllables—the seventh, eighth, ninth, and tenth; and the weapon (astra) with the eleventh, which is the final syllable.

Thus, one should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) upon the tips of the hands with the root mantra divided into six parts according to its birth; as it is said later in the ninth chapter (p.
126): "In the eyes, ears, the pair of nostrils, the tongue, heart, navel, and the secret place."
By way of pervasion, [one should contemplate it] in all limbs, from the head down to the tips of the feet.

Immediately thereafter, one should assign the syllables of the vidyā to these locations; indeed, one should perform the all-pervading assignment (vyāpaka) with the entire mantra according to the stated sequence.
Now I shall explain the meditation prescribed for daily worship, by which the Goddess, being well-pleased, grants one's desires without effort. (7)
Resembling ten million rising suns, radiant with a crown of rubies, and adorned with necklaces, half-necklaces, girdles, rings, anklets, and other ornaments; || 8 ||
Adorned with red garments and beautified by jewel ornaments,
she has six arms and three eyes, and her head is graced by a digit of the moon.
She resides within the five, eight, sixteen, two, six-cornered, and four-cornered [mandalas];
her face shines with a gentle smile, and her gaze is languid with compassion. (10)

He himself will explain how one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*): from the thumb to the little finger, in order from bottom to top, on the five fingers of both hands, one should perform the mutual wiping with the *astra-mantra* starting from the heart and ending with the eyes; then, with the palms of both hands, one should place [the mantras] as follows: *aiḥ* to the heart, *namaḥ*.
By such [passages] as these. || 4 ||

With these two verses beginning with "dṛk" and ending with "vai," in sequence, one should touch [the body] with both palms, starting from the top of one's own head down to the nails of the toes of both feet, by means of the eleven-syllable Vidyā; then, beginning from the tips of the two feet...

One should touch [the body] upward, ending at the heart. At the heart, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpakanyāsa*) with the palms joined, according to the procedure shown by the Lord. Thus, the meaning is that for all mantras, one should perform the pervasive placement at the conclusion of all other placements.

He teaches the sequence for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra syllables. Therein, "in the secret place" means at the *mūlādhāra*. "From the head down to the tips of the feet"—this is what is meant: [the placement] with the entire root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) in these ten aforementioned locations and throughout all the limbs; and it is pervasive (*vyāpaka*), as before.
The meaning is that one should perform it once again. || 6 ||

Now, with six verses beginning with "atha dhyānam" and ending with "tatra vai," he teaches the visualization for the daily worship of the Goddess. In that context, by means of which visualization... [verse 7] ...the *ūrmikā* is a ring. [verse 8] She whose head is adorned with a digit of the moon refers to her having the crescent moon as an ornament.
The name common to the fifteen Nityās is [as follows]. || 9 ||

[The mandala] consists of five, eight, sixteen, two, and six, situated within squares. This is what is meant: two lines with equal intervals [are drawn], along with a noose (*pāśa*) and a goad (*aṅkuśa*), a lotus (*puṇḍra*), a sugarcane bow (*ikṣu-cāpa*), and a flower-arrow (*puṣpa-śilīmukha*).
Holding in her hands a blood-cup filled with nectar and granting boons.
Having meditated in this manner, one should worship the Goddess for the sake of accomplishment during daily rites;
I shall indeed describe the meditations for all applications and so forth therein.
Madanonmādana, followed by Dīpana and Mohana, and Śoṣaṇa— these are declared to be the five arrows previously mentioned.
Kusumā, Mekhalā, Paścāt, Madanā, and Madanāturā; those [preceded by] Anaṅgapada, with the fifth being Madaveginī. (14)
Then there should be Bhuvanapālā, and immediately after her, Śaśirekhā; another line, beginning with Gaganā, is to be worshipped on the eight petals. 15.
Having made it square with equal sides by means of an external division, having drawn two circles within that,

and having fashioned a hexagon therein according to the sequence to be described, one should fashion two circles within that with an interval of one finger-breadth, and within that, a circle with an interval of four finger-breadths.

Having drawn a circle with a measurement of one finger-breadth within that [space], and having thus performed this three times by way of entry, one should draw five petals on the inner circular path; then, outside of that, one should draw eight petals on the circular path; and further outside, one should make sixteen petals on the circular path. Thus...

The meaning is that [the worship] proceeds within the five-petalled, eight-petalled, sixteen-petalled, six-cornered, and square [mandalas]. Since the specific measurements of these will be explained further below, they are not elaborated upon here. || 10 ||

"Regarding 'the noose and the goad'": one should arrange these weapons and so forth, starting from the upper left hand and ending with the lower left hand, following the sequence of left and right, and for the two lower hands, following the sequence of right and left. || 11 ||
In those very places where the instructions for practice are located. || 12 ||

With the verse beginning "madanonmāda" (Madanonmāda), he teaches the five Śaktis of the Five Arrows (*pañcabāṇa*) who are to be worshipped on the five petals. Therein, "previously mentioned" means those spoken of earlier.
[He teaches] the five Śaktis of the Five Arrows. This is what is meant: by means of the five arrows of Śiva mentioned in the fourth chapter.
One should worship the powers of the five arrows with the names beginning with "Madanonmādanī" (the Intoxicator of Lust), preceded by each individual syllable-mantra. || 13 ||
With the two verses beginning with "Kusumā" and ending with "aṣṭasu," [the author describes] on the eight petals of the second and third enclosures:
Śraddhā, Prīti, Rati, Dhṛti, Kānti, and Manoramā.
She is proclaimed as Manoharā-aṣṭamī; she is the Goddess Manorathā here.
Then Madanonmādinī, Mohinī, Dīpanī, Śoṣaṇī, Vaśaṅkarī, Siñjinī, and Subhagā. (17)
The sixteen Sasvarās have been declared to be lovely to behold and radiant;
they are to be worshipped on each leaf, upon every one of the sixteen petals.
Pūṣoveśā, Sumanasā, Rati, Prīti, Dhṛti, Vṛddhi, Saumyā, Marīci, and beyond that Aṃśumālinī. (19)
Śaśinī, Aṅgirā, Chāyā, and then Sampūrṇamaṇḍalā; these are said to be the digits (kalās) of the Moon, together with Tuṣṭi and Amṛtā, accompanied by their respective vowels.
One should worship them in due order upon all sixteen petals;
likewise, one should worship Ḍākinī and the others in the corners of the outer hexagon.
He teaches the powers (śaktis) who are to be worshipped. In that context, "those preceded by the word *anaṅga*" refers to the four previously mentioned;
this means: Anaṅgakusumā, Anaṅgamekhalā, Anaṅgamadanā, and Anaṅgamadanāturā. "The line (*rekhā*) preceded by the sky (*gagana*)" means Gaganarekhā. The others...
The eighth [chapter]. || 15 ||

With the words beginning with "śraddhā" and ending with "ṣoḍaśacchade," he teaches the powers (śaktis) to be worshipped on the sixteen petals of the third enclosure; therein, the eighth is to be connected as "manorathā. || 16 ||

One is Madanonmādinī, meaning she who brings [others] under her control. || 17 || The sixteen "possessing vowels" (sasvarāḥ) are preceded by each of the sixteen vowel-syllables; they are the sixteen Priyadarśanakāntikās, meaning those of lovely appearance. || 18 ||
With the two and a half verses beginning with "Pūṣā" and ending with "yathākramam," he teaches the powers (śaktis) to be worshipped on the sixteen outer petals of the fourth enclosure. || 19 ||

*Tuṣṭyāmṛtā* means *amṛtā* together with *tuṣṭi*; thus, there is one *amṛtā*. These [syllables] also possess vowels as before. Among the vowel-syllables, each is preceded by a single consonant; this is the arrangement of the moon (*vidhodha*).
With the latter half of the verse beginning with "bahiḥ," he teaches the powers (*śakti*) to be worshipped in the six corners of the fifth enclosure:
"Outside of that, one should worship the World-Protectors (*lokeśa*) situated in the square, equal to them. (p. 129)
One should worship Baṭuka, Gaṇapa, Durgā, and Kṣetreśa on all sides.
One should offer bali to them— Agni and the others— using their names situated within the seven-syllable mantras beginning with "vidyā," along with the prescribed offerings of fragrance and so forth.

Then, having prepared the water offering (arghya) through the two sciences of the limbs (aṅgavidyā), one should worship Śivā with the previously mentioned services and so forth; thereafter, one should likewise perform the fire sacrifice (homa).
In that regard, one should worship in this manner; that is to say, following the sequence taught in the subsequent *Nityānityā-paṭala*,

one should worship the triad of powers— *Ḍākinī*, *Rākinī*, and *Lākinī*— in the corners of Nirṛti, Vāyu, and Vasava according to the stated order, and then in the three corners of Agni, Īśa, and Varuṇa according to the stated order.
One should worship the triad of powers as Kākinī, Śākinī, and Hākinī. || 21 ||

With the two verses beginning with *tadbahis* and ending with *coditaiḥ*, he teaches that in the sixth enclosure, within the square, one should worship the powers (śaktis) beginning with Pūjyā in the four corners; *tadbahis* means outside the hexagon. The word *loke* implies "the powers" (*śaktīḥ*) as the ellipsis; they are equal to those [previously mentioned].

One should worship all these common powers of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-śakti*), who bear colors, ornaments, hands, and weapons identical to those of the principal deity, in the eight directions starting from the east and ending with the northeast, as well as below and above,
proceeding clockwise; and the others...

The traditional meaning is that one should worship the surrounding powers within the hexagon, beginning from the front of the Goddess and proceeding clockwise. [Verse 22] In the triangles starting with the southeast (Agni), which are situated in the space between the square and the outer circle of the hexagon, [one worships] by means of those residing within the seven syllables beginning with the Vidyā.

By their respective names. This is what is meant: for all the previously mentioned powers (śaktis) of the letters beginning with 'A', one should [worship] on both sets of sixteen petals, following each syllable of the Vidyā, with their respective names preceded by the first syllable of the root-vidyā (mūlavidyā) and ending in seven syllables, accompanied by the sixteen vowel-syllables.
One should worship according to the stated sequence. "To them" means to Baṭuka, Gaṇapati, Durgā, and Kṣetrapāla.
"With substances such as sandalwood and the like" refers to the materials to be mentioned hereafter; this is the implied meaning. || 23 ||

With these three and a quarter verses beginning with "tataḥ" and ending with "siddhyanti," he teaches the sequence of the Goddess’s daily worship and its fruit. In that regard, having prepared the *arghya* offering by means of the *aṅga-vidyās*, this is what is meant: as before, [one prepares] the base, the cup, and the water.

Having understood [the deities] as consisting of fire, sun, and moon, and having worshipped them with their six limb-mantras (*ṣaḍaṅgamantra*) according to the prescribed order, one should touch the *arghya* vessel, recite the root-vidyā eleven times,
and perform the worship as before using the prepared *arghya*. Thus for all [of them].
The meaning is that the preparation of the *argha* for the *nitya* [offerings] to be described hereafter must be performed.

(p. 130) One should offer oblations with auspicious reddish flowers smeared with ghee or honey, along with food and other offerings; thereafter, one should conclude the rite as previously described. || 25 ||
Thus, for one who worships constantly, there shall be longevity, health, and prosperity;
the winning over of people, and the act of captivating both women and kings. 26.
They are established as non-different from that; listen, O beautiful one, to how they produce great wonder and are capable of shaking the three worlds through their union. (27)
In former times, the Goddess created her own five arrows consisting of the five objects of desire and the five forms of knowledge, as well as the three types previously mentioned.

The remainder [of the phrase] is "by means of the specific modes of worship, such as the previously mentioned offerings (upacāra) and so forth. Likewise, it should be concluded as before, according to the sequence prescribed for the fire-offering (homa) of the Lalitā-vidyā. This is what is meant: having realized that the powers of her retinue have entered the body of the deity in the form of light, and having realized [that state], one should conclude.

Having brought her, who is of the nature of light, into one's own heart by means of the path of the *pravaha-nāsā* (the central channel) through the *khecarī-mudrā*, one should conclude as before. Regarding the specific instructions for the fifteen *Nityās*, at the commencement of the worship (*saparyā*), the offering of the oblation (*bali*) is performed with the sixteen-syllable mantra; likewise at the conclusion.

The meaning is that one should perform the offering of the bali with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā, and likewise perform the worship of the nine lords arranged in three rows as previously described, located to the west of the deity, at the beginning of all obstructions and so forth. || 25 ||

"Attraction" (*āvarjanam*) means bringing under control (*vaśīkāraḥ*). "Not separately" (*apṛthaktvena*) means by way of non-attainment. Here too, having recited one hundred thousand syllables (*akṣara-lakṣam*) according to the [specific] age (*yuga*), one should perform the libation (*tarpaṇa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), and so forth, consisting of a tenth part of that.

With the first verse of the three-quarter section, beginning with "tadyogāt" and ending with "prāgudīritān," he introduces these [five] by way of praising the five desires (*pañcakāma*). In that context, "tadyogān" refers to the yogas consisting of the mantras and yantras of the goddess who is the essence of the five desires; they are those which produce great wonder.

Because it bestows the desired object, there is *camatkāra*, which means wonder. "Capable of agitating the three worlds" and "causing renown throughout all the realms"—these are adjectives for "those [mantras] connected with this. (27) The Goddess refers to the tradition (*sampradāya*) of Kāmeśvarī.

She created those who are described as the powers (*śakti*) beginning with Madanonmādanā and so forth—consisting of the five types of knowledge and having the form of the five sensory cognitions—because they all consist of the cognition of the sense organs.
The meaning is that she transformed herself into their form. She created them in three ways, according to their gross, subtle, and supreme natures.
Those which were previously mentioned in the fifth chapter with the words "the arrows shall be," and so forth. || 28 ||
Hear their names, forms, and mantras in sequence, by which the entire universe is brought under control in an instant through meditation and other means. (29)
The first was named Kāmarāja, the second was Manmatha,
the third became Kandarpa, and after that came Makaraketana.
The fifth is Manobhava; these indeed are their names in sequence.
O wise one, hear now of the meditation upon them, who cause the agitation of the universe. (31)
Three have yellow, white, and reddish forms, while the other two are smoke-colored and blue;
all are two-eyed, two-armed, and possess lotus-faces like those of Smara.
Bearing the Puṇḍra, the sugarcane bow, and the flower-arrows, they consist of the elements in due order;
they possess universal forms and have as their essential nature the regulation of the agitation of the minds of all beings. || 33 ||

O wise one, hear these mantras, even those consisting of a single syllable, in their proper order; by means of each one of them, both individually and in combination, there shall be various distinct yantras.
The Kāmarāja [bīja] is impelled by its own [seed], the letter *sa*, the letter *ha*, the letter *sa*, the letter *da*, the letter *ha*, and the fire (*ra*).
Likewise, Manmatha consists of the vital breath (*pra*), the chest (*āṇa*), the fire (*ra*), and its own [seed]. (35)
With two and a half verses beginning with "Their names" and ending with "in sequence," he teaches their names preceded by an introduction to their names, forms, and mantras.
In that context, "of those" refers to the five desires; "by which" refers to the names, forms, and mantras.
"By means of the meditation on those," etc., refers to those [mantras] in the form of name-mantras;
the word "etc. (ādi) refers to topics such as consecration (abhiṣeka) and ritual placement (nyāsa). || 29 || "The third among them" means the third among those. || 30 ||

With the passage beginning with "meditation" (dhyānam) and ending with "of restricted nature" (niyatātmakāḥ), he teaches their forms as objects of meditation (dhyeya). Among them, three have yellow, white, and red forms; two are smoky and blue. Because they are the embodiments of the powers (śakti) of the five elements, they possess the respective colors of those elements.

They consist of the elements (*bhūtātmaka*), their forms being the power of the elements; they possess universal forms because their nature is the power of the elements. And their capacity to cause agitation in the minds of all beings arises precisely from their consisting of the elements. || 33 ||

With the verse beginning with "eṣām" and so forth, he introduces their mantras and yantras; therein, from each individual syllable conjoined with each individual yantra, when combined, five [mantras] produce three yantras. || 34 ||
With the two and a half verses beginning with *sahaṃsa* and ending with *manobhava*, he teaches those five one-syllable mantras. (p.
132) Śuci joined with its own [vowel] is taught; Kandarpa is joined with *ambu* and *rasa*.
He, this very god whose banner is the makara, was addressed by Kṣmā herself.
The God of Love was addressed by his companions, who were themselves like the fires of fever:
"By means of ritual placement (*nyāsa*), you [should be installed] in the forehead, face, heart, navel, and private parts. (37)
One who would constantly place these very arrows, from the root up to the forehead, shall bring all women under his control and become a Smara (the god of love) to them. 38.
All these machines are capable of shaking the three worlds;
I shall describe them to you in order, so listen with a concentrated mind. (39)
In that context, the syllable *hrīṃ*—composed of the letters *sa*, *ha*, *sa*, *dā*, *ha*, and *va*, along with fire (*ra*) and its own [vowel]—is the meaning of the Kāmarāja mantra.

The syllable *klīṃ*—consisting of the letter *ka*, the letter *la*, and the letter *i* with the nasal drop (*bindu*), joined by the vital breath (*pra*), the chest (*u*), and fire (*ra*), as well as its own [vowels]—is the Manmatha mantra. (35) The syllable *śuciḥ* (the pure one), conjoined with itself and the twelfth vowel together with the nasal drop (*bindu*).

The mantra of Kandarpa consists of the syllables *va*, *la*, *ū*, and the nasal bindu (*aṃ*). The mantra of Makaraketana consists of the syllables *ha*, *ra*, *ya*, *da*, *ha*, *va*, *hi*, *sa*, *ta*, *ra*, *repha* (r), *ī*, and the nasal bindu (*strīṃ*). This is the mantra of Manobhava.

With the first half-verse beginning with "bhāla" and ending with "smara," he teaches the sequence of placement (*nyāsa*) for those mantras and the *bāṇa* mantras. Therein, "bhāla" refers to the forehead; "guhya" refers to the location of the *mūlādhāra*. These...

The mantras of the five Kāmas (37). [One should place] the seed-syllables of the Śaiva Bāṇas—the kūṭa-mantras consisting of single syllables—into these very locations already mentioned, starting from the root, that is, beginning from the *mūlādhāra*. This is what is meant: of those five Kāmas...
Having performed the placement (*nyāsa*) of the five mantras— which have been declared to consist of single syllables each, are of the *kūṭa* form,

and are joined with their respective names— at the five aforementioned locations from the forehead down to the *mūlādhāra*, and having likewise performed the placement from the *mūlādhāra* up to the forehead as previously described;

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) of the five Śiva-bāṇa mantras—consisting of single-syllable forms in their condensed (kūṭa) state as described in the fourth chapter—which are directed toward their respective locations and end with the word "namas. || 38 ||
With these five and a half verses beginning with "eṣām" and ending with "śive," he teaches five yantras for each of those desires respectively.
Therein, "in order" means according to the sequence of the previously mentioned *kūṭa* mantras. || 39 ||
Within those five seed-syllables, one should join the sixteen vowels with those various eight [consonants], avoiding repetitions, by means of *māyā*. (40)
Thus, there are indeed one hundred and twenty-eight [mantras];
by means of these, O Śivā, the yantras for the five [deities] should be prepared in their proper order.

Having drawn a hexagon situated within three circles, one should write one's own syllable in the center, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and that same [syllable] again in the six corners.
By means of the eight letters—ha, ra, ka, la, ai, va, sa, and ta—which are free from redundancy and whose nature is non-return;
such are the letters [to be used], as is understood from the context. Here, the "joining of the vowel ai" refers to the sixteen vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga.

The utterance is according to the sequence. Thus, in all cases, there is the joining of vowels with vowels, and this is due to the independence of the vowels. By means of *māyā* (the vowel *ī*), by the visarga (*ḥ*), and by the joining of those [consonants] with the sixteen vowels—this is what is meant: in those five *kāma*-mantras.

One should join each of the sixteen vowels ending in *visarjanīya* with the eight non-repeated syllables beginning with *ha*; by this, the syllables become the stated number [thirty-five]. These are, for example:
*haḥ*, *hāḥ*, and so forth. Furthermore, among these thirty-five syllables, the *visarjanīya* is joined again. By means of these...
By means of syllables whose vowels are modified. || 41 ||

With two and a half verses beginning with "situated in three circles" (vṛttatrayastha) and ending with "in Śiva" (śive), he teaches the nature of the five yantras. Therein, "one's own syllable" (svamakṣara) refers to one specific syllable among the five syllables of the *kāmakūṭa*. This is what is meant:
Having produced a circle with a rotation of the desired measurement, preceded by the central line,

one should mark points on both sides of the circle using the measure of half its diameter, supported by the two junctions of the Brahma-line and the circle; then, extending beyond the circle through those points, [one draws] a north-south line.
Having stretched two threads, and having fixed them upon the circular junction of the two tips of the eastern thread,

one should stretch two threads from that point to the circular junction at the western tip of the central thread; likewise, from those two points, one should stretch them as far as the western thread.
Having drawn two lines from the midpoint of the central axis to the front and rear junctions of the circle,
thus forming a hexagon, one should then draw a circle through the center of that hexagon such that it touches and does not touch the diagonal lines.

Outside the circle drawn outside the previously written hexagon, having successively produced two circles with an interval of one *aṅgula* between them, one should write the *hṛllekhā*— the first syllable among the five mantras consisting of the *Kāmakūṭa* letters— accompanied by the *bindu*, in the center of the innermost circle; then, of that...
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within the letter *ra*, the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) within the fourth vowel (*ī*),
and the ritual action (*karma*) between the two, one should write [the seed-syllables] outside in the six downward-pointing corners.

Having divided [the space], one should write [the letters] sequentially from below upwards with the *bindu* and *māyā* [vowels]. Outside the two circles, one should write twice with sixty-four [letters].
Thus, O Śivā, there are five yantras for the five [elements] respectively;
and by means of these five, there is another single yantra, which is exceedingly great and marvelous.
One should write the first name together with the second inside the belly;
then, one should enclose both of them externally in the form of a third hexagon.
O Pārvatī, one should draw the fourth [syllable] in these six corners;
one should encircle that entire yantra with the fifth [syllable], which is the deluder of all.
Having written that *hṛllekhā* with the *bindu* in the three [inner] corners,

and having written that same [syllable] ending in the *visarga* in the upper triangles, one should [place] the letters modified by the aforementioned vowels in sequence, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, upon the path of the circle outside the hexagon.
Having inscribed the first sixty-four [syllables] in the outer enclosure and the third sixty-four syllables as well,
one should employ them in the desired rites. In this same manner, having likewise inscribed the other four *kūṭākṣara*s in such a yantra according to the stated sequence, [one should proceed].

As before, one should draw the sixteen seed-syllables (*bīja*) and so forth within each [square], along with two sets of sixty-four on the outside. In this manner, one should employ these five yantras for the desired purposes. (42–43)

With the first half-verse beginning with "by five" and ending with "the delusion of all," he teaches the sixth yantra, which consists of the collection of the five previously mentioned *kūṭa*-mantras. Therein, within the womb of the second *kūṭa*— that is, within the womb of the *Kāmadeva-kūṭa*— is the first [kūṭa], the *Kāmarāja-kūṭa*.
"Accompanied by the name" means together with the name of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*).

"In the third form" refers to the form of the *kandarpa*-syllable (*kūṭa*). By virtue of the script of the twelve vowels which constitute the *kandarpa*-mantra, it possesses the nature of a triangle through its six-angled [arrangement]; this is due to the union of those two pairs.

The state of being a hexagon. || 45 || The fourth is the *makaraketana* (Cupid) peak; with the fifth, the *manobhava* (mind-born) peak. The remainder [of the sentence] is that the yantra is constructed in this manner. This is what is meant: having written the *hṛllekhā* along with the name as before, one should place that [name] as the first element.

Having placed the second seed-syllable (*kūṭākṣara*) within the womb [of the triangle], one should encircle it with a hexagon formed by doubling the triangle, using the second and third syllables as a single syllable; then, having written the fourth seed-syllable of the Fish-bannered One (*makaraketana*) in its six corners, that hexagon—
Having drawn the [corner] so that it resides in the fire-position of the fifth peak-syllable, according to the sequence taught by the Guru, one should employ it for one's desired aims. || 46 ||
(135) Outside that as well, one should generate another yantra, encircling it with those previously mentioned [syllables] and also with the Mātṛkā on the exterior.
Thus, there are eight instruments; indeed, five of them consist of desire.
By means of these, nothing in this world is ever unattainable for them.
One should meditate upon a human being, whether a lord of men or a woman clouded by passion, as situated within the eight hymns by means of one's own splendor.
One should mutter these five syllables as a single unit;
by that means, they will certainly come under one's control quickly for as long as one lives.

With the two verses beginning with *tasyāpi* and ending with *kadācana*, he teaches the seventh and eighth yantras, the conclusion regarding their number, and their respective powers. Therein, *tasya* refers to that aforementioned sixth great yantra; *parataḥ param* means the seventh.
The meaning is "the yantra. By those eight syllables previously mentioned, increased by the vowels—the meaning is this:

having drawn a circle that touches and does not touch the outer syllables of the sixth yantra, and having fashioned two circles outside of that with an interval of one finger-breadth each, as before; |||
On the two rows of the three outer circles of the diagram, one should draw two sets of sixty-four [squares] as before.
This is the seventh diagram; the other diagram is the eighth. The remainder is that it is surrounded by the aforementioned two sets of sixty-four [squares], using the *mātṛkā* [alphabet].

The meaning is that it is encircled by the fifty-one letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. Furthermore, the word "api ca" (*apiceti*) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). What is being said is this: having fashioned a circle outside the nature of the seventh yantra with an interval of one finger-breadth, in that path (*vīthyām*), [the letters are placed].
One should draw the letters from *a* to *kṣa* as before; this is the eighth yantra. || 47 ||

The grossness of those five objects of desire is established by the aforementioned forms of the objects of meditation, while their subtlety is established by the forms of the five aforementioned mantras; [and their nature is] the knowledge arising from the five sense organs, which consist of the power of the five aforementioned elements.

Having understood that the nature of the other [the object] is constituted by the fivefold body, and that it cannot be accomplished by those [means], and so forth—this is the secret meaning of the tradition. || 48 ||

With the five verses beginning with "manujam" and ending with "mudrayā," he teaches the attainment of results through the application of desired objects and the internal contemplation of knowledge regarding the eight yantras previously mentioned. Among them, [the verse] beginning with "sadāvilām"...
Like a scent-elephant (*gandhagaja*). The word "each" is to be supplied after "in the eight hymns. "By his own splendor" means by the nature of his own self. || 49 ||

Among those, the central one is neutral; it is red like a hibiscus flower in the act of accomplishing one's own purpose, and it is surrounded by the radiance of the letters of that mantra, which are likewise even more intensely red. (51)
Meditating upon them as being swallowed by oneself, one should mutter those very syllables;
thereby they will quickly come under one's control and bestow both life-force and wealth.
One should encircle that sixth [syllable] within the seed-syllable situated in the center with the mantra;
as before, one should cause it to enter into one's own suṣumṇā by means of the yonimudrā.
Having thus prepared the pitcher situated in the center of the eight according to the prescribed rite,
one should perform the consecration with it for the sake of liberation from misfortune, disease, and poverty.
Having fashioned eight wheels on the ground, on a wooden board, or on stone slabs, using either fine sandalwood paste, vermilion, red ochre, or minium; || 55 ||

Regarding the phrase "become one" (*ekībhūta*), the method of meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) should be understood from the mouth of the Guru. The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that [the practitioner] has become one with those mantras; the meaning is that he has become one with the splendors of the mantras. By means of that ritual application (*prayoga*).
The verse beginning with "In them" (*teṣu*) is clear in its meaning. [He should give away] his vital breaths and his wealth.

The meaning is: "how much more so other objects? (verse 52). The meaning is that within the central seed-syllable (*madhyabīja*) there are two peaks (*kūṭa*) of Kāmarāja and Manmatha. By the mantra—that is, by the *Kāmeśvarī-vidyā*—the specific meaning obtained from the mouth of the Guru is here stated by me; for example, regarding the central seed-syllable of the sixth [chapter].

By this statement, one should surround the seed-syllable situated in the center of the eight yantras previously mentioned with the mantra of Kāmeśvarīnityā; by that means, there are also eight yantras. Thus, in total, there shall be sixteen yantras. This is because of the context concerning the five desires (*pañcakāma*).

The connection with the encirclement by the *Kāmeśvarī-vidyā* has been indicated; thus, as previously stated, it is according to the manner described in the passage beginning with "by the manifestations of the mantra-syllables" (*mantrārṇaprakāśaiḥ*). By means of the *yonimudrā*, which will be described further below, [one should contemplate] from the *mūlādhāra* within the *suṣumṇā* up to the *brahmarandhra*.

The conventional terminology is that the "binding of the Yoni-mudrā" (yonimudrābandha) refers to the contemplation of the coming and going [of breath] by means of one's own nature as the triad of lights consisting of fire, sun, and moon; according to the tradition, this constitutes the common form for these sixteen [yantras] and other yantras as well.

With this verse beginning with "etad" (this), he teaches the installation of the water-pot (*kumbha-sthāpana*), the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) by means of those eight yantras mentioned [previously], as well as their fruit— both in these yantras obtained through tradition and in those [others] taught here; in that regard, it is stated according to the rule as follows.

Having first performed thirty-eight ritual windings (*kalāvartana*)— consisting of wrapping with thread, placing three metals, grains, and nine jewels, inserting a root and a sprout, covering the opening, and wrapping with a pair of garments— one should worship the intended deity according to that sequence. || 54 ||
Having surrounded the center with the Vidyā and having worshipped her there with offerings both internal and external,
one who subsists on a milk-vow should stand before her as Kāmeśvarī and recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times.
By this, his evil deeds from previous births indeed perish;
having attained excellent fortune in this life, he prospers in happiness.
Having drawn within that [mandala] a man, a woman, another king, a city, or a town, as well as a country, a district, and the entire universe; 58.
One should worship with reddish flowers and scents blended with saffron,
and with food offerings such as plantains, milk, sugar, and milk-rice (pāyasa).
Whether it be for a full mandala, half of that, or even for seven days,
a man will certainly become equal to Kandarpa in good fortune.
By engraving [this] on gold and other materials or by wearing it upon the surface of the earth, one shall obtain full lifespan through prosperity, beauty, wealth, and health. (61)

With these three verses beginning with "With *kucandana*" and ending with "*edhate*," [the author] teaches the fruits [attained] through the specific substances for drawing the yantra, according to the sequence of the daily worship of Kāmeśvarī therein. Among those, by the phrase "the eight wheels" (*cakrāṣṭaka*), that which consists of the secret yantra is also indicated.
