It comes to pass. || 55 || In the center, surrounded by the Vidyā as before. There, in the centers of each of the sixteen yantras, having worshipped according to the stated sequence, one who observes the milk-vow—that is, one whose diet consists of milk—[attains purification]. || 56 || [This purifies] the evil deeds of previous births, those wicked actions accumulated over a long period of time.
This is the meaning: "in this birth," that is, at that particular time. || 57 ||

With these four verses beginning with "naram" and ending with "āpnuyāt," he teaches the means for bringing the entire world under control by means of those very same yantras. In that context, "in the middle of that" means in the center of the aforementioned sixteen yantras; "that yantra" [refers to the specific one]. [The offering is made] with milk-rice and other such substances.

Here, by the word "etcetera" (ādi), he refers to cakes and so forth. (59) Regarding the phrase "maṇḍala, maṇḍala," since each of the seven days is sevenfold through the relationship of part and whole, forty-nine days are spoken of by all. (60)

In the phrase "on gold and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to silver, copper, birch bark, and other such materials; the remainder of the sentence is "having inscribed the sixteen yantras. || 61 ||
By joining the sixteen vowels with the unobstructed letters of knowledge, one hundred and ninety-two syllables arise, born from mantra. (62)
O Supreme Lord, for what reason is the application of vowels performed in all mantras? Tell me that now. (63)
O Goddess of the gods, there are sixteen vowels and likewise thirty-five consonants; these are declared to be produced through their mutual conjunction.
O Supreme Goddess, know that the joining of vowels with those consonants, which are the very body of Bhāratī, is the secret of the joining of their vital breaths (prāṇa). 65.
The two eyes of Bhāratī, who consists of the phonemes (varṇa), are said to be *ha* and *sa*;
the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) are declared to be the vowels (*svara*), while the *bindu* and *visarga* are her consciousness (*cetana*).
O Supreme Goddess, the constituent parts [of the phonemes] are distinct from one another;
therefore, by that method of conjunction, the phonemes become manifest, and not otherwise.
Know that the emission of the *bindu*, the *ha* and *sa*, and the fifth, the fourth vowel (*au*), constitute the unfolding of consciousness within the body of the Mother, Bhāratī. (68)

By means of these ten verses beginning with "anāvṛtaiḥ" and ending with "siddhidāḥ," [it is taught that] for the mantra of Kāmeśvarī, there is the addition of the sixteen vowels to the twelve syllables beginning with *e* (ekāra) which are not enclosed by other letters; and likewise for all other mantras as well.
He teaches the application of the vowels and their corresponding mental impressions (*vāsanā*). In this context, "by those that do not return" means by those from which there is no returning.

"By the syllables of the Vidyā" refers to the twelve syllables of the *Kāmeśvarī-nityā-vidyā*; this is the remainder [of the sense]. What are they? *Ai / sa ka la ha ra na ta ya ma da va*. Here, because the previous *la* is accepted [as part of the sequence], the letter *la* is omitted [from the explicit list].

Because there is no difference between *la* and *la*. (62) "The conjunction" refers to [the conjunction] with the imperishable (*akṣara*) syllables from which there is no returning; this is the ellipsis. "Tell the cause of that"—this is the syntactical connection. (63) The consonants (*vyañjana*) are those beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*. "Thirty-five" is an adjective qualifying the consonants. It has been fully explained for those two.
The meaning is that it is designated as such precisely through the mutual conjunction of vowels and consonants. || 64 ||
In response to the inquiry "How so?", he says: "Of Bhāratī. This means of the Mother (mātṛkā) who is Bhāratī.
"By those that have become her body" means by those that have become her limbs. "The joining of her vital breaths" means the joining of the vital breaths of Bhāratī.
65 || *Hasau* refers to the letters *ha* and *sa*. The two eyes are so called because they are of the nature of Śiva and Śakti. *Cetanā* is the form of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*). 66 ||
For that reason, through that method, by means of the conjunction of the vowels with the letters *ha* and *sa*. || 67 ||
Therefore, those mantras and other vidyās that are deficient in form are considered to be like lifeless bodies, incapable of performing any function. (69)
Therefore, I proclaim the application of vowels everywhere;
one should join them with whichever mantras are devoid of the stated letters.
By that, they shall be powerful and endowed with success in their undertakings;
therefore, through their conjunction everywhere with the vowels, they grant the accomplishment of all goals.
In this way, indeed, powerful mechanical devices (yantras) are produced by those very [means].
I shall now describe their thirty-two applications in their proper sequence.
Having drawn a hexagon within two circles, one should write one's desired object in the center,
encased by the syllable *māyā* (hrīṃ), and then surround it with the letters of the *mātṛkā*.

With the verse beginning with *bindusargau*, he concludes the meaning already stated: "The blossoming of consciousness" (*caitanyajṛmbhaṇam*) means the expansion of consciousness. (68–69) By those five [vowels], which are the form of the deity consisting of supreme light, [the consonants] are "devoid of the aforementioned letters," that is, devoid of the five aforementioned groups of letters.

One should join those five phonemes—this is the remainder [of the verse]. "Those" refers to the mantras and so forth. Here, by means of these ten verses, the following is stated: although all the syllables exist as constituent parts within the form of Bhāratī, whose body is the Mātṛkā consisting of the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, [the mantras are extracted from them].
The fourth vowel, the nasal bindu, and the vowels of the letter *ha* and the sixteenth vowel *sa*—

like the manifestation of vital breath (*prāṇa*), consciousness (*caitanya*), and so forth within the bodies of embodied beings— exist everywhere through the application of those five [elements] to those [bodies] which are devoid of the five [ordinary] phonemes, due to their relationship as cause and effect.
And through the application of the musical notes (svaras), there occurs the bestowal of strength for all of them. || 71 ||
With this verse beginning with "evam," he introduces thirty-two yantras by means of the letters of the Kāmeśvarī-vidyā modified by vowels. In that regard,
by those [modifications] of the Kāmeśvarī-vidyā...
The meaning is: by means of one hundred and ninety-two syllables, which have been increased by musical notes (svaras). || 72 ||

With the verse beginning "vṛttadvaye" (in the two circles), he teaches the common nature of the thirty-two yantras. Therein, "māyāgarbham" means within the *hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*). Having drawn it as before, this is what is meant: having produced a circle by means of a rotation as before, there [within it], as before...
Having drawn a hexagon and having written the *hṛllekhā* mantra in its center according to the prescribed sequence—

with the syllables of the desired object placed within it— one should [place] the vowels modified by the *kāmeśvarī-vidyā* in the six corners of the hexagon, starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise.
Having written the first group of six among the one hundred and ninety-two syllables:
(p. 140) "In the first [syllable] there is the acquisition of gold; in the second, the appearance of ornaments;
in the third, the attainment of a maiden; in the fourth, the acquisition of land. (74)
In the fifth [year], there is the acquisition of a vehicle; in the sixth, mastery over women is proclaimed.
In the seventh, there is the acquisition of a house; in the eighth, union with a cow.
In the ninth [house], one shall subjugate a king; in the tenth, an elephant or a horse;
by the eleventh, a man becomes victorious on the field of battle.
In debates, legal disputes, and various kinds of gambling, there is the attainment of one's desires in the twelfth year, and the destruction of enemies by the supreme [deity]. (77)
It brings about the swift destruction of elephants, horses, camels, humans, cattle, deer, birds, serpents, goats, buffaloes, and mules. (78)
And that very [mantra] was written in red ink upon its skin in various places;
it was installed from the mandala for either one month or even seven nights. (79)
By the fourteenth [digit], there will be rain; by the following, the enemy will experience yawning, as well as the certain onset of anger, enmity, exertion, departure, and so forth.

Having constructed a circle with a one-aṅgula interval outside the [original] circle, one should write the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' in that path (vīthī) as before; this is the first yantra. Previously, in the six corners of this very yantra...
One should write the group of six syllables above the group of six syllables written in the [first] yantra. This is the second yantra.
Thus, by writing the six syllables in sequence within those six corners until completion, thirty-two yantras are produced in total. || 73 ||

With eighteen verses beginning with "The first" and ending with "the powers of the yantras," he teaches the specific fruits of the thirty-two yantras. In that regard, all the yantras individually bestow every desired object. [The results] begin with "the attainment of the immeasurable," and so forth.

Because of the rule beginning with "the attainment of immortality" (*amitāvāpti*), that [attainment] is unique to this [system]. [This applies] to various [beings], distinguished by the categories of sentient and insentient. (vv. 74–76) By the thirteenth [chapter]; the destruction of elephants and other creatures is effected by the thirteenth yantra. (vv. 77–78)
By the sixteenth [rite] with clarified butter in the fire, one is not oppressed by spirits and the like;
thereafter, by means of the subsequent yantra dug into the surface of the earth. (81)
Protection is certain for all living beings everywhere; [this is so] due to the absence of digging and of both quarreling and agitation. (82)
There will be the destruction of crops and even of trees due to many afflictions; furthermore, there will be suffering for the countries resulting from mutual strife. (83)
There will be conflict among the rulers of the earth due to a neighboring mechanical device, arising from the digging of that country's border for a short time. (84)
By means of the twenty-first yantra, enemies afflicted by disease are certainly [subdued];
by the twenty-second, the disease of cattle; and by the twenty-third, that of elephants.
By the twenty-fourth [digit] there is the acquisition of mounts; by the twenty-fifth, of kings;
and by the twenty-sixth, the acquisition of disease for the principal [persons] becomes certain. (86)
By the twenty-seventh [mantra] among those taught, there is the destruction of afflictions;
by the twenty-eighth yantra, malevolent magic (kṛtyā) is turned back.

Through being carried away by floods, by digging in the earth, by being bound to the tops of trees and the like, or by being cast into tanks, wells, ponds, and so forth, she certainly goes [to her death]. (88)
Thereafter, by means of the subsequent yantra, even a loquacious person becomes mute;
thereafter, by means of the upward-pointing yantra, the paralyzing of an enemy's speech occurs.
By means of the thirty-first yantra, there is protection for draft animals and even for elephants; this occurs both by digging it into their hooves and by wearing it.
In each respective place, at the locations for tethering elephants and so forth; from the mandala, as before. || 79 || 80 || 81 ||
"From digging" means in the locations of crops and so forth. [Verses 82, 83, 84, 85, 86, 87] state here in this section the destruction of afflictions.
(142) By means of the thirty-second [chapter], ships do not ever suffer distress in the ocean;
and through the power of various machines, they reach the further shore without hardship. || 91 ||
Of the sixteen Nityās, however, for each one on its respective lunar day (tithi) in sequence,
there is worship on that specific day by means of recitation (japa), fire-oblation (homa), ritual adoration (arcana), and so forth.
Clarified butter, sugar, milk, cake, plantain fruit, honey, jaggery, coconut, fruit, parched grain, sesame, and curd. (93)
One should offer flattened rice, chickpeas, mung beans, and milk-rice,
beginning from the first lunar day and continuing in sequence through all fifteen days.
All these [mantras] are always prescribed for the first one, Lalitā, as well as for all the other Śaktis beginning with Kāmeśvarī. 95.
One should offer it as an oblation, sacrifice it into the fire,
and also give it to men who possess the power of knowledge, constantly and incessantly for the attainment of their desired goals.
Having ground the medicinal herb prescribed by the syllables of the respective vidyā according to its measure and having formed it into pills, one should accomplish all [aims] with them. 97.

"Because of the wearing of those that have been proclaimed"—the meaning is that in all cases, the *yantras* bestow their fruits through being worn, installed, worshipped, and so forth. (88) (89) (90) (91)

With the verse beginning with "of the sixteen" (ṣoḍaśānām), he teaches the sequence for the worship of the respective Tithinityās on the lunar days starting from the first (pratipad) up to the fifteenth. In that context, by the word "and so forth" (ādi), recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and—by the word "etc. (ādi)—libations and ablutions are meant. || 92 ||

With these four verses beginning with *ghṛtam* and ending with *aniśam*, [the author] teaches the fifteen offering substances for the fifteen lunar days (*tithis*) as well as the methods of their conjunction with those days. Therein,
by the word "successively" (*kramāt*), he demonstrates the sequence for each of the offering substances corresponding to the lunar days of Śakti.
All these items, beginning with the substances for offering, are always present because [the deity] consists of all fifteen Nityās. || 93 || 94 || 95 || 96 ||

Offering libations like those of the *arghya*, daily bathing, drinking, and eating, as well as applying [the substance] mixed with sandalwood paste upon the forehead, brings about all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*). (98)
One should constantly provide special protection for kings by means of these [substances],
through bathing, drinking, wearing, and indeed by the application of medicinal pellets.
Defects arising from the planets, such as disease, untimely death, and malevolent rites, do not afflict one; therefore, one should always worship [the deity] somewhere within one's own home.
This pervasive state consisting of aesthetic flavor (rasa) has been correctly described;
by the churning of this [flavor] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self. (101)
Thus, the seventh chapter of the Śrīkādimata within the venerable Ṣoḍaśanityātantras is fully completed and concluded. 7.

With the verses beginning with *tattad* and ending with *kvacit*, he teaches the preparation of pills (*gulikā*) for all the vidyās using their respective syllables as medicinal herbs, their application, and their results.
In that context, *tatpramāṇataḥ* means according to the measure of the repetition of those respective syllables. *Paṭīram*... [text fragment]
Sandalwood. || 98 || With these medicinal substances made into pills. || 99 || At a certain place for the worship of the deity. || 100 || 101 ||
Thus, in the *Manoramā* commentary composed by Subhagānandanātha, titled *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, within the *Śrīkādimata* among the *Śrīṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
The seventh chapter, titled "The Illumination of the One Known as Kāmeśvarīnityā," has been fully expounded and concluded. || 7 ||
The number of verses in the original text (yantra) is forty-seven;
the explanatory commentary (vyākhyā) consists of two thousand one hundred and three-quarter verses. (1)
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Now, O Goddess, listen as I shall explain in due order the third among the sixteen Nityās, Bhagamālinī, together with her limbs and her enclosures. 1.
Then its limbs, that meditation, the deities who guard it, the sequence of its worship, the fire-oblation (homa), and various types of yantras. || 2 ||
The extraction of its mantra has already been declared by me to you previously;
the limbs [of the ritual] are formed with the syllables of the mantra, and the Heart is said to be formed with the first [syllable].
Then, the head should consist of four [syllables], the crest-lock (śikhā) is declared to have three;
the remaining six limbs are formed by groups of four and three respectively.
She was as red as the dawn, beautiful, with a smiling countenance;
she had three eyes and was endowed with six arms, seated upon a lotus throne.
Now begins the eighth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding seventh chapter the ritual procedure for the second Nityā, Kāmeśvarī, [the author] next [teaches] that of the third, Bhagamālinī-nityā.

He teaches the sequence of the ritual procedure by means of the eighth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "his she. Therein, with two verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "and various," he indicates the subjects of the chapter. || 2 ||

With the two verses beginning with "The extraction of its mantra" and ending with "in due order," he teaches the sequence for the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*). In that regard, as previously stated in the third chapter, the ellipsis is "one should place the six limbs. "With the first" means with the first syllable of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*). || 3 ||

The remaining limbs—the armor, the eyes, and the weapon—consist of three sets of four syllables each. Here too, one should perform the application of the *jāti* mantras as previously described. || 4 ||

With these three verses beginning with *aruṇām* and ending with *madātmabhiḥ*, he teaches the meditation for the daily worship of the Goddess together with her retinue; therein, *kamalāsanām* means seated upon a lotus-throne. By the left arms, in order from the upward direction [proceeding clockwise]... (6)
Holding in her left arms a white water-lily, a noose, a *puṇḍra* flower, and a sugarcane bow, and in her right [hands] a lotus, a goad, and a flowery arrow. (6)
She was surrounded on all sides by such groups of Śaktis who were praised with other imperishable hymns, their very souls intoxicated with the madness of passion.
Having joined the fivefold Rūpiṇī-śaktis and the seven-syllabled mantra with those [mantras] consisting of three hundred and thirty-five syllables, one should worship that same number of Śaktis.
Madanā, Mohinī, Lolā, Jambhinī, Udyamā, Śubhā, Hlādinī, Drāviṇī, Prīti, Rati, Raktā, and Manoramā. || 9 ||

She who causes universal intoxication, who is all-bliss, who is the embodiment of the bodiless god of love, who exerts herself on all sides, who is not small, whose power is manifest, and who exists within the body of manifold agitation.
These powers (śaktis) shall number two hundred and fifty-five;
one should worship that Goddess surrounded by them for the attainment of one's desires. (11)

The expression "by such groups of powers" is used because of [Śiva’s] sovereignty. "By others" refers to those distinct from the phonemic powers (*akṣara-śakti*), beginning with Madanā and so forth. "Consisting of passion, madness, and intoxication" is an adjective describing those whose nature is passion (*smara*), madness (*unmāda*), and intoxication (*mada*).
Common to all the hosts of Śaktis.

With the verse beginning "thirty-five" (*pañcatriṃśat*) and so forth, he teaches the thirty-five powers (*śakti*)—which constitute the retinue of the Goddess—and their corresponding Vidyās, consisting of the syllables of the mantra. This is what is meant: [the mantra] together with the nasal bindu...
Having uttered the twelve vowels, and thereafter having uttered each of the thirty-five hundred mantra-syllables in succession,
one should then utter "I worship the sandals of the Śakti Rūpiṇī"; by that [means].
There exist one hundred and thirty-five Vidyās, corresponding to the number of syllables in the Vidyā-mantra, as well as an equal number of Śaktis. || 8 ||
With these three verses beginning with "Madanām" and ending with "vāñchitāptaye," he teaches the two enclosures by means of twenty Śaktis and the Śaktis of the mantra-syllables.
Among them, [the first two] are "Vividhakṣobhavigrahe," meaning she whose form is various disturbances and she whose form is disturbance. These [are the two].
"Regarding the powers (*śaktayaḥ*): [they are] the twenty powers beginning with Madanā, which arise from the syllables. (p.
146) "Now, O Goddess, hear the sequence of worship that bestows all goals, by which the entire universe, both moving and unmoving, shall come under one's control. (12)
Having constructed two squares, one should make a door in the western direction;
in the center of that, having fashioned a five-petalled lotus, [one should place] it within the pericarp.
Between those two yonis, by means of drawing horizontal lines,
one hundred and thirty-five yonis are situated all around.
Having established those Śaktis moving in reverse order from the top, one should worship them;
in the center, one should draw three circles with twenty lines.
Having produced that many wombs, beginning with Madanā and the others, one should worship them;
then, within the circle, one should worship the six limbs in sequence around it.

"By the powers" means one hundred and fifty-five powers; "the pair" refers to the two enclosures (āvaraṇas), as is understood from the context. The meaning is that the powers, numbering as stated, constitute the two enclosures according to the sequence previously described. || 11 ||
Now, with thirteen and a half verses beginning with "atha pūjā" and ending with "narādhipān," he teaches the sequence of the Goddess's daily worship and its fruits. Therein,
[he explains] by which sequence of worship, starting from "caturasradvayam" and ending with "kramāt," [the results are attained].

By these verses, this is what is meant: having constructed a square pathway with equal sides and an interval of four finger-breadths between the inner and outer sections, and having made a door in the middle of its western side,
one should fashion a five-petaled lotus in the center of that square.

Having constructed a *yoni* of appropriate dimensions within that pericarp— which is joined by two circles and possesses three equal lines whose three corners touch the circle at the center of the pericarp—
one should divide one of its lines into twenty-four parts and mark twenty-three points with those divisions.
Having done so, and having likewise drawn three lines for it, one should leave out a measurement of one part on all sides and, within that, fashion a *yoni* with three equal lines as before; then,
having divided one line of that *yoni* into twenty-one parts, in those [parts]—

Having made twenty marks on each of the lines, one should draw forty-five horizontal lines across both sides, following the sequence of outer and inner marks, such that there is a mark followed by a non-mark. When this is done, the tips of the outer lines and the tips of the inner lines [will align].

There are one hundred and thirty-five triangles. In their center (p. 147), having invoked that Bhagamālā who possesses the aforementioned form, one should worship her with the ritual services, joined with the rites of installation and so forth. || 17 ||
Having prepared the *arghya* with the limbs-mantras and the root-mantra, and having sprinkled it with water from the root-mantra,
one should likewise worship the powers of Attachment (*rāga*) and Aversion (*dveṣa*) on the two sides of the door.
Likewise, one should worship sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as before;
then, between those two inner functions, one should likewise worship the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga).
Within that garland of inner sections, one should likewise worship Madana and the others;
and in the center, one should worship the Goddess, as well as the other weapons surrounding her.
Then, one should worship the Goddess with the sixteen services as they have been described, using the first syllable; one should then fashion two cavities for her.
Having constructed a circle by rotating [the compass] so that its radius touches three rare (widely spaced) lines,
and having constructed another circle within that one by rotating [the compass] with a radius measuring one-fifth of the diameter of the former,
one should multiply by three the diameter-measure of those two circles increased by one-sixteenth of their diameter.
Having divided the entire area into ten parts and assigned a distinct mark to each individual section,

one should draw twenty horizontal lines— ten in each of the two surrounding circles— following the "cow's urine" (gomutrikā) pattern by moving sequentially from the outer to the inner circle, and then from that inner circle back to the outer.

When this is done, twenty triangles in total arise on all sides— those whose tips touch the outer circle and those whose tips touch the inner circle. Within all of these, according to the stated sequence, one should construct a square courtyard (*vīthī*) that is equal on all four sides with an interval of four *aṅgulas* between the internal and external divisions.

"One should worship the Śaktis as described" (verses 13–17). Having sprinkled oneself and the others with water, [one should worship] "from the root," that is, by means of the Mūlavidyā. As before, this includes the three-syllabled mantra "Svarūpiṇī. (verse 18)
Between those two circles, within the pathway of the two circles of the pericarp of the five-petaled lotus;
likewise, in the order starting from the northwest (vāyavya), within the thirty-five triangular spaces situated between the interior and exterior *yoni*s.

Moving clockwise from the first [corner] to the last; within that, in the garland of triangles situated between the two circles—specifically in the twenty triangles located in the center—one should then place the Goddess around [the center].
This is what is meant: in the middle of the circular path within that, the six weapons of the Goddess [are placed]. One should [place] them...

Having divided the circular path— which consists of six lines forming a hexagon— into six parts, one should worship [the objects] in sequence, starting from that which is on the lower left hand of the Goddess and ending with that which is on the lower right hand,
proceeding clockwise from the front. [This is done] with the first syllable.

Together with the first syllable of the mantra, etc.—this is the ellipsis. One should daily recite one hundred and eight times before the Goddess the first syllable of the root mantra, accompanied by the nasal bindu and the twelfth vowel (au). (p. 148)
Having performed the fire-ritual (agnimukha) as before, one should perform the oblation (homa) for a tenth part [of the total]. || 22 ||

Having joined her into the *bindu* and having worshipped her with the root mantra in that same manner, one should dismiss the Great Goddess from within one's own self according to the prescribed method. (23)
The self of the Goddess shall bring the entire universe—men, women, and kings—under her control.
Now, I shall describe the optional fire-oblation (kāmyahoma), which bestows the attainment of various desired objects.
O Brahmins, by means of an oblation of white lotuses smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one brings [the target] under control;
with *āragvadha* flowers, a king; and with *karavīra* flowers, a Vaiśya.

One may bring a Śūdra under control with blue lotuses, and a woman through recitation and burnt offerings; prosperity is attained through oblations of bilva fruits, and land and other riches through the offering of lotuses.
Through white water-lilies one obtains a vehicle; through varada flowers, great fame;
through campaka flowers, good fortune; and with siddha flowers, one should offer the red saugandhika.
With *tagara* one achieves success in obtaining garments; with *punnāga*, for the attainment of ornaments;
with *madhuka*, for the success of obtaining a maiden; and with *palāśa*, for the attainment of gold. (28)
The meaning is that one should transform all the powers of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) into the syllables of the mantra. One should offer two *bali* offerings:

at the beginning of the worship with the sixteen-syllable mantra, and at the conclusion of the worship with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā. The traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) is that in all cases, one should perform the worship of the Lord (*nātha*) both at the beginning and at the end of the ritual worship.

21. After the sequential *homa* performed for one-tenth [of the recitation], one should perform a *homa* with the root mantra (*mūlamantra*) for one-tenth of the recitation (*japa*). This is common to all [deities]. 22–23.
(In the manner described, at the conclusion of the worship of the principal goddess, according to the stated sequence... [The essence of the Goddess...]

The meaning is: by means of the non-dual meditation on the form of the goddesses of the nyāsa as before. Here too, for the sake of the preliminary rite (puraścaraṇa), one should recite the vidyā ten thousand times alone, and then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and other rites with a tenth part of that; such is the meaning of the tradition. || 24 ||

With these five verses beginning with "kāmyahoma" and ending with "parameśvarī," [the author] teaches the attainment of various fruits through oblations of diverse substances. In this context, "trimadhv-akta" refers to the three sweets: honey (kṣaudra), clarified butter (ājya), and milk (dugdha).

O Supreme Goddess, one should perform oblations with *kiṃśuka* flowers for the attainment of fine garments, with *pāṭala* flowers for the mastery over animals, and with red lotuses for the accomplishment of all goals. (29)
Now I shall describe the yantras which bestow desired objects;
one should write them with sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, musk, and saffron.
One who desires the attainment of all desired objects should [employ] all the various yantras on gold, silver, copper, cloth, or birch bark.
One should perform worship by placing all the yantras entirely upon the head, the two arms, the neck, the waist, the forearm, or in some other location. || 32 ||
Having drawn a hexagon between two circles,
and likewise having drawn a *yoni* in its center, one should write the *māyā* syllable, joined with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*), in the middle of that.
Having drawn [the diagram], one should write the syllable *vahni* (ra) in the three corners and also in the six [triangles];
then, between each pair of circles, one should write the remaining syllables.
Having encircled it with the outer Mātṛkā, which is joined with circles, lines,
and dots, the yantras are thus formed by ten mantra-syllables each.

Or [the offerings may be] honey, milk, and curd. The meaning in this context is that one should offer all the aforementioned oblation materials smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). In all optional (*kāmya*) fire-offerings, after first completing one's own regular daily ritual sequence, one should subsequently [offer] the respective *vidyā* into the fire.

Having offered the *parivāra* (retinue) oblations, one should subsequently perform oblations with the aforementioned substances and in the aforementioned number, using the respective root-mantras (*mūlamantra*) for the attainment of the stated results. In all homas, it is the universal rule that at the conclusion of the oblation, one should recite the root-mantra as many times as the number of oblations performed. || 25 || 26 || 27 || 28 ||
With red lotuses and red water-lilies. || 29 ||

Now, with these three verses beginning with *atha yantryaṇi* and ending with *aśeṣataḥ*, he first introduces the description of the yantras and then teaches the materials for drawing the yantras common to all tantras, the substrates for the yantras, and the methods for wearing them. (30, 31, 32)
With these six verses beginning with "the hexagon" and ending with "is prescribed," he teaches the procedure for constructing fourteen yantras. Therein, "māyā" refers to *hṛllekhā*;
[one should place it] there, accompanied by the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*), as before.
O Śivā, in the final [verse], one should worship the remainder with the Amṛta-ṣaṣṭhi alone. [The sequence is:
Jyā, Kāṃ, Dā, Vaḥ, Ambu, Hṛt, Sva, and Māyā; this is the fivefold Amṛta. (36)
That group of five, through its differentiation by the vowels, becomes eighty; likewise, through Māyā, it becomes sixty when the neuter vowels are excluded. Thus it should be. (37)
One hundred [syllables] are specified by sixty [units] as having the form of nectar within the phonemes;
their application is prescribed everywhere in this tantra. (38)
The traditional instruction is that one should write each individual syllable of the mantra within the *māyā*. || 33 || 34 ||

The remaining syllables are one hundred and twenty-five in number, arranged in sequence. In the final fourteenth yantra, [the mantra is formed] by the "sixty nectars" (amṛta-ṣaṣṭi) which will be described as *jyākaṃ dāvombuhṛtsvena*. Here, *jyā* is the letter *ja*; *kaṃ* is the letter *sa*; *dāvaḥ* is the letter *ṭha*; *amba* is the letter *va*; and *hṛt*...

The letter *sa* [is formed] by its own *bindu* and by *māyā*, which is the *visarjanīya*. Likewise, by *māyā*: when the *bindu* is removed from the eighty *amṛta*-syllables—which number eighty due to the differentiation of vowels when accompanied by the *bindu*—and because the *visarjanīya* is joined everywhere [in their place], those very syllables become the eighty syllables.

The meaning is that they come into being. "By those lacking the neuter [vowels]" means by those devoid of the syllables *ṛ*, *ṝ*, *ḷ*, and *ḹ*. And likewise, "by means of *māyā*"—even when joined with the *visarjanīya* (the visarga)—there would be sixty syllables, provided they are devoid of the four neuter vowels;
this is the meaning. The statement "one hundred and sixty are specified" is the expression used.
Because it is endowed with the four neuter [vowels]. Regarding the phonemes in the *mātṛkā*:

the phrase "the five phonemes whose form is nectar" (*amṛtavigraha*) is the remainder [of the statement]. Here, excluding the fourteen neuter vowels, the number of the syllables of nectar is exactly one hundred and twenty. Of those, including the neuter ones—

The sequence for constructing the fourteen diagrams (*yantra*) consisting of one hundred and sixty immortal syllables (*amṛtākṣara*) is as follows: having drawn three circles with an interval of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) between each by means of a compass,
divided into inner and outer sections, [one proceeds] within the middle of the third circle from the inside.

Having fashioned a hexagon according to its measure, one should draw a triangle of equal sides facing oneself in its center; having written the *hṛllekhā* syllable accompanied by the name in its center,
and having written the first letter of the mantra within the *māyā* portion inside that, [one should write] the mantra in the outer triangles.
Having written the second, third, and fourth syllables, and having written the syllables from the fifth to the tenth in the six outer corners starting from the front and proceeding clockwise,
one should [place] the eleventh syllable and so forth on the circular path outside of that.
Having written the one hundred and twenty-five remaining mantra-syllables as before,
and having likewise written the syllables with their bindus on the outer circular path as before,
[one should write] the syllables with their bindus on the outer circular path in the same manner.
One should inscribe [the letters] from *ā* to *kṣa*; this is the first yantra. O Dear One, hear now the application of the fourteen yantras, beginning with the second and ending with the thirteenth:
subjugation, attraction, immobilization, health, victory, and prosperity. (39)
One should effect protection for elephants, horses, cows, rams, and buffaloes in their respective order,
as well as for men, women, and kings, by means of the prescribed yoga.
With the syllables of the ocean of nectar, with those same root-syllables excluding Lalitā,
and also with the fourteen syllables of the Nityās, [there are] one hundred and sixty-one.
Four hundred and fifty-six [yantras] have been proclaimed; O beloved, hear now the application of their arrangement and their fruits. 42.

Having written the ten syllables situated above the first set of ten syllables inscribed on the first yantra upon each of the twelve yantras— in the second, the third, and the fourth [yantras]— and so on in sequence across all twelve,
one should surround them externally with the remaining syllables.
For the sake of accomplishing the one hundred and twenty-five syllables,

starting from the syllable immediately following the tenth syllable among the ten syllables written in the middle of that [diagram], one begins with the subsequent mantra-syllables, namely *hṛllekhā*.
One should write the letters starting from the letter written in the center up to the preceding letter.

In the final fourteenth yantra, having written the five nectar-letters (pañcāmṛta) along with their bindus in the five [angles] beginning with the second angle of the hexagon, [one should place] the remainder of the mantra's letters outside.

On the street [of the yantra], one should write the syllables of that nectar (amṛta) with the nasal bindu, their vowels and consonants distorted and indistinct; then those same syllables joined with the visarga; and then the five syllables of nectar together with the visarga—thus, one hundred and twenty-five syllables in total should be inscribed. || 38 ||

With these two verses beginning with "Of the fourteen" and ending with "one should accomplish," he teaches the fourteen results corresponding respectively to the fourteen yantras. In that regard, "one should accomplish by means of the stated yoga" refers to [the methods of] wearing, depositing, and so forth. (39–40)

With this half-verse and more, beginning with *amṛtārṇaiḥ* and ending with *udīritam*, he teaches the specific number of mantra-syllables and their total sum for the purpose of constructing thirty-three yantras. In this regard, the following is stated:
With one hundred and sixty syllables of the ocean of nectar,
and with one hundred and thirty-five syllables of their own root-mantras— excluding Lalitā and consisting of the other fourteen Nityā-mantra syllables devoid of the root-mantra— one...
And when combined with those numbered as one hundred and sixty, the total number is declared to be four hundred and fifty-six. || 41 ||
With the second half of the verse beginning with "tair" (by them), he introduces the yantras and their results by those [means].
Therein, "by them" means by the syllables of the stated number. (42)
Having drawn a triangle, an eight-petalled lotus, and likewise two outer circles, one should place the syllable *māyā* in the center and the name within the triangle. (43)
Having written the three intermediate spaces situated in a triad— like [the spokes] extending outward to the eight petals—
and having inscribed the fourteen-syllable mantra within the circle, one should place the Mātṛkā therein.
Having drawn it, one should employ the thirty-third yantra, which is perfected through worship, oblations, recitation, and sprinkling, along with the powers and the five nectars.
In cases of severe fever, shivering, and quartan fever; in eruptions, smallpox, and ailments arising from the eyes or the abdomen.

By means of these three verses beginning with "the triangle" (*trikoṇam*) and ending with "by the fivefold" (*pañcakair*), which consist of four hundred and fifty-six syllables— the five-syllabled nectar (*amṛta-pañcākṣara*) and the *hṛllekhā* known as *Śakti*— he teaches the sequence for constructing the yantra in its thirty-three forms. Therein:

This is what is meant: having produced two circles with an interval of one *aṅgula* between them by means of a desired measure and a compass, one should form the pericarp (*karṇikā*) with a circle having an interval of eight *aṅgulas* from that [inner circle],
and [the next layer] with a circle having an interval of three *aṅgulas* from that [pericarp].
Having drawn three lines outside that [square] along the path of the tips of the three fingers, and having fashioned eight petals, one should fashion a *yoni* in the center of the pericarp;
this *yoni* should have three equal lines and its three corners should touch the circle of the pericarp.
In its center, having written the *hṛllekhā* mantra accompanied by the name as before, [one should place it] upon those three corners.

Having written the fourteen syllables as follows—three from the beginning among the previously stated number of syllables for the pericarp (*karṇikā*); three in the three intermediate spaces between the circles, the *yoni*, and the polygons; and the eight syllables on the eight outer petals starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise—one should then [write] the series from *a* to *kṣa* in the outer circular path (*vīthī*).
One should likewise write out the *mātṛkā*. From among these syllables, starting from the beginning, the first diagram (*yantra*) consists of fourteen syllables.
Similarly, the second diagram consists of the fourteen syllables following the aforementioned fourteen syllables.
In this manner, with fourteen syllables each from the subsequent [sections], there are thirty other yantras in sequence, followed by the final yantra.
With the remaining eight syllables not employed in the thirty-three yantras, together with the five-syllable *amṛta* mantra:

One should perform [the rite] with the *hṛllekhā* mantra and likewise with fourteen syllables; having thus prepared thirty-three yantras, one should employ them through worship (*pūjā*), fire-oblation (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), and consecration (*abhiṣeka*).
Here, the worship, recitation, and so forth are performed with the *mātṛkā* and with the specific syllables written therein. Thus...
The procedure for all syllable-machines (akṣarayantresu). || 45 ||
With these fourteen verses beginning with *jvare* and ending with *īśvarī*, he teaches the thirty-three fruits corresponding respectively to the thirty-three yantras.
Among them, regarding the quartan fever (*cāturthika*), there is the pacification of the affliction on the fourth day and subsequent days.
In cases of affliction by yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, piśācas, uragas, and grahas of children; in misfortune, barrenness, and oppression by enemies. (47)
In disputes, in madness, in royal wrath, in fear of thieves, as well as when one is assailed by the six classes beginning with the Ḍākinīs, or by Brahmarākṣasas; || 48 ||

O Goddess, one should apply these thirty-three [medicines] according to the prescribed method for the three types of diseases arising from the humors—diabetes, jaundice, and vomiting—respectively. 49.
Listen, O Goddess! I shall explain the common worship of the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī, according to the application of the relationship between the whole and its parts. (50)
The syllables of those fifteen [mantras] are declared to be two hundred and ninety-six; with them, the wheel there is to be worshipped. (51)
One should draw twenty lines east-west, north-south, and south-north;
by that, O Pārvatī, square compartments are produced.
In the *kāgada* [system], || 46 || 47 || it is said that by means of the sixfold *ākrānti*, there are six kinds of results. || 48 ||

Regarding the three groups of diseases arising from the humors—those born of wind (vāta), bile (pitta), and phlegm (śleṣman)—by means of the prescribed method, such as worship, recitation, and so forth. || 49 ||

With the verse beginning with "Kāmeśvary-ādi," [the author] introduces the fifteen-fold common mode of worship for the other [fifteen Nityās] who constitute the limbs of Lalitā, [in which they serve as mutual principal deities]. Therein:
The phrase "of the fifteen Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 50 ||

With the verse beginning with "tāsām" (of them), having taught the total number of mantra-syllables of those fifteen [goddesses] starting with Lalitā, he introduces their common wheel for optional worship (*kāmyapūjā*) by means of those syllables. Therein, by those...
With the number of syllables as previously stated. || 51 ||
With twenty verses beginning with *prākpratyak* and ending with *pūjayet*,

he teaches the construction of the complete wheel of worship (*pūjācakra*), the sequence of worship, and the specific requisites for worship. Among these, with eleven verses beginning with *prākpratyak* and ending with *krameṇa vai*:
The construction of that wheel is described in verses; therein, the sequence of worship for the fifteen Nityās [is given].
One should draw three hundred and sixty-one [squares], circling from Īśa (the northeast) onwards, following the spatial layout, according to the required number and the appropriate intervals. (53)
Among those, there are sixty-five; in the four directions beginning with the east, there is a group of four;
and when those situated in the directions are combined, the remainder remains among them. (54)
One should draw the Māyā situated within the four [squares] in sequence as desired,
once the forty-nine cells have indeed become unified therein.
Having drawn a fourteen-petalled lotus along with two outer circles,
one should draw a womb (yoni) within the belly of Māyā in the center of the pericarp.
Likewise, one should draw the fourteen powers upon the petals;
having invoked Bhagamālā into the central power, one should worship her on the outside.
But one should invoke and worship the others starting from the west and ending with the northwest;
in this way, this wheel shall be common to them all in due order. (58)
But those who are to be worshipped in the middle [of the petals] are the remaining ones situated there upon the petals;
one should worship them in their proper order, ending with Citrā, possessing the forms as previously described.

He instructs therein that it should be done in such a way that sixty-five squares remain in the interior; this is the meaning. Regarding those sixty-five [squares]: "in the east and so forth" means that in the directions beginning with the east, there should be four [squares] each remaining from the center. Among those—
When the four sets of four squares have been unified—meaning that the three middle lines have been erased. || 54 ||
When forty-nine squares have been unified there, a fourteen-petalled lotus is formed from the center in the shape of a perfect square,
extending as far as the lines at the ends of the four squares located in the cardinal directions that were previously unified— thus comprising forty-nine squares.
The meaning is that one should form a lotus there in the manner previously described by combining [the elements].

(56) In the central power (*madhyaśakti*), the central power is *hṛllekhā*. (57) The others are the fourteen *nityās*. For these—having constructed two squares on the outside and doors in the cardinal directions—(p. 155) [one should proceed].
One should worship twelve [deities] in sequence at the corners on both sides of the doors.
Brāhmī and Māheśvarī are at the western gate on the left and right;
Komārī and Vaiṣṇavī are in the north; and Vārāhī and Aindrī are in the east.
Mahālakṣmī is in Cāmuṇḍā; those located in the south and the corners starting from the northwest are indeed space and time, as well as form and sound, according to the stated sequence.
One should worship them in their prescribed forms, and they [should be worshipped] in their prescribed forms in sequence, with ritual offerings,
spirits, meats, and well-prepared fish.
Of the fourteen Nityās. || 58 || 59 || 60 || "In the eastern gate" is the ellipsis. || 61 || 62 ||
Thus, by these eleven verses, the following is stated:

having made a square with equal sides with an interval of twenty-five finger-breadths, one should draw a smaller inner square two finger-breadths away from that; then, upon that two-finger-breadth border—
Regarding the doors in the four directions: having drawn four lines to form a square measuring one finger-breadth on each side,
one should strike eighteen lines each across the center, from south to north and from east to west, with an interval of one finger-breadth between them.
In the center of all, having combined forty-nine squares into one, one should produce two circles there by rotating [the compass] so that they touch and do not touch the lines of the square; then,
having fashioned a fourteen-petaled lotus with a pericarp in the middle of that, one should [draw] a circle touching the triangle in the middle of its pericarp.
Having fashioned a yoni with three equal lines and having inscribed the *hṛllekhā* in its center,

one should then inscribe the *hṛllekhā* on each of the fourteen petals— starting from the west and ending at the northwest— in a counter-clockwise direction around the outside of that lotus; and [further] outside the square surrounding that lotus.
Having unified the four squares in the four directions starting from the east, as well as the center, by dividing them into inner and outer sections,

one should draw the *hṛllekhā* there as before, containing the desired object within; then, starting from the square of Śiva located in the outermost row on the far left, proceeding in a clockwise direction—

By way of entry, having inscribed in sequence the fifteen letters of the Nityā-mantras— beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā— within two hundred and ninety-six squares according to their respective numbers (despite the unmentioned order),
one should [place them] at the four doors of the outermost square, starting from the west.
Having worshipped the eight Śaktis beginning with Brāhmī in a clockwise direction starting from the south,
two by two on the left and right branches,
and having worshipped the Śaktis of Place, Time, Space, and Sound in the corners starting from the northwest (Vāyu) and ending at the southwest (Nirṛti), [one should worship] within that.
In the previously mentioned squares, proceeding clockwise from the northeast square (īśa-koṣṭha) according to the path of entry,

one should worship the syllables of the fifteen Nityā-mantras with their respective letters; then, in the four directions starting from the west, one should worship the Bhagamālā-mantra within the Hṛllekhā-mantras containing the desired object, and finally in the very center.
Having worshipped that very [deity] with that same vidyā, from west to east (from the exterior to the interior), [he should offer] cakes, milk-rice, well-boiled milk mixed with sugar,
and fruits such as plantains and jackfruit, as well as honey. (64)
One should gratify the Goddess with food offerings, as well as with dance, song, and other such arts, for one night, three nights, five nights, or seven nights.
Whether it be for nine nights, a fortnight, a month beginning with the full moon,
or for a year ending in Phālguna, [this practice] shall be the destroyer of all suffering.
In cases of adverse planetary influences, long-standing passions, or physical deformities;
or when there is a portentous disturbance of the deities, or the threefold practice of malevolent magic (abhicāra). || 67 ||
This worship, which grants all desires, is effective for overcoming poverty, during famines and oppression by enemies, and in other terrible hardships. (68)
Having prepared either a pedestal or a beautifully leveled altar adorned with a platform, one should worship it according to the prescribed form and with the prescribed materials.
One should worship the fourteen Nityās, beginning with Nityaklinnā and ending with Kāmeśvarī, upon those respective outer petals;

likewise, among the other fourteen Nityās as well, one should worship them starting from the Nityā immediately following the central one and ending with the Nityā preceding it. Thus [it is said]. || 62 ||

With these nine verses beginning with "pūjayet" and ending with "pūjayet," he teaches the specific substances to be offered, the duration of the worship there, and the timing and procedure for the ritual of worship. In that regard, by means of the aforementioned forms...

By the words "red fragrance" (*raktagandha*) and so forth, the word "practitioner" (*sādhaka*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Those [deities] possess forms identical to those of the Central Nityā, including her ornaments and weapons;
they are the fourteen Nityās situated on the outer petals. Here, the specific offering substances (*nivedya-dravya*) are those previously mentioned. In this...

They are to be offered in the fifteen cakras taught according to the sequence of worship involving the relationship between parts and whole among the fifteen [deities]. Everywhere, for all sixteen Nityās and others, one should perform the worship and so forth with these specific substances only during occasional (naimittika) and optional (kāmya) rites; this will be explained further below.
With *nameru*, *campaka*, *aśoka*, *punnāga*, *bakula*, and *ambuja* flowers;
with *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jātī*, *śatapatra*, *utpala*, and others. (70)
With fragrant substances and others as well, one whose mind is full should perform worship;
likewise, one should worship others who possess devotion to this vidyā and are endowed with faith. || 71 ||
Whether it be in the bamboo flute, in the resonant chant,
or even in the recitation of the Vedas, one who is devoid of sacrifice and the like should speak only of the Supreme Reality, which is the source of all.
Those who possess wisdom are like a fire; they do not tremble before the rain of calamities. Having crossed over the ocean of illusion, they are remembered as being of three kinds.
The *vitavalī* is said to be free from fear. || 74 ||
Even though he was ground down by the enemy, today he shall be the desired one; today he shall be the one who delights the wicked through his own power,
while the Lord of Gauḍa, whose ear is satisfied with a mere fragment of truth,
shall fall from his high position, and the eye of the world shall be bewildered.
May the one who strikes the banner of desire with his palm be the bestower of great joy. Then, [let there be] the abandonment of delusion; may there be prosperity in that which is truly right.
In all cases of adversity, when a threefold portent is proclaimed—whether celestial, atmospheric, or terrestrial—[may there be well-being]. (67)

During famine when food is scarce, and during hardships such as when Āryas and others have arrived in the country—this fifteen-fold worship is prescribed for all that has been mentioned. The aforementioned form is the common wheel of worship for the fifteen Nityās. [This applies] everywhere among those things mentioned.

The oral tradition (*sampradāya*) states that when there is adverse planetary influence or similar obstacles, one should perform worship in the respective daily worship-mandalas (*nityapūjācakra*) using the specific substances prescribed for those instances; this applies even to other [deities] who are outside of one's own tradition.
From here onwards, up to the ninety-first verse, it is explained in the form of verses.
In the eighth [chapter], there are seventy-three and so forth, ending with sixty-four.
The verses, numbering twenty-one less than ninety, have their syllables disordered.

He who has attained the meaning of the *Devītantra*, who bears its lotus feet upon his crest, who is the essence of the three hundred [verses] of the Āgamas, the sun to the lotuses of the faces of the sages, and whose secret is the end of the sacrificial post (*dhvaja*)— he is the venerable [Guru].
(With tongues of flame) from the sacrificial ladle, O Gādhū! (O Gādhū,
free from doubt,) may this offering of ours reach the beloved Viṣṇu.
One should behold the upper region above the meditation; in this yoga, one should not perceive even a speck of dust, nor the taste of a sprout, nor should one remain with the mind agitated by desire,
nor should there be any wavering of the mind.
The Dayakeli-ūḍadhupaika-limata shines forth with its piercing rays;
in the waning of the moon, when the water-born [lotuses] have perished, it is perceived by the wise as a mass of light.
When the Brahmins have resorted to the mountain, the cloud-like darkness of ignorance is dispelled by the sun of one's own self.
Having joined the pure syllables, one should grind them with the essence of the mantra;
the wise one, having meditated upon the state of the self, should listen to the sound arising from the heart.
Having ascended through the eastern direction, one should perceive the world as if it were a dream.
Born under a double-light [yoga], he is one who bestows wealth upon us without price; his gaze is like that of the sun in the sky.
He shall be a delighter of the world, possessing the splendor of the ocean and the stability of Mount Meru.
His fame shall be as vast as the seven oceans, and his brilliance shall endure for an entire year.
The practitioner should recite the verses in the eighth chapter, which are joined with the *liptakepha-nā-teśa-nā-liyute-śi-sathaṃ-gala* [mantra], following a somewhat disordered sequence.

This is the verse for recitation: "The verses beginning with seventy-three and ending with ninety, as well as eighteen—though their meaning is easily understood, they will be briefly explained here and there;
however, their commentary shall consist of verses with intermingled syllables."
One should draw [the maṇḍala] with six [colors] and cause it to be recited according to the prescribed form:
*ṇaṃ sanistarmātrāvataiḥ raḥpamevī śvatīravrarthamikāmyarcānaimittikāḥ kaṃ ramān svādikā krataḥ || 1 ||* [The text continues with: *lpaguyotastu kīladhāraṇaṃstutugaga*.
The young woman, whose body was as dense as a cluster of black mustard seeds, was like a cloud. || 2 ||
(159) O you who have been nourished by the *rdrakkā* flower, even though you are free from all afflictions,
you are like a physician; though you grant a hundredfold [benefits], O *reṇusa*, you shine through the days,
having dispelled the darkness for the sake of those to be liberated.
One should give what is to be given with a single act; one should not be intent on giving more than that.
If one thinks, "I am wealthy," and becomes arrogant, one should know that this is the work of Māra;
one should not harbor such pride.
That which is made of clay for the sake of purification is pleasing;
how many new ones are there? That [is] the sacrificial post, and others are like the bull. They do not go out, even when they have settled together, ending with the sound *svar*.

And that very Kīja-pā, having spread out the waters of the sky, always maintains the end of the line of the world, adorned with the beauty of the ocean; may you, O Śiva, protect me from the fear of this worldly existence. 90.
Now listen, O Goddess of gods, to another wheel of wondrous appearance, known as the Ocean of Yonis (Yonyarṇava), which consists of women, cows, mountains, and vajras. 91.
That which is born from the Guru’s grace is indeed glorious; it is not attained through mere words, nor by the pride of one who has previously studied the scriptures.
May that stainless elephant-temple [of the heart], which bestows the nectar of immortality upon the world, be attained; may the river of tears flow forth like a stream of pure water. 4.
He who has reached the peak of the mountain, he who has descended from the sky;
he who protects the body of the one who bestows joy, the perfection of the servant of the one who possesses all.

Having drunk from his own wife’s mouth, he should first perform the *ardhakṛtyā* ritual; then, while standing in that place, he should offer fuel or food, or otherwise, he should remain there making various sounds.
Then, with these ten verses beginning with "athānyat" and ending with "sā," having constructed a womb-ocean (*yonyarṇava*)— which is heavy, free from fracture,
and measures twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*)— upon a surface level with the womb;
There, one should apply eleven threads at the measurement of two finger-breadths each.
Therefore, one hundred and forty-four triangles are produced here; within them, however, are the syllables of the mantra.
Entering by way of circumambulation, one should draw [the lines] continuously;
in the center, within the remaining nine squares, there is the group of nine.
Afterwards, one should write the name of the Lord nine times, joined with the name of the target and the ritual action;
one should write this everywhere again and again by means of repetition.
At midnight, however, he should visualize that woman to be won as being consumed by the fire of passion, her heart stolen away, with her palms joined in reverence upon her head.
Her hair was disheveled, her eyes were rolling, and she was of a deep crimson hue;
her body resembled a cloth fluttering in the wind, like a banner.
One should not contemplate or worship the naked Goddess in the center of the maṇḍala, for she is devoid of discrimination, intoxicated, and transcends pride, shame, and fear.
One should worship with *japā*, pomegranate, *bandhūka*, *kiṃśuka*, and so forth, as well as with other fragrant flowers such as *śephālī* and the like. (99)
Within twenty-one nights, she returns in the form described, intoxicated with passion;
until the fall of the body, she remains inseparable from him like a shadow.

It teaches the machine for the agitation of women, its meditation, the procedure for its worship and recitation, and the nature of its fruit. Therein, the syllables of the mantra are one hundred and thirty-five syllables of the Bhagamālinī-vidyā. [Verses 91, 92, 93] It is endowed with the nine groups [of consonants].

The sixteen vowel-syllables beginning with *a* are divided into two groups; the other consonant-syllables from *ka* to *kṣa* should be divided into groups of five. When this is done, the pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of the principle of form (*rūpatattva*), beginning with *ḷ*, *ka*, *ca*, *ṭa*, *ta*, *pa*, *ya*, and *sa*, is correctly proclaimed.
When the mind is freed from this [duality], that very reality is realized as one's own self.
Thus ends the eighth chapter in the venerable Kādimata, among the venerable Ṣoḍaśanityātantras.
The nine groups consist of the nature of the nine lords. (94) (95) (96) The *kalevara* is the body. (97) (98)
99 || By the words "being burned by the fire of passion" (*madanavahninā dahyamānam*) and so forth, [the nature] has been described. "Anapagā" means not going elsewhere.
Here, by these ten verses, this is what is stated:
having made a *yoni* facing oneself with three lines measuring twenty-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*), [one should perform the ritual].
Having divided one line of that [square] into twelve parts and made eleven marks upon them,
and likewise having made marks on the other two lines as well, one should strike eleven threads in succession from mark to mark. When this is done, [there will be] forty-four...

One hundred triangles arise. Within them, having written the one hundred and thirty-five syllables of the Bhagamālinī-vidyā by moving in a clockwise direction starting from the upper-left [corner] of each, in the center of the remaining nine [triangles],...
Having written nine syllables for each of the nine lords endowed with the previously mentioned nine divisions,

and having written the names of the goal (sādhya), the practitioner (sādhaka), and the rite (karma) in all the one hundred forty-four triangles according to the prescribed sequence as before, in their midst—
Having invoked the Goddess and meditated upon her according to the prescribed sequence, and having worshipped her, one shall obtain the stated fruit from the stated time. || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Śrī Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete tantra known as the *Śrīkādimatā* among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
The eighth chapter, dedicated to the elucidation of the ritual procedure for the Bhagamālinī-nityā-vidyā, is fully completed and concluded. || 8 ||
The number of verses in the eighth [chapter] is sixty-three;
furthermore, the diagrams and those following the commentary have been observed to consist of one hundred and eighty-five verses.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Now, O Pārvatī, hear of the fourth among the sixteen Nityās;
the ritual procedure for Nityaklinnā and her mantra have already been declared previously.
Its limbs, that meditation, its powers, and worship by means of them; the varieties of fire-offerings and libations, as well as the mystical diagrams according to their different fruits. || 2 ||
O Supreme Goddess, I shall explain everything in its proper sequence as it has been taught:
the Heart-mantra is declared by means of the first syllable of the mantra.
Then, with two [syllables] for the citizens, two for each of the following, and two for the pair [of gates],
one should perform the remaining limbs and place them on the hands in sequence.
In the Tantra, the six-limbed mantra is taught; one should place it on both hands, starting from the base of the thumbs and ending at the tips of the little fingers, moving upwards.
Having placed the remainder upon the two palms, one should apply the colored powder (varṇaka) to the heart, the two shoulders along with the hymn of praise,
and to the skin, the banner, the anus, and the feet.
Now begins the ninth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding eighth chapter the ritual procedure for the third *bhagamālinī-nityā-vidyā*, [the author] next [teaches] that of the fourth, the *nityaklinnā-nityā-vidyā*.

He teaches the ritual procedure. Then, by means of the ninth chapter consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "from the body" (*vigrahāditaḥ*), he does so. Therein, with two and a half verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "the Supreme Goddess" (*parameśvarī*), he indicates the subjects of the chapter. Therein...

The mantra is that which was previously mentioned; the remainder of the sense is "in the third chapter. "Together with them" refers to the retinue of Śaktis; the remainder of the sense is "the collection of objects already specified. || 2 ||

With the words "by the first," and so forth, he teaches the sequence for the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) through the three and a half verses beginning with that. Among those, [the first two] are by means of two syllables of the *vidyā*;
the remaining five are applied in sequence. Therein, [he begins] with the verse starting "the six limbs," and so on.
(163) She is ruddy, resembling the dawn, wearing ruddy garments, anointed with ruddy blood, and her lotus-face bears a beautiful smile. || 7 ||
Her face shines with three eyes, and she is resplendent with drops of perspiration like pearls upon her forehead; she bears the crescent moon shimmering on the Mandara flower as her crest-ornament.
Seated upon a lotus, languid with intoxication, she holds in her four arms a noose, a goad, a drinking vessel, and the gesture of fearlessness.
Having meditated thus, one should daily worship Klinnānityā with her own powers;
the powers Kṣobhiṇī, Mohinī, and Līlā reside at the corners of the triangle.
Nityā, Nirañjanā, Klinnā, Kledinī, Sadanāturā, Madadravā,
and Drāviṇī— by this arrangement, they reside upon the eight petals.
Madāvilā, Maṅgalā, Manmathārtā, and Manasvinī;
Mohā, Amodā, Mānamayī, Māyā, Mandā, and Manovatī. (12)
Seated in a square formation, they are to be worshipped; their eyes are unsteady and reddened with passion.
They are eternally centered, possessing uniform forms, colors, arms, and weapons. || 13 ||

The meaning of the verse ending with "having placed" (*nyastvā*), which contains one additional quarter-verse, has already been explained by us previously. [The locations are: on the skin (*tvaci*)—that is, on all the limbs; on the banner (*dhvaje*)—that is, on the penis; on the anus (*pāyau*)—that is, on the rectum; and on the two feet—one syllable each, as is understood from the context. || 5 ||

With the three verses beginning with "aruṇām" and ending with "madālasām," he teaches the visualization for the daily worship of the Goddess through these stanzas [and the sequence for the six-limbed ritual placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*)]. Therein, she is described as having four arms, arranged in order from the upper left to the left and right. (7, 8, 9)

With these four verses beginning with *dhyātvaivaṃ* and ending with *anvitāḥ*, he teaches the powers (*śakti*) of that enclosure. Among them, there is one power called *moha* and another called *āmodā*. (10, p.
164) Having constructed two squares joined by doors facing east and west, [one should proceed].
In the center of that is an eight-petaled lotus, and in the center of that likewise is a triangle.

Having prepared the *arghya* with the two root-mantras of the six limbs, he, facing east, should worship her; and within the square, he should worship her starting from the west and ending at the southwest (*nirṛti*). || 15 ||
One should worship those ten [deities] at the sides of the doors, in the corners, and in the cardinal directions;
then, within that [area], on the eight petals starting from the west, one should proceed clockwise.
One should worship those eight Śaktis located within the inner triangles;
then, according to the prescribed rule, one should worship the three Śaktis starting from the front and proceeding clockwise.
In the region situated at the center of the pericarp-source, one should worship the six limbs in sequence in the directions of Vāyu, Īśa, Agni, Nirṛti, and the eastern direction.
Then one should invoke that goddess Nityaklinnā and worship her with ritual offerings, and present the sacrificial oblation (bali) as before.
One should recite the vidyā one thousand or perhaps one hundred times before that;
then, having worshipped Śivā, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the prescribed sequence.
With the verse beginning "two squares" (caturasradvayam), he teaches the wheel for the daily worship of the Goddess;
the implication is that one should worship it after having easily constructed that wheel. || 14 ||

With these eight verses beginning with "arghyam" and ending with "caret," he teaches the sequence for the daily worship of the Goddess; therein, the phrase "facing east" is common to all [the following].

Regarding the phrase "on the sides of the doors," this is what is meant: one should worship the ten powers, beginning with Madāvilā and the others, in the square [mandala], starting from the southern side-chamber of the western door and proceeding toward the directions of Vāyu, Soma, and Īśāna; and on the northern and southern sides of the eastern door, in the directions of Agni, Yama, and Nirṛti.

"From the west onwards in a clockwise direction," beginning from the foremost goddess and proceeding in a circumambulatory manner; this is common to all the powers (śaktis) of the entire retinue. "Those three, Nityā and the others, and Kṣobhiṇī and the others," [are to be worshipped] "according to the prescribed rule," meaning in the sequence already described. 16–17.

The sequence for the worship of the six limbs (aṅga) and the enclosures (āvaraṇa), beginning with Vāyu and Īśa, is common to all procedures for the worship of the six limbs, such as the offering of the arghya water and so forth. [This is performed] before the deity; the phrase "with sixteen services" (upacāra) is to be understood as the remainder; as previously stated.
With the sixteen-syllable mantra and the Kurukullā-vidyā (p.

165), one should offer oblations of clarified butter poured over grain, or with fragrant flowers, according to the previously stated number; having completed that in the same manner as before, [one should proceed]. || 21 ||
Then, having worshipped that Goddess and dissolved her into one's own self as before,
and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) and recited the pair of hymns, one should conduct oneself as being absorbed in her.
O Goddess, listen as I shall explain the proper means of accomplishing the vidyā, which bestows the desired fruit, so that it may become fit for practical application. (23)

Having conquered the senses and subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), one devoted to the worship at the three junctions of the day should perform the recitation (japa) of one hundred thousand [mantras] as before, and should likewise perform the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa) consisting of one-tenth of that amount. || 24 ||
One should offer libations with water scented with Madhūka flowers smeared with honey, or with Bakula flowers, or likewise with water perfumed with camphor, sandalwood, and musk.

Therefore, one who is fit for constant practice, devoted to daily worship, and a reciter of the mantra a thousand times, being a devotee of Him, should perform what has been prescribed and not otherwise.

The meaning is that the offering of the *bali* is performed at the beginning and the end. (19) According to the stated sequence; the meaning is that one should perform the "mouth of fire" (*agnimukha*) and so forth as before. (20) With *andhas*—that is, with food—as before, according to the sequence of the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
The "specified number" refers to the number constituting one-tenth of the recitation (*japa*); that is the oblation (*havana*). (21) Having worshipped.
With the root-vidyā, as before, one effects the internal union with the nature of light.

The pair of hymns consists of five verses and twelve verses respectively. This recitation of the pair of hymns is common to all the Nityās. Being identical with that, one is as previously described. 22.

With these four verses beginning with "of the vidyā" and ending with "otherwise," he teaches the method for the preliminary practice (puraścaraṇa) of the vidyā. Among those, [the first] is "from which means" (yataḥ sādhanataḥ). || 23 ||

Devoted to worship at the three junctions of the day, intent on adoration according to the *Lalitāsādhana*, he should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times as before, following the sequence of one hundred thousand syllables appropriate for the current age. (24)

With the verse beginning "With Madhūka flowers," etc., he describes, in due order, the materials for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), the fire-oblation (*homa*), and the libation (*tarpaṇa*). In that context, the remainder [of the sentence] is: "one should offer oblations with Madhūka flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), that is, sprinkled with the three sweets. [This refers to] the aforementioned applications.

By the passage beginning with "constantly devoted to daily worship" (*nityārcanānirata*), this is what is meant: even after the *puraścaraṇa* rite, the practitioner who is constantly devoted to daily worship, who recites [the mantra] a thousand times every day, who is devoted to the teacher of the *vidyā*, and who is skilled in the ritual applications (*prayoga*) and so forth—[only such a one succeeds], and not otherwise; this applies universally to all deities. || 26 ||
By performing a fire sacrifice with red lotuses smeared with the three sweets, one shall obtain Lakṣmī;
likewise, by means of red night-lotuses, one shall bring women under one's control. (27)
By offering oblations of milk from a white cow that has a calf of similar appearance,
along with jasmine, mālatī, jātī, and śatapatra flowers, [the desired result] shall come to pass.
Through an oblation of *āragvadha* flowers smeared with honey, one attains fame, mastery of knowledge, health, good fortune, victory, and so forth. (29)
The attainment of gold, the paralyzing of an enemy, or even the quelling of the anger of kings and others,
is achieved by offering oblations of red karavīra flowers smeared with clarified butter.
Red garments, subjugation of women, kings, and mortals, as well as success in ornaments, vehicles, and trade, are his desired goals. (31)
Then, by means of a fire-oblation (homa) of white or other mustard seeds mixed with salt,
soaked in that same oil, one shall bring the desired bride at midnight.
If one offers oblations at night with black datura flowers smeared with oil,
the enemy will certainly suffer from intense pain and fever within a month.

By performing a fire-oblation at night with the seeds of the *āruṣkara* tree smeared with clarified butter, wounds shall appear upon the body of the enemy that are difficult for physicians to cure. (34)
Indeed, by those very [embers] set ablaze, the enemy goes to the abode of Yama;
likewise even with charcoal seeds sprinkled with that oil.

With these six verses beginning with "padmaiḥ" and ending with "vadhūm," he teaches the attainment of various fruits through various types of *homa* (fire-offerings). In that context, "of one with a calf of similar form" means of one with a white calf. [Verses 27–31]
Or else, in the alternative case, with other black [seeds], namely mustard seeds smeared with that oil—that is, smeared with the oil of two types of mustard seeds. || 32 ||

With these three verses beginning with "tailāktaiḥ" and ending with "apīti," he teaches the fire-oblation (homa) for the purpose of subduing enemies; therein, through the oblation of their seeds—that is, the seeds of *āruṣkara*—the aforementioned result is attained.

By performing a fire-oblation at night for one month with black pepper soaked in mustard oil and clarified butter, one will certainly bring the desired woman, who is afflicted by the fever of passion, under one's control. (36)
By offering oblations at night for seven times with black pepper and mustard seeds,
along with *dhairya*, *māna*, and *kulāni*, one shall always bring back a bride who is otherwise difficult to obtain.

One should daily offer oblations with food and clarified butter, either one hundred and eight times or simply one hundred; by that, O Dear One, the world becomes filled with food and one becomes its enjoyer. (38)
By offering oblations of śāli rice mixed with clarified butter, one shall obtain a house;
by offering mung beans with ghee, one obtains mung beans; and by offering desired items with clarified butter, one's desires shall be fulfilled.

One should offer as an oblation at night an effigy made from the wood of the tree belonging to the victim's constellation, or fashioned from flour mixed with the dust of the victim's feet, or produced from long pepper, black pepper, and salt.
From the two forefeet, the two shanks, the two knees, the pair of thighs, from below the navel, from the heart, and likewise separately from the neck; || 41 ||
Having cut [the head] with a very sharp sword in due order,
men, women, and kings likewise performed twelve oblations.
