one should then place two [conjunctions] within an eight-cornered figure between the two circles.

With the two and a half verses beginning with *āsām* and ending with *vidhānakam*, he provides the instruction on meditation for the fifteen *Nityās* in their mutual relationship as primary and secondary (*aṅgi-aṅga*) within the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites, and concludes what has been stated. In that regard, they are of such a nature...
The women are of eternal and incomparable form; at other times, they are individually engaged in their respective worship as the presiding deities (*aṅgin*).
[Verses 58–59] That which was taught in the *Paṭala* [of the *Guhyasamāja*], and that which was taught in the *Dhyānapaṭala*, is thus according to the manner described. [Verse 60]

With the first half-verse beginning with "vidyā" and ending with "mantrakāḥ," he teaches the distinction between *vidyā* and *mantra* by means of a question. In that context, those whose deity is feminine are *strīdaivatyāḥ*; those whose deity is masculine are *puṃdaivatyāḥ*. (61–62)
With these five and a half verses beginning with "Again" (*punar*) and ending with "without remainder" (*aśeṣataḥ*),
he teaches sixteen yantras. Among them, for this Vahnivāsinī Nityā-vidyā, there are eight unenclosed syllables.
Having formed the syllables Oṃ, Ha, Ra, Va, Na, Sa, Pa, and Ma, one should place eight letters within each of those, with the eight [remaining] in the center.
Having joined Māyā with the name, one should enclose it with the Tāra (Oṃ). (65)
One should write those letters in groups of ten within the intervals between the ends;
indeed, one should write the fifty [letters] according to their respective functions in the manner previously described.
In the intervals between the verses, as before, the letters from 'a' to 'kṣa' are placed;
in this way, sixteen yantras are produced by them in their proper sequence.
With those yantras, one should constantly accomplish every desired object in its entirety;
first, [one should prepare] in a shallow pan (kharpara) that which is joined with the root-mantra of Raktavahni.

Having ground vermilion with its juice and combined it with the juice of *dhattūra*, one who performs the recitation should write [the name] and heat it over charcoal from the *khadira* tree at night. (69)

Whether it be a woman, a man, a king, or another person who approaches by the power of that [mantra], one should, as before, draw [the figure] on copper or bell-metal using that deity's [mantra]. (70)

The meaning is that there are eight non-repeated syllables. In all cases, the vowels are taken as uncombined. Regarding the vowels, their non-repetition is according to their class (*varga*); regarding the consonants, it is according to the individual letter (*akṣara*).
This is the convention everywhere. Then, "a pair" refers to the pair [of circles] within the octagon and the circle.

"Having done"—this is the meaning. || 64 || "With *tāra*," that is, with the *praṇava*. || 65 || "Those," as before; "by them," that is, by those syllables modified by vowels; "in a clockwise direction. The sequence for the construction of the *yantra* is as follows: having produced two circles with an interval of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) by means of a rotation according to the desired measurement, [one should draw] an eight-cornered figure (*aṣṭakoṇa*) in their center as before.

Having drawn two circles within that [space] and having written the first eight [syllables] in those eight corners, proceeding clockwise from the tip [of each], one should write the *hṛllekhā* in the very center—
accompanied by the name as before and encircled by the *praṇava*— within the space between the inner circles.
Having written the five syllables of the elements corresponding to the [specific] karma ten times each,
one should write the fifty-one syllables from *a* to *kṣa* in a clockwise direction starting from the front on the outer circular path; this is the first [circle].

The Yantra: In the eight corners of this very [yantra], one should write eight sets of eight syllables each, consisting of the eight syllables following the eight modified syllables derived from the vowels of the mantra written previously in succession. By this, sixteen yantras are produced.
One should accomplish what is desired by means of those [mantras]. || 69 ||
O Īśvarī, by heating that [substance] as well, the previously mentioned fruit shall arise.
Having written the second [mantra] on a skull-bowl (kharpara), one should heat it at night. (71)
A woman who transgresses the laws of her birth and conduct becomes submissive;
having written the third [syllable] right there, one should heat it at night. (72)
With disheveled hair, afflicted by the fever of enmity, she [should be visualized] for a moment in the cremation fire;
likewise, the couple should be burned in a fire-chamber made of neem wood.

Having ground it with mercury, written [the mantra], and heated it over a fire, one should then cast it into a cremation ground at the prescribed time; with a mind full of wrath, one should recite [the mantra] against enemies.
One who is agitated by that very mantra becomes an enemy afflicted by a piśāca;
one should write the fourth [mantra] on a black cloth or a dark garment. (75)
One should bury it there as before during the night, according to the stated procedure;
within seven days, the enemy, afflicted by a burning fever, goes to the abode of Yama.
Alternatively, on the fifth or the sixth day, one should write the names of two [enemies] upon two skull-cups using a pen made from the wing of an owl or a crow. (77)
One should bury two [images] as before in a cremation ground or on both banks of a river;
then, by means of the water of a river that is full to the brim, there will be mutual hatred between those two.

By means of the thirty-three and a half verses beginning with "prathamam" and ending with "bhuvi," [the author] describes the methods of suppression (*nigraha*) using six yantras— the third, fourth, fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth— among the sixteen yantras previously mentioned.

With the eleventh [chapter], he teaches restraints and favors; with the remaining [chapters], he teaches auspicious and inauspicious [results]. Therein, "in that rasa" means in the rasa of red fire (*raktavahni*). "Red fire" is the name for *raktacitraka*. "In the charcoal of khadira" means in the charcoal of khadira fuel. (69) "By that" refers to the previously mentioned substance. In this entire section, everywhere...
If the substance is not specified, [the rite] is performed on khadira embers. (70–73) At the prescribed time, it is done as before. (74) "In black garments" connects with what precedes.
(75) As before, having written the name on a board of śiṃśapā wood according to the rule on the seventh [day], (p. 202) [one should proceed].
Having placed it within a skull, one should bury it in a cremation ground at night. || 79 ||
At the previously mentioned time, the enemy shall be seized by piśācas;
having placed the eighth [syllable] in a skull-bowl (kharpara), one should bury it at the enemy's door at night.
Within seven days, the enemy shall depart from that house, driven away elsewhere;
having fashioned the ninth [syllable] into a ring of gold on an auspicious day.

In a Siddha-yoga, at an auspicious lagna, or indeed during the rising of Jupiter (Dhiṣaṇa), a person is liberated from sufferings such as malevolent spells, untimely death, disease, and the like. || 82 ||
Having placed the tenth [tablet] upon a cloth, one should deposit it somewhere within the house and worship it for the pacification of dangers such as falling stones.
Likewise, by the recitation of this [dhāraṇī], those afflicted by spirits and seizing demons shall be protected.
On the eleventh day, one should write it upon birch bark with the liquid of sandalwood and camphor.
Having formed that [liṅga] into a pill according to the sequence previously described, one should then place it upon a liṅga made of white beeswax and worship it once more.
One should place it in the midst of honey and worship it daily at the junctions of the day (sandhyās) with very white, fragrant flowers, according to the prescribed rite.
Within a month, half a month, or at the end of seven days, enemies will certainly become afflicted with disease; by means of that ghee, they shall attain health. 87.
Those afflicted by fever will especially find relief without effort;
when situated in sour sauvīra, it creates enmity between two enemies.

With neem juice and so forth. (76) Regarding the two machines; regarding the two persons to be incited to hatred. (77) Here too, the writing material consists of neem juice and so forth. This very [material] is the substance to be used whenever no specific substance is mentioned in this section on suppression. (78) (79) (80)
By speaking of that very thing, one may even cause disease to arise in those two.
Dry ginger, black pepper, and long pepper, finely ground into a powder— (89)
One should place them, mixed with the juice of the *lakuca* fruit, into its center;
one should heat it at the three junctions of the day where the enemy’s face is directed.
At the prescribed time, [the enemy] will be afflicted by fevers, accompanied by burning sensations and thirst.
Having written the twelfth [syllable] in a skull-cup with the juice of a night-blooming plant, one should then [proceed as follows].
Having placed it between a pair of bricks, one should join it firmly;
then one should install it either in a temple of Caṇḍikā or in a shrine of the Teacher (Śāstṛ).
By placing [the image] within the wall of one's own house, or even by installing it upon a bed, one may paralyze the anger, the exertion, or the very thoughts of an enemy. (93)
Legal disputes, debts, and whatever else is detrimental to her well-being—
by wearing this [amulet] made of birch bark as the thirteenth [item], a woman quickly overcomes them through its power of retention.
Even a barren woman obtains a son by means of this wondrous power of the yantra;
having written the name of one who has gone to the fourteen worlds upon birch bark, [she should place it] at a crossroads.
Having placed it in the middle of a sieve, one should heat it at midnight;
within seven days, women, men, or kings will come under one's control.

Elephants, horses, deer, and whatever other living beings dwell upon the earth—by means of their names joined with another [name] and indeed inscribed on a wooden board (phalaka)—[they are liberated]. || 97 ||

The arising of *dhiṣaṇā* is as before; "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative case. (82, 83, 84) In "consisting of white wax," that is, consisting of white beeswax; "that [is] the *liṅga*" is the ellipsis. (85, 86, 87, 88) "In that very place" refers to sour *sauvīra*. (89, 90) "With the juice of night" means with the juice of turmeric. (91, 92, 93, 94, 95, 96)
Through the honoring and beholding of it, women shall experience an easy delivery;
likewise, by writing the name on the sixteenth [day] and wearing it, the same occurs for living beings. (98)
It provides protection everywhere from the fear of planetary influences, diseases, and so forth;
having placed that very [mantra] upon a gold plate according to the prescribed rite, || 99 ||
Then, one may wear [the mantra] on finger-rings, armlets, ornaments, and so forth, or upon the head;
thereby, one becomes liberated from mental and physical ailments, free from rivals, and has conquered the senses. (100)
He shall be the enjoyer and the recipient of merits, and live for a hundred years on earth; thus has the pervasion consisting of the principle of the womb (yonitattva) been correctly described. 101.
By the churning of this [wisdom], that very reality has been made one's own within the mind.
Thus ends the eleventh chapter of the complete *Kādimata*, known as the *Śrīkādimata*, among the sixteen *Nityātantras*. 11.

By another [verse], the fifteenth. (97) Here, in this section on favor (*anugraha*), when no specific material is mentioned, it refers to gold situated in the word "paṭīra" and so forth; [it is] engraved upon a golden plate. (98–99) Mental anguish is *ādhi*. Here, the twelfth verse is a six-line *gāthā*. (101)

Thus, in the *Manoramā*, so named, composed by the venerable Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, [a commentary] on the complete *Tantra* known as the venerable *Kādimata*, among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
In this commentary, the eleventh chapter, which is dedicated to elucidating the ritual procedure for the *nityā-vidyā* of Bhagamālinī, has been fully examined. 11.

The number of verses is sixteen thousand; with commentaries, it shall be more than half [of that], namely sixty-four thousand. Having observed this, everything has been declared in the eleventh chapter.
The Twelfth Chapter. Now, I shall describe the ritual procedure for that which is proclaimed as the seventh among the sixteen Nityās; listen to it, for it accomplishes all aims.

The Vidyā consisting of twelve syllables has already been declared previously; now [its] limbs, the ritual placement of the letters (lipinyāsa), the meditation, and worship with the Śaktis shall be described. || 2 ||

I shall describe in its entirety, according to the prescribed rule and in the stated sequence, the means of accomplishment, the rites of fire-oblation, and the diagrams for all purposes, along with their various results.
Having encased each pair, then one, then two, then two, and finally two,
with *māyā*, one should perform the six limbs in their proper sequence.
One should perform the placement (nyāsa) with ten syllables of the mantra, each encased by the Śakti-mantra,
in sequence upon the eyes, ears, nose, speech, chest, navel, and private parts.
She is red in color, clad in red garments, adorned with red perfumes, garlands, and ornaments;
she has four arms, three eyes, and is radiant with a crown of rubies.
Now begins the twelfth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding eleventh chapter the ritual procedure for the mantra of the sixth Vahnivāsinī Nityā, [the author] next [teaches that of] the seventh.

He teaches the ritual procedure for the *mahāvajreśvarīnityā* mantra with the twelfth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "for the attainment" (*avāptaye*). Therein,
he indicates the subjects of the chapter with three verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "according to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*).
In that regard, it has already been [stated] previously in the third chapter. 1 | 2 | 3.
With the two verses beginning with "dvayam" and ending with "kramāt," he teaches the sequence of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

In that context, for each [syllable], the remainder is "on the head and on the *śikhā*. By "with *māyā*" is meant with *hṛllekhā*. The "limbs" are the heart and so forth. "In sequence, joined with the *jātis*" means by means of the ten [syllables] enclosed by *śakti*, that is, enclosed by *hṛllekhā*.
In the speech, chest, navel, and private parts—excluding the two *hṛllekhās*—there is one [syllable] each; this is the remainder. "Private part" (*guhya*) refers to the organ of generation. 4, 5.
With these five verses beginning with "raktām" and ending with "nāyikām," he teaches the visualization for the daily worship of the Goddess together with her retinue. (p.
206) [She holds] a noose, a goad, a bow of sugarcane, and likewise a pomegranate as an arrow.
Holding [the world] with her arms and eyes that are exceedingly cool with supreme compassion. || 7 ||
She beholds the practitioner seated comfortably in the center of the wheel— within the city of the earth, the lotus, the hexagon, and the triangle— with her lotus-face smiling.

She is surrounded by her own powers (śaktis) who are identical with her own nature, seated upon a lion-throne situated in the middle of a boat, with her own powers swaying and standing firmly on all sides.
I meditate upon the Mistress of Mantras, who dwells in the crimson ocean, constantly providing diversions through various narratives and the coming and going of beings. (10)
There, the powers of will, knowledge, and action reside in the triangle;
the Ḍākinīs and others reside in the hexagon, situated upon the twelve petals of the lotus.
Hṛllekhā, Kledinī, Klinnā, Kṣobhiṇī, Madanāturā, Nirañjanā, Rāgavatī, and likewise Madanāvatī. (12)
Mekhalā, Drāviṇī, and Vegavatī are the twelve Śaktis.
Thereafter, O Ambikā, hear of the Śaktis residing upon the sixteen petals.
To Kamalā, Kāminī, Kalpā, and Kalā, who are filled with wonder;
to Kirātā, who destroys time, to Kauśikā, and to Kambuvāhinī.
The arrangement of the weapons proceeds from the upper left hand to the lower right hand, following the sequence:

left, right, left, and right. (6–7) [This is done] within the great city of the lotus, which consists of a triangle and a hexagon, in the center of the wheel. This is what is meant: having first fashioned a vulva (*yoni*) consisting of three equal lines.

Outside of that, having fashioned a hexagon according to one's preference, and outside of that, having prepared a twelve-spoked yantra and twelve lotuses, and outside of that, having made a sixteen-petalled lotus,
one should construct two equal squares provided with gates in the four directions; therein is the wheel.
One should meditate upon her as seated comfortably. || 8 || 9 || In the "ruddy ocean," that is, in the crimson ocean. || 10 ||

With these seven verses beginning with "icchā" and ending with "yajet," he teaches the attendant powers (parivāra-śakti) of the Goddess; therein, those situated in the hexagon are arranged in the order starting from the southwest (nairṛtya). || 11 ||
*Madanāturā* and *Madanā*—these two are the powers (*śakti*) known as *Madanāturā*. (12–13) *Kalitākautuke* and *Kalitā Kautukā*—these two are the powers.
[She who is] *Kātarā*, *Kapaṭā*, *Kīrtikumārī*, and also *Kuṅkumā*. (p. 207)
And now listen in due order to the Śaktis who abide in the square. || 15 ||
Jambhikā, named Veginī, Capalā, and the virtuous Peśalā;
Rati, Śraddhā, and the high-minded Bogalobhamadonmattā. || 16 ||
O Great Goddess, one should mutter these twelve [syllables] all around the square, situated in the cardinal directions, the gates (or sides), and the intermediate directions (and so forth). 17.
Having prepared the *arghya* in the manner previously described using the *aṅga* and *mūla* mantras,
he should then worship the crimson ocean, the golden boat, and immediately thereafter the lion-throne.
There, having invoked the Discus and then the Goddess as before,
one should worship them with their names placed within the seven-syllable *māyā* mantra along with the *śaktis*.
Thereafter, one should offer the bali-oblation with the previously mentioned seven-syllable mantra,
and perform the fire sacrifice (homa) for the goddess Kurukullā according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with red flowers smeared with ghee, or with ghee alone;
one should conclude it as before. Thus has your worship been described.

*Kālakadanā* and *Kālākadanā*—these two [are placed] at the gates situated in the directions; that is, on the sides of the gates. First, on the sides of the four gates starting from the west, and subsequently in the intermediate directions starting from the northwest (vāyu). || 14 || 15 || *Madonmattā* and *Madonmattā*—these two [are placed] at the gates situated in the directions; that is, on the sides of the gates. First, on the sides of the four gates starting from the west, and subsequently in the intermediate directions starting from the northwest (vāyu). || 16 || The meaning is "situated in the directions," which refers to the gates. The phrase "on the sides" is to be understood as "on the sides of the gates.
One should worship by proceeding in a clockwise direction. In all the enclosures (āvaraṇas), one should perform the worship starting from the front and moving clockwise. || 17 ||

With these four verses beginning with *kṛtvā* and ending with *samīritam*, he teaches the sequence of the Goddess’s daily worship (*nityapūjā*). In that context, "of the aforementioned form" means endowed with the meditative visualization (*bhāvanā*) consisting of fire, moon, and sun, and so forth. "The crimson ocean" (*śoṇābdhi*) refers to the red sea. || 18 ||

In that context, the ellipsis is "seated upon the lion-throne. As before, by means of the *trikhaṇḍā* mudrā and so forth, [the deities are invoked] with the seven-syllabled *māyā* mantra placed in the middle and joined with the seven-syllabled *hṛllekhā* mantra.
This same sequence for joining the mantras applies to Śoṇasāgara and the others as well, using the seven-syllabled *māyā*.

In all cases where no specific [mantra] is mentioned for the *bali* offering, one should offer the *bali* with the *vidyā* of Kurukullā and others. This is accepted here according to the prescribed rule (20). As before, it is because of the union with one's own self through the form of radiant energy (21).

In the spring or summer season, beginning from the full moon, one should practice the sādhana while subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), consuming only milk, or else eating fruits and roots. (22)
Having bathed in fragrant waters, pure and clad in crimson garments, his body was anointed with moon-like sandalwood and saffron, appearing rosy in hue. || 23 ||
With his pair of eyes anointed with collyrium and his face reddened by betel, he held a crescent of the moon to his mouth; joyful in heart, he had conquered his senses. (24)

Remaining silent during the three daily worship services, having accomplished his practice through formal resolve, eating only at night from the remnants of the oblation, he should recite the vidyā with a concentrated mind. (25)

One who possesses devotion should recite the vidyā constantly, and one who possesses devotion should feed those who are devoted to worship and eager for service with sweet milk-rice (pāyasa), provided it is not deficient in the three [qualities]. 26.
Having prostrated and worshipped [the deity], one should always bid them farewell on those specific days;
however, having approached the preceptor (Guru-jīva), the self-possessed person should prostrate repeatedly.
Having gratified him with wealth, grain, clothing, and other gifts, and with his permission, one should begin the undertaking and worship him constantly with devotion. (28)
And having gratified him with mental offerings and hymns of praise, one becomes successful; yet one must avoid stinginess regarding wealth, pride, hypocrisy, and falsehood. (29)
One should never do so, especially in the presence of the Guru.
Having thus recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times, one should offer oblations with clarified butter ten times that number.

With these eleven and a half verses beginning with "In the spring season" and ending with "the practitioner," he teaches the prescription of qualities common to the accomplishment of all vidyās. Among those, "one who eats sacrificial food" (haviṣyāśaḥ) is one whose diet consists of cooked rice-grains from which salt has been removed. 22, 23, 24.

Having accomplished the means for his resolve, having performed the sequence appropriate to his own vow; [he approached] those who are constantly devoted to worship out of a longing for devotion. On those days—the days of the *puraścaraṇa*—at the conclusion, that is, at the end of the *puraścaraṇa*, with five verses of praise, he [addressed] that guru, [free from] hypocrisy.
And with the blossoms of the *āragvadha*, the flowers produced from the *bakula*, those born of the *madhūka*, or the *campaka*—anointed with the three sweets—one should [worship] constantly. (31)
A devoted and steadfast worshipper should satisfy [the deity] with waters rendered fragrant by moonlight, sandalwood, musk, and saffron, for as long as the day lasts. || 32 ||
Thus, having perfected the mantra, the practitioner— devoted to the guru, performing daily duties, and endowed with firm resolve— should accomplish the rites for specific desires.

O Śivā, he who has performed a thousand recitations, whose intellect is steady, who knows the potency of mantras, and who possesses self-mastery— he alone may perform rites for desired objects, and not otherwise.
If one should act out of ignorance, delusion, or even restlessness, one will certainly encounter misfortunes, the destruction of one's efforts, and suffering. (35)
One should perform a fire sacrifice with reddish lotuses soaked in the three sweets;
from this mandala, one obtains great fortune and a praiseworthy form.
From the full moon day until that same [third] day, one should daily offer one thousand beautiful, fully blossomed *kahlāra* flowers sprinkled with honey, with constant devotion.
On each of those aforementioned days, one should feed [the guests] according to the prescribed form;
and until the end of the fire-oblation, one should perform recitations (japa) as many times as the number of oblations (homa) that have been offered.

The fulfillment of the false nature [of the mantra]. || 29 || Because of the specific injunction "three hundred thousand," the meaning is that one should recite exactly three hundred thousand [times]. || 30 || 31 || "To that extent" means by a tenth part. "Daily" means every day. Here, in this procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), everything stated constitutes the *puraścaraṇa* for all vidyās.
32. Thus, in the manner described; 33. thus.

With the first half-verse and the following verse—beginning with "gurubhakta" and ending with "niścitam"—he teaches, by means of these two verses, that [the practitioner] is fit for the ritual application even without prior preparatory rites (*puraścaraṇa*), as well as the transgression incurred by acting otherwise. In this context, "otherwise" (*anyathā*) means "not possessing such qualities. || 34 || 35 ||

With twenty-seven verses beginning with *aruṇaiḥ* and ending with *bhavet*, [it is taught that] through various substances such as oblations and so forth—specifically by performing one thousand offerings of *campaka* flowers mixed with honey (*kṣaudra*)—the result is certain. (p. 210)
One obtains a hundred gold niṣkas within a month, as before. || 39 ||
Likewise, by offering three thousand *pāṭala* flowers drenched in ghee on the new moon and other such days,
one obtains variegated garments.
For a month, he obtains fragrant substances such as camphor and sandalwood, along with other pleasing articles suitable for enjoyment. (41)
One should offer a hundred oblations of rice grains sprinkled with milk on the seventh lunar days;
by that, there will undoubtedly be an abundance of rice within six months.
By offering oblations of sesame seeds on that day, one shall obtain freedom from disease for a year;
likewise, one should offer oblations with dūrvā grass on the three days of one's own birth.
Free from fear and possessing great enjoyment, he lives for a hundred years;
or one may offer oblations with *guḍūcī*, sesame, and *dūrvā* grass during three lifetimes.

By means of those [offerings], one shall become a possessor of longevity, prosperity, fame, enjoyments, merit, hidden treasures, and so forth, through oblations of ghee, milk-rice, and milk offered respectively in those three [fires]. (45)
Likewise, by honoring the king with longevity, health, and wealth, one becomes respected;
and by performing a homa of plantains on the seventh lunar day, one obtains good fortune and is well-supported.
It teaches the attainment of various kinds of fruits; therein, the mandalas are as before. || 36 ||
"From that day until the full moon day" (v. 37) means: on those respective days, which are the days for all ritual applications (*prayoga*).
"Those previously mentioned who know the *vidyā*" [should be understood] according to the form described, beginning with "mostly sweet substances" (*madhurasa-prāya*) and so forth;
this is common to all ritual applications. That which was stated as "for that long" (*tāvat*) and so forth is common to all *homa* offerings.

38 || 39 || "From the new moon onwards" (*darśādimāsān*) means from the beginning of the new moon until its end; such is the meaning. 40 || 41 || Regarding the seventh lunar days (*saptamī*), the underlying rationale (*vāsanā*) for this should be understood from the mouth of the Guru, since in the eleventh chapter there is a specific prescription for the worship, fire-oblation (*homa*), and other rites of the *Nityās* on their respective lunar days, and here [it applies] even to the sixth lunar days.
A specific injunction must be made: on that day, the seventh lunar day (saptamī), during one’s own three birth-asterisms— that is,
one’s own birth asterism and the tenth and nineteenth asterisms from it—
one should [perform the rite] with three blades of *dūrvā* grass, each a span (*prādeśa*) in length, combined with the three sweets.
One should offer oblations daily in the Ghorā [fire] during the disease of sannipāta fever.

In cases of major diseases, one should daily perform a fire-oblation with dūrvā grass, sesame seeds, and sprouts of unbroken rice— either all three together or individually— conjoined with the three sweet substances.
Within six months or even a year, one shall be freed from disease and become happy;
on those days, one should constantly recite the vidyā while touching water.
One should perform bathing and drinking with its water one thousand times;
one should also prepare cooked food and other items with that very water for the sake of liberation from disease.
Having ground the tree belonging to the victim's asterism, along with cloves, mustard seeds, and sesame,
one should mix the paste with the dust raised from the footprint of the victim.
Having fashioned a doll with their names written upon its heart,
one should cut that doll as before with sharp iron weapons and offer it as a sacrifice.
In this way, within seven days, or three, or even a single day,
the person to be accomplished— whether firm in resolve or situated far away— will quickly come under one's control.
One should bury such a doll in the earth in the middle of a pit;
having placed a fire on top of it, one should offer oblations there daily with the vidyā.

Likewise, one hundred [times]. Likewise, he becomes free from disease (aroga). || 43 || Free from affliction (nirātaṅka), undisturbed (avyākula). Guḍūcī is Amṛtā. One should offer the three substances beginning with Guḍūcī into the fire in their respective order throughout three births. Or, according to another interpretation, the remainder is that this applies to three births. "In order" means sequentially. || 45 || 46 ||

"With three dūrvās" means with three blades of dūrvā grass; "conjoined with the three sweets" means conjoined with the three sweet substances (honey, sugar, and ghee). Regarding "in cases of great diseases," the so-called "great diseases" are the eight [disorders] beginning with wind (vāta);
"with chinnodbhavas" refers to the amṛtā creepers, with the word "each one" being understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
If one performs [this rite] three thousand times during the night with mustard seeds soaked in that juice, one can forcibly bring a woman from as far as a hundred yojanas away. (55)
One should bury that doll, which is filled with half-wax and upon which the rite of enlivening (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) has been performed, in a cremation ground at night.
Having cut off the womb of the victim right there and offered the bali-oblation,
one who has performed the consecration (abhiṣeka) should then mutter that vidyā three hundred times.

If the Arāti [Yoga] occurs in the eighth house, it is certain that one will meet destruction within eight months through various kinds of diseases and afflictions caused by spirits and the like. || 58 ||
If, having extracted it from within, one should dig for it in the water at night, he is liberated from those afflictions and lives happily upon the earth. (59)
Having placed that [image]— which has been prepared with the tree of the person to be accomplished and immersed in mustard oil and ghee—
into the midst of water, one should boil it for the number of days prescribed.
An enemy afflicted by a severe fever will become happy as before once [the rite] is performed;
likewise, one should bury that very [image], accompanied by an offering, in the house of Caṇḍikā.
If the person to be targeted is a man or a woman, one should dig in the temple of the Teacher;
when accompanied by that same procedure, the enemy shall become insane. (62)

By the three [herbs] beginning with *dūrvā* combined together; or, in the alternative view (*pakṣāntare*), on those days—namely, the days of the practice for counteracting great diseases (49). With their waters—that is, with consecrated water—for food and so forth, such as cooked rice; by those very waters alone (50, 51). By them.
By means of the combined powders of the tree belonging to the asterism of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), and so forth. || 52 || 53 || 54 || 55 ||

"Combined with half of beeswax" means made with the previously mentioned ingredients accompanied by a half-portion of beeswax. "Having performed the consecration," and so forth, refers to the rites to be performed after all the cruel applications (*krūraprayoga*). As for the consecration, it is that of the respective deity.
"By means of the wheel of daily worship" (verse 57). The connection is that one should bury [the effigy] in the eighth house;

in all cases of cruel rites, one should perform them in the eighth house of the person to be targeted (sādhya) (verses 58–59). "That effigy" refers to the one buried in the cremation ground. "This vessel of mustard seeds and clarified butter. "By the stated days" refers to the months and so forth.

60 || Having performed the ritual of placing water as before, [one should take] that very [image] which was fashioned from the tree of the natal asterism of the person to be protected (sādhya); likewise, it should be accompanied by the *bali* offering, specifically the *bali* offering belonging to the *yoni* of the person to be protected. 61 ||
(213) I shall also describe the great vajra, the vajra, and other mechanical devices not previously mentioned;
listen with a concentrated mind as I explain these applications as well. 63.
One should cast twenty lines toward the east, west, and south;
by that, three hundred and sixty-one squares are produced.
In those four corners (once they have been taken up), one should erase with the pentad;
there, forty remain so that the form of a vajra may come to be.
Having cleared four squares in each of the directions, one should form a triangle;
the remaining squares shall be one hundred and sixty-five.
Within those [circles], one should write the syllables of the vidyā, beginning from the east and proceeding all around,
differentiated by the vowels as before, according to the previously stated method.
Out of those one hundred and forty-four,
O Ambikā, twenty-one squares remain as the remainder.
For a man and a woman respectively, [the rites are performed] in the house of Caṇḍikā and the Śāstra, according to their respective injunctions,
beginning with the eighth zodiac sign and so forth.

With the eleven verses beginning with "Mahāvajrām" and ending with "according to the requirements of the task," he teaches the sequence for constructing the *yantras* such as Mahāvajrā. Therein, as before,
the eleven non-repeated syllables are [arranged] according to the previously stated rule by way of a clockwise entry-movement.

Among those one hundred and seventy-six modified vidyā-syllables, the remainder consists of six modified syllables; this is the sense. By the word "and" (ca), it is implied that they are accompanied by the modified vidyā-syllables. The rest is easy to understand. [This refers to] the sequence of writing.
Since this must be obtained through the traditional lineage, the method of drawing it here is as follows:
one should lay down twenty lines each toward the east, west, south, and north, with equal intervals between them.
When this is done, three hundred and sixty-one squares are produced. Among those, in the four directions...
Excluding the four central squares, one should erase seventeen squares each on all sides in the outer row, at every corner. Inside that,
in the second row, as before, one should erase one square each on the sides of the previously discarded squares.

Leaving aside the central square, one should erase thirteen squares on each side toward every corner. Within that, in the third row, as before, leaving one square on each side, one should erase nine squares toward every corner. Inside that, in the fourth row—
As before, omitting one [syllable] at each corner (p.
214), one should write in those [spaces] the six syllables of the *paryāya-nityā* along with the pair of syllables for the *ghaṭikā*, according to the previously stated method of conjunction.
In the remaining [squares], one should write the letters of the alphabet and the vowels in the two sets of twelve that remain;
and in the two enclosures, one should write the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) according to the stated sequence.
One should write the elemental syllables (bhautikārṇa) around the four cardinal directions and the corners;
specifically, three each in the eastern and western corners, following the sequence of two and three.
Having written this down among those previously mentioned and having worshipped it according to the prescribed rite,
one should then recite the mantra three thousand times while touching it.
O Śivā, one should employ [the mantras] in their proper sequence for the tasks as prescribed;
furthermore, one should write down the elemental syllables (bhūtākṣara) according to the requirements of the task.
One should erase five squares in each of the five [sections]. Within that, in the central path, as before, one should erase one square in each corner by skipping one square at a time.
When this is done, there will be one hundred and eighty-one squares, arranged in rows of one and so forth in every direction.
It appears in the form of a vajra through the addition of one square at each side.

Among those, having erased the four squares situated in the first and second rows in the four directions, one should construct a triangle there by supporting it upon the two tips of the penultimate lines. When this has been done:
One hundred and sixty-five squares are seen. Among them,
starting from the wooden beam situated in the middle of the five squares located in the first row,
and proceeding clockwise along the outermost path through one hundred and seventy-six squares:
Having first written thirty-six syllables starting from the beginning among the syllables of the *svaravikṛta* vidyā,
one should likewise write thirty-two syllables above the previously written syllables, starting from the central square within that second row, as before.
Having written twenty-eight syllables above the inscribed letters within that [third path],
one should likewise write twenty-four spokes in the fourth path within that, following the sequence of the unliberated syllables.
Having written as before, having likewise written twenty syllables within that in the fifth row, and having then written four [syllables] within that in the sixth row—
thus totaling one hundred and forty-four syllables— thereafter:
Having inscribed the six syllables of the Nityā-paryāya, which will be described in the twenty-fifth chapter, together with twenty-one letters in sequence upon the thirty-two remaining filaments,
one should thereafter, according to the tradition, place two syllables representing the *yuga*-ghaṭikās upon one [filament].

Having drawn the grid, one should then write the twelve syllables of the mantra— which have not been employed in the ritual— in the twelve squares; then, in the middle of the two remaining syllables written in the two leftover squares, one should place the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) below as before, and [the seed-syllable] above.

Having also inscribed the *sādhaka*’s name, one should write the elemental syllables (*bhūtākṣara*) in the triangles in the four directions, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise in groups of two and three; then, the remaining eleven syllables of the modified mantra (*vikṛtavidyā*), which are known as the "Great Vajra" (*mahāvajra*), are invincible everywhere. (p. 215)
In rites for victory, pillars, hatred, subjugation, and eradication. || 74 ||

One should perform protection for the sake of nourishment and pacification, and likewise for the subjugation of enemies, especially for the establishment of regions, kingdoms, cities, villages, and so forth. (75)
When terrible portents have arisen, one should draw [the design] upon the ground with chalk;
having invoked the Goddess Śivā in the center, one should worship her daily.
During the three *sādhyā* [fortnights], one should likewise perform the *naurājana* rite according to the prescribed sequence;
for a period of three nights, it should be doubled or tripled according to the nature of the desired goal.
When the wealth of kings has been reduced to the city alone due to hostility with enemies,
one should draw a great thunderbolt upon his pavilion.
One should worship the goddess of pure smiles in its center with perfumes and so forth, especially during the junctions of the day (sandhyās), accompanied by dance, song, and other such arts. (79)
Thus, as previously stated by the astrologers, the king shall become victorious either through the destruction of his enemies, or through their defeat, or even through their misfortune. (80)

Then, having cleansed that [mark] and placed it upon his forehead, he should surround the city with his forces; by thus circumambulating the guide (the preceptor) first, he shall live long and happily upon the elephant.
Without rival, free from fear, possessing six limbs, and renowned for its majesty—who indeed could describe the full extent of this Vajra’s power? (82)
One should draw three [squares] each in the east and west, and two and three [squares] respectively in the south and north.

With these nine verses beginning with "Mahāvajra" and ending with "should describe," he teaches the specific applications of the Mahāvajra-yāntra and their respective fruits. Therein, according to the stated sequence—that is, the sequence taught by Lalitā—[the results are obtained] as before within [certain] days. 74, 75, 76, 77, 78, 79. As previously [stated], within the days.
"By means of months and so forth"—the words "having established [it] upon the elephant" are to be supplied. || 80 || 81 ||
Now listen, O beloved, to another procedure for the emanation of the vajra, by means of which, once it is held in the hand, even the *siddhis* come into one's own hands. (83)
One should cast ten lines—eastward, westward, southward, and northward—thereby producing eighty-one squares; that [procedure] is as before.
One should wipe [the area] in the ten corners and likewise draw [lines] in the remaining [spaces];
one should draw triangles in the four directions, and within them, as before, in the same manner.
One should write the letters of the mantra in the remaining [spaces] according to their respective divisions;
in one central space, one should write the Śakti, and in the belly, the object of the rite (sādhya).
And this one should apply at will to those previously mentioned;
however, there is no difference between these two in all ritual applications.
Having given this name "Vajramadhyastha" to the king, and having established it upon his heart and head, he engaged in battle. (88)
It is free from fear and possesses six limbs; the six limbs are known as the minister, the kingdom, the fortress, the treasury, the army, and the ally—these being subordinate to the sovereign.
The rest is easy to understand. 82.

With these four verses beginning with "atha" and ending with "ālikhet," he teaches the manifestation of another vajra. Therein, as before, within those ten corners in the form of a vajra, there are ten squares in each of the four corners.

The meaning is that one should erase [the lines]. Regarding the remaining squares: the meaning is that one should likewise erase one square in each direction. This is to be connected with the phrase "one should draw triangles. These are the syllables of the elements corresponding to the ritual action. In the remaining thirty-seven squares...

The remaining [number] of mantra-syllables is twelve. "In pairs" means two by two. Likewise, starting from the east and proceeding clockwise, one writes within the womb of Śakti, that is, in the center of the *hṛllekhā*. As for the sequence of writing:
having first drawn ten lines each, at equal intervals, running east-west and north-south, therein—

As before, having cleared seven squares in each corner of the outer path, two squares in the second path within that, and one square in the third path within that— thus clearing ten squares in sequence on all sides— and having cleared the four squares situated in the four cardinal directions;
There, having constructed triangles, one should write the elemental syllables within those triangles as before;

then, within those thirty-seven squares, one should write the mantra-syllables two by two in six rotations as before, and in the square located in the very center, one should write the *hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
"One should write"—thus [ends verses] 83, 84, 85, and 86.
Having destroyed the fourfold army of the enemy king, he remains with all his limbs uninjured and free from disease, endowed with fame, prosperity, and wealth. (89)
Having performed this, one may live for a very long time on earth as an enjoyer of pleasures according to one's own will;
having fashioned this upon a copper plate, one should install it for the sake of prosperity.
Having fashioned a hexagon between the two lines, one should place the first and last seed-syllables of the Vidyā within its center and on the outside.
Furthermore, one should draw [the syllables] in the six corners;
one each in the front and rear, two each in the side corners, and again within the circles.
One should write the *mātṛkā* (the alphabet) from 'a' to 'kṣa', accompanied by the nasal dot (*bindu*).
One should write that which is desired for oneself in the center of the central seed-syllable.
Whoever wears this on their arm or neck immediately becomes beloved by young maidens who are afraid of being constrained by a husband. 94.
One should fashion sixteen beautiful lotuses using the syllables of the mantra extended by their respective vowels, each provided with eight petals arranged in a circle. 95.

With these four verses beginning with "etad" and ending with "abhivṛddhaye," he teaches its applications and their results. Among them, the "daṃśaka" is the armor (*kavaca*). The rest is easy to understand. (87, 88, 89)

With these four verses beginning with *vidhāya* and ending with *jāyate*, he teaches the yantra that bestows good fortune (*saubhāgyakara*). In this regard, the following is said: having drawn a hexagon according to the prescribed measurement, one should draw two circles outside the inner circle, with an interval of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) between them.

In this regard, one should perform the encirclement by *hṛllekhā* in the inner path according to tradition, and the encirclement by the letters of the *mātṛkā* in the outer path, proceeding clockwise from the front;
the rest is easy to understand. In this tantra, the encirclement by all *hṛllekhās* is for cruel rites.
One should perform it with a portion of the letter *ra*; elsewhere, one should perform it with a portion of the fourth vowel. || 91 || 92 || 93 || 94 ||
With these six verses beginning with "svaraprasāritaiḥ" and ending with "avāptaye," he teaches sixteen lotuses.
One should write one syllable each upon the pericarp and the petals.
One should place one's desired name in the center of the pericarp of the lotus. || 96 ||
One should constantly employ the syllables joined with the ghaṭikās;
having divided the day and night into sixteen parts, one should apply them to those [intervals]. || 97 ||
Then, one should write all the desired objects within their respective [sections]; one should wear it, consecrate it with water, and recite the mantra for the attainment of the wished-for goal. (98)
By laying down five lines each toward the east, west, south, and north, there shall be sixteen squares; within these, one should cause lotuses to be made.
Having performed [the rites] in this manner as previously described, one should worship her in due order throughout the night;
indeed, for the attainment of all prosperity, one should install the Goddess upon the ground. 100.
The pervasion consisting of the reality of the anus has been correctly described.
By the thorough churning of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own. (101)

In that regard, among the previously mentioned bases such as *suvarṇa* and so forth, this is what is meant: through the expansion of vowels (*svaraprasāraṇa*), the eleven syllables of the *vidyā*, when not subject to elision (*anāvṛtta*), become one hundred and seventy-six in number. Among those syllables, from the beginning...

Having written the first syllable in the center of the pericarp, one should write the second syllable in the middle of that syllable; there, in the position of the *ghaṭikā*-syllable below it, one writes the third syllable;
and on the eight petals outside, one writes the eight syllables starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise.

In this way, one should write the syllables of the eleven [units]—that is, the syllable for each respective ghaṭikā of the first segment among the sixteen segments of a day and night—at their respective places; this is the first lotus. Immediately after that, [one should write] the syllable following the previously written set of eleven syllables.
Having written the group of eleven as before, one should write the letters for the respective ghaṭikās of the second half of the day and night as before. This is the second lotus.
Having thus fashioned the other fourteen lotuses in sequence, at each respective place and at those respective times—

Through the worship of the Goddess and other rites, the attainment of desired goals occurs. Having inscribed each of those sixteen lotuses, one by one in each square, within a mandala consisting of sixteen squares made of gold and other materials as previously described, the aforementioned accomplishment is achieved through worship. || 95 || 96 || 97 || 98 || 99 || 100 ||
Thus, in the venerable Kādimata among the venerable Ṣoḍaśanityātantras, the twelfth chapter is fully concluded and has been thoroughly examined. 12.

Thus, in the *Manoramā*, so named, composed by the venerable Śrī Subhagānandanātha— known as the *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*— on the complete *Tantra* called the venerable *Kādimata* among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
In this commentary, the twelfth chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the ritual procedures for the Mahāvajreśvarī Nityā-vidyā, has been fully examined and concluded. 12.
The number of verses is nineteen; the explanatory texts for the yantras are more than a hundred;
and here, in this twelfth chapter, twelve [verses] are likewise recorded.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Now, O wise one, listen to the ritual procedure for that which was declared as the eighth among the sixteen Nityās; it bestows the fruits desired.

The extraction of the mantra was performed previously; now likewise [follows] the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), its protective power (āvaraṇa-śakti), its meditation (dhyāna), and its worship (prapūjana).
Its means of accomplishment, its applications through fire-offerings, yantras, and so forth,
as well as the rite of infusing life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), the mantra-lore, its ritual procedure, and its fruit— [all these shall be explained].
O Maheśvarī, I shall explain in due order and in their entirety those mantras by which one becomes renowned in the world as capable of both subjugation and grace.
One should perform the six limbs as before, according to the path described for the Vidyā-mantra;
with the syllables enclosed by that very mantra, one should perform the nyāsa on the five [senses] beginning with the ears.
Having placed the sixth [syllable] upon the mind, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka-nyāsa) with the Vidyā.
The arghya is prescribed as before; O Pārvatī, listen now to that regarding the Śaktis.
Now begins the thirteenth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding twelfth chapter the ritual procedure for the seventh mantra, the Mahāvajreśvarī Nityā-vidyā, [the author] next [teaches] that of the eighth, the Śivadūtī Nityā-vidyā.

He teaches the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) by means of the thirteenth chapter (*paṭala*), consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "the ritual procedure" (*vidhānakam*). Therein, he indicates the subject matter of the chapter with four verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "is capable" (*kṣama*). In that regard, previously, in the third chapter...
The rest is easy to understand. || 1 || 2 || 3 || 4 ||

With the two verses beginning with *kuryāt* and ending with *pārvatī*, he teaches the procedure for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) as well as the preparation of the offering water (*arghya*). In that context, "by the aforementioned path" means by means of [the syllables] joined with the six long vowels and their respective classes [of consonants]. By that very same [method], [one should perform it] in the five [senses] beginning with hearing, using the *hṛllekhā* [syllable].

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "respectively in those called the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose. (5) In that regard, the meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the skin—on all the limbs and the aforementioned locations—with each individual syllable enclosed by the *hṛllekhā* mantra. (6)
Vihvalā, Karṣaṇī, Lolā, Nityā, Madanamālinī, Vinodā, Kautukā, Puṇyā, Purāṇā, and Caturasragā. (7)
Vāgīśā, Varadā, Viśvā, Vibhavā, Vighnakāriṇī,
Vīrā, Vighnaharā, and Vidyā— these are said to be the eight powers of the yantra.
Sumukhī, Sundarī, Sārā, Samarā, Sarasvatī, Samayā, Sarvagā, and Siddhā— these are said to be the eight corner-shaktis.
The ḍākinīs and the others are in the six corners, all starting from the front and proceeding clockwise,
endowed with forms, colors, and weapons identical to those of the root goddess.
One should worship all around on the six petals the auspicious Speech, which is accomplished from afar, which is formless yet possesses a body, and which consists of sound and mind.
One should worship the powers of will, knowledge, and action in the three corners;
in the center, one should worship the eighth goddess, Śivā, who is surrounded by weapons.
O wise one, hear now of her meditation, of which the entire universe is said to consist;
nevertheless, she has fashioned this supreme body for the sake of protecting her devotees. (13)

With six verses beginning with *vihvala* and ending with *śivām*, he teaches the attendant powers (*parivāra-śakti*) of the Goddess. Among them, there are two powers: Madanamālinī, Madanā, and Mālinī.
Those situated in the square (*caturasragāḥ*) consist of two each on both sides of the pair of gates of the square.
In this manner, there are two [lines] in each of the four corners, making four;

and two in the northern and southern directions. Thus, ten lines reside within the square—meaning they are situated in the square. [These are] the eight powers of the yantras—the powers residing in the eight yantras. By the statement "all," [it is meant that]...

Here, one should worship the Ḍākinīs and others, beginning from the foremost [corner] and proceeding clockwise. Their respective powers (śaktis), however, are situated as before in the corners starting from the southwest (nir-ṛti); thus, the sequence of worship is Hākinī, Rākinī, Sākinī, Lākinī, and Ḍākinī. [The mantras] beginning with "Śivām" belong to the Vidyā.
The powers of the names beginning with the second syllable; "tyaivigrahavatī" means "possessing a body consisting of 'tyai'. || 11 ||
The worship of the weapons is performed with their respective names ending in the seven-syllable mantra, proceeding clockwise from the exterior to the northwest. || 12 ||
(222) She possesses a radiance equal to the midday sun during the summer season;
she wears a crown of nine jewels, has three eyes, and is clad in crimson garments. (14)
Her body’s luster was radiant, interspersed with various ornaments;
she possessed a pure smile, had eight arms, and was being praised by the great sages.
With his left arms he holds a noose, a shield, a mace, and a jeweled goblet; likewise, with his right hands, he holds a goad, a sword, an axe, and a lotus.
Having thus meditated upon the goddess Dūtī, who holds a *ādhukā* fruit, who is endowed with the exertion to grant desired boons, and who destroys wicked conduct, one should worship her. (17)
Two squares, a hexagon, two triangles, a six-petalled lotus, likewise a hexagon, an octagon, and similarly an eight-petalled lotus. (18)
Having placed Śivā in the center of the Bhūpura (the square diagram) within the Vahnivāsinī (the fire-abiding goddess),
one should invoke and worship those Śaktis established according to the previously mentioned procedure.

Having recited the mantra, offered oblations, and paid obeisance, one should likewise dissolve [the deity] into one's own self; and one should perform the practice diligently for one hundred thousand repetitions according to the stated method.
O Goddess, listen to the procedure for the optional fire-oblation (kāmyahoma) which grants the fulfillment of one's resolve, by means of which one certainly attains one's desired object quickly. (21)

With these five verses beginning with "tasyāḥ" and ending with "nāśinīm," he teaches the procedure for the daily worship of the Goddess. In this context, the phrase "hear about her supreme form" connects back to the preceding section.
This [procedure] is common to all deities. On the arms [are placed] the noose, goad, and so forth.
One should arrange them in the sequence starting from the top, moving left and right: the white water-lily (kahlāra) and the small knife (asidhenu).
[She is called] Durnītināśinī because she perfectly bestows discernment (viveka). 13, 14, 15, 16, 17.
With these three verses beginning with "vṛttadvayam" and ending with "atandritaḥ," he teaches the perpetual worship-circle (*nityapūjācakra*),
the conclusion of the worship therein, and the instruction on the means of accomplishing the Vidyā (*vidyāsādhanopadeśa*). Therein, within the *bhūpura*,
one should construct two squares, just as in the worship-circle of the goddess Vahnivāsinī-nityā.
This is the meaning. Furthermore, regarding the construction of the wheel:
(p. 223) One shall bring a woman under one's control through oblations of guggulu mixed with honey;
by means of jaggery combined with coconut fruits, one shall obtain Lakṣmī. || 22 ||
Likewise, with white water-lilies sprinkled with clarified butter, with red lotuses smeared with milk, with campaka flowers and bakula blossoms anointed with the three sweets (trimadhu); || 23 ||
By offering oblations of Madhūka flowers, one shall obtain a daughter;
by offering oblations of Punnāga flowers, one obtains garments; and by offering oblations of Āja flowers, one attains one's desired goal.

By offering oblations of clarified butter made from buffalo products, one obtains buffalo-kingdoms; likewise, by offering oblations of clarified butter made from cow-products, the practitioner obtains cow-kingdoms; and by offering precious gems with clarified butter, he obtains precious gems. (25)
Having fashioned an effigy out of rice flour mixed with white [sugar],
with the syllable of the victim's name placed in the region of the heart, one should cook it in oil and clarified butter at night.
Without eating during the day or night, one should consume that which has been consecrated by the recitation of the vidyā;
through this practice for seven nights, whether it be a man, a woman, or even a king [attains the desired result].
One comes under control like a servant and may surrender one's wealth, life, and so forth;
likewise, one should perform oblations with red or white flowers of the *hayāri* plant.
After twenty-one nights, a man attains great prosperity;
by offering goat meat with oblations consecrated by the three sweets (trimadhu), he shall obtain gold.

This is easy to understand. || 18 || 19 || Likewise, according to the path previously described for Lalitā, one should perform three hundred thousand recitations of the syllables and so forth, in accordance with the respective Yuga, as before. || 20 ||

With these ten verses beginning with *kāmyā* and ending with *dirneḥ*, he teaches the attainment of specific fruits from the oblation of specific substances. Among them, the red lotus (*aruṇotpala*) and the red water-lily (*raktakairava*) are as before; the five substances beginning with honey (*madhūka*) and preceding [the others], starting with jaggery (*guḍa*), bring about prosperity (*lakṣmī*). (21, 22, 23)

"With *punnāga* flowers"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. One should combine the four substances beginning with *campaka* and ending with *punnāga* with the three kinds of honey (*trimadhu*). (24) The words "with buffalo [products]" and so forth are qualifiers for the word "with clarified butter" (*ājyaiḥ*). (25) "Combined with white" means accompanied by sugar (*śarkarā*).
The ellipsis is "of the oil and clarified butter having become mixed together. (26) The ellipsis is "not eating food. (27)

By offering *karavīra* flowers, which are enemies of horses, smeared with milk, one obtains land abounding in crops from the *maṇḍala*. By performing oblations with *padmākṣa* seeds, one attains fortune (*lakṣmī*) within three days. (30)
Now I shall describe the yantras which bestow various desired objects;
listen with a concentrated mind, O Śivā, to the rules for them. (31)
In the *tūtīnityā* syllables, there are indeed ten unchanging [syllables]. When these are joined with the sixteen vowels and uttered one hundred and sixty times, [the mantra is complete]. (32)
Having made two squares, within that a pair of circles;
within that an eight-cornered figure, and within that another pair of circles. || 33 ||
Having done so, one should write the primary mantra together with the name in the center;
the remainder [of the mantra] should be written within the two circles and on the eight outer corners.

One should write two syllables each within the space between the two outer circles; inside the ten-fold city-gate (bhūpura), one should place the letters of the elements corresponding to the ritual action.
One should write the *mātṛkā* (alphabet) in the cardinal directions, twelve by twelve in sequence;
the final letter [ḥ] should be placed in the four corners, and the remaining letters should be written [in the intermediate directions]. (36)

Or, in another alternative: for twenty-one days—that is, three times seven nights—with goat meat soaked in milk; such is the grammatical connection. "Chāga" refers to a goat, and "meṣa" to a ram. || 29 || 30 ||

Now, with seven verses beginning with "atha yantrāṇi" and ending with "vai," he teaches ten yantras. In this regard, the following is stated: having produced two circles by means of a rotation of the desired measurement, one should fashion an eight-cornered figure outside of them as previously described.

Having fashioned two circles by touching their corners at the tips— touching and not touching— and having produced two equal squares with a two-finger interval between them by dividing the space into outer and inner sections,
one should write the *hṛllekhā* mantra together with the syllables of the name in the center of all, within the *vidyā*.
Having written the six remaining syllables of the *adhi-vikṛta-vidyā* within the inner circular path,

one should then place two syllables each— starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise— in the eight outer corners among the one hundred and sixty syllables formed by the modifications of the vowels.
Having likewise inscribed the syllables of the elements (*bhūtākṣara*) on the outer circular path according to the ritual procedure,

one should similarly inscribe the letters of the alphabet (*mātṛkā*) on the outer square path— twelve in each direction, starting from the northeast, southeast, southwest, northwest, and so forth. Regarding their inscription, in those [spaces]:

Having joined the visarga with the vowels at the end of the *mātṛkā* syllables, and having joined the bindu with the fourteen vowel-syllables, one should join the visarga with the vowels and the bindu with the consonants.
In this way, indeed, the mechanical devices that rival the ten supernatural powers are produced.
First, having made [the image] with red ochre, one should invoke Śivā there and worship her;
on the seventh day, at the three junctions of the day, [one should offer oblations] accompanied by white cakes.
Having prepared the milk offering in the morning and likewise at midday, one should offer curd with rice in the evening,
as well as milk and plantains.
In this manner, being composed in meditation, one should perform worship in a mandala or even half a mandala;
by the grace of the Goddess, one shall obtain one's desire with little effort. || 40 ||
Having performed the second [rite] with the Daradas, one should then invoke [the deity] there on that day and offer well-cooked food along with goat meat and honey.
One should serve the protector of the earth so as to bring him under control without effort, and likewise, one should captivate a beloved woman for as long as life lasts. (42)
Having likewise prepared a third [image] with vermilion and having invoked her there,
by worshipping her in that manner for those many days, one shall bring the two kinds of enemies under control.

Having joined the thirty-four letters from *ka* to *la*, one should write the final letter *kṣa*—accompanied by the *visarjanīya*—within the four corners of the square, inside the group of four, and outside the two circles that lie exterior to the eight-cornered figure; this is the first yantra. The second and subsequent yantras are of this very same [nature].
In the eight corners of the yantra, one should write the sixty [syllables] beginning with the second letter as before;
the other ten are well-proportioned (or equal). || 31 || 32 || 33 || 34 || 35 || 36 || 37 ||
With twenty-three verses beginning with "prathamam" and ending with "samīritāḥ," [the author] teaches the ten types of yantra-applications and their results. Among them, regarding the first yantra:
one should worship according to the constant ritual sequence (*nityakrama*). "Sita" means sugar. *Pāyasa* and the other two are the three substances to be offered (*nivedya*).

The meaning is that one should offer [the oblation] in sequence during the three junctions (sandhyās). (39) Thus, "half" refers to half of the mandala. (40) With "daradas" means with those possessing the characteristics of their respective castes. On "that day" means on the seventh lunar day. (41) "To that extent" refers to the previously mentioned mandala and so forth. One should "worship" according to the regular ritual procedure. In this section...
Having prepared the fourth [mandala] with saffron, one should likewise worship there in the center;
by its grace, all calamities depart within seven days. (44)
Having prepared the fifth [offering] with sandalwood, one should worship Śivā in its center;
[one should offer] only milk-rice, plantains, and white sugar combined with ghee.
By offering this at the three junctions of the day for one month, he shall be freed from all diseases without exception;
having conquered them, he shall live long and happily, free from illness, until the end of his allotted lifespan.
Having established the water-pot right there, the sacrificer should perform the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) with those [mantras];
and having performed the sacrifice (*yajana*), he should give a generous sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) to him according to his own capacity. || 47 ||
One should give all one's possessions to that giver of life, or rather, one should offer as much wealth as it takes for him to attain satisfaction. 48.
Then, one should draw the sixth [mandala] combined with camphor and sandalwood paste,
either on a smooth stone slab, a pedestal, or on a floor of white plaster.
One who has attained self-control should offer rice, clarified butter, milk-rice, cakes, and side dishes;
likewise, one should worship during the three junctions of the day while reciting the vidyā.
Within merely twenty-one nights, living beings are liberated from fever born of terrible malevolent magic;
for the powers of mantras and yantras are inconceivable.
Having prepared the seventh [inscription] on a copper plate, and having invoked and worshipped it, one should install it in that temple; therein Lakṣmī dwells most firmly.
Having fashioned the eighth [mark] out of silver, one should wear it for the sake of all prosperity;
having fashioned the ninth out of gold, O Śivā, one should wear it as an ornament and so forth.
The worship of all [deities] is according to the perpetual sequence; likewise, as before, through worship in the second yantra.
42 || For that many days, as before; likewise, together with the second yantra, the worship, and the offering substances.

The two types are the innate (*sahaja*) and the artificial (*kṛtrima*). Among these, the innate is one born of one's own family, while the artificial is one who has committed an offense. 43 || Likewise,
In the tenth [chapter], one should accomplish all undertakings while worshipping Śivā;
for whatever desired task there may be, it should likewise be placed within that [mantra]. (54)
Having performed that [rite], one should worship there while remembering the task in one's heart;
by those very days one attains it—no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 55 ||
Having prepared those ten very same yantras on birch bark and worshipped them,
one should place them in the midst of honey contained within a vessel made of beeswax.

With a concentrated mind, one should worship at the three junctions of the day with red perfumes and flowers, facing the person to be accomplished, while reciting the vidyā and reflecting in this manner: (ret).
Having bound his neck with a noose, he leads him to his own feet—he who has placed his hands with palms joined upon his head and says, "I am your slave. (58)
Within twenty-one nights, men, women, kings, and others shall become submissive;
likewise, by making that same [substance] lukewarm and applying it constantly during the three junctions of the day (saṃdhyās), [the same result follows].
Afflicted by desire, their hearts tormented by the fever of passion, women gradually abandon family, modesty, and discernment to become his servants.
Thus have the applications of the mechanical devices been described.
O Pārvatī, listen as I shall now declare the vidyā for the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). 61.
Accompanied by the previously mentioned offering substances (nivedya-dravya) [44]; milk-rice (pāyasa) and so forth, one of each at every twilight [45] [46];
with those syllables of the Vidyā inscribed upon the yantra; for that consecrator (abhiṣektṛ) [47]; he is the consecrator [48] [49];
food and so forth, everything at every twilight; while reciting [the mantra] a hundred or a thousand times [50] [51] [52].

53. "Situated in the middle of that" means situated in the middle of the tenth yantra; likewise, as before. 54. "That" refers to the eternal messenger (dūtī); "by those days" refers to the maṇḍalas and so forth, as before. 55. The remainder is that there are ten of each of those; having worshipped them, preceded by the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (the installation of the vital breath).
By means of those respective written syllables; *siktha* is beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*). The remainder [of the sentence] is "that yantra. || 56 ||

"In this manner" means by the method that is about to be described (vv. 57–58). "That very [substance] presided over by the Yantra" refers to the honey (v. 59). "Of this practitioner" (v. 60). The word "would become" (*bhaveyuḥ*) is to be construed with what precedes. (p. 228) Touch, conjoined with the pervasive [element], is joined with wind, ether, and earth.
The swift [fire], joined with the wind, and even the sky, joined with the wind.
Agni and Haṃsa are the first two; likewise, the first three [syllables] are at the end.
The sixth and seventh are the meanings joined with Jyā and Agni, and then Ambu.

The Heart-mantra joined with the Fire of the Heart (HṚCCHIKHYA), then the Māyā-bīja (Hrīṃ) followed by the triad beginning with RA-YA-GA; again, the Heart-mantra with the aquatic beings (VA-ŚA-RA-YA-Ū) and its own [name], then the Gotra-mantra with Ā-HĀ and the Fires (RA-YA-Ū). || 64 ||
Pervaded by the wind (marut), followed by space (vyoma), fire (agni), and motion (gamana);
then again, the first triad [of elements] joined with water (ambu), wind (marut), day (dyu), and ether (nabhas). 65.
Then the Void (Śūnya) joined with Māyā, the fourth, and likewise the fifth;
Agni joined with Haṃsa, and Vyāpta joined with Marut. (67)
One's own name, joined with the earth (la), the heart (ha), water (va), and air (ya);
and the *haṃsa* (ha) joined with air (ya)—this mantra consists of forty syllables. (68)

With the second half of the verse beginning with "prāṇa," he introduces the *vidyā* for the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), which is common to all systems (*sarvatantrasādhāraṇā*). || 61 ||

With these six verses beginning with "vāta" and ending with "manuḥ," he teaches the forty-syllable *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā*. In that [mantra], "vātaḥ" is the letter *a*; "nabhodharāyuktaṃ" is *mu*; and "sparśovyāptena saṃyutaḥ" is *ṣya*.

"Javī" (the swift one) is the letter *da*, joined with fire (*ra*) and wind (*ya*), thus *prā*. "Vyoma" (space) is also joined with wind (*ya*), thus *ṇa*. "Agni" (fire) is the letter *ī*. "Haṃsa" is *ha*. "The two preceding syllables" refers to the first two letters of this [word], thus *prāṇā*.
"The first three" of that [word] are *amuṣya*. "Jyā" (bowstring) joined with fire (*ra*) is *jī*. "Ambu" (water) is the letter *va*. The sixth...
The seventh is *iha*. (63) Now, [the mantra] joined with the Heart (*hṛd*), Śikhā (*śikhā*), and Agni (*agni*) is *sthi*. Māyā (*māyā*) is the Visarga (*visarjanīya*).
*Ra* and *ya* situated above the letter *ta* is *ta*. The first three [syllables] are as before.
*Amuṣya* consists of three syllables. The Heart is the letter *sa*. With the "burners," "water-dwellers," and itself—this is one [mantra], the twenty-third syllable.
The twenty-fourth syllable is *gotrādāhāgnibhiḥ paraṃ dri tri*.

Here, at the beginning of *tri*, a nasal dot (*bindu*) is obtained through traditional transmission. [The next is] *vyāptaṃ marutsamopetaṃ yā iti*. Following *vyomāgni* (the sky and fire), there is *ṇi*; this is the twenty-sixth syllable.
The first triad consists of the three syllables *amuṣya*. One should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) by joining the seven syllables beginning with *a*, *b*, *u*, *ma*, *ru*, *t*, and *yā* in pairs.
These same [limbs] should be placed upon the skin and other [constituents], situated within the enclosure of the Śaktis. (69)
One should meditate upon the Goddess, the power of breath (prāṇaśakti), who is ruddy, clad in ruddy garments,
wearing a ruddy crown and possessing ruddy sprout-like lips.
Her face is graced with a beautiful smile and a pair of lotus-eyes as red as the dawn;
she holds a cluster of flowers and a noose in her two hands.
One should worship her from the center of the lotus, surrounded on all sides by ten powers equal to herself, who are endowed with infinite power.
"Accompanied by water and wind" means *i* (ambu = *a*, marut = *i*). "Or" (*vā*) is used as a disjunctive particle. "Joined with heaven and ether" refers to the letter *ṅma*;

the remainder is that it is the thirty-first syllable, namely *jama*. || 65 || "The void joined with *māyā*" means *naḥ* (void = *m*, *māyā* = *visarjanīya*). "The fourth" is *prā*. "The fifth" is *ṇa*. "Fire" (*agni*)...
The letter *ī* [is the seed-syllable]. Joined with *haṃsa* and *marut*, it becomes *hā*. Pervaded by *marut* and joined with *yā*, it becomes *hyā*. || 67 ||

"Syāt" (syā) is joined with the "raya-dharā" (the earth element, *la*), becoming *slā*. "Nnu" is accompanied by the heart (*ha*), water (*va*), and wind (*ya*), becoming *svā*. "Haṃsa" is joined with the wind (*ya*), becoming *hā*. Thus, the forty-syllable mantra for the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) is: *āṃ hrīṃ kroṃ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha la kṣa a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ a ā i ī u ū ṛ ṝ ḷ ḹ e ai o au aṃ aḥ ya ra la va śa ṣa sa ha kṣa slā svā hā*. This [mantra] is used in all Tantras for the consecration of all yantras, figurines, jars, deities, and so forth.
The mantra for the installation of vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā). || 68 ||

With the verse beginning with "yādī," he teaches the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the six limbs and so forth for the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra. In that context, "from the union of two" means from the union of two syllables. For example:
[the letter] *ya* and *pa* for the heart; *ra* and *la* for the head; *la* and *va* for the crest-lock (*śikhā*).

The meaning is that one should perform the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) together with the seed-syllables (*jāti*): from *va* and *sa* comes the armor (*kavaca*), from *ṣa* and *ṣā* comes the eye (*netra*), and from *ṣa* and *sā* comes the weapon (*astra*). Regarding the skin and so forth:
among the seven constituents (*dhātu*)—skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, and semen—it is those very [limbs] [that are assigned].
The seven syllables beginning with *ya* and ending with *sa*, as previously mentioned, are enclosed within *Śakti*.

This is a specific qualification for the three [syllables]. In each of the seven [names], it should be such that every individual syllable is enclosed by *Hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*), joined with their respective names.

The meaning of the tradition is that one should perform the placement (nyāsa) in the locations known as the two roots of the arms, the two armpits, the heart and so forth, and the pair of hands and feet, or else in the heart alone. || 69 ||

With these three verses beginning with "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) and ending with "in the middle" (*madhyataḥ*), he teaches the meditation on the power of breath (*prāṇa-śakti*). In that context, the cluster of flowers (*prasūnapiṇḍa*) is on the right side of the Goddess because it is of the nature of breath (*prāṇa*); from that [breath] comes the vitalizing cluster of flowers by means of the ten powers (*daśa-śakti*).
By means of the vital breaths (prāṇa) and so forth; the phrase "endowed with infinite powers" applies to each one respectively—this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 70 || 71 || 72 ||
The powers of prāṇa, apāna, samāna, vyāna, and udāna;
and [the five vital winds] nāga, kūrma, kṛkara, devadatta, and dhanañjaya. (73)
Having constructed two squares, within them a pair of circles;
