within that, a ten-petaled lotus, and within that, likewise another pair [of circles].
Having performed [the preliminary rites] and having invoked them into the center, one who has offered the *arghya* should worship them;
one should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times while subsisting on milk, and likewise perform oblations (*homa*) ten thousand times as a tenth part of that.

One should offer libations with pure sesame seeds and white mustard seeds mixed with honey, using water scented with saurabha and other fragrances; in this manner, one should perform the rite effectively.
Whatever effigies and yantras have been described in every respect in this tantra, one should infuse the vital breaths into them by means of this vidyā. (77)
O wise one, hear now of her yantra, which produces immediate conviction;
by means of it, a puppet is made to move with the pulsation of life through the power of the mind. (78)
One should lay down eight lines—east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east—so that forty-nine squares are produced; one should then place [the deities] within them.
Beginning from the northeast and proceeding around the perimeter,
one should write the remaining nine [syllables] in the center in sequence, starting with the limbs (aṅgas).
With the verse beginning with "prāṇa," he teaches the attendant powers (parivāra-śakti) of the goddess Prāṇaśakti;
therein, the principal Prāṇaśakti is their collective totality (samaṣṭi). || 73 ||

With the three verses beginning with "catusradvayam" and ending with "sādhayet," he teaches that maṇḍala for worship, the worship itself, and the method for accomplishing its mantra. In this context, "that pair" refers to the two circles; the construction of the other wheels is easy to understand. || 74 ||
Having offered the water of honor (arghya) as before; with white [and] pale-yellow [substances].

With the verse beginning with "In this tantra" (*tantre'smin*), he teaches the procedure for the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) for puppets and other such objects in all cases. Among those [verses], the meaning of the others is easy to understand;
[the rest is explained] by the four and a half verses beginning with "the yantra" (*yantram*) and ending with "may there be" (*bhavet*).

He teaches the construction of that machine and its application. In that regard, one should place the syllables of the *prāṇapratiṣ�ṭhā* mantra—endowed with the vibration of the living soul—following the arrival of the soul of the person to be acted upon; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 78 ||
79 || To the northeast (the direction of Īśāna). Around [the mandala], proceeding clockwise.

(p. 231) Then, having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the remaining two [spaces] and then that of the practitioner (sādhaka), one should recite the mantra a hundred times while touching [the disciple] with the hand, which is "endowed with life" (sajīva). 81 ||
With that [mudrā], one should fashion dolls for the sake of accomplishment; otherwise, it will not come to pass.
Listen, I shall tell you the wonderful method for bringing forth the life-force of the target and so forth. 82.

Maintaining the potency of the mantra through mindfulness, [he perceives] by means of that [mindfulness] the organs of knowledge and action, their objects, the mind, the individual soul, and likewise the body from within that womb. (83)

Therefore, from within the body of the one to be accomplished, one should mentally bring forth those [limbs] by means of the names and the red thread consisting of power, and offer them into the effigy.

One should join the names of those to be accomplished at the ends of the three syllables of the mantra; having thus joined the mantra, one should recite it a thousand times while touching [the object]. 85.
By means of the "living hand" (jīvahasta), the practitioner should [place it] in that mind during the middle watches of the night;
thus, with the vital breaths established in this way, the doll vibrates after a year.

Regarding the entry [into the mandala], the sequence has not been omitted. The seven syllables beginning with *ya* are those mentioned in the *Aṅga*. In the construction of the yantra, the rest is easy to understand. (80) "Touching the yantra"—this is the ellipsis. (81) "With that substance. This is what is meant: those substances by which the making of the seven figurines (*puttalikā*) was described, those [are used].
Having placed the substances inside the mechanical device (yantra), or having placed the mechanical device inside those substances, one should fashion a doll (*puttalikā*) with them—
this is stated in the four verses beginning with "sādhya" and ending with "abdataḥ."
He teaches the invocation of the life-force (*jīva*) of the target (*sādhya*) in effigies and the like.

Since the potency of the mantra will be explained in the thirty-fifth chapter, it is not discussed here. "Together with that recollection" is the ellipsis. "From within the body of that [effigy]" means from the interior of the target's body. "The objects" (refers to the following).
The ten sense objects; the *jīva*, which is the self (*ātman*);

and the body, consisting of the eight constituents (*dhātu*) known as skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and vitality—having first joined these with the eight syllables beginning with *ya* along with the nasal bindu, and following that...

The meaning is that immediately after pronouncing the names of those respective elements, one should bring them [into the object] according to the instruction by means of the recitation of the mantra "ākṛṣya pratiṣṭhāpaya. || 83 || 84 || Regarding the words "at the end of the three syllables," this is what is meant: at the ends of the three syllables of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* vidyā, the names of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) are inserted.
"One should apply [the ritual]," [it is said]. (85) With the "living hand"—that is, the hand positioned at the side of the flow of breath along with the breath—one should say:

"Listen, I shall tell you the birth-constellations (*janmanakṣatra*) of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), primarily consisting of the ninth and eighth lunar mansions (*ṛkṣa*) arising from his birth-ascendant (*janmalagna*). (87) (p. 232)
And there are other nine asterisms associated with the nine planets;
I shall describe them for those various applications in another fire-offering.
One should attach the fingernails, the hair, the dust from the feet, and other body hairs to the effigy at the time of death. (89)
And in all rites such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and others, one should use the aforementioned effigy (*puttalī*);
thus has the entire procedure for the act of drawing in the vital breath (*prāṇākarṣaṇa*) been explained to you. (90)
Having performed the drawing in of the vital breath by means of this vidyā as described,
one should then carry out the prescribed actions in the various parts of the effigy (puttalī) as specified therein.
In all cases of killing, the placement of the victim's asterism and planet is prescribed;
likewise, for the trees mentioned, one should apply the *aṣṭakavarga* system.

"In that mind" means in the mind of the doll; this is what is being said: having placed the doll within the previously mentioned yantra, one should perform the extraction of the life-force (*jīva*) and other elements of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). || 86 ||

With these two verses beginning with *sādhyasya* and ending with *homake*, he teaches the ten types of birth asterisms (*janmanakṣatra*) for the beings to be accomplished (*sādhya*). Among those, the ninth decan (*navāṃśa*) star produced at the time of one's birth-lagna is the primary one. This is what is meant: for whomever...

At the time of birth, the ninth-part (navāṃśa) of the ascendant, the degree distinguished by that ninth-part, and the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) distinguished by that ninth-part are its primary [factors]. The other nine mansions are equal to one another and secondary; this is the meaning, because of the conjunction with the nine planets.

The remainder [of the phrase] is "of the constellations" (nakṣatrāṇām). And that [constellation] is connected to the zodiacal signs (rāśi) in the section on oblations (homapaṭala) within the *Homaka*. || 88 ||

With these three verses beginning with "ripoḥ" and ending with "ācaret," he provides the instruction on the specific qualities for the construction of the effigy (puttalī) and offers a conclusion to what has been stated; therein, "mṛtau" refers to the application of the rite of killing (māraṇa).

Regarding the phrase "in [rites such as] subjugation and so forth" (*vaśyādiṣu*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes attraction, inciting enmity, and the like. By that [image], which is devoid of the nails, hair, and other parts of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), and is fashioned from the substances prescribed for each respective case—the word "application" (*prayoga*) being understood as the ellipsis—[the rite is performed]. || 91 ||

With the two verses beginning with "sarvatra" and ending with "kṣaṇāt," he teaches that in the performance of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), one should observe the favorability of the planets for the victim, and the adverse consequences of disregarding them; therein,
[he describes] the configuration of the planets and constellations of the victim.

The relative strength and weakness of the planets, the primary asterism (nakṣatra), and the zodiac sign; the eightfold division (aṣṭavarga) of those nine asterisms, of that which is to be accomplished, of the nine asterisms at birth during the periods (daśā) of the nine planets, and of the seven planets beginning with the Sun as well as the natal ascendant (janmalagna).
Having carefully observed the state of the ten stages, the self-possessed practitioner should perform the rite of killing;
for if performed without such observation, the ritual instantly destroys one's own self. (93)
One should never employ a righteous Brahmin, a king, a woman, a man who is devoted to the spiritual path, a generous person, or one who is compassionate in the practice of malevolent magic. || 94 ||
If one applies this with hostility, it destroys that very person.
Listen to the objects for which malevolent rites (abhicāra) are intended; I shall tell you. 95.
The most wicked atheists, thieves, revilers of the gods and Brahmins, destroyers of living beings, and those established in all kinds of afflictive actions—[these he should punish]. || 96 ||

One who seizes fields, wealth, property, and women; one who brings about the end of a lineage; one who reviles the sacred conventions; one who is malicious; and one who slays a king—[these are to be avoided]. (97)
One who always harms living beings with poisons, fire, razors, weapons, and the like, should be employed in acts of killing; by these means, one does not become a sinner. 98.

Having swiftly performed the rite of killing, at its conclusion, one should propitiate the preceptor and the Brahmins with half of one's own wealth, or with a quarter, according to one's own regular means. || 99 ||
Having performed the consecration, one should then recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times while subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya);
one should perform this consecration for a period of one year, even if it spans three lifetimes.

He explains that the "eightfold division" (aṣṭavargaka), as taught in the science of astrology (jyotiḥśāstra), is a means for indicating mutual favorability. [He also discusses] the duration of planetary periods (daśāsthiti), the status of the Great Periods of the Wheel of Time (kālacakra-mahādaśā) and so forth,
and the observation of the planets' favorability or unfavorability specifically regarding rites of sorcery (māraṇa).
Not otherwise. || 93 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with "brāhmaṇam" and ending with "tad," he teaches that those who are not to be subjected to sorcery (anabhicāryāḥ) incur sin (pratyavāya) by performing such sorcery (abhicāraṇa). In this context, "dhārmika" is an adjective qualifying "bhūpa. Regarding "abhicāre," it means in the act of killing; the rest is easy to understand. || 94 ||

With these three and a half verses beginning with *abhicāre* and ending with *pātakī*, he teaches the rites of sorcery (*abhicāra*). In this context, "by means of these rites of killing," the remainder is that "the practitioner becomes a sinner" (*pātakī*). || 95 || 96 || 97 || 98 ||
By performing a year-long fire sacrifice with *dūrvā* grass, one is liberated from those sins.
Thus, I have explained to you in its entirety the ritual procedure for the *Dūtīnityā*. (101)
The pervasion consisting of the reality of the feet has been correctly described;
by the thorough churning of this within the mind, that very reality is made one's own. 102.
Thus ends the thirteenth chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, among the *Śrīṣoḍaśanityātantras*.

With these three verses beginning with "Having performed" (*kṛtvā*) and ending with "according to the rule" (*vidhānataḥ*), he teaches the expiation for performing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). In this context, the word division is *āśu* (quickly).
One should eat *haviṣya* food; "haviṣya" refers to cooked rice-grains from which the salt has been removed. 99–100.
By those sins—that is, by the sins of performing malevolent magic—this practitioner [is affected]. 101 || 102 ||

Thus, in the *Manoramā*, the commentary composed by Śrī Subhagānandanātha, titled *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete *Tantra* known as the *Śrīkādimatā* among the *Śrīṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
In this commentary, the thirteenth chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the ritual procedure for the Śivadūtī Nityā-vidyā, has been fully examined. 13.
In this thirteenth chapter, it is stated that the number of verses is eleven hundred, and the explanatory treatises on the Yantras shall be seventeen and a half.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Now, regarding that which is proclaimed as the ninth among the sixteen Nityās:
the twelve-syllable Vidyā known as Tvaritā has already been explained previously.
O wise one, listen to its procedure along with the fire-offerings (homa), the ritual manuals (tantra), and so forth,
by which the practitioner of mantra, radiant as the god of love, agitates the surface of the earth.
One should likewise form the limbs with the seven syllables beginning with the fourth vowel [U] and the others;
one should perform the sixfold assignment of the hands and limbs using pairs of syllables in due order.
Indeed, [one should place them] in sequence upon the head, forehead, throat, heart, navel, and base (ādhāra), as well as upon the thighs, knees, shanks, and feet.

One should perform the placement (nyāsa) with the remaining mantra-syllables situated in the second, penultimate, and middle positions, preceded by the Tāra (Oṃ). Listen now to its meditation (dhyāna), its powers (śaktis), and its worship.
She was dark-complexioned, of auspicious form, and radiant with fresh youth;
she shone with ornaments fashioned by eight serpents arranged in pairs.
Now begins the fourteenth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding thirteenth chapter the ritual procedure for the eighth *dūtī*, the Nityā, [the author] next [teaches] that of the ninth, the Tvaritā-nityā-vidyā.

He teaches the ritual procedure with the fourteenth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "from the mountain. Therein, with two verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "the surface of the earth," he indicates the subjects of the chapter. Regarding that, [it was already explained] previously in the third chapter. || 1 ||
He agitates by means of his own self and brings about establishment. || 2 ||
With these three verses beginning with "Vidyā" and ending with "pūjanam," he teaches the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and other rites.

In that regard, just as in the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā-vidyā*, the application of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga-yojana*) is performed by means of a chain-binding (*śṛṅkhalā-bandha*), [placing] one limb each upon the thighs, knees, shanks, and feet. (3–4)
"By those situated between the second, the penultimate, and the middle": *hṛllekhā* is the second [syllable]; *upāntya* is that which is near the end;
"by those situated between these two," meaning by the other mantra-syllables as well, such as *tāra* (om) and so forth. This is what is meant:
first *hṛllekhā*, and after that...
(236) Likewise, with those of the Brahmin, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes, who possessed terrifying forms and were adorned with earrings, armlets, girdles, and anklets; || 7 ||
Clad in a garment of young shoots,
her arms adorned with beautiful bracelets made of peacock feathers, she shone with a crown of rubies.

She was adorned with a garland of *barha* feathers on the outside, possessing an umbrella and a banner; her chest was graced by a string of *guñjā* berries, and her breasts were beautified with saffron.
She has three eyes and a beautiful face, her lotus-like countenance graced with a gentle smile;
her four arms shine as they hold a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.
Having thus meditated upon the goddess Totalā, who is surrounded by her powers (śaktis), one should worship her;
and [one should worship] Sphāṭkārī, who stands before her, radiant with bow and arrow in hand.
Because she is endowed with haste in bestowing grace and granting fruits to practitioners, this ninth Māyā is called Tvaritā. 12.

Then, one should place the Praṇava, followed by the penultimate syllable, and then "Hṛllekhā," and so on in this sequence, placing the other ten mantra-syllables beginning with *varma* (the armor-mantra) and ending with *phaṭ* upon the ten aforementioned locations. || 5 ||
With these five and a half verses beginning with *śyāmavarṇām* and ending with *vṛtām*, he teaches the visualization for the daily worship of the Goddess. Among them,
by means of the first half-verse beginning with *dvidvikramāt* and ending with *vigrahaiḥ*, this is stated:
Through the doubling of each successive pair, the Lord of Serpents is formed by the eight castes— Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra— in due order,
beginning with the fashioned earrings, up to the girdle and the pair of anklets. In this regard:
It should be understood that the arrangement of ornaments follows the sequence of the origin of the four castes. || 7 ||

Clad in garments of young shoots, wearing a lower garment of tender sprouts, with a crest of peacock feathers— *āpīḍa* meaning a crest— and possessing such a parasol— a parasol made of peacock feathers— and likewise possessing such banners; this is the arrangement of weapons.
From the upper left hand down to the lower right hand, in the sequence from left to right.
Trotalā means swift; the names of the Goddess are Tvaritā, Trotalā, and Tūrṇā.

With these five verses beginning with "tadagrasthā" and ending with "manmathaḥ," he teaches the goddess's retinue of Śaktis and so forth. Among them: "She who is radiant with bow and arrow in hand"—that is, she whose pair of hands is resplendent with a bow and arrows. (11)
(237) He who is black in color, holding a mace in his hand, with hair that is matted and standing erect—his servant (Kiṅkara) should be worshipped at her front for the accomplishment of all aims. 13.
On both sides of that door, two goddesses named Jayā and Vijayā are to be worshipped;
they are similar to her, with lotus-hands holding golden canes.
Huṅkārī, Khecarī, Caṇḍā, Chedinī, and then Kṣepaṇī;
Strī, Huṅkārī, and Kṣemakarī—these are equal to the guardians of the world. 15.

The powers of the syllables of the mantra, stationed upon the eight petals of the lotus, are to be worshipped; by worshipping them constantly, a man becomes like the god of love among both men and women. (16)
Listen, O Maheśvarī, to the procedure for the worship of that Tvaritā.
Having prepared the arghya as before, O Īśānī, [place it] upon an auspicious throne with eight lion-claws.
Upon a seat fashioned of gold, one should draw two *bhūpura*s (fortified enclosures) provided with a western gate, and within them, a pair of circles.
Then, having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus within that space, one should invoke the supreme Śivā there,
surrounded as before by her Śaktis.
"In *prasāde* means in the state of being present before one's eyes. By this verse, the etymological justification for the Goddess’s name is established. (12)

Holding a mace in his hand, he likewise has two hands; *varvara* means curly or twisted. *Kiṅkara* is a specific type of spirit who has become a servant or messenger of the Goddess. (13) In those [hands] similar to that, meaning having a color equal to the deity’s, there are two arms with lotus-like hands holding golden canes (*vetra*). (14) One who is to be addressed with the feminine *hūṃ*...

*Strīkārī* and *Huṅkārī* are two powers (*śakti*). They are equal to the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), with the understanding that this refers to their colors, weapons, and vehicles. (15) The "powers of the mantra-syllables" are the powers of the syllables of the *Tvaritā* mantra;
by means of these syllabic powers, the practitioner (*sādhaka*) becomes [successful], as is understood from the context. [He becomes] like Manmatha [in subduing] all women.
The meaning is that she agitates [him] by perceiving her own self as possessing desire. || 16 ||

With these six verses beginning with *ṛṇvi* and ending with *samāpayet*, he teaches the sequence for the daily worship (*nityasaparyā*) of the Goddess. Therein, as before, [the worship is performed] with the six limbs and the root mantra. *Īśām* means the presiding deity of all. *Aṣṭasiṃhāṅghrike* means provided with eight lion-feet. || 17 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *vidadhyāt* and ending with *vidhāya*, he teaches the wheel of the Goddess’s daily worship (*nityasaparyācakra*). In this regard, the following is intended: having constructed two squares provided with a western door, one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus within them, provided with two circles.
One should fashion it with a pericarp. (18) Here, in this wheel, one should worship her as prescribed, preceded by the display of the mudrās.
The two previously mentioned [deities] are to be worshipped either at the tip of the front petal or in the center of the circle. (20)
One should offer an oblation to the servant (kiṅkara) before the Goddess with the previously mentioned [mantras],
out of devotion, to him who stands within the maṇḍala surrounded by his own like-minded attendants.

Having thus performed the worship, one should recite the mantra a thousand times before it, or a hundred times; then, having performed the fire-oblation (homa), one should conclude the worship as previously described.

Then, having accomplished the vidyā, the person should perform the ritual applications; for the purpose of accomplishment, he should offer oblations with leaves and other materials made of bilva wood, numbering one-tenth of the recitation.
Thus, with water from a handful consecrated by those who have perfected the mantra,
one should revive the snakes by striking their mouths with that water, which is the nectar of their fangs.
One should mutter the vidyā into his two ears, or strike him with a staff for the sake of accomplishing the recitation;
by striking him suddenly on the head, one shall raise the dead. || 25 ||
O Goddess, listen; I shall describe the ritual for the optional oblation according to the rules.
Having fashioned a *yoni* in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one should duly pour [the oblation] into the fire there. (26)
This is what is meant: having invoked [the deity], [one should place it] in the middle of the pericarp; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 19 ||
"Preceded by the display of mudrās" means preceded by the four mudrās beginning with *sthāpanā*.

This applies to all [deities] in common. "As stated" refers to starting from the front and proceeding clockwise. "On the tip of the front petal" means on the very tip of the front petal among the eight petals, specifically in the center of the circle at the front petal of the Goddess.

In the two circular paths situated outside the lotus, one should worship the previously mentioned Phaṭkārī and Kiṅkara respectively at the tip of the front petal and in the middle of the circles within the paths; this is the meaning. "The offering" (bali)—the word "final" (antya) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. It is before the Goddess, as before, in the presence of Tvaritā. The offering of the bali is to be performed everywhere.
In the presence of the respective root-deity, [one should worship] with the aforementioned food offerings (*annādya*) and so forth; "with their respective mantras" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

(The aforementioned mandala is circular in its center. [This is done] as before, until the completion of the worship of Lalitā. Then, by means of these three verses beginning with "tataḥ" and ending with "iti."

By means of verses, he teaches the method for accomplishing the vidyā and the procedure for neutralizing poison by one who has mastered the vidyā. In that context, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in "leaves and so forth," flowers, roots, stalks, and fruits are intended.

The syntactical connection is as follows: when the recitation (*japa*) has reached a count of one hundred thousand syllables, corresponding to the [specific] yuga, one should perform the oblation (*homa*) with a tenth part of that number. || 23 ||
With consecrated sesame, mustard seeds, wheat, rice, grain, and barley—
one should offer these individually or combined with the three sweets for the sake of prosperity. (27)
With *bakula*, *campaka*, *abja*, *kahlāra*, and red lotuses,
with night-lilies, jasmine, *kunda*, and *madhuka* flowers, [he offered] for the sake of attaining Indirā.
With Aśoka, Pāṭala, Bilva, Jātī, and Vicakila flowers, with white blossoms, with fresh blue lotuses, with those born from the enemy of horses (aśvaripu), and with Karṇikāra flowers; || 29 ||
Through this oblation, one certainly attains Lakṣmī, good fortune, long life, wealth, and a treasury of fame;
indeed, whatever is desired, all that is obtained with certainty.
By offering oblations of dūrvā grass, guḍūcī, aśvattha, vaṭa,
āragvadha, white arka, and plakṣa, a person is soon liberated from diseases.
By offering oblations of sugarcane, jambu fruit, coconut, plantain, jaggery, and sugar, one attains unshakable prosperity and will certainly become an enjoyer [of wealth]. (32)
When these [substances] are offered individually, soaked in clarified butter, honey,
and milk, a woman becomes submissive for as long as she lives through wealth and other such means.

"One hundred times" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "In his ears" means in the ears of the one bitten. "Reciting, he would revive" is the ellipsis. Or, as for the alternative: by the perfection of recitation—that is, by the perfection of reciting the Vidyā one thousand times—through the emission from the tips of his hands, he would raise up the dead one who has been bitten by a hooded serpent. This...
The third position. || 25 ||

With these five verses beginning with "kāmyahoma" and ending with "priye," [the author] teaches the attainment of various fruits through various types of material offerings (dravyahoma). In that regard,
having prepared the *yoni* within the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) according to the method to be described in the chapter on the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍapaṭala*),...

The meaning is that one should fashion a *yoni* (vulva-shaped altar) in the middle of that. This applies generally to all fire-offerings (*homa*). There, in the *yoni*—the words "when the fire has been established" are to be supplied—the sense is that one should perform the rites beginning with the "face of the fire" (*agnimukha*) according to rule, as previously described.
26 || "Ekaśaḥ" means individually, one by one. || 27 || "Aruṇotpalam" (red lotus) is as before; "with white *kairavas*" is the implied completion.

|| 28 || The *vicakila* flowers are to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. "With smiles" means with blossomed [flowers]; "born of the enemy of horses" refers to *karavīra* flowers. || 29 || 30 || "*Guḍūcīm*" is the *amṛta-latā* as before; "with white [flowers]. || 31 ||

O Dear One, by offering oblations soaked in clarified butter with those [seeds], kings shall become submissive; when those same [seeds] are offered soaked in milk, mortals remain entirely under one's control. (34)

One should offer oblations of mustard seeds and clarified butter into a fire of *mṛtyu-kāṣṭha* wood for the death of an enemy; likewise, one may do so for that same purpose with the flesh arising from the womb of an enemy, smeared with those same substances.
One should offer into the fire oblations of parched grain cooked in blood arising from the female organ,
mixed with *āruṣkara* oil and clarified butter, using a ladle shaped like a serpent's head.
Having wrapped his head in black cloth and holding a sword in his hand,
one who is full of wrath should immediately offer oblations in the middle of the night to forcibly slay the enemy.
By performing a fire sacrifice (homa) with its fruits and leaves in a fire made of death-wood (mṛtyukāṣṭha),
elephants and horses will contract disease within seven nights.

By performing a fire sacrifice with sticks four finger-breadths long, the enemy's fourfold army will undoubtedly be afflicted by disease and suffering within seven days; of this there is no doubt. (39)
Who indeed could describe the full majesty of this vidyā?
Nevertheless, O beloved, listen as I describe a small portion of it according to its general direction. 40.

"With sugar-candies" (śarkarābhiḥ). || 31 || 32 || With these aforementioned items—of which "sesame seeds and so forth" is the ellipsis—the remainder being "plunged in ghee, honey, and milk," that is, sprinkled with the three sweets (*trimadhu*). Being sprinkled with the three sweets is common to all [the materials]. "With each one individually" is likewise common to every ritual application.

In the phrase "with wealth and so forth" (*dhanādibhiḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the vital breaths (*prāṇa*). The meaning is that one should perform the oblation (*homa*) in the stated sequence with all thirty-six substances, such as sesame seeds and the rest, either soaked in clarified butter (*ājya*) or merely smeared with pure ghee. That is to say, one should perform the oblation in the stated sequence with those [substances] moistened with milk.

This is what is meant: one should offer oblations in the various prescribed rites with the thirty-six substances beginning with sesame and ending with sugar, anointed with the three sweets according to the stated sequence; this is the first position.
One should offer oblations with those same substances anointed with pure ghee alone; this is the second position.

The third position is that one should offer oblations with [substances] smeared solely with milk. *Mṛtyu* is the *kāraskara* tree; [the oblation is made] with its [wood], smeared with mustard seeds and clarified butter. With the flesh arising from the womb of an enemy—that is, the flesh of the animal corresponding to the birth-nakṣatra of the enemy—for the sake of the death of that enemy. || 35 ||
[The oblation] is cooked in blood arising from a womb and cooked in the blood of the victim’s birth-star;
then, with a ladle formed by a severed snake-head, [one offers].
Now, I shall describe the mystical diagrams (*yantra*) for the attainment of all desired goals.
O Goddess of the Gods! contemplate all of these in your mind in their proper sequence. (41)
One should lay down twelve threads extending east, west, south, and north; one should then form three-pointed projections on both sides of their tips, centered upon that [central thread].

Having placed the name in the center of the *tāra* within the enclosure (*koṣṭha*), one should perform twelve repetitions by means of *māyā*, entering [the enclosure] in a clockwise direction starting from Śiva.
Having written out the vidyā and recited it, one should wear it for the sake of all accomplishments—for prosperity, fame, subjugation, good fortune, and the attainment of everything. (44)
One should wear it for the pacification of poison, planetary afflictions, diseases, and insanity; for the attainment of victory in battle;
and for bringing men, women, kings, and others under one's influence. (45)
One should draw nine lines running east-west and north-south;
thus, O Supreme Goddess, sixty-four squares are produced.

The meaning is "with the hood of a serpent. The connection with the preceding verse is: "One should offer [oblations] to slay the enemy, for the destruction of the enemy" (37). "With its fruits" means with fruits that cause death; "with its leaves" means with leaves that cause death (38). "Born from the four-fingered [plant]" refers to the flowers of the *āragvadha* tree (39). That...
The connection [of the words] is: "Listen to that majesty (vaibhava) in its general direction and in part. || 40 ||

Now, with five verses beginning with "atha yantrāṇi" and ending with "tad," he teaches the yantra consisting of one hundred and twenty-one squares, its application, and its results. In that context, "triśikhāni" refers to fresh tridents. [It is] in the central square.
In the central square of all; "together with Māyā, which is Hṛllekhā"—this is the remainder [of the sentence].

43. "That [is] the yantra"—this is the ellipsis. What is meant is this: having drawn twelve lines each with equal intervals, oriented toward the east and west, and toward the south and north, there will be forty-eight points on all sides.
Having made each of their tips into tridents, one should write the *praṇava* containing the name in the very center of the hundred and twenty-one squares; then,
by entering in a clockwise direction starting from Śiva, one should [arrange] the root-vidyā according to the sequence not yet mentioned.

Having written the ten syllables—beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and excluding the first *hṛllekhā* mantra—twelve times within the interior of the second *hṛllekhā*, one should wear it according to the prescribed method. || 44 || 45 ||
Within those [squares], one should write all the deities beginning with Nirṛti and Lakṣmī in due order;
outside, one should surround [the diagram] with the *tūrṇākṣara* syllables ending in *vaṣaṭ*, and [thus] worship it. || 47 ||
O Maheśvarī, listen to the *anugraha-mahācakra*, the *anuṣṭubh* mantra for the *sarvatobhadra* arrangement, which bestows all perfections (*siddhis*). (48)
Then, the ether (viyat) joined with fire (dāhavahni), heart (hṛt), and wind (marut);
and the ether accompanied by wind is pervaded and endowed with that [fire]. || 49 ||
These same [syllables], when reversed, shall constitute the first quarter;
the second [quarter] shall consist of the first [syllable] of the second [verse], while the second [syllable] shall be "bhuvā" followed by a void (śūnya). (50)
The third [pāda] would be that same fourth, and then the *jyā* would move through the clouds;
likewise, the second foot would consist of these [syllables] in reverse order. || 51 ||
With the two verses beginning with "prāk" and ending with "veṣṭayet," he teaches the sixty-four-square yantra for the *anugraha* (graceful) rite. In this regard, the following is stated:
[one should draw] nine lines each, with equal intervals, running east-west and north-south.

Having stretched out the threads and divided them into sixty-four squares, one should draw there the Śrīvidyā Anuṣṭubh in the form of the Sarvatobhadra, as will be described— a configuration of four rows by four rows, beginning from the square of Śiva-Nirṛti and extending southward and northward to its conclusion.

Outside of that, in the four directions beginning with the east, from Īśa to Īśāna, one should surround the Tvaritā-vidyā— which has been repeated four times— by means of the syllables of Tvaritā interspersed with the *vaṣaṭ* (or *phaṭ*) sounds, so as to touch the outermost line. || 46 || 47 ||
With these seven verses beginning with *anugraham* and ending with *saṅkathā*,

[the author] teaches the extraction of the Śrīvidyā and its majesty, preceded by an introduction in the *anuṣṭubh* meter in the form of a *sarvatobhadra*. Among those, [he teaches] the *anuṣṭubh* for the *sarvatobhadra* arrangement:

The quality of being "auspicious in every respect" (*sarvatobhadra*), however, is established by reciting [the mantra] eight times in four rows, both in direct and reverse order. Furthermore, the first syllable of the *Śrīvidyā* is the letter *viyat* (ha) joined with *dāha* (ra) and *vahni* (ra), thus forming the syllable *hrīṃ*.

The meaning is that the first syllable is *śrī*. Then, *sā* is the second, consisting of the heart (*hṛt*) and the wind (*marut*). *Mā* is the third, being space (*nabhas*) conjoined with the wind. *Pā* is the fourth, pervaded by and endowed with that same wind. These very four syllables, situated in the order already stated, are now [to be taken] in reverse.
"By reversing the stated order. *Caraṇa* means "foot. This is what is meant:
those same four syllables that abide in the stated order, when reversed—that is, in reverse order—constitute *yamopāśrī*.
The third and fourth [syllables] are *ilā* and *vanhi* followed by *ilā*;
joined with *marut*, this is the third [mantra], as before, in reverse order. (52)
The fourth, twelfth, twentieth, and the one preceding it—
these, O Maheśvarī, are the fourth quarter of the Śrīvidyā in reverse order.
This Vidyā, possessing forms auspicious in every respect, accomplishes all aims;
wherever she resides established in the wheel, there no talk of inauspiciousness exists.

Thus, these eight syllables constitute the first quarter of the *Śrīvidyā-anuṣṭubh*. "The first [syllable] of the second" means that the second syllable of the aforementioned first quarter becomes the first syllable of the second quarter; "sā" is the [first syllable] of the second quarter.
The first syllable is *ā*. The second is *bhū*, which is empty (*śūnya*). The second syllable is *no* (the letter *ka* is not present).

That third [syllable] shall be the fourth; that is to say, the fourth syllable of the first quarter-verse (*pāda*) becomes the third syllable of the second quarter-verse. Then follows *jyā* and *sābhracarā*.
The syllable *jyā* is the letter *ja*; *abhram* is the letter *jña*. In the word *jñe*, the letter *e* is the fourth syllable.
The "foot" (*caraṇa*) of these four syllables situated in the aforementioned order is as before. This is what is meant: [the foot] of the four syllables situated in the stated order.

One should recite "jñeyānosā" in reverse order as before; thus, it shall become the second quarter of that *anuṣṭubh* verse. Furthermore, the third and fourth quarters [are formed] by taking the third and fourth syllables of the first quarter and the first and second syllables of the third quarter.
The meaning is that they should be [so]. *Ilā* is with *vanhi* (fire); because of its independence, it possesses the state of being a stream (*srotva*).
*Lī* is the third syllable. *Ilā* joined with *marut* (wind) is *lā*; this is the fourth syllable. This is in reverse order;
the third [mantra] is *lālīyāmā*, which is the reverse of the four syllables situated in the stated sequence.
The meaning is that it becomes a quarter (pāda). The word "third" refers to the foot; the sense is "quarter. || 52 ||

The fourth, twelfth, twentieth, and the one preceding that of this vidyā: the fourth syllable is *pā*, the twelfth is *jñe*, the twentieth is *lā*, and the one preceding that—the nineteenth—is *lī*. Thus, these four syllables should occur according to the stated order.
These are the "reverse-moving" (vilomagā): these four syllables, which were established in the stated order, are recited in reverse.
This constitutes the group of eight syllables. The quarter-verse (caraṇa) is as before. What is meant is this:
the four syllables established in the stated order and those same syllables recited in the reverse order of that sequence—*caya*, *jñe*, *lā*, *lī*, *lā*.
"The eight syllables [of the mantra] should be known as such; thus the fourth quarter of that Śrīvidyā Anuṣṭubh comes to be. This is of the nature of the Sarvatobhadra diagram; what is meant is this:
in the previously mentioned sixty-four squares, starting from the top...

Having inscribed the four lines, beginning with *sarva* and ending with *dakṣa*, in the first, second, third, and fourth rows, one should form eighty-one squares (*pada*) by applying ten threads across those same lines.
Having placed [the deity] in the forest situated within that central square, one should place his name in the paths located in the middle of the forest.
One should write that fourth letter of the varga; listen, O blessed lady, to it according to the rule:
[it is] with the bowstring, the lower lip, the māyā, the heart, then water, and Ilā residing in touch. 56.
Then one should draw the Vidyā of Śrī, beginning with the directions starting from the northeast for the protection of Śiva;
as before, one should encircle it with those syllables of the ocean of nectar joined with the vowel *vṛddhi*.

Then, having fashioned a water-pot with its base shaped like a lotus and its upper part circular, by means of those two [verses] joined together with that [mantra] which has taken the form of a *mālā*, || 58 ||
Having fashioned [the thread] from gold or other materials, and having worshipped and honored it again,
one should place it upon those previously mentioned [objects] for the successful accomplishment of the recitation (japa).

Having written it out in reverse order in the four bottom rows so that the first quarter-verse appears at the very bottom, one should observe that the first quarter-verse is seen in the four outer rows,
both in reverse and in direct order; this is the case everywhere in the second rows.

In the four [verses] of that kind, the second quarter is seen; likewise, in the four lines of the third [set], the third quarter is seen; and similarly, in the fourth lines, the fourth quarter is seen. This is Śrīvidyā—this is the remainder [of the statement]. || 54 ||

With these seven verses beginning with "daśa" and ending with "sampada," he teaches the yantra called Amṛtakumbha, which consists of eighty-one words, as well as its application and its fruits. In this context, "dāvaḥ" refers to the letter *ṭha*. The syntactical connection is: "Listen to that."

"Jyādharāsvaiḥ jū" means: the letter *sa* together with the *visarjanīya* [ḥ] taken by means of *māyā* [the vowel *ī*]. "Ambu" is the letter *va*. "Sparśagā ilā ṣala" means the letter *ṭa*. These four syllables are located within the four cells situated on the sides of the central cell, across the four rows.
The traditional meaning is that one should write [the syllables] in sequence by moving outward from the center. Regarding this,

the followers of the pure tradition state that one should write four syllables in each of the four rows, writing one syllable at a time in each of the four [positions] according to the order of the rows.
That is not approved by our venerable teachers. (56) "With the syllables of the *Tvaritāmṛtā*":

[this refers to] the syllables of the *Tvaritāmṛtā*, which are the syllables of the *Tvaritā-vidyā* joined with *phaṭ* or joined with *vaṣaṭ*. (57) "Joined with *ambu* and *sva*" means *vaṃ*; by that...

[It is] together with the syllable *vaṃ* alone, which has the form of a garland and whose written forms are joined to one another; this is the remainder [of the sense]. It is endowed with two lotuses, one above and one below, having upward and downward faces respectively, positioned from the lower to the upper.
The meaning is "the jar" (kumbha). || 58 || Having established [it] there, Lakṣmī becomes exceedingly abundant, and likewise the subjects are free from disease;
elephants, cattle, and other living beings are constantly happy. || 60 ||
One should wear this [amulet] during afflictions caused by spirits, ghosts, piśācas, and the like;
for the pacification of misfortune, for the attainment of power, and for all prosperity.
Listen to the method of subjugation, O Goddess of Gods! By means of this power, one's enemies shall surely lose their lives in a very short time. (62)
Having first divided [the area] into eighty-one squares as before, one should write the name "Dāhagarbha" in the central cell, and likewise [the names] in the paths of the directions in sequence.

The word "the deity" is to be supplied [as the object]. The word "the yantra" is to be supplied [as the object of worship]. The phrase "in the previously mentioned times of the rising of the eleven zodiac signs" means "in the positions corresponding to those respective signs. This is what is meant:
by drawing ten lines with equal intervals running east-west and north-south.

Having arranged eighty-one squares according to the sūtras, one should write the name within the *ṭha* letter joined with a nasal dot (*bindu*) in the very center of the grid. Then, in the four rows situated at the sides of that square, one should sequentially write, starting from the top and proceeding clockwise: the syllable *jūḥ*, the syllable *saḥ*, and the letter *va* six times.

Having thus written in the four squares by way of an outward movement from the center, one should then write the previously mentioned *anuṣṭubh* verse of Śrīvidyā— beginning with Īśa and ending with Nirṛti, and likewise beginning with Nirṛti and ending with Īśa— excluding the four central paths; finally, on the outermost perimeter all around, from Īśa to Īśa.
Having quickly inscribed the syllables of the *tūrṇāmṛta* four times as before, and having occupied the center of the central square,
one should produce a circle by rotating according to the measure of the syllables of the *tūrṇāmṛta* located in the four corners.

Outside of that, having likewise produced a circle with a measurement of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*), and having erased two circles— one in the upper portion and one in the lower portion— with a four-finger interval between them from the center;
then, slightly curved from the four tips of those [circles], with equal intervals, extending four fingers upward.
Having raised [the structure] so that it takes the shape of a pot's mouth,

one should draw two horizontal lines across the mouth of that pot; then, the center of the path of that pot is [to be connected] by a garland in the form of a chain, which has an inward-facing curve and whose ends touch one another.

Having filled [the vessel] completely and drawn a *bindu* above everywhere, one should draw the pitcher beneath it situated within the pericarp of a lotus; likewise, having drawn a lotus at the mouth of the pitcher with its face downward and its stalk upward, according to the prescribed sequence.
And because they are employed for one's desired objects, the aforementioned results shall indeed come to pass. || 60 || 61 ||

With eighteen verses beginning with "nigraham" and ending with "asurairapi," which consist of eighty-one words, [the text describes] the *nigraha*-yantra, the secret syllables (*kūṭākṣara*) to be written therein,
the *sarvatobhadra* diagram, the *Kālī-vidyā*, and likewise the *Yama-mantra*.
One should write the four seed-syllables that have the nature of fire and wind, by which enemies immediately abandon their own bodies. (64)
In the *Tekṣt*, the numbering of the switches proceeds directly from 64 to 66:

"The swallow (*khaga*) is joined with the earth and the three [units] of the burner of *rasa* (*rasodāhakṣmāsvayuta*); the bird (*khaga*) is joined with the earth and the three [units] of the devourer of *grāsa* (*grāsodāhakṣmayā*);

the light (*prabhā*) is joined with the earth and the three [units] of the burner (*dāhakṣmāsvayuta*); and it is conjoined with the beginning of the utterance of the *haṃsa* (*haṃsodāhādisaṃyuta*)" (66).
Then, starting from the northeast and the northwest directions, one should write the line by line the untransmitted Vidyā-mantra of Kālī and Yama in their proper sequence.
O Goddess, the *anuṣṭubh* of Kālī is indeed of a form auspicious on all sides;
listen, O Goddess, as I shall hereafter describe the *anuṣṭubh* of Yama.
Prāṇa (ha), together with Marut (sa), Ilā (la), and Vanhi (ra);
Nabas (na) joined with Marut (sa), and Dāha (ca)—these are the four in reverse order. (69)
Its first foot is [the syllable] *ca*, and its second is indeed *śūnya* (zero);
this second [foot] consists of the swallowing (*grāsa*) of space (*nabhas*) and earth (*bhū*), read in reverse order. (70)
The third [foot] is the eleventh; then follows the *gotra* together with the *cara*;
their speed (*rayas*) is reversed, and the third foot belongs to Manu. (71)

And he teaches its fruit: therein, for whichever application of suppression [is used], [it is] within the womb of burning, with the letter *ra* joined by a dot (*bindu*) above. It possesses the form of fire and wind, both in terms of the syllables of the name and in terms of its experiential manifestation. By which four peak-syllables (*kūṭākṣara*), the body—

The body (śarīra) is *bhrūṃ*, joined with fire, earth, and ether. The morsel (grāsa) is *kṣū*, consisting of fire, earth, ether, and air. The radiance (prabhā) is *vlū*, joined with fire, earth, ether, and air. The swan (haṃsa), joined with fire and the others, is *hū*. The vital breath (prāṇa), accompanied by wind, is *kā*.

The syllable *lī* is endowed with *ilā* (the letter *i*) and fire (*vahnī*, the letter *r*). The syllable *mā* is joined with space (*nabhas*, the letter *h*) and wind (*marut*, the letter *y*). "Burning" (*dāha*) refers to the letter *repha* (*r*).
The first quarter-verse (*caraṇa*) shall consist of these four letters in reverse order. This is what is meant:
as before, [the mantra is formed] from the four letters situated in the aforementioned sequence.

From reading [the mantra] in reverse order, a quarter-verse of the *anuṣṭubh* of the *Kālī-vidyā* shall arise. The meaning of "the second" is that the second syllable of the first quarter-verse of this *vidyā* becomes the first syllable of the second quarter-verse; namely, *lī*. The second syllable is "void," which is the letter *na*.
The third syllable is *mo* with *nabhobhū* [i.e., *o*]. (p. 247) The fourth, twelfth, and twentieth [syllables] are reversed from the *rayobāla* [i.e., *bālayora*];
this is declared to be the fourth quarter. This is the *vidyā* that destroys everything.
Vyāptam, Kālī, and the third [syllable] joined with Marut and Ambu;
Nāda is the reverse of these, and it is the first quarter in Yama.
The second and fourth [syllables] are *nabhas* and *bhū*, and *nādaka*;
the second foot is the reverse of these, namely *manāḥ*.

The letter *kṣa* is the fourth syllable. This means that, by reversing the order, it is the second [syllable] among the four syllables situated in the stated sequence; thus, according to the previous method of reversal, it constitutes the second quarter-verse (*pāda*). The third [syllable] is the third syllable of the first quarter-verse, namely the syllable *mā*.
The first syllable of the third quarter is *bhavati*. The eleventh [syllable] of this *anuṣṭubh* is *ekādaśamo*, which is the second syllable. *Gotrā carānvitā de* is the third syllable.
*Rayaḥ* with the letter *ta* is the fourth syllable. And the third quarter consists of these [syllables] in reverse order.

The meaning is that the third quarter consists of the recitation in reverse order of the four syllables situated according to the stated sequence. Regarding the word *manuḥ*: the term *manu* is a common designation for both a mantra and a vidyā. (71) The fourth [syllable] of this vidyā is *va*.

The fourth syllable is the first syllable of the fourth quarter; this is the meaning. The twelfth is the letter *kṣa*, the second [syllable]. The twentieth is the letter *ta*, the third syllable. *Rayaḥ* is the letter *ta*. *Abā* means "possessing water" (*ambuvān*); by virtue of its independence (*svātantryāt*), it becomes *tva*, which is the fourth syllable. It is reversed (*vilomaka*).

The meaning is that by reciting these four syllables, which abide in the stated order, in reverse, the fourth quarter [of the verse] is formed. This [verse] has thus been described as "all-destroying" (*sarvanāśinī*), with the word "through its application" (*prayogāt*) being understood as the ellipsis. In this way, as before, this *anuṣṭubh* of Kālī in the form of the *Sarvatobhadra* has been declared.

With these four verses beginning with "vyāptam" and ending with "śive," he teaches the *yamānuṣṭubh* in the form of a *sarvatobhadra*. Among them, the letter "ya" is the first syllable; "kālī" is the third, meaning the third syllable of the *kālyanuṣṭubh*.

The second syllable of this [mantra] is *mā*. The third syllable is *vā*, accompanied by the water of the Maruts (*marut*). The fourth syllable is the resonance (*nāda*), which means the letter *ṭha*. By reciting these four syllables in reverse order, as before, the first quarter-verse (*pāda*) is formed.

Regarding *yama* and *yamayantra*: || 73 || "And the second and fourth [syllables] of this"—the second and fourth syllables of this *yama-mantra*, which are the first and second syllables of the second quarter, become *sāṭa*.
*Nabhasā bhūḥ saḥ* is the third syllable. *Nāda* and the letter *ṭha* are the fourth syllable.
From the reverse recitation of these four syllables arranged in the stated order, as before (p. 248),
the mantra joined with water (ambuyukta) is indeed this eleventh [mantra].
The taste [is produced] by the earth; from the reverse order [of elements], there is burning by fire and the third [element]. (75)
"Nāda, nāda, dāha, vahnī, and īra— immediately after those,
O Śivā, the fourth quarter shall consist of them in reverse order."
Having thus written the two mantras within the compartments, one should then encircle them on the outside with the Vyāpta and Dāha mantras, according to the stated sequence.
One should place a stone smeared with *markaṭī*, *daṇḍī*, and poison,
over which mantras have been recited, either into the opening of the axle or at a crossroads.
In an anthill, in a mother’s abode, or in a temple of the Teacher, or in a cremation ground—at the prescribed time and endowed with the prescribed sequence—[one should perform the rite]. (79)
Wherever the yantra is located—in whatever country or place—there misfortune dwells together with diseases;
and the pestilence (mārī) becomes firmly established there, such that it cannot be overcome even by all the gods and asuras combined.

The meaning is that this is the second quarter (pāda). "Marut joined with water" (ambuyukto marut) is the first syllable of the third quarter. In this [sequence], the eleventh [syllable]—in this *yamayantra*, the syllable *mo* is the eleventh; it is the second syllable of the third quarter. "Rasa, kṣmayā, abhra" [are the remaining syllables].
The third syllable is *tṛ*. From the reverse order, the fourth syllable is *agni-dāhau ri*.

This means that by reciting these four letters—which exist in the previously mentioned sequence—in the reverse order as before, the third quarter-verse (*pāda*) is formed. [The fourth syllable] is *nāda-nāda* and the two *ṭa*s.

In the first and second syllables of the fourth quarter, there are *ga* and *ga*. The third syllable is *rī*, representing the fire of burning. The fourth syllable is *yo* (or *yoṃ*), representing loftiness (*uccatva*). And these four syllables, which abide in the order previously stated, are [to be arranged] in reverse order as before.

The meaning is that by reciting [the mantra] in reverse order, the fourth quarter would arise. By the pervasive *yakāra* and *repha*, which signify burning; it is endowed with the aforementioned sequence and has the intermediate space (*antarāla*) performed. Daṇḍī refers to Brahmadaṇḍī. He himself will explain the method of applying the poison later on.
Having performed the ritual installation of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) as before, one should place [the deity] upon a single seat. || 78 || 79 ||
In the phrase "deśādi" (regions and so forth), the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to villages, cities, market towns, hamlets, and the like.
"Mārī" is the power that destroys the countryside. The sequence for the arrangement of the restraints and the yantra is now demonstrated:
as follows, with ten [lines] having equal intervals, directed toward the east, west, south, and north.

Having produced eighty-one squares with threads, O Śivā, and having formed a group of eight times eight squares there— just as before— with nine threads in the central square which is marked above with a dot (p. 249), one should [place] the mantra of Kālikā in them, beginning from the northeast and the southeast directions.
Having written [the diagram] with the Yama-mantra and the two aforementioned seed-syllables,
and having surrounded the wheel on the outside, one should place it face downwards.
And this, O Supreme Goddess, produces the fruit mentioned for the previous wheel;
one should also apply the names from the middle of the grid even to those not explicitly mentioned. (82)
Salt, pungent substances, urine, soot from a house, and fire—these combined with the resin arising from *nimba* wood and charcoals from a cremation ground are declared to be poison. (83)

Having written the name in the center of the *repha* (the letter *ra*), one should, as before, write the four syllables *bhū*, *kṣra*, *vrū*, and *hrū* in the four squares on the four rows at its sides, according to the previously mentioned sequence, surrounding them by moving from the interior outward; thus should the practitioner perform the rite.

If it is a man, he should write the Kālī-anuṣṭubh mantra inside and the Yama-mantra outside; if it is a woman, she should write the Yama-mantra inside and the Kālī-vidyā outside. In the process of writing, however, having written the Kālī-mantra starting from the northeast (īśa) and ending at the southwest (nirṛti), and in other cases likewise having written the Yama-mantra [in the same manner].

Having written one [series] continuously from the exterior starting at Īśāna and ending at Nirṛti, and again from Nirṛti to Īśāna, and having written outside that the letter *pa* joined with a *bindu* and the letter *ra*,
continuously and without gaps from Īśāna to Īśāna according to sequence, distinguishing between the interior and the exterior, for the sake of one's desired aims—
One should employ [this method]. And this applies to the case of a woman as well. If it is a woman, one should dig below the very top of the Teacher’s āyatana;
if it is a man, one should dig below the very top of the āyatana of Kālī and so forth. || 79 ||
With the three verses beginning with *prāgvat* and ending with *koṣṭhamadhyataḥ*,
[the author] teaches the *nigrahayantra* consisting of sixty-four squares,
as well as the specific results of its application; therein is the description of the encircling with the *Yama-mantra*.

This concerns the subject of the restraint of men. By this, it should be understood that in the case of the restraint of women, there is an internal wrapping with the *antaryama* mantra and an external wrapping with the *kālī* mantra; such is the meaning of the tradition. || 80 ||
One should encircle it as before with the two seed-syllables, namely the letter *ya* together with the *repha* (the letter *ra*) accompanied by the *bindu*. || 81 ||

The statement "even in the case of those not mentioned" refers to the female subject (*strīviṣaya*). Here, having described the infallible subjugation through the *Kālīya-mantra* and the *Amantra*, its remedy is achieved by means of the application of the *Tvaritā-vidyā* and the *yantra*. It is for this very purpose that [the text says...].

The description of the suppression [of the enemy] by means of the syllables of the mantra: The sequence for constructing the yantra is as follows. As before, having divided [the space] into sixty-four squares with nine lines, one should place the Kālikā-mantra inside if the person to be acted upon is a male, starting from the northeast (īśa) and ending at the southwest (nirṛti).

If [the practitioner] is a woman, one should draw the *antaryama* mantra on the outside and the *kālīvidyā* on the inside as before; then, having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) within the belly of the first letter of the *vidyā* using the letters *ya* and *ra* accompanied by the bindu as previously described, one should write it outside of that.
One should inscribe the syllable *phaṭ* at the eight divisions; thus it is the eight-syllabled [mantra].
Then one should surround the lotus situated upon the pericarp with Māyā,
and thereafter one should fashion the pitcher (kumbha) on the outside according to the prescribed rule of syllables.
In this manner, one should fashion nine yantras with the other nine syllables of the Vidyā in their proper order; now hear the fruit of these ten! || 86 ||
One shall obtain all forms of protection, victory, subjugation of men, women, kings, and others, as well as paralysis [of enemies], fortune, fame, gold, and garments. (87)

Having encircled it according to the previously mentioned sequence, one should place it face-down in the aforementioned locations according to the stated order; by that means, the very same results as previously described shall come to pass. || 82 ||

With the verse beginning with "lavaṇa," he teaches the nature of the poison for the purpose of drawing the diagram of the restraint (*nigrahayantra*). In this context, *ūṣaṇa* means salt (*ūṣa*); *mehāmbu* means urine; *agni* means *citraka*; and the rest is to be understood from the mouth of one's chosen deity (*ārādhya*). || 83 ||
With two and three-quarter verses beginning with "vidyā" and ending with "yantrāṇi," he teaches the method for ten yantras using ten syllables each from among the syllables of the root-vidyā;
therein, according to the prescribed arrangement of syllables:
This is due to the encircling by the garland of the syllable *va*, which has the form of a chain (*śṛṅkhalā*) together with the nasal bindu as previously described.

This is what is meant: having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus, one should place the first *hṛllekhā* of the Vidyā in the center of its pericarp (*karṇikā*), the *praṇava*—which is the first element of the Vidyā—in its interior, and [the remaining syllables] in the middle of that.

Having written the name, one should then inscribe the remaining eight mantra-syllables— devoid of the two *hṛllekhās* and the *phaṭ*-kāra— in sequence, proceeding clockwise from the tip [of the petals] upon the eight petals; then,
having encircled that lotus with the second *hṛllekhā* in the manner previously described, [one proceeds] outside of that as before.

One should fashion a jar accompanied by a garland of *takāra* syllables joined by bindus and linked together, and provided with two lotuses above and below; this is the first yantra. Likewise, in the center of the pericarp of this very same yantra, within the interior of the *hṛllekhā*, one should place the third syllables of the Vidyā in sequence.

Having inscribed each [name] as the core, one should then write the previously mentioned sequence from the beginning to the end using these aforementioned syllables situated on the petals; together with what was stated before, one should draw nine yantras within the *hṛllekhā*, inscribing the name along with the syllable *phaṭ* in the center.

With the remaining syllables beginning from the third, excluding the *praṇava*, situated on the petals as before, one should likewise fashion the tenth [yantra]; thus, one should make ten yantras. || 84 || 85 ||
With the first verse beginning with "Of the ten" (*daśānām*) and ending with "one would obtain" (*āpnuyāt*), he teaches the ten uncommon fruits of the ten yantras in their respective order;
therein, the meaning is easy to understand. (86–87)
p. 251) The syllables at the end are eleven, and they are not repeated;
when combined with the vowels, the number is traditionally held to be one hundred and seventy-six. || 88 ||

O Goddess of the gods! Listen as I shall describe, in due order, the construction of those machines and their respective fruits for the sake of accomplishing the desired goals of the practitioner. (89)
Having fashioned a sixteen-petaled lotus situated between two circles,
one should place the Śakti, together with the object of the rite (sādhya), in its center, within the pericarp.
One should encircle those sixteen syllables with others on the outside using the Māyā-bīja;
between the two circles, one should draw a pitcher (kumbha) as prescribed on the exterior.
Thus, eleven celebrated yantras have indeed been described;
now listen, O Pārvatī, to their applications in due order. || 92 ||
The first is for the protection of horses, the second for the protection of elephants,
the third for the protection of the king, and the fourth for the protection of the army.
He performs the protection of the royal palace on all sides.
With four and a half verses beginning with *anāvṛttāni* and ending with *iti*, he teaches eleven yantras using the syllables of the root-vidyā modified by vowels. Therein, the *śakti*...

The *hṛllekhā* [mantra]. (88) (89) (90). This means on the other petals. That lotus. By *māyā*, that is, by the *hṛllekhā*. Between the two circles, that is, in the path between the two outer circles of the lotus. The syntactical connection is:
"One should encircle it with *māyā* between the two circles. On the outside, that is, on the very outermost part. Thus it has been stated.
"Accompanied by a garland of *va* syllables, linked together and provided with the nasal bindu as before. This is what is meant:

having fashioned a sixteen-petalled lotus and drawn two circles around it, one should likewise, as before, place a garland of *va* syllables—linked and endowed with the bindu—both above and below that outer circle.

Having fashioned a jar accompanied by two lotuses, one should write the *hṛllekhā* mantra containing the name [of the disciple] in the center of the pericarp of that lotus; then, among the one hundred and seventy-six syllables of the Vidyā— which are formed from the sixteen vowels modified by the consonants— one should take the first sixteen syllables and place them upon the sixteen petals.

Having drawn [the diagram] in a clockwise direction starting from the top, one should encircle the space between the lotus and the outer circle with the *hṛllekhā* mantra; this is the first yantra. In the same manner, one should write the other sixteen syllables upon the sixteen petals of this very yantra. Thus, according to what has been stated...
Thus, there are eleven and a half yantras. || 91 ||
The sixth protects the ministers, and the seventh protects the city. || 94 ||
The eighth [chapter] shall be on the protection of the home for everyone at all times,
from dangers such as serpents, thieves, and malevolent spirits, as well as from enemies.
O Goddess of gods! when joined with the previously mentioned procedure, this ninth [mantra] shall always be the deliverer from all afflictions caused by disease for everyone. 96.
Having fashioned the tenth [linga] out of birch bark as before, with its characteristic marks described for beeswax,
one should then place it in cool water within a jar or similar vessel nearby.
One should worship them and recite [the mantra] while touching that [object] with the "life-giving hand" (jīvakara);
thus, a burning fever arising from terrible malevolent rites and the like will vanish in an instant.
Having released it, O Dear One, one should destroy that practitioner at that very moment!
In this way, these yantras, by their names, accomplish all tasks. (99)
O Pārvatī, for the prosperity of all the eternal ones, one should offer an oblation at the beginning of the worship and other rites in the early morning with the sixteen-syllable mantra.
The pervasive state consisting of the reality of breath has been correctly described;
by the thorough cultivation of this within the mind, that very reality is made one's own. (101)

With these seven verses beginning with "viniyoga" and ending with "kāryakṛt," he teaches the application (*viniyoga*) of those yantras. In that context, "daṇḍarakṣaka" means that which effects the protection of the army. [Verses 92, 93, 94, 95. "Endowed with the previously mentioned procedure" means...
The consecration of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā), the empowerment (abhiṣeka), the dhāraṇa, and the worship (arcana) are now described. || 96 ||

Because the application [of the ritual] is the same for the tenth and eleventh [chapters], it is not stated separately. "In the presence of the one afflicted by disease" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "That jar" (verse 97). "Those written syllables" (verse 98). "That one afflicted by disease. "The performer"—the ellipsis to be supplied is "of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and so forth"—"by name."
The meaning is that all these machines accomplish every task; by means of the skillful arrangement of the letters of one's name in the center, they perform all activities.

With the verse beginning "Of all [the Nityās]," he extends by analogy (*atideśa*) the mantra for the offering of the *bali* at the commencement of the morning worship of all the Nityās. In this context, "of all" is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
"With the sixteen-syllable mantra" refers to the mantra stated at the conclusion of the third chapter; this is the ellipsis. (99–100)
Thus ends the fourteenth chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, among the *Śrīṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
Thus [ends] the commentary titled *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa* on the complete *Tantra* known as the *Śrīkādimata* within the *Śrīṣoḍaśanityātantras*.

Thus, the fourteenth chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the ritual procedure for the Śivadūtī Nityā-vidyā, has been fully expounded in the commentary named Manoramā composed by Śrī Subhagānandanātha. 12.
In this fourteenth chapter, the number of verses is twenty-six, the diagrams are two hundred and twenty-one and a half, and the explanatory texts are [the same].
Now begins the fifteenth chapter.
Now, regarding that which is proclaimed as the tenth among the sixteen Nityās—
the Vidyā known as Kulasundarī— listen to the procedure for her worship.
He [taught] that meditation, that ritual placement (nyāsa), those powers, that worship,
as well as that means of accomplishment, the various forms, and the sacrifices that bestow speech.
She is red, attended by a multitude of powers of red appearance,
clad in red garments, smeared with blood upon the ground, and possessing six lotus-like faces.
She has three eyes on each face and is endowed with a beautiful smile;
she is radiant with a crown of rubies set with priceless jewels.
Resplendent with earrings, necklaces, armlets, girdles,
and anklets, her auspicious chest was adorned with clusters of red blossoms.
She whose seat is a red lotus supreme with compassion and bliss,
endowed with twelve arms, and who embodies all speech for all beings.
A rosary of coral beads, a lotus, a water-pot fashioned from jewels,
a cup filled with wealth, and a ring inscribed with the *Luṅgivyākhyāna*.
Fifteenth Chapter.
Having taught in the preceding fourteenth chapter the ritual procedure for the ninth, the Nityā Tvaritā, [the author] next [teaches] that of the tenth, the Kulasundarī-nityā-vidyā.

He teaches the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*) by means of the fifteenth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "he plunges" (*vigāhate*). Therein, with two verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "the offering" (*pradāna*), he indicates the subjects of the chapter. Regarding that, the phrase "stated in the third chapter" is to be understood as the remainder. That meditation (*taddhyāna*)...

The word "for the purpose of constant worship" is to be supplied as the remainder. "Its means" refers to the means for attaining knowledge. "Of those two" refers to the knowledge and the deity. || 1 || 2 ||

With nine verses beginning with *lohitām* and ending with *apekṣayā*, [the author] teaches the meditation for daily worship (*nityapūjādhyāna*) and the varieties of meditation for specific desires (*kāmyadhyāna*). (p.
255) [She is] holding in her right and left hands a book and a beautiful red lotus.
And in his arms he holds a golden pen, a garland of jewels, and a choice conch shell.
And she was being praised on all sides by gods, gandharvas, and kinnaras,
as well as by yakṣas, rākṣasas, celestial sages (devarṣis), siddhas, vidyādharas, and others.
Having meditated thus, one should worship daily for the sake of attaining mastery over speech, fortune, and beauty;
for the sake of mastery over speech alone, one should worship her as white, and for the sake of fortune, as having the luster of gold.

One should visualize her as having the appearance of smoke for the purpose of causing enmity with enemies, for death, and for subjugation; and one should visualize her as blue when aiming at the silencing [of speech]. || 11 ||
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) using those three root syllables beginning with *la*,
sequentially at the beginning, middle, and end of the rite of worship and recitation.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands, limbs, and faces with each of those three seed-syllables conjoined with the long vowels, according to the prescribed rule.

In that regard, concerning the arrangement of the faces—six lotus-faces [located] above, in the east, south, north, west, and behind—he himself will explain this later. (3) (4) (5) "Consisting of all speech" means consisting of the sounds of all Vedic languages. (6) "That cup" refers to a jeweled cup; *luṅgī*...
The *mātuluṅgī* (citron). || 7 || The connection is with "by the right arms. The *aruṇotpala* is the red water-lily (*raktakairava*).

Here, the arrangement of weapons begins from the top on both sides. || 8 || 9 || 10 || For the sake of manifesting [the form] (*prativigrahāya*), that is, for the affliction of diseases and so forth; according to each respective requirement, in accordance with the application of each specific [rite]. || 11 ||

With these five verses beginning with "tribhiḥ" and ending with "varṇakaiḥ," he teaches the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). In that context, at the beginning, middle, and end of the procedure for recitation and worship, the conclusion of the recitation occurs when one-half of the intended number of recitations has been completed. Therein lies the placement (*nyāsa*).

Having performed [the preliminary rites], one should recite [the mantra] for half the remaining portion. The ritual placement (*nyāsa*) occurs during the recitation. For this very Kulasundarī, apart from the time of the invocation prior to worship and the time of the placement during the recitation, all other times for placement are common to everyone. This is done in sequence, according to the proper order. || 12 ||

In the first *kūṭa*, the addition of long vowels (*dīrghasvarayojana*) consists of the utterance of the six pure long vowels—*ā, ī, ū, ai, au, aḥ*—because that [first *kūṭa*] is composed of vowel-syllables (*svarākṣara*). Thus, in all cases where there are vowel-syllables, there is the addition of long vowels; for the other two [kūṭas], it is as previously stated.
In the hands, limbs, and faces— specifically in the hands and limbs— with the names "upward," "east," "south," "north," and "west" (along with their respective opposites),
one should [place them] in due order within those [deities] who abide in the interior of purity. 14.
This [first] is in the foundation-cavity (ādhāra), the heart, and the three eyes;
the second is in the two ears and the chin; the third is in the nose and the palate. || 15 ||
Then, one should place [the syllables] five times on the shoulders and the navel, and then on both hands and feet;
thus, by means of the root-syllables, one should assign them ninefold according to their roots, middles, and tips.

As before; for the faces, however, in the manner that will be described [in verse 13]. By those names of the faces, which are pure, situated within the *natya* (the syllable *namas*), and contain the word *namaḥ* in their midst—by those names of the faces, in their respective forms located on those specific planes (*talas*), according to the sequence of the previously mentioned seed-syllables (*bījas*) of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*).

One by one, decreasing by one each time—*ai*, *r*, *ū*—one should place [the seed-syllables] upon the upward-facing mouth with the mantra: "Obeisance to the upward-facing mouth" (*ūrdhvavaktrāya namaḥ*).

The same applies to the others. The traditional teaching is that one should likewise place them upon the five mouths—the eastern, southern, northern, western, and rear ones—in the specified order, using the respective name-mantras of that kind.

At the time of worship, after the invocation, one should worship the deity in its respective faces with the six syllables of the first peak (kūṭa) using their respective mantras. This is what is meant:
the three seed-syllables of the Kulasundarī-vidyā are each made long according to the sequence already stated.
By joining the six vowels in a sixfold manner, and having thus combined them into eighteen syllables,
the procedure for the worship and recitation of the nine triangles of the first peak-syllable (kūṭākṣara) is to be performed at its commencement according to the stated sequence.

One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands, limbs, and three faces. In the center of that, one should perform the ritual placement of the hands, limbs, and three faces upon the hexagon of the second seed-syllable (kūṭākṣara) according to the prescribed sequence. At the conclusion—
One should perform the threefold nyāsa according to the sequence prescribed for the hexagon of the third peak-syllable. || 14 ||

With the verse beginning with "ādhāra," he teaches the sequence of placement (*nyāsakrama*) consisting of nine coverings (*navāvaraṇa*) by means of the three syllables of the root-vidyā. In that context, "one" implies "once";
likewise, "the second" and so forth also denote times. [The placement is] on the two hands and feet—that is, on the pair of feet.

And likewise for the two feet, and for all four [limbs]: in each one, at the three locations—the root, the middle, and the tip—one should perform the placement ninefold, together with those previously mentioned; that is, six times, seven times, eight times, and nine times. This is what is meant here.

One should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) nine times with the three syllables of the Vidyā in their respective locations, according to the prescribed sequence, within the nine triangular groups beginning with the *ādhāra*.
These aforementioned [syllables] should be applied at the beginning, middle, and end of the performance of worship and recitation, up until the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*).
One should perform the ritual placements (nyāsa); such is the traditional teaching. || 16 ||
Speech is Sarasvatī, the voice, whether refined (Sanskrit), natural (Prakrit), or supreme;
