she takes the form of the sword and the form of wealth, being delightful and full of joy and wonder. (17)
These eleven have been declared; one should worship them within the nine wombs (navayoni).
Furthermore, one should worship Brāhmī and the others on the external eight-petaled lotus.
In the square, one should likewise worship the world-protectors (lokapālas) in the form of spears:
Indra, Agni, Yama, Rakṣas, Varuṇa, Anila, Soma, and [Iśāna]. (19)

For the sake of all accomplishments, one should worship Īśāna and the rest in the eight directions starting from the east, arranged from bottom to top, using their names ending with "Śakti," as previously described.
Having constructed two squares joined by doors in the east and west, one should fashion an eight-petalled lotus situated within a pair of circles in their center.
Having divided [the area] into nine parts consisting of four, three, five, and four [squares],
and having invoked her there as before, one should then worship her perfectly.

With these four verses beginning with *bhāṣā* and ending with *siddhaye*, he indicates the attendant powers (*parivāra-śakti*) of the Goddess; therein, in the *Ānandakautuka*, there are two powers: *Ānandā* and *Kautukā*.
Among the nine *yonis*, in the central *yoni* and in the three corners, [he places] the first.
One should worship the tenth and the eleventh [lunar days] in the manner that will be described hereafter.
With names ending in "śakti," such as "Indraśakti" and so forth as before, up to those ending in the seven-syllable [mantra]. || 20 ||

With these four and a half verses beginning with "caturasradvayam" and ending with "vai," he teaches the mandala for daily worship and the sequence of worship. In that context, the phrase "from four, three, five, and four parts" refers to the diameter of the circle; the word "four" [refers to the number of parts].

This is a statement of independence. What is meant is this: having first drawn a Brahma-sūtra (central line) in the form of east-west and north-south across the square, one should divide it into sixteen parts;
then, having marked points at the fourth, third, and fifth divisions starting from the east and so on, one should [draw lines] in groups of three at those marks.

Having completed two circles ending at the circumference, one should draw two lines starting from the two points where the southern and northern circumferences of the middle circle intersect, extending to the point where the western circumference meets the Brahma-line (the north-south axis); then, regarding the western line—

Starting from the two junctions of the eastern and western circles with the southern and northern circles, draw two lines extending to the two junctions of the eastern circle with the Brahma-line; then,
starting from the two junctions of the southern and northern circles with the eastern line, [draw two lines] to the western line.
Having stretched out the two threads— the Brahma-sūtra and the boundary-sūtra— one should worship the powers ending with Antaśakti on both sides of the central womb in the eleven [sections],
and likewise worship the powers ending with Lokapāla at the two doorways. (23)
O Ambikā, this is the specific [rite], while the other is the general worship:
at the conclusion of the pūjā, one should offer a bali-oblation to Kurukullā with the seven-syllable mantra.
In this manner, one should perform the daily worship and indeed the daily fire-oblation with clarified butter;
and for the sake of attaining the realization of the Self through knowledge, one should drink water in the morning.
With sandalwood, ushira, camphor, musk, and gorocana, as well as with saffron, black agallochum, and the secretions from the temples of deer; || 26 ||
One should wipe away the Brahma-line that was first struck. When this is done, a perfectly level nine-yoni wheel is produced, consisting of eight triangles touching the circle.
Having drawn an eight-petaled lotus outside of that, one should draw [the rest] outside of that, provided with gates in the east and west.
Having constructed two squares, one should worship her there according to the stated sequence. || 21 || 22 ||
The phrase "in the eleven powers" refers to the powers beginning with Bhāṣā; [this includes] the tenth power, Antaśakti, known as Ānanda, and the eleventh power, Kautuka.
Regarding the sides of the central yoni, this refers to the north and south of the yoni situated in the center.

One should worship in the two corners. Following the worship of the three central yoni-śaktis, one should perform the worship of the eight-cornered [diagram] for the first power called Bhāṣā, located in the middle of the yoni and the corner positions. The powers ending with the world-protectors (lokapāla) are the powers of Ananta and Brahmā.

"At the two doors" means at the eastern and western [doors], as is understood from the context. This is what is meant: on the southern side of the eastern door is the power of Indra (indra-śakti), on the northern side is the power of Ananta (ananta-śakti);
at the western door, on the southern side is the power of Varuṇa (varuṇa-śakti), and on the northern side is the power of Brahmā (brahma-śakti).

"And one should worship others in their respective directions"—this is the specific detail mentioned [in the passage] beginning with "on the two sides of the central yoni. Here, in the eight-petaled lotus and in the nine yonis, one should worship starting from the front and proceeding clockwise. In the square [mandala], however, one should worship according to the stated sequence, beginning from the eastern gate.
This means that one should worship by circumambulating clockwise; "in the general manner" means as previously described. || 24 ||
In this manner,
by the latter half of the verse beginning with "at dawn" (*prātaḥ*) and so forth, he teaches the means for accomplishing knowledge; therein,
for the sake of accomplishing the nature of the Vidyā, [one should act] by means of this *Kulasundarī* Vidyā alone.
The meaning is that by drinking a mouthful of water over which the mantra has been recited three times, there shall be purification of the self through the attainment of perfect knowledge. || 25 ||

With one and a half verses beginning with *candana* and ending with *siddhaye*, he teaches the prescription of qualities for the practitioner at the commencement of worship, as well as the fragrant substances for the worship of the Goddess. In that context, "with the sweat and musk of deer" means with the sweat of deer and with the musk of deer. (26)
With his body anointed, his inner heart joyful, and observing silence, wearing variegated ornaments and garments and garlanded with flowers, he should recite the vidyā at the onset of night. (27)
And one should worship Śivā with these fragrances for the accomplishment of all aims,
together with all the Nityās and likewise with the Mātṛkā at dawn.
O Śivā! One should drink water over which [the mantra] has been recited three times for the sake of attaining mastery of speech;
it is also accomplished through other mantras and vidyās. (29)

Having recited [the mantra] three hundred thousand times as before, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) with fragrant waters ten times that amount; likewise, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with substances soaked in the three sweets (trimaṭhura).
With blossoming *pālāśa* flowers that are unblemished and unbroken,
the practitioner should again perform the rites for desired goals once the vidyā has been mastered.
The distinctions in results arising from the different colors of the Goddess have been proclaimed;
now listen as I shall duly describe the distinctions in the essential nature of the Vidyās. 32.

With a delighted inner organ—*the remainder being that this is done through the contemplation of one's identity with the deity*—and by means of the word "ca" (and), he should also worship; "at the beginning of the night" is drawn in [from the previous context]; *with these fragrances*, such as sandalwood and so forth, consisting of ten kinds of substances.

With the first half-verse beginning with "sarvābhiḥ" and ending with "prasiddhyati," and with the following single verse, he teaches the application of the accomplishment of speech (*vāksiddhi*) by means of all the *nityā* goddesses, other vidyās, and all mantras.
In that context, "by all" means by the sixteen [goddesses]; this is the ellipsis. "By other vidyās" is the ellipsis for the second part.

This is what is meant: at the conclusion of the morning *saṃdhyā* rite, having taken a handful of water in one's cupped palms (*culuka*), one should visualize within it the *mātṛkā*-yantra to be described;
then, for each syllable of the fifty-one letters of the *mātṛkā*, beginning with the letter 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'—

Having recited the *bindumatī* [mantra] three times, and subsequently having recited one's own chosen *nityā*, another *vidyā*, or a *mantra* three times, while contemplating that water as consisting of nectar (*amṛta*),
one should visualize the channel of Sarasvatī extending from the *mūlādhāra* to the tip of the tongue in the form of a lamp flame.

Having meditated upon her with the intent of performing a fire sacrifice, one should sip water (ācamana). For one who performs this every day in the morning, the fourfold scholarship and self-knowledge of the Self certainly come to be; such is the secret oral tradition (*upahvara*). || 29 ||
With the two verses beginning with *prāgvat* and ending with *sādhakaḥ*, he teaches the method for accomplishing the Vidyā. In that context, *prāgvat* means "as before," i.e., like Lalitā.
*Tāvat* means "that [number] plus its tenth part. *Aduṣṭaiḥ* means "unblemished," i.e., not damaged by insects and the like. *Avikhaṇḍitaiḥ* means "unbroken."
By those established in virtuous conduct. || 31 ||
(260) Thus, through the conjunction of phonemes, the Vidyā consists of the three Vedas, as does the infinite expansion of the world in the form of the signified and the signifier. || 33 ||
O wise one! Listen as I describe, in due order, their causality, their nature as the Supreme Self, and their immeasurability—the majesty of the detailed ritual procedures. (34)
The Sāmaveda begins with the letter 'a', the Ṛgveda begins with that [same letter], and the Yajurveda begins with the letter 'i'; from the conjunction of these, one becomes pure. (35)
O wise one, hear now its accomplishment as it has been explained according to the sequence of what precedes and what follows:
first, one should write [the letters] and join them in accordance with the science of grammar (śabdaśāstra). || 36 ||
From that, through the conjunction of the qualities and the Ṛg and Yajus [Vedas], another [form] arose;
and from the union with Vṛddhi-sandhyā, the pure body was produced.
Therefore, through the connection between cause and effect regarding the knowledge consisting of the three Vedas,
all other [sciences] were indeed produced from the initial syllables by him.

With these three verses beginning with "Of the Goddess" (devyāḥ) and ending with "the majesties" (vaibhavāḥ), he introduces the majesty of the pervasiveness of the Vidyā and so forth. Therein, "by the differentiation of the colors of the Goddess" refers to the differentiation of the colors of the Goddess's forms as previously mentioned in such passages as "white for the sake of attaining the perfection of speech alone. (32)

"Consisting of the threefold [Veda]" means consisting of the Vedas; the word "of knowledge" (vidyāyāḥ) refers to Kulasundarī, as is understood from the context. "In the form of the signified and the signifier" means by way of the nature of sound and the nature of meaning. || 33 || "The state of being the supreme self" means the state of being supremely exalted. "Immeasurability" means not being constrained by space, time, or form. || 34 ||

With these four verses beginning with "akārādi" and ending with "vai," he teaches that the first peak (kūṭa) of the Vidyā, which consists of speech, is composed of the three Vedas (trayīmaya). In this regard, the following is stated:
the letter *a*, which is the primordial element of the Sāmaveda, is situated at its side.

Having written the letter *a*, which is the beginning of the Ṛgveda, and above both of them the letter *i*, which is the beginning of the Yajurveda, the vowel *e* (*ekāra*) is formed through the *guṇa* sandhi by the union of the preceding *a* with the *i*;
and the vowel *ai* (*aikāra*) is formed through the *vṛddhi* sandhi by that same *a* and that same *e* according to the aforementioned method.
And having thus established [the syllable *ai*], because the syllable *ai* is produced from the first letter of the three Vedas (*trayī*),

and because the subsequent arrangement of letters originates precisely from the first letter of the three Vedas— just as a sprout arises from a seed— and because they are the cause of those [subsequent letters] and the syllable *ai* is composed of them, it is said that the syllable *ai* consists of the three Vedas. || 35 || 36 || 37 ||
The Mātṛkā [consists of] the vital breath situated within the middle vowel, beginning with the consonants;
through its connection with the relationship of cause and effect as before, it takes the form of the signifier. (39)
The conjunction of those phonemes, digits, and flavors is to be designated as the "beginning of the elements" (bhūtādi);
thus is declared the nature of the universe as consisting of both the signifier and the signified. (40)

The form of the other [deity] is said by the thirtieth [verse] to consist of three, being composed of the three [times]; thus, this auspicious differentiation of the forms of Vidyā is composed of the universe. 41.
The first is the pure Speech (Vāk) by nature; the second is said to be Fire (Vahni).
She, whose form is the unity of the Bindu and the Sarga, is our own body. 42.

With these two verses beginning with "madhyamā" and ending with "uditāḥ," having described the nature of the Vidyā as consisting of the three Vedas (*trayīmaya*) in the form of a specific composition,
[the author] explains how all words and all meanings possess a state of mutual pervasion, and [how this applies to] the Vidyā as well.

It teaches unity. In this regard, the following is meant: because the letter *ka* is the primordial source (*mātṛkādi*) of the consonants situated between the two letters *ka* and *la* within the second syllable of the Vidyā.

In the third section beginning with the five elements, it is taught that consonants have the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), vowels have the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), and the *visarjanīya* has the nature of the knower (*jñātṛ*).
Thus...

This third section also possesses the nature of being the universal self, consisting of the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; for, as previously stated, it consists of the element earth and the syllable *la*, and by virtue of including such [elements] at the beginning, the entire remainder—
the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) consisting of the five elements in the form of the signified and the signifier— is the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).
Thus, that which is of undifferentiated form is pervaded by this Vidyā. || 39 || 40 ||

Having previously taught the pervasion of the first and second syllables of the Vidyā by means of the verse beginning with "parārūpam," he now teaches the pervasion of the third syllable and so forth.
In this regard, the following is stated:

Because this third section of the *avidyā* consists of the nature of the *parā-vidyā* as proclaimed in the scripture known as the *Triṃśikā* previously taught [therein], it has been stated that the consonant (*vyañjana*) is of the nature of the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), the *visarga* is of the nature of knowledge (*jñāna*), and the *visarga* [as well] is of the nature of the knower (*jñātṛ*).
Thus,
it has also been stated that this third section consists of Viṣṇu, whose nature comprises the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; such is its nature.

Through its three sections, the Vidyā has demonstrated in a threefold manner its nature as the entirety of the universe. Since its nature as an object of knowledge (*meyatva*) has been so well established, it is evident that there is nothing impossible to achieve for a practitioner through this Vidyā when following the authentic tradition (*satsampradāya*). This is the meaning. Such is the differentiation of its form.
The meaning is: "Listen to the distinctions in the nature of knowledge. || 41 ||

With these three verses beginning with "The Pure One" (śuciḥ) and ending with "consisting of the Self" (ātmikā), he teaches the Vidyā which is the root of the entire mass of Trika knowledge and which contains the supreme secret known as the Saṅketa-vidyā; therein, the first [verse] concerns the Pure One.
By that seed-syllable, she who is the nature of speech (p. 262) and the universal self is properly invoked. The third forest is said to be joined with Māyā or with herself. (43)
This is the Traipurakanda, which is declared to be the Saṅketā;
it consists of the triad of the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge, as well as defect, quality, and splendor.

But by the application of the vital breath (prāṇa) to the essence (rasa) within its central seed-syllable, one indeed becomes the self consisting of both the signified and the signifier within the cause of the phenomenal world. || 45 ||

In the third [center], through union with the heart, she is declared to be the self of the triad and the universe; among those, the yoga of the *haṃsa* in the heart constitutes the nature of the mobile and the immobile.
O Supreme Goddess, due to the combination of one, two, or more consonants, as well as in the three [vowels], it is impossible to know the number of vidyās.

The first is called Vāgbhavā, whose form consists of the twelve vowels. The second is Vahni (the Fire), which is the fourth vowel, consisting of the essence of Śiva and Śakti in the form of the unity of the Bindu and Visarga, which are the causal source of all the letters of the Mātṛkā. By that seed-syllable, which is the nature of the fourth state (turya), she is the embodiment of the universal self.

The meaning is that by means of the fourth vowel, which has been established as the form of Śiva and Śakti, that Vidyā is said to be the nature of the universal self (viśvātman). "Vana" refers to the third [vowel]; the third Vidyā consists solely of the fourteen vowels.
By "māyā," it means either by its own [form] or by the visarga or the bindu. || 43 || Regarding the term "traipurakanda":
And its designation is "ignorance" (*avidyā*). In that regard, it is called a "bulb" (*kanda*) because it is like a bulb.
Within this ignorance, there are innumerable [mantras] produced by the combination of one, two, or more consonants across its three sections, which will be described hereafter.
The meaning is that she is the fundamental source of the masses of mantras belonging to the three cities (Tripura).

She consists of the triad of light—namely, the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge, as well as defects and virtues. What is meant by this is that she exists in the form of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.
It remains pervading the entire universe, filling it completely by way of its nature as wind, bile, and phlegm, and as the essence of fire, sun, and moon. || 44 ||

With these two verses beginning with *asyāḥ* and ending with *ātmatā*, [the author] teaches the previously mentioned pervasion (*vyāpti*) of this ignorance (*avidyā*) through its connection with the middle *ka* and *la*, and its connection with the *sa* at the conclusion; furthermore, he teaches the impression of pervasion (*vyāptivāsanā*) through the connection of *ha* and *sa* within the three sections (*trikhaṇḍa*). In that context, *asyāḥ*...
The statement "the cause of conventional knowledge" is an expression of sovereignty; the meaning is "the causality [of that sovereignty]. || 45 ||

The state of being the universal self of the three [principles] is the state of being the universal self consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; this refers to those three *kūṭas* (syllabic clusters), as is the remainder of the sense. It is the state of being the self of both the moving and the stationary. This is what is meant: in each of those three seed-syllables (*bījas*), through the conjunction of the letter *bha* and the letter *sa*, and of this...
It is stated that the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of the mobile and immobile nature [of things] arises from the knowledge of conventions (*saṅketa-vidyā*). || 46 ||
(263) Thus, how could she, whose power is infinite, be described in its entirety?
Nevertheless, for the sake of protecting my devotees, I shall speak to you something of it. 48.
It bestows longevity, fortune, fame, enjoyment, beauty, and health;
it consists of knowledge pertaining to this world and the next, and it grants all perfections.
Through the union with Haṃsa, from the three [syllables] of the Kulasundarī-vidyā in sequence, arises the Great Vidyā named Vijayā, who is intent upon the protection of the universe. (50)

Through the union of our hearts within them, that which is called the individual soul (*jīva*), consisting of universal consciousness, arises from the joining of the two; it becomes the body of us both. (51)
The Vidyā beginning with *hṛd* consists of you; the Mantra beginning with *haṃsa* consists of me.
Through their union in burning, she is known as Viśvā and has a universal form.

With the verse beginning with "one, two," etc., he teaches that this *saṅketavidyā* possesses innumerable forms through its association with one, two, or more consonants (*vyañjana*). In this regard, the following is meant:
within the three sections of that *saṅketavidyā*, [the forms are infinite].
Whether lacking the second and third [syllables] in the first [position], or lacking the first and third in the second,
or lacking the first and second in the third, or lacking any one of them in the others,
or lacking all of them together among the thirty-five syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*.

Whether in sequential, reverse, or non-sequential order, through the combination of one, two, and so forth, it is impossible for anyone to know or describe the number and essential nature of the vidyās that thus arise. || 47 ||

With these two verses beginning with *evam* and ending with *siddhidāḥ*, he introduces [the subject] by means of a praise of the Vidyā, which is the jewel of Tripuṛa, both as previously stated and as yet to be described. In that context, *sā saṅketā* refers to that Saṅketavidyā; he praises it as being produced from one, two, and so forth, and as being innumerable.

Regarding the sciences (*vidyā*): by stating that she is "consisting of knowledge pertaining to this world and the next" (*aihikāmuṣmikajñānamayī*), he distinguishes her from those sciences which teach what is incorrect regarding those two [worlds]. || 49 ||

With these six verses beginning with "vidyāyāḥ" and ending with "smṛtāḥ," he provides the instruction on the nature of the eleven vidyās and concludes by stating the total number of those vidyās which constitute the jewels of Tripura. Therein:

This is what is meant: by adding the letter *ha* to each of the three sections above [the syllables] of Kulasundarī, there arises the one called Vijayā; because she bestows knowledge pertaining to both this world and the next, she is the Vidyā that provides all protection.
By removing the letter *ha* from those [three] and adding the letter *sa* there, [the result is the Vidyā of Sarvarakṣākarī].

The seed-syllable *viśvacaitanyarūpiṇī* is the ignorance (*avidyā*) known as the individual soul (*jīva*). Among those [three], by joining the letter *ha* before the letter *sa*, there is the mantra known as "mantra"; by joining the letter *sa* before the letter *ha*, there is the knowledge (*vidyā*) known as "vidyā" among those three.
Each Vidyā, when encased by Śakti, is the deluder of the universe;
but when that [Vidyā] is encased by both Māyā and Khecarāmburasa, it is likewise so. (53)
She is known as Tripurāmṛtā, whose form is the dissolution of all things;
she is called Māyā and Mohinī, while the one in their midst is considered Kṣobhiṇī.
Ending with that, the fifteen [syllables] beginning with *vā* are declared to be of great prosperity;
these thirteen are said to be the ritual procedures (*vidhi*) known as Tripurā. (55)
From these, through the reversal of their sequence, seventy-eight types of ignorance arise;
their complete classification has been declared by you in the *Lakṣasāgara*.
There exists a certain lore called Sampatkarī, whose majesty is inconceivable;
I shall speak of it, O Goddess of gods, so that you may hear it for the sake of attaining all desired perfections. 57.

In the *kūṭas*, because of the application of the letter *ha* below the first [syllable], the letter *sa* below the last two, and other intervening consonants, there is the Vidyā named Viśvā, which consists of the universe. In the Kevala-krama, one should enclose each of the three sections of Sundarī with the two *hṛllekhās*; that is the Viśvamohinī.
The Vidyā || 53 || Furthermore, by enclosing that very same [Vidyā] with the two *hṛllekhā*s (the syllables *hrīṃ*),

there is the Vidyā known as Tripurāmṛtā || 54 || [She who possesses] the union, nourishment, and form arising from the knowledge of reality and the attainment of all things; having removed the first *kūṭa* of that Kulasundarī, therein—

By joining the *hṛllekhā* [syllable] to the first part, there is the *vidyā* named *Mohinī*. Likewise, by discarding the middle section and joining the *hṛllekhā* there, there is the *vidyā* named *Kṣobhiṇī*. Similarly, by joining the *hṛllekhā* in place of the final section, there is the *vidyā* named *Kledinī*. Furthermore, of that *Kulasundarī*...
By omitting the first section and joining the letter *a* there, the Vidyā named Mahodayā arises.

Thus, the Saṅketa-vidyā called Tripurākaṇḍā, together with the two Vidyās Kula-sundarī and Vijayā, beginning with Vijayā and ending with Mahodayā, constitute the ten Kaṇa-vidyās; these, combined [with the previous three], amount to thirteen Vidyās in total.
Thus, it is proclaimed as the Tripurāratnākhya [Tantra]. || 55 ||

By means of this verse beginning with "āsām" (of these), the detailed exposition is given of those seventy-eight mantras— resulting from the combination of the thirteen vidyās with the direct, reverse, and inverted sequences described in the thirty-fifth chapter, each having six variations.
And he teaches that the ritual procedure is taught in the scripture known as the Lakṣasāgara. || 56 ||

With these eleven verses beginning with "saṃpatkarī" and ending with "samunnayet," [the author] provides, preceded by an introduction, the instruction on the *vidyā* named *Saṃpatkarī* according to its etymological meaning, the instruction on its meditation (*dhyāna*), and the instruction on its ritual procedure (*vidhāna*).
He also establishes the sequence of worship for the seventy-eight vidyās previously mentioned.
In that regard, the first [vidyā] is said to arise from the union of *prāṇa*, *rasa*, *amarut*, and *vahni*; it consists of the letters *ka*, *la*, *ā*, *ī*, and the *bindu*.
(265) O Pārvatī, the first [mantra] is said to arise from the union of *prāṇa*, *rasa*, *amarut*, and *vahni*; the second likewise arises from *vāta*, *cara*, and *sva*. 58.
O Supreme Goddess, the third [form] consists of the *haṃsa-hṛd-vana* and the *māyā*;
thus that Vidyā has three syllables, and its ritual procedure is now being told. (59)
One should perform the ritual for the limbs on the hands and body in sequence using the third seed-syllable joined with the long vowels, as before; then one should meditate upon her in this manner.
Her body, garments, and ornaments resemble the filaments of a pomegranate flower;
she has four arms, three eyes, and a face with a gracious, smiling expression.
She is perfected by the jewel-consecration, seated upon a swastika within a triangle at the center of an eight-petaled lotus, and is the abode of the bliss of compassion.
Holding in her hands a rosary of coral beads, a jeweled goblet filled with gems, and a book that grants boons— she is Sarvamangalā.

In the seat of Kula (kulāsana), which is conceived as three times sixteen [letters] beginning with 'a' and ending with 'sa', situated in the midst of the letters from 'ha' to 'kṣa', and endowed with that Vidyā; || 64 ||
The first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) has been stated; that is to say, here there is no *guṇa* sandhi between the vowels *ā* and *ī*.
With *vāta* (the letter *ha*), *cara* (the letter *ra*), and *sva* (the letter *a*), the second [syllable] is formed; with *a*, *e*, and the *bindu*, the second peak-syllable is formed.
Here too, there is no *vṛddhi* sandhi. [57–58] The third [peak-syllable] is formed by *haṃsa* (the letter *ha*), *hṛt* (the letter *ka*), *vana* (the letter *la*), and *māyā* (the letter *ī*).

The third *kūṭa* consists of the letters *ha*, *sa*, the vowel *au*, and the *visarjanīya*. "O Supreme Goddess" (*parameśvarī*) is the vocative address to the Goddess. [The phrase] "of the hand and limbs" refers to the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the hands and limbs;
the meaning is that one should perform this with the third seed-syllable (*bīja*), joined with a nasal dot (*bindu*) and a long vowel. Thus...

In the manner that will be described [in verses 60 and 61]. (60) (61) "Seated in the svastika" means situated by means of the posture known as the svastika. The expression "the temple" (*mandiram*) is a statement of independence; it means "the temple" (*mandira*). (62) One should arrange the objects to be held in the hands, starting from the upper right and ending with the lower left, according to the sequence of the sides. (63)

In that which is fashioned from the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *sa*, there is the construction of a triangle everywhere by means of three lines, commencing with the letters *a*, *ka*, and *tha*, and concluding with the *visarga* and the letter *sa*; in the center of that [triangle].
The supreme Śakti remains, her body being the manifold expansion of the meanings of words such as *śiṣṭa*, *hala*, *aṅghri-dvaya*, and *akṣa*.

Within the Śakti-mantras, this is the supreme secret, the meaning of the oral tradition (*sampradāyārtha*). That which is called the *Kulāsana* is a specific wheel (*cakra*) in the form of a triangle; it is conjoined with that Vidyā.
Having invoked [the deity], one should worship her in due order, preceded by the formal declaration (*saṅkalpa*) regarding the water offering (*arghya*);
in the center and at the corners of the triangle, one should worship Rati, Prīti, and Manobhava. (65)

Likewise, one should worship the Mothers on the eight petals starting from the northeast and moving counter-clockwise; and in the square, one should worship the world-protectors and the Śaktis as previously described.
The procedure has been correctly explained as being with seventy-eight [verses];
one should likewise determine the two offerings and the fire-oblation (homa) as before.
Clarified butter prepared for three days by boiling it with four times as much *brāhmī* juice, *vacā*, and milk, combined with an equal amount of [the previous] base, [is thus prepared]. (68)
Accompanied by that vidyā; this is a specific qualification of the *kulāsana*. (64) The ritual intention (*saṅkalpa*) for the *argha* is as before.
(65) Moving to the left, in a counter-clockwise sequence. Likewise, from the tip [of the blade] in a counter-clockwise sequence.
The eight Mothers, beginning with Brāhmī, are as before. The powers (*śakti*), those whose form is power.
The meaning is that they are situated in the east and so forth. (Verse 66) "With seventy-eight vidyās"—the word "vidyās" is to be understood as the remainder.

The meaning is that this very procedure applies to the seventy-eight types of vidyās. "Two offerings"—the word "at the beginning and the end" is to be understood as the remainder. "Homa" refers to the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) as before. This is what is being stated:

At the beginning of the worship and so forth, one should offer two *bali* offerings according to the prescribed sequence—using the sixteen-syllable mantra at the start and the seven-syllable *Kurukullā* mantra at the end—and then perform the fire sacrifice (*homa*) according to the procedure for daily worship. Furthermore, there is the application of the two seed-syllables and the seven-syllable mantra to the beginning and end of the mantras; this applies to these [mantras].

The procedure for arranging the cycle of daily worship (*nityasaparyā*) is as follows: having first constructed two equal squares provided with gates facing east and west, and having then fashioned an eight-petalled lotus within them,
one should construct a *yoni* (womb) of three equal lines according to the proper measure in its pericarp (*karṇikā*), and therein—
One should worship the Śaktis as described, according to the stated sequence. || 67 ||

With these two verses beginning with "caturguṇa" and ending with "kaviḥ," he teaches the procedure for preparing *brāhmīghṛta* (clarified butter from *brāhmī*) and the application of that clarified butter for the attainment of speech by one who is mute; in this context, *brāhmī* is to be obtained from the mouth of a guru, and *sarpiḥ* means clarified butter (*ghṛta*).
This is what is meant: one should combine four parts of *brāhmī* juice equal to the quantity of ghee to be prepared, one-fourth part of the quantity of *vacā*,
and milk equal to the quantity of ghee, according to the sequence of measurements thus described.
Having cooked it over a mild fire for three days, one should cleanse it in a vessel of smooth ghee, remove it, and once it has cooled,
place upon it the *mātṛkāyantra* to be described later on a silver plate;
having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) upon that yantra, one should immerse it in this ghee.

Touching clarified butter with any one of *kuśa*, *dūrvā*, or *darbha* grasses, one should diligently recite the *mātṛkā-vidyā* together with its *yantra* ten thousand times, including the *mātṛkā* with its drops (*sabindukā*). (p. 267) One should recite it ten thousand times with devotion.
If one licks it every morning for a year, one who was mute shall become a poet. || 69 ||
Śiva, Ambikā, Kumāra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, as well as Ramā;
Kubera, Ravi, Candra, Maṅgala, Budha, Guru, Śukra, and Śani. || 70 ||
On those respective days, one should worship, satisfy with libations, and pacify those lords of the days by means of the mantra of that day, employing the seven-syllable name-mantra.
With ashes produced from colored medicinal herbs and consecrated by mantra, one should touch [the disciple] while performing the Mātṛkā-nyāsa for the sake of protection, reciting the mantra. (72)
One should perform this rite especially for kings and for those who are afflicted;
by that, they, along with their lineages, shall become happy again for as long as they live.
Having recited [the primary mantra], one should subsequently recite any one of the aforementioned vidyās that same number of times,
place it securely somewhere, and worship it at the three junctions of the day with both the Mātṛkā and the vidyā.
Every morning, having consecrated it three times with both the Mātṛkā and the vidyā, [one should offer] a measure of three niṣkas.
For one who licks that clarified butter, the attainment of the stated results occurs within a year. || 68 || 69 ||

With the two verses beginning with "Śiva" and ending with "huned," [the author] teaches, for each of the seven days starting with Sunday, the pair of deities, their worship and so forth, as well as their purpose. In that context, "Ramā" is Lakṣmī. "Āraḥ" is Bhīma. Regarding "sitasaurayaḥ," due to the author's independence [in usage], the meaning is "Sita and Sauri."

Sita is Venus. || 70 || The ellipsis is "among those seven [planets] beginning with the Sun. Those lords of the days; "of two kinds" means by means of the *vidyā* of that specific day—that is, the *nityā-vidyā* of that particular day—and by means of the application of the seven-syllable name, meaning that each respective name is joined at the end with the seven-syllable mantra. One should offer oblations (*hunet*, i.e., *juhuyāt*). By that—

The ellipsis is "the desired success shall be attained. This is what is meant: among the seven days beginning with Sunday, for each day, one should worship the two types of lords of the day mentioned in the prescribed order—two for each—using their respective name-mantras joined with the seven-syllabled mantra of the daily Nityā of that specific day.
In each respective maṇḍala, one attains the desired accomplishments through worship, libations, fire-offerings (homa), and so forth. || 71 ||

By means of the two verses beginning with "varṇauṣadhī" and ending with "yāvadāyuṣam," [it is taught that] by means of the *mātṛkā* syllables, medicinal herbs, and ashes, preceded by the drawing of the *mātṛkā*-yantra and the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā*, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of the *vidyā-mātṛkā*.

He teaches that by means of this combined *mātṛkā*, when touched in sequence at the locations of the *mātṛkā* syllables to be described during the two junctions (*sandhyā*), protection from all calamities is secured for everyone. (72, p.
268) When cruel diseases have arisen, one should worship thus within the mandala.
In a nine-square grid, one should place the nine [planets] as prescribed, including Rāhu and Ketu.
In the central [cell], Indra, Yama, Varuṇa, the Moon, Agni, Rakṣas, Vāyu, and Īśvara—by worshipping them in these cells, one shall immediately be freed from disease and become happy. (75)

In times of affliction by malevolent planets, distress caused by enemies, famine of three kinds, as well as during portents and preparations for war, one should perform the prescribed worship and other rites.
Having worshipped those who know that [mantra] properly, one should give a cow, gold, and clothing;
by that, liberated from all calamities, one lives happily on this earth. (77)
"O Supreme Lord, tell me the nyāsa of the Mātṛkās and its yantra.
"I shall tell you both today; I will explain it all in that chapter. (78)
One should form the six limbs using the six groups of consonants, excluding the sibilants (ṣaṇḍha), encased by pairs of short and long vowels, consisting of five and fifteen syllables respectively.
With these four verses beginning with "krūreṣu" and ending with "bhūtale," he teaches the crossing over calamities through the worship of the nine planets (*navagraha*). In that regard,
it is to be performed in the manner to be described in the twenty-eighth chapter, once one has entered the mandala consisting of nine squares.

The meaning is "in their respective maṇḍalas. By the words beginning with "in the center" (madhye), he recalls the directional division of the planets that is about to be described. "According to the sequence of auspicious and inauspicious [results]" refers to those nine planets.
"By them" means by the nine name-mantras of the aforementioned type situated within the seven-syllable daily mantra (dinanityā). || 75 ||

The word "trividhe" (of three kinds) is connected with the word "utpāte" (in the case of a portent). "Tadvidām" means those who know that [science], i.e., those who possess the knowledge. "Gām" means a cow. "Tenārcanādinā" means by that [act] of worship and so forth. This is what is meant:
[one should draw] four lines with equal intervals, directed toward the east, west, south, and north.

Having prepared nine squares and having constructed the mandalas of the nine grahas within them according to the stated sequence— as will be described in the twenty-eighth chapter— one should [worship] therein with the nine name-mantras situated in the midst of the seven-syllable mantra of the daily Nityā for each respective day.

By means of worship, libations, fire-offerings, and the like, as well as by honoring those who know that mantra and giving gifts such as gold, one becomes liberated from all calamities and attains happiness. || 77 ||

With these eight verses beginning with "brūhi" and ending with "nyaset," he teaches the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) of the Mātṛkās and the placement of the Mātṛkās themselves. In that context, "that yantra" refers to the Mātṛkā-yantra. "The two" refers to the placement (*nyāsa*) and the yantra. "Here" means in this chapter.
In that chapter, namely the Mātṛkā chapter; "everything else" is the understood remainder. || 78 ||
By means of this single verse consisting of three and a quarter lines, beginning with "short" (hrasva) and ending with "thus" (ittham), the following is stated:
among the vowels, there are four neuter syllables—ṛ, ṝ, ḷ, and ḹ;
excluding these, there are twelve others: a, i, u, e, o, and aṃ.
p. 269) Among the vowels, the four neuter forms are said to be in the middle. Having thus assigned the letters from *a* to *kṣa* to the hands and limbs, indeed— (80)
One should place the vowels one by one on the forehead, the covering of the face, the eyes, the ears, the nose, the cheeks, the lips, the teeth, the head, and the tongue. (81)
One should place the four groups [of letters] at the roots, the middle, and the joints of the hands and feet, as well as at their tips; the fifth group should be placed on the sides and the back.
Having placed [the mantras] at the navel and the heart, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) throughout the ten constituents,
extending through the skin, blood, flesh, fat, bone, marrow, semen, and the internal organs.
In this manner, being well-composed, one should likewise perform the placement (nyāsa) upon the vital breaths, the powers, and the selves;
then, recollecting those [mantras] that touch the heart, one should place them within the constituent elements (dhātus).
Alternatively, one should place [the syllables] on the heart, the pair of shoulders, the two armpits, below the heart, as well as on the feet, the belly, and the face. (85)
Having enclosed the five-syllable groups *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa* and the ten-syllable group beginning with *ya*, along with the six short vowels (*a, i, u, ṛ, lṛ*) and the six long vowels (*ā,
ī, ū, ai, au, aḥ*) accompanied by the bindu (anusvāra), in the manner previously described, one should finally [proceed] with those six.
One should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs with mantras joined by the [seed] syllables of birth. || 79 || 80 ||

With the five verses beginning with "From Ā to Kṣa" (ādikṣānta) and ending with "one should perform the placement" (nyaset), he teaches the sequence for the arrangement of the letters of the Mātṛkā upon the body. Among those, "at the root and middle joints" (mūlamadhyasandhyoḥ); "at the root joints" (mūlasandhau) refers to the two elbows (the roots of the arms).

The "middle joints" (*madhyasandhi*) are said to be at the wrists and the bases of the fingers; however, for the feet, by the term "base and middle," the hips and knees are meant. Therein, the "two middle joints" refer to the joints of the forefoot and the toes. The phrase "the fifth group" is the remainder [of the sentence]. || 81 || 82 ||

The ellipsis is "the pervasive phonemes. The pervasiveness of the phonemes from *ya* to *kṣa* is due to their being the very nature of the elements (*dhātu*) and so forth. Even the vital breath (*prāṇa*), power (*śakti*), and self (*ātman*) are intended as elements;
[the genitive] "of those elements" is used in the sense of the accusative.

This means the elements (dhātu). Or else, in another interpretation: when the triad has passed away, while touching from the heart to the tips of the hands and feet—that is, touching from the heart up to the tips of the two hands—one should place the letter *sa*;
and while touching from the heart to the tips of the pair of feet, one should place the letter *ha*. This is the meaning.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus above the earth, surrounded by two circles, one should write in the center the syllable produced from *haṃsa*, *hṛd*, *vana*, and *śakti*. (86)
One should write the vowels upon the filaments and the consonant groups (vargas) upon the petals;
those consisting of five syllables each, along with *dāru*, *cāmbu*, and the [directional] quarters, should be placed in the directions.
Furthermore, there are five other [syllables] among the vowels that are non-repetitive;
indeed, due to the distinction between being with consonants and without consonants, there was a twofold recurrence. (88)
Together with the powers of wind, fire, and the self, that becomes the pentad;
the other eleven [powers] arise in Śiva from the mere junctions and so forth.
With these seven verses beginning with *vṛttadvaya* and ending with *vitanvate*, [the author] teaches the construction of the *mātṛkā*-yantra, its application, and its fruits. Therein,
the *kūṭa* born from the Haṃsa, the Heart, the Forest, and Śakti consists of the letters *ha*, *sa*, the vowel *au*, and the *visarjanīya*.

The single *kūṭākṣara* (compound syllable) is formed by their combination. One should write the sixteen vowels on the filaments (*kesara*). At the base of each petal, one should write pairs [of letters]. Regarding the "groups" (*varga*), the connection is that they consist of five letters each, beginning with *ka*. There is a specific rule regarding the number seven. *Dāva* refers to the letters *ṭha* and *va*. These are to be placed in the cardinal directions.

Some say that one should write the letter *ṭha* in the intermediate directions and the letter *va*; however, that is not our view. The meaning of our tradition is that both should be written in all eight directions.
(87) The meaning is that one should write the five vowels and syllables, which will be mentioned below and are non-repetitive, on the eighth petal.
Furthermore, the other five [vowels] are written with five syllables each upon the other seven petals;

"vai" is used here as a particle indicating reason (*hetu*). The placement of the vowels is twofold, based on the distinction between being accompanied by consonants (*savyañjana*) or not (*avyañjana*): one type is conjoined with consonants, while the other shines forth by itself, according to the etymological derivation of the word *svara* ("that which sounds by itself"). Thus, it is independent (*svatantrā*).

And another [method] follows. Therefore, the two [syllables] should be repeated on the filaments of the eight petals. This is what is meant: one should write the five non-repeated syllables to be mentioned among the vowels on the eighth petal.
Regarding that, as for the writing of the five syllables on the eighth petal, [it is to be done] while the other seven petals [remain blank].

Because five groups of five syllables have been written, and because the vowels exist in two ways—both accompanied by consonants and devoid of consonants—there is a double recurrence here. [The mantra is:
*savātāgnidharāsvena śaktiḥ*, which consists of the vowel *a*, the vowel *i*, the vowel *u*, and the *bindu*.

The *visarjanīya*. That pentad consists of five vowels and consonants that are not repeated. This is what is meant: the letters *a*, *i*, *u*, the *bindu*, and the *visarjanīya* are the non-repeated vowels;
the other four [vowels] have arisen from these very [five] through processes such as vowel-lengthening (*savarṇadīrgha*).
Having placed the name of this yantra in the center of the neuter syllables (p. 271), one should employ it;
at dawn, one should meditate on the moon’s orb situated upon the head for the sake of all prosperity. (90)
Through consecration, wearing, worship,
and installation in a place such as one's home, the yantra fashioned from metal bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
All the deities situated within the center of this yantra bestow their presence and the granting of fruits upon the practitioners.

The distinct forms [of the letters] are produced by the letter *la* together with the *ra* that is devoid of the vowel *a*. Therefore, among those [sixteen vowels], these five alone hold primacy within the vowels; the other eleven syllables are redundant, as they arise merely from the conjunction of [the primary vowels] and so forth. The sequence for the arrangement of the *yantra* is as follows:

Having drawn a circle with one's own preferred measure, and having drawn another circle outside that with a measure of one *aṅgula*, and having drawn yet another circle outside that with a measure equal to half the diameter of the second circle,
one should fashion eight petals within the space between them according to the cardinal directions, and [fashion] the location for the filaments within that.

Having divided [the circle] sixteenfold by means of sixteen lines at equal intervals, one should draw a fourth circle outside that measuring one *aṅgula*. Outside that, at a distance of three *aṅgulas*, one should construct a square provided with eight spikes at the ends of its lines; in the pericarp [of the lotus], the letter *ha* [is placed].

Having written the single-syllable Vidyā known as Śaktiprasādā, which is endowed with the letters *sa*, *au*, and the *visarjanīya*, and which possesses a name situated between the letters *ha* and *sa*, one should write the sixteen vowels in the sixteen filaments starting from the east and proceeding clockwise; then, on the eight petals outside, [one should write...]

Having inscribed the five-syllable groups of seven consonants— *ka-ca-ṭa-ta-pa-ya-śa*, and so forth— in the seven petals in a clockwise sequence starting from the front, and having inscribed the five syllables *a-i-u-aṃ-aḥ* in the eighth [petal],
one should likewise place the letter *ṭha* and the letter *va* in the eight directions outside the fourth enclosure.

One should draw all the aforementioned syllables with the *bindu* (nasal dot), excluding the syllable situated within the pericarp (*karṇikā*). This refers to the *yantra*. [Verse 90] The phrase "in a *yantra* fashioned from metal" is the ellipsis; it connects with the end of the word "from worship. The phrase "from the installation" is the ellipsis for "of the *yantra*."
The word "etcetera" (ādi) has as its referent the village and so forth. || 91 ||

By the verse beginning with "etadyantrasya" (of this yantra), it is taught that for the consecration of the entire circle of deities, one should carve a yantra out of gold, silver, or stone, and having inscribed the name-syllables in the center with the words "be present here" (*sannidhehi*), it should be worshipped for one month while being endowed with the rite of vitalization (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*).

First, the knower of reality, whose self is perfected, having well-worshipped the Mātṛkā-mantra recited one hundred thousand times, should install the image of the deity with all its limbs (sakaladevatāvera) in the center of that [mandala]. When this is done,
the manifestation of those deities within that image becomes perfect, as does the fulfillment of the desires of the installer.
He teaches that it is possible. || 92 ||
Even a foolish, dull-witted, mute, or great sinner among men shall, by means of constant recitation, worship, and other rites at the proper time, attain equality with me. (93)
One should repeatedly contemplate these syllables on the tongue with the intellect;
having entered the assemblies of the learned, one is joined by eloquent people. (94)
Visualizing [the deity] situated in the center of the moon-disk upon his head, bestowing a rain of nectar, one should recite this mantra with a one-pointed mind. (95)
From the mandala, the perfection of poetry shall arise, consisting of all languages;
and in all debates and the like, one who has become the very self of the deity shall be victorious.
The instruments of both the eternal and the non-eternal are identical due to their connection with the single Self;
one should perform the various applications of these in mutual unity through the yoga of oneness.
Therefore, O Śivā, these [yantras] spoken by the Self indeed grant all accomplishments;
among even the sixteen Nityās, it is impossible to describe anything other than the yantra.

With these four verses beginning with "of the vidyās" and ending with "would become," he teaches the specific results arising from specific applications of the Kulasundarī-vidyā. In that context, "that Kulasundarī-vidyā" refers to the mantra. "Mūrkhaḥ" means ignorant; "jaḍaḥ" means a child.
The word "first" refers to the libations, fire-offerings, and so forth; [it leads to] equality with Matsya and equality with Śiva. 93.

"These syllables" refers to the mantra of Kulasundarī; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. (94) The syntactical connection is: "visualizing the mantra—the Kulasundarī-vidyā—as one that causes a shower of nectar through the agitation of the lunar orb, one should recite the mantra. (95) The word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to matters such as worldly affairs, gambling, and the like.

"Identified with the deity" means through the contemplation of being the deity. The meaning is that in all activities such as debate and worldly discourse, victory will be achieved by performing each action while maintaining the contemplation of being the deity. || 96 ||

With the verse beginning with "yantrāṇi" (the yantras), [the author] extends by analogy the yantras taught in the sixteenth chapter for the Nityānityā, because of the identity of form between the two Vidyās; thus, those yantras are also common to her. In that context, through the extension of those yantras, there are two additional yantras as well.
It is common to both the eternal and the non-eternal. || 97 ||

With the verse beginning "In all sixteen," he analyzes the specific and general prescriptions for all the *nityā* goddesses. In that context, "other" refers to recitation (*japa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), worship (*arcā*), sprinkling (*seka*), meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and so forth. This is due to their unity (*aikyayogataḥ*).
By means of the union of the sixteen [energies] into a single form of ultimate reality,

having formed a pair of circles and a hexagon, and having written the names from the center to the middle and so forth, one should place that triad externally in the six [petals] by means of one's own *māyā*. (99)
Having written the Mātṛkā within a circle and placed it in one's mouth,
by meditating upon it on the tongue, one enters as a leader into all assemblies.
The pervasion consisting of the reality of speech has been correctly proclaimed;
by the churning of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self. (101)
Thus, the fifteenth chapter of the Śrīkādimata within the venerable Ṣoḍaśanityātantras is fully concluded and has been thoroughly examined. 15.

This is what is meant: for all sixteen Nityās, the various diagrams (yantras) taught in their respective chapters—whether defective or belonging to specific ritual applications—are common to one another due to their uniform nature. || 98 ||

With the passage beginning with "the pair of verses" (*vṛttayugmam*) and ending with "he plunges into" (*vigāhate*), he teaches the yantra that bestows victory in the assembly of the wise (*vidyā-goṣṭhī*). In this context, "from the middle of the first middle" means: in the middle of the first peak (*kūṭa*) of the *Kulasundarī* mantra, specifically within the letter *ka*. That triad...

The three peaks of knowledge (*vidyākūṭa*) [are formed] by means of the *māyā* [vowel] and the *visarjanīya*. It penetrates the forefront; that is to say, it becomes a leader, it becomes most eminent. The sequence for constructing the diagram (*yantra*) is as follows: having fashioned a circle with a radius of the desired measure by means of a compass, one should [mark] within its center, as before, according to the intended measure...
Having drawn a hexagon, one should draw a circle outside the [first] circle at a measurement of one *aṅgula*; then,
having written the middle syllable of the *vidyā* in the center of the hexagon,
and having inscribed the name within the belly of that initial letter *ka*, [one should write it] in its six corners.

Having sequentially inscribed the three syllables of the Vidyā, together with the bindu, in the three lower [triangles] starting from the middle and proceeding clockwise; and having inscribed those same syllables, accompanied by the visarga, in the three upper corners starting from the "unreleased" (amukta) and proceeding clockwise; [one should then proceed] along the outer circular path starting from the front and proceeding clockwise.
Having written down the fifty-one letters from *a* with its bindu to *kṣa*,
having formed them into a pill, and having placed that pill in the mouth according to the prescribed sequence while visualizing it upon the tongue,
one obtains the aforementioned fruits. || 100 ||

Thus, in the *Manoramā*, the commentary composed by Śrī Subhagānandanātha, titled *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśā*, on the complete *Tantra* known as the *Śrīkādimatā* among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
In this commentary, the fifteenth chapter, which is devoted to illuminating the ritual procedure for the Śivadūtī Nityā-vidyā, has been fully examined. 15.
Regarding the number of verses here, two yantras have been described; the explanatory text for this fifth chapter consists of three hundred and nineteen verses.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter. Now, O wise one, listen to that which is called the eleventh among the sixteen Nityās— the Nityā Nityā— upon whom this entire world depends.
The extraction of the mantra was performed previously; now its ritual procedure is being described here—that [power] which establishes the bodily existence of all living beings.
Then [he performed] the ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), the powers (śaktis), worship with them, and the practice;
as well as the diagrams (yantras) in the form of vajras, situated within the six supports (ṣaḍādhāra).
Suppression and favor, as well as the pervasion of time by the six [syllables], are performed in sequence;
the six-limbed rite is formed with the syllables *haṃsa* and *hṛt* joined with long vowels.
Now begins the sixteenth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding fifteenth chapter the ritual procedure for the tenth *Kulasundarī-nityā-vidyā*, he subsequently teaches the ritual procedure for the eleventh, *Nityānityā*.
Now, by means of the sixteenth chapter consisting of one hundred verses, beginning with "Then, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "from all sides" (*sarvataḥ*),

[the author] indicates the subject matter of the chapter through three and a half verses starting with "sixteen" and ending with "in sequence. Therein, "dependent on the eternal and non-eternal" refers to the world (*jagat*), which is that which moves (*jaṅgama*).
Because it maintains the body (dehasthitikaratvāt) [as stated] previously in the third chapter. "Its procedure" means the procedure for the Vidyā.

"Of all living beings" means of all sentient creatures. It is that which effects the maintenance of the body because it resides in the six supports (ṣaḍādhāra) and so forth. "The deity's abiding" refers to the remainder [of the text]. This is what is meant:
I shall now describe the abiding of the six deities, beginning with the Ḍākinīs, within the six ādhāras, as well as the presence of Nityānityā in the form of their presiding deity. || 3 ||
Through the six supporting deities, namely Ḍākinī and the others, one attains the fruit in due time and the pervasive unity with the deity.
With the half-verse beginning with *dīrghasvara* and ending with *yutam*,

he teaches the sequence of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). In that regard, by means of the mantras joined with *haṃsa* and *hṛt*— that is, the syllables *ha* and *sa*— preceded as before by the long vowels, such as *hsāḥ*, *hsīḥ*, and so forth.

The meaning is that one should perform the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) as previously described. (4) The syllables of the Vidyā, which are said to be the *kūṭas*, [should be placed] in the middle of the eyebrows, the throat, the heart, the navel, the secret place, and the foundation (ādhāra), respectively.
One should indeed place the syllables of the Vidyā in sequence, joined with the bindu. (5)
Having pervaded [the universe] with the entire [mantra] according to the prescribed rule,
one should meditate upon Śivā, who is the soul of all, for the sake of attaining all prosperity.
Resplendent with a crown of rubies resembling two rising solar discs,
she is adorned with ornaments made of ruby and wears garments of crimson hue.
She is resplendent with six lotus-like faces adorned with beautiful, smiling expressions,
each face possessing three eyes, and she is endowed with twelve arms.
She carries a noose, sugarcane, a bow of lotus fibers, a shield, and a trident in her right hands, and she grants boons while holding a goad and a book with her left hands.
One should meditate on the Goddess with undivided attention as holding a flower, a sword, and a human skull, as well as the gesture of granting fearlessness, in her right hands. 10.
The powers of the Goddess are infinite; listen as I describe them to you.
This group of Lalitā-śaktis consists of two seed-syllables (bījas) in their sequential order.

The six syllables beginning with *ha* and ending with *ḍa*, devoid of the secret mantra (*saṃketavidyā*), are each joined with a nasal drop (*bindu*). This means that the syllables of the mantra from *ha* to *ḍa*, each accompanied by a *bindu*, [are to be placed] in the six aforementioned locations.

"One should place them one by one in succession" (verse 5). The pervasive [placement] is as before, with the whole [mantra] consisting of the three peaks (kūṭa) endowed with the secret code (saṅketa-vidyā).

With the four verses beginning with "one should meditate" (*dhyāyet*) and ending with "other-minded" (*anyadhīḥ*), [the author] teaches the meditation for the daily worship of the Goddess. In that context, she is "consisting of all" (*sarvātmikā*) because her nature is universal consciousness (*caitanya*).
Her nature as consciousness, moreover, pertains to those whose bodies consist of the elements (*dhātu*).

Because she is the very nature of one's own self, which is the presiding form of the Ḍākinīs and others. [Verses 6 and 7] "Resplendent with a lake of six faces" means resplendent with a lotus of six faces. [Verse 8]
One should arrange the weapons in the arms starting from the upper one; *kheṭa* means a shield made of leather. || 9 ||
The tip of the *maṇḍala* is a particular kind of six-sided [jewel]. A human skull is a cranium. || 10 ||

With these five verses beginning with "Anantā" and ending with "Ānatā," he teaches the surrounding powers (*āvaraṇa-śakti*) of the Goddess. Here, regarding the word "Anantā," because the powers have the nature of syllables (*akṣara-vigraha*), it is not possible to speak [of them as having further attributes]; however, the Goddess's state of being surrounded by an infinite retinue of powers is [established].
They possess the colors of the full mandala and are joined with the [term] "śakti.
When combined with the seven-syllable [mantra], these twelve-syllable mantras are known as the Vidyās. (12)
One should also worship Śivā, who is surrounded by one hundred and seventy-six [deities], seated within the corners of the hexagon; likewise, one should worship the Ḍākinīs and the others.
And these [powers] are respectively located in the guardians of the directions—Rakṣas, Vāyu, Indra, Agni, Īśa, and Varuṇa;
namely, Ḍākinī, Śākinī, Lākinī, and Kākinī.
At the base are Sākinī and Hākinī, whose forms resemble those of the Goddess;
surrounding her are the weapons in the form of Śaktis, bowing with their heads toward her crown.
Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), the offering of water (*argha*), and the formal resolve (*saṅkalpa*), one should worship according to the prescribed sequence;
one should also perform the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) and recite the mantra as instructed.
Because they are the very nature of one's own self. "Listen to some [of them]"—the remainder of the sentence being "to the powers that are about to be described"—is the implied sense. || 11 ||
The colors of the full mandala consist of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, numbering as previously stated.
By joining each of the thirty-six letters from *a* to *kṣa* with the sixteen vowels, there are five hundred and seventy-six [variations]. Of these:

The nature of the *pūrṇamaṇḍala* is not discussed here, as it will be explained in the twenty-fifth chapter. The *saṃjñā-vidyās* are the names and forms of the *vidyās*, consisting of twelve syllables: *hrīṃ śrīṃ aṃ śaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth, up to *hrīṃ śrīṃ kṣaḥ śaktipādukāṃ*.
The meaning is that they consist of twelve syllables, ending with the word "pūjayāmi" (I worship).

Having fashioned sixteen petals—thirty-six lotuses in total—outside the hexagon according to the sequence of the groups (*varga*) of those powers (*śakti*), one should worship those powers upon those petals; such is the tradition (*sampradāya*).

Alternatively, having fashioned thirty-two petals and eight-petaled lotuses according to the sequence of the two groups [of consonants], one should worship them therein; this is the meaning of one's own lineage. The locations for Ḍākinī and the others within the hexagons have already been explained previously. (12, 13, 14)

Their forms resemble those of Mūladevī; they possess forms that are eternally identical to Nityā. They wear her crowns—that is, crowns equipped with her respective weapons. They are bowed (with palms joined and humble), bent by the weight of their breasts, and stationed in their respective positions on the arms. This [description] is common to all. 15.

With these five verses beginning with *kṛtā* and ending with *gatāḥ*, he teaches the threefold sequence of worship by means of specific wheels (*cakra*) and specific powers (*śakti*). In this regard, the ritual resolve for the *arghya* offering is as before. "By the stated sequence" means by the previously mentioned sequence. "As declared" means as before. (16)
"Endowed with fifty-one petals" means possessed of fifty-one petals. (p.
278) Having drawn [the lotus] outside the hexagon, ending with the lines, and endowed with fifty-one petals, one should perform the worship in the middle circles with those [same lines]. 17.
In a six-cornered [diagram] surrounded by lotuses having two, four, six, ten, twelve, eight, and two petals, one should worship according to the rite remembered for the *Laghvī*.
Having constructed two squares on the outside provided with four doors, one should worship the twenty Śaktis upon those door-frames (śākhās).
Those known as Brahmā and the other World-Protectors are stationed at the sixteen gates;
they are censured for being forms of infinite Brahman, Niyati, and Kāla.
By means of those powers of the fifty-one letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'. || 17 ||
"With sixteen petals having eighteen segments" (18). Regarding the twenty powers:

there are eighteen powers beginning with Brāhmī and ending with the world-protectors (*lokapāla*); these become twenty by adding the two powers of *niyati* and *kāla*. This is what is meant: having drawn a circle using a radius of the desired measure by means of a compass...
Outside of that, having drawn a circle provided with a hexagon, and outside of that, according to tradition, having drawn sixteen petals—
that is, twenty-six lotuses— and outside of that, having drawn two squares with an interval of three finger-breadths between them,
and then having fashioned doors with their side-branches in the four directions, [one should place the deity] there in the very center of all.

One should place the Goddess outside in the six corners according to the stated sequence, followed by the group of six beginning with Ḍākinī; and further outside, the powers of the letters of the Full Mandala (pūrṇamaṇḍala) in the order of the consonant groups and the order of the individual letters,
within the thirty-six lotuses and their respective sixty-four petals.

One should worship according to the prescribed sequence by means of a path of exit from the interior; outside of that, in the four directions of the square, starting from the right side of the western door and ending at its left side,
one should worship in a clockwise order at the eight locations situated at the sides of the four doors.
One should worship the eight powers, beginning with Brāhmī, in a clockwise sequence. Then, there,
starting from the northern branch of the eastern door and ending at the southern branch of the [respective] door as previously described,
one should worship Indra and the others, ending with Īśāna, in a clockwise sequence upon the eight branches.

One should worship the eight powers of the World-Guardians (lokapāla). Following that, one should worship the powers of Ananta, Brahmā, Niyati, and Kāla in the four intermediate directions starting from the southeast (āgneya) up to the northeast (īśāna), proceeding in a clockwise order; such is the meaning of the tradition. Alternatively:
Outside the aforementioned hexagon, according to the tradition as before,

one should fashion eighteen lotuses with thirty-two petals each; having worshipped there the powers of the letters of the full mandala in the sequence of the two groups [of consonants], within the square—

One should worship as before; this is the supreme method. The middling method, however, consists in drawing a fifty-petaled lotus outside the previously mentioned hexagon, and then placing the fifty powers of the letters from *a* to *kṣa* upon its petals; the rest is as before.

"One should worship" means: according to the *Laghuprakriyā*, one should construct outside the hexagon a sixteen-petalled lotus, outside that a twelve-petalled one, and outside that a ten-petalled one;
the ritual practice (*sādhana*) is as before, [consisting of] a hundred thousand recitations of the syllables while observing a vow of milk.
Likewise, the oblation was performed with reddish lotuses sprinkled with the three sweets.

A person whose mantra has been perfected through recitation, libation, fire-offering, worship, and sprinkling may perform the prescribed ritual applications; otherwise, the deities presiding over those bodily constituents will [cause obstacles].
O Śivā, his vital breaths are indeed devoured by [the goddesses] in an instant when they are provoked;
there is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished through this vidyā. (23)
There are seven syllables of the Vidyā; with these, joined with the vowels as before, there are one hundred and twelve [mantras]. I shall describe to you the yantras formed by them.

Having drawn a hexagon within two circles, and then another pair of circles within that, one should place in the center a single syllable consisting of the *māyā* (the letter *hrīṃ*) together with its name.
Outside, one should draw six [circles]; within the six circles, having arranged the elements and the Mātṛkās, there will thus be sixteen yantras in sequence by means of nine [components].
Having drawn a six-petalled lotus outside of that and a four-petalled lotus outside of that,

and having written the rest as before, one should [place] the fifty syllable-energies from 'a' to 'kṣa', excluding the energy of the letter 'la', upon those lotuses and their respective petals, as described for the six ādhāras.
"One should worship according to the sequence of worship as before"—thus there are three positions. || 19 || 20 ||

With these three verses beginning with "vidadhyāt" and ending with "kvacit," he teaches the procedure for accomplishing the Vidyā, the transgression incurred in performing the ritual application by one who has not attained success, and the majestic power (*anubhāva*) of the Vidyā. In this regard, as before, it is like the Lalitā-vidyā. One who observes the milk-vow (*payovrata*) is one whose diet consists of milk.

Likewise, [the rite is performed] from the tenth part of the recitation (japa). (21) If not, then regarding the phrase "those deities of the elements" (taddhātudevatāḥ), the word "that" (tat) refers to all [of them], because they are the presiding lords of the six elements. (22) Of that practitioner (prayoktuḥ). (23)

With the verse beginning with "vidyā," he teaches the expansion of the meaning of the yantra through the combination of the vowels and consonants of the *vidyā* syllables. Among those, the first seven unenclosed syllables are the syllables of the first *kūṭa*. 24.

With the two verses beginning with *vṛttadvaya* and ending with *ṣoḍaśa*, he teaches sixteen yantras by means of the syllables of the Vidyā modified by the vowels. Among these, "situated in Māyā" means situated in Hṛllekhā. This is what is meant: by means of a circle of the desired measurement...
Having divided the two circles into inner and outer sections with a space of one finger-breadth between them,

and having likewise constructed a hexagon outside that, as well as another such figure outside that, [one should place] the first of the syllables of the Vidyā— numbering one hundred and twelve among those syllables modified by vowels which have been specified— in the very center.

Having written the name as the seed-syllable (*nāmagarbha*) within the *hṛllekha* (the heart-line), one should write the six syllables beginning with the second one in the six corners starting from the front, proceeding clockwise; then, within the inner circle and the enclosure, one should write [mantras] according to the specific rite.
By holding the first [syllable], there shall be the destruction of abdominal diseases.
By the second [mantra], O Supreme Goddess, diseases of the head are destroyed. || 27 ||
By the third [mantra], there is the pacification of eye diseases; by the next, those born of the ears;
by the fifth, diseases of the arms depart; and by the last, those born of the feet.
By the seventh [mantra], which is sustained by the intermediate empowerment, those diseases residing in the vital breaths (nidhana) are held;
by the eighth yantra, the ailments located in the organs of cognition are held.
By the tenth [day], those arising from the action-faculties (karmendriya) occur;
by the eleventh, those born of bile (pitta); and by the twelfth, those born of phlegm (kapha). || 30 ||
By means of the thirteenth [mantra], those ailments arising from the conjunction of the humors (doṣas) are instantly brought to dissolution through the majestic power of the yantras. || 31 ||
O Śivā, by means of the fourteenth yantra, all bhūtas, pretas, piśācas,
and even all other grahas, flee in terror in an instant.

Having written the elemental syllables (*bhūtākṣara*), one should write the *mātṛkā* together with the *bindu* in a clockwise direction starting from the outer circular path and so forth; this is the first yantra. In this same manner, by means of the seven [syllables] situated in the center of the hexagon and those situated in the corners—each placed above the previously written ones—[the subsequent yantras are formed].
By means of the syllables of the *svaravikṛta* vidyā, there are fifteen other yantras;
thus, together with those previously mentioned, there are sixteen yantras. || 24 || 26 ||

With these nine verses beginning with *prathamā* and ending with *anyathā*, [the author] teaches the application of the sixteen yantras for the pacification of all diseases, as well as the procedure for consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth in every case. Among these, *audaravyādhi* refers to abdominal ailments such as *gulma* (tumors), and *parameśvarī* is an address to the Goddess.

27 || The phrase "of diseases born of the ears" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "By the subsequent fourth instrument" is the ellipsis. "By the upward sixth instrument" is the ellipsis. As before, "diseases born of the feet" is the ellipsis. 28 ||

*Antarādhi* refers to the region of the body situated above the hips and below the two hands; the diseases located therein are what is meant by the term *antarādhistha*. The phrase *nidhanāśrayāḥ* (those which have death as their locus) is to be construed with *antarādhistha*.
The diseases residing in the organs of perception—those arising from the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—are called *gadā*.

(Verse 29) By means of the ninth instrument, the word "following" (*pareṇa*) is to be supplied as the remainder. Those residing in the organs of action—those arising from speech, hands, feet, anus, and genitals—and those arising from wind (*anilodbhavāḥ*), meaning those originating from wind-diseases (*vātaroga*).
The word "gadā" (diseases) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Those arising from the head (kapodbhavāḥ) are those originating from the disorder of phlegm (śleṣmadoṣasamudbhavāḥ).
In this context, for the subjects not explicitly mentioned, the term "diseases" (rogāḥ) serves as the subject. 30.
O Īśvarī, by holding [the breath] for sixteen [mātrās] with that supreme [concentration], the eight great diseases are not afflictive;
through holding it for sixteen [mātrās], there shall be long life and health.
One should employ these sixteen mechanical devices for the pacification of diseases, even for those ailments not explicitly mentioned, for the sake of all living beings. (34)
In every case, the wearing of the yantra—accompanied by consecration, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā), salutation, and full confidence—surely bears fruit; otherwise, it is otherwise.
O Śivā, that Vidyā called Pañcakūṭā, when deprived of the [specific] action, accomplishes everything else, including the perfection of speech; there is no difference between those two.
From the twenty varieties of those vidyā-mantras, there are seven hundred;
by means of them, the construction of the vajra-machines occurs—listen, O beloved, to their results as well. (37)
"With the thirteenth machine"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "Of the humors" (*doṣāṇām*) means the three humors, wind and the others, which have arisen from their combination (*sannipāta*).
"By its power" (*vaibhavāt*) means by its excellence. Regarding the phrase "with the machine," since no specific machine is mentioned in this context, it refers to that [general] machine.

It follows everywhere. "Grahas" refers to spirits (*bhūta*) and so forth. "O Śivā" is an address to the Goddess. (Verse 32) By the fifteenth [verse] which follows that; "great diseases" refers to wind (*vāta*) and the others. "By the sixteenth, by the supported"—the meaning is "by the sixteenth yantra. In this context:
The traditional meaning is that one should employ [these mantras] for common worship, consecration, installation, and so forth.
(33) "For the pacification of disease" means for the pacification of all diseases. This is what is meant:
all these sixteen yantras are to be worn and so forth for the pacification of those respective diseases when other [specific] diseases have not been mentioned.

"One should perform [it]"—by this it is meant that all the *yantras* individually become removers of all diseases. "In this tantra" is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*).
