Otherwise, if they are performed differently than as they have been taught, they do not bear fruit at all. This is what is being said: it is common to all.

Having performed the placement of the yantra and the consecration by means of the yantra, and having given wealth to the consecrator to his complete satisfaction, one should worship him and place faith that "this indeed bears fruit," and then perform the wearing of the yantra.
When done in this way, it certainly bears fruit; otherwise, it does not bear fruit at all. || 35 ||

By means of the verse beginning with *kurvihīnā*, [the author] teaches the ritual procedure for the five-peak (*pañcakūṭa*) vidyā, the ritual procedure for this vidyā, and the fact that it consists of this very vidyā. In that context, *kurvihīnā* means devoid of the letter *u*; there is no difference between these two, namely the six-peak (*ṣaṭkūṭa*) and five-peak vidyās.
By the verse beginning with "tadvidyā," [the author] explains the essential nature arising from the various arrangements of the syllables of the *nityā*, *anityā*, and *avidyā* mantras.
First, one should cast eighteen threads toward the east, south, and north.
By those [channels], two hundred and eighty-nine cavities are produced.
As before, one should gradually erase thirty-six squares in the corners;
one should arrange them on all sides so that a vajra appears in the center. (39)
The Vajraka [mandala] consists of one hundred and forty-five squares;
the four corners are triangles, each consisting of four squares, as described previously.
Having meditated [upon it], one should write [the letters] starting from the lower central cell of that [grid],
entering in a clockwise direction, beginning with those born from the first section of the *kūṭa* (the syllable *a*).
In the remaining nine squares in the middle, within the two groups of three on the left and right, one should then write the two Vidyās consisting of the reverse and direct orders.

In the remaining three compartments, one should write the name of the practitioner (sādhaka) in the one above that; in the middle of the action-compartment (karma), and in the one below, one should likewise inscribe the name of the person to be acted upon (sādhya) on all sides.
He introduces the construction of diagrams (*yantra*) in the form of vajras preceded by numerical designations. In that regard,
the various divisions of that vidyā consist of the syllables of the six-peak vidyā (*ṣaṭkūṭavidyā*), according to the sequence to be explained in the thirty-fifth chapter.
Due to the sequence of priority and posteriority, there are distinctions in their essential natures. Because of the sequence of the three sections of the Saṅketavidyā,
among the four thousand two hundred [divisions] produced by those modes, there are indeed the distinctions arising from the sections of the Saṅketavidyā.
The construction of the six mechanical devices (*ṣaḍyantra*) is taught here by means of those various combinations (*kūṭabheda*). "O Dear One" (*priye*) is an address to the Goddess.

With these eight verses beginning with "prāk" and ending with "śive," he teaches six yantras in the form of vajras within a grid, distinguished by the various syllables of the *kūṭa* of the present vidyā; in this context, the remainder is that there are thirty-six [syllables] for each corner. (38–39)

The meaning is that one should make the four tips of the *vajra*-mechanism triangular; that is, the four tips should be made into triangles. "By means of four squares" means, as before, by means of four squares in each direction. [This refers to] the square at the bottom of the center of that mechanism.
The central square among the five squares situated in the upper row of the downward-pointing triangle;
"in six" refers to those born from the first section—this is the remainder. Those *kūṭas* are one hundred and twenty in number; [they are arranged] in sequence for those six.
The state of being divided [into sections] arises because it begins with the six syllables of the Vidyā. "In the middle" refers to the remaining nine;
that is, in the nine central squares situated in three rows, arranged in an upward and downward sequence, consisting of two sets of three on the left and right.
(283) Situated in the center of four triangles, renewed by two lines, one should draw it like the central [triangle] within those; this is called the Vajra-yanttra. || 44 ||
In this way, one should fashion five [more] with the other five sections;
thus, O Śivā, the six vajra-machines have been described in sequence. (45)

The meaning is that one should form three sections of the two-fold Vidyā— consisting of the *pratiloma* (reverse) and *anuloma* (direct) orders— of the Nityānityā-vidyā, either upon a plate made of the three metals, on a stone slab, or on four [surfaces]. The meaning is that one should write them in the order of *pratiloma* and *anuloma*.
The meaning is that one should form nine triangles with six lines by means of two lines drawn at each corner, equally spaced apart,
and following the proportion of three lines in the middle, proceeding in groups of two; one should draw them in those various places just as in the center.

The meaning is that one should write the Vidyā as before within the nine triangles situated in the belly of the triangle, as well as in the three triangles located on the left and right sides; and one should write the syllables of the name of the practitioner (sādhaka) and others within the three central triangles.
This is done with the five sections of the Nityā-vidyā.
The remainder [of the sentence] is that each [of these] consists of one hundred and twenty *kūṭākṣara*s of the forms previously described.
This is what is meant: having drawn eighteen threads with equal intervals running east-west, north-south, and south-north, within the two hundred and eighty-nine resulting squares—

In the four corners of the grid, having divided each corner into thirty-six squares, one should erase them in the center according to the vajra-pattern as before. Afterwards, in the remaining one hundred and forty-five squares that form the vajra-shape, in the four [corners]...
Having cleared away four squares in each of the four directions,

one should construct four equilateral triangles in each direction according to the previously mentioned sequence, one by one; then, having divided each of those three lines of the triangles into three parts, [one should place] in the middle of each of those...
Having made two marks, one after the other, in accordance with two threads,
one should draw six lines in the sequence of two by two. When this is done,
there appear three triangles in an upward and downward order, and on their sides, two [forms].
Two triangles [are formed], with one triangle on each of their sides; thus, nine triangles come into being.
Therein, beginning from the central square situated within the five squares of the row above the lower triangle—

Having written the same number of *kūṭākṣaras* as there are squares from the outer row up to the square where the entry begins, within the *kūṭākṣaras* of the first section according to the previously stated sequence,
and having entered inside and written them in the second row as before;

Having thus written the letters of the first *kūṭa* of the science (vidyā), numbering one hundred and twenty in total, one should place the letters of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the ritual action (*karman*), and the goal (*sādhya*) in sequence from top to bottom within the nine remaining central squares— specifically, within the three middle squares.
Having written [the letters], in the three squares located in the row on the left side of those [squares],
from the bottom square up to the top square; and in the three squares situated in the row on the right side,
from the top square down to the bottom square.
On a cloth or on a wooden board, one should arrange the sixfold [set] in six places. || 46 ||
One should perform worship of the fruit and the cloth daily;
having installed the other [images], one should worship that Śivā right there. (47)
In the place where that [image] is to be installed, one should construct an auspicious pavilion,
nine cubits in length and breadth, adorned with banners and archways.
One should fashion it as being endowed with canopies of fruits and flowers;
and in the center, a sacrificial altar (vedi) measuring one cubit in height, length, and width.
If one should perform a single set of six, then likewise the [six] beginning with Vedyā;
[one should place them] in the directions of Īśa, East, Fire, and South, and in the directions of Vāyu and so forth, in due order.
First, one should offer to the Rākṣasa, and then to the others in the order previously mentioned,
having presented them with perfumes, flowers, and so forth, as well as with dance, song, and the like.

Having thus propitiated [the deity] for three days as instructed by the Śaktis, and having performed the fire-oblation and recitation during the exaltation of Jupiter (Jīva), or the exaltation of the Sun, or at the rising of a fixed sign, || 52 ||

And having drawn the three-sectioned Vidyā, one should also write the syllables of the Vidyās within the nine triangles situated inside the triangles drawn in the four directions outside, just as in the center. This is the first Vajra-yantra. In the same way, the others [are to be constructed] as well.
One should construct the five vajra-machines with the five sections of the Vidyā;
thus, together with the previously mentioned one, there are six vajra-machines that come into being. || 45 ||
With these thirteen verses beginning with "lohatraya" and ending with "vā," [the author describes] the construction of the pavilion and the altar for the purpose of empowering those vajra-machines,
their installation therein, and the consecration of the seven forms of the deities within them.

Having drawn the method of worshipping Him, the fruits thereof, and the diagrams (*yantras*) for those two types of receptacles—the fruit-bearing tree and the stone slab—he teaches the fruit of that worship. In this context, "on the stone" means on a rock; "the hexagon" means on six surfaces, that is, on six substrates such as one, two, and so forth, or individually upon each of the six.

The meaning is that one should fashion six yantras in the form of vajras—either one by one, or all of them, or in every case—respectively. The word "of the yantra" is to be understood as "of the worship. The other six yantras are those drawn on the three metals and on stone. [One should perform] that [worship] upon the vajras installed right there.

[The goddess] Nityānityā. || 47 || In that place of installation, in the place where the six *vajra*-yantras are installed; having established [the yantra] on the earth in its own left side (*vāmabhāga*) at the rising of the ground, O Supreme Goddess.
Having firmly bound the soul of the Goddess there with slabs of stone, indeed.
O Ambikā, having produced and installed the seven forms of the Goddess who is surrounded by those six, beginning with the Ḍākinīs, one should worship her.
One should also cause the constant worship of that knowledge (Vidyā) to be performed; for wherever there may be misfortune, poverty, enemies, malefic planets, or piśācas, [it destroys them].
Afflictions arising from famine or minor misdeeds, even when instigated by others,
never occur through the power of this vidyā-mantra.
For all people, everywhere, and at all times, only auspicious things arise;
and there are righteous kings, endowed with the full seven limbs of sovereignty. || 57 ||
Having performed worship with a leaf or a cloth in one's own home,
one attains one's desired object even from a mandala after a month.
The width [is as stated]. || 48 || "In the middle" refers to the pavilion; this is the ellipsis. || 49 || "One yantra" is the ellipsis.

"A group of six yantras" is the ellipsis. || 50 || By the aforementioned sequence, the meaning is that the Ḍākinīs and others are to be installed in the directions previously mentioned—namely, the southwest, northwest, east, southeast, northeast, and west. || 51 ||
By the aforementioned Śaktis, who constitute the retinue of Ḍākinīs and the others;
when Jupiter is in its own exaltation, in a dual exaltation, or in its constant exaltation; likewise when the Sun is in its exaltation;

during a stable rising (sthirodaya), that is, at the rising of a fixed zodiac sign (sthira-rāśi); and during the rising of Earth (bhūmyudaya), which refers to the rising of Earth as described in the *Śvāsapaṭala*.
The word "yantra" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Therein, on the altars (*vedikā*)—the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the *rākinyas* and so forth.
The "seven forms" (*mūrtisaptaka*) refers to the six goddesses beginning with *ḍākinī* and the [central] Goddess; this is the remainder [to be supplied]. 54.

"Before them," that is, in their presence; "one should cause the worship of the Vidyā"—the meaning is that one should cause the worship of the root-vidyā—to be performed. (55) "Afflictions arising from minor rites" refers to the distresses produced by the employment of spells such as those for inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). "[By the power] of the Vidyā-yantro" means by the efficacy of both [the Vidyā and the yantra]. (56, 57)

"From the performed worship" means from the worship of the six prepared yantras; "from the mandala" as previously described. This is what is meant: having engraved the aforementioned six vajra-forms and the *devī-nityapūjā-cakra* (yantra) upon three metals or on stone according to the stated procedure, for the purpose of installing them—
Having constructed a pavilion (maṇḍapa) with the prescribed length and width, adorned with banners and other decorations, one should place the yantra therein;
if there is only a single yantra to be installed, one should construct a single altar (vedikā) in its center with the prescribed height, length, and width, and upon it the yantras are to be placed.
If there are six, there are six vedikās (p.
286). I shall describe their location within the body, which bestows all goals; listen!
They reside in the six lotuses of the supports situated in the middle of the suṣumnā. (59)
The goddesses abide within living beings; when worshipped with knowledge, they grant success.
And externally, in the mandala, their worship consists of grace and restraint.

In the region of the throat, known as Viśuddha, upon a lotus of smoky color with sixteen petals inscribed with the vowels, one should visualize the goddess Ḍākinī, whose form is identical to that [of the central deity].
One should worship her there as surrounded by the Śaktis whose forms are the vowels;
through her, the accomplishment of omniscience occurs without a doubt. || 62 ||
Having arranged [the yantras] in the directions previously specified and having constructed a single altar in their center,
one should place the six yantras there according to the prescribed sequence; then, having placed the perpetual worship-circle (nityapūjācakra) of the Goddess upon the central altar,
[one should worship] within those yantras with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth.

Having propitiated the Goddess for three days with the ḍākinīs and other attendant śaktis to be described hereafter, and having recited [the mantra] one thousand times every day, and having offered oblations amounting to one-tenth of that number,
[one should perform this] during the exaltation of Jupiter, or during the two-fold exaltation of the Sun, or likewise during the exaltation of the Sun at the rising of a fixed zodiac sign.

Or, when the breath arises in the earth-element located at one's own left nostril, having installed those mechanical devices (*yantra*) upon those altars (*vedikā*) according to the prescribed sequence and having secured them firmly with stone slabs,
[one should worship] the six goddesses beginning with Ḍākinī and the [central] Goddess upon each of those altars.

Having fashioned the seven forms, having installed them, and having worshipped them thoroughly, one should also perform the recitation of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) in their presence. Wherever this is performed, the aforementioned inauspicious events do not occur; rather, the aforementioned auspicious events surely come to pass.

Having fashioned all of these, or each one individually, either on a wooden board or on a cloth, and having installed them in some place within one's own residence, one obtains every desired object through worship after the prescribed time. || 58 ||

With these thirteen verses beginning with "āsām" and ending with "āspadam," [the text describes] the six locations of the supports (ādhāras), their names, the lotuses situated therein, the syllables residing in those lotuses, the deities located in those lotuses, and their respective colors.

He teaches the sequence of worship for the sake of their respective grace, and the sequence of worship and so forth for the sake of their respective restraint. In this context, "of these" refers to the Ḍākinīs and others. "The state of abiding in the body" means their presence within the bodies of all living beings. The connection is with the word "those goddesses," and the ellipsis is "the Ḍākinīs and others. || 59 ||

"Worshipped by knowledge" (jñānapūjitāḥ) means that they have been worshipped after one has learned from the mouth of the Guru their ultimate nature as the presiding deities of these [mudrās]. And "externally" refers to the form of the mandala which is about to be described;
the connection is with the phrase "I shall describe the worship. "Having that same form" (tatsamākṛtim) means having the same form as the root deity (mūladevatā).
Their color is identical to that of their respective supporting lotuses; their form, however, is identical to that of the root deity. || 61 ||
In the region of the heart, within the lotus red as vermilion known as Anāhata, one should [worship] Rākiṇī upon its twelve petals, which consist of the letters from *ka* to *ḍha*. (63)
One should worship daily with the Śaktis for the attainment of fame, long life, prosperity, and wealth,
in the lotus of ten petals located at the navel, known as Maṇipūraka.
One should worship Lākinī—who possesses a self-power consisting of ten colors beginning with sapphire-blue—for the sake of victory over enemies and the attainment of prosperity. 65.
At the base of the banner, for the sake of crossing over all transgressions and for the attainment of desired success,
one should worship Ḍākinī, who is surrounded by the powers of the six vowels of the Vādis.
In the six-petaled lotus called Svādhiṣṭhāna, possessing the luster of the rising sun,
and in the four-petaled lotus called Ādhāra, which has the brilliance of gold.
One should worship Śākinī, who is surrounded by the powers (śaktis) of the vowels, consonants, and semi-vowels (vādi-śāntārṇa),
endowed with splendor in the center of a triangle situated between the anus and the penis.
Likewise, one should worship Hākinī, who has a beautiful form and resides in the two-petalled lotus called Ājñā between the eyebrows, served by the powers Ha and Kṣa.
A man who knows the three times effortlessly bestows the power of creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe, as well as the vision that removes all anxiety.
By reversing the stated sequence, there is likewise internal and external defeat;
yet worship [performed correctly] is the destroyer of all suffering and affliction, and the source of all prosperity.
By that worship. || 62 || 63 || 64 || 65 || 66 || At the base of the banner, that is, at the base of the phallus. || 67 ||

Between the anus and the penis, in the region between the anal aperture and the urethra; in the center of the triangle, she who is endowed with fire, whose form is the splendor of Kuṇḍalinī. (68) "And likewise" (tathā) [indicates] a conjunction. (69)

The construction here is: "Hākinī, who effects the vision of thoughts. The meaning is that she bestows upon the minds of practitioners the capacity for knowledge of past, future, and present events. || 70 ||

The meaning is that worship—both internal and external—is performed according to the sequence already stated and to be stated hereafter, within the six ādhāras (internal supports) whose nature will be described, as well as in the external yantra. This is what is meant:
[worship is performed] in the six ādhāras beginning with the throat and ending with the space between the eyebrows, which have been previously mentioned.
Having placed on the ground, within the lotuses of the described form, the deities beginning with Ḍākinī and ending with Hākinī according to the sequence of the directions in a set of seven hexagons,
one should worship that Nityānityā in the center there with perfumes and other offerings. (72)
One should worship that group of six in the six corners surrounding it, in their respective order;
and one should also worship those [deities] in the outer [corners] as before, using the prescribed syllables.
Likewise, in the six corners of those [six], there are thirty-six Śaktis; they are identical to the Goddess in all respects, including their forms, weapons, and so forth. (74)

In the vowels as before, there should be five [groups], beginning with 'a' and ending with 'ma'; in the subsequent [consonants], they are devoid of the letters ya, va, la, and kṣa. One should worship with those in that same manner.

The six deities possess bodies identical to those of the root deity; their forms and colors correspond to the colors prescribed for the respective lotuses that serve as their seats, and they are accompanied by syllabic powers (*akṣaraśakti*) whose shapes and colors match their own.

One should perform the worship of the sequence of emanation known as Anugraha, according to the prescribed order, surrounded by the lotuses of the bases, each having the number of petals previously stated. In that regard,
the mantras for their worship consist of two seed-syllables and so forth, up to the seven-syllable mantra, using their respective names.
At the conclusion of the worship, one should worship each respective name-vidyā with the root-vidyā;
and for the powers of those respective enclosures (āvaraṇa), such as those consisting of syllables and so forth,
one should perform the worship— whether daily or occasional— with the twelve-syllable vidyā as prescribed.

Among these, the worship beginning with Hākinī as the conclusion and ending with Ḍākinī as the commencement is called the worship of restraint (nigraha), which is the worship according to the sequence of withdrawal (saṃhārakrama). Thus, one should perform the worship of grace (anugrahapūjā) both internally and externally. || 71 ||

With these four verses beginning with "On the ground" and ending with "one should worship with these," he teaches the external circle of grace (*bāhyānugraha-cakra*), the meditation on the powers (*śakti*) to be worshipped therein, and the sequence of their worship. Therein,

according to the previously stated order of directions— that is, the order of the directions starting from the center and proceeding through Nairṛti, Vāyu, Śakra, Agni, Īśa, and Varuṇa— in the center...
And there, in that wheel, in the center of the six spokes situated in the middle;

by the word "beginning with fragrance" (*gandhādibhiḥ*), the sixteen types of offerings (*ṣoḍaśopacāra*) are indicated. In the midst of those six corners—that is, within the hexagon—one should [place] that group of six, namely the group of six powers (*śakti*) beginning with Ḍākinī, in their respective order.

In the directions starting from the southwest (nir-ṛti) according to the stated sequence; and also in the external [locations], the word "also" (api ca) being used for conjunction. In the six external hexagons, those [deities] beginning with Ḍākinī, as before, have the stated colors according to the sequence starting from the southwest; they possess the colors assigned to their respective supports. Likewise, in the sequence starting from the southwest.

The meaning is that they possess forms, colors, and weapons identical to those of the respective central goddesses of the Samādevis. As before, there are five among the vowels; this is the eighth [section] of the Mātṛkā-yantra described in the Kulasundarī-paṭala.

Those five letters—*a*, *i*, *u*, *aṃ*, and *aḥ*—are unprecedented; that is, they are not repeated among the remaining fifty phonemes. Among the other ten phonemes from *ya* to *kṣa*, those four letters *ya*, *va*, *la*, and *kṣa* are excluded because they are repetitions. Of these [remaining letters]...
Furthermore, there is a repetition of four [letters] because the substitution of *yaṇ* (*ya*, *va*, *ra*, *la*) is possible for both *yakāra* and *vakāra*;
and because of the non-difference between *ra* and *la*, and because the letter *kṣa* consists of the forms of *kakāra* and *ṣakāra*. By means of those thirty-six syllables:
p.

289) Likewise, by means of the previously mentioned twelve syllables: therein, one should worship the six powers beginning with *ā* and ending with *ka* in the first wheel; similarly, [one should worship] the other [six] in the remaining [wheels] in due order.

One should worship the six powers. This is what is meant: seven hexagons, interconnected by mutually conforming lines, are situated in the directions of the center, the Rakṣas, Vāyu, Śakra, Agni, Īśa, and Varuṇa.

Having established the tips [of the lines] touched by Varuṇa, Vāyu, Īśa, Śakra, Vahni, and Nirṛti, one should invoke Nityānityā— whose form was previously described as ruddy— into the center of the six-cornered figure in their midst,
worship her with the sixteen services (ṣoḍaśopacāra), and [then worship] the deities beginning with Ḍākinī and ending with Hākinī within those six triangles.

Having meditated upon the six Śaktis situated in the center, who possess forms and weapons identical to those of Nityānityā, and whose lotus-petals are the colors of their respective supports, one should worship them in sequence with the sixteen services (upacāras), and then [worship] those very [Śaktis], beginning with Ḍākinī, up to Vahni...
Having invoked [the goddesses] in the centers of the six hexagons located in the directions beginning with the East according to the prescribed order,
and having meditated upon them facing westward as being like the *ādhāra* [support], and having worshipped them,
one should likewise invoke the thirty-six Śaktis of their respective enclosures within the hexagons surrounding them, facing toward each of those [central goddesses].

One should worship [the deity] according to the sequence taught in the *Ṛtyādi* and other texts, using the six respective twelve-syllable vidyās in groups of six, accompanied by the specific offerings of the various oblations (nivedya) to be described hereafter.
Thus, this worship of grace (*anugraha-pūjā*) brings about the attainment of all prosperity. This is the [nature] of this wheel.
The sequence of construction is explained by thirteen verses with their numerical annotations:
"Having first drawn a circle with a diameter of twenty-four finger-breadths, one should then establish the Brahma-thread (the central axis) at its center, measuring half of that [diameter]. (1)
Having made a pair of marks on both sides of that circle, and likewise having made another pair of marks from one mark to the other in both [directions], || 2 ||
Having laid two threads diagonally between the ends of the pair of western-pointed [threads],
there should be two threads reaching as far as the eastern points situated upon the Brahma-thread.
Then, from the two tips of the initial thread, one should likewise draw two threads reaching as far as the western Brahma-thread; in this manner, a hexagon is formed.
Then, from the southeast corner to the northwest corner, and likewise from that direction to the northeast corner, there shall be two Brahma-threads ending at the southwest corner. || 5 ||
Having divided each Brahma-thread into three parts and made a mark,
one should then draw circles on both sides by rotating through their respective half-portions.
Having divided one of those [lines] into twenty-four parts according to the Brahma-sūtras,
one should drop six lines at the tenth parts thereof.

From the cardinal points to the corners, up to the edge of the circle, one should drop a pair of lines touching the circle at their ends into each of the six wind-circles, intersecting them in the middle.
Then, having drawn six lines among them— three along the sides, one at each corner, and one through the center— one should erase [the remaining lines] to form the supreme wheel.
Furthermore, when the worship of these wheels and powers is performed in reverse order, it is known as "suppression" (nigraha); that leads to the ruin of one's enemies.
Having prepared six jars at the six wheels, filled with the decoction-water of the enemy-tree and wrapped in black cloth; (77)
One should worship them at midnight by offering oblations (bali) into their respective wombs;
thus, the bodies of the enemy will quickly become filled with skin and other [tissues].
One should offer the oblation consisting of the enemy’s blood mixed with sacrificial porridge (caru);
and with that very substance, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (homa) in anger, using a ladle shaped like a serpent’s head.
One should meditate on the goddesses as being enraged, biting their lips with their own arms,
striking at the piśācas and scattering their bodies about.
With ears adorned by swaying clusters of *jayā* flowers and uttering terrifying cries of distress—one should meditate thus and perform the suppression of enemies for their destruction. (81)
And those belonging to the Rakshasas, Maruts, Shakra, Agni, Shiva, and Varuna;
and those possessing the luster of smoke, vermilion, the rising blue sun, gold, and the moon.
Having thus prepared the central square, one should worship the Ḍākinīs and others;
and in the center, one should worship Nityānityā, who possesses the luster of the rising orb of the sun.
A man who is a practitioner of mantras, not knowing this manifestation of the wheel,
perishes while striving in the rites of subjugation and grace.
In times of illness or affliction, in dual combat, in the overthrowing of enemies, and likewise in the attainment of one's desires, success shall come through his worship. (13)
From this point forward, [the following sections] are to be explained. || 75 ||

With these six verses beginning with "eṣām" and ending with "maraṇāya vai," he teaches the worship-circle called *nigraha* (suppression) within these very wheels. Therein, the remainder is that there are seven wheels in the form of hexagons; and "of the powers" refers to the six powers mentioned in their respective places.

"In reverse order" means in the reverse sequence of the worship procedure described for the favor of the *cakra* and the *śakti*. (76) "Filled with the decoction-water of the enemy-tree" means filled with water boiled from the astringent extract (*kaṣāya*) of the tree belonging to the [astrological] asterism of the enemy. (77) "By offering the oblation (*bali*) to its source."
Having cut away the birth-stars of the enemies, the wheel for suppression is said to be of a terrifying vajra-form;
having fashioned it from bell-metal or lead, one should place it upon the lands of the foes. (82)
By laying down ten lines—east, west, south, and north—there shall be eighty-one squares; among these, in the four corners, [one should place the guardians].
One should erase ten squares in each [direction] using the remaining vajras;
one should fashion triangles in the four directions using four squares each.

"From the offering of the *bali* sacrifice. Those jars; "corpses" means bodies. (78) "In the blood of the wombs" means with the blood from the birth-stars (*nakṣatra*) of one's enemies; "with that very sacrificial porridge" (*caru*).
"With a ladle [formed from] a serpent's head" means having cut off the hood of a snake, [using] that hood which has become the ladle (*sruc*). (79)

*Tattanuṃ* means the body of the enemy. *Gulucchuḥ* refers to Kālikā. This is what is meant: having invoked the respective Śaktis, along with their retinues (*sāvaraṇa*), who abide in their terrible forms within the seven previously mentioned hexagonal wheels (*ṣaṭkoṇacakra*), and having meditated upon them facing [the practitioner], they remain stationed in their respective locations within those wheels.

Having offered the *bali* to be described according to the sequence of grace (*anugraha*) and worship (*pūjā*)— both in direct and reverse order— to the powers (*śakti*) of the wheels (*cakra*) and their enclosures (*āvṛti*), one should perform worship accompanied by fire-offerings (*homa*). Then, having placed six jars in the centers of those same seven hexagonal wheels, excluding the central wheel, among the six [remaining wheels]...
Having filled those jars with water boiled with the decoctions of the tree belonging to the enemy’s birth-star,

one should visualize all the presiding deities of the bodily constituents— skin and so forth— as having the terrifying forms previously described; standing before them as before, they extract the respective constituents, such as the skin and others, from that enemy.

Having filled the respective jars and having dismembered that body with one's own weapons, one should visualize those [weapons] scattering it among the Piśācas so that their bodies are being devoured by them; then,
by means of one's own consciousness, one should [dissolve] the senses, mind, and vital breaths of that [body] according to the procedure taught in the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā.
Applying [the ritual] to the central deity, worshipping according to the reverse order of the sequence prescribed for the worship of grace,
severing the *bali* offering of the enemy’s asterism and birth-sign, presenting the oblation (*nivedya*) with the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) prepared as described,
and performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) with a ladle made from the hood of a serpent— worshipping in this manner, it is said.

"One obtains the fruit"—thus it is said. Regarding these castes, such as the Ḍākinīs and others, and the [bodily constituents] such as the skin and so forth, the secret meaning concerning their relationship with the Nityā and Anityā Vidyās, their substrata, and their respective rites of suppression, favoring, and worship, must be understood solely from the mouth of one's own Guru. || 81 ||

With six and a half verses beginning with *cakra* and ending with *mardana*, [the author] teaches the construction of the Vajracakra of the suppression-compartment (*nigrahakoṣṭha*), its specific application, and its result. In that regard, having cleared away one compartment in each of the four directions by means of four compartments...

In that regard, the meaning is that one should construct triangles. (82–84) In those [triangles], one should write the object of the rite (*sādhya*) and the ritual action (*karman*) within the central square;
in the remaining squares, starting from the lower-middle square, one should write [the syllables] in reverse order. (85)
One should draw thirty-six Vidyākūṭas in a clockwise direction,
smeared with the powder of the tree belonging to the victim, ground together with its blood and excrement.
One should install [the deity] at the prescribed time in the houses or fields of enemies;
however, if installed in a cremation ground or a temple of Caṇḍikā, it will cause the destruction of one's own lineage.
Thus has been declared the method of suppression, which crushes all enemies;
now listen, O wise one, to the method of grace according to the ritual of the worship-circle. 88.
Having meditated upon those goddesses in the forms previously described, one should worship them in the wheels; their sacrificial food (naivedya) is said to be that which is pleasing to them. (89)
The meaning is that one should write starting from the central square and beginning from the square situated below it,
proceeding counter-clockwise (apradakṣiṇya) in an unmentioned order by way of exit;
[these are] those produced in reverse order.

In the various sequences to be described in the twenty-fifth chapter, [one should perform the rites] in reverse order according to the sequence of forms. (85) With the blood from the womb of the victim and the blood from the womb of the asterism of the enemy, one grinds the powder of that tree—the powder of the tree belonging to the enemy's asterism—into a paste. (86) At the prescribed time...

"In the *arāti* or *vaināśika* asterism, at the rising of the eighth house; the word 'ādi' (and so forth) refers to [inauspicious] places and other such factors. In each of those cases as well, it refers to the position of the eighth house. (87) Thus, in the manner described, "the crushing of enemies" means that which effects the destruction of foes. This is what is meant: as before, one should draw eighty-one squares.
Having divided those squares into ten squares each at every corner, and having cleared them in the shape of a central vajra,

and having cleared one square in each of the four directions, and having fashioned triangles in each of those places, and having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) both in those triangles and in the center;

Starting from the middle cell of the bottom row of the central square, proceeding clockwise in the manner not yet described— that is, by way of exiting— the [syllables] formed by the reverse order of the *vidyākūṭas* to be taught in the thirty-fifth chapter [are to be placed].

Having sequentially inscribed the thirty-six *kūṭas* according to the six types of relationships produced by the knowledge of the six conventions, one should then inscribe them using the blood and clarified butter from the womb of the victim’s birth-constellation, along with the mud from the tree of that constellation.
Having established [the deities] at the prescribed times and in the prescribed places, one shall obtain the prescribed fruit.

With the six verses beginning with "anugraham" and ending with "laghuvigrahaḥ," which describe the [sixfold] powers such as *ṛddhi* and so forth, [the text describes] the previously mentioned worship of the Wheel of Grace (*anugrahacakra*) and of those respective deities.
Having offered special oblations to them, the worship of the women consists of the Vajra-mechanism of the treasury of grace (p.
293): milk-rice, jaggery-rice, as well as rice with split mung beans, turmeric-rice, sesame-rice, and pure rice—these six indeed. (90)
Likewise, having established seven young women of beautiful form, possessing the colors corresponding to those [seven] wheels, and having worshipped them in sequence as before; 91.
One should satisfy them with ornaments, garments, perfumes, blood, food, and so forth;
for when they are satisfied, those Śaktis who are equal to them will likewise be satisfied.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished upon the previously mentioned vajra, one should then inscribe the kūṭas born of the direct order (anuloma), beginning from the unspoken [syllable], proceeding clockwise.
One should establish [the deity] in the aforementioned locations in the manner prescribed;
thus, the aforementioned fruits shall indeed be attained. This yoga is of a concise form. || 94 ||

Therein, he teaches the sequence of worship and its fruits: by means of the arrangement of the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*), the arrangement of the worship (*pūjāvidhāna*), and the arrangement of the circle (*cakravidhāna*). Therein, the arrangement of the worship refers to the *ḍākinīs* and other young women; the arrangement of the circle, however, refers to the *vajrayantra* and so forth. (88) These...

The *ḍākinīs* and so forth. By the phrase "of the form described," it is stated that they possess the colors mentioned for the *ādhāra-cakra*, as well as arms and faces equal to those of the Root Goddess (*mūladevī*). The remaining six [goddesses] are red, including the goddesses with their sons; this refers to the goddess situated in the center. Their color is [as follows].

Having worshipped, as before, those Śaktis—whose colors correspond to those of the root-deity of the presiding deity mentioned in the *Ādhāra*—starting from the center and ending with the east; [one should offer] food prescribed for each respective deity.
By the word "etc. (*ādi*), wealth in the form of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) according to one's capacity is also meant. [One should worship] those young women; those...

The *ḍākinīs* and so forth. This is what is meant: having invoked and worshipped the aforementioned powers (*śaktis*) in the seven previously mentioned wheels according to the stated sequence, and having offered each respective oblation (*nivedya*) to its corresponding deity, one should offer that entire collection of six oblations to the central deity. In those very [wheels]...
Having established seven young women upon the seven wheels, each possessing a complexion identical to their respective deities,

and having invoked those Śaktis into them according to the prescribed sequence and worshipped them, the various Śaktis become fully satisfied by pleasing those young women with offerings such as food, ornaments, and other gifts.

"They shall grant all desired objects. Thus [it is said]. In the previously mentioned *vajra* diagram, known as *nigraha*, consisting of eighty-one squares (*koṣṭha*) which has been extracted as a *vajra*-yantra—one should take the thirty-five *vidyās* born in direct order (*anuloma*), which consist of the *vidyās* in reverse form according to the sequence stated in the thirty-fifth chapter.
The thirty-six *vidyākūṭas* [are to be placed], beginning from the aforementioned starting point— that is,
beginning from the central square of the row below the center of the entire grid— within the previously mentioned squares for gold and so forth.

(294) With the letters from *a* to *kṣa*, joined with the power (*śakti*) whose form is as before, [and] with the fifteen-syllable [mantras] beginning with the two seed-syllables and ending with the seven syllables. || 95 ||
The fifty Śaktis are to be worshipped along with the fifty Kṣetrapālas;
likewise, there are fifty pairs [of deities] corresponding to the Ghaṭikās during the days.
Their two seed-syllables, conjoined with the letter, the formless one, the Lord of the Field, and the seven-syllabled [mantra], constitute fifteen-syllabled mantras. (97)
In the center of the sixty-four squares, having written the desired object within a group of four using the science of days, one should place those pairs of couples within them.
One should worship the center of the heart-illusion through the application of the sequence of the ghaṭikās;
thus, within half a month, one certainly attains what is desired. (99)

The meaning is: in the asterisms beginning with Maitra, during the rising of the eleven zodiac signs, and in the positions of those eleven signs; and in the aforementioned locations such as houses and pavilions. The aforementioned results—consisting of the attainment of longevity, fame, victory, and so forth—will indeed occur. Yoga is the application. By this, there is a concise exposition.

It is of the same form. This is what is meant: in the previously described Vajra-yanttra, starting from the middle of the bottom row of the central square and proceeding clockwise, one follows the sequence of emergence without interruption.

Having written the thirty-six *kūṭas*— numbered thus, consisting of the thirty-five *vidyās* whose sequence will be described in the [thirty-fifth] chapter, which take the form of both *anuloma* and *viloma*, and which are joined with the six types produced by the six conventions (*ṣaṭsaṅketa*)— one should place them as before in the center and in the triangles situated in the four directions.

Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) according to the prescribed method, and having engraved it at the stated times, in the stated substrates, on the stated grounds, and in the stated locations, the attainment of the stated results will occur; thus, this [rite] among the applications is also to be accomplished with effort. || 94 ||

With these six verses beginning with "From Ā to Kṣa" and ending with "from all sides," he teaches that the attainment of the desired fruit results from the worship of the fifty pairs (mithuna) in the form of the ghaṭikās of time within that maṇḍala. In this regard, the following is stated:
Having stretched nine threads across the intermediate spaces from east to west and south to north, one should then,

within that wheel of sixty-four squares, combine four squares into one by proceeding two steps up and down from the center; therein, according to the procedure to be described in the twenty-fifth chapter.
Having first written the three syllables of the daily *nityā-vidyā* intended for the desired prayer in the middle [cell],
one should then proceed from the right-hand cell of the middle pair located in the bottom row on the outside, moving clockwise in the manner previously described, following the path of exit.
From the left row of the *cakravāla* down to the lower square,
one should constantly invoke the deities beginning with Akṣa, as will be described in the thirty-fifth chapter (*paṭala*), and by worshipping them within that wheel—
The attainment of all desired objects occurs at all times and forever. || 100 ||
The pervasion consisting of the principle of breath (prāṇatattva) has thus been correctly described.
By the thorough clarification of this within the mind, that very principle is realized as one's own self.
Thus ends the sixteenth chapter in the *Kādimata*, within the *Śrīṣoḍaśanityātantra*. 16.
Having written the fifty letters proclaimed in the *Mātṛkā*, excluding the letter *kṣa* and either excluding the *visarga* or including the letter *sa*,

situated within the heart of the *hṛllekhā*; and having further written the ten syllables beginning with *udaya* in the remaining squares, [one should proceed] according to the order in which they were written therein.

During the sixty *ghaṭikās* beginning from sunrise and so forth, having worshipped the respective pairs with sixteen types of offerings (*upacāras*), one shall obtain their respective fruits. As for their mantras, following the two seed-syllables (*bījas*) and the interval between the forms and the field (*rūpa-kṣetra-antara*), they are: "I worship the sandals of the formless power (*arūpiṇī-śakti-pādukā*)," and so on.

There are fifty *tacchakti* mantras. Furthermore, following each pair of seed-syllables (*bīja*), there are exactly fifty mantras for the respective *kṣetrapāla*, beginning with "I worship the sandals of the formless *kṣetreśa*" and so forth; thus, each consists of fifty syllables.

One should worship those couples with the *vidyās* and mantras consisting of fifty and fifteen syllables respectively. The traditional meaning (*sampradāyārtha*) is that subjugation (*nigraha*) occurs through the drawing and worship of this wheel in an anti-clockwise direction, starting from the previously mentioned commencement. || 95 || 96 || 97 || 98 || 99 || 100 ||

Thus, in the *Manoramā*, the commentary composed by Śrī Subhagānandanātha— entitled *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*— upon the complete *Tantra* known as the *Śrīkādimatā* among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
In this commentary, the fifteenth chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the ritual procedure for the Śivadūtī Nityā-vidyā, has been fully examined. 16.
The number of verses is thirty-six, and the explanatory texts on the diagrams are remembered as two hundred and eighty-five and a half quarters in the sixteenth chapter.
Now begins the seventeenth chapter.
Now, regarding that which is proclaimed as the twelfth among the sixteen Nityās,
the ritual procedure for her, Nīlapatākā, bestows all accomplishments.

The procedure for the sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation, the powers, worship, the practice of one who has mastered the vidyā, victory, and the power of assuming any form at will. || 2 ||
I shall describe to you sandals, collyrium, the sword, vetālas, piśācas, yakṣiṇīs, servants, magic, and mechanical devices.
By means of the ten accomplishments (siddhis) taught in their entirety according to the sequence of the ritual applications, a mortal becomes another Vidyādhara.
One should perform the six limbs with the syllables of the root-vidyā in sequence, as stated,
using two, four, and six syllables respectively.

The seventeenth chapter. Having taught in the preceding sixteenth chapter the ritual procedure for the eleventh *nityā-vidyā*, Nityānityā, [the author now teaches] that of the twelfth, Nīlapatākā-nityā-vidyā.

He teaches the ritual procedure (*vidhāna*). Therein, with four verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "the Supreme" (*para*), he indicates the subject matters of the chapter. Since the *vidyā* was already taught in the third chapter, it is not mentioned here; the syntactical connection is: "I shall state the ritual procedure. || 1 ||

The forms [of the mantras] consist of the procedures beginning with "the sequence of nyāsa" and so forth. "Śaktis" refers to the powers of the enclosures (*āvaraṇa-śaktis*); the word "in the vidyā" is to be understood as the ellipsis for "as the means. The phrase "of the person who has mastered the vidyā" is also to be understood as the ellipsis. Since the ten accomplishments (*siddhis*) such as Vijayā and others will be described by the author himself later on, their specific forms are not detailed here.

They are not mentioned [here]. || 2 || "Machines" refers to the mechanical devices for the purpose of accomplishing those [rites]. || 3 || "Of the instructed" refers to the success (siddhi) and so forth. || 4 ||

With these three verses beginning with "mūlavidyā" and ending with "yathāvidhi," he teaches the method of ritual placement (*nyāsa*). Therein, by means of the two, four, six, and three syllables respectively—
specifically, by the first and second syllables of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*)— the heart [is to be placed].
With the four [syllables] immediately following that, the head; with the six above those, the crest-lock (śikhā);
with the one immediately after that, the armor (kavaca); and then, in sequence, upon the ears, eyes, pair of nostrils, speech, throat, and heart.
And in the three joints of the feet, respectively, upon the support of non-existence. || 6 ||
One should sequentially place all seventeen mantra-syllables, and one should also perform the pervasive placement with the entire mantra according to the prescribed rule.
Resembling a sapphire, adorned with a crown of radiant jewels,
she has five faces and three eyes, and wears garments of reddish hue.
Ten cubits in height, adorned with ornaments consisting mostly of shimmering pearls, her body interspersed with clusters of gems, and her face graced with a beautiful smile. (9)
Holding a noose, a banner, shields, and the excellent Śārṅga bow in her hands,
which are adorned with all ornaments and positioned on her left side.
Holding a goad, a spear, a sword, an arrow, and likewise the gesture of fearlessness with her right hands, she is seated upon a lotus throne.

With one [syllable] the eye, and with the next one the weapon; since the two remaining mantra-syllables have already been employed in the heart-mantra, they are not taken up again for fear of redundancy. Thus, by the sequence of divisions as stated—“by the six uttered in order”—the six limbs [are formed] by means of the syllables of different classes.

The meaning is that one should perform the placement (*nyāsa*) upon the limbs of the hands. Since the repetition of the word "six" (*ṣaṭ*) is intended for the purpose of indicating both contraction and expansion, there is no fault of tautology. || 5 ||
With the two verses beginning with *śrotra* and ending with *yathāvidhi*,
he teaches the sequence for the placement (*nyāsa*) of the mantra-syllables along with the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*). In that regard,
one [syllable] is placed in each of the five locations— the speech-center, throat, heart, navel, and foundation— and [one syllable] in each of the other six.

The meaning is that there are two [syllables] each at the ears, eyes, nose, feet, and the three joints; therein, after placing three steps with one foot, one places three steps with the other foot— thus one should place the seventeen syllables of the root-vidyā according to the sequence of the indicated locations.

And one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka-nyāsa*) with the entire [mantra] according to the rule; that is to say, one should perform the pervasive placement with the entire root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) as before. || 6 || 7 ||

With these five verses beginning with "resembling sapphire" (*indranīlanibhām*) and ending with "in sequence" (*krame*), he teaches the visualization for the constant worship of the Goddess together with her retinue. In this context, *mauli* means a crown;
as for the manner in which the five faces are situated, the meaning is that they are located above and in the four directions.

The oral tradition states that her upward-facing face is directed toward the practitioner. "Three-eyed" means she has [three eyes] in each face. "Ten-armed" is the remainder of the phrase, meaning she is born with ten hands. || 8–9 ||

In the sequence of daily worship, one should meditate upon the Goddess as having a single Śārṅga bow (p. 298), endowed with her own characteristic form, color, attire, face, hands, weapons, and ornaments, and surrounded by multitudes of Śaktis. 12.
Outside of that, there is an eight-petalled lotus joined with three hexagons;
then an octagon, followed by two sets of four-walled enclosures (bhūpura) within two circles.
Having constructed it with four gates on the cardinal directions and provided with archways,
and having surrounded it there with hosts of Śaktis, one should worship Śivā therein.
One should worship the powers of will, knowledge, and action in the three corners;
starting from the front, one should worship the fivefold enclosure by proceeding clockwise.
Because the bow is made of horn, one should fashion their heads and so forth, arranged in sequence on both sides.
On a lotus-seat of the form to be described [later] (verse 11); "āsya" means the face (verse 12).

With the two verses beginning with *triṣaṭ* and ending with *śivām*, he sets forth the procedure for the maṇḍala of the daily worship (*nityasaparyā*) and introduces the ritual of worship therein. In that context, "endowed with three hexagons" means it is joined with both a triangle and a hexagon; beyond that [is the outer portion].

Outside the eight-petaled lotus, from the corners formed by the cardinal and intermediate directions of the pair of square enclosures (bhūpura)—the word "vṛte" is in the dual number—meaning having made that subsequent pair of two square enclosures; the word "having made" (kṛtvā) connects with what precedes. There, in that mandala—the meaning is as follows: according to the desired measurement.
Having divided two equal squares into inner and outer sections according to the method to be described,

one should form four corners by joining the tips of the lines of the inner square with the outer square; then, in the four directions, from the center of each, one should form [sections] provided with two branches.

Having fashioned four doors, one should immediately thereafter fashion a square situated within [the mandala] touching [the perimeter], and within that as well, a circle with an interval of one finger-breadth; then, having drawn four threads at equal intervals within that circle, reaching the edge of the circular line and terminating in eight points directed toward the cardinal and intermediate directions.

Among those, having formed eight corners by drawing lines from one thread-tip to another at intervals of one, through the stretching of eight threads, and having erased four of the threads, one should produce two circles— touching the middle of the eight lines of the octagon within— that interval— as before, [measuring four finger-breadths in diameter].
Having constructed two circles as before, one should fashion eight petals there according to the proper measure; then, in the center of that, a hexagon as before, and in its center two circles.
Within those, by drawing equal divisions according to the method taught by the Guru, one should form [the design] with three equal lines.
Having drawn a corner there, one should worship the Goddess together with her retinue according to the sequence to be described.
One should worship the Ḍākinīs and others in the six corners all around in sequence;
likewise, one should worship Brāhmī and the others on the eight petals and in their corners on the outside. (16)
One should worship those Śaktis previously mentioned, as described in the Nityānityā and other [tantras]; one should offer two oblations (bali) and conclude the worship as before.
In all cases, one should perform the perpetual fire-oblation (nityahoma) with food, clarified butter, or even sesame seeds and rice; this is declared when no specific materials are mentioned.
Having separated all the syllables of the vidyā— including vowels, consonants, and bindus—
and having calculated them, they indeed amount to fifty-three.
Therefore, one who observes a vow of milk should recite that vidyā one hundred thousand times;
one should offer oblations into the fire one-tenth of that amount for every hundred-thousand recitation of the syllables.
In daily worship and in spiritual practices, the practitioner should face the east;
this has been declared for all daily rites as well as for the process of mental cultivation (vāsanā).

With these three verses beginning with "icchā" and ending with "samāpayet," he teaches the sequence for the worship of the five enclosures (*pañcāvaraṇa*) of the Goddess. Therein, by the expression "successively around," it is meant that for *Ḍākinī* and the others, who are situated as before, the order proceeds from the front and so on in a clockwise direction.

This means "worship. The sequence for that worship has already been explained by us previously in the tenth verse of the thirteenth chapter. "In its corners" refers to the eight corners; "outside" refers to the square. || 15 || 16 ||
Because this refers to the previously mentioned extension (*atideśa*) stating that [the rites] have been taught regarding the eternal, the non-eternal, and so forth, there is no fault of redundancy.

In that context, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the *dūtī*s are indicated; by that, the eight corner-energies (*śakti*s) such as Samukhā and the rest, which are taught in that chapter, are expressed. Those energies [are to be placed] in the square according to the sequence of commencement taught therein.
The meaning is that one should worship. By this, the double worship of Brāhmī and the others is established here.

With the sixteen-syllable and seven-syllable Kurukullā mantras, respectively at the beginning and the end—this is the ellipsis. As before, it means accompanied by the visualization of the three fires within the three supports (ādhāras). || 17 ||

With the verse beginning with "sarvatra" (everywhere), he teaches the materials for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) that are common to all deities when no specific substance is mentioned; there, "prokta" means "stated in the manner previously described," and "substance" (*dravya*) is to be understood as the ellipsis.

With these three verses beginning with "vidyā" and ending with "udīritam," he teaches the means for attaining knowledge (*vidyā*) and so forth. In that context, "pṛthakkṛtya" means having separated or distinguished each [element] individually; "hi" indicates the reason. 19. In that regard:
The first, fourth, sixth, eighth, sixteenth, and seventeenth syllables have four variations each;
the fifth, seventh, ninth, eleventh (twelfth), and fourteenth syllables have two variations each. (p.
300) Thereafter, the practitioner who has mastered the mantra should apply curiosity toward the various accomplishments (*siddhis*).
O wise one, listen to its ritual procedure; I shall explain it according to the different divisions of the Vidyā.
The ten Vidyās corresponding to the ten Siddhis, their divisions, their enumerations, and their respective fruits have been proclaimed in due order.
One should join [the syllables] in sequence within the ten [sections] beginning with the first peak of the Vidyā;
then, one should enclose those mentioned above by means of those two [syllables] themselves in reverse order.
Listen now to the syllables of the ten mantras and their respective numbers;
thereafter, I shall declare the specific mantras for each of those divisions according to the prescribed rule.

The meaning is that the syllables of the Vidyā—consisting of ten, thirteen, and fifteen syllables respectively—are of three varieties, totaling seventeen. Because of the specific injunction "that [number] in its lakṣas," the meaning is that in all yugas there are fifty-three lakṣas. One who observes the milk-vow (payovrata) is one whose diet consists of milk. Its tenth part...
This means one-tenth of a hundred thousand syllables (ten thousand). || 20 || In the *Vāsanā*, in the chapter on *vāsanā*, the reason for facing eastward was previously stated. || 21 ||
With the two verses beginning with *tataḥ* and ending with *phalāni ca*, [the text] first teaches the fitness for accomplishing the ten siddhis of one who has mastered the vidyā,
and then [teaches] each of the ten siddhi-vidyās in the form of the seed-syllables (*bīja*) of the root-vidyā.

He introduces the subject, saying: "I shall explain the enumeration of the internal subdivisions of the accomplished sciences (*siddhividyā*), their essential natures regarding success and failure, and their respective fruits. In that regard, concerning the ten accomplishments (*siddhi*) such as *vijayā* and the rest, there is "curiosity" (*kautuka*), meaning reverence.

Their "procedure" (*vidhāna*) refers to the procedure for the ten accomplishments. This is according to the "distinctions of the sciences" (*vidyāvibhedataḥ*), [starting] from the root science (*mūlavidyā*).

Of the syllables that constitute its own nature; "through division" means by dividing and subdividing according to the method to be described later. Of those *siddhis* and *vidyās*; "the division reached" refers to that which will be clearly explained by the author himself further on. Those [are as follows].

The accomplishments (*siddhi*s). Of these accomplishments: this is what is meant. From the specific varieties of knowledge produced by the different modes of application of the essential form of the Root-Mantra (*mūlavidyā*), there arise ten accomplishments; for each of those mantras, there are numerous intermediate subdivisions, which constitute those accomplishments and their respective fruits.
He introduces all those things that will be explained in the remainder of the chapter. (Thus, 23.)

With the two verses beginning with "vidyādītyādinā" and ending with "yathāvidhītyantena," he teaches the common *kūṭākṣara* (cryptic syllables), the *paṭala* (sections), and so forth, which constitute the essential nature and application for all the specific accomplishments (*siddhi*) and sciences (*vidyā*) that are about to be described. Among those:

In the *vidyādikūṭa*, there are two conjoined syllables that constitute the beginning of the root-vidyā; here too, the dual number is used for the first [pair]. (p. 301) Victory is fourfold in a duel involving four divisions.
In deceptive warfare and in sieges of fortresses, their fourfold types of counsel are employed. || 26 ||

The power to assume at will any desired form, which is called "the state of being able to take any form" (kāmarūpatva), is said to be that one mantra alone by which one is capable of creating such a body for oneself.
Having placed a pair of sandals, obtained through the power of the vidyā, upon one's feet, one should meditate upon the desired place; then one's residence shall be there.
Its mantra shall be of a single kind, and likewise the collyrium is described;
anointed with which one may behold the treasure-trove as well as the gods and others moving in the intermediate space.
And such is the sword said to be: by means of it held in the hand, enemies flee in an instant, or they fall at one's feet, having come under one's control. (30)
There are innumerable vetālas who are accomplished through this single vidyā;
having placed it upon one's shoulder, they move according to his will.

The meaning is that one should join the first two syllables of the *siddhimantras*. The phrase "in the ten attainments" (*daśasu siddhiṣu*) implies "of the vidyās. "By those two joined syllables" means one should encase [the mantra] or join them at the end of the *siddhimantra*. "Those mentioned above" refers to those which will be described further on. || 24 ||

The phrase "and of the ten" connects both to what precedes and what follows, like the eye of a crow. "Those respective numbers" refers to the numbers of the specific designations for the accomplishments (*siddhi*) and their corresponding vidyās. "Those accomplishments" [refers to] those very siddhis. "Subsequently" means after the instruction on the nature of the accomplishments according to their numerical count. "Of their subdivisions" refers to each one individually.
Of the intermediate subdivisions of the accomplishments, [one should know] the mantras by their respective numbers and so forth. || 25 ||

With fifteen verses beginning with "fourfold" (caturvidha) and ending with "in propitiation" (prasādane), he teaches the nature of the ten accomplishments (siddhis), their subdivisions and numbers, and the numbers of the divisions of their vidyās. Therein, [he begins] with "fourfold," etc.
With this verse, he teaches the nature of victory and success and so forth. In that context, "in a duel" implies "in battle" as the remainder of the sense.

Regarding those enemies bearing such names, when the two principal ones, along with their armies, engage in mutual combat—provided it is complete with the four divisions of the army—the rest is as before. When it arises from a fort (*durgaja*), meaning produced within a fort, the rest is as before.
Of those four kinds of Vijayas. || 26 ||
With the verse beginning with "kāmam" (at will), he teaches the attainment of the ability to assume any form and so forth;
therein, "śakti" means capacity. He is the bestower of forms at will. || 27 ||
Some had distorted limbs and faces, some had faces and limbs turned sideways, and some were Vetālas with terrifying bodies and many forms. (32)
All become subject to his word and devour his enemies; by performing what he commands, they shall remain as his servants for the duration of their lives.
Such beings are called Piśācas; they possess emaciated and deformed bodies, are wrathful, possess base intentions, act according to their descriptions, and are said to be innumerable.
One of these should be their vidyā; by means of it, they shall always be servants [to him]. With those very [mantras], he may strike the enemy unawares and incessantly in battle.
Thirty-six yakṣiṇīs, endowed with beautiful forms, bestow whatever is desired; they possess lovely countenances, have two arms, and are adorned with variegated garments and ornaments. (36)

With the two verses beginning with "pādukā" and ending with "antarikṣagān," he teaches the nature and other characteristics of the accomplishment of the sandals (*pādukāsiddhi*). In that context, "attained through the power of the Vidyā" means bestowed by the grace of the Vidyā of the accomplishment of the sandals; "on his own feet"—this is the ellipsis. "In that place" refers to the location [of the sandals]. || 28 ||
That mantra is the *pādukā* mantra; furthermore, it is according to how the *pādukā* is obtained, or the number of its mantras, or by which ointment [it is applied]. || 29 ||

With the verse beginning "And the sword is likewise," he teaches the nature and other qualities of the accomplishment of the sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*). In that context, "likewise" refers to [the attainment] through the mantra and vidyā; the ellipsis is "with the sword held in one's hand. "Ahitāḥ" means enemies.

With these three verses beginning with "vetālā" and ending with "āyuṣam," he teaches the nature and other characteristics of the *siddhis* such as the *vetāla*. In that context, "of this" refers to the practitioner (*sādhaka*). "Those *vetālas*" [are described]. (31) "Tiryaṅmukhāṅgakāḥ" means those with faces and limbs of animals—those with the faces and bodies of deer.

The many compounds [should be understood] even through the previously mentioned alternative analysis of compounds. "All these vetālas belong to him"—this connects with both the preceding and the following [words].

With the two verses beginning with "piśācā" and ending with "raṇe," he teaches the forms and other characteristics of the accomplishment of the Piśācas. In that context, "tādṛśāḥ" means "of such various kinds.
"Kṣudrāśayāḥ" means those of small resolve or little courage. The phrase "in their accomplishment" is the ellipsis to be supplied. [This is] by means of that vidyā.
They are the piśācas; by those piśācas; unknown, that is, not perceived directly. || 35 ||
With these three verses beginning with "thirty-six" and ending with "are agreed upon," he teaches the forms and other characteristics of the yakṣiṇī-siddhis.
In this context, "endowed with thirty-six forms" means that they are numbered at thirty-six. || 36 ||
(303) Those women, who are without companions, rich in youth, and fragrant with garlands and unguents, shall indeed assemble and grant all desired objects to the practitioner. 37.
I shall now declare their thirty-six vidyās; listen to them, O beloved, by the constant perfection of which practitioners become honored by all. (38)
There are sixty-four Cetakas, and their mantras are equal in number;
they too are of various forms, and once perfected, they grant whatever is desired.
Mayas, numbering in the millions and possessing diverse forms, might incessantly bring various riches to him by his mere will; yet, there is but one science for the accomplishment thereof.
From the six syllables beginning with the ninth letter of the Vidyā that have been declared, ten Vidyās are produced; listen, and I shall describe them in order. (41)
"Without companions" means devoid of a retinue; "those" refers to the yakṣiṇīs. [Verse 37] "Of those" refers to the yakṣiṇīs;
"those" refers to the vidyās; "by which" refers to the vidyās. [Verse 38]

With the verse beginning with *ceṭaka*, he teaches the form and other details of the *ceṭaka* [attendant] accomplishment. In that context, "of them" refers to those *ceṭakas*. "Equal to those" means numbering sixty-four. "Those *ceṭakas*" refers to them as previously described. The phrase "the desired [object] of the practitioner" is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 39 ||

With the verse beginning with "māyā," he teaches the nature of the accomplishment of *māyā* and so forth. In that context, the expression "innumerable *māyās*" is a statement regarding sovereignty; the meaning is that the *māyās*, which are powers (*śaktayaḥ*), are innumerable.
This is to be connected with the phrase "variegated objects. [This refers] to this practitioner; those are the *māyās*.
"Gratifying them" means gratifying the *māyās*. "Gratification" (*prasādana*) means attainment. This is what is meant:
for the *vijayā* yakṣiṇīs and the *ceṭakas*, there are four, thirty-six, and sixty-four vidyās respectively; for each of the other seven, there is one form each.
The sciences are seven; together with the ten accomplishments (siddhis), the number of sciences is one hundred and eleven. || 40 ||

With thirty-one verses beginning with "vidyāyāḥ" and ending with "vyākulakramāt," he teaches the nature of the mantras for the *siddhis*, numbering one hundred and eleven as previously stated. Among those:

Of *vidyā* means of the root-vidyā. "By those declared" means by those that will be described hereafter. "The ten vidyās" is a statement made with reference to the attainment of supernatural powers (*siddhi*). Those are the vidyās. || 41 ||
With this verse beginning with "nitya," he teaches the fourfold *Vijayasiddhividya*.
In that regard, having said "nitya" (p. 304), [one should say] "O Vijaya, grant [me success]," and then enclose it within the *sampuṭa* (the encapsulation).
That is the Vidyā for the attainment of victory; it consists of eleven syllables among the four [Vidyās]. || 42 ||
"Intoxicate my Kāmarūpa; grant it to me"—thus one should encapsulate [the mantra].
This thirteen-syllable vidyā is proclaimed as the bestower of Kāmarūpa. (43)
Having said, "O Nityā, give me the sandals," one should perform the *sampuṭa* (encasement).
This twelve-syllable mantra becomes perfected (*siddha*), and one should then bestow the sandals.
Likewise, having said "nityaprada" (ever-bestowing), one should utter "dehyañjanam" (ointment for the body);
one should worship with that pair here, and this is declared to be the twelve-syllable mantra.
Having said, "O melting one, come, O glowing charcoal," one should likewise perform the *puṭa* rite;
thus the twelve-syllable mantra becomes perfected and true, and it shall bestow great splendor.

The application of the mantra: regarding "in the attainment of victory," the grammatical connection is "in the attainment of victory in the four types of dual combat and so forth. There are four modes of the eleven-syllable *vijayasiddhi* vidyā.

By applying specific names mentioned [in relation] to dual combat (*dvandvayuddha*) and so forth— just as in the cases of "dual combat," "fourfold combat" (*caturaṅgayuddha*), "treacherous combat" (*kūṭayuddha*), and "fortress combat" (*durgayuddha*)— these terms should be placed before the word *vijaya*. Thus, there are three [mantras] consisting of fifteen syllables each, and one consisting of seventeen syllables.
Because they are extremely secret, the vidyās are not written down explicitly. || 42 ||
With the verse beginning with *mada*, he teaches the *vidyā* for the accomplishment of the form of desire (*kāmarūpasiddhi*).

In that context, the phrase "the application of the mantra is stated" is the understood remainder (*itiśeṣaḥ*). In this section, where it is said "is stated" and so forth, the phrase "is stated" is the understood remainder even when not explicitly mentioned.
Likewise, the meaning is "by means of the two *kūṭas*. The rest is easy to understand. || 43 ||

With the verse beginning with "nitya," he teaches the *vidyā* for the accomplishment of the sandals (*pādukāsiddhi*). In that context, "nitya" [is used] because of its application to the mantra; "vidyā" connects with both the preceding and the following [words]; and "pāduke" is in the dual number. || 44 ||

With the verse beginning with "tathā," he teaches the science (*vidyā*) for the accomplishment of the collyrium (*añjana*). In that context, "tathā" means the application [of the method] as in the case of the sandals (*pādukā*); "nityamada" is the application of the mantra; "by that pair" refers to the pair of *kūṭas*;
and the remainder is that this is the twelve-syllable *vidyā*. (45)

With the verse beginning "dravanityā," he teaches the *vidyā* for the accomplishment of the sword (*khaḍgasiddhi*). In that context, the application of the mantra is "dravanitye. It is likewise as before. The remainder is that the *vidyā* consists of twelve syllables formed by the pair [of mantras]. The remainder is that it is accomplished as before. || 46 ||
With the mantra "O you who are eternally liquid," one should likewise enshroud the Vetālas with the word "Dehi" (give);
then, having perfected the thirteen-syllable Vidyā, one should cause them to manifest in that manner. || 47 ||
"Grant me the Piśācas," [one should say] at the beginning; this is always in the *adadrava* meter.
One should enclose it as before with two [mantras]; thus the Vidyā consists of seventeen syllables. (48)
Thirty-six yakṣiṇīs have been mentioned; they all bestow whatever is desired.
Listen as I shall declare their names and mantras according to the prescribed rule. (49)
Vicitrā, Vibhramā, Haṃsī, Bhīṣaṇī, Janarañjikā, Viśālā, Madanā, Rūddhā, Kālakaṇṭhī, and Mahābhayā. (50)
Māhendrī, Śaṅkhinī, Cāndrī, Maṅgalā, Vaṭavāsinī, Mekhalā, Sakalā, Lakṣmī, Mālinī, and Viśvanāyikā. || 51 ||
Sulocanā, Saśobhā, Kāmadā, Savilāsinī, Kāmeśvarī, Nandinī, Svarṇarekhā, and Manoramā. || 52 ||
Pramodā, Rāgiṇī, Siddhā, Padminī, Saratipriyā, Kalyāṇadā, Kalādakṣā, and thereafter Surasundarī. (53)

With the verse beginning with *nitya*, he teaches the vidyā for the accomplishment of the vetāla. In that context, the application of the mantra is *nityadrava*. Likewise, as before, by means of the pair; the ellipsis is "those vetālas. || 47 ||

With the verse beginning "piśācān" (the piśācas), he teaches the vidyā for the accomplishment of the piśācas. In that regard, first, from the word "piśāca," the mantra-formation is "nityam adadrava"; the remainder is "by means of two seed-syllables. || 48 ||

With these five verses beginning with "thirty-six" and ending with "Sundarī," he teaches the names of the Yakṣiṇīs, preceded by an introduction to the *nāmavidyā* (the science of names). Among them, [he speaks] of those Yakṣiṇīs. 49.
With the verse beginning with "vicitrā," he teaches twelve names; therein, "Mahābhayā" is the tenth.
With the verse beginning with "māhendrī," he teaches ten names. || 51 ||

With the verse beginning "sulocanā," he teaches eight names. Among them, "sulocanā" is a name of four syllables. In the word "saśobhā," the letter *sa* has the sense of "together with. In "savilāsinī," the *sa* functions in the same way. || 52 ||
Thus, thirty-six yakṣiṇīs who grant desired boons have been declared.
Their vidyās [mantras] follow in due order, enclosed by their respective pairs of seed-syllables (bījas). (54)

By means of the thirty-six Vidyās declared by me through the six syllables beginning with *nitya*, *drava*, and *mada*, which are their own stated names, these perfected ones shall grant whatever is desired.
Listen as I shall describe the number of syllables in those vidyās in their proper order:
the fifth, the fifteenth, the twentieth, and likewise the last. (56)
The third [pāda] consists of four fifteen-syllable units;
likewise, the eighth, thirteenth, eighteenth, twenty-second, and twelfth [syllables] consist of twelve syllables each. || 57 ||
Likewise, there should be thirty-one [deities] endowed with fourteen;
and similarly, the ninth, the tenth, and the twenty-first immediately thereafter.
With the verse beginning with *pramoda*, he teaches eight names.
In that regard, in the term *saratipriya*, the letter *sa* is also as before. *Kalādakṣa* is one name; the other names are easy to understand. (53)

With these two verses beginning with *iti* and ending with *īpsitam*, he provides the conclusion of what has been stated and teaches the *yakṣiṇī-siddhi-vidyā*. In that context, "of those *yakṣiṇīs*" refers to them; "in sequence" means by the order to be described; "enclosed within the pair of their seed-syllables" means encapsulated by the pair of seed-syllables at the beginning and end of the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
