The phrase "with the six syllables of one's own names" is to be connected with the following verse. The application of the mantra is "nityadravamada. By the statement that "these [syllables] are at the beginning and end of the root-vidyā," these six syllables—consisting of the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) flanking the instruction of one's own essential nature—are common to all *yakṣiṇī* vidyās.
The differentiation of the mantra occurs through the very names mentioned— beginning with Vicitra and ending with the six-syllabled Vidyā— conjoined with those thirty-six names themselves.

With these four verses beginning with "tāsām" and ending with "parā," he teaches the number of syllables for each of the vidyās. Therein, "tāsām" means of those yakṣiṇīs. "The last one" refers to the thirty-sixth. "Four vidyās"—this is the ellipsis. "Pañcadaśakāḥ" [means consisting of fifteen].

The meaning is that they consist of fifteen syllables. [In the phrase] "saikatriṃśacca" (and thirty-one), the connection is with "dvādaśa" (twelve), meaning twelve syllables. Thus, there are six vidyās consisting of twelve syllables in total. Likewise, they should be endowed with fourteen, just as [previously].
The meaning is that they likewise consist of twelve syllables and fourteen syllables. || 58 ||
The twenty-fourth, the twenty-fifth, the twenty-seventh, and those following it;
the thirty-third and so forth—these three are followed by another group increased by thirteen. (59)
I shall tell you of the sixty-four servants and their respective measures;
listen with purity, for they will always accomplish your desired aim.
Vibhrama, Vāhaka, Vīra, Vikarṣa, Kroka, Kavi, Siṃhanāda, Mahānāda, Sugrīva, Markaṭa, and Śaṭa. || 61 ||
Cat-eyed and cat-faced, the youth born of the sky-traveler,
he is the peacock, auspicious, formidable, leopard-mouthed, and six-faced.
Mātaṅga, Niśācārī, Viṣagrāhī, Vṛkodara, Sauribhāsya, Gajamukha, Paśuvaktra, and Gajānana. || 63 ||
Kṣobhaka, Maṇibhadra, Krīḍaka, Siṃhavaktraka, Śyenāsya, Kaṅkavadana, Kākāsya, and Hayavaktraka. || 64 ||
"Those moving upwards" means twenty-eight.

"The three beginning with the thirty-three" means the three starting from the thirty-three and ending with the thirty-five. Together, there are ten vidyās consisting of fourteen syllables; the others are joined with thirteen.
The sixteen vidyās consist of thirteen syllables each; and these [syllables] are the first, second, fourth, sixth, seventh, eleventh, twelfth, fourteenth,
sixteenth, seventeenth, nineteenth, twenty-third, twenty-sixth, and twenty-ninth.

(Thirty-second): Regarding that, the names of those [goddesses] are to be joined with the forms of the *sambuddhi* (vocative singular) at the end of the six syllables of the Vidyā; then, at the end of those, the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) are to be joined as before—this is the meaning of the oral tradition. || 59 ||
With these eight verses beginning with "ceṭakānām" and ending with "kīrtitā," he teaches the names of the *ceṭakas*, preceded by an introduction to their mantras.
In this context, "te" means "to you"; those are the *ceṭakas*. (60)
With the verse beginning with "vibhrama," he teaches eleven names. || 61 ||
With the verse beginning "Viḍālākṣa," he teaches ten names.
With the verse beginning with "Mātaṅga," he teaches eight names. || 63 ||
Mahodara, Sthūlaśiras, Vikṛtāsya, Varānana, Capala, Kukkuṭāsya, Māyāvī, and Madanālasa. (65)
Charming, long-shanked, thick-toothed, ten-faced, fair-faced, afflicted, enraged, boar-faced, and maned-faced. (66)
Kapaṭa, Kautukī, Kāla, Kiṅkara, Kitava, Khala, Bhakṣaka, Ubhayada, Siddha, and Sarvaga are thus proclaimed. (67)

With those names ending in the accusative case and joined with the word "dehi," placed within the enclosure of two seed-syllables and conjoined with the liquid [vowels] *ma*, *na*, *ti*, and *a*. || 68 ||
Thus, O Maheśvarī, the sixty-four mantras have been declared in sequence;
likewise, listen as I shall explain their enumeration according to the prescribed rule.
Among those, nine mantras are declared to have fourteen syllables;
likewise, there are twenty-six [mantras] that consist of fifteen syllables. (70)
With the verse beginning with "Kṣobhaka," he teaches eight names; therein, "Siṃhavaktraka" is a five-syllable name, and "Hayavaktraka" is a five-syllable name.
With the verse beginning with "Mahodara," he teaches eight names. || 65 ||
With the verse beginning with "manoharā," he teaches nine names. || 66 ||
With the verse beginning with "kapaṭa," he teaches ten names. Therein, the word division is *bhaya-da*. The rest is easy to understand. || 67 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with *bīja* and ending with *maheśvarī*, he teaches the mantras of the *ceṭakas*. In that context, the application of the mantra is *madanityadrave*.
[The names] are the sixty-four, such as *vibhrama* and so forth, ending in the accusative case.

These [syllables], ending in the second case (accusative) and encapsulated [by the seed-syllables], constitute the introductory forms of the root-vidyā. These six syllables are common to all mantras; thus, the distinction between mantras lies solely in their names.
The sequence for joining the mantras is as follows: the two seed-syllables followed by the six syllables of the root-vidyā.
The respective names are in the accusative case; at the end of each is the word *dehi*, and at the end of that are the two seed-syllables in reverse order.
68. Thus, in the manner described.

With the passage beginning with "of them" (*teṣām*) and ending with "in sequence" (*kramāt*), the first half [of the verse] teaches the number of syllables in the name-mantras of the servants (*ceṭaka*). (p.
309) "The mantras are said to consist of sixteen syllables; twenty-five [servants] are proclaimed."
Likewise, there are seventeen syllables and four [syllables] in a disordered sequence. (71)
The fourteen syllables not covered by the Vidyā-syllables,
together with their vowels, constitute a total count of two hundred and twenty-four.
There are seven yantras; one should worship the deities within them with devotion, in sequence, for the seven days starting from Sunday (Bhāskara).
Regarding those mantras therein [verse 69]: "Among them, nine mantras are declared to have fourteen syllables.
The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is that among those mantras, nine mantras consist of fourteen syllables.
And these are the third, sixth, eleventh, sixteenth, nineteenth, fifty-second, and fifty-seventh [mantras].
The fifty-first, fifty-seventh, sixtieth, and sixty-third [verses] consist of fifteen syllables;
these are the twenty-six [syllables] belonging to the first, second, fourth, fifth, ninth, tenth, fourteenth, fifteenth, and seventeenth [pādas].

The [kalpas] numbering eighteen, twenty-two, thirty, thirty-two, thirty-four, forty-two, forty, fifty, fifty-one, fifty-five, fifty-six, fifty-eight, fifty-nine, sixty-two, sixty-two, and sixty-four. 70.
There are twenty-five mantras consisting of sixteen syllables each;
these are located at the seventh, eighth, twelfth, thirteenth, twentieth, twenty-first, twenty-third, and so on, up to the twenty-ninth,
then at the thirty-first, thirty-eighth, thirty-ninth, fortieth, forty-first, and [forty-second].
The forty-fourth, the forty-third, the forty-sixth, the forty-seventh, the forty-eighth, the forty-ninth, the fifty-third, and the fifty-fourth;
these are the seventeen syllables, and they are four.

The thirty-third, thirty-fifth, thirty-seventh, and fortieth [chapters] follow a disordered sequence rather than the stated order. The rest is easy to understand. Here, the primary tradition holds that the mantra for the accomplishment of illusion (*māyāsiddhi*) is not mentioned because it is included within the *ceṭaka* section. Therefore...
By substituting the word "māyā" in place of the word "sarvaga," that mantra consists of fourteen syllables. Thus,
there are one hundred and eleven root mantras in number.
These have been correctly shown as being distinct from their own essential natures. || 71 ||

With twenty-four verses beginning with "vidyākṣaraiḥ" and ending with "naram," [the author] explains the seven [mantras] for the purpose of accomplishing the previously mentioned one hundred and eleven *siddhimantras*,
by means of the root-vidyā syllables modified by the vowels of the seven days.

It teaches the mechanical devices (*yantras*), their respective locations for practice, the various modes of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) associated with them, and their fruits. In that regard, there are two hundred and twenty-four [mantras] each, purified by the sixteen vowels as before, together with the vowels.
The meaning is "two hundred and twenty-four. By those [mantras], in those yantras;

"proclaimed" means proclaimed as the ten kinds of accomplishments previously mentioned; on the seven days of the week, beginning with the Sun—that is, on the seven days starting from Sunday—all the deities of accomplishment have been proclaimed for each respective day.

In each of the seven yantras, one should write the name of the day of the week (vāra), joined with its ordinal number (saptamī), along with the respective means of accomplishment and so forth, saying "grant what is desired. In the center of the yantra, situated within the *māyā* syllable, one should worship the *siddhis*.
Having formed a ninefold womb within two squares and an eight-cornered figure on the outside, one should duly fashion a pair of lotuses— one of sixteen petals and one of eight— on the exterior.
Having drawn those [lines], one should inscribe the thirty-two syllables in sequence upon them—
on the petals, on the corners, and likewise again in the three centers of the circles.
One should indeed write the Mātṛkā, the Makāra, and so forth, according to the internal sequence;
then, within the intermediate corners of that [diagram], one should write the letters of the *ha-la-kṣa* group in order.
Thus, by performing seven circumambulations starting from the front with those [yantras],
one shall attain success with the yakṣiṇīs and likewise with the ceṭakas, each individually.
This is the specific characteristic of the servants: in their midst is an eight-petalled lotus.
Their means of accomplishment (sādhana) and their fruits are indeed according to the sequence already stated. (79)

The meaning is "one should sacrifice" (yajet). [The word] "joined with the seventh" means ending in the seventh (genitive) case. "Residing in Māyā" means situated within the *hṛllekhā* [syllable]. "And one should write the desired [word] 'dehi' (give)" is to be connected with the preceding [verse]. Therein, within the belly of Māyā, are the *siddhis*, the deities who grant all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhidevatās*). [This is] outside of the two circles (*vṛtta*). Outside.

From the eight-cornered [figure], one draws a sixteen-petaled lotus (*kalābja*) according to the prescribed rule and measurement; this connects with what precedes. "In those petals" connects with what follows, namely "in the corners.
Outside the three circles, outside the nine-yoni figure, and outside the sixteen-petaled lotus located outside the eight corners...

The meaning is: "in the three paths situated between the two previously mentioned [rows]. (76) The meaning is: the sixteen letters beginning with 'a' and ending with the visarga; the sixteen letters beginning with 'ka' and ending with 'ta';
and the sixteen letters beginning with 'tha' and ending with 'sa'. Of that [which has been written] outside of it...

Regarding the pair of squares: the meaning is that one should write the three aforementioned syllables in the four intermediate corners of the pair of earth-squares (bhūpadas), placing the syllables *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* in sequence within those intermediate corners. || 77 ||
"From the front, clockwise"—the remainder is "all the syllables. "There shall be seven yantras"—this is the remainder.

"By those yantras"—the remainder is "the practice and so forth for each one individually. The word "should be" (bhavet) is to be construed with this remaining portion. || 78 || "In the center, an eight-petaled lotus."

The meaning is that in the place of the nine sources (navayoni), there is an eight-petaled lotus. (79) By means of that as well, O Goddess of Gods, hear the ritual applications (prayoga) together with their pericarp (karṇikā), by which, once perfected, one is honored on earth as my equal by all people everywhere and at all times. (80)
At the foot of a banyan tree in the forest, on mountain peaks, in caves, in the midst of gardens, in the wilderness, and at the root of a mother-tree (mātṛpādapa). || 81 ||
One should accomplish these yakṣiṇīs three times in a forest on the banks of the Indus;
for each one, one should recite a hundred thousand syllables according to the prescribed method.
There are nine positions for those [deities] beginning with Vijaya and ending with Ceṭaka, by means of which [ritual] applications.
"Equal to me" means "the Supreme Lord. By these nine verses, this is what is stated:
through the delusion of the desired measurement, one should [construct] a path with an interval of one finger-breadth between the internal and external divisions.
Having drawn two circles, one should fashion a ninefold source (*navayoni*) between them according to the previously stated measurements;
then, outside that, having fashioned an eight-cornered figure by means of two squares with corners aligned to the cardinal and intermediate directions,
and having drawn two more circles outside that with a one-finger wide intervening path between them, [one proceeds] beyond that.
Having fashioned sixteen petals along with two outer circles, and having made two squares outside of those, divided into inner and outer sections,
one should [pray] in the *yonis* situated in the very center: "O Hṛllekhā, grant this accomplishment on this lunar day."

Having written "svasaṃjñāyām" in the portion for *māyā*, "vārākhyām" in the portion for the letter *ra*, and "tadantarāle siddhiṃ dehi" in the space between them, one should then write, outside of that, in the eight corners starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise,
the letters of the root-vidyā modified by the vowels, numbering one hundred and twenty-four.

First, having written the group of eight [syllables] within that [central area], then the group of eight on the eight petals outside of it, and the group of sixteen on the sixteen petals— thus having inscribed thirty-two syllables— one should place them in the three paths between the circles: specifically, in the path between the two circles located outside the inner nine-yoni diagram.
Having written the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarjanīya*,
one should write the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and ending with the *visarjanīya* in the path between the two circles located outside the eight-cornered [figure], situated in the center.
In the middle [section], having written the sixteen syllables from *ka* to *ta* in the path between the two outer circles of the eight-cornered [figure],
one writes the [syllables] from *tha* to *sa* in the path between the two outer circles of the sixteen-petaled [figure].

One should write the sixteen syllables outside that [square], and the three syllables *ha*, *la*, and *kṣa* within the four corners of the square; one should also write them within the interior of each triangle. This is the first yantra.
Regarding the other six yantras:

One should write the thirty-two syllables above each of the previously written sets of thirty-two syllables. Having thus prepared seven yantras, one should employ them according to the stated sequence for all seven days, beginning with Sunday. [This is done] from the root of the mother-tree.
The eight [deities] beginning with Mātṛpāda were previously mentioned in the discussion on the primary, eternal, and optional [forms];
therefore, there are eight locations or abodes (āyatanas). "In the forest on the bank of the Sindhu" means in the forest situated on the riverbank. Thus, in total, twelve locations arise. Threefold.

In each of the twelve locations, one should perform the propitiation and the fire-oblation (homa) with flowers for three yakṣiṇīs in each individual spot; the oblation should consist of one-tenth of that [number] using red *kadamba*, *bandhūka*, *jayā*, and *hayamāra* flowers. (83)
Then, having assembled, those pleased [deities] who grant desired objects appeared before his eyes,
[bestowing] gold, garments, ornaments, and fruits.
They should provide various kinds of foods to be relished and drunk, as well as ointments and garlands, until the end of life. 85.
"Whenever they arrive, one should always accept what is desired from perception and the other means of knowledge";
having said this, one should constantly worship them and likewise perform recitation.
With single-minded concentration, one should recite each of those vidyās one thousand and eight times;
in this way, all those yakṣiṇīs shall grant the desired fruit.
When all those servants had been mentioned in due order,
there were indeed five perfected ones (siddhas) for each one, and nine on the shore of the Sindhu.
And for them, the number of recitations according to their respective colors should be performed according to the prescribed rule;
one should maintain constant silence during the days for the sake of success and must not break it. 89.
It is taught that at midnight, one should always perform the fire-oblation (homa) and the libation (tarpaṇa);
it is prescribed that one should recite [the mantra] day and night in the practice of all [deities]. 90.

The meaning is that one should accomplish [the goal]. "A hundred thousand repetitions of the syllables" refers to the specific vidyā. By the phrase "by that and that," the number of recitations (japa) is indicated. "With hayamāra flowers" means with red karavīra flowers.

The meaning of the text beginning with "tat" and ending with "itīpsitam"— which describes the direct perception of the Yakṣiṇī, the objects to be given by her, and the constant worship of her— is easy to understand. (84, 85, 86, 87)

In those places: in one place there are five, and in each of the others five servants (*ceṭaka*). Along the bank of the Indus, in the twelfth place, there are nine servants. In the eleven places previously mentioned by the Yakṣiṇī, there are five in each place.

The meaning is that one should accomplish each of the nine *ceṭakas* in the five locations on the banks of the Sindhu and the twelve forest sites, according to the stated sequence; thus, there are sixty-four in total. According to the tradition, these places are common for the accomplishment of all other groups of eight siddhis as well. || 88 ||
The mantra consists of one hundred thousand syllables.
On the [prescribed] days, those servants, having arrived at midnight, extremely terrifying, will agitate this practitioner;
if he does not tremble, then they shall come before him. (91)
Appearing before them at night, he would say, "What do you desire? I shall do that for you.
Each of them replied, "So be it," and added, "Do not abandon me."
One should constantly worship them with recitations and offerings, and furthermore, one should perform [the rites].
When they have been summoned, they will remember what was commanded and accomplish the desired goal.
They cause the defeat of enemies in battle and inflict blows upon their foes, while bestowing desired objects day and night. 94.
They would certainly bring back desired women in that very instant;
they can even make a rutting elephant, a horse, or a man stand still. 95.
When the eternal Ṣoḍaśaka was accomplished, it was mastered by gods, sages, ancestors, and rākṣasas;
by piśācas, uragas, siddhas, kinnaras, and hosts of apsarases. || 96 ||
By the Maruts, the Vasus, the seven Ṛṣis, the Yakṣas and Dānavas, the eleven kinds of Rudras, the nine Sādhyas, and the planets. || 97 ||
On the days of practice, this is common to all; that is to say, day and night at all times.
It applies to all those previously mentioned, as well as to the other eight beginning with Vijayā and ending with Māyā, and to others as well. [This refers to] this practitioner.
"Before that" means before the practitioner (*sādhaka*). (91) "Each one" means one *ceṭaka* each;

this connects with the phrase "he should speak to him. Those *ceṭakas*. The remainder of the verse beginning with "in that manner" (*tathā*) is the speech of the practitioner's request. (92) "Constantly" (*nityaśaḥ*).

Immediately after the accomplishment of each respective *ceṭaka*, when [the deity] is remembered according to the stated sequence, the *ceṭakas* [appear]; "the desired object of the practitioner" is the ellipsis. (93) The passage beginning with "of enemies" describes the method for accomplishing the desired goal.
This is what is meant: among the *ceṭakas*, one should choose whichever one is most desired, and that single *ceṭaka*...

"One should accomplish [the goal] according to the stated sequence. Regarding this, the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) holds that the plural forms [used for the mantras] apply to all *ceṭaka* spirits alike because they share the same method of accomplishment and so forth. In this same way, the procedure for the accomplishment of *māyā*, as well as the procedures for the seven [deities] beginning with Vijayā, are likewise [to be understood]. || 94 || 95 ||
With these five verses beginning with "nityā" and ending with "bhavet," he teaches the characteristics of the accomplishment of the sixteen Nityās. (p.
314) [She is] by the twelve suns, the world-protectors, and likewise by other deities.
By kings, by women, by other men, and likewise by animals. (98)
He is always honored as the abode of happiness desired by the perfected ones;
he is joyful in disposition, generous, compassionate, pleasant-faced, and patient. (99)

One whose heart is full, who is ever-blissful, who is endowed with detachment from fruits [of action], who is wealthy, an enjoyer, free from hatred for others, and born of love—such a person shall become one of us two. (100)
The pervasion consisting of the reality of the tongue has been correctly described;
by the churning of this within the mind, that very reality is assimilated into one's own self. (101)
Thus, in the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*, within the *Śrīkādimata*, the seventeenth chapter has been fully expounded and concluded. 17.
In that regard, [it is] with others, such as the ten Prājāpatya offerings and so forth. 96 || 97 || 98 ||
The meaning is: "the abode of happiness desired by the Siddhas" and "the one who is both the Siddha and the desired abode of happiness. || 99 ||
"His intention is fulfilled" because of his indifference toward that which is to be known. "Indifferent" refers to objects such as wealth and the like.
The word division is *apara-dveṣaḥ*. The meaning is: one who is averse to causing hatred in others. "Of us two" refers to Śiva and Śakti. || 100 ||

Thus, in the *Manoramā*, the commentary composed by the venerable Subhagānandanātha— entitled *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*— upon the complete *Tantra* known as the venerable *Kādimata*, among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
In this commentary, the seventeenth chapter, which is devoted to illuminating the ritual procedure for the Śivadūtī Nityā-vidyā, has been fully examined and concluded. 17.
The number of verses in the treatise is said to be seven; the commentary, according to the count of verses,
consists of two hundred and sixteen in this seventeenth chapter.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Now, O wise one, listen to the procedure for that which is proclaimed as the thirteenth among the sixteen Nityās; the Vidyā has already been declared to you previously.

I shall now describe the placement of syllables upon its limbs for the purpose of meditation and worship, along with the powers [of the mantra], and the application of its yantras, which bestow victory. (2)
One should form the four [syllables] of the Vidyā with the consonants joined with long vowels;
with the remaining two, one should form two more, thus making the six limbs for the hands and the body.
Then, one should place the syllables, joined with the nasal bindu, in sequence upon the organs of perception beginning with the ears, and also upon the mind; the rest is as before.
Now begins the eighteenth chapter.
Having taught in the preceding seventeenth chapter the ritual procedure for the twelfth Nityā-vidyā, Nīlapatākā, [the author] next [teaches] that of the thirteenth, the Vijayā-nityā-vidyā.

He teaches the ritual procedure with the eighteenth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "are proclaimed. Therein, with two verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "the offering," he indicates the topics of the chapter. Among those, the thirteenth [verse]...

The meaning is "Vijayā is impermanent. [This was explained] previously in the third chapter. Regarding the phrase "dhyānārce," it is a dual form in the accusative case; the meaning is "meditation and worship. Regarding "tadyantraviniyogān," the meaning is "those yantras and their applications."
With the two verses beginning with *vidyāyāḥ* and ending with *pūrvavat*,

he teaches the procedure for the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) of the syllables of the root-vidyā upon the hands, the limbs, and the six cognitive faculties, and so forth. Therein, regarding the *vidyā*:

With the consonants joined with the long vowels, one should form four [limbs]; and with the remaining two, one should form two more—thus, by the verse ending with "the six limbs of the hands and body," this is what is meant: with the four syllables consisting of consonants joined with the long vowels of the internal root-vidyā, namely *bhā*, *mī*, *rū*, and *yai*.

Having performed the placement of the heart, head, crest, and armor with the [seed-syllables] of their respective classes accompanied by the bindu, one should likewise perform the six limbs— beginning with the ritual placement on the hands— using the two remaining vowel-syllables of the Vidyā (the letter *au* in the form of *ū* with the bindu) for the eyes and the weapon, each joined with its respective class.

"One should perform [the placement]" (vidadhyāt) || 3 || "In the organs of knowledge," etc., refers to the ears and so forth—namely, the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose. Among these, the placement on the skin is like that of the pervasive [deity]; the others are pervasive. As before, this is done with the entire Vidyā-mantra.
She has five faces and ten arms, with three eyes in each face, and she is resplendent with a crescent moon placed upon her shining crown. (5)
Adorned with all ornaments, radiant in her yellow garments,
with the splendor of her body resembling the rising, shining orb [of the sun], and possessing a pure smile.
With his left arms he holds a conch, a noose, a shield, a bow, and a white lotus;
likewise, with his right arms he holds a discus, a goad, a sword, an arrow, and a citron.
Holding [attributes] with her right hands that appear fearsome during her ritual application,
yet exceedingly gentle during worship, she is seated upon a lion.
She is surrounded on all sides by Śaktis mounted upon tigers;
she sits upon a comfortable throne during battle, worship, and other ritual applications.
The Śaktis also, in the worship, are seated upon comfortable seats;
they all possess forms, faces, hands, and weapons identical to those of the Goddess. 10.

The meaning is: "by the method previously described. This is what is being said: in the six locations—namely, the five organs of cognition beginning with the ear, together with the mind—at the three pairs of locations among the ears and so forth, one [syllable] is placed in each pair, and one [syllable] is placed in each of the other two. Thus...

Having sequentially placed these six syllables of the root-vidyā—namely *bha*, *ma*, *ra*, *ya*, *au*, and *ū*—along with their nasal bindus, one should perform the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*) using the vidyā in its entirety. || 4 ||

With these six verses beginning with "pañcavaktrām" and ending with "apīti," he teaches the visualization for the daily worship and the visualization for ritual application (prayoga-dhyāna) of the Goddess together with her retinue.
Among these, the five-faced state of Nīlapatākā is according to the manner previously described; [and she is] "ten-armed."

And likewise [in the other hands]. The weapons in the left arms should be understood as starting from the upper-left and proceeding clockwise, and those in the right arms starting from the upper-right and proceeding clockwise. (5, 6, 7) "In practice" (*prayoge*) means in the practice for victory in battle and so forth;
"in worship" (*upāsane*) means in constant devotion. "Seated upon a lion" means mounted on a lion. (8) [This applies] during worship in battle.

The meaning is that worship is for the sake of victory in battle. Having meditated upon her as mounted on a lion, terrifying, and surrounded by Śaktis of equal form mounted on tigers—for the purpose of victory in combat—one should worship her; this is the meaning. In other cases, such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth, [the procedure is different]. || 9 ||

Regarding the daily worship (*nityāpūjā*): the word *api* (even/also) is used here with a shifted position [in the verse]. The meaning is "all," and the word "powers" (*śaktayaḥ*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence.

What is intended is this: in ritual applications such as subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth, as well as in the daily worship of regular practice, one should meditate upon the Goddess seated comfortably together with her retinue. || 10 ||
Having constructed two squares adorned with four gates and provided with eight petals, one should perform worship there as previously described. (11)
Then, having fashioned an eight-cornered [figure] within that pair of inner lines,
one should likewise fashion a sixteen-petalled lotus within that.
In the same manner, having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus and invoked her there, one should duly worship her, surrounded by her respective Śaktis, with the various ritual offerings.
One should perform the daily fire-oblation (nityahoma) with rice and clarified butter, or with sesame seeds and rice;
one should also offer two bali-offerings and likewise complete the worship.
The fifteen Nityās, excluding Lalitā, are the Lords of the lunar days (tithis);
she is considered to be identical with them, her head adorned by the beautiful crescent moon. 15.
One should worship with names situated within the seven-syllabled *māyā* mantra;
these are the powers (*śakti*) belonging to that enclosure, possessing powers of identical form. (16)
With fifteen verses beginning with "two squares" (caturasradvayam) and ending with "happy one" (sukhī),

[the text describes] the sequence for constructing the maṇḍala for the daily worship of the Goddess, the procedure for the four-fold enclosure therein for the daily worship, and [the rites] of the other fifteen Nityās.

He teaches the *vāsana* for the retention of the digit of the moon (*candrakalā*), the *vāsana* for the retention of that [digit] belonging to Lalitā, and the names of the powers of obscuration (*āvaraṇa-śakti*). In that regard, "as before" means as in the worship of the Nityās within the square (*caturasra*). "Within that" means within the square. There, in the wheel (*cakra*).
"In that manner" means by the method that will be described. As for the sequence for constructing the mandala for daily worship (*nityasaparyā*):
having fashioned two squares, each with two projections and four gates, according to their respective measurements and distinguishing between the interior and exterior;

Having fashioned two internal curved lines within that [square], touching and not touching the lines of the inner square, and having formed an eight-cornered figure within that as before, one should fashion a sixteen-petalled lotus within that,
and having constructed an eight-petalled lotus within that, [one should worship] the [Goddess] with her retinue in its pericarp.

"Having invoked the Goddess, one should worship her"—the word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. "Two offerings (*bali*) as before"—this refers to the two offerings previously mentioned. || 13-14 ||

By means of the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of the threefold radiance (*tejas*), she is composed of that; the meaning is that she is Lalitā, whose form consists of the imperishable digit of the moon (*akṣayacandrakalā*). By this verse, the following is stated:
elsewhere, the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) consist of the fifteen digits of the moon which are subject to waning and waxing.

All [the deities], though individually distinct, should be worshipped within them by means of the sixteenth *kalā*, which is imperishable and whose form is woven through all [other] *kalās* as their cause; one should worship all of them starting from the front and proceeding clockwise.
Listen as I shall duly declare their names in sequence. (17)
In the square [mandala], worship is declared to be both permanent and impermanent;
one should worship the deities in their prescribed forms within the eight inner angles.
And [he should worship] Jayā, Vijayā, Durgā, Bhadrā, Bhadrakarī, Kṣemā,
Kṣemaṅkarī, and Nityā with devotion in the eight corners.
Within that, one should worship those sixteen Śaktis on the sixteen petals surrounding [the center], endowed with devotion and provided with perfumes, flowers, and so forth. || 20 ||
Vidārikā, who consists of the universe, who is the universe itself, who shatters the universe, the Heroine, the agitator, the Vidyā whose form is graced by playful diversion. || 21 ||
Free from sorrow, with a neck like poison, vast, bestowing victory, prosperous, manifold, and excellent—these [names] are endowed with the forms as they have been declared. || 22 ||

Within the intervals between the petals of the eight-petaled lotus, the self-controlled practitioner, whose intent is fixed in devotion, should worship the eight Śaktis on all sides with perfumes and other offerings according to the prescribed order.

They are indeed joined together. Therefore, for the fifteen Nityās who are devoid of Lalitā, because they consist of the fifteen lunar days (tithis), there occurs the maintenance of the inexhaustible sixteenth digit of the moon;
but Lalitā, being composed of all lunar days, is uninterrupted.

The sixteenth digit (kalā) is imperishable and consists of the form of the cause of all digits; therefore, it is devoid of the lunar digits. (15) [This refers to] by means of names—that is, mantras—beginning with Hṛllekhā and ending with the seven-syllabled Māyā, situated within the seven-syllabled Māyā. (16)
Those powers [are located] in those places, such as the square and so forth; [this refers to] those encircling powers (āvaraṇa-śakti). || 17 ||
"In the eight inner triangles"—the remainder [of the phrase] being "of the square and so forth.

Their "described forms" are those to be mentioned in the subsequent verse beginning with "Jayā" and so on. The double mention of "in the eight triangles" is not a fault, as it serves both a concise and an expanded purpose. [This is done] out of devotion.

The word "should worship" (pūjayet) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 19 || "Within that" means within the eight-cornered [figure]. "Those various ones" refers to those who will be described in the two subsequent verses beginning with "Vidārikā" and so forth. || 20 || "Vidārikā" means the one who rends asunder; "Viśvavibhañjikā" means the one who shatters the universe. || 21 ||

"Vividhām" means that they possess the forms described in the fifteenth [chapter] and are equal to the root deity; this is the meaning. The syntactical connection is "one should worship. (22) Within that [mandala], [he should worship] Manoharā, Maṅgalā, Madotsiktā, and Manasvinī.
She is the proud one, the sweet one, the illusory power, the enchantress, who has cast off all conflict.
Thus, he who, having gained self-mastery through worship, recitation, meditation, fire-offerings, and service, constantly honors the Goddess, shall be happy in every respect. (25)
Following the previously mentioned sequence, the self-controlled practitioner should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times according to the number of syllables;
having performed the fire-oblation with red lotuses, he becomes endowed with the arising of the perfected mantra.
The practitioner of mantras should perform the ritual applications according to the rules for the fire-sacrifice and the construction of the yantra,
as well as through recitation, libation, and worship in accordance with the prescribed rites.
With lotuses, white water-lilies, red and white fragrant utpalas,
and sweet-smelling śephālikā flowers, all anointed with the three sweets according to the prescribed rite.
One should perform the oblation for seven days using the seven [mantras] that have been taught;
and indeed, the two aforementioned lords of the days [should be worshipped] from their respective mandalas alone.
"Within the sixteen petals" refers to the powers (śaktis) that will be described in the subsequent verse beginning with "the captivating one" (manoharām).
23. The etymologies have been stated as before. The sequence for the worship of her enclosures proceeds from the outside toward the inside. 24. Thus, according to the form described. 25.

With the two verses beginning with *pūrva* and ending with *yathāvidhi*, he teaches the procedure for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) and the fitness for the ritual application (*prayoga*) only for one who has completed that preliminary practice. In this context, "by the previously mentioned sequence" means by the sequence declared in the *Nīlapatākā*. By that...

It is stated that one should recite the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) a number of times equal to the total count of its syllables after having separated and counted the vowels, consonants, and bindus. The number of those syllables is seven.
The rest is easy to understand. || 26 || 27 ||

With three and a half verses beginning with "kamalaiḥ" and ending with "niścitam," [the author] teaches the attainment of victory as previously described, according to the sequence of the ritual for worship and fire-offering (*homa*) with the seven flowers mentioned for the seven days of the week.
In that context, the phrase "raktaiḥ sitaiḥ" (with red and white) connects with both "kamalaiḥ" (lotuses) and "kairavaiḥ" (lilies); therefore, [it means] with red...

It is stated that [the offerings consist] of white lotuses, red lotuses, and white night-lotuses (*kairava*). Their being smeared with the "three sweets" (*trimadhu*) occurs specifically in the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*). The ablative case in *homāt* (from the oblation) is used in the sense of the elision of a verbal root, meaning "having performed the oblation. [The offering is made] on the seven days of the week, beginning with Sunday, using the aforementioned seven [mantras].
"By flowers" is the ellipsis. "Of the two lords of the aforementioned days" refers to the *Kulasundarī* chapter;
"from their mandalas" means those [mandalas] are also stated in that very place, and should be consulted in the twenty-eighth chapter.
This is what has been said.
One attains victory in a battle, in a duel, in wrestling, in debate, in both types of gambling, and in both types of dice-play. (30)
In all legal disputes, he will certainly obtain victory;
by performing a fire-oblation with flowers produced from four-fingered branches, he shall paralyze his enemies.
Likewise, with flowers produced from the Karṇikāra, the Punnāga, and the Nameru, as well as from the Campaka, the Ketaka, the Ājavṛkṣa, and those originating from the Māgandha; || 32 ||
As before, one should offer oblations at the gates in sequence with seven flowers;
by this, the certain paralyzing or breaking of the enemy occurs as previously described.
By performing oblations in the fire of the Śatānaka tree using its fuel-sticks soaked in ghee and clarified butter, they indeed bow down at his feet.

One should properly offer oblations into the fire of the wood of death with the leaves, flowers, and fruits of the tree of death, using sacrificial fuel-sticks, preceded by the worship of the lord of the day.
It occurs through the seven flowers named the red lotus, white lotus, red *kairava*, white *kairava*, *saugandhika*, blue lotus, and fragrant *śephālikā*— beginning with *karṇikāra* and so forth—
as prescribed in order for the seven days starting from Sunday, corresponding to the two lords of those respective days.

The attainment of the stated results occurs through worship in that maṇḍala with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) and through oblations (homa) performed by them. (29) "In battle" refers to the seven topics to be described hereafter. "In duels" refers to what was previously mentioned. "In the two types of gambling" refers to those involving living beings and inanimate objects. (30) "Everywhere" means even in other disputes.

With the first half-verse of the two verses ending with "dhruvam," beginning with "caturaṅgulajaiḥ" and so forth, he teaches the paralyzing of enemies and other rites by prescribing the performance of *homa* at all times with *āragvadha* [flowers] over seven days using seven flowers. In that regard:
[One should worship] with flowers arising from the *caturaṅgula*, the aged *āragvadha*, and the *nameru*; with *suparṇī* flowers;

and with *rājavṛkṣa* flowers—that is, *āragvadha* flowers—as before, preceded by the worship of the lords of the days (vāreśas) during the seven days beginning with Sunday, using the seven [deities] starting with Karṇikā. Here, regarding the *āragvadha*:
The repetition [of the term] is for the purpose of prescribing the *homa* on all days of the week;
and regarding the aforementioned battles between two armies and so forth— it is said that with the seven flowers previously mentioned,
one should always perform the worship preceded by the *āragvadha* tree on each respective day of the week, as before, throughout the seven days.
The attainment of the proclaimed fruit results from the fire-oblation (homa). || 33 ||

With twenty-one verses beginning with "śatroḥ" and ending with "saṃśayaḥ," [it is taught that] on specific lunar days, weekdays, and so forth, by means of particular substances, the fourfold army of the enemy shall become afflicted by disease. (p. 321)
Therefore, may victory be his, whether by life or even by death. || 36 ||
On a Sunday, when the fire has been kindled with fuel-sticks produced from the Arka tree,
one should offer oblations in sequence with the leaves, flowers, fruits, stems, and roots arising from that same source.

Having turned his face toward the direction of the enemy, he should [perform the rite] according to the rules in a triangular pit (kuṇḍa) with oblations of ghee poured from a vessel containing a calf of the same color as the cow's body. || 38 ||
Even an enemy, though fully endowed with strength and possessed of pride in his valor, either flees from the afflicted one or bows down, overcome by fear. (39)

On a Monday, by performing a fire sacrifice in a fire fed with fuel-sticks of *palāśa* wood, using the five limbs of that [plant] soaked in ghee, one will become as before; of this there is no doubt. (40)
By performing a fire sacrifice on a Tuesday with fuel-sticks of khadira wood in a blazing fire, using its five parts soaked in that ghee, one certainly attains that [result]. (41)
Likewise, one should offer oblations with its fuel-sticks into a fire produced from Apāmārga wood on Wednesdays,
using ghee mixed with [milk] from a white cow that has a calf.

By prescribing specific types of oblations, he teaches the methods for attaining victory. In that context, "with those fuel-sticks" means with fuel-sticks from the trees associated with the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). "Those" refers to the enemies. [Verse 34. "With fuel-sticks, of Death"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. [Verse 35.]
"By the destruction of the enemy's force"—this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. (36) "Arising from that" means originating from the sun. "In sequence" means according to the order specified;
the meaning is by the five limbs beginning with the leaves and ending with the root. (37)
"Of one having a calf of the same color" means of a cow that has a red-colored calf and is herself red-colored;

"sprinkled with clarified butter" means with the previously mentioned five limbs; "from the mandala as before" means after forty-nine days; "in a triangle" means in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 38 || 39 ||

Of that *palāśa* tree: with its five limbs—leaves, flowers, fruits, stems, and roots—and furthermore, those drenched in ghee from a red cow whose calf is of the same color, drenched in ghee. "As before" (*prāgvat*) is a displaced construction;
the meaning is that "it should be as before," i.e., victory shall be attained. (40) Of that *khadira* tree: the five limbs.

As before. With those [offerings] soaked in clarified butter, as before. That is the fruit of victory. (41) With its fuel-sticks—that is, with the fuel-sticks of *apāmārga*—(42) the attainment of the previously mentioned fruit indeed occurs within those days. (p. 322) The attainment of the previously mentioned fruit certainly comes to pass in those days.
Indeed, your birth was already [determined] during the days of the carpenters; that was indeed your prior action.

In all rites—whether recitation, fire-offerings, worship, silent chanting, or mantra-repetition—one must perform the specific daily worship and the worship of the two door-keepers for each respective [deity]. (44)
Having first performed these preliminary rites, one should then carry out those [main] actions with a concentrated mind;
for the swift attainment of their fruit occurs in this way, whereas otherwise it happens differently.
On a Wednesday, during the Pippala-lagna, one should offer oblations into the fire with [offerings] soaked in ghee, produced from that [tree];
by doing so, the attainment of those fruits will undoubtedly occur within those very days.
On a Thursday or a Friday, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) in a fire of udumbara wood using materials produced from that tree and sprinkled with its [juice];
by doing so on those days, that [goal] is accomplished.
One should offer oblations into a fire of *śamī* wood using the ghee of a black cow produced from that;
on those days, the fruits of that [rite] will be obtained throughout the seven weekdays.
Victory has been correctly explained through the oblation of the lunar day and the asterism;
now hear of Viyaya, O Goddess of Gods, which I shall describe to you in due order. (49)

"Siddhi" means the accomplishment of victory; "by those days" means by the days of the mandala; "that rite should take place" is the ellipsis to be supplied. (43) "In every tantra" is the meaning. "That specific daily worship" (tattannityārcana) signifies that one should worship the specific Nityā who corresponds to the particular lunar day (tithi) occurring on that specific day. (44) Otherwise—

Regarding the performance of the two daily worship services (*nityārcā*): otherwise, they are fruitless. This is what is meant: in all tantras and in all ritual applications (*prayoga*), one should first worship the *Nityā* appropriate for the specific day of the application as well as the two lords of its respective lunar days (*tithi*), and only thereafter perform the ritual applications. || 45 ||

In the *pippala* fire—that is, in a fire fueled by *aśvattha* wood—with oblations produced from that, meaning with *aśvattha* fuel-sticks; soaked in its clarified butter—that is, saturated with the pure cow’s ghee from a cow whose calf is of the same color—the attainment of that fruit, namely the attainment of victory, occurs in as many days as [previously stated] from the mandala. In the *udumbara* fire... [46]

As before, in a fire with *udumbara* wood; "produced from that" means by means of *udumbara* fuel-sticks; "smeared with that" means smeared with the previously mentioned pure cow's ghee; "for those days" as before; "that" refers to the fruit of victory—this is the ellipsis. (47) In a *śamī* fire, as before, in a fire with *śamī* fuel; "arising from that" [refers to the fuel].

The meaning is "with fuel-sticks of *śamī*"; "on a Saturday" is the ellipsis to be supplied. With the clarified butter of a black cow and its calf of the same color—with the clarified butter of a black cow and its calf of the same color.
Starting from the first lunar day (*pratipad*) and proceeding in order up to the fifth day—thus it is said. (p. 323)
And by means of oblations of śāli rice, chickpeas, mung beans, barley, and black gram; || 50 ||

With those same [offerings] soaked in buffalo ghee, one shall obtain [the results] on the lunar days from the sixth to the tenth; likewise, with the ghee produced from goats, one obtains them on those same days.
Through oblation with the aforementioned dehusked [grains], one shall obtain the previously mentioned fruit;
thereafter, at the end of the fifteenth [day], [one obtains it] with all [the grains] and two sesame seeds.
By offering oblations of white rice, milk-rice (pāyasa), sprinkled offerings, and sheep's ghee,
one obtains that fruit which has been described as resulting from such a sacrifice.
Likewise, by offering oblations soaked in honey into a fire produced from a tree under a lunar mansion (nakṣatra), that attainment certainly occurs; of this there is no doubt. (54)
From that day until the [concluding] maṇḍala; the fruits thereof are the fruits of victory; thus, according to the form described. || 48 ||

"Victory has been declared"—this connects with what precedes. "From the oblation" (havanāt) connects both to what precedes and what follows. The former means that victory has been declared in the seven days in the manner thus described. The latter means: "Listen to the victory to be described hereafter from the oblation performed on the lunar day (tithi) and the asterism (ṛkṣa). || 49 || 50 || By those [days].

By means of the five lunar days beginning with the first (pratipad) and ending with the fifth, one shall attain victory—this is the ellipsis. Likewise, by means of the five lunar days beginning with the sixth and ending with the tenth. || 51 ||

"With the five [grains] previously mentioned, such as śāli rice and so forth," means with those that are "husked," i.e., stripped of their husks and the like. "The previously mentioned fruit" refers to the fruit of victory (*vijayaphala*). "Beyond that, at the end of the fifteenth day" means during the pentad of lunar days (*tithi*) beginning with the eleventh up to the end of the fifteenth. "With all [the grains] beginning with śāli rice."

The meaning is that one should offer oblations with five [sesame seeds] on the eleventh day; with two types of sesame seeds, black and white, on the twelfth day; and with black sesame seeds on the twelfth and with white sesame seeds on the thirteenth day. || 52 ||
With white rice and pure grains on the fourteenth day; with milk-rice (pāyasa) on the fifteenth day;

and with irrigated rice and other such grains, including all five types and so forth—by means of those lunar days, the fruit is declared to be "victory" (vijaya); this is the meaning. [In the fire] produced from the tree of the lunar mansion...

In the fire kindled by the fuel of the respective trees corresponding to those respective asterisms (nakṣatras), such as the poison-tree and others—with "those respective" meaning with the limbs and sacrificial wood (samidh) of those respective nakṣatra-trees—by means of the oblation (havana) of honey (madhu, i.e., *kṣaudra*), there is constant attainment; that is, the attainment of victory (*vijaya*). This is what is meant: in [the rites performed under] Aśvinī and the other asterisms...

In each of the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*s), one should perform oblations (*homa*) with the sacrificial wood (*samidh*) of the specific tree prescribed for that mansion, soaked in honey, into a fire kindled by the fuel of that same tree; through this, the respective fruits are obtained. || 54 ||
(324) One should apply the five syllables of the *vidyā* with the vowels as before; [thus] the *vidyā* consists of eighty syllables. Listen, O beloved, to the yantras formed by them. 55.
By laying down ten threads—east-west, north-south, and south-north—one hundred and one squares are formed; upon these, one should write those [syllables] in sequence.

Having inscribed the name in the central square and joined it according to the previously stated rule, one should form a trident by extending the ends of the lines, and having invoked and worshipped that [deity] therein; || 57 ||
One should worship the Purovidyā, recite it constantly, and perform its regular adoration;
by worshipping that sequence of knowledge within the yantra, one shall obtain its fruit. || 58 ||

With these four verses beginning with *vidyāyām* and ending with *āpnuyāt*, he teaches the attainment of victory (*vijayā*) through the worship of the yantra-grid constructed from eighty syllables, which are produced from the five root-mantras (*mūlavidyā*) modified by vowels. In this context, the meaning is that, as before, they are not redundant.

Those five syllables—*bha*, *ma*, *ra*, *ya*, and *au*—will be explained below. The omission of *ū* and *viṃdu* is because they are already included among the vowels (*svara*) and to avoid redundancy. [The phrase] "with the sixteen vowels" means according to the sequence previously stated. That, moreover, applies to each individual syllable.
It consists of the application of the sixteen vowels; by means of those syllables, the diagrams (yantras) will be described hereafter. || 55 ||
The phrase "from the ten lines" implies that there is an equal interval [between them]. In those squares;
the phrase "those letters of knowledge" implies they number eighty. "In sequence" means by entering and moving clockwise from the front. In the central square, the eighty-first.

The designation of the rites to be accomplished by the practitioner [is as follows]: according to the previously mentioned rule, in the intervals between the upper and lower [lines]—that is the meaning—the tips of the lines number forty.
Herein, in this yantra, one should worship that eternal Vijayā with ritual offerings, recitation of mantras, and so forth, constantly. 57. One should worship her eternally.

The daily ritual sequence (*svanityakrama*) and the sequence of the Vidyā (*vidyākrama*) for the purpose of its application. The meaning is that one should worship both the daily ritual sequence and the sequence of the Vidyā within this Yantra for the sake of its application. One should sacrifice (*yajet*) according to the prescribed method.
Its fruit is the fruit of victory. The procedure for the construction of the Yantra here is as follows:
Having drawn ten lines— east, west, south, and north— at equal intervals, and thus having produced eighty-one squares,
one should begin from the square situated in the middle of the bottom-most row and proceed in a clockwise direction with an inward movement.

Having written the eighty syllables of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) with their vowel-modifications (*svaravikṛta*), one should write the names of the three [persons] beginning with the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in the single remaining central square according to the previously mentioned method of writing; [then, regarding] the twenty lines of the yantra...
Having slightly opened out the forty tips on the outside and made each of them a trident,
one should invoke Vijayānityā into that yantra, discard the previously mentioned maṇḍala of daily worship, and then constantly perform one's own regular ritual sequence.
In that [mandala], one should worship the sequence of vidyās for the sake of practice; by that, there is the attainment of the fruit of victory. || 58 ||
(325) By the laying down of four threads—east-west and north-south—nine squares arise here, O Supreme Goddess. (59)
Upon each of these, one should draw eight-petaled lotuses;
in the center of those, one should draw [the deity] within the pericarp of the central lotus.

One should write that vidyā with the name in its interior, and outside of it on an eight-petaled lotus; having first inscribed the eight [syllables] upon those petals, one should likewise surround them with the bindu.
One should write the name once in the pericarp, and likewise eight times on each of the eight petals;
having thus inscribed it upon the eight [petals], one should encircle it with the letters of the Mātṛkā.
One should draw [the letters] in reverse and in direct order, combined with the *māyā* (ī) and the *bindu* (ṃ),
within three outer squares at the front of the yantra.
Having done this, one should place that jar, measuring two cubits,
and fill it as before with water consisting of the decoction of the mantras, seeds, and medicinal herbs.
With fifteen and a half verses beginning with *prāk* and ending with *puṣkalām*,

[the author] teaches the attainment of results such as victory through the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and worship of the lotus-mantra diagram situated within nine compartments. In that regard, by the laying down of four threads—
The phrase "with equal intervals" (*samāntarālam*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, in the place where the thread is cast;

|| 59 || in those—namely, in the nine squares (*koṣṭha*) and in those nine lotuses (*padma*). || 60 || Containing the name within—the letter *bha* being in the interior (due to the practice, the phrase "with equal intervals" is the remainder)—[one places] the practitioner's [name] in the portion of the letter *ra*, and the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*) in the space between them.
And from the non-writing of the *karma* [mantra]. That *vidyā* is transformed. "Outside of that" means outside of the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

In those eighty syllables of the *vidyā*, which are all modified by the vowels—[one should place] eight letters; the remainder is that they are accompanied by the *bindu*. "Outside of that" means in the lotuses situated outside the central lotus. One.

Above each of the eight [syllables] written previously; outside the pericarp (*karṇikā*). Within the pericarp, above each of the syllables already written, there is another group of eight. In the eight petals—thus, in the manner described—excluding the central lotus.

"In the middle squares of the bottom-most row" means in the squares within the wings [of that row]. (62) "Māyā" refers to the *visarga*. "In the three squares" means in the two paths (*vīthī*) situated between the three squares. That is the location of the *mātṛkā*. "On the outside" means outside of the three squares. "In front of this yantra."
The connection is with the word "outside" (*bāhye*) here [verse 63]. The phrase "in a nine-square grid measuring two cubits" is the ellipsis;
the meaning is that one should construct a nine-square grid measuring two cubits.
Having worshipped and recited the Vidyā ten thousand times according to the prescribed rule by means of those [materials], (p. 326) ...
Then, having been consecrated, he becomes liberated from the afflictions and happy. || 65 ||
May victory be everywhere, even in those seven aforementioned situations:
when afflicted by the nine planets, by enemies, or when suffering arises from all sides.
For the sake of exertion in battle, for the attainment of fame and prosperity,
or for the birth of a son or the fulfillment of one's desires, one should have [the rite] performed during three lifetimes.
Having drawn this yantra on a seat with red ochre,
one should invoke the Goddess there, worship her, and likewise recite the vidyā ten thousand times.
That jar [should be placed] at each pericarp; as before, it is adorned with fruits, sprouts, and so forth. || 64 ||

Having worshipped the unmodified Vidyā according to the daily ritual sequence and so forth, one should then perform the consecration with those waters, reciting the mantra ten thousand times because it consists of a single syllable. This refers to any one of the seven [substances] previously mentioned in the thirtieth verse of the preceding chapter.

And in the seven [arts] beginning with hand-to-hand combat (handvayuddha). Regarding "fame and prosperity," these two desired objects are to be attained in three births, as previously stated. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "one should cause the consecration (abhiṣeka) to be performed. What has been stated by these nine verses is this: in a space measuring two cubits extending eastward, westward, southward, and northward.
Having divided the intervening space by the laying down of four lines into nine squares,

and having fashioned nine lotuses provided with eight petals within them, one should write the unaltered Vidyā— enclosing the name as before— in the center of the pericarp of the lotus situated in the middle square.

Among the eighty syllables of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) modified by vowels, one should write the first eight, each accompanied by the bindu, on the eight petals starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise— one on each petal. Outside of that,
one should [write them] in the eight [cells] starting from the central cell of the bottom row, proceeding clockwise.

From each preceding group of eight written [letters], one takes the successive letters from above; [one places] the letter from the center of the *sādhya* in the pericarp, and the eight letters from the successive squares above that in the eight petals, starting from the front of each set of eight petals.

Having drawn [the diagram] clockwise with these eighty syllables, one should construct a nine-compartment yantra consisting of nine lotuses; then, having made two squares outside of that with an interval of one finger-breadth between them,
one should place the Mātṛkā in reverse order within the inner of the two intermediate paths.

Having written [the mantra] with the *visarga*, and having written that same [mantra] with the *bindu* in reverse order on the path outside of it, and having written the two syllables "lakṣa" at the front on the exterior of the entire yantra,
[one should place them] in the center of the pericarp of the nine-petaled lotus situated within those nine squares.
Having placed one jar upon each lotus leaf,

having filled them with water consisting of the decoction of medicinal herbs and the syllables of the Vidyā, having worshipped them as before, and having placed fruits, sprouts, and so forth according to the daily ritual sequence, one should invoke the Goddess there and worship her according to the daily ritual sequence.
Having consecrated him with the three empowerments throughout his births, the attainment of the proclaimed fruit occurs. || 67 ||
Thus, by repeating this twenty-one times over a period of three weeks, one shall bring the entire universe under control—the king, women, mortals, and all other living beings. (69)
Having prepared [the image] on a cloth of turmeric, or having placed it in a jar, or in two shallow bowls, or in the middle of a wall, or in one's own sleeping place; || 70 ||
Having worshipped with the Vidyā, one should perform recitation daily during the twilights;
by reciting it a thousand times for the prescribed duration, one may firmly paralyze everything.
Likewise, one should avoid causing harm to an enemy through exertion or anger;
one should avoid legal disputes, military preparations, harsh speech in debate, and thoughts of wrath. (72)
Having drawn her there with the fragrant substances previously mentioned,
one should worship her daily at the junctions of the day (sandhyās) and likewise recite the mantra a thousand times.
By practicing at the prescribed time, one attains abundant prosperity. Now, I shall describe another yantra in the form of a vajra, which possesses great power.
Just as before, by the dropping of fourteen lines, one should likewise produce sixty-nine squares;
thus it is clearly established that there are one hundred and sixty-nine.

This [yantra], which has the form of nine squares like the opening of a fresh lotus, should be worshipped there according to the daily ritual sequence, just as in the case of initiation. "For three, seven, or twenty-one nights" means it is said to be [accomplished] after three nights, seven nights, or twenty-one nights. The universe...

This is a summary statement regarding the kings and others to be mentioned hereafter. "All" refers to the remaining living beings, including animals and so forth (verse 69). The ellipsis [to be supplied] is: "having constructed a yantra of nine compartments. "Of two bowls" means of two [bowls] placed one above and one below, with their openings joined to each other. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative.
"Having placed [it] in the place of rest"—this is the ellipsis. || 70 || A thousand [times] at each junction (sandhyā).

By the stated time, such as three nights and so forth. "Entirely" means all that is about to be described. || 71 || In debate, that is, in logic (tarka). [He should silence] the speech of the opponent. || 72 || This yantra, with the fragrant substances previously mentioned...

With sandalwood, agallochum, musk, and saffron as described in the eighth chapter, [one should worship] that Vijayānityā within that yantra. On the days of ritual application, one thousand [times] at each twilight; prior to the prescribed time, [she is] abundant like the glory of sovereignty, as before.

Then, with twenty-six verses beginning with "Now, another" (*athānyat*) and ending with "are proclaimed" (*samīritāḥ*), consisting of half-verses and so forth, he teaches the construction of the *vajra*-yantra of eighty-one squares using the syllables of the root-vidyā modified by the vowels, as well as its applications and their fruits. Among those, [the phrase] "of exceeding majesty" (*ativibhavam*) means [superior] to others. As before.
East, west, south, and north—one should erase twenty-one square compartments.
And in the center, exactly eighty compartments shall be formed according to the rule. (76)
One should draw triangles in the four directions starting from a single square;
likewise, in the central square and in the four directions in front of it.
Having formed the *vidyā* in the center, one should write the syllables as before;
by touching the four corners of this [square], a triangle or a quadrangle is formed. (78)
Having prepared it there, one should inscribe the Mātṛkā according to the previously mentioned procedure;
by means of this single Vajra-yantro, the Vijayas grant victory. (79)
Having written this out among those prescribed [sites], one should install it according to the prescribed form;
thus one attains victory even in the seven [places] that have been mentioned.

Of the fourteen lines [formed by] two sets of seven lines; the remainder is that there are twenty-one [squares] per corner. In the center is a vajra in the form previously described. From each single square in every direction [is the mantra]; the vidyā is unaltered, with the name in its interior as before.

The meaning is: by entering in a clockwise direction starting from the middle square of the three squares located in the bottom-most row, according to the aforementioned sequence; [one should place] the letters modified by the vowels, numbering eighty, by touching the four squares at the front of this [group].
The meaning is: by touching the tips of the four triangles located in the four directions at the front of the *yantra*.

"Three squares" (*tricaturasraka*) means three squares due to the internal and external divisions. (78) Therein, in the two paths (*vīthī*) between them, according to the previous rule, [one should write] the [syllables] ending with the visarga in reverse order.
The meaning is "together with the anusvāra (bindu) and in direct order. By means of one [line], independent of others;
the sequence for constructing the diagram (*yantra*) is as follows: having struck out fourteen lines each toward the east, west, south, and north, with equal intervals between them.
Having constructed one hundred and sixty-nine squares according to the previously mentioned sequence,
one should erase twenty-one squares in each of the four corners so that a vajra-shape is formed in the center; then, in the remaining eighty-five squares...
Having formed four triangles by clearing one square in each of the four directions,

one should write the root-mantra— unaltered and encapsulated by the name as before— within the remaining eighty-one squares, specifically in the four triangles situated in the cardinal directions of the very center. Thereafter...
In the remaining eighty-one squares,
one proceeds by moving clockwise starting from the middle square of the bottom row,
following the sequence of the "liberated" (muktakrama).

Having written the eighty syllables of the root-mantra according to the sequence of the modifications of the vowels, and having fashioned three squares by touching the tips of the four sets of three triangles located in the cardinal directions, thereby distinguishing between the interior and exterior,
[one proceeds] within the two intermediate paths.
Having inscribed the yantra on the surface of an *aśvattha* plank with red sandalwood paste, one should install it—once perfected through recitation and worship—in empty dwellings. (81)
In that region, prosperity increases daily and remains unshakable;
indeed, no piśācas, rākṣasas, kṛtyās, or vetālas shall exist there.
Having inscribed this according to the prescribed rule upon a plate of Palāśa wood, one should place it anywhere; that spot becomes a sacred field, an abode for Brāhmaṇas.
By performing the previously mentioned ritual of installation, the royal capital becomes firmly established;
by drawing [the diagram] on a banyan tree and digging there, a city will certainly be founded. (84)
By performing the installation in this manner upon an Udumbara tree, that place will indeed, without delay, become a refuge for those who have taken up residence; of this there is no doubt.
From within the triangular space of the directions of the vajra, one should fashion a trident;
when it is pervaded by fire and joined with its own [nature], one should draw [the syllables] in the middle of its prongs.
Having established the wielder of the mace there by means of the power of the recited mantra,
the mace, having entered him through the empowered mark on his forehead, shall speak.

Having written the Mātṛkā in reverse order along with the *visarjanīya* (ḥ) and that same [Mātṛkā] in direct order with the *bindu* (ṃ), by means of this yantra—which functions through internal and external movement and is independent of anything else—one attains all fruits, such as victory, through its application. Thus it is said regarding those [yantras] previously mentioned. || 79 || Prokteṣu.
The meaning is: in the three metals and so forth mentioned in the eighth chapter; in the seven [topics] mentioned in this chapter;
and in the seven [topics] such as duels and battles mentioned by the thirtieth verse. || 80 ||

The *yantra* is of the form of a vajra. With red sandalwood (*kucandana*), as before; the word "in a vacant place" (*śūnye deśe*) is to be supplied as the remainder. There, in both the house and the region [it is applied]. (82) This *yantra* is of the nature of a vajra. "In whatever field" (*yatra kutrāpi kṣetre*) is to be supplied as the remainder.
Because of the previously mentioned installation, the royal capital is the established ground, and the city (*pattana*) is the established region. (84)

The place is presided over by the *yantra*. (85) "From the intermediate space of the three corners of the directions of the *vajra*" means from the space within the middle of the triangles situated in the four directions. The letters *repha* (Ṛ) and *yakāra* (Y) represent the pervasion of burning. "Its own" refers to the *bindu*. [These are] in the middle of its two prongs.
Regarding the two tips at the side-regions of the central line of the trident situated within the interior of the triangle:

this is what is meant—having fashioned a trident in the central space of the triangle located in the direction of Vajra as previously described, one should write the syllables *ra* and *ya*, which consist of fire and wind respectively and are accompanied by the bindu (*ṃ*), upon its two tips. Therein...
One should perform the ritual application (prayoga) that is about to be described. In that regard, [he is] with a thunderbolt (vajra) provided with a trident; him, who holds a mace (gadī). 87.
Just as one establishes the sequence for the cause of self-possession through ritual action, so indeed do the grahas, bhūtas, piśācas, and others enter into and depart from this person. (88)
At that very moment, by the power of this, he comes under one's control like a slave;
having drawn this yantra on a stone and worshipped it, one should place it somewhere.
In that king's palace, the royal patience does not fail him;
having established nine elephant-stables and nine horse-stables in their respective places, he maintains them all.
One should likewise worship these [deities] daily when they have been installed in their respective places—
in the cardinal directions and in the center— for therein diseases and malevolent spells sent by enemies [are neutralized].
However, due to his power, they would not be able to even look upon him,
as if he were a fresh painting made with moonlight, sandalwood, and saffron on a new canvas.
Having worshipped it and spread out that cloth upon which the mantra has been recited, one should lay the patient down;
he who is afflicted by a burning fever will soon be freed from that fever.
One should likewise cause this to be done for the sake of liberation from other diseases as well;
this machine has been described for kings in battles. (94)
One should draw [the deity] upon a sharp-edged drum, other drums, or musical instruments;
then, having invoked her into the center of that with red lead (darada), one should worship her. || 95 ||
One should march while striking Vijayā simultaneously for the sake of attaining victory;
upon hearing that sound, the enemy army flees.
Agitated by fear, he never ventures out in the ten directions;
this machine was constructed for the times of gambling with living beings. 97.
Just as with *gada* || 88 || the *yantra* is devoid of the trident || 89 || *kṣamā* is the earth || 90 || with respect to nine locations; in nine locations || 91 || by its power.
With *candana*, *kāśmīra*, and *candra* combined || 92 || [it cures one] afflicted by burning fever. || 93 ||

The connection [of the verb] is with "he should cause to lie down" (*śāyayet*). He is possessed of a staff (*sa-gadī*). For the sake of liberation from that—that is, for liberation from disease—this [is] the form of a thunderbolt (*vajra*). Striking means expelling; the word "that sound" refers to the sound of expulsion.
Having made it into a pellet and tied it around his neck, one should then apply [the mantra].
By the mere sight of this, they flee in the ten directions. (98)
And that machine, O Pārvatī, achieves victory in every respect even against lifeless objects;
there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by means of that Vajra-machine.
One should meditate upon the yantra or the lore (vidyā) in the form of blood within the mouth of the enemy;
by that power, he immediately comes under one's control like a servant. 100.
Thus have been described for you the manifestations of the impermanence of victory;
the pervasion consisting of the reality of the Eye has also been correctly explained.
By the churning of this [citta], that very reality is made one's own within the mind. (101)
Thus, in the Śrīkādimata among the sixteen Nityātantras, the eighteenth chapter has been fully expounded. 18.
On his neck—that is, on the neck of a cock or similar bird—the person who wears it attains victory; this is the implied meaning.
"Vidyām" means the root-vidyā (mūlavidyā) without conceptual differentiation (*avikalpena*). "Having a red form" (*lohitākṛtim*) is also an adjective for the *yantra*;

thus, it connects with "having a red form. "Of that" refers to the element (*dhātu*). "He becomes an enemy"—this is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). "By its power" means by the power of meditation (*dhyāna*). "In the manner described" [refers to the aforementioned method]. || 100 ||

Thus, in the *Manoramā*, so named, composed by Śrī Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, [a commentary] on the complete *Tantra* known as the venerable *Kādimata* among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
In this commentary,
the eighteenth chapter, which is dedicated to illuminating the ritual procedure for the Śivadūtī Nityā-vidyā, is fully completed and thoroughly refined. 18.
The number of verses: there are twelve treatises (yantras) and one hundred and eighteen commentaries;
they are recorded as being ninety-two thousand, three hundred and fifty-four [verses].
The Nineteenth Chapter.
Now, among the sixteen Nityās, she who is declared as the fourteenth is called Ekākṣarā; that Vidyā is Sarvamaṅgalā.
The sequence of ritual placement (nyāsa), the method of meditation, the powers residing in the enclosures,
the order of worship, the means of accomplishment, and the applications and so forth, in their proper sequence.
One should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅgaka) using the syllables of the root-mantra differentiated by the long vowels;
these, likewise differentiated by those same vowels, one should place upon one's own limbs until the mind reaches its limit.
Resplendent with a golden complexion, adorned with pearls and rubies,
wearing a crown of rubies, and possessing a weight of compassion shimmering from her two eyes.
Having taught the procedure for the thirteenth [deity], Vijayānityā, in the eighteenth preceding chapter, he now teaches the procedure for the fourteenth [deity], Sarvamaṅgalānityā,
with a hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen... and ending with "api ca."

By the nineteenth chapter. Therein, with two verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "in sequence," he teaches the subject matter of the chapter. Therein, it was stated in the third chapter;
the remainder is "the application and so forth of the yantras and other [ritual objects]. || 2 ||
With the verse beginning "The root-vidyā" (*mūlavidyā*), he teaches the sequence for the performance of the ritual placement (*nyāsa*).

In this context, "by the syllables of the root-vidyā" means by the letters *sa*, *va*, and the *bindu* of the root-vidyā when they have been combined into a single unit (*piṇḍībhūta*). Here, the plural number is used with reference to the three intermediate [components].

"With long vowels distinguished as before" means this: one should perform the placement of the limbs (*aṅganyāsa*) preceded by the placement of the syllables (*akṣaranyāsa*), using the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) joined with the long vowels in the sequence beginning with *svāṃ* and so forth, according to its own class (*sajātika*). These...

The forms of the sixfold sciences, joined with long vowels, are to be placed within one's own five organs of knowledge—namely, hearing and the rest—with the mind as the sixth; this is the meaning.
