Among those, in the four beginning with hearing, even though they occupy pairs of locations, the meaning is that one should place one syllable for each corresponding pair. In that regard:
The placement on the skin is as before. Following all the various types of placement, one should perform the pervasive placement (vyāpaka) as before; such is the traditional teaching. || 3 ||

With these five verses beginning with *suvarṇa* and ending with *sthitā*, he teaches the meditation on the perpetual worship and so forth, which has within it the construction of the maṇḍala for the perpetual service of the Goddess together with her retinue. Therein, [he describes her] as possessing the weight of a swinging compassion from her two eyes...
She has two arms and is seated upon a lotus with eight, sixteen, or thirty-two petals;
she resides within a temple possessing four doors and a pair of courtyards.
Holding a mātuluṅga fruit in her lotus-like right hand,
she bestows wealth and other blessings with her left hand upon her own devotees.
She is surrounded on all sides by her own similar powers,
and accompanied by seventy-six others who have arisen from the syllables.
O Goddess of the gods, hear now of those powers who reside in the eternal enclosure— powers whose capacity has been declared for other ritual applications and for the daily services.
One should worship Bhadrā, Bhavānī, Bhavyā, Viśālākṣī, Suvismitā, Karuṇā, Kamalā, and Kalpā upon the eight petals.
The meaning is that she has two eyes which are like the sun and the moon of compassion, being reddish and crimson respectively.
"Seated on her own seat" means she is comfortably situated upon a lotus within the mandala whose form will be described.
"With eight, sixteen, and twice that many petals"—the phrase "twice that many" refers to twice sixteen.

The meaning is "with thirty-two petals. This is what is being said: one approaches [the mandala] by means of eight petals, sixteen petals, and thirty-two petals according to the internal sequence. "Situated in the middle of two squares joined together with four gates and the ground" means situated in the center of two quadrangles possessing four gates in the four directions.
The procedure for constructing the maṇḍala for its perpetual worship is as follows:

having fashioned two equal squares, one within the other, with internal and external divisions and provided with four gates situated in the four directions, [one should place] a thirty-two-petalled lotus in their center. Inside that—

The meaning is that having fashioned a sixteen-petaled lotus and an eight-petaled lotus within it, one should invoke the Goddess in its pericarp and the attendant Śaktis upon the petals and other parts, and then worship them. The phrase "with the lotus-hand" refers to the left hand (as the context implies). By "Śaktis" is meant the Śaktis of the eternal enclosure (*nityāvaraṇa*). [There are] seventy-six of them.
"With thirty-eight forms in the shape of couples" means with others; this is a qualification of the specific powers arising from the syllables (*akṣarottha-śakti*).

"Endowed with those arising from the syllables" refers to those beginning with Amṛtā, which will be described later—the powers of the syllables that take the form of the Moon, Sun, and Fire. This is to be connected with the phrase "in ritual applications" (*prayogeṣu*).

The connection is that [this occurs] "at other times during the daily worship" (*nityasaparyā*). The remainder of the context is that one should "remember" her who possesses the aforementioned powers as well as the powers such as Bhadrā which are to be described hereafter. "Powers" (*śaktīḥ*) refers to the powers that constitute the retinue (*varaṇa*) of the daily worship. This is what is meant: in the daily worship, [one remembers] the power Bhadrā and so forth.

Together with those [energies] to be described later— beginning with Amṛtā and arising from the letters of the Mātṛkā, known as the digits of the Moon, Sun, and Fire— in the form of thirty-eight pairs, which constitute seventy-six [energies], [the practitioner should perform the practice] in the ritual applications and so forth.
Having meditated upon her as endowed with powers (śaktis) according to the described form, one should worship her. || 8 ||
With the nine verses beginning with *bhadrām* and ending with *sahasrakam*,

[the text] provides the names of the five powers (*śakti*) of the enclosure of the daily worship (*nityasaparyā*), as well as the eternal, immortal, life-sustaining, and compassionate *kalā* known as Pūriṇī.
[She was] free from sorrow, stainless, full, meritorious, fortunate, and ever-radiant. || 10 ||
One should worship the eight powers— Vivekā, Vibhavā, Viśvā, and Vitatā— in the eight pairs, surrounding [the central deity] in a clockwise order.
To the passionate one, the sky-farer, the all-encompassing, the ancient, the supreme sovereign;
to Gaurī, Śivā, the immeasurable, the stainless, the victorious, and the transcendent.
The pure, divine lotus-lake, the sovereign of the universe, beloved of Śiva,
possessing infinite forms, blissful, lotus-eyed, and beyond reproach.

I bow to Sarasvatī, who grants boons, who bestows speech, who is the goddess of eloquence, whose form is the various Vedas, who is knowledge, the mistress of speech, the twilight, and who has attained union.
One should worship Nirmalā and Dānarūpā in the two sets of sixteen;
as before, all [the goddesses] are worshipped by Indra and the others in sequence, according to their etymological names. || 15 ||
He also teaches the conclusion of the worship and so forth. Therein, with the verse beginning with "Bhadrā," he teaches the names of the eight powers (śaktis) to be worshipped on the eight petals.
With the verse beginning with "Kalā," he teaches the names of twelve of the powers to be worshipped among those on the sixteen petals.

With the verse beginning with "Vivekā," he teaches that one should worship all the remaining four powers by their names, starting from the front (the east) and proceeding clockwise; this refers to the sixteen petals within the group of eight [circles]. With the verse beginning with "Kāminī,"...
With the verse beginning with "pavitrām," he teaches the names of eleven of the powers to be worshipped on the thirty-two petals;
with the verse beginning with "varadām," he teaches the names of nine of the remaining twenty-one powers.

He teaches the names of ten out of the twelve powers. Therein, "Vāgīśvarī" is the name of the twenty-seventh power. With the verse beginning with "nirmalām," he teaches the remaining two powers as well as their worship and so forth. In that context, "in the pair of sixteen" means on the thirty-two petals.
As before, by way of circumambulation from the southeast (Agni), there are eight powers known as the world-protectors, beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna;
these are in female form. At the four doors, including both sides, there are four [powers] starting from the west;
that is, four at each of the four doors located in the four directions starting from the west.
The meaning is that one should worship. Because the word "four" has two meanings, it is connected twice;

thus, on another occasion, the phrase "the four" refers to the powers of Ananta, Brahmā, Niyati, and Kāla. The meaning is that one should worship the twenty powers together with those previously mentioned forms.
The meaning is that they are situated at the corners and the sides of the gates located in the four directions, as described in the *Nityānityāpaṭala*.
One should worship the powers known as the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), beginning with Brāhmī, at the gates. (p. 336)
In the four directions beginning with the west, there are four [deities] described as having the aforementioned forms. || 16 ||
One should perform the two valid rites and the fire-oblation (homa) as before, concluding in the same manner;
one should always perform a thousand recitations (japa) in front of her.
One should accomplish that vidyā as before, by means of thirty-two lakṣas [of recitations];
one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) with food, clarified butter, or ghee, amounting to one-tenth of that number.
Thus, one who has perfected the vidyā should perform the prescribed applications in their entirety;
otherwise, there will be fruitlessness, infamy, and death for him.
Having worshipped her with devotion according to that prescribed sequence and having accomplished the rite, he should thereafter perform the auspicious acts proclaimed for the sake of prosperity.

This is what is meant: having thus combined the eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī and the sixteen powers of the eight world-protectors (lokapāla) beginning with Indra and ending with Īśāna— four at each of the four doors of the square mandala—
in the sequence of worship, there are the eight [Mothers] beginning with Brāhmī.
Having performed worship on the eight sides, starting from the right side of the western gate and ending at its left side,
one then proceeds from the northern side of the eastern gate of the square to the end of the northeastern side.
Having worshipped the eight powers of the world-protectors, beginning with Indra,
one should then worship the powers of Ananta, Brahmā, Niyati, and Kāla in the corners starting from the southeast (āgneya) and ending in the northeast (īśāna).
When the worship has been performed in this manner by repeating it three times, [one should proceed] at the doors located in the four directions, beginning with the west.

There are twenty powers (śakti) situated thus, four in each of the corners and so forth, and one each [in the center]. The two offerings (bali) are completed as before, through the meditation on the three fires and so forth, as previously described. Of that Goddess... (17)

With these three verses beginning with "prāgvat" and ending with "uditāni," [the author] teaches the procedure for the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*), the fitness of one who has performed the preliminary rite for the performance of the ritual application (*prayoga*), and the transgression that results from doing otherwise. Among these, [the first verse begins with] "prāgvat": 1. As before, one should worship the Lord of the Discus (Viṣṇu) in the heart-lotus, and likewise the mantra, the rosary, the ground, the seat, and the water-pot. 2. Having worshipped the deities of the directions and the guardians of the quarters, one should perform the fire-sacrifice (*homakarma*) with oblations of sesame seeds, clarified butter, and so forth. 3. One should recite the mantra ten thousand times; this is declared to be the preliminary rite. Having performed it thus, one becomes fit for the ritual application. 4. Otherwise, the mantra will not grant success; rather, it will bring about misfortune. Therefore, one should perform the preliminary rite according to the prescribed rule. 5. By means of the preliminary rite, one attains the fruit of all mantras. Without the preliminary rite, there is no attainment of the fruit. 6. For one who has completed the preliminary rite, the mantra bestows success. Otherwise, it brings about misfortune and even death. 7. The preliminary rite is said to consist of four parts: japa, homa, tarpaṇa, and brāhmaṇabhojana. 8. Japa is said to be ten thousand repetitions; homa is one-tenth of that. Tarpaṇa is equal to homa, and feeding Brahmins is equal to that. 9. Or else, the japa is said to be one hundred thousand repetitions; homa is one-tenth of that. Tarpaṇa is equal to homa, and feeding Brahmins is equal to that. 10. The preliminary rite is said to be of two kinds: with obstacles and without obstacles. That which is performed with obstacles is difficult to accomplish. 11. The preliminary rite without obstacles is easy to accomplish and grants success quickly. It should be performed by those seeking the fruit of the mantra. 12. One should perform the preliminary rite during the bright fortnight, under an auspicious lunar mansion, on an auspicious day, and at a favorable time. 13. One should avoid the following: the dark fortnight, the new moon, the conjunction of planets, the eclipse of the sun or moon, and the period of impurity (*aśauca*). 14. One should avoid a place where there is a corpse, a funeral pyre, a cremation ground, a village boundary, a crossroads, or a temple of a heretic. 15. One should avoid a place frequented by outcasts, a place of public assembly, a marketplace, a riverbank, or a place of slaughter. 16. One should avoid a place infested with insects, a place with many stones, a place with much dust, a place with much grass, or a place with much mud. 17. One should avoid a place with many thorns, a place with many pits, a place with many snakes, a place with many scorpions, or a place with many ants. 18. One should avoid a place with many crows, a place with many owls, a place with many vultures, a place with many jackals, or a place with many dogs. 19. One should avoid a place with many cranes, a place with many herons, a place with many hawks, a place with many cormorants, or a place with many water-fowls. 20. One should avoid a place with many monkeys, a place with many bears, a place with many tigers, a place with many lions, or a place with many elephants. 21. One should avoid a place with many horses, a place with many camels, a place with many donkeys, a place with many goats, or a place with many sheep. 22. One should avoid a place with many cows, a place with many buffaloes, a place with many pigs, a place with many deer, or a place with many birds. 23. One should avoid a place with many trees, a place with many creepers, a place with many shrubs, a place with many bushes, or a place with many hedges. 24. One should avoid a place with many stones, a place with many pebbles, a place with many sands, a place with many shells, or a place with many salt-flats. 25. One should avoid a place with many fires, a place with many sparks, a place with many flames, a place with many smokes, or a place with many ashes. 26. One should avoid a place with many clouds, a place with many lightning-bolts, a place with many thunderclaps, a place with many rain-showers, or a place with many winds. 27. One should avoid a place with many mountains, a place with many valleys, a place with many caves, a place with many peaks, or a place with many ridges. 28. One should avoid a place with many rivers, a place with many streams, a place with many lakes, a place with many ponds, or a place with many wells. 29. One should avoid a place with many tanks, a place with many pools, a place with many marshes, a place with many swamps, or a place with many bogs. 30. One should avoid a place with many forests, a place with many jungles, a place with many thickets, a place with many thickets of reeds, or a place with many thickets of cane. 31. One should avoid a place with many thorny plants, a place with many poisonous plants, a place with many medicinal herbs, a place with many fragrant plants, or a place with many flowering plants. 32. One should avoid a place with many fruits, a place with many flowers, a place with many leaves, a place with many buds, or a place with many seeds. 33. One should avoid a place with many roots, a place with many stalks, a place with many joints, a place with many nodes, or a place with many fibers. 34. One should avoid a place with many fibers, a place with many threads, a place with many ropes, a place with many nets, or a place with many snares. 35. One should avoid a place with many hooks, a place with many bars, a place with many bolts, a place with many locks, or a place with many keys. 36. One should avoid a place with many doors, a place with many windows, a place with many lattices, a place with many screens, or a place with many curtains. 37. One should avoid a place with many walls, a place with many fences, a place with many hedges, a place with many ditches, or a place with many moats. 38. One should avoid a place with many ramparts, a place with many towers, a place with many gateways, a place with many arches, or a place with many turrets. 39. One should avoid a place with many watchtowers, a place with many sentries, a place with many guards, a place with many soldiers, or a place with many weapons. 40. One should avoid a place with many drums, a place with many conchs, a place with many trumpets, a place with many horns, or a place with many bells. 41. One should avoid a place with many gongs, a place with many cymbals, a place with many lutes, a place with many flutes, or a place with many harps. 42. One should avoid a place with many songs, a place with many dances, a place with many instrumental performances, a place with many theatrical shows, or a place with many festivals. 43. One should avoid a place with many crowds, a place with many assemblies, a place with many gatherings, a place with many processions, or a place with many pilgrimages. 44. One should avoid a place with many merchants, a place with many traders, a place with many artisans, a place with many craftsmen, or a place with many laborers. 45. One should avoid a place with many beggars, a place with many mendicants, a place with many ascetics, a place with many renunciants, or a place with many devotees. 46. One should avoid a place with many heretics, a place with many atheists, a place with many skeptics, a place with many nihilists, or a place with many materialists. 47. One should avoid a place with many atheists, a place with many skeptics, a place with many nihilists, a place with many materialists, or a place with many hedonists. 48. One should avoid a place with many libertines, a place with many profligates, a place with many debauchees, a place with many lechers, or a place with many adulterers. 49. One should avoid a place

"Or"—that is, as an alternative—by performing the worship of the three junctions (*sandhyā*) and so forth; otherwise, if the prescribed means (*sādhana*) and other rites are not performed, the *vidyā* would bring about fruitlessness and the like for that practitioner (*sādhaka*). This is the remainder [of the sense]. For that reason, having propitiated that root *vidyā*, [one should proceed].
Having first accomplished [the goal] through daily worship and other such means, one should subsequently perform the auspicious applications (*maṅgala-prayoga*)—this is the ellipsis.
That is to say, one should perform the auspicious applications mentioned in all the *Maṅgala* chapters;
the meaning is that these are the auspicious applications taught in the entire *Sarvamaṅgalāpaṭala*. || 20 ||

(337) O Dear One, listen as I describe the powers of the phonemes which serve the purpose of ritual application; they are goddesses, and they consist of the forms of the Moon, Sun, and Fire, numbering thirty-eight. 21.
Amṛtā, Mānadā, Pūṣā, Tuṣṭi, Puṣṭi, Rati, Dhṛti, Śaṃsinī, Candrikā, Kānti, Jyotsnā, Śrī, Prīti, and Aṅgadā. || 22 ||
Pūrṇā, Pūrṇāmṛtā, and the wish-granting Kalās together with their vowels—these sixteen are the digits of the Moon, comparable to the wish-fulfilling tree. (23)
Tapinī, Tāpinī, Dhūmrā, Marīci, Jvālinī, Ruci, Suṣumnā, Bhogadā, Viśvā, Bodhanī, Dhāraṇī, and Kṣamā. || 24 ||
These are declared to be the Śaktis, corresponding in order to the twelve suns;
they consist of the pronunciation of the letters from *bha* to *ḍa* in reverse order.

With thirteen verses beginning with *prayoga* and ending with *bhavet*, he teaches the powers of the letters of the Mātṛkā, which were previously introduced as being conjoined in the form of the thirty-eight *kalās*, for the sake of practical application (*prayoga*). Among these, the purposes of the application are as follows:

He causes [the practitioner] to remember up to the point "in the preliminary practices" (*pūrvaprayogeṣu*). The powers of the phonemes (*varṇaśakti*) of Mātṛkā—those previously mentioned in number and form—are, by virtue of their being in union (*mithunarūpataḥ*), of the nature of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni;
they follow the sequence of Mātṛkā to be described hereafter, and through the division of syllables (*akṣaravibhāgataḥ*), they take that form as they become conjoined in pairs.

Regarding the powers (*śaktayaḥ*): with the verse beginning "Amṛtā" and so forth, he teaches fourteen powers among the sixteen digits of the moon (*somakalā*). Therein, *pūṣā* ends in the feminine nominative suffix *ṭāp*. The word division is *puṣṭīḥ*, *ratiḥ*, *puṣṭiḥ*, and *ratiḥ*.

With the verse beginning with *pūrṇe*, he teaches the names of the two remaining digits (*kalā*) and the sequential application of each of the sixteen vowels to each of them. In that context, "bestowing desires" (*kāmadāyinī*) means granting what is desired; the plural number here is used in view of their being sixteen.
The *sasvaras* are formed by sequentially prefixing each of the sixteen vowels to the beginning of every one of the [consonants].

With the verse beginning with *tapinī*, he teaches the twelve names of the solar digits (*sūryakalā*). The meaning is that one should join the twelve syllables beginning with *bhā* and ending with *ḍā*— which are listed in reverse order from the sequence previously mentioned— at the beginning of those [names] according to the root-text sequence, as before.
With the verse beginning with *dhātā*, he teaches ten names among the twelve names of the Sun;

therein, *samanantara* means the tenth [name] following the ninth. With the verse beginning with *tvaṣṭā*, he teaches the remaining two names and their constituent syllables; therein, they are bodies formed from the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*.

The meaning is that one should apply the twelve syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *ṭha*, in their direct order (*anuloma*), at the beginning of its name. In that regard, the sequence for joining those mantras is accompanied by the previously mentioned powers (*śakti*) such as Tapinī and their corresponding syllables; namely, *kaṃ* and *bhaṃ* in due order.
"Salutation to Dhātṛ and Tāpinī," and so forth; [the syllables] *ṭhaṃ* and *ḍaṃ* belong to Viṣṇu. (p.
338) Dhātṛ, Aryamā, Mitra, Varuṇa, Śaubhaga, Vivasvān, Indra, Pūṣan, Arka, Parjanya, and immediately after him [Aṃśu]. || 26 ||
Tvaṣṭṛ and Viṣṇu are declared to be the twelve Ādityas in sequence;
their bodies consist of the letters from *ka* to *ṭha*, they are all-pervading, and they bestow all spiritual accomplishments.
Dhūmrārcis, Ūṣmā, Jvalinī, Jvālinī, Visphuliṅginī, Suśrī, Surūpā, Kapilā, and also Havyavahā and Kavyavahā. (28)
The ten powers consisting of the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa* have been proclaimed;
O Śivā, their names as they appear in the *Vāsanā* have been told to you. (29)
Having worshipped the twenty-two pairs of letters from Ka to Kṣa according to the prescribed order, one should apply the ritual procedure in every respect.
Because the vowels are independent, the Śaktis are likewise independent;
their Lords (Nāthas) are declared to have names and forms similar to theirs. (31)

The twelve mantras ending with "Obeisance to Kṣamā" thus constitute the twenty-four solar digits (arkakalā) as deities in the form of twelve pairs. With the verse beginning with "Dhūmrā," he teaches the names of the ten digits of fire (vahnikalā). Among those, Havyakavyavahe refers to Havyavahā.

And [the goddess] Kavyavahā. This means they are composed of the letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa*; that is to say, preceded by the ten letters starting from *ya* and ending with *kṣa*.
The purificatory essences (*vāsana*) of those ten fires are stated in the thirty-fifth chapter, the Vāsanā-paṭala.

These are those mentioned starting with "Agni" and "Vahni," and so forth. This is what is meant: one should join each of the ten letters beginning with *ya* and ending with *kṣa*, in sequence, to the beginning of each of the fire-energies (*vahnikalā*), and likewise join them to the names of the fires. Their mantras are as follows: *yaṃ*.

The ten mantras beginning with *agnidhūmrārcirbhyāṃ namaḥ* and ending with *kṣaṃ grāsakavyavahābhyāṃ namaḥ* constitute twenty [deities], because they consist of ten pairs of deities who are the digits (*kalā*) of Fire. Thus, there are twenty-two solar pairs and twelve fiery ones; such is the count.
The meaning is that, taken together, there are twenty-two pairs of letters from *ka* to *kṣa*.

The sequence therein has been shown by us according to the aforementioned order. They are called "autonomous" (*svatantra*) because they shine forth by themselves due to their independence; and because they consist of vowels, their names and forms are similar to those [of the vowels], and thus they are named after the powers (*śakti*).

The meaning is that one should join them with masculine endings. This is what is intended: because the vowels are independent, their presiding powers—the previously mentioned sixteen lunar digits (kalās) beginning with Amṛtā—are themselves independent; therefore, their lords possess forms and names similar to theirs.
Therefore, the meaning is that one should apply the names of the powers ending in the masculine gender. This is what is being said:
"The pairs beginning with the vowels have thus been declared in the sequence of thirty-eight. (p. 339)
Having worshipped those [elements] in the auspicious water, which consists of the essence of that triad of energies, || 32 ||
Having invoked and worshipped the forms of the deities as they have been described, one should [perform the rite] with those waters.
But through consecration, those three splendors become identical with the Goddess.

One should join that Vidyā, which is Sarvamaṅgalā, with the five Nityās by means of one hundred and seventy-six [syllables] consisting of the vowels beginning with *vā* (the *vāta*-letters) and so forth. 34.
Then, one should join sixteen vowels in the place of her [the consonant's] base;
thus, there are sixteen [syllables] by nine thousand and two hundred.

These should be applied exactly as ending with the female deities (*stryantāni*). Their mantras are sixteen, beginning with *aṃ amṛtāmṛtābhyāṃ namaḥ* and ending with *aḥ pūrṇāmṛtapūrṇāmṛtābhyāṃ namaḥ*. These couples of the lunar digits (*somakalā-mithunāni*) are to be worshipped at the beginning of all couples. Here—

The fact that each of the couples consisting of the Sūrya-kalās and Śaktis is composed of two syllables is justified by the intention to express their distinction; whereas the fact that the other couples consist of a single syllable each is justified by the intention to express their unity.
"Thirty and eight" means thirty-eight. What is meant is this:

by means of the sixteen couples of lunar digits and powers (*kalā-śakti*), the twelve couples of solar digits, and the ten [couples] of fire-digits, there are thus thirty-eight couples, which constitute seventy-six digits (*kalā*).

The letters of the *mātṛkā* exist; one should employ them according to the stated sequence. This is said by means of the worship of the aforementioned couple within the nature of those three fires (*tejas*). "O Śivā" is the vocative. The meaning is that they are those intended by oneself, as taught in all the Tantras. Having worshipped them in that order, [one attains] the state of being the Goddess herself through those three fires.

The meaning is that because all deities consist of the letters of the Mātṛkā which are composed of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni, they are identical with the essence of those respective deities; the word "of the one to be consecrated" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. || 33 ||

With these three verses beginning with "vātādyaiḥ" and ending with "vadāmi te," he provides instruction on the nature and multiplicity of the root-vidyā, as well as an introduction to its application. In this context, "vātādyaiḥ" refers to the vowels beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa'.

The meaning is "by the syllables of the expansion of the *mātṛkā*s" as they have been stated; that is, by five hundred, meaning five hundred [syllables]. This is what is meant: for each of the sixteen vowels beginning with *a* and the thirty-five consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*.
By joining each of the sixteen vowels with each of the [consonants], there are thus, in total,
five hundred and seventy-six letters of the expanded *mātṛkā*;
by joining these one by one in sequence at the beginning of the root-vidyā—
There are five hundred and seventy-six forms of the Vidyā. In its place of power (*valasthāna*), one should join the sixteen vowels to the fourteen vowel-positions of the root Vidyā;
that is, the sixteen vowels in their proper sequence.
(340) O Supreme Goddess, forms are born from eternal ignorance;
I shall describe to you the yantras, the ritual applications, and the fruits resulting from them. || 36 ||
Having fashioned two circles for this [mandala], one should draw a hexagon outside;
outside that, an eight-petaled lotus, and outside that, likewise those three [circles].
Having done so, one should place the *vidyākūṭas* within them according to the prescribed sequence;
among those, one should write the first one in the center, accompanied by the *sādhya*, and [the others] on the outside.
Then, one should draw four [syllables] in each of the outer corners;
thereafter, one should write five in each of the eight petals.
In the pair of outer enclosures, one should properly draw the Mātṛkā, joined with Māyā,
both in reverse and in direct order, together with its own [seed-syllable].
One should apply each [mantra] individually. This refers to the *Nityāvidyā* and the *Sarvamaṅgalānityāvidyā*.
What is meant is that, by joining these with the previously mentioned mantras and so forth, using the five hundred and seventy-six letters from the expansion of the *Mātṛkā*, one obtains—

In the final stage, through the sequential application of the sixteen vowels to each of the divisions of the numerical forms, there arise nine thousand two hundred and sixteen forms of the *vidyātattva*.
By means of these aforementioned numbers of *vidyā*-forms, one performs the ritual applications (*prayoga*) with yantras—this is the implied meaning. || 36 ||

With these six verses beginning with "vṛttadvayam" and ending with "kramāt," which describe the forms of the vidyās according to the stated numbers, he teaches one hundred and forty-four yantras for each individual vṛtti. Among them, of this...
"Of the two circles": outside that hexagon; "outside that": outside the eight-petaled lotus.

The construction "having made those three"—meaning the three circles—applies to all instances. In those locations, one should place the *kūṭas* (syllabic clusters) of the Vidyā, meaning the forms of the root-vidyā according to the previously stated conventions, in the order described.

According to the sequence to be described: among those aforementioned numbers of *kūṭas*, one should write the first [syllable] from the very middle— that is, from the center of all— conjoined with the *sādhya*, and having written the letter *va* beneath the letter *sa*, in the intermediate space between those two.
The meaning is that one should write the triad beginning with the *sādhaka*. From the center to the outside, there are four [syllables] in each corner;
these, together with the syllables written in the center, amount to twenty-four syllables to be written within the hexagon. Outside the hexagon, there are five [syllables] on each petal.
The meaning is that one should write five syllables. Taken together, there are forty syllables to be written on the eight petals.
Thus, including these, there are sixty-four syllables to be written in this yantra. "Outside" means outside of the eight-petaled [lotus], within a pair of circles.
In the two intermediate paths between the three circles situated outside the eight petals— by means of *māyā* with the *visarjanīya*,
and by its own *bindu*— within the six internal spaces, that is, within the six internal spaces of the inner hexagon,
when the days of the cycle occur.
When the days of the [six] cycles occur within the six internal intervals, one should write them constantly in front, proceeding clockwise in every direction. (41)
In this way, the yantras are produced from those aforementioned varieties of *kūṭas*,
numbering one hundred and forty-four respectively.
In this manner, one should draw the other *kūṭas* in sequence as they have been described;
those containing the name should be placed in the center, while the others should be drawn around it.
In the eternal [mantra], the two sciences (*vidye*) consist of six syllables, each being composed of three syllables.
"Everywhere" means in all locations of the yantra. The connection is with the phrase "by the aforementioned yoga. By this, the meaning of "by the aforementioned yoga" is explained.

From each preceding set of sixty-four written syllables, each subsequent set of sixty-four is placed further and further outward; in this manner, by means of the syllables of the vidyā in the stated number, yantras are produced in single rounds according to the stated number. The procedure for constructing the yantras is as follows:

Having first constructed a hexagon according to the previously mentioned measurements, containing two circles within it; having then constructed an eight-petaled lotus outside of that; and having fashioned two circles outside the two outer circles—then, in the very center of all these, among those numbering nine thousand two hundred and sixteen...

Having first written the name as before within the forms of the Vidyās— which have arisen from the conjunction of the various sounds of the Mātṛkā and are produced through yoga— one should then write four letters each, beginning with the letter written in the center, in each of the six corners surrounding it.

Having written twenty-four syllables, one should then write forty syllables in total by writing five syllables on each of the eight petals outside of that— five syllables being those following the [first] twenty-four written within the hexagons— and thus, having combined them, [one writes] forty syllables in all.
Having written the sixty-four syllables, one should write the *mātṛkā* in reverse order, including the *visarga*, within the inner lane between the three circles, and in the outer lane,
in forward order.
One should write them together with the nasal bindus. This is the first yantra.
In this manner, from among the sixty-four [syllables] written in the previously mentioned yantras, one should proceed with each successive group of sixty-four;
thus, by means of a single rotation of the stated number of mantra-syllables in this sequence—
By drawing [the figures] outward and outward, one hundred and forty-four yantras are produced. || 42 ||

By means of these four verses beginning with "evam" and ending with "vadet," [the author] describes the yantras— which arise from the different locations for the placement of syllables— that are produced from the previously mentioned one hundred and forty-four yantras.

He also teaches that, in this same sequence, other machines arise even for the fifteen [syllables] that were previously considered numerically distinct. In that regard, in the manner thus described, other *kūṭas* (cryptic syllable-groups) are taught for the aforementioned number of previously mentioned machines.
Above the peak-syllable written in the center,
there are thirteen lakṣas, twenty-seven thousand, and four hundred in number. (44)
O Goddess, the yantras are produced; by means of them, she is Sarvamaṅgalā.
Thus, there shall be separate yantras for each of these Nityās. 45.

The meaning is that one should write the "peak-syllable" (*kūṭākṣara*) amidst the aforementioned number of upper diagrams. The others [the remaining syllables] are sixty-four in number, beginning with the syllables written in the middle of each respective first diagram.

"By twenty-seven thousand" means by twenty-seven thousand [yantras]. By those yantras. This is what is meant: just as in the case of the previously mentioned one hundred and forty-four yantras, [the rule applies] to the first yantra.

Having first written in the center the first of the nine thousand two hundred and sixteen syllables of the *vidyā* in the form of *kūṭa*-syllables, one should [proceed] with the sixty-four *kūṭas* beginning with that first syllable written in the center, as they are written in the locations specified outside of it.

The first yantra. The second [yantra] is formed by the sixty-four [syllables] beginning with the sixty-fifth peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) written on the exterior; in this manner, in sequence, the aforementioned number of yantras are written within the pericarp itself of the very first peak-syllable. Likewise...
Having written the second *kūṭa* in the center of that first machine,
and having written sixty-four [units] each starting from that [second *kūṭa*] on the outside,
one hundred and forty-four machines are produced. Thus, of those...

By writing them in such a manner, with each one situated in the middle of a single peak (kūṭa), there are exactly the stated number of yantras; likewise, by writing all the peaks in their stated order from the center, revolving according to the sequence of those respective numbers of peaks.
When the one hundred and forty-four machines, numbering nine thousand two hundred and sixteen,
are combined, there are one million twenty-seven thousand four hundred and four machines in total. Among these:

From the *kūṭa* written in the center of the ground of each successive first yantra among the one hundred and forty-four yantras, the letters of the preceding *kūṭas* become the respective final letters of each successive final yantra; thus it continues until the end.
The yantras of the Nityās should be distinct for each. This is what is meant: for each of the sixteen Nityās, including the ten Hṛllekhāvatīs, within that very Hṛllekhā, it is thus—

By joining the sixteen vowels of the Mātṛkā in their full expansion at the beginning and end of all the *maṅgala* verses, there arise forms of that [Goddess] equal in number to those mentioned in the *Sarvamaṅgalā*. Likewise, one should fashion yantras of that same number. Regarding the five yantras that are devoid of the *hṛllekhā*:

By joining the vowels of the *mātṛkā* expansion to the beginning and end of all the syllables starting with the word "maṅgala," there arise forms equal in number to those [syllables], and from them, yantras of that same number come into being.
From these various [yantras], those respective supernatural attainments (*siddhis*) also arise. In that regard:
Therefore, there are never, at any time or place, any [goals] that cannot be accomplished by these [mantras].
Whatever exists within them, I shall speak of; who could possibly describe the remainder? (46)
O Goddess, by means of those nine sequences, one should divide those [mantras] which have the Lord as their essence into sixteen parts and perform their ritual application.
Having arranged nine compartments with a wide central layout,
joined with the directions starting from the east up to the center, [one should place] the Lords and the Goddesses in their respective order.
Whatever action one desires, that one should apply toward them;
one should perform worship on the prescribed day, whether on a pedestal or even upon the ground.

Because there is no [fixed] measure of syllables (*halamātrā*), the instruction is that one should begin with the expansion of the *mātṛkā* and, by joining each of the sixteen vowels to the place of that *vidyā*-syllable, bring about those respective numbers.
Thus, although this is an extreme secret, everything has been analyzed here at the command of the Lord.
What we have said is correct. By means of these fifteen Nityās, there are certain tasks that cannot be accomplished at any time or in any place, even partially.
Therefore, who could speak of the remainder? I myself am not able to describe those tasks that are to be accomplished in their entirety.
The meaning is "I am able. || 46 ||
With thirteen verses beginning with *nāthātmakāni* and ending with *japādinā*, he teaches the methods of application for the previously mentioned yantras. Among these,
those yantras which consist of the Nāthas are nine in number, because [the yantras] are exhausted by that count during their extraction.

"Having pierced with nine steps" means having divided each group of nine. "Having pierced into sixteen parts" is to be construed as "having combined. One should perform the application by dividing each previously divided group of nine into sixteen parts. Thus, one performs the application with groups of nine [parts] consisting of sixteen [sub-units] each.

It is said that one should construct it as follows: having prepared a nine-square grid with a wide central arrangement and sufficient expansion in the middle to be suitable for the construction of the yantra,
by means of four threads drawn east-west and north-south.
One should form nine squares by striking along the intermediate spaces.

One should write [the letters] starting from the east and ending at the center, proceeding in a clockwise direction. Among the nine, one should begin from the central square of the three squares situated in the row facing the east.

The meaning is that one should write nine yantras in a clockwise sequence, ending at the corner of the middle-middle square. Within those nine yantras, the three syllables [of each] correspond respectively to the nine constellations beginning with Aśvinī in the first group of nine, and to the nine [constellations] beginning with Maghā in the second group of nine.
In the third group of nine, there are the nine constellations beginning with Mūla; thus it continues through the subsequent groups of nine until the attainment of the fruit.
Then, when the desired object has been obtained, one should perform the ritual dismissal (*udvāsana*) of the deities within oneself.
Having washed the discus, one should pour that water onto fields and the like.
Thus, O Śivā, other yantras have been declared in due order;
one should employ them in accordance with their sequence for one's desired undertakings, O Śivā.
This same procedure applies to each of those [rites] involving the enumeration of others;
by this means, all gentle rites certainly succeed in every respect. (53)

For the attainment of knowledge regarding those things to be brought under control, for the pacification of all obstacles, for the acquisition of prosperity as well as health, and for the pacification of the afflictions of disease; || 54 ||
For victory, for the crossing over all calamities, for the attainment of perfection,
for the acquisition of sons, and for protection from all [dangers], one should worship them in that sequence.
For the protection of elephants, horses, cattle, donkeys, and camels, as well as for the pacification of their afflictions such as diseases, [these rites should be performed] in due order. (56)

In all rites, one should repeatedly write the nine constellations (*nakṣatras*) in their proper sequence. This means that the writing of the constellations should be done in the seventh case (*saptamī-vibhakti*), ending in the seventh case. Regarding the term "the lords" (*nāthān*), it is singular; however, "the goddesses" (*devīḥ*) is plural because of the multiplicity of the diagrams (*yantras*).

The syntactical connection here is with the phrase "one should worship the Lords and the Goddesses. According to that sequence—that is, starting from the east and so forth—on the aforementioned day, one should worship those mandalas and deities, using the plural number as before. In the expression "in Kedāra and so forth," *kedāra* refers to a sacred field (*kṣetra*). The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to gardens, pleasure groves, and the like.
The meaning of the passage beginning with "evam" (thus) has been stated. "Auspicious rites" refers to the subjugation (*vaśya*) and other rites to be described hereafter.
"By this [method]" means by the procedure already explained. By the words "by another number," etc., the following is intended:
without this *Sarvamaṅgalā*, among the other fifteen *Nityās*...

The sequence of application for these machines—which have been fashioned according to the stated order and whose total number is combined with the previously mentioned count—is also this very same sequence as described. Likewise, for the attainment of Lakṣmī, [one should apply them] to those machines in that sequence;
and when afflictions arise, [it is applied] according to the previously stated order for their pacification.

The meaning is: for the pacification of afflictions, in those respective yantras employed for subjugation (*vaśya*) and other purposes, as well as in others, according to the sequence of nine-by-nine [grids] respectively;
that is to say, sixteen groups of nine, each consisting of nine enclosures, starting from the first lunar day (*tithi*).

The connection with the subsequent phrase is "one should worship. Having fashioned nine yantras in the first group of nine (p. 345), one should place Śivā there in each respective location for the sake of attaining those specific results mentioned in those various rites. || 57 ||
In those [days] beginning with the first, on each lunar day (tithi), there are sixteen [forms] endowed with nine walls, described according to their stated forms; therein is that Sarvamaṅgalā.
One should worship her for the attainment of one's desires; at the outset, one should always bestow [offerings].
In this way, through worship, recitation, and other rites, she brings about great accomplishment.

This mandala, obtained through traditional lineage, is drawn for the purpose of arranging the nine sets of sixteen yantras of Sarvamaṅgalā. As follows: having laid out five lines each toward the east, west, south, and north at equal intervals according to one's desired measurement, [one proceeds] within those sixteen squares.
In each [square], having created nine compartments by drawing two parallel lines horizontally and two vertically at regular intervals,
one should [place the letters] in those sixteen [squares], starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and ending in the center, following a clockwise path, within each of the nine [sub-groups].

One should arrange the yantras in all those squares, proceeding in order from the east and moving clockwise through the interior until the center. What is meant by this taken together is that, by extracting nine yantras at a time from the aforementioned total number until they are exhausted, there are nine [groups] of nine.

Having inscribed the diagrams (*yantra*) in the previously mentioned nine-square mandala, proceeding clockwise from the east to the center, one should write within the middle of that diagram the names of the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī, Maghā, and Mūla, ending in the seventh case (locative) inflection.
Having written the nine-by-nine grids of constellations together with their respective *sādhya*s in this sequence,

and having written them again and again, one should perform the worship of the respective yantras and so forth within those specific constellations in the upper nine-by-nine grids until the attainment of the fruit. Furthermore, there is the previously mentioned yantra consisting of nine times nine times sixteen.

Having drawn the sixteen-square mandala with nine inner squares as previously described, and having worshipped according to the aforementioned sequence on each of the fifteen lunar days from the first (pratipad) to the fifteenth (pañcadaśī), one should worship within each of the nine squares— starting from the second set of nine squares among the fifteen sets of nine— for each respective lunar day.

On all lunar days (tithis), one should first worship in the first group of nine squares situated in the eastern direction. In this manner, until the attainment of the fruit, one should draw the subsequent sixteen groups of nine as well; by worshipping on the lunar days, this "All-Auspicious" (Sarvamaṅgalā) [arrangement] brings about the attainment of all fruits. Herein—

The secondary number, consisting of one hundred and forty-four, is exhausted by the nine ornaments of number; and the primary number is likewise [exhausted] in that same manner. Therefore, it is the tradition that these possess the nature of the Lord (Nātha) and the nature of the sixteen Nityās. || 59 ||
O Śiva, tell me the concise ritual of mantra for their worship, which grants the accomplishment of all aims, is complete yet not overly prolix, and is auspicious. (50)
O Goddess, O captivating one, I shall describe to you the secret worship which is the refuge of celestial sages, perfected beings, gandharvas, yakṣas, and divine women; listen! 61.
Having first performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) on the hands and limbs with the Kulasundarī Vidyā,
and having worshipped her, one should then establish that Cakra upon the pedestal.
Among sandalwood, agallochum, camphor, gorocana, frankincense, and so forth,
one should properly worship them there with a single substance according to the prescribed form.
Having drawn [the design] upon the aforementioned gems and other materials and having consecrated it, one should worship it here;
[the altar] should be one-fourth of the length and width of the circular [mandala].

With the four and a half verses beginning with "laghumantre" and ending with "ittham," preceded by an introduction in the form of questions and answers, [the author describes] the hand-gestures (karāṅga) and limbs (aṅga) for the worship to be described— the worship consisting of the practice of the *laghumantra*, which is common to the sixteen *Nityās*.
It teaches the ritual of placement (*nyāsa*), the procedure for the offering (*argha*), the materials for drawing the diagrams (*yantra*), the empowerment (*adhiṣṭhāna*), and so forth.
In that regard, "short mantra-rites" means short mantras and short rituals.
Among these sixteen *Nityās*, [the author describes] the *Pūrṇā* and the *Maṅgalā* in order to avoid brevity.

It is auspicious and secret because of its divine nature. By means of that Kulasundarī, the *cakra*—which will be described as having the form of twelve angles—is [to be formed]. The word "that" (*tat*) is an adjective qualifying the *cakra*. The phrase "having prepared it with a single substance" connects with what precedes. In that *cakra*, those Nityās [are to be placed] in the aforementioned manner.

Having installed [the deity] in the form to be described—just as it was stated regarding the jewels and so forth, which were declared to be the primary, eternal, and optional [forms]—one should install the wheel; this is the remainder [of the sentence]. Here, on the wheel. || 63 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *vṛttasya* and ending with *samāsrakām*, he teaches the sequence for constructing the twelve-spoked wheel. Here, the phrase "from one-fourth of both the length and the width" means by the measure of one-fourth of either the length or the width.

Regarding those marks, the remaining [details] are that there are twelve lines; the remaining [details] are that the three marks form a twelve-cornered wheel. At their vital points—that is, at the locations where the pairs of lines of the twelve [sides] intersect—in the very center, one should [draw] the *yoni*.

A triangle facing oneself. This is what is meant: having produced a circle by means of a rotation according to the desired measurement, one should divide its radius into twenty-four parts, and within those divisions—
Having fashioned the circle and marked the signs upon it, one should drop the lines;
by releasing three [lines] from the interior, a twelve-cornered [figure] is thereby produced. (65)
One should place a pair of circles among their vital points (marmas) and in their center;
in the middle of that central circle, one should fashion a yoni with equal sides.
As before, one should worship the three Nityās in the corners, proceeding clockwise;
one should then worship the other twelve [deities] in the remaining corners in sequence.
First, one should perform a circumambulation from left to right and then offer the bali-oblation according to the prescribed rite;
one should worship Lalitā alone with the seven-syllabled mantra alone.
Having drawn two circles— one from the interior of the seventh part of the circumference and another from the interior of the sixth part—
and having divided the diameter of the very outer circle, or either its length or width,
into eighty-four parts, one should mark twelve points around the entire outer circle starting from the fourth part.

Having marked those points with signs such that each sign is separated from the next by three intervals, one should strike twelve lines in this sequence; then, in the center of the central circle, one should fashion a *yoni* facing oneself, with its sides equal as before. When this has been done:

Thus, the twelve-spoked wheel (dvādaśāsracakra), which consists of the twelve vital points (marmas) accompanied by the inner triangle (adhyonivṛtta) and contains the central triangle within its center, is said to have the form previously described. || 66 ||

With the two verses beginning with *prāgvat* and ending with *yajet*, he teaches the abbreviated worship (*laghupūjā*) for the remaining [deities] in that wheel. Therein, as before, those situated above the central one are [worshipped] in the corners;
in the three triangles situated in the very center, [the order is] clockwise, starting from the front (*agra*). The others [are worshipped] after the three.

To the other Nityās located in the external corners—meaning, twelve Nityās in each of the twelve [corners]—the remainder [of the instruction is as follows]: "in order," meaning sequentially from the front in a clockwise direction; this connects with what precedes.
One should offer the *bali* at the very end of the worship, according to the rules, using substances such as food and so forth, along with the appropriate mudrā.

"With the seven-syllable [mantra] alone"—the remainder being "Kurukullā. The syntactical connection is that one should offer the oblation (*bali*) with this phrase. Between the worship [of Kurukullā] and [the next], "Lalitā alone" means her whose name is Lalitā, namely the third section of the *Lalitānityā* [Tantra]. This is the meaning.

The meaning is that when performing the worship of the principal [deity] as the primary member (*aṅgin*) in this constant practice, one should recite the respective *vidyā* when performing the worship of the other fifteen [deities] as the primary members. That the *Lalitā-vidyā* consists of three parts (*khaṇḍa*), while the other two consist of two parts each, is stated in the third chapter.

He has taught this himself. This is what is meant: having worshipped Lalitā with the third segment of the Vidyā in the center of the central *yoni* within the previously mentioned twelve-spoked wheel, one [should worship] the three [deities] in the three corners of that *yoni*, proceeding clockwise from the front.
In all worship rituals, the vidyās should always be [recited] by means of the names of the sixteen Nityās, beginning with Lalitā, and by means of the seven-syllabled mantras of the Nityās. (69)
One should constantly worship those sixteen Nityās with those sixteen Vidyās.
Listen now as I shall state, in due order, the number of syllables in each of those Vidyās.
The first and the seventh [mantras] shall be the sixteen-syllable Vidyā;
those of the second and the fourth shall consist of fourteen syllables.
And from the third, the sixth, the tenth,
the twelfth, the fourteenth, and the fifteenth [tithis], there are indeed fifteen [units] in sequence.
Having propitiated Kāmeśvarī, Vajreśvarī, and Bhagamālinī with their respective vidyās,

one should worship the other twelve Nityās— beginning with Nityaklinnā— in the twelve corners, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, using their respective vidyās; and having offered the bali at the end with the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā.

One should recite only the third section. Regarding the worship of the limbs and the principal deity among the other fifteen [Nityās], one should worship the three [sections] following that as before with those Vidyās;
then, the twelve Nityās following that are to be worshipped in sequence within the twelve corners.

Having worshipped with their respective vidyās and having offered the bali-oblation to all of them with the seven-syllabled mantra of Kurukullā, one should recite those respective vidyās. In that worship, "in the inner-twelfth" means one should worship her situated in the center within the twelve-angled [mandala]. || 68 ||
By means of these five verses beginning with *nityānām* and ending with *uditāḥ*, [the author] explains the names and forms of each of the sixteen *nityās*,
as well as the number of syllables for each, and how by means of those names, forms, and vidyās, [they reside] in that twelve-spoked wheel (*dvādaśāra-cakra*).

And he teaches the procedure for worship (*pūjāvidhāna*). In that regard, by name, [the mantra] consists of the seven syllables beginning with "Tripurasundarī" as proclaimed in the third chapter; [specifically], the two syllables "Nityā" followed by the aforementioned seven-syllabled mantra—these constitute the [mantra].

There is a syntactical connection (*anvaya*) with the preceding and following [words]. By this, the meaning is that there should be the aforementioned types of *vidyās*. "Always" (*sarvadā*) means eternally; by those names and forms, is the meaning. The phrase "the triad of *vidyās* also [consists of] the five tens" is the connection here. The three words beginning with "of the fifth" (*pañcamyāḥ*) and so forth [are to be understood as follows].

The thirteen syllables preceding the specific qualification of the mantra are as before. The phrase "of the eleventh," and so forth, refers to the three [syllables] as previously stated; the remainder is that twelve letters have been declared. This is what is meant:
in the instruction on the sixteen Vidyās in the third chapter concerning the sixteen Nityās, of whichever [Vidyā]...

Regarding the names such as "Tripurasundarī" and others that have been proclaimed, at the end of each of them, one should join the seven-syllable mantra of the Nityās to form a nine-syllable mantra for all of them, according to the tradition. First, for all [the goddesses], [one joins the Nityā-mantra]; then, for each individually, [one applies it] to the fifth, the ninth, and the thirteenth [syllables]. The thirteenth [syllable] of the thirteenth [group]—p. 349).
The [fingers] of the eleventh, eighth, and sixteenth [tithis] are said to be twelve.
In this very wheel, one should likewise worship with twenty-four [deities],
and for the sake of accomplishment, one should recite those various Vidyās one hundred and twenty times.
There are another twenty-seven hundred [mantras]; worship is not performed with those yantras.
Regarding these [mantras], the performance of worship, japa, and so forth, as well as their application in yantras, has been explained.
This is the concise method of the machine that bestows all aims;
by means of it, one who possesses the vajra-form should accomplish everything taught in the tantra. (76)

[Verse 36] The hundred-and-forty-first mantra has one hundred and seventy-one syllables; the hundred-and-forty-second has one hundred and seventy-two; the hundred-and-forty-third has one hundred and seventy-three; and the hundred-and-forty-fourth has one hundred and seventy-four. [Verse 37] The hundred-and-forty-fifth mantra has one hundred and seventy-five syllables; the hundred-and-forty-sixth has one hundred and seventy-six; the hundred-and-forty-seventh has one hundred and seventy-seven; and the hundred-and-forty-eighth has one hundred and seventy-eight. [Verse 38] The hundred-and-forty-ninth mantra has one hundred and seventy-nine syllables; the hundred-and-fiftieth has one hundred and eighty; the hundred-and-fifty-first has one hundred and eighty-one; and the hundred-and-fifty-second has one hundred and eighty-two. [Verse 39] The hundred-and-fifty-third mantra has one hundred and eighty-three syllables; the hundred-and-fifty-fourth has one hundred and eighty-four; the hundred-and-fifty-fifth has

"By means of the letters of the names occurring in sequence through these sixteen syllables— [which are] like mountains [unshaken] by the song of non-attachment to all worlds— the number is thus determined. Thus,
the sixteenth Vidyā is seen to consist of names with the aforementioned number of syllables, appearing in their respective forms as names according to the preceding Vidyās.
One should worship the sixteen Nityās in the previously mentioned twelve-spoked wheel according to the sequence stated before. || 73 ||

By means of these two verses beginning with "asmin" and ending with "samīritam," [the author] describes the six syllables of the *khaṇḍa* of the mantra of Lalitā— the primordial *Nityā*— by means of the phonemes that will be explained further below.

By means of the twenty-four *vidyās* produced from the divisions of the four-syllable [mantra], by the twenty-four *vidyās* produced from the twenty-four divisions, by the one hundred and twenty *vidyās* situated within the subdivisions of those five syllables,
and by the [vidyās] produced from the six syllables— more than twenty...
In this very wheel of twelve spokes that has been described, he teaches the propitiation of that Lalitā by means of seven hundred vidyās; therein,
by those various vidyās, through those specific forms of the vidyās worshipped within the yantras.
"In the various chapters to be described" refers to those [chapters]. "Of these" refers to the aforementioned number of vidyās.

In the phrase "worship, recitation, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to libations (tarpaṇa), fire-offerings (homa), and the like. The phrase "the prescribed procedure" is the ellipsis to be supplied. This applies to the worship and other rites of these aforementioned number of vidyās, as well as to their yantras.

The meaning is that the procedure has been stated. Here, the double mention of "in the yantras" serves the purpose of providing both a summary and an elaboration. What is intended is as follows: regarding the ritual of worship for Lalitā, the principal Nityā, within the center of her twelve-spoked wheel (*dvādaśāracakra*).
One should worship with the prescribed number of vidyās generated from the various divisions of the syllables of the third section of that [Vidyā].
With these, one should perform the worship and other rites even upon the yantras to be described in the chapter on yantras. || 75 ||

With these eight verses beginning with "etad" and ending with "koṇataḥ," [it is said]: "The Vajra of those sixteen Nityās is declared to be twofold, according to the division of its nature as consisting of squares and corners. (p. 350)
The applications for the emanation of the vajra of the self at the corners [are taught] further on, O Śivā. (77)

I shall now describe, according to the rule, the form of the *vajra* for those two storehouses (*koṣṭha*), which, like the celestial tree (*surāṅghripa*), brings about the attainment of whatever the practitioner desires. (78)
By means of twenty-four lines drawn east-west, north-south, south, and north,
there will indeed be five hundred squares by twenty-nine [lines].
In the corners, one should erase sixty squares using six lines as before;
in the remaining spaces, there are two hundred and sixty-five squares forming the faces of the vajras.
He teaches the procedure for constructing the Vajra-machine in the form of a grid (*koṣṭha*) through the twenty-four varieties of *Lalitā*.

In this regard, the remainder of the sense is: "I shall tell you that which is about to be described. By means of that machine, one should accomplish everything taught in the Tantra, because it consists of the syllables of the sixteen *Nityā* mantras. Hereafter...

In the chapter on the Yantras: regarding those two [yantras] consisting of squares and corners, the phrase "the yantra is equal to the feet of the gods" means that its independence is equal. Within those squares, numbering five hundred and twenty-nine, and in the corners—that is, in the directions of the corners—by means of six...

The word "combined" (*sahitāni*) is to be supplied; the meaning is "sixty-six squares. "As before" means that it should be such that the form of a vajra appears in the center. And within those two hundred and sixty-five squares, by groups of four, starting from the bottom, the middle, and the outside in each direction.
Starting from the outer square in the middle of the five squares located in the bottom-most row,
the syllables of the name-mantra (nāmavidyā), beginning with Citrā and ending with Lalitā, are combined.

The meaning is "numbering two hundred and twenty-five. The meaning is "in the remaining twenty-four squares. The phrase "produced from the fourfold division of the letters of Lalitā" is to be construed with the word "twenty-four. [It refers to] the interior of the *hṛllekhā* syllables situated within those twenty-four, joined with the name and the *śakti*.

The meaning is that one should write the name as before. One should write the third [syllable] of Lalitā containing the *sādhya* (the object of the rite) within it, as before, with the *sādhya* situated in the *hṛllekhā*. "From the middle corner" means in the center and in the triangles.
By this, the meaning is that one should write the Vidyā in its twenty-four forms in reverse order. When this has been done:
The meaning is that the twenty-four *anuloma* forms are to be written in the middle;
that is to say, one should write them within the four sets of triangles. This is what is intended:
having first stretched out twenty-four threads with equal intervals running east-west and north-south.

Having prepared five hundred and twenty-nine squares, and having placed sixty-six squares in each of the four corner directions— thus totaling two hundred and sixty-four squares— one should arrange them in the center in the form of a vajra.
Having cleansed [the area], one should draw a vajra in the center (p.

351). Within those, having fashioned four triangular fields in the four directions using four squares each, starting from the outer edge and proceeding clockwise, one should place them below the center.
One should draw [the grid] starting from the entry-point up to the end of the "Lalita" section;
then, in the remaining central space, one should write the twenty-four syllables of the *khaṇḍārṇa*.

One should write the goddess Lalitā from the middle corner, joined with the power (śakti) of her name, which is produced by the fourfold division of the letters of Lalitā, and containing within it the object of attainment (sādhya). 83.
Having thus drawn this yantra on stone, the three metals, or other materials,
and having installed it in some location, one should worship it for the attainment of one's desires.
In whatever region the Vajrayantra is installed, for a distance of one yojana, only auspicious things arise; no talk of inauspiciousness shall occur. (85)
In the remaining two hundred and sixty-five squares, having cleared sixteen squares— four in each of the four directions as before—
therein one should draw four equilateral triangles with equal lines, and in what remains...
In the two hundred and forty-nine squares [of the grid],

beginning from the central square of the five squares in the bottommost row and proceeding in a clockwise, inward-moving manner, one should place [the letters] starting with *Citrā* and ending with *Lalitā* according to the liberated sequence (*muktakrama*).

Having written the syllables of the sixteen Nityās, which are the letters of the Vidyā numbering two hundred and twenty-five, until their total count is completed, [one should fill] the remaining twenty-four squares in between.
Taking the first syllable from each of the subsequent squares written previously and proceeding by a clockwise entry-path,

one generates the twenty-four-fold Vidyā produced from the variations of the four syllables of Lalitā; this [Vidyā] is in its natural (anuloma) form, accompanied by the triad beginning with the practitioner situated within the *hṛllekhā*, with Lalitā herself as the first element positioned in the center, as follows:
Likewise, having written it in reverse order, one should write the *Lalitā* in its natural (*anuloma*) form located in the center of all;

then, having written the three names as before within the belly of the *Hṛllekhā*, one should write that very same [mantra] within the four triangles situated in the four directions, with the *sādhya* (the object of the rite) placed inside. Thus ends verse 83.

With the two verses beginning with *evam* and ending with *bhavet*, he teaches the fruits of the previously mentioned application of the yantra. In that context, in the phrase "the three metals, etc.," the word "etc.
(*ādi*) refers to gems and so forth. Having established—that is, having placed [the yantra]—preceded by the ritual of infusing life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other rites...
"An inauspicious discourse" means the word "inauspicious"; "in that" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. || 85 ||
And in the worship-circle (pūjācakra), having written their names in each corner, one should draw Lalitā in the center, containing the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). || 86 ||
One should place the Mātṛkā and that wheel on the ground outside the enclosure;
by that means, as previously stated, there shall be no misfortune in the region.

Having inscribed that most auspicious Vidyā everywhere upon it, one should place it in the center accompanied by the syllables of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), for the attainment of its fruit. || 88 ||
Having placed the pitcher, filled with the decoction of a tree of that same color, upon either the previously mentioned Vajrayantra or upon a twelve-spoked [yantra] of Śiva; 89.
One should perform an auspicious consecration with waters over which the Vidyā has been recited according to the prescribed rule,
especially on the days of one's birth-star, for the sake of pacifying all dissolutions.
For the sake of the perfection of previous merits and for the pacification of planetary afflictions, diseases,

and so forth, [the ritual is performed] in the previously mentioned twelve-cornered wheel (*dvādaśakoṇacakra*) by means of sixteen verses beginning with "In the circle of worship" (*pūjācakra*) and ending with "unmanifest" (*abhavyakta*), according to the sequence of worship described above.
In each of the aforementioned locations, one should write down the mantra of each individual name;

outside of that, on the circular path (*vṛttavīthī*), he teaches the respective application (*viniyoga*) pertaining to the writing of the *mātṛkā*. In this regard, the following is intended: in the twelve-spoked wheel, one should place Lalitā in the very center as previously described.

Having depicted the one to be accomplished (the sādhya), and having written the name-mantras (nāmavidyā) of the fifteen Nityās in the other locations according to the order of worship, and having inscribed the Mātṛkā in direct order along with the bindus on the outermost circular path, the attainment of the previously mentioned fruit results from installing [the yantra] in the aforementioned place. || 87 ||

With the verse beginning with "In that" (*tasmin*), he teaches that by writing the *Sarvamaṅgalā-vidyā* in all locations within the previously mentioned twelve-cornered wheel (*cakra*) and applying it (*viniyoga*), the aforementioned results are accomplished; specifically, [the mantra] should be written there together with the syllable of the object to be achieved (*sādhya*) in the center, and not elsewhere. 88.
With one and a half verses beginning with *prāgukta* and ending with *śāntaye*,

he teaches the auspicious results arising from the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) of the previously mentioned twelve-cornered wheel of the vajra-mechanism (*vajrayantra*). In that regard, the tree of that color...

Then, for the sake of increasing previous prosperity and for the attainment of the previously mentioned fruits, one should employ the medicinal herbs prescribed according to the letters of the *vidyā* of Lalitā herself— which exists as the very limbs (*aṅga*) of her *vidyā*— in a twelve-angled *vajra* diagram during the birth asterisms or the three [other] births. || 91 ||
Likewise, O Goddess of the Gods, there is another practice that purifies all. (91)
It is a forest fire for the jungle of poverty, a submarine fire for the ocean of sin,
a sun for the darkness of contraction, and the rising of the moon for the ocean of contentment.
Being composed and observing silence, one should recite the eternal Vidyā, which was previously described as being interspersed with syllables, and worship it with fragrant flowers. (93)
One should satisfy [the ancestors] with auspicious waters originating from rivers flowing to the ocean,
and one should offer fragrant white sesame seeds and rice according to the prescribed rite.
Having established the water-pot filled with the prescribed water and having recited the mantra over it with devotion,
one should perform the entire consecration by means of those [waters] once, following the proper sequence.
One is instantly liberated from the sufferings of terrible sorcery, malevolent rites, and the like, as well as from the afflictions caused by bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and so forth. (96)
The Kumāras, Guhyakas, Vīras, and the fierce Ḍākinīs and others, becoming terrified, release [the victim] at that very moment and depart elsewhere in an instant. (97)

With the six verses beginning with "tathānyadapi" and ending with "kṣaṇāt," he teaches the fruit resulting from the recitation (japa) and other practices of the aforementioned number of Vidyās— which are produced by joining the Mātṛkā-letters and the sixteen vowels at the beginning and end of the Nityā Sarvamaṅgalā.

In this context, the remainder of the sentence is "I shall explain it in the application" (*prayoga*). Poverty is a forest fire for the forest of poverty; that which is called "poverty" is dissatisfaction (*atuṣṭi*). That which is called "sin" (*pāpa*) is acting without reflection. "Contraction" (*saṅkoca*) refers to negative latent impressions (*durvāsanā*).
"Contentment" (*santoṣa*) is the experience of one's own true nature (*svarūpānubhava*). [This refers to] that which is intermingled with the syllables previously mentioned.

"Intermingled at the beginning and end with the sixteen vowels of the *mātṛkā* expansion"—this [phrase] breaks the sequence to indicate that one should make the *vidyā* "All-Auspicious" (*sarvamaṅgalā*). And one should worship the eternal All-Auspicious One with fragrant substances and water; this is the connection with what precedes. "With pure [substances]"—thus [it is said].

This is an adjective qualifying sesame and rice; the meaning is that one should place [them] in any one of the twelvefold mixtures and so forth. It is filled with the aforementioned water—that is, filled entirely with water consisting of decoctions of the root, the vidyā-mantra syllables, and medicinal herbs, or with water from ocean-going rivers.
The syntactical connection here is: "having recited [the mantra] once, according to the number prescribed for that [deity].

By means of those waters, one is protected from the miseries of terrible malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and the like; the word "and the like" refers to planetary afflictions and similar matters. *Tam* refers to the one who has been consecrated. || 97 ||

Standing in the water of a river flowing to the ocean, one should cause those [waters] to circulate; by immersing oneself up to the neck, one is liberated from the sins of previous births and so forth. (98)
In the same way, through oblations of ghee, libations, and pure waters, she who is proclaimed as the source of all auspiciousness becomes Sarvamaṅgalā. 99.
May he grant, through his compassion, the fruit corresponding to the names of those who take refuge in him—by being ever-quickly gracious and by constantly generating joy. (100)
The pervasive extension consisting of the reality of smell has been correctly explained; through its refinement within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self. (101)

Thus, in the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantra* according to the *Kādimata*, the nineteenth chapter is fully concluded. Furthermore, by means of the three verses beginning with "Samudragā" and ending with "api ca," [the nature] of Sarvamaṅgalā is described.

He teaches the fruit, such as the destruction of sins, resulting from the recitation (*japa*) of the mantra according to the stated number of times. In this context, "by long-standing evil tendencies" refers to those originating from previous births and so forth. Likewise, the meaning is that one is liberated by means of [the mantra] originating from previous births and so forth.
Thus, in the manner described, she is "possessing all auspiciousness," meaning she is of the nature of all blessings.

This is the meaning. The word "by compassion" (kṛpayā) connects with both what precedes and what follows. The phrase "by bestowing the fruit," and so forth, connects with the statement that the names of the perfected states (siddhānāṃ padānām) correspond to their actual nature. [These names are so called] because they produce joy and because they consist in the experience of one's true nature. || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha— entitled *Prapañcasārasihārājaprakāśa*— upon the complete *Tantra* known as the venerable *Kādimata*, which is among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The nineteenth chapter, which elucidates the ritual procedures for the eternal *Sarvamaṅgalā-avidyā*, is thus fully concluded and examined. 19.
Regarding the number of verses:
in the nineteenth chapter,
three hundred and eighteen and a half verses have been correctly counted through careful examination.
In this regard, there are one million three hundred thousand yantras,
as well as one thousand two hundred and twenty-six more.
As far as has been sent: 26/5/08, Chapter Twenty-six.
Now, regarding the sixteen Nityās, that which is proclaimed as the fifteenth—
Listen, O wise one, to its ritual procedure; it is proclaimed as Jvālāmālinī. || 1 ||

Listen now in due order to the ritual placement (nyāsa), meditation (dhyāna), the powers (śaktis), the worship (pūjā), the means of accomplishment (sādhana), the diagrams (yantras), the applications (viniyoga), and the fruits [of these practices]. || 2 ||
One should form the limbs (aṅgas) with one, two, four, five, four, and ten syllables;
first, with the six root-syllables, one should perform [the nyāsa] on the hands and the limbs.
Resembling a blazing fire, radiant with a crown of rubies,
she has six faces and twelve arms, and is adorned with all ornaments.

(26 la 27 sa 1 Śaddīśrīḥ) Having taught the procedure for the Caturdaśī Sarvamaṅgalā Nityā-vidyā in the preceding nineteenth chapter, he subsequently teaches the procedure for the Pañcadaśī Jvālāmālinī Nityā, beginning with the words "Now, the sixteen Nityās," and so forth.
By means of the twentieth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "vaibhavāt" and ending with "iti," [the author] explains the contents.
