Therein, by means of two verses beginning with "atha ṣoḍaśa" and ending with "kramāt," he indicates the subject matter of the chapter. In that context, "Jvālāmālinī has been cited" means that the Jvālāmālinī-vidyā was taught in the third chapter.

The powers (śaktis) reside in the coverings (āvaraṇas); "of those machines" (yantrāṇām)—this is the ellipsis for "viniyogas" (applications). "In order" means according to the sequence previously stated. || 2 ||

With the verse beginning with "eka," he teaches the ritual placement (nyāsa) of the hands and limbs. In this context, "from the beginning" refers to the root-mantra (mūlavidyā). What is meant is as follows:
the heart is [assigned] by means of the syllable *praṇava* which constitutes the beginning of the root-mantra, and [the head is assigned] by means of the two syllables following that.

One should worship the head with the four syllables situated above that, the crest-lock (śikhā) with the five syllables situated above that, the armor (kavaca) with the four syllables situated above that, the eyes with the [three] syllables situated above that,
and the weapon (astra) with the ten syllables situated above that— in this sequence, using distinct [mantras] belonging to their respective classes.

Having first combined [the syllables] from the beginning of the root-mantra syllables into six mantras consisting of twenty-six syllables each, one should perform the assignment of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), preceded by the ritual placement on the hands (karanyāsa). || 3 ||

With these three verses beginning with "jvalat" and ending with "anvitām," he teaches the visualization for the daily worship of the Goddess together with her retinue. Here, she has six faces— these being the upward direction, the transcendent direction, and the four cardinal directions—
and twelve arms.
Holding in her lotus-like hands a noose and a goad, a sword and a shield, a bow and arrows, a mace, a trident and fire, and displaying the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness. (5)
She is surrounded on all sides by Śaktis equal to herself,
possessing a lotus-face with a beautiful smile and endowed with three eyes.
Having meditated thus, one should worship her constantly with those ritual offerings;
having constructed two squares provided with four gates.
Having fashioned an eight-petaled lotus with its stalks, then an eight-cornered [figure] within it,
a hexagon, and a triangle in the center, one should worship Śivā there.
One should worship the powers of will, knowledge, and action, situated in the triangle in their respective order;
then the Ḍākinīs and others in the hexagon, and the Ghasmarīs and others in the octagon.
The voracious one, who swallows the universe, with restless eyes and a flickering tongue;
she who devours all, the thousand-eyed one, free from attachment, and fond of dissolution.

The arms [are arranged] two by two for each face. Here, the sequence of weapons should be understood as starting from the upper left and ending at the lower right, with each one alternating. "Endowed with three eyes" applies to each face; the word "one should meditate" is to be supplied. || 6 ||

With the two verses beginning with *dhyātvaiva* and ending with *yajet*, he teaches the construction of the wheel for daily worship (*nityasaparyā*) preceded by a conclusion. Therein, *evam* means in the manner described; *taiḥ* means by those sixteen [deities]; *tām* refers to that root deity; and *saśākham* means along with the four branches at the four doors.
The meaning is "accompanied by two branches. "Inside" means within the yantra; from that, an octagon [is formed], with "inside" being the understood remainder.
"In the middle" means in the very center. This is what is intended:
two squares, divided into inner and outer parts as before.

Having constructed [the mandala] provided with two branches and four doors, one should fashion within it an eight-petalled lotus with two surrounding circles; within that, likewise, an eight-cornered [figure] with two surrounding circles;
and within that, as before, a six-cornered [figure] with two surrounding circles.
Having fashioned an equilateral triangle with three lines according to the proper measurement, one should perform worship there.
With these five verses beginning with *icchā* and ending with *samīritam*,

he teaches the five-fold enclosures of power (*pañcāvaraṇa-śakti*) and their worship within the perpetual ritual service (*nityasaparyā*). Therein, in due order, proceeding clockwise from the front [corner], one should [install them] in the corners of the hexagon, as described in the chapter on Nityānityā.

In the order of the corners starting from the northeast (īśāna) direction, one should worship Ghasmarā and the others on the eight outer petals, proceeding clockwise in the following verse (p. 357): "One should worship Acintyā, Aprameyā, Pūrṇarūpā, and Durāsadā. (11)
One should worship those previously mentioned [deities], who are all-pervading, the very form of accomplishment, purifying, and of a single nature, at the outer doors and corners.

Having performed the worship as before, one should worship that [wheel] in the stated sequence as described, up to the conclusion of the offerings and oblations; thus it has been correctly explained. (13)
One who has conquered the senses and subsists on sacrificial food (haviṣya) should recite the vidyā eight hundred thousand times;
one should then perform the libation (tarpaṇa) and the fire-oblation (homa) with cow’s ghee, each being a tenth part of that [recitation]. 14.
Thus, one whose mantra has been perfected should fashion the yantras in due order.

With the verse beginning with "ghasmare" (the devourer) which is about to be spoken, he teaches the eight Śaktis to be worshipped in the eight corners; therein, the worship proceeds clockwise starting from the front. From the outer eight-cornered [figure]...
On the eight outer petals are these [deities] to be described, beginning with Acintyā; they are arranged clockwise starting from the front.

This arrangement, excluding the Ḍākinīs and others, is common to all. With the two half-verses beginning with "Acintyā" and ending with "ekarūpiṇīm," he teaches the Śaktis to be worshipped on the eight petals.

"At the outer gates" means at the square gates. "As previously mentioned" means that it is stated in the chapter on ritual procedures (*vidhānapaṭala*) regarding Nityānityā that one should place the eight powers of the world-protectors (*lokapāla*), beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Īśāna (i.e., Indra), as well as the four powers of Ananta, Brahmā, Niyati, and Kāla, within the square.

In this regard, it is said that one should worship according to the sequence of commencement. As before, with the limb-mantras (*aṅga*) and the root-mantra (*mūla*), in the previously mentioned wheel, one should worship that Goddess according to the stated sequence—by way of moving from the interior to the exterior, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise—up to the conclusion of the *bali* offering and the *homa*. What is meant by this is as follows: first...

The meaning is that, having offered the bali with the sixteen-syllable mantra at the end followed by the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) according to the stated sequence; "the worship" has been described—this is the ellipsis. || 13 ||

With the verse beginning "eight hundred thousand" (*aṣṭalakṣam*), he teaches the procedure for the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) of the Vidyā. In this context, "eating sacrificial food" (*haviṣyāśī*) is as previously described; "having conquered the senses" (*jitendriyaḥ*) means being devoid of indulgence in women, conversation with them, and so forth.

Then, by the word "and" (*ca*) in the phrase "the number of recitations and the libation," it is drawn that the libation should consist of one-tenth of the recitation count. [The libation] is performed with cow's ghee.
The mention of "cow" is for the purpose of excluding the clarified butter of goats and other animals. || 14 ||

With these seven verses beginning with *evam* and ending with *dhruvam*, [the author] provides the instruction for the construction of the ten yantras and introduces their application and so forth. (p.
358) On the worship-circle, outside [the central area], on an unbroken square: || 15 ||
Having prepared that [space], one should inscribe the syllables according to the rule: in the very center, within the *tāra*, one should place the *śakti* accompanied by the name. (16)

And the yantra [is arranged] with six [squares] in three corners, then eight in six [corners], and likewise an octagon outside; thus, on the exterior, nine [squares] are placed in sequence in the directions.
Having thus prepared the yantra with the root-syllables, one should accomplish all that is desired through worship, wearing, and installation, O Śivā. (18)
Within the letters beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa' joined with vowels,
one should write the fourfold [groups] in the yantra according to their respective positions by means of those letters.

He performs [the rite]. Regarding that, the *yantras* will be described hereafter. Having made a square that is undivided—meaning having fashioned two squares within a four-doored [mandala] without breaking the internal lines—therein, the syllables of the *jvālāmālinī-vidyā* [should be placed] according to the prescribed rule.

According to the method to be described: in the very center, that is, within the triangle; in the womb of the *tāra*, that is, in the midst of the *praṇava* which is the first of the mantras; the *śakti*, which consists of the forty-five syllables of the root-vidyā and the three *hṛllekhās*.

"Vidyā" refers to the second syllable and so forth. "In the three corners" means in the corners of the triangle; the word "in the six corners" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. The "group of six" is that which follows the previously mentioned group of three. "In the eight corners" is the syntactical connection; the "group of eight" is that which follows the previously mentioned group of six, and likewise externally. [This applies] to the eight petals.

This means that one should write the group of eight syllables following the previously mentioned eight; externally, in the cardinal directions, according to the sequence of nine, within the square, in each direction, by the sequence of nine, there are thirty-six syllables in total across the four directions.
The meaning is that one should write [the syllables] excluding the previously mentioned forty-sixth syllable, *hṛllekhā*.

This is done with the sixty-three root-syllables. By means of that yantra—by this half-verse beginning with "accompanied by the letter 'a' and so forth" and ending with "samanvitam"—the following is stated.
By means of the five hundred and seventy-six letters of the *mātṛkā*-expansion, consisting of thirty-six syllables from *a* to *kṣa*, each conjoined with the sixteen vowels.
By means of the sequence of the sixty-four syllables of the four groups (*caturvarga*) as previously described in the yantra, combined with the syllables of the Vidyā,
there are nine yantras formed by writing the sixty-third syllables in their respective positions and writing the sixty-fourth syllable in the very center, according to the previously stated method.

By means of the syllables of the root-vidyā alone, one yantra was produced, which then resulted in ten yantras. The connection [of the sentence] is: "from the application of those yantras. That is, the attainment of the fruit is from their application; by means of which applications.
One should write the remainder thus in the center, accompanied by the syllable of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*).
In this way, ten yantras are produced; [I shall describe] them in their proper order. (20)
I shall now proclaim the attainment of results through ritual application; listen, O beloved, by which means a practitioner certainly obtains every desired object even without a yantra. (21)

The procedure for constructing the tenfold yantra is as follows: having drawn two unbroken squares, one inside the other, with equal dimensions according to the prescribed measurement, and having made an eight-petalled lotus within that space together with its circle,
one should then construct an octagon from the inner circle, touching the cardinal and intermediate directions and their corners, as previously described.
Having drawn a circle within that and a hexagon as before, and having drawn a circle within that and an equilateral triangle within it,
one should write the first syllable of the root-mantra, the *praṇava*, in the center of the central triangle, and within its interior, the mantra.
Having written the *hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) in the form of the forty-sixth letter, containing the name within it,

one should write the three letters beginning with the second letter of the *vidyā* in a clockwise direction starting from the tip of each of the three corners of the triangle; then, outside of that, in the corners of the hexagon—
Having written the six syllables previously mentioned above in the six [triangles] by proceeding clockwise from the top,
one should then write the eight syllables following those written in the hexagon, in the same order as before, upon the eight corners of the outer octagon.

Outside of that, having written the eight syllables following the previously written syllables in clockwise order upon the eight petals of the eight-petaled lotus starting from the front petal, [one should place them] in the path between the two outer squares.

Having written nine syllables in each of the four directions— starting from the west and proceeding as before, excluding the *hṛllekhā* written in the center— above the syllables previously written in the east,
totaling thirty-six syllables in this manner; thus:
Having written the sixty-three syllables of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*), one should accomplish all desired objects by means of that yantra; this is the first yantra.
Together with the syllables of the root-mantra situated in the previously mentioned yantra—
Among the five hundred and seventy-six letters of the alphabet, the letters of the first four groups— numbering sixty-four— are to be placed in the sixty-two positions of the *vidyā* syllables;
then, starting from three, up to sixty, they are repeated again in the middle.
One should write the remaining single syllable. When this is done, two syllables are seen in the center.
This is the second yantra. In the same way, other syllables from the expansion of the Mātṛkā should be placed above each of the four sets of sixty-four syllables previously written.

From the drawing of the sixty-four syllables until its completion, ten yantras come into being together with the two previously mentioned yantras; one should perform the applications in desired matters by means of them. || 21 ||
The second and subsequent diagrams, indeed joined with the letters of the Mātṛkā, shall belong respectively to the nine planets in their respective directions on their corresponding days. (22)
Because they worship those deities, they are pleased and do not cause you any misfortune,
even when Rāhu and Ketu are situated in the lord of that lunar mansion or on its day.
In the spaces between the six and eight spokes, one should correctly write the names of the planets in the second case, followed by "I satisfy [them] properly in this vessel. (24)
Having first inscribed [the mantra] upon the yantra according to the prescribed sequence,
one should then worship it on all days of the week for the sake of attaining the favor of all.
O Dear One, one should certainly worship those planets for the pacification of misfortune;
thus, they are worshipped together with Nityā within the ten yantras.
With fifty-nine verses beginning with "dvitīya" and ending with "vidhānataḥ," he teaches the specific applications of the ten yantras previously described. Among those,
[he explains] with six verses beginning with "tatra dvitīya" and ending with "vitanvate."

He teaches the applications in ten yantras through the worship of the nine planets on their respective days together with Jvālāmālinīnityā. In this context, the meaning is that the second and subsequent [yantras] consist of nine yantras, excluding the first yantra which is composed solely of the syllables of the Vidyā.
Endowed with the letters of the Mātṛkā, that is, accompanied by the syllables from the previously mentioned expansion of the Mātṛkā; in that direction,

according to the sequence to be described in the twenty-eighth chapter, one should place the Sun in the center and the auspicious planets beginning with the Moon in the cardinal directions, proceeding clockwise starting from the east.

The meaning is that [one should worship] the nine planets in the four intermediate directions starting from the southeast (vahni) and ending with the northeast (īśāna). The phrase "in those nine yantras" implies "in the positions situated above the *hṛllekhā* located in the center.
From the worship of the Goddess—that is, from the adoration of Jvālāmālinī—those nine planets [are propitiated]. This is indicated by the passage beginning with "Rāhu," and so forth.
By the second half of this verse, the following is intended: on whichever zodiac sign Rāhu and Ketu reside, the day of that respective sign’s lord is their [day].
Therefore, on those respective days, after performing the worship of the lords of those days, one should perform the worship of these two when they have reached those signs.

"In the intervals between the six and the eight [spokes], the names of the planets"—the word "in each interval" (*pratyantarālam*) is the ellipsis; the syntactical connection is that one should draw them "upon the vessel. What is meant is this: in the intervals of the hexagon and in the intervals of the octagon, the name of each respective planet who has attained the status of lord of the quarter (*vārādhipati*) [should be written] in every interval.
One should write the second-case form [of the name] followed by the end of the sentence, "I perfectly satisfy. || 24 ||

In the first [section], which is devoid of the expansion of letters from the *mātṛkā*, one should perform the drawing of the directions according to the previously mentioned sequence for each respective planet; in the center, the worship of the Goddess and so forth for all nine planets; and those planets [should be placed] in their respective locations for writing their names.
(361) Those who are pleased, even if they are cruel or always situated in cruel places, bestow only auspicious results upon those who have gone to auspicious states. || 27 ||
And when the ten yantras have been drawn by Daradas or with red ochre, and have been worshipped in this manner, [one should worship] either Kumāra or a maiden.
Having established and worshipped with the Vidyā either a beautiful maiden of very auspicious limbs who has bathed and wears clean garments, or a boy of similar qualities; || 29 ||
Having touched [the disciple] on the head, one should recite the vidyā one hundred times and likewise worship with flowers that are reddish,
white, or fragrant.
One should offer guggulu incense until the completion of the rite;
then, once the deity has entered into him, one should worship him with great care.

By the eternal Jvālāmālinī. The cruel ones are the five—Āditya, Aṅgāraka, Śani, Rāhu, and Ketu—who are cruel when situated in cruel places, such as the birth sign, the twelfth, the eighth, and so forth;
this applies generally to all nine planets. The gentle ones are the four other than the five previously mentioned.
The phrase "of those moving in auspicious [houses]" is the ellipsis; "auspicious houses" refers to the eleventh house and so forth.

This is what is meant: in the nine yantras beginning with the second, which are situated in their respective directions as previously stated, one should write the names of the planets that are the lords of those days in their respective positions on those specific days.

Having drawn [the diagram] according to the prescribed sequence and having worshipped the Goddess in the very center, one should worship the respective planets in the locations where their names are written, and then worship the powers of the eternal enclosure (*nityāvaraṇa-śakti*) in their respective places.
First, having placed the first yantra in its corresponding direction for each day of the week, one should [pronounce] the name of that respective planet.

Having drawn [the diagrams] in the previously mentioned locations as before, the attainment of the stated results occurs through the worship of each individual planet there at every session, and by the worship of the Goddess in the very center. || 27 ||

With these seven verses beginning with "In the ten" (*daśasu*) and ending with "happy" (*sukhī*), he teaches the methods for self-immersion (*svasthāveśa*) and so forth by means of the ten yantras previously mentioned. In that context, the phrase "in each one of the ten" is the intended sense; "when worshipped" means by means of the syllables of the respective vidyās written therein. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. [The term] *mugdhām* refers to the deluded [state].
"Skhalitendriyām" means one whose senses have faltered; that is, one possessed of such qualities as having very beautiful limbs and faltering senses.

"Having worshipped her a hundred times with the *jvālāmālinī* vidyā" is the meaning. "Having touched the head" means having caused possession (*āveśa*), one should worship her in that manner—a hundred times, according to the previously mentioned method of worship. "Or even so" (*athāpivā*)...

This is the meaning of the conceptual elaboration (*vikalpa*). The connection with the preceding [text] is as follows: until the completion of the ritual task—that is, up to the limit of the deity’s immersion (*samāveśa*)—one should worship that deity with offerings (*upacāra*) within those two bases in which the deity has entered, using the sixteen [offerings] previously mentioned and the *vidyā*, namely the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
"Reciting" means reciting the *vidyā*, with the understanding that it is accompanied by the ritual formulas (*upacāramantra*).

(p. 362) Then, having brought her under control by means of those aforementioned ritual services and the *vidyā*, one should worship her; thereafter, one should ask her what is desired, and she shall speak it.
O you who are fully honored, one may speak of all that has been, is being, or will be, as well as whatever else resides in the mind and all past lives in other births. (33)

Then, having worshipped her as before and dissolved her into one's own self, one should recite her mantra a thousand times with a steady mind; thus, being full of the Self, one may move about in happiness.
Likewise, having drawn the burner [mantra] in the middle of the corners of a hexagon,
and having placed the wielder of the mace there, one should worship him according to the stated sequence.
Having entered the patient, one should inquire about the disease, its cause, and its pacification;
once all of that has been explained, it departs at his command. (36)
That deity; that deity; or whatever else is desired—that deity.

"Having worshipped that deity with the sixteen offerings as before"—this is the ellipsis. "That mantra, [realizing] his full self through identity with the deity. This is what is meant: in any one of the ten previously mentioned yantras.
Having worshipped as before, one should place the youth or the maiden in the center in the form described,
honor them with the root-mantra,
and while touching their head, recite the root-mantra one hundred times with the aforementioned flowers, perfumes, and other offerings.
Having again worshipped as before and offered guggulu incense until the deity has entered,
once the deity has entered into whichever of those two substrates [is chosen],
one should worship that deity with the sixteen types of offerings using the root mantra and recite that mantra.

One should inquire of one's chosen deity regarding the past, present, and future; when that deity has explained the entire range of questions, one should worship her with offerings as before, dissolve her into one's own self as before, and then move about happily, with one's intentions fulfilled. || 34 ||

With the two verses beginning with *tathā* and ending with *apayāti*, he teaches the construction of the hexagonal yantra for the purpose of inducing disease, as well as its ritual application and so forth. In that context, the "burning" [syllable] is the letter *ra* belonging to the Vidyā, which is to be pronounced seven times. Therein, in the center of the hexagon...

The syntactical connection is as follows: having caused the disease to enter the sick person by means of the two sets of seven syllables written in the *vidyāyantra* according to the stated procedure; "the cause of that" means the cause of the disease, which is the cause of its entry into him;
"of that practitioner"—the remainder of the sentence being "the disease departs. This is what is meant:
Having completed the circle by means of the desired measure and having drawn a hexagon therein according to the previously stated sequence,
one should write the seven *repha*s (the letter *ra*) found in the *mūla-vidyā* both in its center and in its six corners; then,
having worshipped that yantra with those [syllables] and the vidyā, one should place the sick person there in the center.
First, one should heat the center of a woman’s skull at night while reciting the vidyā and remembering the person to be acted upon; then she is immediately drawn forth. (37)
Free from fear, shame, pride, and the like, with trembling limbs and having cast aside all other states of being, she approaches, afflicted by the god of love. (38)
One should heat that yantra placed in a human skull and likewise perform the recitation;
[this applies to] kings, princes, or whoever else [may be the target]. (39)
Devoid of discernment, deluded, and having abandoned the traditions of their birth and lineage, they remain on earth as slaves under the control of others until death, certainly. (40)
Then, for the instruction on all the eternal [mantras], the Guru [should place] that [deity] situated in the center of each respective wheel, accompanied by the recitation of the encircling vidyā.

Having established [the deity] one hundred times and worshipped it with the root-mantra, and having likewise recited that same mantra one hundred times while touching its head, one should cause the disease to enter the patient; then, having asked the cause of that possession, and once the cause has been explained by him, one should say, "Depart! (apehi).
By the command of the practitioner, that disease departs. || 36 ||

With these four verses beginning with "First" (*prathamam*) and ending with "Firmly" (*dhruvam*), he teaches the first yantra for attracting, subjugating, and so forth. Therein, the first yantra is situated in the center of a woman's skull; [it is drawn] within the woman's skull using the previously mentioned substances.
The meaning is: having first drawn the yantra. One should heat it over coals;

according to the tradition, one should heat it over coals preceded by the recitation of the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* mantra one hundred times. While heating it, one should recite and remember the *vidyā*, and at that time, one should likewise [remember] the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*).
Thus: the woman to be won over (*sādhyā*), having cast aside all other attachments and being single-minded, "approaches," meaning she advances of her own accord.
She is the one to be won over. One should first heat that [substance] which is placed in a skull-cup (*puṃkapāla*) as before.
As before, one should mutter the mantra (*vidyā*) accompanied by the ritual of vitalization (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and so forth. Likewise...

Just as [it is] when placed in a female skull; by this it is meant that one who has written that yantra in a male skull, performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and so forth, and is reciting the vidyā at night while remembering the target and heating it over embers, brings the following under control. Having become like a servant, [they submit] to this practitioner.
Kings and others constitute the group of those to be converted. || 40 ||

With these three verses beginning with *sarvāsām* and ending with *tataḥ*, he teaches the *yāmala-vedha* (the piercing of the couple), which is the common form of the two types of piercing (*vedha*) whose nature is about to be described. In that context, because of the identity of the *vidyā* and the deity in the teaching of all sixteen *nityās*, [he addresses] that disciple.

Meditating upon [the deity] whose limbs are enveloped by flames of fire—whether it be that specific *cakra*, or the *nityasaparyā-cakra*, or any one of the ten yantras mentioned here (p. 364)—one should, as before, draw back the senses, including the mind as the sixth, into oneself by means of the mind. (42)
When this has been done, he will instantly fall unconscious upon the ground;
then, having raised him up and poured the arghya water into his mouth, one should speak as follows.
This piercing (vedha) is declared to be threefold,
producing immediate realization through the two divisions of Śākta and Śāmbhava, and by means of their union as a single essence.

"Recall the seven burning syllables in the disciple’s locations beginning with the *mūlādhāra* up to the *brahmarandhra*," having said this, [the teacher] proceeds as before from the act of gazing. (45)

This is the meaning. Here, the inclusion of the wheel of the perpetual worship (*nityasaparyācakra*) refers to the disciple’s realization of the Guru’s state of being perfected through meditative cultivation (*bhāvanāsiddhi*). Accompanied by the recitation of the *vidyā*, one should contemplate each of those *Nityās* as having their limbs enveloped by flames of fire;
if they are situated within the wheel of perpetual worship, one should contemplate them as having a form surrounded solely by a circle of fire-flames.

The meaning is that if the disciple has entered any one of the ten previously mentioned yantras, [the teacher] should contemplate him as being enveloped by the flames of fire in the form of seven *repha*s (the letter *r*) situated within those respective [yantras]. The sense-faculties (*indriyāṇi*) are those of hearing and so forth, which consist of the nature of cognition (*jñāna*).

The sixth [senses] follow from the fifth; those for whom the mind is the sixth are thus referred to as "ending with the sixth. Having drawn [the consciousness] into one's own self by means of the mind and meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*) according to the previously described procedure for the installation of life-force (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*), and then having cast the water of the *arghya* offering into the mouth of that [effigy] which has been rendered unconscious and laid upon the ground, one should then rise up from there.

Having invoked and established her—whose form consists of the threefold light of the Vidyā—within the three substrates according to the previously described procedure, one should recite the Vidyā into the ear of that living being. || 43 ||

With these seven verses beginning with "eṣa" and ending with "sama," he teaches the forms of the two-fold piercing (*dvivedha*) and so forth within the three-fold piercing (*trividhavedha*). Among these, "this" (*eṣaḥ*) refers to the previously mentioned *yāmalavedha* (coupled piercing) in its general form; [it is further characterized] by its own nature as described in the three-fold manner and by the two [piercings] that are about to be explained.
"Creating conviction" means creating the conviction that the Guru, the deity, and the self are one.

"Of the two" refers to the Śākta and Śāmbhava [upāyas]. The meaning is: from the *yāmala* (union) which is the nature of their oneness—that is, from the union consisting of the nature of the oneness of the two aforementioned forms, the Śākta and the Śāmbhava.

The phrase "in the six locations beginning with the *mūlādhāra*" is an ellipsis; the meaning is that, including the *brahmarandhra*, there are seven locations in total. Having said, "Remember the seven burning syllables," [the teacher instructs] according to the guru’s instruction for the disciple to contemplate them within himself. The "burning syllables" refers to the seven *repha*s (the letter *r*) contained within the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*).

As before, because his body is enveloped by flames of fire from this point on, one should perform this [rite] common to all initiations (*sarvavedha*) according to the described form, using the perfected *vidyā* that is to be imparted. This is what is meant:
the disciple situated in the center of the previously mentioned yantra—

Having instructed [the disciple] to contemplate the seven *repha*s belonging to the Vidyā located in the seven sites beginning with the *mūlādhāra* and ending at the *brahmarandhra*, the Guru should, as before, gaze upon him with the Vidyā to be taught and, through visualization and other means, perform the Śākta-piercing (*śāktavedha*) upon the ground by means of the perfected Vidyā.
O wise one, hear now about Śambhu, whose form is wondrous and piercing.
Having established the disciple in silence within each respective cakra through its own essence,
he himself enters that body, becomes one with it, and returns again to his own.
Having arrived in his own form and having indeed meditated upon that Self,
one who has performed the ritual placements (nyāsa), recitation (japa), and worship should burn that body with fire.
This may be the Śāmbhava piercing; the Yāmala piercing was already explained previously.
Thus, the three piercings have been described, which indicate the accomplishment of your own state.
However, this specific distinction is established in the *Yāmala*: "Afterwards, one should transmit all other knowledge heard from the Guru; by this, one becomes equal to him. (50)

Having raised up [the disciple] who was previously cast down, one should utter the respective vidyā; this is called Śāktavedha. Therein, with the remaining four verses beginning with "śāmbhavam" and ending with "sama," he teaches the Śāmbhavavedha, which effects non-return [to saṃsāra], as well as the fruit of Yāmalavedha.
In that regard, the Śāmbhava [state] has a form to be described hereafter, possessing a wondrous body because it brings about immediate non-return [to saṃsāra]. It is established in silence,
by means of the absence of the previously mentioned Śākta piercing, contemplation, and so forth, within each respective wheel, such as the wheels of perpetual worship and the like.
"In that form" means in the form of the disciple's self; the connection is that the Guru himself,

having entered by means of the contemplation of being the Self of all, enters that body— the disciple's body— and then, having become one with the disciple's self and so forth, [unites] again with his own self and so forth.

After the stabilization of the unification of the disciple’s self and so forth, the teacher—this is the remainder of the sense—having arrived at his own body, [the word] "in his own" is to be construed here. "In the form of the Self" means in the form of one's own Self, that is, by means of the dissolution of one's own Self. Then, that Self is the disciple’s Self.

Having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*), recitation (*japa*), and worship, [the teacher] should burn his own body—and by extension, the body of the disciple, meaning it is as if dead—with fire; that is to say, he should reduce it to ashes because of its state of death. This is the "piercing" (*vedha*) of Śambhu, whose nature has been previously described. What is meant is this: the true Guru [should perform this] within those respective wheels (*cakras*) and so forth.

Having established the disciple in silence, devoid of the previously mentioned meditative cultivation (*bhāvanā*), [the teacher] enters the disciple's body by means of his own essential nature through the contemplation of being the self of all; having become one with that [disciple's] self and so forth,
he returns again to his own body and visualizes the disciple’s self as completely dissolved within his own self.

The meaning is that the disciple, having performed the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) and so forth, should take the deceased body to the cremation ground and consign it to the fire. This *śāmbhava* piercing is for one who desires liberation alone; it was already described previously with the words "he would fall unconscious," and so on. As for the three piercings, however, [the piercing] is by means of one's own self.

By means of the unification of the disciple’s contracted self with the nature of the supreme *ahantā* (I-consciousness), which is full and consists of the radiance of *saccidānanda*, one effects the appropriation of one's own self known as the aforementioned supreme *ahantā*.
Having first written [the mantra] upon Śivā with red sandalwood paste— (p. 366) — [one should proceed].
On a slab fashioned from iron, on a wooden board, or on a surface of stone; || 51 ||
Or, on ground that is perfectly level, pure, and free from clods of earth and charcoal,
one should invoke the Goddess right there and worship her together with the Śaktis.
By practicing for one day, three days, seven days, or even seven weeks; or for a month, or a full year (maṇḍala), one shall obtain the desired goal in that respective order.
Through this wondrous worship, one attains subjugation, attraction, immobilization, restraint, desired gain, and all other things that are wished for. (54)
Then, O Śivā, one shall conquer all the aforementioned diseases as well as all others;
one shall accomplish [this] with effort by means of the very first yantra alone.

These three names, beginning with Śāmbhava, belong to these [three types of piercing] and are established by their respective Siddhāntas. The phrase "of the Guru" is to be supplied as the remainder for the indication of success through contemplation (*bhāvanā*). By the words "in the Yāmala," etc., this is what is meant:
having drawn forth the soul of the disciple within the piercing that takes the form of the *Yāmala*, one unifies it with one's own self.

Furthermore, by means of the rite of installation (*pratiṣṭhāpana*), all [qualities] such as knowledge that reside in the Guru are transferred into that specific body of the disciple. Therefore, the disciple becomes equal to the Guru; this is the distinction of this [initiation] over the other two. || 50 ||
With twenty-three verses beginning with "raktacandanam" and ending with "sādhayet," he teaches the ritual applications for subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth by means of ten yantras. Among those,
with five verses beginning with "raktacandanam" and ending with "śive," [he teaches] regarding them...
He teaches the rites to be accomplished by means of the first yantra; in this context, "the first yantra" is the understood subject.
On a cloth fashioned from metals, and there too, the substance is indeed red sandalwood (*kucandana*); it is the same for both the wooden board and the stone surface.
*Vā* (or) indicates an option. There, in the center of the yantra, [one should worship] with the *śaktis*, beginning with those mentioned in the section on the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).

"One day" is the remainder [of the sentence]. "The mandala" is as before; "desired" refers to the subjugation (vaśyādi) and so forth to be described; the connection is that it is the desired gain. "Other than" means other than those previously mentioned, according to the sequence of worship stated for the daily rite. "Previously mentioned" refers to those taught in the sixth chapter in the section on optional rites (kāmyaprakaraṇa).

And the *prameha* (urinary disorders) and so forth that will be described; and "all other" (*anyāni cākhilān*)—the coreferential construction (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is established because of the scriptural authority—and "others" (*anyāni*), with "objects" (*arthān*) being the understood supplement. "O Śivā" (*śive*) is an address to the Goddess.
Having placed the second [syllable] in *Darada*, when the sun has risen high over the aforementioned [place].
One should worship at the prescribed times; thus one shall obtain the fruits that have been described. || 56 ||

Having inscribed it on a metal plate and recited the Nityā-vidyā one thousand times daily, one should touch it; then, with water consecrated by that [mantra], [one should perform the ritual]. // 57 //
Then, on the prescribed day, one should perform bathing, drinking, and the preparation of cooked food;
[he shall be freed] from the three types of terrible prameha and the most dreadful dysuria (mūtrakṛcchra).
Freed from diseases such as urinary stones and dysuria, he shall become happy;
free from illness and with a healthy mind, he shall live for a very long time upon this earth. (59)
Having fashioned a third [image] out of red ochre from the wood of a tree belonging to an enemy’s asterism,
one should then dig a pit in the ground at its base and always kindle a fire there.
Within those aforementioned days, the enemy perishes from diseases such as burning fevers;
and if that [image] is lifted up but not cast into water, he likewise perishes.

With these four verses beginning with "the second" (*dvitīyam*) and ending with "mental" (*mānasa*), he teaches the [mantras] to be accomplished by means of the second yantra. Among them, the second yantra:

the substance is *darada* (mercury/cinnabar) alone, even among those previously mentioned materials such as iron and so forth for the first yantra. When [the planet] has reached its exaltation (*ucca*).

The meaning is that when the Sun is situated in Aries, which is its exaltation sign, it is the month of Caitra. Even then, one should worship the Goddess at the time of her exaltation according to the sequence of daily worship; this is the implied sense. By the aforementioned time, starting from the beginning of the day, the rites of subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth are performed. Having drawn the second yantra, in that case as well, these very same substances [are used].

Touching the *yantra*; the *nityāvidyā* is the *jvālāmālinīvidyā*. With those perfumed waters—that is, with water infused in the *yantra*—one prepares cooked food, such as rice and so forth. The "stated day" uses the accusative case to denote duration; it refers to the days as previously described. "By the threefold" means due to the persistence of the three defects. "The urine-rim" (*mūtrapālī*)...
In this context, *ākāra-meha* is a specific type of urinary disorder. One whose mind is healthy (*svastha-mānasa*) is so because of the absence of mental anguish (*ādhi*). || 59 ||

With the two verses beginning with "the third" and ending with "perishes," he teaches the subjugation of enemies through the application of the third yantra. In that context, "the third yantra" refers to [one] on a surface, meaning on a wooden board (*phalaka*). "Therein" means at the place where the yantra is to be engraved. "By the aforementioned days and so forth" refers to that [time].
The meaning is that when the *yantra* is not destroyed in the water—that is, in a reservoir of water—then the enemy perishes by means of a fever of burning heat. || 61 ||
By drawing the fourth [mantra] with *rocanā* paste and performing the aforementioned worship, one certainly attains victory in all the matters previously mentioned. (62)
In debates, in the two kinds of gambling, and in all other planetary influences, everyone always becomes victorious through his majesty. (63)
Having prepared the fifth [maṇḍala] with saffron, by worshipping it there for those days,
men, elephants, horses, and women come under one's control.
Having drawn the sixth [letter] together with the name upon a cloth using turmeric,
one should place it somewhere in a well-sealed brick-pot located in a low or high position.
One will certainly paralyze the tongue of the enemy, their movements, their remaining strength, the divine efforts of kings, their desire for speech, and all other undesirable things.
Likewise, one should draw the seventh [mandala] with sandalwood mixed with camphor;
there, one should worship her daily at the three junctions of the day within one's own home.

With the two verses beginning with "The fourth" and ending with "by its power," he teaches victory in gambling and other such activities through the application of the fourth yantra. In that context, regarding the phrase "the fourth yantra," the expression "from the aforementioned worship" refers to the subject matter concerning the number of days, the deities of the retinue, and so forth, for the specific ritual occasion.

In this regard, the tradition holds that the *adhikaraṇa* and other such elements were taught in the first yantra. Regarding the planets mentioned or yet to be mentioned— such as those involved in debate (*vāda*) and so forth— in the context of wagers (*paṇabandha*), one should employ the fifth yantra of this honored [text], according to the verse beginning with "pañcamā" and so on.
It teaches [the method] subject to mortals and so forth. In each respective yantra, the bases and other elements are as before.
From worshipping that according to the daily ritual sequence, [the results are attained] in days as before. || 64 ||

With the two verses beginning with "the sixth" and ending with "firm," he teaches the paralyzing of enemies through the application of the sixth yantra. In that context, the sixth yantra is joined with the [enemy's] name;
this is common to all yantras. [When] Saturn is in its *mandocca*...

The traditional teaching is that even when situated in a heap of cotton, it is the time of its exaltation (*uccakāla*). However, it is well-established that within a brick enclosure (*iṣṭakāpuṭa*), one should create a cavity in the middle of the bricks according to the arrangement of the instrument,
having made a hole measuring half the height of the brick, and then [filling] it with another brick.
The meaning is that it was bound very firmly with a smooth, well-knit [garment]; [he displayed] divine exertion. || 66 ||

With the two verses beginning with "The seventh" and ending with "the powers," he teaches the attainment of Lakṣmī through the application of the seventh yantra: "On those days, Indirā [abides] for him, surpassing all the worlds. (p. 369)
O Great Goddess, the powers of the yantras are indeed manifold.
On the eighth day, when the sun has ascended high, one should draw that goddess upon a wooden board or a pedestal using powdered aṣṭamaṇḍūka and aguru.
At that time, one should likewise worship with fragrant flowers;
one shall obtain diverse garments and ornaments as well.
Having drawn the ninth [mantra] with the sweat of a deer and having worshipped it there,
one smeared with that [substance] may go anywhere among a gathering of people.
If all women, regarding him as their guru, become submissive to him,
then by his power they will accomplish his desires for as long as they live.
One should draw the tenth [mandala] with all the aforementioned substances, as well as each one individually;
whatever has been declared by them, one should successfully accomplish all this.

Therein is the seventh yantra. "In that manner" means according to the previously stated sequence for the worship of the locus (*adhikaraṇa*). Therein, in the yantra, one should [worship] that Goddess during those days, beginning with the days previously mentioned. "O Maheśānī" is an address to the Goddess. || 68 ||

With the two verses beginning with "the eighth" and ending with "he shall obtain," [the author] teaches the attainment of garments and ornaments through the application of the eighth yantra. Therein, "the eighth yantra" refers to [the one made] with powdered aguru and aguru paste. In that yantra, when Jupiter has reached its exaltation (*ucca*).

When Jupiter is situated in Cancer, at that time of its exaltation, when it has reached the middle of the sky in that sign—thus the time for the Sun and the other planets is also stated; likewise according to the regular sequence. || 70 ||
With these two verses beginning with *mṛgasvedaiḥ* and ending with *anubhāvataḥ*,
he teaches the accomplishment of subjugating worldly women by means of the ninth application. Therein,
having drawn the ninth yantra and worshipped it in the previously mentioned locations according to the daily ritual sequence, that...

Jvālāmālinī. Anointed with that [substance], one should go at the end of the worship; having wiped away that yantra, one is anointed with the sweat of a deer. All the people present there [will be affected]. If the woman to be won over is the object of this practice, she will approach that practitioner. [This is] of this application. 72.

With the verse beginning with "vilikhet" (one should draw), he teaches the ritual application (*prayoga*) and so forth by means of the tenth yantra, in order to attain the results expressed by the previously mentioned ninth yantra.
In that regard, [the drawing is performed] with all the aforementioned substances.

Having inscribed [the syllables] upon those ten [circles] mentioned [in the text], using the nine substances—beginning with *kucandana* as stated in the first yantra and ending with *mṛgasveda* as stated in the ninth yantra—and using the substances mentioned for those [ten circles]; (p. 370) [one should proceed].
Having established the water-pot according to the ritual procedure and having performed the recitation during that fierce planetary influence, he then— || 74 ||
One should consecrate [the disciple] with the fruit located in the position of the defect of that planet;
thus it shall not come to pass, and everything will indeed be brought under control through the yantras without exception. || 75 ||

Likewise, having offered worship to that [deity] on a high place with oblations, mantras, clarified butter, and milk-rice, and having presented the offering, prostrated, and worshipped, one should give [the gift]; thus one shall attain the state of Śiva. || 76 ||
Due to their power, those planets quickly cease causing affliction from their respective planetary influences;
moreover, through constant worship, they grant the fruits of being situated in the eleventh house.
O Śivā, having engraved one or another [of these] upon gold or silver, or upon their respective yantras, and having worshipped it, one should give it, well-honored, to a knower of that vidyā.

The meaning is "by those combined. The word *ekaśaḥ* signifies "alternatively" or "one by one. By means of those nine yantras, through the various arrangements of the letters of the name in the very center, this is the tenth yantra. || 73 ||

With the two verses beginning with "prokteṣu" and ending with "aśeṣataḥ," he teaches the pacification of planetary afflictions through the rite of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) performed upon the ten yantras previously mentioned; in this context, the word "in the ten yantras" is to be understood as the ellipsis. "By the rule" means preceded by the worship of the thirty-eight pairs of *kalās* and so forth.
Having recited the mantra (*vidyā*) against the fierce and adverse [spirit], [one should act] so as to completely [overcome] that spirit;

the meaning is that this applies to all *yantras* in the same way. What is meant is this: when the respective spirit has entered the *yantra* among the ten *yantras* according to the previously stated sequence.
Through the consecration performed according to the sequence prescribed for each respective adverse planet, there is the pacification of that specific planetary adversity.

With the two verses beginning with *tathā* and ending with *api*, he teaches the worship that pacifies the adverse influence of the nine planets, according to the sequence previously stated, among the yantras already mentioned. Therein, *taducce* means in the exaltation (*ucca*) of the adverse planet; *tatpūjām* means the worship of that adverse planet; *nivedya* means having offered.

By the word "ca" (and), "with milk-rice offerings" (*pāyasa*) is drawn forward. They are "constantly adverse," meaning even apart from regular sacrifice (*nitya-yajana*), even without the occasional sacrifice (*kāla-yajana*). This is what is meant: in the ten previously mentioned diagrams (*yantra*), in the diagram obtained for each respective planet according to the sequence stated before, at the specific time of the exaltation (*ucca-kāla*) of that particular adverse planet.

Apart from that specific time, by the constant worship of those respective planets, by the worship of the Goddess with their individual name-mantras, by oblations (homa) of food, clarified butter, and milk-rice,
and by the offering of those respective planetary gifts preceded by the water of honor (arghya), those planets become pleased and immediately favorable.
They come into being. || 77 ||

With the three verses beginning with *suvarṇa* and ending with *vidhānataḥ*, [it is taught that] by the gift of a gold plate or similar object inscribed with the yantra, that [merit] is prepared in sixteen, twelve, nine, six, or three *niṣkas*. (p. 371)
Or for one who performs daily worship, it is for the purpose of worshipping even one among the eternal [deities]. || 79 ||

Having worshipped that embodiment of the planets with fragrances and other offerings, and having bowed down to it as it sits facing west, one should present [the image] to him according to the prescribed ritual.

By drinking water consecrated with the recitation of the mantra, the digestive fire within the stomach increases; and it is certain that this also occurs by touching the abdomen while reciting the mantra after eating. 81.
While the sun is in the zodiac signs beginning with Aries, throughout all twelve months,
one should perform [the practice] for three days each in the ten yantras previously described.
One should worship the Goddess for a year with wealth, grain, houses, and other such things;
thus enriched, one lives long on earth, free from disease and with a joyful mind.

It teaches the attainment of the fruit. In that regard, the phrase "in those ten yantras" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Having worshipped whichever one among them has been attained as supreme—that is, having worshipped the yantra well for one who knows the vidyā, meaning for one who knows the Jvālāmālinī-vidyā.

The measurement of sixteen and twelve [units] is for those who lack the capacity; it is an option for one who worships a single [deity] among the sixteen *Nityās*. The repetition of the word "should give" (*dadyāt*) is not a fault, as it serves the purpose of expanding the exposition. It faces west because its nature is that of a planet (*graha*). To him—
"To the one who possesses knowledge, whose form is the planets. This is what is meant:
among the aforementioned yantras, whichever yantra corresponds to a particular planet should be cast upon a plate of gold or other materials at the prescribed time;
that golden plate, marked with the yantra and worshipped with the Vidyā, [is to be used].
Having seated either one who knows the *Jvālāmālinī-nityā-vidyā*, or one who knows the *Ṣoḍaśanityā-vidyā*,

or one who knows any one of these *Nityās*, facing west upon that yantra drawn on the ground, and having worshipped him after meditating on his form as that [planetary] graha with perfumes and other offerings while reciting the respective mantras;
One should give it to him; thus [it is said]. || 80 ||

With the verse beginning with "vidyā," he teaches the means for increasing the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*). In this context, "vidyā" refers to the recitation (*japa*) of the *Jvālāmālinī* mantra; the number of recitations there is one hundred and eight.
With the two verses beginning with "meṣādi" and ending with "bhūvi," [the author] explains the ten [elements] that have been mentioned.

He teaches the fruits to be obtained through the worship of deities such as Bhāskara (the Sun) over twelve months, sequentially for three days at a time on each of the yantras. In that regard, by the statement "when the Sun is in the zodiac signs beginning with Aries," it is understood that starting from the month of Caitra, one should perform [the worship] for three days on each [yantra].

The meaning is that it lasts for three days on a single yantra. In this way, there is one cycle every month. One should worship the Goddess together with Bhāskara; in that regard, the place for the worship of Bhāskara is as previously described. || 83 ||
Whichever planet resides in whichever zodiac sign—whether one, two, or many—if one worships that [planet] on those days and at those times when it is in its exaltation, [the result follows]. (84)
The respective planets, being well-pleased, protect him constantly;
likewise, through libations, fire-offerings, recitation of mantras, gifts, and so forth. (85)
Furthermore, in all nine yantras, having diligently inscribed the respective agitation caused by each of the nine planets within them, one should perform worship for the crushing of enemies.
Having written down the numbers associated with the enemy's name and those of the Sun and Moon, one shall obtain victory day by day on the ground during an eclipse. 87.
Having placed one karṣa each of the mantras, seeds, and medicinal herbs into a new vessel containing five products of the cow (pañcagavya) measuring one khārī, one should cook that mixture.

With the two verses beginning with *yadrāśau* and ending with *api vā*, he teaches the fruit resulting from the propitiation of all the planets within those yantras. In that context, *athavā* (or) signifies an alternative;
it means on the days when the respective planets are situated in their respective signs, that is, at their respective gates. [This applies] when they are in their exaltations (*ucca*).

"At the times previously mentioned" means during those specific periods. "By worshipping them" means by worshipping the respective deities together with their corresponding planets at the conclusion of each [period]. In this section, in all worship of the planets, there is worship together with the root deity (mūladevatā). That practitioner [should be honored] through recitation (japa), giving (dāna), and so forth, according to the sequence previously described.
The gift of a gold plate engraved with a mechanical design. || 85 ||
With the two verses beginning with *navasu* and ending with *āpnuyuḥ*,
he teaches the crushing of enemies through the worship of the planets as before in the nine yantras starting from the second; therein,
having written the respective agitation (*kṣobha*) within, one should place the planet adverse to the enemy who is the target (*sādhya*).

"At the place of the pericarp, may the Sun agitate Devadatta," and so forth. In the ritual for the crushing of enemies, the syntactical connection is "during the eclipse, that is, the seizing of the Sun and the Moon. The enemies shall suffer [the consequences]. || 87 ||

With these five verses beginning with "vidyā" and ending with "vibhañjakaṃ," he teaches the means for all vidyās, syllables, medicinal herbs, and ashes, as well as their application and so forth. In that context, "karṣa" refers to three niṣkas; this is the measure for the non-repetitive vidyā-syllables and medicinal herbs.
For the repeated [mantras], as before, they are multiplied by the number obtained;

having offered that medicine into a new vessel consecrated by the *vidyā*—consecrated by its root *vidyā*—into the fire arising from within that vessel, at least one thousand times; there, in those ashes. There.
When the machine has been reduced to ashes, one should worship that Goddess constantly according to the sequence;

that ash [is empowered] by all sixteen Nityās. In that house presided over by the ash, [one should anoint it] with śrīkhaṇḍa and so forth, such as sandalwood and saffron. This is what is meant: in a new vessel, [one should place] a measure of one *khāri*.

Having placed all five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) in equal portions therein with their respective worship-mantras (*upāsya-mantra*), vidyās, and so forth; and having further added all mantras, vidyās, repeated syllables, and medicinal herbs into that [mixture] according to the prescribed measure, accompanied by the recitation (*japa*) of those respective vidyās, [one should offer it] into the fire consecrated by those respective vidyās.
Having consecrated the fire with the Vidyā, and then, once it has arisen from within that [fire],
having offered ghee with the Vidyā, one should indeed take those ashes from there.
Having prepared the ten yantras, one should worship the Goddess therein;
then, having collected that ash, one should deposit it and perform worship every day.
That ash provides all protection; one should accomplish everything with it.
Diseases, thieves, malevolent spirits, calamities, and afflictions shall not exist in that person's home.
Constant wearing [of the ashes] on the body, anointing with Śrīkaṇṭha and other [substances], and consuming [them] for all rites and so forth, destroy misfortune and affliction. (92)
Within the ten syllables of fire, one should sequentially join the three vowels with each of the seven consonants; by that means, they become twenty-one.
Having drawn two triangles, joined externally and internally, and having fashioned a hexagon situated within the circle in their center; 94.
Having cooked it with the mouth of the vessel firmly sealed, one should then offer oblations into the fire described as being within the interior of that vessel,
using the respective vidyā, at least a thousand times. Afterwards, taking those ashes,
one should then take cow dung while remaining in the air without touching the ground, and mix the ashes with it.

Having formed it into a mass, purified it, and burnt it along with cow-dung, one should then take the ash from that fire together with the medicinal herbs; having ground it in a cloth and fashioned ten yantras for her,
and having likewise fashioned the respective daily worship-yantras for the other goddesses, one should invoke those respective deities therein.
Having worshipped according to the daily ritual sequence and recited the mantra one thousand times, one should place that ash in a casket;
by offering handfuls of flowers every day with the respective vidyās according to the prescribed method, the attainment of the stated fruits occurs. || 92 ||

With these eight verses beginning with "In the letters of fire" (*vahnyakṣareṣu*) and ending with "thus" (*iti*), twenty-one yantras are produced by the mutual combination of the ten fiery syllables previously mentioned as belonging to the five elements.

By means of those [syllables], he teaches the practice for increasing the digestive fire (*jaṭharāgni*) and so forth. In that context, "among the syllables of fire" means among the syllables of the five elements; these are ten, beginning with *ī* and ending with *kṣ*. [The practice is performed] with seven [of these], excluding the three vowels located at the beginning.

By means of the second letters of the consonant groups beginning with *kha*— namely *kh*, *gh*, *ch*, *jh*, *ṭh*, *ḍh*, *th*, *ḍh*, *ph*, *bh*, *th*, *dh*, *ph*, *bh*, *kh*, *gh*, *ch*, *jh*, *ṭh*, *kh*, *gh*, *ch*, *jh*, *ṭh*, *ḍh*, *th*,
Thus ends [the section]. "Within that" means within the two triangles. The phrase "together with the name" is the ellipsis;
this refers to the names of those to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth.
(p. 374) One should write the first letter of the name in the center, and the six [letters] in the six hexagons in sequence.
O Pārvatī, one should draw [the diagram], beginning from the northeast and proceeding in a clockwise direction.
Having written fourteen [syllables] in sequence within the interior of the triangle,
one should write the syllable of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the remaining space, as well as in all fifteen [triangles].
By gradually inserting the others in the middle, twenty-one yantras come into being; likewise, by means of them, the digestive fire in the abdomen is activated.
Having indeed inscribed those [syllables] upon a copper plate in the shape of a triangle,
one should recite the vidyā one hundred thousand times while touching it, with each syllable forming an enclosure.
The first syllable is *khi*. Among the twenty-one fiery consonantal syllables joined with the three vowels, it is the first. Respectively, in each one by one in succession;
"Pārvatī" is the vocative case. Likewise, fourteen [syllables] are in order on its own left side.
One should draw five [syllables] each from the bottom to the top on the right side;

five from the top to the bottom at the front; four from the right to the left at its end; and finally, in the fifteenth position, one should write the triad beginning with the practitioner (sādhaka), or alternatively, [the other two].

"In the fifteen [yantras]" means in the twenty yantras at the fifteen locations. "Of others" refers to the second and subsequent syllables. "By those twenty-one" means on a cloth in the shape of a triangle, which serves as the basis for twenty-one suitable applications for the purpose of the *kukṣyagnivardhana* (increasing the digestive fire in the stomach) practice.

Those are the diagrams (*yantra*). The meaning is that one should recite the previously mentioned twenty-one syllables of the *vidyā*, having joined them in forward and reverse order within an enclosure (*sampuṭa*) formed by those [syllables].
That diagram-cloth (*yantrapaṭṭa*), having been consecrated by recitation (*japa*) with the aforementioned *vidyā*, is the "cooking" (*pāka*).
The connection here is that "there is an intensification [of power] through food and so forth, as before.

Due to the destruction of sins from previous lives—that is, from the eradication of the misdeeds of prior births—brought about by the performance of consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) and other rites, "intensification arises; it arises" is the form of the conclusion. By the statement "of the eternal [mantras]," the meaning is that this application is common to all.
The phrase "thus declared" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The sequence for the application of the construction of the twenty-one yantras is as follows:
among the syllables of the five elements, there are twenty-one in number produced by the mutual combination of the fire-syllables; these are the syllables of the form previously described.
On a copper plate shaped like a triangle, having drawn two equilateral triangles— one external and one internal— both with their apexes pointing east,
and having constructed within them a circle that touches and does not touch the three lines of the inner triangle, [one should place] inside that...

Having constructed a hexagon according to the previously mentioned measurement, one should write therein as follows: having inscribed the first syllable containing the name in the very center, one should then inscribe the six syllables in the six corners outside of that, proceeding clockwise starting from the front corner.
Outside that, in the path between the two triangles (p.

375), one should daily place a water vessel that has been consecrated with mantra-recitation; by sprinkling the food being cooked with that water, [the desired result] certainly comes to pass. || 99 ||
O Supreme Goddess, the kindling of the digestive fire occurs through the destruction of the sins of previous births;
this indeed arises from the majesty of the eternal ones. (100)

The pervasion consisting of the reality of hearing has been correctly explained; by the thorough cultivation of this [pervasion], that very reality is assimilated into one's own self within the mind. (101)
Thus ends the twentieth chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, a tantra of the sixteen *Nityās*.
[The sequence is as follows: beginning from the lower part of one’s own left side up to its upper part—this constitutes five [positions];
and beginning from the upper part of the right side down to its lower part—this constitutes another five.

Starting from the right side and ending at the left side, there is a group of four; among them, the syllable of the *sādhya* (the target) is placed in the last position, the fifteenth place. Having thus written the remaining fourteen syllables ending with the syllable of the *sādhya*, one should write a total of twenty-one syllables.

This is the first yantra. In this very yantra, starting from the center, there is the placement of the twenty syllables beginning with the second [syllable] and so forth; and among the others, there is the placement of those beginning from above the syllable written in the center, ending respectively with each preceding syllable.

By arranging twenty syllables externally according to the previously mentioned sequence, twenty-one yantras are formed together with the previously described yantra. Any one of these yantras, when encased by the Vidyā and its syllables, should be consecrated with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and worshipped after being recited one hundred thousand times.

If one daily recites this mantra a hundred times without fail, using the Vidyā encased within the syllables of that [person's] name, and having consecrated water-vessels with it and worshipped them, then drinking, cooking, and bathing with those waters will destroy one's long-standing sins and increase the digestive fire. || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete tantra known as the venerable *Kādimatā* among the venerable *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.
The twentieth chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the ritual procedure for the eternal Jvālāmālinī-vidyā, is thus completed and fully examined. 20.
Regarding the number of verses:
in the twentieth chapter, thirty-two diagrams have been explained; the total number of verses is three hundred minus one and a half quarters.
The Twenty-First Chapter. Now, O Śivā, listen to the ritual procedure of Citrā, who is the sixteenth among the sixteen Nityās; it has been proclaimed, and it bestows the accomplishment of all aims.
The Vidyā has already been taught, along with its application of the limbs (aṅganyāsa), meditation, the Śaktis, worship, the means of accomplishment, and its fruits. || 2 ||
I shall describe to you the fire-oblation (homa), libation (tarpaṇa), yantra-worship, and meditative visualization (bhāvanā);
by means of these various fivefold methods, one may accomplish every desired object.
One should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) in sequence with the Vidyā-mantra joined with the long vowels as before; then one should install the Mātṛkā using the Vidyā.

Having taught the ritual procedure for the fifteenth *jvālāmālinīnityā* mantra in the preceding twentieth chapter, he subsequently teaches the ritual procedure for the sixteenth, the *citrānityā* mantra, beginning with "Now,
the sixteenth" and ending with "the leader."

By means of the twenty-first chapter, consisting of one hundred verses, [the author] teaches the subject matter of the chapter there with three verses beginning with "atha ṣoḍaśa" and ending with "īpsitam. Therein, "O Śiva" is the vocative address. "Tatkalpam" means that procedure. [This was already explained] previously in the third chapter. "Śaktīḥ" [refers to the powers].
Those who abide in the obstructions; the means is the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*); their fruits are the fruits for one whose knowledge has been perfected.
By these [means], such as fire-offerings (*homa*) and so forth. || 3 ||

With this verse beginning with "vidyā," he provides the instruction for the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and extends the application of the *mātṛkā* placement [to it]. In that context, "with the syllable 'ca' which is the first of the Vidyā and the element" means with the letter *ca*, which is the first of the Vidyā-mantra and corresponds to the element [air]. "Joined with the long vowels" is as before; thus, in the form *cā*, *cī*, and so forth.

Just as in the case of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣivat*), this [syllable] follows both the preceding and the following according to the requirements of the sense; therefore, the meaning is that once it has been joined in the preceding [position], one should place it together [with the next];
and if it is to be joined in the subsequent [position], one should place it in those respective locations previously mentioned. By means of the *vidyā*.

The meaning is that one should place [the letters] joined with each individual syllable at the end, according to the extension of the previously mentioned sequence of placement (nyāsa), following the order stated in the chapter on Kulasundarī. || 4 ||
She has the luster of the rising orb of the sun, is adorned with the nine precious gems, wears a crown of the nine precious gems, and is radiant with variegated silken garments. (5)
Four-armed and three-eyed, with a face radiant with a pure smile,
she is eternally composed of all bliss and the bestower of every desired object.
Four-armed, holding in her hands a noose, a goad, and the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
she resides within the fresh source [the lotus] at the center of the auspicious lotus.
The worship of that wheel by means of those powers has been described in the same manner;
one should worship Brāhmī and the others, accompanied by the nine *yonis* and the eight groups [of letters].

With these three verses beginning with "udyad" and ending with "navayonigām," he teaches the visualization of the Goddess’s daily worship (*nityasaparyā*), which contains within it the extension of the maṇḍala for the specific daily worship. Therein [is the image] resplendent with variegated silken cloths.

The meaning is that she is clothed in variegated silken garments. She is "consisting of all bliss," meaning her very form is composed of bliss. The repetition of the term "four-armed" should be understood as being for the purpose of introducing the description of her weapons.
Here, the sequence of weapons follows the order from the top, left, and right.
[The worship] of Sarvamaṅgalā, who resides in the nine *yoni*s within the pericarp of the lotus of Maṅgalā, is superior to this wheel of the eternal and non-eternal worship of Nityā.
[It is] precisely within the ninefold source (navayoni) situated in the center of the pericarp. This is what is meant:
therein is the aforementioned pair of squares accompanied by four gates; inside that is a thirty-two-petaled lotus;
inside that is a sixteen-petaled lotus; inside that is an eight-petaled lotus; [and it is] in its pericarp...
One should construct it according to the measurement declared for the nine-fold womb (navayoni). || 7 ||

With the two verses beginning with "By her powers" (*tacchaktibhiḥ*) and ending with "in the vicinity" (*antike*), he teaches the sequence of the Goddess’s perpetual worship (*nityasaparyā*) consisting of six enclosures (*ṣaḍāvaraṇa*). Therein, "by her powers" means by the powers of the four enclosures of Sarvamaṅgalā. Likewise, from the interior...

By the process of external emission, they are joined with the eight groups, preceded by the eight groups beginning with *a, ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa*. By this, the double worship of Brāhmī and the others is established. "On all sides" means outside the central triangle. "Near its arms."
The meaning is "in a clockwise direction," starting from the lower right arm and ending with the lower left arm.

What is being stated is as follows: in the center of all, within the *Sarvamaṅgalā-nityapūjā-cakra*, specifically in the middle of the nine-yoni (*navayoni*) located in the central pericarp (*karṇikā*) of all that was previously mentioned.

Having invoked Citrānityā and worshipped her with the ritual offerings (*upacāra*), one should worship the row of the nine lords (*navanātha*) on her back in the previously mentioned intermediate space, following the sequence of three groups of three as before. Then, in the corners of the central womb (*yoni*), one worships Her powers of Will, Knowledge, and Action; and outside of that, near each of the Goddess’s respective arms, starting from the lower right and so forth.

Having worshipped those weapons in a clockwise direction starting from the end of the left lower [corner], one should worship Brāhmī and the others, accompanied by their respective groups (*vargas*), in the eight outer corners starting from the front in a clockwise direction; then, one should worship the powers of Will (*icchā-śakti*), Knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*), and Action (*kriyā-śakti*) from the central corner.
And one should worship the weapons around the Goddess, near her arms.
One should worship all the eternal protectors to the west of the Goddess, in their respective forms, with their respective mantras according to the prescribed rule.
The worship of the maṇḍala of the Guru and other such rites have been declared as common to all [the Nityās], since these [Nityās] are born from the outflow of the Primordial One (Ādyā). 11.
The means of accomplishment (sādhana) has been declared in that manner, as well as the oblation of its limbs;
thus, when the Vidyā has been successfully accomplished, it becomes fit for ritual application (viniyoga). || 12 ||

Outside of that, in the same manner, having worshipped the eight Śaktis beginning with Bhadrā as described in the Sarvamaṅgalā-paṭala upon the eight petals; outside of that, likewise, having worshipped the sixteen Śaktis of Kalā mentioned therein upon the sixteen petals; and outside of that, likewise, upon the thirty-two petals—

Having worshipped the thirty-two Śaktis, beginning with Kāminī, as described therein, one should worship outside that [mandala], within the square, as before: the [goddesses] beginning with Brāhmī at the western gate, those beginning with Indra at the eastern gate, and those beginning with Ananta at the southeast (Āgneya) corner. Therein, two *bali* offerings are performed upon the completion of the worship.
As before. || 9 ||
With the two verses beginning with *sarvāsām* and ending with *imāḥ*,

[the author] provides the instruction for the common worship of the nine lords (*navanātha*) for all the Nityās, as well as the extension of that worship to be performed on every festival day (*parvan*) within their respective mandalas and so forth. In that regard:

[One should visualize] their respective forms, such as the physical appearance and so forth, resembling that of the Central Goddess, by means of their respective mantras as stated in the second chapter, arranged in three rows according to the prescribed ritual order. These are "born from the initial outpouring" because the first [Goddess], Lalitā, is the nature of the spontaneous manifestation of her own will. Of these, the entire circle of gurus...
The meaning is that the ritual service and so forth are exactly the same. || 11 ||

With the verse beginning with "sādhanam" (the means of accomplishment), he teaches the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*). In that context, "tathā" means as [prescribed] for Lalitā. "Tadaṅgahavana" refers to the fire-oblation (*homa*) which is a limb of the means of accomplishment.
