Likewise, according to the previous statement, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) of three hundred thousand syllables in the Kṛta Yuga, or one hundred and twenty thousand in the Dvāpara Yuga.
The meaning is that one should perform a fire-oblation (homa) consisting of food, clarified butter, and other substances, amounting to one-tenth [of the total]. || 12 ||
(379) I shall now describe the ritual procedure for the optional oblation (*kāmyahoma*), which bestows all aims;
by means of it, even one of extremely meager fortune may become illustrious, an enjoyer of pleasures, and happy. 13.
One attains prosperity through oblations made with red lotuses sprinkled with the three sweets from the mandala, and great fame through those same flowers when they are white.
By performing oblations with red lotuses smeared with honey at the prescribed time,
one obtains gold, or a treasure, or even nectar.
By performing a fire oblation with white water-lilies smeared with milk at the prescribed time,
that man shall quickly obtain various kinds of grain and become fortunate.

Through oblation with blue lotuses smeared with clarified butter, one shall obtain one's desire; likewise, through offering oblations with white water-lilies smeared with that same [butter], one becomes a favorite of the king.
By performing oblations at that time with *palāśa* flowers combined with the three sweets, the fourfold scholarship is surely attained; of this there is no doubt. (18)
By offering parched grain mixed with the three sweets at that very time,
one obtains through effort a maiden endowed with all excellent qualities.
Likewise, one who is like the Lord of Wealth (Kubera) should effortlessly offer the powder of coconut fruit mixed with sugar or molasses, and anointed with honey. || 20 ||

With seventeen verses beginning with "kāmyahoma" and ending with "cetana," he teaches thirty auspicious homa-rites using various homa-substances. In that context, by which rule: "with those lotuses" (ambujaiḥ) means with water-lilies (utpalaiḥ); "red" (raktaiḥ) means with red water-lilies (raktakumudaiḥ); [and] with white lilies (kairavaiḥ).

The word "white" (*sitaiḥ*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the description]. "With *utpala*s" means with blue lotuses. "Anointed with that" means anointed with clarified butter (*ājya*). It is fourfold, as before: by way of instrumental skill, poetic composition, eloquence, and knowledge. The word division is: "obtains through effort" (*yatnāt*) and "without effort" (*ayatnāt*). "With white" (*sasitam*) means mixed with candied sugar (*khaṇḍa-śarkarā*). "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. And likewise (*tadvat*).
The meaning is that, for the sake of attaining conceptual power (*vikalpa*), he is like the Lord of Wealth (*Dhanada*) in that very way.

Similarly, as before, by performing oblations (*homa*) with rice, clarified butter, sesame seeds, rice grains, all red flowers, and *bandhūka* flowers, one becomes like the Lord of Wealth; this is the meaning. [One may also use] white and red flowers, or *guḍūcī*.
As before, with the offering of amṛtā-latā (p. 380), and likewise with oblations of food and clarified butter, as well as with rice grains and sesame seeds;
similarly, with reddish flowers, and likewise those produced from the bandhūka plant. || 21 ||
Through oblation with white flowers, one shall obtain perfection of speech;
through those that are both white and red combined, one shall obtain long life and health.
By offering oblations of three types of dūrvā grass smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one shall conquer diseases;
likewise by an oblation of guḍūcī, or milk-rice (pāyasa), or sesame seeds.
By performing oblations with hundred-petaled lotuses mixed with sandalwood paste and camphor, one attains prosperity; that prosperity shall belong to his lineage as well. (24)
Having ground saffron with snow-water and mixed it with camphor, one should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with beautiful, blooming kahlāra lotuses rubbed with that paste. || 25 ||
May the king be abundant in glory; may he live for a hundred years on earth, without rivals, free from affliction, beyond dualities, and pure in intention. (26)
By offering all the stalks of sugarcane, one shall obtain clothing;
likewise by means of red or white flowers produced from the *karavīra*. (27)
By offering oblations of *pāṭalī* flowers smeared with honey, one shall subjugate a maiden;
likewise, by offering oblations of *campaka* flowers, one may bring a courtesan under one's control.
By performing oblations with milk from a cow that has a calf of the same color and is white, even one whose mind is most sinful attains incomparable fortune. (29)

By the word "ca" (and), it is drawn out that one should conquer diseases. Śrīkhaṇḍa is sandalwood. "Śatapatraka" is its name, which should be understood from the mouth of the Guru. "Sā lakṣmīḥ" means she is Lakṣmī; the sense is that one belonging to her lineage attains peaceful fortune. "With auspicious [flowers]" means those free from insect damage and the like, and unbroken.
"Free from dualities" means incomparable; the sense is that one would obtain clothing in that very manner. "Rūpājīvās" refers to courtesans.
"From the white oblation" (sitahomataḥ) means from the oblation of sugar. For one whose consciousness is most sinful—that is, one who lacks discrimination—fortune is easily attained. || 29 ||
O Ambikā, by performing a homa at that very time with cotton seeds smeared with *sauvīra* salt in a crescent-shaped (*ardhendu*) fire-pit, enemies will certainly become hostile.
By offering oblations with the leaves and seeds of the ariṣṭa tree smeared with that oil,
and by performing homa with the seeds of death (mṛtyubīja) sprinkled with neem oil, elephants [are subdued].
Likewise, by offering oblations of the five limbs smeared with red lac,
or of *akṣa* seeds smeared with oil, the fire-sacrifice certainly brings about the destruction of everything.
By offering oblations of *karañja* seeds that have been sprinkled [with mantras], one destroys enemies;
likewise, by offering the five limbs (roots, bark, leaves, flowers, and fruit) produced from an *akṣata* tree.
By performing a fire sacrifice with seeds of the akṣa tree soaked in nimba oil on that very day, the enemy will certainly become possessed by epilepsy.
When the birth asterism and tree of the enemy have not descended to the base,
an oblation performed with the flesh belonging to those [elements] brings death to the foe.
Likewise, by performing oblations with the seeds of *yakṣākṣa* and *vijā*, smeared with mustard oil, enemies arise as leprosy diseases that destroy the body. (36)
By performing a fire-oblation at midnight with black pepper and mustard seeds smeared with oil,
an enemy seized by burning fever will certainly perish within those same days.

With eight verses beginning with *sauvīra* and ending with *bhuvam*, he teaches the ninefold fire-sacrifice (*nigrahahoma*). In that context, it is performed in the *ardhendu* (half-moon) hearth which is to be described; "with their seeds" means with the seeds of the *ariṣṭa* plant; "smeared with their oils" means smeared with neem oil. The meaning is that [the enemies] thus become mutually hostile.

In that same way, as with elephants; by its five limbs, meaning the five limbs of death; smeared with those, meaning smeared with neem oil; possessing total destruction, meaning causing the destruction of all living beings;
by those days smeared with neem oil, such as the mandala and so forth; and with the flesh of its womb.

[One should perform the rite] with the flesh of animals born under the enemy constellations and with the trees corresponding to those constellations; furthermore, the seeds of the *yakṣākṣa* tree are to be learned from the mouth of the Guru. [The image should be smeared] with oil produced from sesame, that is, sesame oil. || 37 ||

Thus, during the fire-offerings for suppression, as well as for one's own protection, one should daily have the recitation of mantras, fire-offerings, and so forth performed by those who are affectionate and have acquired true knowledge. (38)
Or likewise, one may perform the ritual with the Mṛtyuñjaya mantra and those very same vidyās;
otherwise, it will quickly destroy even a perfected mantra.
One who desires prosperity should never practice the suppression of those previously mentioned out of one's own anger or out of a desire for wealth. (40)
One should accomplish those [rites] by means of the libations (tarpaṇa) prescribed in the ritual of Nityaklinnā;
O Great Goddess, by means of this vidyā, all rites without exception are accomplished.
Now I shall describe the yantras which indeed bestow various desired objects, by means of which everyone may always obtain everything they wish for. (42)
O Supreme Goddess, one should duly inscribe the mantra, which contains a multitude of letters joined with their respective vowels, in all the places mentioned according to the prescribed rule.

With these two verses beginning with *evam* and ending with *nāśayet*, he teaches the sequence of the ritual for self-protection for one performing malevolent magic (*abhicāra*). In that context, "with those who are affectionate" means with those whose happiness and suffering are equal to one's own.
"By Mṛtyuñjaya" refers to the [mantra] to be described in the thirty-fourth chapter; "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative; "otherwise" (*anyathā*) [indicates the opposite].
By way of the reversal of the rules for self-protection. || 39 ||

With the verse beginning with "prāgukta" (previously mentioned), he teaches the prescription of the qualities for the rite of exorcism (*abhicāra*). In this context, "of those previously mentioned" means specifically those stated in the three verses beginning with the ninetieth [verse] of the thirteenth chapter;
"he should perform the suppression" means [the suppression] of those [beings] mentioned therein who are subject to the rite of exorcism. || 40 ||
With the verse beginning with "nityaklinnā," he teaches the libations; those [libations] are explained there [in that context].

Now, with six and a half verses beginning with "atha yantrāṇi" and ending with "vicakṣaṇaḥ," [the author describes] the first among the five hundred and seventy-six forms produced by the application of the letters of the *mātṛkā-visara* to the initial [syllable] of the Vidyā.

By means of those [syllables] numbering four hundred and sixteen, he teaches twenty-six types of yantras according to the sequence of their classes (*varga*). In that regard, all practitioners [should know] the five hundred and seventy-six syllables of the Vidyā, beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, which contain within them the entire collection of letters joined with vowels.

At the beginning, one should join them one by one; the meaning is that by this, as many forms of the Vidyā arise as there are [syllables]. Regarding those already mentioned and those yet to be described: "O Supreme Goddess" is an address to the Goddess. "That pair" refers to the two circles. "Outside of that" means outside of the hexagon.

Therein, one should draw three circles, a triangle, a pair of circles, a hexagon, and likewise a pair of those; outside of that, one should draw a six-petalled lotus and each of those three [enclosures]. (44)
One should write the first *kūṭa* containing the *sādhya* (the name of the person to be accomplished) in the center according to the prescribed rule;
one should likewise write it within the triangles, the hexagon, and on the six petals.
And fifteen other kūṭas have been mentioned there;
within the pair of internal circles, one should place the elements and syllables appropriate for the ritual action.
"In the triangles" means in the three central triangles of the yantra; "others" refers to the second and subsequent ones.

"Therein" means in fifteen locations. "Within the pair of inner circles" means in the path between the two outer circles surrounding the corners and in the path of the outer circle surrounding the hexagon.
[One should write] the colors of the earth and so forth, which are appropriate for rites such as *stambhana* (paralysis) and *vaśya* (subjugation).

Regarding the sequence of writing there: ten by ten along each row; and at the end, it is accompanied by the letters of the rite together with the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*). [These letters] are joined with the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) and the *bindu*, both in direct and reverse order. This is what is meant.
Having written the *mātṛkā* in reverse order, with each syllable joined by the *visarga*,

all around both the outer and inner paths— specifically surrounding the inner circular path— and having written it in forward order, with each syllable joined by the nasal dot (*bindu*), all around the outer path.

Thus, there are twenty-six varieties [of diagrams] according to the sequence and reverse sequence of the classes (*varga*). The procedure for constructing the twenty-six yantras is as follows: having produced a circle by revolving [the compass] to a desired dimension, one should then draw two circles at intervals of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) each; the space between them...
Having reduced [the circle] by a measure of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) and drawn six petals there,

one should fashion a circle within that with a measure of one finger-breadth; then, from the measure of half the diameter of that circle, having fashioned a hexagon as before, one should construct a circle within it that touches and does not touch those junctions.

Having produced a circle with a measurement of one *aṅgula* from that [point], and having fashioned an equilateral triangle whose sides touch the line of that circle, one should [place] there, in the very center, at the beginning of the root-vidyā,
among the five hundred and seventy-six [syllables] produced by the combination of the expansion of the Mātṛkā.
Having written the first *kūṭa*, including the name of the practitioner to be accomplished (*sādhya*), within the [central] triangle;

then having written the three subsequent *kūṭa*-syllables in the [other] triangles of the [central] triangle, starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise; and then having written the syllables beginning with the fifth in the six outer corners, starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise—
Having written the six-peaked syllables, and having written the six-peaked syllables beginning with the eleven syllables in the six yantras outside of that,
and thus having written the sixteen syllables of a single class and type,
[one should place them] in the path between the two circles outside the triangle.

And having written ten syllables of the elements, appropriate for the ritual, in a counter-clockwise direction starting from the front in each of the two paths between the two outer circles of the hexagon,
[one should do the same] in the two paths between the three outer circles of the lotus.

Having first prepared the primary yantra by writing the *mātṛkā* in both direct and reverse order, joined with the *bindu* and the *visarjanīya*, together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and other elements, starting from the outer path as before,
one should thereafter [proceed] in this very same [manner].

On the two outer and inner circles, using the letters of the syllables of the rite together with the object to be accomplished, one should write the Mātṛkā, joined with Māyā and the Bindu, in both forward and reverse order. (47)
Thus the wise one should construct the twenty-six-fold yantra;
thereafter, he should write the thunderbolt (pavi) with one hundred and sixty peak-syllables (kūṭas).
One should cast eighteen lines—east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east—by which two hundred and eighty-nine squares are produced. (49)
There, one should likewise erase thirty-two squares in the corners;
then, in the center, there shall be a vajra consisting of one hundred and sixty-one [squares].
One should construct triangles for it starting from a single square in each of the directions;
in the central square, one should write the Vidyā together with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) and the ritual action (karman).
One should write those peak-syllables (kūṭa) together with the objects to be accomplished within the triangles;
starting as before, one should write them by entering in a clockwise direction.

By writing each letter of the alphabet in sequence, up to the twenty-sixth letter including the vowels (the *savargas*), within the diagrams, twenty-six diagrams in total come into being, together with the previously mentioned diagram. || 47 ||
With five verses beginning with *parastāt* and ending with *śubham*, starting from the first half-verse,

the construction of the Vajra-casket yantra is described using the one hundred and sixty remaining *kūṭa*-forms of the root-mantra that were not employed in the twenty-six previously mentioned yantras.

And he teaches its significance: therein, beyond the previously assigned forms of the *kūṭas*, *pavi* means the thunderbolt (*vajra*). By those lines—[the remainder is] "thirty-two per corner"—it is so that the remaining [space] in the center takes the form of an uneven thunderbolt.
We shall explain this specific arrangement in the commentary on the construction of the yantra.

"Consisting of a hundred" means consisting of one hundred squares. From each individual square, in every direction, one should write the Vidyā in its pure form—the root-vidyā. Therein, the writing of the letters of the name to be accomplished (*sādhya*) occurs within the letter *ka*.

As before. Regarding the term "kūṭas" (peaks): it means that one should write the first four syllables from the beginning among those previously mentioned and numbered, starting with the first letter of the twenty-seventh group, in the four corners beginning from the front corner and proceeding clockwise. Starting as before...

The meaning is as follows: starting from the central square within the five squares of the upper row of the front triangle, one writes the four syllables located above the four sets of three triangles.
This is the aforementioned form. The sequence for constructing this Vajra-yantra within these squares is as follows:
By striking eighteen lines— running east-west, north-south, and at right angles to each other—
one obtains eighty-nine [squares].
This great *vajra* diagram is the warder-off of all calamities.
It bestows all desired objects, grants the glory of universal victory, and is auspicious. || 53 ||
Having constructed two hundred and one squares, one should erase the entire outermost row thereon; then, in the four directions,
[one should erase] the tips of the two outer lines of the two rows extending up to the central row.
Having formed them in the shape of triangles, then, within those, having cleared nine square cells in each of the four corners along the visible outer path,
then, within those, in each of the four corners along the visible outer path, five...
Having cleared five squares, then inside that, having cleared three squares each in every one of the four corners along the visible outer path,
there are thus thirty-two squares in each corner in total.
Having combined [the elements] in this yantra, one should erase one hundred and twenty-eight squares consisting of triangles and vajras. When this has been done, in each of the four directions,
there are five squares in each row situated within the intervals between the four triangles.
In the two rows situated within that interval, there are seven squares in each direction;

in the row situated within those intervals, there are four squares in each of the four corners— exceeding those seven squares— which extend outward individually from each corner in a single-unit sequence.
Then, within that space, there are forty-nine squares arranged in an unequal quadrangle; these,
together with the four external triangles,
constitute one hundred and sixty-one [squares] in this odd-numbered Vajra Yantra.
They arise. At the base of this *vajra*, there is the aforementioned discrepancy intended by the word "likewise" (*tathā*):

namely, that in the four directions, externally, the second and third rows consist of an equal number of squares. Therein, in the very central square, [one should place] the *vidyā* of the syllable *śat*.
As before, having written [the syllables] containing the names of the three— beginning with the one to be accomplished (sādhya)— within the belly of the letter *ka*,
one should place them in the four corners situated in all the outer directions, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, within the previously mentioned number of forms of the root-vidyā.

From among the four hundred and sixteen syllables consisting of the twenty-six groups written in the twenty-six yantras produced by the sequence of the previously mentioned groups, the first four syllables— which are in the form of *kūṭas*— among the one hundred and sixty syllables consisting of the remaining ten groups, are as before.

Having written down the syllables containing the *sādhya* [name] within [the central triangle], one should place the one hundred and fifty-six *kūṭākṣara*s— beginning with the five *kūṭas* situated above them— into the remaining equal number of squares located in the row above the topmost triangle.

Starting from the central square of the five-row grid and proceeding in a clockwise direction by way of entry, one should write the entire mantra containing the essence of knowledge (*vidyāgarbha*) according to the prescribed order, excluding the very center square.
This is the Great Vajra Yantra of the Odd-numbered Type, which bestows the attainment of the aforementioned results. || 53 ||
(386) Thus, O Maheśvarī, twenty-seven yantras have been described;
although these are equal in number to the twenty-seven lunar mansions.
O Supreme Goddess, I shall now declare their fruits in due order according to the sequence already mentioned, as well as the sequence of their application with perfect clarity.
By worshipping with the first [mantra], diseases are destroyed without remainder;
having performed this in one's own house upon a pedestal or even on the ground. (57)
Having thoroughly ground the aforementioned substances together with their paste,
[one should apply it] for three nights, seven nights, or twenty-seven nights.

Having worshipped the water-pot there, which is filled with water containing mantras and medicinal herbs, and having placed it down and honored the wielder of the mace (Viṣṇu), one should then be consecrated; thereafter, one becomes happy.
In this manner, one should employ other yantras among those already mentioned;
now listen as I tell you the materials for drawing them. (60)
Kucandana, candana, sindūra, along with gorocanā, kāśmīra, aguru, kuṣṭha, and with elā, kakkola, and jāti; || 61 ||
With the twelve trees of one's own asterism ground with snow-water, or with auspicious waters produced from the trees of the asterisms finely ground; || 62 ||
One should perform the second [rite] for the sake of attaining victory according to the prescribed form;
one shall become victorious in debate, dispute, battle, and at dice. (63)
With sixteen verses beginning with "saptaviṃśati" and ending with "āpnuyāt," [the text] describes,

collectively by means of twenty-seven yantras, the worship and so forth in the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) as being of that nature, as well as worship on the days of the week (*vāra*), and subsequently the sequence of worship for the lunar days (*tithi*).

He instructs: "Therein, twenty-seven instruments" means that together with the one previously mentioned immediately before, there are twenty-seven instruments. For that reason, those very same twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*) [are to be applied] along with the case-endings;
this is the ellipsis. In the phrase "those very same," the word "very" (*eva*) is connected to "those" (*tāni*). The goal (*sādhya*)...

The aforementioned yantras [are to be used] on those respective days when those specific yantras are obtained during the asterisms beginning with Aśvinī. "Of them" refers to those yantras. "O Supreme Goddess" is the vocative address.
It should be so.
In the first nine [months] of the third [period], one should worship the nine planets;
because they are of the same nature as the Goddess herself, there will certainly be no affliction for him from them. (64)

One should quickly paralyze [the enemy's] march to battle, the onset of rain, military exertion, or obstinate speech by means of the twelfth [mantra], according to the prescribed sequence of ritual procedure. 65.
By means of the yantras beginning with the thirteenth and ending with the vajra, which consist of the lunar days (tithis),
one will certainly obtain one's desires on those respective lunar days, just as before.
Having worshipped the respective lords of the lunar days (tithis) and the lords of the days (vāreśas) within those various yantras, one shall obtain their respective fruits.

When tasks have arisen, whether they be desired or otherwise, one should employ that [mantra] in the machine prescribed for the day, the asterism, and the lunar date, along with their respective deities. (68)
One should worship [the fire] in a counter-clockwise direction, situated in the quarters of Agni, Rakṣas, Vāyu, and Īśa;
thus one shall attain the pacification of disease and obtain the desired fruits of one's endeavors.
This is an indeclinable particle (*avyaya*) used as an insertion into the verb, serving the purpose of emphasis (*avadhāraṇa*). "Or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative.

"The aforementioned substances" refers to those yet to be mentioned, such as *kucandana* and so forth. "Or" (*vā*) again signifies an alternative. Having placed [the substance] there in the yantra, immediately after the worship on the prescribed day, [he becomes] happy or afflicted—this is the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). Regarding those [substances] that have been mentioned...

In due order, for the constellations (*nakṣatras*) and the rites (*kāryas*) to be described and previously mentioned, [one should perform the rite] with water containing moonstone (*sendu*) and camphor (*sakarpūra*), using twelve waters derived from the trees of the constellations such as red sandalwood (*kucandana*) and others—either auspicious and pure in form, or, according to the alternative (*vā* as an option), with substances finely ground; this is the remainder [of the sense]. This is the second [part].

The word "yantra" (diagram) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. By means of the aforementioned form, through the worship and consecration on those respective days corresponding to those particular asterisms and so forth; in the nine diagrams beginning with the third—that is, the first three diagrams and so on—ending with the eleventh; from that which has the nature of the Goddess's own self, meaning from her body consisting of the Goddess. By that...

For this reason, for this practitioner, by those planets—this worship of the planets should be performed on their respective days; such is the traditional instruction (*sampadāya*). The days of Rāhu and Ketu are as previously stated. "By the twelfth" refers to the yantra following the previously mentioned ninefold [arrangement]; the remainder is to be understood according to the prescribed sequence of rules.
From the worship of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra) attained at that time and the day itself, and so forth— by means of the thirteen and others previously mentioned,
which consist of the lunar days (tithis) and are distinguished by the number fifteen— the remainder is that they are "properly worshipped" as before.
[One should worship] the lords of the lunar days and the days, whose forms will be described later, and the lords of the weekdays as stated in the *Kulasundarīpaṭala*.

Of two kinds; that goddess; by those deities situated in the directions of fire, the rākṣasa, wind, and Īśa (northeast)—namely, the lords of the lunar days, constellations, and weekdays, who are to be worshipped in pairs and positioned in the directions according to the stated sequence.
The connection here is with the word "by the deities. "The entire pacification of diseases" refers to that previously mentioned;
"the fruits of diligent effort" refers to the fruits of undertakings already commenced. || 69 ||

O Supreme Goddess, the presiding deities of the lunar days (tithis) and the lunar mansions (nakṣatras), as well as the trees and the womb-sources (yoni) of the constellations, have been declared; now they shall be recited. (70)
Agni, the two Aśvins, Umā, Vighna, the serpents, Ṣaṇmukha, Ravi, the Mātṛs, as well as Durgā, the quarters, Dhanada, and Keśava. (71)
Yama, Hara, and Śaśin are proclaimed as the lords of the lunar days (tithis).
Now listen as I shall duly declare the deities of the constellations (nakṣatras) as well. 72.
The Aśvins, Yama, Vahni, Dhātṛ, Candra, Śiva, Aditi, Guru, the Sarpas, the Pitṛs, Aryaman, and Bhaga as well. || 73 ||
Dinakṛt, Tvaṣṭṛ, Māruta, Indra, Agni, Mitra, Indu, Nirṛti, Toya, the Viśvedevas, and Hari; || 74 ||
The Vasus, Varuṇa, Aja Ekapāt, Ahirbudhnya, and Pūṣan are declared to be the deities of the lunar mansions. || 75 ||

With these eleven verses beginning with "vārāṇām" and ending with "gajāḥ," [the author] teaches the lunar days (*tithi*), constellations (*nakṣatra*), trees, deities of the constellations, and the origins (*yoni*) of the constellations, preceded by the recollection of the deities of the days previously mentioned. Among those, what was stated...

In the *Kulasundarīpaṭala*, the phrase "the wombs" (*yonīḥ*) means the lunar mansions (*nakṣatrayonīḥ*). With the verse beginning with "Fire" (*vahnī*), he teaches the twelve deities among the fifteen lunar-day deities (*tithidevatā*). Having taught the remaining three lunar-day deities with the verse beginning with "Yama,"...

And he introduces the section on the deities of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). With the verse beginning with "The two Aśvins" (*aśvināv*), he teaches twelve names among the twenty-seven lunar mansion deities, which correspond to that number.
In that context, the word division is *śivo 'ditiḥ śivaḥ aditiḥ*. With the verse beginning with "The maker of day" (*dinakṛt*)...

Among those remaining fifteen in number, he teaches the names of ten deities. Therein, Indra and Agni are the two deities of one lunar mansion. With the verse beginning with "The Vasus," he provides the instruction on the names of the five remaining deities and offers a concluding summary of what has been stated.

With the verse beginning with "kāraskara," he teaches the names of ten trees among the twenty-seven lunar mansion-trees (*nakṣatra-vṛkṣa*) that correspond to their number. In the phrase "āmalakodumbara," the elision (*sandhi*) occurs because of its divine nature;
the meaning is "āmalaka and udumbara. With the phrase beginning with "palāśa," [he teaches] the remaining seventeen in number.
Among them, he teaches the names of the eleven trees: (p.
389) Kāraskara, Āmalaka, Udumbara, Jambuka, as well as Khadira, the two types of Kṛṣṇavaṃśa, Pippala, Nāga, and Rohiṇa. || 76 ||
Palāśa, plakṣa, kāmbaṣṭha, bilva, arjuna, vikaṅkata, vakula, sarala, sarja, vañjula, and likewise panasa. (77)
Arka, śamī, kadamba, cūta, nimba, and finally madhūka—these trees are declared to be the measures in their respective order. (78)
A horse, an elephant, a goat, a snake, a female serpent, a dog, a cat, a she-goat, a male cat, a rat, mice, a bull, and a buffalo-cow; (79)
A tiger and a buffalo, a tigress, a doe, a female deer, and a monkey;
a gokarṇa, a female monkey, a lioness, a mare, a lion, a cow, and an elephant. (80)
When suffering from diseases and other ailments occurs, its cessation shall happen after half the number of days,
muhūrtas, or days as indicated by the count, or else after double that time.

With the verse beginning with "arketi," he provides the instruction on the names of the remaining six trees and concludes what has been stated; here, the connection is "madhūka" at the end, meaning that *madhūka* is [the tree] for Revatī. [The word] "bhānām" means of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). With the verse beginning with "aśvam," etc.,...
Among the twenty-seven lunar mansion origins (*nakṣatrayoni*), he teaches the names of thirteen origins.

Therein, "dog and cat" (*śvaviḍālikā*) means both the dog and the female cat; "bull and buffalo" (*vṛṣamahiṣī*) means both the bull and the buffalo. With the verse beginning with "tiger," he teaches the names of the remaining origins.

In this context, "mahiṣavyāgrhī" means a buffalo and a tigress; "mṛgaśanī" means two deer and two dogs—this refers to the latter half of the verse. Here, the names of all [the deities], beginning with the lunar-day deities and ending with the womb-beings of the asterisms, are to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. || 80 ||

With the verse beginning with "yadā" and so forth, he teaches the means for knowing the time for the pacification of diseases by means of knowing the time at the onset of fevers and other ailments. In this regard, the following is meant:
when there is the onset of a fever or other disease, then in whichever lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*) [it occurs]...

One should know that liberation from the disease will occur after a number of days equal to the number of *ghaṭikās* elapsed, or after half that number of days. In this regard, if the onset of the disease occurs under gentle (*saumya*) constellations, there will be a pacification of the disease according to the stated sequence; however, if it occurs under cruel (*krūra*) constellations—
If it is the case that the sick person abandons the body, such is the tradition. || 81 ||
One should meditate upon five yantras in the *ādhāra*, four in the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, and as many as have been mentioned in the *maṇipūraka*. (82)
Then, one should meditate upon five yantras in the Anāhata [cakra], four in the one called Viśuddha, and five in the Ājñā, in this sequence. (83)
On each of those respective lunar days, one should thus meditate upon the auspicious Śoḍaśī;
one should meditate upon all those who reside within the respective cakras for the sake of all prosperity.
One should meditate upon the cakras in the locations beginning with the ādhāra according to the stated yoga;
however, one should never meditate upon all [cakras] everywhere at all times. (85)
For those who are unable to perform meditative cultivation (bhāvanā), one should likewise fashion the aforementioned support-lotuses outside of those respective yantras and worship Śivā there.
Thus, by worshipping the Goddess in due order on the [specified] days, weekdays, and lunar mansions, one shall obtain desired objects within the stated number of days.

With these four verses beginning with "ādhāra" and ending with "kadācana," he teaches the attainment of the fruit for one who visualizes the twenty-seven yantras— previously mentioned— according to the sequence of their specific divisions within the six centers (ādhāras), starting from the Mūlādhāra.

In that context, among the twenty-seven [yantras] previously mentioned, there are as many as four; this is the meaning. Thus, in sequence, according to the order of the first yantra and so forth, on those specific lunar days when the respective yantras are obtained—this is what is meant:
of the first and other yantras, which are divided according to the stated number.

On the lunar days and days corresponding to each respective yantra, one should perform the meditation on each [deity] individually in the Mūlādhāra and other centers every day. This is for one meditating upon Citrānityā Śivā as the sixteenth [deity]; it is not that all [deities] should be meditated upon everywhere, nor all [yantras] in all the substrates according to one's own whim.

These are to be meditated upon according to the division of the stated numbers; following the sequence of the divisions beginning with the first as described, those very things mentioned for each case are to be meditated upon. || 85 ||

With the two verses beginning with "In meditation" (*bhāvanāyām*) and ending with "in days" (*vāsaraiḥ*), [the author] describes how for those who are unable to perform meditation within the supports (*ādhāra*), one should first construct the respective lotuses of those supports externally as before; then, having inscribed the specific yantra obtained therein, one should worship the Goddess on the corresponding lunar day, weekday, and asterism.
It teaches that by propitiating [the deity] for the previously mentioned twenty-seven days, one shall obtain the aforementioned fruits. || 87 ||
And on those very days, one should offer the *vali* oblation according to the prescribed rule;
and at midnight, [the offering] for the fifty pairs in the aforementioned circle should be performed. (88)
O Īśvarī, at midday and during the two twilights, for those situated within the wheels [of the maṇḍala],
the procedure for those moving through the wheels follows the sequence of the couples, just like that of the Śakti-mantras.
O Īśvarī, the mantra-forms of the kūṭas have been clearly declared;
with those [mantras], one should offer bali to them at those respective times, as has been described.
Having prepared a large wick with the offerings prescribed as a favor from the Goddess,
one should place a lamp soaked in ghee in its center.
Having performed [the rites] with their respective mantras, one should arrange those [offerings] in sequence,
either for each individual deity or for the couples.
One should offer cakes, jackfruit, and plantains, combined with ghee and jaggery;
along with boiled millet and milk-rice, there should be a side dish accompanied by goat meat.
Thus, depending on the gravity or lightness of the task,
one should accomplish it in seven days, or in a fortnight, or in a month, or even from a maṇḍala.
One should offer an oblation to the couples and worship them in the home every month;
or, the practitioner of mantra may worship them in the home once a year, and thus live until the great dawn of liberation.

With the nine verses beginning with *valim* and ending with *narāḥ*, [the author] teaches the method of offering oblations (*validāna*) to the Goddess and the fruits thereof, as well as the previously mentioned fifty pairs. In that context, "on those very days" refers to the days for the application of the aforementioned yantras; furthermore—
The traditional teaching is that one should constantly perform the offering of fifty pairs [of couples] for the sake of auspiciousness and for the purpose of warding off inauspiciousness;
these fifty pairs are those mentioned in the sixteenth chapter, located in the wheel described in that very same place.

This is what is meant: in the wheel of sixty-four squares mentioned in the ninety-eighth verse of the sixteenth chapter, having combined the four central squares into one, one should write the daily *nityā* goddess containing the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) therein; then, on the outside, starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise in the order of exiting, according to the sequence of *ghaṭikās*.
One should perform the worship, the offering of oblations (bali), and so forth for the pairs [of deities].

Regarding the phrase "at the two twilights," this refers to the morning and evening twilights. The grammatical connection here is that one should offer an oblation to the powers of the *kūṭa-vidyās* situated in the *cakra*, together with the Root Power (*mūla-śakti*). "O Sovereign Lady" (*īśvarī*) is an address to the Goddess.
Like the mantra of Śakti, like the mantra of Śakti spoken for the couple (mithuna);
thus, by worshipping through the offering of the oblation to the couple whose nature is Time (kālātmamithuna), and by remembering and glorifying [them], men shall obtain all their desires. (96)
O Maheśvarī, listen to the offering materials for the couples, by which they, having attained satisfaction, swiftly bestow whatever is desired. (97)
One should give milk-rice (pāyasa) for ten [deities], molasses with rice (guḍodana) for ten,
split-mudga beans with food for five, and curd-rice (dadhibhakta) for five.
One should offer five cakes, five portions of milk and sugar,
and five pieces of coconut pulp mixed with jaggery.
The fruit of the plantain (mochāphala) is said to be obtained by those who offer five white oblations;
he who is constantly devoted to the worship of the Gemini [deities] shall become the foremost among practitioners of mantras.

The syntactical connection here is with the phrase "of the peaks belonging to those who move within the wheel. What is meant is this: just as previously there were fifty pairs of powers and vidyās, so too here, for the powers of the vidyā-peaks contained within the described yantra, there are fifteen-syllable vidyās—each accompanied by a peak—as have been taught.

One should perform worship and the offering of oblations (*balidāna*). Those *vidyās* are as follows: first, having uttered each respective *kūṭa* preceded by the two seed-syllables, then saying "Rūpiṇī Śakti," and then reciting the seven-syllabled mantra; thus they consist of fifteen syllables.
There are five hundred and seventy-six vidyās. By means of those mantras,

at those times previously mentioned— such as the three junctions (sandhyās) and so forth— and by means of the offerings for grace described for the goddess Citrānityā in the sixteenth chapter, [the rites are performed].

The meaning is: with the milk-rice (*pāyasa*), rice with jaggery (*guḍānna*), various other foods, turmeric-rice (*haridrānna*), sesame-rice (*tilānna*), and pure, unadulterated rice (*kevalaśuddhānna*) mentioned in the ninetieth verse. "A *śikthaka*" means a morsel or ball of food.
By the words "to each" and so forth, this is what is intended: that [the offering] for the principal deity alone consists of six [morsels].

Regarding the offering of the *bali*, three or four alternatives have been stated: [the offering] may be made to her alone, or to her retinue, or to her retinue together with their consorts, or to each individual couple separately. The nine substances, such as cakes (*apūpa*) and so forth, [are to be used].

It is accompanied by the previously mentioned offering substances (*nivedya-dravya*). Their names are to be learned from the mouth of the Guru. Alternatively, *api vā* signifies an option; *vā* has the sense of an alternative. This is because of the recollection of the couples (*mithuna*), that is, through the contemplation of their nature as being identical with Time (*kāla*). || 96 ||

With these four verses beginning with "mithunānām" and ending with "agraṇīḥ," he teaches the sacrificial substances for the couples that are to be offered regularly, as well as the fruit of worshipping them. Among those,
there are sacrificial substances to be offered regularly and those to be offered on specific occasions.
"The pervasion consisting of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) has been correctly explained. By the refinement of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own. (101)
Thus ends the twenty-first chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, the *Nityātantra*.
"Dadhibhaktaka" means food mixed with curd. "Sitabhaktābhyāṃ mocāphalaṃ" means plantain fruits along with rice and sugar. These very items are also used for the offering of the daily *bali*.
The materials for the couples; this is the officiating priest. 100.

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete tantra known as the *Śrīkādimata* within the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantra*.
The twenty-first chapter, which elucidates the methods for the practice of variegated and impermanent ignorance, is fully concluded and examined. 21.
The number of verses: twenty-seven yantras and two hundred and one and a quarter verses of commentary in this twenty-first chapter.
The Twenty-second Chapter. Now, that which was declared as the deity of power (*validevatā*) among the sixteen *Nityās* is the *vidyā* of Kurukullā, proclaimed to consist of twenty-five syllables.
That very same Vidyā, consisting of three sections, is proclaimed there by its numerical count;
the first was previously said to consist of seven [syllables], joined with thirteen.
That third [form] consists of twenty-five syllables and grants all desired objects;
thus, through these three forms of Vidyā, she bestows what is wished for.
One should worship that Lalitā, who is eternally delighted by amusements, on the island of nine jewels situated in the midst of an ocean of sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, and milk.

Having taught the ritual procedure for the sixteenfold Citrānityā in the preceding twenty-first chapter, he next teaches the ritual procedure for Kurukullā— the offering deity who is non-different from each and every Nityā— beginning with the word "atha" (now).
By means of the twenty-second chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "The sixteen constant [deities]" (*ṣoḍaśanityā*) and ending with "that" (*tat*),
[the author explains] therein— through three verses beginning with "Now, the sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "bestowers of desired fruits" (*abhīṣṭhadā*)—
the threefold nature of the *Kurukullā* vidyā as described in the third chapter, and of those...

It teaches the number of syllables stated for each of the three sections therein, as well as the way those [sections] cause the deity to grant one's desires. In that regard, the remainder is that the twenty-five-syllable [mantra] is mentioned in the third chapter; therein, it consists of twenty-five syllables.
The meaning is that the root-vidyā consists of the nature of the first and second sections and constitutes the third section;

it is precisely that [vidyā] of twenty-five syllables. It is "three-sectioned" (trikhaṇḍā), meaning it has a threefold division of forms. "In that very [place]" means in the third chapter itself. "That third one" means that vidyā which is the root of the two preceding sections constitutes the third section.
She is Kurukullā. || 3 ||
With the one and a half verses beginning with *ikṣu* and ending with *tīrapālikām*,
[the author] recalls here the sequence of worship for Lalitā— the goddess whose body is composed of all [deities]— as taught in the three chapters starting from the fourth. Regarding her:

He intends for Kurukullā to be an ancillary part (*aṅga*) of that [Lalitā]. In that context, she is delighted by constant diversions such as music and the like. By the first half of the verse beginning with "tattīre" (on its bank), he incidentally indicates her who is an ancillary to that Lalitā, whose ritual procedure will be described in the subsequent chapter.

Since Kurukullā is to be worshipped first, he introduces [the rite] with the words, "one should worship Vārāhī as the fifth. In that regard, she is on its shore—that is, on the shore of the ocean of sugarcane juice—because she is the first of the four. Furthermore, this is because it is stated in another scripture: "Then, one should worship Vārāhī at the edge of the ocean of sugarcane juice. Therein:
The tradition holds that her station is in the south-western corner, facing Lalitā. || 4 ||
On its bank, one should worship the goddess Pañcamī Tīrapālikā;
one should worship Ratnapotacarī all around those oceans.
By his command, one should worship the jewel-boat (ratnapota) using that very name;
and by that same [name], one should worship the wheel of Bali (valicakra) in its center. || 6 ||
Having fashioned a square [mandala] provided with gates in the eastern and western directions,
one should draw within it a lotus with eight petals and a pericarp.
Having fashioned a beautiful pericarp, one should worship the nine-fold source (navayoni).
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with the *vālā* [mantra], one should also prepare the *arghya* offering with it.

With the first half-verse beginning with "tatsāgareṣu" and ending with "samarccayet," he teaches the worship of the jewel-vessel, the bali-offering, and the maṇḍala for this Kurukullā, preceded by an introduction to her worship; therein, "tatsāgareṣu" refers to those [oceans] presided over by the fifth [Tārā].
On its shores, in the ocean, and so forth, one should perform the practice of Ratnapotacarī Kurukullā. There, by her command and with the permission of Tīrapālikā Pañcamī,
the worship and installation of that Kurukullā takes place in the oceans, specifically in the northwestern corner of the Ikṣusāgara.

By the expression "the course of the jewel-boat" (*ratnapotacarī*), the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) holds that it faces toward the practitioner. This is because the fifth [vow] is situated in the southwest corner. The "jewel-boat" (*ratnapota*) is a vessel constructed of jewels, having a form similar to a modern ship.

The tradition: one should worship with the name itself—namely, "Ratnapota" followed by "namaḥ"—preceded by the *hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīḥ*) which is to be used for dismissal as will be described later; for example: *hrīḥ ratnapotāya namaḥ*.

And the *valicakra* (wheel of the folds) is of the form to be described hereafter; with that very name, as before, ending in "namas" and preceded by the power of the letter *visarjanīya*, one should worship it, for example: "Hrīḥ, obeisance to the *valicakra*.
In the middle of that, in the center of the jewel-throne.
With the one and a half verses beginning with "pūrva" and ending with "samarcayet," he teaches the ritual cycle for the daily worship (*nityasaparyā*) of the goddess Kurukullā. In that context,
regarding the phrase "endowed with eastern and western gates," although the construction of the door-frames (*śākhā*) is not explicitly mentioned, [it is understood].

According to the tradition, by the statement "to the north, the branch of Dakṣa," etc., it is indicated that each door is provided with two branches, thus describing the square [mandala]. "Charming" means according to the proper measurement. This is what is meant:
in the corners, there are two equal squares, each having a pair of doors with two branches, from east to west.
Having marked the directions with the signs for the positions of the deities,
one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus provided with two central spaces; then, in its pericarp,
one should construct a nine-yoni wheel according to the previously mentioned proportions of four, three, five, and four parts.
One should worship that [deity] with its name-mantra. || 8 ||

With the second half of the verse beginning with "six-limbed" (*ṣaḍaṅgam*), he teaches the ritual placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and the preparation of the *arghya* offering. In that context, the phrase "with the *vālā*" refers to the *Kulasundarī* mantra; the ellipsis "of the same class" (*sajātikayā*) is to be supplied. Thus, [one performs] the six-limbed [placement] with the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*).
And one should worship [it] with the twenty-five-syllable [mantra], three times without fail.
One should invoke her with the first root mantra and the *trikhaṇḍa-mudrā*.
Having meditated thus upon that Goddess together with her retinue, one should worship her in due order with perfumes and other offerings. (9)
One should meditate upon her with disheveled hair, naked, red in color, and the embodiment of bliss,
holding in her hands an arrow, a bow, a noose, and two quivers.
The goddesses who stand outside possess weapons, forms, and complexions identical to his;
they have bathed after their menses, their vulvas quiver with desire, and their eyes are perpetually red with bliss. (11)
One should perform the ritual services, beginning with installation, using the *hṛllekhā* mantra;
then, by her command, one should worship *Bhrāmiṇī* and *Drāviṇī* upon the sprout.
Beginning from the western door, one should worship the right branch and so forth:
Sūrya and Soma, the lunar day (tithi), the day of the week (vāra), as well as the yoga, the asterism (ṛkṣa), and the karaṇa.

With these three verses beginning with "trikhaṇḍā" and ending with "īkṣaṇā," he teaches the visualization of the Goddess together with her retinue, preceded by the invocation mudrā and mantra. Therein, [the first] is by means of the seven-syllabled mantra.

The ellipsis [is to be supplied]. "In this manner" means by way of the form that is about to be described. "One should worship with perfumes and so forth"—this is the ellipsis to be supplied. As for the nakedness of the Goddess, meaning she is sky-clad (*digambarā*): her being sky-clad is due to her consisting of consciousness, bliss, and *ānanda*. "Unveiledness" is the supplementary explanation; this is the meaning according to the oral tradition (*sampradāya*). She whose body is bliss (*ānandavigrahām*).

Because its nature is the bliss of consciousness (*sambid-ānanda*). As for the sequence of the weapons, it proceeds from the lower right of one's own [body] to the end of the north, moving counter-clockwise (*apradakṣiṇya*). "Having bathed after their menses, with throbbing vulvas"—this is common to these goddesses as well;
the mention of her having bathed after her menses and possessing a throbbing vulva is [for this reason].
The traditional teaching is that she possesses the previously mentioned nature of being composed of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), as well as an excellence of eternal radiance.

Furthermore, the traditional teaching is that even when performing the worship of her graceful limbs (*lalitāṅga*), this very same visualization (*dhyāna*) is to be used, and not one identical to that [of the main deity]. || 12 ||

With six and a half verses beginning with *hṛllekhā* and ending with *pūjayet*, he teaches the sequence of the daily worship (*nityasaparyā*) of the Goddess, preceded by the ritual offerings (*upacāra*),
along with her fourfold enclosure (*sāvaraṇa*). In that context, [the first is] with *hṛllekhā*.

The traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) is that [the mantra] includes the *visarjanīya*. Likewise, one should worship all the powers (*sarvaśakti*) present within each respective mantra and so forth. The word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the rites of installation (*sthāpana*) and others, such as the rite of withdrawal (*sannirodha*).
"Offerings" (*upacāra*) refers to the water for honor (*argha*), the water for the feet (*pādya*), and so on. "By her command" means by the command of the Goddess. [One should worship] Bhrāmiṇī.
One should worship Drāviṇī. Their positions, however, are at the eastern and western extremities of the jewel-boat.
For the goddess facing westward, they are located starting from the right branch [of the boat] and proceeding clockwise along the branches on her right side. Regarding the phrase "and the Yakṣiṇīs":
The plural ending is used because they are characterized by the number thirty-six. Their mantra is as follows:

*hrīḥ yakṣiṇīrūpiṇīśaktipādukāḥ pūjayāmi* (I worship the sandals of the powers in the form of Yakṣiṇīs). For the others, [the word] "pādukām" (the sandal) [is added] at the end of each respective name.
Likewise, one should worship Yakṣiṇī and Tārā on the two doorposts of the eastern gate, together with the Śaktis who have the forms of ether, air, fire, water, and earth. (14)
One should worship sound, touch, form, taste, and smell as before, and likewise the sense of smell, the intellect, and the power, upon the eight petals. || 15 ||
In the intermediate octagonal corners, one should worship the eight goddesses of speech (Vāgdevīs).
Then, one should worship the arrows, the bow, the noose, and the goad around it.
Having worshipped the powers consisting of will, knowledge, and action at the corners of the central triangle,
one should then worship the seat of consciousness (sambidāsana) in its center.
Then he should worship her with the root mantra consisting of twenty-five syllables.
Then, by her command, he arrived at an island surrounded by ships.
Having obtained the western Puṣparāga stone, one should descend in due order;
while circumambulating, one should indeed worship these [stones] here and there in their respective directions.
One should first worship the oceans of sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, and milk, starting from the west and proceeding in reverse order,
using their names ending in "namaḥ" along with perfumes and flowers.

"I worship Hrīḥ, the Sandal-powder Śakti" and "I worship Vyomarūpiṇī, the Sound Śakti"— these and similar [formulas] are to be understood as the mantras for sound and the other [objects of sense]. As before, one should worship them in a clockwise direction starting from the front,
together with Rūpiṇī-Śakti and the others, all around in a clockwise direction starting from the front.
As before, outside the central triangle, on both sides near each of its arms, [one should place them] counter-clockwise;

or else, as before, in sequence within that, namely in the middle of the triangle. Regarding "the seat of consciousness" (*saṃvidāsana*): according to the tradition, this refers to the Person whose nature is consciousness, who serves as the husband of the deity. In that regard:

The manner of the stations of the deities and the manner of the abiding of the veiling powers (āvaraṇa-śakti) must be understood solely from the mouth of the Guru. Its mantra is as follows: *hrīḥ saṃvidāsanāya namaḥ*.
This consists of twenty-five syllables, serving as the root-mantra (*mūlamantra*) which constitutes the nature of the two sections.
The meaning is "by the third. || 18 ||

With the two and a half verses beginning with *tataḥ* and ending with *puṣpakaiḥ*, he teaches the Goddess’s abiding as an auxiliary limb (*aṅga*) of the principal deity Lalitā, as well as the worship [of the ocean] starting with the letter *ikṣu*.
In that context, the remainder is: "by her command" means "by the command of Kurukullā," and it should be performed. The western...

The term "puṣparāga" (topaz) recalls that specific portion at the forefront of the island of nine gems (*navaratnadvīpa*) mentioned in the *Nityapūjāpaṭala*, since that section consists of topaz. Regarding the phrase "being surrounded," it refers to what was previously described as "the island consisting of nine gems" and so forth.
Thus was it worshipped by the Goddess, bringing delight to Lalitā.
Thus, for the one who worships the Goddess, many desired things are quickly fulfilled;
therefore, O Sovereign Lady, one should worship her in this manner.
O Supreme Goddess, at the conclusion of the worship, one should worship Kurukullā among the goddesses above the water with the root mantra consisting of twenty-five syllables.
The offering for the Goddess has been declared through the mantra of Tārāśakti;
listen to it, O beloved, as I shall speak that ten-syllabled Tārā-vidyā. (24)

The syllable *bhūḥ* joined with its own [seed-syllable], followed by *rayaḥ* accompanied by *dāha* (the letter *ra*) and *cara* (the letter *sa*), then *rayaḥ* joined with *dharā* (the letter *la*), and finally a pair of *rayas* joined with *marut* (the letter *ya*). || 25 ||
This third [syllable] becomes the sixth; the fourth shall become the seventh.
One should know that the sixth then becomes the eighth, accompanied by the heart, water, and air. (26)

The phrase "wandering here and there" implies various locations. "From the west and so forth in reverse order" means according to the previously stated sequence. By saying "with names ending in *namaḥ*," it recalls the two seed-syllables (*bīja*) as being "each preceding one. The meaning is that one should first join the two seed-syllables with the names, and [worship] with those.
Their mantras are as follows: *hrīḥ śrīḥ ikṣusāgarāya namaḥ* (Hrīḥ Śrīḥ, obeisance to the Sugarcane Ocean), and so forth. || 20 ||

With these two verses beginning with "consisting of the nine gems" and ending with "the Sovereign Lady" (īśvarī), he teaches the specific fruits resulting from the special worship of Goddess Lalitā. In this regard, it is as previously stated in the instruction on the daily worship of Lalitā according to the described form. Thus, as before, she becomes gracious and bestows [the fruit].
The word "devī" is to be supplied [as the subject]. "Īśvarī" is an address to the Goddess. || 22 ||
With the verse beginning with "devīnām" and so forth, he teaches the independent sequence of worship for the goddess Kurukullā. || 23 ||
With these four verses beginning with "Of the Goddess" (devyāḥ) and ending with "Supreme Sovereign Lady" (parameśvarī),

he teaches the bali offering for the independent daily worship of the Goddess Kurukullā, as well as her ten-syllable mantra and the procedure for presenting the bali. In that context, regarding the phrase "of the Goddess Kurukullā, the earth [is] joined with herself":

The remainder is *oṃ*. *Raya* joined with *marut* is *tā*. *Dāha* accompanied by *carā* is *re*. *Raya* joined with *dharā* is *tu*. A pair of *raya*s joined with *marut* is *tā*. This is the third [syllable] and it shall be the sixth. Of this very *vidyā*, the third syllable is indeed *re*.
The ten-syllable Vidyā is said to be *haṃsa* joined with the wind (*marut*).
O Supreme Goddess, one should offer an oblation to this [deity] by means of this Vidyā. (27)
O wise one, listen to the meditation of the Goddess, which cuts through all afflictions;
when remembered, there shall be no obstruction anywhere in her waters. (28)
She is dark-complexioned, three-eyed, and two-armed, holding a boon-granting lotus; she is surrounded by [attendants] of many colors and many forms. || 29 ||
One should meditate upon her whose face is like that of Smara, who is adorned with jewels and pearls,
and whose pair of lotus-feet rest upon jeweled sandals.
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) daily with red flowers smeared with ghee,
or with fragrant white flowers, or with food and clarified butter, or with ghee alone.
Endowed with the vow as before, having recited the mantra twenty-five hundred thousand times, one should worship during the twilights, and then perform the libations and fire-offerings.

The meaning is that it should be the sixth syllable. "The fourth is the seventh": the meaning is that the very fourth syllable of this same *vidyā*, namely the syllable *tu*, shall become its seventh syllable. "The sixth is the eighth": [the meaning is] of this same *vidyā*, the sixth...
One should know—that is, one should understand—that the eighth syllable of this [mantra] is the syllable *repha*, which is simply *re*.

The ninth syllable is *svā*, accompanied by the heart (*hṛt*), water (*ambu*), and wind (*marut*). And the *haṃsa* joined with the wind becomes the tenth syllable, *hā*. By means of these ten syllables thus declared, [one should worship] her.

The offering for Kurukullā is made with this very mantra; for Tārāśakti, the tradition holds that the offering at the beginning of all worship is made with the sixteen-syllable mantra. "O Supreme Goddess" (parameśvari) is an address to the Goddess. || 27 ||

With these three verses beginning with "dhyānam" and ending with "smaret," he teaches the visualization for the time of the offering (bali-samaya-dhyāna) of the offering deity, the power Tārā. In that context, "from her"—
meaning from the recollection of this power Tārā, which is to say, from the visualization to be described— [she resides] in the excellent lotus.
"With the left and right [hands]"—this connects with "surrounded by Śaktis" from the preceding passage.
The meaning is that she has placed her pair of lotus-feet forward, approaching face-to-face for the purpose of accepting the offering.
With the verse beginning with "homaṃ," he teaches the materials for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) of the goddess Kurukullā; in that context, the word "vā" signifies an alternative. || 31 ||
With one and a half verses beginning with "as before" (prāgvat) and ending with "the ritual action" (kriyām),
[it is taught that] one should perform the oblation rite (havanakriyā) using any one of those [mantras] prescribed for daily recitation, based on the root-vidyā of twenty-five syllables.
Thus, having perfected the vidyā and being likewise devoted to the daily worship, || 33 ||
One should indeed practice the optional rites with devotion according to the prescribed order;
listen now to those [rites] through fire-offerings, worship, and the contemplation of the yantra. (34)
By performing a fire-oblation with mustard seeds smeared with ghee, one may bring women under control;
and by offering black pepper soaked in mustard oil, one may summon them.
By performing oblations at midnight according to the prescribed rite with sesame seeds smeared with oil,
one shall bring women, men, kings, and others under one's control for as long as they live.
By performing oblations at midnight with Bandhūka flowers smeared with goat’s ghee, one may enchant all women with love and passion.
By offering oblations of mallikā flowers soaked in milk, one shall bring brāhmaṇas and kings under control; likewise, by means of auspicious śatapatra and vicakila flowers.
By performing oblations with coconut-derived pulp mixed with sugar and combined with the milk of a cow and its calf, one shall obtain gold. (39)
By offering oblations of crushed coconut kernels mixed with jaggery, honey, and ghee, one shall obtain an accumulation of wealth within the time frame previously mentioned. (40)
Through the oblation of plantain fruit one becomes foremost; through the oblation of lotuses one attains [prosperity];
and through the oblation of white water-lilies and the two kinds of night-lilies, one obtains all that is desired.

He teaches the *puraścaraṇa* (preliminary rite). In that regard, the vow consists of the formal resolve (*saṃkalpa*). One should [recite] the twenty-five-syllable *vidyā* with any one of the [mantras] prescribed for daily recitation, and with any one of the red flowers and so forth prescribed for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*). || 32 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *evam* and ending with *śṛṇu*, he teaches that only one who has completed the preliminary practice (*puraścaraṇa*) is fit for the ritual application (*prayoga*), as well as the methods of that application. In this context, "devoted to daily worship" means even after the completion of the *puraścaraṇa*. "Those applications" refers to the rituals. (34)

With these seven verses beginning with "ghṛta" and ending with "kumudadvayaiḥ," he teaches the attainment of various fruits through oblations (*homa*) performed with fourteen substances. In that context, "those women" refers to [the aforementioned]. "Anointed with oil" means anointed with the oil of sesame seeds. "The others... [and so forth].
O Goddess, one should worship with blue lotuses for liberation from all calamities;
one should worship with white and red lotuses for the attainment of Indirā. (42)
Likewise, one desiring the acquisition of wealth should worship with *kumuda* flowers, as well as with *bandhūka* blossoms and those born from the *dāḍima* tree. (43)
One should worship Śivā with *saugandhika*, *vicakila*, *kuṭaja*, *śatapatraka*, *punnāga*, *pāṭala*, and flowers arising from the *campaka* tree.
One should worship [the deity] during the seven days of the week, beginning with the Sun, at the prescribed times; thereby one obtains wealth, land, grain, garments, and other such things.
One should constantly worship with camphor, and likewise with the liquid of black aloe-wood; in the time prescribed, one obtains every desired object.
One should constantly perform worship with saffron for the attainment of good fortune;
with camphor for the attainment of longevity, and for the attainment of subjugation, women, and wealth. (47)
And by worshipping for just one month with deer-sweat and *mada*, a man shall possess a charm equal to that of Kandarpa among women. (48)
One should constantly worship with cardamom, cloves, kakkola, and nutmeg;
for as long as a year, he will then become renowned in the world through his riches. (49)
Worship performed with pieces of camphor shall grant all desired objects;
by worshipping with them and consuming them, a man becomes beloved by everyone. (50)

One should also [subjugate] the vassals and others through affection and curiosity, through endearment and longing; this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*) regarding the Brahmins, that is, the *vipras*. Likewise, there is an alternative (*vikalpa*): "combined with white" means mixed with sugar;
"from the previously mentioned time" refers to the mandala and so forth; and "the first" is also the subject for the lotus and the *kahlāra* lily.
With pairs of red and white water-lilies. || 41 ||

With these nine verses beginning with "utpalaiḥ" and ending with "priyaḥ," he teaches the attainment of various fruits through worship with diverse substances. Therein, the grammatical connection is with "sitaiḥ padmaiḥ" (with white lotuses).
Likewise, with red [lotuses] and with two types of water-lilies (kumuda), as before, even through recitation and other rites, there is the attainment of prosperity (śrī).

With *saugandhika* and *kahlāra* lotuses—meaning with all seven types beginning with *saugandhika*—there is likewise the attainment of all desired objects; this is the meaning. For the accomplishment of subjugating women and acquiring wealth, the connection is "with camphor" (*karpūraiḥ*).
Furthermore, there are three circles, as well as an eight-spoked [wheel] and a lotus, and likewise in their center.
Having fashioned the ninefold womb (navayoni) here, one should place Māyā together with the object of accomplishment (sādhya) in its center.
Having drawn [the mandala], one should write the eight syllables of the mantra in the eight corners;
likewise, one should indeed write them on the outer petals in the sequence of two by two.
Having encircled it in reverse order with the external Mātṛkā and the Māyā-svagā, one should accomplish [the rite] by means of that yantra. || 53 ||
Having written the entire desired mantra upon birch bark or a piece of linen cloth with yellow pigment (rocanā), using methods such as worship, wearing, or installation, [one should place it]. 54.

"By musk and ichor" means by musk (mṛgasveda) and by musk-deer secretions (mṛgamada). "Then from that sacrifice" means by those [substances] such as camphor and so forth, having been consumed—that is, eaten. || 50 ||

With three and a half verses beginning with *vṛttatrayam* and ending with *sthāpanādibhiḥ*, he provides instruction on the construction of the yantra using the third root-vidyā consisting of twenty-five syllables, as well as an introduction to the method of its application. Therein:
"In the middle of that" means in the center of the eight-petaled lotus; likewise, according to the procedure described in the *Kulasundarīpaṭala*.

"Here in the middle" means in the center of the *yoni* (vulva) which is the center of all. "Māyā" is as before, the *hṛllekhā* with the visarga, which constitutes the eleventh syllable within the twenty-five-syllable vidyā.
In the eight corners—excluding the central corner—one should write the eight syllables of the mantra;

that is to say, the first eight syllables from the beginning of the twenty-five syllables of the root-vidyā, which constitute the nature of the first and second sections. One should write them starting from the front.

The tradition holds that this is the clockwise direction. "Outside" means outside the nine-yoni diagram. Likewise, it indicates the previously mentioned sequence. By a process of two by two on each petal, the remaining sixteen syllables—those following the nine syllables of the Vidyā written within the yoni—are to be placed; this is the sense. "Outside."

Within the two corridors situated between the three circles that extend outward from the eight-petaled lotus, [the syllables] are arranged by means of *māyā* (the letter *ī*), *khaga* (the letter *ha*), the *visarjanīya* (the letter *ḥ*) joined with [the former], and the *bindu* (the nasal dot), respectively, both in direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*pratiloma*) order.

Regarding the phrase "by means of installation and so forth" (*sthāpanādibhiḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and other such rites. This is the sequence for the construction of the *yantra*.

Having constructed three circles with equal central lines by rotating according to the desired dimensions through the division of interior and exterior, and having fashioned an eight-petalled lotus there,
one should fashion a wheel of nine triangles within its pericarp as previously described.
In the midst of the womb situated in the center of all,
within the third root-vidyā consisting of twenty-five syllables which constitutes the nature of the first and second sections,
[one should contemplate] the *hṛllekhā* consisting of eleven syllables, including the visarga.
Having drawn [the diagram] joined with the triad beginning with the practitioner (sādhaka),

one should first write the eight letters of the root-vidyā in the eight outer corners, starting from the top and proceeding clockwise; then, outside of that, in the eight petals, according to the previously mentioned sequence, [one writes] the *hṛllekhā* written in the very center.

Having written the remaining sixteen syllables, two at a time in sequence on each petal, one should form pellets from wax and place them within the two intermediate bands between the three outer circles. (p.
403) Having thus prepared that which is situated in the center of the wax, [one should proceed].
One should cause her to suffer during the nights for the number of days previously mentioned, and then bring the woman under one's control. || 55 ||
Having engraved this upon a copper plate, or having written it on a cloth or inside a wooden board, one should invoke the Goddess there and worship her; by those days, success shall be attained.
The entire three worlds—including men, women, kings, and others, as well as elephants, horses, guards, and even species of animals—will certainly come under his control. (57)
One should draw that yantra either on the bank of the ocean or on the bank of a river;
having invoked the Goddess there with white pigment, one should worship her right then and there.
Through the days that have dawned, there shall be the pacification of all diseases, sufferings, and afflictions;
and from worship there, there shall be gains of livestock, female slaves, wealth, and so forth.
By fashioning that yantra out of sandalwood and worshipping it on its pedestal for that day, one shall become possessed of sons, grandsons, a wife, authority, wealth, grain, and so forth. (50)
By writing this yantra on gold, silver, or birch bark and wearing it, one becomes free from all diseases, miseries, and afflictions, and prospers in happiness. || 61 ||

Having first encircled [the center] within the inner path (antarvīthi) in reverse order with the Mātṛkā joined with the Visarga as before, and having likewise encircled it on the outer path in direct order with this same [Mātṛkā] joined with the Bindu as before,
one proceeds to the application [of the mantra] according to the sequence of worship and so forth to be described.
"The accomplishment of all fruits. || 54 ||

With seven verses beginning with "yantram" and ending with "sukhī," consisting of half-verses and so forth, he teaches the fivefold application of that yantra. Therein, the yantra has been described. The word division is either "ālikhya" (having drawn) or "ālikhya" (having written) as an alternative. "Sikthasya" means of beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*). "Gulikīkṛtya" means having made the yantra into a pill.
By means of the previously mentioned mandalas and so forth; with vermilion (darada) as before. This is the yantra. Or (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative.

There, one should worship in the center of the yantra according to the regular sequence (*nityakrama*). "By those [means], it shall come under control as before"—this is the connection with what precedes. *Tarakṣu* is a tiger; [it refers to] the four-footed species of the animal kingdom.

The word "should subjugate" (*vaśayet*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "On the shore of the Sindhu" means on the shore of the ocean. "Or" (*vā*) has the sense of an alternative; that is to say, "or else.
One should draw [the diagram] there, on a very level ground—this is the ellipsis. There, one should worship in the machine (*yantra*) as before. The syntactical connection is:
"there, by means of the worship with those [mantras] mentioned previously. "There" refers to that place.

The region beginning with Sindhu-tīra [is the subject]. (p. 404) By the laying down of six lines—east-west and north-south—there are twenty-five squares; one should erase three [squares] in the corners. || 62 ||
Then, the vajra is said to be formed by the remaining thirteen cells;
in its center, one should write the śakti, the māyā, and the sthāna, and then the name all around it.
Then, at midnight, one should write the vidyā upon that [surface] and worship it,
[thereby obtaining] the desired woman who has transcended pride, family honor, and modesty.
Having fashioned a yantra upon a leaf of the king of grass (palāśa), one should prepare [the medicine] with mustard seeds and *riṅgu*,
combined with cinnamon, ginger, *māgadhikā* (long pepper), black pepper, and the juice of *arka*.
At night, one should heat a wax-sealed amulet over the flame of a lamp while reciting the thirteen-syllable mantra facing that direction; within days, one will obtain a woman.

And the acquisition of wealth and so forth—this is the grammatical connection (*anvaya*). "Obedient" (*ājñācara*) means having speech that cannot be transgressed by force. The particle *vā* has the sense of an alternative (*vikalpa*). || 61 ||

With these ten verses beginning with "prākpratyak" and ending with "sannibhāḥ," [the author] teaches the construction of the *koṣṭhavajrayantra* by means of the second root-vidyā consisting of thirteen syllables, as well as the fourfold application of that yantra.

In that context, "three" is the remainder for each corner; this is to be construed with the phrase "by the remaining thirteen squares. "In the middle of that" refers to the central square of the yantra. "Śakti" is a name for both the *visarjanīya* (the final *m*) and the vowel *ī* of the *hṛllekhā* mantra, according to established tradition (*sampradāya*) and the context (*prakaraṇa*).
The name of the *visarjanīya* is "māyā," and the names of the previously mentioned [syllables] are here as before;
the name of *hṛllekhā* is "māyā. Therefore, it should be so that within the *vidyā*, the *visarjanīya*—which constitutes the eleventh syllable—is situated within the *hṛllekhā*.

"Thus" is the meaning. "The name" refers to that of the practitioner and so forth. "Then," from the central square, "outside"—this is the ellipsis. "The Vidyā," devoid of the *Hṛllekhā* with its powers, consisting of twelve syllables.
"In that Yantra, one should worship the Goddess"—this is the ellipsis. The sequence for the construction of the Yantra is as follows:
Having drawn six lines— east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east— forming equal intervals,
one should produce twenty-five squares; within those squares, in each corner, that is,
in the four corners, three squares each, totaling twelve squares in the center.
Having cleansed it so that it becomes the form of a vajra,
