one should place the thirteenth syllable of the second root-vidyā consisting of thirteen syllables in the middle of the thirteenth remaining square, which is the very center of all.

One should attract the *hṛllekhā* mantra consisting of eleven syllables including the *visarjanīya*, as before; (p. 405) otherwise, [the victim] will not come. There, by the gradual onset of the fever of passion (*kāmajvara*), he will certainly meet his death through the ten stages (*avasthā*). || 67 ||
Having clearly drawn that form on birch bark or a palm leaf,
one should likewise heat it straight with images made of beeswax.
They cause men, women, kings, and other living beings to be overwhelmed with affection until the end of their bodies, and they speak in opposition to them.
Having drawn the yantra with soot on birch bark, or on white silk, and having performed the recitation (japa), one should wear it; this destroys all diseases, miseries, and afflictions.
Then, having drawn [the image] upon a spotless cloth with red chalk mixed with sandalwood paste, the women who were lying there became like enemies appearing as servants. (71)
Having formed a hexagon within the space between two squares,
one should write the name situated within its center, and [the syllables] *bhūḥ* and *svaḥ* in all three of the six [triangles].
Having written [the syllables] joined with the three designations beginning with "sādhaka" (the practitioner),
one should proceed from the middle square of the triad in the middle row below that, following the proper sequence in a clockwise direction as they exit, into the remaining twelve squares.

Having written the twelve syllables of the second root-vidyā— accompanied by the *hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) with its *visarga*, which is inscribed in the central square— one attains the accomplishment of the results to be described through the worship and other applications to be explained therein.

"On a leaf of the king of grasses" means on a palm leaf; this is what is called the *yantra*. "Sharp salt, *māgadhikā*, and long pepper with beeswax" is as before. "In the lamp-fire" means in the fire in the form of a lamp.
"Facing that direction" means facing the quarter where the target resides. "In days," such as those required for the *maṇḍala* and so forth. "If he does not come."

The word "sādhyāpad" (the victim's state) is to be understood as the ellipsis. In that diagram (*yantra*), she is situated through ten states, beginning with "delight of the eyes" and ending with "death. "Death" refers to the nature of the tenth state. Or, as for the alternative (*vā*): that *yantra*, having been fashioned from beeswax (*madhūcchiṣṭa*) in the likeness of the victim...

That emanation is according to the portions to be described in the thirty-first chapter; likewise, it is accompanied by the recitation of the Vidyā in the lamp-fire on the day specified. The word "other" refers to vassals and the like. Those are the living beings; "hostile" means adverse. "With soot" means with ink.

This is a qualification of the cloth (*kṣauma*). Alternatively (*athavā*) is used in the sense of an option. "Having recited" refers to the root mantra (*mūlavidyā*) together with the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* and other rites. "Having drawn the yantra" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "One should wear" refers to the garment together with that yantra; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 71 ||

With these ten verses beginning with *vṛttadvaye* and ending with *bahiḥ*, [the author] teaches the procedure for constructing the yantra by means of the first root-mantra consisting of seven syllables, as well as the ritual application (*prayoga*) using that yantra. Therein, regarding that hexagon:
One should indeed inscribe the six syllables in sequence within the seven-syllable mantra;
this yantra [should be drawn] on palm leaf, birch bark, linen, or the leaf of the *arka* tree. (73)
Having recited the mantra ten thousand times, one should deposit it in an anthill;
then, on that very day, the serpents residing there shall flee.

Having inscribed it on a wave-patterned cloth or similar material, having recited the mantra over it and worshipped it, one should place it somewhere within the house, provided with daily worship, for the sake of protection. (75)
Indeed, ghosts, spirits, piśācas, apasmāras, vetālas, rākṣasas, yakṣas, gandharvas, serpents, scorpions, and the like do not exist there at all. || 76 ||
Having smeared [the patient] and having recited this vidyā over the water in a jar one thousand times,
sprinkling with those waters destroys the poison.
When that [medicine] is drunk and reaches the stomach, it destroys poison entirely—whether residing in the body, O Supreme Goddess, or of the three terrifying types. (78)

*Bhūḥ* means "contained within its own womb. *Bhūḥ* refers to the syllable *o*; *svam* refers to the *bindu*. The meaning is that it is contained within the thirteenth vowel (*au*) together with the *bindu*, which constitutes the first letter of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*). The name is as before. The six syllables are written in the middle.

One should write these [syllables] in sequence upon the seven-syllable root-mantra (mūlavidyā), excluding the first syllable which is the root-om (praṇava), in a clockwise direction starting from the tip; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Alternatively, the word "vidyām" (the mantra) should be understood as referring to the seven-syllable one, and "tadyantram" (that yantra) refers to that specific day.
To the one who receives the deposit: the procedure for the construction of this yantra is as follows—
having fashioned two circles, one inside and one outside, by rotating according to the desired measurement,
and having constructed a hexagon within the inner circle as before, [one proceeds] in the center of that hexagon.

Having written the *praṇava*— which consists of the first syllable of the seven-syllabled root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*)— as before, with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) placed within it; then, outside in the six corners, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise,
one should write the seven syllables of the root-mantra, excluding the *praṇava* written in the center.

One should write the six syllables of the *ṣaḍakṣarī*. Having thus written this yantra on one of the materials such as birch bark (*bhūrja*) and having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-breath), one should recite the ten-thousand-fold mantra of the seven-syllable vidyā. By burying that yantra in an anthill, the serpents residing there [will perish] on that very day.
Thus they become eradicated. Regarding that yantra: "on the ring, etc."—here "ring" (*ūrmmikā*) means a finger-ring;
the word "etc. refers to ornaments such as bracelets and armlets. For the person who wears it: "scorpions, etc."—here the word "etc.
refers to spiders, rats, and other such creatures. In that regard:

The specific house has been established. That [house] contains a yantra inscribed with rings and other [symbols]. By means of this first [mantra] consisting of seven syllables, there is sprinkling (āseka), that is, consecration (abhiṣeka). It destroys poison (kṣveḍa) and removes all venom.
With limbs empowered by that yantra, one should sprinkle.

Having written that [mantra] on a coconut leaf with the tip of one's fingernail while recollecting the form of the serpent, one should first perform the recitation of the vidyā using the fingernails and so forth. (79)
By pressing and by tearing, the serpent becomes pressed and torn;
in this way, it destroys all three types of poison. || 80 ||
Having drawn the yantra upon sands and worshipped the deity therein, one should encircle the serpent with those [mantras] seven times; thus it shall not go outside.
There are thirteen unobstructed syllables in the Vidyā;
together with the sixteen vowels, they number two hundred and eight.

The term "dehaga" (located in the body) is a qualification of poison; it is of three kinds, as previously stated: stationary (*sthāvara*), mobile (*jaṅgama*), and artificial (*kṛtrima*). This is what is meant: water that has been consecrated by a *yantra* and empowered by mantra, when drunk, [removes] the poison located in the stomach and situated within the body.

"And one should destroy it in three ways" refers to that *yantra*. The construction here is: "recalling that *yantra* in its form as a drawn coconut leaf. It is to be accepted that it is "crushed" or "split" because of its divine nature; [the deity] is "crushed" by the crushing and splitting of the *yantra*.
The meaning is "split open. Thus, in the manner described, it is of three kinds as before.

This machine is [placed] in sands (*vālukāsu*), that is, in grains of sand (*sikatāsu*). It is called a "machine" (*yantra*); [the word refers to] that machine. [The pronouns] "by them" (*taiḥ*) and "by those" (*tābhiḥ*) have this meaning, because they are qualifiers of the sands. Here too, due to its divine nature, one would go [there] inconceivably; even one who is awakened remains an enjoyer (*bhogī*).
Outside, it is surrounded by sand. || 81 ||
By means of these two verses beginning with *anāvṛttāni* and ending with *maheśvarī*, [the author] explains,
as before, by means of thirteen non-repetitive syllables within the third root-vidyā, which consists of twenty-five syllables and serves as the source for the two sections.

By means of those [syllables] numbering two hundred and eight through their own expansion, he teaches the eight yantras. Among them, within the root-vidyā consisting of twenty-five syllables—which is the source of all [vidyās]—there are thirteen [of these]; namely, the letters *ka*, *u*, *ra*, *la*, *ya*, *o*, and *k*.
The letters *ha*, *sa*, *va*, *ja*, *na*, and *śa*—

even when a vowel is conjoined with [these] non-nasalized (*avāma*) consonants— the number thirteen is stated with great force on account of the inclusion of even a conjoined vowel by overriding the previously mentioned [rule regarding] the primary cause.
The non-returning nature of those two syllables indeed exists. By means of those non-returning syllables—
those syllables numbering two hundred and eight— in the first yantra among the previously mentioned yantras, that is, in the first yantra within this very chapter, as stated before.

Regarding the three verses beginning with *vṛttatrayam* (the fifty-first verse), the connection is as follows: "In the middle" means from the very center; "two" refers to two syllables; "from the outside and the middle" means one should draw [the lines] as before. By those syllables numbering two hundred and eight, eight [triangles] are produced in total.

O Maheśvarī, one should draw those [mantras] starting from the east in the yantra; however, two should be written in the center. Then, as before, on the outside, there shall be eight yantras by means of them, O Maheśvarī. (83)
Of these, one should employ the first [yantra] on all days when it is prescribed;
the second and the other six yantras are for the days starting with Sunday (Bhānu).
One should employ [the mantra] in the prescribed rites after first writing down its name;
one should write the name of the weekday joined with the seventh case-ending, followed by the word "sādhaya" (accomplish). || 85 ||
One should perform subjugation, attraction, pacification, and attainment by means of the first yantra,
according to the prescribed sequence and ritual, as well as through worship for the sake of peace.

This is the perfect awakening (*sambuddhi*). This is what is meant: among the previously mentioned yantras, in the first one—which consists of three circles, an eight-petaled lotus, and a ninefold *yoni*—and which proceeds from the exterior toward the interior, in the very center is the twenty-five-syllable mantra modified by the vowels.

Having written the first two syllables— each accompanied by the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) and so forth— at the beginning of the two hundred and eight syllables produced from the thirteen syllables of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) that are not obscured, one should [place them] in the eight corners located outside of that.
Having written the eight syllables following the two syllables written in the center,

proceeding clockwise from the top, one should then write, in order, two syllables on each of the eight petals outside of that, using the ten syllables remaining after those written in the nine-yoni diagram.

Having written the sixteen syllables as before, and thus having written twenty-six syllables in total in sequence, one should perform the encirclement with the Mātṛkās as before within the two paths between the three outer circles. This is the first yantra. In this very same yantra, likewise...

Having written the subsequent sets of twenty-six syllables in sequence above the previously written set of twenty-six syllables, one should produce eight yantras together with the previously mentioned yantra. || 83 ||

With these six verses ending with "teṣvādibhijanminām," he teaches the application and so forth of those eight yantras. Therein, "teṣu" means in those eight yantras; the word "the first yantra" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This refers to the sixty-eighth verse beginning with "udīrite vaśyākarṣaṇa... and so on.

Regarding what is to be said [later]: the word division is *sapta* (seven). In the phrase "on the day of the Sun and so forth" (*bhānvādivārake*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to Soma, Aṅgāraka, Budha, Bṛhaspati, Śukra, and Śanaiścara; the meaning is "on their respective days. Regarding "in the aforementioned rites," this refers to the rites that will be described later. [This is done] preceded by writing down their names.

The meaning is: as before, preceded by the writing of the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth. "The name of the day" means "accomplish [this] below the *sādhya*. "That" refers to the form of the sentence to be written. What is being said is this:
within each day, between the two syllables situated in the very center, one should write "accomplish this" (*etatsādhaya*).
The seventh [type], when worshipped and placed somewhere within the hold of a ship, causes that entire ship to perish in the ocean; likewise, O Śivā, [it destroys] everything. (87)
Likewise, having written down those [mantras] prescribed for the respective days of the week, one should worship Śivā;
through those days, one shall obtain all desired things.
It brings about the pacification of diseases, victory, gain, and the fulfillment of various desired objects;
it effects the defeat of enemies and the subjugation of women, kings, mortals, and all living beings. (89)
One should strike the lines running east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east in succession,
numbering twenty-two, then forty-one, and four hundred.
In those corners, one should wipe around them in sequence as before;
O Maheśvarī, there are fifty-five other squares [forming] the vajra.
Among those, there are two hundred and twenty-one triangular figures in the directions;
in the center, within the middle of the remaining nine, one should write the name in the belly [of the triangle].
"One should write the syllables from the base up to the end" means that from the first yantra, one should write them in the eight [yantras];

"in the prescribed order" is an adjective for "by the rule. That rule consists of the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) preceded by the placement of the support (*ādhāra*), and so forth. "From worship" refers to that [yantra].

"From the worship of the Goddess. The word "tathā" (thus) is used as a conjunction; [the Goddess] has been worshipped. "They destroy" is in the plural number in view of the count of the seven *yantras* on their respective days. "O Śivā" is an address to the Goddess.
"In those" is an adjective qualifying the days. The ellipsis is "the *yantras* mentioned. By them—
"By means of the mandalas and so forth, as previously described. Those [mandalas] are for the pacification of diseases and other such purposes, which will be explained hereafter.
In the phrase "of mortals and other beings," the word "and others" refers to the entire range of living creatures, including ministers, vassals, and so on. (89)

By means of the six previously mentioned verses beginning with *prākpratyak* and ending with *śive*, [the mantras] are expanded by the vowels into two hundred and eight in number; these consist of the syllables of the root-vidyā in their unmodified form, along with twenty-five unmodified syllables of the root-vidyā, making two hundred and twenty-one.
It teaches the construction of the hundred-compartment Vajra-mechanism (vajrayantra) and its applications.

In that regard, "in sequence" means twenty [lines] from east to west, twenty from south to north, and twenty from west to east; such is the meaning of "in sequence. Then, by means of striking [the lines].

In those four hundred and forty-one squares, in the four corners, as before, there should be a vajra-shape in the center; that is to say, in sequence, fifty-five squares for each corner, and so on in order.

The meaning is: "having combined" refers to the four corners, specifically within the two hundred and twenty squares; "by means of four squares" means by erasing one square in each direction; "the others" refers to those remaining after the erasure. In them—

The meaning is: "in squares numbering two hundred and twenty-one. The meaning is: "by clearing one square in each of the four directions. The meaning is: "starting from the central square among the squares in the row extending toward the eastern limit. Those [squares].

One should write the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) numbering two hundred and eight times around that [central point], and then the letters of the mantra three times each in sequence within the triangles; these are what are called the "thunderbolt" (*vajra*) objects to be accomplished. || 93 ||
Likewise, having drawn that vajra-yantro on a cloth, a linen garment, or a very white and auspicious material,
and having worshipped that yantro, it protects [the vessel] in the ocean.
O Śivā, one should constantly accomplish all that was previously mentioned by means of this vajra-form yantra, using the time-periods as they have been described.

One should write the syllables of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā) with their vowel-modifications (*svaravikṛta*), up to the end of the syllables. The phrase "in the middle of the yantra" is the ellipsis to be supplied. This means in the central square of the nine-fold grid (*navaka*).
It should have the name within its belly—that is, containing the name of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) and so forth—and contain the *māyā* [syllable].
Of the twenty-five-syllable root-vidyā, [one takes] the eleventh syllable; surrounding that,
starting from the central square of the eastern row immediately adjacent to the interior,
one proceeds clockwise in an outward direction, moving in groups of three by three, excluding the central square.

The word "in each compartment" (*pratikoṣṭham*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the phrase "and in the triangles," because of the word "and" (*ca*), one should write the letters of the *sādhya* (the name to be accomplished) in the four triangles, which are the locations of *māyā*. The ellipsis for "that yantra" is "the Vajra-yantra.
The sequence for constructing the yantra is as follows: [draw] lines with equal intervals running east-west and north-south.
Having stretched out twenty-two threads each,
he produced four hundred and forty-one squares; in those [squares],
there are fifty-five squares in each of the four corners, totaling...
Having cleared away two hundred and twenty squares as before so that a diamond (vajra) shape is formed in the center,
and having then created four triangles by clearing away one square in each of the four directions, [one proceeds] with the remaining seventeen...
In the two hundred chambers, starting from the middle chamber of the three chambers situated in the easternmost row and proceeding by way of clockwise entry,
there are two hundred and eight syllables of the root-vidyā modified by vowels, arranged in their proper sequence.

Having written [the mantra] up to the end of the syllables, then, in the nine remaining squares starting from the center— specifically in the middle of the central square— one should write the *hṛllekhā*, which consists of the eleventh syllable of the twenty-five-syllable root-vidyā and contains the *sādhya* within it; [and then] in the remaining eight [squares].

In the squares, starting from the middle square of the eastern row immediately following the central square, and proceeding according to the prescribed order by moving clockwise in a counter-clockwise exit-pattern, there are twenty-five syllables in each square.

Having written the three syllables of the root-vidyā, excluding the *hṛllekhā*, three times each within four triangles situated in the four directions—and having likewise written the *hṛllekhā* together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the central square—one should perform the applications (*viniyoga*) to be described hereafter by means of that yantra. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. "Very white" (*susite*)... [refers to the ground].
This is a qualification of *kṣauma* (linen). It connects with the phrase "which protects the machine" (*yantra*); thus, it refers to the machine acting as the agent.

The tasks mentioned here are those previously described. "By what was spoken" (*proktena*) refers to the previously mentioned mandala and so forth. "O Śivā" (*śive*) is an address to the Goddess. || 95 ||

[He visualizes] that goddess drawing the person to be accomplished (sādhya), who is bound by a noose, toward her own feet by striking him with a goad, while [the sādhya] repeatedly bows with palms joined in reverence. (96)
Recalling this while muttering the vidyā at night, saying "Protect! Protect!", the person to be acted upon—whether man or woman—will certainly come under one's control. (97)
Alternatively, with palms joined in añjali, one should recite [the mantra] over the target as before while he is drawn by his hair in the goad-mudrā; as before, he will become submissive.

Or, surrounded by the splendors of the syllables of the mantra, he should himself bring her who is of such a nature; then, while recollecting her, he should bring her under control through the repetition of the mantra.
Thus has that Kurukullā been described to you as the accomplisher of all aims, who possesses a graceful form and is endowed with Vaśinī and the others. || 100 ||
The pervasion consisting of the reality of consciousness has been correctly proclaimed;
by the polishing of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self. (101)
Thus ends the twenty-second chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, within the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantra*. 22.

With these four verses beginning with *tām* and ending with *tataḥ*, [the author] teaches the threefold practice of meditating upon, attracting, and subjugating the mantra-deity, as well as the mental cultivation (*vāsanā*) regarding how that goddess Kurukullā is surrounded by the eight powers (*śakti*) such as Vaśinī and the rest.

In this context, the word "tām" (her) is syntactically connected with "smaran" (remembering) in the subsequent verse. The word "sādhyam" (the object to be accomplished) is syntactically connected with "ākarṣantīm" (attracting) found in the second half of that same verse. "Vidyām" refers to the mantra consisting of twenty-five syllables. "Prathavā" (or else) serves to exclude the alternative view. "Prāgvad vādinam" (as before, the speaker).
"Protect, protect!"—as before. The meaning is that one should recite the vidyā while visualizing the goddess as drawing [the target] toward her.

The group of objects to be accomplished (sādhya) is as previously described. Regarding the "twenty-five syllables of the mantra," this refers to the syllables of the root-vidyā; likewise, [one should recite] "protect, protect" in that manner.

[She is] endowed with speech and so forth; [this occurs] by her own accord, without being drawn [by force]. This is what is meant: [the practitioner], being surrounded by the splendor of the syllables of the mantra of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), and because [the deity] is unable to withstand that splendor, [the deity]—endowed with speech and so forth as before—enters within [him] as if being drawn by the deity herself.

"Remembering and reciting the vidyā, one brings [others] under control"—thus it is according to the form described. "Them" refers to the Goddess. "By which" means by that cause which consists in possessing the form of Lalitā. "From that cause" [is the meaning]. || 100 ||

Thus, in the *Manoramā*— so named— composed by the venerable Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, [a commentary] upon the complete tantra known as the *Kādimatā* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
In the commentary,
the twenty-second chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the ritual procedure for the vidyā of Kurukullā— the form of the deity who is the offering to the sixteen Nityās— is fully examined.
The number of verses:
Twelve yantras are contained in the twenty-second chapter concerning manifest activity;
the total verses amount to two hundred and forty-one and a quarter.
The Twenty-third Chapter.
Now, the fifth [deity] among the sixteen Nityās is indeed an ancillary (aṅga) [of the system].
She was previously described as being twofold, along with her ancillaries and her worship.
I shall explain the practice of the perfected mantra through ritual applications, meditations, worship, fire offerings, and yantras, for the sake of accomplishing all desired goals. (2)
Having performed the ritual placement of the limbs (aṅga-nyāsa) with the seven mantra-syllables and the six pairs [of syllables],
it is endowed with the ten, the seven, and the sevenfold classes [of phonemes].
Having fashioned a wheel consisting of a triangle, a circle, a hexagon, and two circles, one should invoke [the deity] there by its own name and worship it.

Having taught in the twenty-second preceding chapter the ritual procedure for Kurukullā, the offering deity of the sixteen Nityās, he subsequently teaches the ritual procedure for Vārāhī known as the Fifth, who constitutes a limb of the sixteen Nityās. Now...
By means of the twenty-third chapter, which consists of one hundred verses beginning with "The sixteen" and ending with "by this method," [the author] teaches the subject matter of the chapter.

Therein, with two verses beginning with "Now, the sixteen" and ending with "for the sake of accomplishment," he teaches the meaning of the chapter. In that regard, previously in the third chapter, the word "accomplishment" (sādhana) is to be understood as referring to the "vidyā" (mantra). || 2 ||
With the verse beginning with "the limbs" (*aṅgāni*), he teaches the mantras for the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*).
Here, the word "having made the six limbs" (*aṅgāni ṣaṭ kṛtvā*) is syntactically connected to the word "one should worship" (*pūjayet*) found in the latter half of the following verse.
[The limbs are formed] by means of the mantra-syllables from the beginning of the root-vidyā, distinguished by the numbers and sequence to be described hereafter.

Combined with forty-three syllables—meaning the *śiras* mantra consists of six syllables and the *śikhā* mantra consists of six syllables—and accompanied by the six *jātis*, such as "hṛdayāya namaḥ" and so forth; this is an adverbial modifier for the action. || 3 ||
With these six verses, beginning with *trikoṇatya* and ending with *itītyantaiḥ*, [the author] teaches the wheel for the daily worship of the Goddess Śākaradevī,
the procedure for the worship of the two enclosures (*āvaraṇa*), the sequence of daily devotion, and its fruit. Among these, it is an adjective for the phrase "the wheel is endowed."

The procedure for arranging the wheel of daily worship (*nityapūjācakra*) is as follows: having fashioned two circles with an interval of one finger-breadth between them by means of the desired measurement (due to the error of [standard] proportions) divided into internal and external parts,
and having fashioned a hexagon within the middle of the inner circle according to the previously mentioned measurement, from the center of that [hexagon]—
O Dear One, having drawn a circle touching and not touching the junction-lines (sandhirekhā),
one should worship everything in the center with the hundred-and-ten-syllable Vārāhī-vidyā, starting from the left and right upper corners. (5)
Then one should worship Krodhinī, Stambhinī, Caṇḍā, and Uccaṇḍā by their own names, joined with the first seed-syllable, the final letter, and the vital breath (ha).
In the six corners, beginning from one's own front, one should worship Brāhmī and the others counter-clockwise; and on the circle, one should likewise worship Mahālakṣmī as the fifth, in the center.
Having fashioned a bali offering with sixteen syllables and having worshipped it with ritual services (upacāras),
one should recite that vidyā before it a thousand or a hundred times.
One should perform a fire-offering daily with well-purified sesame seeds and rice, or with ghee; thereafter, the vidyā shall become perfected within eight days.

In the center of that, having constructed a triangle with three equal lines as before according to the instruction, one should invoke the Goddess there and worship her in the sequence to be described. One should invoke her by her own name—namely, the name beginning with *Hr̥llekhā* and accompanied by the *bindu* (the nasal *m*)—in the accusative case and joined with the verb of action; such is her mantra.

One should worship [her] with "Hrīṃ, I invoke Vārāhī," according to the sequence to be described by means of the hundred-and-ten-syllable mantra mentioned in the third chapter. "O Dear One" (*priye*) is an address to the Goddess. "In the very center of the wheel" means in the middle of the triangle at the very center of everything.

From the left and right upper corners of the Goddess, one should worship her attendant Śaktis by uttering "Caṇḍoccaṇḍā" and so forth, using their respective names in the dative case with the word "namaḥ" at the end;
this is the traditional teaching (sampradāya). By the phrase "with the first seed-syllable and the last [syllable] together with the vital breath," this is what is meant.

Having uttered "Kroṃ" for Krodhinī and "Staṃ" for Stambhinī, each with their respective initial syllables accompanied by the bindu (anusvāra), and having worshipped them with their names in the dative case followed by "namaḥ," one should then [worship] Caṇḍoccaṇḍā.

Having pronounced "kṣo," which is the letter *kṣa*— the final letter of the *mātṛkā*— conjoined with the bindu obtained through the section on the vowel *o*, and immediately thereafter having pronounced "kroṃ" as taught in the tradition, one should worship by saying "caṇḍoccaṇḍāyai namaḥ. In this regard:
According to the tradition, the three powers beginning with Krodhinī are devoid of the *hṛllekhā* syllable because they are preceded by their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*).
One should worship from the left, that is, in counter-clockwise order, using the names beginning with *Hṛllekhā* and ending with *namaḥ*. Here, regarding these seven powers—

The tradition holds that [the mantras] beginning with Hṛllekhā lack their respective seed-syllables (bīja) at the beginning. "In the circle" means on the path of the two circles situated furthest outward. "In front of her" means in front of the Goddess. "Facing her" refers to the infinite celestial attendants, such as those holding chowries, fans, and whisks, and those engaged in music and other arts.
According to the tradition (p. 414), [he is surrounded] by Mahālakṣmī and others, who stand on all sides in the two rows of the enclosure of Śaktis;
thus, with his senses conquered, subsisting on sacrificial food, and observing silence, he worships during the twilights.
One should recite the mantra one hundred thousand times and perform libations with a tenth part of that number.
Having performed worship and oblations, being one whose mantras are perfected, full of compassion, devoted to the guru, well-contented, peaceful in mind, and endowed with forgiveness. || 11 ||
One should practice the applications with devotion, by which everything desired is accomplished instantly,
effortlessly, through the grace of the Goddess and her sovereign power.
And one should meditate upon the goddess Kolāsyā, who resembles molten gold, who has the form of a woman up to her neck, and whose tawny hair is ablaze. (13)

The fifth [deity] is Vārāhī, the root deity; she is in the center as before. Likewise, with the root mantra (mūlavidyā), one should worship her three times without omission—this is the implied meaning. "One should worship" is supplied from the preceding context.
What is meant is this: having invoked the Goddess into the center of the wheel, immediately thereafter, with [the mantra] accompanied by the bindu...
Having worshipped with the *hṛllekhā* mantra and names ending in *namaḥ*, outside of that, in the six corners,
one should worship the six Śaktis beginning with Brāhmī and ending with Cāmuṇḍā; and on the path of the two outermost circles, one should worship her seated facing the front of the Goddess.
Having thus worshipped Mahālakṣmī— who possesses the aforementioned royal insignia and retinue—

along with the seven Śaktis, using their respective mantras beginning with *Hṛllekhā* and ending with *namaḥ*, one should again worship the Goddess in the center with her own Vidyā three times without omission. As for the *bali* offering, it is performed with the sixteen-syllable mantra.

The meaning is that at the beginning and end of the worship, one should offer the *bali* as before with the sixteen-syllable *bali-mantra*. According to the tradition (*sampradāya*), the offering of the two *balis* is always performed in the area in front of the principal deity. [This is done] with the sixteen services (*upacāras*) following the invocation (*āvāhana*) and so forth, at the conclusion of the worship.

And here, although the placement of the *arghya* vessel has not been explicitly mentioned, it should be understood as already established by what was stated previously regarding the general procedure.

According to the primary tradition (*mukhyāgama*), one should place it as before with the root-mantra and its six limbs. "That" refers to the hundred-and-ten-syllable mantra. Alternatively, the word "or" (*atha vā*) signifies an option; "or" (*vā*) indicates another alternative.
From the practice of the prescribed daily worship. || 9 ||

With these three verses beginning with "jitendriya" and ending with "vaibhavādapi," he teaches the preliminary rite (*puraścaraṇa*) for the root deity and the eligibility for ritual application (*prayoga*) for one who has completed that preliminary rite. In that context, one should recite [the mantra] one hundred thousand times; worship alone—
One should perform the oblation (*havana*) and the libation (*tarpaṇa*), which is one-tenth of the number of recitations (*japa*), and then the oblation again;

this is the general rule for all mantras. A "perfected mantra" (*siddhamantra*) is characterized by such qualities as being endowed with compassion in the manner described. "By its majesty" (*vaibhavāt*) means by the Goddess's universal form (*vaiśvarūpya*). The word "api" (also/even) [is used here].
In the case of conjunction (samuccaya). || 12 ||

With thirty-four verses beginning with *dhyāyet* and ending with *viśrutaḥ*, [the author] teaches the visualization (*dhyāna*) and invocation (*āvāhana*) for the Goddess together with her retinue during independent daily worship (*svatantra-nityapūjā*). Therein,
with the verses beginning with *dhyāyet*, [he teaches it] regarding Śiva.
She has three eyes and eight arms, holding a discus, a conch, and a lotus; likewise a noose, a mace, a plow, as well as the gestures of granting fearlessness and bestowing boons. (14)
One should contemplate her seated comfortably upon the shoulder of Garuḍa;
O Śivā, during the concluding rites of worship, one should likewise remember her powers as being equal to her.
In the ritual applications, one should remember the Goddess as seated upon a lion,
or mounted on a tiger, or mounted on an elephant, or mounted on a horse, or mounted on Garuḍa, accompanied by her Śaktis.
Whether she be dark, ruddy, yellow, black, or smoke-colored in form,
one should likewise meditate upon her in those specific applications for the attainment of those respective goals.

Meditating upon the fifth [wheel], which is surrounded by powers (śaktis) that are reddish, resembling Aruṇa, and red in hue, one should recite [the mantra] incessantly for the attainment of subjugation (vaśya). || 18 ||

With these three concluding verses, [the author] teaches the specific meditations, invocations, and so forth for the independent daily worship of the Goddess and for certain ritual applications. In that context, regarding the phrase "one should meditate upon the Goddess," the word "and" (ca) implies the worship of the limbs of the Goddess along with her retinue in the *Lalitāṅga-pūjā*.

The meaning of the tradition is that, in independent daily worship and other rites, one should meditate according to the sequence to be described hereafter, without the meditation on the form of the deity possessing the same weapons and appearance [as the practitioner].
This is indicated by the passage ending with: "Kolaśyā, who has the face of a boar, and whose form is that of a woman up to her neck."

The meaning is that he avoids [this description] by implying that one should not even out of negligence contemplate the form of the one whose body is below the neck as being of the nature of a boar (*varāha*). [She is] "with flaming tawny hair," meaning she has upward-pointing, tawny locks that seem as if they were burning. (13) Here, however, is the sequence of the weapons:
"Having eight arms"—the ellipsis is "holding [objects] with her arms," starting from the top and proceeding in order from right to left.
One should meditate on her holding a plough (*sīra*) according to the daily rituals (*nityapūjā*).
There is no fault of tautology here, because this is for the purpose of describing the meditation on the vehicle other than Garuḍa and the retinue that will be described later.
"One should remember those powers, the powers of the retinue"—this connects with what precedes it, namely "in the daily worship" (nityapūjāsu). || 15 ||

With the two verses beginning with "In the ritual applications" (*prayogeṣu*) and ending with "for the attainment" (*avāptaye*), he teaches the general characteristics of the vehicle, its color, and so forth, for all ritual applications. In that context, "with the powers" (*śaktibhiḥ*) means with the retinue powers; the word "together" (*saha*) is to be supplied [as the object of the verb]. This is according to the sequence that will be described. || 17 ||
With the verse beginning with "aruṇām," he teaches the meditation upon her specifically; therein, "aruṇākalpām" means adorned with ornaments made of rubies and the like. || 18 ||

One should always meditate, for the purpose of paralyzing, upon her who is yellow, clad in yellow garments, adorned with yellow ornaments, garlands, and unguents, and surrounded by yellow Śaktis. (19)
And [he saw] Śyāmā on the impassable path, seated upon a lion, possessing a terrifying form, and accompanied by female attendants equal to herself in power and standing at her sides. || 20 ||
Meditating and reciting the vidyā, the mantra-practitioner should worship her within the midst of her power; contemplating his own self in this way, he shall proceed with unimpeded majesty.
With lions, leopards, śarabhas, horned antelopes, dogs, and boars;
with gayals, terrifying serpents, and elephants sluggish with rut. || 22 ||
In a perilous forest crowded with thieves bearing cruel weapons, with other fierce and terrifying beings, and with ghosts, spirits, and piśācas; (23)
In a forest where the path is not found, or on such a mountain peak,
one who remembers the Goddess in her liberated form shall proceed happily and free from fear.
Even in terrifying battles where chariots and elephants are falling, and amidst insurmountable perils, one will become victorious by recollecting this. (25)

With the verse beginning with "pītām" (yellow), he teaches the application for immobilization (*stambhana*). In that context, "surrounded by yellow powers" means surrounded by powers (*śakti*) of yellow color. || 19 ||
With these five verses beginning with "śyāmām" and ending with "sukhī," he teaches the method for protecting the difficult path. In that context, [it refers to] the infinite—
meaning individually innumerable— wrathful goddesses (krodhinī) and others stationed in the enclosures.
"Of unimpaired majesty" means he is endowed with an entourage and other necessities that remain untainted even by the fatigue of the journey and similar hardships.
"By terrifying ones" is an adjective qualifying all [beings] such as lions and the like; "by others" refers to monkeys and so forth.
"In the tumultuous" means in a dense [thicket]. "In the forest-crisis" means on a path obstructed by forests. "Having lost his way" means from this point...

The phrase "previously" implies "because it was beyond the range of non-human beings. The term "in such a place" connects with the previously mentioned "on the mountain peak. The phrase "of the aforementioned form" refers to the verse beginning with "Śyāmā," etc.
"Free from fear" means entirely devoid of distress. "One should go" [is the instruction].
Because it serves the purpose of concluding the section, there is no fault of redundancy. || 24 ||

With these five verses beginning with *samareṣu* and ending with *madoddhataiḥ*, he teaches the meditation on victory in battle. In this context, "distressful" (*duranteṣu*) refers to death, suppression, and lamentation;
these are specific types of chatter (*jalpa*). Thus...
Holding a claw, a knife, a sword, an arrow, a trident, a mace, a goad, and a discus in her right arms, she possesses a terrifying form. (26)
She holds the tarjanī (threatening gesture), a shield, a shield-skin, a bow, a hand-drum, a plow, a noose, and a conch, and she is blue with her other innate powers.
Having struck down the entire enemy army upon the ground with iron clubs, she—mounted upon elephants and surrounded by elephants ridden by warriors armed with spears—[prevailed]. 28.
Above that, it was crowded on all sides with swaying plantain-tree banners,
and it moved along with throngs of Śaktis who were arrogant with pride and making terrifying roars.

One should meditate upon the Goddess as standing in the center of the solar disc, with the bodies of her enemies impaled upon her trident, and with the trident itself smeared by the blood flowing from their bodies. (30)
Standing in water reaching only to the neck, one should recite the vidyā with undistracted mind;
by practicing this for seven nights, one shall cause the enemy to die from fever.

In the manner that will be described: "the small dagger" (*churikā*) refers to a knife; "of terrible form" (*bhīmavigrahām*) is an epithet of the Goddess. With "others," namely eight arms—the ellipsis being understood—therein the names of the weapons are to be learned from the mouth of the one to be propitiated. As for the sequence of the weapons here:
It should be understood that this extends from bottom to top on both sides as well. "Blue" is the color;
"with" is the ellipsis. This means she is accompanied by her own powers (śaktis), which possess that same color.
[This applies] to the bars (parighas) of the Goddess and of her retinue of powers.

[The army] is situated on the third arm starting from the upper right side; above that, over the army, is the region crowded with plantain-tree banners and filled with elephant-pennants resembling plantains—this is the remaining sense. || 29 ||

With the two verses beginning with "bhānumaṇḍala" and ending with "jvarādityanta," he teaches the ritual application for slaying enemies by means of fever. In that regard, by the words beginning with "bhānumaṇḍala," the following is stated:
[one should visualize] the goddess, who is dark-blue in luster and holds the aforementioned sixteen weapons in her hands.

Meditating thus with undistracted mind: [he sees] his own enemy’s body impaled upon a trident, which originates from the fourth [syllable] starting from the right and upward within the center of the solar disc; that trident is smeared with blood streaming out from the enemy’s body.
With a one-pointed mind. || 31 ||
One should visualize the body of the enemy, shattered into pieces by the weapons of the Goddess together with her retinue, being devoured by jackals, *kaṅka* birds, carnivorous beasts, and dogs. (32)
While being devoured, one should recite the vidyā while standing in water for three days;
having heard that [the victim] has been killed by the water over those same number of days as before, one should emerge.
Visualizing her with two arms, having the luster of smoke-colored light, tearing out the tongue from the heart-lotus of the victim, one should lead the enemies to Yama while reciting the mantra.
Having thus recollected her yellow form and having performed the recitation [of the mantra] against an enemy, one may quell anger in debate, dispute, and even in battle. (35)
Mounted upon Tārkṣya and surrounded by Śaktis stationed on a host of Tārkṣyas,
she was fanned by the intense wind from the wings of that multitude of Tārkṣyas.

With these two verses beginning with "of the Goddess" (devyāḥ) and ending with "should cross over" (samuttaret), he teaches a specific ritual application for the slaying of enemies. In this context, the phrase "of the Goddess" implies her form as distinguished by sixteen hands, weapons, a blue complexion, and so forth. *Pheru* means a jackal.

Flesh-eaters such as *piśācas* and others, and the dog (*kukkura*, *sārameya*), devour [the victim] who has been previously mentioned along with the jackals and other creatures. As before, this occurs in water reaching only up to the neck for seven days or three days. In that context, "in another fortnight" is said in comparison to the water reaching only up to the neck.
"Slain by water" means the enemy who has died in the water; this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 33 ||
With the verse beginning with "dvibhujām" (two-armed), he teaches the visualization for the ritual application of slaying an enemy.
In that context, [the phrase] "on the tongue and heart-lotus of the one to be accomplished" (*sādhyajihvāhṛdambuje*) uses the dual case ending. "Yama" means death.
This is what is meant: having cast the enemy to be accomplished down upon the ground, lying flat on his back.

Having placed two feet upon his belly and throat, one should meditate upon the smoke-colored goddess as tearing out his heart-lotus with one hand and his tongue with the other; by reciting [the mantra], one shall kill the enemy—this is the meaning of the tradition. || 34 ||

With the verse beginning with "tathāvidhām" (of such a kind), he teaches the meditation for the immobilization of anger (*krodhastambhana*). In that context, "of such a kind" refers to the goddess who has four arms, having drawn out the tongue and heart-lotus of the target (*sādhya*) and having dragged the target upward by means of the plow held in her upper left arm.
One should meditate on her as striking with the mace held in her right arm and uprooting [the enemy] as before; such is the meaning of the tradition. || 35 ||
With the half-verse beginning with "mounted upon Tārkṣya" and ending with "in an instant," he teaches the routing of the enemy army. In that context, regarding the phrase "that Goddess...
fainted by the wind from the powerful wings of the host of Tārkṣyas," [the description continues] later on.
The word "army" (senām) is to be construed with this [verb]. "In an instant" means by mere recollection. || 36 ||
Having recollected [the goddess], one should mutter [the mantra] over an enemy's army; she will cause it to flee from afar in an instant.
Likewise, one should visualize her with eight arms, wielding swords and surrounded by spears. (37)
In that very manner, scattering his hair and wearing a reddish-brown lower garment, he would destroy the enemy host in battle in an instant, mounted upon horses. (38)
[The space was filled] with multitudes of spears mounted by hyenas, lions, monkeys, bears, and Garuḍas, upon which foot-soldiers, horses, and elephants were impaled by their tips.
Meditating upon the enemy while engaged in play and diversion in a pavilion of rubies upon a lion-throne, the king shall destroy the enemy's army with his own forces. (40)
O Supreme Goddess, for the purpose of immobilization (stambhana), one should worship her who has a yellow luster with yellow flowers,
using the previously mentioned mandalas and so forth on the appropriate days.
The practitioner can, in an instant, paralyze the movement, the army, the thought, the tongue, and the exertion of enemies, as well as everything else they desire.

With the two half-verses beginning with *tathaiva* and ending with *kṣaṇāt*, he teaches the meditation on the destruction of the enemy army. In that context, "in the same way" means mounted upon the shoulders of Garuḍa; "by the Śaktis mounted upon Tārkṣyas" [is the meaning].
The remainder is as before; likewise by means of recitation (*japa*) and so forth, [it occurs] in an instant. || 37 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *vikīrya* and ending with *nṛpa*, he teaches the meditation for the destruction of the enemy army. In that context, *aruṇavāravāṇadharaḥ* means "wearing a reddish-brown loincloth" (or garment); the word *nṛpa* follows this later on.
The connection is with this [phrase]. "Accompanied by horses" is the ellipsis.

"With foot-soldiers, cavalry, and elephants impaled on the tips of tridents" is an adjective qualifying the host of Śaktis. "The Goddess seated upon a lion-throne" is the ellipsis. This is what is meant: [she is surrounded] by those mounted on the six vehicles beginning with the hyena.

Meditating upon the Goddess seated on the lion-throne within a pavilion of rubies— she who displays playful pastimes with hosts of Śaktis by impaling enemy generals, horses, and elephants upon the tips of the tridents held in their respective hands— one wearing a reddish-brown bodice should dishevel one's hair.
Accompanied by a troop of horses and mounted upon a horse, the king shall destroy the enemy army with his own forces. || 40 ||

With these two verses ending with "in an instant" (*kṣaṇāt*), beginning with "yellow" (*pītā*) and so forth, he teaches the specific flowers and other items for the offerings, as well as the five limbs (*pañcāṅga*) and so on to be paralyzed (*stambhanīya*). In that context, "the goddess of yellow luster" is the ellipsis; "for the purpose of paralyzing those who are desired" is the ellipsis.
The word *arātīnām* (of the enemies) is connected individually with each of the five [verbs], beginning with *gati* (going), as before; [this occurs] in an instant. || 42 ||
One who desires to destroy all enemies should worship with reddish flowers at midnight; he will certainly bring them under his control. (43)
During the Viṣanāḍī, the Dagdhayoga, the Mṛtiyoga, or the Sanāśaka,
or at the time of Yamakaṇṭaka, one should perform such [a rite] with black flowers.
Worshipping him with those flowers for those days, one leads one's enemies to the city of the Lord of Life;
likewise, by worshipping Śyāmā with those same fragrant flowers for those days.
One born under the Uditas becomes wealthy as Indra, free from disease, virtuous-minded, and self-controlled;
renowned on earth, he lives happily for a hundred years.

With the verse beginning with "aruṇām," he teaches a specific mode of worship using particular flowers for the purpose of subjugating enemies. In this context, the phrase "having meditated upon the goddess" (dhyātvā) is to be understood as "the reddish one," meaning the goddess of reddish hue. "With reddish ones" means with flowers of reddish color; "at midnight" means at the middle of the night. || 43 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with *viṣanāḍyām* and ending with *nayet*, he teaches the ritual application for slaying an enemy through specific worship at particular times; therein,
during the *yamakaṇṭaka* period accompanied by the *nāśaka* yoga, on the seven days of the week starting from Sunday, respectively:

At times accompanied by the numbers five, four, three, two, one, seven, six, and half; and as for the poisonous hours (*viṣanāḍī*), for example, after fifty *ghaṭikās* of the asterism Aśvinī, the next four *nāḍīs* are poisonous hours. The same applies hereafter.
And so it has been said:
"For horses and the others, the four poison-veins (viṣanāḍikā) should be known in sequence as fifty, twenty-four, thirty, and forty-eight."
From twenty-one (21), thirty (30), ten (10), and thirty-two (32); from eighteen (18), thirty (30), and ten (10);
then from twenty-one (21), twenty (20), ten (10), and fourteen (14);
from ten (10) and fourteen (14); from fifty-six (56), twenty-four (24), twenty (20), ten (10), and twenty (20).
From Smṛti (10), from Nṛpa (18), and from Jina (24); likewise, from Khāgni (30), those nāḍīs are situated thereafter. Thus it is said.

With "kṛṣṇaiḥ" means with those that are black in color; likewise, "tathāvidhām" means one who is of such a black complexion; "taddinaiḥ" refers to the previously mentioned mandalas and so forth. || 45 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with *śyāmām* and ending with *viśrutaḥ*,

he teaches the ritual application for attaining Lakṣmī through specific offerings such as flowers. In that context, *śyāmām* means "dark-complexioned," referring to those days that have arisen with a dark color.
The connection is with what precedes. || 46 ||
Likewise, one should perform the *homa* at night in a square sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍaka*) with food mixed with turmeric, sesame seeds, black gram, and rice grains. (47)
Having performed the ritual of sakalīkaraṇa with yellow flowers, yellow fruits, and even palm leaves, which are inscribed with the letters of the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya), || 48 ||
One should paralyze those previously mentioned [effects] with offerings combined with turmeric and ghee;
likewise, a fire-oblation (homa) with turmeric powder mixed with ghee will similarly cause paralysis.

At midnight, in a fire kindled under an enemy tree with flesh produced from the body of one born of that same [enemy] womb, and smeared with the fat produced from that same body, by means of oblations performed for a number of days... [50]
One may slay an enemy by means of disease, weapons, horns, serpents, water, fires, elephants, or other such things, as well as through favors or thorns and the like. || 51 ||
Even through the collapse of thunderbolts, trees, or walls, from the ingestion of poison, or by the employment of enemies, they do not become fragile at all. (52)
With fourteen verses beginning with "homam" and ending with "bhūtale," he teaches the specific fruits resulting from the specific materials for the *homa* and other details. Among those,
[he does so] with three verses beginning with "homam" and ending with "tathā."

He teaches the specific substances for the *stambhana* (paralyzing) fire-oblation (*homa*). In that context, "there" means at midnight. "In a square" refers to the characteristics of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) which will be described in the section on the ritual manuals (*paṭala*). "Mixed with turmeric" means accompanied by turmeric powder; this is an adjective qualifying the four substances beginning with food.

The *sakalīkaraṇa* (the ritual of making [the deity] whole) consists of the inscription of the names of the target (*sādhya*) and so forth; this is performed specifically on palm leaves (*tālapatra*) using *tāla* leaves mixed with turmeric powder and clarified butter (*niśā-ghṛta-samopeta*). The phrase "as previously mentioned" refers to the fivefold [process] beginning with the movement of the enemy (*arātigati*). [This is done] with the powders of *niśā*.
With offerings smeared with ghee and drenched in ghee, as well as with mandalas and other such rites. || 49 ||

With these three verses beginning with "at midnight" (ardharātre) and ending with "fickle" (bhaṅgurā), he teaches a specific fire-offering (homa) procedure for the rite of killing (māraṇa), as well as the specific methods of common killing applicable therein. In that context, [it refers to] a fire kindled with wood from an enemy tree.

In a fire kindled by wood produced from the tree of the enemy’s asterism, [one should perform the rite] with fuel-sticks born from the body of that [enemy's] birth-asterism— meaning those produced from the body of the birth-asterism of the enemy— and smeared with oil produced from the body of that [same enemy], meaning drenched in oil produced from the birth-asterism of the person to be acted upon (sādhya), for a number of days as previously described through the mandala and other rituals.
"By others" means by tigers and the like; "by negligences" means by lack of attention;
in the phrase "by thorns and the like," the word "and the like" (ādi) refers to things such as spikes; "nirghāta" means a thunderbolt;
regarding "prayogāmī prayogāḥ amī," the word division is *prayoga-āmī* because of its divine nature; "bhaṅgurāḥ" means fruitless.

Meditating upon her as smoke-colored, mounted on a heron, and equipped with weapons such as claws, [one should perform the rite] in the eighth house from the enemy's [ascendant], using oblations soaked in goat's ghee. (53)
By means of oblations of black pepper and mustard seeds performed on those specific days, one shall slay enemies,
seizing them with a violent burning fever, rendering them unconscious and deforming their limbs.
Recalling Śivā, who possesses the luster of the rising sun and is joined with her primordial weapons,
[one should worship her] with auspicious, reddish-colored items smeared with red cow's ghee and accompanied by a calf of similar hue.
With flowers produced from the *kiṃśuka*, as well as those arising from the *vandhūka*, with *japā* flowers, *pālāśa* flowers, and those originating from the *karavīra*; || 56 ||
With white water-lilies, blue lotuses, red lotuses, those born from the *pāṭala* tree, flowers produced from the *aśoka*, those arising from *kusumbha*, and other red flowers. || 57 ||
From the oblation, he shall certainly become equal to a king in sovereignty, command, wealth, and other qualities that depend upon those very things. (58)

With the two verses beginning with *dhūmrām* and ending with *vikṛtāṅgakam*, he teaches a specific fire-oblation (*homaviśeṣa*) for the purpose of killing. In that context, *dhūmrām* means smoke-colored;
[she is] endowed with weapons such as claws and so forth.

As before, the phrase "with the thirty-six [substances] beginning with *nakha* (nails)" and so forth is to be understood as referring to those residing on the sixteen arms; this is the ellipsis. *Chāgaḥ* refers to a specific type of goat. *Marīcaiḥ* means with black peppers. These two [black peppers and mustard seeds] are the qualifiers for the term "drenched in ghee" (*ghṛtāplutaiḥ*). By means of those days, as previously described, one becomes *vikṛtāṅgakaḥ*, that is, one whose limbs are no longer under one's own control. || 54 ||

With these four verses beginning with "vālārkābhām" and ending with "suniścitam," he teaches the *homa* (fire sacrifice) that brings about the attainment of sovereign power (*aiśvarya*). Therein, [he refers to] the fifth [deity], Śivā, who is joined with the primary weapons and endowed with the eight weapons mentioned in the *svatantra-nityapūjā*.

"With flowers that have the color of a red cow with a calf of similar appearance, soaked in the ghee of such a cow; auspicious [flowers], free from those that have fallen buds, those that are withered at the tips, those defiled by insects, or those touched by feet"— this [description] should be understood as a qualification for the word "red" (*aruṇaiḥ*) mentioned previously.
"Produced from *karavīra* flowers"—the word "red" (*aruṇaiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis.

"Red" (*raktaiḥ*) is an adjective qualifying the blue lotuses (*utpala*), red lotuses (*kamala*), and *pāṭala* flowers. "With limbs" refers to the regalia and attendants, such as the parasol, fly-whisk, and so forth. || 58 ||

Meditating with a concentrated mind on [the goddess] Aruṇā, who is endowed with claws and other [attributes], one should offer oblations at midnight with black pepper while facing the direction of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). || 59 ||
Within the days prescribed, the king, as well as the world of men and women, shall come under his control;
endowed with fame and fortune, he shall live for a long time upon the earth. || 60 ||
Having drawn the Bhūpura (the outer square enclosure), one should write one's own sādhya (target) in the center;
outside of that, one should write the letters of the Earth-mantra (Bhaumākṣara) all around, starting from the tip of the eastern spoke.
Having drawn an eight-petalled lotus on the outside, one should write the syllables of the mantra there in sequence, one for each season; outside of that, a pair of circles [should be drawn].
Therein, one should draw a hexagon outside the letters of the king’s name;
in its corners and intermediate spaces, one should place the letters of the mantra accompanied by the ten earth-syllables (bhūdaśa).

With the two verses beginning with "aruṇām" and ending with "bhūtale," he teaches the procedure for the fire-offerings (*homa*) for subjugation and other rites. In that context, "with the claws and so forth" refers to the sixteen weapons, such as the claws, mentioned in this thirty-sixth chapter; "composed" means having a mind focused on nothing else.
"Or even by means of the previously mentioned days, mandalas, and so forth"—the word "api" (even) has the sense of "also. || 60 ||
With forty verses beginning with *vilikhya* and ending with *ānayet*,

[the author] teaches eight yantras produced from the syllables of this vidyā that perform acts such as immobilization (*stambhana*), as well as the majesty of the vidyā. Among these, [the first group] begins with *vilikhya* and ends with *vāhinīm*.

With five verses, he teaches the yantra that causes the immobilization of a world-protector and an enemy army. Therein, "in the center" means in the middle of the outer square (bhūpura). "Outside of that" means outside the outer square. The syllables of Bhauma (Mars) [are to be placed there].

The third letters of the consonant groups beginning with *ka*, preceded by the fifth, sixth, and thirteenth vowels, together with the *bindu*, are ten in number. Surrounding [the center] in a clockwise direction— [that is, from the outside,
due to the encircling of the earth-syllables]— on those petals, in order starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, there are six syllables for each season (*ṛtu*).
The word "per petal" (*pratidalam*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence]. "Outside of that" means outside of the lotus.

There, in the circular path (*vṛttavīthyām*), one should write the letters of the Earth-element (*pārthivān varṇān*) as before. Outside the pair of circles, in the corners—that is, in the six corners of the hexagon—in the intermediate spaces, namely in the six intervals between the corners, one should place the letters of the mantra accompanied by the ten earth-syllables (*bhūdaśānvitān*).

Having inscribed the remaining syllables of the root-vidyā—accompanied by the ten-syllable mantra of Bhūta mentioned previously—upon the eight petals, according to the six-fold sequence as before at each station; having placed [them] there in the path surrounding the outer hexagon, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise; and having done so outside the two circles. Thus it is said.
In the previous case, the connection is with the root-vidyā; this is the ellipsis. (p.
424) One should draw two circles around [the center] as before, and having placed the reversed Mātṛkā there, one should draw the enclosure of the earth on the outside.
Having written the Mātṛkā in direct order along with the root-mantra,
and worshipping it, one may paralyze the entire world and the army of enemies.

"Worshipping the Goddess" is the ellipsis [to be supplied], according to the sequence prescribed for daily rites. "The army of enemies" means the hostile force. The word "and" (ca) is to be supplied here. This is the procedure for drawing the yantra: having drawn the square enclosure (bhūpura) with the desired dimensions and the aforementioned characteristics, outside of that, by touching or not touching the tips of its corners...

Having drawn a circle, and having drawn two circles outside of it with an interval of one and six finger-breadths respectively, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus there within the outer prong-path; then,
having drawn another circle outside the outer circle with a measurement of one finger-breadth.

Having drawn a circle outside that [first circle] with a radius equal to half the diameter of the middle [circle], and having fashioned a hexagon within the space between them as before, one should draw a circle outside the tips of the hexagon at a measurement of one *aṅgula*,
and then draw a square outside that [second circle] at a measurement of one *aṅgula*.
Having written the object of attainment (*sādhya*), the practitioner (*sādhaka*), and the ritual action (*karman*) within the central city-gate (*bhūpura*) in the sequence of the inner intervals,
one should write the terrestrial mantras (*bhaumāni*) in the path between the two outer circles outside that city-gate, proceeding clockwise starting from the east.

Having written the ten syllables *uṃ ūṃ oṃ gaṃ jaṃ ḍaṃ daṃ vaṃ laṃ vvaṃ*, one should [place] the hundred and ten syllables of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) upon the petals of the lotus outside of that, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise, with [one syllable] on each petal.
Having written the forty-eight syllables by way of six groups of six,

one should write the ten syllables of Bhauma in sequence as before upon the circular path outside that; and outside of that, in the six corners, starting from the eastern corner and proceeding clockwise as before.

First, having written the letters of the root-vidyā upon the eight petals, one should write thirty-six of the remaining sixty-two letters— six in each corner— in successive order; then, in the six intermediate spaces between those corners, one should write [the letters] in each space as previously described.

In sequence, from the upper corner and the northern side up to the southern side of the hexagon, there are thirty-six syllables in total: the twenty-six remaining syllables of the Vidyā written within the hexagon,
together with the ten syllables of the Earth (Bhauma), making six groups of six syllables each.

Having drawn [the diagram] according to the six-fold sequence, one should write the *mātṛkā* with the visarga and in reverse order, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise along the path of the outer circle; then,
on the path within the space between that outer circle and the square (*bhūpura*), one should proceed clockwise from the northeast to the northeast.
The fifty-one letters of the Mātṛkā with their bindus and the one hundred and ten letters of the root-vidyā,
totaling one hundred and sixty-one letters, [are arranged] forty in each direction.
Having written forty syllables in the northern direction and forty-one syllables [in the other],
and having invoked the Goddess there, one who worships her according to the sequence of the independent daily worship (svatantra-nityapūjā) attains the stated fruit. || 65 ||
Having drawn a nine-pointed star and a pair of circles, and outside that a pair of eight-pointed stars and a square, one should write six mantra-syllables in each of the [sections]. (66)
One should write one [syllable] in each of the eight intermediate spaces, the Mātṛkā on the outer circle, and in the square, both in reverse and direct order.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished all around [the diagram], one should worship the eight-armed Śivā;
by this procedure previously mentioned, O Supreme Goddess, there shall be immobilization (stambha).

With these three verses beginning with "navāsram" and ending with "parameśvarī," he teaches the yantra that effects the immobilization of all beings. In this context, "navāsram" means nine-spoked (nine triangles) and "navayonim" means nine-yonis;
"vasvasram" refers to an eight-cornered [figure] as previously described; "taddvayam" refers to two circles; and "ṣaṭ ṣaṭ" [refers to six and six].
"In each of the nine corners" means in each of the eight corners. "In the eight intermediate spaces" means in the intermediate spaces between the eight corners;

the meaning is that one should place one syllable of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) in each intermediate space, using the remaining eight syllables written in the corners. "On the outer circle" [refers to the placement of the remaining syllables].
In the path between the two outer circles of the eight-cornered [figure], the word "tu" (but/and) serves as a conjunction.

"Pratilomānulomakam" means in reverse order in the circular path and in direct order in the square. "Sarvataḥ" means in all the places where the letters are to be written. This refers to the previously mentioned [movements] such as the "enemy's movement" (arātigati) and so forth.
"O Supreme Goddess" is the vocative address. This is the procedure for drawing the yantra:
having drawn a circle with the desired measurement, having fashioned a nine-yoni [triangle] in its center as before, and having drawn two circles outside that with a one-finger interval between them;
Having fashioned an eight-cornered figure outside of that, consisting of two concentric square enclosures with corners extending toward the cardinal and intermediate directions;

having then drawn a circle outside of that, touching and yet not touching those eight corners; and having made a square outside of that at a distance of one *aṅgula*; then, beginning from the *yoni* situated in the very center of all—

Having written the fifty letters starting from the beginning among the previously stated number of syllables of the root-vidyā— six in each corner in sequence across the nine corners by way of exit and clockwise rotation— one should likewise [proceed] in the eight outer corners as before.

Having written the forty-eight syllables by placing six syllables in each corner in sequence— using the fifty-six remaining syllables of the root-vidyā previously written, starting from the first syllable and proceeding clockwise— one should then [place them] within the intervals between those eight corners.
Having written one syllable of the remaining Vidyā-mantra in each intermediate space, starting from the northern side of the outer corner and ending at its southern side,
[one should proceed] in the same manner as before, moving clockwise from the tip along the path between the two outer circles.

Having written the Mātṛkā in reverse order including the *visarga*, one should then, in the space between the outer circle and the inner square, as before, write the letters starting from the northeast (Īśāna) and ending at the northeast, proceeding clockwise: thirteen letters in each direction in sequence, and twelve letters in the northern direction, making a total of fifty.
Having written the fifty-one letters of the *mātṛkā* along with their *bindus*,

and having inscribed the three names of the practitioner and others in all twenty-seven places where letters are to be written, one should invoke there the eight-armed Goddess as described in the sequence of the daily worship (*nityapūjā*).
By worshipping [it], one causes the movement of enemies and so forth to be paralyzed. || 68 ||
Having fashioned a circle, then a triangle, again a circle, a hexagon, a pair of circles,
and an octagon outside that circle, one should perform the ritual placement (vinyāsa) here.
Having drawn one [line] in the center, and three each in the outer corners and the intermediate spaces in sequence, the remainder outside should be filled with earth.
Having written even the name in the center, the practitioner, after reciting it and worshipping,
should install [the image] somewhere there and daily offer an oblation (bali).

With these three verses beginning with *vṛttam* and ending with *kṣipet*, he teaches another yantra for immobilization (*stambhana*). Regarding that, the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) is that in this yantra, one should write the first syllable of the root-mantra (*mūlavidyā*) in the form of a triangle in the center—that is, in the very middle. In the center...
In the center of the triangle, which has the form of the first syllable situated in the middle of all [the others]; or on a wall or similar surface;

in that very place where it has been established. This is the sequence for constructing the yantra: having drawn a circle with a radius of the desired measure by means of a compass, one draws another circle outside that [first] circle with a radius equal to half the diameter of that [first] circle.
Having done that, one should draw a hexagon in the middle as before; having drawn a circle outside that with a measurement of one *aṅgula*,
and having drawn an octagon outside that as before,
one should draw a circle outside that which touches and does not touch the tips of its corners, and [then] one *aṅgula* outside that.

Having drawn a square (vṛtta) within a square, one should inscribe there— in the middle of the square situated in the very center— the first syllable of the root-mantra (mūlavidyā), which takes the form of a triangle, together with the three [deities] beginning with the practitioner (sādhaka),
topped with a bindu; and outside of that, in the three corners of the triangle, [one should place] the [syllables] of the root-mantra.

Having written three syllables each in every corner— starting from the front and proceeding clockwise— from the second syllable up to the tenth syllable, one should then write, as before, the eleven syllables starting from the eleventh up to the nineteenth in the three intermediate spaces between those corners.

Having written the nine syllables in a sequence of three by three, starting from the upper corner and the left side up to the right side, one should write the seven syllables beginning with the twentieth syllable of the Vidyā and ending with the twenty-seventh syllable in each of the corners of the hexagon outside that, proceeding clockwise starting from the front corner.

Having written eighteen syllables in groups of three by way of triple succession, and having likewise written eighteen syllables— beginning with the thirty-eighth syllable and ending with the fifty-fifth— in the intermediate spaces between those corners as before;
Outside of that, in the eight corners of the octagon,

one should write twenty-four syllables— beginning with the fifty-sixth syllable and ending with the seventy-ninth syllable— in groups of three according to the previous method, within each of the eight intermediate spaces.
Having written the twenty-four syllables beginning with the eighty-first and ending with the one hundred and third, according to the previously mentioned order of commencement,
[one should then write] at the end of that the seven remaining syllables of the root-vidyā, beginning with the one hundred and fourth syllable.
Having written the seventeen syllables— consisting of the twelve syllables of Bhauma and the five others—
around the perimeter within the space between the two outer circles of the eight-cornered figure as before,
one should invoke the Goddess there, worship her as before, and place that yantra inside a casket made of shallow bowls or similar vessels.
Having installed [the image] on walls and other such places, and having worshipped it there every day and offered the bali-oblation, one obtains the previously mentioned fruit. || 71 ||
Having drawn six and eight-sided figures and separate hexagons, one should sequentially draw the spaces between the triangles and circles, joined with hexagons. (72)

From the outside, proceeding in order toward the center, one who knows the scripts should write all the letters of the Mātṛkā joined with the Śaktis, conjoined with the lunar mansions, lunar days, and days of the week. (73)

O Goddess, one should write the object of accomplishment (sādhya) clockwise among the seven middle [circles]; situated in the center of the Māyā [syllable], it should be worn for the sake of attaining all perfections.

One should wear [this] for the pacification of ghosts, spirits, and piśācas, for the pacification of all afflictions, and for the pacification of diseases of elephants, horses, donkeys, camels, and so forth. 75.

With these four verses beginning with *kṛtvā* and ending with *dvārayet*, he teaches the yantra that pacifies all diseases. In this context, the word division is *ṣaḍ-aṣṭakoṇāni*, meaning "six and eight corners"; that is to say, there are six corners within and eight corners on the outside.
One should draw six hexagons individually and in sequence within the spaces between the triangle and the circle,
each hexagon joined to the previously drawn hexagon and octagon, occupying the regions between the triangle and the circle.
"One should perform [this]"—such is the sequence for the arrangement of the text. From the exterior, in due order, up to the center:
from the corners of the eight external triangles and so forth, up to the six-cornered figure situated in the very center of all; from the middle of the corners up to the end.
The phrase "in the places for writing the letters of the *sādhya* joined with the lunar mansion, lunar day, and weekday" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Regarding the term "lipiśaḥ":

The word "endowed with Śakti" (śaktiyutām) is to be construed here. Regarding the *mātṛkā*—which consists of fifty syllables but is devoid of the *visarjanīya*: its state of being devoid of the *visarjanīya* arises from the fact that a *visarjanīya* is joined to each individual syllable [in the subsequent stage].
The two syllables of the phrase "joined with Śakti" (śaktisaṃyutām), which were learned from the mouth of the venerable teacher, are now written down.

Namely, together with the *visarjanīya* and together with the syllables of the root-vidyā. "In the seven centers" means in the seven centers of the seven hexagons. And by the word "likewise" (*ca*), one should write the remaining ten syllables of the vidyā and the ten syllables of the earth-mantra (*bhaumā*), just as in the previously mentioned yantra.

One meaning is that one should draw [the letters] along the outer path of the lines; "is drawn together" (samākṛṣyate) is the traditional sense. All the aforementioned syllables are arranged clockwise, situated within the *māyā* (the syllable *hrīm*), and embraced by the *hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*). This is for the pacification of ghosts, spirits, demons, and the like.
