By the word "etc. (*ādi*), epilepsy and other such ailments are meant. For the pacification of the afflictions caused by these, the phrase "elephants, horses, donkeys, camels, etc.

includes, by the word "etc.," four-footed animals such as cows, buffaloes, goats, and so forth. This is the procedure for drawing [the mandala]: having first drawn a circle with a radius of the desired measure, using a compass.
Therein, having drawn seven hexagons according to the sequence of the *anugraha-cakra* as taught in the *Anityānityā-paṭala*,
and having constructed an eight-spoked [figure] outside of that as before,
one should then draw a circle such that it touches and does not touch the tips of the outer eight spokes.
Outside of that, at a measurement of one *aṅgula*, one should draw twelve lines— east-west and north-south—
at the tips of all the lines there should be tridents, as well as at their centers and on both sides. (76)
Having written "stambhaya" (paralyze) and the name of the enemy in the central square,
one should write the syllables of the mantra, accompanied by the letter *bha* (for Mars), all around it.
One should draw it on birch bark, a cloth, metal, or stone;
when placed upon a house or a city, it bestows the attainment of desired goals through iron and sight.

Having drawn a circle, one should write the eight letters of the Mātṛkā beginning with the first, along with their visargas, in the eight outer corners starting from the front corner and proceeding clockwise; then, in those very corners,
one should write one letter each from the sixteen syllables at the beginning of the root-mantra.

And having likewise written the eight syllables at the beginning, one should write, as before, the eight syllables starting from the ninth up to the sixteenth of the Mātṛkā and the Vidyā respectively within the eight intermediate corners; and inside that—
Beginning from the sixth corner and proceeding clockwise, in each of the six corners and in the six intermediate spaces between them— thus totaling eighty-four locations—
one should place the letters of the Mātṛkā and the Vidyā, beginning with the seventeenth letter and ending with the fiftieth.
Having written the thirty-four syllables in thirty-four places,
one should again write the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā alphabet— beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', excluding the *visarga*— each endowed with a *visarga*, in the remaining fifty places.
Having written them in sequence as before, together with the fifty letters beginning from the fifty-first letter of the root-vidyā and ending with the hundredth letter,
one should likewise [arrange] the remaining ten letters of the vidyā and the ten letters of the earth (bhauma) as previously described.
Having drawn seven hexagons along the entire outer perimeter, one should write within the seven central [hexagons] the asterism,
lunar day, and weekday occurring on each respective day of practice, ending with the seventh case-ending; above each of those,
one should write the triad beginning with the practitioner as before, and then place that entire yantra within the *hṛllekhā*.

Having made sport with the fourth vowel situated above [the letter *ha*], one should invoke and worship the Goddess therein; through maintaining the concentration according to the stated sequence, the attainment of the stated fruit occurs. || 75 ||

With these five verses beginning with *prāk-pratyak* and ending with *dvayoḥ*, he teaches the grid-mandala (*koṣṭhayantra*) for performing the rite of immobilization (*stambhana*). In that [grid], one should place the respective tridents at the center, the tips, and the sides; specifically, the respective tridents at the tip of the central line, and at the center and the sides of that central line.

The three syllables "stambhaya" are to be placed in sequence at the tip of the central line of the trident and on its right and left sides; specifically, in the middle cell, in the very center of that middle cell, and below the entire middle cell.
Starting from the central square of the row, meaning by way of the path of exit;

"endowed with Mars" means endowed with the letters of the color of Mars; the remaining sense is that this applies to the construction of a house or a city, or to the immobilization of inauspiciousness occurring therein; [this is done] with iron and stone.

Among the four previously mentioned sections, one should perform the auspicious and captivating rite with *tāla* and *haritāla*— in the sequence of placing them within the covers of bowls and so forth— until the attainment of the fruit is achieved.
Then, O Śivā, one should inscribe auspicious [mantras] with yellow orpiment and *tāla* on a stone slab; one should then install them in sequence upon the wall and the ground. (79)
One should constantly worship with fragrant flowers and likewise perform recitation;
one should do this regularly during both twilights until the attainment of the fruit. 80.
One should draw sixteen lines—east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east—which produce two hundred and twenty-five squares by those [lines]. (81)
O Goddess, one should wipe around those corners as before;
then, among the remaining squares in the cardinal directions, there are twenty-eight cells.
As before, one should construct the triangles one by one according to the prescribed rule;
in the middle, within the three squares, [one should place] the object of attainment (sādhya), the practitioner (sādhaka), and the rite (karman).

O Śivā, one should write [the letters] above, below, and in the middle, as well as in the remaining [spaces] as before; starting from the top, one should inscribe the syllables of the mantra all around.
The meaning is: recitation, worship, and so forth; "regularly" means every day. As for the sequence for constructing the diagram (*yantra*):
having drawn twelve lines each toward the east, west, south, and north, one should produce one hundred and twenty-one squares.
Having drawn a trident around each of the forty-eight squares at the tips of those respective lines,
one should write the triad beginning with the practitioner as before in the center of the square situated in the very middle;
then, starting from the central square located in the row below that square...
Having written the syllables of the root-vidyā by moving in a clockwise direction until the completion of the syllables, one should write the ten syllables of Mars in the remaining ten squares,
[and then] upon the outer tridents and the central tridents.
Having written the three-syllable mantra "stambhaya stambhaya" on the central line and at its right and left sides for each trident,
one should draw this yantra upon any one of the four substrates such as birch bark, using the prescribed substances.
Having performed the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of the vital breath) and so forth, having invoked the Goddess there and worshipped her,
and having enclosed [the vessel] with bowls as previously described and placed it in the two aforementioned locations,
one should [worship] there every day during both twilights with fragrant flowers until the attainment of the desired siddhi.
By worshipping him, one obtains the desired fruit. || 80 ||
With these eight verses beginning with *prākpratyak* and ending with *dhruvam*, he teaches the Great Vajra Yantra, which bestows all desired fruits. Therein, by those lines;
in those squares—meaning twenty-eight squares per corner—the remainder [is as follows].

In [a mandala] consisting of one hundred and thirteen squares, from each individual square— O Śivā, this vajra, the great yantra which accomplishes all desired aims, should be installed when it has been inscribed upon metal, stone, or other materials. (85)
In that regard, there are calamities arising from thieves, robbers, diseases, enemies, and serpents, as well as those born from the wrath of bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, and other such spirits. (86)
In such a place, prosperity never arises, yet calamities do occur;
however, that house can pacify the suffering caused by defects in the vital points (marman) of the site and so forth.
In whatever house this yantra is installed, for those residing in that house, there will certainly be no affliction from sorcery, malevolent spells, or minor evils. || 88 ||

The term *sādhyasādhakakarma* means "the actions of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and the agent who accomplishes (*sādhaka*). It is to be construed with the phrase "one should draw starting from the top. The terms "above, below, and in the middle" are to be construed with the preceding phrase "the actions of the object to be accomplished and the agent who accomplishes. As for the specific methods for those [drawings], they are [described] in the upper section.

The practitioner (*sādhaka*) is in the lower square, the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is in the middle square, and the ritual action (*karman*) is likewise [placed]; then, in the remaining squares numbering one hundred and ten, one should write the letters of the mantra—one hundred and ten syllables—in the same manner as before, by way of a clockwise movement of entry; such is the connection [of the sentence].
In the phrase "stone and so forth" (*śilādī*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to birch bark, cloth, and palm leaves.

In the phrase "piśācas and so forth" (*piśācādī*), the word "and so forth" refers to epilepsy and similar conditions. The connection with the preceding clause is that "disturbances" (*upaplavāḥ*)—that is, calamities—do not occur. Regarding the phrase "vital points and so forth" (*marmmādī*), the word "and so forth" [refers to...]

The scope [of the diagram] includes the doors, walls, and so forth. "House-treasury" (geha-gañja) means that the yantra is placed within the house. The word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "minor spirits and so forth" (kṣudrādi) refers to piśācas and other such beings.
Herein is the sequence for drawing: by stretching sixteen lines—east-west and north-south—one should proceed.
Having constructed two hundred and twenty-five squares, within those squares— at each of the four corners— twenty-eight squares per corner,
totaling one hundred and twelve squares, [one should draw] a vajra-shape in the center as before.
Having cleared away [the squares] in that manner,
one should then clear away four squares in total— one square in each of the four directions— from among the remaining one hundred and thirteen squares; therein, one should draw triangles as before.
Having drawn three parallel lines, one should write the ritual action (*karman*) in the very center square,

the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in the square above it, and the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) in the square situated below it; then, in the remaining hundred and ten squares, which are accompanied by four triangles facing the four directions...

Having written the syllables of the root-vidyā, numbering the same as those [triangles], by moving clockwise through the primary triangle and so forth, and having placed this yantra in any one of the aforementioned locations, one should worship it in the prescribed places preceded by the rite of *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (consecration of life-force); from its installation, the attainment of the stated fruits occurs. || 88 ||
One should draw twelve lines toward the directions of Vāyu, Agni, Nairṛti, and Īśa;
by means of those, there shall be one hundred and twenty-one squares in the form of vajras.
Having written the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya) in the midst of those [syllables],
one should then write the other letters all around, starting from the tip.
O Śivā, by means of its removal, [the sins] beginning with those of the color of the earth are gradually established as written on iron, stone, and so forth, or even as worshipped. 91.
It shall destroy diseases, elemental spirits, planetary seizures, madness, demons, epilepsy, enemies, and whatever other things cause affliction. (92)

With these seven verses beginning with "vāyu" and ending with "bhūtala," he teaches the *yantra* named Vajravajra and its application and so forth. Therein, "with those lines" refers to those [lines] within the square compartments (*koṣṭha*) in the form of vajras; "in the center" means in the central vajra-compartment; "the name of the person to be accomplished" (*sādhyanāma*).

The rites of the practitioner [should be performed] starting from the lower square situated beneath the central square, proceeding all around in a clockwise direction. "Other squares" means that one should write the letters—the letters of the root-mantra—in the other squares. First, those preceded by the letter of the earth (ma).

The meaning is that one should write the terrestrial syllables and then write the syllables of the Vidyā in the remaining squares. "O Śivā" is a vocative. In the phrase "on stone and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to objects such as clay images, leaves, and cloth.
Other things, such as the *kṛtyā* spirits established by enemies, the ashes of the unseasonable, and so on, [are to be used] against the aforementioned afflictions such as diseases.

"In afflictions" means when afflictions such as the aforementioned diseases have arisen. "That *vajra*" refers to the *vajravajra*, specifically the central square located in the very middle of all [the squares]. It is filled with the decoction of milk-trees—that is, with the bark of the four milk-trees: the *aśvattha*, *udumbara*, *plakṣa*, and *vaṭa*.

It was filled with water measuring one *khārī*, boiled and cooled; "having placed [the vessel]" connects to what precedes. The "Goddess" refers to the fifth [vessel]. The words "in the water contained in the jar" are to be supplied.
The self-possessed one attained [this state] through the transmission of power from those waters by means of the science of mechanical devices (*yantra-vidyā*) and so forth.
[This is] by means of the determined measurements. Herein is the procedure for drawing [the mandala]:

having produced a circle with the desired measurement, one should strike two Brahma-lines upon it—east-west and north-south—extending to the limits of that circle. Then, of the east-west Brahma-line...
From the eastern tip [of the north-south Brahma-thread] to the southern tip of the south-north Brahma-thread;
from that tip to the western tip of the east-west Brahma-thread; from that tip to the northern tip of the south-north Brahma-thread; from that tip—

Having stretched four cords in the form of bowstrings from the eastern tip to the western end of the Brahma-line, and having formed a perfect square with four corners at the cardinal directions by erasing the two Brahma-lines and the circle;

By stretching ten parallel lines from the line situated in the direction of Vāyu (the northwest) to the line situated in the direction of Agni (the southeast), and from the line situated in the direction of Nairṛta (the southwest) to the line situated in the direction of Īśa (the northeast), one forms a vajra-and-vajra-shaped grid consisting of one hundred and twenty-one vajra-patterned squares.
Having constructed a yantra there, even in the aforementioned afflictions, one should likewise draw that vajra on the ground with white pigments;
in its center, however, a water-pot filled with a decoction of milky trees [should be placed]. (93)
Having placed the Goddess in the water, having invoked her and worshipped her,
the self-possessed practitioner, touching the water, should mutter the Vidyā three thousand times.
Then, one should sprinkle that patient, who holds a staff and faces the east, with those waters;
having his body liberated from those afflictions, he lives happily upon the earth.

Regarding the empowerment for the attainment of knowledge (vidyāprāpty-abhiṣeka) in this Vajra-koṣṭha-vajraka, one should also establish the ritual jar (kumbha) within the one hundred and twenty-first [section] and perform the consecration. || 96 ||
Having made a circle by rotating [the cord] four finger-breadths (vedāṅgula) from there,
one should then draw eleven [lines] outward, each at an interval of two finger-breadths, in succession.
Upon those [lines] measuring two finger-breadths, one should cast transverse threads; then eleven [threads], starting from the middle of the east, proceeding clockwise among them. 98.
One should write that vidyā with eighteen syllables according to the sequence of emanation;
having formed the tips of the lines as tridents, one places the sādhya in the center. (99)
Having written the practitioner’s name, the object to be accomplished, and the ritual action as before in the center of the central square,
one should write the ten earth-syllables in the ten vajra-squares, beginning from the vajra-square situated below that and proceeding clockwise in a path of exit, and then in the remaining [squares].
Having written the root-mantra syllables, numbering one hundred and ten, within as many vajra-shaped compartments, and having placed this yantra in any one of the aforementioned locations,
its accomplishment of the stated results occurs through its installation and worship, or by means of the consecration performed upon that yantra according to the prescribed sequence.

By means of the verse beginning with "vidyā," he extends the application of three among the seven yantras mentioned to the initiation for the attainment of the Vidyā; and here, specifically, in this "vajra" [yantra],
that is, in the seventh yantra named Vajra-vajra which was immediately previously described, [and] in the "vajra-cells" (koṣṭha-vajraka).
"In the sixth yantra, which consists of sixty-four cells (*koṣṭha*) in the form of a vajra;
or in the fifth yantra, which consists of one hundred and twenty-one cells in number; or—'or' being used as an alternative—meaning in any one of those three yantras. (96)

With these four verses beginning with *vedāṅgula* and ending with *anayā*, he teaches the yantra that bestows all spiritual accomplishments (*siddhi*) as well as the majesty of the Vidyā. Therein, by a rotation of four finger-breadths (*caturaṅgula*) in each direction— that is, by a rotation measured at four finger-breadths from each cardinal point— from that circle, [at a distance of] two finger-breadths...
In each measurement of two finger-breadths (*dvyaṅgula*), there are eleven circles; this is the remainder [of the description].
This yantra, when employed as before in all its applications, has nothing that cannot be accomplished in this world by means of this perfected *vidyā*. (100)
The pervasion consisting of the reality of the mind has been correctly described;
by the refinement of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is assimilated into one's own self. (101)
Thus ends the twenty-third chapter in the Śrī Kādimata, among the venerable Ṣoḍaśanityātantras.

In those squares, which measure two finger-breadths each and include their own eleventh part—this being the remaining sense—the measurement stated here refers specifically to the inner circle. The horizontal lines (tiryak-sūtra) are those running from the very center of the circle to the very edge of the outer circle; that is the meaning. Within those compartments, starting from the eastern center...

The meaning of the tradition is that one should write the names of the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of practice (*sādhya*), and the ritual action (*karman*) in the outer ring immediately adjacent to the pericarp— which consists of the central portion included within the middle— and specifically in the northern square of the eastern central cell, as previously described.
[This is performed] preceded by the *prāṇapratiṣṭhā* (invocation of the vital breath), through worship, retention, installation, and so forth;

the phrase "in all prescribed applications" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Herein is the sequence for drawing: having produced a circle by means of a compass with a measurement of four finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in every direction.

Outside of that, having produced eleven circles at intervals of two finger-breadths each as before, one should triple the respective diameter for both the innermost circle and the outermost circle, divide each of those measurements into eleven parts,
and mark eleven points at those respective locations.

Having performed the procedure starting from the west and so forth, beginning from the eleventh mark situated on the central circle and extending through the space between that and the eleventh mark situated on the outermost circle, one should strike eleven lines;
then, slightly extending the tip of each of those eleven lines so that it touches the outermost circle.

Having fashioned it in the shape of a trident, one should thus produce a circular yantra outside the central pericarp (karṇikā), consisting of one hundred and twenty-one squares and surrounded by spikes; then, having written the practitioner's name and other details within that pericarp as before, [one should proceed].

Immediately thereafter, on the outer circular path (vīthī), beginning from the central eastern square and proceeding by the previously mentioned sequence in a clockwise direction with an outward movement, one should write the syllables of the Vidyā— one hundred and ten in number— into that same number of squares; then, in the remaining eleven squares:

Having written the ten syllables of the Earth-mantra, and having written the triad beginning with the practitioner (sādhaka) as before in the one remaining [space], and having placed it within any one of the aforementioned substrates, one should proceed as before in the prescribed applications,
preceded by the consecration of life-force (prāṇapratiṣṭhā) and worship and so forth.
"Thus, the accomplishment of the stated fruits shall come to pass.
Thus [ends the section] from the *Śrīkādimatākhyam*, the complete tantra among the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*,
by the illustrious *Subhagānandanātha*, under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*.
In the commentary titled Manoramā,
the twenty-third chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the procedure for the fifth Vidyā that constitutes a limb of the sixteen Nityās, has been fully examined and completed. || 23 ||
The number of verses: In the twenty-third chapter, there are twenty-one yantras;
the explanatory text consists of one hundred and eighty-two and a half verses.

The Twenty-Fourth Chapter. Now, O wise one, listen as I describe to you the various meditations upon the sixteen Nityās, which are like celestial wish-fulfilling trees for the attainment of desired goals.
Each one of them [is established] through the relationship of limb and possessor of limbs by means of their respective powers,
in all ritual applications, both externally and internally, in due order.
For the sake of prosperity, fame, the attainment of victory, and for the accomplishment of irresistible attraction,
one should meditate upon all the goddesses, adorned with red-colored ornaments.

For the attainment of knowledge and for rites of pacification, one should visualize [the rays] as resembling pearls, drops, and camphor; for inciting enmity, eradication, killing, and suppression, one should visualize them as black.
Or, for the sake of achieving the aforementioned [attainments] such as hatred (dveṣa), one should visualize all [the goddesses] as smoke-colored;
in every case, they are surrounded by their own forms, colors, and powers.

Having taught in the twenty-third preceding chapter the ritual procedure for Vārāhī, who is a limb of the sixteen Nityās, he subsequently teaches the various meditations on the sixteen Nityās, as well as their respective roles as limbs or the principal deity, along with their sequential applications and so forth.

Now, by means of the twenty-fourth chapter consisting of one hundred verses, beginning with "Then, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "accomplisher of success" (*siddhikṛt*), [the author] teaches the subject matter of the chapter.

Therein, by means of two verses beginning with "Then, sixteen" and ending with "in sequence" (*kramāt*), he teaches the meaning of the chapter. In that context, "divine trees" (*suradrumān*) refers to things resembling divine trees.
This means by way of being unwearied in the bestowing of desired objects and so forth. "Each one" means in a successive order;
the phrase "with their powers" refers to the powers of those Nityās, namely their respective retinue-powers—this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
"Externally and internally" means according to the distinction between the gross and the subtle. The term "meditations" (dhyānāni) is to be construed with what precedes.

With the verse beginning with "For Prosperity" (*śriyai*), he teaches the general visualization for the purposes of prosperity, fame, victory, subjugation, and attraction. In that context, for the sake of achieving subjugation and attraction—
meaning for the accomplishment of subjugation and the accomplishment of attraction— the entirety of the sixteen Nityās along with their retinues [should be visualized].
In the phrase "adorned with red forms," the word *maṇḍana* refers to clothing, ornaments, garlands, ointments, and so forth. (3)

With the first half of the verse beginning with "vidyāptau" (in the attainment of knowledge), he teaches the general meditation which brings about the acquisition of knowledge, pacifies [obstacles], and accomplishes liberation; therein,
"resembling the moon and camphor" means resembling the moon and resembling camphor.

The words "by means of beauty and color" (*kāntivarṇābhyām*) are to be supplied as the remainder. By the first half-verse beginning with "hatred" (*vidveṣa*) and ending with "possessed" (*vṛtāḥ*), [it is shown that] the elements such as earth and the qualities such as *sattva* are each combined together. (p. 435)
The powers [are manifested] by means of phonemes and forms initiated by single [phonemes], dyads, and so forth.
These [powers] are innumerable; who indeed could describe them in their entirety?
Or who could hear them in their totality? Therefore, I shall tell you something of them.
All those of the nature of earth are yellow in color and effect immobilization;
all those of the nature of water are said to possess the quality of goodness (sattva) and are white in appearance. || 8 ||
All of them bestow knowledge, peace, glory, fame, good fortune, and liberation;
they are all fiery, characterized by the quality of rajas, and endowed with a red appearance. || 9 ||

He teaches the general visualization for the rites of inciting enmity, eradication, destruction, and suppression. In that regard, "dark" refers to [the goddesses] by virtue of their form, clothing, garlands, ornaments, unguents, and so forth; "smoky-colored" refers to them as before by virtue of their form and so forth. The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. All [these] are the Nityās. This applies everywhere to those previously mentioned.
Regarding the distinctions among the meditative absorptions (dhyāna). || 5 ||

With these two verses beginning with "Earth and so forth" and ending with "I shall tell you," [the author] explains the cause for the perception of various colors and other qualities through the limited form of the supreme power (*parā śakti*), which itself possesses a limited nature.

It also teaches that the powers perceived therein are innumerable and so forth. In this context, by "elements" (bhūta) such as earth and the rest— namely earth, water, fire, air, and ether— and by the qualities (guṇa) such as *sattva* and the rest—
namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— each being combined individually and connected separately with one another.

The remainder [of the sentence] is as follows: they have arisen through colors and forms conceived by means of one, two, or more equal or unequal portions of the distinct, interconnected qualities of the elements, which are themselves initiated in groups of one, two, or more; this is the remainder. Of these powers, in their entirety—

Who indeed could describe meditation in its entirety, or who could hear it in full? This is because both speakers and listeners are impermanent; that is to say, for that reason, the statement "something [of it]" refers to those mantras with their various powers (*śakti*), as they constitute only a single part of the form that is about to be described. This is what is meant:

Of the elements such as earth and so forth, which are eternally connected with individual qualities such as *sattva* and the rest, and which possess various colors and forms distinguished by the conceptualization of one, two, or more equal or unequal parts;

Since the powers (*śakti*) are innumerable, it is impossible to describe or hear their various forms and manifestations; therefore, regarding those distinctions of power, I shall speak of them briefly from the perspective of power itself for the sake of protecting the universe. || 7 ||

With three and a half verses beginning with "bhīmākārā" and ending with "smṛtā," he teaches the visualization and the practical applications of the powers of the five elements, each endowed with its respective quality. Among these, "bhaumākārāḥ" means having the nature of the earth.

They are yellow in color, [as is understood] from the context regarding their bodies, garments, ornaments, unguents, garlands, and so forth. All these attendants are eternal and effecters of immobilization (*stambhana*), because the earth element is by nature immovable.
The water-based powers (*śaktis*) are of the nature of water; they possess the quality of *sattva*, and all are as previously described.
Their white forms, as before, consist of bodies and so forth;
they bestow subjugation, attraction, pacification, fortune, good luck, and victory.
Those whose form is wind and who are smoke-colored cause all [such things] as hatred. (10)
Those [lines] which are ethereal and blue in color are prescribed for killing and expelling;
O Pārvatī, hear now the description of their faces, arms, and bodies. 11.
Some have one face, some four faces, and others nine; some have sixteen mouths, and even some with twenty-five faces. (12)
In some places she has thirty-six faces, in others forty-nine;
likewise, she has sixty-four mouths, and even one hundred and eighty-one faces.

All those powers are of the nature of water; the bestowing of knowledge and other qualities by the water-powers arises from their being essentially of the nature of *suṣṭhu* (the well-formed). They are joined with a red form, as before, through their bodies and other attributes.
The fire-powers bestow subjugation (*vaśya*) and other effects because they are essentially of the nature of *grāsa* (the devouring/consuming).

The remaining [words] are "the powers have the form of wind. They are smoke-colored, with bodies, garments, and so forth, as before. Regarding the phrase "causing hatred and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to such matters as eradication (uccāṭana). Wind causes eradication and other such effects because its nature is movement.

The *nābhasā* powers are of the nature of space (*ākāśātmikā*). They are blue in color and [are associated] with the two forms and so forth as previously described. Together with their retinues, these eternal (*nityā*) powers are remembered—that is, meditated upon—for the acts of killing (*māraṇa*) and eradication (*utsādana*). "Eradication" (*utsāda*) means being rendered as ineffective as a corpse; this refers to the result of those two activities, as is understood from the context. They are "remembered" (*smṛtāḥ*), meaning they are visualized in meditation.

The tradition holds that the powers whose nature is space (ākāśa) bring about the perfection of dissolution (nidhana-siddhi), because space is formless; furthermore, it is said that wind and space consist of the quality of rajas. || 10 ||

With the second half of the verse beginning with "āsām" (of these), he introduces the prescription of the distinctions in the nature of the faces, arms, and bodies of those powers produced by the combination of one, two, and so forth, of even and uneven parts. In this context, "Pārvatī" is the vocative address. || 11 ||

With these two verses beginning with "ekavaktrāḥ" and ending with "śatānanāḥ," he teaches the visualization of their different numbers of faces based on the combination of the qualities (guṇas) and elements (bhūtas) in equal or unequal proportions, such as one, two, and so forth. In that context, "ekavaktrāḥ" means those endowed with a single face.

"Four-faced" is as before. "Others" refers to the remaining powers (*śakti*). Some powers have sixteen faces—that is, sixteen mouths—as before. In certain specific applications, they have forty-nine faces—that is, forty-nine mouths—or eighty-one hundred faces.

They have eighty-one faces and hundreds of faces; and according to the sequence of equal numerical parts, they possess portions of the qualities (guṇas) of the elements— from one to ten— by means of portions ranging from one to ten.

Thus, by means of multiplication alone, the tenfold Śaktis, possessing as many faces as the resulting number, are revealed. As for the sequence of their faces: on top of the throat-seat (kaṇṭhapīṭha), there is one face;
however, in the case of four faces—
(437) What is the use of much talk with the desire to establish the number of mouths and arms? Nevertheless, something has been shown: two faces and two pairs of arms. (14)
Transcending name and form, she possesses infinite forms;
by her own will, she dwells there in various forms according to desire.
Of the first, Lalitā, there are fifteen others who reside in her limbs; by virtue of Lalitā being their principal body, they are the embodiments of all [the goddesses]. 16.
For each of all those [goddesses], there were female attendants whose inner natures corresponded to theirs,
and who were perfectly endowed with complexions, weapons, forms, and vehicles identical to their own.
Even though they are surrounded by their respective multitudes of powers of such a kind, O Maheśvarī, these gross variations in their meditative forms have thus been described. 18.
Above the first face, there are three faces arranged horizontally; together with that, there are four faces.

In the case of nine faces, however, above those there are five faces arranged in a horizontal row; together with them, there are nine faces. The same applies to the subsequent cases, each time adding more faces above.

The meaning of the tradition is that by imagining faces numbering seven, nine, eleven, thirteen, fifteen, seventeen, and nineteen, they become deities with the aforementioned number of faces. || 13 ||

By means of the two verses beginning with *bahunā* and ending with *vāñchayā*, it is taught that for Lalitā, who transcends name and form, even in the subsequent [sections], because the elemental portions (*bhūtāṃśa*) and the qualitative portions (*guṇāṃśa*) are multiplied by equal numbers, and because they are multiplied by single, double, and so forth, up to tenfold parts, those [results] which have arisen—

Because the powers (*śakti*) are innumerable, he teaches that their forms—distinguished by variations such as faces and arms—are to be conceived in accordance with the practitioner's own inclination. In this regard, there are many [forms] characterized by specific bodies, and even by hundreds; among these, those described as having multiple faces and two arms— [The text continues: ...of those [powers] thus described...

One should imagine as many faces as there are, assigning two arms to each face in succession. The phrase "transcending name and form" (nāmarūpātigā) implies that this is because names and forms are unlimited, and because the supreme power (*parā śakti*) is manifold. Of these...
Of the eternal [things]. || 15 ||

With these three verses beginning with "Of the first" and ending with "Maheśvarī," he teaches the sequence of the relationship between limbs and the possessor of limbs (aṅga-aṅgin) among the sixteen Nityās. In this context, "residing in the limbs" means residing in the limbs of the central Nityā; "having their own forms" means having the forms of those respective Nityās; and "ending in their own [names]" means [ending] with their own [names].

"Ending with each respective Nityā" means ending with the remaining Nityās. "By those having the colors, weapons, forms, and vehicles of each respective [Nityā]" means by those having the colors, weapons, forms, and vehicles of the Nityā situated in the center. "By such [beings]" means by those having the colors, weapons, forms, and vehicles of each respective [Nityā]. "O Maheśvarī" is the vocative address. This is what has been stated.

O sinless one, I shall likewise describe to you how Lalitā, who stands in the center, exists in the form of the limbs within the meditations on the limbs and the possessor of limbs among the sixteen Nityās; and how Kāmeśvarī and the other fifteen Nityās exist as her retinue in their subtle forms.
By which all those practitioners may attain their desire in an instant. || 19 ||
Having meditated upon her whose form is identical with the red [element] within the previously mentioned foundational lotuses,
one should contemplate success within that mass of light.
By that, one attains everything desired without effort, indeed through meditative visualization alone, even without worship, libations, fire-offerings, and the like. || 21 ||
But meditation is considered joy arising from the unbroken self-reflection [of the Self], resembling a lamp in a windless place, through the self-perception of the Self by the Self. (22)

They possess external forms, weapons, vehicles, and so forth, similar to those of Lalitā. However, when Nityā Kāmeśvarī is the principal (aṅgin), Lalitā herself exists in the form of a limb (aṅga) consisting of this very nature—possessing the form and other attributes of Kāmeśvarī. Immediately after that:
The fourteen Nityās, beginning with Bhagamālinī and ending with Citrā, along with Kāmeśvarī at their conclusion,

together constitute the fifteen Nityās who stand outside as the retinue. Thus, although Bhagamālinī and the others serve as the primary members (*aṅgin*) of the group, Lalitā alone— possessing the very form of each respective Nityā— is the central primary member.

Outside of that [central deity], immediately following it, fifteen Nityās—extending to the end of each respective Nityā—are to be meditated upon as standing in the form of her attendants, each possessing the specific form of the deity they accompany. || 18 ||

With these three verses beginning with "sūkṣmarūpa" and ending with "bhāvanena vai," he teaches the meditation on subtle forms along with its preliminary application and so forth, preceded by an introduction.
In this context, "subtle forms" refers to their meditations—this is the ellipsis. "O Sinless One" (*anaghe*) is a vocative address.

By that subtle meditation on the connection—[the phrase] "among those taught" refers to the *Nityānityāpaṭala* [as the remainder]. [The deity] whose body is one with the red self possesses a body identical in form to the color red.
Therein, in that mass of fire, [one attains] success (*siddhi*), [the word] "desired" being the remainder; this connects with the phrase "by that contemplation."

This is what is meant: having visualized within the aforementioned foundation-lotuses a mass of fire in the form of red light, inseparable from oneself, one should contemplate the desired fruit in the midst of that light through the visualization of the essential nature of the goal, the practitioner, and the ritual action.
He attains it. || 21 ||
With the verse beginning with "param," he teaches supreme meditation (*paradhyāna*). In that context,
through the reflective awareness of the indivisible Self (*akhaṇḍātma-vimarśa*),
[one perceives] all particular ornaments such as bracelets and crowns as non-different from it, in their respective forms.

In all objects perceived as having these various forms, there exists— non-different from them— a supreme power abiding in the form of each respective aspect; this is realized through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of that power,
which is like a lamp in a windless place, being undivided by space, time, and other such conditions.
The remainder [of the sentence] is that it is perceived as having the nature of unwavering, full radiance.
This is because, through the self’s observation of itself, the self has the nature of not being illuminated by anything else.
(p. 439) One should accomplish each respective desired object, whether auspicious or inauspicious, by means of the gross [form].
O Goddess of gods, this should be performed constantly by the practitioners and those seeking success according to the prescribed sequence. || 23 ||

Once perfected, however, through meditation in its subtle form, one shall accomplish every desired object; but for the sake of achieving the means of accomplishment, the object to be accomplished must be realized in its supreme form.

Speak, O God Maheśāna, regarding the various accomplishments through the ritual action of meditation upon the two forms— the gross and the subtle— along with the application of their respective fruits.
O Maheśānī, listen as I shall now describe to you, in due order, all the weapons that are said to be in their respective hands. (26)
In the two-armed form, the left and right hands should display the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness;
in the four-armed form, they hold a noose and a goad; and in the six-armed form, they hold a bow and arrows.

This is what is meant: that which is perceived through the contemplation of the Self by means of the indivisible self-reflection—that is, the observation of the Self as the Self—is the supreme meditation (paradhyāna), resembling a lamp in a windless place. || 22 ||

With the two verses beginning with *sthūla* and ending with *siddhaye*, he teaches the sequence for the classification of meditations regarding the objects of accomplishment (*sādhya*) and so forth within the three types of meditation already mentioned. In this context, "by means of gross meditation" is the implied sense; "one should accomplish" means "one should accomplish [it]"; and the particle *tu* indicates a distinction.

"Other form" (*pararūpa*) means consisting of reflective awareness (*vimarśātmaka*). "But" (*tu*) indicates a distinction. "To be accomplished" (*sādhya*) means that which is to be attained, the form of the goal (*upeya*), the ground of rest; this is the meaning. The phrase "by means of the contemplation of non-separateness" is to be supplied [as the method]. [This occurs] within the unlimited Supreme Power (*parā śakti*), as being non-different from oneself.

Even when it is accomplished, because there is no other state to be reached and because of the scriptural statement that "nothing exists beyond the attainment of the Self," that very [Self] is what is to be attained; such is the meaning. || 24 ||

With the verse beginning with "Speak," the Goddess asks about the sequence of success through ritual action (*karma*) in both gross and subtle meditations; therein, by means of the application of results, one attains the desired fruit. With the verse beginning with "Of those," [she asks] about the specific weapons that are to be described.
And he introduces the explanation of the matter asked about. Regarding that, according to the tradition (*sampradāya*), it is said that by the word "also" (*api*), he means:
"I shall also speak of the various accomplishments (*siddhis*) of the rites you have asked about. "O Maheśānī" is the vocative address. [This continues] in sequence.
In the sequence of having two, four, and so forth, arms. || 26 ||

With the two verses beginning with *vāma* and ending with *vāñchayā*, he teaches the general rules for the weapons, their sequence, and so forth. In that context, the phrase "of the left and right hands" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. Regarding "in the two-armed [form]," this refers to the meditation on the two-armed [deity]. [The mudrās are] *varābhaye*.
The gestures (mudrās) are those of granting boons (varābhaya); this is the dual form of the first word.

Regarding the "noose and goad with four arms," this refers to the meditation on the four-armed [form]: the meanings are that the noose and goad are in the upper left and right hands, while in the other two [hands] they are as before, namely, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness.

When [the deity] is described as having eight arms, there are a shield and a sword; when ten arms are mentioned, there are a mace and a trident. This is according to the desired number and form of the weapons held in the hands for the sake of ease. (28)
O Goddess, in whatever rite the practitioner remembers her, she appears before him and protects him with devotion accordingly. (29)
In all auspicious rites, they have smiling faces and eyes;
in cruel rites, they have fierce fangs and terrifying eyes and faces.
Whether seated, standing, or even mounted on a vehicle, they are always engaged in auspicious deeds, while all others are always engaged in inauspicious ones.
All of them were resplendent with bracelets, armlets, and jeweled rings,
and they were also clad in divine garments.

In the meditation on the six-armed [form], there are a bow and an arrow as before; in the two upper arms are a noose and a goad, and in the two below them are the gestures of boon-granting (*varada*) and fearlessness (*abhaya*) as before. In the eight-armed [form], there are a shield and a sword; in the meditation on the eight-armed [form], [the attributes] in the upper arms are as before.
Below those two are the noose and the goad; below those, as before, are the bow and arrow; below those, in order from left to right, are the shield and the sword;

below those, as before, are the gestures of granting boons (varada) and fearlessness (abhaya); and in the visualization of the ten-armed form described [in the] Daśodita, there are the mace and the trident.

As before, [he holds] a noose and a goad in his two upper arms; below those, a bow and an arrow; below those, a shield and a sword; below those, a mace and a trident in the left and right [hands] respectively; and below those, the gestures of granting boons and fearlessness as before.
In the phrase "the number of forms, etc.," the word "etc. refers to objects other than those already mentioned. || 28 ||

With the verse beginning with "yasmin" (in which), he teaches that they bestow the accomplishment of desired goals in the rite intended; therein, for that practitioner, the word "bhūtvā" (having become) is connected with "tathā" (thus), meaning "having manifested. || 29 ||

With these four and a half verses beginning with "In all [cases]" (*sarvatra*) and ending with "the Great Goddess" (*maheśvarī*), he teaches the general visualization regarding auspicious and inauspicious rites. Therein, the word "in all" (*sarvatra*) is common to the entire system; the first half-verse beginning with "in all" refers to the visualization for auspicious rites.
With the second half-verse beginning "daṃṣṭrogrā," meditation is prescribed for inauspicious actions. (30)

By the verse beginning with "In auspicious [acts]," the first quarter of the first half of the verse refers to meditation on virtuous deeds; by the remaining three quarters of the verse beginning with "Established," it refers to meditation other than that. The word "api" has the sense of "also. The term "made of jewels" applies to all three, beginning with the bracelets.

This is the qualification. Regarding the phrase "wearing divine garments," their divinity is due to them being perceived by certain knowers of reality with their [divine] vision. All of them are eternal and accompanied by their retinues. Here, among the ornaments, there are necklaces, neck-chains, gems, signet rings, anklets, and so forth.
And all of them were adorned with clusters made of the nine precious gems. || 33 ||
Thus, O Maheśvarī, the general meditation for them has been declared;
now hear the specific [meditation] which I shall describe, granting success in their respective rites. (34)

Mounted on elephants, horses, and chariots, or stationed in celestial palaces (vimānas), or riding upon lions, tigers, and Garuḍas—these should always be meditated upon for the sake of protection. (35)
For the attainment of victory in battles, for the protection of kings, kingdoms, and so forth, and on forest paths difficult to traverse due to Piśācas, thieves, serpents, and the like; (36)
One should meditate upon all those deities, surrounded by all their powers, either individually or collectively; thus one will certainly become happy. (37)
For rites of eradication, all those [deities] should be meditated upon as terrifying and most formidable, mounted upon bears, monkeys, brown bears, donkeys, buffaloes, and boars. (38)
The names [of the deities] are to be understood from Ārādhyapāda. These ornaments are common to all ritual applications. "O Maheśvarī" is an address to the Goddess. || 33 ||

With seven verses beginning with "The distinction" (*viśeṣam*) and ending with "are proclaimed" (*samīritā*), starting from the half-verse onwards, he teaches the meditation on the various types of general vehicles within the specific applications, preceded by an introduction to the specific meditations (*viśeṣadhyāna*). Among these, [the first] half-verse begins with "The distinction."
He introduces the specialized meditation (*viśeṣadhyāna*). Here, "specialized" means [distinguished] from the form generally described; this is the sense.

With these three verses beginning with "gaja" and ending with "niścitam," he teaches the meditation on specific vehicles for the *akṣas* and so forth. In that context, regarding "rakṣās," the word "ātmarakṣāsu" (for self-protection) is to be supplied as the remainder.

In the phrase "the kingdom and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to cities, villages, towns, ports, market towns, houses, and the like. In the phrase "wild beasts and so forth," the word "and so forth" refers to lions, hyenas, and the like. Whether individually or collectively, among the sixteen Nityās, one should [visualize] the desired Nityā together with her own retinue and all [the others].
Or [they may be] accompanied by their respective retinues. By the phrase ending with "niścitam" (certainly), the unfailing nature of the fruit is expressed. || 37 ||

With the verse beginning with "ṛkṣa" (bear), he teaches the visualization of the specific mounts for the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*). In that context, "fierce by virtue of their physical forms and so forth"—the ellipsis is to be supplied as "are extremely terrible in their ritual action. (38)
(442) Those who ride upon herons, hawks, curlews, crows, and owls—all of them, intent on causing enmity, are crowded with terrible weapons. (39)
The practitioner should visualize a rhinoceros, a jackal, a porcupine, a gavaya, a deer, and a horse in all minor rites. 40.
Piśācas and Vetālas are to be meditated upon in all cases of killing.
Thus have the differences in results been declared according to the differences in the mounts. || 41 ||
All of them are mounted upon Garuḍas, possess two hands holding fire and wind, have two eyes and one face, with fierce fangs and terrifying forms. || 42 ||
Scorching the multitude of enemies with the powers of their own forms,
they are to be meditated upon as being surrounded on all sides by those of terrifying roar at the forefront of the battle.
One quickly becomes victorious through the destruction of the enemy army, whether by causing them to flee in great numbers or by making them fall at one's feet. || 44 ||

With the verse beginning with "kaṅkā," he teaches the visualization of specific mounts for acts of inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). In that context, *kauśika* refers to the owl (*divābhīta*). They are "crowded with terrible weapons" (*ghorapraharaṇākulā*), meaning they are densely packed with fearsome armaments. || 39 ||

With the verse beginning with "khaḍga," he teaches the specific vehicles for rites such as subjugation and attraction. Regarding "minor rites" (kṣudrakarmasu), these refer to subjugation, attraction, and so forth. (40)

With the verse beginning with "piśāca" (the flesh-eater), he teaches the meditation on the various mounts and so forth for rites of slaying (*māraṇakarman*). In this context, the phrase "by means of the various mounts through meditation" is the ellipsis;
[this is taught] by the twenty-five verses beginning with "all" (*sarvā*) and ending with "sixteen" (*ṣoḍaśa*).
Through verses, he teaches the meditation on victory in battle and so forth, according to the distinctions of their vehicles, faces, weapons, and other attributes.

In that context, all the Nityās are accompanied by their retinues. Regarding the phrase "endowed with fire and wind in both hands," this means that the right and left hands hold fire and wind respectively. They are burning.

"By the fire kindled by the bows held in their respective hands"—that is the meaning. "With terrifying roars," meaning those making a dreadful noise. "Surrounded"—this connects with the word "all" (*sarvāḥ*) in the preceding passage. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. [This refers to] the army of the enemy.

"By any one of [the four ways], namely: destruction, flight, crushing, or falling at the feet. This means: "cutting down" or "crushing" by any one of the four methods, such as the destruction of the enemy army, according to the sequence mentioned. "Having twice that many arms" means having eighteen arms. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative; [it means] "with nine left arms."
The remainder: Having visualized [the goddesses] with four faces and eight arms, cutting down a vast army with swords, one indeed attains victory in battle according to the stated sequence. (45)
Having nine faces and eighteen arms, they possess terrifying forms;
with their left hands they hold a multitude of bows, and with the others, they bear swords.
Having meditated upon the entire army of enemies with their bodies pierced by arrows and vomiting streams of blood, one shall obtain the victory described.
Alternatively, she may hold a sword along with nine other weapons,
cutting down the fourfold army of the enemy with her blades.
Having reflected and fought for victory against that one of terrifying form who was exceedingly difficult to conquer,
[the field] was tumultuous with the clamor of infantry, horses, elephants, and chariots, and the sound of musical instruments.
One quickly attains [the goal] without effort through the application of the previously mentioned sequence;
or else, by means of nine maces held in the left and likewise in the other hands. (50)
Remembering those terrible women holding claws in their hands during the battle, and [remembering] his own fourfold army destroyed by them, one shall attain victory. (51)
Likewise, by felling the enemy's force with floods of spears and axes at the gate on the field of battle according to the prescribed method, one becomes victorious.
Likewise, by meditating on [the goddesses] striking with force using multitudes of leather-bound swords, one shall become victorious in a hair-raising battle. (53)

The swords held in each of their respective right hands are to be construed with the word "chindantyaḥ" (cutting) from the preceding verse. "Āṭopaḥ" means agitation or fury. The verb "prāpnoti" (attains) is to be construed with "vijayam" (victory) from the preceding verse. This occurs through one of the aforementioned methods, such as the destruction of enemies and so forth.

Alternatively, as before, in another sense, "by the destruction of enemies and so forth" means as previously stated. The word "by others" (itaraiḥ) in the phrase "by the other right hands" connects with the word "others" (itaraiḥ) from the preceding passage. "Terrible" (bhīmāḥ) refers to their physical forms and so on.
These powers, distinct from those [previously mentioned], are pierced by the claws of the nine right hands, ending with the fourth limb.
"Endowed with four limbs"— this connects with the word "likewise" (*tathā*) in the preceding [verse],

meaning "in the same manner as before," following the sequence of the multitude of left and right arms. "With multitudes of tridents and axes" means with multitudes of tridents (*śūla-ogha*) and multitudes of axes (*kuṭhāra-ogha*), according to the stated order.
Or, having meditated on [the goddess] who bewilders the army of enemies with the hand of the darkness of sleep, a king certainly attains victory in battle. (54)
Or, remembering that his army is being crushed by those with the hands of *piśācas* and serpents, he, resembling Śaṅkara, eternally enjoys victory in battle. (55)
Or, by slaying the enemy host in battle with nooses and razors, a king certainly attains victory by recollecting [the deity] according to the prescribed sequence. (56)
And by tearing apart the armies in an instant with a hook and a saw, one who meditates thus in battle will certainly be victorious. 57.
Constantly striking the enemy's forces with plows and pestles while recollecting his victory in battle, he attains complete victory through the power of meditation. (58)
Likewise, one should meditate upon those [goddesses] with sixteen faces and endowed with thirty-two arms, crushing the hosts of enemies as before, while reciting the mantra. (59)
Or they may have twenty-five faces and be endowed with fifty arms;
by means of those eleven varieties of weapons, they strike fiercely.

By means of any one of the ways beginning with the destruction of the army; likewise, by means of a multitude of shields and daggers—that is, by means of multitudes of shields and multitudes of daggers—following the sequence of the left and right arms;
"the strength of the enemies" is the ellipsis; or (*vā*) is used as an alternative particle; "hair-raising" is the ellipsis, referring to [the state] of the heroes.

The meaning is that [she holds] the hands of sleep and darkness in the order of left and right. The phrase "the hands of a piśāca and a serpent" refers to the sequence of the left and right hands; this is the ellipsis. She "encompasses" or attains [them] by means of the noose and the knife held in the multitude of her left and right hands, according to the stated order.
As before, by means of any one [of the acts] such as the destruction of the enemy army; with the goad and the saw held in the multitude of left and right hands—this is the ellipsis;
with the ploughs held in the multitude of left arms—this is the ellipsis; and with the maces held in the multitude of right arms.

The remainder [is as follows]: likewise, they hold, in the sequence of their hands, the eleven types of weapon-pairs beginning with fire and wind and ending with the plow and the pestle; that is to say, those Śaktis [are to be visualized] according to the previous method for any one of the purposes, such as the destruction of the enemy's army.
"By eleven divisions," the remainder being "by those such as Vahni, Vāyu, and so forth. "The strength of the enemies," the remainder being [the same].
Regarding the word "having reflected" (*vicintya*), in the preceding passage (p.
445): "Having reflected, the king always attains victory in battle."
Likewise, one should worship them at that time in the sacred enclosure (agraha) with those [mantras] joined with recollection.
One should visualize the goddesses as having thirty-six faces and seventy-two arms;
likewise, they are endowed with those ten forms, colors, and weapons.
Visualizing her with forty-nine faces and twice as many hands, thus striking down her enemies, one shall attain victory. (63)
One should meditate upon the goddesses with sixty-four faces, endowed with twice that number of hands, striking [the enemy] in battle; one will certainly become victorious. 64.
By remembering the goddesses with eighty-one faces, joined by twice that number of arms, and likewise endowed with such weapons, one shall be victorious in battle. (65)
Having remembered those sixteen [goddesses], who have a hundred faces, twice as many hands, and are equipped with their respective weapons, one attains victory in battle.
Thus, they are endowed with many faces and hands according to their desired forms,
as well as with those multitudes of weapons, their hands moving in a bewildered succession.
They would become innumerable, granting the desired accomplishments of the practitioner; thus, one should contemplate them during fierce battles, crises, and the like. (68)

This connects with the word "nighnatīḥ" (striking down). Likewise, the practitioner should worship those Nityās— who are characterized by their forms and so forth— with recollections joined with the aforementioned meditation on their forms.
The meaning is that one should cause [it] to be made. "Then" means at the time of battle.
Likewise, as before, by any one of the [means] such as the destruction of the enemy's army; by those doubled, numbering eighty-eight;
by those doubled again, numbering one hundred and twenty-eight.

"Endowed with twice that number of arms" means endowed with arms numbering one hundred and sixty-two. "By such [beings]" refers to those beginning with Fire (Dahana). "Having twice that many hands" means having two hundred arms. "By their weapons" refers to the eleven types of paired weapons mentioned previously. || 66 ||

With these four verses beginning with "evam" and ending with "niścitam," [the text describes] the application for victory in battle there, which is accompanied by the desired number of faces, arms, and so forth— even without the previously stated number— and involves the visualization of weapons and other attributes in a disordered sequence.
And he teaches the specific types of practitioners: "In that regard, by means of the aforementioned sequence,
a person who crosses over those goddesses with the gestures of the disordered order quickly overcomes calamities."
Whether a god, a rākṣasa, a yakṣa, a kinnara, or a bhujaṅgama; || 69 ||
Whether he be a Piśāca, a Guhyaka, a Siddha, or a Dānava, one who constantly remembers [this] shall certainly never suffer defeat. (70)
In a forest fraught with dangers such as thieves, on a path through mountain fastnesses, amidst hardships caused by various kinds of enemies, or in fear of the king; (71)
In times of minor afflictions, during crises caused by spirits, epilepsy-demons, and rākṣasas, and when tormented by hosts of piśācas, ḍākinīs, and brahmarākṣasas; || 72 ||
Moreover, even in other difficult, extensive, and great calamities, one who remembers this [mantra] shall overcome all misfortunes through the power of meditation. (73)
Having one face and two arms, fulfilling the desires of the practitioner, they arrived wearing sandals and adorned with all ornaments. (74)
They were surrounded on all sides by their own equal powers (śaktis),
who sang and performed dances, and they were adorned with forest garlands (vanamālās).
Meditating upon them, one shall obtain all that is desired, even those sixteen;
O Maheśvarī, there is nothing in the world unattainable through meditation on these.
The phrase "in the manner described in the *Vāsanāpaṭala*" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
In the expression "in great battles, in perils, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to matters such as musical contests and other types of conflict.
The term "the goddesses" (*devīḥ*) is to be construed with the preceding word "contemplating" (*cintayan*).
Thus, by means of the forms of his desired face, hands, weapons, and so forth, [he perceives] *bhaṅga*, that is, defeat. || 70 ||

With these six verses beginning with *corādibhiḥ* and ending with *maheśvarī*, he teaches the application for crossing over all calamities through specific meditations on the Nityās. In that context, in the phrase "in danger from thieves and so forth" (*corādisaṅkaṭe*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to tigers and the like. [The calamities are] of two kinds: those that are innate (*sahaja*) and those that are natural (*prākṛta*), etc.

In minor afflictions— afflictions arising from enemies, the manipulation of time, and so forth; in others— consisting of the three types of suffering such as the internal (ādhyātmika) and so on— in this manner,
by means of the method of meditation to be described, [the goddesses] holding their desired objects with two arms.

Bestowing the desired objects of the practitioner—[accompanied] by forms possessing two eyes and so forth that are identical to their own; these are the Nityās. [The word] "of these Nityās" is the vocative address "O Maheśvarī. || 76 ||
Having recollected those women who are mounted on adorned horses, surrounded by female attendants (śaktis), with smiling faces and singing, one should bring the entire universe under control. (77)
Mounted upon elephants in such a manner and likewise surrounded by female attendants,
they stood in the midst of throngs of women intent on singing.
By remembering [her], one attains a stable fortune that is honored by kings, endowed with various enjoyments, and renowned for its own majesty. (79)
Mounted upon such chariots, surrounded by such Śaktis, and accompanied by such throngs of Śaktis closely attached to them; || 80 ||
By remembering it, a king indeed conquers the circle of his enemies;
likewise, from that threefold meditation, one attains incomparable good fortune and fame.
With the verse beginning with "alaṅkṛta," he teaches the meditation for the subjugation of the universe. In that context, "surrounded by Śaktis" means surrounded by Śaktis mounted on adorned horses.

With the two verses beginning with *tathā* and ending with *vaibhavām*, he teaches the visualization for the practice of attaining Lakṣmī. In that context, "of such a kind" means characterized by the previously mentioned forms possessing two eyes and so forth. "Mounted upon elephants" means mounted upon decorated elephants.

Likewise, they were surrounded by Śaktis— mounted upon decorated elephants and possessing forms identical to their own— and surrounded by groups of female practitioners (yoginī) devoted to music. It was exceedingly stable, impervious to kings, thieves, and others.
"Endowed with various enjoyments" means possessed of various objects of enjoyment, specific articles, and the respective capacities for such enjoyment and so forth.
"Renowned for her own majesty" refers, as is understood from the context, to her form, qualities, learning, pride, manliness, and other such attributes. (79)

With the two verses beginning with *tathāvidha* and ending with *yaśas*, he teaches the meditative application (*prayogadhyāna*) for attaining the stages (*bhūmi*) and so forth. In this context, "mounted on such chariots" means, as before, mounted on chariots that have been adorned. Likewise...

Surrounded by Śaktis means surrounded by Śaktis mounted on decorated chariots; likewise, accompanied by groups of Śaktis engaged in music means accompanied by groups of Śaktis devoted to music and other arts who are mounted on decorated chariots. "The earth" is the understood object [of their movement].

The "circle of enemies" (*vairimaṇḍala*) refers to the kingdom of the foe. Thus, from that threefold meditation—namely, the meditation on [the enemy] mounted upon horses, elephants, and chariots adorned with the aforementioned sequence—one attains the incomparable, which is beyond comparison. || 81 ||
(448) Recalling them thus in a secluded forest grove of plantains, they arrive with their own powers, their feet fixed upon the sandals. 82.
Having recited the vidyā for a month or half a month within the maṇḍala, one should then enter it;
having obtained a treasure in the world, one shall be an enjoyer of pleasures for as long as life lasts.
Likewise, by recollecting [the mantra] in a betel-nut grove, one obtains a treasure without effort;
the same applies to *campaka*, *puṃnāga*, *nameru*, and *vakula* trees. 84.
Likewise, by remembering them in mountain groves, one shall obtain wealth from a king, a wealthy man, or others, by which he may remain happy for a long time. (85)
By constantly remembering [the Lord] with his intellect on the shores of the ocean or in the forests, one obtains many priceless jewels through the power of meditation. (86)
By thus recollecting those [goddesses] in groves of trees situated amidst rivers flowing to the ocean, one obtains gold of preeminent color in incalculable quantities.

With the two verses beginning with *kadalī* and ending with *āyuṣam*, he teaches the meditative practice (*dhyāna*) for the application of attaining the treasure (*nidhi*). In that context, "those" refers to the eternal [goddesses]. Likewise, the ellipsis is to be supplied as "together with the Śaktis characterized by the previously mentioned forms such as Dvinetrā and so forth. The mandala...

As before, there are fifty-one days; half [of that] for the mandala and the months. "Or" (vā) means as an alternative, up until success is achieved. "Vidyā" means one's own desired eternal Vidyā. "Yāvadāyuṣam" means for as long as one lives. || 83 ||

With the verse beginning with "pūga" and so forth, he teaches the specific characteristics of the five gardens upon the attainment of the treasure through the aforementioned meditation. In that context, "tathā" means in the manner just previously described. || 84 ||

With the verse beginning with "tathā," he teaches the specific application for attaining wealth through the previously mentioned meditation. In that context, "tathā" means in the manner previously described;
"in mountain bowers" means in mountain caves; "those" refers to the eternal [energies]; "from the king" means from the presence of a king; "by which" refers to that [means] by which he [attains it].
The meaning is that the practitioner should possess as much wealth as would allow him to be happy for a long time; that is, he should be happy for as long as possible. || 85 ||

With the verse beginning with "In the ocean," he teaches the practice for obtaining priceless jewels through the previously mentioned meditation. In that context, "in that way" means by the aforementioned method of meditation. 86.

With the verse beginning with "samudrageti," he teaches the practice for attaining immeasurable, supreme gold by means of the previously mentioned meditation. In that context, "tathā" (thus) means in the manner of meditation as before. || 87 ||
By recollecting [the deity] in a solitary forest, one obtains auspicious women who are rich in beauty, youth, and virtuous character, who are overcome by love and devoted to no other. (88)
A man who, mounted on a horse, remembers [the deity] in those aforementioned places, brings the king under his control through the actions of his mind, speech, and body. (89)
When those [mantras] have been uttered, one who is mounted upon an elephant— having remembered women, men, kings,
and especially all living beings in the world— brings them under control.
Likewise, those mounted on chariots who remember the goddesses as they have been described shall attain their desires and be liberated from fetters and other bonds. || 91 ||
Having clearly drawn those [goddesses] upon nine cloths—each with a hundred faces and twice that many arms—and having depicted their desired weapons upon them; 92.
Likewise, one should place those cloths at both the middle and the two ends,
provided with curtains for the chariots, elephants, and horses.
When facing the enemy forces, however, one should properly display those [instruments]:
the vajra, the alikhita, the niśāna, the bherī, the paṇava, and the maddala drums.

With the verse beginning with *nirjana* and so forth, he teaches the visualization for the practice of attaining a woman through the previously mentioned meditation. In that context, "having remembered" implies "in the manner described. "Subdued by love" means being under the sway of love. || 88 ||

With these three verses beginning with "ukteṣu" and ending with "āditaḥ," he teaches the meditation for the release from shackles and so forth, together with the subjugation of kings and others. In that context,
"in those aforementioned places" refers to the previously mentioned locations such as the groves of plantain trees.
In those ten locations at the edges of uninhabited forests— in those aforementioned places as before—

and all living beings without distinction, that is, all creatures including gods, humans, beasts, birds, reptiles, and so forth, in those aforementioned places as before; and regarding the phrase "from shackles and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to [punishment] by kings and others.
The object [of this] consists of specific types of bonds and so forth. || 91 ||
With these five verses beginning with "śata" and ending with "anaghe," he teaches a specific application for victory in battle. In this context, "desired things" refers to those conceived by oneself;
"they" refers to the Nityās. "In nine" means in those numbered as nine. "Clearly" means very manifestly, in the two pairs at the center and the periphery.

One should establish them; likewise for the chariots, elephants, and horses. Among those three—horses, chariots, and so forth—on each of the nine cloths, one should place [the figures] on both the left and right sides at the two extremities.
Beating and sounding trumpets, conchs, kettledrums, and other instruments, the enemy, utterly defeated, flees swiftly toward the vajra. (95)
"Once it has come face-to-face with that army, it will certainly never turn back;
thus, O sinless one, have the meditations been explained to you in their entirety. (96)
Through subtle meditation, the fruit arises for both the perfected ones and the practitioners;
therefore, listen as I shall speak of that which accomplishes all desired goals. (97)

Meditating with the intellect upon her form, whose splendor resembles the filaments of a pomegranate flower, one should likewise visualize within that [heart] the form of the person to be accomplished (sādhya), according to one's own desire. (98)
One obtains all desired things, both auspicious and inauspicious;
likewise, one should contemplate the coming and going within the Suṣumnā.
By the power of meditation, he attains his entire desired goal;
likewise, both the practitioner and the perfected one achieve swift success through those two alone.
And one should arrange three by three, together with *tiraskaraṇikās*—the remainder of the sentence being that they are accompanied by *tiraskaraṇīs*.

A *tiraskaraṇikā* is a covering cloth positioned facing the opposing army. [One should place] those nine cloths—the remainder of the sentence being that they are the cloths—as well as drums (*bherī*) and small drums (*paṇava*) inscribed with vajras, and *maddala* drums.

O sinless one, with the multitude of drums such as the *niśāna*, *bherī*, *paṇava*, and *mardala*— inscribed with the *vajra*-yantra according to the method described in the three verses beginning with the ninety-fourth verse of the *Vijayānityāpaṭala*, starting with "In battles..."— and including the *kāhala* and so forth (where the word "and so forth" refers to the *bherī* and other instruments), that army [confronts] the enemy army. O sinless one!
Thus ends the section on the vocative case. || 96 ||

With these four verses beginning with "subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and ending with "accomplishing success" (*siddhikṛt*), he teaches subtle meditation (*sūkṣmadhyāna*) along with its preliminary introduction and its application (*prayoga*). In this context, the phrase "in the supports" (*ādhāreṣu*) is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence] for that subtle meditation; [it occurs] in their midst.

In the midst of the light consisting of a stream of eternal [flames], according to one's own desire—that is, in accordance with the action intended by oneself—and likewise in the form of that light, within the *suṣumnā*, meaning in the middle of the *suṣumnā* channel; that which is in accordance with one's own desire is one's own goal (*svasādhya*). Or (*vā*) is used as a particle of option.

The meaning is that one should perform the going and coming repeatedly in the sequence of ascending and descending from the *mūlādhāra* to the end of the *brahmarandhra*, and from the *brahmarandhra* to the end of the *mūlādhāra*. By that, it means by the aforementioned two methods.

By the word "only" (*eva*) in the phrase "of those two only," it is stated that they lack qualification for the practices of meditating on the subtle form of the object of attainment (*sādhya*). || 100 ||

The all-pervasion consisting of the self by its very nature has been correctly proclaimed. Through the refinement of this [pervasion] within the mind, that reality is realized as one's own self. (101)
Thus, the twenty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, within the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantra*, has been fully examined and completed.
Thus [ends] the complete *Tantra* named *Śrīkādimata* among the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.

The twenty-fourth chapter, dedicated to illuminating the expansion of the meditation on the sixteen Nityās, from the commentary named Manoramā composed by Śrī Subhagānandanātha, whose title is Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa.
It is complete and thoroughly grasped. || 24 ||
The number of verses: In this twenty-fourth chapter, there are no yantras;
the explanatory verses shall be sixteen more than two hundred.

The Twenty-fifth Chapter: Now, [the description of] the nature of Time (kālātmatā) for the sixteen Nityās, in due order, through the bodies of the thirty-six principles (tattva), the phonemes, the mantras produced from them, and the yantras.

I shall describe the ritual applications which are the means for attaining various desired goals, through which the mantras of the student are perfected by means of both knowledge and the different modes of worship. (2)
The sixteen vowels are eternal; [the consonants] from Ka to Kṣa are accompanied by the vowels.
Within them are the twenty-six principles (tattvas), consisting of the nine groups of letters headed by Nātha. || 3 ||

In the twenty-fourth preceding chapter, having taught the meditations and other practices for the applications of the sixteen Nityās, [the author] subsequently [teaches] the arising of the colors through the pervasion of the sixteen Nityās by the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), and the various distinctions of the elements produced by those respective yogas.

Then, by means of the twenty-fifth chapter consisting of one hundred verses, beginning with "Now, sixteen... and ending with "Śiva," he teaches the nature of time through mantras and yantras, as well as their ritual applications and so forth; therein, starting with "Now," [he describes] the student.
With these two verses ending thus, he teaches the subject matter of the chapter and its power. In that regard,

the ellipsis is to be supplied as "by the pervasion" of the sixteen vowels of the sixteen Nityās with the thirty-six consonant-syllables, which are the embodiments of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*).

"By the colors" means by those whose number will be stated hereafter; "arisen," is the ellipsis. "Produced from them" means produced from the various combinations of those [colors]. "The nature of time" means the essential form of time, which is attained through the distinction between knowledge and worship—that is, through the distinction in internal contemplation.
