And by means of the distinctions of external worship, consecration, fire-offerings, and so forth, those belonging to the [four] castes possess merely the characteristics of their respective castes;
they are devoid of the qualities such as *sattva* and are characterized by the layers of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which will be described hereafter. (2)

With the verse beginning with "The vowels" (*svarāḥ*), he teaches the identity (*tādātmya*) of the sixteen vowels with the sixteen *Nityās*, of the thirty-six consonants with the thirty-six *Tattvas*, and of the nine groups of the *Mātṛkā* with the nine *Nāthas*. Among these, those accompanied by the vowels...
They are conjoined with the letter *a*; because the thirty-five letters from *ka* to *kṣa*, together with the vowel,
consist of the thirty-six principles (*tattvas*) and thus possess a dual nature, they are of that very essence.
Since even the first vowel possesses a dual nature by virtue of consisting of both vowel and consonant, and according to the oral tradition (*upaskara-sampradāya*),
it is intended here that the first vowel alone is meant by the designation "vowel" (*svara*); the particle *tu* is used for emphasis.

This is what is meant: those sixteen vowels are themselves the sixteen Nityās; those thirty-six consonantal phonemes are themselves the thirty-six Tattvas; and those nine groups of the Mātṛkā are themselves the nine-fold Nāthas. || 3 ||
In each vowel, there are eight groups; thereafter, there are indeed five by five.
For the Mothers, however, one group is formed with the vowels, as before, followed by the subsequent one.
In the conjunction of the principles (tattvas) of the eternal ones, the number of syllables is proclaimed as five hundred and seventy-six; through years of that same number, fullness is attained.

The completion of the machines (yantras) numbering that same amount occurs over as many years; this is the recurrence of the full cycle of time, which bears the names of the yugas, kalpas, and so forth.
The duration of the Kṛta Yuga is said to be three thousand [divine years] multiplied by four;
through a reduction of one-fourth of that [period] for each subsequent quarter, the Tretā and following ages arise.
With the first half of the verse beginning with "eight," he teaches the nature of the nine groups of the *mātṛkā*. In that context, "eight by eight is a group in the vowels":
each individual group among the vowels consists of eight letters.

With the second half-verse beginning with "mātṛṇām," [the author] teaches the pervasion of the eight groups by the Mothers, Vaśinī and the rest, as well as the nature of the eight groups of the letters of the Mātṛkā. In this context, "mātṛṇām" refers to the Mothers, Vaśinī and the rest; "tu" is used for emphasis; and "with the vowels" implies "with the sixteen vowels" as the understood remainder.
As before, among the thirty-five consonants beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, each group consists of five [consonants] according to the form described for the groups.
With the two verses beginning with "of the Nityās" and ending with "the portion of the names," [the author describes] the vowels.

And he teaches the number of syllables arising from each individual conjunction, the pervasion of those syllables and their respective numbers by years corresponding to the number of *mātṛkā* wheels, as well as the designations of intermediate *yugas*, *kalpas*, and so forth, resulting from the rotation of those same number of years.

In that regard, regarding the eternal [mantras], their perfection is achieved through the conjunction of each of the sixteen vowels with each of the thirty-six consonant syllables from *a* to *kṣa* during union with the principles (*tattva-saṃyoga*). This refers to those aforementioned numbers of phonemes within the yantras.

The meaning is: of those wheels whose number has been stated by the two and a half verses beginning with "In the chapter" (*paṭale vṛttam*) and ending with "have been proclaimed" (*samīritā*). This is what is intended: starting from each respective Yuga among the Kṛta and other ages, [the total] is five hundred and seventy-six (576).
Through their respective natures as the numbers of the phonemes, the numbers of those [cycles], and the *mātṛkā* wheels, fullness is attained in years equal to those respective numbers.
Thus, the designations such as "yuga," "kalpa," and so forth, correspond to their respective durations. || 6 ||

With the verse beginning with "trisahasra" (three thousand), he teaches the number of years of the four yugas—Kṛta and the others—by means of the revolutions of the years of the aforementioned maṇḍalas. Therein, "of that" refers to the Kṛtayuga. This is what is meant: [the number] of the full years of time is five hundred and seventy-six.
The Kṛtayuga consists of seventeen lakhs, twenty-eight thousand, and three hundred years (1,728,300), produced by three repetitions [of the preceding number].
454) The syllables of the Kṛta and other ages are said to be represented by the numbers five, four, three, and two.
One should inscribe those [syllables], joined with the letters of the day, within the central womb.
In the placement of vowels within the dīnāras, they are to be arranged in sequence in the form of bindus;
five each are prescribed for the left, upper, and right sides.
The syllables of the respective ages (yugas) are established in their own forms in their respective places;
however, in all instances among the consonants, they are well-integrated and conjoined with their own [vowels]. || 10 ||
By subtracting one-fourth of the Kṛta Yuga from its years—namely, 32,000 years—one obtains the Tretā Yuga, which consists of twelve hundred and ninety-six thousand years (1,296,000).
This is calculated by subtracting those 32,000 years from the total years of the Kṛta Yuga.
Thus, the Tretā Yuga measures 1,296,000 years.

Furthermore, by subtracting from the years of the Tretā Yuga those years equivalent to one-fourth of the Kṛta Yuga, the Dvāpara Yuga consists of 864,000 years. Again, by subtracting from those years of the Dvāpara Yuga one-fourth of the years of the Kṛta Yuga, the remaining half of those years constitutes—

The Kali Yuga consists of four hundred and thirty-two thousand years (432,000). When these are combined, one cycle of four yugas (Caturyuga) consists of forty-three lakh and twenty thousand years (4,320,000). || 7 ||

By means of these three verses beginning with "māyā" and ending with "saṃyutā," [the author] describes the phonemes of the bodily forms of the Kṛta and other yugas, along with those phonemes, in conjunction with the ghaṭikā-phonemes to be described later in this chapter within the ghaṭikā-cakras.
He also teaches the sequence of writing and so forth. In that regard, by means of *māyā*, *dharā*, *agni*, *vāta*, and *sva*:
*māyā* is the visarga; *dharā* is the vowel *u*; *agni* is the vowel *i*; *vāta* is the vowel *a*; and *sva* is the bindu.
What is meant is that these four syllables—*aḥ*, *uṃ*, *iṃ*, and *aṃ*—are used in their respective order.
They become the embodiments of the four ages beginning with Kṛta. These [are] the syllables of the ages conjoined with the syllables of the days, because the ghaṭikās are parts of the day;
that is to say, they are conjoined with the syllables of the ghaṭikās to be described. In the central womb (madhyayoni).
The phrase "of the ghaṭikā-yantaras to be described" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "In the letters of the day" means as before;
"in the letters of the ghaṭikās" refers to the fifteen vowels to be described, which constitute the ghaṭikās and exclude the visarga.

"Having the form of a drop" means having a form drawn in the shape of a drop (*bindu*). On the left, upper, and right sides—just as before—in the central *yoni* of the water-clocks (*ghaṭikāyantra*) to be described; the word "of the deity" is to be supplied [as the object].
"In that place" means in the center of the central *yoni* of all, just as before. This is what is meant:

When, among the *ghaṭikā*-syllable yantras to be described hereafter, it occasionally happens that a syllable in the form of a vowel (*svara*) must be written as a *ghaṭikā*-syllable, and when five [syllables] each are assigned to the left, back, and right sides of the deity in the central *yoni* of those yantras, one should place those letters [there].

Beginning from the left side, having designated the positions for the fifteen vowels starting with *a*, one should write a single dot in the position of the vowel occurring at that time as the syllable of the *ghaṭikā*, identifying it as being of that same nature.

In all matters—whether for the installation and consecration of the arrangement of yantras, for grace-bestowing worship, for subjugation, for the layout of a dwelling site, or for the placement of the foundation—it brings about the desired success. (11)
Beginning from the rising of the sun, one by one in the sequence of ghaṭikās,
there is a rotation through each of the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā.

Then, one should write the syllable of the *yuga* (pair) that has arrived at that time in its own form in the middle, in the place of the deity. The remainder [of the instruction] is that among the consonants (*vyañjana*), they are to be written as the syllables of the *ghaṭikā*. Throughout this chapter, when writing the syllables of the *ghaṭikā* and the syllables of the *yuga*, one should write them in their own forms among the consonants.

"Well-joined" (*suśliṣṭāḥ*) means well-connected, that is to say, those groups which have undergone the euphonic changes (*sandhi-kārya*) appropriate to each respective case, such that their forms are not divided. This is what is meant: throughout this chapter, in the writing of both the *ghaṭikā*-syllables and the *yuga*-syllables, if the *ghaṭikā*-syllable is of the nature of a vowel (*svara*), [it is joined].
Having written the syllable of the *ghaṭikā* in the form of a vowel on the left side and so forth according to the stated manner,

and having written the form of a *bindu* in its own portion, one should write the pair of syllables (*yugārṇa*) in its own form in the center of the central *yoni*. If it is a consonant, then [one should write it] in the center of that central *yoni* in the form of that *ghaṭikā*-syllable.
One should write the consonant joined with the vowel as before, well-joined and connected; in the Kṛta age it should be written with the visarga, and in the other ages with the bindu. || 10 ||

With the verse beginning with "sarvatra" (everywhere), he teaches the application of the *ghaṭikā-cakras* and their respective fruits. In that context, the word division for "garbhanyāseṣṭasiddhikṛt" is "garbhanyāse iṣṭasiddhikṛt" (in the placement of the embryo, it effects the desired accomplishment).
Because of its divine nature, the euphonic junction (*sandhi*) of the scriptures need not be analyzed by us. || 11 ||
With the two verses beginning with "starting from" (*ārabhya*) and ending with "proceeds" (*pravartate*),

he teaches the sequence of pervasion of the *mātṛkā* syllable-wheel by means of the wheel of light (*jyotiścakra*), which consists of *ghaṭikās*. In that context, the phrase "the rising of the sun" implies [its rising] in Laṅkā.

"From fifty revolutions" means from the fifty revolutions of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*, excluding the final vowel. This refers to that Mātṛkā which consists of such revolutions.
What is meant is this: in every age, on the first day of the age...

Beginning from sunrise at Laṅkā, fifty letters of the Mātṛkā—from *a* to *kṣa*, excluding the vowel *visarga*—arise in the sequence of one *ghaṭikā* each over the course of fifty *ghaṭikās*. These constitute the fivefold Mātṛkā: *a, e, ca, ta, ya*.
These are to be known in the *ghaṭikā-pārāyaṇa*. Furthermore, on the first day, ten syllables beginning with *a* and ending with *ḷ* arise by means of the remaining ten *ghaṭikās*. On the second day,
As before, starting from sunrise, the remaining forty syllables beginning with the letter *e* (ekāra) arise over forty ghaṭikās.
Then, on the second day, the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ṅa* arise over the remaining twenty ghaṭikās.
Twenty syllables arise; then, on the third day thereafter (p.
456), they are uttered by her through six repetitions over five days.
Thus, beginning from the start of the Yuga, it proceeds by means of the letters that are the nature of Time. || 13 ||
Having drawn a triangle within a yoni, one should draw a yoni within that;
having written the letters of the Nityārṇava in their respective sequences upon those [triangles], one should place them on the outside.

O Goddess of the Gods, having placed the syllable of the Yuga (the letter *ya*) in the middle of the syllable of the Ghaṭikā (the letter *ra*), the worshipper should constantly worship the sixteen Nityās there.

The thirty letters beginning with *ca* and the thirty letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ṇa* arise. Immediately thereafter, on the fourth day, the twenty letters beginning with *ta* and the forty letters beginning with *a* and ending with *ma* arise. On the fifth [day]...

On the day immediately following that, the ten syllables beginning with *ya* and the fifty syllables from *a* to *kṣa* arise. Thus, in sequence, over five days at a time, there is the manifestation of the Mātṛkā in the form of the aforementioned cycle of revolutions.
Thus, six sets of six transformations occur. || 13 ||
By means of these three verses beginning with "yonau" and ending with "ayogyatā," [the text explains] the sequence for constructing the ghaṭikā-cakra, and therein,
the sequence for writing the Vidyā according to the divisions of yugas, cycles (paryāya), days, and ghaṭikās within that cakra.

This teaches the necessity of performing the worship of the sixteen *Nityās* and the unfitness of the practitioner (*sādhaka*) for the practice if it is not performed. In that context, "in the womb" (*yonau*) means in the center of a triangle whose apex points toward oneself;
"triangle" (*trikoṇam*) refers to a triangle whose apex points away from oneself; "in that" (*tasmin*) means in its center; and "the womb" (*yonim*) is as previously described.
Among those, in the three corners of the outer and middle enclosures— which take the form of a triangle—

there are the letters of the "eternal ocean" (nityārṇava) according to the sequence; that is, the triad of letters of the Vidyā obtained at the specific sequence-number within the total number of Vidyās to be mentioned hereafter, as well as the triad of letters of the Vidyā obtained on the specific day.
"Externally" means beginning from the outer enclosure; this is the ellipsis. "In the center" means in the middle of the central womb (*yoni*).

"Constantly" means every day. By stating "the supreme [worship] is constant," he teaches that daily worship must necessarily be performed. "On every festival" refers to those occasions already mentioned.

"At every festival" (*parvasu pratiparvam*) means as long as [the practice continues]. "Within a month" (*māsamātreṇa*) means at one of those festivals each month. Here, the prescription for the middling and inferior options applies only during times of distress, such as national upheaval, famine, or disease; otherwise, there is unfitness [for these], as stated in the second chapter.

By the latter half of the seventieth verse, beginning with "a thousand," it is implied that for the practitioner who has failed to perform the prescribed expiation (*prāyaścitta*) during daily worship and other rites—this is the remainder of the sense.
Herein is the sequence for constructing the wheel of *ghaṭikās*: having produced a circle by means of a radius of the desired measure, therein...

Having stretched the east-west Brahma-sūtra, and taking half its measure, one should fix the point at the junction of the eastern end of the Brahma-sūtra with the circle, mark two points on the two sides of that circle,
and then stretch a horizontal sūtra connecting the two ends of those two marks.
Starting from those two tips (p.
457), the superior [practice] is indeed constant, the middling at every joint, and the inferior within a single month; beyond a month, there is unfitness.
In the first [circle], the syllables of the colors of the full mandala should be placed in order from the beginning;
in the second, the syllables of the thirty-six principles (tattvas) should be placed in order by means of the winds.
The third [syllable] is fire on all sides; thus, these three-syllabled vidyās are declared in sequence to be the Tripuras, the mines of all siddhis. || 18 ||

Having laid down two threads from the western end of the Brahma-thread to its limit, one should fashion the womb (yoni); then, having drawn a horizontal line through the middle of the lines on the left and right sides of that womb,
[one proceeds] from those two ends of that womb.
Having formed a triangle by laying down two threads from the middle to the ends of the horizontal line,
one should draw a horizontal thread through the two points located at the centers of the sides of that triangle; then,
starting from those two points, [one should draw] a thread to the center of the horizontal line of that triangle.
Having formed the central womb by striking the two [lines] together and having cleared away the circle of the Brahma-thread, one thus completes the wheel consisting of the time of the ghaṭikās; then,
starting from the tip of the outer womb and proceeding clockwise, [one places] the previously mentioned [syllables] from the Vidyā into the three corners.
Having written the three syllables of each respective Vidyā in succession,
one should write the three syllables of the Nityā-vidyā within the corners of the triangle— starting from the eastern corner and proceeding clockwise— and then,
in the center of the yoni within that, [place] the syllable of the specific ghaṭikā accompanied by the method previously described.

Having written the *yugārṇa* (the number of years in a Yuga) therein, one should know that the various forms of knowledge residing within the mind are contained in the wheel whose nature is Time (*kālātmake cakre*).

This refers to the number produced by the eleven-syllable statement (*ekādaśākṣaravākyajanitasaṃkhyā*), which is 94,675,000,000. Within this time-period, which is divided according to its distinctions, one should worship the sixteen *Nityās*. Thus [ends verse 16].

With the two verses beginning with *pūrṇamaṇḍala* and ending with *kramāt*, [the author] teaches the nature of the three-syllabled *Tripurā-vidyās* that arise by virtue of the specific procedure of the application of syllables (*akṣarayoga*) within the colors of the full mandala, as well as their power (*anubhāva*). In that regard:

The letters beginning with *a* and *ā* and ending with *kṣaṃ* and *kṣaḥ*, numbering five hundred and seventy-six, possess the colors of the full mandala; the meaning is that these are the first letters of the Vidyās in the first [group], existing as the *vāgbhava* [seed-syllable] from the beginning in their respective order.

The thirty-six *tattva*-letters beginning with *a*, previously mentioned as the letters starting from *a* up to *kṣa*, are the second set of letters; they consist of the *Kāmarāja* [mantra] and have been joined with the letter *ā* by means of *marut* (the wind-vowel), this being the remainder [of the sense]. The third script is the remainder. Of those *vidyās*, it is the third.

The *lipi* (script) among all these sciences whose numbers will be mentioned hereafter is the "Fire-script," namely the letter *i*; the meaning is that it exists as the seed-syllable of power (*śakti-bīja*) for those sciences. Thus, in the manner described, the *Tripuras* [are established] by name and by their essential nature—this is the ellipsis.
This is what is meant: having placed these [mantras] in a book and established it upon a pedestal in this chapter (p. 458), one should worship it;
wherever [this is done], pestilence, misfortune, planetary afflictions, famine, and enemies [shall cease]. || 19 ||
For him who worships constantly, untimely death, sorcery, and other such evils do not occur in his city or elsewhere, and his desired goals are accomplished. (20)
The number of those [breaths] is declared to be twenty-one thousand six hundred and seventy; their repetition brings about the attainment of that [state]. (21)

As for the full maṇḍala syllables mentioned as the first letters in the extraction (*uddhāra*) of each of the Tripurā-vidyās—consisting of three syllables each and numbering thirty-six, as will be stated in the twenty-first verse: [The text continues with the specific syllables: ... *pūrṇam*, *maṇḍalam*, *lavarṇam*, etc.

Having first uttered each syllable in its respective order, one should then, as the second syllable in sequence, utter the previously mentioned thirty-six syllables consisting of the *tattvas* with the vowel *ā*, joined by euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*).
Immediately thereafter, one should everywhere utter the vowel *ī* as the third syllable. By that—

Among the colors of the full mandala, each single syllable is the first of thirty-six, the first syllable of thirty-six vidyās; by means of that, the vidyās of the number to be described come into being. || 18 ||

With these two verses beginning with *etāḥ* and ending with *nityaśaḥ*, he teaches their application (*viniyoga*) and the fruits [of their practice]. Therein, *etā vidyāḥ* means "these mantras. *Āropya vilikhya* means "having inscribed [them]. The syntactical connection is: "one should worship them on the pedestal" (*pīṭhe pūjayet*). *Saṃsyāpya* means "having established [the deity]" by performing the rite of consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*).
"Śātravāḥ" means enemies (*śatravaḥ*). In the phrase "kṛtyādyāḥ," the word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to *hatyā* (murder) and the like.
In the phrase "purādike," the word "ādi" refers to villages, towns, cities, market towns, hamlets, houses, and so forth. "Tasya" refers to that worshipper (*arcaka*). || 20 ||

With the verse beginning "thirty-six," he teaches the number of the aforementioned vidyās, the fruit for one who contemplates them, and the synonyms of that tantra, such as "eternal" (nitya) and so forth. In this context, "their repetition" (tadāvṛttiḥ) refers to the rotation of those vidyās according to the sequence to be described; it is that which effects their attainment.

It means that it effects the state of being the Self of the Goddess. Here, the meaning of the tradition (*sampradāyārtha*), which serves as an introductory supplement, is written by the command of the Lord (*nātha*). Since these *vidyās* consist of the Goddess, the word "that" (*tat*) refers to the *vidyā*. Therefore, because they consist of the daily *Nityā*, there is a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of them. Of those...

That is to say, it effects the attainment of each individual *vidyā* among the daily obligatory rites (*dinanitya*) by way of their being performed in alternation (*paryāya*). Furthermore, there is repetition (*āvṛtti*) of those *vidyās* by way of their being performed in alternation;
that is, it effects the attainment of each individual *vidyā* precisely by way of its being performed in alternation.

In the places for writing the alternating mantras (*paryāya-vidyā*) within the *ghaṭikā-cakra* and other such [diagrams], one should write the mantra consisting of the alternation together with each respective alternating mantra. At the end of the ages (*yugānta*), when there are two mantras by virtue of being daily [mantras], then those two [should be written] in those very same places.
One should write [it]. || 21 ||
In rites such as immobilization (stambhana), those [deities] possess their respective colors, forms, weapons, and vehicles;
by reciting the mantra according to these knots, practitioners attain success. (22)
The repetition of the Lord within the mass of mantras is known to be two thousand two hundred and four; this is declared to be the repetition of the principles (tattva).
The constant repetition [of the mantra] is said to be exactly the number of the full mandala, performed a thousand times;
specifically, two hundred and ninety-six repetitions are declared to be complete.
In each day of the Yugas beginning with Kṛta, those Vidyās, whose nature is that of the Tattvas, are assigned one by one in sequence; however, at the end, they are recorded as two each.
By means of these three verses beginning with "In [rites such as] stambhana" and ending with "are proclaimed," the manner of application for those aforementioned numbers of Vidyās,
the sequence of pervasion by the nine Nāthas, the sequence of pervasion by the thirty-six Tattvas, and the sixteen Nityās [are explained].

And he teaches the sequence of pervasion (*vyāptikrama*). In that context, regarding *stambhana* and the other rites, the word "first" refers to the six rites and so forth mentioned in the twenty-fourth chapter.
Their respective colors are the colors of those specific vidyās, as well as the yellow and other colors mentioned in the twenty-fourth chapter.

Those [mantras] consist of thirty-five forms, which are the sixfold varieties to be described in the chapter; by means of these mantras, which take the form of the first variety, through "knotted" recitation (*granthitajāpa*) or "single-intervened" recitation (*ekāntaritajāpa*), all the mantras [are accomplished]—this is the remainder [of the sense]. The *varṇins* are as before. This is what is meant: regarding the *nityā* vidyās.
One should recite the desired *vidyā* with these *vidyās*, each separated by one [of the others].

This method of recitation (*japa*) is common to all mantras because, according to the stated method, all syllables are of the nature of the eternal (*nitya*), and all mantras are composed of syllables. Of this...

The secret meaning, however, should be understood from the mouth of the venerable Guru. The repetition of the Lord (nāthāvṛtti) consists of nine recitations; the repetition of the principles (tattvāvṛtti) consists of thirty-six recitations;
the number of the full mandala is five hundred and seventy-six; [and] the eternal repetition (nityāvṛtti).
The repetition sixteen times each constitutes the complete and total pervasion without remainder. || 24 ||

With these two verses beginning with "kṛtādīnām" and ending with "siddhaye," he teaches the sequence of the pervasion of the aforementioned vidyās throughout the days of the four yugas— Kṛta and the others—
as well as the necessity of performing worship on each respective day during ritual applications (prayoga), and their fruits. Therein, [he explains] one by one...
Each [of these] is a *vidyā*. Each has the form of a *tattva*, and each consists of the syllables of the *tattvas*.

This is because, as the remainder implies, all *vidyās* without exception consist of three syllables each, and thus possess the nature of the knower (*jñātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*jñāna*), and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). At the end...
The word "of the ages" (*yugānām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "In pairs" means two sciences each day. This is what is intended:

in the four ages beginning with Kṛta, according to their rotation, one science per day occurs in the order stated for that specific number of sciences. This applies during certain days at the ends of those respective ages.

Every day, two sciences (vidyās) arise. However, in all practical applications, worship on that specific day must be performed with particular care for the sake of attaining victory, health, and other such accomplishments. (26)
All of that is illustrated: just as when thirty-four thousand three hundred and thirty-seven (30,437) cycles have passed according to the sequence prescribed for the Kṛtayuga,
in the cycle immediately following [that].
When the nine thousand two hundred sixty-four (9,264) daily *nityā-vidyās* have passed, one should then begin from the *vidyā* whose form is *tāṭā ī iti*,
and for the remainder of those cycles as well as the subsequent cycle, recite two *vidyās* each day.
In the Kṛtayuga, when taken together, the cycles amount to thirty-four thousand three hundred and thirty-nine (30,439). And in the Tretāyuga...
When twenty-two thousand eight hundred and twenty-eight (22,828) cycles have passed according to the stated sequence, in the immediately following cycle,
there are six thousand nine hundred and forty-eight (6,948).

When the daily *nityā-vidyās* have passed, immediately thereafter, beginning with the *rūpiṇī-vidyā* "Ṭhāthā Ī," there occurs two *vidyās* each day— one from the remainder of that cycle and one from the remainder of the subsequent cycle; together, these constitute the cycles of the *tretā-yuga*.
The number [of years] is twenty-two thousand eight hundred and twenty-nine (22,829). And in the Dvāpara age,
according to the stated sequence, it is fifteen thousand two hundred and eighteen (15,218).
When the cycles have passed,
and after the daily *vidyās* numbering four thousand six hundred and twenty-two (4,622) in the immediately following cycle have elapsed, one begins with the *rūpiṇī-vidyā* "Jaḍā Ī".
In each daily cycle, there are two sciences consisting of the *tatparyya* and the subsequent *paryya*;
taken together, these cycles of the *dvāpara* period amount to a total number of fifteen thousand two hundred and twenty (15,220).
And in the Kali Yuga, when seven thousand six hundred and nine (7,609) cycles have passed according to the stated sequence, in the subsequent cycle,
there are two thousand three hundred and sixteen (2,316) daily Nityā-mantras.

Immediately after [the previous cycle] has passed, beginning with the *dinanityā-vidyā* (daily mantra) whose form is "ghaḍā ī," there are two mantras each day for the remaining cycles and the subsequent cycle.
Taken together, the number of cycles in the Kali Yuga is seven thousand six hundred and ten.
They come into being. Taken together, the cycles of the four ages amount to a number of ninety-six thousand and ninety-eight (76,098).
At the end of the ages, every day, there arises the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of practicing the two daily *nityā* mantras.

This should be understood from the mouth of Pūjyapāda. The calculation of the number of days in a yuga is also to be found in the *Siddhāntaśiromaṇi* within the field of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*). The meaning of the verse "pañcāṅgarāmāstithayaḥ khavahnī sārddhadvidasrārkadinākhyamabdaiḥ" is as follows: in one solar year (*sauravatsara*)...
There are three hundred and sixty-five days (365), fifteen daṇḍas (15), thirty palas (30), and twenty-two and a half vipalas (22|30).
In that Kali Yuga, which consists of a total of 432,000 years,
there are 157,680,000 [units] corresponding to three hundred and sixty-five days, based on the number of days in the Kali Yuga.
In the Kali Yuga, there are days consisting of sixty-four lakhs and eighty thousand daṇḍas related to fifteen daṇḍas; that is,
there are one hundred and eight thousand (108,000) days.
In the Kali Yuga itself, there are 3,600 days consisting of thirty-six lakh and ninety-three thousand and sixty thousand *pala*s, which relate to the thirty *pala*s [of a day].

In the Kali Yuga, there are forty-five days related to the [solar] days, corresponding to ninety-seven million two hundred thousand (97,200,000) *vipalas*— which relate to twenty-two and a half *vipalas* per day. These are the days related to the solar days within this Kali Yuga.
The days associated with the *daṇḍa* are 108,000; the days associated with the *pala* are 3,600;
and the days associated with the *vipala* are forty-five (45). Thus, when combined, they total seventy-seven thousand nine hundred and six hundred and forty-five (77,9645).
The number of days in the Kali Yuga is fifteen crores, seventy-seven lakhs, nine thousand, six hundred and forty-five (15,779,1645).
Then, by multiplying the twenty thousand seven hundred and thirty-six (20,736) mantras seven thousand six hundred and nine (7,609) times, [one obtains the total].
There are 15,778,022,424 days (157780224), after which,
in the tenth cycle, among those remaining...
In eleven thousand four hundred twenty-one days (11,421),
one science (*vidyā*) occurs every two thousand one hundred six days (2,106). In nine thousand three hundred fifteen days (9,315), two sciences occur every [two thousand one hundred six days].

"May you possess knowledge! By that, the completion of the tenth cycle [is achieved]. It should be inferred through the doubling [of days] starting from the Dvāpara age and so forth. In numerical figures, they are as follows: 3,155,832,900 days for the Dvāpara age; 4,733,749,350 days for the Tretā Yuga; and 6,311,665,800 days for the Satya Yuga. Regarding this, here are the summary verses:"

In the solar year, the time from the beginning of the day until the end of the *vipalas* consists of five limbs (5), three Rāmas (3), fifteen lunar days (15), zero (0), three fires (3), two and a half eyes (2½), and two eyes (2).

The number of days in the Kali Yuga is said to be five arrows (5), four Vedas (4), six waves (6), one lord of nights (1), nine planets (9), and seven mountains (7), followed by five arrows (5) and one moon (1).
In that regard, the synonyms should be known as: sky (0), moon (1), taste (6), and mountain (7);
furthermore, the days of the synonyms are nine (9), zero (0), limb (6), and the underworld (7).

In the remaining days, the numbers are one, two, four, one, and one, corresponding to the count of the moon (1), eyes (2), oceans (4), earth (1), and earth (1). These are to be added to the total of the Vedas (4), twice the eyes (2), zeros (0), eight (8), horses (7), sages (7), and moons (1).
and ||
One should perform worship of the elements (dhātu), the field (kṣetra), and the lords (īśa) for the attainment of their respective [results].
The method for that will be properly explained in the chapter on ritual applications (prayoga). || 27 ||
Among those, fifty pairs of the fifty phonemes indeed undergo transformation through their association with the sequence of the ghaṭikās.
Now, the yantras, numbering as previously stated, will be described in sequence:
the circle, the thirty-six-sided, and likewise the eighteen-sided.
Furthermore, my dear, when a number of days equal to zero,
one, and two have passed in succession, one should know that on each individual day, two vidyās are to be mastered in order.
"Having understood the days and so forth in the year, as well as the days of the yugas and so forth— in the Dvāpara age and others, all of that [is calculated] as double, triple, and so on. Thus,
in the ritual applications (*prayoga*), on the specific days of those applications, there is the worship of each respective day on that particular day.

On the day when the ritual applications (*prayoga*) are performed, there is the worship of the lords of those days. By that [worship], the lords of the days are sixfold: the daily *nityā* of the day, the *tithi-nityā*, the lord of the lunar day (*tithy-adhipa*), the two lords of the weekday (*vāsareśau*), and the lord of the lunar mansion (*nakṣatreśa*). The worship of these, together with the daily *nityā* of the day, is described in this chapter.
He will say: "The worship of each respective Tithinityā has been taught in its respective chapter;

the worship by the names of the Lords of the Tithis and the Nakṣatras has been taught in the Citrānityā chapter; and the worship by the names of the two Lords of the Days (Vāreśas) has been taught specifically in the Kulasundarī chapter. In the event of not performing that..."

Fruitlessness [would result] due to the consequence of afflicting the performer. This is what is meant: on the days of performance, the worship of the six types of lords of the day mentioned above must necessarily be performed according to the stated order.
This is stated in the two verses beginning with *dhātu* and ending with *parivartanam* later on.

The worship of the *dhātu* (element) and the *kṣetrapati* (field-lord), which will be described in the manner to be explained in the *Prayogapaṭala*, is introduced here within the *Mātṛkāvyāpti* as something that must necessarily be performed on the days of ritual application (*prayoga*).
In this context, the *dhātveśas* are Ḍākinī and the others; the *kṣetrapatis* have been previously mentioned. [This concludes] the transposition.
The act of making circular. || 28 ||

Now, with nine verses beginning with "atha yantrāṇi" and ending with "anyavat," he teaches one wheel for each year, numbering as many as there are syllables in the five hundred and seventy-six complete mandalas, corresponding to that same number of years.
In that context, the stated number refers to five hundred and seventy-six. (p.
463) "The twelve-sided, the nine-sided, or the sideless within the vowel, and the nine-sided;
then the four-sided and the three-sided—these are the nine divisions in sequence. (30)
These [mantras] are each eightfold due to the different arrangements of their phonemes;
thus, there are seventy-two varieties among them based on the distinctions of the eternal syllables (nityārṇa).
Thus, these have been declared with the stated number of eight varieties for each;
from the arrangement of the first of these meters, the others may be inferred.
One should draw a single circle by rotating [the compass] six finger-breadths;
in this manner, one should repeat it again and again, increasing outward by one finger-breadth at a time.
When seventeen [squares] have been formed, one should then divide that by thirty-six spokes; thereafter, one should place the syllables within them starting from the beginning.

By the second half of the verse beginning with *vṛttamitthādi*, there is one three-fold wheel; by the half-verse beginning with *dvādaśāstra*, there is a four-fold wheel—meaning, in that context, within the sixteen-spoked wheel (*ṣoḍaśāra-cakra*) which is the *khara*; and by the first quarter of the second half of the verse beginning with *caturasram*, there are two moving wheels (*cara*). These are the nine wheels that have been described.

Due to the different arrangements of phonemes (*varṇavinyāsabheda*), as will be explained in this chapter by the thirty-fifth verse beginning with "anuloma" through the different arrangements of the phonemes of the principles (*tattva*) to be discussed; among those seventy-two varieties,
[the numbers] stated are due to the different arrangements of the sixteen vowels (*nityārṇabhedataḥ*).
The number is five hundred and seventy-six. This is what is meant:

for each of the aforementioned meters and so forth, and for the nine wheels (*cakras*) which are without end, there are distinctions based on the arrangement of the *tattva*-syllables and the eternal syllables (*nityākṣara*) in the manner that will be described.

Because they consist of sixty-four forms, their combined number becomes that which has been stated. Among these nine wheels (*cakras*), regarding the circular wheel—that is, the wheel in the form of a circle—any other wheel different from the circle should be inferred; its arrangement of eight spokes, its dimensions, and so forth, are to be understood from the *Kuṇḍalapaṭala*.

The meaning is that one should write after having inferred [the pattern] in the manner to be described. "By a rotation of six finger-breadths in each direction" is the ellipsis. One should "turn" or rotate [the compass] when there are seventeen circles;
"circles" is the ellipsis. "In the corners at the ends of that wheel," meaning in the squares numbering the full mandalas. The "syllables" (arṇān).
[He should visualize] the colors of the full mandala, beginning from *a* and *ā* in their proper sequence, ending with *kṣaṃ* and *kṣaḥ*.

As for the procedure for arranging the circle: having drawn a "swan's foot" (*haṃsapāda*) on a level surface, one should draw the Brahma-line from east to west through the center of the junction of its two prongs.
Using that as a support, one should produce a circle by rotating a thread measuring six finger-breadths; then,

outside of that, having combined sixteen circles with an interval of one finger-breadth between each, one should thus form seventeen circles according to the sequence to be described in the twenty-ninth chapter.
(464) Furthermore, there are the forward and reverse [orders], the external and internal encapsulation, the external and internal reversal, and likewise the "scattered" [order]. || 35 ||
Having produced thirty-six spokes on all sides with equal intervals and having erased the Brahma-thread (the central axis),

one should place the corresponding number of syllables in the squares situated along those paths— numbering as many as the full mandala— in the manner to be described; thus, within this very wheel in the form of a circle, there are sixty-four wheels.

One should accomplish it as follows: in all the wheels (cakras) having thirty-six spokes and so forth, according to the previously mentioned method described in the chapter on Sarvamaṅgalā, one should place the respective signs corresponding to the stated number of spokes within the surrounding circles; then, having drawn lines from each sign in the form of bowstrings (jyā), one should stretch the threads.

By erasing the segments of those circles, the wheel becomes composed of various [polygonal] sides; an eight-sided wheel is formed by thirty-seven circles. One should likewise construct it with sixteen spokes as before.

With the verse beginning with "anuloma" and so forth, he teaches the sequence of the different arrangements of syllables within those nine wheels. Therein, the word "ca" (and) has the sense of conjunction for both "anuloma" (direct order) and "viloma" (reverse order); by that very [conjunction], the various arrangements of the vowels are drawn in.
The outer and inner enclosures (*saṃpuṭa*) are formed by the two halves, outer and inner;

due to the difference in their positions, there are two mutual enclosures. During the reversal of the outer and inner [halves], as before, from the two central cells on both sides of the two halves, [the syllables are arranged] in reverse and direct order.
The drawing is twofold, according to the distinction between the outer and inner positions. This is what is meant:

within the nine previously mentioned wheels (*cakras*), there arise thirty-six paths (*vīthīs*) consisting of sixteen squares each, extending from the exterior up to the pericarp (*karṇikā*) on all sides.

And those paths (vīthīs), proceeding from the front in a clockwise direction through the eight divisions of each wheel— which consist of the direct and reverse orders— become nine paths for the inscription of the letters of the respective principles (tattvas).
Among those paths, in the sixteen squares situated on the front path:
Having written the sixteen vowels by means of their movement from the exterior into the interior,

one should then, following the sequence of circumambulation, write the sixteen forms of the letter *ka*— distinguished by the sixteen vowels— in the sixteen squares located in the subsequent row, just as before, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
In each row, one should draw the various forms of the consonants from *ka* to *kṣa*, differentiated by their combination with the sixteen vowels, within sixteen squares in each row as before.
This is the sequence of direct and reverse order (*anuloma-anuloma*). This wheel is known as the Full Mandala (*pūrṇamaṇḍala*) during the Yugas.
It consists of the first year. In this very wheel, the forms of the thirty-six *tattva*-syllables are fully present, each syllable being differentiated by the sixteen vowels.
Starting from the innermost square among those situated in the paths of their respective direct (*anuloma*) sequences—
By erasing up to the outer enclosure, there arises the wheel known as *anuloma-viloma*, which consists of two years. In this very wheel, within those same paths (*vīthī*),
for each of the thirty-six letters of the principles (*tattva*), there are forms differentiated by the vowels.

Having written the eight forms in the eight outer compartments and so forth, in successive order, by way of entry and following the clockwise direction (*anuloma*), one should then write the remaining sets of eight forms in the other eight compartments, starting from the innermost compartment, by way of exit and in successive order.

Having written the names of the winds and fires all around the pericarp (karṇikā), one should join them with those situated in the outer compartments in due order according to the previously stated rule. (36)
This wheel, known as the *anuloma-vāhya-sampuṭa*, consists of the third year of the aforementioned pair of years;
in this very wheel, within those same paths, the letters of the principles (*tattva*) appear in sixteen forms as before, of which the first eight forms occur in sequence.
In all eight compartments beginning with the innermost one, one should write the remaining eight forms in sequence, starting from the outermost compartment, by way of exit and entry;
this is the wheel known as the "inner reverse-enclosure" (*anulomābhyantara-saṃpuṭa*), which consists of the pair of fourth-year [cycles].

In this very wheel, on those same paths, among the sixteen forms of the previously mentioned syllables as before, one should place the first eight forms in sequence within the eight squares starting from the eighth square up to the outermost square, following the path of exit.
And one should write the remaining eight forms in sequence, by way of entry, in the eight squares starting from the ninth square up to the innermost square;
this is called the *anuloma-bāhyaparāvṛtta* (the reverse-turning outward in direct order), consisting of the five years of the aforementioned yuga.

It becomes a wheel (*cakra*). On this very wheel, within those same rows, among those sixteen vowels which are the syllables of the principles (*tattva*), there are eight forms in sequence starting from the beginning;
then, from the commencement of the ninth square until the end of the innermost square, [they are] in eight squares.
By way of entry, one should write the remaining eight forms in the eight remaining squares, starting from the eighth square and ending with the outermost square, by way of exit;
this is called the "reverse inward rotation" (*anulomābhyantaraparāvṛtta*), which consists of the six-year cycle of the yugas.

The Wheel. On this very wheel, as before, the sixteen forms of the letters of the *tattvas* are placed in sixteen squares along each path: in the first [square] in the sixteenth, in the second in the fifteenth, in the third in the fourteenth, in the fourth in the thirteenth, in the fifth in the twelfth, and in the sixth in the eleventh.
One should write [the letters] starting from the beginning in sequence within the seventh, tenth, eighth, and ninth compartments.

This constitutes the wheel known as *anuloma-vāhya-vyākīrṇa*, which consists of the years of the aforementioned yuga-sequence. In this very wheel, within those same paths, [one should place] the letters of the aforementioned *tattvas*.
The forms have been declared for each street within the sixteen squares: in the sixteenth [square] in the first [street],
in the fifteenth in the second, in the fourteenth in the third, in the thirteenth in the fourth, in the twelfth in the fifth, in the eleventh in the sixth,
in the tenth in the seventh, and in the ninth in the eighth square from the beginning.
One should draw it in sequence. This is the wheel known as the "Anuloma-abhyantara-vyākīrṇa" (the inwardly interspersed in direct order), which consists of the eight years of the Yuga.
In this very wheel, which consists of thirty-six spokes and seventeen circles, for each row—

In the thirty-six pathways consisting of sixteen squares, having sequentially inscribed the forms of the letter *kṣa*— distinguished by the sixteen vowels— within the central pathway, starting from the outer square and proceeding by way of entry into the interior;

In the thirty-five paths (vīthīs), beginning with the path immediately following that which extends in a clockwise sequence, one should inscribe, as before, the forms of the remaining principles (*tattva*)— the consonants *ḷ* and so forth— differentiated by the sixteen vowels. This is known as the "reverse-and-forward" (*vilomānuloma*) [arrangement].
p.

466) There is a wheel (*cakra*) consisting of nine years corresponding to that [cycle]. Within this very wheel, by means of the previously mentioned procedures, there are the forms of the phonemes of the principles (*tattva*), differentiated by their vowels.
By gradually erasing [the syllables] in reverse order, there arise what are known as: the reverse external enclosure (*vilomabāhyasaṃpuṭa*),
the reverse internal enclosure (*vilomābhyantarasaṃpuṭa*), the reverse external reversal (*vilomabāhyaparāvṛtta*),
the reverse internal reversal (*vilomābhyantaraparāvṛtta*), and the reverse external scattering (*vilomabāhyavyākīrṇa*).

That wheel consists of sixteen years, beginning from the tenth year of the yuga and so forth, with each year occurring in sequence as one year at a time, scattered within the reverse order. Furthermore, in that very same [wheel]...
Having inscribed the sixteen forms of the letter *a* on the front path (*agravīthī*) of the wheel described above, following a movement from the outside toward the inside,
one proceeds through the seventeen subsequent paths in a clockwise sequence.
Having written, as before, the forms of the seventeen syllables from *ka* to *tha*, each differentiated by the sixteen vowels,
[one should place them] in the remaining eighteen paths, beginning with the nineteenth path occurring immediately after each respective sequence.

In the rows, one should write, as before, the forms of the eighteen syllables beginning with *kṣa* and ending with *da*, differentiated by the vowels, according to the previous method. This is the wheel known as the "External Encasement in Direct Order," which consists of seventeen years of that yuga. In this very wheel, of those...

By writing out the forms of the syllables of reality (*tattva*), accompanied by the sixteen vowels as before, according to the previously mentioned procedures, there arises what is called the "external encapsulation in reverse order" (*bāhyasaṃpuṭaviloma*) and the "external encapsulation within an external encapsulation" (*bāhyasaṃpuṭabāhyasaṃpuṭa*).
The outer enclosure and inner enclosure;
the outer enclosure and outer reversal;
the outer enclosure and inner reversal.

There is the wheel known as the "outer enclosure" (*vāhyasaṃpuṭa*) and the "outer scattered" (*vāhyavyākīrṇa*), as well as that known as the "inner enclosure" (*abhyantarasaṃpuṭa*) and the "inner scattered" (*abhyantaravyākīrṇa*); this wheel consists of individual years beginning from the first year of the yuga up to the twenty-fourth year. Within this very wheel—
In the foremost path (agravīthī) of the described form, having written the sixteen forms of the letter *da* as before by means of a movement entering from the outside toward the inside,
[one proceeds] through the seventeen paths beginning with the one immediately following that, arranged in a clockwise sequence.
Having written, as before, the forms of the seventeen syllables beginning with *dh* and ending with *kṣ*, each differentiated by the sixteen vowels,
[one should place them] in the eighteen paths (vīthīs), starting from the nineteenth path following immediately after each respective sequence.
One should write the eighteen syllables beginning with *tha* and ending with *a*, each differentiated by the vowels as before, according to the stated sequence;
this is known as the "inner encapsulation in direct order" (*ābhyantara-sampuṭānuloma*), which corresponds to the cycle of twenty-five years.

It becomes a wheel (*cakra*). On this very wheel, by inscribing the forms of the phonemes of reality (*tattvākṣara*)— distinguished by the sixteen vowels— as before, according to the previously stated procedures, it is called the "inner encapsulation in reverse order" (*ābhyantarasaṃpuṭaviloma*).
The inner casket and the outer casket;
the inner casket and the inner-inner casket; the inner casket and the outer reversal; the inner casket and the inner reversal; the inner [casket].
It consists of the outer *saṃpuṭa* called *vyākīrṇa*, and the inner *saṃpuṭa* called *vyākīrṇa*;
each is composed of one year, beginning from the twenty-sixth year of the pair and ending with the thirty-second year.

The wheel is formed. Furthermore, in that very wheel of the aforementioned form, one should write the sixteen forms of the letter *tha* on the front path (*agravīthī*), as before, by moving from the outside toward the inside.
The arrangement of petals for others is declared to be thirty-six.
In an eight-sided figure, there should be sixteen spokes; the circle of thirty-six is as described otherwise.
In the seventeen pathways (vīthīs) beginning with the one immediately following the sequence of circumambulation,
one should write the sixteen forms of the seventeen syllables starting with *ta* and ending with *a*, as previously described, in the same manner as before.
In the eighteen paths (vīthi) beginning with the nineteenth path immediately following that sequence, one should write the sixteen forms of the letters starting from *da* up to *kṣa*, as before.
This is known as the "outer reversal in direct order" (*bāhyaparāvṛttānuloma*), which consists of thirty-three years.

It becomes a wheel (*cakra*). Within this very wheel, by drawing those sixteen forms of the syllables of reality (*tattvākṣara*) according to the previously mentioned procedures, there arise what is called the "external reversal in reverse order" (*vāhyaparāvṛttaviloma*) and what is called the "external enclosure with external reversal" (*vāhyaparāvṛttavāhyasaṃpuṭa*).
That which is called the "outer reversal with inner enclosure," that which is called the "outer reversal with outer reversal," and that which is called the "outer reversal with inner reversal."

The [periods] known as "external transformation" (*bāhyaparāvṛtta*) and "externally scattered" (*bāhyavyākīrṇa*), and those known as "internal transformation" (*abhyantaraparāvṛtta*) and "internally scattered" (*abhyantaravyākīrṇa*),
last from the thirty-fourth year up to the fortieth year.
In successive order, there is a wheel consisting of one year for each [vowel]. Furthermore, in that very wheel,
on the foremost path (agravīthī), one should write the sixteen forms of the letter *kṣa* as before, by means of a movement entering from the outside toward the inside.
In the seventeen paths beginning with the one immediately following that which proceeds in a clockwise direction,
one should write the sixteen forms of the seventeen syllables starting with *ḷ* and ending with *ḍ*, as previously described, in their respective order.

Immediately thereafter, in the eighteen streets beginning with the nineteenth, one should write the sixteen forms of the eighteen syllables starting with *a*, *ka*, and so on, ending with *tha*, as before.
This is known as the "inner reversal in direct order" (*ābhyantaraparāvṛttānuloma*), consisting of forty-one years.

A wheel (cakra) is formed. Within this very wheel, by inscribing those sixteen forms of the letters of reality (*tattvākṣara*) according to the previously mentioned procedures, there arises what is called the "inner reversal" or "regressive order" (*ābhyantaraparāvṛttaviloma*).

The [mudrās] known as internal reversal and external union (ābhyantaraparāvṛttabāhyasaṃpuṭa), known as internal reversal (ābhyantaraparāvṛtta), known as internal union (ābhyantarasampuṭa), known as internal reversal and external reversal (ābhyantaraparāvṛttabāhyaparāvṛtta),
known as internal reversal and external scattering (ābhyantaraparāvṛttabāhyavyākīrṇa), and known as internal reversal and internal...
And that wheel known as *vyākīrṇa* consists of a single year for each [unit], spanning from the forty-second year of the yuga to the forty-eighth year. Furthermore, in that very same wheel,
on the foremost path (*agravīthī*), there are sixteen forms of the letter *a*, as before.

Having written [the letters] by moving from the exterior into the interior, one should place them in sequence within the thirty-five successive rows and so forth, proceeding clockwise: *kṣa, kla, kha, ha, ga, sa, gha, ṣa, ṅa, śa, ca, va, cha, la, ja, ra, jha, ya, ña, ma, ṭa, bha, ṭha, ba, ḍa, pha, ḍha, pa, ṇa*.
For these thirty-five syllables beginning with *na ta dha tha da*, one should write their forms, each syllable distinguished by its vowel as before, according to the previous method.
This is known as the "External Intermingled in Direct Order" (*bāhyavyākīrṇānuloma*), which consists of forty-nine years.
It becomes a wheel (*cakra*). In this very wheel,
there are the forms of those syllables of reality (*tattva*), differentiated by the sixteen vowels.

By means of the previously mentioned procedures, through the process of drawing out, there arise what are known as the "externally scattered inverse," the "externally scattered external casket," and the "externally scattered internal casket."
That which is called the external scattered and external transformation; that which is called the external scattered and internal transformation;
and that which is called the external scattered and externally scattered.

And that which is called "externally scattered" and "internally scattered" constitutes a wheel consisting of one year each, in sequence, from fifty years up to fifty-six years; furthermore, within that very same [cycle].

Having written the sixteen forms of the letter *kṣa* on the foremost path by means of a movement entering from the outside toward the inside, one should [place] *a, ḷ, ka, ha, kha, sa, ga, ṣa, gha, śa, ṅa, jha*, and so forth, in due order upon the thirty-five paths beginning with the path immediately following that one, proceeding in a clockwise direction.
For these thirty-five syllables— *ava-maca-bha-ṭa-vala-pha-ḍa-ṭa-pa-na-ṇa-dha-ta-ch-ava-ṭha*— one should draw sixteen forms for each individual syllable as before.
This is called the "intermingled in reverse order" (*ābhyantaravyākīrṇānuloma*).
That wheel consists of fifty-seven yugas and years. Within this very wheel,

by inscribing the forms of those syllables of the principles (tattva)— distinguished by the sixteen vowels— as before, according to the previously stated procedures, it is called the "inner reverse" (ābhyantaraviloma).
The one called "internal-intermingled-external-casket," the one called "internal-intermingled-internal-casket," and the one called "internal-intermingled-external-reversal."
That which is called "internally mixed," "internally transformed," that which is called "internally mixed and externally mixed," and that which is called "internally mixed and internally mixed."
Thus, from the first year of that *yuga* up to the sixtieth year,
there is a wheel consisting of one year for each [year] in sequence. In this way,
within this very wheel composed of circles, there are [the years] consisting of the first sixty-four years of that *yuga*.
There are sixty-four wheels (*cakras*). Thus, by means of the various methods of drawing the eight wheels— beginning with the thirty-six-spoked and ending with the triangle— as previously described,
each wheel corresponds respectively to the sixty-four years of that [Yuga] cycle.
When combined, there are five hundred and seventy-six wheels (*cakras*) consisting of the years of that *yuga*, known as the "Full Mandala. Among these, in the eight-spoked wheel (*aṣṭāsracakra*),
within sixteen paths (*vīthi*), each path consists of thirty-six squares (*koṣṭha*).

On the outer path (agravīthī), by moving from the exterior toward the interior, one should write the forms of the letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *kṣa*, which consist of the thirty-six principles (*tattva*), for each letter, differentiated by the first vowel among the sixteen vowels.

In the fifteen paths (vīthi) following immediately after that, proceeding in a clockwise direction, one should write their forms— numbering thirty-six and differentiated by the remaining fifteen vowels— by means of the entry and movement according to the sequence previously described. This is the first wheel within this eight-spoked wheel.

It occurs as follows: by means of the exchange of positions for consonants, vowel-syllables, and written characters, one should likewise conceptualize the remaining sixty-three wheels according to the previously mentioned varieties of classification.
This refers to the wheels of the full mandalas mentioned in the pericarp (*karṇikā*). [The elements] wind and fire...

The remaining portion [of the instruction] is that the letter *ā* and the letter *ī* are joined by euphonic combination (*saṃdhi*). The remaining portion is that [the name] is accompanied by the name [of the practitioner], as well as the ritual action to be accomplished (*sādhya-karman*). As for the method of writing it:
according to the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*), one should write it in three lines within the interior of the letter *ī*, just as before.
Having painted this upon a cloth, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus outside;
then, having arranged it, one should inscribe the eight Goddesses of Speech (Vāgdevīs) sequentially upon the petals.
Then, having properly performed its consecration according to the form described, one should worship it daily for the sake of attaining the success mentioned in the *pustakapūjā*. (39)
For one who performs both, Lakṣmī remains firm in his lineage;
never shall there be a loss of prosperity in that family.

One should join [the letters] everywhere, in all the wheels (*cakras*) and all the rows (*vīthis*). The grammatical connection is "wind and fire. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "by means of the thirty-six letters of the principles (*tattvas*) located in the outer compartments. This is according to the previously mentioned rule, in sequence, by the method of the aforementioned sixty-four divisions, proceeding clockwise from the front.
This is what is meant: having written the two syllables "ā" and "ī"— joined by sandhi— along with the practitioner and others in the center of the pericarp (karṇikā) within the aforementioned wheels,
[one should proceed] with the initial syllables situated in the outer compartments of the rows at the tips of those respective wheels.

One should sequentially join the two syllables located in the pericarp with the syllables situated in all the outer compartments of the grid, which are divided according to the previously mentioned sixty-four variations. Regarding the eight-spoked [wheel], however, one should arrange the outer compartments of the front row; this is the meaning derived from oral tradition (*ānuśravika*). It is "like the others," meaning as it is in other wheels.
The meaning is that the sequence for applying the *pārāyaṇa* mantras is likewise divided into sixty-four varieties.
In this verse, everything else has already been explained by us previously. || 37 ||
With these three verses beginning with *etad* and ending with *kule*, he teaches the common residual form, their applications, and their fruits for those aforementioned wheels (*cakras*).
Therein, *etad* refers to each individual wheel; *bahis* [refers to] each of those wheels externally.
The meaning is "outside of the form described. "Eight-petaled lotus" means a lotus with eight petals.

By the mention of "lotus," since the previously mentioned wheels are to be constructed within the pericarp (*karṇikā*) of that lotus, one should first draw a single circle for the sake of the pericarp outside of those wheels.
The meaning is that one should draw eight petals outside of that.

"In sequence" means in the order of clockwise rotation starting from the front. The connection with the preceding text is that one should draw the eightfold group of Goddesses of Speech—the eight mantras of Vaśinī and the others—in their previously described forms. This is for the purpose of the worship of Lalitā.

The remainder [of the sentence] is as follows: the meaning is that [the mantra] is joined with the seven-syllable name of the seed-syllable (bīja) of each respective group (varga). "Of that" refers, as before, to the subject of each cakra; the phrase "stated in the second chapter" is the remainder.
This is what is meant: in the second chapter concerning the installation (pratiṣṭhā), within the described form and the described cakras, in the very center of all—
Having invoked the deity into the center of the pericarp and worshipped them with perfumes and other offerings,

and having worshipped the powers of Śrīnātha and the fifteen Nityās behind the deity according to the prescribed procedure, one should worship the weapons all around and Vaśinī and the others on the outside.
Having filled a large pitcher with water consisting of a decoction of thirty-six medicinal herbs,
he should duly invoke the Goddess therein and worship her at night according to the prescribed rites. (41)

Having recited the mantras of the eternal principles (tattvas) and the Vidyās, on the following day, having worshipped [the deity] upon his seat and seated the disciple there, he should consecrate him according to his capacity.
In this manner, on the full-moon days of each successive birth,
the practitioner should offer a ring made of one karṣa of gold and cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Thus, for one who has been consecrated for a full year without interruption, that practitioner will undoubtedly become either a sovereign king or one worthy of being honored. || 44 ||
By consecrating him for two years, Lakṣmī becomes firmly established in his lineage;
by consecrating him for three years, the siddhi of the Vidyādharas shall be attained. (45)

One should worship twenty thousand seven hundred and thirty-six (20,736) mantras according to the sequence extracted from that wheel. This applies daily, every day, to the auspicious clockwise wheel and so forth; for the other wheels, however—

At the time of each respective rite, having performed the installation, worship, and so forth, and upon the completion of that rite, one should dismiss the deity along with his retinue; then, having cleansed the *cakra* depicted on the cloth, one should perform the prescribed expiations and other rites for the sake of attaining the success described for the worship of the book,
and for the sake of attaining the fruit of the previously mentioned writing and worship of the book.
Both are the worship of the wheel of the Mother (mātṛkā) and the worship of the book. || 40 ||

With these eight verses beginning with *varṇauṣadhi* and ending with *āpnuyāt*, he teaches the method of consecration by means of those vidyās and others, as well as the attainment of their fruits. In that regard,
[the method] with the decoction-water of the *varṇauṣadhi* [is described] in the thirty-fifth chapter.

With water boiled with the medicinal herbs whose syllables will be mentioned hereafter— [the vessel] being filled with a great quantity of water measuring one *khārī*— one should, in that water, according to the rule and by means of the procedure for the previously mentioned *cakra*, [perform the rite] at night on the preceding day (this is the ellipsis). [One should recite] the *tattva-vidyās* of the *nityās*, which are the *vidyās* produced from the conjunction of the vowels with the thirty-six *tattva*-syllables.

The phrase "having established him on the seat" is to be connected with what follows. The ellipsis is to be supplied as "together with a woman who has been chosen as a deity according to one's capacity. "Him" refers to the disciple. Regarding "birth, subsequent birth, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to special days such as the equinoxes, solstices, the beginning of the yugas, and so on. The word "full moon" (paurṇamāsī) [is used here to represent these auspicious times].
The subject matter of the remaining festivals: *karṣa* is three *niṣkas*; *mudrikā* is a ring.

"As a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)"—the remainder [of the sentence] is "for the consecrator. "In this manner" means according to the stated method. "Continuously" means without transgressing the stated times. "For a year"—the accusative case is used to denote duration.
Through initiation at four years of age, there occurs union with the Khecarīs;
through initiation at five years of age, one does not undergo death. (46)
By initiation for six years, one becomes equal to a world-protector;
by initiation for seven years, one becomes equal to the sun. || 47 ||
By initiation at eight years of age, one becomes like the moon;
by initiation at nine years of age, one attains the same form as the Goddess.
For the sake of victory, one should properly accomplish the thirty-six or indeed fifty-one vidyās through repetitions, recitations, fire-offerings, worship, and libations.
Having conquered all enemies by that means, he prospers like the sun;
likewise in all portents, as well as in afflictions such as disease and the like. (50)

He is to be venerated by that king; this refers to the Brahmin caste. For him who is to be consecrated, "union with the sky-farer" (*khecarīmelana*) means conversation with the *yoginīs* who move through space, and so forth; "death" (*pañcatva*) means the lack of recognition of one's own true nature. The second [line], "for six years," is as before. He is equal to a world-protector (*lokapāla*).

By virtue of the majesty of his respective qualities, he is equal to the sun in terms of his splendor and so forth; he is like the moon because of his capacity to bestow delight and other such traits; and he attains identity with the Goddess, which is the nature of the supreme *aham* (I-consciousness). Om.

By means of these five verses beginning with "jayāya" and ending with "sampradāyataḥ," [the author] explains that through the fourfold distinctions of worship one attains the fruits; that the phenomenal world (prapañca) is of the nature of those respective cakras; and that once the realization of that knowledge is perfected, all desired fruits are accomplished.

He instructs: therein, the Vidyās are of the number previously stated, being the Kālanityās; "thirty-six" and "fifty-one" are specific qualifications for their repetitions (*āvṛtti*). The word "or" (*vā*) denotes an alternative.
"Properly" means with a mind not directed elsewhere; by that means, one prospers through all [mantras], whether innate (*sahaja*), natural (*prākṛta*), or artificial (*kṛtrima*).

The meaning is "it shines as if. In this context, the word *tathā* (thus) refers to the previously mentioned methods such as the *japa* [of mantras] and so forth. Regarding the phrase "in all [cases], whether terrestrial, atmospheric, or celestial," the word *ādi* (and so forth) in the expression "diseases, etc. refers to spirits, *vetālas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, *apasmāras*, and the like.

Regarding the warding off of *kṛtyā* (malevolent spells), the turning back of *kṛtyā* raised by others, and the non-arising of *kṛtyā*—the remaining sense being for the purpose of self-protection. "In this manner" refers to the aforementioned subjects. Having established this wheel (*cakrāra*), the planets, constellations, and so forth proceed; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the zodiac signs (*rāśi*) and other such matters. This is what is meant:

The stellar sphere (jyotiścakra) consists of twelve zodiac signs, each composed of its respective sign, decan (drekkāṇa), and so forth; likewise, each of those individual wheels consists of twelve zodiac signs, each composed of three spokes (āra).
Therefore, just as in the stellar sphere consisting of twelve zodiac signs, the planets, constellations, and so on [move] from time to time...

In that same way, for the sake of accomplishing one's desires, for the warding off of malevolent rites (*kṛtyā*), and for the prevention of the arising of such rites— it is thus the bestower of the accomplishment of all aims. (51)
Relying upon this wheel-spoke, the planets, constellations, and so forth proceed;
and the earth is seen as having the form of the arrangement of this wheel-spoke. (52)
Therefore, all this is composed of that; and by worshipping Him, all desires are fulfilled through worship according to the tradition. (53)
One should first practice the sequence according to the arrival of time, and then resort to another sequence;
during the dark fortnights and the bright fortnights, one should follow the sequence as it has been stated exclusively.
This same sequence applies to recitation, satiation, fire-oblation, worship, and ritual bathing;
having understood this, one should perform [the rites], for otherwise it would bring about misfortune. (55)

Because these [wheels] consist of the circle of luminaries (*jyotiścakra*), within each and every one of these wheels, the planets, lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*), and so forth—which are composed of the letters of the *mātṛkā*—proceed according to the sequence of the specific years of their respective ages (*yuga*).
This is the "earth" (*bhūmi*). Because the wheel of the earth consists of the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*), [it proceeds] from the east...

This means that, according to the sequence already established, even that [perceptible world] becomes identical with each respective *cakra*. All that is visible consists of this—that is, it consists of the *mātṛkā-cakra*. It was stated previously that this occurs through the worship (*bhajana*) of any one of the aforementioned *cakras*. Worship must be performed by means of the attainment of perfection (*sampad*).
The meaning is that the fault of tautology does not occur. || 53 ||

With these two verses beginning with *kālaprāptā* and ending with *āvahet*, he teaches the specific manner of practicing those vidyās according to the different times of the moon’s waning and waxing, their necessity, and the transgression incurred by failing to perform them. In that regard:

The sequence of the time-attained order refers to the specific sequence of the various types of years attained in each respective year, among the distinctions of methods such as *anuloma* and *pratiloma* shown in the previously mentioned wheel of years; the "other sequence" refers to that which is prescribed for those respective rites.
The sequence has been stated in its entirety; that is, the sequence corresponding to each specific rite, excluding those sequences obtained according to the particular time [of performance].

What is meant is this: when commencing optional rites (*kāmyakarman*) or the regular daily worship (*nityopāsanā*) during the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), one should first rotate the sequence shown by the wheel consisting of those respective years.

Thereafter, one should follow the sequence prescribed for each respective rite. However, during the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), one should follow only the sequence appropriate for that specific rite. Thus, this distinction between the dark and bright fortnights has been demonstrated. This sequence, as shown by the distinction between the two fortnights, is to be observed.

The remainder [of the sentence] is "whether it be a compulsory rite (nityakarman) or a rite performed for a specific desire (kāmyakarman). Otherwise, [the fault lies] in not performing it in that manner. 55.
In the accomplishment of tasks, in the defeat of enemies, and in subjugation, it is prescribed as contrary [to the usual rule]; otherwise, it is declared to be appropriate at all times. (56)
For subjugation and protection, the two pairs of enclosures (sampuṭa) are used in sequence;
for the conquest of diseases and enemies, they are indeed prescribed in reverse order.
And it is prescribed for the acquisition of cattle, land, gold, vehicles, and so forth;
it is scattered [applied] in rites of eradication (uccāṭana), while one should worship according to the sequence for the sake of pacification (śānti) among those [other rites]. (58)
Gods and asuras alike bow down to one who is proficient in this ritual procedure;
against such a person, afflictions caused by enemies, such as malevolent spells (kṛtyā) and the like, do not even appear before him.
On the contrary, they turn back and surely destroy the doer;
wherever he dwells, that place is a sacred field, a grove of asceticism.

With these three verses beginning with *kṛtyotpattau* and ending with *yajet*, he teaches the results— consisting of the arising of hostile acts, the defeat of enemies, and so forth— as well as the ritual prescriptions and expiations for those born through inverse (*pratiloma*) and natural (*anuloma*) unions. Among these, that which is obtained by time...

In all the rites to be described hereafter, there are those suitable for inauspicious acts such as *pratiloma* (reverse order) and others, as well as those suitable for auspicious acts such as *anuloma* (direct order). What is meant is this: by resorting to the sequence beginning with *pratiloma* and so forth, which bestows inauspiciousness at the time of the commencement of an action and so on, one engages in auspicious acts.

When various actions are being performed, because one resorts to them according to the sequence appropriate to their respective times as things that must necessarily be done, they do not become sources of inauspiciousness.
Thus, even in the case of inauspicious rites, by resorting to the sequence that yields auspicious results— such as the *anuloma* order and so forth— [the same applies].

When [the rites] are being performed, because they are undertaken as necessary duties according to the sequence appropriate to the time, one does not become a destroyer of the fruits of those respective inauspicious [results]. There are two types of *saṃpuṭa* (enclosures), distinguished by the external and internal [positions] of vowels and consonants; in the case of reversal (*parāvṛtti*), there is likewise a distinction as before.

The word "ca" (and) serves to conjoin the two previously mentioned sequences of reversal; the ellipsis is "the sequence of the two types of reversed order. "Intermingled" is as before, according to its divisions. Within those aforementioned inauspicious [sequences], even when employed by others, the sequence is of the nature of *anuloma* (direct order).

Regarding the sequence of constant worship within these eight divisions, such as the *anuloma* and others, there is a single type of division involving vowels and consonants, beginning with *anulomānuloma*. This certainly bestows swift results in those respective rites and is unfailing. This will be explained further later in this chapter.
By the passage beginning with "all scattered," etc., the infallibility of the scattered and non-scattered wheel is established, both through reasoning and from tradition. || 58 ||

With these two verses beginning with *etad* and ending with *tapovanam*, [it is said]: for one who is proficient in these sciences, [the places are] a cremation ground, a mountain, a deserted forest, or a place of minor affliction. (p. 474)
When the king of machines is established, that shall become a great realm.
O Goddess, by establishing the Sarvavyākīrṇacakra, Amarāvatī was utterly destroyed;
and furthermore, it is no longer protected even by me.
Having engraved [the inscription] on a stone slab, a copper plate, or one made of silver or gold,
