one should bury it in the ground within villages, kingdoms, cities, and so forth.
Having constructed a temple there and installed the discus within it, one should fashion the image in the center of its pericarp for the sake of achieving the deity's presence.

He teaches the majesty [of the field]. Therein, the practitioner is one who is proficient. "In that practitioner" means in that person who is the agent or the performer. "This practitioner" refers to him; the word "this" (eṣaḥ) is connected here with the word "that" (asau). "Field" means a sacred field (puṇyakṣetra). || 60 ||

With the verse beginning with "In the cremation ground" (*śmaśāne*), he teaches the method for constructing villages, cities, towns, and so forth, in empty lands such as cremation grounds and the like. In that regard, concerning the "King of Machines" (*yantrarāja*) in a region abounding in minor afflictions— such as the ashes of time and other such small-scale calamities—

In the wheel known as Anulomānuloma, it possesses the status of the "king of machines" because it is the cause of all other machines. The word "that" (tat) is an adjective qualifying the region; the meaning is that such a place constitutes a *janapada* (province). || 61 ||

With the verse beginning "sarvavyākīrṇa," he teaches the majesty of the wheel of eradication (*uccāṭana*). In that context, by means of the "all-dispersed" (*sarvavyākīrṇa*) wheel—whether through vowels and consonants or through the distinctions of outer and inner—there are four wheels which are the objects of all words; they are eradicated.
"The entire race of gods has been uprooted by me, the Lord"—the word "even" (api) implies: how much more so by those of little power and the like. || 62 ||

With these five verses beginning with "On a stone" (*śilāyām*) and ending with "bestowing success" (*siddhidāyakam*), he teaches the procedure for installing that wheel in villages and other locations for the sake of protection, as well as the attainment of the presence of all deities through the installation of that wheel. In that regard:
"In the alternative" (*vakalpe*): the remainder is that one should draw the wheel called *anulomānuloma*. "One should bury it" (*nikhanet*):

the remainder is that this is for the sake of protection, according to the method to be described by the three verses beginning with the sixty-fifth verse of this chapter, starting with the words "in villages and so forth" (*grāmādau*). Regarding the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in cities and so forth" (*purādiṣu*), [the list continues].

The domain [consists of] cities, market towns, ports, and so forth. There, in the temple, one should install the *cakra*—meaning the *mātṛkā-cakra*, which consists of both direct and reverse orders—at the single location where the deity is to be installed, in the manner that will be described. Of that *cakra*:
The phrase "in the center of the pericarp" is the ellipsis to be supplied. One should fashion—that is, install—the image (*vera*) of one's chosen deity; this is the meaning.
For the sake of achieving the presence (*sannidhya*) [of the deity], [one should do so] there in the center and also in the eight directions for the protection of the village and so forth. (p. 475)
Having dug a pit, they then firmly constructed it with stones.
Then, having invoked and worshipped [the deity], one should establish [it] with the root-mantra (mūlavidyā);
then, having covered it with stone, one should make the pedestal (pīṭha) firm upon it.
One should worship [it] constantly with perfumes, flowers, incense, and so forth, equally;
one should perform this at the three junctions of the day, for otherwise it does not bestow success.

The word "of the deity" is to be understood as the ellipsis. This is what is meant: having constructed a temple for the chosen deity in the desired location among the aforementioned sites, one should dig a single pit in the center of the place where the deity is to be installed, and having secured it with stones in the manner to be described, therein—

The wheel consisting of the *anuloma* and *anulomānuloma* [mantras], as previously described, should be engraved upon the aforementioned substrates such as stone; having performed the installation of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other rites as before,
one should establish and worship it, cover it with that stone, and [perform the rite] there, above the location in the center of the pericarp (*karṇikā*).
By means of the installation of the respective deities' bodies (*vera*), the accomplishment of the presence (*sānnidhya*) of those respective deities within those bodies is achieved.

Regarding the protection of the village and so forth previously introduced, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) is as before. In that [context], in the middle of all of them—that is, in the center—one should dig a pit (*avaṭa*). The words "in the middle and in each direction" are to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). Within those [pits]...
"In the pits"—the remainder of the sense is "in their respective inner spaces.

"Having invoked"—the remainder is "the desired Nityā into the center of the pericarp of the aforementioned wheel. "Having worshipped"—the meaning is "according to the sequence for the daily worship of that Nityā and according to the sequence of the Vidyā residing in that wheel. "Internally" [is the end of the sentence].

The phrase "of those fashioned from stone" is to be understood as the ellipsis [for the pedestals]. One should install the established *cakra* belonging to the root-vidyā of one's chosen *Nityā*. That *cakra* situated within the pit is the pedestal (*pīṭha*), constructed from stone and other materials, having the form of a base (*dhiṣṭya*). It is stable upon the covered surface above.

Because it is fashioned from stone and other materials, one should worship the Nityā, who has been invoked into the wheel (cakra), within that consecrated site (dhiṣṭhya) in the manner described—that is, with perfumes and so forth. Otherwise means apart from the stated procedure.
This is what is meant: in the protection of the dwellings of villages, cities, towns, hamlets, market towns, ports, and so on.
In each of those respective sites, having dug nine pits— eight in the cardinal directions and one in the very center— within these nine locations, and having filled their interiors with stones,
[one should perform the rite] in one of the aforementioned bases, consisting of nine bases in a manner that is favorable to both.
Alternatively, having engraved nine wheels in the form of a double-enclosure (*ubhayasampuṭa*), and having performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other rites upon it,
one should invoke the desired *Nityā* and worship her according to the sequence of that particular *Nityā*;
then, worshipping her with the various divisions of the wheels (*cakrabheda*) and with the *Kālanityās*, one should proceed thus for three days without fail.
Having worshipped each of those nine circles individually and established them one by one within each pit, having covered the top of each pit with stone slabs,
[he should construct] nine very firm pedestals in the form of stones and so forth upon those respective levels.
The sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) prescribed for that time are all [required] for the nine types of fire-offerings (homa).
The priests (hotṛs) should be rewarded with fees consisting of garments, land, ornaments, female slaves, cattle, and wealth.
Whatever one desires, whether it be difficult or easy to accomplish, one who is steadfast should achieve it through recitation, libations, fire-offerings, or sprinklings. (69)
No knowledge like these exists anywhere in the worlds;
therefore, one should accomplish all that is desired by means of them.
By reciting it fifty times, endowed with devotion to the Vidyā,
one is released from shackles, hardships, and most terrible enmities with enemies.
By reciting it a hundred times, women endowed with various powers of knowledge—even those who are barren—obtain sons possessed of all excellent qualities. (72)

Having established the *dhiṣṭyas* here and there, by performing worship at each *dhiṣṭya* every day according to the prescribed sequence during the three junctions of the day, the accomplishment of protection for the aforementioned villages and other places is achieved. There exists no other circle (*cakra*) equal to this. || 67 ||

With the verse beginning with *tatkāla*, he teaches the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) and the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the officiant within the nine types of sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) shown according to the sequence of pervasion in the previously mentioned wheel. Among those, there are nine pits described for that specific time.

The meaning is that one should construct nine wheels in the shape of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), as prescribed for each respective year, beginning with the conduct (vṛtta) and so forth. "In all respects" means in all obligatory (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and optional (kāmya) rites.
"With wealth consisting of cattle" means with cows and with riches. This is what is intended: [these should be performed] in numbers equal to those of the full mandalas.
In the sixty-four years of the *yuga*,

nine fire-pits (*kuṇḍas*) should be constructed according to the sequence to be described in the chapter on fire-pits, having the shapes of the previously mentioned thirty-six types beginning with the *vṛtta* (circular) and the nine types beginning with the *astra* (bow-shaped).
Having fashioned [the altar] excluding the placement of letters for the second, third, and subsequent diagrams,

and having performed the fire-oblation (homa) in all rites within the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) appropriate for each respective year, one should give the prescribed materials as the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the officiating priests (hotṛ). || 68 ||

With the two verses beginning with "Whatever" (*yadyat*) and ending with "desired" (*īpsitam*), he teaches the attainment of one's desired goals and the majesty of the knowledge (*vidyā-vaibhava*) through the fivefold worship by means of those aforementioned sciences. In that regard, each respective desired object is difficult to accomplish and exceedingly great.

"Even that which is to be accomplished with effort"—the word "tu" (but/then) is used for emphasis; "vā" (or) is used as a conjunction. "Firm" means one whose mind is certain that [it] will surely bear fruit. "By these sciences" means by these aforementioned fivefold means of accomplishment. || 71 ||
With these seven and a half verses beginning with "pañcāśat" and ending with "avāpnuyāt," one should, out of devotion, repeat those vidyās one hundred and fifty times. (p.

They obtain a wife endowed with virtues, beauty, and other qualities without any effort.
By repeating this [mantra] that many times, young women obtain a husband endowed with all virtues;
and, possessed of wealth, they prosper through sons, grandsons, and other descendants.
Having performed them two hundred times, one is certainly released from poverty;
with three hundred, one becomes rich in land and grain, and with four hundred, one becomes wealthy.
With five hundred [beings] one becomes a chief (bhūpa), with six hundred a king (nṛpa);
but with seven hundred, the goddess Ramā does not abandon his lineage.
With eight hundred of these [arts], all kings are his servants;
with nine hundred, however, he is Cupid among women. (77)
Having thus recited nine hundred times, one shall obtain all desires.
O beautiful one, now hear the ancillary limbs of these eternal Vidyās. 78.

It teaches that by increasing the number of repetitions from fifty times up to nine hundred times, there is a corresponding increase in the fruit. In this context, the word division is "vidyā" (the vidyā-mantra). "By hardships and calamities" refers to the various manifestations of power (*vaibhava*) as previously described, due to the diversity of the fruits. [This is done] one hundred and fifty times.
The meaning is "one hundred and fifty times.

In the phrase "qualities, form, and so forth" (*guṇarūpādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to noble lineage and the like. The ellipsis is "the practitioners obtain" (*vindanti labhante sādhakāḥ*). "That many" means one hundred and fifty times. "Maidens" (*kanyāḥ*)... [is the subject].

The nominative plural. *Vā* means "in combination. *Edhante* means "they increase. "Endowed with prosperity"—this is an adjective qualifying "maidens" (*kanyā*). Those [maidens] are the sciences (*vidyā*).
"Due to poverty," meaning due to having nothing and due to dissatisfaction. "Three hundred times. And by four...
The construction is with "four hundred" (śataiścaturbhiḥ). The particle *tu* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*), as before; the remainder [of the verse] follows the previous pattern.

With "five hundred," however, the construction and the remainder are as previously explained. "Bhūpaḥ" means a lord of the earth; with "six hundred," the remainder is as before. "Nṛpaḥ" refers to a king who is preeminent due to his servants, female slaves, attendants, and so forth. The particle *tu* [is used here as well].

And the remainder is as before. Of this practitioner; "tu" (but) is as before, and the remainder is as before. Of these vidyās; the kings are those previously mentioned. Of this practitioner; this practitioner; by the words "in this manner," etc., it is stated that [this should be done] by repeating nine hundred times in this section.
It has been stated that other rare and desired [attainments] are accomplished. || 78 ||
By repeating [the mantra] twice, one should perform the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with those syllables on the hands and limbs;
having performed the placement (nyāsa), one should recite the vidyā ending with the Mātṛkā, one by one.
One should visualize them as red, clad in red garments, adorned with red ornaments, garlands, and unguents, and holding nooses, goads, sugarcane bows, and flower-arrows.
Then, one should visualize the powers of the five squares as being similar to them;
having constructed two squares adorned with two doors. (81)

With the first half-verse beginning with *āsām* and ending with *ekaśaḥ*, he teaches the threefold nyāsa and other rites for the worship of each of all those vidyās mentioned therein. Therein, *sundari* is an address to the Goddess. By the repetition [of the term],...

By means of a double utterance; this is a qualification of the word "those syllables" (arṇaiḥ). The meaning is that one should perform the placement of the Mātṛkā, conjoined with the six limbs, according to the sequence taught in the chapter on Kulasundarī. "One by one" (ekaśaḥ) means each individual Vidyā. This is what is being said regarding these aforementioned [Vidyās]:

Among the Kāla-, Nityā-, and Vidyā-mantras, having first performed the placement of the Mātṛkā along with its six ancillaries according to the method described in the *Kulasundarīpaṭala*, one should subsequently apply the heart-mantra with the first syllable of each respective three-syllabled mantra, and the head-mantra with the second syllable.

With the third [syllable], the *śikhā*; again, with the first syllable of that respective *vidyā*, the *kavaca*; with the second syllable, the *netra*; and with the third, the *astra*. Having performed the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) together with the [respective] *jātis* by repeating these three syllables of the *vidyā* twice, preceded by the ritual placement on the hands (*karanyāsa*), and having likewise performed the pervasive placement (*vyāpaka*), [one should proceed].
"One should recite that vidyā. Its mantras are as follows: *aṃ* hṛdayāya namaḥ; *āṃ* śirase svāhā;
*īṃ* śikhāyai vaṣaṭ; *aṃ* kavacāya huṃ; *āṃ* netratrayāya vauṣaṭ; *īṃ* astrāya phaṭ. In this same manner, one should apply [these] to other vidyās as well. Of these vidyās...

Regarding worship in a collective manner, the tradition is that one should recite [the mantra] after having performed the placement (nyāsa) of the Mātṛkā preceded by one's own six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga), as previously described. Furthermore, regarding worship together with any one of the sixteen Nityā-vidyās, the tradition is that one should recite it preceded by the set of nyāsas prescribed for that specific Nityā-vidyā. || 79 ||
With the half-verse beginning with "raktā" and ending with "smaret," he teaches the visualization (*dhyāna*) of all those Vidyā-deities together with their surrounding Śaktis.
In that regard, the sequence of weapons should be understood as proceeding from the top downwards, and then from left to right.
The traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) is that by meditating on their forms as identical to those of the meditation on Lalitā—who consists of the sixteen *Nityās*—one achieves identity with them;
they are "similar to her," meaning similar to the root deity (*mūladevatā*) in terms of color and other attributes, as is understood from the context. || 80 ||
One should worship her in the center of an eight-petaled lotus within the ninefold source (navayoni);
the enclosure of the limbs (aṅgāvṛti) is in the central source, while the enclosure of the weapons (āyudhāvṛti) is in between.
Behind [the central deity], one should worship the lineage of gurus, and in the eight corners in due order; likewise, on the outer petals, one should worship with the letters in reverse order.
One should worship the powers of Brāhmī and the others outside of that, within two squares, accompanied by the Rūpiṇī-śaktis joined with the seven-syllabled Māyā-mantra.

With the four verses beginning with "caturasradvayam" and ending with "smaran dhiyā," [the author] describes the general arrangement of the lines in the form of the mandala for the daily worship of those deities, which will be explained in detail immediately hereafter.
In each of those various eternal worship-mandalas (*nityapūjācakra*),
he teaches the procedure for the sequence of worship for the respective deities. Therein,
two squares are arranged with an inner and outer division, adorned with two doors.
The words "in the eastern and western directions" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. "In the middle" refers to the interior of the square;
the word "and" (ca) in the phrase "and in the nine-yoni" draws forward the word "in the middle" from the preceding context. Therefore, it means:
in the nine-yoni drawn within the pericarp (karṇikā) of the center of that eight-petaled lotus. "Tāḥ" refers to those deities.

In the middle womb (*madhyayoni*), within the central triangle of the nine-womb wheel (*navayonicakra*) according to the previously mentioned sequence starting from the exterior; "inside" means all around the outside of the middle womb as before; "behind" means behind the central deity; the word "and" (*ca*) is for conjunction, referring to the sequence of writing the syllables that will be described below; likewise.
In the manner that will be described; "in reverse order" means counter-clockwise, starting from the tip;

"accompanied by the Rūpiṇī-śakti" means together with the five-syllable mantra "Rūpiṇī-śakti"; "Māyā" is Hṛllekhā, the seven-syllable [mantra] as before. This is what is meant: having first uttered Hṛllekhā...

Then, having uttered each one of the forms of that unmanifest syllable (avyākṣara) as differentiated by the sixteen vowels in their proper sequence, and subsequently having uttered the five syllables "rūpiṇī śakti," one should then join the seven-syllable mantra. Thus, all the mantras consist of fourteen syllables.

The mantras are as follows: *hrīṃ arūpiṇīśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, *hrīṃ ārūpiṇīśaktipādukāṃ pūjayāmi*, and so forth; likewise, as before, their mantras are *hrīṃ brahmāṇīpādukāṃ pūjayāmi* and so forth. Here, in the worship circle (*pūjācakra*).

The method for arranging the layout of the lines common to all [mandalas] is as follows: having first produced two squares by dividing them into inner and outer sections, one should fashion an eight-petaled lotus in their center, and within its pericarp a ninefold source (*navayoni*) according to the procedure described in the *Kulasundarīpaṭala*; then, therein...

In this chapter, having written the syllables according to the sequence to be described starting from the subsequent verse, one should worship each of them there in the prescribed order. And one should perform the offering of the *bali*; the word "at the end of the worship" is the ellipsis. By the word "and" (*ca*), it is indicated that [this should be done] with the sixteen-syllable mantra common to all in this tantra.
This summarizes the meaning that one should offer the *bali* at the beginning of the worship and so forth:
"And let him perform the offering of the *bali* for these [deities] with Kurukullā alone, using the seven-syllable mantra, while mentally recollecting her in the form described. (85)
Having written the Vidyā by name in the center, and [the syllables] in pairs on the outer [petals],
one should write the syllable in the middle differentiated by the vowels, and [the syllable] with Māyā on the [three] corners.

Having written the *haṃsela* syllables in a garland starting from the southwest (Nirṛti) and proceeding in reverse order, there should be twelve [syllables] each, ending with the heart-syllable (*hṛt*), beginning with the letter *va*. 87.

By means of the seven-syllabled mantra of Kurukullā, which is the first vidyā, alone— being devoid of the second and third [mantras]— one should [visualize her] in the form described, that is, in the form stated in the meditation (dhyāna) of that chapter. For here, among these Kālanityās, there is the prescription of two specific offerings (bali) not common to the sixteen Nityās.
The meaning understood from the mouth of the venerable teacher (Ārādhyapāda) is that he demonstrates identity with them. || 85 ||

With these three verses beginning with "vilikhya" and ending with "samudvaset," [the author] describes the differentiation of the forms of those vidyās through the placement of the syllables of the vidyā— which serves as a specific feature introduced previously— within the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) in the form of lines that was previously mentioned as common to all.

It teaches their respective applications and the completion of the worship. In that context, "with the name" refers to the *vidyā* [mantra] of the triad beginning with the *sādhya*; "together with" is the ellipsis. In the wheel of daily worship (*nityapūjācakra*), one should employ whichever *vidyā* is appropriate among those of the *Kālanityās*. Indeed, the very act of writing the *vidyā* constitutes the daily worship wheel.
It is stated that [the mantra] should be written. "In the middle" means within the central *yoni* among the nine *yoni*s;
"externally" refers to the eight pairs—that is, in the eight triangles situated outside the central *yoni* and in the eight petals situated outside of those. The syllable in their center is...

Having written the central syllable of the *vidyā* situated within the respective central *yoni*, differentiated by the vowels as before and modified by the sixteen vowels, [one proceeds] from the top corner clockwise; on the corners— specifically on the three corners located within the space between the circle and the square— one places the *grāsa*, the letter *ha*, by means of *māyā* and *haṃsa*.

The syllables *la*, *kṣa*, and *hṛllekhā* [are to be written] starting from the southwest (*nirṛti*) in reverse order; this phrase connects with both the preceding and the following [clauses] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye. In that regard, in the case of connection with the preceding, one should write the aforementioned group of four beginning with the letter *ha* respectively in the corners of Nirṛti, Agni, Īśa, and Vāyu. In the case of connection with the following...

The syllables to be described should be written in the manner to be described within the square grid (*caturasravīkṣyā*) starting from Nairṛti and proceeding inward in reverse order. The syllable beginning with "vāta" (the letter *a*) and ending with "heart" (*hṛt*, the letter *s*) should be [placed there]. "Beginning with vāta" means beginning with the vowel *a*;
"syllable" (*arṇa*) here refers to the letters; "ending with heart" means ending with the letter *s*. This is the meaning.
In the *mātṛkā*, the remainder consists of the three syllables beginning with *haṃ* that were previously written;
the use of the neuter form "arṇam" and the change in grammatical number are due to its divine nature.
[One should contemplate] the letters from *a* to *sa* in groups of twelve each.
The meaning is that one should write twelve syllables in each row within the forty-eight square grids. O Īśvarī, by means of those [mantras] mentioned in the second chapter, beginning with Gaṇeśa,
one shall accomplish every desired object consisting of the six rites.
Having praised them with those twelve verses, one should dwell within them in one's own heart.
When the self-controlled practitioner, situated in the center of these wheels, recites the vidyā, at that very moment he will attain equality with the circle of deities. || 89 ||
Having placed the radiant Śrīcakra in the center of the great wheel,
one should invoke the Goddess right there and worship her for the attainment of all perfections.
"In one's own heart" means in the heart. "Those" refers to the root deities and the retinue deities. This is what is meant:

in the previously mentioned *nityapūjācakra*, which consists of lines common to all, one should [worship] whichever one among the *kālanityā* vidyās resides in the center of the *yoni* located in the middle of the nine *yoni*s.
Having inscribed [the mantra] during daily worship, and having inscribed it during rites for specific desires joined with the triad of names beginning with the *sādhya*,

one should place the sixteen forms derived from the vowels of the middle syllable of that vidyā within the eight corners of the nine-yoni wheel and upon its eight petals, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise.

Having drawn [the diagram] in due order, one should write the forty-eight syllables from *a* to *sa* in each direction, moving clockwise within the corridor between the two outer squares, starting from the southwest (*nirṛti*) and ending there.

Having drawn twelve sets of twelve in sequence, and having written the three remaining letters beginning with *ha*— from the southwest (*nirṛti*) to the northeast (*īśāna*)— within the spaces between the lotus, the outer enclosure, and the inner square, and having also written the *hṛllekhā* in the northwest corner;

Having invoked her in the manner previously described, meditated upon her, worshipped her, and praised her with the *Dvādaśaślokī*, one should dissolve her, along with her retinue, into one's own heart. In this way, even in rites performed for specific desires (*kāmyakarman*), the attainment of those respective fruits occurs through such worship. In that regard, there is a distinction: the writing of the three names in the center together with the *vidyā*. By means of that—
The wheels are as many in number as the syllables produced by the five-syllable phrase "Caṇḍī Sunetrā. || 88 ||

With the verse beginning with "etāsām" (of these), he teaches the specific fruits resulting from specific modes of worship within the wheels of the Kālanityās, which have been stated in the aforementioned number. Therein, "vidyām" refers to the knowledge of the sixteen Nityās and the Kālanityās. "Asya" refers to this practitioner. This is what is meant:

In the worship of the sixteen *nityā* vidyās, as well as in the worship of the specific *nityā* assigned to each particular day, one should perform the recitation (*japa*) while situated within the wheel (*cakra*) of the *nityā* for that specific time. In the worship of any one of the *kāla-nityā* vidyās, one should always perform the recitation while situated precisely in the center of that wheel.

One should recite while abiding in the worship of the collection of the sixteen eternal [deities] within the assembly of the eternal ignorance of time, or in the worship of the sixteen eternal [deities] within whichever specific wheel is attained during that particular year, or in the wheels of direct and reverse order, or in the circular wheel of direct and reverse order which is the cause of all wheels of time. By that—
"The accomplishment of the stated fruit. || 89 ||
Having acted thus and having established [the deity], one should worship it with due ritual;
thereby, the most wondrous accomplishments of the Command manifest in the world. || 91 ||
Having done so, one should place there a beautiful young woman, red in complexion and clad in red garments, in the midst of that [circle], and worship her according to the prescribed rites.
One should perform this every year when the sun and the moon are situated in Pisces on the full-moon day;
by that, the Goddess becomes pleased and grants one's desires.
With these four verses beginning with "Of the great wheel" (*mahācakrasya*) and ending with "would come to be" (*bhavet*),

he teaches the worship-circle of Lalitā within the aforementioned great wheel, the worship thereof, its fruit, and the specific fruits resulting from specific modes of worship at specific times in that very place. Among those, [the passage concerning] the great wheel...
Of the wheels (*cakra*) consisting of the previously mentioned pairs of years of the full mandala— the first form of which consists of clockwise and counter-clockwise circles,
or which is attained in its respective year— the Śrīcakra, the wheel for the worship of Lalitā, [is described] in the thirty-third [chapter].

As will be described in the [next] chapter: "Radiant" means having a clearly manifest form; by that, it is established that the diameter of the pericarp of the Great Wheel (mahācakra) has expanded—this is the traditional teaching (sampradāya). Therein, in the center of the Śrīcakra situated in the middle of the Great Wheel. This is what is meant: among the previously mentioned wheels.

Having prepared either a wheel (cakra) corresponding to the specific year attained, which is circular in form consisting solely of *anuloma-anuloma* [arrangements], or one that provides the expansion for the pericarp (*karṇikā*) suitable for the construction of the *Lalitā-cakra*, and having fashioned within that pericarp the *Śrī-cakra* for the worship of Lalitā, endowed with the characteristics to be described, one performs the worship of the Goddess therein.

"Attainment of all desired goals" means that the Śrīcakra, situated within the aforementioned form, is the Great Cakra (Mahācakra). Having prepared it according to the rule— the procedure described in the second chapter— upon any one of the substrates such as gems, the three metals, or glass, one should worship the Goddess together with her retinue.

The remainder [of the commentary] is as follows: "In which place" means in whatever location; "in that place" refers to the state of the mobile and immobile world being subject to one's command (*ājñāsiddhi*). Having done so, as before, the meaning is that one should construct the Śrīcakra situated in the center of the Mahācakra. In the middle of that [is] what resides within the Mahācakra.

In the center of the *śrīcakra*, within the *yoni*; by the "stages" (*krama*), meaning by the stages of the worship of Lalitānityā; when the sun is situated in Pisces, during the solar month of Phālguna, on the moon being full—that is, on the full-moon day (*paurṇamāsī*);
"tu" is used for emphasis; by that worship, the Goddess Lalitā [is pleased]. This is what is meant by what was stated above.

In the month of Phālguna, on the full moon day, having seated within the *yoni* at the center of the *Śrīcakra*— which is situated in the middle of the aforementioned great *cakra* fashioned with vermilion and other substances— a beautiful young woman adorned with garments and ornaments of the colors prescribed for her; in her...

Having invoked the Supreme Goddess, one should worship her every year according to the sequence of the daily rite; then the Goddess Lalitā, being pleased, shall become the bestower of desired boons. || 93 ||
A claw, a razor, a sword, a bow, a trident, a mace, arrows, or any other weapon whatsoever—all these are situated within the center of the great wheel. (94)
Having performed worship with mantras and having first offered the *sādhya-yoni-bali*, and having slain the enemies in battle by means of those [mantras], one shall attain victory. || 95 ||
Whether recited daily, by the week, by the fortnight, by the month, or for thirty-six days—
reciting them even for a single time, those vidyās become eternal in nature.

With the two verses beginning with *nakharam* and ending with *āpnuyāt*, [the author] teaches that victory in battle is attained by worshipping the weapons within the centers of that great wheel (*mahācakra*). Therein, *nakhara* refers to a sword, *dhenu* to another [weapon], and *kunta-prāśa-laguḍa-ādi* to a spear, a javelin, a club, and so forth. Of the great wheel...

In the wheels (*cakra*s) composed by Śrī Cakravartin, which consist of the aforementioned years, there is a tetrad consisting of "return and non-return" (*parāvṛtta-aparāvṛtta*) attained in each respective year. [The phrase] "having placed it in the middle" is to be construed with the final quarter-verse of the preceding *śloka*. [This is done] by means of the *vidyā*s obtained through the sequence of those wheels.

The phrase "with those that are eternal in time" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "The womb of the sādhya" means the womb previously mentioned for the lunar mansion of the sādhya. "In front" (puraḥ) means before the deity who has been invoked. "Having given," the ellipsis is "he cuts as before. "By them" means by those weapons residing in the wheel which have the nature of the deities. This is what is meant: among those [weapons] previously mentioned...
In the *mātṛkā* wheels of the various years, or when that specific year arrives,

in any one of the thirty-six wheels consisting of the *jaya*, *prokta*, *parāvṛtta*, and *parāvṛttātman* types, or in a wheel whose form is a rotation consisting solely of *anuloma* and *anuloma*, [one should perform] all [the rites], beginning with those of the nails (*nakha*).

Having placed the weapons upon them, having invoked the eternal Kālanityā who is desired together with her retinue and worshipped her according to their respective sequences, and having worshipped the Kālanityās in the form of the sequences obtained from those respective wheels,
one should [worship] the Yoni as described by the characteristics and the manner prescribed for the asterism of the enemy to be overcome.
Having offered the *bali* sacrifice before the deity in the form of that weapon while reciting the prescribed *balimantra*,

and having performed this for no fewer than seven days in consideration of the relative strength or weakness of the enemy to be subdued, one slays all enemies in battle through those various deities and attains victory. || 95 ||
With these three verses beginning with *dinataḥ* and ending with *kalpyate*,

[the author] teaches the specific fruits resulting from the repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the previously mentioned mass of mantras (*vidyārāśi*) at specific times, as well as the fact that the Lalitā-vidyā possesses an authentic tradition (*satsampradāya*) through its identity with all these mantras. Among those, regarding *dinataḥ*:

The construction here is with the word "once" (vāramekam). The meaning is that one should recite the previously mentioned vidyās once every day. In this way, by means of the days of the week, fortnights, months, and thirty-six days, it means to perform each one once. Regarding the rotation of the syllables of the weekdays, first [the recitation occurs] on Sunday (Bhāskara-vāra).

The vidyās arising from the groups [of letters] beginning with Vaśinī and Kāmeśvarī; and in the other six [groups], at each turn, the vidyās arising from the six groups of the Mātṛkā beginning with Modinī (p. 484). [These grant] longevity, health, sovereignty, victory, and the desired object, respectively.
They obtain those [mantras] by which one becomes possessed of the tradition. || 97 ||
If recitation, fire-offerings, worship, and so forth are performed outside of the proper tradition, they become perfectly conducive to the [right] tradition in a future birth. (98)
In the sequence of recitation, satiation, fire-offering, and worship, one should devote oneself to these Vidyās;
by that, because the syllables have been mastered, the mantras are accomplished in their entirety.

One should recite [the mantra] in due order. However, in the case of a single cycle during a fortnight, on the lunar days (tithis) of the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth—which constitute the three full [days]—one should recite the Vidyā arising from four sets of four lines;
on the other [days], one should recite the Vidyā arising from two sets of two lines. This applies to the month consisting of two fortnights.
In a single rotation, when the previously mentioned six groups are complete, one should recite the Vidyās arising from two rows each;

for the other twenty-four lunar days, one should recite the Vidyās arising from one row each—this is the tradition. These are of the nature of the Nityās, consisting of both direct and reverse orders, [granting] longevity and so forth.

The "five fruits" are the respective objects for each of the five previously mentioned modes of recitation (*japa*). "In sequence" means according to the order of non-delayed succession. This connects with the verb "they obtain" in the first half-verse. "Lalitā" refers to the primordial *Nityā*, by whom [the] *Kālanityā* vidyās [are presided over].

It possesses a tradition because it is uninterrupted through the succession of lineages in the form of ages (yuga), cycles (paryāya), days, and ghaṭikās; and these vidyās [are so called] because they pervade the forms of the nine Nāthas.

Through the uninterrupted continuity resulting from the practice of those respective lineages, all of this is characterized by the eternal ignorance of the All. Otherwise, because it would lack a tradition—this is the word-division: *asampradāyatvāt* (due to the absence of a tradition).
Otherwise, in the case of practicing these [teachings] in isolation, there would be a lack of a tradition (*asampradāyatvāt*).
Because it is impossible to worship the pervasive form that constitutes the beginning of the Yugas, and because it is impossible to worship the lineage of the pervasive forms of the Lords;
[the phrase] "done without the tradition" (asampradāyena) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
[This may occur] in another birth, at another time, or among one's sons, grandsons, and so forth. This is what is meant.

Through these vidyās, because they are maintained without interruption by means of the knowledge of the previously mentioned pervasive form (*vyāpti*) of the sixteen Nityā-vidyās beginning with Lalitā,
they constitute a true tradition (*satsampradāya*). [Otherwise], in the absence of worship in the aforementioned manner, [the tradition would not be authentic].

Because it is severed, this [lineage] is devoid of sequence and lacks the order of syllables; however, for a practitioner who has performed worship, there will arise in the course of time a true tradition among his sons, grandsons, and so forth. || 98 ||

With these two verses beginning with "japa" and ending with "śiva," he teaches that for those who practice, the attainment of all mantras and the fruit of liberation (*bhava*) result from the worship of that mass of vidyās. In this context, the phrase "by that worship" refers to the vidyā of Kālanityā; this is the ellipsis to be supplied.
For one who worships them in this world, there is no spiritual practice that is difficult to accomplish; he becomes auspicious and beloved by kings and women alike. (100)
The pervasion consisting of the nature of the Puruṣa has been correctly described; by the refinement of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self. 101.
Thus ends the twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Pervasion of the Mātṛkā," in the *Śrīkādimata*, a tantra of the sixteen *Nityās*.

Because they are established through identity (*tādātmya*), all these—without exception—of these *vidyās* such as Kālanityā and others, are established even by the mere absence of a vessel for the practitioner (*sādhaka*) who performs the worship. For him, nothing is unattainable (*asādhya*) or impossible;
nothing is difficult to accomplish. Śiva is the self whose nature is perfect I-consciousness (*paripūrṇāhaṃtā*). || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary titled *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha— known as *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*— on the complete tantra named the venerable *Kādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The twenty-fifth chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the temporal pervasion of the sixteen eternal Mother-letters (mātṛkā), has been fully examined and completed. 25.

The number of yantras: The yantras, established according to the rules for the arrangement of names and hymns with delightful and accessible meanings, are equal in number to the syllables of the Rudrārṇava, excluding those associated with the Śrīcakra.
Thus, in the twenty-fifth chapter, the explanatory treatises are indicated as numbering five hundred and ninety-seven.
The Twenty-sixth Chapter. Now, O Goddess, listen according to the rule as I shall describe the majesty of the mantras of the sixteen Nityās, by way of the nature of the pervasion of their vidyās.
The arising of the sound (nāda) and its form, and through the attainment of its locus, its state as phonemes (varṇa);
thereafter, certain words and sentences in the form of mantras. || 2 ||
One should likewise know their number, the sequence of the purification of one's own self through the Vidyā,
and [the procedure] by means of the syllables and the couples of the goddess Amṛteśvarī.
In the preceding twenty-fifth chapter,

having taught the pervasion of the sixteen Nityās by the Mother-letters (mātṛkā) and Time (kāla), [the author] next [teaches] the pervasion of the mantras which reveals the majesty of the pervasion of the sixteen Nityās.

He then teaches the *Tanmayāmṛteśvarī-vidyā* and so forth by means of the twenty-sixth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "the moving and the unmoving" (*sacarācaram*). Therein,
he teaches the subject matter of the chapter with four verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "without remainder" (*aśeṣataḥ*).

In this context, the phrase "of the sixteen Nityās" has a double application: namely, in the expressions "by way of the nature of the pervasion of Vidyā" and "by way of [their] majesty. Regarding "by way of the nature of the pervasion of Vidyā," the meaning is: by way of the nature of the pervasion of all mantras through these Vidyās.
The majesty (*vaibhava*) of the sixteen *Nityās*. This is what is meant:

since all mantras are, by their very nature, pervaded by the *vidyās* of the sixteen *Nityās*, I shall describe the majesty of those *Nityās* by way of their pervasive nature. In that regard, [I shall describe] the majesty of the mantras and the arising of the *nāda*.

In this very chapter, that which is to be described—the form of *nāda* consisting of *paśyantī* and so forth—[is attained] through the acquisition of its locus, by means of connection with the locations such as the throat. Of that *nāda*, [it is said] "then by means of phonemes" (*varṇaiḥ*);
the sense is "by means of phonemes. The ellipsis is "sentences by means of words" (*vākyāni padaiḥ*). These are the forms of mantras, the manifestations of mantras.

They exist by means of phonemes (*varṇa*), words (*pada*), and sentences (*vākya*). Among them, some mantra-forms are born from phonemes, numbering five hundred and seventy-six crores; this statement is made because the mantras born from phonemes and so forth are innumerable, and the stated number represents only a portion of them.
The sequence of the purification of one's own self by means of the knowledge (*vidyā*) numbering as many crores as there are [mantras] in that [system];

and the sequence of the purification of one's own self through consecrations and so forth by means of the knowledge desired by oneself—this refers to the Goddess Amṛteśvarī; the word "sequence" (*krama*) is to be construed here with both [phrases].

With those syllables of the color of nectar—along with the couples (mithuna) as mentioned in the *Nityānityā-paṭala*—[one should perform] the pervasion (*vyāpti*) and the ritual applications (*prayoga*) correctly for the sake of attaining one's desired goal. (p. 487)
All this has been explained in its entirety, exactly according to the sequence previously indicated. || 4 ||

Through the impact of the power of one's own will, arising from the nature of the vital breath (prāṇavāyu) at the mūlādhāra, there emerges that which is called the "supreme" (parā), born of sound (nāda). || 5 ||
That very [power], when led upward and expanded within the Svādhiṣṭhāna, attains the name Paśyantī; likewise, it proceeds gradually further upward.
The pervasion of eternal [mantras] is [effected] by those mantras beginning with the *praṇava*, numbering 576,000,000; this is the syntactical connection for the "applications" (*prayoga*). || 4 ||

With the verse beginning with "svātma" (one's own self), he teaches the arising of the *nāda*. In that context, "by the striking of the power of one's own will" means by the striking—that is, the impelling—of the Self in its supreme form (*pararūpa*) by its own power of will consisting of time; [this occurs] from the nature of the vital air (*prāṇavāyu*), namely that which is called *prāṇa*.

Due to the single form of the wind (vāyu) which will be described in the thirty-sixth chapter, there is the "origination of nāda"— meaning the arising of nāda, its first state— within the mūlādhāra of living beings, in the form described in the *Nityānityā-paṭala*. This is the implied meaning.
The nature of *nāda* (sound) is to be understood from the mouth of the venerable teacher (*ārādhyapāda*). This is what is meant:

for all living beings, within the *mūlādhāra*—which exists in the form described in the chapter on the eternal and the non-eternal—the power of *parā*, which is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), through the power of time (*kāla-śakti*) that takes the form of her own will (*svecchā-rūpā*), [manifests].
The state known as Parā, whose nature is the impelled vital breath (prāṇavāyu), arises as the first stage consisting of Nāda and Bindu. || 5 ||

By means of these four verses beginning with "sa eva" and ending with "kṣakābadhi," [the author] first describes the three remaining states— beginning with Paśyantī and ending with Vaikharī— of the *nāda* designated by that name.

He teaches the places of origin for the fifty-one phonemes beginning with *ma* and ending with *kṣa*. Therein, that *nāda* is in the state of *parā*. By means of that power of will (*icchāśakti*), in the *svādhiṣṭhāna* at the base of the genitals; likewise, just as the *nāda* is led upward by the power of one's own will.

In the *svādhiṣṭhāna*, it becomes expanded and is known as *paśyantī*. In the *anāhata* at the region of the heart, it is accompanied by the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*); in that place, there is the perception of the intellect. Just as it is in the *anāhata*, so too, by that same power as previously described, in the *viśuddhi* at the region of the throat, it is designated as *viśuddhi*.
The meaning is "in the region of the throat. Then, after the state of *vaikharī*, [the letters] reside at the root, tip, and back of the tongue;
that is to say, they reside at the root of the tongue, the tip of the tongue, and the back of the tongue. Furthermore, the syllable *la* resides at the back of the tongue.

The phrase "situated" (sthita) is to be understood as the ellipsis following the sequence mentioned. The ablative case in "from the throat and lips" (kaṇṭhauṣṭhāt) is used in the sense of "omission of an action" (lyablope), meaning "situated merely in the throat and lips. The expression "from both teeth and lips" (dantauṣṭhadvayataḥ) means "situated in both the teeth and the lips."
At the *anāhata* [cakra], conjoined with the principle of the intellect (*buddhitattva*), it is called the "Middle" (*madhyamā*).
Likewise, impelled upward from those two, it reaches the region of the throat in the *viśuddhi* [cakra]. (7)
Then, that which is called Vaikharī arises sequentially from the head, throat, palate, lips, and teeth;
likewise from the root, tip, and back of the tongue, and from the tip of the nose. || 8 ||
The phonemes, beginning with 'a' and ending with 'kṣa', have arisen in succession from the throat, palate, lips, and throat-lips, as well as from the teeth and both lips. (9)

The state of being syllables (akṣaratva) is declared for these [phonemes] from 'a' to 'kṣa'. Among them, the vowels (svaras) are independent; by means of them, the consonant (vyañjana) is manifested. || 10 ||

This is what is meant: in the aforementioned locations, the *nāda*— which consists of the four states beginning with *parā*— by its own will, being joined with the aforementioned locations starting from the head,
consists of the fifty-one phonemes beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.
It comes to be. || 9 ||

With these six and a half verses beginning with "From A to Kṣa" (ādikṣānta) and ending with "in that direction" (taddiśā), [the author] establishes the existence of the Mātṛkā as consisting of vowels and consonants, preceded by an etymological definition of the word "syllable" (akṣara).

He teaches the specific forms produced by the mutual union of those two, as well as the infinity and other qualities of the expansion of sound (*śabdaprapañca*). In that regard, the *mātṛkā* consisting of the letters from *a* to *kṣa* is the previously mentioned supreme form (*parārūpa*). Among these syllables, she is independent (*svatantrā*).

Because even in the absence of phonemes (*vyañjana*), the essential nature of the syllables (*akṣara*) is accomplished; by means of those vowels (*svara*), they are manifested because they are made manifest through the completion of their status as syllables. Their forms are those of the syllables of the full mandala as described in the chapter on the *Mātṛkā*. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. By way of number...

The connection [of the sentence] occurs later. By those syllables of the aforementioned number and by those words—[the phrase] "and the mantras" implies "by means of syllables, words, and sentences"—is the meaning. Regarding the expression "due to the distinction between Vedic language and others," the word "others" refers to the *ārṣa* (sage-derived) and other such forms; the connection here is that these are the designators (*vācakāḥ*) of this [reality]. [This applies to] grammar and the other sciences.

[The practitioners] are endowed with the observances (*niyama*) and so forth. Here, the first "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to etymology (*nirukta*) and the like; the second "and so forth" refers to grammar (*vyākaraṇa*), and the rest—the collection of indeterminate technical terms, mantras, and so on. From those syllables, the resulting divisions are produced by taking them in pairs, by threes, and by ones.

The number of full mandalas is indeed 576; these varieties produced by two [syllables] are multiplied by that same number of full mandalas, resulting in 331,776, which is the number generated by the six-syllable mantra. These same varieties produced by three syllables...
The steadfast one remained having multiplied [the number] by the count of the full mandala;

thus, the numbers produced from the nine-syllable sentences become 191,102,976. In the same way, in subsequent cases as well, one should multiply each respective variety by the count of the full mandala.
By multiplying up to the number of the full mandala, infinite divisions arise.
These are formed by the sixteen vowels of that nature [the *mātṛkā*s] combined sequentially with the thirty-six consonants.
They arise through conjunction alone, but their specific forms are determined by number.
By means of those [syllables], there are indeed five hundred and seventy-six words;
and from them, through the various divisions of the Vedic speech, arise both sentences and mantras.
They are the expressers of the manifold universe as well as of the Self;
likewise, they are endowed with the rules and so forth of grammar and other sciences of words. (13)
It is impossible to calculate the number of those forms—consisting of three and so forth—which arise from the mutual combinations of those [elements] taken two at a time. (14)
Because its forms are infinite and inconceivable, they cannot be fully described;
indeed, no one at all is capable of declaring the full majesty of the Word (Śabda). 15.
Nevertheless, O beloved, although you possess such power, I shall tell you something; listen to its direction.
Within each of the nine wheels of Lalitā, there are Śaktis, O dear one. (16)
Those sixty-four crores previously mentioned, when combined, constitute the total number of crores;
I shall now describe those Vidyās in their proper sequence.

The power (*śakti*)—meaning the capacity—of those forms consisting of the mantras of the *siddhayoginīs* produced by the conjunction of the previously mentioned types and the conjunction of letters; "of this" connects with the preceding verse; "by way" means by means of the method. || 15 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with "Lalitā" and ending with "in sequence," he introduces the teaching of the number of deities in the Lalitā-cakra and their corresponding mantras (vidyās).
In that regard, within the nine-fold Lalitā-cakra is the Śrīcakra of the form to be described hereafter.
In each individual wheel— from the Trailokyamohana-cakra up to the Sarvānandamaya-cakra,

including all nine wheels from the outer square to the very center— there are powers (śaktis) known by secret names; those secret-named powers are said to be in the millions (koṭis), as previously described.
Five hundred and seventy-six crores (576,000,000).
From that sequence, from the sequence of the nine wheels; of those aforementioned powers numbering one crore;
sequentially, according to their order. || 17 ||
By means of seventy-six [syllables], there are five hundred initial syllables;
and those same [syllables] shall be the second ones in sequence from the beginning. (18)
And one should join those very same third [syllables] from the beginning in sequence;
by means of those thirty-six syllables ending in *kṣāṃ*, which are equal in number to what has been stated, [the mantras are formed]. (19)

Having taught the mantras consisting of three or four syllables through these three verses beginning with "seventy-six" and ending with "three or four syllables," he teaches the mantras numbering five hundred and seventy-six crores that exist apart from those mantras consisting of a single form. Therein:

"Five hundred and seventy-six are indeed the first letters. This means that the five hundred and seventy-six letters beginning with *a* and *ā* and ending with *kṣaṃ* and *kṣaḥ* are the respective initial letters of the vidyās whose numbers have been generated according to the sequence to be described.
They come to be; and those same [syllables] would again be the second ones in sequence from the beginning. This is what is meant:
those very syllables, numbering five hundred and seventy-six, [serve as the basis] for each of the Guptayoginī-mantras whose number is to be stated hereafter.

These become the second syllables; and those very same syllables, as previously stated in number, each become the third syllables of those [mantras] whose numbers will be mentioned below. One should join them from the beginning in sequence with the letters ending in *kṣa*.

"By thirty-six syllables. This is what is meant: one should join the aforementioned number of second syllables to the beginning of those [mantras] by means of the thirty-six letters starting with *a* and ending with *kṣa*. By means of those combinations, there arise the stated number of *vidyās*. This is what is meant.

By means of those forms of the Vidyā extracted according to the stated method, and ending with the Visarga, there arise Vidyās consisting of letters of a single form, numbering one crore as previously mentioned; the remaining [letters] are indeed of a single form by virtue of those [Vidyās]. This is what is meant: among the Vidyās extracted according to the stated method...

The remaining sciences become identical in form through those syllables; the meaning is "without those [sciences] being identical in form. Those numbering ten million (koṭi) as previously stated—consisting of three or four phonemes, namely those in the form of four syllables—are the Traipuras.
This is the meaning: "they become. From among those, one should fashion each *kūṭa* by means of two middle syllables.
This is the method for extracting the mantras here from these aforementioned *guptayoginī* vidyās.

Since the letters of the full mandala, beginning with *a* and so forth, exist as the first, second, and third letters [of their respective groups], for each one of those letters situated as the first letter—
The first syllable of each of the vidyās numbering in the millions (koṭi) becomes [the seed-syllable].
By joining the visarga to each of those syllables— which reside as the third syllable within their respective millions— those thirty-six syllables become possessed of the visarga.

Since it is prescribed that all vidyās end with the *visarga*, the thirty-six syllables ending with the *bindu* and the thirty-six syllables ending with the *visarga* constitute the vidyās; the remaining [syllables] would be of a single form, but they are excluded by those [two sets].
By means of those [mantras], there are ten million such vidyās consisting of three or four syllables.
And by adding the *visarjanīya* to the neuter vowels (*ṣaṇḍākṣara*), since the letter *ra* is included within the letter *la*,
those four [vowels] become redundant; thus, when combined,
these seventy-six syllables result in five hundred syllables remaining as a single unit.

Each one consists of the third syllables among twenty thousand syllables of the *vidyā*. At the end of those syllables which stand as the second syllables, there is the rule for joining each with the thirty-six syllables of the *tattvas*.

There are twenty thousand seven hundred and thirty-six varieties of forms. Among those forms of the aforementioned number, when the conjunction of *tattva* and syllables is to be performed, it is because without the conjunction of their vowels, no other form of mantra capable of achieving the goal (*atisiddha*) is possible.

Regarding the phrase "the conjunction with their respective vowels": those five hundred and seventy-six forms are further produced by the four letters [of the *ṣaṇḍha* group], because they possess identical forms through the addition of the letter *ra* to the first two groups of consonants and the addition of the letter *la* to the latter two groups.

There are one hundred and forty-four forms. Furthermore, by joining the class of the letter *kṣa* with the letter *kṣa*, those sixteen forms are added together, resulting in twenty thousand forms— specifically,
seven hundred and thirty-six in number.
Excluding twenty thousand forms, there remain [eighty thousand] forms.
When those twenty thousand forms are multiplied by the five hundred syllables mentioned previously— which exist as the third syllable— the result is a number in the tens of millions (*koṭi*).
By multiplying the forms of the Vidyās, which exist as the first syllables, with five hundred and seventy-six syllables,
there arise distinct forms numbering ten million full mandalas.

The forms of the Vidyās consist of the Tripura [mantra] in the form of four syllables. Here, the number of Vidyās to be discarded due to their identical form and the method of their multiplication are written down.
For example, among the forms produced by the variations of the central syllable:

By multiplying the seven hundred and thirty-six syllables— which have abandoned their individual forms through the uniformity of the previously described method— by the number of syllables in the full mandala as stated for the third vowel, [the result is] "tuṅgadhīgurur vaḥ."

There are forms numbering the same as the syllables produced by the six-syllable mantra. The intermediate forms, which are of distinct shapes, number twenty thousand; this is obtained by multiplying them by the seventy-six syllables resulting from the single form being excluded from the third set of syllables.
The forms produced by the seven-syllable phrase *nānājñānāśramo'yam* amount to 1,520,000;
when combined with the forms produced by the seven-syllable phrase *tuṅgadhīgarbhadhanya*, which amount to 1,943,936, these are the total forms. Of those forms...

Because of the union with the essence of the Knower (Saṃkhyājña), who abides as the first syllable within the full maṇḍala, the aims of human existence (puruṣārtha) are accomplished for all of them through meditation, ritual worship, yantras, and offerings. This has been stated by those whose weapons are the Mātṛkās. (21)
Listen, O Goddess of gods, to the ritual procedures for the protection of the disciple by the Guru;
even though the Guru and the disciple are equal in their physical bodies and other such activities.
I shall now quickly demonstrate to you, through direct perceptual examples, how [the world] arises from causes such as the relationship between the worshiped and the worshiper.

The wise and lofty Sādhu, who was ever stainless and knew the paths, stood before Caṇḍikā; having multiplied the number produced by the words "nityākalaṅka" (123456789) by means of the syllables of reality (*tattva*),
he [perceived] the sciences (*vidyā*) produced by the ten-syllable phrase "sadocce" (6879707136).

"By abandoning the single-form vidyā, the aforementioned innumerable forms arise. This means that the forms produced by the ten-syllable mantra, "Caṇḍikā sanāthārddhakāya" (111,970,713,6), must be abandoned as being of a single form. Herein lies the nature of the differentiated vidyā.

A small portion is shown by us: for instance, from the abandonment of the yoga of the *svaratattva*, the forms of the first group of thirty-five *vidyās*—beginning with *a a ka aḥ*, *a a kha aḥ*, and so on, ending with *a a kṣa aḥ*—are the forms of the second group of thirty-five *vidyās*:
*a ā ka aḥ*, *a ā kha aḥ*, *a ā* [and so forth].
The [syllables] beginning with *ga aḥ* and ending with *kṣa aḥ* come into being. || 20 ||

With the verse beginning with "tāsām api" (of these also), he extends by analogy (*atidiśati*) the previously mentioned meditations on these aforementioned sciences (*vidyā*) characterized by their specific numbers, as well as the worship of their respective deities along with their enclosures (*sāvaraṇa*), and the individual applications of the *yantras* and so forth. In that context, regarding those sciences...

And that [is attained] through meditation, worship, and the adoration of the *yantras* of the deities; by means of meditation, worship, *yantras*, and their adoration. In this context, the *yantras* consist of the syllables of the respective *vidyās*, differentiated by the vowels.
Regarding the meditation and so forth, they are described in the chapter on the *Mātṛkā*. This is what is meant: of those [mantras] whose number has been stated...
In the worship of each individual Vidyā among these four-syllabled Vidyās,

one should conceptually form a single-syllable shape from the middle syllable or the pair of middle syllables of these [Vidyās], and having performed the placement of the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) by repeating [the mantra] twice as before, [one proceeds] to the construction of the respective worship yantras.
In the chapter on the Mātṛkā, having constructed the wheels described in the Kālanityā— consisting of two squares, an eight-petaled lotus, and a nine-yoni diagram—
one should place each respective Vidyā, together with the object of accomplishment (sādhya), as before, in the center of the central yoni within each of those nine-yoni diagrams.
Having arranged [the syllables] outside of that in the eight corners and outside of those in the eight petals,
having arranged the vowels differentiated from the central syllable of the tattva-syllable as before,
and having performed the remainder as before, one should invoke [the deity] in its center as before, meditate upon it as before, and [proceed] as before.

Having worshipped thoroughly as before, having offered the two *bali* offerings, and having performed the previously mentioned applications (*prayoga*), one obtains the previously mentioned fruits. || 21 ||
If the body is refined by means of mantras, yantras, worship, consecration, and so forth, it will not be touched by the afflictions of old age, disease, and death; otherwise, it will be. (24)
Indeed, from that point on, there would be permanence for the vital breath (prāṇa) of embodied beings;
however, for the formless self (ātman), such refinement (saṃskāra) is simply not tenable.
If there were equality between the sense organs and the vital breath (prāṇa), or if there were equality between the intellect and the self, then whose would the observation of the Guru be? (26)
For those whose minds are distressed by such doubts as these, yet whose sins have been exhausted, the Guru provides instruction through the sprinkling of water and other means. (27)

With these five verses beginning with "The consecrations" (*saṃskārān*) and ending with "by means of the contemplation on impermanence and so forth" (*anityādibhir vīkṣaṇam ityantaiḥ*), the Teacher introduces the mantra-consecration being performed for the disciple, preceded by an exposition of the various rituals and so forth. In this context, "consecrations" (*saṃskārān*) refers to the empowerments (*abhiṣeka*), the glances (*kaṭākṣa*), and the instructions (*upadeśa*).

The connection here is with the *saṃskāras* (purificatory rites) which will be described later in this chapter by the Guru for the sake of protecting the disciple and bestowing grace upon the disciple.

Regarding the phrase "in the activity of the body and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the vital breath, the senses, the intellect, and other such faculties. This refers to the activity [of these].

The six waves—hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death—are in pairs; they exist in that [reality] which takes the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the intellect (*buddhi*), the body, and so forth. Here, the syntactical connection is with the "reasons" consisting of the relationship between the worshiped and the worshiper, and with "examples. *Pratyayam* means conviction or trust. This is what is being said:
He teaches as follows: "Even though the attributes of the body, senses, vital breath, intellect, and so forth are common to both the teacher and the disciple,

I shall demonstrate through illustrative examples— serving as the logical grounds for the teacher's worshipability by means of prostrations and the like, and the disciple's role as the worshiper— the production of direct conviction and certainty."

Refinement (*saṃskāra*) consists in the production of a specific excellence of good qualities in a certain object by means of a specific action that removes its inherent bad qualities. By this, the refinement of a disciple consists in the establishment of the knowledge of ultimate reality through the removal of evil tendencies (*durvāsanā*).
[This occurs] through mantras, yantras, worship, initiation (abhiṣeka), and so forth; the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to such matters as a glance or oral instruction.

[The phrase] "of the body" (tanoḥ) means "of the disciple's body"—this is the ellipsis. That is the disciple’s body. Otherwise, it is indeed touched [by grace]; this is the meaning. [The phrase] "of the breath" (prāṇasya) means "of the disciple's breath"—this is the ellipsis. If there is a purification (saṃskāra), [the word "purification"] is drawn back [from the previous sentence].

The phrase "there would be permanence for embodied beings" implies those who have performed the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*). [This refers to] the self in its form as the individual soul (*jīva*). Its "equality with the vital breaths" means its permanence due to its similarity to the self, that is, its similarity in being formless.
Of whom was this stated, other than [the one] excluded? || 26 ||
With these nine verses beginning with "iti" and ending with "bhavet," he provides a reasoned resolution for the matter he himself has raised, accompanied by illustrative examples:
"Therefore, I shall explain clearly and correctly that which is most secret and supreme."
Having attained which, one quickly abandons the great impurity known as doubt. || 28 ||
O beloved, the witness of the body, senses, mind, and vital breath—the Self—is properly purified by a Guru who knows the reality. (29)
By sprinkling, whatever impurity exists in the body is removed;
by gazing upon oneself, the cutting away of the intellect's false conceptions occurs. (30)

However, that deeply ingrained latent impression (vāsanā) of his which has persisted for a long time through instruction, he should destroy with his intellect by means of self-investigation, for it is difficult to overcome. || 31 ||

In that context, by the phrase "beginning with doubts" (*ityādi-saṃśayaiḥ*), the word "beginning" (*ādi*) refers to subjects such as the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), muttering (*japa*), worship (*pūjā*), and the enjoyment of their fruits;
[this applies] to those whose sins have been exhausted, through doubt in the manner described.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is: "I shall speak of those [distinctions], because the discrimination (*viveka*) of the body, senses, intellect, self, and so forth, culminates in the attainment of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). That which brings about a specific state: having attained that, and having known that which brings about a specific state, one realizes the great impurity, because it destroys one's own self.
Of the Self, which is the witness of the body, senses, mind, and vital breath,
and which is perceived within the body, senses, mind, and vital breath that serve as its limiting adjuncts— due to beginningless latent impressions (vāsanā),
the qualities belonging to those adjuncts [appear] through their own respective qualities during the states of waking, dreaming, and deep sleep.

In the state of continuity regarding those things whose nature is pleasure and pain, there exists a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of the consciousness called the *jīva*, which will be described below. By one who knows the reality— the knower of the ultimate truth regarding the two principles, namely the self and its limiting adjuncts— through the sprinkling of consecration according to the method taught by the *Seka*, [this occurs] within the body, which serves as the limiting adjunct.
"Impurity" refers to affliction by disease and the like. "By means of observation" means according to the sequence prescribed for piercing the array of *Jvālāmālinī*;

"of the Guru" is the ellipsis. "Of oneself" means of one's own intellect; that is to say, of one's own consciousness. "Cutting away what is not as it is" means the destruction of the cognition of something as being what it is not. [This occurs] through the instruction of the *Vidyās*, such as the *Śrīvidyā*.
And for the sake of those objects—of which the remainder is "of the three qualities" (traiguṇya)—as will be described in the section on the veil of latent impressions (*vāsanā*).

Of that disciple; "long-established" means attached to the mind from birth onwards. "Latent impression" (*vāsanā*) means habitual familiarity. "Difficult to cross" means that latent impression which is difficult to abandon. [One should cross it] with the intellect (*dhiyā*), that is, with the awakened understanding (*buddhyā*).
By means of self-reflection as taught by the Guru— that is, by the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) in the form of the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhaṃtā*)—
when this has been performed, that is, when the aforementioned purification has been effected,

there occurs the destruction of the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*) which consists of the ignorance of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), [and] of that [modification] whose nature is the knowledge of transmigratory existence.

The meaning is that through the exclusion of māyā and the like from the activity of the intellect (buddhi-vṛtti), there occurs a destruction consisting in the absence of the cognition of saṃsāra. "Apprehension of one's own nature" (svarūpālambha) means resting in identity with that [nature] through the cessation of activity, because one's own nature is not an object of grasping. "Both" (ubhe) means "the two"; thus, "both [of them] come to be."
The connection is with what precedes. This has been stated [on p. 495]:
"When this is done, both the destruction of the mental state (buddhivṛtti) which consists of the ignorance of saṃsāra, and the attainment of the nature of the eternally pure Self, [occur]. (32)
O Pārvatī, behold there a visible example for you:
sprouts have grown from seeds of grain through contact with fire.
In that case, his power simply does not exist; rather, it is consumed by fire.
Likewise, that which is the cause of his ignorance, birth, and so forth, is likewise destroyed.

For the individual self (jīvātman), who is of the nature of consciousness and who— deluded by the experience of qualities belonging to various adjuncts as if they were its own qualities— is perceived through the adjuncts consisting of the aggregate of body, senses, mind, and vital breath like the moon reflected in water, the process known as "the refinement of qualities" is performed by a teacher who knows reality.
By means of the consecration described in the aforementioned form,
there occurs the removal of the impurities acquired through the limiting adjuncts (upādhi) of previous births and so forth; and by his glance,
the destruction of false knowledge— which consists of the mind’s natural tendency toward error— takes place through further instruction.

Furthermore, through the contemplation of one's own Self according to the method thus taught, the destruction of long-established, difficult-to-eradicate latent impressions (*durvāsanā*) will occur. When this is done, there occurs the destruction of the mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*), which by its very nature tends toward external objects, in the form of the absence of modifications directed toward those objects.

Therefore, when this [intellect] proceeds toward the westward direction, because its own nature has become an object of perception, both [its] dissolution— in the form of resting in identity with that very [object]— and [its] transformation occur. In that regard,

when the latent impressions (*durvāsanā*) of the intellect are destroyed through the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) and other means performed by the Guru according to the form already explained, [the state of liberation is attained].

And since there is no sprouting therein despite its being established through one's own experience, the meaning is that the power (*śakti*) of this seed-form is the "power of sprouting," not the seed-form itself. Likewise, regarding its [the seed's] production of ignorance, birth, and so forth—
here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to old age, death, and the like.

Otherwise, there would be birth, old age, death, and so forth, resulting from ignorance. The meaning is that just as seeds do not sprout when touched by fire, so too birth and other states do not arise for the disciple due to ignorance.
The reason is precisely this: just as [seeds] do not sprout from their seed-form when touched by fire...

The meaning is that even when [the body] has perished previously, the power (*śakti*) which is the cause of its regrowth is burnt away; likewise, that which is the cause of ignorance, birth, and so forth—namely, the form of evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*)—is also burnt away.
Furthermore, by means of purification (*saṃskāra*) and so on, the cause of the manifestation of one's own Self [is realized].
The meaning is that it is seen from another illustration. Its sprouting refers to the sprouting of a cotton seed.

The word "etcetera" (ādi) in "flower etc. refers to fruits, roots, and so forth. Thus, the meaning is that it becomes red with the dye of lac. This is what is being said: just as in the case of seeds of grain...

Just as the sprout, which is the effect, does not arise because its causal power for germination is destroyed by the mere touch of fire, so too, through the refinement performed by the guru, that mind of the disciple— which constitutes birth and the engagement in saṃsāra— is [transformed].

Due to the destruction of the evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*) which serve as the causal seed for the operation of *saṃsṛti*, the operation of its effects—such as *saṃsṛti* itself—also ceases to exist. For example, just as cotton seeds dyed with lac [do not produce red flowers]:
Furthermore, when cotton seeds are dyed with lac... (p. 496) ...[they do not produce red fruit].
Its sprouting is seen, and likewise its flowers and so forth shall come to be. || 35 ||
This supreme secret is the wish-fulfilling gem of all accomplishments, steadfast,
easily mastered when obtained from a true guru, and free from the association of sins.

Today I shall describe to you those infinite mantra-vidyās which are devoid of preliminary rites (puraścaraṇa), fire-offerings (homa), worship (arcā), libations (tarpaṇa), hymns of praise (stuti), and mystical diagrams (yantra). || 37 ||
Listen to them, O Maheśānī, for the constant attainment of all desired goals by practitioners and perfected ones, but never by others. (38)
It is entirely free from the threefold distinctions of being the Veda, its commentary, or something else;
it possesses virtuous latent impressions and is always devoid of thoughts regarding the good or the bad.

Just as a seed that has been processed with lac results in sprouts, flowers, and so forth that appear red with the color of lac, likewise, the mental activity of that disciple— whose mind has been refined by the teacher’s purificatory rites and other means— becomes the very nature of his own experience in the form of the teacher’s instruction. || 35 ||
With these eight verses beginning with "The secret" (*rahasyam*) and ending with "always" (*sadā*),
he teaches that all syllables, words, sentences, and so forth, possess the nature of mantra. Here,
there are six accusative-case nouns beginning with "the supreme" (*paramam*) and ending with "devoid of" (*rahitam*).
The syntactical connection here is that I state "the secret of the words" as the predicate.
As for the phrases "mantras and vidyās," the meaning is that there exist infinite mantras and vidyās due to combinations of one, two, and so forth, in the manner previously described. These...
