The *mantravidyās* [belong] to practitioners (*sādhakas*) and perfected ones (*siddhas*). This connects with the phrase "for the attainment of their desired goal. It does not belong to others—that is, not to those who are still to be accomplished (*sādhya*)—because, in any way whatsoever, they lack knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). "Being of another nature" means being of the nature of an ordinary person (*ārṣya*).

It possesses a pure latent impression (*sadvāsanā*) and is always free from the thought of what is good or bad, because the correctness or incorrectness of words is purely conceptual. Its meaning is that it consists of you, in the form of *śakti*.
It is the resting place of the "assemblage" (*samudaya*) of *nāda*, namely the previously mentioned forms of *parā*, *paśyantī*, and so forth.

Of those very [elements] mentioned previously; "consisting of me" means having the nature of Śiva; "consisting of both" means having the nature of Śiva and Śakti, whose forms are emergence and repose; "the nature of the Self" refers to the previously mentioned form of the "I-consciousness" (*ahaṃvitti*). The phrase "together with those syllables" is the ellipsis to be supplied. "In time" means by way of sequence.

Through the destruction of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of suffering arising from otherness— the dissolution of the latent impressions of pain produced by the nature of duality— it becomes composed of supreme *ahantā*,
consisting of perfect *ahantā*, the embodiment of one's own self in its entirety.

The essential natures of all categories of existence (padārtha) are identical with You; their emergence rests within Me, and the nature of the Self consists of both. Such is the relationship of that Nāda with them. (40)

In time, through the destruction of the impressions of otherness, suffering, and affliction, one certainly attains that which consists of supreme I-consciousness, whose very form is the self-nature of all things. (41)
Consisting of existence, known as vibration, free from all limiting adjuncts, and having the nature of light—that supreme reality shines forth as the very Self. (42)
Since this is so, there is nothing in the world that is not mantra, not even a single syllable; therefore, O Mantrin, protect me from all quarters, from the enemy and from every danger. 43.
Because all Vaiṣṇava mantras— whether consisting of six, eight, or twelve syllables— denote the meaning of the supreme reality, they are non-different from one another.

That whose own form is its very body; the meaning is that all these various forms of objects exist in a state of identity with that which has the nature of the secret sound (nāda). It is of the nature of Being (*sadātmaka*), having the form of existence (*sadbhāvarūpa*), and is known as "vibration" (*sphurattā*)—that is to say, it is known as the pulsation (*sphuraṇa*) called consciousness (*cit*).

Free from all adjuncts (*upādhi*), devoid of all modifications produced by adjuncts, and consisting of light—[the meaning is] "as the identity of each and every object," this being the ellipsis. Regarding its being the Self, that is, its being the essential nature (*svarūpa*)—"that which is the reality" (this being the ellipsis)—it shines; that is to say, it becomes the Supreme. Since it is thus:

"Thus it is" means "because of this. Therefore, from this [it follows that] the syllable which is without mantra—that is, distinct from other mantras—the meaning is as follows: of all mantras, whether in the form of syllables, words, sentences, and so forth...

Because the phonemes have as their ultimate reality Śiva in the form of power (*śakti*), whose nature is the repose of emergence, and because they culminate in that repose of emergence, there occurs— through those mantras— a gradual process of clarity in contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of one's own self, which is the ultimate reality of consciousness consisting of both [emergence and repose], as being non-different from them.
Because they possess the essential nature of the supreme reality, which consists of the supreme I-consciousness (parāhaṃtā) as previously described, all phonemes (varṇas) become mantras. || 43 ||

With these five verses beginning with "ṣaṭ" and ending with "āpnuyuḥ," he teaches the pervasion of the Lalitā-vidyā by means of eleven mantras— namely, Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Vaidika mantras— which serve as the primary elements. Therein:

The grammatical connection is as follows: "of the three aforementioned Vaiṣṇava mantras consisting of six, eight, and twelve syllables"—namely, those of six syllables, eight syllables, and twelve syllables. "In their entirety" means even in the form of their words and word-meanings. This is because they express the meaning of the supreme reality (*paratattva*) and because they denote the nature of the Supreme (*parasvarūpa*).

Non-difference (*abhedatā*) is the pervasion (*vyāpti*); the word "non-difference" is to be construed here with "by means of the *lalitā-vidyā*. What is meant is this: for the sake of the pervasion of the form of the deity expressed by one's own [mantra], namely the six-syllable mantra in the form "Oṃ namo viṣṇave," there is the presentation of the essential nature of Viṣṇu.
In the same manner, [the worship] of the threefold Prāsāda [mantra] is performed with the Lalitā-vidyā;
likewise, that of Parā and Gāyatrī is performed according to the form already described. (45)

Through the application of the *vyāhṛtis*, the great sentences (*mahāvākyas*), and the *praṇava*—which have the Supreme Self as their essence and consist of silent recitation—one attains identity with each of those respective selves. (46)

The pervasion by means of the eight-syllabled mantra [is established] because Nārāyaṇa, who is the deity expressed by his own name, is the abode— that is, the locus— of the entire universe denoted by the word *nāra* (which signifies a multitude of men),
since this deity exists as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) within that universe denoted by the word *nāra*.

And because of the demonstration of his established nature: by means of the twelve-syllable mantra, [one meditates] on the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, who is the form of the deity expressed by the mantra, using the word *bhagavat* which denotes his being the cause of all powers,
and the word *Vāsudeva* which denotes his abiding in a state of identity with all things.
Because their sovereignty is thus established, and because they denote the nature of the Supreme,
they are pervaded by the Lalitā-vidyā, which is the ultimate reality of the Supreme nature. Similarly,
because it denotes the meaning of the Supreme Reality, the mantra of the Prāsāda— which is the root of the Śaiva Tantra— [is likewise pervaded].

The meaning is: "because it consists of three, it has a threefold nature. This threefold nature consists of the knower (*jñātṛ*), the means of knowledge (*jñāna*), and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*). Of that mantra, the *bindu* is the form of the knower, the fourteenth vowel (*au*) is the form of the means of knowledge, and the letter *ha* is the form of the object of knowledge. This is what is being stated.
By means of the Prāsāda mantra, because it describes the ultimate nature of one's own deity— as being free from conceptual constructs in the form of the knower, the knowledge, and the known—
its pervasion by the Lalitā-vidyā occurs; the meaning is that this is likewise due to its denoting the supreme form.

Of that Parā, who is the form of the third seed-syllable of the Kula-Sundarī-vidyā, there is the status of denoting the ultimate reality (paramārtha) due to the threefold nature previously mentioned. This is what is meant:
by the Śrī Parā-vidyā, in its aforementioned form, [there is the denotation] of her own deity who is signified by it.

The pervasion by the Lalitā-vidyā occurs through the non-separation of the knower, knowledge, and the knowable— represented by the visarjanīya, the fourteenth vowel, and the letter *sa*— which constitutes the nature of the unsurpassed ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is similar to the case of Gāyatrī and Sāvitrī as previously described.

In the three Vaiṣṇava mantras, the word "in its entirety" (aśeṣataḥ) means even in the form of the words and their referents as they have been described. This is what is being said: by means of this Gāyatrī, the state of being the progenitor of the entire phenomenal universe belongs to the deity who is its own expressed meaning.

It is said that [these] consist in the nature of the activity of mere vibration, the possession of the power capable of negating all dualistic cognition, and the state of being the self of the universe—
referring to the three [syllables] which are the causes of the three feet of the Gāyatrī.

This is what is meant: by those [mantras], the state of being pure existence (*sanmātratva*) of the deity expressed by their own words, their being the cause of the entire phenomenal world (*sakalaprapañca*), and their non-difference from that cause are declared.
[This applies] to the Great Sentence (*mahāvākya*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and the *ajapa* self. Regarding the Great Sentence:
Regarding the mantra of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and the *ajapā* mantra: what is meant by this is that, through the Great Saying (*mahāvākya*),

the true nature of the deity expressed by one's own [mantra]— which is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the form of existence (*sat-rūpa*) and the ultimate reality of the nature of non-duality— is the *ajapā*.
By means of the supreme mantra of the *paramātman*, which is the cause of the entire phenomenal world (*sakalaprapañca*) for the deity expressed by one's own [mantra],
[one perceives] that *māyā* as well as those two [bindus] as a single embodiment of their identity.
The vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) in the form of a swan, arising from that very state of stillness.
He who understands the Praṇava, which is eternally proclaimed, is liberated;
others, if they possess devotion, shall attain that knowledge in due course of time. || 48 ||
In this world, devotion to that which is unworthy of devotion constantly brings about suffering;
tell me, moreover, of the distinction in devotion by which one certainly attains everything.
Through the connection with which there is the attainment of results from deities, mantras, yantras, meditations, and so forth, entirely; and in separation from which effort is in vain. (50)

By means of the *ajapā* mantra, [one realizes] the ultimate nature of the Supreme Self— which is of the essence of consciousness— as being non-different from its own power of will (*svecchā-śakti*), which consists of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) as various effects; this is the manifestation of that very power of will in the form of the world, which is the deity expressed by the mantra.

The manifestation of the supreme form (*pararūpa*) is called the ultimate reality (*paramārtharūpa*). This refers to the *praṇava* (the syllable Om), whose nature will be described in the immediately following verse. Through its connection with that form—that is, through the relationship of identity with the supreme form—there is identification with that [reality] by means of the *Lalitā-vidyā*; this is the implied meaning.
This is what is meant: among the Vaiṣṇava, Śaiva, and Vaidika mantras,
these eleven root mantras [arise] from that which is the cause of all— whose nature is pure consciousness (cinmātra)— and which unfolds through the expansion of its own power of will (svecchā-śakti).

The meaning is that, by demonstrating identity through conceptual elaboration (*prapañca*), it becomes a means of conveying the significance of Lalitā. From the reversal of those [two], the *praṇava* arises;
this refers to the euphonic combination (*sandhi*) produced by reversing the *ha*-kāra and *sa*-kāra—which are identical to that [Lalitā]—once they are freed from the *bindu* and the *visarjanīya*.
The origin is the *praṇava*. This is what is meant:

within the *kāmakalā*, which is the ultimate nature of the eternal Śrī Mahātripurasundarī—the supreme reality whose form is the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) between Śiva and Śakti—there is [this origin].

By knowing the vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*), which consists of the ultimate recitation (*paramārtha-japa*), through the union of the *bindu* in the form of Śiva and the *visarjanīya* in the form of Śakti in their direct order (*anuloma-yoga*), and by knowing the *praṇava* through their reverse order (*vailomya-yoga*),
one becomes a knower of reality (*tattva*) and eternal. Others...

Those devoid of the knowledge of this state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) are [nevertheless] devoted to the *nityās*. Gradually, over time, that knowledge—the knowledge of equilibrium—[arises]. This is what is meant:
even without the knowledge whose form is this equilibrium, merely through those *nityās*...
Through worship with very firm devotion, that devotion—namely, the worship—gradually bestows the knowledge of the supreme reality, which consists of identity with Him. || 48 ||

With these five verses beginning with "abhakti" and ending with "duḥkhinaḥ," [the author] teaches the praise of devotion (*bhakti*), the nature of devotion, and the transgression incurred by worshipping without devotion.
In this context, the phrase "worship without devotion" (*abhaktibhajana*) is to be construed with the word "of the obligatory rites" (*nityānām*).
(500) I shall declare to you that devotion, which is secret, most wonderful of the wonderful, consisting entirely of its fruit, perfected, and unattainable by those of little merit. (51)
Firmness of mind regarding the teacher who possesses the aforementioned characteristics, as well as regarding the knowledge and practice taught by him, arises from the destruction of doubt. (52)
Devotion, which bestows all goals, has been described as that which leads to liberation and vigilance;
those devoid of it are certainly miserable both in this world and the next. (53)

She who is like a ship for the ocean of all afflictions and calamities, possessed of great splendor; she who is the sovereign of nectar, providing rain against the great forest fire of mental and physical ailments.

Listen, I shall describe the embodiment of the life-force of all living beings, which is sixfold [and is realized] through recitation, fire-offerings, worship, libations, meditation, and yantras. (55)
The first [mantra] is formed with *dāvāmbusvaiḥ*; the other is formed with *hṛddhaṃ samāyayā*. The third is *jyākaṃ dāhavanasvaiḥ*, which is Sāmṛteśvarī.

"It brings affliction to the practitioner"—this is the ellipsis. "By which devotion" means by that yoga of devotion through which all desired fruits arise; "in its absence," meaning in the lack of devotion, there is only "exertion," that is, practice.
[This results in] the attainment of the perfectly fruitful accomplishment of the previously mentioned deities, mantras, and so forth.

Because it is the cause for the accomplishment of all fruits. [This refers to] one endowed with the characteristics described above, complete with the characteristics stated in the first chapter, such as "handsome," "fair-faced," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "from the destruction of doubt in the intellect concerning those two taught by the true guru": this follows the logic of the crow's eye (i.e., it applies to both).

It follows both the preceding and the following [verses]. It bestows all objects and grants the perfection of one's true nature; "by whom [the goddess] is devoid," the word "people" is to be supplied as the subject. || 53 ||
With the two verses beginning with *sarvakleśa* and ending with *yantrarkaiḥ*, he introduces [the subject] preceded by a hymn of praise to the Vidyā of Amṛteśvarī; therein,
she is the form of a boat for the ocean of all afflictions and calamities (*sarvakleśāpad*).

The meaning is that she is the boat-like deliverer from afflictions such as those caused by elemental spirits and celestial deities, which are like oceans. She is the Vidyā known as Amṛteśvarī, whose splendor is my own and whose majesty is unsurpassed;
the word "Vidyā" is understood from the context. She is the embodiment of the vital breath of all living beings, because she consists of nectar.
The word "together with" (saha) is the ellipsis [to be understood] with recitation, fire-offerings, worship, libations, meditation, and yantras. || 55 ||

With the verse beginning with *dāva*, he teaches the *Amṛteśvarī-vidyā*. In that context, the meaning is that the first mantra consists of the syllables *da*, *va*, *a*, *u*, *r*, *sva*, along with the letter *ṭha*, the letter *va*, and the nasal bindu; the remainder is that the other is the second mantra.
(501) That [mudrā] is said to be sixfold according to the manner described for the *vāsanā*; the limbs of the first among them arise from the application of long vowels. (57)

Having first performed those three [mudrās] with the hands and limbs, one should then join them with the sixteen vowels and install them as abiding in nectar; the other [mudrās] are likewise situated therein.
The second Vidyā consists of the *hṛdaya* (heart), *haṃsa*, *māyā*, along with *sakāra*, *hakāra*, and *hṛllekhā*; this is the meaning.
The third [Vidyā] consists of *jyā*, *kaṃ*, *dāha*, *vana*, and *svaiḥ*;
that is, the third Vidyā consists of *jakāra*, *hakāra*, *repha*, *ukāra*, and the *bindu*; this is the meaning. Of these seed-syllables (*bījas*)...
Each one of the three possesses the nature of a *vidyā*. The meaning is that *Sāmṛteśvarī*—the *Amṛteśvarī-vidyā* previously introduced—is thus described. || 56 ||

With these six verses beginning with "vāsanā" and ending with "kṣīṇakalmaṣaḥ," he teaches the sixfold divisions of this [practice], its constituent parts, the nectar-essences (*amṛtakalā*) within the body, and the sequence for the method of their placement upon the bodies. Therein, according to the manner described as "vāsanā"...

The meaning is that this sixfold Vidyā of Amṛteśvarī becomes sixfold through the distinctions of form described in the manner of all the Vidyās to be mentioned in the *Vāsanāpaṭala*. As for those forms:
therein, the first form is the sequence of extraction (*proddhārakrama*), while the second form is...

The first form arises through the sequence of joining the first, third, and second peaks; the third form, however, arises through the sequence of joining the second, third, and first peaks; the fourth form arises through the sequence of joining the second, first, and third peaks; and as for the fifth form—

The third form arises through the sequence of joining the first and second peaks; the sixth form, however, arises through the sequence of joining the third, second, and first peaks. Thus, it is the reverse form of the first form. Of those six vidyās, [this applies] to the first.

In each of those respective divisions, the addition of long vowels to the form of the first *kūṭa* is as before, and [the assignment] to the hands and limbs is as before. This is what is meant: among the six divisions of the forms of the *amṛteśvarī-vidyā*, because the first *kūṭa* residing in the first and second forms is the primary one, it is placed therein.
By joining long vowels:

one should perform the ritual placement (*nyāsa*) on the hands and limbs by means of forms such as *ṭhvāṃ* and *ṭhvīṃ*, which are endowed with the *jāti* vowels, through the division of those two types of forms.
Among these, because the second peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) itself constitutes the beginning of the third and fourth [syllables], one joins long vowels to that [second peak-syllable].

One should perform the placement of the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and so forth by means of forms associated with the classes [of consonants], such as *sth-n-ām* and *sth-n-īm*, through the division into those two types of forms. Among those,
because the first [consonant] of the third peak (*kūṭa*) is used for the fifth and sixth [limbs], one should join a long vowel to that [consonant].

One should perform the six-limbed placement (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) and other rites by means of forms associated with the seed-syllables (*jāti*), such as *jphāṃ*, *jphīṃ*, and so forth, through the division of those two types of forms. Having joined that triad—the three peak-syllables (*kūṭa*)—with the sixteen vowels, [one should apply them] to each peak-syllable; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. This is because they abide in nectar (*amṛta*).
The meaning is: beginning from the essential locations where the digits of nectar (amṛtakalā) reside according to the sequence that will be explained immediately hereafter.

[These locations are] sequentially on the back of the big toe, its joint, the genitals, the navel, the heart, the breast, the throat, the nose, the eyes, the ears, the eyebrows, the temples, and the crown of the head. (59)

This sequence applies to both men and women, beginning from the right and the left respectively; in the bright fortnight it ends with the full moon, while in the other [the dark fortnight], it proceeds in reverse order starting from the head.
By the transposition of the two Bhagas, [the breath] reaches the thumb at the end of the Darśa;
thus, it constantly begins and ends its movement from the station of Mṛtaka.

The meaning is that one should place another form, which consists of a vowel joined with a *visarjanīya*, in the position of nectar (*amṛtasthāna*) which serves as the starting point for the locus of the deposition (*nyāsasthāna*). This is what is intended:
for each of the first, second, and third *kūṭas* of the Amṛteśvarī-vidyā, [one should perform this].
Through the conjunction with the sixteen vowels, each *kūṭa* (peak-syllable) possesses sixteen forms.

Having arranged fifteen of those sixteen forms— beginning from the station of nectar (*amṛtasthāna*) according to the sequence to be described, and following the movement of the nectar-constituents (*amṛtakalā*) to be described— one [places] the sixteenth.

Furthermore, one should place *rūpa* again in the station of immortality (*amṛtasthāna*), namely on the back and the forefoot. Its junction is at the junctions of the ankles and knees; [it is placed] in the *śaṅkha*, which is the bone on the side of the forehead.
This sequence applies to both men and women, beginning from the right and the left respectively. [This continues] until the end of the full moon in the bright fortnight.

This is what is meant: in the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa), beginning from the big toe of the right foot up to the crown of the head, on each lunar day (tithi) from the first to the fifteenth, [the breath flows] through the fifteen aforementioned locations situated at those respective sides.
In due order, according to the sequence of ascent, the abiding of the digit of nectar (*amṛtakalā*) occurs. For a woman, however,

beginning from the big toe of the left foot up to the crown of the head, it resides in the fifteen aforementioned locations situated on her sides, corresponding to the fifteen lunar days (*tithis*) starting from the first and ending with the full moon.

On each lunar day (*tithi*), the nectar-portion (*amṛtakalā*) abides according to its sequential order of ascent. Thus, for both male and female [practitioners], even though there is a reversal in the sequence of the sides during the commencement of the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*), there is no reversal in the sequence of the locations. In the other case, the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*), [the sequence begins] from the head and so forth.

"Up to the thumb" means in reverse order, that is, by way of descent. "By the transposition of two parts" implies [the distinction between] male and female. "Residing in the thumb" refers to the nectar; this is the sense. What is meant is as follows: during the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa), for a male, [the movement is] from the top of the left side down to the left thumb.
In the fifteen locations previously mentioned, starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) up to the new moon (darśānta),
the presence of the digits of nectar (amṛtakalā) occurs in each lunar day respectively, according to the descending order, throughout the fifteen lunar days. As for the woman, however—

Beginning from the top of the right side down to the right thumb, in the fifteen aforementioned locations, the presence of the nectar-portion (*amṛtakalā*) occurs according to the sequence of the lunar days (*tithi*), starting from the first day (*pratipad*) up to the new moon (*darśa*)— that is, throughout the fifteen lunar days— in a descending order. This is constant.
By this first half-verse, beginning with "ityādinā" and ending with "kalmaṣaḥ," the following is stated:
among the six varieties of the Amṛteśvarī-vidyā, one should install those six types at the end of the prescribed sequence for each individual deity who is to be worshipped, but not permanently.
Through this placement (nyāsa), the practitioner, with his impurities destroyed, shall become one whose nature is nectar.
I shall proclaim their meditations; listen indeed according to the stated order, by the mere remembrance of which all afflictions perish without remainder. (63)
Resembling pure crystal, their bodies were moistened by the nectar flowing from the crescent moon upon their crests; they were adorned with stainless ornaments.
Holding white and red lotuses that resemble the nectar of the full moon with their hands,
they have smiling faces and are adorned with ornaments of pearls.
By joining the sixteen vowels to each peak of the three peaks that constitute the division itself,
sixteen forms of sixteen types are produced; thus, totaling forty-eight forms,
they reside in fifteen locations, beginning from the station of the Amṛtakalā according to the stated sequence.
Furthermore, one should place fifteen forms again at the starting point as the sixteenth form;
thus, by dividing them sixteen by sixteen, one should assign them thirty by thirty. By that means, the practitioner becomes of the aforementioned form. || 62 ||
With these four verses beginning with "Dhyānam" and ending with "parivāritā," he teaches the meditation on Amṛteśvarī, her worship, and the multitude of powers that constitute her retinue.
In this context, regarding those [powers] who belong to the sixfold division of the vidyās of the forms of Amṛteśvarī— of whom...

Regarding the "forms" (mūrtīnām): the afflictions (kleśāḥ) consist of the threefold suffering (tāpatraya). The phrase "the form resembling pure crystal" (śuddhasphaṭikasaṅgāśāṃ mūrtim) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The word "bearing" (dadhānāḥ) is syntactically connected with the first quarter-verse of the second half of the subsequent verse. As for the singular number used for "form" (mūrteḥ), it refers to those six [forms] collectively.
Because their ultimate reality is unity (*aikya-paramārthatva*). The plural number in "anvitāḥ" (endowed) is used by way of accepting their differentiated forms.

Here, the weapons are [placed] in the sequence of upward, right, left, right, and left. "With smiling faces," as before; the qualification of the forms is to be connected with the phrase "as before, bearing... from the previous passage.

"Adorned with pearl ornaments" means decorated with ornaments made of pearls. "Residing in the middle of the petals" refers to those sixty-one hundred powers (*śaktis*), meaning the aforementioned one hundred and sixty immortal syllables (*amṛtākṣara*). This is what has been stated.

Having completed the circle according to the desired measurement by means of a compass, one should draw a circle outside it measuring one *aṅgula*, then a circle outside that measuring five *aṅgulas*,
and again a circle outside that measuring one *aṅgula*; thus, by means of the internal and external divisions.
Having fashioned twenty circles together with the four previously mentioned,
and having created sixteen petals in each of the ten paths (vīthi) which have an interval of five finger-breadths between them, [one should place] there in the central pericarp (karṇikā) of all...
The principal deity is Amṛteśvarī (p. 504),
who is surrounded by those [deities] situated in the middle of the petals of lotuses possessing sixteen petals, namely by those powers consisting of one hundred and sixty syllables.
Accompanied by the syllables of the respective vidyās, that syllable is the word *rūpiṇī*;
the two-syllabled word *śakti* is declared to be joined with the seven-syllabled mantra.
Having thus performed the fourteen-syllable vidyā, one should worship with those [mantras],
using fragrant substances, by entering from the outside and proceeding clockwise.
One should worship her outside with white flowers sprinkled with the liquid of sandalwood and camphor, and one should offer a pair of oblations (bali).
Having offered milk-rice (pāyasa), coconuts, plantains,
and sugar, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) with those same items and the libation (tarpaṇa) with water scented with camphor.

One should worship her surrounded on the outer petals by the one hundred and sixty powers consisting of the nectar-syllables mentioned in the *Bhagamālinīpaṭala*. This is common to all five [deities] other than this one.

With these four verses beginning with "tattadvidyā" and ending with "vāsitaiḥ," he teaches the worship-mantras (*pūjāvidyā*) of the enclosure-deities (*āvaraṇaśakti*), as well as the Goddess’s articles of worship, the offerings (*bali*), the fire-oblations (*homa*), and the libations (*tarpaṇa*). Among these, [the mantra] is accompanied by the syllables of each respective vidyā.

The meaning is that this should be joined as the initial syllable for each of the previously mentioned numbers. That syllable [is to be placed] among the previously mentioned number of nectar-syllables (amṛtārṇa), one by one; [this refers to] the second syllable of the previously mentioned seven-syllabled mantra—this is the remainder [of the sense]. "A fourteen-syllabled [mantra] for each vidyā"—this is the remainder [of the sense]. Having done thus...
The meaning is "having thus extracted. By means of those vidyās. "In a clockwise direction," with the words "beginning from the front" being understood as the ellipsis.

This is what is meant: having first uttered the first kūṭa of the form to be worshipped—which consists of the sixfold division of the forms of the Amṛteśvarī-vidyā—one should [then proceed] among the syllables of nectar (amṛta).

Having thus combined the eighty [letters] with the *bindu*, and having uttered one letter at a time according to the stated sequence out of the one hundred and sixty, one should then utter the twelve syllables: "I worship the sandals of the Śakti Rūpiṇī. In this manner, for each vidyā, they are combined.

One should worship with the fourteen-syllable vidyās by means of the movement of entry and exit, starting from the front and proceeding clockwise. This is to be construed with the phrase "with fragrant flowers. *Śrīkhaṇḍa* is sandalwood. *Vahis* means outside the daily worship mandala. Of these...

Regarding the sixfold Amṛteśvarīs, their nature as being of the essence of Lalitā is also stated. The pair of offerings at the beginning and the end are performed respectively with the sixteen-syllable mantra and the seven-syllable mantra of Kurukullā; these are offered with the four items, such as milk-rice (pāyasa) and so forth. || 70 ||
One should recite the vidyā one million times while subsisting on milk and remaining concentrated.
When the mantra-practitioner has thus achieved perfection through recitation and other means, [he should enter] the water. (71)
Touching the ocean-born [water] with the palm of his hand, he should mutter those [mantras] one hundred times each; thus that water becomes like a thundercloud.

Within those very [squares], one should write the hundred-syllable [mantra] joined with each respective syllable of the vidyā and accompanied by the sixty; one should write that first [syllable] in the middle and [the rest] from the center.
With these two verses beginning with "ten lakṣas" and ending with "resembling," he teaches the procedure for accomplishing the *vidyā* and the characteristics of one who has mastered the *vidyā*.
In this context, the phrase "ten lakṣas per *vidyā*" is the understood remainder; here, the libations (*tarpaṇa*) and fire-offerings (*homa*) are likewise performed for each *vidyā*.
The traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) is that these constitute ten directions.

In the phrase "japa and so forth" (*japādīti*) mentioned in this manner, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to libations (*tarpaṇa*), fire-offerings (*homā*), worship (*pūjā*), and the like. The phrase "water born of the ocean" is to be construed with the term stated in the preceding verse. These are the sixfold sciences (*vidyā*). [Recite them] one hundred times each.

The meaning is that one should mutter each of those six vidyās, which have been established for oneself, one hundred times. By means of recitation in the manner thus described, that water—the ocean water—becomes like milk in its flavor and other qualities. || 72 ||

With the two verses beginning with "In those" (*teṣu*) and ending with "infinite" (*anantakā*), he teaches the method for constructing the lotus-mandala and its nature as having infinite numerical units. In that context,
within each of those [petals] situated in internal and external divisions, which have been declared to be the mandala for the perpetual worship (*nityasaparyā*):
In the ten lotuses having the form of sixteen petals, [one should place] those [syllables] accompanied by the respective letters of the Vidyā;
that is to say, among the sixfold Amṛteśvarī-vidyās, they are accompanied by each individual *kūṭa* (peak-syllable) of the chosen Vidyā.
These consist of one hundred syllables joined with sixty—the meaning being the previously mentioned nectar-syllables (*amṛtārṇa*)—in the center.

The word "of the pericarp" (*karṇikāyāḥ*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "One should write that first [syllable] in the center, accompanied by the syllable of the target" means that one should write the form of the first [syllable] among those written on the exterior, positioned in its own center and accompanied by the syllable of the target.
"Of them" refers to those syllables of the stated number, which are the forms of the letters.

"Because they do not delineate mutual interpenetration"—that is, because they do not delineate the sequence of distinctions belonging to the layers of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) which will be described later.

"Infinite" means "infinitely many"; the word "yantras" is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. This is the procedure for the arrangement of the yantras here: each of those [circles] situated in internal and external divisions according to the previously stated sequence [is to be treated].

Having fashioned sixteen-petaled lotuses, upon those one hundred and sixty petals, proceeding from the outside toward the inside, moving from tip to tip in a clockwise direction, [one should place] the nectar-syllables (amṛtārṇa) accompanied by the first peak-syllable (kūṭa) of the first vidyā among the sixfold Amṛteśvarī-vidyās.

Having written down the one hundred and sixty [syllables], one should write in the pericarp in their midst the form of the syllable written on the first petal among those syllables written on the outer petals— namely,
the first peak (kūṭa) of the vidyā-syllables, accompanied by the syllable of the object to be accomplished (sādhya) situated in its middle. This...

The first yantra: In this very yantra, among the ten [types] described, the yantra endowed with the syllables of the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) brings about the attainment of one's desired goal.
By drawing them in mutual combination, they become infinite. (74)
Having drawn twenty lines running east-west and north-south,
one should produce three hundred and sixty-one perfectly equal squares.
One should erase forty-five [squares] from that corner;
the remainder, consisting of one hundred eighty-one squares, shall indeed be the vajra.
There, in the directions as before, one should form a triangle with four [lines];
within those [triangles], one should write the respective vidyās, joined with the names of the six objects to be accomplished.
In each lotus among the ten immortal syllables,

according to the sequence of divisions to be described in the section on latent impressions (*vāsanā*), the number of yantras produced through the application of the sixteen vowels is stated in a sentence of fourteen syllables within the ocean of the bliss of knowledge.

The king of the essence of wisdom (dhīdasārarāṭ) is 20,922,389,888,000; each one of these [numbers] is a yantra according to the sequence of divisions to be described in the chapter on the *vāsanā*, situated within and outside the ten lotuses (*daśapadma*) through the distinction of the syllables of the ten nectars (*amṛta*).
It bestows knowledge, being the deer of the destroyer: 3,628,800.
The number produced by sentences of seven syllables occurs [as follows]. Taken together, the number of yantras produced by a single *kūṭa* is expressed by a sentence of twenty syllables:
"ananajñānabhāvaḥ somaśambhudhīrdhanyaścidvaro dharmmastha."

756,921,994,557,440,000; in this manner, for each syllable of the other two *kūṭas* as well, there are this many yantras. Therefore, because the number of yantras arising from each individual *kūṭa* exceeds even the number of a *parārdha*, they are infinite.

For the other five vidyās, which arise from the reversal of these two *kūṭa*-yantras, there is no other *kūṭa* [to serve as their source]; therefore, they have these very same yantras. Consequently, in the ultimate sense, no difference exists between them. || 74 ||

With these eight verses beginning with "east and west" and ending with "the attainments," he teaches the sixfold *vajra*-machine of the grid (*koṣṭha-vajrayantra*) and its applications. In that context, "even" means each one is individually a perfect square relative to the others. "From its corners" refers to that [grid].
In the four corner directions of the yantra consisting of the stated number of squares,
there are forty-five squares— meaning forty and five— each direction having four, as is understood from the context. In those four corners, they are each established according to their own nature.
"Endowed with the name of the person to be accomplished" (sādhyākhyāsamāyutām) means being joined with the name of the practitioner, the person to be accomplished, and the name of the rite.
"From the beginning of the middle [square]" (prāṅmadhyamārambhāt) means starting from the middle square of the five squares situated in the row directly to the east.

By the statement "the five situated in the middle of the corners," one should write [the letters] in the seventh enclosure, which consists of eight squares, in the corner located in each of the four directions.
As before, starting from the center of the east and proceeding clockwise upon entry.
O Dear One, one should draw one hundred and sixty oceans of nectar in their proper sequence.
In the remaining five located in the corners and the center,
one should indeed write the other five [syllables] according to the stated sequence, from the outermost to the middle.
The six vajra-diagrams, each joined with the syllables of the name of the person to be protected,
serve as yantras that provide protection against diseases and other afflictions everywhere.
One should perform the pacification of portents and other auspicious rites;
for in whatever region this group of six yantras is thus well-worshipped, [there shall be prosperity].
The first [set] consists of the squares starting from the outer fire-corner (southeast);

"the others," however, refers to those distinct from the self-perfected *vidyās* written in the five triangles. The syllables of the *kūṭas* of those respective *vidyās*, joined with the letters of the target (*sādhya*), are associated with the six *vidyās*. Of those yantras—

The protection against diseases and the like is the result; this is the implied meaning. Other auspicious results include the attainment of longevity, prosperity, sons, wealth, and so forth. In that region, *mārī* refers to the power that causes destruction through a single disease across the entire territory. This is what is meant here.

Regarding the sequence for drawing the diagram: having struck twenty lines—ten each oriented east-west and north-south, with equal intervals between them—one generates three hundred and sixty-one squares;
within those, in each of the four corners, there are forty-five [squares] in every corner.
Having combined the compartments to form one hundred and eighty compartments and erased them in the shape of a vajra as before,
one should then combine four compartments in each of the four directions from among the remaining one hundred and eighty-one compartments, resulting in sixteen compartments in total.
Having cleansed those respective places and drawn three-cornered triangles there as before,
one should write the first of the six Amṛteśvarī-vidyās within those triangles, incorporating the three *kūṭas* joined with the *sādhya* and other elements according to one's own intention.
In one hundred and sixty-five remaining squares, as before,
starting from the central square of the five squares situated in the eastern row along with the *sava*,
and proceeding by way of clockwise entry, [one should place] the one hundred and sixty "oceans of nectar" (*amṛtārṇa*) as previously described.
Having written up to one hundred and fifty-six syllables as far as the end of the sixth enclosure (*āvaraṇa*),

one should write the remaining four syllables in the eight squares of the seventh enclosure, placing them in the four squares located in the cardinal directions starting from the east, while excluding the four corner squares.

In the five squares consisting of the four squares located in the corners to be avoided and the central square, one should write the remaining five mantras of Amṛteśvarī— starting from the fire-square (southeast) and proceeding clockwise up to the center— as previously described, with the three triangles inscribed at the cardinal directions.

One should draw [the name of] the person to be accomplished (sādhya). This is the first yantra. In this same manner, for each of the five vidyās beginning with Amṛteśvarī-dvitīyā, one should insert the vidyā of one’s own choice. Furthermore, there [in that context], thieves, planetary spirits (graha), diseases, pestilence (mārī), famine, and enemies [are to be averted].
Prosperities do not always exist, yet they also inevitably come to pass. || 82 ||
Having drawn twelve lines running east-west and north-south,
one should gradually erase the one hundred and twenty-one squares on all sides in sequence.
In the remaining fifty-one squares of the sixty-one-fold grid,
one should write in the center the mantra born on that day, accompanied by its name.
Having formed triangles one by one in those directions according to the rule,
one should draw them from the eastern triangle as before, starting from the letter of emergence (udayākṣara).

Having drawn [the figures] in the three outer triangles as before, one should then produce five yantras by drawing five central squares for each of the remaining five groups starting from the one immediately following that; thus,
together with the previously mentioned one, six yantras are completed, and through them, the prescribed applications [are to be performed].
Having performed [these], one shall obtain the fruits that have been described. || 82 ||
With these eight verses beginning with *prākpratyak* and ending with *saṃyutaḥ*,
[the text describes] the construction of the vajra-mechanism consisting of sixty-one squares, the worship of the couples therein,
the general fruit thereof, the attainment of specific fruits through the worship of specific substances, and the specific times.

And he teaches the specific fruit resulting from worship. In that context, "on all sides" (abhitaḥ) means as before, in each of the four corners; this is an adverbial phrase meaning "endowed with ten and five.
The meaning is that one should erase fifteen squares. [Regarding] "vajraikaṣaṣṭike":

This means in the sixty-first square of the Vajrarūpa yantra. "In the center" means in the very middle square. "The mantra born on that day" refers to the mantra obtained as the daily deity for that specific day among the Kālanityā mantras taught in the fifteenth chapter. It is accompanied by its name, as previously described.

"Containing the triad beginning with the practitioner (sādhaka)" means from each individual square; "in every direction" is the ellipsis; "according to rule" means with three lines on all sides. "As before, within the *hṛllekhā*" means starting from the western triangle, that is, beginning from the front triangle. "From the letter of arising (*udayākṣara*)"—

The meaning is: beginning from the syllable obtained at the moment of sunrise on each respective day, according to the sequence stated in the twenty-fifth chapter; "in order" means through the successive rotation of five or six days; "pairs" refers to those mentioned in the chapter on the Nityā and Anityā [mantras]; here, in this yantra, by means of the application of the sequence of ghaṭikās, [one should proceed] during those respective ghaṭikās.

"Pratighaṭikam" means by way of the sequence of pairs (mithunaka) obtained from each respective hour (ghaṭikā). "Tathā" means by those [methods] such as those stated in the chapter on Nityānityā. "Anyajāsu" means those arising from spirits, ghosts, planetary influences (graha), and so forth. The other [terms] are locative plurals.
One should worship the sixty syllables here as pairs in their proper sequence, using perfumes, flowers, and other offerings according to the progression of the *ghaṭikās*. (86)
In intense afflictions arising from battle, from disease, or from other causes, those sufferings indeed quickly reach pacification through worship performed there. (87)
One should worship the deities for the sake of prosperity with reddish fragrant flowers, or with white ones endowed with fragrance; from the maṇḍala, one shall obtain fortune. || 88 ||
Having thus propitiated the couples during the full moon days according to the prescribed rite, one certainly obtains every desired object within a year. || 89 ||
Thus, by worshipping for three lifetimes, one shall live happily for a hundred years—
free from disease, devoid of mental anguish, and endowed with the conduct of renunciation.
In cruel rites of malevolent magic (abhicāra), one should indeed worship couples day and night within a vajra-diagram accompanied by the object to be accomplished (sādhya).

There are three steps, which are qualifiers of the steps in cases of intense suffering. Therein, in the case of a mechanical device (*yantra*), it is by means of days as before; in the three types of full offerings (*pūrṇā*) during the three births, it is as before. This is what is meant:
having stretched twelve threads with equal intervals running east-west and north-south.
Having prepared one hundred and twenty-one squares, and having erased sixty squares— fifteen in each of the four corners, totaling sixty—
to form the shape of a vajra as before, [one proceeds] with the remaining sixty-one squares in the four cardinal directions.
Having cleared one square in each direction and fashioned equilateral triangles there with three equal lines, [one should proceed] starting from the triangle situated in the western direction,
within the twenty squares of the outer enclosure accompanied by triangles, and within the sixteen squares of the second enclosure.
In the twelve squares of the third enclosure, the eight squares of the fourth enclosure,
and the four squares of the fifth enclosure— thus, in sixty squares in total—
one proceeds according to the sequence of *ghaṭikās* from the syllable of the *ghaṭikā* attained at sunrise on that particular day.

Having written the letters of the sixty *ghaṭikās* currently in operation within the womb of the *hṛllekhā* by way of clockwise entry, one should write in the central square, within the womb of the *hṛllekhā*, the daily *nityā-vidyā* for that specific day,
containing the three names beginning with the practitioner's name; then, for each successive *ghaṭikā* starting from that day...

The attainment of the respective results occurs through the worship of the pairs (mithunas) reached during those specific ghaṭikās at the prescribed times and for the duration of the prescribed times, by means of the mantras and other elements taught in the chapter on Nityānityā. || 90 ||
(510) The king was [attended] by mantrins who were assigned to specific days, who were constant devotees, excellent, affectionate, and had received their sacrificial fees. || 92 ||
After some very auspicious days have passed, it destroys the practitioner;
likewise, having fashioned a very large diamond upon a surface of three metals and stone... (93)
One should draw the śaktis all around and write those [syllables] within their respective compartments;
having written the object of the rite (sādhya) in the center, one should bury it in houses and other locations.
Therein, his desired prosperities shall be constant, free from disturbance, without rivals, incomparable, endowed with right policy, and uninterrupted. (95)
O wise one, hear now the vidyā-mantras of those śaktis who are said to be worshipped in the wheel during the full consecration (pūrṇābhiṣeka), by means of which one attains a perfected body.

With these five verses beginning with "krūreṣu" and ending with "nirantarāḥ," he teaches the method for countering malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) by means of that very [mantra], as well as the method for protecting the house and so forth through its installation. Therein, one should worship as previously stated...

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "by means of the sequence of mantras for the food offering (naivedya) and so forth. In the previously described Vajrayantra, "according to the watches" (yāmataḥ) means by eight rounds, each consisting of one watch (yāma) from among the eight watches of a day and night, which are assigned to the respective days of the week (vārakalpitaiḥ). "By those who are very skillful" (sudakṣiṇaiḥ).

By those skilled in the practices taught in the *Nityātantra*, depending on the gravity or lightness of the task, within a few days—by means of one, two, or more mandalas—the practitioner [achieves] the performer of the *abhicāra*.
That *abhicāra* is the "vajra," the *mithuna-vajrayantra*. In every respect...
In the sixty-one squares of that yantra, [one should place] the Śakti Hṛllekhā.

In its enclosure, in the portion of the letter *ra* of Hṛllekhā, are those Ghaṭikā-syllables. In the center, within the Ghaṭikā-syllables, one should bury that yantra as before, together with the Prāṇapratiṣṭhā, worship, and so forth, according to the Mātṛkā-paṭala.
In the manner previously described; in that location; continuous, being extended without interruption. || 95 ||
By means of these five verses beginning with "The full consecration" (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) and ending with "the moving and the unmoving" (*carācara*),

[the text describes] each of those deities to be worshipped in the wheel of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣekacakra*) taught in the second chapter, numbering one thousand four hundred and forty-four.

He also teaches the nature of the sixteen-syllable mantra. In that regard, it is as described in the second chapter concerning the wheel (*cakra*): by means of those powers (*śakti*)—that is, by means of those power-mantras (*vidyā*)—one becomes the perfected body, the very self of the Goddess.

(511) But by means of those arising from the consonants (*khara*), which arise together with the eternal ignorance (*avidyā*) and are impelled by the [vowels] that have been endured, [the mantra is formed] entirely without exception, excluding the vowels (*svara*). || 97 ||
Combined with one thousand four hundred and forty,
it is endowed with the two seed-syllables mentioned in the worship of Lalitā-Śakti.
O Ambikā, one should worship [the deity] together with the power of form (rūpaśakti), ending with the seven-syllable mantra, using those vidyās consisting of sixteen syllables for each. 99.
Thus has been told to you in its entirety the pervasive majesty of the Vidyā,
of which this entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, is seen to consist.
Together with the fifty-seven [Nityās] arising from vowels— namely, the Nityā-mantras produced from the *Vaśinī* group among the *Kālanityā* mantras mentioned in the twenty-fifth chapter—
and together with the fifty-seven [Nityās] arising from those [consonants], namely, the Nityās produced from the letters *sa* and *ha* within them.

The term "eternal vidyās" (*nityāvidyābhiḥ*) is the object to be qualified. "Proclaimed" (*samīritāḥ*) refers to the vidyās that are devoid of the six vowels and the group beginning with *vaśinī*, and which are free from the one hundred and forty-four eternal vidyās produced by the four sets of four neuter syllables consisting of the letters *sa* and *ha*.
The meaning is as follows: "forty-four hundred" means four hundred and forty, that is, five hundred and seventy-six.
This refers to the number five hundred and seventy-six produced from the *Vasini* group of the *Kalanityavidya*, as stated in the twenty-fifth chapter [of the *Tantraraja*], namely 20736.
Among those sciences arising from the letter *sakāra* which have been stated to be that number,
the four hundred and forty-four sciences produced by the neuter (*ṣaṇḍa*) syllables are excluded;
the remaining number is four hundred and thirty-two.
The *vidyās* are the syllables of pride (*ahaṃkāra*) numbering as many as those [deities], namely the *nityā-vidyās* numbering one thousand four hundred;
these *vidyās*, which are said to be limbs (*aṅga*) of that Śrīcakra, consist of uncommon three-syllable forms. They are endowed with two seed-syllables (*bīja*).

"Endowed with the seed-syllable of Māyāśrī" means that at the very beginning of all [mantras], this is the remainder [of the instruction]. "Accompanied by Rūpaśakti" means endowed with the four syllables "Rūpaśakti. This refers to the end of the previously mentioned uncommon three-syllabled vidyās of Kālanityā. At the very end of all [mantras], there is the seven-syllabled [mantra].

The meaning is that it is accompanied by the seven-syllable vidyā mentioned in the second chapter. All of this is an adjective qualifying the form of the uncommon three-syllable Nityā-vidyā. By "those," one refers to the ones previously introduced; those vidyās are as follows: Hrīṃ Śrīṃ A Ā I.
"I worship the sandals of Rūpaśakti," and so forth, ending with "hrīṃ śrīṃ haḥ kṣa ī,
I worship the sandals of Rūpaśakti. These aforementioned number of Śaktis belong to the Śaktis residing within the Śrīcakra of Lalitā, beginning with Aṇimā and ending with Mahātripurasundarī.
The obscuring powers (*āvaraṇa-śaktayaḥ*) of the ninety-six [deities] exist through a division of fifteen for each.
Thus, the pervasive pervasion (*vyāpti*) consisting of the nature of the Rule (*niyama*) has been correctly explained.
By the constant cultivation of this [meditation], that very reality is made one's own within the mind. || 101 ||
Thus, in the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*, within the *Śrīkādimata*, the twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Majesty of Mantras" (*Mantravaibhava*), is fully concluded and examined. 26. Oṃ.
Therefore, each of those [deities], beginning with Aṇimā, possesses the nature of the sixteen Nityās, just like the root deity. Consequently, when taken together,
they constitute one thousand five hundred and thirty-six manifest Yoginīs.
Up to: "That which consists of the Vidyā, that is, the Lalitā-vidyā, is 'vidyāmaya' (composed of the Vidyā). || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete tantra known as the venerable *Kādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The twenty-sixth chapter, which is devoted to revealing the pervasive power of the mantra that illuminates the pervasiveness of the sixteen Nityās, has been fully considered. Oṃ tat sat.
The number of yantras is 2,277,738,598,367,232,000,000. By means of knowledge, Śrī Gaurī, Sitāṅgā, Dugdhā, Śabdagā, Svātmā, Suraśrī, and so forth— these are the twenty-one-syllable yantra-numbers.
The number of verses— stated in the twenty-sixth chapter, the commentary consists of four hundred and thirty-eight verses in total,
clearly by that count.
The Twenty-Seventh Chapter. Now, the Prāṇatoḍaka is declared according to the sequence of the sixteen Nityās,
together with the Mātṛkās, the Bhūtanāthas, and so forth, as well as the Śrīcakra and the Śaktis.
However, because time is difficult to perceive for those beginning with the *lava*,
it has been stated that one should begin with a single breath and proceed gradually by counting its repetitions.
Having explained its pervasion throughout the day and night, one should infer other [details] from it—
both internal and external particulars— which serve to establish the respective accomplishments.

In the preceding twenty-sixth chapter, having taught the pervasion of the sixteen *Nityās*— which is intent upon revealing the majesty of their pervasive power— as well as the pervasion of the mantras and the *Vidyā* of *Amṛteśvarī* who consists of that [pervasion], [the author] next [teaches] of the sixteen *Nityās*.

The twenty-seventh chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" (*atha ṣoḍaśa*) and ending with "would come to be" (*bhavet*), teaches— through [the teachings of] Mātṛkā, Bhūtanātha, and others, along with the Śrīcakra and the Śaktis— the state of being the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇātmatā*) and so forth by means of Time (*kāla*). In that [chapter], [it begins] with "Now, sixteen," etc.

He teaches the meaning of the chapter with three verses beginning with *rūpāpādaka*. In that context, "by time" means by the three times whose nature is breath (*prāṇa*), [attaining] identity with that; "by the lords of the elements, the Mothers, and so forth" means by the fifty letters of the Mātṛkā, from *a* to *kṣa*, excluding the visarga.
By the five elements, the nine lords, and by the term "and so forth" (ādya), [it is] by the thirty-six principles and the rest;
by the Śrīcakra consisting of nine wheels, and by the powers (śaktis) located therein, numbering ninety-six and ninety-one;
and by the divisions of time beginning with the lava and ending with the truṭi, since the measure of the [subtler] moments and so forth is difficult to perceive.

The phrase "its stated nature" (tadīritaṃ svarūpam) is the ellipsis, because it is impossible to know [otherwise]. By those numbers—that is, by the numbers of breaths that have arisen in the form of ghaṭikās, days, nights, and so forth—[it occurs] sequentially, according to the sequence to be described. The word "of the day and night" (ahorātrasya) is to be construed with the preceding term "by those numbers" (tatsaṃkhyābhiḥ).

Having stated that its pervasion consists in being of the nature of breath (*śvāsa*), one should infer other things by means of it. "Different agency" arises from autonomy (*svātantrya*). "Other" refers to the specific forms of time such as months and years; the remainder is that these are the movement and function of the breaths. This is [inferred] from the internal, consisting of the rising of the elements (*bhūtodaya*) and so forth, and from the external.

From the regions of the right and left sides and so forth, [one perceives] those factors that bring about various accomplishments and produce auspicious or inauspicious results. This is what is meant: by way of the nature of the sixteen Nityās—which are identical with them—such as Mātṛkā and the rest, in their form as breath and as time.
(514) The wind arising from the *mūlādhāra* assumes the names of *prāṇa* and so forth through its two-fold pervasion of both the internal and external;
it is fivefold according to the distinctions of the elements and the locations of its emergence. (4)
In the two nostrils, the winds—consisting of air, fire, wind, water, and ether—flow respectively from the sides, the top, the middle, the lower opening, and the center. (5)
Jupiter and Ketu, Venus and Mars, Mercury and the Sun, and the Moon and Saturn [preside over] the four elements in order; space (vyoman) is the soul of all.
Rāhu should be situated on both sides of the Moon and the Sun according to the sequence of the nostrils;
his entry and exit are through their left and right [nostrils] respectively.
The soul, the moon, and the sun; the void, as well as the female and the male; earth, water, the moon, and the sun—the other three shall likewise be so. (8)
Because those breaths bestow auspicious and inauspicious results as will be described hereafter, it follows that he shall state their external and internal distinctions. || 3 ||
With the two verses beginning with *mūlādhāre* and ending with *yathākramam*,

he teaches the arising of the breaths, how they acquire their respective designations due to the differences in their functions, and the specific sequence of their arising as they consist of the elements. Among these, [the first] is the arising from the *mūlādhāra*.
Arising from the region of the *mūlādhāra*, which has the form described in the chapter on the eternal and the non-eternal,

that wind— whose nature has been explained— takes the name "prāṇa" and so forth; the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the other distinctions such as apāna, vyāna, and the rest, according to their respective sites of origin.

In the locations of perception, which are situated in the two nostril cavities as will be described immediately below— specifically within the two *puṭas*, that is, the two apertures— the flows proceed respectively through the lateral, elevated, central, lower, and apertural [channels], moving transversely, upwards, as a staff, downwards, and through the middle. The elision of the visarga is due to poetic license (*svātantryāt*).

By means of these seven verses beginning with "guru" and ending with "īritau," [the text] explains how the breaths (*śvāsa*), through their specific modes of arising and the specific times of the five desired locations, possess the nature of the elevenfold Moon and Sun.
He indicates the nature of Rāhu along with that [of Ketu] by means of the verse beginning with "There, Guru and Ketu... What is meant here is as follows:
when the four elemental breaths (bhūtodayas)—consisting of air, fire, earth, and water—flow through both nostrils in the sequence of left and right, respectively.
At the emergence of the void (*vyomodaya*), there occurs the state of being composed of the pairs of planets mentioned in the sequence,
as well as the state of being composed of the eight planets including Rāhu and the Moon. Being situated in both— that is, residing within both channels—
the cause for the flow of the breaths in such and such a manner is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
The phrase "left and right" is to be construed with "the two nostrils" from the preceding context. Within each of those two nostrils, there are likewise the moon and the sun;
[as for the planets] in the houses: the Moon is in Jupiter's house, Jupiter, the Moon, and Mercury are in [Jupiter's], while the Sun is in the others.
And likewise the Mātṛkā-vidyā, according to the distinction between vowels and consonants. || 9 ||
The moon should be at the bottom and on the back, while the sun should be at the top and in front;
likewise, within the body, the jar is said to have the moon above and the sun below.
The statement "it exists" refers to the Moon, while that which is said to be "it does not exist" is known as the Sun;
likewise, the two sides, white and black, are the Moon and the other periods (daśās). || 11 ||
Thus, O illustrious lady, the ten Suns have been declared according to their external and internal aspects;
the elevenfold forms of the Moon and the Sun have been correctly described.
Of these two, the moons are bringers of joy, while the suns cause affliction;
Rāhu and the void everywhere lead to destruction in an instant. (13)
Everything is auspicious under the Sun; however, eating soft foods and sexual intercourse are recommended everywhere.
Under the Moon, all other undertakings are accomplished without effort.

The word "bhāga" (portion) is to be construed with what follows. Thus, the meaning is "the Moon and the Sun. The other triad consists of Fire, Wind, and Space; the others are Mars, Saturn, Rāhu, Ketu, and the Sun. Likewise, "the Moon and the Sun" are at the top-front;
this is the first dual number. Likewise, the Moon and the Sun are the internal ones.

They are devoid of the nature of being [mere] sides. In the manner described above, the word "ten" is to be construed with the preceding term "internal. With the external moon and sun, which consist of the white and black forms respectively—the particle *ca* indicating a collective compound—[the total is twenty]. || 12 ||

With the verse beginning with "tayoh," he teaches the general result for the moon, sun, Rāhu, and the void as previously mentioned. In that context, the "suns" (bhāskarāḥ) are devoid of the form of the void. || 13 ||
With these four verses beginning with "In the suns" (*sūryeṣu*) and ending with "the Supreme Goddess" (*parameśvarī*),

[the author] teaches the rites to be performed when the Moon, Sun, Rāhu, and the Void are present, as well as the specific results according to the particular mode of questioning. Among those, "in the suns" refers to the eleven types of solar positions.

The phrase "with eating, sexual intercourse, and battle" (mṛdha-bhojana-maithunaiḥ) implies "eating, sexual intercourse, and battle" (yuddha-bhojana-maithunaiḥ). The word "saṃgraha" (collection/summary) connects with the preceding term "śasta" (praised). All other remaining actions are of an auspicious nature. [This applies] when the Moon is in its elevenfold [divisions].

It has been stated that one becomes determined regarding what is real, whether desired or undesired; having determined "it exists" or having determined "it does not exist," the truth is declared regarding the living soul (*jīva*), and the vision of the pure (*medhya-darśa*) is accomplished.
It is said that it exists having been determined; otherwise, it would be otherwise.

If the rule is not determined, one should firmly declare the result after due deliberation: "In the question regarding a maiden's pregnancy, if [the relevant factor] is from another [sign], it is a male; if it is empty, there will be a miscarriage," and so forth.
O Supreme Goddess, when Rāhu is in the empty sky, even auspicious [planets] become inauspicious;
there, all auspicious things perish.
When the wind flows through the left [nostril], the teacher,
having placed [the disciple] in that position, should whisper the mantra into his ear.
Alternatively, one should impart the mantra into the ear of that person when he is in the position of the living soul (jīvaga);
otherwise, it leads to the destruction of both the teacher and the disciple, like a Rāhu in an empty state.
This means that the stated result comes to pass. Otherwise, if it is otherwise, then if it is stated in the void (*śūnya*), it becomes void.

Regarding the phrase "in uncertainty" (*aniścaye*), which is a qualifier for "the query concerning pregnancy" (*garbhapraśna*), the word division is *garbha-praśna*. If [the calculation] is from elsewhere in the Sun, excluding the void (*śūnya*), then in the void—
In the phrase "when the sun is of the nature of emptiness" (*śūnyarūpasūrye*) and so forth, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the subject matter of a question regarding an uncertain effect.
What is meant is this: when the effect is uncertain, if it is the moon, then whatever is desired occurs; if it is the sun, then whatever is undesired occurs. In that regard:
The meaning is that inauspicious things perish and cease to exist within the void of the sky-like Rāhu. || 17 ||

With the two verses beginning with "on the left" (*vāme*) and ending with "of the two disciples" (*śiṣyayoḥ*), the Guru teaches the specific time for imparting the mantra to the disciple and the transgression incurred by failing to do so. In that context, the phrase "of the teacher and the disciple" (*deśika-śiṣyayoḥ*) is to be construed with the preceding word "on the left" (*vāme*); that is, in its place, on the left side.

That [mantra] is placed in the ear of that disciple—that is, in the left ear; or else, in another sense, in the place of the *jīva* (the vital breath), according to the distinction between left and right—that is, in the ear of the *jīva*. Otherwise, by way of the reversal of the two aforementioned methods, this is the placement of the *jīva* on the left side.

In the instruction on the entire mantra-cycle that is eternally free from ignorance, we have already previously stated that for the Nityās— namely, Svacchandā, Vārāhī, and Kurukullā— their respective installation in front [of the practitioner] occurs within their respective worship-circles (pūjācakra). Here, regarding those who reside in their own seats...
The other means for understanding the arising of the true nature of the elements and so forth should be understood from the mouth of one who has attained [realization].
Three hundred and sixty breaths are considered to be one nāḍikā;
sixty of those constitute a full day, and that day occurs again and again. (20)
But on a single day, there are twenty-one thousand and six hundred breaths; now listen to their true nature, O beautiful one. (21)
Beginning from sunrise in the morning, there are two hundred and seventy breaths in sequence;
[the elements] air, fire, water, and earth [correspond to these], while elsewhere the transition occurs at ninety [breaths].

In that case it is thus, and elsewhere it is likewise; according to the sequence of the ten [days], one should proceed through the day in this manner, beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight (darśa-pratipad).

With the two verses beginning with "sixty" and ending with "Sundarī," he provides an instruction on the nature of time through the specific numbers of one's own breaths in the form of *ghaṭikās* and days, and introduces the form of those breaths. In that context, regarding those *nāḍikās*, that day—
[This] consists of sixty nāḍikās due to their repeated revolution; [this refers to] those breaths. "O Sundarī" is an address to the Goddess. || 21 ||

By means of these three verses beginning with "ārabhya" and ending with "bhavanti hi," the time of the rising [of the breath] in the two nostrils— beginning from the first day of the lunar fortnight (pratipad) and so forth— and the sequence of the transition to the other nostril are explained, following the reversal of the previously stated conclusion.

And he teaches the result: therein, two hundred breaths correspond to seventy [units]. With ninety breaths, there is a transition to the other nostril; this is the time of transition from one nostril to the other.
Because it flows through both nostrils simultaneously, that is Rāhu—this is the meaning. Therein also:

Even within the interval of the transition (*saṃkrānta-puṭāntara*), it is thus according to the previously stated limit of time. Beyond this, the transition occurs within another interval of transition, according to the previously stated limit of time.
Thus, by the rotation of the aforementioned modes, there are fifteen rotations; the phrase "at the beginning of the ages" (*yugānām*) is to be understood as the remainder.

The grammatical connection is "at every new moon" (*darśa*), "at every first day" (*pratipad*), meaning "at every first day of the bright fortnight. What is being stated here for all living beings is that, on the first day of the bright fortnight at the beginning of the Yugas, starting from sunrise, within one *puṭa* (cycle).

One thousand three hundred and fifty (1,350) breaths constitute the arising of the five elements. Thereafter, with ninety breaths, there is a transition into another channel. Thus, one complete cycle consists of one thousand four hundred and forty (1,440) breaths. In this manner...

The established conclusion is that in fifteen cycles there are twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths; this begins at sunrise on the morning of the first day of the bright fortnight during the commencement of a Yuga,
proceeding through the left and right nostrils in succession.
(518) Thus, the arising of the vital breath for all has been described in this sequence;
indeed, by reversing this order, they become unfit. 24.
Those with strength in excess are mobile on the left side and strong and stable on the right;
those possessing both natures are present on both sides for the examination of the auspicious and the inauspicious. (25)
From the sequence of twenty-two and a half breaths, the twelve zodiac signs arise; therein, by a sequence of four and a half [breaths] each, the elements occur in order. (26)

In all the syllables of the *ghaṭikā*, when the breaths arise one by one starting with air (*vāyu*) and so on, the breaths produced from those respective syllables are said to be three hundred and sixty. (27)

Within each of the five elements, the flow and transition of breaths occur for the duration of the time specified. Thus, fifteen such cycles constitute one day. On the following day, it proceeds in the same manner, beginning from the right nostril.

In this manner, sequentially up to the new moon, the rising of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) for all occurs through the process of beginning with the reversal of the *puṭas* every day; however, if this sequence is inverted, great misfortunes arise. || 24 ||

With the verse beginning with *valādhikā*, he teaches that during the flow of the breath through the left, right, or both nostrils, there is an increase in the strength (*bala*) of the substances such as the *cara* and others. In this context, "when the wind flows in the left" or "in the right" is to be understood as previously explained.
"In both cases," as before, refers to the examination of the auspicious and inauspicious; the ellipsis is "of actions" characterized as mobile, fixed, or both. (25)
With the verse beginning with *sārddha* and so forth, he teaches that the elements and the zodiacal signs possess a mutual pervasion through the sequence of breaths. In that regard,
from the sequence of twenty-two and a half breaths, there are the twelve signs.

The meaning is that, by combining the previously stated number of breaths according to the sequence of the zodiac signs (*rāśi*), each individual element (*bhūta*) becomes twelve zodiac signs consisting of that same number of breaths.
In this context, the phrase "in each one of those zodiac signs" is the ellipsis; [this occurs] by means of four and a half [breaths] per sign.

The remainder [is as follows]: This is what is meant: within each of the twelve zodiac signs, which consist of the aforementioned number of breaths, the elements arise individually in each sign, becoming composed of the aforementioned number of breaths for each element. || 26 ||

With the two verses beginning with *ghaṭikā* and ending with *akṣaraiḥ*, he teaches the syllables of the rising *ghaṭikās* each day, the fact that those *ghaṭikā*-syllables consist of breaths, and the sequence of the arising of the elemental syllables within those breaths. Therein:

p. 519) Among those, for the ten syllables that have become those [deities], the first ten [are formed] by a sevenfold repetition; thereafter, the remaining [syllables] are [formed] by the syllables of breath (prāṇa), fire (agni), water (ambu), ether (kha), and the eye (akṣi). || 28 ||
O beautiful one, hear from me the pervasion of the breaths by means of numbers, through which, when practiced, the practitioner of mantra shall always possess divine vision. (29)

The word division is: "sarvatra," "sarveṣu dineṣu," "vāyvādi," and "ekāntarā udaye. This is what is meant: in all the days of the *yugas*, with respect to the syllables of the *ghaṭikās*, [the sequence] is at intervals of one. Therefore, "ya" refers to the five syllables of the wind (*vāyavya*), which, through the sequence of the five days, constitute the syllables of the rising *ghaṭikās*.
"Proceeds" means that those [breaths] arise from their respective *ghaṭikās*, consisting of the letters (*varṇa*) of those respective *ghaṭikās*. This is what is meant:
the breaths, which consist of *ghaṭikās* according to the previously mentioned method, become both the nature of those respective *ghaṭikās* and the form of letters. Within those breaths...

Among the three hundred and sixty *ghaṭikā*-syllables consisting of those elemental letters (*bhūta-varṇa*) that have been mentioned, there are ten breaths (*śvāsa*) for each respective elemental letter obtained per syllable; this is the remainder. The remaining [letters] number three hundred and fifty. This is what is meant:

In the sixty-fold *ghaṭikās* consisting of syllables such as those previously mentioned for the rising [of breath], within each *ghaṭikā* there are three hundred and sixty breaths; among these, the first ten breaths correspond to the elemental syllables and phonemes obtained through the respective *ghaṭikā* and syllable.
Then, ten [letters] beginning with *t* and ending with *d* arise in their own form.

The remaining three hundred and fifty, however, consist of the *śva* [consonants] alone; thus, by a sequence of ten each, they correspond respectively to the five groups of letters beginning with *t* and ending with *bh*, for each individual element (*bhūta*).

The forms consisting of ten syllables each arise seven times in their own nature. This being the case, for every ghaṭikā, there are eight revolutions of the ten elemental syllables obtained from those respective syllables, and [four revolutions] of the remaining four elemental syllables.
And thus, there are seven cycles; in this manner, by the sequence of one ghaṭikā each, they consist of the phonemes whose nature is the five elements. || 28 ||

With these four verses beginning with "By numbers" (*saṃkhyābhiḥ*) and ending with "the Sovereign Lady" (*īśvarī*), [the author] provides, preceded by an introduction, a detailed sub-classification of the eleven types of intermediate pervasions— ranging from time (*kāla*) and constancy (*nitya*) up to the powers (*śakti*) situated within the *śrīcakra*— of the breaths (*śvāsa*) whose stated quantities include the days and nights and so forth.

It teaches the pervasion (pṛti), the equal pervasion (samavyāpti), and the majesty of their contemplation. In this context, the connection with what follows is "by means of the numbers of breaths. "The pervasion of latent impressions" (vāsanāvyāpti) means both the latent impression and the pervasion, that is to say, the pervasion consisting of latent impressions. [This refers to] the eleven types that are about to be described.

The remainder [is as follows]: "O Sundarī" is an address to the Goddess. By which pervasion—among the twenty-five vidyās of that eternal non-pervasion mentioned in the twenty-fifth chapter, and among the numbers of breaths of the preceding day and night—one by one...
