The meaning is that [the breaths] are to be known individually in each of these. Therefore, the meaning is "beyond" the previously mentioned number of breaths.
(p. 520) The numbers of the *nityā*, the *avidyāpti*, and the *tattvas* were previously [stated] one by one.
From that, the vowels of the days (dinārṇa) arise as the junctions (sandhyā), and from that, the consonants of the ghaṭikās (ghaṭikārṇaka).
There are twelve zodiac signs, then the planets, the five elements, the fifty Mātṛkās, and the Śaktis residing within the Śrīcakra. || 31 ||
The syllables of the *dināṇṛ* are the syllables of the full mandala. The *sandhyās* are those whose number is sixty-one, obtained through the three junctions (*sandhyā*).
The phrase "beyond the number of breaths of the full mandala" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. From that, [it follows] from that number.
"Beyond": the remainder is that there are sixty letters for the *ghaṭikās*. "Beyond the twelve zodiac signs":
the remainder is that they correspond to the number of letters of the *ghaṭikās*. "From that": from the number of the zodiac signs.
"The planets": nine. "From the elements": five. "The *mātṛkās*": from the number of the elements.

The word "param" (beyond) is to be supplied [to complete the sense]. The syllables are to be understood as being devoid of the fifty *visarjanīya*s. The powers (*śaktayaḥ*) are beyond the number of the *mātṛkā*s; the word "param" is to be supplied. They are ninety-one, because the eight weapons are taken as four pairs and because of the absence of the central deity. Thus says the Goddess.
Lalitā exists in her entirety as the collective totality of the breaths. This is what is meant:
from the beginning, there are twenty-one thousand six hundred breaths that constitute the day and night;
of these, the forms of the Kālanityās number twenty-seven hundred and thirty-six.
Breaths arise. Among the remaining breaths, numbering eight hundred and sixty-four,
those breaths numbering five hundred and seventy-six take on the form and color of the full mandala.
Among the remaining two hundred and eighty-eight breaths (*śvāsa*),
sixty-one breaths consist of the nature of the Lord (*nātha-tattva*) and the Nityās, which take the form of the three junctions (*sandhyā*).
Among the remaining two hundred and twenty-seven breaths, there are sixty breaths.
They consist of sixty letters per day and night. Of the remaining one hundred and sixty-seven breaths, twelve breaths constitute the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*).
Of the remaining one hundred and fifty-five breaths, nine breaths...
They consist of the nine planets (*navagraha*). Of the remaining one hundred and forty-six breaths (*śvāsa*), five breaths consist of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*).
Of the remaining one hundred and forty-one breaths, fifty breaths [consist of the five vital breaths].

The letters of the Mātṛkā, excluding the Visarga, constitute [the remaining breaths]. The ninety-one breaths that remain, corresponding in number to the sequence of the Śrīcakra as previously described, become the form of its power (śakti).
Thus, in this order, the breaths comprising a day and night constitute the collective totality (samaṣṭi).
They possess a universal form with distinct bodies and are of a graceful nature. Herein, the meaning understood from the mouth of Pūjyapāda is written down by his command as follows:
the breaths (śvāsas) mentioned for a day and night consist of fifty syllables of the Mātṛkā.
Through four hundred and thirty-two repetitions, they become composed of that [essence]. O Goddess, these are said to be ninety-one, abiding as the very soul of all.
O Supreme Goddess, he who thus meditates upon the Vidyā and its latent impressions (vāsanā)— || 32 ||

The wheel of channels (nāḍīcakra), the vital points (marmāṇi) within the body, the activity of the vital airs (marut), the practice of yoga along with its ancillaries, and the method for voluntary departure from the body (svecchotkrānti). || 33 ||
Entering another's body is a characteristic of one perfected in yoga;
I shall now describe the signs of approaching death in their proper order.
Situated in the center of the previously mentioned mūlādhāra, from the middle of the triangle,
the suṣumnā runs through the center of the spinal column, which is called the neck of the lute.

The channel named Alambushā is said to extend from the base of the spine to the aperture of Brahma at the crown of the head, reaching twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose, and from its tip, it goes down to the anus.

Furthermore, through four thousand three hundred and twenty revolutions, they consist of the five elements (*pañcabhūta*). Again, through two thousand four hundred revolutions of the nine lords, the Śrīcakra, and the planets, they consist of those respective [entities]. Those, in turn, again...
By repeating the thirty-six principles six hundred times, they become identical with them; furthermore,
by repeating the vowels consisting of the sixteen Nityās one thousand three hundred and fifty times, they become identical with them.
Furthermore, they consist of sixty syllables of the sixty *ghaṭikās* through three hundred and sixty repetitions;

furthermore, they consist of the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśis*) through one thousand eight hundred repetitions; furthermore, they consist of the ninety-six powers (*śaktis*) situated within the Śrīcakra.
Through two hundred and twenty-five repetitions, they become identical with that [reality].
Here, another secret should be understood from the mouth of the Venerable Guru. || 32 ||

With the two verses beginning with "the channels" (*nāḍī*) and ending with "in due order" (*yathākramam*), he teaches the remaining topics of this chapter. In that context, the word "marmas" implies "locations.
"Voluntary departure" (*svecchotkrānti*) means the relinquishing of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) by one's own will. "Entry into another's body" (*parakāyapraveśaṃ*)...
Either the entry of one's own life-force into a dead body, or the entry of that [life-force] from there back into one's own body. || 34 ||

With these ten verses beginning with "prāk" and ending with "pare," he teaches the nature of the wheel of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) and the location of Kuṇḍalinī therein. There, [she resides] in the center of the jewel of the previously mentioned *mūlādhāra*, which was described in the chapter on Nityānityā.

The meaning is that it is sewn through the central opening like a thread in a cloth. The connection with the preceding text is: "the Suṣumnā extends as far as the Brahma-randhra, ending at the Brahma-randhra.
(p. 522) The channel that has arisen from the apex of the triangle is named Kuhū, reaching to the end of the penis.
On its left and right sides are Saviśva and Udārava-raṇa. (37)

The *jaṭharāntā* and *sarvagā* are said to be in the same locations as those [previously mentioned]; likewise, the *hastijihvā* and *yaśasvinī* are located at the respective big toes of the feet. (38)
Likewise, iḍā and piṅgalā are situated at the two nostril apertures;
and similarly, gāndhārī and pūṣā are situated at the two eyes in due order.
By her, the Śaṅkha and Payasvinī [nāḍīs] are indeed located in the ears in succession;
however, that which is the Sarasvatī nāḍī goes to the tip of the tongue.
Thus, fourteen principal channels (nāḍīs) are said to exist in the body;
in the junctions of those very channels, other channels are likewise situated within the physical frame. (41)

"At twelve finger-breadths from the tip of the nose" means at the location starting from the tip of the nose and extending to a distance of twelve finger-breadths; that is, the *brahmarandhra*. "From its tip" means starting from the front portion where the *suṣumnā* begins, down to the anus, ending at the opening of the rectum (*gudarandhra*).

From the tip of the triangle—that is, from the corner of the triangle in the form of the *mūlādhāra*—it extends to the end of the penis (*mehana*). From its left and right sides, it reaches to the end of the abdomen;
that is, it extends to the middle of the belly and reaches everywhere, [flowing] through the channel known as *kuhū*. This is the implied meaning.

"Extending downwards and upwards, all-pervading, the warding-off [is performed]"—this is what was stated; its connection with the preceding is "the warding-off of the belly of the universe. Likewise, in the subsequent [sections], situated to the left and right of that which follows:
"located on the respective big toes of the feet," meaning reaching as far as the big toes of the left and right feet.
The meaning is "it belongs to you. Likewise, immediately following that, starting from the left and right sides, it reaches the ends of the two nostril apertures. This is what is meant:
beginning from the left side of the *suṣumnā* situated in the center of the triangle of the *mūlādhāra*.
Having a protruding curved form at the base of the *dhvaja*, it goes to the right side by adhering to the *suṣumṇā*;
then again from there, by a curved course, it reaches the region of the navel; and once more, by adhering to the *suṣumṇā* and moving in a curve toward the left side, it reaches the heart.

By means of a curved movement resting upon the eight parts of the right side adjacent to the *suṣumnā*, it reaches the region of the throat; then again, by means of a curved upward movement from the left shoulder arising from the side adjacent to the *suṣumnā*, it reaches the region of the *brahmarandhra*; and once more, by means of the side adjacent to the tip of the *suṣumnā*...
The Suṣumnā, which has a downward-facing course by way of a rightward curvature,
becomes the channel named Iḍā, which, by adhering to the Suṣumnā, extends as far as the left nostril; Piṅgalā, however, begins on the right side as before.
Moving in a curved course through a sequence of alternating right and left passages,
[the vital energy] reaches the middle of the vital points (*marman*) at the joints by embracing the upward path of the *suṣumṇā*.
The number of these principal channels (*nāḍī*) is three hundred thousand and fifty thousand.
The secondary vessels in the body are indeed innumerable, by which alone—
Enveloped by all those [elements], the man remains for an eternal night;
the channels, which are hollow and pervade the entire body, are filled with blood and vital air.
The Vajra channel is situated in the middle of the Suṣumnā;
within that is another, called Citrā; and situated in the middle of that is the supreme Kuṇḍalinī.

And she becomes [present] at the end of the right nostril. Likewise, beginning from the immediately following left and right [nostrils], she reaches the two eyes and terminates at those respective two eyes; likewise, beginning from the immediately following left [ear], she reaches the ears and terminates at those respective ears. Sarasvatī.

The one remaining between the two previously mentioned channels, starting from the nose and reaching the tip of the tongue, terminates at the tip of the tongue. Among those fourteen principal channels, [one is located] at their junctions—that is, at the junctions of those principal channels. Of those...

The meaning is that there are three hundred and fifty thousand (*sārddhatrilakṣaka*)— that is, three hundred and fifty thousand— beginnings of junctions (*sandhyārambha*) for the fourteen principal channels (*pradhānanāḍī*) and those called their junctions (*tatsandhyā*). By means of these,
both principal and non-principal, all the channels (*nāḍyaḥ*) are said to be *nāḍikās*.

"Suṣirāḥ" means possessing apertures. "Suṣumnāmadhyagā" means situated within the central aperture of the Suṣumnā. "Tanmadhyagā" means situated within the central aperture of the Vajra-nāḍī. "Sā" (she) is situated in the middle of that, residing within the Citrā-nāḍī.

In the thirtieth chapter, by means of six verses beginning with the sixty-fourth, [the form] to be described is as follows: having drawn a triangle on the ground and having drawn another triangle three finger-breadths outside of it, one should draw twelve horizontal lines between the two, and in the very center of all—

The first letter of Suṣumnā is in its lower part; the first letter of Alambuṣā is in the part preceding it; the first letter of Kuhū is in the central square between the two triangles. Thus, by proceeding clockwise, the first letters of the channels (nāḍīs) are placed in the intervals between the squares. Vāyuṣī.

The tradition is that one should write and display fourteen syllables— namely *pūṣarśa*, *saṃjñāṃ*, *ihayi*, and *vāpapi*— along with the previously mentioned ones, while being apprehensive of the consumption of pus (*pūyasa*). Here,
three summary verses (*saṃgrahaśloka*) are written.
Between the Suṣumṇā and the Alambuṣā is the one known as Kuhūccāraṇa;
the Payasvinī is the Piṅgalā, while the Suṣumṇā is the highly illustrious Suyaśasvinī.
Sarasvatī, Śaṅkhinī, Gāndhārī, Īḍā, Dvipāsyagā, and Viśvodarā are the channels (nāḍīs); this is their order of location.
"Those located in the anus, the genitals, the penis, the navel, the mouth, the eyes, and the ears;
and those ending at the tongue, the ears, the eyes, the nose, the feet, and the belly, [are to be pierced] in a clockwise direction. Thus [it is said]. (44)

The vital points (*marmans*) are located in the thumbs, the ankles, the backs of the feet, the calves, the knees, the thighs, the groin, the testicles, the penis, the navel, and the two sides of the torso. (45)
In the heart, breasts, throat, shoulders, nape of the neck, ears, and head;
in the two temples, and from the outer corners of the eyes, the nose-tip, the middle, the end of the mouth, and the cheeks—46.

Thus, thirty-eight [types] have been declared; by means of the concentration (dhāraṇā) on the wind among these others, entry into another's body and voluntary departure from the body are accomplished.
Listen now to the functions of the ten vital airs (vāyu) residing within the body:
Prāṇa and Apāna are always engaged in moving upward and downward within the body.
The *nāga* wind is said to cause belching, while the *kṛkara* causes hunger;
the *devadatta* causes yawning, and the *dhanañjaya* causes sound. (49)
The *udāna* wind is said to perform the opening of the eyes (*unmeṣa*), and likewise performs two functions;
the *samāna* wind kindles the bodily fire (*kāyāgni*) for the purpose of digestion.
That which is called vyāna takes up the rasa and causes it to pervade the entire body.
Of these ten winds, there are indeed infinite subdivisions. (51)

With these three verses beginning with "The vital points" (*marmāṇi*) and ending with "is accomplished" (*sidhyati*), [the author] teaches the thirty-eight locations of the vital points (*marman*) and the fruit of fixing the breath (*vāyu-dhāraṇa*) therein.
Among these, the *sovanikā* is the channel situated between the scrotum and the anus; the *kṛkāṭī*...
The elevated bony region on the side above the ear;

the temples (*śaṅkha*), which are the elevated bones on the sides of the forehead; and the cheeks (*kapola*). Among these thirty-eight vital points (*marman*), there are twenty-six locations where they occur in pairs; the remaining locations are [single].
Twelve [of these] combined make thirty-eight vital points (*marmas*). In these vital points... [47]

With these five verses beginning with "Of the ten" and ending with "is conceived," preceded by an introduction, he teaches the names, functions, and effects of the ten winds situated within the body; therein, regarding their upward and downward movement, [he says]:
Bound to one another like a chain, they exist simultaneously; "out of envy" is the implied sense.

The two are called *prāṇa* and *apāna*. *Nāga* is a name for the wind (*vāyu*), as are *kṛkara*, *devadatta*, and *dhanañjaya*. *Kūrma* is also a name for the wind. *Udāna* is the one that performs the two functions of opening and closing the eyes.
The *samāna* wind (p. 525):
through its expansion, the body attains a healthy state;
in its perversion, due to the deformity of the limbs, it leads to destruction by the world. || 52 ||
Yoga is to be understood as the union of the individual soul with the Supreme Soul through the mind in a state of non-difference; its limbs are indeed eight.
Then comes restraint (yama), followed by observance (niyama); after that, posture (āsana);
likewise, breath control (prāṇāyāma), then withdrawal of the senses (pratyāhāra), and thereafter concentration (dhāraṇā). || 54 ||
Dhyāna and samādhi—these are said to be the eight limbs in their proper order.
Listen, O wise one, as I describe them, by means of which a mortal may become equal to me. (55)
Their six obstacles have been declared: desire and anger, as well as greed and delusion, pride and arrogance; like fire, they are the destroyers of all.

The wind called *samāna* [is so named because] it digests the food consumed; that is to say, the fire of the body, the digestive fire located below the stomach. The remainder of the sentence is "the wind called *vyāna*.
The remainder of the sentence is "the essence (*rasa*) of the food consumed. "Parts" means the constituent elements. "From expansion" means according to their proper nature.
By way of favorability to movement; in the case of the reverse, by way of unfavorability to movement as it truly is, due to deformed limbs, harmfulness, and so forth. || 52 ||

With the verse beginning with "jīvātma" (the individual self), he provides the definition of yoga and introduces its constituent limbs. In that context, "this single state" refers to the non-dual nature of the individual self (*jīvātman*), with the word "together with the mind" being understood as the remainder of the phrase.
"Of the Supreme Self" means of the Consciousness (*cit*) whose nature is the manifestation of pure existence (*sanmātra*). This is *yoga*.

The relationship is one of identity (*tādātmya*). Of that *yoga*. This is what is meant: *yoga* is the unity consisting in the dissolution of the sense of "this-ness" (*idantā*) among the individual soul (*jīva*), the mind (*manas*), and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), which are perceived as having distinct forms. || 53 ||

With the two verses beginning with *yama* and ending with *bhavet*, he teaches the names of the eight limbs of yoga (*aṣṭāṅga*), introduces their essential nature, and describes their power. In that context, *tathā* functions as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).
Regarding the term *aṣṭāṅgāni*, it is understood from the preceding [verse] by way of the "crow's eye" maxim (*kākākṣivat*).

"I shall tell" is to be connected with what follows. "In its true nature" is the ellipsis for "I shall tell. "By which" refers to those eight-fold aspects; "equal to me" means consisting of me, having the form of Śiva. || 55 ||

With the half-verse beginning with "tat-pratyūha" and ending with "yama," he teaches the obstacles (*pratyūha*) and the nature of *yama*. In this context, "tat-pratyūhāḥ" refers to the obstacles to yoga; they are called "destroyers of all" because they constitute obstacles to the attainment of one's true nature (*svarūpa-lābha*).
But Yama is the restraint of the activities that obstruct the direct realization of the Self.

Yama is the withdrawal from the exertions toward the six—desire and the rest—that have been mentioned as obstacles to the direct realization of one's true nature; it is the limb known by the name of Yama. 56.
Yama is the one whose function is to obstruct the direct perception of the Self;
likewise, Niyama is proclaimed to have eleven forms. (57)
Non-violence, truthfulness, faith, straightforwardness, equanimity, fortitude, forgiveness, compassion, threefold purity, contentment, and service to the guru. (58)
The lotus, the svastika, the hero’s posture, and the auspicious posture have been described in sequence; these postures are indeed effective for achieving stability of mind. (59)
Having placed the soles of the two feet upon the thighs in reverse order, by touching both outer sides [of the thighs], that is declared to be the *padmāsana*. (60)
Likewise, O Īśvarī, when the lower parts of those two [feet] meet at their inner sides in the form of a svastika, that is declared to be the bhadrāsana.

With the first half-verse beginning with "tathaikādaśa" and ending with "sevanam," he teaches the nature of the eleven-fold *niyama* (observances) in a single verse. In that context, "tathā" means that as is *yama*, so too is *niyama*; this is the limb known as *niyama*. *Samatā* (equanimity) refers to [remaining balanced] amidst gain and loss. *Śauca* (purity) is threefold.
Through the forms of mind, speech, and body, contentment is fullness. || 58 ||

With these four verses beginning with "Padma" and ending with "is remembered," he teaches the nature of the eightfold postures (āsanas), preceded by their names. In this context, the remainder [of the meaning] is that "yogic practice" consists in achieving stability of the mind. They are "efficacious" (sādhakāni), meaning they are beneficial.

By the verse beginning with "ūrvorupari" (upon the thighs), this is what is meant: [the left foot] is placed upon the middle of the right thigh, specifically the side connected to the little toe of the sole of the left foot, while [the right foot] is likewise placed upon the side connected to the little toe of the sole of the right foot.
By stepping upon the left calf and placing it across the middle of the left thigh, and by the reverse placement— namely,
by stepping upon the right calf with the left calf— the two types of *padmāsana* are formed through these arrangements as previously described. Likewise:

Due to a twofold reversal of sequence: from the joining of the inner sides of those two thighs. This is what is meant: the lower part of the right thigh connected to the big toe of the left sole is placed upon the side connected to the big toe of the right sole, and the lower part of the left thigh [is likewise placed].
As before, by means of an inverted placement, and again as previously,
by means of the placement of mutual treading upon the two shanks,
and by means of the placement of mutual treading on the sides connected to the two big toes of the soles of the feet.

The *svastikāsana* is of two kinds. By the verse beginning with "talānte" (at the end of the palms), this is what is stated: one should place one foot beneath either of the thighs, joining its side with the side connected to the big toe of the other foot. Furthermore—
One should perform it by exchanging the left and right; thus, this *bhadrāsana* becomes twofold.
One [hand] should be placed on the inner side of the palm, while the other is placed on the outer side.
When the legs are positioned both below and above [the knees], it is known as the Bhadrāsana in two ways.
When the two soles are inverted and the shanks are raised high due to their upward contact,
the position of the feet at the region of the knees is indeed called the *vīra* posture, as it is from the *yogapaṭṭa*.
Prāṇāyāma is said to be of three kinds: superior, inferior, and middling.
In the superior [type], there is lightness, the leaving of the ground, and the tranquility of the mind.
An increase of perspiration over the entire body occurs in the lowest and likewise the middling stages;
trembling of the whole body is said to result from practice performed for the appropriate duration. (65)
Even these supreme qualities shall arise through practice over the course of time;
therefore, one should indeed practice regularly both in the morning and in the evening.
One should fill [the lungs] through the left nostril with the essence of nectar;
then, while recollecting the water-mantra, one should expel the air through the right nostril.
Taken together, there are eight postures. Regarding this, the traditional teaching (sampradāya) is that by the statement "of two kinds," all postures are twofold. || 62 ||
By the verse beginning with "vyatyasta" (crossed), this is what is meant:
[the posture] is formed by the upward extension resulting from the contact of the shins,
while the sides connected to the little toes have their soles crossed and press against the ground.

Due to the binding of the meditation band (yogapaṭṭa) at the feet, the region of the knees, and within the middle of the chest; due to the placement of the forearms with extended arms above the knees;
and again, as before, due to the specific arrangement of the contact between the two shanks, both externally and internally.
The heroic posture (vīrāsana) is of two kinds. || 63 ||

With these five verses beginning with *prāṇāyāma* and ending with *turīyata*, he teaches the varieties of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*), its meditation, and its essential nature. In that context, "lightness" refers to the body; "leaving the ground" refers to either the cotton or the jar [rising] one at a time.

The meaning of the tradition is as follows: having placed objects of equal measure to one's own [height] to the east, and standing on the other side, [one observes] the elevation of one's own jar through *prāṇāyāma*. The words "in the highest *prāṇāyāma*" are to be supplied; likewise, "in the lowest *prāṇāyāma*" and "in the middling *prāṇāyāma*" are to be supplied. This is due to practice (*abhyāsāt*).
"Joined with time" means from practice performed over a long period; [the result] would become superior, middling, or inferior.
When it has been thus well-mastered, one should subsequently extract [it] by means of thirty-two measures (mātrā).
One should retain it for sixty-four [counts] and exhale it through the fourth [nostril]. || 68 ||
Trembling, horripilation, bliss, purity, steadiness, lightness, as well as luster and radiance—these are the characteristics of one perfected in yoga. (69)
Having fixed the mind in the *mūlādhāra* and filled [the body] from the base with the vital air (*vāyu*),
one should lead it through the interior of the network of channels (*nāḍīcakra*) and cause it to circulate through all the limbs.
When the vital airs have been thus fully mastered within the thirty-eight vital points (marmas), one can,
by means of concentration, restrain the limbs in every direction according to one's will.

Having thus fixed the mind upon the *ādhāra* and joined it with the vital air (*pavana*), one should pervade the body with the essences (*rasa*)—which are like clouds of fire—along with the *haṃsas*. (72)
The meaning is "may they become divine. One should practice the *prāṇāyāmas*. "Ambu" refers to the syllable *va*;

because it is divine like the wind (*marut*), it means "wind. This term has two meanings: in one case, it connects with the preceding [verse], meaning "resounding with the syllable *ya*"; in the other case, it refers to the breath (*śvāsa*).

The connection with the subsequent [verse] is "one should expel" (apasārayet); the meaning is "one should exhale. A *mātrā* is the duration of time required for eight snaps of one's own fingers. The phrase "with sixty-four *mātrās*" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].
"From the fourth" means with sixteen *mātrās*. || 68 ||

With the verse beginning with "trembling" (*kampa*), he teaches the characteristics of one who has attained yoga. "Purity, stability, and lightness": purity pertains to the mind, while stability and lightness pertain to the body.
"Radiance" (*prakāśa*) refers to the manifestation of one's own internal luster externally, like that of a seed or similar object. (69)
With the verse beginning with "mūlādhāre," he teaches the nature of pratyāhāra (withdrawal). In that context, "from the root" means from the mūlādhāra. || 70 ||

With this verse beginning with "evam," he teaches the essential nature of *dhāraṇā*. In this context, the phrase "one should cause [the breath] to move" (*cārayet*) is to be understood as "one should cause the *vāyu* (vital air) to move. This occurs by the power of one's will, that is, by the power of fixing [the breath] upon whichever limb is desired. || 71 ||

With nine verses beginning with "tathā" and ending with "vrajet," he teaches the fruits of the perfection of *dhāraṇā* together with the nature of *samādhi*. Among these, with two verses beginning with "tathā" and ending with "bhuvi," he teaches the means for attaining the perfection of knowing the three times and so forth through *samādhi*. Thus:

As before. Together with the letters *la*, *va*, *ra*, *ya*, and *ha*— which are pervaded by the oceans of flavors (*rasa*) and fire (*āha*), accompanied by *haṃsa*, and each endowed with a nasal bindu— the remainder of the sentence being "together with"—
when the body has thus been made identical with those syllables by means of the vital breath (*vāyu*).
Knowing the three periods of time, with a purified self, he shall live long and happily on earth. || 73 ||
Moving at will and traveling through the sky, he may associate with the gods;
remaining within his own body by his own will, he is like one who has entered a chamber within a house.
Thus, one whose yoga is fully perfected may, by his own will,
draw the vital breaths of his body through the central aperture of the suṣumnā situated within.
Having emerged through the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), one becomes possessed of the Self by means of the universal self;
or else, one becomes self-controlled through the tasting of the powder as described above.
With a mind free from attachment, one should abandon one's own body by that means; this, O Dear One, is called "voluntary departure" for those whose souls are united with yoga.

"One should pervade with the wind"—this is the ellipsis. "Made of that" means made of each respective element through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) in which the distinctions between the meditator, the meditation, and the object of meditation have been dissolved. This is what is meant: having joined the mind at the *mūlādhāra* as before, one should sustain the vital air (*vāyu*) there.

By means of the five aforementioned elemental syllables together with that vital air (pavana), through its pervasion of the entire body, one's own body is made to consist of those respective elements; thus, the attainment of the stated fruits occurs. || 73 ||

With the verse beginning with *svecchā*, he teaches the means for attaining supernatural powers such as traveling through the sky. In that context, one who acts according to his own will (*svecchācārī*) possesses unimpeded movement; even while remaining at home, he is like a person staying at home, yet remains free from attachment to the body. || 74 ||

With these three verses beginning with "evam" and ending with "priye," he teaches two methods for voluntary departure (utkrānti). In this context, the phrase "he should abandon the body" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the first verse].
"The vital breaths" refers to the breaths; "from the central aperture of the Suṣumnā" is to be supplied as the remainder of the phrase "of the network of channels" (nāḍīcakra).
Likewise, as before; having completely abandoned the limitation of the body by means of the self, one becomes possessed of many forms that are unlimited. Or else, in another sense:
through the tasting of the powder (*cūrṇa*) described later—in the thirty-fourth chapter below.

"By means of that," which consists of the tasting of the powder described in the three verses beginning with *ugre* and ending with *ātmavān*. This is what is meant: having drawn back, by means of the mind, the vital breaths (*prāṇas*) previously circulated through the [lower] stations without remainder, via the path of the aperture of the *suṣumnā*, from the aperture of Brahmā (*brahmarandhra*).
Having brought [the breath] forth, by means of the continuous connection arising from tasting the powder to be described, one becomes one whose essential nature is uninterrupted. || 77 ||
O Goddess, I shall now describe the most wonderful entry into another's body; for in the Kali age, O Sovereign Lady, success is generally difficult to attain among mortals. (530) 78.
Having renounced his own life and body without affliction, he beheld before him, through the power of yoga, [the goddess] endowed with all her limbs complete.
One should enter that body according to the prescribed rite for the consecration of life (prāṇapratiṣṭhā);
then, one should protect one's own body with one's own [mantras] and likewise proceed toward them.
O Great Goddess, listen to those eight characteristics of one who has attained perfection through the constant practice of yoga, as well as the other qualities that arise from them. 81.
The cessation of dualities, the attainment of happiness, health, and self-control;
mastery over the senses, freedom from anger, and the protection of people through compassion. (82)
O beloved, listen as I describe the signs of one whose death is imminent;
by these, both the practitioner and the subject, remaining vigilant, may know the time for casting off the body. (83)
Then, devoted solely to worshipping the deities, those two attained a happy rebirth; from the very moment of their birth, they became established in spiritual perfection.

With these three verses beginning with *parakāya* and ending with *vrajet*, [the author] introduces the subject and teaches the entry into another's body (*parakāyapraveśana*) and, subsequently, the re-entry into one's own body. In this context, the connection with the preceding [verse] is that the entry into another's body is "difficult to clothe" (*duḥśāṭaka*), meaning it is difficult to perform; [this is done] without affliction (*akleśataḥ*).

By virtue of the absence of suffering caused by cruel diseases and the like; "he should enter through yoga" is the syntactical connection with what follows. "According to the prescribed procedure for the installation of the vital breath (prāṇapratiṣṭhā)"—this refers to the chapter on the Dūtīs and Nityās. This is the ellipsis. "With his own affectionate men"—this is the ellipsis. "Then" means from that.

Having projected that [divine] body from his own body, he teaches the characteristics of one perfected in yoga— preceded by an introduction and a count [of verses]— in two verses beginning with "tathā prāgvat prāṇapratiṣṭhāvidhinā siddhasya" and ending with "śocitaḥ. Among those [characteristics]:

The characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). By "characteristics" is meant by way of qualities (*guṇa*). The "destruction of duality" (*dvandvahāni*) refers to the destruction of transformations such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, and so forth. The "attainment of happiness" (*sukhāvāpti*) occurs through the eighteen verses beginning with "by the contemplation of one's own nature" (*svarūpānusandhānena*) and ending with "it would come to pass" (*āsannetyādibhir bhavet*).

He teaches the signs of approaching death, preceded by the fruit of knowing the introduction. In that regard, for a person whose death is near, by which signs [it is known], those two, the object to be accomplished and the means of accomplishment—(p.
531) a man, abandoning his own former nature without cause.
If he relies upon that [falsehood], his death will certainly occur within three years. || 85 ||
One does not perceive Arundhatī or Dhruva in the sky beyond that midpoint;
nor does one see the two pupils of the eyes if they do not extend as far as the bridge of the nose. (86)
If the throbbing of the two arteries below the ankles does not occur, it is certain that death will come within half a month for that person. (87)

The destruction of that [mind] is said to occur swiftly when one perceives the sun as a severed trunk, provided that the sound of Kuṇḍalinī is not heard while the openings of the ears are blocked. (88)
If smoke is seen rising from the top of his head or even from his house or field, or if birds are perched and clinging to his head—who would not declare him to be dead? (89)
If, after the sun has set, a man does not see a rainbow in his mouthful of water,
he should know that he himself will certainly die immediately.
One who, with his hand upon his own head, can see his own thick forearm,
or one who can see from his eyes down to his ankles, perishes thereafter.
The meaning of the phrases "the tradition of the Sugatas" and "from the moment of birth" is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.

One should resort to the eastern direction, whether gentle or cruel; the remainder is that one should not resort to the opposite of the east. From that point of resorting, "fixed" refers to the form of the lunar mansion (nakṣatra). "From half of that" means from six months.

"By stepping to the edge of the nose" means by stepping with two fingers to the edges of the nose. "In the moon" refers to the light in the form of a moon situated in the center of the peacock's eye. The word "if not" (na cet) connects with "he looks" (*vilokayati*) in what follows; the word "looks" (*vilokayati*) connects with "in the moon" (*candrake*) in what precedes. From its half...

After three months, for one whose two channels below the ankles have ceased to throb, there is a *ruṇḍa*—that is, a headless trunk (*kavandha*). The word "ca" (and) is displaced in the sequence. "Of one who sees" refers to another alternative case.
Regarding "houses, fields, and so forth," the word "etc. includes cities, towns, and other such locations. Even smoke is seen.
Thus it is drawn. "Vā" indicates an alternative. That person: with the sun turned behind him (paścātkṛtārka), meaning with the sun cast to his back;
in a mouthful (gaṇḍūṣe), meaning water filled in the mouth and then expelled; a bow-like light (cāpakaṃ jyotiḥ), resembling the rainbow of Indra;
the forearm (prakoṣṭha), meaning the elbow; the region between the elbow and the wrist; those two hands (tau janau).
When phlegm, semen, and impurities become submerged in water, in that very fortnight one departs for Yama, abandoning life. (92)
One who gazes upon an image made of gold certainly goes to the abode of Yama;
even one who gazes upon the sun amidst the constellations goes to the abode of Yama. (93)
Having observed one's own body-reflection distorted in water and other such media for a month,
or seeing a fissure in the orb of the sun, one goes to one's death.
If the chest of one whose body has been bathed and anointed dries up first,
he shall meet his death within a fortnight, even if protected by all the gods.
He constantly reviled, without cause, his gurus, the assembly of mothers, the Brahmins, the deities of the moon and sun, and those who were believers. || 96 ||
From the crushing of one's own enmity toward dogs, from abandoning [one's vows] out of anger, and even from the abandonment of the guru and the mantra, death occurs before long. (97)
One who constantly insults and curses the guru, the Vidyā, one's father, one's mother, or any deity, perishes swiftly.
A man who, without cause, rejects a book, his own home, a seat, or a bed, quickly perishes. (99)

In that case, it is within half a month; the phrase "along with the lunar mansions" (bhagaṇaiḥ saha) is to be understood as the ellipsis. "Vikṛtām" means having a deformed or loathsome appearance and lacking luster. "Bhānau chidram" means a hole or cavity in the sun. The word "sarvair api," meaning even by Brahmā and the others, connects with the subsequent phrase "akāraṇataḥ," which is linked later with "in the crushing of the enemy's army" (śvāśvaverasya dalane).

In the event of abandoning the enmity toward dogs and horses, there is death within a month due to insults and curses, resulting in the discoloration of the eyes, body, and facial features. If one meditates upon the deformity of one's own deity, death shall occur within a month. (100)
The pervasion consisting of the reality of time has been correctly explained;
by the refinement of this within the mind, that very reality is assimilated into one's own self. (101)
Thus ends the twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Form of the Breath," in the *Śrīkādimata*, a tantra of the sixteen *Nityās*.
By means of censure and unpleasant speech, he rejects and abandons them. "Discoloration" refers to roughness;
the remainder implies the deformity of one's own deity through [loss of] complexion, physical form, serenity, and so forth. || 100 ||

Thus, [this concludes] the section on the sixteen Nityās within the *Manoramā* commentary— composed by the venerable Subhagānandanātha, under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, upon the complete tantra known as the *Śrīkādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.

The twenty-seventh chapter, which is dedicated to elucidating the methods for the pervasive expansion of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) that constitutes Time, has been fully considered and completed. Om. That is the Truth.
Regarding the number of verses:
in the twenty-seventh [chapter], there is one yantra, and the explanatory verses are recorded as two hundred and fifty-five and a half.
The Twenty-eighth Chapter.
Now I shall declare to you the nature of the sixteen Nityās as being the very self of the world— that of which the entire universe, including all that is moving and unmoving, consists.
I have already explained to you the pervasion between Kāla and Bhairava,
as well as that between Mātṛkā and the world, by way of the relationship between the signified and the signifier.
Today I shall correctly declare to you the pervasiveness of Time and the World;
this entire universe is dependent upon them, for those forms of Time are eternal.
Indeed, the sixteenfold form of time is clearly perceived through the waxing and waning of the moon by means of its first digit.
In the twenty-seventh preceding chapter,

having taught that the sixteen *Nityās* consist of time and have the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), he subsequently teaches that the sixteen *Nityās* consist of the worlds, beginning with the words "Now, the sixteen" and ending with "the body."

By means of the twenty-eighth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses, [the text proceeds]. Therein, beginning with the verse starting "Now, sixteen," it teaches—preceded by an introduction concerning the statement that the sixteen Nityās and others are the very nature of the world—that the entire universe, including the moving and the non-moving, exists as being composed of that [divine essence]. In this context, "being the nature of the world" refers to...
Identity with the world: that which consists of this world, which is eternal by nature, exists and is perceived. || 1 ||

With this verse beginning with "kāla," he recalls the pervasion (*vyāpti*) of the *Kālamātṛkā* taught in the twenty-fifth chapter and the *Mātṛkāloka* taught in the twenty-sixth chapter. In that regard, it was already stated previously in the twenty-fifth chapter: "By means of the union of the signified and the signifier, [this applies] even to the *Mātṛkāloka*s."

The meaning is that I have also explained to you in the twenty-sixth chapter the pervasion of the *mātṛkā* and the world, through the non-separation of the world from the *mātṛkā*, which consists of the forms of sound and their corresponding objects. || 2 ||

With this verse beginning with "vyāpti," he teaches that eternal entities possess time as their very form, preceded by an introduction concerning the description of the pervasion (*vyāpti*) between time and the world. In that regard, on which this entire universe depends in this present chapter—

Because the universe, through its identity with them, is dependent upon time; the meaning is that time alone—which is the cause of the entire universe—is the eternal form (*vigraha*) of those eternal [entities]. || 3 ||
With the verse beginning with "of time" (kālasya), he teaches that Mahānityā consists of time that is unlimited, while the others consist of time that is its constituent parts.
The form of the world is its measure, and the Kālacakra is likewise; the mutual eternal pervasion of these two, and their abiding state accordingly, [is explained]. (5)
Listen now to the measurement of their constant luminous state and the form of their armor, as well as the nature of the planets as the Mātṛkās, explained in due order.
In the center of the earth stands Mount Meru, golden in form;
on its great sides, it extends for five hundred yojanas.

In this context, "of Time" refers to that which will be described in the thirty-sixth chapter. The meaning is that even that which is not the ultimate reality (aparamārtha) is indeed perceived as manifesting. The phrase "by means of increase and decrease" refers to the fifteen digits (kalās); "tathā" is used in the sense of conjunction. This is what is being said:

Of the lunar orb consisting of sixteen digits (*kalā*), [there is] the Great Eternity (*mahānityā*) whose nature is time indivisible and whose form is the imperishable digit (*akṣarakalā*), as well as those whose natures are intermediate times consisting of the other fifteen digits.

For the eternal [lights], there arises the perception of their rising and resting sequentially on each lunar day (tithi), beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight up to the full moon, and beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight up to the new moon. || 4 ||

With the two verses beginning with "loka" and ending with "vai," he teaches the remaining topics of the chapter in sequence. Therein, "the form of the world" refers to the arrangement of the continents and oceans;
"its measurement" means the dimensions of the continents, oceans, and so forth—meaning it is endowed with such measurements.

The mutual pervasion of eternity between those two, the pervasion of eternity of the world, and the pervasion of eternity of time; likewise, their stability— the mutual pervasion of the world and the wheel of time (*kālacakra*) by way of sixteen aspects each— and the stability of the eternal light.

The state of the Nityāloka to be described hereafter; "of the Nityāloka" is the ellipsis for "the measure. Their state as armor-forms—that is, the state of the Nityās existing as armor—for the sake of practitioners, is the ellipsis.
Of the nine planets, beginning with the Sun; "nine" is the ellipsis. The form of Mātṛkā.
The nature of being the *mātṛkā*.
With the two verses beginning with "Hemamaya" and ending with "āvṛta," consisting of three additional syllables, he teaches its world-form and its measurement. Therein, "of that" refers to Meru.
"Five hundred yojanas" means five thousand yojanas. This is what is meant:
In the center of the earth, which is circular in form, Mount Meru, consisting of gold, stands like the pericarp of a lotus.
Surrounding that Meru, the earth extends for five thousand yojanas on each side. Of that...
The measurement of the intervals between them is ten thousand yojanas everywhere.
"By the rivers" means by the oceans; "by the islands" refers to those specific regions of land situated between the respective oceans, whose names will be mentioned later.

By those [oceans] numbering twice as much as each preceding one, according to the measurement of the earth at the side of Meru, each succeeding one is double the size of the one before. This is what is meant:
[the oceans] consist of salt water, sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, curd, milk, and fresh water.
[It consists of] seven oceans and as many continents, each double the size of the preceding one. || 8 ||
It is enclosed on its outer sides by the external ocean of water;
having been measured for its width in the middle, it is then enclosed again on the outside.
The wheel of time, together with the supreme power (parāśakti), indeed always revolves certainly from the west,
moving downwards in a counter-clockwise direction.
On each side surrounding Mahāmeru, extending five thousand yojanas on every side,
there is the Salt Ocean, measuring ten thousand yojanas on each side; beyond that, it is as before.

Plakṣadvīpa consists of twenty thousand by twenty thousand yojanas. Outside of that is the Ikṣurasasamudra, consisting of forty thousand by forty thousand yojanas, as before. Outside of that also is Śālmalīdvīpa, consisting of eighty thousand by eighty thousand yojanas, as before.
Outside of that, as before, is the ocean of wine (*surā-samudra*), measuring one hundred and sixty thousand *yojanas*.
Outside of that, as before, is Kuśadvīpa, measuring three hundred and twenty thousand *yojanas*. Outside of that, as before, [is the ocean] exceeding forty thousand...

The ocean of clarified butter (*ghṛtasamudra*) measures six hundred thousand *yojanas*. Outside of that is Krauñcadvīpa, measuring a number of *yojanas* produced by the seven-syllable phrase "beginning with Nūna-nidāra" as previously described. Outside of that is Śauri, brought by Agni, [measuring] 1,280,000 [yojanas].

The Ocean of Curd consists of a measurement equal to the number produced by a seven-syllable sentence. Outside of that, as before, Śākadvīpa consists of a measurement equal to the number produced by a seven-syllable sentence, being composed of the individual souls (jīvāṇu) characterized by action (kriyātman). Furthermore, outside of that...

As before, the Ocean of Milk consists of a number of *yojanas* produced by the eight-syllable phrase "nānājñānabharo nityam. Outside of that, as before, the Puṣkara Continent consists of a number of *yojanas* produced by the eight-syllable phrase "nūnaṃjñānadovinnara. Furthermore, outside of that...
As before, the wise one has taught that the "Ocean of Water" consists of a numerical arrangement produced by the eight-syllable phrase *dhunir bhūḥ*;
here, the word *āvṛtā* (surrounded) connects with *mahī* (the earth) from the preceding verse. || 8 ||

By means of the two verses beginning with "the external water" (*vāhyasalilam*) and ending with "by the bodies" (*vigrahaiḥ*), which consist of five syllables per line and three lines each, [the text explains] the region situated between the external waters and the ocean of the wheel of time (*kālacakra*),
the cause of the revolution of that wheel of time, the manner of its rotation, and the distinctions of its orbits.
He teaches its measurement and its nature as a mass; therein, from the outer ocean of water—
the outermost ocean of all waters— enveloping it from the outside according to its middle width measurement, that [measurement] again and again...

And that [wheel] is joined with eight wonderful paths of the measures (tanmāna), and it is endowed with twelve spokes consisting of light, having the forms of Aries and the other [zodiacal signs]. (11)
In those streets, the seven planets are situated facing the eastern direction;
they are described as being above and below according to the time conjoined with the zodiac signs.

From that measurement of the diameter across the assembly of the seven continents and seven oceans (16,383,700), there arises the form of the earth consisting of the continents and so forth, which is the Kālacakra— the wheel whose nature is time.
Its nature as time is due to its revolution being the cause of all transformations in the universe.

Impelled by the wind of the Supreme Power—that is, by the wind in the form of the power of will (icchā-śakti) of Mahānityā—the meaning of the word "only" (eva) is that there is no other cause. To the west, below, and on the left (apasavya), facing westward, it proceeds upward and downward in sequence, moving clockwise; that is the Kālacakra.

By means of its paths of measurement, which increase successively on each side by double the respective measurements; wonderful, because it consists of all marvels and because it was created by no one; consisting of light, having the nature of luminosity; [it has] twelve spokes.

From the center of the earth up to the supreme ether (paravyoman), by means of forms expanding upwards from the crown of the head—with equal intervals being understood as the remainder—[and] by means of the bodies of Aries and so forth, that is, the natures of the zodiacal signs beginning with Aries and ending with Pisces. This is what is meant: the measurement of the diameter across the middle of both sides of the outermost ocean of water.
Having encompassed all that which extends beyond it, [the mandala] takes the form of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), impelled by the vital wind (*māruta*).

Measured from the previously mentioned outer ocean of water, there are eight courtyards (*vīthī*) on each side, each doubling in size in succession as before, together with eight intermediate spaces between them.

The Wheel of Time (Kālacakra), which has the form of light and consists of twelve spokes representing the twelve signs beginning with Aries, revolves from top to bottom in a clockwise direction while facing westward. || 11 ||
With the verse beginning with "In those" (*teṣu*) and ending with "the stability" (*sthitiḥ*), consisting of one and a half verses,

he teaches the location of the seven planets within the paths of that wheel of time (*kālacakra*), as well as the stability of the world through their movement through the zodiacal signs contained within that wheel according to the time-periods stated by himself. Therein, in those paths...

"In those paths" means in those zodiacal signs (*rāśi*). "Situated" refers to [the planets] of the Moon, Mercury, Venus, the Sun, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn, by way of leaping over their respective lower and upper orbital paths (*vīthi*) as they proceed through the signs situated within those paths. This is according to what is stated in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*. Likewise, they face only toward the eastern direction.
They proceed and move; the state of these planets consists of birth, existence, transformation, growth, waning, and destruction. This is what is meant:
they remain by traversing the eight paths within the aforementioned wheel of time (kālacakra) according to the stated sequence.

Facing the east, those respective planets, by means of their own stated motions within their respective zodiacal signs, bring about the state of the world consisting of its creation and so forth. || 12 ||
By their movement, the stability of the worlds is maintained;
the immensely radiant Lalitā always resides upon Meru, situated in the center. (13)
On all sides of that, the remaining fourteen [worlds] are situated within the waters;
beyond that, however, these [other worlds] are established in the supreme ether (parame vyoman). || 14 ||
Beginning from the Kṛta age and so forth, they remain established year by year;
in the second and subsequent ages, they proceed in sequence through their revolutions.
In the sixteenth year, Lalitā is in the supreme sky, while Citrā is in the ocean of water;
thus indeed do they undergo their cyclic rotation.
By means of these three verses beginning with *dhyastha* and ending with *rūpataḥ*,
[the text describes] the sixteen Nityās in sixteen types of locations, starting from Merudvīpa and ending with Paramavyoma,
throughout the four-yuga cycles of each Yuga, beginning from the Kṛtayuga.

He teaches the sequence of transformation. In that regard, "he always abides" means that he remains at all times in the form of the Pradhāna, which consists of all things. "Of great splendor" (mahādyuti) is because his nature is a light unconditioned by space, time, and so forth. "Of that Meru," [meaning] on all sides.

"From all sides": [this refers to] those situated in fourteen locations, starting from Jambudvīpa, which is immediately adjacent to Meru and situated within the waters, and extending outwards as far as the outermost ocean of water. The remaining ones are the fourteen [goddesses] beginning with Kāmeśvarī.

Ending with Jvālāmālinī. Outside of that, beyond the outermost ocean of water; here, sixteen [goddesses] for each *varṣa* (region), for each *kṛta-yuga* and so forth. The connection with what follows is that "those Nityās become Lalitā. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). Thus, in the manner described.
The word "evam" (thus) is to be construed with the phrase "prokta-rūpataḥ" (in the form described). "In others" refers to the Tretā and subsequent ages. What is meant is as follows:
[the sequence consists of] Meru, Jambūdvīpa, the Salt Ocean, Plakṣadvīpa, the Sugarcane Ocean, Śālmalīdvīpa, the Wine Ocean, Kuśadvīpa, the Ghee Ocean, Krauñcadvīpa, and the Curd Ocean.

In the sixteen locations known as Śākadvīpa, the Ocean of Milk, Puṣkaradvīpa, the Ocean of Water, and Paravyoman, during the first years of the four ages beginning with the Kṛtayuga, the sixteen Nityās— beginning with Lalitā and ending with Citrā— abide as their very essence; then, in the second years of each respective age, they abide likewise.

In sixteen locations, beginning with Jambūdvīpa and ending with Meru, the sixteen Nityās, starting with Lalitā and ending with Citrā, reside. Likewise, in fourteen years each, beginning from the third year of their respective yugas and ending at the sixteenth year, they abide.

Lalitā resides sequentially in each of the fourteen specific regions, beginning from the Salt Ocean up to the Supreme Sky (Paramavyoma). Starting from the interval between the locations where Lalitā resides and extending back to each respective preceding location, there are other goddesses, beginning with Kāmeśvarī and ending with Citrā.
The fifteen Nityās abide thus; in this manner, every sixteen years they undergo one revolution each. || 16 ||
Thus, O Īśvarī, it exists in other ages as well in the form described,
and throughout the periods of time from the middle [of the age] up to the limit of the supreme void.
Those who are neutral resort to transformation and move about according to their own portions;
all others indeed move about there and there by themselves.
In that way, those [constellations] undergo revolution according to the sequence of time;
when, through time, place, and the cycle [of the zodiac], their conjunction occurs, [the result follows]. (19)
Then the kings become righteous due to timely rains;
and the subjects shall be happy, free from disease, and subject to death only at the proper time. (20)

By means of these five verses beginning with "In the times" (*kāleṣu*) and ending with "has been proclaimed" (*samudīritam*), [the author] explains: the manner in which the sixteen *Nityās* consist of the wheel of time (*kālacakra*);
the fruit of sovereignty over both time and space; and the existence of the *Kālacakra* within the supreme ether (*paravyoman*) in the form of the external path.

He also teaches the conclusion previously stated: therein, among the times, the orbits (*kakṣā*) of the Moon of Kālacakra—within the sixteen locations beginning from the space between the earth and [the heavens] up to the end of the orbit of the stars—are contained within the middle sky, starting from the center and ending with the lunar orbit; these are the sixteen *Nityās*.

The one situated in the center is Līlitā. By her own portion (*svāṃśataḥ*), she exists through another form identical to herself. The other fifteen Nityās are likewise present in various places and at various times. Thus, according to the sequence of time—specifically by way of the sixteen-year cycles beginning with the years of the previously mentioned *yuga* and so forth—there is a particular distinction.

"By time" means through the sequence of the cycle of time; "by place" means by the circle of the region, [moving] with the *kālacakra*. "Again" (*bhūyuḥ*) is as before. "Deaths of time" (*kālamṛtyavaḥ*) means deaths that are beneficial. "On the outer path" (*bāhyasthavīthyām*) means on the path situated outside the orbit of Saturn (*śanaiścara*). "Stars" (*tārakāḥ*).

The constellations; "outside of that" means outside the orbit of the constellations. "The state of the Kālacakra" is to be construed with what precedes. Therein, in the Kālacakra, "ending at that" means having that as its limit, reaching to the end of the supreme void (*paravyoman*). By the word "also" (*api ca*), the term "state" (*sthiti*) is drawn over from the preceding verse.

"By that sequence" means by the sequence of sixteen years for each successive Yuga as previously described. "Consisting of that" means eternally free from disease. This is what is meant: Lalitā and the others, ending with Citrā, [arise] according to the sequence of sixteen, sixteen years beginning from the first year of each of the four Yugas, starting with Kṛta.

The sixteen *nityās* are, in sequence, within the *Kālacakra*: the lunar orbit; the region between that and the next; the orbit of Mercury; the orbit of Venus; the orbit of the Sun; the orbit of Mars; and the orbit of Jupiter.

Then, according to the division of the orbits of the intermediate constellations within that interval, they revolve in sixteen locations around the revolution of the regions in successive order of revolution. By that sequence,
whichever [constellation] is eternally situated in the lunar orbit becomes the presiding deity of that particular wheel of time.
The stars abide upon the outer stationary path of the Kālacakra;
beyond that lies the supreme void (paramavyoma), which is situated in close proximity to it. (21)
And of those sixteen eternal ones as well, that [nature] arises in due order;
thus, with respect to both place and time, it is declared to be composed of that.

One should worship with special care that [deity] who has attained unity through the conjunction of the country, the year, and the lunar day, and one should recite her mantra for the attainment of all goals. (23)
Through the instruction of that knowledge to them, its presence shall arise;
and by the glory of the unity of the three, the Great Power (Mahāśakti) is born.
One should worship her when she has reached her [proper] time on the day of one's own birth;
but when she has reached her [proper] place, O Śivā, one should worship her on the full moon of that month.
For one who performs this every year, the goddess Ramā does not abandon his fame;
moreover, he shall always be long-lived, free from disease, wise, and happy.

Therefore, through the distinction of changes in place and time, the eight locations— beginning with Jambudvīpa and ending with Paravyoman— are established as having a single permanent sovereignty over each of the eight years in successive order, just as in the case of Jambudvīpa.
Kāmeśvarī and Kulasundarī are respectively in the first and ninth regions of Plakṣadvīpa; Bhagamālinī and Nityānityā are in the second and tenth regions of Śālmalīdvīpa;
and Nityaklinnā and Nīlapatākā are in the third and eleventh regions of Kuśadvīpa.

In the fourth and twelfth regions of Bheruṇḍā’s Vijaya [continent], there are Vahnivāsinī and Sarvamaṅgalā in the fifth and thirteenth regions of Krauñcadvīpa; Vajreśvarī and Jvālāmālinī are in the sixth and fourteenth regions of Śākadvīpa; and [these are] for Puṣkaradvīpa.

In the seventh and fifteenth years, the dūtīs are Citrā and Parā; in the eighth and sixteenth years, they are Tvaritā and Lalitā. Thus it is stated that place and time are of the nature of the eternal (nitya). || 22 ||
With these five verses beginning with *deśa* and ending with *pūjanāt*,
[the author] teaches the worship of the Nityā as it occurs according to place, time, and lunar day (*tithi*), as well as the specific characteristics of that time and its fruit.
In this regard, there are three— place, year, and lunar day— or two, namely place and the wheel of time (*kālacakra*).

That *tithinityā-vidyā* [is to be understood] in those [specified] places, years, and lunar days (*tithi*). Of her—the sovereign of that place and so forth—it is the "great power" (*mahāśakti*) for the practitioner; this is the ellipsis. [This applies] to the triad of the place and the others. || 24 ||

[He is] the sovereign of the Wheel of Time, attained at the [proper] time; on the completion of that month, [that is,] on the completion of the month of his own birth. For one who acts in this way, he is [honored] by kings, by men, by women, and even by other living beings.
All mantras are honored, and they shall become perfected through worship there. || 27 ||
The Jambū, Plakṣa, Śālmalī, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śāka, and Puṣkara are the trees that stand respectively upon the seven continents.
From their very mouths, those respective names should emerge;
having worshipped with those various names, one should then honor that island.
The practitioner should worship each of those eternal [deities] there and then at their respective times; for one who worships in this manner, there is no equal in the world, nor anyone superior.
In the center is that earth, and surrounding it is the Kālacakra;
outside of that is the great void (mahāvyoma), which is without a periphery, and therein exists this pair.

This practitioner performs worship, recitation, fire-offerings, and so forth, along with others such as animals and the like. At that time, when the conjunction of place and other factors occurs—this is what is meant: on the full moon day of one's own birth month, preceded by the worship of the island (dvīpa-pūjā), [one should worship] the Nityā who is the sovereign of each respective island among the seven continents.

By worshipping both Kālacakreśvarī and Nityā on the day of one's birth in their respective years, as well as on each lunar day (tithi) attained during every fortnight, one becomes a partaker of the attainment of the aforementioned fruits. || 27 ||

With these three verses beginning with "jamvi" and ending with "adhika," he teaches the names of the seven continents derived from the names of the seven trees located in those continents, the worship [to be performed] for each respective continent, the perpetual worship to be attained there, and its fruit. Among them:
"Bhūruhāḥ" means trees; "teṣāṃ pādapānām" means of those trees. Their respective names are the names of the islands.

Through the expertise regarding those various trees, by means of their respective names—namely the names starting from Merudvīpa and ending with Paramavyoman, beginning with the *praṇava* (Om) and ending with the fourth case-ending and the word "namaḥ"—[the offering is made].

For example: *oṃ merave namaḥ*, and so forth. Therein, among the sixteen locations headed by Meru, having first worshipped him at each respective place where he resides from time to time, [one worships him] in that year—that is, in each particular year. This is what is meant: among the sixteen *nityās*.
Those who are worthy of their own vessel and are eternal, residing within the sixteen locations— having first worshipped them there,

and then meditating upon them as situated in those respective places during each particular year, worshipping according to the sequence of the daily ritual (nityārcana), one shall attain the aforementioned form of power. || 30 ||

With these three verses beginning with "In the center" and ending with "is found," he teaches the sequence of the abiding of the Great Space of the Bhūmika-cakra, the position of the planets within the Kālacakra, and its cause. Therein, "in the center of the Great Space":
In the center of the very stable earth, as the wheel revolves incessantly, the planets—whose movements and dwellings therein are governed by fixed laws—[abide]. (32)
O Supreme Goddess, the cause is your will alone;
there exists nothing else anywhere that can serve as a support for those two.
Outside of those two, in the supreme sky, is the fourfold ocean located somewhere;
and on its shore is the fifth [face], Kolavaktra, whose form has been described previously.
In the water [he should visualize] Kurukullā, mounted upon a boat and possessing a pure smile;
in the midst of that, indeed, are the nine jewels and a great island.
Her body was served by the six seasons in the garden of the Kalpa tree;
in its midst, she was surrounded by countless forms of the Śaktis of song.
She was being incessantly entertained by those deeply attached to singing, instrumental music, dancing, and the like,
her glances languid with the intoxication of her radiant joy.
Seated upon a jeweled lion-throne in the center of a pavilion of gems,
she possesses a pure smile and is delighted by the songs of attraction sung by the multitude of Śaktis.

"Staying on that ground"—this is the ellipsis. "From that Kālacakra" means from the limitless (niḥsīmam), that is, without boundary. "Therein," meaning in that great void (mahāvyomani). "The abiding of this dyad" refers to the persistence of both the ground and time.
"In the middle of the great void" means therein, in the Kālacakra.

For those whose selves are fixed in their respective modes of movement through association—that is, for those who possess a fixed rule of movement within the various zodiacal signs (rāśis) associated with their own specific pathways—there is the command of Your supreme power of will. This refers to those two: the terrestrial sphere and the wheel [of time]. This is what is meant: [The following verse: "O Goddess, by Your will, the planets, having entered the twelve houses, move according to their own nature; they do not deviate from their own paths. This means that by Your will, the planets enter the twelve houses and proceed according to their own inherent nature, never straying from their respective orbits. They do not act independently, but rather follow the law established by You. Thus, the entire cosmic order is governed by Your sovereign will.

The state of perfect stability of the Bhūmika-cakra situated in the center of the great void, along with the elements and planets residing therein, during their revolution; the constant uniformity of their measurement due to the aforementioned causes of their cohabitation and movement; and their support, belong solely to the Supreme Goddess (Parā).
"From power comes desire. || 33 ||

With these nine verses beginning with "tayoh" and ending with "suniścitam," he teaches the eternal abiding of light, the presence there of the Goddess together with her retinue, and the fruit for the one who worships each of them; therein, "of those two" refers to Mahī and Kālacakra in a certain location.

The "four oceans" refers to the ocean of sugarcane juice and so forth. She possesses the form previously described, with a body resembling Lalitā as mentioned in the *Aṅgapūjā*. She has the face of a boar (*kolavaktrā*), meaning Vārāhī in her twenty-fourth aspect in the form of Potrī.
Her form is born from the innate, the savoury, and the enjoyment, consisting of the bliss that has arisen;
she is the excellent practitioner through her compassionate and fierce side-long glances. (39)
He likewise saw elephants and horses shining with various ornaments, such as golden chowries and the like.
She beheld her before her, manifesting a universal festival through her powers,
and likewise attended on all sides by eternal attendants who were her own equals.
The worshiper of them gradually attains a form identical to theirs;
he will certainly become their companion and a dweller in their presence. (42)
That most wonderful island, measuring ten million yojanas in both breadth and length,
is composed of the nine precious gems and is surrounded by oceans of the same dimensions.
In the pavilion situated in the middle of the third part of Ratnadvīpa, which measures one-third of that [city] and possesses the brilliance of a thousand suns— 44.
Meditating upon her who is endowed with countless powers on all sides at the edges of the radiance of ten million suns, a man becomes equal to me. (45)

The fifth [verse] refers to the group of eight Mothers beginning with Brāhmī situated within the Śrīcakra; here, the mention of the "fifth" is for the sake of establishing similarity with the form of Lalitā. "In the water" means in the ocean of sugarcane juice, specifically in the midst of the four oceans.
"In its center" [refers to the center of that].
"Within the jeweled pavilion situated in the center of a ruby fragment located in the very middle of a garden of [myriad] aeons"—this is the intended meaning. The word division is *asaṃkhyarūpābhiḥ*.
"With glances languid with passion" refers to the three types of bliss that will be described in the third verse following this one.

And by Saṅgītānanda, the meaning is that she is situated above. "Susādhakām" means a practitioner belonging to the true lineage; likewise, "tathāvidhān" means adorned in such a manner. "Tathā" is used as a conjunction. In this context, the words ending in the second case singular refer to Lalitā.
The substantive [object] is to be supplied; the meaning is "having meditated upon her.
Their diversion—that is, their special diversion consisting of music and so forth—is that of the Nityās together with their retinues. || 42 ||

With these nine verses beginning with *koṭi* and ending with *te*, [the author] teaches the measurement of the Nityāloka and so forth, the fruit resulting from worshipping the two deities therein, and the majesty experienced by those who know the eternal glory of Paramavyoman. Among these:

The circumference and the width of the inner enclosure (koṣṭhī) are as follows: by means of oceans, each measuring ten million (*koṭi*) *yojanas*— that is, by oceans whose measure is thirty-three thousand three hundred and thirty-three,
plus one-third of a *yojana* (the third part of the total measure).

Having thus meditated upon the Goddess, whose extent of width and length is three million three hundred and thirty thousand yojanas, a man who has conquered his senses and whose ignorance— the root of saṃsāra— has been cast away, should worship her with supreme devotion as described. (46)
He was skillful and adept in the arts, possessed of equal wealth as those who were happy, sinless, virtuous in character, and endowed with truthfulness and straightforwardness. (47)
The preceptor, exalted by his own lineage and possessing a self esteemed by all, is born;
for a distance of one yojana around him, the area becomes purified. || 48 ||
By the destruction of their evil karma through beholding, conversing with, or touching him, men shall become equal to him, being freed from those [sins]. (49)
The eternal state of Kālacakra and of the world exists outside [of them]; that which is of the nature of space, without beginning or end, is the consciousness-nature (cinmaya) of us two. 50.
He who knows thus this entire eternal glory as it has been described is indeed liberated while living; that is what its characteristic has been told to you.

For the sake of liberation from all calamities, for the attainment of all prosperity, for the pacification of afflictions caused by spirits, ghosts, and demons, and for the acquisition of happiness. (52)
In the third part of the central ruby section located in the middle of the central Ratnadvīpa,
[the measurement is] eleven lakhs, eleven thousand, one hundred and eleven, plus nine-tenths of a yojana.

In a pavilion measuring one *yojana* in both width and length—the *māṇikya-maṇḍapa*—at the edges, that is, on the sides of the pavilion (this is the ellipsis), and likewise as before; one who is equal to me, having become Śiva, [should act] according to what was stated in the twenty-sixth chapter. Ignorance (*ajñāna*) is, by name, a wicked latent impression (*durvāsanā*). Straightness (*ārjava*)...

The term *nāma* refers to the uniformity of the actions of mind, speech, and body. "Around him" means around the dwelling place of the practitioner; "there would be men"—this is the ellipsis. Of the eternal [Mahānityā], who consists of all that is eternal; her form is that of space, composed of consciousness (*cinmaya*).
Consisting of knowledge that is free from objects; of us two, Śakti and Śiva; "thus" means in the manner described;
"proclaimed" means it will be explained in the thirty-fifth chapter. || 51 ||

With twenty verses beginning with "samasta" and ending with "matsama," preceded by an introduction to His manifestations (*anubhāva*), [it is taught] for the destruction of all diseases and for victory in battle. (p. 545)
In that place terrifying with lions, tigers, elephants, gavayas, and other beasts of prey.
In the forest, in mountain thickets, on the road, during famine, as well as in afflictions of mind such as [lack of] water, or in the perils of ships and the like upon the ocean; || 54 ||
Having recited the Nityā-kavaca once, he transcends everything within;
he lives happily, free from dualities, without rivals, and with his senses conquered. || 55 ||
Listen, O Goddess, I shall now declare that armor which is identical with my own self, by means of which even I am always victorious over the gods and asuras in battles. (56)
May Lalitā, who is omnipresent, protect me from all sides and at all times;
may Kāmeśī protect me in front, and Bhagamālā immediately thereafter.
May she protect the direction; likewise, may Nityaklinnā and Bheruṇḍā always protect my right side and my direction forever. 58.
In the same way, Vahnivāsinī shall protect the western quarter,
and Mahāvajreśvarī shall always protect the intermediate direction.
May the messenger Tvaritā always protect my left side;
may Kulasundarī protect the other direction and guard me. (60)

He teaches the eternal armor and its fruit. In that context, by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "piśācas and so forth," epilepsy and other such conditions are meant. For the sake of attaining happiness, because of the attainment of one's true nature (*svarūpa*). In the phrase "gavayas and so forth," the word "and so forth" refers to the *śarabha* and other such creatures. Terrifying...

"Frightening" (bhayaṅkaraḥ). Its connection with the subsequent phrase is "his path. "During famine" refers to the decline resulting from the loss of boundaries and so forth. "And likewise" (tathā) indicates a conjunction. In the phrase "from ships and so forth" (potādī), the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to boats and the like. "This reciter" (asau japitā). "Free from dualities" (nirdvandvaḥ) means devoid of the affliction of dualities such as cold and heat.

Alternatively, it is "incomparable" (*nirūpama*). The meaning is that it consists of that [reality] and consists of you. By means of which armor even I and even Śiva—everywhere, in all the locations to be described hereafter—are omnipresent because we consist of the universe. "In front" means in the eastern direction. The particle *tu* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*). Immediately thereafter...

The phrase "the southern direction" is to be connected with what follows later; likewise, "tathā" (so too) indicates a conjunction. "May Nityaklinnā protect my right side"—this is to be connected with what precedes.
"May Nityā protect me from above; may Sādhu protect me always. (p. 546)
May the eternal one named Nīlapatākā and Vijayā protect me from all sides.
May she who is the embodiment of garlands of flames, the bestower of all auspiciousness, always grant me blessings; may she [protect] my body, senses, mind, and vital breaths. 62.
May she protect my mind incessantly; may the variegated one protect my mind at all times from desire, anger, greed, delusion, pride, and even arrogance. (63)
From evil, from envy, from grief, from doubt, and always from all [these], as well as from inertia and from exertion toward unwholesome actions; 64.
May they always protect me from untruth, cruel thoughts, violence, and likewise from theft; and may they cause my will to be directed toward auspicious things. (65)
May the sixteen eternal goddesses, mounted upon elephants with their own Śaktis, protect me;
likewise, may those mounted upon horses protect me always from all sides.
May they protect me while mounted on lions, and likewise even when situated in the intermediate spaces;
may they protect me from all sides at all times in battle while mounted on chariots.
