The meaning is "then immediately after," that is, toward the *naiṛti* (southwest) direction. The word "tathā" (*tathā*) is used in the sense of conjunction. She, whose majesty was previously described, [protects] the subsequent direction, the *vāyavya* (northwest) direction. The phrase "the left side" refers to the northern direction;
the connection with the subsequent clause is that "Tvaritā protects" it. The particle "tu" is used for conjunction. [She protects] the other direction, the *aiśānī* (northeast).

The word "mām" (me) is intended to indicate the directions situated between above and below. The term "nityānām" means "of the ten Nityās," specifically the tenth Nityā. The word "sā" (she) connects with what follows, meaning "the one called Nīlapatākā.
Thus, "nityā-nīlapatākā-ākhyā" means "the Nityā known as Nīlapatākā. [The mantra continues: "May she protect me from below."

The connection with what precedes is as follows: by the word "and" (*ca*), the phrase "may she protect" (*pātu*) from the preceding [verse] is drawn in for all eleven directions mentioned. The meaning is that Jvālāmālinī is the eternal one whose form is garlanded with flames.
The verb "may she protect" (*pālayet*) connects with what precedes; likewise, the particle "and" (*tathā*) indicates a conjunction, and the word "also" (*api*) likewise signifies a conjunction.

From evil, from lack of discrimination, from doubt, and from ignorance in the form of indecision—this applies everywhere and at all times. From "always" [comes] "in the form of non-doubt," meaning through mental stillness; the word "in auspicious actions" is to be supplied as the remainder. The particle *tu* (but) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*), and it connects with "from exertion in inauspicious actions. Thus, it is used in the sense of conjunction.

May those sixteen deities mentioned previously, ending with the word *kāma* and so forth, who are mounted upon Tārkṣya, protect me; likewise, those who move through the sky and those who dwell on the earth—may they always protect me everywhere and at all times. (68)
May they dispel my diseases caused by spirits, ghosts, piśācas, apasmāra, kṛtyās, and the like, with their own terrifying weapons according to their powers. || 69 ||
May the innumerable powers (śaktis) of the Goddess—mounted upon elephants, horses, leopards, lions, and eagles, and bearing all weapons—protect me always from every side. (70)
Chanting daily this protective armor (*kavaca*) which grants all protection at dawn and dusk,
one who is equal to me shall never see nor hear anything inauspicious.
Since the form of the planets is the embodiment of the Mātṛkā-vidyā,
I shall therefore describe their maṇḍala-abode for the purpose of their worship.
The orb of the moon would consist of the sounds of nectar, while that of the sun would take the form of the consonants of nectar; for the others are composed of those very elements. (73)

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) here is "may they protect me. "Those" refers to the *nityās* (eternal goddesses). "Together with their own powers" (*svaśaktibhiḥ saha*) is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Likewise, as before, the meaning is "together with their own powers. "Those situated on leopards" means even those mounted on tigers are together with their own powers;
by the word "and" (*ca*), the meaning is "together with their own powers. By the word "and," [the same] is implied.

The meaning is "together with their own powers. Likewise, "those situated in the sky" means "together with their own powers," that is, "standing in the sky. Regarding the phrase "the kṛtyās and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to the ḍākinīs and others. "Diseases" (gadān) means from suffering. "Equal to me" (matsamaḥ).
He has become Śiva. || 71 ||

By means of these four verses beginning with "Of the planets" (*grahāṇām*) and ending with "consisting of that which brings about the highest good" (*śreyaskarātmakam*), [the text] teaches the nature of the nine planets as being identical with the *mātṛkās*,
the instruction for the general construction of their respective mandalas composed of those [syllables], and their identity with the moon and the sun.
And he treats the other planets, as well as the introduction to the specific mandalas of the moon and the sun;
therein, the "form of the Mātṛkā-vidyā" refers to the form of the vidyā known as the Mātṛkā, which consists of the letters beginning with *a* and ending with *kṣa*.

The meaning is "of the planets. "Body" (vigraha) means body because of its divine nature. For that reason, their abode-mandala—their essential form which serves as their dwelling—is a mandala consisting of the sixteen vowels, which are of the nature of nectar (*sudhā*), and whose form will be described below. The particle *tu* indicates a distinction.
"Having the form of nectar and its manifestations" means, as before, having the form of the manifestation of the essential nature of nectar. (p.
548) Therefore, I shall describe their mandalas with their respective syllables to you;
in the worship of those nine, there is a ninth mandala consisting of them. (74)
O Goddess of the Gods, having performed the separate worship of the mandalas of the Moon and the Sun, listen now in due order to that which consists of all that brings about supreme welfare. (75)
By laying down four lines—east-west, north-south, south-north—one should produce nine squares, each measuring three cubits in size. In those [squares], indeed: || 76 ||
Having clearly drawn three circles in the middle of the two forearms, one should drop two threads across and upwards in their center. (77)
Having divided [the space] ninefold, one should write in sequence starting from the center and the northeast;
in the center, one should place the eight vowels beginning with *a* (representing wind and the other elements), joined with the *praṇava* (oṃ) and the letter for space (*ha*).

The phrase "of this maṇḍala" connects with what precedes. "The others" refers to those beginning with Bhauma (Mars). "Consisting of that" means consisting of the Moon and the Sun. For that reason, by means of those respective [deities] whose nature is the Moon and the Sun; in the worship of the nine, that is, in collective worships, [it is] "consisting of that," which is of the nature of the Mātṛkās, [whereas in] individual worships [it is otherwise].
In independent worship rituals, those two, the Moon and the Sun, [are worshipped]. || 75 ||
With these fourteen verses beginning with *prāk* and ending with *anugraham*, he teaches the construction of specific mandalas for the collective worship of the nine planets (*navagraha*),
as well as the worship and other rites to be performed therein. In that context, [the area] is three cubits in both length and width.
Among those nine compartments, in the central compartment of the middle [group],

and in the central compartment of the three outermost compartments situated in the eastern direction, and in the center of the three circles within that— specifically in the center of the central circle— one should proceed from Īśa (the northeast) through the nine compartments beginning with Īśa and ending with the northern compartment.

In successive order and by way of circumambulation, one should place the eight vowels beginning with *a* and ending with *ṛ*, starting from the wind [direction] and so forth; in the center, within the middle square situated at the very heart, one should place the "sky" (*nabhas*), which is the letter *ma*.
This sky is endowed with the vowels belonging to the two paths situated between the three circles—that is, the two paths within the interval of the triple circle.

The syllable *akāra* is extended by the sixteen vowels. In that mandala, [the deities] are described twelvefold by means of the twelve [syllables] beginning with "Dhātā" and so forth, as stated in the twenty-sixth verse, the first half of which begins with "Dhātā," in the nineteenth chapter. By the phrase "ending with *namaḥ*," their state of being in the dative case is indicated.

This is already indicated by their names. Those mantras begin with "Oṃ dhātre namaḥ" and so forth, ending with "Oṃ viṣṇave namaḥ. The first [syllable] of Soma is the initial letter of the word *saumya*, namely *so*.
This is joined with its own [vowel], that is, conjoined with the *bindu* (anusvāra). By means of that, it is his name.
Thus is the connection with what follows. By that name ending in the dative case and the word *namaḥ*,

together with its previously mentioned name-mantra, [one should place it] there— in the nine squares situated within the circle located in the middle square of the three squares standing in the eastern row.
One should draw [the mandala] as before, enriched with points (bindus) starting from the northeast, and write the Mātṛkā along with the vowels within the two circular paths;
there, one should worship the Sun with its twelve names that have been proclaimed. (79)
In all cases and at all times, one should worship the Sun with [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava (Om) and ending with "Namaḥ";
likewise, having joined the first [syllable] of Soma (Sa) with its own [vowel], one should worship with that as well.
There, under that name, one should draw the eight vowels beginning with *bindu*,
as well as the sixteen vowels and the *mātṛkā* letters according to their respective combinations.
One should draw it within the two circles and also write it in the central square;
one should worship it there in the mandala together with the fire of burning and the letter *sva*.
Always, at the times prescribed, according to the very sequence taught by Soma, one should offer oblations along with services consisting of sugar, milk, and milk-rice (pāyasa). || 83 ||
Having likewise drawn three circles within the other seven squares,
one should place the letters beginning with each respective class-consonant (varga) and also that Mātṛkā composed of vowels.
Having drawn the center in that manner and having arranged those [squares] in their proper sequence,
one should also write the letters of each respective group (varga) using three-syllable designations.
The letter *ha*, which is enriched by the *bindu* (the nasal dot), ends with the vowel *ṛ*, and is joined with the sixteenth vowel (*au*),

extended by the sixteenth vowel; joined with its own *yoga* (the *bindu*)— that *ha*— is placed in the central square, within the very center of all the squares, accompanied by the fire of burning, the letter *ra*.

The syllable *hrīṃ*, consisting of the vowel *ī* together with the *bindu*, [should be used] during the aforementioned times when there is adverse planetary influence and so forth. [One should worship] with five or sixteen types of offerings. In the remaining squares, starting from the southeast (āgneya) and ending with the northeast (īśāna), as well as in the central and eastern squares, one should place the respective letters beginning with those specific groups (*varṇas*).

In the squares beginning with Bhauma (Mars), the seven consonant groups consisting of those seven planets—namely the seven syllables *ka, ca, ṭa, ta, pa, ya, śa* and so forth—are each expanded by the vowels as before; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. Having written them as before, one should fill the space between the circle and the path.

The middle of all the rows is the middle of the row; having done so, the meaning is that one should divide it into nine parts as before. Within those nine squares produced by the mandalas, "in that order" means in the clockwise sequence starting from the northeast (Īśa) and ending in the north, as previously described.
The syllables of each respective class [of consonants] are designated by three-syllable names; within this [system], there is a pentad of syllables from each class,
along with the three syllables of the name of the planet ending in the dative case, which will be mentioned later in the seventy-eighth verse.

Thus, taken together, there are eight times eight syllables; this is the meaning. "In the middle" means in the center of the central square among all the nine squares of those respective [sections]. "The first syllable of each group" refers to the seven previously mentioned syllables that constitute the beginning of each respective group.
In the center, one should write the first letter of each group [of consonants] situated within the *praṇava* (oṃ).
When these nine have been thus prepared, one should worship the nine planets.
One should write their names in order around [the diagram], starting from Agni (southeast) and ending with Īśāna (northeast);
one should worship them with those [names] in the dative case, consisting of three syllables each.

The phrase "in the nine mandalas" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The expression "from Agni to Īśāna" connects with both the preceding and the following [clauses], like the eye of a crow. "He should worship at one time" refers to the former [clause], while "he should draw [the names] at another time" refers to the latter.
"In sequence" means according to the order that will be described. "By those" refers to the name-mantras beginning with *praṇava* (oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
"Those planets"—thus, according to the manner previously described. "By these name-mantras"—in this way, according to the manner stated.
"In those mandalas"—of those planets. "Those planets"—their favor, which is the favor toward the worshippers. This is what is meant: [the directions] east, west, south, and north.
Having stretched four lines with an interval of one cubit between each, and thus produced nine squares,
one should draw a circle in each of those squares that touches but does not cross the four lines of the square, at a distance of one finger-breadth from them.

Having constructed two circles, one should draw two threads with equal intervals— one east-west and one north-south— through the center of the pericarp of the central circle situated in the middle of all;
thereby, having formed nine compartments, [one should place] therein the compartment situated in the very center.

Having written the syllable *soṃ* together with the name of the person to be protected (*sādhya*) in the central square of the nine-square grid located within the three concentric circles at the center, one should write the eight syllables *aṃ, āṃ, iṃ, īṃ, uṃ,
ūṃ, ṛṃ, ṝṃ* in the remaining eight squares, starting from the northeast and ending in the north.
Having written, in a clockwise direction, the row of *makāra*s— each extended with one of the sixteen vowels and joined with a bindu— as before, within the inner path between the two outer paths;
and having written the *mātṛkā* with bindus on the outer path as before.

Then, in the center of the nine-squares located in the central pericarp of the three circles situated in the eastern row, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and other details;
then, in the remaining eight squares, as before, one should write from the northeast to the north: *ḷṃ*, *ḹṃ*, *eṃ*, *aiṃ*, *āṃ*, *auṃ*.

Having written the eight syllables "aṃ aḥ," one should then write the row of the syllable *u* modified by the vowels and joined with the *bindu*, proceeding clockwise within the inner path between the two outer circular paths;
and having likewise written the *mātṛkā* joined with the *bindu* on the outer path as before.

Then, having written the *praṇava* (oṃ) in the central square of the nine-square grid located in the middle of the three circles within the seven squares extending from the southeast to the northeast, one should write the individual letters of each respective group—
*kaṃ*, *caṃ*, *ṭaṃ*, *taṃ*, *paṃ*, *yaṃ*, and *śaṃ*— one by one, in sequence, in the center of that *praṇava*.

Having written that, outside of it, from the northeast square (īśakoṣṭha) to the end of the northern square, one should write the five groups of five syllables— the *ka*-group, *ca*-group, *ṭa*-group,
*ta*-group, *pa*-group, *ya*-group, and *śa*-group—
corresponding respectively to Bhauma, Budha, Sauri, Guru, Rāhu, Śukra, and Ketu.

Having combined each of the seven names one by one in their respective order and thus written eight groups of eight syllables in total, one should place the initial letters of those respective vargas, modified by the vowels, as before, within the two outer circular paths and within the inner path.
Mars, Mercury, Saturn, Jupiter, Rāhu, Venus, and Ketu—with these [planets], worship is performed everywhere even when no specific mantra is mentioned. (88)
Thus, the mandalas of the nine planets have indeed been declared; by worshipping them within those very mandalas, one should effect their favor.

O Pārvatī, listen now to the description of the maṇḍala for the worship performed on the two days of the sun and moon, as well as on the new and full moon, when they are situated in their respective exaltations.
Having drawn two circles, one should write within them— in the center, by means of eight lines drawn horizontally and vertically— within eighty-one squares.

By entering from all sides starting from the northeast cell (īśakoṣṭha), one reaches the eighty syllables ending with Māyā (Hrīṃ) located within the ocean of nectar; and that [ocean] is situated in the center.
Having written them out in successive order, one by one in each row, and having inscribed the Mātṛkā as before on each successive outer path, thus having completed the nine maṇḍalas,
[one should employ them] for the aforementioned planets during their respective stated periods of adversity and so forth.

Through worship with the prescribed substances and other offerings using the name-mantras of the Sun consisting of twelve names as previously stated, preceded by *praṇava* (oṃ), the dative case, and ending in *namaḥ*; and for the Moon, with *soṃ somāya namaḥ*; and for Mars and the others, with *ūṃ bhaumāya namaḥ* and so forth, up to *ūṃ ketave namaḥ*, the attainment of the stated fruits occurs.
In this manner, in sequence, the auspicious planets are located in the cardinal directions and the inauspicious planets are in the intermediate directions.
With these nine verses beginning with "Bhāskara" and ending with "Īśvarī," he teaches the time for worship,
preceded by its introduction, as well as the worship-mandala for the Moon and Sun individually,
the materials for its construction, and the manner of worship therein; this occurs twice during that [period].
Respectively, on Sunday and Monday; "at the full" (pūrṇikā) means at the time of the full moon.

When the two are situated in their respective exaltations: when the Sun is in the tenth degree of the sign Aries and has reached midday, and the Moon is in the third degree of the sign Taurus and has reached the middle of the sky. Between those two—

The ellipsis is that [the grid] is produced by eight lines within the circle situated between the two verses. Its connection is with the phrase "in the eighty-one squares. "In the middle" means in the center of each respective square.
"The syllables of nectar" refers to those mentioned in the second half of the thirty-sixth verse of the eighth chapter, beginning with *jyākam*.
The letters ja, jha, ṭha, va, and sa, modified by the sixteen vowels;
those numbered eighty ending with *māyā* (the letter *m*), and those numbered eighty ending with the *visarjanīya* (the letter *ḥ*). In the middle:
in the center of the square situated in the very middle of all.
Having placed the *mātṛkā* between the two rows and having woven it with those five, one should write there; then, within that *bimba*, one should worship Soma.
Then, one should draw the orb of the moon with camphor and sandalwood;
on one side, the orb of the sun [should be drawn] with red sandalwood, vermilion, and red ochre.
Having fashioned an image there, one should worship it according to the prescribed form.
Having drawn lines at equal intervals, two horizontal and three vertical, [forming a grid]. (95)
In the middle of those [squares], one should draw the nineteenth [letter], as previously described— namely,
the letters beginning with *pra* (prāṇa) and ending with *na* (nabhas), each joined with its own vowel and combined with the vowels.

Having placed the letter *ṭha*, which has entered the [mantra], in the middle, and having first placed the syllable *hrīṃ*—as previously stated—in the center of the lunar-maṇḍala cell; this indicates a reversal of the sequence, meaning "having intertwined" them.
"Intertwined" means separated by one [letter] each. By those...

With the five nectar-syllables ending in the *visarjanīya* and devoid of vowel modifications, one should form the disc of the sun with any one of them; "of the sun" is to be connected with what precedes. There, in that disc, one should [worship] that Sun according to the described form, using the aforementioned mantras, offerings, and so forth. "Up to two circles" means two circles (*vṛtta*).
"Having placed it within that" means having placed it inside that. "The nineteenth" means nineteen.
The phrase "its lines" connects with what precedes. "In their centers" means in the midst of the four hundred squares produced by those lines. As before.

By means of the movement of entering and circumambulating starting from Īśa [the northeast], one takes the twenty-five letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ma*, starting from *prāṇa* [the east] and ending with *ākāśa* [the center]. These are joined with their respective vowels and bindus, each modified by the sixteen vowels; by means of those letters from *ka* to *ma*.

"By those distinguished by modifications of vowels," meaning by vowels joined with *bhānta* (the letter *ha*) and accompanied by the vowel-modified *a*. "By ten syllables of fire and elements" means by the ten syllables consisting of fire (*ra*) and the elements (*la, va, ya, sa*). Regarding the phrase "having written the script" (*lipim*), the word *lipim* connects both to the preceding term "in a clear form" (*viśadākāram*) and to the subsequent term "in the middle of that" (*tanmadhye*), like the eye of a crow looking in both directions. Thus, the construction is: having written the script (*mātṛkā*) in a clear form, [one should place it] in the middle of that.
In the center of the mandala, by means of the name-mantra, ritual services, and so forth, as previously described. This is what is meant:

having constructed a circle with a measurement of three cubits in length and breadth, and having constructed another circle outside that at a measurement of one finger-breadth, [one should perform the rites] in the pericarp in the very center of the central circle.
Having produced eighty-one squares by means of eight lines each drawn east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east with equal intervals,
one should proceed in a clockwise direction starting from the square located in the northeast corner of those squares.

Having written the eighty syllables of nectar (*amṛta*) as previously described, modified by the vowels and ending with *māyā* (the letter *ha*), one should write the letter *ṭha* in the central square of all the remaining [squares]. Inside that, as before, one should write the syllable *hrīṃ* together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth; then, outside of that, on the circular path (*vṛttavīthī*).
One should contemplate the script woven from the five nectar-like syllables devoid of vocal modification (*svaravikāra*), situated between the two meters (*vṛtti*) by those twenty-five phonemes;
and [the script] woven with the vowels joined by *bhānta* and the ten-syllable [mantra] of Fire (*vahni*). (97)
Having drawn a clear form measuring three cubits in length and breadth,
O Goddess, one should invoke the Sun into its center and worship him as before.
Having prepared images as prescribed on a pedestal, or on a floor smeared with lime, or on a stone slab, or on a well-levelled covered ground, one should worship them.
Thus, in this tantra, the worship of the planets is prescribed for all cases; however, where no specific instruction is given, one should worship them according to that sequence.

Having thus laid out the *mātṛkā* and fashioned this maṇḍala with camphor and sandalwood, one should worship Soma at the prescribed times with the previously mentioned name-mantra and the aforementioned offerings and so forth. Then, having produced two circles according to the previous measurement, as before, in their pericarp—
Having drawn nineteen lines each running east-west and north-south with equal intervals,

one should produce four hundred squares; within those squares, starting from the northeast (Īśa) and proceeding clockwise in a counter-clockwise entry-pattern, one should place the letters from *ka* to *ma*.

Having written the twenty-five syllables, each modified by the sixteen vowels so that they number sixteen times sixteen— totaling four hundred— with the *bindu*, one should write them on the outer circular path.

The *mātṛkā* [is] strung with single intervals by fifty-one syllables— consisting of the twenty-five syllables from *ka* to *ma* which are devoid of vowel-modifications (*svaravikāra*), the sixteen forms of the letter *ma* modified by vowels, and the ten syllables of the elements and fire— each accompanied by the nasal bindu.

Having written [the syllables] with the nasal bindu and having thus drawn this maṇḍala with the aforementioned red sandalwood and other materials, one should worship the Sun there at the prescribed times with the twelve aforementioned name-mantras and the aforementioned offerings and so forth. By that, one becomes a partaker of the attainment of the aforementioned fruits. || 98 ||

By means of these three verses beginning with "pauṭhe" and ending with "vigrahāḥ," [the author] provides instruction on the specific locations for drawing the maṇḍala of the nine planets common to all tantras,
the extension of the previously mentioned worship, and the conclusion of the chapter's subject matter regarding the planets.

And he provides the teaching on its eternal nature. In that regard, within that alternative [view], it is "unobscured" (anāvṛte), meaning free from the veils such as birth and so forth; and "devoid of specific instruction" (viśeṣādeśarahite), meaning devoid of the sequence of specific teachings regarding that.
Thus, by the sequence of the specific teachings of that knowledge, [it refers to] "of the eternal ones" (vidyāyā nityānām).
Thus, O Goddess, this Vidyā has been declared according to its time, place, and nature;
she alone, who possesses all forms, is to be worshipped at all times with one’s whole being. (101)
The pervasion consisting of the reality of passion has been correctly proclaimed;
by the refinement of this within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self.
Thus ends the twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Exposition on the Identity with the World and Other Matters," within the *Śrīkādimata*, among the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*. 28.
The remainder: she alone, Lalitā herself, is to be worshipped as possessing all forms—that is, as possessing the forms of all deities. || 101 ||
Oṃ.

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete tantra known as the *Śrīkādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*, [concerning] the sixteen *Nityās*...
The twenty-eighth chapter, which is devoted to revealing the identity between the world and time and so forth, has been fully considered. Oṃ tat sat.
Regarding the number of verses: twenty-eight yantras are taught here;
as for the explanatory text, it consists of two hundred and eighty-four verses.
Now, the twenty-ninth chapter: O Śiva, [I shall explain] the ritual procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) of the sixteen Nityās,
as well as the division of the directions beginning with the East and the characteristics of the pavilion (maṇḍapa) and other structures.

By means of constructing the locations of the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one obtains the characteristics of the navel, the womb, and so forth; their measurements, the meditation on Agni, his tongues, and the manner of his worship. || 2 ||
The materials for the fire-oblation, both general and specific, the performance of the oblation, the commencement and conclusion, and the fruits, in their proper order.
Listen, O wise one, I shall tell you by what means a mantra-practitioner may attain success;
if he should act contrary to what has been observed, he will perish and go to hell. (4)
Having ascertained the directions by the movement of the sun, the preceptor should perform the rites;
listen as I explain, according to the rules, how the knowledge of the directions is derived from that movement.

Having taught in the twenty-eighth preceding chapter the identity [of the sixteen Nityās] with the world and time, and so forth, he now teaches, immediately thereafter, the sequence for the construction of the pavilion, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and so on, for the purpose of the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*) of the sixteen Nityās. Now:
By means of the twenty-ninth chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Of the sixteen Nityās" and ending with "the desired," [it is explained]. Therein,
by means of the four verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "should go,"...
Having stated the summary of the meaning of the chapter and the instruction regarding the transgression incurred by performing it otherwise, [the author explains]:

therein, in the phrase "of the pavilion and so forth" (*maṇḍapādeḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and other such items. In the phrase "the womb and so forth" (*yonyādi*), the word "and so forth" refers to the girdle (*mekhalā*) and other such items. Of those, namely the pavilions and so forth—this is their visualization (*tad-dhyāna*).

The meditation on each [deity] proceeds from the classification of them as cruel, gentle, and so forth; their worship consists of the worship of the tongues of the fire. The commencement and conclusion are those prescribed by the rules concerning the qualities of the pavilion and other elements in the earlier Tantra and the later Tantra, exactly as they were observed.
"Excluding the previously mentioned qualities and prescriptions. "Niraya" means hell, which signifies being adverse to the deities.

With these five verses beginning with "of the sun" (bhānoḥ) and ending with "one should calculate" (kalpayet), he teaches the sequence for determining the directions by means of the shadow of the gnomon (śaṅku), along with an introductory context. In that regard:
"By the movement of the sun" (bhānoḥ gatyā) means, in effect, by the shadow produced from the difference in the sun's (ādityasya) course during the sequence of its southern and northern solstices.
"Rituals" (karmāṇi)—the word "such as pavilions and sacrificial pits" (maṇḍapakuṇḍādīni) is to be supplied as the remainder. "By that movement" (tad-gatyā) means by the movement of the sun.

"Having made [it] on a perfectly level ground"—the phrase "by means of water-machines and so forth" (jalayantrādibhiḥ) is to be supplied as the remainder. The word "having made" (kṛtvā) is to be understood as displaced in the sentence structure.
Having fashioned a circle by means of rotation on a perfectly level ground,
one should indeed place a gnomon at its center, which is the center of the point.
Having marked the two points, east and west, on the circle according to the sequence of the shadow’s progression in the forenoon and afternoon, one should likewise mark the center on both sides.
Having again constructed two circles with their own respective radii,
[one] situated to the south and the other to the north of the center produced by the intersection of those two.
And at the two junctions, one should lay down the thread between the eastern and western lines;
for those [threads], one should determine the directions starting from the east by means of their tips, with the southern and northern threads.
"Having made a circle" means up to that point. "In its center" refers to the center of the dot (*bindu*); this is an adverbial modifier. The meaning is:
in such a way that the middle of the half-dot situated in the center of the circle coincides with the middle of the gnomon (*śaṅku*).
The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. The phrase "in the circle of that gnomon" connects with both the preceding and the following [clauses].

In the two directions, east and west—that is, having made marks as before in the two directions consisting of the east and the west—the construction follows. "On both sides of that" means on both sides of those two marks. Likewise, having fixed those two [ends], one should rotate [the cord] with its own equal length.

Having rotated two circles by means of a measurement equal to one's own desired radius plus a half-measure, which is equal to the distance between the two marks; that is to say, having made two circles. Of those two circles, the eastern and western ones: [this refers to] "situated in the middle of the junction, in the south and north."

In the two subsequent junctions, this is the object to be qualified. "Between the eastern and western threads" means between the threads consisting of the east and the west. The particle *tu* indicates a collective sense. "To the south and north" (*dakṣottaram*) means to the south and the north.
By the "threads" (*sūtraiḥ*), meaning by the tips of those threads of the pavilion and so forth—by the tips of the threads—the following is what is meant:
On a day when the sun is surrounded by a mass of clouds, in a place not covered by roofs or the like,

having leveled the ground with water-machines and other means so that it resembles the surface of a mirror, one should mark a central point and, from that support, measure twelve finger-breadths in each direction.

Having constructed a circle there, one should place a gnomon that has a base with a circumference of six finger-breadths, which gradually decreases in circumference until its tip is needle-thin, and which is straight in shape.

Having placed a circular disc, twelve finger-breadths in measure and provided with a shadow, fashioned by a master craftsman, such that its center— containing a central point— is situated at the middle of the base's circumference, one should [observe] the tip of the shadow of that gnomon in the forenoon.
Having marked a point where the shadow-tip of that gnomon meets the western side of that circular line in the afternoon,
and having likewise marked a point where it meets the eastern side of that circular line,
the thread reaching both those marks constitutes the east-west line.

Having established two circles, one in front and one behind, which are slightly joined to each other, equal to one another, and with a diameter greater than half the desired [diameter] by means of a measurement that exceeds the measure of the interval between those two marked points by relying on the two imagined marks;
The line that runs transversely, reaching the two points where the eastern and western lines meet the southern and northern lines, and passing through the center, is the north-south line. (p.
558) For the purpose of performing rites such as the fire-oblation (*homa*) and consecration (*abhiṣeka*) for kings, however, there is the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*).
One should construct it with a new cloth, provided with its proper width and length.
It was provided with sixteen pillars, four gates, and beautiful archways,
and its roof and garlands were made of udumbara, vaṭa, aśvattha, and plakṣa trees.
Having covered all the corners, one should construct an altar (vedī) there, measuring one-third of that area, with a height of one cubit, centered in the middle.
One should likewise fashion [the central area] in the middle, resembling the surface of a mirror,
and then [the surrounding areas] in the directions starting from the east, as well as in the corners starting from the southeast.

Having mentally projected that [space], one should determine the four directions— east, west, south, and north— of those [structures] such as the pavilion and the sacrificial pit, by means of the intersection of the two lines running east-west and north-south, using the tips of the lines to be described later. || 9 ||

With these ten verses beginning with "rājñām" and ending with "lakṣaṇam," he teaches the sequence for constructing the pavilion (*maṇḍapa*) and the locations for constructing the altar (*vedī*) and the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) therein;
there, [the pavilion] is joined with a width and length of nine cubits, and a width of nine cubit-measures.

It is endowed with a length of nine cubits; it is provided with sixteen pillars, with four threads stretched out at equal intervals toward the east, west, south, and north—the remainder [of the description] being that there are sixteen junctions; and it has four doors in the cardinal directions.

The remainder: with a garland of *darbha* grass as a covering; with all corners completely covered, meaning the decorative divisions of all corners are concealed. Therein, from one-third of the pavilion—that is, from one part out of three parts—from the center.
In the midst of the four pillars situated in the center of the pavilion (maṇḍapa), and around them, on all sides of the altar (vedi)—

as will be described in the thirty-first chapter— within the locations corresponding to the twelve zodiac signs beginning with Aries and ending with Pisces; the word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction.

The word "kalpayet" (one should construct) connects with the subsequent term "kuṇḍāni" (pits). The ellipsis to be supplied is "a set of four pits. This is what is meant: one should draw nine lines each of nine cubits in length, extending east-west and north-south, and [construct] four [pits] in each of the four outer corners.
By proceeding in twos across the four directions with eight pillars on each side and four in the middle, and likewise with four in the four corners,
it is joined by sixteen pillars in total; thus, the four corners are completely covered, and at the four doors of the pavilion starting from the east, etc., [the structure is established].

Having constructed a pavilion (maṇḍapa) measuring three cubits in width and length, provided with nine bays (bhakti), and endowed with four archways (toraṇa) fashioned respectively from the milky trees known as udumbara, vaṭa, aśvattha, and plakṣa, which form a surrounding canopy;

In the center of the four pillars within that [structure], in the middle of the partition, one should construct [a hall] with a height of one cubit and a length and width of three cubits; [therein are] eight sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and a group of four, along with their forms and names.
O sinless one, I shall describe to you the entire process of emanation according to the prescribed rule.
One should construct circular fire-pits (vṛttakuṇḍas) according to the location for Libra, Cancer, Aries, and Capricorn— these being the four movable signs (cararāśi).
In the fixed signs of Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius,
one should then construct square sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) in their respective order.
In Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces— respectively,
in both types [of lunar days]— one should construct Yoni-shaped sacrificial pits for auspicious rites.

Having constructed an altar (vedī) that is wide and resembles the surface of a mirror, one should arrange eight sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) around it in the eight external divisions corresponding to the twelve zodiac signs, two in each direction, and four sacrificial pits, one in each corner; thus, in total...

One should construct twelve sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*) according to the sequence to be described hereafter, for the purpose of auspicious rites such as fire-offerings (*homa*) and consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) for kings.
The form of those twelve pits consists of squares and other shapes; by the word "crab" (*kulīra*), [the shape is indicated].

The sign of Cancer is thus described. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of a collective aggregate. "Deśataḥ" means according to location. "Vṛttakuṇḍāni" refers to circular-shaped sacrificial pits. In the four fixed signs beginning with Taurus as previously mentioned, one should construct square ones; that is to say, one should fashion a set of four squares. One should perform [this].

Those four pits (kuṇḍas) are square; the meaning is that one should construct the pits according to the sequence to be described hereafter. In the four positions of the zodiac signs—namely the two natures (ubhayātman) and the aforementioned pairs (mithuna, etc.)—there are yoni-pits, which are pits of the shape of a yoni with characteristics to be described later.
"In auspicious applications"—this is the ellipsis. "In inauspicious applications"—this is the ellipsis.

"In the *caras*," meaning in the places of the *cara* (movable) signs, [the shapes] are half-moon-shaped (*ardhaśaśāṅkaka*). "In the *sthiras*," meaning in the fixed signs; by the word "also" (*api*), the phrase "the previous *kuṇḍas*" is drawn in [from the preceding context]. [The shapes] are triangles (*trikoṇāni*).
They are triangular in shape. "In the others" refers to the two remaining zodiac signs. "Tur" (indeed) signifies a distinction. "In the fourfold" refers to the corners; this is the ellipsis.
"In the eight-cornered" means in the octagon. This is what is meant:
in the eight divisions situated outside the aforementioned pavilion, in the four [divisions] located in the four directions starting from the east...

In each of the lines situated at the corners and cardinal directions, proceeding by groups of two, and then sequentially in each line, having combined [the counts], one should proceed from the northern position in a clockwise direction through the two positions located in the eastern row,
up to the line in the northeast corner.

Having conceptualized the twelve zodiacal signs beginning with Aries as locations, for the performance of auspicious rites in those places, there are four circular *kuṇḍas* in the signs of Aries, Cancer, Libra, and Capricorn;
four square *kuṇḍas* in the signs of Taurus, Leo, Scorpio, and Aquarius; [and] Gemini...
In the case of inauspicious movements, one should employ the half-moon diagram;
in fixed signs, the triangles; and in the other [dual] signs, the four-sided figure. (18)
The five-cornered and the six-cornered [fire-pits] should have eight corners with a pericarp;
now hear the characteristics of the measurements and so forth for these nine fire-pits.
In this tantra, the circumference of the middle joint of the middle finger shall constitute one-third of an angula; and in all cases, the angula is measured in this manner.
O Śivā, four of those [finger-breadths] make a muṣṭi; three times that [muṣṭi] is a vitasti; two of those [vitastis] would be an aratni, and from two of those [aratnis] comes a hasta.
Two of those [vyāmas] shall constitute a vyāma; that measure shall be the height of a man.
That [height] shall be ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas); by those measures, the construction of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) is prescribed.
In the signs of Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces, there are four fire-pits (kuṇḍas) shaped like a womb;
furthermore, in the practice of inauspicious rites, there are four half-moon-shaped fire-pits in the four movable signs beginning with Aries,
and triangular [fire-pits] in the four fixed signs.
Having constructed four sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) for each of the two groups of four [signs] in sequence—
consisting of five-sided, six-sided, seven-sided, and eight-sided [pits] respectively— and having combined them all together,

"Listen to the characteristics of the measurements and other features of the nine types of sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), which are circular, square, semi-circular, crescent-shaped, triangular, pentagonal, hexagonal, heptagonal, and octagonal. || 19 ||

With these three verses beginning with "madhyamā" and ending with "kalpanam," he teaches the sequence of measurements for the finger-breadths (aṅguli) and the underlying rationale for the measurement of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). Therein,
by the verse beginning with "madhyamāṅgulī," the following is stated:
Having divided the circumference of the middle joint of the middle finger of the sacrificer’s right hand into three parts,
one of those three parts shall constitute the measure of one *aṅgula* throughout this entire tantra.

By those parts measured at four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), it is called a *muṣṭi*; by three times that—that is, by the measure of twelve finger-breadths consisting of threefold the measure of a *muṣṭi*—it is known as a *vitasti*. By two of those, meaning by two *vitastis*, which amounts to twenty-four finger-breadths, it is termed an *aratni*.

A *hasta* is a measure; from those two [hands], it is by means of two *aratnis*, which amounts to forty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgulis*). "O Śivā" is an address to the Goddess. Those two hands constitute a *vyāma*; its measure is called the *vyāma*-measure. This is the height of a man; that is to say, it is the measurement of men. That...
"By the measures of a man" means by the dimensions of his limbs, which are ninety-six finger-breadths (aṅgulas) in measure.
This is what is meant: since each of the dimensions—length and width—of all the fire-pits (kuṇḍas) specified here is distinguished by twenty-four finger-breadths, [the total] amounts to...
And since each of those girdles (mekhalā) is specified as being twelve finger-breadths (aṅgula) in both height and width,
they together constitute ninety-six finger-breadths.
Having stretched a cord from east to west and having made a mark in its center, one should then [measure] twelve finger-breadths from that point toward the east and the west. (23)
Having wiped it thoroughly, one should also mark two signs there; using the measurement of the east-west signs, one should hang [the cord] from those two very points.
Having made two *haṃsapada* marks from south to north, one should then stretch a cord between those two and erase them according to the stated measurement.
Then, taking hold of those tips according to the measurement of the central mark,
one should form a *haṃsapada* (swan’s footprint) and cast squares on both sides of it.

And because their circumference consists of ninety-six finger-breadths, the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) are equal in size to the height of a human body measured in that same number of finger-breadths. || 22 ||

With these five verses beginning with *prāk* and ending with *mānataḥ*, [the author] teaches, along with the introductory context, the procedure for constructing a square fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the construction of any other type of pit within that square pit. Therein:

The meaning is: having made a mark in the middle of the line running east-west through the center of that [square], that is, having made a mark; "from that" means from the eastern and western marks; "to the east and to the west" by a measure of twelve finger-breadths each—this is the ellipsis; "furthermore" (paraṃ) means additionally, even there.

Even when the measurement of twelve and twelve finger-breadths is stated for both [sides], the meaning is that it is produced by rotation from the support— that is, from the fixing— of those two marks at the east and west.
From the measurement of the horizontal line between those two "swan-steps" (haṃsapada) at the south and north, [the center is determined].
The word "more" (*adhika*) is the ellipsis [to be understood] after "measuring twelve finger-breadths twice" (*dvādaśāṅguladvādaśāṅgulamānataḥ*). The phrase "one should drop those tips"—
meaning the four tips of the four lines running east-west and north-south—
from the central mark at a measurement of twelve finger-breadths, is to be construed with the word "four" (*catuṣṭayam*) here.

This is what is meant: having first established a thread extending east-west according to the previously conceived sequence of directions, and having made a mark at its center, one should then make marks twelve finger-breadths each to the east and west from that central mark, and [measure] the portion exceeding those [marks].
Having wiped it clean, by means of the support of those two marks, one should fashion two circles slightly touching each other from east to west with equal measurement and circumference;
then, reaching the "swan's footprint" (haṃsapada) at their southern and northern points—
Having struck the north-south thread from the intersection of the swan-mark situated in the center of the east-west Brahma-thread,
one should likewise measure twelve finger-breadths and twelve finger-breadths from the central mark there as well.
Having established two marks to the south and north and having erased the respective excess portions,
one should then establish four *haṃsapada* (swan’s foot) marks in the four corners by suspending the four ends of the respective threads at a measurement of twelve finger-breadths each.

Having drawn four lines in total— two lines from each respective end reaching the corresponding *haṃsapada* marks, one oriented east-west and the other north-south— a square of equal dimensions shall be formed.
Within that [area], I shall describe other sacrificial pits to you according to their measurements. || 27 ||
O Śivā, I shall now describe very clearly the procedure for measuring and constructing those [temples] within the movable and other signs of the zodiac, according to the sequence already stated.
One should extend the tip of the eastern thread by an eighteenth part of that [central distance];
likewise, one should rotate [the compass] outside the transverse thread by that same measure.
By relying on the central mark, that circular kuṇḍa should be formed;
however, that ground surrounding the square as well as the other [surrounding] ground must be abandoned.
By that [measure], all [offerings] are obtained in all sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas) from every side;
they become exactly equal by means of the ninety-six-finger dimension. || 31 ||
Having set aside a tenth part from the middle, both below and above,
one should likewise rotate [the circle] from their center according to the measurement of the moon.
"One should make it a perfect square. Within that perfect square, other shapes such as circles and so forth should be made according to measurement;
that is to say, they should not deviate by even a fraction from the sixty-nine finger-breadths (aṅgula) measurement prescribed for the square fire-pit (kuṇḍa).

With these four verses beginning with "teṣām" and ending with "ātmanā," he teaches, along with an introduction, the procedure for constructing the *vṛtta-kuṇḍa* (circular sacrificial pit) and so forth. Therein, "teṣām" refers to those *kuṇḍas*;
"susphuṭa-gamakaṃ" means clearly understood; "śive" is a vocative address; and "tanmadhyāṣṭādaśāṃśena" means by an eighteenth part of its center.
By means of an eighteenth part of the measurement of the middle cord of the square;
outside the transverse cord, on the three transverse cords extending south and north; likewise outside the eastern cord;
similarly on all sides, that is, around the four corners—that is the ground. On the other side, that is, in the other [direction].

The meaning is "in the four directions. By that, [it means] according to the procedure to be described. All the *kuṇḍas* are equal to that, being equal in their square dimensions and circumference. This is what is meant: having made a regular square as before, one should divide the measurement of its central diameter into eighteen parts.
From one of those [measures], having projected a cord extending eastward from the southern [corner] outside the previously laid transverse cord,

and having drawn out an east-west oriented cord with its tip pointing east, one should form a circular shape by rotating [the cord] while suspending it from the center of the "swan's foot" situated in the middle of the square, using that same measure.

One should calculate the measurement of the *kuṇḍa*. When this is done, the area extending outside the circle in the four corners is obtained in the four cardinal directions; therefore, all *kuṇḍas*, according to the procedure to be described, are equal to a square field in circumference of ninety-six finger-breadths (*aṅgula*).
They come into being. || 31 ||
O Śivā, that by which the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) takes the form of a half-moon is so described; by which there may be two [pits] for each of the signs of the zodiac in their proper order.
One should expand that very sixth part on both sides; then, using that measurement, one should draw two lines for each of the western threads.
By laying out [the lines] up to the Brahma-sūtra and by supporting the tips of those two [lines],
the triangular pit (kuṇḍa) is declared to be [constructed] during the four fixed zodiac signs.

With the two verses beginning with *tanmadhye* and ending with *śive*, he provides the instruction for the method of constructing a half-moon-shaped (*ardhacandra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and concludes that this circular pit (*vṛttakuṇḍa*) consists of the aforementioned movable zodiac signs (*cararāśi*). In that context, *tanmadhye*:

The tenth part of the measurement of the square Brahma-thread; "tu" denotes a collective conjunction; [it is measured] below, above, east, and west. From the center of that, at a distance of eight parts below the horizontal thread extending toward the western direction—
"From the center of the imaginary north-south and east-west threads, likewise up to the southern and northern ends of those threads"— this means that by this procedure,
one [extends] two ends of the south-north and east-west threads three parts each outside of the square.

The meaning is that one should extend [the line]. This is what is intended: having divided the measurement of the diameter of the center of the square into ten parts, and having set aside one part each from the east and the west, one should make two marks; then, from the western mark, a horizontal thread should be drawn extending toward the south and north.
Having extended [the cord] outward from that square by three additional parts on each side,

one should fashion a semi-circular *kuṇḍa* by means of a rotation, using a measurement of eight parts from the center of the junction of the imaginary western line and the *brahmasūtra*— which is determined by hanging down from the two tips [of the cord] up to the marked points at its ends.

"May it be so. These two—the circular pit (*vṛttākārakuṇḍa*) and the half-moon-shaped pit (*ardhacandrākārakuṇḍa*)—are for auspicious and inauspicious rites respectively. "O Śivā" is the vocative case. || 33 ||

With the two verses beginning with *tasyaiva* and ending with *rāśiṣu*, he teaches the procedure for constructing a triangular sacrificial pit (*trikoṇakuṇḍa*). In that context, *tasyaiva* means "of that very [square]";
*pārśvayoḥ* means "on the two sides, the southern and the northern"; and *tanmānena* means "by that measurement," i.e., by the measurement of the extended cord.
"From the grasping of the two tips of that [line]" means from the grasping of the two tips of the two posterior lines that have been extended.

This is what is meant: having first made a square as before, one should extend that Brahma-line with its tip pointing eastward outwards, and then divide the measurement of the diagonal of that square into six parts.

From each of those [points], having extended two outer lines from the tips of the western transverse lines toward the two sides, one should strike [the cord] starting from the point where those two lines meet the previously extended Brahma-line— using cords equal in measure to those two lines— to form a triangle.
One should fashion a pit (kuṇḍa). This is declared for inauspicious rites when performed during the four fixed signs (sthirarāśi) [of the zodiac]. || 35 ||
Having expanded the Brahma-thread by one-fifth of that [measure], [one should draw] a pair [of lines] from the east to the west through the middle of the two squares. (36)
O Dear One, one should rotate [the cord] according to the measurement of that corner, reaching as far as the western tip,
then to the northern tip, and likewise to the southern tip.
By supporting the two tips of the transverse thread in the middle of that [central line], there should likewise be two threads extending as far as the Brahma-thread that has been opened out. (38)
O auspicious lady, this Yoni-kunda exists within the four signs that possess a dual nature;
it brings about the accomplishment of the goals of the Vedic hymns and auspicious rites prescribed for those signs. (39)
Having extended the Brahma-sūtra by a seventh part of that [central portion], and then having drawn a circle around it using that measurement as a radius; ||| 40 ||

With these four verses beginning with *tanmadhye* and ending with *siddhikṛt*, he teaches the construction and joining of the yoni-pit, the conclusion regarding what was stated therein, and its fruit. In that context, by means of the fifth part of the middle of that square...

By means of a fifth part of the middle measurement, by the measurement of its corners, and by the measurement of the interval between those two middle corners— from the western end up to the northern end,
and likewise from the western end of the Brahma-thread up to the northern end of the horizontal thread situated in the middle— [mark the points].
From the southern end of the Brahma-sūtra up to the western end,
and from the middle transverse sūtra up to its southern end— “O Dear One” (*priye*) is an address to the Goddess.
[The measurement is] by means of supporting the two ends of that central transverse sūtra.

By supporting [the cord] on the two tips of the north-south line situated in the middle of the square; "O Bhadre" is an address to the Goddess. This is what is meant: by means of a fifth part of the measurement of the central line of the square, [one marks] the Brahma-line.
Having expanded it outward with its tips pointing eastward,

[one should proceed] from the southwest to the northeast and from the southeast to the northwest within the two southern and northern squares of the western portion of that square consisting of four compartments.
By stretching the two diagonal threads, one identifies the central point as the intersection of those two threads; then,
by taking that central point as a support and measuring out to the respective corners, one first [establishes] the inner compartments.

From the western end of the Brahma-sūtra to the northern end of the middle transverse sūtra extending southward and northward, and from the western end of that same sūtra within the southern square to its southern end, one should rotate [the thread] starting from both ends of the middle transverse sūtra therein.

By stretching two threads from the tip of the previously extended Brahma-thread and thereby demarcating four positions consisting of two pairs of heaps for that auspicious ritual action, it is said that the Yoni-shaped sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) brings about the attainment of the aforementioned results. || 39 ||
With the two verses beginning with *tanmadhye* and ending with *kuṇḍakam*, he teaches the procedure for constructing a five-cornered sacrificial pit (*pañcāsrakuṇḍa*). In that context,
by means of the seventh part of the center— that is, by means of the seventh part of the measurement of the central cord of the square—
The word "tat" (that) is an adjective for "brahmasūtra" (the Brahma-thread). "Having made it expanded by measurement" means having drawn a circle using that measurement.
Having made that circle with a measurement of three parts, one should indeed place marks there.
One should drop five lines; that shall be a five-cornered sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa). || 41 ||
Having expanded the Brahma-thread by a sixteenth part of that [diameter], and having likewise drawn a very clear circle using that measurement; 42.
One should draw the middle line of that [square] with half its length as a mark;
there, by the casting of six lines, a six-cornered (ṣaḍasra) sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) shall come into being.
Having extended the Brahma-thread by one-tenth of that middle portion, and having then drawn a circle with that measurement without confusion; || 44 ||
Having marked the signs on the circle according to the measure of thirty-three parts out of its sixty-four divisions, one should drop seven lines.
The meaning is: likewise, by hanging down from the center of the swan-foot (haṃsapada) situated in the middle of that square;
"by the measure of one-third of that" means by the measure of three-quarters of the thread across the middle of that square; "therein" means at those aforementioned marks.
This is what is intended: having constructed a square as before, [one should proceed] with the measurement of its center.

Having extended the eastern end of the Brahma-thread outward by one-seventh [of its length], and having produced a circle by rotating [the thread] from that measurement while supported by the *haṃsapada* situated in the center of that square,
one should divide the thread through the middle of that square into four parts, and [mark it] at each of those three parts.
Having marked five points around that circle, starting from the eastern tip of the Brahma-thread,
and having stretched five threads in the form of bowstrings from each respective mark to the next,
one obtains a five-cornered sacrificial pit (*pañcāsra-kuṇḍa*) by erasing the portions of the circle corresponding to those bow-shaped segments.
In rites for auspicious purposes, it is declared that the southeast direction corresponds to the position of the Gemini zodiac sign. || 41 ||
With the two verses beginning with *tanmadhye* and ending with *ṣaḍasrakam*,
he teaches the procedure for constructing a six-cornered (*ṣaḍasra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). In that context,
"having expanded [the line] by a sixteenth part of the measure of the Brahma-line of the square" means outside of the square, having extended it by a sixteenth part.

The remainder is as before. From the center of the *haṃsapada* (swan’s footprint) in the middle of the circle, according to the measurement of the Brahma-thread, there is the marking—that is, the sign. This is what is meant:
having constructed a square as before, one should divide its central measurement into sixteen parts.

From one of those [lines], having extended the tip of the Brahma-thread outward by that same measure, and having produced a circle by rotating it while suspending it from the center of the *haṃsapada* situated in the middle of the square,
[one should mark] from the southern end of the transverse thread at its center by half the measure of the diameter of that [circle].

Having marked six points on a circle drawn all around, and having stretched six threads from each respective mark to the next in the form of the arc between them, one should erase the circular segments corresponding to those arcs; thus, by erasing the inauspicious portions, there shall be a hexagonal sacrificial pit (*ṣaḍasrakuṇḍa*) located in the southwest direction (*nairṛti*), which is said to be the position of the Virgo (*kanyā*) zodiac sign for inauspicious rites. || 43 ||
With these three verses beginning with "tanmadhye" and ending with "śive," [the text describes] the procedure for constructing the seven-pointed sacrificial pit (*saptāsra-kuṇḍa*).
That seven-pointed pit should be situated in the western direction, facing the wind.
O Śivā, this sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) has been prescribed for the destruction of all enemies.
Having likewise constructed a square on the outside with a measurement of twenty-four units in the middle of that [area], starting from half the measure of the eastern corner; || 47 ||
Having indeed made eight marks all around its corners,
O Śivā, one should draw eight threads around those marks.

And it also teaches the result: there, having expanded [the measurement] by a tenth part of that [square], specifically by a tenth part of the central diagonal line of the square—meaning, outside of the square—and having drawn a circle (the meaning being "having made a circle"), one proceeds as before; thereafter, the word "then" implies "immediately after that."

Regarding the sixty-four divisions: among the sixty-four divisions of the central line of the square, by a measure of thirty-three parts—that is, by a measure of thirty-three parts—the [mark] reaches the bow, meaning it reaches the position of the zodiac sign Sagittarius (Cāpa). This is what is meant: having first constructed a perfect square as before...

Having divided that middle portion into ten parts, one should expand the Brahma-sūtra outward by the measure of one part; then, using that same measure, one should draw a circle centered on the *haṃsapada* situated in the middle of that square.
Next, having divided the measure of the central sūtra of that square into sixty-four parts, among those...
Taking one-thirtieth-third as the measure, starting from the eastern tip of the *brahmasūtra*,

one should mark seven points on the circle; then, by stretching seven threads from each point to the next in the form of chords (*jyā*) and erasing the respective circular segments in the shape of those arcs, this becomes a heptagon.
It is stated that a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) situated in the direction of the wind, at the location of a mass of bows, shall effect the destruction of enemies.

With the three verses beginning with *tanmadhye* and ending with *vai*, he teaches the procedure for constructing the eight-cornered (*aṣṭāsra*) fire-pit (*kuṇḍa*), together with an introduction to the description of the construction of the girdles (*mekhalā*) and other features of the aforementioned pits. Therein:

"Of that middle" refers to the central line of the square. "In the measure of twenty-four" means in the measure of a twenty-fourth part. "On the outside" implies from the square. "From half the measure of the eastern corner" means by half the measure of the line of the corner of the square previously drawn in the east.

"From each corner," meaning from all four corners on both sides; "having made marks," is the meaning of the phrase. "O Śivā" is a vocative. This is what is intended: having fashioned a square as before, one should divide the measuring-line of its center into twenty-four parts.

From each of those [corners], having extended a thread outward in every direction by a measure of one part and having constructed a square there as before according to the prescribed method, one should [draw] on both sides of each line, using half the measure of the diagonal thread of that [inner] square as a support, by shifting the four corners of the outer square.

Having produced two marks in succession and then eight marks, one should strike four lines there from mark to mark as before; then, by clearing away the corners extending outside that, one should fashion an octagonal sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) located in the northeast direction, as described for the sign of Pisces.
For these sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas), one should construct an eight-cornered pit; I shall explain their girdles (mekhalā) and so forth—listen, O wise one, as they are set forth in due order. (49)
One should divide the measurement of the middle ground of the square by three in succession;
indeed, its sides will then be according to one's desired measurement.
Thus, this procedure applies to the thirty-six [rites] mentioned, such as those involving mechanical devices (yantra),
and likewise to the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) and the ten-million-fold oblation (koṭihoma) and so forth, as has been proclaimed.
In any one of the aforementioned fire-pits measuring nine cubits,
one should cause a *koṭi-homa* to be performed by eight men.
For the sake of attaining all perfections, one should offer oblations to those [deities] located in the cardinal and intermediate directions over five days in sequence,
preceded by worship and prostration, and give them their sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
In the phrase "the girdle and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to the womb and other such [parts]. "O Wise One" (prājñe) is a vocative address. || 49 ||

With the two verses beginning with *vṛtta* and ending with *samīritam*, he provides the instruction on the method for constructing the eight-cornered yantra, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and so forth, and concludes what has been stated. In that context, *vṛttamadhyabhuvaḥ* refers to the diameter of the center of the circle.
"Threefold" means multiplied by three. "By its own desired [measurement]" means by the measurement of the sides desired for it.
"Its sides" refers to the eight-sided yantra-kuṇḍas. This is stated in the twenty-fifth chapter. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction.
Regarding the "Koṭihoma and others" that will be described, the word "etc. (*ādi*) here refers to homas involving very large numbers and so forth.

This is what is meant: having drawn a circle according to the stated sequence, one should divide its diameter by the number of sides desired; then, marking points all around the circumference at those respective intervals, one should proceed from each mark to the next.
Having stretched out threads in the form of radii according to the number of desired spokes,

and having erased the circular segments in the form of those respective arcs, one should proceed thus with the diagrams of thirty-six spokes and so forth mentioned in the Mātṛkāpaṭala, as well as in their respective sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas).
And the procedure for the sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) prescribed for great numbers of oblations, such as ten million and so forth, has thus been declared. || 51 ||

With these six verses beginning with "prokteṣu" and ending with "āstikair," [the author] describes the dimensions of the sacrificial pit for the *koṭihoma*, the number of officiating priests (*hotṛ*), the method of that homa,
the fees for the priests, and the fee for the preceptor (*guru*).

It teaches the specific times for performing the *koṭi-homa* sacrifice, the relevant mantras (*vidyā*), and the characteristics of the officiating priest (*hotṛ*). Among those times previously mentioned, one should choose any one that is either auspicious or inauspicious according to its nature, provided it is suitable for the particular rite.
Furthermore, the sacrificial ground should measure nine cubits in both length and width. Likewise...
By those who know the sciences, as defined by the characteristics to be described [later]: (p.
567) "Land measuring two *gocarmas*, a cow with flowing udders, a buffalo-cow with her calf, along with horses, male and female slaves, and ornaments. (54)
Then, for each of them, there were garments and a hundred gold coins;
likewise, those very same things were declared to be equal to those of the preceptor.

In the event of celestial portents, during the affliction of disease, in the face of a terrible enemy assault, likewise upon the conquest of another's territory, or when the occurrence of hostile magical rites and the like takes place; (56)
One should cause the *koṭihoma* to be performed with the primary *nityā-vidyā*, by means of those who are handsome, virtuous, constant devotees of the *Nityās*, and likewise full of faith. (57)
Of all the aforementioned sacrificial pits (kuṇḍas),
the pit for a koṭi-homa should indeed have a depth of only one aratni, while its upper portion [should be shaped] accordingly.
"Successively" means according to the sequence of the fire-offering (homa) procedures to be described in the thirtieth chapter. This is what is meant:

having constructed, day by day, a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) measuring nine cubits and provided with the aforementioned girdles (mekhalā) and other features—selecting a pit appropriate to each case among those described in the *Samudbhava*—as stated in the passage beginning with "to be described," etc.

For five days, one should cause the oblation (homa) to be performed by eight men stationed in each of the cardinal and intermediate directions— men endowed with the characteristics to be described— who perform the rite according to the vidyā to be described until the attainment of their desired success; such is the case for those sacrificers (hotṛ).

In the phrase "one should give" (*dadyāt*), each of the eight subsequent words beginning with "earth" (*bhuvam*) and ending in the accusative case is to be construed individually. One should give [this] on five days at a time. "Two *gocarmas* in measure" refers to the measurement of earth equal to two *gocarmas*.
Bṛhaspati said:
"A nivartana consists of thirty plots measured by seven cubits; ten such [nivartanas] constitute a gocarma."

Twice that amount for each individual Hotṛ; those same substances; by those Hotṛs; the same as what was uttered and declared regarding the collection of materials. In the case of celestial portents, such as abnormalities in the planets, constellations, and so forth; with the first Lalitā; by those devoted to the Nityā.
By those devoted to the sixteen Nityās; by theists who are intent on the sequential worship of the daily (nitya), occasional (naimittika), and other rites. || 57 ||

With the verse beginning with "prokta" (stated), he teaches the measurement of the excavation for the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍas*). In that context, "an *arātna*" is a measure of twenty-four finger-breadths (*aṅgulas*);
this refers to the pit of nine cubits mentioned in the *Koṭihoma*. || 58 ||

p. 568) One should construct the measurement of the girdle for all [the altars] at eight, four, and two *vitastis* respectively in width and height, in front of the *yoni*, the *hotrāsana*, and the tip [of the altar]. || 59 ||
Furthermore, for the great pit (mahākuṇḍa), the girdles (mekhalā) are one cubit in measure;
the width of each of the three is sixteen finger-breadths (aṅgula).
Their heights and numbers are indeed sixteen in sequence;
now listen, O beloved, to the formation of the womb and its latent impressions (vāsanā).
Starting from the middle of the most excellent girdle,
one's own stalk [should be visualized] as a square measuring one *vitasti* in size, resembling the leaf of an *aśvattha* tree.

With the verse beginning with "sarveṣām" (of all), he teaches the measurement of the girdles for all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) as well as the construction of the womb (*yoni*). In that context, by "eight *vitastis* and half of that," [he means] measurements of twelve finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) and four finger-breadths; this sequence of measurement applies to the width and the base, and so forth.

The height and so forth of the upper [girdle] should also be understood. This is what is meant: for all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) except the *mahākuṇḍa*, one should construct a girdle (*mekhalā*) outside on all sides, measuring one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) [in width], with a height of four finger-breadths, and a width of twelve finger-breadths each.
Having joined [the first girdle], one should leave a space measuring four *aṅgulas* all around on the exterior above it; then,
having left a space measuring four *aṅgulas* on the exterior as before, one should construct a second girdle with a width of eight *aṅgulas* and a height of four *aṅgulas* within that interval.

Having fashioned a third girdle measuring four finger-breadths in both width and height, one should construct within that girdle— at its front, side, and middle— the *yoni* (vulva-shaped cavity) characterized by the features to be described for the Hotṛ priest's seat. || 59 ||

With these two verses beginning with *mahā* and ending with *priye*, he teaches the measurement of the girdle (*mekhalā*) of the great sacrificial pit (*mahākuṇḍa*), as well as the procedure for the construction of the womb (*yoni*), together with an introduction to the explanation of its underlying rationale (*vāsanā*). In this context, *tu* signifies a distinction; [the measurement is] from one cubit (*hasta*).
The measure is forty-eight finger-breadths; this refers to the three girdles (*mekhalā*), as is understood from the context.
Because those girdles are divine, the word "of them" (*tāsām*) is used. The measure is sixteen finger-breadths; this is understood from the context.
What is meant is that [the space] all around the great sacrificial pit (*mahākuṇḍa*)—
The lower girdle (adhomekhalā) is forty-eight finger-breadths in width and sixteen finger-breadths in height; above that,
leaving a space of sixteen finger-breadths on the outside, its interior width is thirty-two finger-breadths.
One should construct a second girdle sixteen finger-breadths in height above that;

then, leaving sixteen finger-breadths on the exterior, one should construct a third girdle measuring sixteen finger-breadths in both its internal width and height. This is according to the nature of the *yoni*.
"Her emanation" refers to the emanation of the womb from its latent impression (*vāsanā*). "O Beloved" is an address to the Goddess. || 61 ||

With the four verses beginning with *bahiṣṭhā* and ending with *samūhataḥ*, [the author] describes the nature of the womb (*yonisvarūpa*) and the sequence of its construction: "One should make it one span (*vitasti*) in length and half of that in width. (p. 569)
It should be one finger-breadth high all around above the girdle.
One should fashion the yoni from the root, slightly tapered at the tip, and small on all sides;
for the yoni is the great abode of the fundamental principle (tattva) that serves as the cause.
Therefore, because he is identical with that very [reality], the ritual procedure for oblations is performed right there;
he bestows full fruits without effort and without delay.
He teaches the measurement and arrangement of the *tadvāsanā* by means of the emergence from the womb of the great pit (*mahākuṇḍa*). In that regard,
starting from the center of the outer girdle (*mekhalā*)— that is, from the ground area which constitutes the center of the first girdle— one [should mark] a space of two or three *mātrās*.
It should have a tube fashioned with a height of twelve finger-breadths, resembling and shaped like an *aśvattha* leaf, measuring one span in length,
twelve finger-breadths in length, and half of that in width.
[It should be] six finger-breadths in width on all sides in all the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*). "Slightly" means a little.

The connection with what follows is: "on all sides of this which has become the cause of everything. What is meant is this: in all the fire-pits, on the ground in the middle of the first girdle (*mekhalā*) at the place where the officiant sits.
Having fashioned a square pedestal out of clay measuring two finger-breadths in length and width and one finger-breadth in height,

one should then fashion a circular stalk (nāla) that reaches from the top edge of the first girdle to the middle of the upper girdle; this stalk should have a perforation made for the purpose of spreading [the material] over the upper girdle and should touch the inner girdle.
Above the upper girdle connected to that stalk, there is a leaf of the *aśvattha* tree, six finger-breadths in width at its middle,
with its length measuring twelve finger-breadths— tapering gradually from that region toward both sides— and one finger-breadth in height.
One should fashion the *yoni* from the base, gradually tapering toward the tip;
