this is the traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) that one should understand the *yoni* for all sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) except for the circular ones.
It is the station (*pada*) of the causal reality (*tattva*), specifically the reality of gold (*jātarūpa-tattva*), which is the cause of the universe.

The place of rest for arising is "great" because of its fullness. Therein, in the womb (*yoni*), that [womb] is of an undivided nature. Regarding the measurement of the "great pit" (*mahākuṇḍa*)—that is, the pit described for the *koṭi-homa*—the word "of the womb" (*yoneḥ*) is to be supplied.
"From the collection" (*samūhataḥ*) means by a correct gathering. As for "gathering" (*ūha*), it is as follows:
For a pit with a girdle measuring one *vitasti*, the height of the neck (*nāla*) is one *vitasti*;

the measurement of the width of its base (*yoni*) is six *aṅgulas*, the length is one *vitasti*, and the height is one *aṅgula*. For a great pit (*mahākuṇḍa*) with a girdle measuring one cubit (*hasta*), [the proportions are as follows].
To determine what the respective measurements are, the measurements for that context are written here:
the measurement of the *nāla* (tube) is forty-eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*); the width of the *yoni* is one cubit (*aratni*);
the length measurement is one hand (*hasta*); and the height measurement is four finger-breadths. This refers to the *yoni-kuṇḍa*.
The traditional teaching is that even without constructing a yoni above that girdle, it brings about the attainment of its fruit. || 66 ||
One should perform this measurement for the great pit (mahākuṇḍa) by combining [the dimensions];
however, one should fashion the navel (nābhi) in the center of every pit according to the prescribed rule.
One should fashion a beautiful lotus with eight petals;
one should make both the pericarp and the petals four finger-breadths in size.
The height is also declared to be six [parts] for every six [parts] of the width;
and in the case of a large pit, one should perform it accordingly by means of inference, as previously described.
Meditation on the fire is said to be twofold, according to the division of gentle and fierce.
The gentle meditation has the form of Nityā; hear now about the other, O beloved. (69)

With the first half-verse beginning with *nābhim* and ending with *tathā*, these two verses teach the method for constructing the *nābhi* (navel) in the center of all fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*), its characteristics, and the application of the rules for the great pit (*mahākuṇḍa*) as previously stated. Therein, "according to the rule" (*vidhānataḥ*) means by the manner that will be described.

"Of beautiful form" means having a measurement that is neither deficient nor excessive. "With four" [each]—the word "each direction" is understood as the remainder. The conjunction "ca" (and) is used for accumulation.
By the phrase "also with six by six," the word "with finger-breadths" (*aṅgulaiḥ*) is drawn forward from the previous verse. This is what is meant: of all the fire-pits (*kuṇḍa*) mentioned...
Having produced a circle by rotating ten finger-breadths in each direction while supported by the swan-foot mark situated in the center of the pit,
one should construct a pedestal within that circle with a height of six finger-breadths.
Having established a circle by measuring four finger-breadths in each direction from the support of the swan-foot situated in the center of that [square],
and having made another circle outside that measuring six finger-breadths,
one should conceive of the center of the inner circle as the pericarp (*karṇikā*).

Outside of that, by means of an eight-petalled arrangement within the intermediate path (vīthī) situated between them, one should construct the navel-lotus (nābhipadma), which measures twenty finger-breadths (aṅgula) in its center. This applies when there is a large sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa),
or a pit prescribed for a *koṭi-homa*, or when, by adaptation (*ūha*), there is a pit with a width and length of one cubit (*aratni*).

On a couch measuring six *aṅgulas* in height, the measurement of the pericarp (*karṇikā*) at the base of the navel-lotus is four *aṅgulas*. Thus, in a great sacrificial pit (*mahākuṇḍa*) nine cubits in width and length,
one should write down the numerical measurements of the respective parts of that navel-lotus by means of inference as to how many [units] they are.
Just as the measurements for the elevations amount to one hundred and eight finger-breadths (aṅgulas),

the measurements for the petals in each direction are one hundred and eight finger-breadths, and the measurements for the width of the pericarp (karṇikā) are seventy-two finger-breadths; these together constitute the measurements for the diameter of the lotus in finger-breadths.
There are three hundred and sixty in number; the navel-lotus is likewise of that same measure.

With the verse beginning with "Dhyānam" (meditation), he introduces two types of meditation for Fire by distinguishing between the gentle and the cruel; having extended the application of the gentle meditation, he now introduces the cruel meditation. In that regard, the meditation on the form of Nityā is as follows:
The meditation on the gross form as proclaimed by each respective Nityā; "O Dear One" is an address to the Goddess. || 69 ||
Having two heads, seven hands, three feet, and seven tongues, he possesses a form of three aspects with six exceedingly cruel, reddish eyes. (70)
With his four right hands, he holds a spear, a rosary, a *sruk* ladle, and a *sruva* ladle; with the others, a javelin, a palm-leaf fan, and a fine vessel for clarified butter.
One should meditate upon the Fire-god with his mouth wide open, as if incessantly intent on devouring;
this is declared to be the power of meditation for all cruel oblations.
If one should offer oblations into the head of the fire, or into the body, or likewise into the ears or the eyes, then that [sin] will swiftly destroy his transgressions.
Then, one should properly worship the seven tongues in those two mouths and offer oblations; thus, one attains every desired object in an instant.
The tongues—Hiraṇyā, Kanakā, Raktā, Kṛṣṇā, and Yathārthakā—are situated in the right face; they grant all accomplishments through worship. (75)

With these three verses beginning with *dviśīrṣa* and ending with *īritam*, he teaches the visualization of the fierce form of Agni. In this context, the remainder is that his form is threefold according to the distinction of the qualities (*guṇas*), such as *sattva* and the rest.
With the right hands (*savyair dakṣiṇaiḥ*) and the other left hands (*itarair vāmaiḥ hastaiḥ*), [he holds] a fine vessel of clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*).
A golden vessel filled with clarified butter.
Here, the sequence of weapons should be understood as starting from the upper arms and ending with the lower arms. "Vyāttavaktra" means having a wide-open mouth. || 72 ||

With the verse beginning with "of fire" (vahneḥ), he teaches that there is an offense in performing a homa in parts of the fire other than the tongues; or, in that context, [the word] "there" (tatra) signifies a conjunction. [The word] "him" (tam) refers to the practitioner. || 73 ||

With the verse beginning with "tataḥ," he teaches the worship of the seven tongues, the oblation (homa) therein, and its fruit. In that context, "therein" means one should offer oblations into the two faces of Agni; by the word "and" (ca), the meaning is "into the seven tongues. "In an instant" (kṣaṇāt) means without transgressing the prescribed time for the mandala and so forth. || 74 ||

With the verse beginning with "Hiraṇyā," he teaches the names of the four tongues of the mouth on the right side of Agni. In that context, "yathārthakā" means [endowed] with forms and so forth; she is the bestower of all accomplishments (*sarvasiddhidā*), meaning the giver of desired fruits. || 75 ||
By means of the verse beginning with "Suprabhā," [the author] states the names of the three tongues of the left face;
of those, the tongue at the end is for all rites:
"Suprabhā, Atiraktā, and Bahurūpā are located on the left. (p. 572)
An oblation performed upon the multiform tongue accomplishes all aims. || 76 ||
One should offer oblations in the other [fingers] during rites of a cruel nature as desired;
however, having first worshipped whichever finger one offers into seven times, [one should proceed]. (77)
Then one should offer oblations upon the tongue when it has been invoked in that rite;
O beautiful one, hear now the substances for the general daily homa.
Clarified butter, cooked rice, milk-rice, and sesame-rice—these two pairs are declared and prescribed for the daily rites. (79)
Having strewn auspicious darbha grass everywhere in all auspicious rites,
O beloved, as well as in malevolent incantations and other cruel or various other rites.

In cruel rites, one should use the constellations, trees, sacrificial porridge (caru) produced from their blood, and their respective meats, along with the substances prescribed for each specific case.

And it teaches the bestowing of accomplishment (*siddhi*). In that context, "going to the left" means situated at the left face. "The accomplisher of all aims" means that which effects various accomplishments in all fire-offerings (*homa*). The traditional teaching (*sampradāya*) is that one should perform the daily fire-offering (*nityahoma*) in that very [face]. || 76 ||

With the two verses beginning with *itarāsu* and ending with *sundarī*, [the author] generally explains the necessity of performing the hand-homa (*karahoma*) within the group of six other tongues, the worship of those other tongues preceded by their respective [primary] tongue and ending with the preceding tongue for each specific rite, and the prescription for the homa of that [tongue].

And he introduces the discussion on the materials for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*). Therein, among the other six tongues— excluding the one called Bahurūpa— in whichever tongue [is intended], then after the worship of the tongues, in that which has been described as corresponding to each respective rite, [she is called] Sundarī.
The address of the Goddess. || 78 ||

With the verse beginning "ājyam" (clarified butter), he teaches the materials for the daily fire-oblation (*nityahoma*). Therein, five materials are mentioned in the first half-verse; among them, "that pair" refers to rice mixed with sesame seeds.
This applies to the *nityaka*, that is, the daily oblation. 79.

With the verse beginning with "subhaiḥ" and so forth, he teaches the different types of ritual strewing (*paristaraṇīya*) for auspicious rites, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and the like. In that context, "in all [tantras]" refers to every tantra; "in others" refers to rites such as eradication (*uccāṭana*).
"O Dear One" (*priye*) is a vocative address. || 80 ||
With the verse beginning with "nakṣatre" and so forth, he teaches the substances for the fire-oblation (*homa*) in rites of a cruel nature. In that regard, it is stated:
"In all cases, one should likewise offer flowers and fruits individually. (p. 573)
One should offer all substances, such as rice and clarified butter, in sequence, measuring exactly one niṣka each.
Having bathed, wearing clean garments, and being perfumed with incense, garlands, and scents, the practitioner, with a serene mind and countenance, should perform the fire oblation (homa). || 83 ||
Facing the east and seated upon a grass mat, preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma),
and having performed the ritual placement of mantras on his limbs (nyāsa), he should sprinkle the center of the sacrificial pit with the arghya water.

For the sake of complete purification, one should draw four lines with a blade of *darbha* grass in the center of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), thereby purifying all other substances located therein without exception.

Regarding "with the nakṣatra-trees," this refers to what is stated in three verses beginning with the seventy-sixth verse of the twenty-first chapter; the word "of the enemy" (*ripoḥ*) is to be supplied as the object. "With the sacrificial porridge (*caru*) produced from the blood of its [the enemy's] *yoni*" refers to the sacrificial porridge cooked with the blood of the *yoni*-constellation of the enemy, as described in the two verses—the seventy-ninth and eightieth—of that same twenty-first chapter.
Likewise, in the case of a combination: "with their meats" means with the meats of the birth-constellations of one's enemies; this is explained in various places in the respective chapters. || 81 ||
With the verse beginning with "prasūnāni," he teaches the quantity of each individual offering substance.

In that context, "tathā" means one by one. Regarding the phrase "annājyādi," the word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to milk-rice, sesame, rice-grains, and the like. By the expression "niṣkamātram" (the measure of a niṣka), [the quantity] of the clarified butter and other substances is indicated.
This means that one should perform ninety-six oblations with a measure of one *prastha*. || 82 ||

With the verse beginning with "snāta" (having bathed), he teaches the preparatory rites for the Hotṛ priest at that time. Among these, the phrase "with a serene mind and face" refers to the context of the regular, occasional, and auspicious *homa* offerings.

With ten and a half verses beginning with "prāṅmukhaḥ" and ending with "udīritaḥ," [the author] teaches the general procedure for all *maṅgala-homas* both before and after [the main rite], as well as the common application of this same method to the *krūra-homa*. In that context, "having placed his limbs [upon the seat]" (*nyastagātraḥ*).

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "with the mantras of the nyāsa prescribed for each respective Nityā. Therein means "situated in that [yantra]," specifically situated in its source (the *yonipada*) and situated around the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). Therein means "in the nine compartments" (*navakoṣṭha*), specifically in the compartments starting from the east. Of the word "seven," the term "tongues" (*jihvā*) is the substantive. In the center means "in the central compartment. Thus, one should meditate upon the Fire.

Recalling the fire in its respective form of the daily [rite] according to the method prescribed for the *nityahoma*, it is to be construed with the word "should worship" (*pūjayet*) in the following verse. The phrase "with the names of the fire" mentioned previously is the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*). The word "and" (*ca*) serves as a conjunction (*samuccaye*).
"Consisting of two syllables, etc. refers to the two seed-syllables of Śakti and Lakṣmī, and so forth. Of the eight...
And for Agni and his seven tongues, the mantra is as follows: *hrīṃ śrīṃ agnaye svāhā hrīṃ śrīṃ*. (p.
574) One should worship the tongues there in the east, west, south, and north.
But remembering the seven [deities] in the east and other directions, as well as Agni in the center, || 86 ||
One should worship with clarified butter and perform seven oblations (homa) in sequence,
offering to each of the tongues of Fire individually, beginning with their two-syllable names.
O Śivā, having uttered the mantras for the eight [deities] ending with "svāhā" in their respective order,
one should take the fire along with its vessel and the charcoal in one's hand.
Having uttered "Homage to the flesh-eaters," he should then take another vessel,
circumambulate the pit, and place it in its center.
Having kindled the fire and performed the sprinkling with the mantras beginning with Lalitā,
and having strewn it around with *darbha* grass and leaves of the *palāśa* and *aśvattha* trees.

"Hiraṇyāyai svāhā" and so forth. "Sabhājana" means together with the vessel; "namaḥ kravyādebhyaḥ" (homage to the flesh-eaters) is the remainder [of the mantra]. "Anyat" refers to the remaining charcoal that has been discarded. "In the midst of that" means in the middle of the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*).
With *darbha* grasses, they are placed with their tips pointing north in the east and west, and with their tips pointing east in the south and north.

The phrase "on the middle girdles" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "With leaves of *palāśa* and *aśvattha*" means with leaves from either the *palāśa* or the *aśvattha*. Likewise, regarding the oblations of clarified butter (*ghṛtāhuti*), [the procedure is described] by the second half of the fifty-ninth verse and the first half-verse of the following verse in the fifth chapter.

According to the aforementioned sequence, preceded by the recollection of each respective tongue, one should offer nine fresh oblations for each sub-tongue (*pratijihvā*) and one oblation for each of the surrounding powers (*parivāra-śakti*), using the root mantra and the specific *nityā-vidyā* for each, as well as those born from the Nātha, the *Nityā*, and the *Ātmabhūta*.

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "by means of mantras consisting of the nine Nāthas, the fifteen Nityās, the Ādinityā, the eight-syllable [mantra], and the five elements. [One should contemplate] the great fire in the form of the Śakti situated within one's own seat of ignorance, located in the center of the two-petaled lotus within the middle of one's own eyebrows.

[The mantra] has attained identity with its own essential form. Following the preliminary strewing—meaning the strewing starting from the east and ending at the north—one [should perform the rite] with ashes over the darbha grass used for the strewing that has been burnt. This is what is meant:
seated upon the seat facing the east, having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) preceded by breath control (prāṇāyāma),...
Having sprinkled the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and the oblation materials with the water set aside for the *argha* offering,

one should produce nine squares by drawing four lines— east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east— with a blade of *darbha* grass upon the pericarp of the navel-lotus situated in the center of the pit, and then [sprinkle] with the *argha* water.

Having sprinkled [the area] and taken the charcoal placed in the vessel with his hand, he should cast the entire mass of charcoal toward the south with the mantra "Obeisance to the flesh-eaters" (kravyādebhyo namaḥ). Then,
having offered sixteen constant oblations of clarified butter according to the root mantra, [he proceeds].
One should offer oblations one by one with [mantras] born from the Lord, Nityā, the Self, and the Bhūtas. || 91 ||
Then, having sprinkled oneself and meditated upon her,
one should perceive her as situated in the place of one's own command (svājñā), preceded by the act of strewing the sacrificial grass (paristaraṇa).
Having applied ashes from the Dandhvan fire as a tilaka and having smeared his limbs,
that man, possessing that very form, shall complete his worship and wander about happily.
Having cast the embers toward the [southern] direction, having circumambulated the pit three times clockwise,

having established that fire in the central square and kindled it, one should sprinkle it with water using the mantra of one's own chosen deity from among the respective Nityā-mantras, such as Lalitā and the others.

Having strewn around the middle girdle of that sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) with *darbha* or *kuśa* grass whose tips point northward and eastward, and having envisioned the Goddess within using the leaves of either the *palāśa* or *aśvattha* tree, one should place the fire in the center and the seven tongues of flame, such as Svāhākṛti and the others, in the compartments of the pit starting from the east and proceeding clockwise.

Having meditated, one should worship the fire in the center with the mantra *hrīṃ śrīṃ agnaye namaḥ*, and then worship it thoroughly with the seven-tongued mantras, such as *hrīṃ śrīṃ hiraṇyāyai namaḥ* and others according to one's preference,
while recollecting each respective tongue during the *Lalitā* oblation.
Having offered nine oblations for each tongue with the daily *nityā* mantras of the third section of the *Śrīvidyā*,

and having offered nine oblations for each of those [other] tongues in the homa of the respective *nityās* using their individual tongue-mantras ending in *svāhā*, [one should worship] the fire in the daily, occasional, and auspicious homas.

Having offered one oblation for each [deity] according to the sequence of their worship using the mantra of the respective deity to be venerated— thereby offering the eternal formless [deity] and the form prescribed therein for auspicious rites— and having offered sixteen oblations with clarified butter for both the daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites, [one should proceed] in the case of optional (kāmya) rites.

Having offered oblations of the specified number of times with the substances prescribed for each respective rite, and having offered in the *Lalitā-homa* with the *Nātha-mantras*, the *Tithinityā*, the daily mantra of that specific day, the eight-syllabled *ātma-mantra*, and the *bhūta-mantras*;
and having offered in the homa of the other *Nityās* with the *Nātha-mantras* alone; then, as before, having sprinkled water around the fire, [one worships] the Goddess.

Contemplating [the self] as the Great Fire in the form of the Power (Śakti) residing within the support of one's own Command (svājñā), and having meditated upon identity [with that], one should burn the sacrificial grass for strewing (paristaraṇa-darbha) and other materials in that fire; then, having applied a tilaka with those ashes and having repeated the respective Nityā-vidyā as many times as the number of oblations offered, one should perform the ritual placement (nyāsa) as before.
"One should perform" refers to cruel rites such as malevolent magic (*abhicāra*) and the like. || 94 ||
This procedure has been proclaimed for homas involving cruel rites;
in those [rites], the performance of that homa is likewise constant once it has been completed. (94)
One should perform anointing upon oneself with the mantra and likewise worship; thereafter, one should daily perform the regular ritual sequence with the specific mantra for that particular day. (95)
One should worship fifty pairs and also prostrate;
when the auspicious [planet] has first risen, one should utter: "Protect me! || 96 ||
Thus everything has been told to you regarding the sacrificial pits and so forth as they have been proclaimed;
that fire sacrifice (homa) is said to be threefold, according to its gross, subtle, and supreme natures.
The gross and the supreme [forms] have been correctly explained in the subsequent chapter;
however, those things which are to be known regarding the procedure for the other [the subtle form] shall now be stated.
Thus all [the rites] have been declared; through these oblations one shall obtain prosperity, and by means of these oblations one shall destroy enemies and one's own sins.
With these six verses beginning with "teṣu" and ending with "vāñchitam," consisting of half-verses and so forth,
a fire-oblation (homa) should be performed after the cruel oblation (*krūrahoma*) for the purpose of pacifying its effects; for that purpose,
it should be accompanied by the recollection of the worship of the previously mentioned daily couple (*dinanityāmithuna*).

He teaches the conclusion, accompanied by the introduction stating that the two subtle supreme homas will be explained in the subsequent chapter, as well as their fruit. In this context, "constantly" means every day; "likewise" means in the manner already described; "by the Vidyā" means by the respective Nityā-vidyā.
One should worship that respective Nityā—this is the ellipsis. The "constant ritual" (*nityakrama*) refers to the sequence for the daily worship of each respective Nityā.

"Then" (*tataḥ*) means after that worship of the respective Nityā. "With the mantra of that specific day" means with the mantra for the particular day as stated in the twenty-fifth chapter—this is the ellipsis. As previously mentioned:

In the sixteen-petalled [mandala] consisting of sixty-four squares as described, the mantra consisting of the syllables "pāhi mām" (protect me) is to be used; this is the remainder [of the instruction]. Everything that is to be performed by the practitioner after the cruel *homa* sacrifice is prescribed for the sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth. It is taught regarding the sacrificial pits and so forth.
The procedure for the construction of the girdle, the navel, the yoni, and so forth has been declared.

This is specifically in the thirty-second subsequent chapter. Regarding "of the other," namely the gross fire-oblation (*sthūlahoma*); the word "those" (*tāni*) is to be qualified by the phrase "declared further on. Thus, from the oblation—that is, from the oblation performed in the manner previously described.
(177) O Īśvarī, there is nothing that cannot be accomplished by means of the *homa*, nor is there anything unattainable;
therefore, one should accomplish everything desired through the *homa*. 100.

The pervasion consisting of the principle of knowledge (vidyātattva) has been correctly described. Through the refinement of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very principle is assimilated into one's own self.
Thus ends the twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Construction of the Fire-pit," in the *Śrīkādimata* among the Sixteen *Nityātantras*. Oṃ.
"Evils" refers to inauspicious things. "Nothing is unattainable" refers to that which is not within the domain of enemies; "nothing is unobtainable" refers to that which is desired. || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha— entitled *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*— upon the complete tantra known as the *Śrīkādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*, [concerning] the sixteen *Nityās*...
The twenty-ninth chapter, which is devoted to illuminating the identity between the world and time and so forth, has been fully considered and completed. Om, that is the Truth.
Regarding the number of verses: there are no yantras composed in this twenty-ninth chapter;
the commentary text consists of three hundred and thirty-one verses.
Chapter Thirty.
Now, the common deities of the site (vāstudevatā) belonging to the sixteen Nityās are present there; I shall correctly describe their wheel and the sequence of their worship to you. (1)
Their fruits, as well as the rules for their oblations, likewise the ritual offerings (bali), the subtle rules for oblations, their fruits, and furthermore the supreme [methods]. || 2 ||
Listen in due order, O Goddess of gods, to those [methods] proclaimed for the attainment of the fruit, without which all mantras in this world would certainly be fruitless. (3)
In ancient times, there was a certain asura of square form who brought about the destruction of all; for his very slaughter, all the gods made an effort.
Having done so, they were intent on killing him, but he became invulnerable to them by virtue of a boon;
then, in order to repel that [threat] for both of us, he spoke thus to me.

In the preceding twenty-ninth chapter, having taught the procedure for constructing the pavilion, the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), and so forth for the purpose of the fire-oblation (*homa*) of the sixteen *Nityās*, [this chapter] subsequently teaches the general deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*) of the sixteen *Nityās*, their wheel (*cakra*), the worship thereof, and the respective fruits [of such worship].

Then, with the thirtieth chapter consisting of one hundred verses, beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "without remainder," he teaches the prescriptions for that *homa*, the offerings (*bali*) for that, the prescriptions for subtle *homa*, and the procedure for the supreme *homa*. Therein, first—

With these three verses beginning with "sixteen" and ending with "certainly," he teaches the subjects of the chapter and the fruitlessness of all mantras due to a deficiency in the practice of that knowledge. In that context: "of those" refers to the deities of the site; "therein" means in the wheel; "those" refers to you.

The "fruits thereof" are the fruits of the worship of the Vāstu deity; the "prescriptions for its oblation" are the prescriptions for the oblation to the Vāstu deity. Likewise, "bali" refers to the bali offering to the Vāstu deity; the "fruits thereof" are the fruits of the subtle oblation. Furthermore, the fruits resulting from the supreme oblation have been described in their proper sequence.

The remainder [of the verse] follows. "O Queen of the Gods" (*deveśī*) is the vocative address. By those who have performed the meditation as described, it is certain (*dhruvam*), that is, definite. || 3 ||
By means of these seven verses beginning with "caturasrākṛtiḥ" and ending with "te," [the author] explains the cause of the origin of the Vāstu deities, their origin, their number,
the transgression incurred by failing to perform their worship and so forth, and the fruit of their worship.

He teaches this together with the introduction to the description of the procedures for the wheels (*cakra*) and so forth. Regarding that, [he says]: "Now tell us about that *vāstupuruṣa*, who causes the destruction of all and is intent on the injury of all living beings. (p. 579)
If he had not pacified his pride, the entire universe would have been overwhelmed by calamity.
When they had spoken thus, I said that his death would be difficult to accomplish;
one should bury him in the earth and likewise place [the weapon] upon his body.
And constantly, for the sake of subduing those fifty-three who were devoid of movement, he appointed [the gods]; however, by those among them who were averse to worship, [these things] were done.
They would take upon themselves good deeds and perform evil ones;
therefore, one should always perform their worship every day.
Only auspicious things arise quickly, and not even a mention of anything inauspicious;
now listen to the procedure for that wheel and so forth, which I shall explain to you correctly. (10)
Having drawn ten lines east-west, north-south, south, and north,
eighty-one equal squares are thereby produced.
Of that Asura; "the gods," namely Brahmā and the others. The word *kṛtvā* (having made) connects with *samudyamam* (an exertion) in the preceding clause.

By those gods, [they acted] against us two, Śakti and Śiva. For the purpose of repelling him—that is, for the sake of slaying the Asura—they [approached] me, Śiva. Among us gods, *tu* (but/indeed) serves to distinguish.

The "pacification of pride" (*darpaśānti*) means the extinguishing of the arrogance born from the conceit of being invulnerable. If you do not speak of the pacification of pride, then by that *Vāstupuruṣa* Asura—[the phrase] "when this has been said" is the ellipsis—by those gods, by me, Śiva, [his] destruction, that is, his death, [shall occur]. Of that *Vāstupuruṣa*.

Difficult to perform, difficult to do; that asura; of that asura; "sthāpayet" [is used] with the causative suffix (*ṇic*) for its own sake because of its frequent occurrence, meaning "he would remain. The connection of "fifty-three" (*tripañcāśat*) follows later.
The word "of the gods" (*devānām*) is to be supplied [as the object], completing the phrase "fifty-three gods. The syntactical connection here is: "of that asura, of the destruction..."

"Because it is difficult to perform, I have instructed and declared to the gods that they must remain for fifty-three days upon his body after digging him into the earth, in order to effect a state of motionlessness; [this was said] regarding those gods,
by those gods who were averse to performing the worship."
The term "performed" (*kṛtāni*) is qualified by the term "well-performed" (*sukṛtāni*) which follows later. Therefore, for that reason, [the result accrues] to those gods.
In the phrase "that wheel and so forth" (*tac-cakrādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the abiding of the respective deities, their worship, the consecration of their wheels, and so on.
ḥ | those [are] yours || 10 ||

With these four verses beginning with *prāk* and ending with *īritam*, he teaches the procedure for constructing the wheel of the deities of the site (*vāstudevatācakra*). In that context, by those stretched lines, they become equal, meaning having equal intervals. The syntactical connection is that within those squares there are nine squares.
"One should make one" means that one should unify them. Outside of that—that is, outside of the nine squares already unified—one should make nine single squares in their center.
Outside of those, one should unify three squares in each direction, starting from the east, in due order. (12)
Then, by means of four horizontal lines in the four corners, one should divide the corner squares into eight; then, on both sides of those again—
Likewise, one should combine two by two in the middle of the directions within that path; thus, one remains as a remainder, and thirty-two are said to be outside.
In the very center, one should properly worship Brahmā, who is seated upon a lotus,
possessing a golden luster, four faces, and being devoted to the study of the Vedas.

The word "in the street" (*vīthyām*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. Regarding the phrase "in the four corners," the ellipsis is "nine squares formed by combining [the lines] in the two outer streets. The grammatical connection is: "squares [formed] from the four horizontal threads.
On each side of those [squares], there is one horizontal thread for each pair of squares at every corner.

"On both sides of the middle path's squares"—the remainder is "two squares each. "In that path" means in the middle path. "From the middle"—the remainder is "of the two pairs of squares joined together.
"Outside" means in the outer path; the remainder is "thirty-two squares. This is what is meant:

Having produced eighty-one squares by stretching ten lines each toward the east, west, south, and north with equal intervals, and having unified the nine central squares therein, [one proceeds] around the inner and outer paths within that space.
In the [mandala] consisting of sixteen squares, having combined three squares each in every direction,
there remain four squares in that path, one by one at each corner.
In the twenty-four squares situated in the outer row, four squares are assigned in sequence for each corner;
likewise, in order, two squares at each corner are divided in two by a horizontal line, making a total of...
Having designated the eight squares of two half-squares each located at the four corners as the positions for the eight deities in successive order, one should again, in the second row,
combine the two squares on each side of those respective corners into single units, and then, in that same row, in the center of each direction.

Having set aside each remaining single square for the purpose of arranging the syllables according to the sequence to be described, one should likewise designate thirty-two squares in the outer row as the locations for the thirty-two deities.
Thus, including the combined placement of syllables, there are fifty-three locations for deities, excluding the four squares used as the bases for the syllable-arrangements. || 14 ||

With twelve verses beginning with *sarvamadhye* and ending with *samīritāḥ*, he teaches the names of the fifty-three deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*), their order of placement within the previously described wheel at the specified locations, and their respective name-mantras. Among these, [the first is] *sarvamadhye*.
In the space consisting of nine squares made into one, and outside of that in the immediately adjacent row, one should worship these [deities] starting from the east and proceeding clockwise:
Āryaka, Vivasvat, Mitra, and the other Mahīdhara. (16)

O Dear One, one should worship one [deity] in each of the two half-cells at the corners, and eight [deities] in those two [central squares], surrounding them from the southeast to the northeast as before.
Sāvitra, Savitṛ, Śakra, Indrajit, Rudra, Tadjaya, Āya, and Apavatsaka—these are declared to be the eight by name. (18)
One should worship the eight [deities] in sequence, starting from Agni and ending with Īśāna, located at the corners, half-corners, and sides,
using their names preceded by the syllable *Tārā* (Oṃ) and ending with *namaḥ*.
One should likewise worship all the others mentioned in this wheel:
Sarva, Guha, Aryamaṇa, Bhañjaka, and Pilipicchaka. (20)
O Maheśvarī, one should worship Carakī, Vidārī, and Pūtanā in each of the eight directions, starting from the northeast and proceeding around the exterior.
Īśāna, Parjanya, Jayanta, Śakra, Bhāskara, Satya, Vṛṣa, and Antarikṣa are, in order, those who occupy the compartments of the eastern direction. (22)

In the four locations consisting of three squares each—formed by combining [the central] three squares—one should place these [deities] beginning with Āryaka. The "other" refers to the fourth [set]. The phrase "eight deities" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. In that pair [of squares], from the southeast (Agni) to the northeast (Īśāna), in the two half-squares on both sides...

The meaning is: from the two half-squares located in the fire-corner (south-east) up to the two half-squares located in the Īśa-corner (north-east). "In the same manner as before" means in a clockwise direction. "O Dear One" (*priye*) is a vocative address. "Rudra and Rudrajaya" refers to Rudra and Rudrajaya; these are the deities. "Eight" refers to [the deities] beginning with Sarva, which will be mentioned in the immediately following verse.

"With Tārā and others" means beginning with the *praṇava* (oṃ). By the phrase "ending with *namaḥ*," it is indicated that each respective name should be in the dative case. Likewise, "in a clockwise direction. "The others" refers to those previously mentioned, such as Brahmā and the rest. "In that manner he should worship" means he should worship them according to the stated sequence using their respective names as mantras.

By the second half of the verse beginning with "sarvam," five names [are given]; by the first half beginning with "carakī," three names [are given]. "Maheśvarī" is the vocative case. "Vahiḥ" means on the outermost external path. "Aṣṭau devān" means the eight deities. "Diśaṃ prati" means in every direction. By the [verse] beginning with "īśāna,"...
Agni, Pūṣan, Vitatha, Yama, Gṛharakṣaka, Gandharva, Bhṛṅgarāja, and Mṛga are situated in the southern chamber. (23)
Likewise Nirṛti, Dauvārika, Sugrīvaka, Varuṇa, Puṣpadanta, and the one called Asura, as well as Śoṣa and Roga. (24)
In the compartments situated in the western direction, these should be worshipped in due order:
Vāyu, Nāga, Mukhya, Soma, and likewise Bhallātaka. (25)
Argala, Diti, and likewise Aditi—
these deities are declared to be situated in the compartments arranged in order from the north.

Having divided the square situated in the middle of the second row into four parts by means of diagonal lines, [one should proceed] in those very [sections], starting from the east and so forth, in due order.
The eight names are given by the verse beginning with *agni*.
The eight names are given by the verse beginning with *nirṛti*. These are the deities starting with Nairṛti.
The five names are given by the second half of the verse beginning with *vāyu*. The [remaining] five names are given by the first half of the verse beginning with *argala*.
The three names: therein, the word division is *argalaḥ* and *ditiḥ*. These refer to Vāyu and the others. This is what is meant:
in the center of the aforementioned wheel consisting of nine combined squares, one should place Brahmā in his prescribed form;
and on the outer path surrounding it, in the four locations consisting of four sets of three combined squares in each direction.

Starting from the east and proceeding in a clockwise sequence, one should place the four [deities] beginning with Āryaka in the eight squares formed by the two half-squares produced by drawing the transverse lines at each corner within those two rows— that is, the inner row and the outer row.
From the southeast (vahni) to the northeast (īśāna) in clockwise order, one should place the eight [deities] beginning with Sāvitrī;

then, in the intermediate corners of the central path, and in the two sides of the remaining corners— within the eight [squares] produced by combining pairs of squares— one should likewise place them.
In the positions from Agni to Īśāna, one should [worship] the eight [deities] beginning with Sarva in clockwise order; then,

on the outermost path, in the thirty-two squares starting from the square of Īśāna, one should [worship] the thirty-two deities beginning with Īśāna in clockwise order with their respective name-mantras.
One should worship with [mantras] beginning with the Praṇava and ending with "namaḥ. || 26 ||

With these three verses beginning with "dvitīyā" and ending with "tāni," [the author] describes the remaining four squares in each direction, one by one, along the central path of the previously mentioned vastu-cakra.

He teaches the sequence for the placement of the letters at the beginning of the Yugas. Therein, starting from each of the four squares situated in the middle of the second row, one proceeds in each direction according to the order of the individual squares;

by means of the diagonal lines (*koṇasūtra*) and the two diagonal lines, one follows the sequence of the four positions located within those very same individual squares, moving clockwise as before, toward the east.
In the four positions situated within the eastern compartment (p.

583), one should write the letters of the *nityārṇa* in their sequential order, corresponding to the number of ages (*yuga*). Likewise, in the east and so forth, as well as on the right, one should write the *nityārṇa* and the letters of the rising breath (*aṇudaya*).
In the west, one should draw those whose occupations involve earth, water, fire, and wind;
in the north, having written "I worship," one should perform sacrifice to them there.
Facing the direction of Indra (the east), he should offer oblations individually into each square pit with rice,
mung beans, and barley, sequentially soaked in honey, clarified butter, and milk.
One should offer oblations one hundred and eight times, or twenty-one times each, with those respective substances and likewise with milk-rice (pāyasa) while reciting the mantras.
And one should offer them a bed (vali) accompanied by milk-rice (pāyasa) with various side dishes,
mixed with sugar, and combined with milk, plantains, cakes, and so forth.

The *yugārṇa*, the *paryāyanityārṇa*, and the three *tattatkālīnayugārṇa* and *paryāyanityārṇa* syllables; these are to be placed, as before, in sequence and in a clockwise direction. Likewise, in a clockwise direction, they are to be placed in the four positions located in the square on the right side.
The meaning is: the syllables of the eternal [mantra], the syllable of non-arising, and the syllable of arising, as well as the three daily syllables for that particular day.

In the west, within the four locations situated in the western corner, there is also the grasping of the essential nature of "Bhūmi" and so forth. [One should take] the words ending in the second case (accusative) from the end of the ritual action. In the north...

In the four positions situated within the northern square, there are the four syllables "pūjayāmi" (I worship). In this wheel, [one worships] those aforementioned deities beginning with Brahmā. || 29 ||

With the two verses beginning with *pratyekam* and ending with *pāyasaiḥ*, he teaches the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and other requirements, the sacrificial materials, and the number of oblations for the purpose of the *homa* of the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*). In that context, "with those" means with the previously mentioned name-mantras ending in *svāhā*; "one should sacrifice" (*hunet*) means one should perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*).

"Facing the directions beginning with Indra" (caturasrandradiṅmukhaḥ)—here the *sandhi* is due to the divine nature [of the context]. "Indra’s direction" means facing east (*prāṅmukha*). "In sequence" (*kramāt*) means one by one. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. "In that manner" (*tadvat*) means by exceeding the stated number. This is what is meant: in a square (*caturasra*) sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*), one faces the east.
Having performed [the ritual] there according to the stated method, preceded by the installation of the fire and so forth,

one should offer to Brahmā and the others— using each of the three substances such as honey and so on, along with the three types of rice-puddings (pāyasa)— one substance for each deity, according to whichever of the stated numbers is appropriate.
"One should offer oblations of clarified butter," thus [it is said]. || 31 ||
With the verse beginning with "valim" and so forth, he teaches the offering of oblations (bali) for them and their respective materials.
In that context, "for them" refers to Brahmā and the others. "Combined with milk, plantain fruit, cakes, and so forth" is an adverbial modifier of the action.
Thus, when the sun has entered Leo, on the full moon day of every year, one should perform the worship of Vāstu in one's own home within a mandala, following the sequence in all respects. (33)
On that day, one should feed the Brahmins who are regular devotees according to one's ability;
one should provide them with various kinds of sweet foods and other delicacies, ensuring they are not fewer than three.
Having honored them according to one's ability, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to those who have eaten;
for one who acts in this manner, nothing inauspicious ever occurs in the home.
There shall be no premature death from disease, spirits, ghosts, and the like;
nor shall there be affliction by snakes, mutual quarrels, or inauspicious events. (36)
He becomes a possessor of sons, grandsons, wealth, health, cattle, and female slaves;
free from disease and victorious, he lives for a long time, renowned in his home. (37)

In the phrase "apūpādi" (cakes and so forth), the word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to ghee and other such items. This is what is meant: having invoked the fifty-three deities mentioned for the fifty-three locations previously described, and having worshipped them individually with perfumes, flowers, incense, lamps, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), or substances prescribed in the *tantra*, [one should proceed].
Having offered the *valisikthas* (rice-ball fragments) immediately thereafter, and having placed the foods in another vessel according to their proper positions,

[the practitioner], wearing red garments and a turban, holding a sword in hand, and surrounded by men likewise holding swords, should go to one of the following locations: a crossroads, a temple, a riverbank, or the foot of a well-known tree.

Having placed [the offerings] on the sacrificial ground (sthaṇḍila) in their respective places, the reciter of the Śrīvidyā mantra should then return home with guards who are indifferent [to worldly concerns], and having performed the ritual placement (nyāsa) upon his limbs, he should become one whose very self is the deity. || 32 ||

By means of these seven verses beginning with *evam* and ending with *bhavet*, [the author] explains: the time for the worship of the Vāstu deity in one's own home every year; the sequence of the daily worship of the *nityācakra* on those respective days; the fruit thereof;
the necessity of performing this worship in the houses of kings and others; and the consequences of its non-performance.
And he teaches the transgression [of failing to do so]. In that regard, according to the sequence thus declared: "in one's own home" means in the house of the practitioner;

"in the mandala" means in the aforementioned house (or the mouth of the Śakti). The word "should perform" connects with the preceding term "in the worship of Vāstu. "On that day" means on the day of the propitiation of the deity Vāstu. "The regular devotees..."
"Devotees of the sixteen Nityās"; "not lacking three," meaning not lacking the three *puruṣas*;

in the phrase "with sweet and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the other five tastes; in the phrase "those devotees, such as *bhūtas*, *pretas*, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to *apasmāra*, *kṛtyā*, and the like; [these are] inauspicious things.
In all royal palaces, as well as in the quarters of the queens, in the residences of ministers, counselors, and generals, and likewise in the city— (38)
The preceptor should perform [the rite] every year for the sake of the aforementioned success;
otherwise, there will be constant suffering through results contrary to what was taught. (39)
On a surface made of one of the three metals or stones, measuring one cubit in size,
one should inscribe the names of the respective deities within the womb of the *māyā* syllable.
There, one should worship them for seven, five, three, two, or one day;
and one should indeed install them permanently in some dwelling or other.
One should remember them with the thought that they are deities and offer three handfuls of flowers;
that brings auspiciousness to their house, as well as to villages, cities, towns, and the like.
One should perform all these rites for the pacification of minor afflictions and for prosperity.
"Inauspicious things" refers to poverty and the like. "In his house" means in a residence protected by the deities of the site (vāstu-devatā) who have been worshipped.
"Everywhere" refers to royal residences, pavilions, and so forth; likewise, in the case of the queen's quarters.

"In the residences and dwelling places of the queens," that is to say, in all the cardinal and intermediate directions and in the center; "tu" (but/however) is used for emphasis. If the worship of the deities of the site (*vāstudevatā*) has not been performed according to the stated sequence—[as described] in the two and a half verses beginning with "triloha... and ending with "...samṛddhaye"—then [the following occurs].

In these chapters, by means of verses, he teaches the procedure for constructing the *vāstu-cakra* (site-plan) and so forth for houses and other structures, as well as their consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*) and their results. In that regard, "on surfaces of three metals and stone" refers to surfaces made of gold, silver, copper, and stone; it is to be one cubit in measure in both width and length.
The names of those respective deities are stated [to be] ending in the accusative case; this is the remainder [of the sense].

Their state of ending in the accusative is because it is taught that they are to be written within that wheel following the words "I worship" (*pūjayāmi*), and also because the rule regarding the accusative ending is prescribed for the writing of the four names beginning with Earth (*bhūmi*). [This occurs] within the womb of *māyā*.
Within the interior of the *hṛllekhā*; in that wheel; those deities; somewhere in an undisturbed location; in that established place;

three times, meaning not less than three repetitions; in places such as market towns (*kharvaṭaka*)—here the word "etcetera" refers to cities (*pattana*) and the like; one should perform [the rite] in the prescribed manner within the *vāstudevatācakra*.
The word "such as the consecration" (pratiṣṭhādikam) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 42 ||
Thereafter, O beloved, hear [about] the accomplishment (*siddhi*) through subtle and supreme oblations (*homa*). (43)

One should likewise offer as oblation into the fire at one's own *mūlādhāra*, which has reached the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī, the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) in the form of both the signified and the signifier.
"O wise Śambhu, tell me now correctly that procedure by which, O Goddess, an equality between us two may indeed arise through the act of oblation. (45)
O Lord, tell me clearly about the location of the fire in the foundation, the abiding state of Kuṇḍalinī thereafter, her form, and all her activities. (46)
Listen, I shall now explain to you in full detail the procedure which is heard as the supreme "Science of the Fire-Sacrifice of Vital Breath" (prāṇāgnihotra-vidyā) in the three Vedas.

With the half-verse beginning with *tataḥ* and ending with *vai*, he teaches, preceded by an introduction to the description of success (*siddhi*) through subtle and supreme oblations (*homa*), the procedure for the subtle homa in brief as well as its majesty; therein, the *ca* denotes a conjunction (*samāhāra*). *Priye* is the vocative case.

In one's own *mūlādhāra*, which has the form described in the sixteenth chapter, [resides] that which consists of both the signified (*vācya*) and the signifier (*vācaka*), and is of the nature of both signified and signifier; in the manner that will be explained, by whatever procedure, [this is the union] of us two, Śakti and Śiva. This is what is meant.

One should offer the phenomenal world, consisting of both the signified and the signifier, as an oblation into the fire that enters the mouth of the Kuṇḍalinī power situated at the Mūlādhāra; by means of this method of offering, a practitioner equal to us two shall arise. || 44 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with "tadvidhānam" and ending with "prabho," the Goddess asks about its procedure— the location of the fire in the *mūlādhāra*, the state of Kuṇḍalinī, her form, and her activity. Therein, "its procedure" refers to...

The detailed procedure for the subsidiary rites of the fire-sacrifice (*sūkṣmahomāṅgavidhāna*). The two words "O Wise One" (*prājña śambho*) are an address to the Lord (*īśvara*). Now, in this chapter: "that form" refers to the form of Kuṇḍalinī; "her activity" refers to the activity of Kuṇḍalinī; "clearly" means very distinctly.
"O Lord" (prabho) is an address to the deity. || 46 ||
With these four verses beginning with "Listen" (*śṛṇu*) and ending with "something" (*kiñcana*), [the author],

preceded by an introduction to the exposition of their ritual procedures, teaches the praise of those vidyās in the Vedas and their majesty and so forth; [this serves as the introduction] to the remainder of that majesty which is to be declared in this chapter.
Having known that [method], a man will certainly never again enter a woman’s womb;
it is free from expense or exertion, and its fulfillment requires no dependence on others. (48)

That state where the mind rests from afflictions, which is entirely free from defilement, the abode of bliss, heaven itself, consisting of the universe, [arises] from the consciousness that knows the object of knowledge. 49.
All that remains to be said here will be clearly demonstrated in the thirty-sixth chapter;
therefore, I shall describe a portion of it there.
In the center of the *mūlādhāra* of all living beings, there is the fire that arises as both eternal and non-eternal; likewise, in their hearts, there is the sun.
At the crown of the head, below the aperture of Brahmā (brahmarandhra), the moon is situated;
that very essence shall be the first Nityā, consisting of three parts (trikhaṇḍaka).

He explains that [the ritual] will be described in the thirty-sixth chapter. Therein, the procedure is a subsidiary part of the subtle fire-offering (*sūkṣmahoma*). Now, in this chapter, the procedure is supreme and unsurpassed. It concerns the womb of a woman—that is, the mother’s belly—which is free from expense and exertion.
Because it does not depend on the exertion of performing rituals, offering clarified butter, giving priestly fees (*dakṣiṇā*), or practicing penances such as the *Cāndrāyaṇa*,

and because it consists of mantras for reconnection (*anusandhāna*); and because its fulfillment is independent of others— since it requires no specific *ṛc*-verses, officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), supervisors (*upadraṣṭṛ*), and so forth— the perception of its own distinctness occurs within itself alone.

And because it consists merely in the contemplation of dissolution: that which is the mind (*manas*) is the place of rest for the afflictions (*kleśa*), because its nature is the dissolution of conceptualization and discursive thought (*saṅkalpa-vikalpa*). It is entirely free from impurity (*niḥśeṣakalmaṣa*), because there is nothing apart from itself.
It is the abode of bliss (*sukhāspada*), because within itself the mind brings about the dissolution of all emergence (*nirvyutthāna*). It is self-abiding (*svagaṃ*), within itself.

Because it is contained within; because it consists of the universe, since consciousness consists of the object of knowledge and the act of knowing, and because it consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; here, in this chapter; therefore, from that.

With these five verses beginning with "nityā" and ending with "tair," he teaches the subtle nature [of the mantra], its contemplation, and the method of its oblation (*homa*). In this context, "nityānityodite" means as described in the *Nityānitya-paṭala*; "tadvat" means as stated in the Tantra; and "sthite hṛdaye" refers to its abiding in the heart, namely, the *anāhata-cakra*.
In the skull of the head, below the *brahmarandhra*, at the lower portion of the site of the *brahmarandhra*,

in the center of the downward-facing lotus, is that which consists of the triad— the primordial *Nityā* consisting of three parts, the three sections of the *Śrīvidyā* composed of Fire, Sun, and Moon. [This is indicated] by the words "of them," and so forth.

By this verse, the following is meant: at the *mūlādhāra*, one should contemplate with the mind the oneness of those three—the nature of fire belonging to Śrīvidyā—and their mutual arising through their splendors by means of their coming and going, O Śivā. (53)
Having thus understood that triad of fires to be kindled and composed of those [elements],
one should meditate upon that which is wondrous and free from the conceptual constructions of the mind.
Having formed any one of those three previously mentioned classes [of mantras] by means of two [others] in sequence, one should perform the oblation with them in an encapsulated manner (puṭita).

With a steady mind, one should offer oblations into the fire at the mouth of Kuṇḍalī, consisting of the vowels enveloped by the syllables "bhānu-hṛt" (the sun's heart, i.e., *ra*), along with the *tāra* (the *praṇava*) and *huṃ* sounds.

Because the first segment has its radiance extending upward, it begins from that [point] and extends to the *brahmarandhra* within the heart; because the middle segment of Śrīvidyā has its radiance extending in both directions, it begins from that [point] and extends from the *mūlādhāra* to the *brahmarandhra*.

In the pericarp of the downward-facing lotus located in the region below the *brahmarandhra*, there is the third section of the Śrīvidyā, which is lunar in nature; because it consists of nectar, its radiance flows downward.
Beginning from that point and extending as far as the *mūlādhāra*, these three sections consist of the threefold fire.

One should contemplate one's own self as having become unified with that [object] through the continuous flow of going and coming, by means of a mind absorbed in that [object]. This is according to the manner described above. The phrase "absorbed in that" (*tanmaya*) implies being like a mirror that is distinct from gold and other materials; it is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) and devoid of duality.
The genitive case in *teṣām trayāṇām agni-sūryya-somānām* (of those three: fire, sun, and moon) expresses a different substratum (*vyadhikaraṇa*).
It refers to the previously mentioned letters, which were intended [as the subject] by the sixtieth verse beginning with "starting from the letter *a*" (*akārādi*) in the fifteenth chapter.

By means of two [syllables] from among the three groups of letters consisting of fire, sun, and moon, one [syllable] from those groups of letters is enclosed according to the sequence to be described hereafter. This is what is meant:
of those [letters] mentioned in the fifteenth chapter...
Among the letters intended as the three lines of the *kulāsana* consisting of the nature of the Sun and Moon, [there are] the sixteen vowels of the lunar nature,
and the sixteen [consonants] from *ka* to *ta* of the solar nature.

Among the groups of letters, from the sixteen-letter group beginning with *ka* and ending with *sa*— which consists of the fire-element (*tejomaya*)— one should [use] those respective letters, encapsulated according to the sequence to be described by two such fire-element groups other than the one in question.

One should offer oblations, according to the sequence to be described, into one's own non-conceptual radiance—which has been declared to consist of sixteen aspects comprising the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge. || 55 ||
With these five verses beginning with *puṭitān* and ending with *samam*,

he teaches the mantras for the Prāṇāgnihotra and so forth. Here, by means of the syllables of the Sun and the Heart on the Kulāsana, [the letters] from *ka* to *ta* situated upon the solar lines [are indicated].
One should offer oblations in sequence with lunar syllables situated within the cavities of fire-rays, and likewise with fiery syllables situated within the cavities of moon-rays. (57)
Likewise, one should offer oblations with the letters of fire situated between the letters of the sun and moon;
and one should also offer oblations with the letters of the sun situated between the letters of the moon and fire.
Then, one should likewise offer oblations with those [syllables] situated between the fire (RA) and moon (SA),
and also by reversing the order of those sixteen.

There are sixteen [syllables] with the color of the sun. "Hṛt" refers to the letter *sa*. On its seat, among the fiery syllables situated on the line of fire (*vahnirekhā*) in reverse order, since *sa* is the first, by means of the word "heart" (*hṛt*), which expresses that [letter], [the sequence begins] starting from that [sa] and ending with *tha*.

The sixteen letters are said to have the form of fire. Therefore, by means of the sixteen solar letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ta*, and by means of the sixteen fiery letters beginning with *sa* and ending with *tha* in reverse order, [one should place] the vowels upon their respective family-thrones (*kulāsana*).

One should [visualize] the letters such as *ka* and *ā*, which reside on lines consisting of the nature of *soma* (the moon), as being of the nature of the moon. Regarding the phrase "with the *tāra*, the *praṇava*, and the *huṃ*s," the meaning of *huṃkāra* is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru.
One whose intention is steady (*niścalāśayaḥ*) means one whose mind is not distracted by anything else; such a thinker [produces sounds] such as *ka āso* or *kha āṣo*. Thus [it is said].

Or else, there are sixteen [syllables] ending with *it*. [These are formed] by means of the vowels belonging to the Moon (the short vowels) situated within the "enclosures" (*puṭa*) of Fire (three) and Sun (twelve), combined with the letters from *tha* to *sa* in direct order (*anuloma*), and the letters from *ka* to *ta* in reverse order (*pratiloma*). It is the same for the others.
The meaning is "by means of the *praṇava* (OM) and the *huṅkṛta* (HŪM). "In sequence" means in the order beginning with the letter *A* and ending with the *visarga*.
Those mantras are as follows: *tha ato*, *da āṇo*, and so forth, ending with *sa aḥ ko*; thus there are sixteen.
They are situated within the "sheaths" (*puṭa*) of the Moon and the Sun—that is, between the letters starting with *A* and ending with the *visarga*.
Of the sixteen gentle letters beginning with *ta* and ending with *ka*,

and of the sixteen solar letters situated within the cavities [of the palate] beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa*— that is to say, by means of the *Tāra* (Oṃ) and the *Huṃ* sounds— their mantras are as follows:
Now, from "atha ato" up to "aḥ sakaḥ," there are sixteen [syllables].
Within the enclosure formed by the letters *bhā* and *candra*, there are the earth-colored letters beginning with *ka* and ending with *ta*;
the moon-colored letters beginning with the *visarga* and ending with *a*; and within those enclosures, the fire-colored letters.
[The syllables] beginning with *tha* and ending with *sa*; likewise, as before, with the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *huṅkṛta* (huṃ). Those mantras are as follows:
*oṃ khadaṃ*, *oṃ gadhau*, *oṃ*, and so forth, ending with *tasa oṃ*; these are sixteen.
[They are formed] by placing the vowels from *a* to *visarjanīya* (*aḥ*) between the moon (*a*) and fire (*ra*).

The mantras consisting of the letters from *sa* to *tha*, combined with the vowels situated within the clusters (*puṭa*), as well as those from *ka* to *ta* joined with the vowels, and likewise with the *tāra* (oṃ) and the *huṃ*-sounds— these very mantras,
thus described in twelve ways by means of the syllables, constitute the fire-oblation (*homa*).
Having composed all that was to be said, both in words and in meaning, together with them.
The form consisting of the threefold fire belongs to both of us as well;
indeed, our other forms are assumed through our own will.
And those [bodies] belonging to other deities are under the control of the power of one's correct will;
liberation is said to be simply the stability of being absorbed in that [Supreme Reality]. (62)
Just as there are sixteen [syllables] beginning with *ākāśa* and *ākāṣa*, and ending with *atatho*;

likewise, by means of the syllables from *tha* to *sa* placed within the enclosure of fire (*ra*) and moon (*u*), and the syllables from *visarjanīya* (the visarga) to *a* also placed within that enclosure; and similarly, by means of the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*) accompanied by the sound *huṃ*.

The syllables beginning with *ka* and ending with *ta*, along with the solar letters (*bhānvarṇa*), constitute their mantras; for example, *thakaḥ*, *oṃ dakhaṃ oṃ*, and so forth—these sixteen [mantras] end with *oṃ*. Thus, by means of the *tāra* (the syllable *oṃ*), there are the mantras of the various divisions described in the sixfold manner according to the stated method.
Even though they consist of four syllables each, they have been written with sandhi applied according to tradition.

Of those sixteen mantras—of which it is said there are sixteen types through sixfold variations—the remainder [is understood] as being in reverse order (*prātilomyāt*). Thus, by means of both direct (*anuloma*) and reverse (*viloma*) order, one performs the *homa*.
The meaning is that the oblation (*homa*) should be performed because of its divine nature; the phrase "by means of the syllables" implies "consisting of the three-fold light.

By means of the sixteen desired mantras—spoken of as being in the form of one hundred and ninety-two—as uttered [in the aforementioned manner], [one attains] the entirety consisting of the knower, the knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

By means of those three syllables each, which consist of the nature of the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable, and which take the form of designators, that [reality] is non-different from them. This is what is meant: among the twelve divisions thus mentioned, by means of the forms of the mantras of the desired division, there is a triad.

Having made all objects of expression— which consist of the threefold energy (tejas) and are composed of the three syllables each in the form of expressive sounds consisting of knowledge— non-different from their own nature, one should perform the oblation (homa) in the great fire of the Self, which resides in the *mūlādhāra* and is of an undifferentiated nature. || 60 ||

With these two verses beginning with *tejastraya* and ending with *samīritam*, [the author] teaches the true nature and essential form of Śakti and Śiva: their identity with the triad of fires (*tejastraya*), their alternative nature as possessing bodies composed of the five elements assumed by their own will, and the nature of liberation.

In that regard, "of us two" refers to Śakti and Śiva. "That body" is the imperishable body; other [bodies] are composed of the five elements. "Of us two" is as before. "Stability in the state of being identical with that" is explained as stability in the state of identity with the aforementioned triad of lights. || 62 ||
"In that regard, O Supreme Lord, tell me clearly about Kuṇḍalinī.
I shall speak of her; listen, O wise one, for it is a most wonderful secret. (63)

Situated in the midst of the fiery splendor residing at the *mūlādhāra*, the power of the individual soul (*jīva-śakti*), known as Kuṇḍalinī, exists there in the form of the vital breath (*prāṇa*). (64)
Having the form of a sleeping serpent, with three coils and great luster, she has Māyā as her head; roaring, she is constantly uttered by us within our own [minds]. (65)
When, having blocked both ears with that [thumb] in the middle of the *suṣumnā*, one does not hear its sound, then death occurs. (66)
In this way, when that vital power (jīva-śakti), being struck by the staff of its own will, abandons its state as Kuṇḍalinī and attains straightness; 67.
Then there would be the perception of the universe by living beings; otherwise, however, their own existence would be like the state of the world in the darkness of night. (68)
With the first half of the verse beginning with "tatra" (there), the Goddess asks about the nature of Kuṇḍalinī;

"tatra" means clearly and very distinctly. With the second half of the verse beginning with "tām" (her), he introduces the description of the nature of Kuṇḍalinī; "tatra" refers to that Kuṇḍalinī, the secret.

Because it is impossible to know [it] without the side-glance of the Guide (deśika), it is supremely wonderful, owing to its nature as knowledge and its nature as identity [with that knowledge]. || 63 ||

With these six verses beginning with "In the *bhūlādhāra*" and ending with "the practitioner," [the author] teaches the nature of Kuṇḍalinī and her power. Therein, "by that" means by that form of vital breath (*prāṇa*).
She is Kuṇḍalinī. She is of "great luster" because she illuminates the entire universe. She has "Māyā as her head."

Having the *visarjanīya* as its head, uttering that *māyā*, and moving higher and higher by means of that very self—[the phrase] "in *svage*" is a qualification for the subsequent [phrase] "in the middle region of the *suṣumnā*.
That is *kuṇḍalinī*. Then, due to extreme proximity, she who has the aforementioned form attains straightness; "tu" indicates a distinction. She attains straightness.
Having emerged from the *bhūlādhāra* and proceeding upward toward the sense organs such as the ears,
it is impelled by its own will and remains under the control of that self-willed impulse. At other times,
while it remains in the form of a sleeping serpent within that [channel], it exists like the state of the world in the darkness of night.

By way of non-manifestation. This is what is meant: when the Kuṇḍalinī power, whose nature is the intellect and whose form is the vibration of one's own self, departs from the Mūlādhāra, abandoning its state as a sleeping serpent, impelled by its own will.
Thus, the practitioner who knows her within the body as revealed by the instructions of the teacher knows the supreme Brahman, as well as me and you. (69)
He should be known as liberated while living (jīvanmukta), whose mind is attached to the pure Self,
untouched by merit or sin, and who has transcended the realms of sorrow and joy.
Freed from passion and hatred, having renounced the fruits of all actions, content without external conditions, he is endowed with a will that is subject only to his own desire. || 71 ||

He was content with his own body alone as his only possession, remaining equanimous toward praise and blame; he was impartial toward friend and foe, and endowed with auspicious qualities, virtuous conduct, and compassion. (72)
Thus has been described the one liberated while living (jīvanmukta), the adept among people;
the other is full of eager curiosity for the worship and devotion of the Goddess. || 73 ||
In due time, one shall partake of success, while the other becomes a vessel of suffering;
the latter, a fool, remains afflicted through many births for the sake of learning and wealth.
Having ascended and pervaded, she emerges from the body of the void (*viladeha*) through the various doors of the senses and devours the universe;

at that time, the perception of the universe arises. Again, when by her own will she returns to the *mūlādhāra* and assumes the form of a mere sleeping serpent, then it is as if in the darkness of night.

"Otherwise, like the stability of the universe, the perception of that entire world would not occur. Thus [he speaks of] her, the Kuṇḍalinī, who makes [everything] manifest; she who is shown through the instructions of the Guru (deśika), and who shows me as well—both Śiva and you, Śakti. || 69 ||

With these two and a half verses, beginning with "one who is liberated while living" (*jīvanmukta*) and ending with "the practitioner" (*sādhaka*), he teaches the characteristics of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*). In this context, the word division is *asakta-mānasaḥ*.
"Having gone beyond the extremes of sorrow and joy" means having reached the further shore even of sorrow and joy.

Content without external conditions, endowed with natural contentment; possessed of a will governed by his own desire, his intellect is not impelled by others; equal toward friend and foe due to the absence of attachment and aversion; he is liberated while living (jīvanmukta), meaning that even while alive, he is liberated from the perspective of ultimate reality because of the absence of notions such as "self" and "other. || 72 ||

With the half-verse beginning with "itara" and ending with "yoniṣu," he teaches that even for one devoid of the aforementioned knowledge, perfection is attained through time by worshipping the Goddess; furthermore, he teaches the transgression incurred by one who lacks such worship and devotion.
With a mind intoxicated by pride, he goes downward into various wombs;
yet when his sinful karma is exhausted, devotion arises eternally within the world. (75)
By the power of which a man is born in this world with the previously described characteristics, having attained that devotion, he becomes a deity among men in the worlds. (76)
The sun, moon, Mars, Mercury, Jupiter, Venus, and Saturn are seen, as well as other world-protectors and others who have attained prosperity through devotion to Him. (77)
What more need be said, O Goddess? O sinless one, there are no deities or vidyās equal to the Nityās; therefore, they alone should always be worshipped. (78)
"Even today, I meditate [on her] at the three times of day, endowed with a physical form;

whereas the other is one who lacks the aforementioned knowledge. [This is done] for Lalitā, the Goddess who is the cause of all, according to the time—due to the gravity or lightness resulting from devotion, service, and so forth, or due to the swiftness or delay of time."
The other is devoid of that speech and so forth. Through many births—that is, through various births consisting of the entire essence of non-ultimate knowledge—he is a fool, lacking discernment.
The phrase "arising from the wealth of learning" is a qualifier for "joy" (*mudaiḥ*) which occurs later. His mind is deranged.

Devoid of knowledge regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, he goes lower and lower through various wombs; the meaning is that he becomes increasingly subject to external control amidst sense objects. || 74 ||

With these three verses, beginning with "nityāsu" and ending with "anvitaḥ," consisting of two halves and one full verse respectively, he teaches the rarity of devotion to the Nityās, the majesty of that devotion, and the worship of the Lord who is endowed with the form of the majesty of the Nityās; therein, when sinful karma has been destroyed through the grace of a true guru and other means.

The grammatical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: by the power of that devotion—which overcomes karma afflicted by ignorance, evil tendencies, and so forth—a person possessing the previously mentioned characteristics, namely the characteristics of one liberated while living (*jīvanmukta*), shall become such. That devotion, whose nature will be described in this chapter, [is the means].

The word *devatāḥ* (gods) is connected with the word *bhavanti* (they become). In the phrase "the world-protectors and others," the word "others" (*ādi*) refers to the thirty-three crores of deities. "Having attained prosperity through devotion to them" means having attained sovereignty through the aforementioned form of devotion. By speaking at great length, [it is meant that they are] similar, O sinless one.

And this is the word-division (*padaccheda*). The phrase "I meditate" (*bhāvayāmi*) is connected with the preceding "those very [mantras]" (*tā eva*). "I am Śiva. "At the three times" (*trikāle*) means at the three junctions of the day (*sandhyātraye*). "Endowed with form" (*vigrahānvitaḥ*) means having performed the ritual placement of the deity's form (*nyastavigrahaḥ*).
By this, it is stated that even for those who have attained knowledge, the worship during the three junctions is a necessary duty.
The meaning of the tradition. || 78 ||
The planets situated within the wheel pervaded by those colors have also been shown to you. || 79 ||
By their own will, they themselves possess the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva;
and whatever other deities there may be, they all have bodies composed of those very [deities]. (80)
I shall now describe the supreme form, which is a great wonder at the conclusion of the fire-oblation (homa);
by means of this, the previously mentioned forms of the Siddhas shall always attain perfection.
The state that belongs to no others belongs thus to that Great One who is all-encompassing;
devotion arises in those who have destroyed all their sins and serve the Knower of Truth.

With the second half of the verse beginning with "tadvarṇa," he recalls the planetary periods (*daśā*) and their mode of abiding for the planets situated within the *mātṛkā-cakra* as described in the twenty-fifth chapter; therein, they are "situated in the wheel pervaded by those respective letters."
They abide in the wheel pervaded by the letters of the Mātṛkā, which are eternal in nature. || 79 ||

With the verse beginning with "vidhi," he teaches that the sixteen eternal Nityās, as well as other deities, possess bodies formed by their own will; therein, "the nature of Vidhi, Viṣṇu, and Śiva" refers to the nature of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra. Of those sixteen Nityās, [it is said] "by their own will."

"By her own will. "The others" refers to those taught in other systems. "Embodiments consisting of that" means embodiments consisting of the sixteen Nityās residing within the [respective] wheels. || 80 ||

With the half-verse and more beginning with *pararūpam* and ending with *mahān*, [the author] introduces the discussion of the *pararūpa-homa* (supreme-form oblation) and explains that among the triad of the accomplished (*siddha*), the seeker (*sādhya*), and the practitioner (*sādhaka*),
only the accomplished ones are fit for that supreme oblation, whereas the other two categories are not.
