And it teaches its unsuitability for that [lower level]. In this context, "tu" (but) indicates a distinction. It is a great marvel because it consists of the dissolution of all dualities. Its accomplishment is the accomplishment of the state of being an oblation in the form of the Supreme (Parā).
This refers to the accomplished forms mentioned previously in this very chapter.

The state of those for whom the subtle homa has been proclaimed as accomplished, and of other practitioners and their goals, pertains to the homa of the supreme form; this is the ellipsis. Likewise, it is like that of the perfected ones. || 81 ||

With the second half of the verse beginning with "prakṣīṇa" (completely destroyed), he teaches the means for attaining devotion to the Nityās by taking to heart the spiritual power (*anubhāva*) of those who have accomplished the state of being intent upon that supreme oblation (*parahoma*). In this context,
[it refers to] those whose every sin has been exhausted and whose evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*) have been removed by the glances and other graces of the Guru.
For those who serve the Knower of That, being entirely devoted to serving the Lord who has realized the ultimate reality. || 82 ||
O beautiful one, hear now the characteristics of those devotees who possess eternal ignorance: freedom from doubt regarding the hereafter, contentment, and perpetual fullness. (83)
Happiness, renunciation, wisdom, gratitude, lack of greed, absence of meanness, freedom from dejection, and the lack of effort toward the concerns of others; || 84 ||
The creeper of compassion consists of mental nobility, equanimity in the stability of the mind, the absence of joy or anger toward gain or loss, and a virtuous character. (85)
Devotion to what is auspicious, constant proclamation of the auspicious, turning away from conversation and talk of what is inauspicious, and remaining in a state of natural spontaneity. (86)
Everlasting sovereignty, the state of being an enjoyer, steadfastness, straightforwardness, favorability toward all, a love for song, and the attainment of desired objects. || 87 ||

With these six verses beginning with *nityā* and ending with *taiḥ*, preceded by an introductory context, he provides the instruction on the characteristics of a constant devotee (*nityābhakta*) and offers a conclusion to what has been taught. In this regard, "in the *nityāvidyās*" refers to the sciences of the sixteen *nityās*. "O Sundarī" is an address to the Goddess.

Freedom from doubt regarding the next world arises from the thorough knowledge of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). Contentment arises from the absence of desire for objects yet to be attained. Eternal fullness arises through a state that is unconditioned by space, time, and so forth. This is blissfulness.

Renunciation is the savoring of the experience of the supreme bliss of one's own self; knowledge is the constant contemplation of reality; gratitude is devotion to the service of the pair of lotus feet of the Guru;
lack of greed is indifference toward others; and lack of miserliness refers to being free from attachment regarding material objects.

It is accompanied by great effort; it is freedom from dejection and lack of meanness. It is free from the exertion of worrying about others due to the absence of divisiveness. It is compassion toward all living beings. It is mental steadfastness and a sense of contentment. It is impartiality in the mind's state regarding both gain and loss.

Alternatively, the syntactical connection is: "There is no unevenness in the stability of the mind. Affection (*prīti*) means the absence of anger; it is affection toward all living beings and the absence of hostility. A virtuous disposition (*kalyāṇaśīlatā*) is the nature of performing auspicious conduct.
Devotion to what is auspicious (*kalyāṇābhiniveśitva*) is devotion to auspicious actions.

The proclamation of auspicious fame is the recitation of the names and majestic power of great beings whose nature is auspicious. Aversion to unwholesome discourse and conversation is the turning away from talk concerning inauspicious deeds and those who practice them. Abiding according to one's own will.

Existence independent of others; perpetual sovereignty, which is the state of having a majesty unassailed by kings, thieves, wicked people, enemies, and the like; the state of being an enjoyer, which is the possession of the power of enjoyment; and finality.
It is the state of being an inseparable, eternal self-nature permeating the forms of all deities;

it is straightforwardness, which is the absence of a crooked heart; it is universal conformity, consisting of the honor shown by kings, women, lords, and the wise—without distinction among gods, humans, animals, and so forth—and the absence of envy.
And the desire for supreme excellence—these have been declared as your defining characteristics. || 88 ||
That which is the nature of conceptual construction is the mind; that [mind] is deposited within the non-conceptual.
The supreme oblation consists of that which is composed of both the gross and the subtle.

Because of its identity with them, the gross oblation (sthūlahoma) is said to be of a unitary nature, resulting from the burning by fire of various objects characterized by diverse conceptual distinctions.
Because he realizes that all forms are essentially of the nature of the eternal formless;

because his love for music arises from the fact that the nature of sound is eternal; because he attains his desires due to the absence of any object distinct from himself; and because he receives great honor from royal women, lords, and the wise.
Because the state of being one's own delight has been established; "free from envy" (amatsara) because of the absence of anything co-located with oneself;
and the desire for supremacy over all is the desire for the realization of identity with the deity. 88.

With the verse beginning "yadvikalpa" (that which is conceptual construction), he teaches the nature of the supreme oblation (*parahoma*) and how both the gross and subtle oblations are composed of that [supreme reality]. In this context, the nature of conceptual construction is the nature of the cause of all conceptualizations of the universe. [This is to be dissolved] into the non-conceptual supreme nature (*nirvikalpaka parasvarūpe*). This is the "deposition" (*nidhāna*).

"Dissolution" (*vilāpana*) means this: the dissolution of the mind—which is the cause of conceptualization and discursive thought—into its own self, which is of a non-conceptual nature; this is called "offering to the Supreme" (*parahoma*). This [dissolution] consists of the Supreme offering, as expressed by the four verses beginning with "yanmayaṃ parahomamayaṃ" and ending with "samīritaḥ."

He teaches the cultivation of the impression of identity and the contemplation thereof between the gross and subtle homas through the supreme homa (parahoma). This refers to the various objects of diverse conceptualizations— such as sacrificial fuel, flowers, fruits, and so forth— which constitute the materials for those homas.
Because it consists of that, because it consists of the oblation (*homa*), and because it consists of fire (*agni*); "the form of unity" means non-separateness.

This is what is being said: the fact that all things, such as the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) and so forth, are of a single form by virtue of consisting of fire through the gross oblation has been proclaimed. Thus, the meaning is that one should unify them.

This is what is meant: through subtle fire-offerings (*sūkṣmahoma*), [one offers] by means of words expressing various forms into the great fire accompanied by the *visarga*, which resides in the mouth of Kuṇḍalinī situated in the center of one's own *mūlādhāra* and is the locus of rest for the arising of all sounds.
"One should unify those objects denoted by that [mantra] with the self consisting of the object of knowledge, the knower, and the act of knowing.

By the first half-verse beginning with "sthitih" (the state), another view is stated: that through the dissolution of all dualities, the very state of abiding becomes the supreme oblation (*parahoma*) within those things whose form is the flame of the great fire of one's own essential nature.

The Great Power (mahāśakti), which is non-different from one's own essential nature, is the fire of one's own essential nature; its flame is the will of that [fire], meaning the will of the Great Power whose form is one's own self.
Thus, one performs the subtle oblation (sūkṣmahoma) by means of words of various forms that serve as its designators.
By means of the objects of expression in their entirety, through the nature of the object of knowledge, the knower, and the giver [of knowledge]. || 91 ||
Stability becomes the supreme oblation through the dissolution of all dualities, always within those whose form is the flame of the great fire of one's own essential nature. 92.
When the nature of the fuel-less fire is stable within the ultimate Self,
that which is free from the elaborations of emergence is declared to be the supreme oblation.
In those aforementioned fire-pits, one should perform the entire auspicious sacrificial rite (homa) prescribed for the square-shaped pit. || 94 ||
When the blood has been emitted, one should perform that which is of an impure nature;
for other [rites], other actions are prescribed according to the forms previously described. (95)
Facing the northeast or the north, one should perform an auspicious homa;
facing south, one performs abhicāra (sorcery); and facing the fire (southeast), one performs it against enemies during illness.

Those very forms which belong to them are of the nature of the flames of their own internal fire; within those forms, which consist of the great flames of the fire of one's own self, which are like fires burning without fuel, which are manifestations of light not presided over by anything else, and which are the ultimate Self whose essential nature is pure existence— within these, [one should remain] steady.
It is without modification and free from the lamentation of emergence; it is the state of dissolution without remainder. This is what is meant:

in that which is changeless—whose essential nature consists of the Great Power (mahāśakti) in the form of Will (icchā), which is the supportless Light (prakāśa) manifesting as all forms, and which, in the ultimate sense, is the very nature of the throbbing Reality (sphuritatattva).
"The state of their total dissolution within one's own self, which consists of mere existence (*sattāmātra*), is declared to be the 'offering to another' (*parahoma*).

With these two verses beginning with "in them" (*teṣu*) and ending with "by form" (*rūpataḥ*), [the author] teaches the procedure for the fire-offering (*homa*) of auspicious rites in general, specifically in the square sacrificial pits (*caturasra-homa-kuṇḍa*). Regarding that square [pit]:

In the aforementioned form; in the triangle, in the form described; [this applies] to the other sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa)—this is the ellipsis—according to the aforementioned form, that is, by the prescribed method. || 95 ||

With these two verses beginning with *prāk* and ending with *kṛtsnaśaḥ*, he teaches the specific directions facing which the officiant (*hotṛ*) should stand during rites such as those for auspiciousness (*maṅgala*). In that context, there are four specific [directions]: facing east, facing north, facing the direction of Śiva, and facing all [directions] together.

Facing south means having one's face turned toward the southern direction. *Tur* is used for emphasis. *Gade* means at the commencement of the matter concerning the mace. Facing fire means having one's face turned toward the eastern direction. Facing wind means having one's face turned toward the western direction.
(p. 598) One facing wind performs the rite of eradication (*uccāṭana*); one facing the direction of the Rākṣasas performs the rite of inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*).
But he whose face is turned westward should perform all other cruel rites in their entirety.
One should perform those rites while seated in the direction of one's own country, village, house, and so forth; otherwise, it would bring about misfortune.
If one is unable to prepare a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) and so forth, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) upon a leveled and auspicious ground smeared with cow dung. 99.
Having spread sand there, measuring one cubit in both width and length, one should perform the fire-oblation (homa) in the center; thus it has been explained in its entirety.
The pervasion consisting of the reality of time has been correctly described;
by the refinement of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own. (101)
Thus ends the thirtieth chapter in the Śrīkādimata among the sixteen Nityātantras. || 30 ||
Facing the Rākṣasa direction means facing the south-west; facing west means facing the western direction.

The others have been explained previously. What is meant is this: even when there is a difference in the directions relative to the face of the Hotṛ-priest, one should construct the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) by designating each respective direction as the east (prācī), and then perform the oblation. || 97 ||

With the verse beginning with "svadeśa" (one's own country), he teaches the necessity of performing the prescribed rites in one's own country and so forth while facing the prescribed directions, as well as the sin incurred by failing to do so.
In the phrase "gehādau" (in the house, etc.), the word "etc. refers to cities and other such locations. The rites are those previously mentioned; [they are to be performed] in that direction.
In the direction previously described; otherwise, in the case of performing it contrarily. || 98 ||

With these two verses beginning with *kuṇḍādī-* and ending with *śeṣataḥ*, [the author] teaches, along with a concluding summary, the procedure for constructing the sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*), preceded by the injunction for performing the fire-oblation (*homa*) on that mound for those who are unable to construct the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) and so forth. In this context, the particle *tu* indicates a distinction.

In an auspicious place, free from bones, clods of earth, and the like, and undisturbed by smoke and other such things; there, having constructed a grid of nine squares according to the prescribed method, [one should place it] in the center—that is, in the middle of the central square. || 100 ||
Thus, in the commentary titled *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha— known as *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*— upon the complete *Tantra* named *Śrīkādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.

The thirtieth chapter, which is devoted to elucidating the wheel of the deities of the site (*vāstudevatācakra*), its worship and so forth, as well as the methods for the subtle and supreme fire-offerings (*sūkṣmaparahomavidhāna*), is thus fully concluded and examined. Oṃ tat sat.
O Supreme Goddess, I have explained to you the subtle and supreme fire-offering (homa) in the thirty-first chapter;
now I shall describe the gross fire-offering which crushes enemies.
In a sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) activated by the respective rites,
one should perform, according to the prescribed injunctions, the subjugation of enemies, the destruction of foes, the suppression of diseases, and the propitiation of deities.
Having ascertained the life-span of the enemy [planet] according to the asterisms mentioned for the ascendant,
one should also examine the positions of the planets constituting that [enemy] and their Aṣṭakavarga.
If one is in accordance with the three [qualities], one should not perform that malevolent rite (abhicāra);
for otherwise, such rites, when performed, surely bring about destruction.
One should perform those very same actions in such a way as to avoid opposition to that triad [of guru,
deity, and scripture], maintaining devotion to that deity, faith, and conduct toward the guru.

In the preceding thirtieth chapter, having taught the mandala of the deities of the site (vāstudevatācakra) for the sixteen Nityās along with the procedures for their worship and so forth, as well as the subtle and supreme rules for fire-offerings (homa), [the author] next [teaches] for those devoted to the practice of the sixteen Nityās...

He teaches the procedure for the fire-offerings (*homavidhi*) and other rites for the subduing of enemies (*arimardanakarman*) by means of the thirty-first chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Subtle" (*sūkṣma*) and ending with "according to the procedure" (*vidhānataḥ*). Therein,
by means of two verses beginning with "Subtle" and ending with "the incantation" (*cāṭana*), [he provides] the conclusion together with what has been previously stated.

He introduces the exposition of the procedure for the subduing of enemies according to the prescribed method within the prescribed sacrificial pits (*kuṇḍa*). In that context, "your" refers to yours. It was stated previously in the first chapter: "Hatred, destruction, suppression of disease, and incantation. Here, the word "hatred" (*dveṣa*) pertains to the subject of killing (*māraṇa*), while the word "suppression" (*nigraha*) pertains to subjects such as defeat in battle and the like.
Cāṭana is eradication. || 2 ||

With these four verses beginning with "āyurddāyam" and ending with "ātsanāśanam," [the author] teaches the portion to be known at the time of performing the rite of malevolent magic (abhicārakarman), as well as the transgression incurred by failing to observe it; therein, in accordance with the asterisms mentioned for the ascendant in the thirteenth chapter—

By the two and a half verses beginning with "tajjanma" (verse 86), starting from the latter half of the verse, [the results] are stated according to the correspondence of the names of the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*). This refers to the results of the *aṣṭakavarga* of the planets constituting that [birth-mansion] and of the planets occupying their positions at the time of its application; the word "ca" (and) indicates a conjunction. The phrase "the result of the *aṣṭakavarga*" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

Having consulted with those standing by his side who are knowledgeable in mantras regarding the three aforementioned [methods]—the calculation of life-span (*āyurdāya*), the planetary periods (*daśā*), and the results of transits (*gocara*)—one should perform the suppression of enemies according to one's power;
otherwise, there will be fruitlessness or even self-destruction. (6)
When the eighth house from the ripu (the sixth) is the ascendant, and the time [of the planet] is situated in the eighth sign,
the practitioner should perform inauspicious rites for its destruction.
In the east are Aries and Taurus; in the southeast is Gemini; likewise, Cancer and Leo are in the south, and Virgo is situated in the southwest.

"In accordance" (*ānuguṇye*) means being favorable; [it refers to] being contrary to the enemy who is the subject of the malevolent rite (*abhicārya*). "If he were to act otherwise"—the word *eva* (only) here has a shifted position in the syntax; the meaning is: "only by being contrary to those three. This is what is meant: at the time of performing a malevolent rite against an enemy, according to the science of astrology (*jyotiḥśāstra*)...

Having examined the positions of the planets in his *tātkālika-āyurdāya*, *gocara*, and *aṣṭakavarga* according to the methods taught in the *Horā-skandha*, one should not perform malevolent rites (*abhicāra-karman*) unless those three are favorable;
for those very same rites destroy one who performs cruel acts without regard for them.
One should perform those cruel rites for the destruction of the enemy’s form only when there is opposition to one's own essential nature (*tattva*).

Having reflected upon the enemy’s devotion to their deity, their devotion to the deities [of others], their faith (*āstikya*)— that is, their steadfastness toward the gods, Brahmins, and so forth— and their conduct (*vartana*), which is their behavior (*ācāra*).

The meaning is that those who know [the enemy] understand his power and so forth. "Otherwise" (*anyathā*) means in the case of acting contrary to what has been prescribed. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. This is what is being said: in the performance of malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) against an enemy, one must know his devotion to deities, his faith, his conduct, his guru, and the knowledge of mantras held by those in his vicinity.

Having understood their power and so forth, and having deliberated upon them by those who know such things, one should not perform rites such as sorcery when they are predominant; for if one acts otherwise, the fruit of that action becomes fruitless or leads to the destruction of the performer. || 6 ||

With the verse beginning with "ripoḥ" (of the enemy), he teaches the time for commencing cruel rites (*krūra-prayoga*) and specific locations such as houses; therein, "in the eighth ascendant" refers to the birth asterism (*janmarkṣa*), the birth sign (*rāśi*), or the sign of the moon-ascendant (*candra-lagna-rāśi*). "At that time" means at the time of its [the ascendant's] rising.
In the twelfth house, that is, in the twelve houses consisting of the signs to be described in the two subsequent verses; for their destruction, meaning for the destruction of the enemy. || 7 ||

With the two verses beginning with "In the east" (*prācyām*) and ending with "well-established" (*susthitam*), he teaches that all objects, such as the pavilion and the house, consist of the twelve zodiac signs (*rāśi*). Therein, "in the fire [corner]" refers to the corner of Agni; "in the south" refers to the region of the southern direction; and "to its southwest" refers to the direction of Nirṛti.
The scales and the scorpion are situated in the west; the bow is located in the northwest.
The crocodile and the pitcher are in the north, while the fish is situated in the northeast. (9)
Having thus understood the sequence of the zodiacal signs, one should perform the rites according to the region;
however, at that time, there would be five ghaṭikās for each [sign] in successive order.
In all twelve months, beginning with Caitra,
the Sun moves through the zodiac signs starting with Aries, accompanied by the other planetary spheres.

Likewise, within the bodies of living beings, one should perceive those [energies] extending from the head down to the feet through their division into twelve parts, each measuring eight finger-breadths.

In the intermediate direction (Vidiś); from the west, in the western direction; in the northwest corner (Vāyu); from the north, in the northern direction; in the northeast corner (Īśa). The meaning is that it remains well-established and does not rotate, like the wheel of zodiac signs situated within the Kālacakra. || 9 ||

With this verse beginning with "evam," he provides the conclusion of what has been stated and teaches the number of ghaṭikās for the rising time of each individual sign among the twelve signs situated on the circle. In that context, "evam" means according to the aforementioned sequence; "rāśikramam" means the order of the positions of the signs; and regarding "karmāṇi," the word "krūrāṇi" (cruel actions) is to be supplied as the remainder.

By location, [this is] by way of being the nature of the location; but in time, it is in the wheel of time (*kālacakra*). There would be five times five for each single zodiac sign (*rāśi*) through the application of the sequence. However, the state of being situated in the retrograde wheel (*apakramacakra*) results from the disparity between time and location.
According to the sequence prescribed in the treatises on calculation (*gaṇitaśāstra*), this occurs in one's own country.
By means of the duration in ghaṭikās of the rising of the zodiacal signs, according to the method to be described, through the sequence beginning with the sign occupied by the Sun. || 10 ||
With the verse beginning "Caitra and so forth," he teaches the sequence of the movement of the planets in the Kālacakra.

In that context, because they are celestial, the term "Caitra and so forth" refers to solar months; the word "tu" (but/and) indicates a distinction. The ellipsis is to be supplied as: "it moves through each solar month by means of the sequential traversal of each successive zodiacal sign (*rāśi*). Likewise:

"Of such a kind" means together with other [luminaries] such as the moon; "by the circles of planets" (grahamaṇḍalaiḥ) means by the specific times prescribed in the science of astronomy (jyotiḥśāstra) for the revolutions of those respective planets. || 11 ||

With the verse beginning with "In bodies" (*deheṣu*), he teaches that the body of all living beings consists of the twelve zodiac signs (*dvādaśarāśi*). Therein, in that same manner, [the signs] starting from Aries (*meṣa*) and ending with Pisces (*mīna*)—those signs—in twelve locations. || 12 ||
One should perform all actions, whether auspicious or inauspicious, in accordance with these three [factors] and not otherwise; for when performed in this way, they certainly bear fruit. (13)
Likewise, having identified the locations of poison and the locations of nectar during the day, one should fashion the effigy (puttalī) accordingly, applying the *prayāga* everywhere.
On the forehead, the heart, the breasts, the throat, the nose, the eyes, and likewise the ears;
on the eyebrows, the temples, and the middle of the head—there, specifically between the eyebrows and the temples.
It resides in the ears, the eyes, and the nose of a person; likewise in the left throat, the region of the breast, the heart, the navel, and the private parts.
Likewise, on the joints of the knees, the sides of the feet, and the right big toe;
on the foot, the joint, the knee, the private parts, and the navel—these are the most brilliant white spots.

With the verse beginning with "Of the three," he teaches that the performance of auspicious or inauspicious acts depends on the influence of time, form, and the zodiacal sign as previously described. Therein, "of the three" refers to those consisting of place, time, and form. "By way of conformity" means by way of suitability; otherwise...

By means of the aforementioned transgression; thus, when this has been done—that is, when the application of auspicious and inauspicious [actions] has been performed through the aforementioned method of transgression. || 13 ||

With the verse beginning with "tathā" (thus), he teaches that for the purpose of the application of the effigy (puttalī), one must know the locations of poison and nectar within the body. In this context, the word "tathā" (thus) is to be construed with the phrase "the locations of nectar. According to the sequence explained in the twenty-sixth chapter:
The meaning is that they are situated on the right and left sides, respectively, according to the sequence of fifteen distinct positions for each side.

"On the day" refers to the day of the ritual performance (*prayoga*). "Poisonous places" (*viṣasthānāni*) are those which will be described in the immediately following verse. "In every respect" (*sarvataḥ*).
In actions; likewise, in the manner that will be described. || 14 ||

With three and a half verses beginning with *site* and ending with *varttate*, he teaches the conditions resulting from the transposition of poison among men and women. Therein, by the verse beginning with *site*, he teaches twelve locations: *site* means in the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*); *stanagale* means in the breast and in the throat.

"In the middle of the eyebrows, the temples, and the head"—there, "in the middle of the head" means [the crown]; "from the middle of the temples and the eyebrows" means [the locations] in the middle of the temples and in the middle of the eyebrows. By the verse beginning with "the ears," eight locations are indicated there: on the right neck and the left neck. By the verse beginning with "the knees," etc. [the remaining locations are indicated].

There are ten locations according to the verse. Among them, by the term "side of the foot" (*aṅghripārśva*), the region of the back of the foot is meant. "In the big toe" (*aṅguṣṭhe*) refers to the big toe of the left foot; "in the right" (*dakṣiṇe*) refers to the big toe of the right foot. "In the foot" (*aṅghau*)...

The portion of poison (viṣakalā) remains in the man, while in the woman it proceeds from the left [nostril] and so forth; one should pierce with a thorn at the time of poison, within the poisonous channel and at the place of poison. || 18 ||
Then, indeed, by that intense [torture] called Saṅkocaka, which consists of bone, or likewise by iron needles produced from jujube wood and other such materials; || 19 ||
Whichever limb of the effigy is pierced,
that very limb of the enemy's body will certainly be afflicted by disease and, in due course, become uncontrollable.
There, afflicted by that suffering, he shall go to the city of the Lord of Life (Yama).
I shall now describe the ritual of making a doll for the sake of achieving subjugation; listen. (21)

On the back of the foot; at the joint, that is, at the joint immediately following; at the knee and the secret place, that is, at the knee and the private parts—in this manner. "Siteta" means in the dark fortnight (kṛṣṇapakṣa). "Vāmādi" means starting from the left side, beginning with the previously mentioned location of the heart. This is what is meant: on the first day and so forth of the bright fortnight (śuklapakṣa).

During the thirty lunar days ending with the new moon of the dark fortnight, for men, [the breath] moves through nine locations starting from the heart region and ending at the head on the right side; then, on the left side,
it moves through fifteen locations starting from the head and ending at the big toe of the foot.

Furthermore, from the big toe of the right foot up to the navel, in six locations— and counting all together, in thirty locations— the movement of the poison occurs for women on their respective lunar days (tithis) in those specific locations, following the sequence of alternating between the right and left sides. || 17 ||
With the three and a half verses beginning with *viṣanāḍyām* and ending with *siddhaye*,

he teaches— along with the introduction to the description of the *puttalī* (effigy) rite— the time for piercing that [effigy], its constituent parts, the means of accomplishment, and its results. Therein, regarding *viṣanāḍyām*:
Among the twenty-seven lunar mansions (*nakṣatras*), during the time of the four *nāḍīs* said to consist of poison for each individual mansion,

at the previously mentioned location of the object— namely, the *puttalī* (effigy)— specifically by means of the one called Saṅkocaka, which is a particular kind of fish, and by means of the intense [poison] consisting of bone.

[He should pierce him] with bone known as *taddehaja-tīvra* (the intense [bone] born from that body); the word "with thorns" (*kaṇṭakaiḥ*)—such as those produced from the *badara* tree and so forth—is to be supplied.
The word "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. The meaning is that he should pierce him in such a manner.
Whichever limb is thus pierced—that is, pierced by thorns and the like—that limb will be afflicted by disease; this is stated later on.

The term "born from the body of the enemy" is the substantive [of the compound]. Due to the gravity or lightness of the application over time, there is either hastiness or delay of that time. "Dhruvam" means certain.
The word "ārttyā" implies [suffering] produced by a disease in his limbs; the remainder [of the sense] is "the making of a puppet" (puttalīkaraṇa).
The procedure for the construction of a mechanical doll. || 21 ||
Mars, Venus, Mercury, the Moon, and the Sun; Mars and Venus; Mars, Jupiter, Saturn, the Sun, Jupiter, and the Moon are the lords of the navāṃśas and the rāśis respectively. (22)
The constellations consist of four quarters; one hundred and eight [syllables] make up this number. And there are this many effigies (puttalī), according to the sequence of the Aśakas. (23)
In the first group of nine, the measurements for the portions of the moon and the sun are sixteen and twelve, respectively, in terms of finger-breadths (aṅgula).
In all other divisions, fourteen [degrees] are prescribed;
in the second division, nine, and for the others, thirteen and a half. (25)
In the third [section] consisting of nine, thirteen others are proclaimed;
likewise, the sequence of the stated numbers for the moon and the sun is of one kind.

With the verse beginning with *bhauma*, he teaches the lords of the twelve signs and the twelve degrees (*dvādaśāṃśaka*) arising from the three constellations starting with Aśvinī, respectively. Therein:
The lords of the portions and the lords of the zodiac signs beginning with Aries;
by the verse beginning with "the constellations," [it is shown] according to the sequence of four portions for each constellation.
Having combined one hundred and eight parts, he introduces the specific detail of one hundred and eight small figurines (*puttalī*).
In this regard, there are exactly this many, numbering one hundred and eight. (23)

With these three verses beginning with "In the first" and ending with "likewise," he teaches the specific types of human effigies (*puttalī*). Among them, in the first group of nine, [the procedure applies] to the nine lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī and ending with Āśleṣā; in the other divisions, [it applies to the remaining ones].

Regarding the portions of the other planets: the meaning is that all the *puttalīs* (effigies) are measured at fourteen finger-breadths (*aṅgula*). In the second group of nine—that is, in the nine asterisms beginning with Maghā and ending with Jyeṣṭhā—the others, namely the portions of the planets excluding the Moon and the Sun, shall be one and a half [times] thirteen.

The remainder is that the number of fingers for the *puttalīs* is [the measure]. The third [set] is in the nine [asterisms], meaning in the nine asterisms beginning with Mūla and ending with Revatī. For the others, as before, the measures of thirteen fingers for the portions (aṃśakas) of Mars and the rest have already been stated. Thus it is said.

This is the meaning. The phrase "of one kind everywhere" is the ellipsis to be supplied. Furthermore, the sequence of the stated numbers means that the very same measure of the number stated for the first group of nine applies to the second and third groups of nine as well.
(p. 605) For the fashioning of the effigy, the material is clay from the hand of a Cakrin.
Cremation-ground earth, ashes, salt, along with ginger and long pepper. || 27 ||
O Īśvarī, it is said that the substances for the effigy (puttalī) consist of marīca, soot from a house, garlic, asafoetida, rock salt, and red ochre.

An effigy (puttalī) is fashioned from the wood of the tree belonging to the victim's asterism, ground together with powdered mung beans, beeswax, and hair and other substances taken from the body of the enemy.
Having determined the total height of the doll, one-eighth of that should be set aside;
from there, three parts constitute the head above the waist, and likewise two parts constitute the two feet.
Having fashioned a doll with one part [of its body] extending from the hips to the feet, a person should perform all ritual applications according to the tantra. || 31 ||

With these three verses beginning with "puttalī" and ending with "kriyā," he teaches the materials for the construction of the effigy (puttalī). Among those, "endowed with the clay from the potter's hand" means accompanied by the earth from the hands of a potter; "cremation-ground clay, ashes, and salt" [is as follows].

Salt together with cemetery earth and ashes; combined with ginger and long pepper—that is, joined with the powders of ginger and long pepper; black pepper—that is, black pepper powder; house-soot—that is, house-soot powder; garlic—that is, the juice of garlic. These [are the ingredients].

The eight substances beginning with ginger (śuṇṭhī) are common to all the small figurines (puttalikā). "With the trees of the victim's asterism" means with the trees specified for the victim's lunar mansion. "Ground" is an adjective qualifying "with powdered black gram" (māṣacūrṇaiḥ). "With beeswax" (sikthakaiḥ) means with the residue of honey (madhūcchiṣṭaiḥ).
In the phrase "by means of the hair, etc., produced from the body of an enemy," the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the nails, feet, sides, and so forth.
The term "endowed with" (*upetaiḥ*) applies to the three [materials] other than wood—namely, those consisting of clay and those held in the hand of one who possesses the discus. || 29 ||
With the two verses beginning with *puttalī* and ending with *nara*,
he teaches the measurements of the various limbs by means of dividing the length of the doll (*puttalī*) into its respective parts; therein,
the measurement of the doll's length [is determined] by virtue of those specific portions.
The measurement in finger-breadths for the length of the aforementioned doll is as follows: by one part on one side; by three parts [on the other];

and "from the three" means as before. By half a part for the hips and the forefeet—that is to say, half a part for each of the two hips and half a part for each of the two forefeet—this applies everywhere in the application of the doll.
The applications have been declared. || 31 ||
In the *pātāla-yoga*, in that called *nīca*, in the *viṣa-yoga*, in the *mṛtyuja*, in the *nāśa-yoga*, in *dinaja-mṛtyu*, and in the *krakaca-yoga* [the birth is unfavorable]. (32)

With these three verses beginning with "pātāla" and ending with "avāpnuyāt," he teaches the time for commencing the performance of cruel rites (*krūrakarma*) and so forth. Therein, by the verse beginning with "pātāla," he teaches the sixfold cruel times. Among those, "mṛtyuje" refers to the conjunction of death (*mṛtyuyoga*).
Regarding "at the eighth portion of the respective sign" within the asterismal degrees located in the signs beginning with Aries for one's daily birth and death:
by the verse beginning with "Caṇḍīśa," he teaches the ten-fold time for cruel rites (*krūrakarma*).
In that context, "in the *caṇḍīśacaṇḍāyudhaka* yoga," "in the *kāṇaka*" means in the asterism of the one-eyed (*kāṇa*) [planet]. In the *kāṇaka*...

By this [statement], the meaning is: "How much more so in the case of an *andhaka* nakṣatra? The statements from the *Jyotiḥśāstra* are written here: therein is the yoga called *nīca*, known as *pātāla*:
"When the Moon, situated in the portion of the sign of Libra (Tulā) at thirty degrees, rises..."
Then, O auspicious one, the yoga called Nīca (the "low") occurs, which is the Pātāla (hell) and is censured.
The planetary conjunctions: the fourth and seventh [houses] belong to the Sun; the sixth and eighth to the Moon;
Indra (the tenth), Ahi (the fifth), and Dharma (the ninth) to Mars; and Viki (the second), Ādi (the first), and Erava (the third) to Mercury.
On the auspicious day of Ekādaśī, when the moon is in Mandeha, these lunar days (tithis) become poisonous.

The five, two, six, seven, one, six, eight, and fifteen [tithis] are inauspicious; Aśvinī, Citrā, Jayā, Svātī, Indrā (Jyeṣṭhā), Śroṇā (Pūrvabhādrapadā), and the last (Revatī) are inauspicious when starting from Sunday.
The death-yogas, the asterisms of Yama, Maitra, Citrā, Maghā, and the Uttarās;
Citrā, the three Uttarās, Āṣāḍhā, and Śraviṣṭhā follow in sequence.
Citrā, Uttaraphalgunī, Anurādhā, Svātī, Jyeṣṭhā, Śravaṇa, Revatī, Puṣya, Punarvasu, and Śatabhiṣaj—these are the lunar mansions; and Sunday, Wednesday, and Friday are the days of the week.

The Nāśa-yogas: When the asterisms Pitṛ, Indra, Agni, Īśa, Mūla, Vāruṇa, Ājapya, and Bhairava are joined respectively with the days of the Sun and the other planets, they are declared to be the Nāśa-yogas.
Daily deaths occur as follows: in Vasu-hasta (Dhaniṣṭhā), Viśākhā, and Ārdrā; in Budha (Śatabhiṣaj), Bradhna (Pūrvā-phalgunī), Ahi (Āśleṣā), Yāmya (Bharaṇī), and Nairṛta (Mūla).
In these pairs of asterisms, deaths occur on the fourth quarter of each day in successive order.
In Caṇḍīśa, Caṇḍāyudha, Mahāśūla, and Kāṇaka; in Raktasthūṇa, the one called Kaṇṭaka, Sthūṇa, and the one known as Pañcārka. (33)
The applications of the saw:
where, when the numbers of the lunar day and the weekday are added together, they become thirteen.
That yoga known as Krakaca is certainly to be avoided in all auspicious rites.
The fierce weapon of Caṇḍīśa [is to be worshipped] in the asterisms presided over by Sūrya, Bhujaga, Pitṛ, Tvaṣṭṛ, Maitra, Śruti,
Pauṣṇa, and Kramaśas, joined respectively with the Sun and the Moon.

In the constellation Dhiṣṭya (Pūrvaphalgunī), the fierce weapon of Caṇḍīśa falls infallibly upon the traveler. When that [weapon] is joined with the stars of Ātman (Pūrvaphalgunī) and Icchā (Uttaraphalgunī), the wise should not undertake their own welfare or any undertaking; it is a great trident. Seven stars each, beginning with Kṛttikā, are situated in the directions starting from the east in succession.
The asterism Bharaṇī has the mouth of the planets and the like; therein, the great trident (Mahāśūla) is inauspicious.
The nakṣatras beginning with Ajaikapāda (Pūrvaphalgunī) are known as the "half-blind" (kāṇārddha).

One should avoid them for twenty-one days; however, after that period, six of them become "blind" (āva), while the others remain "half-blind. This exception applies except when the commencement occurs on its own weekday.
*Raktasthūṇa*: One should discard the four heaps of grain at the end of the *ruta* [period];
that constellation obtained by adding one to it is known as *raktasthūṇa*.
When Mars is conjoined with the Sun, starting from the asterism Dakṣa (Punarvasu) up to Mūla,
and ending at Mūla within a three-asterism span, these two are respectively called Kaṇṭhaka and Sthūṇa.
As long as there is smoke and so forth, and as long as there is the root of the flame and the thorny *gharghaka* sound,
for that long this triad— the thorn, the pillar, and reality— is free from fault.

The five *arka*-defects: *vālāt*, *koṅga*, *gopālesā*, *arkaśe*, and *sarvasāraṣe*. One should avoid [a birth] when these five, beginning with *dhūma*, are present in the *tvarka* or in the ascendant (*lagne*) conjoined with them.
One should perform ritual applications for the purpose of defeating an adversary or for his destruction; having thus scrutinized [the situation], one should act and thereby attain success. (34)
One should properly fashion four effigies for the purposes of subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, paralyzing, driving away, and killing, according to the prescribed method.
Likewise, [the images] should be made from flour, from clay, or even from the mud of the potter’s wheel,
using wood from the tree of the victim's birth-star, and endowed with the characteristics previously described.
The practitioner, having dug into the seat, the place for the feet, and the middle of the sacrificial pit using flour, clay, or earth, should place beeswax within the vessel.
Having thus prepared the common foundation by placing the feet upwards and the head downwards in the middle of the pit, one should perform the ritual action as prescribed.

This is what is meant: when the planets in the enemy's *āyurdāya*, *gocara*, and *aṣṭakavarga* are unfavorable, and on a day corrupted by the aforementioned defects such as *pātālayoga* and others, or in the eighth house from that [enemy], or during a *viṣanāḍī*, a cruel rite (*krūrakarma*) commenced at such a time bears fruit immediately. The word "vā" (or) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
In the manner thus described. || 34 ||

With these four verses beginning with "vaśye" and ending with "samīritam," he teaches the procedure for employing the effigy (puttalī) in the six types of rites, such as subjugation (vaśya) and the rest. In that context, "samyak" means beautiful in all its limbs; [it should be made] according to the prescribed proportions by the aforementioned method.

"Due to the connection with the hair, nails, and so forth from the body of the enemy"—the word "api" (even/also) is used in the sense of conjunction. "On the seat" means in the place where the sacrificer’s seat is located. "In the place of the feet" means in the region below the spot where the sacrificer places his feet. "Figures made of flour, clay, or wood" refers to effigies (*puttalī*) produced from flour, clay, or wood. "Having dug [them]"— [The remainder of the verse: "...having buried them in the ground, one should strike them with a sword, etc., while reciting the mantra *kṛtye kṛtye*. This is the meaning. The ritual procedure for this is as follows: having fashioned an effigy of the enemy out of flour, clay, or wood, and having inscribed the name of the enemy upon it, one should bury it in the earth at the aforementioned location. Then, while reciting the mantra *kṛtye kṛtye*, one should strike that effigy with a sword or similar weapon. It is said: "One should strike the enemy with a sword, etc., while reciting the mantra *kṛtye kṛtye*. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "by means of the connection with the hair, nails, and so forth from the body of the enemy": the term "and so forth" (*ādi*) includes teeth, skin, blood, flesh, bone, marrow, and the like. The meaning is that one should take these substances from the body of the enemy and fashion the effigy (*puttalī*) by mixing them with flour, clay, or wood. One should then bury that effigy in the earth at the aforementioned location. Afterward, while reciting the mantra *kṛtye kṛtye*, one should strike that effigy with a sword or similar weapon. It is said: "One should strike the enemy with a sword, etc., while reciting the mantra *k

"In the three locations beginning with the seat of the Hotṛ priest, in due order"—the word "api" (also) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "In this manner," meaning by the method thus described;
the remainder [of the sentence] is "in the aforementioned rites such as the common subjugation (*vaśya*) and so forth. What is meant is this:
without transgressing the prescribed measurements and so on, [one should perform the rite] with the eight common substances, the hair from the body of an enemy, and the like.
Having prepared four effigies in total— three made of flour, wax, and clay respectively,

and one made from the wood of the tree associated with the victim’s birth-star and smeared with the eight aforementioned substances— one should place the flour effigy beneath the seat of the officiant in due order.

Having placed a clay image in its proper place beneath the spot where the Hotṛ priest sets his foot, a wooden image in its proper place beneath the navel-lotus situated in the center of the sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa), and a wax image above the pit,
spanning the horizontal archway (toraṇa).

For inauspicious rites, one should perform a fire sacrifice (homa) using a sacrificial ladle (sruk) with a serpent’s head, made from the wood of the *arka* tree, while [the deity] hangs in the sky with feet upward and head downward, suspended by a cord made of *arka* wood, upon a crossbeam of *dāruṇī* wood.
Having fashioned a sacrificial ladle from the wood of the Vairī tree, one should likewise offer oblations with it.
Facing the direction of Yama (the south) at midnight, one should perform the rite of malevolent magic (abhicāraka) in a triangular sacrificial pit (kuṇḍa) in a cremation ground or a desolate place.
Wherever the practitioner performs an oblation for malevolent rites on the earth,
he should have guards stationed all around that place for the sake of his own success.
If King Arāti does not discover him through his spies and slay him,
one should form an alliance with him in one's own kingdom, but not within one's own territory.
If a practitioner of mantras should act through negligence or due to delusion regarding knowledge, then enemy kings will surely afflict that kingdom gradually. (43)
Having thus increased [the mantra] and made it common, one should perform the rites of subjugation and so forth as described, according to the sequence of procedures to be explained. || 38 ||

With the verse beginning with "sarpa," [the author] prescribes the *sruk* and *caru* for cruel rites. In that context, "with a snake-headed *sruk*" means with a *sruk* fashioned in the shape of a snake's head. This is for inauspicious rites such as inciting enmity (*vidveṣa*), expulsion (*uccāṭana*), and killing (*māraṇa*). [The offering is made] with the blood of an enemy.
"With the blood [of the victim] whose birth-nakṣatra is declared to be an enemy's; by her"—this is qualified by the phrase "with a ladle having a serpent's head. (39)

By means of these four verses beginning with "trikoṇa" and ending with "bhūbhṛtaḥ," [the author] describes the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) for the rite of malevolent magic (*abhicārakarman*), the direction facing which the officiant (*hotṛ*) should be situated,
the specific location thereof, and the protection to be provided by the king for the officiant; as well as the consequences for the practitioner should such protection not be afforded.

By mentioning the "kingdom" (*rāṣṭra*), he teaches that the performance of that rite is mandatory for the sake of the kingdom, as well as the sin (*pratyavāya*) incurred by the kingdom if it is not performed. In that context, "facing the direction of Yama" means facing the southern direction. There, on the ground for malevolent rites (*abhicāra*), [the rite is performed] for the sake of the practitioner's own success.
For the sake of achieving [victory] over life and so forth, the enemy king—the hostile monarch—should perform [the rite] against this practitioner;

the word "abhicāram" (malevolent rite) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. His kingdom—the kingdom where the application of the malevolent rite takes place—[will perish] gradually, in the course of time. || 43 ||
By performing oblations in a fire kindled with *akṣa* wood and fueled by its fruits—or likewise with those [fruits] smeared with the juice of golden leaves—one shall destroy the enemy. (44)
When oblations are offered with its fruits into a fire kindled with *naktamāla* wood, even a formidable enemy, afflicted by disease, goes to the abode of Yama. || 45 ||
Having kindled a fire with the wood of the *unmattaka* tree, one should offer oblations with its seeds soaked in water from its leaves; within a month, an enemy shall fall into a state of delusion.
By offering oblations into a fire kindled with *āragvadha* fuel-sticks and its fruits—each measuring a span (*vitasti*) and smeared with oil—the death of an enemy is ensured. (47)
By performing a fire sacrifice (homa) in a fire kindled with *aruṣkara* wood, using its seeds soaked in its own clarified butter, death will certainly occur due to a fever of intense agony. 48.

With the verse beginning "akṣadruma," etc., he teaches the sacrificial oblation (*homa*) for causing the madness of an enemy through grief. In that context, "in a fire kindled with *akṣadruma* wood" means in a fire fueled by sticks produced from the *akṣadruma* tree; "with its fruits" means with *akṣa* fruits.
With [flowers] sprinkled with the juice of golden leaves, and drenched with the water of golden leaves. || 44 ||

With the verse beginning with *nakta*, he teaches the fire-offering (*homa*) for the practice of slaying an enemy. In that context, "kindled at night" refers to a fire fueled by *naktamāla* wood; "with its fruits" means with the fruits of the *karañja* tree.
With the verse beginning with *unmatta*, he teaches the fire-offering for the procedure of causing madness in an enemy.
In that case, with its seeds—that is, with the seeds of the *unmatta* plant—and with those soaked in its leaf-water—that is, soaked in the juice extracted from the *unmatta* leaves. (46)

With the verse beginning with "āragvadha," he teaches the ritual application for the slaying of enemies. In that context, "with those fuel-sticks" means with fuel-sticks of *āragvadha*; "with those fruits" means with fruits of *āragvadha*;
"measuring a span" means measuring twelve finger-breadths. || 47 ||
With the verse beginning with *aruṣkara*, he teaches the ritual application for killing an enemy by means of a violent fever.

In that context, *in a fire kindled with aruṣkara wood* means in a fire fueled by the fuel of *aruṣkara* wood. *With its seeds* means with the seeds of the *aruṣkara*. *Drenched in its ghee* means saturated with *aruṣkara* oil. (48)
By performing a homa with cotton seeds smeared with *sauvīra* (sour gruel), a mutual quarrel among enemies arises, leading to their destruction. (49)

One should offer oblations of ginger, long pepper, and black pepper soaked in mustard oil and clarified butter into a fire made from the wood of the enemy’s birth star; within the circle [of the ritual], death from fever will occur.
Having fashioned a doll from the aforementioned substances according to the prescribed method,
one should offer oblations at night with mustard seeds, aruṣkara fruits, and clarified butter, all sprinkled together.

As previously described, having cut [the effigy] with its limbs, one who is wrathful in mind, wearing crimson garments and adorned with red garlands, perfumes, flowers, and so forth, shall destroy the enemies.
By performing oblations with three seeds of the *Aruṣkara*— which have the shape of a serpent’s head and are anointed with ghee— the enemy will suffer from a burning fever within three days.

With the verse beginning "sauvīra" and so forth, he teaches the practice for killing an enemy through a quarrel; therein, "sauvīrāktaiḥ" means smeared with fermented gruel and soaked in sour gruel. || 49 ||

With the verse beginning with "tarṣapa" (mustard), he teaches the fire-offering (*homayoga*) for the purpose of killing an enemy by means of inducing fever. In that context, "saturated with mustard and clarified butter" means saturated with oil produced from mustard seeds;

"with ginger, *māgadhī* (long pepper), and black pepper" refers to the three pungents (*trikaṭuka*); and "in the fire of the tree belonging to the birth-constellation of the enemy" [is the locus of the rite].
In a fire kindled with wood from a tree produced under the birth asterism of one's enemy, there occurs the death of that enemy—the death of the foe.

With these two verses, beginning with "prāgukta" and ending with "vināśayet," he teaches the ritual application for destroying an enemy by means of a burnt offering (*homa*) using an effigy (*puttalī*). In that regard:

"By those previously mentioned" is a qualification of "by these substances. "According to the stated procedure" means according to the stated measurements and so forth. "Sprinkled with mustard and aruṣkara oil and ghee" means sprinkled with the oils of mustard and aruṣkara. "At night" means at midnight.

As previously stated, having cut [the thread] in twelve ways according to the method described in the forty-first and fortieth verses of the ninth chapter, one should— possessing a wrathful mind, that is,
a cruel mind directed toward the enemy (as is understood from the context)— be clad in reddish garments, meaning wearing saffron-colored robes.
Endowed with red garlands, perfumes, flowers, and so forth; that is, endowed with red garlands, red perfumes, red flowers, a red seat, and so forth. || 52 ||

With the verse beginning with "aruṣkara," he teaches the fire-sacrifice (homa) practice for causing the enemy to suffer from burning fever; therein, "with those seeds" means with the seeds of *aruṣkara*;
"with serpent-headed ladles" means with ladles fashioned in the shape of a serpent's head. || 53 ||
By offering oblations of meat arising from the enmity-nakṣatra-yonis, drenched in their blood, and also by offering oblations of fuel-sticks produced from those same trees; (54)
Within a few days, an enemy who has been brought into being will certainly meet his destruction,
whether through trees, walls, snakebites, or being struck down by a rutting elephant and the like.
By means of the destruction of trees and walls, and by the hurling of water and fire, [one is protected] from yakṣas, rākṣasas, gandharvas, piśācas, and brahmarākṣasas. (56)
Or by other means, the enemy will certainly meet with swift destruction.
[This is achieved] by using neem leaves, cotton seeds, and those produced from them, as well as those from the karañja tree. (57)
From an oblation of mustard oil, enmity shall arise;
one should offer it into the fire during the conjunction of the Nīca yoga, when fueled by wood from the trees of one's enemies.
Struck by the power of the mantra, that enemy will indeed be driven away within days by means of fragments of those trees smeared with oil in the middle of the night.
One should offer oblations into the fire during the auspicious period using the leaves, stalks, and seeds of the *mṛtyu* plant;
by this, the enemy's elephants and mounts will certainly perish from disease.

With these three and a half verses beginning with *vairi* and ending with *dhruvam*, he teaches the fire-offering (*homam*) as a means for the destruction of enemies under the pretext of felling trees or knocking down walls; therein,
"saturated with their blood" means saturated with the blood of those born from the womb-sign (*yoni*) of the enemy's birth-star (*nakṣatra*).

The phrase "tattarūdbhūtasamidhām api" means "also [by means of] sacrificial fuel-sticks produced from those very trees. [This occurs] by a thunderclap (nirghāta), by the falling of a lightning bolt (aśanipāta), by immersion in water, by casting into fire, or by other [causes] such as epilepsy (apasmāra) and so forth. The word "vā" indicates an alternative. || 56 ||

With the two and a half verses beginning with "nimbapatraiḥ" (by means of neem leaves), he teaches the ritual application for inciting enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). In this context, "ca" is used as a conjunction. "Born from that" (*tajjaiḥ*) means born from the neem tree; "seeds" (*bījaiḥ*) is the ellipsis. "Born from *karañja*" (*karañjajaiḥ*) refers to leaves and fruits; "and" (*ca*) is the ellipsis. "Sprinkled with mustard oil" (*sarṣapasrehasiktaiḥ*) means saturated with oil produced from mustard seeds. || 57 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with "nīca" and ending with "tāḍita," he teaches the fire-offering (homa) for the rite of eradication (uccāṭana). In that context, "in the conjunction of the base" (nīcayoge) means in the conjunction known as the base, namely the conjunction of the netherworld (pātālayoga). "One should sacrifice" (hunet) means one should offer oblations; [the materials] are from the fragments of those trees.
By means of the enemy's asterisms, trees, and groves, as well as by the days and the aforementioned mandalas and so forth. || 59 ||

With the verse beginning "By means of death-leafs" (*mṛtyupatraiḥ*), he teaches on page 613 the fire-offering (*homam*) for the application of destruction through diseases against the enemies' mounts and elephants,
when the enemy is in the eighth astrological sign (*aṣṭamarāśike*): having fashioned a doll (*puttalī*) out of red ochre (*gairakaiḥ*).
When one should gradually pierce the body with the previously mentioned thorns and other such instruments. || 61 ||
One should strike slowly and gradually at the poison-channel, at the location of the poison, as well as at the twin-thorn, at the half-watch, or at the head.
Death may come through those very limbs of the enemy by means of a blow or the like, or through knots, or through the aggravation of wounds from thorns and such, or through dreadful diseases. (63)
Having placed a doll made from the wood of the tree specified for that constellation,
along with a piece of cloth, into the urine of a donkey, one should boil it slowly.
Afflicted by a burning fever, that enemy goes to the abode of Yama;
having fashioned an image of him from beeswax, one should heat it slowly at night.

There, with the leaves of poisonous trees (*mṛtyupatra*), with the twigs of those poisonous trees as fuel (*tatkāṇḍa*), and with the seeds of those poisonous trees (*tadbīja*), one should offer oblations (*hunet*) into a pure fire kindled by the wood of poisonous trees;
[the targets are] the elephants (*dantinaḥ*), the mounts—the horses (*vāhāḥ hayāḥ*). || 60 ||

With these three verses beginning with "gairikair" and ending with "dāruṇaiḥ," he teaches the fire-offering ritual for the destruction of enemies by means of diseases and other afflictions arising from the desired limbs [of the enemy's body]. In that context, "when the eighth house is rising" refers to the moment of the ascendant of the eighth house.

In the phrase "by thorns and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to bones, needles, and the like. "Gradually" means step by step. "In the place of poison" refers to the limb corresponding to the day of that specific date. "At the time called Yamakaṇṭaka" refers to the period known as Yamakaṇṭaka. "At the time called Arddhaprahara" refers to the period known as Arddhaprahara.
The nature of the two specific times known as *yamakaṇṭaka* and *ardhaprahara* is now described according to the method taught in the *Jyotiḥśāstra*:
"One should know the *yamakaṇṭakas* to be half a watch (*yāma*) after sunrise and likewise half a watch after sunset."
During the day, one should worship [the deities] in sequence according to the order of the weekday, starting from the half-yāma following the slow (Mandā) gati.
"Upon the head of the effigy"—this is the ellipsis. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. And [it is done] with the head struck by those respective limbs.
In the phrase "by striking and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to cutting and other such acts. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. || 63 ||

With this half-verse beginning with *tannakṣatre* and ending with *yamālayam*, he teaches the ritual application for killing an enemy by means of a burning fever. In that context, *sthāpiterakām* means "having established the life-force" (*sthāpitaprāṇām*). *Gardabhīmehasalile* means "in the urine of a she-ass. *Śanaiḥ*...
In a few days. || 65 ||
Seized by that madness-fever, he will gradually meet his death.
One should dig up her [image], whose limbs are pierced by its thorns, at night in a cemetery. (66)
From that wound, the enemy, possessed by a piśāca, goes to the abode of Yama;
likewise, one should fashion an effigy using all those very same materials previously mentioned. (67)
Having fashioned that [image] within the sacrificial pit with trees belonging to one's enemies,
one should offer oblations at night into the kindled fire using fuel-sticks smeared with oil.
The deluded mind of one suffering from a fever of the combined humors (sannipāta) seizes his mouth and tongue;
gradually meeting its end, he leaves his body and goes to the abode of Yama. (69)
One should bury such an image during the dark fortnight,
on the ninth day of the month of Aṅgāra (Mārgaśīrṣa), at the threshold of the mother’s house.

With the half-verse beginning with *madhūcchiṣṭa* and ending with *yamālayam*, he teaches the procedure for killing an enemy by means of the "insanity fever" (*unmādajvara*). Therein, [he refers to] that effigy (*puttalī*) at night, specifically at midnight. That effigy, by means of that heating (*tāpana*). With the two half-verses beginning with *tām*... [and so forth].

He teaches the procedure for killing an enemy through the practice of making an effigy (*puttalī*). In that regard, "that effigy" refers to one whose limbs are pierced by thorns—that is, whose body is pierced by any one of the aforementioned thorns and so forth—at the father's house, in a cremation ground, at night, specifically at midnight; the word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of a collective conjunction. || 66 ||

With the first two verses beginning with "prāguktaiḥ" and ending with "yamālayam," he teaches the ritual procedure for the *homa* (fire sacrifice) for slaying an enemy by means of the *sannipāta* fever. In this context, "prāguktaiḥ" refers to [the substances] mentioned in the twenty-seventh and following verses of this chapter; "taddravyaiḥ" means "with those substances."

With all twelve substances prescribed for the rite of the effigy (*puttalī*), and according to the specified measurements; that effigy fashioned from the wood of the tree belonging to the enemy’s birth-constellation (*nakṣatra*); with the woods of the trees belonging to the enemy, that is, with the timber of the trees of the enemy’s birth-constellation; and with the fuel-sticks (*samidh*) of those same trees belonging to the enemy’s birth-constellation.
"At midnight" means at the middle of the night; "the enemy goes to the abode of Yama"—this is the ellipsis. || 69 ||
With the two verses beginning with *tathāvidhām* and ending with *lakṣitam*,

he teaches the ritual application for the destruction of an enemy by means of a specific method of drawing a doll (*puttalī*). In that context, "of such a kind" (*tathāvidhām*) refers to a figure or doll (*pratimām*) constructed from the twelve substances mentioned, according to the stated sequence and other details.

On the ninth day, on a Tuesday coinciding with the ninth lunar day, at the mother’s house— that is, in a temple of Caṇḍikā— at the base of the principal pedestal, in the middle of the night, the enemy, struck down during that night, goes to his destruction within seven days.
By the Bhūtādya and others, it was perceived on his own head like a thunderclap.
Having ground mustard seeds, black gram flour, sesame, and rice from the *śāli* variety,
one should also combine them with the bark-shavings of the tree belonging to the deity to be propitiated.
Then, having mixed castor seeds together to form a small image,
one should place the name of the enemy written on a palm leaf inside its chest.

While reciting that mantra a thousand times, touching it and generating the Vidyā produced by the third [syllable] in reverse order, [he should do so] when the moon is in the constellation of the victim's death or when it is situated in the eighth house.

Having bound her by the feet with a thread made from the fibers of the bhānu tree, and having grasped her with the "life-hand," one should recite the mantra and offer sacrifice while remaining pure. (75)
Having offered them into the fire by the thousands, with her head downward and feet upward,
he was on that day overwhelmed by a fever distressed by the agony of heat and thirst.
In the phrase "by the spirits and so forth" (*bhūtādyaiḥ*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to ghosts (*preta*) and others. Like a thunderclap or a lightning bolt;
"unobserved" (*alakṣitam*) is an adverbial modifier of the action. || 71 ||

With these six verses beginning with "mustard seed" (*sarṣapa*) and ending with "in Śiva" (*śive*), he teaches a specific ritual application using an effigy (*puttalī*) for the destruction of enemies by means of a fever of torment. Among them,
the phrase "mustard seed" and so forth, consisting of one and a half verses, refers to four substances [and] the tree of the victim's lunar mansion (*sādhyarkṣa*).

"With fragments" means with pieces. "Api" (also) is used as a conjunction. "Having made" (*kṛtvā*) is a word whose position is displaced; it means "having fashioned a doll. Then, subsequently, "having placed" (*nidhāya*)—this too is a displaced word—with the six aforementioned substances inside its chest, that is, within the region of the chest of the doll. [The name of the enemy...]

The meaning is "having performed. In the phrase "patragam" (on the leaf), "the name of the enemy" is the substantive. The word "saṃjapya" (having recited) is connected with the word "vidyām" (the mantra). "Puttalīm" means a doll whose life-force has been installed.
"Tārtīyapratilomajām" refers to the four [mantras] consisting of the reverse-order divisions of the third section.
One of the sciences; of the person to be accomplished or of the asterism of the one to be accomplished;

"in the asterism of death" means in the seventh asterism; "having bound" that effigy—this is the meaning of "nivadhya"; "tu" indicates a distinction; "with a thread from the *bhānu* tree" means with a thread produced from the *arka* tree; "with the hand of life."
With his hand on the side of the nostril from which the breath flows out, [he should recite] that *pratilomajā* vidyā into a pure fire with those substances such as mustard seeds. (p.
616) His body seized, rolling on the ground, unconscious, and muttering repeatedly—
O Śivā, through the power of its application, it swiftly proceeds to its destruction.
Having fashioned a doll from the wood of the tree belonging to the asterism of the person to be accomplished,
and having smeared it with the milk of the *arka* plant or the milk of the *vajrī* plant, one should bind it as before, facing downwards.
One should suspend [the vessel] above the fire-pit (kuṇḍa), joined with the name of the person for whom the rite is intended;
then, during the night, one should offer oblations of sacrificial wood (samidh) soaked in its milk.
Then, within three days, his enemy shall become afflicted with fever;
if he has any desire for protection, one should bury it within the interior of a pond.
Therefore, from being in the midst of the mire, he gradually attains happiness;
for if he were not to act thus, he would remain afflicted by disease for a long time. (81)
Likewise, having placed that [image] in a secondary vessel on a Tuesday,
one should dig it up at the temple of Caṇḍikā and offer an oblation before its womb.

A thousand times means a thousand repetitions. *Tu* is used for emphasis. *Tām* refers to that doll. *Taddine* means on that day, the day of the ritual performance. *Saḥ* refers to the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*). *Śive* is a vocative address. || 77 ||

With these four verses beginning with *sādhyarkṣa* and ending with *bhavet*, [the author] teaches the ritual application for inducing fever and insanity, as well as the methods for protecting against them. In that context, *arkadugdha* means with the milk produced from the *arka* tree; *vajrīkṣīreṇa* means with the milk of the *vajrī*.
With the milk produced from the *vajrīlatā* plant—or "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative—[one should bind] the wooden beam of the archway (*toraṇaviṣkambhadāruṇi*).

As before, with a thread made of *arka* fibers, [one should write] the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) joined with the initial letter of that name, together with the name of the rite to be accomplished written upon the chest. Above the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍāt ūrdhvam*), that is, over the pit.

"With those fuel-sticks" means with fuel-sticks produced from the tree corresponding to the birth-star of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*); "specifically" (*tu*) [indicates] this distinction. "Anointed with its milk" means smeared with the milk of the *arka* or *vajrī* plant. "In the middle of the night" (*niśāntara*) means at midnight.
"Specifically" (*tu*) is used for emphasis. "Then" (*tataḥ*) means by that ritual application. "Of him," namely the enemy. "That" hanging [limb].
The doll; in the interior of the pond—that is, within the water of the pond—by that digging; from this application; of him who was afflicted by fever; in the manner thus described. || 81 ||

With the half-verse beginning with *tathā* and ending with *upasargakaiḥ*, he teaches the specific ritual application for slaying an enemy through various particular ways of drawing the effigy (*puttalī*). In that context, *tathā* means that [effigy] constructed from the tree corresponding to the natal asterism (*nakṣatra*) of the victim.
Having struck it and placed it at a distance, one should strike it again with the *upasarga* mantras.
Having dug a trench in the ground beneath one's own house, one should increase the fire above it. (83)
For one whose enemies are not severed, there will arise old age and other ailments;
such a woman, having thus assumed that form, [should be joined] with the thigh-bone of Ruru. (84)
Having tied [the object] with the previously mentioned thread, one should dig it into the house of the enemy at night;
within eight months from that zodiac sign, he departs for another place.

Having fashioned a pair of such puppets according to the prescribed method, they should be bound with the skins of a cat and a mouse and inscribed with the name of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). || 86 ||
If one buries it on the banks of a river, or in the father’s house,
or in the mother’s house, or at the confluence of rivers, then enmity will arise between the two.

"At the temple of Caṇḍikā" means in the place situated beneath the foremost pedestal (agra-pīṭha); "its womb" refers to the womb of the asterism of the person to be accomplished (sādhya). "In front of that" means at the foremost pedestal of Caṇḍikā. The word "having struck" (nihatyā) connects with "its womb" in the preceding clause; the word "having given" (dattvā) connects with "the offering" (bali). The particle "tu" indicates a distinction.
By means of the afflictions that are like calamities. || 82 ||

With the two and a half verses beginning with *svagehe* and ending with *sambhavaḥ*, he teaches a specific ritual application for inducing diseases such as fever in a doll (*puttalī*). In that context, the word "having dug" (*khātvā*) is understood to mean "having dug [the ground]," and "upon that" (*tadupari*) means "upon the doll. Regarding the term *avicchinnam* (uninterrupted):

The connection applies to both cases by way of the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*): with the former [phrase], "by increasing the fire," and with the latter, "by the non-occurrence of diseases such as fever. (83)

With the half-verse beginning with "tām" and ending with "itthantena," he teaches the ritual application for eradication (*uccāṭana*) through the construction of a specific effigy (*puttalī*). In that context,
"tām" refers to that effigy produced from the tree corresponding to the [victim's] natal asterism (*sādhyarkṣa*), fashioned in such a manner.

"From the stated measurement onwards"—the word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction. "Joined with the thigh-bone of a ruru deer" means joined with the thigh-bone of a tiger. "By the previous sūtra" means by the thread made from the fibers of the *arka* tree.
"At night" means at midnight. "In the [eighth] zodiac sign"—the remainder of the sense is "of the enemy. || 85 ||

With the two verses beginning with *tathāvidham* and ending with *tadā*, he teaches the application of the rite for causing enmity (*vidveṣaṇa*). In that context, *tathāvidham* means constructed from the specific tree corresponding to the particular lunar mansion (*nakṣatra*); *uktamārgataḥ* means according to the measurement appropriate to its respective *aṃśaka*.

"Bound with the skins of a cat and a mouse" means encircled by the skins of a cat and a mouse; the remainder [of the meaning] is that these correspond respectively to the two, namely the oppressor and the oppressed. "Endowed with the name of the one to be accomplished" means endowed with the three names beginning with the name of the one to be accomplished (sādhya). This [phrase] is to be connected with the verb "one should bury," which refers to the pair of effigies (puttalikā).

In the preceding [verse], there is a connection (*anvaya*). "In the father's house" means in the cremation ground; or alternatively, it is an option. "And in the mother's house" means in the temple of Caṇḍikā. The phrase "when there is a flood of the river" is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣa*). || 87 ||

p. 618) Having arisen as before, those [mantras], accompanied by the name of the target person and so forth, and perfected through the recitation of their respective vidyās, one should then dig them up in the house of the enemy. 88.
Likewise, in the intermediate and cardinal directions, there shall be the destruction of that family;
thus has the malevolent rite (abhicāra) for those residing nearby been described. || 89 ||
"How can there be an act of sorcery against enemies situated at a distance?
Listen, O wise one, as I explain to you regarding an enemy who is very far away. (90)
The ritual application for destruction is swift and even malevolent;
by it, the enemy who stands nearby shall go to his death even before [one can approach him]. (91)
Having fashioned eight hundred effigies from trees suitable for that purpose,
one should sequentially water them with the two types of milk previously mentioned and provide them with their respective names.
Having bodies of the respective measures of those [digits], they should be struck one by one from midnight onwards, facing the directions of the enemies, until they are entirely destroyed.

With this half-verse beginning with *tāḥ* and ending with *bhavet*, he teaches the ritual application for the destruction of the enemy clan through the specific method of drawing effigies (*puttalī*). In that context, "those" refers to the effigies, numbering nine each; they are [to be made] according to the previously mentioned measurements based on the lunar mansions (*nakṣatra*) and trees.

In the phrase "beginning with those called *sādhya*," the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to the objects of the ritual action (*karma*). One should know that those effigies (*puttalī*), which have been empowered by the recitation of the [respective] *vidyās*, are consecrated with the third *vidyās* consisting of reverse order (*pratiloma*). "The destruction of their family" means the destruction of the enemy's clan. || 88 ||

With the half-verse beginning with "evam" (thus), he teaches that those [rites] previously mentioned are to be employed when the object is nearby. In this context, "evam" means by means of the aforementioned procedure for drawing the effigy (*puttalī*) and so forth. (89)

With the two verses beginning with *dūre* and ending with *vrajet*, the Goddess asks about the employment of *abhicāra* (malevolent rites) against enemies situated at a distance. In that regard, [she asks] "how" (*katham*), meaning by what method.
With the first half-verse beginning with *vadāmi* (I shall speak), [the Lord replies].

He teaches that power [of the mantra] together with an introduction concerning the narration of the death of an enemy situated at a distance. In this context, the word "tatra" (therein) connects with "prayogam" (the application) in the subsequent clause. "Te" means "your. "Prājñe" is a vocative address meaning "O wise one. "Yena prayogena" (by which application) refers to [an enemy] who is nearby—"from the enemy"—is the ellipsis. || 91 ||

With the one and a half verses beginning with *tatsādhyā* and ending with *nāśabhāk*, he teaches the fire-offering (*homa*) for the destruction of a distant enemy. In that context, *tatsādhyavṛkṣaiḥ* means by the trees belonging to the asterism of the distant enemy; *aṣṭau śatam* means one hundred and eight; *tāḥ puttalīḥ* refers to those effigies.

If [the roots] are previously sprinkled with the two milks mentioned above, or with the milk of the Arka and Vajrī plants, then even from a great distance, one does not suffer destruction at the time of those respective planetary divisions (*aṃśaka*). Or how could a person protected by a mantra-adept ever become subject to being killed? (94)
Listen to that, O Śivā; I shall tell you the method for his suppression.
