First, those practitioners of mantras should cause enmity to be instigated against him. (95)
When he is hated by them, his destruction would be easily accomplished due to his lack of support;
however, one who possesses superior fortune, provides great protection, and is allied with his mother’s kin [is otherwise]. (96)
"O Lord of Gods, tell me how one might kill a king or a royal scion by means of a stratagem; if such a method exists, please explain it to me. (97)
I shall tell you; listen, O wise one, to this unfailing and terrible form, the supreme incantation that swiftly brings about the destruction of enemies. (98)

These are the effigies (puttalīs), endowed with consciousness and bearing the names of those to be accomplished; they possess the proportions and dimensions of their respective [corresponding] asterisms, beginning from the first degree of Aśvinī and ending with the final degree of Revatī, their bodies constructed according to the measurements prescribed for the one hundred and eight degrees. These are the effigies.

"Facing the direction of the enemy" means facing the direction of the region where the enemy dwells. "At the time of that respective portion" means at the time of the portion corresponding to the measurement of that specific doll. With the half-verse beginning with "How," the Goddess asks for a means to slay an enemy who has been protected by powerful practitioners of mantras. In that regard:

Or how, by what manner? "An enemy"—this is the ellipsis—protected by powerful mantrikas, that is, by those possessing great magical spells; "may he go to being slain," meaning he may go to the state of being killed. || 94 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with *tat*, he introduces the discourse on the means for the destruction of that enemy.

Therein, *śive* is an address to the Goddess. With the two subsequent half-verses beginning with *tasya arāteḥ* and ending with *anāśrayāt*, he teaches the means for the destruction of the enemy. By those...
By those intent on the performance of the rite for the protection against the enemy— [the phrase] "from the time of the commencement of that enemy's own application" is the ellipsis;

[the phrase] "he should cause it to be done by those standing at the side of that enemy" is the ellipsis— by those mantra-experts, when that enemy has become hostile, it is easily accomplished, being easy to perform due to the lack of support [for the enemy].
Because of the absence of a protector. || 95 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with "bhāgyādhikam" and ending with "vidyate," the Goddess asks about the method of performing the *nidhana* rite for kings and others who possess an abundance of fortune (*bhāgya*) and so forth. In that context, "possessing an abundance of fortune" refers to being in accordance with the three types of planetary favor, such as the stated lifespan (*āyurdāya*).

And [the result] is superior through the worship of deities and so forth. How? By what means? Through application (*prayoga*). Or, in the case of application: "O Lord of Gods" (*deveśa*) is an address to the Lord (*īśvara*). Because they are divine, they are called "means" (*upāya*). || 97 ||

With the verse beginning "I say" (*vadāmi*), he praises that subject matter by first introducing the explanation of the meaning asked about. In this context, "O wise one" (*prājña*) is the vocative; the phrase "superior to the manner previously described" (*paraṃ proktaprakārāt*) is to be understood as the ellipsis. || 98 ||

Having [selected] those whose mantras are perfected, who are not overly affectionate, and who possess extremely stable intentions—sixteen of them—one should perform the fire-oblation (homa), dispelling their pride, according to the sequence of the watches of the night and so forth. (99)
Therefore, one should declare that to be his destruction even though he was protected without effort;
thus, one should effect the suppression of the enemy according to the prescribed method.
The pervasion consisting of the principle of *māyā* has been correctly described;
by the refinement of this within the mind, that very principle is assimilated into one's own self.
Thus ends the thirty-first chapter, titled "The Arising of Desired Fruits through Fire-offerings," in the *Śrīkādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.

With these two verses beginning with *siddha* and ending with *vidhānataḥ*, he teaches the application of malevolent rites (*abhicāra-prayoga*) against an enemy protected by a great mantra-master, together with its conclusion.
In this context, the phrase "having appointed those who have mastered the mantras as officiating priests" is the implied ellipsis; [he should appoint] those whose resolve is exceedingly firm.

Those whose hearts cannot be pierced by means employed by others; by those [means] through which mantras have been mastered; "in the sequence of the watches" means in the sequence of two watches at a time, that is to say, every watch in the order of two persons each; by that application;
"his death" refers to the death of a king or similar person of superior fortune, even though he has been protected.
The meaning is "by great mantra-experts and others. The word "without effort" (ayatnataḥ) is to be construed with the verb "should perform" (kuryāt) which follows later.
In this manner. || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, for the complete tantra known as the venerable *Kādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The thirty-first chapter, dedicated to the manifestation of the Subduer of Enemies, is thus completed and concluded. Oṃ tatsat.
The number of verses [in this chapter] is 268.
However, no yantra is taught in the thirty-first chapter;
the number of verses in the commentary there is two hundred and sixty-eight.
The Thirty-second Chapter. Now, O Śivā, I shall proclaim the fire-oblation (homa) by means of the Lalitā-vidyā,
by which even a mortal becomes renowned in the world as equal to a deity.
O wise one, listen to the rules for that [consecration], according to the distinctions of substances, time, and so forth,
as they are prescribed for the nine sacrificial pits (kuṇḍa) enjoined for their respective rites.
One should perform the oblation according to the prescribed method, preceded by meditation on the fire therein;
beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight until its conclusion, one should offer lotuses.
During those days, one may obtain prosperity by offering white water-lilies (kairava) sprinkled with the three sweets, or even with auspicious reddish flowers.
By performing this for an unbroken period of one year, a man becomes like a king;
and by offering white lotuses soaked in ghee on those very same days, he attains that same status.
By offering oblations with white water-lilies (kahlāra) on those days, one becomes possessed of wealth and grain.
Having taught the procedure for the fire-sacrifice (homa) for the crushing of enemies in the preceding thirty-first chapter, [the author] subsequently...

The thirty-second chapter, consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, the oblation" (*atha homam*) and ending with "by those uttered" (*udīritaiḥ*), teaches the procedure for the gentle fire-oblation (*saumyahoma*) for those who have attained perfection through the mantras of the sixteen *Nityās*. Therein, [the procedure] starting with "Now" (*atha*) is [explained] according to its divisions.
With this one and a half verse ending thus, he introduces the manner of explaining the subject matter of the chapter and its majesty.

In that context, "by the Lalitā-vidyā" means by the Śrīvidyā. "O Śivā" is an address to the Goddess. "By which oblation" is stated; "O Prājñā" is an address to the Goddess. Regarding the phrase "due to the difference in substances, time, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) [is used].
The object is the sacrificial pit and so forth. || 1 ||

With the two half-verses beginning with "prokteṣu" and ending with "pūrvakam," he teaches the general procedure for the fire-oblation (homavidhāna). Therein, "prokteṣu" refers to those [fire-pits] mentioned in the twenty-ninth chapter;
the word "kuṇḍe" (in the pit) is to be supplied as the remainder; and "uktamārgeṇa" means according to the stated method.
According to the procedure for sprinkling water and strewing grass, etc., as prescribed in the twenty-ninth [chapter], verse 1.

With seven verses beginning with "śuklā" and ending with "jīvati," starting from the first day of the bright fortnight up to the full moon, [the author] teaches the fire-oblations that bring about accomplishments such as sovereignty (*aiśvarya*) through various types of aquatic flowers. In this context, the term *hunet* means "one should offer oblations."

Sprinkled with the three sweets—milk, ghee, and honey—or with curd, ghee, and honey; auspicious; free from buds, fallen [parts], withered, decayed, or infested by insects; untouched by a limb and not stale.
One becomes like a king;
by offering blue lotuses into those very fires, one obtains abundant prosperity. (6)
By offering oblations of red lotuses, one obtains a maiden;
furthermore, through worship, one attains good fortune, fame, and health.
By means of those six [offerings] soaked in saffron powder, from that day's fire-oblation,
one attains unshakable prosperity and lives happily upon the earth.
By offering oblations with those [sticks] anointed with sandalwood on those specific days according to the prescribed rule,
a human being lives for a long time accompanied by sons, female slaves, and male servants.
By performing oblations with those very [substances] melted with moon-essence (indudrava),
one lives upon this earth resembling Kandarpa, delighting the throngs of women.
Beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight until the new moon, one should offer oblations with white substances smeared with ghee;
within a single year, one shall obtain prosperity free from rivals.
On those very days, one should offer oblations into the fire with jaggery soaked in honey;
thus endowed with splendor, fortune, victory, and health, he lives upon this earth.

The word "with riches" (*sampadbhiḥ*) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. In those [days] consisting of the lunar dates beginning with the first of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad-ādi-tithi*), [one should worship] with *abja*s, i.e., lotuses;
with white ones, i.e., those of light color. In those days, as previously stated, [one should worship] with reddish ones, i.e., blue water-lilies (*utpala*) or red night-lilies (*aruṇa-kumuda*).
In those days, by means of this phrase "even from worship as previously described," [it refers to] the aforementioned ritual applications of flower-homa.

Worship with those respective flowers in their respective places is also prescribed. With those six—namely, two lotuses (one red and one white), the kahlāra, the indīvara, and the two types of kairava—and by means of the oblation performed on those days, that is, on the days corresponding to the lunar dates beginning with the first day of the bright fortnight; "with those aforementioned six" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

On those days, namely the lunar days beginning with the first of the bright fortnight; according to rule, by means of the prescribed procedures such as strewing [the sacrificial grass] and sprinkling water; with those six [substances] as before; "with moon-fluid-anointed" means anointed with camphor-fluid; the particle *tu* indicates a specific distinction. || 10 ||

With nine and a half verses beginning with "kṛṣṇa" and ending with "hunet," he teaches the ritual procedure for performing oblations that bring about prosperity, such as the attainment of Lakṣmī, using specific sacrificial materials on the days corresponding to the fifteen lunar dates from the first day of the dark fortnight until the new moon.

In that context, "with white substances" means with sugar and the like. On those days, which take the form of the fifteen lunar days (*tithi*) of the dark fortnight, one should offer oblations—that is, perform *homa*. By means of those days, which consist of the fifteen lunar days of the dark fortnight, a person [attains success] through the offering of grapes sprinkled with milk on those very days.
Subsisting on milk, he lives for a long time upon the earth with a stainless disposition. || 13 ||
By performing oblations of dates mixed with the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar) for that many days,
one enjoys prosperity endowed with long life, health, and victory.
Likewise, by performing oblations with plantain fruits on those specific days,
one shall possess meritorious fame, be honored by kings, and live happily for a hundred years.
By performing oblations with the pulp of coconut fruit combined with white honey for those specific days,
one shall obtain every desired object.
By offering oblations on those days with those [leaves] sprinkled with sugarcane juice,
he shall indeed obtain garments of various colors that are most precious.

One shall obtain prosperity by offering oblations with those six [substances] smeared with the three sweets; likewise, by offering oblations with those same substances mixed with cow’s milk and sugar along with a calf.
By offering oblations with these [materials] sprinkled with buffalo milk, one shall obtain the desired result;
likewise by those joined with goat's milk or drenched in sheep's milk. (19)

One whose intention is unstained and whose heart is serene. "By those days" means by the same days as before. By the word "tathā" (thus), the immersion in the three sweets is indicated. On those days, as before. The word "tu" (but) indicates a distinction. "By those days" means as before. "By them" refers to the powder of coconut fruits. On those days, as before.
On the lunar days of the dark fortnight, that practitioner [should offer oblations] with those six:

namely, white sugar, jaggery, grapes, dates, plantains, and the powder of coconut fruit—these being the six mentioned. Furthermore, [he should offer] cow's milk along with its calf, together with a calf of the same color.
With [the substances] smeared with the milk of a white-colored cow—the word *api* (also) is used in the sense of conjunction—with those six substances as previously described;
likewise, as before, with those six substances. The word division is: *avikṣīrasaṃplutaiḥ* (drenched in sheep’s milk). [They should be] smeared with coconut powder and milk.
"With those [offerings] moistened with milk produced from the powder of coconut fruit"—
by the word "also" (*api*), the phrase "one shall obtain the desired object" is drawn in here as well. With those six, as before,
one should offer oblations even with those [substances] moistened with the milk of coconut fruit powder.
Likewise, [it arises] from twelve substances, whether combined individually or together. || 20 ||
By offering oblations daily with milk, honey, and clarified butter,
as well as by giving cows, land, gold, and garments, he lives on this earth endowed with all prosperity.
Likewise, on a Sunday, one should offer oblations of white rice mixed with milk;
from this, there will be an abundance of food within a year. Or, one may offer oblations of rice smeared with ghee or saturated with honey.
By offering coconut fruits mixed with sugar on Mondays, one certainly obtains a land abundant in crops. (23)
On a Tuesday, by performing a fire sacrifice (homa) with food smeared with honey, one shall obtain prosperity;
by sacrificing with those same materials when they are combined with what is desired and pleasing, one shall obtain that earth.
By performing a fire sacrifice on Wednesday with sesame seeds and rice grains smeared with ghee for one year,
one obtains Śrī, the abode of all auspiciousness.
On Thursdays, by offering oblations for a full year with the pollen from jackfruit seeds sprinkled with milk, one obtains an excellent house within just one year.
On a Monday, one should offer oblations with coconut kernels mixed with sugar or with molasses; by doing so, one prospers for a very long time.
By means of the first half-verse beginning with *tathā* and ending with *kṣitau*,

[the text teaches] that through the twelve substances combined— the six flowers prescribed for the bright fortnight (*śuklapakṣa*) together with the six substances such as white [sandalwood] prescribed for the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇapakṣa*)— and through all their forms, one performs the perpetual fire-oblation (*nityahoma*).

It teaches that [this practice] brings about the attainment of cattle, land, gold, clothing, and supernatural powers (*siddhi*). In that regard, "likewise" means by means of the twelve lunar days (*tithi*) declared for the bright and dark fortnights; "or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative; and "constantly" (*nityaśaḥ*) means every day.

With these seven verses beginning with "ravivāra" and ending with "manoharām," he teaches the sacrificial materials for the *homas* that bring about prosperity on the seven days starting from Sunday. In this context, "sitānnaiḥ" means with white foods, such as rice accompanied by sugar; "tu" indicates a distinction; and "kṣīrāktaiḥ" refers to those smeared with milk, such as the cow's milk and other types mentioned.

With any one of these four, according to the prescribed method: by offering oblations on a Saturday with pure sesame seeds smeared with ghee, or with other [seeds] sprinkled with oil, one obtains most enchanting prosperity within a year. (28)
One should offer oblations with all of those combined and smeared together, in sequence, for seven days;
through the power of this vidyā-homa, one shall become Lakṣmī and the other goddesses.
And on those days, he should well feed three or two devotees of that vidyā,
providing them with ghee, milk, sesame, honey, molasses, and cakes.
One should offer oblations in sequence into all nine lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī,
using śāli rice, taṇḍula rice, mung beans, māṣa beans, and sesame seeds other than white.
With such mustard seeds, kodrava grains, ghee, sesame, and dundhuka flowers, all soaked in molasses and sugarcane juice, for the sake of attaining Indirā (Lakṣmī).

With any one of the aforementioned products of the cow (gavya) and so forth, smeared with ghee; or—in the sense of an alternative—with those foods accompanied by sugar (sitopeta), that is, mixed with sugar; with sesame and rice (tilataṇḍula), meaning rice mixed with sesame;
and with the pollen of jackfruit seeds sprinkled with milk (dugdhasiktapanasāsthiparāgaka), meaning the pollen of jackfruit kernels mixed with milk. || 28 ||

With this verse beginning with "tair" (by those), he teaches that [the rite] brings about prosperity and other benefits through the oblation of all the substances over seven days. In this context, "tair" means "by those"; "samastāktaiḥ" means "smeared with all the substances for sprinkling. "Over seven days" is the ellipsis to be supplied.

By those days—meaning the days prescribed for the initial maṇḍala starting from this day—through the majesty of the Vidyā-homa, that is, through the majesty of the Lalitā-vidyā and the majesty of the fire-oblation (homa). || 29 ||

With the verse beginning "On those days" (*taddineṣu*), he instructs what should be performed on the days of the fire-offerings (*homa*) for the various rites that bring about specific attainments. In this context, "on those days" means on the days of the respective rites. "Devotees of that Vidyā" means devotees of the Lalitā-vidyā. "Three or two, or three or two" is the meaning; one should feed them well. || 30 ||

By means of these two and a half verses, beginning with "Aśvinyādi" and ending with "kramāt," [the author] sets forth the ninefold materials for the *sampatkara* oblation corresponding respectively to the nine lunar mansions beginning with Aśvinī.
He teaches [the rite] together with the nine substances for immersion. Therein, one should sacrifice (*hunet*); that is, one should offer (*juhuyāt*).

"In sequence" means in the order of one by one. By the words beginning with "rice" (*śālī*) on page 626, [it is meant] by those [substances] soaked in the milk of buffalo, goat, and sheep, respectively, in the nine [vessels].
Likewise, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed with nine [offerings] during each of the nine asterisms beginning with Maghā.

With chickpeas and dishes of chickpeas, with dishes of mung beans and likewise with *kṛsara*, with dishes of black gram and dishes of turmeric, as well as with molasses-rice and milk-rice (*pāyasa*). || 34 ||
For the attainment of fame, fortune, and victory, one should offer oblations of milk-rice and pure rice smeared with the three sweets;
likewise, one should offer oblations with the nine [mantras] beginning with the Mūla-mantra, using clarified butter.
With parched rice flakes, barley meal, fried grain, and stalks of sugarcane soaked in milk;
with preparations derived from śāli rice, chickpeas, and mung beans, as well as those produced from black gram flour and sesame.

The six substances are mentioned in the second half of the verse. Among them, "with white and other sesamums" refers to white-colored sesamums and black-colored sesamums. By the phrase beginning with "in such a manner," the third set of substances and their results are indicated. Therein, "with such mustard seeds" refers to white mustard seeds and black mustard seeds.

By the second half of the verse beginning with *kṣaudra*, the six substances for immersion are indicated; therein, by the word *keronda*, coconut water is meant. By the second half of the verse beginning with *mahiṣī*, the three substances for bathing and their sequence are indicated; therein, [the bathing is performed] with those soaked in the milk of buffaloes, goats, and sheep.

With those aforementioned substances—soaked in buffalo milk, cow milk, goat milk, and sheep milk—in the nine aforementioned [asterisms] beginning with Aśvinī, [one should bathe] in sequence, using each substance one by one in order. || 32 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *maghā* and ending with *āptaye*, and with the second half-verse, he teaches the sacrificial materials for the *sampatkaraṇahoma* in sequence for the nine [asterisms] beginning with Maghā. In that regard, one should offer oblations in such a manner: with the nine [substances], namely chickpeas (*caṇaka*) and so forth, which are to be mentioned immediately hereafter; the word *api* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*).

By the first half-verse beginning with "caṇakaiḥ" (with chickpeas), four substances are mentioned; by the second half-verse beginning with "māṣānnaiḥ" (with black gram rice), another four substances are stated; and by the third half-verse beginning with "dugdhānnaiḥ" (with milk-rice) [or "śuddhānnaiḥ"], one substance is mentioned, as well as the liquid in which that substance is soaked and its fruit. || 34 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *tathā* and ending with *dhruvam*, consisting of two verses, he teaches the nine substances for the *sampatkara-homa* (the oblation that brings prosperity) in the nine constellations beginning with Mūla;

[he does so] "in that manner" (*tathā*), meaning in each successive order, and "in that way" (*tathā*), meaning according to the prescribed procedure. [He further explains] with the half-verse beginning with *pṛthukaiḥ*.

There are four substances, as well as the substance for immersion. Among these, "with those soaked in milk" means those saturated with milk. By the latter half of the verse beginning with "śālī," the five substances for the five cakes used in the oblations during the remaining five days are indicated; among these, they are produced from the flour of *māṣa*, sesame, and so forth, as well as from the flour of these [other grains].
These items, beginning with *śāli* rice, are qualifiers for the word "with cakes" (*apūpaiḥ*) mentioned later. (p.
627) With cakes soaked in sweet [syrup], one will certainly obtain victory, fame, fortune, health, long life, good luck, and honor. (37)
One who possesses those specific substances should offer oblations during the Siddhayogas;
likewise, one should offer oblations during the yogas known as Amṛta for the pacification of disease.
In the Uccha yogas, one should diligently offer oblations of guḍūcī, taladūrvā, and utpala flowers— each smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu)— using auspicious reddish-pink lotuses.
In the yoga called Parvata, one certainly becomes preeminent among all of one's own kinsmen; for whatever substances are offered in the sacrifice, that indeed becomes a mountain [of wealth]. (40)
O Supreme Goddess, this shall come to pass for him in a very short time;
now listen to another wonderful oblation which I shall describe to you. (41)

For the satisfaction of the planets, one should perform oblations with milk-rice mixed with white substances and sprinkled with ghee, using the Vidyā-mantra, when the planet is situated in its own domain or its exaltation.
The sevenfold fruit beginning with victory is common to the fire-oblations prescribed for the nine constellations starting with Mūla. || 37 ||

With these four verses beginning with "siddhe" and ending with "te," he teaches the performance of the *sampatkara-homa* (the prosperity-bestowing oblation) during the auspicious conjunctions of the *siddha* and other yogas, together with an introduction explaining the nature of the oblation (*homa*). In this context, "in the *siddha*-yogas" refers to those produced by the conjunction of lunar days (*tithi*), weekdays (*vāra*), and so forth.

"With substances" means with those desired substances that one wishes to obtain; "possessing the abundance of those substances" means possessing the abundance of the substances offered in the oblation. The word "tathā" (likewise) is used for conjunction.
Regarding the "yogas called Amṛta" produced by the conjunction of lunar mansions, weekdays, and so forth: *guḍūcī* is the *amṛtalatā* (the immortal creeper).

With reverence and devotion; when one of the planets, beginning with the Sun, is in its own exaltation degree and situated in the tenth house from the ascendant; with red lotuses—that is, red water-lilies; "auspicious" means as before, free from the eight defects such as being unopened buds and so forth; "highly" means excessively; [this applies] to that which is called "Parvata."

In this context, "in yoga" is the term to be qualified. When the Sun has risen in its own sign, its exaltation sign, or its portion (bhāga), or when Mars, Venus, and the Moon are situated respectively in Aries,
Libra, and Cancer— at which time, that is to say, during the rising of the sign Capricorn— one should sacrifice, that is, perform oblations, with whatever substances are desired to be obtained.
That substance fills the mountain; "Parameśvarī" is the vocative address. || 41 ||
With the two verses beginning with *svakṣetre* and ending with *tatkule*, he teaches the time for the fire-oblation (*homa*) that satisfies the planets and the substances for the oblation. (p.
628) Whoever should always perform this rite of oblation according to the prescribed rule...
At the specific times prescribed for each, there shall be affliction from the planets, but not within that [particular] family.
One should perform the fire-oblation according to the prescribed rite during the three months of one's birth;
by doing so constantly with dūrvā grass, amṛtā, and sesame seeds for as long as one lives, one shall be happy.
On those days, one should recite the vidyā a thousand times daily;
for such a person, no affliction whatsoever shall ever arise anywhere at any time.
On that day, one should perform a libation with sweet waters scented with camphor, or otherwise worship [the deity] with flowers rich in fragrance.
The three births of a practitioner of mantras shall never be fruitless;
however, if such a person should suffer from disease or other afflictions, it will certainly come to pass. (47)

In that regard, regarding the thirty-first chapter on one's own domain (*svakṣetra*), by the verse beginning with "Bhauma" (Mars) and so forth, it is meant that when any one of the planets, such as the Sun and others, has gone to its own sign; [specifically] the signs of Aries, Taurus, Capricorn, Virgo, Cancer, Pisces, and Libra are the exaltations (*ucca*) for the seven planets beginning with the Sun.
The signs of rising (*udayarāśi*) in succession. When any one of those planets, such as the Sun and so forth, is situated in its own respective sign of rising—at that time;

or (the word *vā* indicates an alternative)—for the satisfaction of the planet, that is, for the satisfaction of that specific planet, with white [substances] mixed [with sugar], that is, mixed with sugar-candy; specifically (*tu*), by means of the *vidyā*, namely the *Lalitā-vidyā*, in each of those places prescribed.
When the planets are situated in their own proclaimed fields, exaltations, or signs, then—within those [planets] and within the family of the practitioner—that [is the case].

With these four verses beginning with "In the months" and ending with "is determined," [the author] teaches the procedure for fire-offerings (*homa*), recitation (*japa*), libations (*tarpaṇa*), and worship (*pūjā*) throughout three lifetimes; the necessity of performing at least one of these among them; and the transgression incurred by failing to do so. In that context, the phrase "in the months" implies "in twelve months."
"With *dūrvā*, *amṛtā*, and sesame seeds"—the meaning is: with any one of these substances. "Constantly" means throughout three successive births.

"On those days" refers to the three days of birth. "Knowledge" (*vidyā*) [refers to] a thousand times; the phrase "along with the daily [recitation]" is to be supplied as the remainder for the thousand repetitions.
"Of him" refers to the reciter. "In some place" means that for someone, there may arise suffering.

This is the object to be qualified. "Scented with moon" means mixed with camphor. "Or" (*vā*) indicates an alternative. On that day, during the three births; the remainder [of the sense] is that the triad of births becomes not fruitless through any one of the acts of *homa*, libation (*tarpaṇa*), or worship. If the triad of births should be fruitless, [it is so] for that practitioner of mantras (*māntrika*).
In the phrase "from disease, etc.," the word "etc. refers to the elements and so forth. || 47 ||
When the Moon or the Sun is situated in its exaltation sign or its own sign, one should recite the mantra of Vidyā a thousand or a hundred times, or worship Śivā. (48)
He for whom no affliction from disease shall ever certainly arise—by acting thus at the times prescribed, he shall become happy. (49)
For a practitioner afflicted by planetary influences, diseases, poverty, and distress, his status as a mantra-expert in this world will become an object of both sorrow and ridicule. (50)
By offering oblations with Palāśa flowers, fruits, leaves, stalks, and roots,
even one who is dull-witted shall become eloquent within a single year.
By performing oblations with *arka* flowers smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*), one obtains the desired result;
likewise, by means of its leaves, sacrificial fuel sticks (*samidh*), and even its roots from the mandala.
One should offer oblations with bilva flowers, fruits, leaves, and stalks, as well as roots, for the attainment of Lakṣmī; may she never depart from that lineage. (53)

With these three verses beginning with "uccastha" and ending with "bhavet," he teaches the sequence of worship when the Sun and other deities are situated in their own signs or their exaltations, the fruit thereof, and the transgression incurred by failing to perform it. In this context, the particle "vā" signifies conjunction (*samuccaye*). "Vidyām" refers to the *Lalitā-vidyā*.

A thousand times means a thousand repetitions. Or rather, "vā" implies an alternative. A hundred times means a hundred repetitions. "Śivām" refers to the eternal [goddess] as previously described. "Yaḥ māntrikasya māntrikasya rogataḥ" means by the diseases of whichever practitioner of mantras. Acting in that manner means performing the worship according to the stated method. "Śokahāsāspadam" means a source of both grief and laughter.
Of one's own side and the opposing side. || 50 ||

With the verse beginning "palāśapuṣpa," he teaches the injunction for the fire-oblation that bestows eloquence. In this context, "with fruits, leaves, stalks, and roots" means those produced from the *palāśa* tree.
"Even one of dull speech" means even one who is mute. || 51 ||

With the verse beginning with "arka," he teaches the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) for the attainment of desired objects. In this context, "with *arka* flowers" means with the flowers of the *arka* tree. "Desired" (*iṣṭa*) means that which is intended. "From the mandala" refers to forty-nine days as previously described. "From the root of that *arka* tree" means with its roots.
In the form of fragments. || 52 ||
With the verse beginning with "vilva," he teaches the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) that brings about the attainment of *lakṣmī*.

In this context, the noun phrase ending in the third-case plural—consisting of the four words beginning with "phalaiḥ"—is qualified by the term "vilvaprasūnaiḥ" (with bilva flowers). By means of the word "vilvaprasūna," [the meaning of] the genitive form "vilvasya" (of the bilva) is conveyed.
The connection [is as follows]: likewise, with those [offerings] smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one should sacrifice—that is, one should perform oblations. "Mā" refers to Lakṣmī;
she shall follow that lineage, meaning she will belong to the family of the practitioner. || 53 ||
By performing oblations for that many days with lotus seeds smeared with honey, a man obtains beautiful fortune that causes wonder in all the worlds. (54)
One should offer oblations of *campaka* flowers mixed with honey until that day;
thus, one who is wealthy but childless shall obtain sons of superior qualities.
By performing oblations with those very same offerings saturated with clarified butter when the auspicious planet is situated in its exaltation,
one obtains land rich in all kinds of crops and becomes a consumer thereof.

When the Moon is in its exaltation, by offering oblations of those [seeds] soaked in milk for that many days, the practitioner becomes a hundredfold [powerful]; likewise, by offering them soaked in the three sweets (honey, ghee, and sugar), he obtains the triad [of powers].
By performing oblations with *pāṭala* flowers sprinkled with honey, one shall obtain a maiden;
likewise with *tagara* flowers, parched grain (*lāja*), or *kuṭaja* flowers. (58)

With the verse beginning with "padmākṣaiḥ," he teaches the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) that brings about the attainment of prosperity (*lakṣmī*). In this context, "with lotus seeds" means with the gems situated inside the fruits of the lotus; "smeared with sweets" means smeared with the three sweets (*trimadhu*).
"By so many days" means by as many days as there are days in the mandala. || 54 ||

With the verse beginning with "campakaiḥ," he teaches the procedure for the fire-offering (homa) that grants success to the son of Lakṣmī; therein, "taddināvadhi" means up until the day of the mandala. || 55 ||

With the verse beginning with "tereva" (56), he teaches the oblation that brings about the acquisition of fertile land. In this context: "taiḥ" means by those *campaka* flowers; "eva" is used for emphasis; "maṅgale" refers to Mars (*bhauma*); "tu" indicates a distinction; "uccasaṃsthite" means situated in its exaltation, namely in the sign of Capricorn (*makara-rāśi*); and "ca" denotes a conjunction. || 56 ||

With this verse beginning with "taireva" (by those very [flowers]), he teaches the prescription for two types of oblations that bring about the acquisition of a hundred cows, of fortune, of a son, and of land. In this context, "taireḥ" means by those *campaka* flowers. "When [the Sun] is in its exaltation" means when it has entered the sign of Taurus (*vṛṣabha-rāśi*). "By those days" means from the [completion of the] mandala. "Possessing a hundred" means endowed with a hundred cows.

Likewise, from that maṇḍala; with those campaka flowers smeared with the three sweets—this is the ellipsis—the practitioner shall obtain [the fruit], meaning he shall obtain it due to its divine nature: the triad consisting of cows, land, and groups of sons. || 57 ||

With the verse beginning with "pāṭalaiḥ," he teaches the substances for the fire-oblation (*homadravya*) that brings about the accomplishment of a maiden (*kanyāsiddhi*). In this context, "tagara-origins" refers to the previously mentioned aquatic flowers or *nandyāvarta* flowers;
"kuṭajas" refers to *girimallikā* flowers; and the word "api" is used in the sense of conjunction. (58)
By performing oblations with those four [substances] mixed with milk, one obtains wealth; and within those same days, one acquires various and highly precious garments. (59)
By offering oblations of hundred-petaled lotuses smeared with honey, one shall obtain Lakṣmī;
likewise by means of saffron filaments, kadamba flowers, and vicakila blossoms.
One should perform the initial commencement of the sacrifice with *mallikā*, *mālatī*, *jāti*, *puṇnāga*, and *nameru* flowers, ending on the fifth day, all drenched in honey.
One shall obtain Mahālakṣmī by performing oblations with each [substance] individually as well as all together;
likewise, one obtains prosperity through ornaments from offering oblations with clarified butter.
By performing oblations for several days with Karṇikāra flowers smeared with honey, one certainly attains unshakable prosperity that has arisen. (63)
With white water-lilies, red night-lotuses, blue lotuses, and pairs of lotuses—
either individually or all five together— one should worship, as before, from Nanda up to Pūrṇa.
With this verse beginning with "tair" (by those), he teaches the fire-oblation that brings about the acquisition of wealth and clothing. In that context, "taiḥ" means by those [flowers]:
the pāṭala, tagara, jalaja, and kuṭaja; "ca" denotes a collective aggregate; and "taddinaiḥ" means from the mandala on that day. 59.

With the verse beginning "With hundred-petaled [lotuses]," etc., he teaches the five flowers for the purpose of a fire-oblation (*homa*) that brings about the attainment of Lakṣmī. In this context, "with *keśara*, *vakula*, and *vicakila*"—where *vicakila* is a specific kind of jasmine (*mallikā*)—"also" (*api*) draws in the word "on those days" (*taddinaiḥ*) from the preceding [verse]. (60)

With these three verses beginning with "mallikā" and ending with "suniścitam," he teaches the various types of *sampatkara* oblations for the lunar days from the first through the fifth. Among them, by the first half-verse beginning with "mallikā," five flowers are indicated; therein, "namerubhiḥ" refers to the flowers of the *suraparṇī*.

On each individual lunar day (*tithi*), there is a collection of five flowers for each [deity]. The word *ca* (and) has the sense of an option (*vikalpa*). "By those very [flowers]" means by the five kinds of flowers already mentioned. "Likewise, individually" means up to "by all together. The phrase "along with ornaments" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. "By the days" refers to those that have arisen [in sequence].
From the mandala that has been described; this [instruction] regarding the limit of the time for the fruit concludes the section. || 63 ||

With these two verses beginning with "kahlāraiḥ" and ending with "sādhakottamaḥ," he teaches the general procedure for the fire-oblation (*puṣpahoma*) that brings about prosperity, to be performed on each of the five lunar days starting from Nandā and ending with Pūrṇā, both individually and collectively, as previously described.

From the oblation, the best of practitioners obtains fortune along with land, ornaments, and vehicles—either by offering each of the three sweets individually or by offering all of them together. (65)
By performing oblations with ketakī flowers soaked in honey for that many days,
one obtains many diverse, priceless garments.
By performing a fire-oblation with white flowers sprinkled with milk for those many days,
one obtains white garments, as well as strings of pearls and silver.
For the attainment of one's desires, one should offer oblations with *kuruvaka* flowers soaked in honey;
likewise, by offering oblations with *damanaka* leaves, one enjoys prosperity.
O Dear One, if the practitioner offers flowers of a particular color while reciting the vidyā, he will certainly obtain garments of that very same color. (69)
By performing oblations at night with black pepper and mustard seeds soaked in oil,
one may bring back a beloved woman who has become fickle in abandoning her shame and modesty.

In that regard, "with pairs of lotuses" means with red and white lotuses, smeared with honey as before. From Nanda up to Pūrṇā—that is, from the first lunar day (pratipad) through the sixth, eleventh, and so on, up to the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth—or alternatively; likewise, with kahlāra flowers and others.
By means of five [factors]. || 65 ||

With the verse beginning with "ketakī," he teaches the ritual procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) that accomplishes the siddhi of priceless and variegated garments. In this context, "tu" signifies a specific distinction. "From those days" means from the mandala as previously described. The phrase "the practitioner obtains" is the ellipsis to be supplied.
Priceless and of excellent value. || 66 ||

With the verse beginning with "sitaiḥ" (white), he teaches the ritual procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhāna*) that brings about the attainment of white garments, strings of pearls, silver, and supernatural powers (*siddhi*). In this context, "he obtains in that manner" means as much as that. || 67 ||

With the verse beginning with *hunet*, he teaches the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homavidhāna*) which grants one's desires and brings about the attainment of prosperity (*lakṣmīsiddhi*). In this context, "one should offer" (*hunet*) means one should perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*). Likewise, "with leaves soaked in honey" (*kṣaudraplutaiḥ*) refers to the leaves of the *tamāla* tree. || 68 ||

With the verse beginning "yadvarṇāni" (of whatever color), he teaches the ritual procedure for the *homa* that accomplishes the attainment of garments of one's desired color. In this context, "by the Vidyā" refers to the Lalitā; "O Dear One" (*priye*) is a vocative address; "of that color" (*tadvarṇāni*) means having the color of the flowers offered in the *homa*. || 69 ||

With these four verses beginning with "marīcaiḥ" and ending with "sitānvitaiḥ," he teaches the procedure for the fire-oblation (homa) that effects the attraction of women, the subjugation of men, the attainment of royal fortune, and the subjugation of all living beings.
With flowers produced from the *pāṭalī*, *kunda*, *mandāra*, and *śephālī*, and with the auspicious blossoms of the *campaka*, *aśoka*, *puṃnāga*, and *nameru* trees. (71)
By offering oblations mixed with honey, one may subjugate all women;
by offering oblations of those same materials mixed with clarified butter, one may subjugate even men.
By offering oblations at night with these [seeds] smeared with ghee, one obtains royal fortune;
by those same [seeds] combined with sugar, one may bring the entire world of living beings under one's control. 73.
By constantly offering oblations of food soaked in ghee, one shall become possessed of food;
likewise, one should always offer oblations with sesame seeds and rice for the sake of longevity.
At midnight, by offering oblations of salt that have been well-mixed and finely powdered, and anointed with the three sweets, one shall bring all women under one's control.
Likewise, by offering oblations with salt mixed with curd, one brings an enemy under control;
similarly, by offering oblations with [substances] soaked in the juice of red sugarcane, kings shall become submissive.
By performing oblations with clarified butter alone for the number of days specified, one becomes wealthy;
by offering ghee daily, one becomes prosperous and an enjoyer of pleasures.
In that context, "during the nights" refers to the middle watches of the night. "The beloved, cherished woman" refers to the female partner.

Regarding the phrase "with *nameru* flowers," the word "flower" (*kusuma*) here implies the practice for subjugation (*vaśyayoga*) arising from the first half [of the verse]. With those eight flowers, beginning with *pāṭalī*, the word "also" (*api*) serves as a conjunction.
With those eight flowers; at night, as before, at midnight; with those flowers, as before; accompanied by white [sugar], that is, mixed with sugar-candy. || 73 ||

With these three verses beginning with "annaiḥ" and ending with "nṛpāḥ," he teaches the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) that brings about the power of subjugation (*vaśyasiddhi*). In this context, "from daily offerings" means by means of the oblation performed every day;
likewise, "with those soaked in ghee" [is used]; "with sesame and rice" means with both sesame seeds and rice grains; "tu" indicates a distinction; and likewise...
At midnight; likewise, as before. || 76 ||

With the verse beginning with "ājyaiḥ" (by means of clarified butter), he teaches the fruit of the homa performed with clarified butter alone. In that context, *tu* signifies a distinction; *dinaiḥ uktaiḥ maṇḍalāt* means "from the mandala within the stated number of days"; and *ca* denotes conjunction. || 77 ||
Having bathed, anointed himself, and wearing a garland, white perfumes, flowers, and garments, he, with a joyful heart, should worship the Goddess in the consecrated sacrificial fire. (78)
One should cook one *prastha* measure of white rice grains grown from *śāli* paddy in twice as much milk from a white cow that has a calf. (79)
Having prepared a large amount of wax mixed with white milk and ghee,
one should take it in the hand and recite the mantra a hundred times.
Having recited "O Goddess, grant me prosperity," and having offered oblations into a fire kindled with wood,
he should complete the worship and likewise spend that day in eating.
One should offer oblations continuously and constantly according to that lineage;
the wondrous powers of the mantras never abandon Lakṣmī.
On Sundays, the practitioner should offer oblations of milk-rice (pāyasa) during the full moon;
he should also present it in worship, and within a year he shall become most wealthy.

With these five verses beginning with *snātaḥ* and ending with *śaktayaḥ*, [the author] teaches the fire-oblation (*homa*) that brings about the attainment of Lakṣmī, together with its preparatory rites, the appropriate time, and the duties of the performer. In this context, the word *ca* (and) functions as a conjunction (*samuccaye*). In the phrase *sitagandhasnānāmbaraḥ*, the word *sita* (white) applies to each member of the compound. [He should worship] the Goddess...

*Lalitām* [is offered] to *Sitā*, who is white in color. *Dviguṇe* means in a measure of two *prasthas*. *Tu* indicates a distinction. *Sita* is an adjective qualifying *taṇḍula* (rice). *Vā* denotes an alternative. It is accompanied by white milk, ghee, sugar, milk, and ghee. The word *siktha* (boiled rice) is connected to both [parts of the compound] according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*).

Having performed [the rite] as stated previously, and having "taken" [the materials] as stated subsequently; having offered oblations with the seven-syllable mantra, "O Goddess, grant me prosperity," using the *vidyā* of Lalitā; and having likewise consumed that *sikthaka* (wax/residue) along with food cooked in the white milk of a cow with its calf, accompanied by white milk and ghee—for that day...

"Every day" means continuously, on each and every day; "constantly" means for as long as one lives; "that lineage" refers to the family of the practitioner; "Ramā" is Lakṣmī; "wondrous" means possessing immeasurable majesty. || 82 ||
From the milk of a reddish-brown cow with her calf, one should extract fresh butter; on that very day, one should then cast it into a white water-lily flower. (84)
Having extracted that [mantra], one should offer oblations into the fire on a Tuesday when Mars is in its exaltation;
at that time, within those many days, one will certainly obtain wealth abundant with land. 85.
Likewise, having placed fresh butter into a white lotus of pure form and taking it up, one who observes silence should offer it into the fire on a Saturday.
By practicing this for seven cycles, one shall obtain great fortune—honored by kings, pleasing to all, auspicious, and endowed with various enjoyments. (87)
Likewise, having placed the butter produced at sunrise within the pericarp of a blossomed lotus on that day of the Sun, one should then [proceed] with it.
O Śivā, by offering oblations eight times, the practitioner shall become wealthy;
likewise, one should offer flowers of the karṇikāra and those born of the campaka.

With the verse beginning with "pāyasaiḥ" (verse 83), he teaches the oblation that brings about the attainment of Lakṣmī, to be performed on full moon days and Sundays. In this context, the phrase "one should offer" is to be understood as "one should offer milk-rice (pāyasa)," and the word "ca" (and) serves as a conjunction for inclusion.

With these seven and a half verses beginning with *savatsā* and ending with *gāminī*, he teaches the fire-oblation (*homa*) of *kahlāra* and other flowers together with fresh butter (*navanīta*), which brings about the attainment of prosperity. In that context, *taddina-annaṃ* means "food from that day"; *tu* indicates a distinction; [and] *kahlāraprasūne* refers to the *kahlāra* flower.

In the interior of a blooming white water-lily (*kahlāra*) in a long pond—from that long pond—one should take up the fresh butter and white water-lily flower placed therein; "silently," is the ellipsis. One should offer it (*hunet*), that is, perform the oblation (*juhuyāt*), into the consecrated fire; this is at the time when [the planet] is in its exaltation (*ucca*).
At the time of the rising of the fourth sign from the sign presided over by Maṅgala (Mars), for that many days [one should worship] from the mandala.
Likewise, from that same day, one should take the fresh butter (*navanīta*) of a white-colored cow with a white calf;
"from that day" is the meaning. On a Friday (*bhṛgordine*), as before, on a white lotus (*sitāmbuja*). There too—

"At that high time" means by the practice of seven days, specifically by the practice of seven Saturdays (Bhṛgu-vāra). Likewise, "produced from a ruddy [cow]" refers to butter produced from a ruddy cow with its calf on that very day;
the remainder of the sense is that it is taken from a large pond. The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction. That...

"Padmam" means silently, as before; "with eight times" refers to the sun (the remaining word); "O Śivā" is the vocative. Likewise, on Thursday, they should be smeared with fresh butter (*navanīta*). "In exaltation" (*ucce*) means situated in the tenth sign from the ascendant occupied by the sun.
When Jupiter has risen in the sign of Leo, one should offer oblations of clarified butter; thus, one becomes free from disease and highly esteemed by kings, thieves, and plunderers. (90)
One attains great fortune that follows one's lineage simply by performing oblations with fresh butter mixed with sugar. (91)
Through oblations of bandhūka, kiṃśuka, and mango flowers smeared with the three sweets (trimadhu), one shall obtain fame, fortune, wealth, health, victory, and long life.
It shall bring about good fortune, prosperity, victory, splendor, and wisdom;
by performing oblations of curd and rice, the practitioner will become abundant in food within three months.
Having written one's own desire on moist pieces of palm leaf, one should offer them into the fire at night together with fresh butter.
Within a month, a fortnight, or even a day from the mandala, one certainly attains one's own desire;
likewise, having inscribed [the mantra] upon Palāśa leaves with red lead (darada), one should perform oblations.
Or, having written [the mantra] on mango leaves with saffron, one should offer oblations at night;
likewise, having written it on jackfruit leaves with sandalwood paste, one should perform the fire sacrifice.
When [the sun] has entered the zodiac sign of Cancer, she who follows that lineage, she who belongs to the family of the practitioner; || 91 ||

With the two and a half verses beginning with "kevalam," he teaches the fruit of the oblation of fresh butter (navanīta) combined with white [sugar]. In that context, "kevalam" means devoid of flowers;
"sitopetena" means combined with sugar (śarkarā). The ellipsis to be supplied is "together with fame, fortune, wealth, health, and victory. || 92 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with "vandhūkaiḥ" and ending with "māsataḥ," he teaches the fruit of the oblation of *kiṃśuka* and mango flowers along with curd-rice. In this context, "cūtaiḥ" means with mango blossoms; "dadhyannahomāt" means from the oblation of rice mixed with curd. || 93 ||

With these seven verses beginning with "ārdreṣu" and ending with "udīritaiḥ," he teaches the procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*) of that written leaf— which brings about the accomplishment of one's own desired aims— as well as the majestic power of the sacrificial offering of that vidyā. Therein, "at night" means at midnight.
By offering oblations of powdered *pakṣaka* mixed with betel leaves, one obtains one's own desired object within the time specified. (97)
It is desired that [the name] be written with musk upon a leaf of the campaka tree;
by offering those [leaves] according to the prescribed rite on those days, one attains that [result]. 98.
Having written one's own desired object upon a lotus-born leaf with white [pigment] combined with cardamom, cloves, kakkola, and nutmeg, || 99 ||
One should perform oblations for its complete accomplishment; what is the use of speaking much here?
There is nothing in this world that cannot be achieved through the aforementioned oblations of the Vidyā. 100.
The pervasion consisting of pure knowledge has been correctly proclaimed;
by the refinement of this within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self.
Thus ends the thirty-second chapter, titled "The Arising of Desired Fruits from the Fire Offering," in the *Śrīkādimata* among the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantras*.

This means: from the mandala, for a month, or for a week, according to the gravity or lightness of the task; likewise, together with fresh butter; having inscribed one's own desire—this is the ellipsis; "or" (vā) is used as a conjunction; at night, specifically at midnight; by those [means], namely the betel leaves; from the aforementioned time.

From the previously described maṇḍala and so forth; of the *campaka* tree—that is, of the *campaka* plant—with those *campaka* leaves; for those days as before; according to that procedure—that is, according to the prescribed procedure for the fire-oblation (*homa*); with white things—that is, with sugar—he should offer into the fire his own desired object—that is, whatever he wishes—with those lotus petals.
The remainder refers to that which is intended by him [the author]. || 100 || Om || 0 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete tantra known as the venerable *Kādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The thirty-second chapter, dedicated to the exposition of the procedure for the peaceful fire-sacrifice (*saumyahoma*), is thus fully concluded and examined. Oṃ tat sat.

Regarding the number of verses: it is stated in the thirty-second chapter that the explanatory text consists of more than one hundred and seventy-one verses; however, there are indeed no yantras here.
The Thirty-third Chapter. Now, the yantras of the first among the sixteen Nityās, who is proclaimed as Lalitā, are described, arising from the various divisions of her vidyā.
Through nine hundred and sixty forms according to the prescribed rule,
these are the causes for the attainment of all desired objects by those who have purified their selves.
In the daily worship of Lalitā, there is a yantra which is the embodiment of the Universal Soul;
it is the wheel of time for the sixteen [deities] and for her worship.
The vessel called Amṛta, the Yantra, and thereafter the Siddhavajra;
the Koṣṭhavajra, the Vajraliṅga, and the Meru-setuliṅga according to the prescribed rule.

In the thirty-second preceding chapter, having taught the procedure for the gentle fire-oblation (*saumyahoma*) of those perfected in the mantras of the sixteen *Nityās*, [the author] next [teaches] those [mantras] arising from the various forms of the *Lalitā-vidyā* which bring about the attainment of one's desires.

He teaches certain yantras by means of the thirty-third chapter, which consists of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, of the sixteen Nityās" and ending with "in the scripture that declares the accomplishment of the yantra.
Therein, [he teaches] by means of five verses beginning with "Now, of the sixteen" and ending with "in due order."
Introducing the discourse on the meaning of the chapter, he indicates its contents:
therein, "the first" means that which is the cause of all, i.e., the *pradhāna*; "Lalitā" is the name [of this energy], as is understood from the context;
she was described in the third chapter. Of that Lalitā, [the following arises] through the various manifestations of her vidyās.
This refers to the nine hundred and sixty forms arising from the divisions of the third section of the Śrīvidyā;
that is to say, there are twenty-four four-syllable variations of the third section of the Śrīvidyā.

The varieties of that five-syllable vidyā are one hundred and twenty; the varieties of that six-syllable [vidyā] are seven hundred and twenty. Since there are six non-repeated syllables, each joined with the sixteen vowels, there are ninety-six varieties in total.

"By those [which have] nine hundred and sixty divisions"— the manner of dividing these will be explained in the thirty-fifth chapter. "According to rule, with neither less nor more measure" refers to the *yantra*, the Śrīcakra, for those who have prepared themselves through the worship of the lotus-feet of the Guru and whose minds are fit [for it].
The body is the form of the Universal Soul because it consists of the five elements, the three abodes, and Time.

The genitive case is used for the selection from among the sixteen eternal ones. Of that Lalitā. The word "ca" (and) denotes a collective aggregate. *Pūjā-kamala-cakrakaṃ* refers to the worship-circle in the form of a lotus.
The great liṅga, the womb-mechanism (yoniyantra), and likewise that vajra-vajraka; that very same [device] of great form, and the chamber-mechanisms (koṣṭhayantra) in succession. (5)
For the consecration, one should prepare a Śrīcakra measuring nine cubits or three cubits;
for the worship on the sacrificial mound (sthaṇḍila), it should be exceedingly beautiful, measuring just one cubit.
However, in the fashioning of images made of jewels and other materials, pride may arise from the influence of desire;
yet, when well-executed, worship is always auspicious, whereas it is otherwise in the case of an inferior one.
Having constructed a perfectly level square by means of a circle,
one should wipe it clean and lay down a cord situated at the center, extending crosswise.

By the verse beginning with "called Amṛta," the fivefold yantra is described. Therein, "the jar called Amṛta" refers to the jar known as the Amṛtaghaṭa. "After this" means following the instruction for the procedure of the Siddhavajra-yantra. "According to rule" means as previously [stated]. "The Great Liṅga" refers to that which is designated as the Mahāliṅga. The "Yoni-yantra."
The *yonisaṃjña* is a yantra; that which is *vajravajraka* means the *vajravajra-yantra*. And that very thing is the *mahākāra*, the *mahāvajra*, meaning the yantra designated as *mahāvajra*.
The *koṣṭha-yantras* are infinite yantras consisting of the *sama*, *viṣama*, *bhadra*, and so forth, in their respective order.
In the order previously indicated. || 5 ||

With sixteen verses beginning with "nine cubits" and ending with "bestowing success," he teaches the collection [of rites] for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*), daily worship (*nityapūjā*), and the construction of the Śrīcakra of Lalitā, including their measurements and so forth. Among these:

With the verse beginning with "nine cubits" (*navahasta*), he teaches the measurement of the *śrīcakra* for both the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) and the worship of the sacrificial ground (*sthaṇḍilapūjā*). Therein, the word "or" (*vā*) signifies an option or a combination. The meaning is: on a sacrificial ground measuring one cubit.
This [measurement] is common to all forms of worship of the wheel (*cakrasādhāraṇa*), including those of Śrīnātha and others not explicitly mentioned; it is exceedingly beautiful.
The meaning is that one should act without transgressing the measures and so forth that will be described hereafter.

With this verse beginning with "ratna" (jewels), he teaches that the construction of the Śrīcakra upon substrates such as jewels is entirely according to one's own will, as well as the fruit resulting from its proper construction and the transgression incurred by failing to do so. In this context, "tu" signifies a distinction; "suvihite" means properly constructed or well-fashioned Śrīcakra.
In another [place] that is devoid of the aforementioned characteristics and so forth, worship is likewise performed; otherwise, it is inauspicious. || 7 ||

With these seven verses beginning with "bhrameṇa" and ending with "uttamam," [the author describes] the forty-three yonis situated within the pericarp (karṇikā) of the Śrīcakra; there are nine threads (sūtras), two of which have both ends touching the circle.
Having established those two ends, [one should proceed] in sequence from the end of the middle line.
When four lines have been drawn, there shall be a hexagon consisting of twenty-one [squares].
Starting from the two eighth-points, the ninth [square] lies between the first and the last.
One should draw four lines according to the four vital points (marmans),
extending from the first and ninth [points] at the top horizontally to the seventh [point].
One should perform [the drawing] by piercing the eight vital points (marmans) within the four lines;
then, by starting from both ends of the sixty-fourth square, one likewise reaches the eighth.
Likewise, one should cast a group of four threads for the second square;
then, in accordance with the four vital points (marmans), [one should do so] between the fifth and the last [squares].

He teaches that each of the two middle wheels is likewise threefold, consisting of the nature of maintenance (*sthiti*) and withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), due to the fivefold process (*pañcīkaraṇa*). Among these, the square [wheel] is of the form described in the twenty-ninth chapter. Therein, within the circle, [one draws] a line running horizontally from south to north.

The phrase "nipātayet" (one should drop) connects with "sūtrāṇi" (the lines) in what follows. "Nava" means nine in number. Among those nine transverse lines, there are two—the third and the seventh counting from the west—whose both ends touch the circle, meaning their two tips touch the circumference. Of those two...
Regarding the two lines that touch the circumference: the ellipsis is "starting from the four tips" [of the corners].

From the end of the central line—that is, from the eastern tip and the western tip of the Brahma-line which extends east-west—one proceeds respectively according to the stated order of alternation across the four lines.
The meaning is "having come together. The word *tu* (but/then) is used for emphasis. There shall be a hexagon consisting of twenty-one [lines];

from the eastern and western tips of the Brahma-line, by means of the pairs of horizontal lines that are third and seventh [from the center], there shall be a hexagon extending to the southern and northern tips—this is the meaning of "having come together."

The word *tu* is used for emphasis. By means of the four vital points (*marman*) in accordance with the four [points] previously written within the hexagon— by piercing the four vital points through the two tips of the ninth and first [lines],
from the two tips of the western and other ninth transverse lines, and from the two tips of the first transverse line.
The meaning is "starting from. "Up to the fourth and seventh" means up to the middle of the two lines, the fourth and the seventh;
that is, starting from the two tips of the fourth line and starting from the two tips of the sixth line.
Likewise, "reaching the eighth and the second" refers to the second line ending at the middle of the eighth line.
And the middle and the end:
one should draw a pair of lines for the third [section] resting upon two vital points (*marman*).
One should erase the central Brahma-line; thus there shall be the supreme wheel. (14)
Having fashioned an outer eight-petaled lotus and likewise one with twice that number of petals,
[one should do so] with six circles and likewise with eight squares.
Having laid out that very [mandala] with cords, provided with gates to the east and west, and likewise from two positions by means of three lines drawn to the south and north; || 16 ||
O Supreme Goddess, one should divide those four squares into two parts each, in due order, by means of four diagonal threads drawn from the corners.

Likewise, by way of inverted order, starting from the ends of the fifth lines—the tips of the two horizontal fifth lines—one reaches that which goes to the third, situated in the middle of the third sūtra. || 14 ||
With these three verses beginning with *vahiḥ* and ending with *parameśvarī*, he teaches the construction of two squares and two lotuses characterized by emanation situated outside that [mandala].
Therein, *vahiḥ* means outside the circle located beyond the previously mentioned wheel. By the expression "an eight-petalled lotus,"...
Since the previously mentioned wheel cannot be drawn within the interior of its pericarp (*karṇikā*), one should first produce a circle outside of that for the sake of the filaments (*kesara*);

beyond that, up to the eight petals. Likewise, there is a sixteen-petaled lotus with double the number of petals [as the previous]. This is on the exterior of the circle situated outside the eight-petaled lotus.
Having produced one circle for the filaments of a sixteen-petaled lotus,

[one should produce] sixteen petals with six circles; for the purpose of constructing the two aforementioned central wheels within the interior of the pericarp, one [circle], and outside that, one for the pericarp itself, attached to it.

Outside of that, one [square] for the sake of the filaments of the eight-petalled lotus; outside of that lotus, one [square] for the sake of equality with its perimeter; outside of that, one [square] for the sake of the filaments of the sixteen-petalled lotus; and one for the sake of the surrounding circle—altogether, these amount to [four].

The meaning is "by six lines. By "eight lines" (aṣṭasūtraiḥ), it is meant together with the previously mentioned four lines of the square; this connects with the subsequent phrase "by its lines" (asya sūtraiḥ).
Of that square, [it is] provided with doors facing east and west.
The meaning is that it is joined with two doors at two locations, having a square width on the eastern and western sides.
"From south to north" means by means of three lines of the square, that is, by means of three horizontal lines in the middle of that [square] running east-west. Having prepared it in such a manner.

By means of four diagonal threads in the corners, one should divide those [spaces] into four squares in successive order; by this [passage], it is meant that within each of the four corner squares of the square [grid], one should divide each individual square into two by stretching a thread. [The term] "Parameśvarī" [is used].
Perfect enlightenment. || 17 ||
This circle of the worship of Lalitā is to be obtained from a true guru in due succession;
it is beautiful, perfectly level, and endowed with all auspicious characteristics. (18)

With these four verses beginning with "Lalitā" and ending with "siddhidam," he teaches that the Lalitā-cakra is obtainable through the grace of a true guru, as well as its characteristics and so forth. In this regard, it is said:
"This [cakra] which has been described is obtainable from a true guru through the lineage."

[The disciple should seek] a Guru who is devoted to the conduct of the *samaya* according to the lineage of the tradition (*kramāgama*) that has been perfectly established through an uninterrupted succession;

who has received the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*); and who knows reality (*tattvavit*). [This is described] by the six verses beginning with the fifty-second, starting from the words "possessing the characteristics mentioned in the second chapter" and ending with "with wealth and so forth."

By means of verses according to the stated sequence; that is to say, by a practitioner who has acquired the vidyā. "Well-levelled" means having equal dimensions, neither deficient nor excessive. "With all characteristics" refers to those which will be described immediately hereafter.
"Downward-facing triangles," nine in total, situated along a single thread.

With its tips resting upon the Brahma-thread, this Śrīcakra is exceedingly beautiful. For this very reason, it is a hexagon touching a circle; that is, the six corners of the first-drawn hexagon [are located] at the tips of the fourteen outer spokes according to the method described. It does not touch the eight [inner triangles].

It is untouched by the other eight [lines] due to its circularity; likewise, in the manner described, it is [formed] at the junctions of the six lines—meaning the locations of the junctions of the lines—by means of the *marmas* (vital points) endowed with the characteristics that will be explained immediately hereafter;
"from the union of two" refers to the union of two lines; it is joined with twenty-four.

Endowed with twenty-four joints; this is the sequence for constructing a wheel measuring three cubits in size according to the method of installing the *kumbha* (vase) here. On a perfectly level and pure ground, having fashioned a *haṃsapada* (swan’s footprint) in the center, one should proceed from that corresponding point toward each side.

Having produced a circle by means of a radius measuring thirty-six, three, and ten finger-breadths respectively, one should produce a circle outside that, touching it, and then another outside that; thus, by the sequence of measurements of three and ten finger-breadths, together with the first circle produced, there are six circles within which [the lotus is formed], from the interior to the exterior.

Having established there the Brahma-sūtra running east-west and the central cross-sūtra running north-south, and having drawn lines from each of the four cardinal directions outside the outermost circle at a measurement of ten finger-breadths each, [one should mark] the four tips of those sūtras.
Wherever there is an intersection on the outermost circumference of all those [circles], the measurement is determined by the touching and non-touching of those respective points;
and by means of eight threads, each measuring one hundred and forty-four finger-breadths (aṅgulas), which touch and do not touch the four tips of those threads.

Having made it a perfect square with two doors, including the corner compartments, by distinguishing between the interior and exterior, one should [mark] on each of the two rows— the western and eastern— of the square,
five finger-breadths (aṅgula) to the south and north from the central line, for each [door].

Having drawn a horizontal line and having fashioned two square doors between them with a measurement of ten finger-breadths, one should strike a single horizontal thread each to the south and north of those two doors at a measurement of ten finger-breadths each.
Having drawn one transverse line each, measuring ten finger-breadths to the east and west from the central thread between the eastern and western paths of that square,
[one should draw] one diagonal corner-thread each within the four corner-cells of that square.

Having combined those four and arranged them both externally and internally, [one should place them] with five facing downwards and four facing upwards within the outer path of the circle measuring ten finger-breadths in diameter, in the cardinal and intermediate directions, as well as in the spaces between them. (p. 643)
However, with nine [syllables] situated within a single sūtra, this would be exceedingly beautiful. (19)
A wheel with well-defined characteristics consists of a circle, a hexagon touching it, and likewise an octagon not touching it, joined by eighteen vital points (marmans).

Having combined these and produced sixteen petals of equal measurement, including the intervals between them— making sixteen with their interstices— and having fashioned eight petals in the cardinal and intermediate directions within a circular path of ten finger-breadths (aṅgulas) as before, one should then draw a north-south line in the center of the circle situated in the very middle of all.
Having cleared away that entire area measuring seventy-two finger-breadths,

one should divide it into forty-eight parts according to the sequence to be described starting from the twenty-fourth verse of this chapter; then, along the Brahma-thread, one should draw three horizontal lines at intervals of fifty-six units starting from the east.

Having done so, one should again draw three horizontal lines at intervals of six-six-sixths of the measure starting from the west; then, between the third line and the seventh line starting from the east,
the positions for the three horizontal lines corresponding to the vital points (*marman*) to be described later must be established.
Having mentally visualized these together with the nine horizontal lines, one should first visualize the line situated at the very end; then, by transferring that [measurement],
one should draw two pairs of lines— the third and the seventh— among them so that they touch the circle.

Having drawn four lines— two lines from the two tips of the third [east-west] line to the points where they intersect the circle on the eastern side of the Brahma-line, and two lines from the two tips of the seventh [east-west] line to the points where they intersect the circle on the western side of the Brahma-line— and having thus formed a hexagon;
Furthermore, by means of the movement conforming to the western vital point (*marman*) of the hexagon previously drawn from the center of that ninth line,
one should extend two threads as far as they reach both sides of the second line;
this is done by means of the movement conforming to the two eastern vital points of the hexagon from the center of the first line.
Having struck two threads together from the tips of the eighth lines until their ends, thus forming four threads in accordance with the four vital points (*marmma*),
one should again [strike] upon the two lines extended from the eastward direction of the Brahma-thread.

From the intersection on both sides of the sixth line, extending two lines toward the center of the ninth line, and likewise from the intersections on both sides of the seventh line, following the directions toward the ninth line and so forth up to the Brahma-line, these together—

One should strike two threads in accordance with the four vital points (*marmman*). Wherever the intersection of those two threads occurs upon the Brahma-thread, that is the location of the fourth transverse thread starting from the west. Furthermore, from the middle of that seventh thread toward the west...

In accordance with the two vital points (*marman*) situated on both sides, one should draw two lines following the first transverse line on both its sides; then, in accordance with four vital points, having drawn these two lines, one should again begin from the center of the eighth transverse line.
From the center of the first line, one should lay down two lines extending toward the ends of the two horizontal fourth lines that stretch as far as the two centers of the extended lines;
then, from the west of the center of the eighth line, [one lays down] two lines that have been extended.

From the center of the fourth line and so forth, following the two points of intersection of the two previously extended lines, there arise the junctions of the six lines known as the *marman*s; from the union of these two pairs of junctions, this wheel, endowed with twenty-four [spokes], bestows the accomplishment of all aims. (21)
Otherwise, one should worship the wheel as being joined with severed vital points (marmans) and so forth;
[for otherwise] there would be death by weapons, great disease, poverty, infamy, and death.
Therefore, having indeed fashioned the wheel according to the described form endowed with its characteristics, one who worships it there constantly shall become equal to me.
Having established the middle of the two rows with forty-eight [units],
one should draw horizontal lines from east to west at intervals of six, six, and five [units] respectively.
From the middle of the ninth line, extending westward from the center of both lines that extend westward, one should stretch a horizontal thread as far as the limit of the center of both lines.
That is the sixth thread; it extends from its two tips to the end of the middle of the second line.
One should strike two threads in accordance with the two vital points (*marman*). From the center,

following the intersection of the two threads extending from the middle of the seventh thread, one should [draw] from the center of the eighth thread toward the west, in accordance with the two points of intersection where the tips and sides of those two threads meet.
One should draw a horizontal line extending from the limit of the two extended threads; that is the fifth line.
Then, having stretched two threads starting from its two ends up to the middle of the third line, and by erasing the Brahma-thread, there arises a six-cornered figure touching the circle.

Thus, the Śrīcakra comes to be that which is untouched by the eight corners (aṣṭāsra), endowed with the eighteen vital points (marmans), and purified by the twenty-four joints (sandhis). Herein, the human mental disposition (mānavāsanā) is to be seen in my *Vāsanāvimarśinī*. 21.

With the verse beginning with "anyathā" (otherwise), he teaches the specific misfortunes that befall those who construct the wheel as it has been seen [in other traditions] and worship therein, rather than in the manner previously described. In that context, "anyathā" means by way of deviation from the stated characteristics; here, the word "ādi" (and so forth) in the term "marmādi" (vital points and so forth) refers to the joints.
