The meaning is that he bestows upon the worshipper the fivefold fruit beginning with "death by the sword" and so forth. || 22 ||

With the verse beginning with "tasmāt" (therefore), he teaches the fruit for those who worship in the manner described within the *śrīcakra*. In this context, "therein" refers to the *śrīcakra*. The word "eva" (indeed) is used for emphasis. By constantly—meaning every single day—worshipping and adoring her, Lalitā, one shall become equal to me, that is, equal to Śiva. || 23 ||

With the two verses beginning with *vidhāya* and ending with *sundaram*, [the author] teaches the measurement-convention for the fourteen-spoked wheel and the others situated within the central circle of the Śrīcakra during the construction of Lalitā’s [mandala]. Therein, the "middle of the two circles" refers to the eastern side of the central circle of all.

The phrase "between the two western lines" means the Brahma-sūtra. "Forty with eight" means forty-eight. This word is to be construed with the word "having laid out. The ellipsis is "three horizontal lines starting from the east. [This applies] in each of the six and five [sections].
The word "in each and every part" (aṃśeṣvaṃśeṣu) is understood as the remainder.

From the west, likewise in the three groups of six, one should apply three threads in the middle of that [space] according to the principle of the vital points (marmma); by this, one should make it exceedingly beautiful. (25)

"From the west" means starting from the point of intersection between the tip of the western Brahma-line and the central circle. "In the three sets of six" refers to the three locations at the measurement of six-sixths.
The word "api" (also) is used for conjunction. Thus, there are three lines; in their midst is the third line, beginning from the east.

And in the middle of the third sūtra from the west, by means of the logic of the vital points— that is, by virtue of the logic for piercing the vital points— at the point of intersection of that respective sūtra and the Brahma-sūtra, according to that procedure. Thus,
because the instruction on measurement is given specifically for the wheel situated at the very center, its measurement is equal to that of the central wheel.

The external area as well, having been divided into twenty-four parts on each side, the intermediate measurements for the filaments, petals, enclosures, squares, and so forth, within eight of those parts, should be made according to the tradition— suitable for the placement of the water-pots (kalaśas) and as aesthetically pleasing as possible.

In all consecrations, such as the attainment of knowledge (*vidyāprāpti*), when following the procedure of placing a single water-pot (*ekakumbha*), a mandala (*cakra*) measuring three cubits must be constructed. In the case of the consecration for the attainment of knowledge (*vidyāprāptyabhiṣeka*), when following the procedure of placing either nine or four pots, [the same applies] for the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*).
In the case of the arrangement of ninety-six jars, the wheel (cakra) should be conceived as measuring nine cubits.

In the case of the arrangement of a single jar, all the positions for the deities—excluding the nine lords and their consorts—are contained within the center of the entire circle; these include the two filaments (keśara), the perimeter (pariveṣa), and the petals (dala).
One should color the secondary petals and the square area excluding the two doors with the prescribed powder.
In the case of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) involving the placement of ninety-six jars,
one should [draw] a single line on each side of every triangle facing oneself in the very center, with equal intervals between them.

Having marked [the ground] with three threads—one in the middle and three around it—one should thereby form four triangles. One should proceed in this same manner even in the case of the installation of four jars for the consecration (*abhiṣeka*) upon attaining the *vidyā*. Furthermore, in the case of the full consecration (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*), however—

Having formed two triangles facing each other with a single horizontal line between them, and having constructed triangles at the four locations where the four weapons are to be placed, one should likewise construct triangles extending from the square to the eight petals and color those as well.
In the case of the installation of the Mahāśaṅkha jar, having constructed the Great Wheel (mahācakra) according to the stated sequence,
one should— as before— construct triangles at all four locations of the weapons in the center,
at the door-areas, on the eight petals, and at the positions of the eight deities situated within the square, with their points directed outward.

Having constructed triangles and combined them to form ninety-six triangles, one should place three marks at equal intervals along each side. Then, by drawing nine lines from mark to mark, one should create sixteen triangles—extending from the exterior to the interior within each corner—and should also color them. Therein:
The method of drawing for the center of all [the diagrams] has been explained by us in the second chapter.

Here, whether in the placement of nine jars within the nine *yoni*s, or in the placement of four jars within the four triangles situated in the central *yoni*, in every case, it is the jar to be placed in the very center of all that [is primary].
It is to be filled with water measured by a *khārī*; the tradition holds that the other jars are to be filled with water measuring two *prasthas* each. || 25 ||
A triangle and a circle, and fifteen petals outside of that;
then an eight-petaled lotus on the exterior, and a ten-petaled lotus.
Then again, a ten-petalled lotus, then a fourteen-petalled one,
an eight-petalled lotus, one with double that number of petals [sixteen], and an eighteen-petalled one.
Having prepared that [mandala] and having invoked her into its center, one should worship her in that manner;
thereafter, one should likewise worship the Lords on the two sides and the other weapons.
With these four verses beginning with *tryasram* and ending with *āpnuyāt*,

he teaches the worship-circle (*pūjācakra*) of Lalitā, which is complete with the enclosure of all powers (*sakalaśakti*) in the form of a lotus, as well as the fruit of worship therein. In this context, "triangular" (*tryasram*) means facing toward oneself.
"Outside the circle and triangle," meaning by touching and not touching the three corners [of the triangle].
By the phrase "and fifty petals outside of that," this is what is stated:
outside the circle, a circle for the filaments; and outside the triangle, having formed its corners, there [is the space] on the exterior.

The meaning is that one should draw fifteen petals. By the expression "an eight-petaled lotus," the meaning is that having drawn a circle for the filaments, one should then draw eight petals outside of it. Outside—that is, outside the eight-petaled lotus—one should further draw a fourteen-petaled lotus.

A sixteen-petaled lotus with twice that number of petals (thirty-two) should be distinguished as before; in all the wheels (*cakra*), one should determine the intermediate measurement of the petals according to the measure of the eight-sided figure described in the section on the sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*). There, in the eastern portion, is the Brahma-thread (*brahmasūtra*).

One should fashion the interior in such a manner. The word "vidhyāya" (having pierced) is construed with the accusative case endings in "tryasram" and so forth. Of that lotus-wheel (*padmacakra*): in the center, meaning in the middle of the central triangle; her, Lalitā; thus, as the eternal one.

Subsequently, according to the sequence stated by Ṛtikā and others, [one should proceed] likewise. "Between the two sides" means between the two side-lines of the inner triangle, that is, in the middle of the two side-lines of the inner triangle. "The others" refers to the Tithinityās and Aṇimā and the rest. "Likewise" means by the appropriate method. This is what is meant: on a perfectly level ground...

Having made the *haṃsapada* mark, starting from the location of the pincers (*sandaṃśa*), one should produce a circle by rotating in each direction with a measurement of eighteen finger-breadths; then, in the center of that circle, one should produce a straight-lined *yoni* facing oneself.
Outside of that, having produced seventeen circles— including the previously produced circle— by means of a sequence of measurements of two and five finger-breadths respectively,
one should [proceed] from the inside toward the outside through the eight five-finger-breadth paths, skipping each single interval.
In a fifteen-petalled lotus, one should arrange the Tithinityās starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise;

having designated the two petals at the east and west as the location for the door situated on the outer eighteenth petal, one should thus proceed in order through the cardinal and intermediate directions.

As before, [worship] Aṇimā and the others with four repetitions; within that, on the sixteen petals, worship the Nityakalās as before; within that, on the eight petals, worship Anaṅgakusumā and the others as before;
and within that, on the fourteen petals, worship Saṃkṣobhiṇī and the others as before.
By worshipping them in the center of this lotus-wheel, one attains great prosperity and, through knowledge, shall attain me. || 29 ||
In the east, one should worship the Goddess according to the stated sequence;
O Supreme Goddess, through such knowledge of Śrī, one likewise attains the supreme state.
Having drawn two pots, distinguished by outer and inner,
one should divide the space between them into nine parts and write the first [syllable] in the corners.
Having drawn the second [set of lines] in the directions, one should draw the third in the center;
having made transverse lines everywhere between the two pots.

In the ten inner petals, as before, [worship] Sarvasiddhipradā and the others; in the ten inner petals, as before, [worship] Sarvajñā and the others; in the eight inner petals, as before, [worship] the Goddesses of Speech (*vāgdevatāḥ*) within the space between the central circle and the side-lines of the triangle in its center.

As before, one should worship the Mistress of the Pīṭha (pīṭheśvarī) in the triangle within that [space], and the Goddess herself in the very center, both according to the previous method; thus one should worship them in sequence according to the stated order. By worshipping these in this world (*aihika*), one attains the glory of this state—this is the syntactical connection with the following phrase. Of those...

Of the queen together with her retinue; "great" means not to be disregarded by kings and others; "from knowledge," that is, from the ultimate reality (paramārtha)—this is the ellipsis; "me," Śiva. || 29 ||

With the verse beginning with "pūrvasmin" (in the former), he teaches the fruit of worship in the previously mentioned Śrīcakra. Therein, "pūrvasmin" means in the previously described Śrīcakra; "endowed with the stated sequence" means endowed with the sequence of worship taught in the three chapters of fourteen [verses].

"Prosperity" means in this world; "from knowledge" refers to that which will be taught in the thirty-sixth chapter; "likewise" means in a non-distinct form; "us two" refers to Śakti and Śiva; "and" (ca) is used as a conjunction; "he" is the practitioner;
"O Supreme Goddess" is the vocative address to the Goddess. || 30 ||

With these nine verses beginning with *ghaṭadvayam* and ending with *apamṛtyujit*, he teaches the diagram known as the Amṛtaghaṭa (the Nectar-Pot), its applications, and its results. In that context, "two pots" refers to two circles, one outer and one inner; having divided the space between them into nine parts, [he proceeds].

The ellipsis [to be supplied] is "by means of two pairs of lines running east-west, north-south, and south-north. "In the corners" means in the squares at each corner. First, the first section of the Śrīvidyā;
the second section is in the squares in the cardinal directions as before; and the third section is in the central square as before.
A fragment. Regarding the two jars with their outer and inner circles: the meaning is that there are seven horizontal lines.
"On all sides" means throughout those squares; one should place the seven syllables of the Vidyā-tṛtīya [mantra] within them, moving clockwise through those squares.
One should draw the lotus of the five nectars on the face with a bindu and a visarga.
Having fashioned [the base] consisting of the primordial *nāla*, with its pair of petals, filaments,
and pericarp, one should perform the ritual application (*viniyoga*) beneath the pot.
Having placed that jar of nectar in the center, adorned with the syllable of the person to be accomplished,
one should carry it and perform the consecration during the birth-constellations for the attainment of longevity.
For the pacification of all defects arising from the eclipses of Kuhu and Parāga,
one should perform the consecration for the sake of alleviating every affliction, for spiritual success, and for the attainment of prosperity.
The remainder is that there are seven individual syllables of the third section of the Śrī-vidyā, together with the *bindu*, the *visarga*, the *anusvāra*, and the *visarjanīya*.
The "lotus of the five nectars" (*pañcāmṛtāmbuja*) is [described] in the eighth chapter by the verse beginning with "jyāka" and so forth.
The lotus described by the second half of the thirty-seventh verse is accompanied by the five nectar-syllables;
its stalk consists of the first [syllable] and is joined with the stalk of the first nectar-syllable.
It possesses petals, filaments, and a pericarp in pairs; here, the word "pair" (dvandva) refers to the collective totality of the petals.

The same [application] should be joined for the other two in their individual forms. This means that the pericarp is accompanied by the second and third nectar-syllables, the filaments are accompanied by the fourth nectar-syllable, and the central circle (karṇikā) is accompanied by the fifth nectar-syllable. The word "ca" (and) indicates a collective aggregate.

Therefore, it is drawn as "the lotus" (*ambuja*). "Below the jar" means in the place situated beneath the jar. "In the middle" means within the interior of the third segment located in the central square; having placed therein the syllable of the *sādhya*, accompanied by the practitioner's name, the *sādhya*, and the ritual action, that [segment] is called the "jar of nectar" (*amṛtaghaṭa*).

The meaning is: "having constructed that machine. The sequence of its construction here is as follows: having drawn a circle on a perfectly level surface with a radius of the desired measure, and having drawn another circle outside it at a distance of one finger-breadth, [one should draw] within the middle of that [inner circle] parallel lines toward the east-west and south-north directions.

Having produced nine compartments by stretching two threads each, one should place the first part of the Śrīvidyā in the four corner compartments, the second part in the four compartments in the cardinal directions, and the third part— accompanied by the practitioner, the object of practice, and the ritual action— in the central compartment of all.

It should be drawn. Then, in the middle of the square located in the east, having divided the space between the two circles— measuring four finger-breadths and situated at equal intervals— as before, into seven parts,
one should place the seven syllables of the third section of the Śrīvidyā, in the form of a triangle, starting from the east within those seven squares.

Having drawn [the diagram] by way of circumambulation from left to right, one should fashion the mouth of a jar facing east within the central square of the eastern section, measuring four finger-breadths; then, having drawn a downward-facing lotus at the mouth of that jar and an upward-facing lotus in the position below the jar, [one should place the two] upon those two lotuses.
In sequence, the two syllables *jaṃ jaḥ* are on the stalk; on their two petals are *ūṃ jaḥ* and *ūṃ ṭhaḥ*. (p.
649) For the pacification of untimely death, great diseases, consumption, and epilepsy, one should likewise perform the consecration for three years during the three [relevant] births.
Completely liberated from all afflictions, that person becomes happy on earth for a hundred years; healthy, victorious, and worthy of universal veneration. (38)
Having fashioned this [image] as a *sikthaliṅga* in gold, silver, or copper, and having placed it in honey, one should install it and worship it; thus one conquers all untimely death. (39)
Having written the name encased within the third Vidyā,
the practitioner should wear it on a ring or similar object for the sake of all prosperity and the pacification of misfortune.

One should write these four syllables at the location of their filaments; two syllables, *vaṃ* and *vaḥ*, at their pericarp; and two syllables, *saṃ* and *saḥ*, [at the center]. This constitutes the Yantra consisting of the Amṛtaghaṭa (the Nectar-Pitcher).
[This should be done] during the three birth-asterisms—this is the ellipsis—to bring about all-encompassing peace.

In this context, by the word "entire" (*akhila*), [the states] such as "under the influence of a cruel planetary period" (*krūradaśāgocara*) and so forth are expressed. The particle *ca* denotes a collective compound (*samāhāra*).

By the term "great disease" (*mahāroga*), the eight diseases beginning with wind (*vāta*) are meant. The accusative case in "three years" (*trivarṣam*) expresses duration (*atyantasaṃyoga*). The particle *tu* indicates a distinction. Likewise, [he becomes] victorious according to the method of consecration (*abhiṣeka*) described in the second chapter.

The phrase "in debates, gambling, battles, and so forth" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. Regarding "gold, silver, and copper," the meaning is on a plate made from any one of those three metals. "A *siktha* linga" means a linga contained within beeswax.
"In the honey" means inside a jar of honey. This is what is being stated:

Having fashioned that pair of nectar-pots as a mechanical device upon a base made of any one of gold, silver, or copper, and having formed them into pills, performed the consecration of the vital breath (*prāṇapratiṣṭhā*) and other rites,
and placed them inside a wax linga, he should install that linga in the center of the ritual jar (*kalaśa*).

Having filled that pitcher with honey, having covered the mouth of that pitcher with a shallow bowl, having placed it somewhere and constructed a clay pedestal over it, one should worship the Goddess along with her retinue there according to the prescribed rite until the desired fruit is attained; then again—
When the accomplishment of the stated fruit has occurred, one should dismiss [the deity] with "Forgive me" and then discard that honey and other substances;
by means of this verse beginning with "tārttīya," he teaches the procedure for all protective rites regarding the *ūrmikā* (ring) and other items.
In that context, "encased within the third Vidyā" refers to the Śrīvidyā—this is the remainder [of the sense]. "Name" [is to be supplied].
Regarding the rites of the practitioner and the goal to be accomplished: the word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction. In the phrase "on a ring, etc.," the word "etc.
refers to armlets and other such ornaments. This is what is meant:
on a golden plate, one should write the third section of the Śrīvidyā in both forward and reverse order, with each *repha* [the letter 'ra'] joined to the other by means of its own *repha*.

Having drawn the illusory portion (māyāṃśa) in such a way that it is enclosed by another illusory portion, and having placed the practitioner within that illusory portion, one should likewise place the yantra in the center of a stone, a pond, or similar location. (p. 650)
One should establish it there so that those men who bathe therein may be happy forever.
By striking with eight lines—east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east—one obtains forty-nine squares; among these, one should erase [the central grid] at the corners.
One should draw twenty-four squares in the remaining spaces in sequence; then, starting from the east and proceeding with entry, one should draw single and triple triangles.

One should draw the twenty-four [syllables] arising from the divisions of the third [wheel] in reverse order; then, one should write that [mantra] together with the object of accomplishment (sādhya) in the center.
The Yantra called Siddhavajra bestows all auspiciousness, destroys all that is undesirable, and grants victory and good fortune. || 45 ||

Having written the object of accomplishment (*sādhya*) within the portion of the letter *ra* of that [mantra], and having inscribed the ritual action (*karma*) as before in the space between those two, one should enclose it within the ornament of a ring, establish the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) therein, and worship it; by wearing it, one becomes a partaker of the attainment of the aforementioned fruits. || 40 ||

With the verse beginning with *kṛtvā*, he teaches the installation of the machine called the Amṛtaghaṭa in ponds and other such places, as well as its fruit. In that context, *tathā* means "in the manner previously described.
Regarding the phrase "in ponds and so forth" (*taḍāgādiṣu*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to rivers, wells, and the like. *Madhyataḥ* means "in the middle."
In those ponds and other water bodies where [the deity] is established. || 41 ||

With these nine verses beginning with "East and West" (*prākpratyak*) and ending with "the conscious one" (*cetanaḥ*), he teaches the construction of the perfected vajra-mechanism (*vajrayantra*), its applications, and its results, along with its praise. In that context, regarding those squares, the word "in the four corners" (*koṇeṣu caturṣu*) is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
The phrase "one should wipe" (*mārjayet*) connects with "twenty-four squares" (*caturviṃśatikoṣṭhāni*) in what follows.

The meaning is that there are six squares for each corner, totaling twenty-four squares. The locative case in "in the remaining squares" (*śeṣeṣu koṣṭheṣu*) is used in the sense of specification (*nirdhāraṇe*). This connects with the verb "one should write" (*vilikhet*).
The connection is with the word "triangles" (trikoṇāni). The ellipsis is "from one side, from the square. "Together" means by four.
"Prior to the commencement" means prior to the commencement of the triangle. "From the entry" means by way of the entry.
Of the third [part], that is, of the twenty-four divisions arising from the third section of the Śrīvidyā.

In the manner to be described in the thirty-fifth chapter, there are twenty-four mantras arising from the divisions of the four-syllable essence. In reverse order—that is, counter-clockwise—one should place them in the central square; that is the third section of the Śrīvidyā.
Accompanied by the ritual action to be accomplished and the practitioner’s own goal; it is named Siddhavajra, meaning "the Vajra of Accomplishment. This is the sequence of its construction here:
by stretching eight threads with equal intervals running east-west and north-south, there are forty-nine [squares].
One should wear it for the sake of attaining victory in battle; in disputes, one should maintain it during every affliction, and thus attain victory and happiness. (46)
And on the full moon day of every month, one should indeed perform an ablution there;
having placed the jar as before, for the sake of all prosperity.

For the sake of obtaining a son, for obtaining a daughter, and likewise for obtaining a bridegroom; for the sake of obtaining land, wealth, and cattle; and for men, women, kings, and others—[one should worship] the maiden [Kumārī]. (48)

One should wear the Siddhavajra for the sake of subjugation, for the unimpeded accomplishment of goals, for the perfection of speech, for the perfection of the household, and for success in all things.
He who considers another mantra to be equal to the Lalitā-vidyā,
or this Yantra to be equal to another Yantra, is a person of deluded intellect.
One should cast eighteen lines— east-west, north-south, south-north, and west-east—
thereby forming two hundred and eighty-nine squares therein.
Having produced the squares, one should erase twenty-four squares— six in each corner, totaling six in each of the four corners— so as to form a vajra shape in the remaining center;
then, in the remaining twenty-five squares, [one should proceed] by adding one square in each direction.

Having fashioned four triangles in the four directions using the four [syllables], one should [place] the twenty-four divisions consisting of the first elements of the third section of the Śrīvidyā mantra within them, proceeding in a clockwise direction starting from the eastward-pointing [triangle].

Having drawn [the grid] in sequence and having written the third section in the central remaining square, one should write the practitioner (*sādhaka*) in its *māyā* (vowel) portion, the object of practice (*sādhya*) in its *repha* (consonant) portion, and the ritual action (*karma*) at the junction between the two;
this is the yantra named Siddhavajra. [It is for the purpose of warding off] undesirable and inauspicious things.
That is the *yantra* called Siddhavajra. Regarding the phrase "in [the case of] arising from dispute," the word "affliction" (*kleśa*) is its qualifier.
One should consecrate that *yantra* there according to the previous method, following the sequence taught in the second chapter.
The phrase "of men, women, kings, and so forth" is connected with the word "for the sake of subjugation" (*vaśyāya*). [The phrase] "of kings and so forth" refers to...

This is a statement regarding independence. The word "tu" (but) is used for conjunction. By means of this aforementioned perfected vajra-instrument (*vajrayantra*), together with its majesty, such a knower—even one of dull intellect—[attains this];
how much more so, then, [one whose] heart is permeated by knowledge otherwise than that? The meaning is: because he perceives others as superior. || 50 ||

With these six verses beginning with "prākpratyak" and ending with "priye," he teaches the method for constructing the *koṣṭhavajrayantra*, together with an introduction to the description of the results of the yantras mentioned in this chapter.
O Dear One, in those corners, one should erase the squares as before;
in the remaining thirty-six [squares] of the vajra, there are four [squares] forming a triangle in each direction.
Having first established [the lines] from the outside to the middle in a clockwise direction,
one should then draw [the pattern] by dividing that second half.
In the three triangles, one should likewise write the third [syllable] together with the object of accomplishment (sādhya) in the center;
then, one should write the three clusters (kūṭa) of the Vidyā nine times in each of the three [triangles].

There, by those lines; there, in the diagram (*yantra*); it is produced in such a way. Two hundred and eighty-nine—that is, two hundred increased by eighty-nine. The locative case [in "those"] is used for specification (*nirddhāraṇa*) regarding the squares (*koṣṭha*). The word "squares" (*koṣṭhāni*) is connected with the word "twenty-six. As before, it is in the form of a vajra.

"It is so" means that it becomes thus. "Thirty-six per corner" means that, taken together, they number one hundred and forty-four. "In the remaining vajra" means in the vajra consisting of one hundred and forty-five remaining squares. "Tu" (the particle) indicates a distinction.

"By four squares" means in each direction. "A triangle in every direction" means one triangle in each direction. The phrase "having made" connects with "a triangle in every direction" in the preceding context.
"From the middle square on the outside toward the east" means from the square situated in the middle of the row that lies on the exterior in the eastern direction.

"An eastern triangle" means starting from the middle square among the five squares situated in the row of those respective elements; "by way of clockwise entry" means by a movement of clockwise entry; "due to the division in its second half."

From the specific division arising from the five-syllable mantra taught in the thirty-fifth chapter of the third section of the *Śrīvidyā*, there are one hundred and twenty [mantras]. The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction; "tataḥ" means immediately after that; and "ca" denotes a collection.
The word "tārtīyakhaṇḍam" (the third section) is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "With the sādhya" means joined with the rite to be accomplished by the practitioner.
"From the center" refers to that vajra-diagram. "In that manner" means according to the sequence to be described in the following verse.
"In the nine remaining squares. "Thirty" means by repeating three times. "In the three right [squares]."
In the three compartments of the right side; in the middle, in the three middle compartments; "likewise" (tathā) means in combination.

In the three on the left is the second peak-syllable (kūṭa); in the three in the middle is the third peak-syllable, which, as before, should be written together with the object to be accomplished (sādhya) and so forth—this is the meaning. "Tu" (but/therefore) indicates a distinction.
This is the procedure for constructing the diagram here:

by stretching eighteen lines each in the east-west and north-south directions with equal intervals, one produces two hundred and eighty-nine squares; within these, there are thirty-six [squares] at each corner.

Having combined the sequence of thirty-six squares so that one hundred and forty-four squares remain in the center, one should erase them in such a way as to form the shape of a vajra; then, within the remaining vajra-shape, [proceed further].
In a grid consisting of one hundred and forty-five squares, proceeding outward in each direction by a sequence of three,
four squares are combined at a time to form each individual [unit].
On the three right sides, the first *kūṭa* is placed, and likewise the third *kūṭa* is placed in the center.
One should write the second [syllable] in the three left [positions], and the third in the [position] of the sādhya.
This machine, known as Koṣṭhavajra, bestows desired objects;
O beloved, hear now the fruits of all the machines in this chapter.
In this regard, whatever fruit is proclaimed for whichever yantra in other tantras, one should apply each of those [fruits] to these [yantras], or indeed all of them together.
Therefore, in this context, I have described only the construction and measurement of the yantras;
one obtains the fruits through desire without effort, by means of the application of the names.
Therefore, the fruits of the tantras have not been stated here in their entirety;
yet [this work] always effects the attainment of every desired fruit for everyone. (59)
By drawing twenty-six threads multiplied by six in the directions east, west, south, and north,
six hundred and twenty-five squares are produced.
Having drawn a triangle, within the remaining one hundred and twenty-nine squares, starting from the central square among the five squares situated in the row proceeding eastward,
[one should place] the one hundred and twenty [syllables] consisting of the second variation of the third part of the Śrīvidyā.

Having drawn [the diagram] by entering and proceeding in a clockwise direction, one should write the first part of the Śrīvidyā in the three squares located in the right row, the middle part in the three squares located in the left row, and [the final part] in the three squares located in the middle row among the nine remaining central squares.

Having written the third segment in each of the four triangles situated in the cardinal directions, and having inscribed the practitioner, the object to be accomplished, and the rite within that third segment as before— this Vajra Yantra, through the aforementioned application of its squares, bestows the desired success, O Dear One.
The address for the Goddess. || 56 ||

With these three verses beginning with "In this tantra" (*tantre*) and ending with "the achiever" (*āptikṛt*), he teaches the results of all the *yantras* mentioned in this chapter by way of extension and in terms of their essential nature. In that context:
"in this tantra" means in this tantra; "in other tantras" means in other tantras; "that result" refers to the result of these [yantras] in this [tantra].

Regarding the mantras mentioned in the previous chapter, each individual mantra yields all fruits; for that reason, here in this chapter, by means of names and applications—that is, the application of the rites of the practitioner and the object to be accomplished—from this [source], every mantra in this chapter [is explained]. 59.
By means of these thirteen verses beginning with "prākpratyak" and ending with "intanta," the procedure for constructing the *yantra* called the Vajra-liṅga is [described] here on page 654.
Within those squares, one should erase seventy-eight [cells] all around.
And with the remaining four [squares], one should construct a triangle in the directions as before.
Among those, one should draw the third vidyā within the meditative absorption as before;
likewise, in the remaining two hundred and ninety-seven [squares], one should draw it from the center.
Having made three squares horizontally on both sides of the central square, and likewise for those two [sides]. (63)
Then, one should likewise equalize two each above and below;
then, one should likewise make two each below and above those two into a single unit.

In this chapter, he teaches the power (*anubhāva*) of the yantras previously mentioned. Therein, "six hundred twenty-five" means six hundred plus twenty-five. Among those squares, the meaning is that there are seventy-eight squares in each corner. In the remainder...

In the *vajra* [diagram] consisting of three hundred and thirteen squares, by means of four squares—in the sense of the previously mentioned sequence of one and three—within those four corners; the word "tu" (but/indeed) is used for conjunction; [one should place] the *sādhya* together with the practitioner, the object to be accomplished, and the ritual action—as before, likewise, in the portions between the *māyā* and the fire (*vahnī*).

"Successively" means as follows: in the remaining squares. Within the twenty-one squares situated in the horizontal row starting from the west of the central square—namely, the central square itself, together with the ten squares to its south and the ten to its north—one should make them equal, that is, unify them. Of those two...
Of those two [squares] made into one; likewise, as before, of those two; likewise, so that they become the bases (adhiṣṭhāna) and the pedestals (piṇḍikā).

"Two squares each across"—this is the remainder [of the sense]. This is what is meant: starting from the west, in the twelfth and tenth rows, on both sides of the central square of each, one [square] each [is to be combined].

"Having left [the center], one should erase [the lines] on the two circles of the intermediate compartments. Then, immediately after that; "likewise," as before; "of those two," meaning of the two compartments made into one; "below and above," because they are divine, meaning from bottom to top;
"and" (ca) is used for conjunction; "likewise on both sides. This is what has been stated.
In the ninth and thirteenth rows, having omitted two squares on each side of the central square,
one should erase the two intervening squares on each side. Below and above that, [one should erase] the two squares that were previously combined immediately before.

In the two central squares, both below and above; likewise, in the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth rows, three squares on both sides of each respective central square [are formed] by erasing only the horizontal lines. The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction: the erasure of the two upper squares.
The meaning is that [the sequence] proceeds only upwards and then transversely. Each one and each pair follow in due order;
likewise below that and above, there is one and two pairs respectively.
Having unified them once more, one should likewise erase two by two from above.
Then one should wipe away the garland from above and on both sides;
with the remaining ten sections, the liṅga should likewise be formed in the center.
Thus, the *liṅga* has been fully described with exactly forty [verses];
the remaining *koṣṭhavajra* meters number two hundred and fifteen.
On both sides of the liṅga, twenty-one pairs [of syllables] should be polished away;
in the central row of that liṅga, one should inscribe the third [set].

This is what is meant: in the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth rows, having omitted three cells on each side of the respective central cell, one should erase the single cell immediately following them. Furthermore, [this applies] above.

The meaning is that previously, in the rows of cells that were unified, there was only one [cell] in the upper row. "Two by two" refers to the cells within the first cell that was erased; thus, it means transversely.
"Then," immediately thereafter, refers to the two upper sides of the nine cells in the form of the *liṅga*.

The word *khaṇḍa* refers to a line because of the act of dividing (*khaṇḍana*) into ten parts; therefore, by means of ten such divisions, nine squares are formed. The meaning is that by erasing the ten lines, the nine squares are unified. [This is done] with the remaining nine squares. The particle *tu* (but/then) indicates a distinction.

"In the middle" refers to the ten segments that have been unified. The word "tathā" (likewise) is connected with the preceding term "mārjayet" (one should erase/cleanse), meaning that the remaining [space] in the middle should become the *liṅga*. Thus, one should unify the nine squares like a garland (*mālā*). In this manner, by means of the forty [squares] described above...

The meaning is: "by means of the squares situated upon the pedestal (*adhiṣṭhāna*), the central mass (*madhyapiṇḍikā*), and the phallus (*liṅga*). The meaning is: "excluding the remaining phalli and the unified squares. Regarding the phrase "two hundred, ten, and five," because the word "and" (*ca*) here has a collective sense, it indicates that the number one is added [to the total].
This is the tradition. Therefore, the meaning is two hundred and sixteen.
"On both sides and above" is the meaning. "Polished" means combined;
"twenty-one pairs" means one pair and twenty pairs, which is forty-one.
In the middle row consisting of ten squares, the third *kūṭa* is located;
the connection here is "in this row" situated from top to bottom in the order of upper-to-lower.
"In the very center" means in the square situated between the *adhiṣṭhāna* and the *piṇḍikā*. [The syllable] together with the practitioner (*sasādhaka*).

The meaning is that it is endowed with the rite of the practitioner and the object to be accomplished, as previously written in the third peak-syllable (*tārtīyakūṭa*). In all cases, in every yantra, within the forms of the *liṅgas*—
starting from the top and so forth— the entire [mantra] situated in the middle of *māyā*, together with the object to be accomplished, is located in the very center.
In all cases, it is declared that the third Vidyā should be written.
In the nine forms of the Liṅga, on the six sides as before,
one should draw the remainder of the Vidyā, starting from the beginning just as previously described.
One should draw one hundred and twenty [squares] arising from the division of the second Vidyā;
there, having invoked the Goddess along with her attendants, one should worship her in pairs.

In the nine compartments above the *piṇḍika*; this [locative case] is used in the sense of selection (*nirdhāraṇa*). In the six sides, by a sequence of three on each side; "but" (*tu*) is for conjunction. As before, like the previously mentioned *vajrayantra*. The remainder of the *vidyā* is that of the *Śrīvidyā*.

The first peak-syllable (*kūṭa*) and the second peak-syllable are to be placed respectively in the three right compartments and the three left compartments; that is to say, starting from the beginning as before, like the *vajra*-machine of the compartments,
one proceeds from the central compartment along the row situated within the previous triangle.

"By way of circumambulation, entry, and movement" means as follows. "That" indicates what will be explained in the chapter on latent impressions (*vāsanāpaṭala*). "One hundred and twenty" means one hundred plus twenty. "In twos" means by way of turns;
[this refers] there, in the *vajra-liṅga* yantra. This is the sequence of its construction here:
Having produced six hundred and twenty-five squares by drawing twenty-six lines each toward the east, west, south,
and north, forming equal intervals, there are seventy-eight squares in sequence at each corner, totaling [the required number].

Having cleared away the remaining three hundred and twelve squares so that they take the form of a vajra, one should then, within the remaining vajra-shape consisting of three hundred and thirteen squares,
construct each triangle by means of four squares occurring in groups of three in each direction.

Having written the third-order vidyā within those [squares] as before, accompanied by the practitioner's and the object of practice's ritual action, one should then write it in the remaining two hundred and ninety-seven squares,
starting from the west in the row consisting of eleven squares that stands in the very center of all.

In both the right and left sides of that central square, three squares are to be drawn horizontally; furthermore, in each of the twelve rows— starting from the west and proceeding upwards and downwards—
two squares are to be placed on both sides of the respective central square.
Excluding [the cells] in the form of a cross as before,
one should leave three cells on each side of the respective central cell within the three rows consisting of the eighth, fourteenth, and fifteenth lines starting from the west.
Furthermore, having merged each individual square, within the rows of merged squares,
one should add two squares horizontally on both sides in the fifteenth row from the top; thereafter, following the sequence of garlands...
By erasing ten lines above and on both sides of the nine-square *liṅga*-shaped grid,
there arise forty-one squares in total, consisting of the five central squares within the eighteen-row arrangement of squares. These constitute the center.

O Supreme Goddess, one should place the *liṅga* together with its pedestal within forty squares on the outer *vajra*, and the remaining two hundred and sixteen squares in the applications (*viniyoga*) as they have been taught.
There is nothing in this world that cannot be accomplished by means of these instruments taught by me. (72)
By increasing the number of squares by one on each side, starting from one,
one should expand the grid up to nineteen squares, and likewise construct the liṅga above it.
Having first performed [the rite] in the center as before with exactly forty [units],
one should then install [the mantras] in them in sequence, starting from the base and proceeding around to the middle.

Having cleansed it in whatever manner is appropriate, one should write the third section of the Śrīvidyā according to the previously described method within the ten squares situated in the vertical sequence— both upward and downward— among the forty squares of that diagram, specifically in its very center square.

Within the interior of the *Hṛllekhā* (the third Vidyā) written [therein], one should place the practitioner (*sādhaka*), the object of attainment (*sādhya*), and the ritual action (*karma*) upon the pedestal;
then, within the nine-square grid, the first *kūṭa* of the Śrīvidyā is placed in the three squares on the right side, and the second *kūṭa* in the three squares on the left side, both combined.
Having written [the letters] in the sixteen squares, one should proceed with the remainder in the two hundred and forty squares combined with the twenty-four squares occupied by the *liṅga*,
starting from the central square within the row situated inside the eastern triangle.

One should draw the three hundred and twenty doors arising from the second division of the third Vidyā by means of a clockwise entry and movement; "O Supreme Goddess" is an address to the Goddess. || 72 ||
With these eight verses beginning with *ekādi* and ending with *tām*, [the author] teaches the method for constructing the Meru-liṅga, its ritual applications, and their results. In that regard,
by increasing [the number of squares] by two starting from one, there is one square and so forth for each successive row.
By increasing the number of squares by two in each successive row— this is the implied meaning—
one reaches nineteen squares at the end; thus, through this gradual increase, there are nineteen squares in the tenth row.
The meaning is "up to that limit. "As before" means according to the sequence stated for the *vajra-liṅga*.

"From the middle" means following the seven squares situated in the middle of the central row; the word "and" (*ca*) is used in a conjunctive sense. "By forty squares" is the meaning; "eva" is used as a restrictive particle. [This refers to] within those squares.

"Beginning from the root" means starting from the first square situated at the very bottom. "Around" (paritaḥ) means clockwise, up to the row above the foundation (adhiṣṭhāna). "Until the center" (madhyāntam) means ending with the central square of the seven rows beginning from the root; in this regard, the "knowledge" (vidyā) is mentioned in the following verse.

This is the connection [of the verse]. Likewise, by way of entry in sequence, there are one hundred and twenty—that is, one hundred and twenty—[units]. "O Dear One" (*priye*) is an address to the Goddess. "Up to the central cell of the *liṅga*" means as far as the central cell of the *liṅga*, [referring to] the cells situated below that.

Having performed the placement (vinyāsa) in all [the squares] according to the stated sequence, up to the end of the central square within that liṅga—O Dear One, the Vidyā arising from the second division of the Vidyā consists of one hundred and twenty [syllables].
One should inscribe the remainder within the corners, ending at the central square of the liṅga. (75)
Having formed a square by the laying down of two threads,
one should draw [the design] upon that which is fixed at the very exterior.
In seven squares arranged in rows, one should place the synonyms and the phonemes in turn; on the right and left sides, there are those produced by the synonyms of the Nityās.

The remaining four sciences [are to be placed] in the corners; the remainder is that they are in the corners of the square to be described, starting from the northwest (vāyavya) and ending at the southwest (nairṛtya). "Having made a square" means having constructed a square. The particle *tu* indicates a distinction, because of the laying down of two lines.

"In every direction" means according to the internal and external divisions. "In the outermost part" means outside of the aforementioned form. "Bound to that" means connected to the lower line of the first square. "Above that square" implies "in the middle of both. This is understood from the subsequent mention of "the series of [squares]" in relation to the verb "one should draw."
The connection [is as follows]: "in seven squares" means in the seven squares situated in the eastern row of the square grid.

Regarding the phrase "the cycles and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to the pairs, the ghaṭikās, the syllables, the days, the daily [deities], and so on. "Arṇakān" means the letters (varṇas). The two vidyās are produced from the cycles and the daily [deities]. [They are placed] in the middle, within the seven squares.

The word "madhyasthe" (in the middle) [is used]; the particle "tu" (but/indeed) serves as a conjunction. The meaning is: starting from the middle square of the row at the top of the *liṅga*, according to the previously stated sequence. The word "abhitaḥ" means clockwise.
This is because the squares situated below that, on the *piṇḍikā* (pedestal), have already been assigned [for other purposes].
The word "saṃlikhet" (one should draw) is connected with the word "vidyā" (the knowledge/mantra) in the following verse. Likewise, [it is done] by way of entry.
Having thus made the Meru-liṅga—meaning, having fashioned the Meru-liṅga—the particle "tu" indicates a distinction.
This is the sequence of construction here: first, one should fashion a single square grid.
Above that, on both sides, by adding one square per side in successive order,
so that two squares are increased in each row, one should arrange it such that there are nineteen squares in the tenth row, starting from the very base.
Then, having left six squares on each side in the tenth row,
one should draw a *liṅga* together with its pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) and base (*adhiṣṭhāna*) above that, using forty squares, following the seven central squares as before.

Connecting that [line] with the line extending from its tip toward the south and north, and also with the south-north line situated beneath the first square, one should draw a single thread each toward the south and north, measuring twenty-two squares.
Furthermore, on both sides, outside the tenth row, from a space measuring one and a half squares,
one should draw a line each toward the east and west measuring twenty-two squares;
and outside that, surrounding it up to the ends of those respective lines, together with eight lines in total.

Having arranged two equal squares on all sides, each provided with one cell at every corner, in such a manner as previously described, one should write there in the center the forms of the one hundred and twenty Vidyās arising from the second division, within the letters of the "Yuga-arising" [group], according to the stated sequence. (p. 659)
One should draw [the lines] all around the top and middle of the liṅga and also upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā). || 78 ||
Having likewise arranged the twenty-four Vidyās arising from the first division,
one should thus form the Meru-liṅga and write that [Vidyā] right there within the Yantra.
For the attainment of one's desires, and for the acquisition of victory, health, and long life,
one should have that [image] painted on cloth or other media and worship it daily.
By means of twenty-one threads drawn east-west, north-south, south-east, and north-west,
there shall indeed be four hundred perfectly equal squares.
Starting from the central cell and proceeding clockwise by way of entry into the one hundred and fifteen cells up to the upper row of the foundation,
[this continues] for each enclosure until reaching the central cell.

In the seven enclosures, [the mantras are placed] in sequence as thirty-six, twenty-eight, twenty, fourteen, ten, six, and one; immediately thereafter, one [mantra] is in the central square within the space between the liṅga-base and the pedestal;
then the remaining four vidyās are in the four corners of the outer square.

Having thus combined [the mantras] in a single sequence from Vāyavya to Nairṛtya, one hundred and twenty *vidyās* are to be installed. Immediately thereafter, within the twenty-four squares of the pedestal (*piṇḍikā*) of that *liṅga*,
beginning from the central square of the row at the top of the *liṅga* and proceeding down to the area situated beneath the pedestal—

Having written the twenty-four variations of the four syllables of the third Vidyā according to the sequence already described, by entering and proceeding in a clockwise direction as far as the end of the row,
one should then divide the eastern path outside the square into seven equal intervals and [proceed] within them.
In the seven compartments arranged in rows, one should place, respectively,
the three syllables of the Paryāya-nityā-vidyā in the three compartments on the left side,
the three syllables of the Dinanityā-vidyā in the three compartments on the right side, and in the central compartment, the syllable of the ghaṭikā together with the syllable of the yuga.
"One should install" means: there, in that yantra; "eva" is used for emphasis; "her," namely Lalitā together with her retinue;

"on a cloth and so forth"—here the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to gold, silver, copper, stone, and other such materials; "that yantra daily," meaning every day; "her," namely Lalitā, as before. || 80 ||

With six verses beginning with "prākpratyak" and ending with "iṣṭadā," he teaches the procedure for the construction of the Great Liṅga Yantra and so forth. In that context, "well-proportioned" (susamāni) means due to the absence of disparity in length and width; "of that" refers to that which consists of a collection of squares.

"On one side, in the lower part" means on one side of the bottom row. "Then" means from that row. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. "Above" means as far as the very top. [This continues] up to seventy-six, one, and eleven.
"Up to the numbers six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven" means as far as that point. "One should erase the squares" is the meaning.
On the lower part of one side of that [figure], one should erase five squares.
And then above that, six and seven—thus up to eleven. || 82 ||
One should then wipe the upper surface of that very [base] in the reverse order;
likewise, one should do so for the two sides, and thereby [prepare] the pedestal and the lotus-base.
And above you, O beloved, by means of twenty-five squares, another liṅga arises from the wiping away of the other [figures] situated at the sides.
Those [rites] arising from the second division are performed upon the pedestal (piṇḍikā) of the base;
that which arises from the first division is for the liṅga; and when situated in the middle of those, one's own desired goal is attained. 85.

"Above" means in the six rows beginning with the eighth; this is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. "Of that" refers to the sequence beginning with five and six. "Eva" is used for restriction. "In reverse order" means according to the sequence from ten down to five; one should act in that manner.
Just as the two bases and the two pedestals consist of sixty cells each,

they are formed there by a number of cells equal to the one hundred and twenty varieties of vidyās that are to be written therein. The other two sides are likewise the bases and the pedestals, according to the sequence.
From the act of wiping (*mārjana*), the two pedestals (*adhiṣṭhāna-piṇḍikā*) come into being. By that same sequence, one should wipe the other side.
The word "and" (*ca*) is used in the sense of conjunction; it means "above the thirteenth row. The particle "but" (*tu*) indicates a distinction.
The connection is that the *liṅga* is formed by twenty-five squares, which occurs later in this [text]. As for the others...

Those squares are in the form of *liṅgas*, meaning they remain after the cleaning of the side-squares—that is, after the removal of the squares situated on the sides. "O Dear One" (*priye*) is an address to the Goddess.
They are the *vidyās* born from that second division. This refers to the *liṅga* consisting of twenty-five squares.

The phrase "arising from the first division" refers to the third [syllable]. "Situated in its center" means situated in the square located in the middle of the *liṅga*. "One's own desire" refers to the object to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth, as previously described.
"In the middle" refers to the three squares situated in the space between the pedestal (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and the base (*piṇḍikā*). "Born on that day" [refers to the specific syllable].

[Draw] either the [mandala] born on the day the Vidyā was obtained, as before, or that born on the day of the ritual application (prayoga), O Sinless One—this is the address to the Goddess. There, in that yantra, this is the sequence of construction:
first, by stretching twenty-one threads each at equal intervals from east to west and south to north.
Having constructed four hundred squares,

one should erase five squares on one side of the bottom row, and on that same side, erase six, seven, eight, nine, ten, and eleven squares extending up to the second through seventh rows; then, once again on that same [side]...
On that same side, in the six rows from the eighth to the thirteenth,
there are ten, nine, eight, seven, six, and five squares; furthermore, on that very same side,
in the five rows from the fourteenth to the eighteenth, there are ten squares in each.
One should erase the two rows above that, consisting of nineteen and twenty [squares] respectively.
O sinless one, it has been declared to you: "In the center is the Vidyā born of that day.
The Yantra named Mahāliṅga, when worshipped there, bestows all desired objects. (86)

Having produced a triangle with three equal sides, one should fashion a yoni in its center; then, by means of those respective lines, one should likewise make ten [triangles] equally in the three directions.
Having done this, one should draw one hundred and twenty squares here all around; then, in the remaining central triangle, one should write one's own desired object.

Immediately thereafter, on the other side as well, one should clear away the remaining cells by means of logic, so that by groups of sixty cells each, there arise two rows above them consisting of nineteen and twenty [cells] respectively, which become the base (adhiṣṭhāna) and the pedestal (piṇḍikā). When this has been done, by sixty...
With sixty squares one forms the base and the pedestal (piṇḍikā); with three squares the space between them;
and with twenty-five squares the liṅga. Having thus constructed the great liṅga in sequence, starting from the middle square of the rear row of the base and the pedestal...
One should know the second set of divisions by entering and proceeding clockwise through the twenty-five squares located within those signs,
starting from the central square of the first row and moving clockwise.

One should write the first divisions of the Vidyā in the central square, and the daily Nityās in a row within the three squares situated between one's own desired [square] and the pedestal (piṇḍikā). || 86 ||

With these three verses beginning with *samatrirekham* and ending with *anubhavataḥ*, he teaches the construction of the *yonicakra* (the vulva-circle) and so forth. Therein, the *yoni* is a triangle facing oneself. Of that *yoni*: the word *tu* indicates a distinction; *madhyataḥ* means in the middle.

One should draw [the lines] according to those respective threads and in accordance with those respective lines. There are ten threads. "In three threads" means in such a way that one hundred and twenty-one *yonis* (cells) come into being.
"Equally" means with equal intervals, for without equality of intervals, the vital points (*marmans*) cannot be established. Here...

In the *yonicakra*, surrounding [the center] starting from the tip and proceeding clockwise, those mantras (*vidyās*) born of the second division are placed; the word "tu" (but/and) serves as a conjunction.
Herein is the sequence of arrangement: having produced the *yoni* consisting of three equal lines facing oneself as previously described, one should mark those three lines with ten marks each.

Having divided the space between the perimeters into eleven parts, one should strike thirty lines from mark to mark, following the respective threads so as to intersect at the vital points (*marmas*); thus, by the striking of these thirty lines, there arises a wheel (*cakra*) consisting of one hundred and twenty-one *yoni*s.

Having performed [the placement] in those matrices (*yoni*) by entering and moving in a clockwise direction starting from the front, one should place the second divisions of the third Vidyā; the remainder in the central matrix, and one's own desired [deity] as well. Therein, in the *yonicakra*, the meaning is that one should place that Lalitā Vidyā together with her retinue.
In the applications previously described, one should worship there as before and likewise install [the deity] in that manner;
there, by the power of the *yonicakra*, one attains one's own desired goal. (89)
Having produced an equilateral triangle together with a conjoined yoni,
one should likewise cast four horizontal lines there from each side.
Having drawn the diagonal line (tiryaṅsūtra), one should then draw twenty-four lines in sequence from the eastern peak (pūrvaśṛṅga) and its surroundings, following the path of entry.
Having drawn [the diagram] with the remaining vajra situated therein, one should draw one's own desired object;
there, one should worship that goddess for the sake of attaining the fulfillment of all goals. 92.
The particle *ca* signifies conjunction (*samuccaye*). "In such and such a way" means in whatever manner it is applied, in that very manner. || 89 ||

With these three verses beginning with "samatrirekham" and ending with "siddhaye," he teaches the procedure for the construction of the vajra and vajra-yanttra, and so forth. In that context, "tryasram" refers to an upward-facing triangle; "yonim" refers to a downward-facing triangle; and "ca" (and) is used as a conjunction.

The meaning is that one should join them together in an upward and downward sequence by means of a single horizontal line; therein, in the wheel, starting from the upper-left corner of the triangle on one side and extending down to the right side of the *yoni* below.

Starting from the southern line and extending to the other northern line—meaning, with equal intervals between them—a horizontal thread is placed in the middle of the two triangular *yonis*. From the eastern peak, as before, starting from the *vajra-vajakoṣṭha* (the diamond-casket square), and likewise proceeding clockwise; those [lines].

The first [set of] divisions are the vidyās. "Situated in the remaining vajra" means situated in the central vajra. This is the sequence of construction here: having established the *haṃsapada* (swan-step) in the center, one draws the east-west *brahmasūtra* through the position of the pincers (*sandaṃśa*), as before, extending through the two fish-figures generated on both sides.
Having stretched the south-north thread, starting from the point of its intersection,
one should mark two points on both sides of the south-north thread at equal distances; then, between those two marks, one should lay down two pairs of threads according to the required measurement.
Starting from those two marks, draw four lines extending eastward and westward up to the Brahma-sūtra; having thus fashioned a wheel consisting of a triangle and a yoni,
erase that Brahma-sūtra and the horizontal line.

Having divided each of the two lines— the left and right lines of the triangle and the yoni— fivefold by means of four marks on each, one should proceed according to the sequence of those marks from the left line of the triangle to the right line of the yoni,
and from the right line of the triangle to the left line of the yoni.

Having joined together and struck out eight lines, one should arrange twenty-five vajra-squares in their midst; then, beginning from the eastern prong and proceeding in a clockwise direction of entry,
one should place the first variety of the third division of the Śrīvidyā in the remaining central space, as well as whatever one desires.
Therein is the Vajra-vajrayantra; on the full moon days—the fifth, tenth, and fifteenth.
Having performed it in that manner, one should draw the second sets of divisions by means of ten lines each, likewise accompanied by the object to be accomplished (sādhya). || 93 ||
Even there, through worship and other rites, one's own desires shall be accomplished;
in this manner, one should also fashion [the ritual] by means of the vidyās arising from the third [day], having inferred [the procedure].
They too will certainly bring about the complete accomplishment of one's desires;
now listen as I describe the various types of storage-vessels (koṣṭhayantras) according to the prescribed rule. 95.
With the first half-verse of the two verses beginning with *tathā* and ending with *suniścitam*,

he teaches the construction of the machine (*yantra*) called the Great Vajra-Vajra, as well as the method for its manufacture and so forth, which is to be inferred from other sources. Therein, having performed it "thus" (*tathā*):

Having first fashioned a triangular source (yoni) joined with another, the second divisions are the *vidyās*. Likewise, in the middle of what remains. This is the sequence of construction here: having fashioned a triangular source-cakra joined with another as before, in its center...

As before, by stretching out ten threads, one should produce one hundred and twenty-one vajra-squares; then, beginning from the eastern triangle and proceeding in a clockwise direction of entry, one should write the second variety of the Vidyā-mantra and one's own desired [mantra] in the remaining central space. In that regard:
In the *Mahāvajravajrayantra*, the word "etc. (*ādi*) in the phrase "by worship etc. refers to [rites] such as installation (*sthāpana*).

In this manner, according to the stated method, [one should perform it] with the third-arisen vidyās—that is, with the specific vidyās belonging to the third part of the Tārtīyavidyā. However, in the method of mental visualization (*ūhana*), there is one [vidyā].
The yantra is written here by way of illustration: having first fashioned a triangular *yonicakra* as before,
one should produce seven hundred and twenty-nine [squares] by stretching twenty-six threads across its center.

Having fashioned the vajra-cells, one should place therein the twenty-seventh variety of the third Vidyā— which will be described in the chapter on ritual preparation (*vāsanāpaṭala*)— by entering and proceeding clockwise starting from the eastern peak; furthermore, within the remaining nine cells, one should do so in the sequence of three cells at a time.

One should place the three *kūṭas* of the *Śrīvidyā*, as before, within the middle third *kūṭa*, and also one's own desired object. In this manner, one should also conceive of the *ūhya* (to-be-inferred) squares for the *vajra* and other [mantras], and place the various *vidyās* in their respective positions. These are the various types of *yantras* conceived by means of inference (*ūhya*).
The particle *eva* is used in the sense of restriction. || 94 ||

Having written the desired number of figures in rows within the odd-even rectangular grids and square wheels, using the five verses beginning with "koṣṭha" and ending with "āgame," starting from the first half-verse.

By writing the *kūṭas* of the vidyās according to their corresponding numbers, he teaches that there are infinite yantras for all of these, and that they are mentioned in other tantras. In this context, by the phrase "according to the rule" (*yathāvidhi*),
he indicates that the writing of the intended number of syllables within the squares is also mentioned in other tantras.

Starting from the nine- and sixteen-compartment [grids], that is to say, beginning with the nine-compartment and the sixteen-compartment wheel; having expanded them around the exterior of each previously mentioned wheel; unevenly.
A square [mandala] consists of an odd number of cells;
having increased the even [number], such as nine, sixteen, and so forth, from odd to even, one should make the numbers equal within them and write them in rows upon those [cells]. (96)

A square consisting of an equal number of compartments; "in those wheels" means having made them equal in number according to the sequence stated in another tantra. This word "in them" connects both with what precedes, "he should draw," and what follows, "in the row. Therefore, it refers to those situated in the row.

"In the squares" (koṣṭheṣu) is one [interpretation]; "in those, one should draw the various divisions of knowledge" (vidyābhedān samālikhet) is another. Of those squares: from the central square in an odd-numbered square grid; in the very center of all in an even-numbered square grid; and in the four central squares.
Because there is no state that cannot be accomplished by all these [means], the sequence of arrangement here is as follows:
by drawing four and five lines respectively toward the east, west, south, and north,
one produces an odd diagram consisting of nine squares and another consisting of sixteen squares.
Having made them equal, and by increasing one row at a time around each of those two in every direction,
there is a combined increase of four rows and four rows.

Having produced wheels that are regular squares consisting of an odd or even number of cells, and having inscribed therein the desired symbols according to one's preference, [one should fill] the cells in each row with the desired numbers and so forth, in the sequence of the desired numbers and so forth.

Having written equal numbers of digits by way of vertical rows (upward and downward), horizontal rows, and various sequences of diagonal corners, one should write one [digit] from among the various forms of the third Vidyā in each of those respective cells according to the corresponding number, and write one's own desired object in the center.

Here, although the sequence for writing the numerical figures (*aṅka*) is an extreme secret, it is written according to tradition by the command of the venerable Śrīnātha’s feet, so that the lineage may remain uninterrupted. In this sequence for writing the *viṣamabhadra*, there is one and a half verses.
On an uneven [square], one should draw [the lines] from the middle of one's own right arm on a auspicious [board],
using desired or undesired odd numbers, or else by increasing the numbers starting from one.
One should fill the compartments according to the movement of the minister; if it falls outside, one should write the subsequent number in the upper compartment above the counter-heap.
"Having drawn two [lines] and established the cell-numbers starting from the front-left," it is said.
Here, the definition of the *viṣamabhadra* and other such patterns will be explained later. In the *viṣamabhadra*, rows are formed by arranging odd-numbered cells both vertically and horizontally.
In the square mandala: starting from the middle of one's own right arm,
one should write the numbers in the squares situated in the row on one's own entire right side, beginning from the central square, using the sequence of desired and undesired [values].

Having first written down the two intended [quantities] in the [first] square, one should then fill each subsequent square with those numbers— either by increasing the preceding number by a constant difference (*uttara*),
or by the sums produced from the desired total wealth using the initial and the differences— or else by the sum of the wealth in a single row.
He will explain the calculation of the initial and subsequent [results]. This means: by means of those initial and subsequent figures.
Having written down the desired [result] arising from the third division of the Vidyā, in accordance with their respective figures, from the central square among them— (97) |||p. 665|||
Likewise, by means of those contrivances thus fashioned, one may accomplish every desired object, such as subjugation, attraction, inciting enmity, paralyzing, eradication, and so forth. (98)

The phrase "one should fill the squares" (kāṣṭhāni pūrayet) is to be construed with the word "by means of numbers" (aṅkaiḥ). By way of the minister’s movement, the meaning is that one should write the numbers one after another in the squares of the row immediately to the right of the previously written row, starting from the top square according to the minister’s path. If it falls outside, [it is excluded].
The meaning is that when [the numbers] have been written in the square of the entire right-hand row and in the square of the entire top row;

and "in both ways" and so forth refers to the method of the minister (mantrin). When the position obtained by the method of the heap (rāśi) has been reached, one should write immediately thereafter, preceded by the numerical figure, in the square to the left of the square already written.

The meaning is that one should write [the numbers]. This is what is intended: having placed the first number in the square situated in the middle of the entire southern row of the Viṣamabhadrā, one should place the second number in the square above the square furthest to the left in the horizontal row.
Having written the third [number] in the central square of the bottom row and the fourth to its left,

and subsequently having written each one in the upper squares by moving like a minister (sacivagatyā), one should then write the corresponding number in the right-hand square; thereafter, by moving like a minister...
One should draw [the lines]. Thus, when no space is obtained on either side, by drawing from the left cell of one's own previously drawn square as before, equality is achieved on all sides.
Regarding the drawing of the uneven interior, there are four verses beginning with "half" (ardha).
In the womb, however, one should write from the vajra in the uneven positions of the four groups.
Having divided the sequence of groups by three, one should set aside a single result;
if there is a remainder, one should transpose the corresponding square in each row.
In the upper and lower rows of the first and last groups [of consonants], this distinction applies respectively;
however, one should know that it is reversed in the rows of the *vidyā* group.
The quotient obtained by dividing the first cell by three is placed in the two corner cells in sequence;
then, having transposed [the values], the remaining cells are filled from the other corner in the same manner.
"Whatever remains as the second result, one should transpose its number into the other two rows; the squares [of the figures] are placed crosswise, and all the rows consist of equal parts."

The meaning of this is as follows: "In the womb" (*garbhe*) refers to the "odd womb" (*viṣamagarbha*), which occurs when there is a meeting of four "odd-bhadra" squares; in that [womb], one should draw from the diamond-pattern (*vajrataḥ*). Within these four wombs, having first determined one desired [square], one should place the second in its corner, and the third on each of its sides.

The meaning is that, having conceived the fourth [number] situated in that corner, one should write the numbers for each group according to the sequence stated for the Viṣamabhadraka, following the aforementioned order. (p.
666) Regarding the phrase "also in the rows of groups," etc.: within these fourfold groups, the number of the single row...

Having divided by three, the resulting quotient should be placed somewhere; if there is a remainder from the division, one should be added to that quotient, and thus the resulting quotient becomes the *ājya*.
In that case, the number of *kāṣṭhas* [sticks] corresponding to the quotient are placed above and below in the first and fourth rows.

The meaning is that one should place [the letters] in the rows, not transgressing the sequence of the individual squares of each respective row. By the first half-verse beginning with "this is the distinction" (*ayaṃ viśeṣa*), the specific arrangement of the reversed squares is described; namely, the number of rows for each group (*varga*).
Having doubled [the number] and divided by three, that result becomes known as the second.
The remainder should be set aside; there, the second result is to be transposed first into the squares of both ears according to the sequence of one and the unmentioned.

In each respective row, the number remaining after subtracting the first number from the penultimate number should be placed somewhere. By means of that [number], one should transpose the digits into the cells other than those of its own operation, sequentially as before. This is established previously in the sequence beginning with "that second," and so forth.

The meaning is that one should transpose the remaining numbers of the second result across as many horizontal rows as there are in the two desired rows of the third square, without overstepping the sequence of the row-cells. When this is done, [the result is] on all sides.
The meaning is that equality occurs. Regarding the easy method for crossing over uneven *garbhas*, there are two verses:
"Alternatively, starting from the row counted by the number of the final fruit, and having shifted transversely by rows according to the number of one's desired fruits, thereafter..."
Thus, from the beginning up to the end of both corners, one should transpose the corners of both [groups] in sequence;
as before, one should transpose them for the first and last groups, and likewise for the other groups.
The meaning of this is as follows: In the horizontal rows of both the first and fourth groups, starting from either the top row or the bottom row and counting within those very rows,
one should [count] the number of results beginning with one less, horizontally and mutually.
Having transposed the rows as before, immediately thereafter, one row should be transposed from the square at one ear to the square at the other ear;
then, in the remaining rows, one should transpose only those numbers situated in the squares at both ears. When this has been done—
In the first and fourth groups, in each row from top to bottom, only the squares corresponding to the number of the first result are reversed.
In the second and third groups, the row corresponding to the number of the remainder of the second result as previously stated is also [reversed].

The meaning is that one should transpose them diagonally. Regarding the drawing of the *samabhadraka*: "In the case of the *samabhadra*, one should first [draw] the squares for the *bhadravata* along the path of the horse; then, one should draw those of the other [the *bhadravata*] again at intervals of one."
"Residing in each respective head, [they proceed] by way of vomiting and so forth, in that same manner, through the path of the elephant."
The meaning of which is as follows: having placed the first number in the square situated below one's own left side within a Samabhadra grid consisting of sixteen squares,
one proceeds from there along the horse-path (aśvamārga) upward and so forth to the second horizontal row on the left.
In the second square, place the second numeral; in the very same row, in the far-right square, place the third;
and in the third square from the left in the bottom-most row (p.
667), longevity, health, victory, prosperity, and so forth are accomplished.
By means of fixing [the mind] and retention, as well as other methods, the practitioner [should practice] constantly. (99)
Having placed the number four and proceeding in reverse order,
one should place the numbers from five to eight in the successive upper cells, starting from the cell above the fourth and ending with the first.
