Then, following the path of an elephant's gait over the squares marked by the first digits starting from eight,
one should write the remaining eight numbers beginning with nine in those eight squares.
This is the first half-verse regarding the arrangement of the equal interior.
Having indeed formed groups within the center, one should write them in sixteen squares, with four cells for each group, according to the previously mentioned sequence.
"The last [syllable] and so forth [should be placed] on each respective head by way of the elephant-path, or otherwise. Thus it is said.
The meaning of this is as follows: having assigned one group (varga) to each set of sixteen cells,
one should place four [letters] for each group— in forward order, reverse order, and regular sequence— according to the method described for the *samabhadraka* meter.
Thereafter, one should write the remaining numbers in sequence, starting from the last number and ending with the first, in reverse order within the respective squares marked by the elephant-paths;
or alternatively, one may write them for each group according to the previous method, following the sequence of the eight squares.
By the latter half [of the verse], this is stated through another method of procedure: in the case of a square diagram (*samagarbha*), however,
having first placed eight sets of eight numbers for each class (*varga*) as described for the *Bhadra* [yantra],
one proceeds from the final number written in the last class to the initial number written in the first class.

One should write those respective remaining digits in reverse order along the elephant-path (gajamārga). Having divided the indicated digit by the number of cells in the row, one should divide the quotient again by half the total number of steps plus one; the result and the remainder are the two "step-based" (pādika) values.
By means of these two half-verses, the method for calculating the first and subsequent terms of a specified sum within each individual row has been described. For example,
having divided the specified number by the count of cells in a single row, that respective quotient [is used].

It should be in every row and square. Having removed one from the total number of those situated in the rows, one should halve that and divide by that same number; the respective result becomes the subsequent [value], and the remainder of the division becomes the first.
Furthermore, having added one to all the first halves [of the numbers] starting from Yama (8), one should multiply them;
the result will be in the square-cells of the row.
Thus, by means of these two halves, the desired [result] and so forth is obtained.
The method for calculating the sum of the figures situated in each individual row among all those written squares has been explained.

This is its meaning: there, having subtracted one from the total number of rows and cells in the *bhadra*, halving that result and multiplying it by that same number, one should add the initial value to it.
One should multiply that by the number of squares in a single row; the resulting product is the total sum of the figures situated in that single row. (p.
668) Thus, the various types of Yantras for the Goddess, which grant all accomplishments, have been described by you.
O Goddess, everything regarding the scripture known as Yantrasiddhi has been told to you in its entirety.
The pervasion consisting of the nature of the Lord has been correctly proclaimed;
by the constant refinement of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self.
Thus ends the thirty-third chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, within the *Ṣoḍaśanityātantra*. 33. 0.
The auspicious *bhadra* [mandala] increases by two starting from three, while the odd [mandala] is formed from the squares of the rows;
the odd-centered *bhadra* consists of four, four, and six.
"Similarly, a set of four rows with equal internal compartments shall constitute a *bhadra*.

Thus, by this half-verse beginning with "ardhādya," the characteristics of the *viṣamabhadra* and other types have been described. [The *prativāhu* consists of three rows of three squares each, and so on, up to] two rows of two squares each, forming a square at the top.
It is known as the Viṣamabhadra (Odd Bhadra). On each arm, starting with a row of six by six squares and increasing by rows of four squares, there is a Bhadra known as Viṣamagarbha (Odd-womb),
likewise starting with a row of four by four squares and increasing by rows of four squares.
And [the mudrā] known as *samagarbhā* is auspicious. Now, the commentary on the root text is written:

"Uccāṭana and so forth"—here the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to rites such as *vidhāna*. In the phrase "vibhūti and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādya*) refers to [substances] such as earth. "By others" means by consecrations (*abhiṣeka*) and the like. "O Goddess" (*devī*) is a vocative.
"It was already stated before"—this is the ellipsis. "In the scripture named Yantrasiddhi" means in the scripture known as the *Yantrasiddhi-āgama*. || 100 || 0 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha— entitled *Prapañcasārasihārājaprakāśa*— upon the complete *Tantra* known as the venerable *Kādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The thirty-third chapter, dedicated to the revelation of the *liṅga*-yantra, is thus fully examined and completed. Om, that is the Truth.
Regarding the number of verses: in the thirty-third chapter, the verses of the commentary are stated to be four hundred and ninety-two and a half.
The eleven yantras, beginning with the Śrīcakra, have been described in sequence;
likewise, there are infinite [yantras] arising from the *u* [vowel] as well as those produced from the squares.
The Thirty-Fourth Chapter.
Now, O beautiful one, listen as I shall proclaim here the mantra that produces wonder for those who take delight in the mantras of the sixteen Nityās. 1.
Siddhasārasvata, Mṛtyuñjaya, Tripuṭa, Gāruḍa, Aśvārūḍhā, Annapūrṇā, Navātman, and Navātmikā. || 2 ||
Then he [taught] the Heart of the Goddess, the Gaurī-vidyā which bestows a hundred thousand [merits],
and the Mataṅginī which grants one's desires and bestows three gold coins.
I shall now describe, in the prescribed order, the varieties of Gopāla, as well as Mahālakṣmī, Rājyalakṣmī, Siddhalakṣmī, and Anantaram, along with their medicinal applications.
Then, from his own [nature], Śuci became joined with Māyā, Vyoman, Dāha, and Svavahni; through the union of Haṃsa, Hṛt, Tejas, Dyuti, Dāha, Cara, and Sva.

In the thirty-third preceding chapter, having taught certain yantras arising from the various forms of the Lalitā-vidyā— which are perfected through the sixteen Nityā-vidyās and yield the fruit of attaining one's desires— [the author] subsequently [teaches] their applications that produce wonders in the world.

He teaches by means of the *vidyās* through the thirty-fourth chapter, which consists of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, of the sixteen *nityās*" and ending with "the self-possessed one. Therein,
by means of the four verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "indeed," in their respective order:
He teaches the meaning of the chapter on the introduction (*prastāvapaṭala*). In this context, the term "Sundarī" is used as a vocative address.

With the verse beginning with "The essence of the Siddhas’ Sarasvatī," he teaches the eightfold *vidyā*. Therein, in the *Tripuṭagāruḍa*, he teaches the *vidyā* of Tripuṭā and the *vidyā* of Gāruḍa. Then, with the verse beginning with "And thereafter," etc.

The sixfold group of sciences (*vidyā-ṣaṭka*); by the half-verse beginning with "the royal fortune" (*rājya-lakṣmī*), the three sciences [are indicated]; "seven varieties of cowherds" is the meaning; it is "sevenfold" because it will be explained later in the sequence of their extraction. The medicinal herbs are those which remove the poison of all serpents and enable one's own departure at will. || 4 ||

With these two verses beginning with "pure" (śuciḥ) and ending with "the body" (vigraha), he teaches the nature of the Siddhasārasvata-vidyā. In this context, "pure" refers to the vowel *ai*, along with its own bindu—this is the ellipsis. "Then," that is, immediately thereafter, "the syllable"—this is the ellipsis.
Furthermore, the Vidyā consisting of five syllables, whose form is the nectar of immortality, has arisen from the union of the two Haṃsas—the heart of the Haṃsa and the burning of the two Haṃsas. (6)
In this chapter, one should provide the limbs for those [mantras] not mentioned by means of one’s own vidyā or by means of Māyā; and the meditation is as previously described.

Having recited the mantra five hundred thousand times while observing the *prāya* vow and having meditated upon Kulasundarī, one whose mantra is perfected should thereafter perform the ritual application (*viniyoga*).
Having purified the maiden with water consecrated by this mantra, and having made her drink it, he, being composed, should say to her: "Recite a verse."

*Māyā* is *hṛllekhā*. The syllable *śrībīja* means the letter *śa*, joined with the sky (*viyat*), burning (*dāha*), and its own fire (*svavahni*), together with the vowel *ī* and the bindu. Following that, through the union of the swan (*haṃsa*), the heart (*hṛt*), and splendor (*tejas*), there are the letters *ha*, *sa*, *sva*, *ra*, *ra*, *e*, and the bindu—these seven.

The meaning is "the seed-syllable. Furthermore, immediately thereafter, by means of seven syllables— namely *ha*, *sa*, *ha*, *sa*, *ha*, *ra*, *au*, and the *visarga* (which constitute the heart-mantra *haṃsa* and its burning [form] *haṃsadvaya*)— together with the *samāya*.

This refers to the fifth seed-syllable. "Amṛtavigrahā" means she whose form is that of the previously mentioned Amṛteśvarī-vidyā as described in the twenty-seventh chapter; the meaning is that a specific visualization is prescribed for a specific application in that very same place. || 6 ||

By means of the verse beginning with "paṭale" (the chapter), the technical definition of the limbs (*aṅga*) and meditations (*dhyāna*) for the mantras (*vidyā*) taught in this chapter is stated; therein, the meaning is "for those mantras not [explicitly] mentioned. By one's own mantra—that is, by each respective mantra—through the first seed-syllable divided into six parts.

The meaning is: "according to the sequence taught by the Guru. "By Māyā" means by Hṛllekhā, which is differentiated by the six long vowels. "Or" (vā) signifies an alternative. "The visualization of the primordial nectar-form" is the intended meaning. "And" (ca) denotes conjunction. The phrase "when visualization has not been described" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This is what has been stated.
When meditation has not been specifically articulated, the meditation upon any particular deity is indeed the meditation upon Amṛteśvarī. || 7 ||

With these three verses beginning with "payobrata" and ending with "mahādbhutam," [the author] teaches the method for accomplishing the vidyā and the divine application by means of the perfected Sarasvatī-vidyā. In that context, "payobrata" means one whose diet consists of milk; [he should worship] Kulasundarī...
"Having meditated" means having meditated upon the form of Kulasundarī as described in the fifteenth chapter.

"One whose mantra is perfected" means one who possesses perfected vidyā. "By this" refers to this perfected Sarasvatī-vidyā. "Consecrated" means, because of their divine nature, consecrated by these [mudrās]. The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction. "A maiden" means one whose senses are undisturbed.
...up to this point; the word *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*). One should speak to that maiden [as follows]: (p.
671) "Her speech shall issue from her mouth like the flow of the Gaṅgā;
and when questioned, she shall declare the most wonderful matters concerning the three times. 10.
Having uttered "Bhūḥ" with its own [seed-syllable], "Jyā," "Dharā," "Sveta," and "Hṛt" conjoined with "Māyā," and having said "Protect" twice, one should then recite that in reverse order.
This vidyā, known as Mṛtyuñjaya, joined with the long vowel and the heart-mantra—
by means of this vidyā, one should regularly contemplate one's own self along with its limbs.
Seated upon a lotus whose stalk consists of the first, middle, and third syllables, his limbs moist with nectar, and his crown joined with the digit of the bindu.
"Recite in verse. Here, the syntactical connection follows a different order: "He should say, 'Recite in verse.
"Composed" means free from other mental activities and the like. "Of her" refers to that maiden. The word "ca" (and) is used for conjunction.
"Objects existing in the three times" refers to things situated in the past, future, and present times. [She] was questioned.
The meaning is "a girl"; it was a great marvel, as if it were a source of great wonder. || 10 ||

With the verse beginning with *bhūḥ svanā*, he teaches the nature of the Mṛtyuñjaya-vidyā. In that context, *bhūḥ* is the syllable *oṃ*; the remainder is that it is accompanied by its own *bindu*. *Jyā* is the syllable *ja*; *dharā* is white (*śvetā*), meaning it is accompanied by the vowel *u* and the *bindu*. *Hṛt* is the syllable *sa*; it is conjoined with *māyā*, which is the visarga.

"Endowed with" [the syllables]. "Protect" (pālaya) should be uttered twice, meaning "protect, protect. That is the three extracted syllables. In reverse order means by way of receding. In these applications, however, one should first utter the three syllables beginning with the *praṇava*, and immediately thereafter, the name of that which is to be protected.

The meaning of the tradition is as follows: having uttered the word ending in the accusative case, one should then utter the pair "pālaya," and thereafter utter the first three syllables in reverse order. || 11 ||

With these three verses beginning with "vidyā" and ending with "edhate," he teaches the nature of the meditation on the Vidyā of Mṛtyuñjaya. Regarding this, the traditional teaching (sampradāya) is that one [meditates] upon one's own self by means of the heart-mantra (hṛdaya) joined with the long vowels, and by the letter *sa* divided by the six long vowels together with the bindu (*m*). One's own self...
"One should contemplate one's own form" means in the manner that will be described hereafter. || 12 ||

By the first half-verse beginning with "ādyā," this is what is meant: having visualized two white lotuses— one with its stalk from the first syllable, its petals from the second syllable, and its pericarp from the third syllable, both facing upward and downward— [one should place] that [deity] upon the white lotus in the space between them, its limbs moist with nectar.
His body is moistened by the nectar flowing from the crescent moon situated upon the crowns of the two lotuses;
he is white in color. Hara holds the four weapons beginning with the deer—[the bow], the deer-skin, the rosary, and the noose—and is white.
One should constantly meditate upon them as one's own identity; thus, victory, long life, and prosperity increase.
The third [syllable] is called Amṛta; immediately after that is the second [syllable].
The vital breaths (prāṇas), together with Rasa, Agni, and Sva, are declared as the Tripuṭa by means of those. 15.
Having performed the ancillary rites with the [mantras] repeated three times,
one should constantly recite the Vidyā at the beginning of the day three thousand times, contemplating oneness with oneself.
By that, a man obtains knowledge, prosperity, splendor, poetic skill, proficiency in singing, and the favor of men, women, and kings. || 17 ||
[She is] ruddy, seated upon Aruṇa, with a serene lotus-face,
[holding] a flower, an elephant-goad, a lotus, a lotus-noose, and a sugarcane bow.
Holding with her six arms a ruby crown,
an ornament of amorous grace, a parrot, a fly-whisk, a mirror, and a chaplet.

From the upper left hand down to the lower [left] hand, in a counter-clockwise sequence: therein, *cintā* is explained as the *vyākhyāna-mudrā*. By way of identity with oneself, that is, by being non-different from oneself. 14.

With the verse beginning with "the third," he teaches the nature of the Tripuṭā-vidyā. In that context, "the third" refers to the third seed-syllable of the Siddhasārasvata-vidyā of Amṛteśvarī, which means the Śrī-bīja (the syllable Śrī). This is the first seed-syllable of this Śrī-tripuṭā-vidyā.

The second [syllable] immediately following that is the second seed-syllable (*bīja*) of the *Siddhasārasvata* lore: the letter *la* together with the "taste" (*rasa*), "fire" (*vahni*), and "self" (*sva*), which are the vowels *i*, *e*, and the nasal dot (*bindu*); the letter *ka* accompanied by these. By this, the "seed of desire" (*kāmabīja*) is expressed. With those three seed-syllables: *śrīṃ*, *hrīṃ*, *klīṃ*.

With these five verses beginning with "tribhiḥ" and ending with "smaret," he teaches the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of the *tripuṭā-vidyā*, the sequence of its practice, the fruits to be attained by one who has mastered the vidyā, its visualization (*dhyāna*), and the visualization of its retinue. Therein:

"By means of the three seed-syllables, uttered twice—that is, recited two times; 'tu' signifies a distinction; 'three thousand' is the remainder, referring to the number of recitations; by that recitation (*japa*); 'ca' is used as a conjunction; 'naraḥ' refers to the practitioner (*sādhaka*).
Here, the sequence of the weapons begins from the lower right hand and ends with the lower left hand."

It should be understood as proceeding in a clockwise direction; that is to say, by means of the six [powers] acting together. The word *dadhānāḥ* (bearing) is to be connected with the latter half of the preceding verse. Of that Goddess:
"The Śaktis also, bearing [her] all around and singing [her praises]... (p. 673).
One should meditate upon her as being surrounded by them, all standing together in a single unity.
The syllable *bhūḥ*, joined with its own [seed-syllable], *haṃsa*, *dāha*, and *marud-vahni-kṣmā*; then the four syllables *vairi-mohī* and *garuḍa*. (21)

"Javī savahnigrāsaśca haṃsahiṃsadvayam tathā | svāhānto gadito mantraḥ tārkṣyasya akhilarakṣituḥ || 22 ||" The mantra of Tārkṣya, the protector of all, is declared to end with "svāhā," consisting of the words "javī savahnigrāsaśca haṃsahiṃsadvayam."
This mantra of twenty-three syllables, when well-mastered during an eclipse,
[liberates] those bitten by serpents, those afflicted by piśācas and other spirits, and other diseased persons.
"Staying" means not sitting; the act of sitting belongs only to the Goddess [herself]. "By those powers" (śaktibhiḥ) refers to those [energies].
"Her," meaning the Goddess. "Through oneness with herself" means by way of non-separation. || 20 ||

With one and a half verses ending with "well-accomplished" (susādhita), beginning with "Bhūḥ svā," he teaches the nature of the Gāruḍa mantra and the method for its accomplishment. In that context, "Bhūḥ" is the syllable *oṃ* accompanied by its own *bindu*; this [phrase] applies to both the preceding and the following [parts], like the eye of a crow.

By "haṃsa" and "dāha," [it is meant] the letters *ha* and *ra*, which are closely joined to one another. "Accompanied by wind, fire, and earth" means together with wind (*marut*), fire (*vahni*), and earth (*kṣmā*)—that is, wind, fire, and earth. These are the vowels *a*, *i*, and *u*; thus, the letters beginning with "wind" (*marut*) are distinct.
"Separately," according to the tradition; by that, the three syllables *hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ* are produced.

Regarding the four syllables *vairimohī*, there is the grasping of the phonetic form (*kharūpa*) of the tetrad of syllables *vairimohī*. And by the word "Garuda," with the letter *ca*, there is also [the inclusion] of the three syllables *garuḍa*.
The nature of grasping its own form is illuminated. The letter *pa* is swift; "together with fire" (*savahni*) means a "swallow" (*grāsa*) accompanied by fire.

Since the letter *i* is the designation for fire due to its similarity in being fiery and according to tradition, the term "swallow" (*grāsa*) refers to the letter *kṣa*. Thus, the meaning is the letter *kṣa* together with the letter *i*.

The pair *haṃsa-hiṃsa* refers to the two syllables *haṃsa* and the two syllables *hiṃsa*. Likewise, there is the inclusion of their own forms. It consists of twenty-three syllables (*trayoviṃśārṇaḥ*), meaning it is composed of twenty-three phonemes. "During an eclipse" (of the moon and sun)—this is the ellipsis. "It becomes well-accomplished"—this is the ellipsis.

The meaning is: by means of recitation (*japa*), satiation (*tarpaṇa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), worship (*arcā*), and so forth. With the first half-verse and the following [half-verse] of the two verses ending with "one should recite" (*japet*)—beginning with *oṃ hrāṃ hrīṃ hrūṃ vairimohi garuḍa prīṃ kṣīṃ haṃsa hiṃsa phaṇī* and so on—[the ritual is performed].

He teaches the fruits and the meditation for one who has attained mastery over the Gāruḍa mantra through its specific application. In that context, in the phrase "by Piśācas and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to Bhūtas, Pretas, Apasmāras, Kṛtyās, and the like; the particle "ca" is used in the sense of conjunction. [The affliction is caused] by three kinds of fierce poisons known as fixed (sthira), artificial (kṛtrima), and mobile (jaṅgama).

One should protect those afflicted by poison—whether they are unconscious from its threefold fierce effects or have lost consciousness—from the moment of sprinkling them with water over which the mantra has been recited a hundred times. (24)
One should mutter the mantra of Tārkṣya while recollecting the Lord who, equal in size to Mount Meru, performs the tāṇḍava dance before Śambhu and devours all enemies.
By means of the seed-oil of *padmākṣa* (lotus-seed), one shall quickly destroy the poison of all serpents without any effort. || 26 ||
The Praṇava, the wind, the Haṃsa, fire, the burning, the two sky-travelers;
the void, water, taste, burning, fire, the heart, water, and joined with air. (27)
The ten-syllable Vidyā is said to be "Haṃsa" joined with the wind (the letter Ya).
Having performed the six-limbed ritual (ṣaḍaṅga) with Māyā (the syllable Hrīṃ), one should recite it one hundred thousand times.

"Rendered unconscious and deprived of sensation," meaning their vital breaths have been constricted by the force of the poison in some part of the body. "With [the mantra] recited a hundred times" means consecrated one hundred times.
Regarding the phrase "while performing the *tāṇḍava*," the syntactic connection is inverted; the meaning is "while he is performing the *tāṇḍava*."

Equal to Mount Meru by virtue of the greatness of his body and its complexion; the all-pervading Lord in reality; "unwholesome things" refers to the poisons and so forth mentioned previously. || 25 ||
With the verse beginning with "padmākṣa," he teaches the medicine that destroys the poison of all serpents and its application. In this regard, oil is obtained from the seeds of the lotus (padmākṣa);
the method [for its extraction] should be understood from the mouth of the Guru. || 26 ||

With the two and a half verses beginning with *praṇavam* and ending with *daśākṣarī*, he teaches the *Aśvārūḍhā-vidyā*. In that context, the compound *carahaṃsāgnī* is a *madhyapadalopa* (middle-term elided) compound; thus, it means *carayutahaṃsāgnī* (the *haṃsa* and *agni* joined with *cara*). Here, *cara* refers to the vowel *e*.

The letter *ha* is "swan-fire" (*haṃsāgni*) when accompanied by the vowel *ī*; the letter *pa* is "swift" (*javī*); the letter *ra* is "burning" (*dāha*); and the letter *e* is "sky-traveler" (*nabhaścara*) when accompanied by the letter *ma*. Regarding "void-water" (*śūnyāmbu*), it means the letters *śa* and *va*, because they possess the nature of the void and water; for here the word *viyat* (space/sky) is a synonym [for the void], and according to traditional usage (*sampradāya*), the letter *śa* signifies the void.

The meaning is that the letter *śa* is accompanied by *va*. "Fire with *sadā*" means the letter *ra* accompanied by *i*. "The heart, water, and wind combined" means: the heart is *sa*, water is *va*, and *sva* is accompanied by *ā*. "Haṃsa" is the letter *ha* joined with wind (*ya*) and accompanied by *ā*. || 27 ||
With the six verses beginning with "ṣaḍaṅga" and ending with "vidyayā," [one should perform] the limbs of the *Aśvārūḍhā-vidyā*. Then,
for whomsoever one performs the recitation at night without effort—
One should bring that performer of the prescribed rites to one's own home until the end of the vow. || 29 ||
Through this perfected vidyā, one constantly attains subjugation, attraction, fortune, gold, and all desired objects without effort. (30)
Red in color, seated upon a red horse, adorned with red garments and ornaments, she has four arms and three eyes, her lotus-like face being serene. || 31 ||
With his right hand he holds a spear, and with his left a brilliantly shining shield-staff;
with his other two hands, having bound his victim by the neck with a golden noose— (32)
Having bound him with golden canes, he made him join his two hands in *añjali* and fall at his own feet, saying, "I am your slave. (33)
By chanting the Svaravidyā, a mortal may effortlessly bring the entire world of living beings under his control through the mantra known as Aśvārūḍhā.
The mantra is formed by the Praṇava joined with "namaḥ," followed by "bhagavati," then "māheśvari," and finally "annapūrṇe svāhā. (35)

It teaches the method of accomplishment, the applications for one who has mastered the vidyā, its meditation, and the specific fruits thereof. In that regard, "by means of māyā as before" refers to the *hṛllekhā* mantra; "a hundred thousand of the syllables" means a hundred thousand repetitions corresponding to the number of syllables in the vidyā—that is, ten lakhs.

"Then, when the vidyā is accomplished" means up to that point. "That sādhya" refers to the one to be mastered. "Until destruction" means as long as the body lasts. "Acting as instructed" means like a servant; this is the meaning. "By this vidyā called Aśvārūḍhā" [refers to] her who stands upon a red-colored horse.

"With the right hand" means with the right arm; "with the left" as before. "Blazing" means multicolored. "With the other two" refers to the two upper hands. "With a golden noose" means with that which is held in their left hands. "Struck with a golden staff."
Remembering the Goddess in the form described above, he was struck by the golden cane held in their right hands.

With the verse beginning with "praṇavam," he teaches the seventeen-syllable mantra known as Annapūrṇā. In that context, by the word "namas" (namely, the word *namaḥ*), there are two syllables, *na* and *maḥ*, following the *praṇava*. The particle "tathā" indicates conjunction. [Then comes] "bhagavatī."
"Bhagavati" consists of four syllables; "Māheśvarī" consists of four syllables;
and "Annapūrṇe Svāhā" consists of six syllables. That mantra is the Annapūrṇā-vidyā. || 35 ||
Having performed the ritual assignment of the limbs through *māyā*, one should recite the Vidyā at dawn a fixed thousand times; for him, there shall be no poverty. (36)
She gazes with eyes intent on the dance that causes terror to serpents;
her face is smiling, and she holds a golden vessel of milk-rice (pāyasa) in her hand.
One who constantly recites the mantra of Bhavānī shall never at any time or in any place be afflicted by hunger.
Likewise, he who daily worships me while I am standing in dance, and you who are curious to behold that [dance], with these two mantras and asks for a boon, [shall obtain it]. (39)
By our grace, whatever he desires shall indeed be swiftly accomplished;
and he shall stand above all, in every way, in every place, and at all times.

Through the union of the earth with those nine— namely, the swan (haṃsa), the heart (hṛt), the seat (āsana), the ether (nabhas), the essence (rasa), water (ambu), pervasion (vyāpta), burning (dāhaka), and the name (nāman)— it becomes ninefold by means of those nine.

With these three verses beginning with "vidhāya" and ending with "kutracit," he teaches the limbs of the goddess Annapūrṇā, the method for accomplishing the vidyā, and the fruits obtainable by one who has mastered the vidyā. In that context, "by means of māyā as before" refers to the *hṛllekhā* [syllable]. The *vidyā* is the one named Annapūrṇā.
At the break of day, in the early morning,
she was gazing at the Supreme Lord who was intent on a specific form of the *tāṇḍava* dance that struck terror into serpents; [she took] from a golden vessel for that reciter.
The ablative case in "hemapātrāt" is used with the elision of a verbal root (lyablope); it means "having filled the golden vessel. This refers to the recitation of the mantra of Annapūrṇā. || 38 ||

With the two verses beginning with *tathā* and ending with *sada*, he teaches the meditation on the two forms of the ninefold self-knowledge (*navātmavidyā*) that will be described immediately hereafter, as well as their fruits. In this context, "thus" refers to standing in the dance posture (*nṛtyasthita*), intent upon the serpent-dance (*bhujaṅgatrāsana-nṛtya*).

By beholding that [deity], one becomes curious; [specifically] curious to behold the dance. "By these two" refers to those which are about to be described. "The boon" means the desired object. "For the petitioner"—the particle *eva* is used here for emphasis. (This is explained) by the two verses beginning with "O Haṃsa" and ending with "bestower of success."

He teaches the nature of the Vidyā within the *navātsaka* [mantra]. In that regard, it consists of the letters *ha*, *sa*, *kṣa*, and *ma*—representing the *haṃsa*, the heart, the seat, and space—conjoined with the letters *la*, *ba*, *ya*, and *ra*, which signify taste, water, pervasion, and burning. By means of those syllables, of that...
Of that very ninefold mantra, having omitted the syllable *kṣma*, one should employ *vahni* (the fire-syllable) there.
That is your ninefold Vidyā; these two [mantras] bestow all accomplishments. (42)
The Praṇava, the final syllable of the Tripuṭā, and the four-syllabled word *namaḥ*—this Vidyā, known as the Heart of the Goddess, bestows the accomplishment of all aims. (43)
Let there be constant meditation upon her, the bestower of all auspiciousness;
[one should apply] white kuṣṭha and the root of svarṇapuṣpī with water from its leaves. (44)
Having ground [the ingredients], being pure, eating only milk-rice, reciting the mantra, and having conquered his senses,
he should sleep on the ground that night in a secluded and very beautiful house.

One who has smeared [the mantra] on the forehead, throat, and heart, and has written the *māyā* [syllable] thereon—she who resides in the command (*ājñā*) shall likewise carry out whatever he desires. 46.
The word *eva* is used for emphasis. *Kṣmā* is the letter *ū*; *vahni* is the letter *ī*.
There, in the place of the letter *ū*, [the syllable] is *navātmikā* as before. *Tu* is used for distinction; thus, *te* means "your," O Goddess, your Vidyā. || 42 ||

With the verse beginning with "praṇavam," he teaches the nature of the *Devīhṛdayavidyā*. In that regard, the first syllable is the *praṇava* (Oṃ); the final syllable of the *tripuṭā* is the third syllable of the *tripuṭā-vidyā*, which is the *kāmabīja* (Klīm). This constitutes the *Devīhṛdayavidyā*.

The meaning is that it is the second syllable. By means of "namaḥ," which consists of two syllables serving as the third and fourth syllables, the four-syllabled mantra is thus produced; such is the sense. || 43 ||

With these four verses beginning with "dhyānam" and ending with "vijayāvahā," [the author] teaches the visualization of the Goddess's heart, as well as the attainment of results such as the narration of dreams by various deities through all the mantras and vidyās. Therein, the visualization of her is described as follows:

The meditation for this *devīhṛdayavidyā* has been stated thus; that is to say, one should meditate upon Sarvamaṅgalā. Here, the names of the two herbs are to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. "With the water of their leaves" means with the water of the leaves of the *svarṇapuṣpī*.

The traditional teaching is that [one should sit] on the ground, on a spread of *darbha* grass, or on the skin of a deer. It should be very beautiful and free from insects and other creatures that obstruct sleep. Having smeared the *ājñā*, throat, and heart with those two aforementioned medicinal substances—the *ājñā* being the space between the eyebrows—one [should remain there]. In that regard:
This Heart-Vidyā of the Goddess, written on a smeared surface (such as a wall), is one that grants immediate results for women;
it brings about good fortune, prosperity, fame, long life, health, and victory. (47)
O beloved of Rudra, this twelve-syllable vidyā is said to consist of the syllable Om, followed by "Yogeśvarī," and ending with "Svāhā. (48)
This is declared to be the Gaurī-vidyā; when recited one hundred thousand times and well-perfected, the Goddess—visualized as before, mounted upon a lion—accomplishes whatever is desired. (49)
In the middle of the night, with focused mind, one should write these [syllables] upon one's own left thigh by means of the ink of the night, accompanied by the name of the person to be accomplished.
Meditating thus, one should recite the vidyā; at that very moment, one shall attract the beloved.
There exists no vidyā equal to this for the purpose of bringing a woman under one's control. (51)
In this world, there are no vidyās for subjugating kings, subjugating the world, or the rites for subjugating women that surpass the pair of Hayagaurī-mantras.

With the *hṛllekha* mantra written [therein], she—the Goddess—residing in the command (*ājñā*) and situated between the eyebrows, [bestows] upon that practitioner the fruit described as the sixfold result beginning with good fortune (*saubhāgya*). || 47 ||

With the verse beginning with "praṇava," he teaches the nature of the Gaurī-vidyā. In that regard, the five syllables "rudradayite," the four syllables "yogeśvarī," and the two syllables "svāhā"—thus, it consists of twelve syllables in total. || 48 ||

With these four verses beginning with *gaurī* and ending with *dvayādityaiḥ*, [the author] teaches the practice (*sādhana*) of the Gaurī-vidyā, its visualization (*dhyāna*), the specific applications for one who has mastered the vidyā, and the distinctions of their results. Among these, by the latter half of the verse beginning with *tatra dhyātvā*, the following is stated:

Thus it comes to pass that the Goddess Gaurī, whose form as the one mounted on a horse was previously described, accomplishes the desired object of the practitioner. The word "tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction. By means of *niśā* (turmeric); from her own left thigh region;

into the left thigh region of the practitioner; accompanied by the name of the person to be acted upon (*sādhya*), together with the ritual action of both the person to be acted upon and the practitioner.

Endowed with these, this Gaurī-vidyā; "with mind fixed on that" means with mind focused on the object to be accomplished (sādhya). Likewise, "according to the traditional method of cultivation"; the word "of Gaurī" is to be supplied after "the vidyā. At that very moment, by means of this Gaurī-vidyā;
[this refers to] the Hayagaurī-mantra, the two-syllabled mantra of the Horse-mounted Goddess.
This means that they are both superior to and similar to the two Gaurī-vidyās. || 52 ||
Agni (Ra), Nada (Sa), and that [consonant] joined with them; then those two, Nabhodhara (Va) and [the same], constitute the second [syllable]. After that, they become Kakaṇṭha (Ka). (53)
"Muṇḍisvāhā"—this fifteen-syllable vidyā has been declared.
Having performed the ritual placement on the limbs (aṅganyāsa) with the Māyā-mantra and having meditated upon that goddess Sarvamaṅgalā, [one should proceed].
One should recite the vidyā while observing silence in the midst of plantain and betel-nut trees;
accompanied by worship at the three junctions of the day, she, being pleased, bestows a hundred thousand [coins] within days.
This twelve-syllable vidyā, beginning with the *praṇava*, followed by *navakeśī* joined with *kanakavatī*, and ending with *svāhā*, bestows three *niṣkas*.

With the half-verse beginning with *agniḥ* and ending with *pañcadaśākṣarā*, he teaches the nature of the vidyā that bestows a hundred thousand pieces of gold. In this context, *agniḥ* is the vowel *i*. And *nāda* is the letter *ra* joined with that [vowel] *i*. These two have been declared. *Eva* is used for emphasis. Of this...

The meaning is that the first and second syllables of the mantra become the third and fourth syllables. "Nabhodharau" means the letter *ma* accompanied by the aforementioned vowel (*u*). This is the second [syllable];
the meaning is that the very second syllable of this mantra becomes the sixth syllable. Those two should be so.

The fifth and sixth syllables themselves shall become the seventh and eighth; that is to say, "kākaṇṭha" consists of three syllables, and "muṇḍisvāhā" consists of four syllables, making fifteen syllables in total, up to the word "sambhūya. || 53 ||

With the first half-verse beginning with *kṛtāṅga* and ending with *dinaiḥ*, he teaches the limbs [of the ritual], the visualization (*dhyāna*), the sequence of practice (*sādhanakrama*), and the attainment of the fruit for one who has mastered the vidyā. In that context, "by means of *māyā*" refers, as before, to *hṛllekhā*. That goddess is the goddess known as *Lakṣaprada*.

She who is the embodiment of all auspiciousness, whose form is equal to all that is auspicious; [located] amidst plantains, in the middle of a grove of plantains, or in the middle of a grove of betel-nut trees; accompanied by worship performed at the three junctions of the day—this is an adverbial phrase. That Goddess is the giver of a *lakṣa*, bestowing a hundred thousand pieces of gold. Within days, as previously stated. || 55 ||
With the verse beginning with "praṇavam," he teaches the nature of the vidyā that bestows the three jewels.

In this context, "navakeśām navakeśām" consists of four syllables; "kanakavatīsaṃyutam" refers to the five syllables "kanakavati"; and "svāhā" consists of two syllables—the word "uccaret" (one should utter) is to be understood as the remainder.
It consists of twelve syllables; it bestows three *niṣkas* as before, both by name and by its meaning. (56)
Having recited the mantra three hundred thousand times, syllable by syllable, at the foot of a banyan tree situated on a mountain peak, one shall constantly obtain the aforementioned fruit. (57)
Cara is prāṇa joined with marut; vyāptam is prāṇa conjoined with dharā;
vyomadvayam is marut joined with [the other] marut; and raya is conjoined with dharā. || 58 ||
Having declared that "the breath is the wanderer," one should privately state the desired knowledge;
Maṅgalā, of auspicious form, is worshipped with jasmine flowers in the middle of the night.
First the three syllables of Siddhasārasvata, followed by "Mātaṅginyai svāhā," and again three [syllables]; such is that mantra. (60)
This twelve-syllable mantra quickly bestows good fortune, poetic talent, prosperity, proficiency in singing, and honor among all people. (61)

With the verse beginning with *nityaśas*, he teaches the method for accomplishing the Vidyā by means of the three *niṣkas* and the resulting attainment. In that context, "having recited three hundred thousand" means having recited the syllables collectively thirty-six hundred thousand times. This refers to the aforementioned measure of three *niṣkas*.
The meaning is "gold. The word "avāpnuyāt" (should obtain) is connected with the word "nityaśaḥ" (constantly). || 57 ||

With the two verses beginning with *cara* and ending with *kṛtiḥ*, he teaches the nature of the Vidyā that grants desired results, its fruit, the sequence of its practice, and its visualization. In this context, *cara* refers to the letter *e*; *prāṇa* joined with *marut* refers to the letter *ā*.

The letter *ka* is joined with [the vowel *a*]. The letter *ya* is pervading (*vyāptam*). The vital breath (*prāṇa*) accompanied by the earth (*dharā*) is the letter *ka* joined with the letter *u*. The two voids (*vyoma*) conjoined with the wind (*marut*) are the two letters *ṇa* pronounced in close union (*suśleṣa*), joined with the letter *ā*. And the speed (*raya*) joined with the earth is the letter *ta* accompanied by the letter *u*. The moving one (*cara*) is the letter *e*.
The letter *ka* is *prāṇa*. "Vidyā" refers to the eight-syllabled mantra. She is of auspicious form, the declared embodiment of the goddess Sarvamaṅgalā. || 59 ||
With the verse beginning with "siddha," he teaches the essential nature of the Mātaṅgeśvarī-vidyā. In that context,
the three syllables of the Siddhasārasvata— namely, the first three syllables of the Siddhasārasvata mantra—
are also the very first syllables of the Mātaṅgeśvarī-vidyā.
Those three are the Vāgbhava, Hṛllekhā, and Śrī-bījas. "Mātaṅginyai" consists of four syllables.
"Svāhā" consists of two syllables. The first three elements, beginning with Vāgbhava, are reversed. That mantra is the Mātaṅgeśvarī-vidyā. || 60 ||
With these five verses beginning with "twelve" and ending with "smiling," [the text describes] the number of syllables of that vidyā and its limbs.
One whose body is fashioned by Māyā should constantly recite that [vidyā] at the rising of the sun.
Having been perfected by him through a thousand repetitions, she bestows everything. || 62 ||
Resembling a sapphire, radiant with red garments and ornaments, and brilliantly adorned with *saugandhika* flowers bound in her long, flowing braid. || 63 ||
She wore a garland of severed heads fashioned therefrom, beautified by clusters of pearls;
her feet were adorned with rings, bracelets, armlets, and anklets.
One should meditate upon the goddess of pure smiles, playing a great lute together with women who resemble her, while being praised from all sides by them. 65.
The second belongs to Mātaṅginī, and the third immediately after that;
then there should be Rasācara, Svaira, and Ambu, followed by Vātāgni.
*Rājyade*, *rājyalakṣmī*, and *hṛnmāyā*—these three, when arranged in reverse order, constitute the sixteen-syllable Vidyā of Rājyalakṣmī. (67)
It teaches the fruits for one who has mastered that vidyā, as well as the method of practicing the vidyā and the meditation upon the deity.

In this regard, this is the Mātaṅgeśvarī-vidyā. Having formed the limbs with *māyā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*) as before, one should perform the six-limbed assignment (*ṣaḍaṅganyāsa*) with *hṛllekhā* (the syllable *hrīṃ*). That is the vidyā. By means of that recitation (*japa*), this vidyā [bestows] everything.

The word "desired" (*vāñchitam*) is to be supplied [as the object]. In the first quarter of this verse, there is an excess of one syllable due to its divine nature. She is radiant with red garments and ornaments, adorned with red clothes and red jewels;
she wears a garland of severed heads fashioned from those [heads], a head-garland constructed of fragrant flowers.

With two verses beginning with "mātaṅgī" and ending with "samīritāḥ," he teaches the nature of the *rājyalakṣmī-vidyā* (the mantra of royal fortune), [describing her] as being accompanied by female attendants equal to herself in form, color, ornaments, and so forth, and as being [manifested] through the *śaktis*. Among those, regarding *mātaṅgī*:
By this half-verse, the following is stated:

the second and third syllables of the Mātaṅginī-vidyā, which consist of the *hṛllekhā* and *śrībīja*, become the first and second syllables of the Rājyalakṣmī-vidyā. [The syllable] *la* is formed by the *rasa* (sixth), *acara* (fourth), and *sva* (fifth) vowels.

O Mother, the letter *va* is endowed with a single *a* and a bindu; thus it becomes *vle*. This means that the letters *a* and *i*, representing wind and fire respectively, are each distinct. || 66 ||

"Rājyade rājyalakṣmī" consists of seven syllables; "sakāra" refers to the letter *sa* together with the heart (*hrīṃ*), *māyā* (*hrīṃ*), and the *visarga*. The phrase "three in reverse order" means that the first three syllables are taken in a retrograde sequence. Thus, it results in sixteen syllables.
Having meditated upon that *vijayā* vidyā, one should recite it daily and worship it;
when pleased, she bestows a kingdom upon the practitioner without delay. (68)
First the Praṇava, then Śrīpuṭā and Māyā, followed by Kamale;
after Kamalā, then Laya, and again the pair of Prasīda. (69)
O Maheśvarī, the first three [syllables] are declared as "Mahālakṣmyai Namaḥ";
this Vidyā of yours consists of twenty-seven syllables and constantly grants all desired objects.
The six limbs are indeed performed with the three seed-syllables repeated twice;
likewise, one should daily meditate upon the form of Vijayā and perform the recitation.
When the sun is situated in Libra, worship on the full moon day bestows all desired things, such as fame, fortune, wealth, health, victory, and so forth. (72)

With the verse beginning with "dhyātvā" (having meditated), he teaches that meditation, the sequence of its worship, and the attainment of the fruit for the worshipper. In that regard: "That Royal Fortune, Vijayā, whose form is eternally identical to that of Vijayānityā... (68).

With the two verses beginning with "praṇavam" and ending with "aniśam," he teaches the essential nature of the Mahālakṣmī-vidyā. In that context, "śrīpuṭāṃ māyām" means the *hṛllekhā* (hrīm) syllable encased by the *śrī*-bīja; "kamale" consists of three syllables; and "kamalāto laye" refers to Kamalā [dissolved] in dissolution.

Beyond the three syllables "laye" are the two syllables "prasīda. The two instances of "prasīda" constitute six syllables. The first triad refers to the *hṛllekhā* mantra encapsulated by the *śrībīja*. "Mahālakṣmyai namaḥ" consists of six syllables. "Maheśvarī" is the vocative address to the Goddess. [Thus,] there are twenty-seven syllables.
"Having come together," so much is meant. || 70 ||

With these two verses beginning with "bīja" and ending with "iṣṭadā," he teaches its limbs, its meditation, the sequence of its worship, its fruits, and the time for practicing that which grants the accomplishment of all desired objects. Therein:

By the half-verse beginning with "bīja," this is what is meant: the six limbs (*ṣaḍaṅga*) of this Vidyā are to be prescribed by repeating the second through fourth syllables twice. Furthermore, the meditation (*dhyāna*) is in the form of Vijayā;
that is to say, the meditation of Vijayānityā is also the meditation of this [Vidyā]. In the phrase "Vijayādi," the word "ādi" (etcetera) [indicates...]

The subject matter concerns various auspicious matters such as houses, fields, and so forth. When the sun is situated in Libra, having entered the zodiac sign of Libra, on the full moon day (pūrṇā). || 72 ||
p. 683) Jyāsaka, Dāhavahni, Svānabha, Haṃsa, Marudyuta, and Caṇḍatejas—these are the colors of Saṅkarṣaṇa that follow immediately thereafter. 73.

With the sky (vyoma) and fire (agni), the letter *ha*; with *kālī* (i) and *manthāna* (la); and with the swan (*haṃsa*) and *māyā* (ī)—this is declared to be the seventeen-syllable Vidyā beginning with Siddhalakṣmī. (74)
Having first performed the ancillary rites (aṅgas), one should constantly recite the vidyā;
in the morning, one should perform the libation (tarpaṇa) one thousand times, and its tenth part [at other times]. || 75 ||
When she is pleased during the daily worship of the practitioner while it rains, she bestows victory in battle and a prosperity that surpasses all others. (76)
It wards off ghosts, spirits, piśācas, epilepsy, and malevolent spells; it protects one on the road from the hardships of deserts and mountains. (77)
O Goddess of the gods, her meditation is equal to Maṅgalā herself in all auspicious matters;
listen as I shall describe, according to the rules, [her role] in the paths of battle and protection. 78.

With the two verses beginning with *jyāsaka* and ending with *akṣara*, he teaches the nature and other attributes of the *Siddhalakṣmī-vidyā*. Therein, by the words *jyāsaka-dāha-vahni-svāt*, it means that one should first utter the seed-syllable (*bīja*) consisting of the letters *ja*, *ra*, *ī*, and the *bindu*s; [the fifth letter is] *nabhaḥ* (the sky).

The letter *ma*. The *haṃsa* joined with the wind (*vāyu*) is the letter *ha* accompanied by the letter *ā*. "Caṇḍatejas" consists of four syllables. "Saṅkarṣaṇavarṇāḥ" refers to the four syllables of "Saṅkarṣaṇa.
The sky (*vyoman*) and fire (*agni*)—the letter *ha* joined with the vowel *ī*. These are the syllables in the *Kālīmanthāna*.
In "kālīmanthāne," there are five syllables; and "haṃsa" is the letter *ha* together with *māyā*, which is the visarga. Thus, they amount to seventeen syllables in total. || 74 ||

With these six verses beginning with "By the first" and ending with "certainly," he teaches her limbs, the sequence of her worship, the respective fruits thereof, her constant meditative worship (*nityopāsya-dhyāna*),
and the meditations for ritual application (*prayoga-dhyāna*) and so forth. Therein, by the first seed-syllable, as before, it is differentiated by its vowels.
"Ten parts of that" means one hundred times. She is Siddhalakṣmī.

In the phrase "kṛtyā and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to diseases, planetary afflictions, fears, and the like. "Of her" refers to Siddhalakṣmī. "O Queen of Gods" (Deveśī) is an address to the Goddess. In the auspicious application, she possesses a form identical to that of Maṅgalā.
Regarding the phrase "the path of battle, etc.," the word "etc.
[refers to her] having a hundred heads and three eyes, being terrifying to behold, endowed with two hundred hands, and accompanied by Śaktis who possess forms identical to her own. (79)
Having meditated upon her, who holds in her infinite hands the weapons desired by the practitioner, one should worship her in this manner; thus, one certainly attains everything that is wished for.
Then, having drawn eight lines— east-west, north-south,
south-east, and north-west— one should erase five by five [squares] in the outer paths, as well as one [square] in a single place.
Then, having combined the three [groups] within the corners of that [square],
one should write the sixteen syllables of the mantra and the name starting from the center.

The word "sound" (śabda) refers to the area adjacent to mountains, forests, and so forth. The phrase "hear" (śṛṇu) is to be construed with "meditation" (dhyāna) from the preceding context. "Terrifying" (bhayānakām) means having a fearsome form. "By infinite [beings]" (anantaiḥ) means, because of her divine nature, by those who are infinite. She is the one whose weapons fulfill the desires of the practitioner.
That is to say, in accordance with each respective application. || 80 ||

With these three verses beginning with "prāk" and ending with "nityaśaḥ," he teaches the construction of the wheel for daily worship and so forth. In that regard, the meaning is: having drawn eight lines with equal intervals; likewise, so that there is one [square] in each corner.

The meaning is that one square should remain [empty]. "Within that" means within the path (vīthī); "three" means three squares. This is what is intended: in the second path, one should erase [the squares] such that one square remains in the center in each direction. This refers to the center and so forth.
This is an adverbial modifier. The meaning is: "just as the first syllable is in the central square.

This refers to the remaining sixteen syllables of the mantra. The name—referring to the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and others—is to be placed, as before, within the seed-syllable written in the central square; that is, in the middle, as stated in the subsequent verse.
Because it will be explained later; the connection with the preceding [verse] is that one should "draw" according to the clockwise sequence.

In that wheel, this is the procedure for its construction: by striking eight sets of eight threads with equal intervals running east-west and north-south, one obtains a grid consisting of forty-nine squares.
Having made it a perfect square, one should combine five central squares in each of the twenty-four squares located in the outer rows for each direction; then,
within that, in the sixteen squares situated in the inner row, one should place one [mark] in each corner.
Having combined three squares each with the two squares situated on either side of them,

[there remain] seventeen remaining squares; in these, one should place the first seed-syllable together with the name of the person to be accomplished (*sādhya*) and so forth in the central square, and [the remaining syllables] in the eight squares located in the outer row surrounding it.
In the four outer compartments beginning with the one at the front, proceeding clockwise as before (p.
685), one should always worship her there in the center according to the clockwise sequence—namely Siddhalakṣmī—for the perpetual attainment of all desired goals. (83)
Sometimes the primordial Lalitā, possessing a male form and a body like that of Kṛṣṇa,
rendered the world helpless through her engagement with all women.
Then he became surrounded by his own powers known as the gopīs;
at that time, for the sake of diversion, he divided his own body into six parts.

The six mantras of these six [deities] bestow all desired objects when employed through the worship of yantras, fire-offerings (havana), recitation (japa), libations (tarpaṇa), and sprinkling (secanam). || 86 ||
They become endowed with fortune, splendor, glory, victory, and health.
Listen now to those six mantras in their proper sequence, along with their meditations, rites of worship, and applications. (87)
The great mantra known as Siddhagopālaka was thus uttered by the forest-dweller Sthirārasavyāpta; it consists of the two *praṇavas* with [the name] situated between them. (88)

Then, one should sequentially write the seventeen syllables of the Vidyā in order within the four corner squares of the outer path, starting from the northwest (vāyavya) and ending at the southwest (niṛti). || 83 ||

With these four verses beginning with *kadācit* and ending with *viniyogakaiḥ*, [the author] teaches that the Lalitā-vidyā is the very nature of Gopāla, along with its various forms, the fruits of its worship, and the introduction to the extraction of its mantra. Among those, the first is the Nityā named Lalitā.

Having a male form and a dark (kṛṣṇa) body, he is in the ultimate sense Kṛṣṇa himself; as before, Kṛṣṇa is accompanied by his eternal powers, such as *aṇimā* and the rest. By that body—meaning by those bodies—and by those mantras, the practitioners (*sādhakas*) become endowed with fortune, beauty, fame, victory, and health. This is the meaning.
This means "together with those employed in the light of meditation. In this verse, there is an excess of syllables in the first quarter due to its divine nature. || 87 ||

With the verse beginning with "sthirā," he teaches the nature of the Siddha-Gopāla mantra. In that context, it consists of the syllables *ga*, *la*, *ya*, *u*, and the bindu—forming a *kūṭa* (compound) shape—which are pervaded by the essences of the "Stable" (*sthira*) and the "Taste" (*rasa*). It is called the "Great Mantra" (*mahāmanu*) both by its designation and by its majesty.
Situated between two *praṇavas*, it is encapsulated by the *praṇava*. || 88 ||

By means of those five Kāma-mantras previously mentioned, one by one in sequence, there is what is called "encasement" (puṭana); therefore, through that encasement with those Bāṇa-mantras, [the rite] comes to be accomplished. || 89 ||
Thus, the great mantra named Sammohana became sevenfold;
the first is a mantra with five limbs, while the others possess six limbs.
One should perform the six limbs (ṣaḍaṅga) according to the rule by means of their respective seed-syllables and so forth;
then, one should worship [the deity] residing in the center of an eight-petaled lotus by skipping over the seventh.
Those yantras, containing their respective mantras in the center,
are to be worshipped in due order on the days of the week beginning with the Sun.
With these three verses beginning with "proktaiḥ" and ending with "kramāt," he teaches the nature of the sixfold Gopāla mantra, its ancillaries, and the sequence of its worship.
In that regard, "proktaiḥ" refers to what was stated in the seventh chapter, beginning with "sahaṃsa."

"By the first thirty-five [verses]" means by the two and a half verses beginning with the first; "from each one" means from each individual seed-syllable (*bīja*); "by name" refers to the names such as Kāmarāja and so forth, which were stated in the seventh chapter by the two and a half verses beginning with the first verse starting with "pathama," belonging to the aforementioned *kūṭa*.

Up to: "with arrows"—that is, with the mantras of the five arrows of the King of Desire (Kāmarāja); by those five seed-syllables of desire (*kāma*). Here, the letter *ca* is to be understood as inclusive; the pair [of *ca*s] signifies conjunction. Thus, according to the stated sequence, this is what is meant: the Great Mantra known as Siddhagopāla is encapsulated by the *praṇava* (the syllable *oṃ*).

The mantra: By encasing each of the five seed-syllables of desire (*kāmabīja*) with the Great Mantra (*mahāmanu*) in succession, there arise five mantras known as Kāmarāja-Gopāla, Manmatha-Gopāla, Kandarpa-Gopāla, Makarakeṭana-Gopāla, and Manobhava-Gopāla; together, these consist of three syllables each.

There are seven Gopāla mantras, including the first mantra; the meaning is that among these, the first is the Siddha-Gopāla mantra. It consists of five limbs (*pañcāṅgaka*), which means it is devoid of the eye-assignment (*netranyāsa*). The other six mantras are those beginning with Kāmarāja-Gopāla and so forth, [to be recited] with their respective seed-syllables (*bīja*) and the Great Mantra (*mahāmanu*).

The remainder [is as follows]: "they may be" (syuḥ) because they are divine; that is to say, they should be so. "According to rule" (yathāvidhi) means by a sequence distinct from the six long vowels. Among these seven, one should place any one of them in the center of the eight petals. || 91 ||

With these three verses beginning with "yantrāṇi" and ending with "avāpnuyāt," he teaches their yantras, the method of worship on the seven days of the week according to the nature of time, as well as the specific offerings and other details; therein, those [yantras] are known by names such as Siddhagopāla and others.
With their centers joined by their respective mantras and their pericarp-inscribed with their own individual mantras,
these [yantras] bestow all desired objects constantly when worshipped on the days of the week with milk, honey, ghee, rice,
milk-porridge, coconuts, and plantains mixed with sugar. (93)
One should offer the food offering (naivedya) at the gates in sequence for the attainment of desired goals;
by means of these seven [offerings] thus described, one shall obtain everything desired. || 94 ||
One should meditate upon him as being ruddy, six-armed, playing a flute, and holding a noose, a goad, a lotus, a sugarcane bow, and flower-arrows, together with his Śaktis.
By rubbing the root of the *suvarṇapuṣpī* with its own juice and applying it to the heart, throat, and *ājñā*-cakra, one shall behold the deity. (96)
Ugragandhā, nīlī, combined with the fruit of dhātakī, āragvadha, muṇḍinī, śākoṭa, and the root of the jambu tree. (97)

Regarding the seven: for those [deities] beginning with Siddhagopāla, the phrase "bestowing all desired objects" is connected with the word "worship" (*pūjā*) in the preceding context. "Constantly" means at every occasion. "With milk, honey, ghee, and food" means with milk, honey, and foods accompanied by ghee; "with sugar" means combined with sugar-candy.
With coconuts, milk, and so forth. || 94 ||

With the verse beginning with "aruṇam," he teaches their visualization (*dhyāna*). Therein, the color is reddish (*aruṇa*). He holds a flute with his two lower hands. Here, the four weapons, beginning with the noose (*pāśa*), are [placed] starting from the top, in the sequence left-right-left-right.
"By the Śaktis wearing the dress of cowherd girls," that is to say. || 95 ||

With the verse beginning with "suvarṇa," he teaches the prescription for the medicinal application of the means for the direct perception of all deities. In that regard, the medicine known as *suvarṇapuṣpī* is to be understood as previously described; [it is to be used] with its own water.
As before; [the application] from the heart, throat, and *ājñā* [centers], as previously [stated]. Herein, this procedure for practice is to be understood from the mouth of the Guru. || 96 ||

With these three verses beginning with *ugragandhām* and ending with *ātmavān*, [the author] teaches the direct departure of the deities at will, or [their removal] by means of the application of medicinal herbs. Therein, [he begins] with *ugragandhām*.
By the verse beginning with "karṇikāri" and so forth, there are seven medicinal herbs; by the [following] verse, there are ten medicinal herbs.
The names of those herbs are to be understood from the mouth of the venerable teacher (*ārādhya*).
"Equal" means that all [the herbs] are in equal proportions. "With white" means with sugar (*śarkarā*). Those three [substances] are smeared with that.
One should powder equal parts of *karṇikāra*, *haṃsapadī*, *vārāhī*, *mṛgarājaka*, *koraṇṭa*, the root of *pippala*, and the three myrobalans (*triphalā*). (98)

Having burnt it with ghee, honey, and clarified butter, and having smeared those three [parts] with that, the self-possessed one, meditating upon it, shall become identical with it within a few days. 99.
The pervasion consisting of Sadāśiva has been correctly proclaimed; by the constant refinement of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self. (100)
Thus ends the thirty-fourth chapter in the *Śrīkādimata*, among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.

[Now follow] those three beginning with the command (*ājñā*) smeared with the seventeen medicinal herbs; he is composed of that, composed of the deity, and possessed of self through the stability of meditative cultivation. 99.
In this chapter, one verse has been omitted after the twenty-seventh verse.

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete tantra known as the venerable *Kādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The thirty-fourth chapter, dedicated to the illumination of the *liṅga* and the yantra, is thus fully concluded. Oṃ tat sat.
Regarding the number of verses: in the thirty-fourth chapter, two hundred and thirty-six explanatory verses are declared,
and eight yantras are indeed contained therein.
The Thirty-Fifth Chapter.
Now, hear the mental cultivation regarding the sixteen Nityās as being one's own self,
by which the accomplishment of identity with them certainly becomes manifest.
The Guru is the primordial Śakti, considered to consist of reflective awareness (vimarśa);
the novelty of his body manifests as the [nine] apertures. || 2 ||
The offering goddesses (balidevyas) are her own manifestations; the fifth is Janakātmikā.
Kurukullā shall be the mother, and the oceans are the human goals (puruṣārthas). (3)
In the preceding thirty-fifth chapter, having taught the applications for the worldly wonders of those perfected in the mantras of the sixteen Nityās,
[the author] subsequently [teaches] the [realization of] the sixteen Nityās and their respective retinue of Śaktis and so forth as one's own self.
He teaches the residual impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth, as well as the varieties of the *prastāra* (grid) and other matters,
through the thirty-fifth chapter consisting of one hundred verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "the accomplishments" (*siddhayaḥ*).
[He does so] by means of twenty-three [verses] beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "is elaborated."

By means of verses, he teaches the underlying intention (*vāsanā*) for the sequence beginning with the worship of the Guru and ending with the display of mudrās, as well as for the installation (*nyāsa*), recitation (*japa*), libation (*tarpaṇa*), fire-oblation (*homa*), consecration (*abhiṣeka*), ritual offerings (*upacāra*), and so forth, pertaining to the nature of the Nityās together with their retinues; therein [he teaches] the sixteen Nityās along with their retinues and other attendants.

Regarding its being one's own self (*svātmatva*), that is, the nature of the Self as it is perceived in the form of the body, senses, mind, vital breath (*prāṇa*), and so forth: by means of which latent impression (*vāsanā*) is there the accomplishment of being composed of that [Self], the accomplishment of eternal selfhood? Without the initial reflective awareness (*ādyavimarśa*), not even the slightest thing can be clearly manifest, for it would be an object of perception (*pratyakṣa*)—that is, within the range of immediate experience.

Because it is impossible to know [it through other means]. The meaning is that its nature is self-cognizable (*svasaṃvedya*). It consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*), having reflective awareness alone as its body. This is what is being said: the Guru is indeed Śakti, whose body is primordial reflective awareness. Of that Guru, "by way of the apertures" means by way of the nine apertures. This is what is being said, just as...
Just as through the apertures [of the body] there occurs the grasping of what is to be accepted and the relinquishing of what is not to be accepted,

so too, by the glance of the Guru whose ultimate reality is discernment (*vimarśa*), practitioners engage with what is beneficial and desist from what is harmful. In this context, the triad consisting of the two ears and speech is divine.

The tradition holds that the two eyes, the generative organ, and the three upper [limbs] constitute the human state. Having produced the cognition of "that" in what is "not that," the powers (*śaktis*) lead one astray.
The fifth is Vārāhī, because she is the fifth among the group beginning with Brāhmī; her nature is that of the progenitor.
The power that paralyzes the subduing [of enemies] for practitioners, like a father;
Kurukullā is the mother. (p.
690) The body shall be Ratnadvīpa, possessing freshness through its elements and hairs.
His volitions are the wish-fulfilling trees, and his own supports are remembered as the seasons.
The self of time, facing westward by means of the wheel of planets, asterisms, and zodiac signs, thereby becomes oriented toward the east; anything else has been explained to you in private.
The knower is one's own self, knowledge is the precious [reality], and the object of knowledge resides externally;
the worship of the Śrīcakra is said to be the unification of these three.
The meaning is that Śakti is the form of the Mother; she is the power that bestows desired objects upon practitioners like a mother.

This is what is being said: when one contemplates [Śakti] as one's own self, merit and demerit (dharma-adharma) are transferred into the body, senses, intellect, and so forth, by virtue of being portions of the progenitor and the progenitress.

One should meditate on [the self] as consisting of Vārāhī and Kurukullā. The goals of human endeavor are dharma and the rest. The word "tu" (but/rather) serves for emphasis. The oceans are so called because of their vastness and their lack of end. The body is an island of jewels (*ratnadvīpa*), for its nature as a body consists in the perception of one's own self. Its "newness" consists in its being composed of nine sections (*navakhaṇḍa*).

"Of the island" means up to that point. By means of the elements, hairs, and so forth—namely, vitality (*ojas*), semen (*śukra*), marrow (*majjā*), bone (*asthi*), fat (*medas*), flesh (*māṃsa*), hair (*roma*), skin (*tvak*), and blood (*rudhira*)—in the sequence starting from the center and proceeding eastward;
"wishes" are the *kalpa*-trees. This is because one engages in action preceded by intention (*saṅkalpa*).

Because the fruit is accomplished. By the ninety-nine verses beginning with "Their own supports are in the sixteenth chapter called Viśuddha," etc., the locations situated within the *suṣumnā*— from the *mūlādhāra* up to the *ājñā*, which were declared to be the dwelling places of the *ḍākinīs* and others— are [described].

Up to this point: the meaning is that the seasons, beginning with spring (*vasanta*), consist of the *ṛtu*s because they are inferred to be of the nature of time through the conjunction of the moon and sun—represented by *iḍā* and *piṅgalā*—within the *suṣumnā*; thus, those things which have their locus in those [channels] possess the nature of the seasons.
This is established by means of the wheel of planets, constellations, and zodiac signs (*graharkṣarāśicakra*).

By means of the wheel of the zodiac together with the planets and constellations; [he is] "one whose nature is time" (kalātmā), meaning one whose essential form is time, facing west—that is, facing the western direction—because the celestial sphere faces westward. For that reason, [there is] an orientation toward the east.
This means that, with respect to the orientation toward the deity who is the essence of time, the practitioner faces the east; this is the point.

The other [aspect] is the real nature of time, which was explained in the thirty-sixth chapter by the first half of the fortieth verse, beginning with the word "time" (*kāla*). *Mithaḥ* means "in secret" or "in a very private place."

"Another [teaching] has been told to you. By the word "in secret" (*mithaḥ*), this is what is meant: the latent impression (*vāsanā*) regarding the self-nature of the senses and so forth, which corresponds to the nature of the respective mantras and objects, has been told to you.
Here, for each of the goddesses beginning with Kālacakreśvarī, [the teaching is given] by means of the fortieth verse.
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the nine elements are explained in the fifth chapter. || 5 ||
The Knower is one's own Self, meaning the worshipper; knowledge is one's own *arghya*, meaning the material for worship. (p.
691) "In the Śrīcakra, the Siddhis are said to be the Rasas together with Niyati."
The waves are merit and demerit, and the Mothers are remembered as Brāhmī and the others. || 7 ||

The elements, the senses, and the mind are indeed the first; then, in sequence, the eternal *akalā*, the organs of action, their objects, and the defects—these eight should be known as the powers (*śaktayaḥ*).
The fourteen channels (nāḍīs) are declared to be the powers (śaktis) beginning with Kṣobhiṇī;
the ten vital airs (vāyus) are fully described as the powers beginning with Sarvasiddhi.
The ten fires are proclaimed to be [the deities] beginning with Sarvajña, while the powers (śaktis) are indeed said to be,
in their respective order, cold, heat, pleasure, pain, and desire.
The object of knowledge (*jñeya*) is situated outside the knower—this is the ellipsis. That is to say, the Śrīcakra is that which is to be worshipped;

worship is that which belongs to the Śrīcakra. The unification of these—the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge—is by virtue of their being of the nature of consciousness (*bodha*). This is what is meant: [it is not as if they were] distinct from one's own self.
Among these three—the cognizer, the cognition, and the cognizable—which are perceived as constituting one's own self-nature:

the cognizer, being perceived as one's own self, is the worshipper; the cognition, being perceived as belonging to oneself, is the instrument of worship, namely the *arghya* offering; and the cognizable, being perceived as external to oneself, is the object of worship.
The Śrīcakra. Their worship consists in their non-separation from the nature of consciousness.

In the Śrīcakra, the "attainments" (siddhis) are the powers such as *aṇimā* and so forth. The "flavors" (*rasas*) are the nine beginning with the erotic (*śṛṅgāra*). "Accompanied by Niyati" means joined with the power of the attainment of Niyati; thus, taken together, there are ten powers.

The waves are hunger, thirst, grief, delusion, old age, and death; merit and demerit, these two types of karma, make eight. The elements, the senses, and the mind—namely, the five elements, the ten senses, and the mind together with them, making sixteen—and the objects of the organs of action.
Speech, grasping, movement, excretion, and pleasure; the defects are wind and the others;

these have been declared in the twenty-seventh chapter—so it is said—and were fully explained in the previous chapter. Here, the extremely secret meanings should be seen in my *Vāsanāvimarśinī*. There are ten fires and seven in the elements.

Regarding the defects (*doṣa*), it is stated in this chapter that they are three, and together with the others, they amount to ten; this will be fully explained later in the fiftieth verse beginning with "fire" (*agni*). The qualities (*guṇa*) are *sattva* and the rest.
The subtle elements (*tanmātra*) are sound, touch, form, taste, and smell, which consist of the five principles (*tattva*). Of these—
The state of being the one whose arrows are flowers exists in the beginning as a manifest form and in the end as the form of Puruṣa.

The essence of the mind is the sugarcane bow; because it impels the senses—which are like arrows whose ultimate nature consists of sense-objects—toward their respective objects, it is the [bow] for the senses and their objects.

And from the mind, in its form of active engagement (p. 692), there arise the powers beginning with Vaśinī; the subtle elements (tanmātras) are the flower-arrows. The mind becomes the sugarcane bow, and attachment is declared to be the noose. || 11 ||
O lady of excellent complexion, hatred is said to be the goad in due order;
[the principles of] unmanifest nature, ego, and the Great One (mahat) follow in reverse order.
The goddesses beginning with Kāmeśvarī are [the powers], while Sambit is known as Kāmeśvara;
one’s own self alone is declared to be the deity, Lalitā, whose form is the universe. 13.
The redness is that very reflective awareness; worship is the contemplation [of it];
perfection is the state of one-pointed mind; and the mudrā is the contemplation of its sovereign power. (14)
Even in the state of movement, there is metaphorical designation, absorption in that [state], and vigilance;
however, the applications consist in the destruction of conceptual constructions within one's own self by means of the cause.

Because both possess the nature of being active agents, they are mentioned separately; therefore, there is no fault of redundancy. This means that the *pāśa* (bond) consists of the principle of *rāga* (attachment); their status as binders is due to their commonality. || 11 ||

Hatred (*dveṣa*) would be the goad, because it acts as the means of restraint toward that which is to be hated. "O lady of excellent complexion" (*varavarṇini*) is a vocative. "Having the forms of the unmanifest, ego, and the great principle" (*avyaktāhaṅkṛtimahadākārāḥ*); the meaning is that, in reverse order, the ego has the form of the Great Principle (*mahat*), and [the Great Principle] has the form of the Unmanifest (*avyakta*) through its sequence. Here, by the word "unmanifest," the principle of primordial nature (*prakṛti-tattva*) is meant.
By the word "mahat" (the Great), the principle of intellect (*buddhitattva*) is expressed; by the word "ahaṅkṛti" (I-making), the principle of egoity (*ahaṅkāratattva*) is expressed.

Consciousness is Kāmeśvara; that is to say, consciousness which consists of all things is Kāmeśvara. Having dissolved his own self—which consists of the manifold conceptual constructions of the universe—into its own essential nature, that reality shines forth as his very self.

The deity (devatā) is so called because of her luminosity; she is Lalitā because of her faultless form; she is Viśvavigrahā because her form consists of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge. Her "contemplation" (vimarśa) is the contemplation of one's own self—that is to say, the continuous reflection upon one's own self. This is what is meant: of everything...

Because of attachment to one's own self, and because of the very absence of stability in the mind due to attachment to some particular object, that attachment is "redness" (lauhitya). This is the contemplation (bhāvanā), which is the accomplishment of the contemplation of one's own self; it means, in short, the fruit of the meditative worship (upāsti). The particle *tu* is used for emphasis.
"State of non-dual-mindedness" means that there is no stability in the practice regarding one's own nature (*svātmatva*).

"Mudrās" refers to all mudrās, such as the *yonimudrā* and others. "Contemplation of the manifestation" (*vaibhavabhāvana*) refers to the contemplation of the Self (*ātman*) in the manner that will be explained later on. "Even in the state of movement" means even during times when there is no continuous mental connection (*ananusandhāna*).

The meaning is "even in dreams and so forth. Because of being composed of that [reality], "heedfulness" (*apramattatā*) is the stability in the state of one's own true nature. This is what is meant: "O Satī" is the vocative; since non-honor (*asatkāra*) is itself a form of ritual service (*upacāra*), therefore, in the case of *Satī*, the vocative is an act of honor (*satkāra*).

Yantras and mantras everywhere serve as the means for establishing steadiness in one's own self-nature; likewise, the worship of the Goddess during the junctions of the day, and immersion at the beginning, middle, and end [of the ritual]. (16)
But those other powers that proceed from the wheel on all sides are declared to be the causes of the manifold conceptual constructions of the universe.
Nyāsa is the conceptualization of one's own self as the body of the deity; japa is correctly described as the contemplation of the form of identity with that [deity]. (18)
The dissolution of all conceptual constructions within one's own self is considered the state of the human being;
the cultivation of their mutual interpenetration constitutes their satiation. (19)

That itself is the ritual practice (*upacāra*). "Applications" (*prayogāḥ*) are specific actions that accomplish what is desired and ward off what is undesired. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. Because of the cause of conceptual constructions—namely, non-discrimination (*aviveka*), which is the cause of conceptual constructions—with respect to one's own self, which consists of reflective awareness (*vimarśa*): this is what is meant.

The destruction of evil tendencies occurs through the impression (*vāsanā*) of one's own true nature (*svātmatva*). "Practices" (*prayoga*) refers to the means for performing practices; that is to say, the meaning is both *yantras* (diagrams) and *mantras*.
