"In all cases" (*sarvatra*) means in the context of one's own true nature, that is, within the impression of one's own true nature. That which is the means for stability (*sthairya-sādhana*) is the cause of stability (*sthairya-karaṇa*).

This is what is meant: *vimarśa* (reflective awareness) is the means for establishing the stability of the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of one's own self-nature. It is the determination of the identity between one's own self and the universal self, established through the sentences of the *yantras* and *mantras*, which serve as the ultimate practical application for stabilizing that very impression.

Because they consist of reflective discernment (*vimarśa*) through the preeminence of definition (*nirūpaṇa*), they are the means for establishing the stability of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*).
In that regard, he will explain later on how the Śrīvidyā— which consists of the totality of mantras— is defined by the determination of its non-differentiation from them.

Since the Śrīcakra, which consists of all yantras, is also of that same nature, it is stated in the *Nityāṣoḍaśikārṇava*: "Time, the abodes, the elements, and the nine cakras in succession [constitute it].
Its beginning, middle, and end are submerged—that is, excluded—by virtue of its continuous, pervasive form.

This refers to the contemplation of one's own non-limitation. What is meant is this: the worship of the Goddess during the junctions (saṃdhyās) is performed within the very self-limitation of one's own self. "The other secret Yoginīs" refers to those powers (śaktis) who move within the Cakra, reside in the Śrīcakra, and are described in the chapter on the manifestation of Mantras.

The particle *tu* signifies conjunction (*samuccaye*). "Causes of all conceptual constructions" means the powers (*śakti*) that bring about the perception of the various transformations of the universe. The particle *tu* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*). "Of one's own self" (*svātmanaḥ*) means of oneself.
This is what is being said: the state of the deity’s form within one's own body is *nyāsa*.
The cultivation of one's own true nature through the meditation on identity with that [Śrīvidyā], both as being of the essence of Śrīvidyā and as being composed of the Mātṛkās,
is correctly described [on page 694] as the firm setting of delusion, ignorance, and other sufferings within the Self.
The consecration (abhiṣeka), however, is the Vidyā; the Self is the great support of all. || 20 ||
The absence of limiting adjuncts (upādhi) is declared to be "instruction" (upadeśa);
freedom from partiality is "the sacrificial fee" (dakṣiṇā), and steadfastness is called "service" (śuśrūṣā). || 21 ||
The observation of the transformation of time in the form of lunar days (tithi)—these fifteen are eternal; thus have the latent impressions (vāsanās) been described. (22)
In the fourth chapter, the nature of Śrīvidyā as the form of Kāmakalā is [explained], and in the first chapter,

the nature of the mantras as consisting of the Mātṛkā through the removal of the twenty defects; and that is for the purpose of the contemplation of the essential nature of the arising and resting [of consciousness] as declared in the twenty-sixth chapter.

"Setting" (astamaya) means rest. This is what is meant: the perpetual dissolution of the world's conceptual constructions within the mere existence of their own nature—just as ornaments and the like [dissolve] into the mere existence of gold—is "oblation" (homa). Of all those aforementioned [constructions].
The cultivation of mutual interpenetration and the cultivation of mutual oneness; "satiating" means the satisfaction born from the experience of one's own self pervading all forms.
[This occurs] because of being possessed by desire, which [otherwise causes] the sufferings of delusion, ignorance, and so forth.
Delusion (*moha*) is the absence of knowledge regarding what ought to be done and what ought not to be done; ignorance (*ajñāna*) is the attainment of a state devoid of consciousness.

The word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to objects such as distorted knowledge (*anyathājñāna*) and rashness (*sāhasa*). Because there is a lack of reflective awareness within the self regarding the internal and other types of suffering that have arisen, it [the self] exists in a form determined to be one with those [sufferings].
Setting (astamaya) is tranquility (upaśānti). Firmly means being incapable of sprouting again. "Tur" denotes a distinction.

It is the support of all because of its identity [with them]. It is great because of its pervasiveness and its possession of all powers. The limiting adjuncts (upādhi) are the qualities such as *sattva* which cause the modifications of the body and so forth; it is of these that [the Lord] is the support.
The word *tu* (but) is used for emphasis. The ellipsis to be supplied is "of one's own self" (*svātmanaḥ*), meaning a state of being devoid [of qualities]. What is intended to be said is this:

the instruction is that there should be a cultivation of the realization that [the Self] is not to be smeared by the qualities such as *sattva*, nor by the modifications produced from them, just as the sky is not smeared by dust, mud, and the like. *Dakṣiṇā*.

The state of being free from duality toward the Guru arises from the surrender of one's self to him. Service to the Guru means steadfastness in the knowledge of the Self. The perception of the transformation of the bright and dark fortnights in the form of lunar days (*tithi*), and the conceptualization of the white and dark portions within the lunar orb—these are the eternal principles (*nityā*).

The fifteen [deities] beginning with Kāmeśvarīnityā and the rest are as follows. This is what is meant: since time, consisting of the lunar days (*tithi*), is the cause for the increase and decrease of the white and black digits (*kalā*) in the lunar orb, therefore the Nityās beginning with Kāmeśvarī have the nature of time in the form of the lunar days. Furthermore:
The lunar days (tithis) consist of intermediate periods of time; by means of these intermediate periods, the phenomenal world—characterized as the lunar orb—is brought into manifestation.
Such is their function.

The meaning of the tradition is that the worship of [the Self] is taught through the contemplation of its non-difference from one's own essential nature, which consists of the Great Eternal (Mahānityā). The fingers beginning with the little finger—earth and the other elements are considered to correspond to the little finger and the others in sequence. (p. 695)
Their state of proliferation arises through various modes of mutual differentiation among them.
O you who are praised by the wise, may that path which leads to the supreme state be attained by me;
may it not be lost to me in this world of mortals.
Then, having gone to the forest, he performed penance; thereafter, having reached the goal, he became a protector of the world and a refuge for all beings.
Who are you? Do not think of me; do not speak of me; do not be near me. O Agni, do not let my life-breath depart;
do not reveal it to anyone. May this [deed] be hidden from view. 26.

Of the five elements whose nature is the fingers: by means of the various modes of mutual interpenetration—that is, the various distinctions in the modes of mutual connection—their "proliferation" (*prapañcatā*) is the specific yoga of the distinctions between the forms of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of the mudrās of one's own self; this is their proliferation. || 23 ||

With these three verses, beginning with "Of Lalitā" and ending with "the manifestation thereof," written in a scrambled order of syllables, he teaches the meaning expressed by the syllables of the primordial Lalitā-vidyā. Therein, of Lalitā...

This refers to the third section (*tārtīyakhaṇḍa*) of the *Śrīvidyā*. "The meaning of the whole" (*sakalārtha*) means the meaning of the word *sakala* as delimited by three [syllables]. "By the remainder" means by the [final] syllable. The particle *tu* is used for conjunction (*samuccaye*).
By that [remainder], the meanings of the parts according to the aforementioned method [arise] from the state of being the aggregate of the third section. This...

The nature of the meaning which is to be explained immediately hereafter: "the entire world without exception" means the whole universe in its collective form (*samaṣṭi-rūpa*), that is to say, in its individualized form (*vyaṣṭi-rūpa*). "Consisting of *hṛllekhā*" means composed of power (*śaktimaya*).
"O Sovereign Lady" (*īśvarī*) is an address to the Goddess. "Of her" refers to that *hṛllekhā*. The particle "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. This is the meaning.
It is expressed by the syllable. The word "tu" (but/then) is used for emphasis. It has been taught in the verse immediately following.
It is concealed in all tantras—that is, in those other than this tantra—because of its extreme secrecy. Through "vyoman," the first syllable of space, there is the manifestation of space.
Because its nature is vibration (*sphuraṇa*). Independence means being without dependence on the manifestation of anything else.

Being "swallowed" means [being absorbed] into one's own essential nature. By means of the second syllable, *agni*, because even fire is of the nature of being swallowed through identity with it. The reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) belongs to those two, which consist of manifestation and swallowing.
The ultimate union of identity (*tādātmya-paramārtha-melana*) is the determination of the reflective awareness of that identity (*tādātmya-vimarśa-nirṇīti*).

This is what is meant: by means of the syllable of space (*vyoma*) situated within the *hṛllekhā*, one's own self possesses the nature of light; by means of the syllable of fire (*vahni*), it possesses the nature of being the devourer (*grāsa*).

By means of the fourth vowel, which consists of the union of Śiva and Śakti and takes the form of the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) of both, and by means of the *bindu* (the point) which is its very essence— the ultimate nature of that [fourth vowel]—
there is effected both the absence of any perception of duality therein and the definitive determination of their unity. || 26 ||
(p. 696) Now, the procedure for the creation of mantras is explained;
it brings about a distinction between those who have successfully mastered the potency of mantras and others. (27)
Mantras consisting of a single syllable are known as *piṇḍas*; those of two syllables are remembered as *kartarīs*.
Starting from three syllables up to nine syllables, they are called *bījas*. (28)
From the eighth mantra up to the twentieth, there are twenty mantras;
beyond that, the garlands have ascended, and no further distinction exists among them. (29)
In the same way, there is a difference between the *piṇḍa* and the *kartarī* mantras in terms of their seed-syllables (*bīja*).
In the case of mantras consisting of words, there is a difference in the number of those words; hear their numbers in due order. (30)
Six, twenty-four, and likewise one hundred and twenty;
seven hundred and twenty, together with forty. (31)
Now, by means of these four verses beginning with "atha" and ending with "kramāt," [the author] explains the threefold nature of the mantras starting from the *piṇḍa* and ending with the *mālā*,
as well as their manifold forms through the arrangement of syllables and words, and their respective numbers.

He teaches this together with its introduction. In that regard, "those well-versed in the potency of mantras" refers to those who have attained mastery through the knowledge of the potency of the mantras to be taught in this chapter; "others" refers to those devoid of the accomplishment of the knowledge of the potency of mantras. "Piṇḍas" means by name; they are the *kartarīs*.

As before, [they are designated] by name. "Seed-syllables" (bījakāḥ) refers to mantras known as seeds. "Mantras" (mantrakāḥ) is as before, by name. "Garlands" (mālāḥ) refers to garland-mantras. Regarding those garlands: the meaning is that they do not exist in that very way. Of those divisions, in sequence—
The remainder [of the sequence] is from the varieties of the three-syllable mantra up to the varieties of the nine-syllable mantra. || 30 ||

With these three verses beginning with "ṣaḍ" and ending with "samunnayet," [the author] explains the sevenfold class of mantras designated as seed-syllables (bīja), starting from the three-syllable mantra up to the nine-syllable mantra.

He teaches the sequence of numbers produced by the conceptualization of the arrangement of syllables. In that regard, these are the divisions of the six-syllable mantra. This is what is meant: by multiplying one by two and three, the number six arises; such are the divisions of the three-syllable [mantra].
The meaning is "twenty-four" because of its divine nature; that is to say, of the four-syllable mantra.

Having multiplied the six varieties of the three-syllable mantra by four, the number twenty-four is obtained—this is the meaning. "One hundred joined with twenty" refers to the fifty varieties of the five-syllable mantra.
The meaning is that [the number] is produced by multiplying the variations of the four-syllable [mantra] by five (120).
"Seven hundred and twenty" means seven hundred plus twenty (720);
that is to say, the variations of the six-syllable mantra.
Subsequently, there are five thousand and forty thousand;
then three hundred and twenty, combined with three hundred thousand. (32)
The number of divisions of these seven [treatises] is thus sixty-two thousand eight hundred and eighty; by means of these, one should calculate the others.
O Goddess, listen to the sequence for their arrangement according to the proper order;
by means of these very [syllables], one should deduce the various divisions of the mantra-words in succession.
Having drawn two horizontal lines, one should then write four vertical lines below and five above them in sequence; thus, there are ten straight-lined squares in total.
The meaning is that the divisions of the five-syllable mantra, when divided by six, result in this number.
"Endowed with forty" refers to the five thousand divisions of the seven-syllable mantra;
as before, the meaning is that the divisions of the six-syllable mantra, when divided by seven, result in this number (5040). Hereafter—
This refers to the number of variations of the eight-syllable mantra. The meaning is forty thousand three hundred and twenty (40,320).
As before, this is the number obtained by dividing the variations of the seven-syllable mantra by eight. Then:

This refers to the number of variations of the nine-syllable mantra. "Endowed with three hundred thousand" means it consists of three hundred thousand, sixty-two thousand, eight hundred and eighty— that is,
three hundred thousand plus sixty-two thousand, eight hundred, and eighty (362,880).
The meaning is that the numbers are produced by dividing the previously mentioned varieties of the eight-syllable [mantra] by nine.

In this manner, according to the stated method, one obtains the numbers for the seven [groups] ranging from three syllables up to nine syllables; by means of those numbers, one finds the other numbers for the varieties of ten syllables and so forth. || 33 ||

With these ten verses beginning with "prastāra" and ending with "coditā," he teaches the sequence of the *prastāra* (matrix) for those various arrangements of mantra-syllables. In this context, "eteṣām" refers to these variations; "devī" is a vocative address; "etaiḥ" means by these methods; and "eva" is used for emphasis.

"Mantrapadabhedān" means the distinctions between the words within the mantras. "Triryyagrekhādvayaṃ" refers to two sets of three lines, meaning two pairs of lines—one on the left and one on the right—with an interval of one finger-breadth (*ekāṅgulāntarāla*) between them. "Tatra" means there, in the middle of those two lines. "Adhordhvāḥ" means vertical; because they are divine, they take the form of being below and above—this is the meaning. There are four such lines.
The meaning is that the space between each finger [of the hand] should be one unit; this is the method for the arrangement of the yantra according to the distinctions of the three-syllable [mantra].

In the case of the arrangement according to the distinctions of four syllables and so forth, up to ten, one should draw five, six, seven, eight, nine, and ten lines respectively, all straight in form. Below that—

One should extend the lines below that [point] for as many finger-breadths (aṅgula) as the respective number; having drawn that same number of horizontal lines, one should inscribe the numbers within them. (36)
In these rows of squares situated on the left and right, one should fill them with the prescribed numbers in sequence, starting from two and increasing by two at each step.
By this [method], one should fill in the remaining digits in all other places according to the sequence;
in the first section of the second row, one should complete the rest.

One should extend the vertical lines above and below; up to the number of finger-breadths corresponding to those respective [divisions], and up to the number of finger-breadths corresponding to the number of those respective variations. Having drawn that many horizontal lines as well,

The meaning is: having drawn that many vertical lines from the ends of the second horizontal line previously drawn, and having drawn vertical lines at intervals of one finger-breadth (*aṅgula*) from the starting point of the second horizontal line previously drawn according to the number of those respective divisions; [then,] in those squares, the mark of the first syllable.

The first number corresponds to the second syllable, and the second number corresponds to the second [syllable]; in this manner, it continues further on, with each number representing the count of the syllables.
This is what is meant: one should first draw four lines—east-west and north-south.

By striking [the grid] in a sequence of seven in a horizontal manner, six rows consisting of three compartments each are formed. In those rows, one should write the six variations of the three-syllable mantra.
The same applies hereafter.

Having arranged rows below one another, equal in number to the specific syllables of the horizontal form, and having conceived therein the various divisions according to their respective counts, one should write those divisions in their respective places— meaning, within these squares situated on the left and right. This refers to the rows of squares, that is, within the sequences of the squares, in due order.

"From top to bottom" means from the first cell downwards, that is, in each successive row. "In pairs" means by way of two rows at a time; that is, having designated one section for each. "Enjoined" means those which serve as indicators of the number of syllables. This is what is meant: [the arrangement proceeds] in this manner.
In the six rows consisting of three horizontal triplets of squares, having conceived each section according to the sequence of two rows below the six lines,
one should place the first number in the very first square of the first row and the first section.

In the first of the two rows of the second section, one should place the second number in the first square; likewise, in the first of the two rows of the third section, one should place the third number in the first square. In this manner, one should place the six letters in their respective positions according to this sequence throughout all other instances.
This refers to the placement of each respective variety from four syllables up to nine syllables; what is meant is that,
in the expansion (*prastāra*) of varieties from four syllables up to nine syllables,
the number of those respective varieties is divided by the number of the varieties of those respective syllables.
Having conceived each individual section by means of rows numbering according to their respective results,
one should place the first number in the very first square of the rows of the first section,
and likewise [the second number] in the second and subsequent squares of that section's row.
In the second and subsequent [rows] as well, one should fill in the remaining [syllables] in the same way within the segments;
likewise, one should write the remaining [syllables] in the third row in this very manner. (39)
In the same manner, one should write [the numbers] from the fourth up to the ninth in the horizontal rows;
thus, the numbers are arranged everywhere in a sequence that has not been previously practiced.

In the first square, one should fill the squares starting from the second with the numbers in sequence; likewise, in the row arranged according to the form of the successive squares, one should fill the indicated numbers in the order of ascending and descending. In the second row, this applies to each individual row.
In the vertical row consisting of the second square,

one should fill in the remaining [numbers] in the first section with the digits not already written in the first section, as before; and having likewise determined the intermediate sections, one should proceed in each individual section that constitutes those respective intermediate parts.

One should fill in the remaining digits by means of a single-digit sequence; likewise, one should fill in the remaining [digits] in the subsequent sections. Furthermore, in the second and following sections, one should likewise determine the intermediate sub-sections as before.

The meaning is that one should fill in all the numbers written immediately after each number starting from the first row of each respective section. In the third row—that is, in the row consisting of the third cells of each successive row arranged in vertical order—the word "tu" (but/and) serves as a conjunction; [one should fill them] with the remaining [numbers].
By means of the numbers written in each section within the first and second squares; the word "tu" (but) is used for emphasis.

This is what is meant: even in the vertical and horizontal rows consisting of the third and third squares, the number of figures written in those respective sectional rows [is determined] by division.
One should draw the various intermediate sub-sections as they are conceived and fill them with the remaining numbers;
in the fourth and subsequent sections, this is done within rows consisting of the fourth, fifth, and other cells, arranged in an upward and downward sequence for each sub-section.

This is the meaning. Likewise, having conceived intermediate sections corresponding to each respective remainder, one should fill those respective sections with those respective remainders; this is the meaning. "Up to the ninth" means thus in sequence, up to the row consisting of nine squares as previously described.
The sequence is not practiced [in the usual way] and is divided into different sequences. Herein is the method of expansion (*prastāra*):

having produced horizontally rows corresponding to the number of each respective variation, consisting of squares equal in number to the desired syllables starting from the first syllable, one should [record] the number of each of those rows.

Having divided [the total] by the number of desired syllables for each [section], one should arrange sections equal in number to those respective syllables in successive order according to the number of lines obtained; then, within the lines of each respective section,
starting from the very first square in each case—
Having placed [the numbers] characterized by the count of syllables from the first and subsequent [sections],
and having again divided the count of each respective row of segments by the count of the remaining numbers for each,
one should likewise [determine] the various intermediate and sub-intermediate segments by means of the resulting quotient.

Having arranged single segments in such a way that they correspond respectively to each horizontal row in the penultimate row of squares— which follows the sequence of ascending and descending— place the numbers within them.

Having placed [the numbers] in their respective rows, one should place the number written in those respective rows within the final cell of the *pariśiṣṭa* (supplement). Here, in the expansion of the six variations (*ṣaḍbhedaprastāra*), the example is that there are six variations for three syllables.
Having divided the group of six by the three numbers, two remain; from those two,
having conceived one section for each of the two rows,
place the first number in the first cell of the first row and section, and the second number in the first cell of the second row and section.
Having placed the second number in the first cell of the third section,
and having again divided the two remaining numbers by the number of rows in each section,
one should determine a sub-section from that [result] consisting of one row for each.

Having placed, in their respective second cells, the second [syllable] which is the remainder of each respective first section, the third [syllable] which is the remainder of each respective second section, and the first and second [syllables] which are the remainders of each respective third section, in due order;

In the six cells of the top and bottom rows, which consist of those respective other squares, one should place the remaining numbers from the horizontal rows as follows: the third number in the first [row], the second in the second, the first in the third, the third in the second, the second in the third, and the first in the fourth.
The placement [of numbers] is also by way of digits in six rows starting from the top; this should be understood in the same manner for what follows.
This sequence of the number of desired varieties and the number of the specified varieties is written down:
having placed the desired number of syllables in some cases in the form of digits, arranged row by row.

Having divided the remainder so that it is not zero according to the number of rows contained within the segments specified for each respective difference— if that is impossible, one should assume the result to be zero—
and having placed those respective results and the zero-results in their appropriate places, [one proceeds] again.

Furthermore, by means of the number of rows contained within each respective intermediate section and so forth, divide the remainder as before until a section consists of a single row; having placed that result below the previous one,
add one to each of those respective results, and in the absence of a divisor, the remainder is one.

Having placed those [results] below the row of their respective products, one should take the digit located in the position corresponding to the number of the first result from among the digits representing the desired number of syllables established in the remaining row, starting from the first position.
In some cases, having placed the digit located in the first position of the specified number of divisions,
one should then sequentially extract the digits located in the positions corresponding to the respective second and subsequent result-numbers from among the intervening digits.

Because they are established in successive rows immediately following that, the *vidyā* consists of the aforementioned divisions. An example for determining the essential form of the seventy-ninth division among the one hundred and twenty variations of the five-syllable [mantra] is as follows: regarding the five syllables—
The placement of the digits in row-form is 12345.
The number of that partial row-series indicated is 24. Dividing by that, the resulting quotients are 3;
dividing the remainder 7 by the number of that intermediate partial row-series, the quotient obtained is 1, with a remainder of 1.
Dividing that by the number of the sequence of intermediate sections (2), the resulting quotient is 0; adding one to this zero result and setting aside the remainder, the arrangement is 45123.
[This applies] in some cases to the numbers corresponding to the count of the established syllables.
The first digit is placed in the fourth position from the end of the first result;
the second digit is placed in the second position from the end of the second result;
and the third digit is placed in the position immediately following the end of the third result.
The numerical figure of the fourth position, beginning from the first fruit; the numerical figure of the position immediately following that;

the remaining numerical figure taken from below that; and the numerical figure of the position directly below that—when this is done, O Goddess worshipped by heroes, the Vidyā shall be formed with all its parts in ascending order.
At the very bottom it has downward-pointing hair; situated in the middle, its sequence is disordered. || 41 ||

By all of these together, one's desired goal is swiftly accomplished; likewise, all the various forms arising from the non-duality of Lalitā, as taught in her yantra, are entirely included therein. 42.
Thus, the arrangement of the nature of the seventy-ninth variety obtained in sequence is complete.

[41235] Immediately following, the method for calculating the number of the indicated variety among the desired number of syllables is written down. The desired number of syllables, in the order of one, two, three, and so forth, are represented in the form of numerical figures.
Having arranged them in rows as 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, and so on,

one should discard the respective numbers located in the second and subsequent positions relative to the position of the indicated permutation in the first position and so forth; furthermore, one should record below each [number] the count of the positions occupied by those respective numbers.
Having arranged them thus, excluding the figure at the very bottom and omitting one by one from each of the figures situated above it,
[the total] is the number of rows contained within those respective segments and their sub-segments, as determined by the remainders starting from the top.

By multiplying [the numbers] and joining them all at the bottom, and by adding the numerical indicators, the total number of variations of the specified mantra (vidyā) is obtained. For example, the placement of the five syllables is 12345;
the placement of the specified variation is 42135. Regarding the first position marked in the specified variation:

Having discarded the digit located in the fourth position, along with the digits in all the subsequent positions starting from the one immediately below it down to the second position, the digit representing the number of those positions is placed beneath that [fourth position]. Then, having subtracted that [digit] by means of the third digit situated in the next position, [the process continues].

The numerical value of that position was placed beneath it; in the position immediately following that, because of the presence of its fourth digit, the numerical value of that position was placed beneath it; and in the next [position], because of the presence of its fifth-position digit, the numerical value of that position was placed beneath it.

It is established. From those very positions, by omitting one from each of the figures situated above it, the arrangement of figures [is made], namely 231. Excluding the figure situated below that, the sequence of numbers within the segments is formed by those upper and lower figures.

Having multiplied and added together the rows contained within those intermediate sections by means of the figures placed in them according to the sequence starting from the top, and having further added one to the figure situated below that, the resulting number constitutes the seventy-ninth variety among the varieties intended therein.

In this manner, it should be conceptualized everywhere; when this is done, it is what is called the *prastāra*. "Vidyā" refers to the nature of the sequence as taught. "All above" means the first line in the first section. "O you who are saluted by heroes" is an address to the Goddess. "At the very bottom" [refers to the final position].
"In the final section" means in the final row. "In reverse order" means in the inverse sequence; that is the Vidyā.

"Situated in the middle" means situated between all the first and all the final rows; "situated in the middle" refers to those whose sequences are disordered or broken. By means of those Vidyās, the various manifestations born of the non-difference from Lalitā [are produced].
This means they consist of fragments. Those [mantras] mentioned in that [specific] yantra are those taught in the chapter on yantras (tadyantrapaṭala);
likewise, those called Nityā and Anityā are also declared in the chapter on yantras.
As for others, they should be sought in their respective places where they are prescribed. || 43 ||
What kind of objects are considered to belong to these five types?
By what means would rightness (samyaktva) arise for all of them without effort? (44)
By what means does incorrectness arise, and how is that corrected?
What are the signs of one who has attained perfection, and what is described as that perfection? || 45 ||
One should draw six lines horizontally; then, one should draw eleven lines vertically in sequence. Thus, the wheel shall consist of fifty squares.
The meaning is that these were taught in the thirty-third chapter.

The names of the Nityās and Anityās are those declared in the chapter on their yantras; they were taught in the arrangement of their yantras in the sixteenth chapter, the chapter on the worship of the Nityās. "Others" refers to the names of the other Nityā-vidyās. The particle *tu* (but/and) is used for conjunction. 43
With these two verses beginning with "eṣām" and ending with "udāhṛtā," he teaches the sixfold question of the Goddess. Therein, "of these" refers to the five types of mantras—
consisting of *piṇḍa*, *kartarī*, *bīja*, and *mālā*— and their "meanings" are in the form of the gross, the subtle, and the supreme.

Thus [it means] up to this point. Of these mantras—of all five types, beginning with the *piṇḍa*—the "correct performance" (*samyakkaraṇa*) refers to the correct performance of the mantras. "Of the perfected one" (*siddhasya*) refers to those who have attained mastery in the mantras, vidyās, and so forth;
or it serves as a conjunction (*vā*). || 45 ||
With these three verses beginning with "rekhā" and ending with "śivātmanaḥ," [the author] intends to establish that the letters of the Mātṛkā— from 'a' to 'kṣa'—
are composed of the five elements, for the purpose of understanding the meaning of the syllables and sentences of the mantras.
He teaches the method of writing them and the elemental sequence for a wheel consisting of fifty squares there; "there" means across, to the right, and to the left.
"In those" means in those [squares], because they are divine; that is to say, in the lines. Because they are divine vertically as well, [the word] "below" [is used].
"Upwards" is the meaning; that is to say, "lines. "Then by that" means by that drawing. "Therein" refers to the wheel (*cakra*).
"From left to right" means beginning from the left square and ending at the right square.
"Syllables" refers to those respective syllables, which is to say, the elemental letters (*bhūtākṣara*).
"In successive order" means one by one in each row, according to the sequence of ten syllables representing the elements; that is to say.

"Named Māyā-śakti" means designated as both *māyā* and *śakti*. "Emission" (*sarga*) refers to the *visarga* (the *visarjanīya* sound), because it arises from the *mūlādhāra* even before the preceding [vowels] are intended to be articulated. Therefore...

Because of that *visarjanīya*, here in the wheel (*cakra*), one should write the phonemes in their proper sequence from left to right, for the one whose self is Śiva—that is, for the one whose nature is Śiva, which is to say, whose self is Power (*śakti*).
(p. 703) Therein, one should write the letters in order from the left to the right.
The five rows are proclaimed to consist of breath, fire, water, earth, and space. || 47 ||
The creation called the power of illusion (māyā-śakti) is the Lord who consists of all beings;
therefore, the arrangement of that [creation] here is not merely a single part of the one whose self is Śiva.
No, ru, raḥ; to, prā, ma, ca, vā, vī, do, yo, yu, ja, rnā, ra, vā;
nirśanāptaḥ, mā, spaśca, vyāśam, tāṃ, rṇādanāṃ, ruva. 49.

Jaḥ hnir cigni ste rva śu atiḥ vaḥ khī bhā dyudā śipra ni sanā homā grāścadā pite sā rṇā manāṃ java || 50 || O you who are swift in mind, the one who bestows gifts, whose face is radiant with light, who is the protector of the earth, the giver of wealth, the one who is praised by the wise, and who is the source of all existence—may you grant us prosperity.
Kūḥ, bhūḥ, rā, rā, jyā, kṣmā, sthi, dha, lā, mī, sā, trā, i, bhū, ra, go, nāṃ, tā, va, mā, rṇā, nye, ni, nā, maṃ, syu, thā, mā, kra, nāṃ, rya, bho. || 51 ||

The syllables *kaṃ*, *ri*, *naṃ*, *laṃ*, *vāḥ*, *vā*, *va*, *ja*, *hṛt*, *yaṃ*, *so*, *tha*, *mbu*, *sto*, *ra*, *pā*, *nā*, *tā*, *va*, *mā*, *rṇā*, *nye*, *ni*, *nā*, *maṃ*, *syu*, *thā*, *pyā*, *kra*, *nāṃ*, *ryya*, *mā*—these are the names of the [deities] of the [respective] directions.
And Svarabhru, Bhraṅkhadyutiyatnyaṃbhomaviśūnavyo, Ninānyesatāścamāhaṇāṃvyorūmepiṇamakrā. (53)
The procedure for its construction here is as follows:

having first fashioned a wheel consisting of fifty squares by drawing eleven vertical and six horizontal lines with equal intervals from east to west and south to north, [one proceeds] in each row across the ten squares on the right and left sides.

According to the sequence previously mentioned, one should write the syllables for air (ya), fire (ra), water (va), and earth (la), each accompanied by the bindu (m), ten by ten, from the upper row down to the lower row respectively. || 48 ||

By means of these five verses, beginning with "vāta" and ending with "vyomarūpiṇām," which are written with a scrambled sequence of syllables, the names of the elements— which serve as the conventions for designating the essential nature of all mantras and vidyās in this tantra— are [revealed].

He teaches ten [deities] for each in sequence. Therein, "of the letters" means of the ten syllables belonging to the Maruts, the winds—that is, the Vāyavyas. "Of the letters of fire" means of the divine fires; that is, of the ten syllables belonging to Agni. "Rasa" refers to Ilā.

No *sandhi* (euphonic combination) has been made because of their divine nature. [This refers to] the *varṇas* (syllables/letters) related to the earth (*bhaumānām*), the *varṇas* related to water (*āpyānām*), and the *varṇas* whose form is space (*vyomarūpiṇām*)— that is, those consisting of ether (*ākāśātmakānām*)— as previously described.
O Śivā, the extraction of the mantra has been performed here using these very names;
therefore, these names must always be kept strictly secret. (54)
Having concealed what was said by means of the method of denial, he should write it there in the book;
then he should whisper a single verse into the ear of the disciple who has been described in that manner.

The syllable *ṅka* (ṅ), followed by *r*, *ṇān*, *khe*, *tta*, *da*, *jā*, *li*, *vṛtaḥ*, *kra*, *yo*, *tya*, *ga*, *sta*, *marvya*, *ryyāt*, *yo*, *neḥ*, *bhe*, *ku*, *da*, *ja*, *tai*, *tarṇāśeṣarbhāmasaṃ*. (56)

By these two verses beginning with "by these" (*etair*) and ending with "of the embodied ones" (*rūpiṇaḥ*), because these names mentioned [therein] are to be kept secret as they concern the extraction of mantras (*mantroddhāra*) within this tantra,
and because this mantra is also to be kept secret as it expresses the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*).

The manner in which the syllables of the verse were written in a scrambled order by the Supreme Lord Himself, so that their unsuitability as a subject matter would not be established, is now presented. In this context, *eva* functions as a restrictive particle (*avadhāraṇe*). *Attra* means "in this Tantra.
*Śive* is an address to the Goddess (*devīsambuddhiḥ*). *Tasmāt* means "for that reason. [This is] by way of the concealment of what has been stated.

[This occurs] by way of the concealment (*nihnava*) described in the verse to be stated immediately hereafter. The particle *tu* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). "A verse" (*padyam*) means that which contains a meaning in the form of concealment. *Eva* is used for restriction (*avadhāraṇa*). [The disciple is] "of the aforementioned form," as described in the first chapter [beginning with] "joined with the four initial [syllables]," and so forth.
That is to say, by means of the two verses beginning with the twenty-third. || 55 ||

With the verse beginning with *vṛtta* and written in a scrambled sequence of syllables, he teaches a single method for both the corruption and the restoration of all compositions— whether in prose, verse, or mixed language. In that regard:
"Vṛttajārṇān" means the syllables produced from meters such as *anuṣṭubh* and others.

"Aṅkaiḥ" means by means of numbers equal in count to the number of syllables. "Vyatyastakramayogataḥ" means by means of a mutual reversal of order—that is to say, through their interchanging. "Bhedayojane" refers to the process of permutation and combination, or the systematic arrangement of the confused elements. This is what has been stated.
Having written down the numbers one, two, three, and so forth in the form of rows, corresponding to the number of syllables in each quarter-verse of the desired meter,
one should multiply each pair of those numbers with every other number.

Having arranged the verses in whatever manner disrupts the sequence, one should compose a verse containing the numerical indicators for those respective sequences, and thereby perform both the jumbling and the correct restoration [of the text].
An example of this is written as follows: "Recite after me"—the syllables of a quarter-verse of the *anuṣṭubh* meter are eight.

Those numbers were written in the form of a row: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8. By mutually transposing the first and eighth, the second and fourth, the third and sixth, and the fifth and seventh among those digits, the resulting sequence numbers were written in the form of a row.

By means of verses containing specific numerical sequences according to the *kaṭapaya* system and other such methods, the teacher may, for the sake of concealment, generate from this single verse an infinite variety of meters and desired meanings through the traditional transmission (*sampradāya*). (57)
Staying in a house or a pavilion that is neither hot nor cold, secluded, very level, and of beautiful form, one should place a seat with a whitened interior.
Having performed the ritual placement (vinyāsa) upon that full vessel during an auspicious lunar mansion or at a favorable planetary rising,
one should [draw the design] with red sandalwood, saffron, or vermilion, according to the instruction.
Having constructed the mandala consisting of the letters, one should invoke Śivā there and worship her;
one should constantly recite the Mātṛkā according to the tradition.
"One who has attained the true meaning of the Goddess's reality and who bears her lotus feet upon his crest should never merely recite the confused verses in this Tantra. (56)

By means of this verse beginning with "ślokena," and through the power of the oral tradition (*sampradāya*) and its experiential realization, [the author] explains that for teachers, it is possible to compose verses containing meanings according to their own wishes within all well-formed meters (*chandah-suvṛtta*), even when those meanings serve the purpose of confusing the context of the respective verses.

It teaches the capacity [of the text]. In that regard, by means of this sequence of mutual transpositions and divisions, it refers to infinite verses containing various sequences of disarray; that is to say, for the purpose of concealing the intended meaning, they serve to illuminate other meanings for the sake of concealing the sequence of disarray.

By means of these four verses beginning with "neither hot nor cold" and ending with "by way of yoga," [the author] establishes the nature of the desired deity for one who is proficient in the Tantra and has perfected eternal ignorance,
through the mantras corresponding to the will of each respective deity.
He teaches the manner of emanation: therein, "neither hot nor cold" means devoid of both heat and cold;

"of beautiful form" means pleasing to the heart. These four qualifiers are intended with respect to the stabilization of the mind and with respect to the suitability as a dwelling for the deity. The word "vā" (or) indicates an alternative.
"Standing facing the east" is the meaning according to the tradition.
The word "pīṭham" (the seat) is to be connected with the word "vinyasya" (having placed) in the verse that will be spoken immediately following.
"Dhavalitodaram" means having its interior whitened by the application of white-colored unguents. "On that seat. "In the full [moon]."
On the full moon day; or "vā" (or) indicates an alternative. At a "subhodaya," meaning at the rising of an auspicious zodiac sign (*rāśi*) and the rising of auspicious planets.

Its traditional meaning (*sampradāyārtha*) is written here: [it refers to] the state of inhalation of the breath flowing through the *iḍā* channel alone. With "kucandana," meaning red sandalwood; or "vā" indicates an alternative; with "darada" (vermilion).
Or, as an alternative, by means of the characteristics of the classes [of letters], according to the sequence of instruction— that is to say, of the venerable Bhūtalipi— the knower of mantras,
having constructed the aforementioned mandala consisting of fifty squares,
should thus offer it to his chosen deity once a year has been completed.
One should perform the mantra that conveys the desired object according to the prescribed method.
Those [planets] consisting mostly of ether, fire, and wind are considered cruel, agitating, and [inauspicious];
those consisting mostly of earth and water are considered gentle, serviceable, and bringers of success. (62)
Due to the great intermingling of these [elements], there are many waves;
through such engagement with them, the perfected ones bear fruit by means of their union as one.
The meanings of the mantras are to be known as threefold by those desiring accomplishment;
the practitioners are likewise to be understood as threefold, as described in the chapter on worship.
The meaning is "having done so. The word *sārṇam* (containing the letters) is connected with the phrase *upadeśataḥ* (according to the instruction) in the preceding verse.

This is what is meant: having constructed the previously mentioned wheel consisting of fifty squares, one should, according to the instruction, [place the letters] in ten squares arranged horizontally within each of the five rows starting from the top.

"Having sequentially deposited the Śrībhūtalipi syllables, one should worship the Goddess"— this means that, according to the tradition, one should deposit the letters from *a* with its nasal bindu (*aṃ*) through to *kṣa* in direct order (*anuloma*), including the visarga at the end; and likewise, from *la* through to *a*, and finally *kṣa*, in reverse order (*pratiloma*).

"In this manner" means by means of daily worship, recitation (*japa*), and so forth. "One should perform the mantra" means one should compose the mantra; that is to say, by way of the path established through etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*) and other means, such that it conveys the intended meaning. "By the aforementioned yoga" refers to the yoga consisting of the contemplation of the essential nature of the potency (*vīrya*) of the mantra, which will be described hereafter. || 61 ||

With the two verses beginning with "nabha" and ending with "svaikyayogataḥ," he teaches the cruelty, gentleness, and mixed nature that pervade all mantras. In this context, "syllables consisting primarily of ether, fire, and air" refers to those syllables abounding in the letters of ether, fire, and air.

Mantras are those which cause agitation of the universe; that is to say, mantras abound in the syllables of earth and water—that is to say, they abound in the syllables of earth and the syllables of water. They are to be served and worshipped by all, at all times, and in all places; that is to say, they bring about the attainment of one's desired object. Of these—

Because of the great variety of mutual combinations between syllables of a cruel nature and syllables of a gentle nature, and because of the great variety of different modes of their mutual conjunction, there are oceans of mantras; by means of those oceans. Thus.
This is said in accordance with their respective natures, such as being cruel, gentle, or mixed. What is meant is that,
due to the conjunction of fewer or more cruel syllables and gentle syllables, there arise many varieties of mantras through their own unification and through their application.
The perfected ones (siddhas) yield fruits according to their respective natures, whether they be cruel, gentle, or a mixture of both. || 63 ||

By means of these three verses beginning with "mantrārthāḥ" and ending with "iṣṭasiddhidāḥ," [the author] explains that when reflecting upon the meaning of all mantras, one should fix the intellect upon the stage of the arising and resting of the phoneme.
(p. 707) *varṇasyodayaviśrāntipade buddhiniveśanam* |
Another [method] is the observation of all things from every side for the sake of achieving complete proficiency.
Through the cultivation of the non-differentiation between the signified and the signifier and other such means, these five types [of mantras] grant the complete attainment of all desired goals. (66)
O wise one, listen to the potency of mantra which I shall describe as a source of happiness;
by experiencing this knowledge, a person becomes liberated while living. (67)
The threefold nature of the modes [of practice] teaches the contemplation of objects and their respective fruits for practitioners of the three types of objects, according to that threefold division.
In this context, "threefold" means according to the distinction of qualified aspirants, such as the *siddha* and others; thus, the meanings of the mantras are to be known.

This is the remainder [of the sentence]. "By those desiring accomplishment" (siddhikāṅkṣibhiḥ) means by those seeking the attainment of mantras, vidyās, and so forth. "Threefold" means as the accomplished (siddha), the to-be-accomplished (sādhya), and the practitioner (sādhaka). "Of the phoneme" (varṇasya) means of each individual syllable of the mantra.
"In the state of arising and repose" (udayaviśrāntipade) means in the locus of arising and repose, which is to say, in the nature of Parā.
The entry [of the object] into the intellect occurs through its subsequent reflection (*anusandhāna*), that is to say, through identity (*tādātmya*). The word "one" (*eka*) refers to the object;

this is the ellipsis. What is meant is this: since all mantras consist of a collection of phonemes (*akṣara-samudāya*), each of those phonemes, too, [is identical] from the perspective of the supreme nature (*parāsvarūpa*) and so forth.

The perfected ones (siddhas) should contemplate that the essential nature of all mantras is indeed the nature of Parā herself—because they arise in the sequence beginning with Paśyantī and so forth, and because they rest within that very [Parā] through identity with it.
This is the meaning of "another sense. It is the observation of the meanings of the words as established by the perfected ones from every perspective.

Through the established grammatical analysis consisting of the distinctions between roots, suffixes, and so forth as proclaimed in grammar, one should contemplate the meaning of each respective mantra; this is the sense of "the object to be accomplished" (sādhya). Furthermore, there is the contemplation of the fusion between the signified and the signifier, [which pertains] to those things that have the form of the signified.

The meaning is that because the five elements are of the nature of the unmanifest (*avyakta*), and because the forms of the signifiers—which are of the nature of syllables (*akṣara*)—have as their ultimate power (*paramārtha-śakti*) the *nāda* which is of that same unmanifest nature, there is a contemplation of identity (*tādātmya-bhāvana*).
This refers to the subject matter for the practitioner (*sādhaka*). "Thus they are proclaimed" means that these are the proclaimed meanings of the Śrīvidyā.
These five types of mantras—
known as *piṇḍa*, *karttarī*, *bīja*, and *mantramālā*— bestow the desired accomplishments through their contemplation, according to what has been taught. || 66 ||
By means of these three verses beginning with "The potency of mantra" (*mantravīryam*) and ending with "is proclaimed" (*īritaḥ*),

[the author] describes the essential nature of that ultimate reality called the "potency of mantra" (*mantravīrya*), which serves as the seed (or the life-force) of the entire multitude of mantras and vidyās, through the knowledge of each respective [aspect].
The three qualities (guṇas), which are said to be the cause of these [elements], are also the cause of the manifestation of the powers of the luminous forms. || 68 ||
The accomplishment of the contemplation of its true nature is declared to be "perfection" (samyaktva).
That is designated as the potency of the mantra; it is said to be the very life of mantras. (69)

He teaches the correct performance of all these. In this context, "mantric potency" (*mantravīrya*) refers to the ultimate nature (*paramārthasvarūpa*) of mantras. "O Wise One" (*prājñe*) is an address to the Goddess;
it is because she has attained the ultimate nature which is the abode of bliss. By means of that mantric potency...

The meaning is: by that which is experienced through knowledge—meaning solely by knowledge alone, culminating in direct experience. "Liberated while living" (jīvanmukta) means liberated even while alive; the meaning is that liberation is indeed non-constriction resulting from the knowledge of reality as it is (yāthātmyajñāna). Of the "lights," namely the forms of Soma, Sūrya, and Agni; and of the forms of Śakti.
The meaning is: of the powers that are the causes of forms and of the forms themselves—namely Vāmā, Icchā, Jyeṣṭhā, Jñāna, Kriyā, and Raudrī;
and of Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Rudra—and of the phenomenal world consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge.

The word *api* (also/even) is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*). The phrase "the cause of the threefold nature of the elements" is the ellipsis to be supplied. [The term] *guṇatraya* refers to *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; the meaning is that these constitute the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of both the forms (*mūrti*) and the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), just as the threefold nature consists of the three qualities (*guṇatraya*) and so forth. [The word] *ca* [is used] with reference to these qualities.
"In the aggregate" (samāhāre). By this, it means [the aggregate] of the qualities (*guṇas*) and of the forms of the powers of *tejas*.
The cause is as before. It was stated in the twenty-eighth chapter: "O Supreme Goddess, the cause is indeed Your will alone. This is the accomplishment of the contemplation of its true nature.

The accomplishment of the realization of non-difference from oneself occurs through *vidyā*, which consists of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*) that is the cause of all things. "Perfection" (*samyaktva*) means bringing about direct orientation (*ābhimukhya*). The individual soul (*jīva*) is the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). This is because mantras that are not oriented toward [the goal] are incapable of performing their function.

Because the knowledge of the sciences of mantra does not produce its effect without the application of the potency of mantra, that method is being written down by the command of the Lord for the sake of ensuring the non-interruption of the tradition. First,
through the yoga of meditation on the *kāmakalā*, according to the ultimate reality to be described in the thirty-sixth chapter.
Having herself become Śakti,

the embodiment of the power of all the splendors that constitute the limbs of Śrīvidyā, she unifies through her qualities all those things characterized by "this-ness" (idantā) as being like that; thus, both of these are neither hot nor cold.

Drawing [the elements] inward from the external, and from the internal toward the external, respectively, by means of one's own intellect, and unifying them, to worship through that very essence is the method for joining the potency (*vīrya*) of the mantra.
In the worship of other *Nityās*, this is done with the constituent parts of the *Hṛllekhā* alone; in the worship of other mantras, it is done with their respective parts.
The traditional teaching is that one should also unify [the elements] with those that constitute the parts of the *praṇava*, as before. || 69 ||
The lack of perfection regarding mantras indeed arises from speaking of what is unfit, from constant practice at improper times, and from doubt. (70)
Due to the sin of disrespecting the guru, through engagement in prohibited conduct, through hostility toward the deity, and through the instability of slandering everyone; 71.
Whether due to lack of tradition, ignorance, or even the worship of many [deities], that by which one's rightness (samyaktva) may be attained has been previously described. (72)
Neither excessive hatred nor excessive passion, no attachment to enjoyments;
neither excessive grief nor excessive joy, no excessive affection nor envy. (73)
Not indulging in excessive attachments, being happy with what one does, acting without affliction, desiring only as much as is required for one’s own body, and avoiding concern for others. (74)
With these three verses beginning with "asamyaktvam" and ending with "īritam," he teaches the thirteenfold causes of incorrectness (*asamyaktva*) regarding mantras, vidyās, and so forth,
together with a concluding summary of the previously mentioned correctness (*samyaktva*). Among these, *asamyaktva*—
It is the performance of what should not be done, or the attainment of contrary results; regarding mantras and mantra-sciences,
by speaking to the unqualified— that is, by instructing a disciple who lacks the characteristics described in the first chapter—
and by constant application, while neglecting the sequence of daily, occasional, and preparatory (puraścaraṇa) worship.

From desire, due to incessant practice; from worship at the wrong time, by performing the obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and optional (*kāmya*) rites at times other than those prescribed while neglecting the proper time; from doubt, regarding both the performance of what has been taught and the bestowal of one's desired fruit; and from contempt for the guru, by performing that which is not approved by the guru.

"From sin" means from the performance of conduct contrary to that described in the three verses beginning with *viśuddha* in the first chapter; "from the practice of prohibited conduct" means from performing the conduct of disciples as taught in various chapters in a manner other than prescribed; "from hostility toward the deity" means from the perception of duality regarding the deity; and "by the constant disparagement of all."

[Failure occurs] through universal censure, or through instability in recitation and other practices; or due to the absence of tradition; or from a teacher who lacks realization, or from merely observing [the text] on leaves and such; or from having acquired only the superficial form;
or through ignorance of the ultimate nature of the deity, the guru, and the mantra.
The "multiplicity of vessels" refers to various mantras, vidyās, and so forth.
Their "perfection" consists in causing those mantras and vidyās that were previously turned away by the aforementioned defects to become oriented toward one's purpose;
the meaning is that this task requires the focused application of those respective mantras and vidyās. || 72 ||

With these three verses beginning with "not excessively hateful" (*nātidveṣa*) and ending with "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*), he teaches the sixteen characteristics of those who have attained mastery through mantras. Among them, by the verse beginning with "not excessively hateful," [he teaches] the seven signs of attainment; by [the verse] beginning with "not being addicted to vices" (*nātivyasanavarttitva*),...
Uniformity of character in both gain and loss, a mind always contented, eating according to one's capacity, and giving from one's power—these are the characteristics of a perfected being. (75)
The untroubled fulfillment of one's desires is declared to be true accomplishment;
the favor of the king, being honored by all, and the attainment of merit are likewise accomplishments.
Renown, the acquisition of vehicles, ornaments, and the like, long life, health, freedom from contradiction, the status of a good disciple, and gratitude; || 77 ||
The digestion of poisons, knowledge, and likewise the perception of things even while healthy—
these are declared to be the direct supernatural powers (siddhis) of a perfected Manu in every respect.
These are declared to be the accomplishments (siddhis) that indicate a mantra has been mastered;
O Dear One, ritual applications (prayogas) must be performed with a perfected mantra, and not otherwise.
O Pārvatī, just as among men, so too among mantras and deities there exists mutual enmity, despite their being joined together as subordinate qualities.
Furthermore, water-mantras are enemies of fire-mantras and earth-mantras; likewise, there is mutual enmity between wind-mantras, water-mantras, and earth-mantras. (81)
By one verse, the five signs of accomplishment are [taught]; by the verse beginning with "ekarūpyam," four signs are proclaimed, as well as the conclusion. || 75 ||

With these four verses beginning with "Of desires" (*manorathānām*) and ending with "O beloved" (*priye*), he teaches the fourteenfold nature of mantra-accomplishment (*mantra-siddhi*) and the prescription of qualities for its applications. Among those, the accomplishments of merit (*puṇya-siddhi*) are those purposes of others that endure for a long time.
Those meritorious deeds and their accomplishments;

here, the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "vehicles, ornaments, and so forth" refers to costly garments and the like. "Non-contradiction" means, in short, between the seen and the unseen. "The state of being a good disciple" means, in short, his own [state]. Of poisons...

[This refers to] moving, stationary, artificial, and so forth; "knowledge" means [knowledge] of the self, that is to say, of the mind, mantras, vidyās, and the like. "From all" means from all [of them]. "Not otherwise" means it should not be performed with an unaccomplished mantra; this is the meaning. "O Dear One" (priye) is an address to the Goddess. || 79 ||

With these four verses beginning with "Of men" (*narāṇām*) and ending with "from the wheel" (*cakrataḥ*), he teaches the mutual enmity among those possessing mantras, sciences, and so forth, along with its cause. In this context, *ca* is used in the sense of conjunction (*samuccaye*).
*Pārvati* is an address to the Goddess. *Eva* is used for emphasis (*avadhāraṇe*).
(711) Those with female deities are generally enemies of those with male deities;
among those with female deities, there is mutual enmity between the gentle and the cruel. 82.
In the same manner, [the worship] of the male deities, of Tvaritā and Narasiṃha,
of the Śastras and Anuyakṣiṇīs, and of the Aghora-weapon, should proceed from the Cakra.
O Goddess, O wise one, listen as I describe the method for creating enmity between mantras and deities, by which the world is brought to ruin. (84)
Whether through ignorance or out of desire, if men partake of inequality, the mantras and deities, becoming enraged by that, shall destroy the practitioner. (85)
Therefore, the potency of mantra is indeed the life-force of the entire world;
for those who are devoted to it, these defects never touch them at any time.

"Because of the association with the subordinate qualities" means because of the association with the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth, and because of the association with the elements (*bhūta*).

"Of those belonging to Agni" means those consisting predominantly of the syllables of Agni; that is to say, of mantras, sciences (*vidyā*), and so forth, whose deity is Agni. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. "Of those belonging to the Earth" is as explained previously.
The *āpyas* (water-related) are as before. *Tu* is used for emphasis. The *vāyavyas* (wind-related) are as before. *Ca* is used for conjunction.
The *bhaumas* (earth-related) are as before—that is, those abounding in earth-syllables and those whose presiding deity is Earth.
"There would be enmity" is the sense. The *strīdaivatyas* (female-deity-related) are the mantras, *vidyās*, and so forth; [this is contrasted with] the *puṃdaivatyasya* (male-deity-related).
This refers, in short, to mantras, vidyās, and so forth; specifically, to those mantras and vidyās whose deities are female.

For those that are gentle (*saumya*), as previously stated, there would be enmity with the mantras and so forth [of the opposite nature]; for those that are cruel (*krūra*), it is likewise. Thus, in short, there would be mutual enmity between the cruel and the gentle.
The word *eva* is used here for emphasis. It means that there would be mutual enmity between Tvaritā and Narasiṃha;
likewise, there is enmity among the Śāstṛs and the Anuyakṣiṇīs. "From the discus" means by means of the Sudarśana. || 83 ||
With these three verses beginning with "Of the mantras" and ending with "never," he teaches that the faults of the practitioner cause enmity toward the mantras and their deities,
lead to their misfortune, and provides the means for avoiding that. In this context, the word "prājñe" (to the wise one) refers to...

The address "O Goddess" [is used] because of that which causes enmity. "Partaking in inequality" means either due to a difference in the sequence of daily worship or due to a difference in states such as excessive meanness;
that is to say, [it occurs] out of ignorance regarding the nature of ultimate reality, and out of expectation regarding the fruits [of practice]. By that [means]:
"By means of partaking in diversity. The word "and" (*ca*) is used for conjunction. Therefore, for that reason, "life" (*jīvita*) is the "basis" (*adhiṣṭhāna*), so to speak.
"Of those who are established in that" means established in the power of mantra because of its divine nature. || 86 ||

Having obtained [the mantra] with reverence at the proper time through service to the guru and initiation, one should, by his command, worship a single form of mantra for the sake of one's own accomplishment. (87)
Otherwise, it would destroy the practitioner through the fear of weapons from an enemy, or through poverty, long illness, or by abandoning him in times of calamity. (88)
Whichever mantra it may be, pills prepared from the medicinal herbs corresponding to its syllables, in a number equal to those syllables, grant the accomplishment of that mantra. (89)
Through that [practice], there shall be consecration, its wearing, its tasting, its smearing, and likewise its worship; this leads to the attainment of siddhi, and not otherwise. (90)

With these two verses beginning with "of the guru" (guror) and ending with "until the final offering" (atisarjanāt), he teaches the sequence for the perfect worship of the guru, the mantra, and the deity. In this context, "of the guru" means of one who is a true guru. "At the proper time" refers to what was stated in the second chapter with the two verses beginning with "in a stable [place]" (sthire) up to the fortieth verse. By initiation (dīkṣayā)...
This means by way of consecration (*abhiṣeka*), a glance (*kaṭākṣa*), and so forth. "With reverence" means with respect between teacher and disciple.

"By his command" means by the command of the Lord (*nātha*). "Of one form" means day after day. "One should strike" refers to the deity. "From the enemy" means out of fear of the enemy; one should strike by some pretext or other, and not merely out of fear.
Or, in the sense of "option" (*vikalpa*); in the sense of "calamities" (*vyasana*) such as women and so forth; that is to say, the seven [types of calamities]. || 88 ||

With the verse beginning with "yo ya" and so forth, he introduces the form of the pill (gulikā) composed of medicinal herbs and syllables, which brings about the perfect accomplishment of all the mantras and vidyās taught in the entire tantra. In that context,
the meaning is that the pill should be fashioned from the medicinal herbs of the letters of that particular mantra.

By means of as many portions of the medicinal herbs corresponding to the number of syllables in each respective mantra—as many repetitions as there are for each individual syllable of those mantras—the pill (gulikā) bestows the accomplishment of that mantra; that is to say, it grants the siddhi of the specific mantra concerned. || 89 ||

With this verse beginning with "tayā," he teaches the sequence for the application of the pill (*guḷikā*). In that context: "by that" means by the pill; "its wearing" means the wearing of the pill; "its tasting" means the consumption of that pill; "its smearing" means the smearing of that pill; and "its worship" refers both to worship performed upon it and worship performed by means of it.

"Likewise, for the attainment of success" means for the attainment of the success characterized as previously described; "and not otherwise, there is no doubt"—this is the meaning. In the first quarter of this verse, however, the addition of one extra syllable is due to its divine nature. || 90 ||
White and red sandalwood, māṃsī, pippalaka, lajjātukā, the crest of a peacock, darbha grass, pāṭala, and bhṛṅgaka. (91)
Śrīdevī is thus designated; indeed, the medicinal herbs correspond to the colors of the ten directions in sequence, and with them one should perform their respective worship.
Laghu, Candra, Mura, Vilva, Udumbara, Plakṣaka, Kṛṣṇa, Śaṅkha, Prasūna, and Citrāphānta are [the names] in sequence. (93)
The medicinal herbs should have the color of fire, and the leaf is proclaimed to belong to Sarga;
one who is devoted to the worship of the Guru's feet should perform their worship with those [herbs]. 94.
Uśīra, kuṣṭha, coraka, guhā, aśmarīka, agnimantha, rohiṇa, tulasī, potrī, and sadāmada—these are the names in sequence. || 95 ||

The colors and medicinal herbs of the earth have been described; with these one should worship them for the successful accomplishment of their respective purposes, and one should offer a fee to the true Guru.
Water, saffron, granthiparṇī, red grass, kuśa, bṛhatī, the drulatā creeper, dūrvā, and lakṣmī—these are the [substances] in sequence. || 97 ||
One should indeed perform the worship of these medicinal herbs with devotion, in their proper sequence, according to the names of the Śrīdevīs beginning with Jalārṇā.

By means of these ten verses beginning with "Sita" and ending with "siddhayaḥ," [the text explains] the syllables from 'a' to 'kṣa' according to the sequence of the five elements as taught in this tantra.

He teaches ten sets of medicinal prescriptions. Among them, for the white and red [deities], there are white sandalwood (*sita-candana*) and red sandalwood (*rakta-candana*). The *pippala* is the *aśvattha* tree. The *lajjātukā* is the *kumbhicandanī*.
With those respective herbs, one performs the worship of those respective syllables.

This is the worship of those respective deities. *Laghu* means *aguru*. Regarding *vilvodumbara*, because it is divine, the word division here is *vilva* and *udumbara*. The letter *s* (visarjanīya) is mentioned separately because it is not included among the "elemental letters" (*bhūtākṣara*). For the letter *kṣa*, there are the letters *ka* and *ṣa*.

Because it consists of yoga, no separate medicinal herb has been mentioned; for those [herbs], it is as before. *Potrī* means *vārāhī*, that is, *muśalī*. With these medicinal herbs, for those [purposes], it is as before.
For the sake of the complete accomplishment of each respective task, that is, for the purpose of achieving each respective task.
Kakkola, as well as Rocanā, Kalakinka (?), Siṃhī, a pair of Dundūka, and Añjali of Apāmārga together; (99)
Thus have the medicinal herbs of the letters of the sky (the vowels) been described in their proper order;
with them, one should perform their worship for the sake of accomplishing those respective purposes.
The pervasive state consisting of Sadāśiva has been correctly proclaimed;
by the constant polishing of this within the mind, that very reality is made one's own self.
Thus ends the thirty-fifth chapter in the Śrīkādimata among the sixteen Nityātantras.

*Añjaliḥ*, *añjalikarī*, and *prasāriṇī*—by means of those medicinal herbs. Regarding them, it is as explained previously. The addition of syllables to the final quarter-verse beginning with "kakkola" is due to its divine nature.
Here, the names of the medicinal herbs, which have not been explained, are to be understood from the mouth of one’s venerable teacher (*ārādhya*).
In that regard, "according to the accomplishment" means by the method previously described. || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, upon the complete tantra known as the venerable *Kādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*, [concerning] the *Nityās*...

The thirty-fifth chapter, which is dedicated to revealing the essential nature of the various expansions and modes of the different forms of those respective Vidyās arising from the latent impression of one’s own Self, has been fully considered.
35 || Oṃ tat sat ||
The number of explanatory texts:
In the thirty-fifth chapter, the eightfold Yantra has been proclaimed;
there are three hundred and ninety-seven explanatory texts.
The Thirty-Sixth Chapter. Now, O Maheśvara, the ritual procedures for the sixteen Nityās have been told by you, and they have been heard by me.
What is the true nature of those [goddesses], of me, and of other deities; how is it so? And what is the form of the universe as it is perceived? (2)

In the preceding thirty-fifth chapter, having taught the purification of latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and so forth regarding the sixteen *Nityās* together with their retinues as being one's own self, [the author] subsequently teaches the respective ultimate nature (*paramārthasvarūpa*) and other attributes of those who have attained perfection through the mantras of the sixteen *Nityās*. Now begins the section beginning with "atha ṣoḍaśa... and so forth.
Thus, by means of the thirty-sixth chapter consisting of one hundred verses, there is— within that [chapter]—

a praise of the twenty-fold inquiry and its forthcoming answer, preceded by a conclusion of the meaning taught in the Tantra, by means of ten verses beginning with "Now, sixteen" and ending with "always."

And by means of the verse beginning with "Now, sixteen," the Goddess concludes the matters taught in the Tantra; therein, those are the injunctions. The word "ca" (and) is used in the sense of conjunction.
"O Maheśvara" is an address to Īśvara. || 1 ||

With this verse beginning with "tāsām" (of them), the Goddess asks about the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārtha-svarūpa*), the means for the manifestation of that nature, and the cause for the manifestation of the nature of ultimate reality. In this context, "tāsām" refers to those sixteen *Nityās*; "tena" refers to you, Śiva; and "atra" [refers to] here.

By the word *tat* (that), he characterizes the Guru as being of the nature of eternal grace; by the word *mat* (my), he characterizes the disciple as one to be graced, because they are fashioned by beginningless *māyā*. [The phrase "from the Guru" refers to this: from me, the Goddess, who have become the disciple. As for others...

"What is the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-svarūpa*), which is the true nature and limb of the essential form taught in all the Vedas and Agamas"—this is the first question. Immediately thereafter, he asks about the means for revealing that ultimate reality: "How [is it revealed]?"—this is the second question.

By the question "In what form is the universe perceived?", this is what is meant: although the manifestation of the ultimate reality alone is logical, nevertheless, the universe— which is not of the nature of ultimate reality—
is perceived as a mere name, like a flower in the sky, even in the absence of any other [objective basis].
"What is its form?"—this is the third question. || 2 ||
What are the forms of the merits and sins of living beings, and by whom are they [incurred]? By what means do their births occur, what is liberation, and what is worldly existence? (3)

Whose is liberation, and how does bondage occur? By what means is there release from it? What is the root of this transmigratory existence, what are the principles (tattvas), and what is the intellect (dhī)? || 4 ||
Which are the sense organs, what are the vital breaths, who is the individual soul, and likewise who is the Supreme?
What is time, and what are the planets? O Lord, tell me everything exactly as it is.
Tell me clearly that which is described by the Vedas, the Śāstras, the Purāṇas, and even the Āgamas— neither too concisely nor too diffusely.
With the verse beginning with "prāṇinām," he asks about the lack of connection between living beings and merit or demerit,
as well as the nature of that merit and demerit, the cause of birth, the nature of liberation,
the nature of the cause of birth, and the nature of cyclic existence (*saṃsṛti*). Among these, regarding "prāṇinām":

The genitive case is used here to denote a relationship. "Of what form" means "by what form," so to speak. This is what is intended: the fourth question is, "By what is the nature of merit and demerit in living beings joined?
The word "by which actions" is to be supplied as the remainder [of the sentence]. Likewise, "the state of being meritorious or sinful," so to speak—this is the fifth question.

"For what reason [do they exist] among those living beings?"—this is the sixth question. "What is the expression 'desire' (kāma)?"—this is the seventh question. "And what is transmigration (saṃsṛti)?"—this is the eighth question. || 3 ||
With the verse beginning with "Of what" (kasya), there is a set of six questions. Among these, "of that" (tasya) refers to that bondage; the particle "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. || 4 ||

With the verse beginning with "kāni," there is a set of six questions. Among them, "Who is the Supreme? means who is the Supreme in reality, that is to say, who is superior to the state of the individual soul (jīva). "Everything" means all twenty kinds of matters asked about. "As it truly is" means according to the actual fact; "for me" means for me, the disciple who am eternally worthy of grace.
"O Lord" is an address to the Sovereign. || 5 ||
