With this verse beginning with "yena," he requests a clear exposition that accords even with the Vedic scriptures regarding matters perceived through direct experience. In this context, "yena" means "in whatever manner it is described. If there is a specific detail, its nature should be clearly stated—suitable for direct experience—and neither too concise nor too prolix.
Because it is impossible to know [the truth] through either excessive contraction or excessive expansion. || 6 ||
(717) Regarding the twentyfold question you have now posed concerning Śivā, I shall provide you with the answers in the very order in which they were stated.
By these subsequent [verses], one's own true nature is correctly and directly known;
for elsewhere, in all other places, it is taught through the cycle of concealment.
In this regard, that which is difficult to express is now directly stated through illustrative examples;
by means of these, one should gradually conquer the hard-to-overcome latent tendencies (vāsanā) according to the sequence I have taught.
One will certainly become the self of the vibration of all things, entirely clear and purified by truth;
one should always conceal this supreme secret and mystery from everyone. 10.

With these four verses beginning with "yat tvayā" and ending with "sadā," he teaches the majesty of that [reality] and its status as a benefactor, preceded by an introductory foundation for explaining the meaning of what was asked. In this context, "yat" signifies the reason; "Śive" is an address to the Goddess.
Regarding those questions: *eva* is used for emphasis. The ellipsis is "therefore I shall speak.

This means by those answers which are about to be stated. One's own nature (*svasvarūpa*)—that is, the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārthasvarūpa*)—is obtained, meaning it is revealed. It is "perfectly" (*samyak*), meaning fit for direct experience; "straightforwardly" (*añjasā*), meaning as it truly is. "Since" (*yat*) indicates the reason.
The phrase "from this tantra" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "Elsewhere" means in all other tantras and Vedas.
"From the wheel of concealment" means because of its extreme secrecy. "Here" means in this tantra. "Directly" (añjasā) means as before, according to the proper way.
"That essential nature" (tat svarūpam) is "difficult to express," being beyond the scope of words. "Tu" (but/then) indicates a distinction.
"By illustrations" means by those intended to reveal each respective point. "By them" refers to the meanings that are to be taught as subsequent [teachings].

"By either of the two methods" mentioned in the sequence—that is, by either the method already explained or the one yet to be explained. "Difficult to conquer" because it has been established from beginningless time. "Gradually" means through the sequence of time and by the power of practice.
Its nature is truth, purity, and the complete radiance of all things. "Truth" is in the sense of being the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*);

"purity" because it is untainted; and "the complete radiance of all things" because it manifests as the very essence of each and every thing. Here, the word "self" (*ātman*) should be applied to all four [qualities]. This is what is meant:

The practitioner, by means of either of the two methods to be described as the answer to the second question, gradually conquers the difficult-to-overcome latent impressions (*vāsanā*) and becomes one whose nature is the true, pure, manifest, and all-pervasive radiance. It is "secret" (*guhya*) because it is deposited within the cave (*guhā*), being luminous within; it is "mysterious" (*rahasya*).
Because it is obtainable solely through the guru’s glance; because it is supreme due to the absence of anything distinct from itself;
"one should conceal it" means from those who are not devotees—that is to say, in every respect. || 10 ||
That knowledge which is the knowledge of "this," that knowledge which is the knowledge of "I," and the knowledge which pertains to both—know that knowledge to be my very body. (11)

For them, for you, and for others as well, the nature of consciousness is, in reality, one thing through the attainment [of truth], and quite another through the destruction of latent impressions (vāsanā). || 12 ||
The self-luminous [consciousness] becomes stable, eternal, unrivaled, and great;
or it may be attained through the clear means taught in the *Nityāhṛdaya*.

With the one and a half verses beginning with "That which is knowledge" (yajjñānam) and ending with "in accordance with reality" (yathārthataḥ), he teaches the essential nature from the perspective of ultimate truth as the answer to the first question. In that context, "that which is knowledge" refers to consciousness (caitanya) which is not an object of speech or mind; it is the knowledge of "this," [not of "that"].
"Apprehension" (*pratīti*) refers to cognition, as previously explained. "Of the 'I' in that manner" means the apprehension of the "I.

Here, the word "in that manner" (*tathā*) is connected to both the preceding and the following [terms] according to the maxim of the crow's eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). Thus, from those two—namely, "this-ness" (*idantā*) and "I-ness" (*ahantā*)—[arises] "this is mine" and "I am this."

This refers to the relationship of cognition such as "I am this very thing" or "this is I," and so forth; furthermore, it means "something more. Know that knowledge to be beyond the reach of speech and mind—that is, you should desire to know it—of me, the Guru Śiva. This is according to reality, meaning according to its true nature.

This is what is meant: just as in heated iron there is no distinct part, so too, for consciousness—which pervades the universe—there arises, through its connection with the elements, senses, and so forth, within bodies that consist of such things, a cognition of pervasion: "I am this very body," which is the locus of perception in the form of the intellect; and "this is the universe," which is the knowledge of its pervasiveness. Furthermore:
One also synthesizes the mutual relationship between those two through such forms as "this is mine.

In each instance, that which flashes forth as pure consciousness alone by way of various specific forms of cognition—that consciousness, know it truly, is my very body. This refers to those sixteen Nityās, and for others...
"Of the deities" means as far as [they extend]. "The body whose nature is consciousness" means its essential form is consciousness; this is the ellipsis to be supplied. || 11 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with "lābhāt" and ending with "bhavet," he teaches,

as the answer to the second question, the means for the manifestation of the nature of ultimate reality (*paramārthasvarūpa*), along with a conclusion and alternative means taught in other tantras. Therein, thus:

In all diverse forms, according to the method taught in the *Vāsanā*, there is the continuous contemplation (*anusandhāna*) of the essential nature of consciousness alone; this occurs through the destruction of [ordinary] mental impressions (*vāsanā*), and not otherwise—meaning precisely through the destruction of evil impressions (*durvāsanā*). Thus, it remains steady amidst transformations such as bracelets, crowns, and the like.

That is to say, it is like the manifestation of the mere existence of gold. It is eternal because it is not delimited by time; it is unrivaled because of its truth; it is great because it is not delimited by space.
"Nityāhṛdaya" refers to the *Nityāhṛdaya* [Tantra] among the sixteen *Nityātantras*, by means of the clear method proclaimed therein.
Because the word of a certain tantra and [the word] of the intellect possess a twofold nature, the proliferation [of phenomena] is seen;
the twofold nature of these two is stated to be due to their being composed of both the real and the unreal. (14)
By that very [consciousness], there occurs the engagement of living beings in meritorious and sinful actions;
just as the activity regarding objects for one who knows the Self is designated as "merit. (15)
Likewise, the mental conception of what is not a true benefit as being a benefit is called "evil";
through these, one undergoes births of various forms, becoming a constant vessel for suffering. (16)

Or rather, by means of the clearly explained method (upāya) regarding that [object], it may become the self-luminous manifestation within conceptual thought (vikalpa); this is to say that because this method is the primary preparation, it must be understood from the mouth of the one to be propitiated. || 13 ||

With the verse beginning with "of sound" (śabdasya), he teaches the cause and other factors of the manifestation of the phenomenal world as the answer to the third question. In that context, the phrase "from its two-fold nature" (dvairūpyāt) means "because it consists of both aspects. This is because, later on, there will be an occasion to provide the answer to the twentieth question.
He recalls the nature of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) which is about to be described; the word "and" (*ca*) is used in a conjunctive sense.
This is because these two—word and cognition—are equally active with respect to both the ultimate reality (*paramārtha-rūpa*) and the non-ultimate reality (*aparamārtha-rūpa*).
What is meant is this: even that which is not ultimate reality functions for word and cognition in exactly the same way as that which is ultimate reality.
The manifold world (prapañca) manifests through name and form. || 14 ||

With the half-verse beginning with "tenaiva" (by that very [means]), he teaches as the answer to the fourth question, preceded by a statement regarding its non-ultimate nature, the manner in which living beings consist of merit and demerit.
In this context, "tena" refers to the duality of word and cognition; "eva" is used for emphasis; and [the term] "prāṇinām" [refers to] living beings.
The genitive case is used here to denote a relationship. "Vartana" means activity. What is meant is this:
the very engagement of living beings in meritorious and sinful actions through the dual nature of words, cognitions, and objects constitutes their merit and demerit. || 15 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with "yathā" and ending with "bhājanaṃ," he teaches,

as the answer to the fifth and sixth questions, the nature of meritorious and sinful karma and the cause of birth for living beings. In that context, "artheṣu" refers to the subtle elements (tanmātras) such as sound and the rest.

The meaning is that this refers to the activity of the sense organs. What is intended is as follows: for one who knows the pursuit of the meaningful (arthārthī) and who, regarding objects, accepts them only in their nature as mere subtle elements (tanmātra-svarūpa-mātra) and remains unattached to them, the activity of the sense organs toward those respective objects is designated as "merit" (puṇya). [This applies] to objects that are not harmful.

Objects are sound and the rest; apart from the mere perception of their subtle elements (*tanmātra*), they are non-objects (*anartha*) when regarded as sons and so forth. "Conceptualization of objects" (*arthasaṃkalpa*) means the cognition of them as having [such] a nature. The word "by the mind" (*manasā*) is connected with the preceding term "conceptualization of objects. This is what is meant: regarding sense-objects—

Without the realization that these [objects] are merely the subtle elements (tanmātra) such as sound and so forth, the very conjunction of the mind with them as sons, friends, wives, and so on, constitutes what is known as sin; that is to say, it occurs through a lack of knowledge of the true nature of the Self. "Of various forms" means having the forms of womb-born beings and so forth.

When there is the true nature of objects, that is knowledge; its opposite is liberation. Transmigration is the bondage of the intellect, while the latent impression (vāsanā) is said to be the bond. (17)
Through the exhaustion of karma and by means of reflecting upon the words of the glance of a true guru, there is liberation for all living beings, and never by any other means. (18)

By whichever distinct forms [the body] becomes a vessel for constant affliction—in those various forms, one possesses such dispositions as "I am a friend" or "I am an enemy," and so forth. This is what is meant: just as sound alone is the object of the auditory faculty, touch that of the tactile faculty, form that of the visual faculty, and taste that of the gustatory faculty.
Odor is the object of the olfactory faculty; sound is the quality of space; sound and touch belong to air;

sound, touch, and form belong to fire; sound, touch, form, and taste belong to water; and sound, touch, form, taste, and odor belong to earth. Therefore, the elements are indeed the subtle potentials (tanmātras) beginning with sound.

The elements themselves, through specific combinations with one another, arise as the forms consisting of the womb-born, egg-born, sweat-born, and soil-born; these very forms, characterized by birth, transformation, decay, modification, and destruction, become various types of births within those respective forms.
In those various forms...
Due to the conceit of "self" and so forth, they experience sufferings through modifications established by that very nature.

With the verse beginning with "yāthārthya," he teaches, as answers to the four questions from the seventh to the tenth, the essential natures of liberation, transmigratory existence, the release of the intellect, and bondage. Among these, liberation is the knowledge of objects according to their true nature (*yāthārthya*).

Just as there is the knowledge of nothing but clay regarding modifications such as jars and bowls, so too liberation consists in the realization of nothing but the existence of consciousness (*cit-sattā*) amidst the various forms that are perceived; conversely, the opposite of that is the knowledge of what is not the true Self.
Up to this point: liberation is the cessation of the intellect's false self-knowledge, because that knowledge is a property of the intellect. Bondage is latent impression (*vāsanā*);
that is to say, false self-knowledge arises solely through beginningless, pernicious latent impressions. || 17 ||

With the verse beginning "From the destruction of karma" (*karmakṣayāt*), he teaches the giver of liberation and the manner of liberation by providing the answer to the eleventh question. In that context, [liberation occurs] from the destruction of karma;
since karma is an effect of ignorance, the cause and its effect are treated as non-different through figurative identification (*upacāra*).

This means "due to the destruction of ignorance. Regarding the term *sadguroḥ* ("from the true guru"), here "true" (*sat*) refers to having received the full initiation (*pūrṇābhiṣeka*) according to the procedure taught in this tantra in the sixty-first through seventy-first verses of the second chapter, as well as possessing stability in the nature of the supreme reality taught in this chapter.

"Guru-ness" refers to the perfection of the characteristics as described by the nineteen verses beginning with "O handsome one" (*sundara*) in the first chapter; the particle *tu* is used for emphasis. Regarding the "expression of side-long glances" (*kaṭākṣokti*), this is discussed in the twenty-first chapter through nine verses beginning with "of all [the goddesses]" (*sarvāsām*). As for "contemplation" (*vimarśataḥ*), it is explained in the twenty-second chapter by the eleven verses beginning with "the contemplation of the Self" (*ātmano vimarśanam*). The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) indicates that the remaining chapters should be understood accordingly. Thus, the entire meaning of the Tantra has been explained. Now, the conclusion is stated: "The essence of the Tantra has been told. This means that the essential meaning of the Tantra has been fully declared. The word "essence" (*sāra*) signifies the core meaning. "Told" (*prokta*) means explained. "Entirely" (*samastam*) means in its totality. "Tantra" (*tantram*) refers to the scripture. "Conclusion" (*upasaṃhāra*) means the final summary. "Now" (*atha*) introduces the topic. "I shall speak" (*vakṣye*) means I will explain. "The supreme secret" (*paramarahasyam*) means the most excellent mystery. "Of the Lord" (*prabhoḥ*) means belonging to the Sovereign. "In the presence of the Goddess" (*devīsamakṣam*) means before the Goddess. "In the assembly" (*parṣadi*) means within the gathering. "Of the Siddhas" (*siddhānām*) means of the perfected ones. "And of the Yoginīs" (*yoginīnām ca*) means and of the female practitioners. "Of the heroes" (*vīrāṇām*) means of the brave ones. "And of the Śākinīs" (*śākinīnām ca*) means and of the female spirits. "Of the Vīras" (*vīrāṇām*) [repeated] means of the heroic ones.
