"And of the Śākinīs" (*śākinīnām ca*) means and of the female spirits. "Of the Vīras" (*vīrāṇām*) [repeated] means of the

Among the three types of methods described in the verses, one is *ukti* (direct statement), which in this chapter is the instruction on the supreme essential nature of Śrīvidyā; *vimarśa* (reflective inquiry), however, is the contemplation of the nature of Śiva according to the aforementioned method of question and answer. Therefore—

By means of glances, speech, and reflection—meaning, in the manner of the questions and answers previously stated—the supreme and great root of transmigratory existence has arisen, which is non-discrimination (aviveka).
Dependent upon this, this world of living beings revolves. (19)

The principles (tattvas) have been described by all [authorities] everywhere and at all times as consisting of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge; otherwise, they are always different.
And as for what was asked—"What is wisdom?"—though it is difficult to express, I shall explain it clearly; listen, O wise one, for upon this depend the twenty [virtues]. (21)
In the disciple, it is the contemplation of one's own true nature; that is to say, by means of glances, speech, and reflective awareness.

This is what is meant: in bodies consisting merely of a particular configuration of elements, the notion of being a living being arises solely through the vibration of consciousness (*cit-sphuraṇa*). From its very modification arises the sense of "I" (*ahaṃtā*) residing in the body, as well as the states of the intellect and the senses.
The activities of the mind, vital breath, and body are merit and demerit; their fruits are the various states of existence.
Since all of this is ultimately unreal through the grace, instruction, and inquiry of a true Guru, the liberation of all living beings is possible—meaning by no other means. At any time.
"Until the dissolution of all that is summoned" means as far as that point. || 18 ||

With the verse beginning with "saṃsṛteḥ," he teaches, as the answer to the twelfth question, the supreme cause of transmigratory existence (saṃsṛti), its essential nature, and its majesty. In this context, because it is divine, the "kanda" means the supreme cause; it is non-discrimination (aviveka).

The absence of discrimination between the body and the self; it is "supreme" because of its transcendence; it is "great" because it extends through all living beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass; "that which is dependent on this" means that which is subject to another, namely, dependent upon non-discrimination; "the world of living beings" refers to the realm of sentient creatures; it revolves.
That is to say, in the form of the delusion consisting of the recurrence of birth, old age, death, and so forth. || 19 ||

With this verse beginning with "tattvāni" (the principles), as an answer to the thirteenth question, he teaches that the triad of the knower, the means of knowledge, and the object of knowledge— which serve as the instruments for the investigation of essential nature—
is of the nature of *tattva* (reality), whereas other natures are of the nature of *atattva* (non-reality). In that regard:
"By means of the [true] reality," that is to say, by means of the *tattvas*. The *tattvas* are the truths, because they manifest through identity with consciousness (*caitanya*).
"By all [means], such as scripture (*āgama*) and so forth," that is to say, by all [means]. "Everywhere," that is to say, in all bodies.
"Consisting of the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable" means having the nature of the knower, the knowledge, and the knowable. "Otherwise" means different [from that].
The others, perceived as having a nature other than that [reality], are unreal; such is the meaning. || 20 ||

With seventeen verses beginning with "And what is intelligence" (kā ca dhīḥ) and ending with "the analysis" (vigraham), [the author] teaches, as the answer to the fourteenth question, the one hundred and seven qualities of the intellect (buddhi) and its power. In that context, the word "in those objects" (tadvastuṣu) is to be supplied as the remainder.

By names such as *manas*, *buddhi*, *ahaṅkāra*, and *citta*, that which has been described everywhere and at all times—both in terms of its diversity of objects and its non-difference—is [the same]. (22)
That is one, imperishable, gross, subtle, difficult to know, and exceedingly manifest;
it is both the unequal and the equal, the universe, transcendent to the universe, and free from affliction. || 23 ||
He is formless and yet all forms; he removes all that produces afflictions;
he removes the source of all thirst for everyone, everywhere, and at all times. (24)
It consists of the forms of sattva, rajas, and tamas, yet is not composed of them;
it is the form of saṃsāra, yet its body has transcended it; it is both perfectly stable and moving.
It is sinless yet appears as sin, the form of the individual soul yet identical with the Supreme Self;
it is beyond the senses yet the essence of the senses, indefinable, and the deity of all. || 26 ||

"Difficult to speak" (durvacam) because it is beyond the scope [of ordinary speech]. "Clear" (sphuṭam) means fit for direct experience. "O Wise One" (prājñe) is an address to the Goddess. "Twenty questions" is the intended meaning. By the word "etcetera" (ityādi) in this context, he indicates that the four names previously mentioned are merely synonyms, just like the terms *dhī* and *prajñā*.
The word "yat" (which) is connected with the word "vastu" (entity) by means of this [phrase]; [it is] "from all," beginning with scripture. || 22 ||
By the verse beginning with "That" (*tad*), eleven qualities are described. In that regard, "that" refers to the Reality, which is one, meaning its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is singular.
It is imperishable because its essence consists of the perception of consciousness (*cid-upalambha*). It is gross because it pervades the entire universe.
It is subtle because it exists as an intense radiance even within the minute bodies of creatures such as ants. It is difficult to know...

It is difficult to know because it transcends the senses; it is exceedingly clear because its nature is consciousness; it is diverse because of the manifoldness that will be described; it is uniform because of the equality of that manifoldness among all living beings; it is the universe because of its identity with it; it transcends the universe in the sense of being the ultimate reality; and it is free from affliction because it is bodiless. 23

By the verse beginning with "formless" (*arūpa*), the six qualities are indicated. In that context, because it is divine, it is "the remover of all that produces afflictions" (*sarvakleśakarahara*) and "the remover of all afflictions" (*sarvakleśahara*). It is also "the remover of all that produces craving" (*sarvatṛṣṇākarahara*), "that which produces all craving" (*sarvatṛṣṇākara*), and "the remover of all craving" (*sarvatṛṣṇāhara*). This refers, in short, to all living beings (*prāṇin*).
"In every way" means in every manner. || 24 ||
By the verse beginning with "sattva," ten qualities are [described]. Among them, "atanmayam" means that which is devoid of qualities (*nirguṇam*). || 25 ||
By the verse beginning with "apāpam," the eight qualities are described. Therein, "apāpam" means that which is of the nature of merit (puṇya). || 26 ||
It consists of all agitation and has the form of universal peace; it is both merciless and compassionate; its nature is non-discrimination, yet its ultimate reality is discrimination. (27)
It is a deliverer, a causer of downfall, and of a fragile nature; it consists of victory and consists of sorrow, yet it is free from sorrow; it possesses curiosity and is devoid of curiosity. (28)

It is effortless yet ever-exerting; it possesses arrogance yet is free from pride; it takes the form of indignation yet is unshakeable; it agitates all things yet is itself beyond agitation; it is both pleasure and pain. || 29 ||
One who is untouched by the six qualities—anger, greed, pride, malice, envy, and sexual desire—is a eunuch; likewise, a woman and a man [who possess these] are so.
It is both base and sublime, clear in form as well as turbid;
it is unfathomable and exceedingly deep, noble as well as wretched.

It is of the nature of fortune yet consists of misfortune; likewise, it is fearless yet fearful; it takes the form of desirelessness yet is the embodiment of desire; it is timid, yet possesses the physical form of a hero.
He is faultless, yet the essence of all faults; he is omniscient, yet has the form of a fool.
He is the contracted form for all, and likewise the illuminator of all. || 33 ||
By the verse beginning with "sarva," the six qualities [are taught]. Among them, *vivekaparamārthaka* refers to the essential nature of the ultimate reality of discernment (*viveka*). || 27 ||
By the verse beginning with "uttāraka," the eight qualities are described; therein, *bhaṅga* means the form of defeat. || 28 ||

By the verse beginning with "nirūdyamam," the eight qualities are described; therein, "pleasure and pain" refers to that which is of the nature of pleasure and that which is of the nature of pain. || 29 ||
By the verse beginning with "krodham" (anger), fifteen qualities are indicated. Among these, "aspṛṣṭa-ṣadguṇam" means being devoid of the six qualities beginning with anger. || 30 ||
By the verse beginning with "apakṛṣṭam," the eight qualities [of the ocean] are described; therein, "agādham" means difficult to fathom. || 31 ||
By the verse beginning with "bhāgyeṇa" (through good fortune), the eight qualities [are described]. || 32 ||

By the verse beginning with "nirddoṣa" (faultless), the eight qualities are described. In that context, "consisting of all defects" means consisting of the three humors—wind and so forth—for all living beings. || 33 ||

(724) Whether one's nature is non-stealing or stealing, self-controlled or uncontrolled, whether one is a spy, gentle, flavorful, tasteless, cruel, or mild—what is the use of all those various qualities? 34.
The intellect consisting of you is fully described, while consciousness consisting of me is proclaimed;
through the discernment of the unity of both, the individual soul (jīva) is that other which possesses such discernment.

But he who knows the true nature of that intellect—its transformations as well as its capacity, its non-difference from itself, and the fruits to be attained once perfection is reached—[is liberated]. (36)

The yogi who is wise, a knower of Brahman, a Śiva-yogi, and likewise a knower of the Self— by him alone is everything ordained, which is the embodiment of the unity of the phenomenal world and the Self.
Indeed, for the sake of the self’s own mind grasping objects through its function,
the sense organs— whose nature consists of the power of the elements and whose forms are composed of the self— were created.
By the verse beginning with "non-stealing" (asteya), the ten qualities [of a yogi] are described. Among them, *avaśya* means independent; by those qualities [he is so characterized]. || 34 ||

"Consisting of you" means, in other words, consisting of power (*śakti*). This is what is meant: cognition (*buddhi*) is the apprehension of the nature of consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*) by its own will. "Consisting of me" means consisting of Śiva, that is to say, being one's own self (*svātmikā*).
This is what is meant: when, apart from the nature of apprehension itself, she [the power] exists as such—like fire within a tree—then [she is my own self].

"At that time, it remains under the designation 'consciousness' (cid). This means that because of the identity of both, the intellect-consciousness (*dhīcit*)—being of the nature of discrimination—is non-distinct from its own essential form; thus, it is said that "it reflects upon the conscious self. Another, the superior one, being possessed of that discrimination, reflects upon the non-distinctness of the essential forms of the intellect and consciousness; this is what is meant.
"Non-differentiation from oneself" means being inseparable from one's own self. "When the true nature of its own essence is established" refers to the state of realization.

"Fruits to be attained" are those results which are yet to be acquired. The particle "ca" (and) is used for conjunction. One who knows is a knower of the true nature of the intellect. The fivefold set of names beginning with "yogī" is found in the Vedas and the Āgamas.

Those who know the ultimate truth have stated all that in accordance with their respective views; the meaning is that all of it is dependent upon the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, [one should act] by one who knows the true nature of the intellect. The word *eva* is used for emphasis. || 37 ||

With the verse beginning with "svātmanaḥ," he teaches the nature of the senses as the answer to the fifteenth question. In that context, "created by one's own self" means perceived through one's own mental activity, that is, through the operation of the mind.
Up to this point: "having the nature of the powers of the five elements" means having the essential form of the powers of the five elements.

The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. What is meant is this: the senses are those whose essential forms are the powers of the elements, perceived for the purpose of grasping their respective objects by means of one's own mental modifications (*manovṛtti*).
The manifestation of consciousness through the power of the aggregate of the elements, the self, the intellect, and the vital breaths is the life-force (*prāṇa*);
for the individual soul (*jīva*) is its witness, while the Supreme is the essence of reality itself. (39)
As for Time (Kāla), which was previously described as possessing all qualities prior to the intellect— whatever is denoted by the two syllables "kā-la" is my very form.
It is not possible to speak or demonstrate it to you directly;
nevertheless, I shall explain to you whatever I can in a coherent manner. (41)
The division of day and night and so forth arises from the conjunction of the moon, the sun, and other celestial bodies;
therefore, it is not appropriate to describe [the Self] as being identical with those. (42)
That which is spoken of as *lava*, *truṭi*, and so forth, are indeed its fragments;
that form of time which has a nature without beginning or end is what is thus described.

With the verse beginning "The self consisting of the elements" (bhūtātman), he teaches the nature of the vital breaths and the individual soul as the answer to three questions— the sixteenth, seventeenth, and eighteenth. Therein:

By the statement, "The vital breaths (prāṇas) are the unfolding of consciousness through the power of the aggregate of the elements, the self, and the intellect," this is what is meant: the various manifestations of the unfolding of consciousness arise through the capacity of the aggregate of the five elemental natures and the intellect.
It is the witness of that [intellect], engaged in the contemplation of the true nature of the body, senses, and so forth. This is what is meant:

the intellect (*buddhi*), whose essential nature is the perception of consciousness (*cid-upalabdhi*), acquires the designation "living being" (*jīva*) when it ceases from its engagement in contemplating the form of the body and other such things due to its state of non-discrimination (*aviveka*).
"By way of its true nature" means by way of its actual reality (*yāthātmya*). This is what is meant:

when the intellect (*buddhi*), whose very nature is the apprehension of consciousness, desists from the activity of identifying itself with the body, senses, and so forth—due to their lack of true reality—by means of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of its own true nature.
Just as fire [remains] because there is no fuel to be burned, it then rests in its own essential nature and attains the designation "Supreme" (para). || 39 ||

With these eight verses beginning with "kāla" and ending with "vai," he teaches the nature of time and so forth as the answer to the nineteenth question. Therein, "tu" is used for emphasis. This refers back to the answer to the fourteenth question, namely the verses beginning with "tadekam."

Since there is a variety of qualities (*guṇa*), therefore he possesses all qualities; that is, he possesses every quality. Nevertheless, even though it is impossible—meaning, even so—and "properly" means "by way of enumeration"—in the phrase "day and night, etc.," the word "etc. refers to the full mandala and so forth; the particle *tu* is used for conjunction.

In the phrase "the moon, the sun, etc.," the word "etc. refers to Mars and the other [planets]. For that reason, there is the description of their nature as being composed of those [elements]. [The disciple says: "Tell me of the divisions such as *lava* and *truṭi*, which consist of day and night and so forth, by means of which time is known by me. (p. 726)
Then, indeed, his [arrow] pierced through the mass of leaves of a lotus plant like a needle. || 44 ||
The state arising from the division of each individual petal is declared to be a *lava*;
thirty times that is said to be a *truṭi*, which possesses a body and so forth. (45)
"What is the nature of that which is called 'time,' and how does it exist?"—when asked thus, I am able to explain that very clearly. (46)
Whatever is obtained through the contemplation of that which has been described by one's own intellect is declared to be its very body; indeed, there is no other way in this matter.

The description of the true nature of time: what is meant is this—that the essence of time, in its ultimate reality, does not consist of the objects such as days and nights which are merely conceptualized on account of the movements of the moon, the sun, and other planets. Therefore, from that [essence], [arise] the lava, truṭi, and so forth;
here, the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to the kalā, kāṣṭhā, and other divisions. That which is its true nature—
They are called "fragments" (*khaṇḍaka*) because they do not consist of that [ultimate reality], meaning they are the delimiters of the universe.
The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. The grammatical connection is: "that is the form of time" (*tat kālasya rūpam*), meaning "the form belonging to time.
Here, by the word *tat*, he recalls the power of time as previously described at the beginning of the *Tantra*. That is the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*).

This is what is meant: that very nature of consciousness (*citsvarūpa*), which is without beginning or end, is itself the nature of time (*kāla*). In the phrase "lava, truṭi, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers, as before, to *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, and other such divisions.
By these—lava, truṭi, and so on—it is known, that is, inferred. [The term] "lava" refers to that [division] of the mass of lotus petals.
The term *saṃjñā* (designation). That [unit], multiplied by thirty, constitutes the nature of the *lava* and so forth; that is to say, it is multiplied by thirty and again by thirty.
"Possessing a body such as *truṭi*" and so on means possessing the designations of *truṭi*, *kalā*, *kāṣṭhā*, and so forth.
What is meant is this: thirty *lavas* constitute a *truṭi*, and thirty *truṭis* constitute a *kalā*.

Thirty *kalās* constitute one *kāṣṭhā*; thirty *kāṣṭhās* constitute one *nimeṣa*; eight *nimeṣas* constitute one *mātrā*, and that *mātrā* is one breath (*śvāsa*). The nature of the period beginning from one breath up to the end of a day is described in the twenty-seventh chapter.

The nature [of time] from the day up to the end of the four yugas has been explained in the twenty-fifth chapter; therefore, it is not discussed here. Thus, in the manner stated, "of that time" refers to its nature—whether as described at the beginning of the Tantra or in this chapter; the word "nature" is to be understood as the remainder. [This occurs] through the reflective awareness (*vimarśa*) of contemplation (*bhāvanā*). That which...
Its own nature (svarūpa) means, in short, the nature of that time; this refers to the description of the nature of time here. || 47 ||
The planets, however, being composed of consciousness, at some point in time, through the rotation of the wheel, again manifest all the elemental beings and other transformations. (48)
Various forms of such appearances are constantly seen as a proliferation;
yet by those very same [appearances], their destruction occurs, just as fire consumes its fuel by means of the wind.
O Lord, O All-pervading One, although the answer to these questions has been told by you, nevertheless, the discrimination between the phenomenal world and the Self has not yet arisen within me. (50)
How and for whom could there be this duality of birth and death? For that formless and all-pervading Lord, if he is the living soul (jīva), how could there be such a state? || 51 ||
With the two and a half verses beginning with "The planets" (grahāḥ) and ending with "O All-pervading One" (vibho), he provides the conclusion to what has been stated,
preceded by an instruction on the true nature and other attributes of the planets, as the answer to the twentieth question. In that regard, they are composed of consciousness (cinmayāḥ).
They possess forms that are inseparable from time, yet are of the nature of consciousness. "In time" means in some place or other, at some time or other, and in some location—this is the sense.
"Due to the rotation of the wheel" implies "by virtue of their respective movements. "Again and again" means repeatedly.
In the phrase "the elements and so forth" (*bhūtādi*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to the sense organs, the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), and the like; [it denotes] their modifications.
The phrase "modifications of the elements and so forth" implies they are known by the name "the manifold world" (*prapañca*). What is meant is this:

here, within the wheel of light (*jyotiścakra*), due to the movement of the planets, various modifications of the elements and so forth are perceived under the designation of the "manifold world"; thus, in this context, the remainder of the answer to the third question [is provided].
The nature of phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*) has been taught by those *grahas*. The word "eva" is used for emphasis.
Of those modifications, such as the elements (*bhūta*) and so forth—"O God," "O All-pervading One"—both are vocatives addressed to the Lord. (49)
With the second half of the verse beginning with "tathāpi" (nevertheless), he establishes the introductory framework for the introduction of another question.
In that context, "tathāpi" means "even though it has been told by me"; the words "even now" (*adhunāpi*) are to be supplied as the remainder; that is to say, "even today. (50)

With these four verses beginning with "jananam" and ending with "upadeśataḥ," he teaches the nature and other aspects of the twelvefold inquiry. Among those, by means of the half-verse beginning with "jananam," he sets forth four questions; and by means of the two half-verses beginning with "arūpasya," [he sets forth another four].

There are three questions. "Of that" means "of one's own self. "From what cause? refers to "Time and the Supreme Self," meaning Time and the Supreme Self, whose forms are without beginning or end. With the second half of the verse beginning with "the liberated," two questions are posed. Therein, "the liberated" implies "the individual soul (jīva)," and "others" implies "other individual souls. "Vā" is used in the sense of an alternative.

This is what is meant: although these individual souls (*jīva*), being each liberated in their respective forms, may logically experience the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) due to the beginninglessness of time, nevertheless, the phenomenal world now unfolds as if it were *prārabdha* (karma whose fruits have begun to bear fruit). Therefore, for the sake of this unfolding—
Whence could there be stability, or how could it exist, for that [individual soul] and the Supreme Self at that time? Is he liberated, or is he born again, or do others come into existence? (52)
Or how is the stability of the five elements within bodies, or from elsewhere?
Tell me such things as: what is the nature of the soul's arrival within bodies? 53.
By means of which hearing my mind may have no further desire to listen to another;
thus, cut through all my doubts by means of a complete instruction. (54)
Birth and death—this dyad arises from the assumption of a body due to the ripening of karma initiated by the various types of intellect mentioned previously. (55)

Just as fire resides within a heated iron ball, the existence of the individual (paru), the universe (viśva), time (kāla), and the Supreme (para) occurs precisely through their identity (tādātmya). 56.

"Are the very same liberated souls born again, or do other souls come into existence?"—this constitutes the two questions by means of the first half-verse beginning with "How" (katham). Therein, "from another" (anyataḥ) means from outside the body. By the first half-verse beginning with "In the bodies" (deheṣu) and ending with "by instruction" (upadeśataḥ), [the second question is posed].
One question is contained in a single verse. In that regard, [the questions concern] what kind [of being], in what state, and in what manner—that is to say, such things.

Here, in the phrase "and so forth" (ityādi), the word "etcetera" (ādi) refers to the subject matter of the questions concerning the method of differentiation from the living bodies, the specific states of happy rebirths, and the time of knowledge. By means of which [verse], when its answer is heard...
The words "of another question" are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 54 ||
With the verse beginning with "prāgukta" (previously mentioned), he provides the answer to the fourfold set of questions. In that regard,

due to the ripening of the karma initiated by the previously mentioned diversity of intellects, the manifestation of the individual soul (*jīva*) occurs within the body— which consists of the union of the elements and so forth— by means of that aforementioned diversity of intellects.

From *prārabdha* karma comes its fruition, and from that, its cessation. This is what is meant: through the previously mentioned diversity of intellects, there arise birth and death—this dyad resulting from the assumption of a body—from the karma of experiencing life as it has begun (*prārabdha-jīva-upalabdhi-karma*) and from its fruition. Thus, this dyad resides in the body.
"Because of the conceit of self-identity. This is what is meant: for the individual soul (jīva), the cause of birth and death is merely the conceit of identifying with the body. || 55 ||
With the verse beginning with *pratapta*, he provides the answer to the fifth question and those following.
In this context, the term *avasthā* (state) is connected both to what precedes and to what follows, according to the maxim of the crow’s eye (*kākākṣinyāya*). What is meant is this:
just as fire resides within a heated iron ball, so too do the Supreme (*para*) and the universe (*viśva*) abide together.

The answer to the fifth [question] has been stated. Regarding the sixth question—namely, "Why is there a cause for the persistence of another in the case of an insentient object?"—the answer has been stated as: "Precisely because of identity (tādātmya).
Furthermore, liberated souls never manifest from anything whatsoever.
Nor do unprecedented things arise; for the function of cognition is entirely [exhausted therein]. //57//

Just as a seal takes the form of the object it seals, or as a figure is formed from beeswax and the like, so too does the intellect (buddhi) distinguish that supreme [Self] by means of the forms of the individual soul (jīva) and other such categories. 58.
The earth alone has a clearly defined location that is always perfectly stable;
whereas for water and fire, their existence is always manifest or unmanifest, both there and elsewhere. (59)

The answer to the seventh question—namely, how the time and the subject of time can exist in mutual dependence, as previously stated—is declared to be that they exist precisely through identity (tādātmya). || 56 ||
With the two verses beginning with *muktāḥ* and ending with *tatparam*, he provides the answer to the eighth and ninth questions. In this context, *jīvāḥ* means living beings.
The particle *tu* is used for emphasis. *Āvirbhūyuḥ* means "they would manifest," because of their divine nature (*divyatvāt*). *Kutaścana*... [text fragment]

The word "hetoh" (of the reason) is to be supplied as the remainder. "Apūrva-jīvāḥ" means, in other words, "newly arisen living beings. "Buddheḥ kṛtyam" means, in other words, "the function of cognition," which is the apprehension [of things] otherwise. "Aśeṣataḥ" means, in other words, "all of that, beginning with birth. "Mudrikārūpamudrā" means a seal whose form is identical to that of a ring.
The phrase "placed upon beeswax, clay, and so forth" is to be understood as the remainder [of the sentence].

"The body of beeswax and so forth" means a body consisting of the nature of beeswax, clay, and the like. "One's own body" refers to the forms of the individual soul (jīva) and so on—that is to say, in the form of light and in the form of one's own living being. "Intellect" refers to that which has consciousness as its essential nature.
"In the specific instances of elemental conjunctions" means "perception. "Distinguishes" means "differentiates.
"That which is other than that" means different from the nature of the material cause (*upādāna*). This is what is meant:
in the case of the *madhūcchiṣṭa* (beeswax) and so forth, a seal-ring that has the same form as the ring superimposed upon it [is perceived].

In particular instances of elemental conjunction, the intellect— whose nature is the apprehension of the essence of consciousness— renders indistinguishable the true nature of its own form, which is the cause of its own body, from the beeswax and other substances that constitute its substratum, as if it were its own essential form.

Because it distinguishes its own nature from other things— by inhering in the elements which constitute its own substratum, by means of its own material cause, and by its conscious nature— it follows that all this is the function of the intellect (buddhi). || 58 ||

With these two verses beginning with "From the earth" (bhūmeḥ) and ending with "always" (sadā), he provides the answer to the tenth question. In that context, "from somewhere" means from the power of the sovereignty of the will (*icchā-śakti*).
"There" refers to on the earth; the conjunction "ca" is used for accumulation. The phrase "elsewhere than the earth" is to be understood as the ellipsis (*śeṣaḥ*).
"Abiding in both the manifest and the unmanifest" means abiding in both a manifest form and an unmanifest form. This is what is meant:

on the earth, water exists in an unmanifest form, yet immediately thereafter it is seen externally in a manifest form through evaporation; likewise, fire exists in an unmanifest form within the earth.
In sun-crystals, wood, and so forth, [fire] is seen through friction and other means;
however, the constant presence of air is observed everywhere in manifold ways.
Space, moreover, must be all-pervading, for it is always identical in nature with time. (60)
The state of those living beings within bodies is clearly fivefold;
the arrival of the souls into a body occurs through the vital seed of the mother and father. (61)
Therein, that identity with the conscious self unfolds in union;
therein, due to the cessation of the prārabdha karma, death is equivalent to sleep.
For the perfected ones (siddhas), there is never any distinction in the act of abandoning the body;
this is especially true for one who has already attained the discrimination between the body and the self within the mind.
And it is perceived in the form of external food and so forth; the remainder [of the thought] is that it appears in many ways through the distinctions of movement and the like.
"By way of identity with time" means by virtue of having time as its essence. || 60 ||
With the first half-verse beginning with "deheṣu" (in bodies), he provides the answer to the eleventh question.

In that context, "of those five elements" [means] "fivefold," with the sense of "in their respective forms" being understood as the ellipsis. This is what is meant: within bodies, earth is in a solid form, water is in a liquid form, and so on.
Fire is of the nature of heat, breath is wind, and the cavities are space.

With the two half-verses beginning with "of living beings," he provides the answer to the twelfth question. In this context, "coming" (āgati) means attainment; "tu" is used for emphasis; and "by way of virility" (vīryataḥ) means through the union of semen and blood.

The word "beginning from" (ārabhya) is to be supplied as the ellipsis. This is what is meant: the attainment of the living being (jīva) in the body begins precisely from the union of the semen and blood of the mother and father. "Tādātmyam" means the state of being the living self; it is called "saṅgatam" because it is conjoined [with the body], that is to say, due to its divine nature. Therein, in that body, it expands (jṛmbhate).
It is perceived; the word "that coming" (*āgati*) is to be supplied as the object. This means: by its own self, that is to say, through its own autonomy.

What is meant is this: when a body has been initiated from the union of the semen and blood of the mother and father, consciousness (*cit*), whose nature is unconditioned, is perceived there in that body having attained the state of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) through its autonomy.
Thus [it is said]. That is the arrival of living beings within the body. || 61 ||

With these four verses beginning with "tatra" and ending with "ayam," consisting of half-verses and so forth, he provides two answers to the question regarding the intent of the word "ādi" (and so forth) mentioned at the conclusion of the twelfth inquiry. "Tatra tatra" means in each respective body.
The perception of "I" arises from the non-cessation of *prārabdha*; with the cessation of that *prārabdha-karma*, there is its absence.

Death, for living beings, refers to the manner of exiting the body. The phrase "death is like sleep" is connected in the subsequent verse with the word "of the perfected ones" (*siddhānām*). This is what has been stated.

For one whose nature is consciousness (citsvarūpa) and who is unconditioned, there is by his own will an appearance within other bodies—both for those to be perfected (sādhya) and for those who are practitioners (sādhaka)—independently of time.
However, during the six months beginning with Puṣya, [this occurs] in the vicinity of Rāka. (64)
Death clearly indicates a good rebirth;
one who is liberated beforehand is established as stable in body, senses, and mind. (65)

When the intellect (*buddhi*), whose nature is attainment, having assumed the state of the living being (*jīva*) and gone outward through the doors of the senses, experiences objects after pervading the universe— that is the waking state (*jāgrad-avasthā*). When, however,
it has withdrawn from those respective senses and, residing in the region of the heart, remembers those respective objects— that is [the dreaming state].

Furthermore, when this [consciousness] has withdrawn even from the heart and rests in the nature of its own supreme reality-consciousness (*svaparamārthacaitanya*), then it is the state of deep sleep (*suṣupti*). Therefore,
because the nature of consciousness is identical to the nature of the intellect (*buddhi*), and because of the similarity in the non-perception [of objects] within the body and so forth, death—

In the phrase "together with sleep," it is established as a firm conviction that, apart from this mere appearance, the perception of the individual soul (jīva) actually undergoing entry into or departure from the body is like the reflection of the moon in a vessel of water; [the word] "difference" implies a difference from its previous state, namely, the time prior to the glance of the true Guru.

The word *eva* is used here for emphasis. Of that perfected one (*siddha*), through the discernment of the body and the self—that is, through the investigation into the true nature of the body and the self—once he has gone to his own state, having attained his own essential nature, there exists no difference from his previous condition at the time of the subsequent abandonment of the body. Thus it is not so.

From the discrimination between the body and the self (*dehātmaviveka*), that is, from the state of such discrimination, the relinquishing of identification with the body occurs precisely through the separation from the body—meaning the absence of ego-identification with the body. For others, namely for common folk (*pāmara*), that relinquishing of identification with the body [is achieved] by means of time; this will be explained later by the phrase "by means of time" (*asya kālataḥ*).
The connection [is as follows]:

for practitioners who, despite the grace of a true guru being present, are averse to the discrimination between the body and the self due to the force of beginningless latent impressions and because they are intent upon dull ritual actions.

Even when there is the experience of the nature of the ultimate reality obtained through the grace of the true guru, for those whose evil latent impressions (*durvāsanā*) have not been entirely liberated, [the result occurs] "in time"—that is, by the law of time, meaning from the destruction of the body. This is what is meant: for ordinary people...

For both those who are to be perfected (*sādhya*) and those who are the practitioners (*sādhaka*), the abandonment of identification with the body occurs only through the separation from the body, due to the absence of discrimination between the body and the self. During the six months beginning with Puṣya— that is, during the northern course of the sun—
starting from the second half of the eighth day of the bright fortnight near the full moon:

This means "on the lunar days ending with the first half of the eighth day of the dark fortnight. By stating that this indicates a bad rebirth (*durgati*), it is implied that dying during the southern solstice (*dakṣiṇāyana*)— specifically on the lunar days beginning from the second half of the eighth day of the dark fortnight and ending with the first half of the eighth day of the bright fortnight— indicates a bad rebirth.

It has been stated: "Siddha" means one who has realized the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The particle *tu* indicates a distinction. Because he was previously liberated, for that reason, the death (*nidhana*) of this Siddha—the separation from the body—occurs at all times, in every place, and in every manner;
this is the remainder of the sense. It is just as it is during the northern course of the sun (*uttarāyaṇa*).
Since, by that [knowledge], his destruction is forever and in every respect thus [non-existent],
this one is indeed liberated while living, because he manifests the state of a Sugati.
O Lord, although all living beings are equally possessed of bodies, tell me: what is the cause of the constant and manifold diversity of their intellects?
Just as there is a difference in the taste of waters even though they are equally situated on the earth,
so too [the difference in the qualities of the elements] arises by virtue of their substrates, and that indeed occurs through karma alone.
Just as fire residing within a *aśvattha* tree cannot be obtained by any other means whatsoever without the exertion of rubbing dry wood; (69)

"At the time of death near a mountain peak, in sacred fields such as Vārāṇasī, and by means of methods such as falling from a cliff"—this is the meaning of "in whatever way. The word *eva* (thus) is used for emphasis; *tu* (but) is used for distinction.
This is established. || 66 ||

With the verse beginning "In the state of possessing a body" (dehavattve), the Goddess asks with supporting arguments for the cause of the manifold nature of the intellect (buddhi) of living beings; therein, the word "sarvataḥ" implies "in every way," and "O Lord" (prabho) is an address to the Sovereign. || 67 ||
With the verse beginning "Because of being situated on the stages" (*bhūmiṣṭhatva*), he explains this further with an illustration.

In that context, "by virtue of the basis" means by virtue of the specific location of the example; that is to say, by virtue of the specific nature of the subject of the analogy (*dārṣṭāntika*). What is meant is this: although they are equal in being situated on the stages...

Just as there is a difference in the taste of waters due to the nature of their substrates, even though they are equally water, so too, although bodies are alike in their physical nature, a diversity of qualities arises in the intellect (buddhi) due to the specific nature of its substrate.
Immediately following this, in response to the doubt as to by what the specific nature of the substrate is produced, he says: "And that..."
The remainder [of the sentence] is that by means of actions alone, both that [result] and that particular substratum (*āśrayaviśeṣa*) are produced there.
By "actions" is meant, in the case of the illustration, by the effects of water such as taste and so forth; in the case of the illustrated subject, by the effects of the intellect (*buddhi*).
This is what is being said: by means of tastes and so forth, [the specific qualities of] waters [are produced].
Due to the influence of specific locations, a particular nature arises for the intellect through its very effects. || 68 ||

With these three verses beginning with "yathā" and ending with "svasvarūpakam," he teaches the proposition— along with illustrative examples— concerning the ritual procedure (*vidhi*) and so forth, which must be received from the mouth of the Guru alone. In that context,
the phrase "situated in the *aśvattha*" refers to a specific [tree] rather than a general mention of trees.

This indicates a specific qualification of the Guru as well. "By others" refers to cutting and so forth; the ellipsis is "in a certain place and time. Regarding the phrase "the activity of dry churning," the word "dry" (śuṣka) implies that the Guru's intent is directed toward the body and other such things, rather than the discrimination between the body and the Self. By the term "activity of churning" (mathanavyāpṛti),...
Without obtaining a true Guru, no disciple whatsoever can ever attain self-knowledge through such practices as worship and the like; this is a universal and eternal proposition. (70)
Just as water situated beneath the earth is obtained through digging,
so too is one's own true nature attained by resorting to a true guru.

For one who has attained the true nature of the self through service at the feet of the True Guru, what other excellence, difficult for others to obtain, could there be—except for the embodiment of Truth? (72)
Beauty of form, freedom from doubt, contentment, fullness, a heart moist with compassion, and a mind that does not take as its object passion or hatred. || 73 ||
Ease of attainment, freedom from pride, constant discipline of character, gratitude, truthfulness, and the turning away from concern for others. (74)

And he indicates the intended meaning (*tātparya*): "of someone" means, in short, of one who is complete in the characteristics described [in the text] beginning with "by the four initial ones" in the first chapter; "my promise" is the ellipsis, meaning the promise of the Lord (*īśvara*). "From all sides" (*viśvataḥ*) refers to the cause. "One's own essential nature" (*svasvarūpaka*) is the knowledge of the Self (*ātmajñāna*). || 71 ||

With this verse beginning with "sadguroḥ," the Goddess asks about the specific nature of one who has attained their true self through service to the True Guru; here, "difficult for others to obtain" means difficult for those who have not obtained knowledge exactly as it is.

With these nine verses beginning with "beauty" (*ābhirūpyam*) and ending with "proceeds" (*pravartate*), he teaches, as a response to that [question], the forty-seven characteristics of those who possess self-control, as well as the absence thereof in others. Among these, by means of the verse beginning with "beauty":

The seven characteristics: therein, *ābhirūpya* means the state of being present on all sides, that is to say, the nature of the entire self; or it means beauty. *Asandeha* means even by means of conceptualizations and scriptural traditions; that is to say, [the absence of doubt].
*Santoṣa* [means] fulfillment through one's own experience, by virtue of having the nature of fullness, and because of being free from dependence.
A heart moist with compassion, a state of mind that finds no footing for passion and hatred—this is what is meant by "non-distinctness.
(73) By the verse beginning with "ease of attainment," the six characteristics [of the Mahāyāna] are presented. (74)

Rectitude, freedom from greed for possessions, lack of excessive attachment to sense objects, absence of prolixity and meanness, and a nature characterized by a depth of disposition that is not overly fathomless. (75)
Avoiding the power for idle talk, abandoning useless activities, being devoid of frivolous amusements, and not associating with those of crooked minds. (76)
The curiosity to contemplate and explain the purpose of human endeavor, the power of non-stealing, faith, and reflection upon the world beyond; || 77 ||
The habit of engaging in conversation regarding the majesty of the worship and hymns of the deities, the constant avoidance of sins, and a perpetual eagerness for performing meritorious deeds. (78)
Abstaining from censuring others, freedom from passion, lack of longing, absence of greed, lack of agitation, and being free from dullness; || 79 ||

By the verse beginning with "straightforwardness" (*ārjavam*), a set of six characteristics is presented. Among these, *avittalaulya* is the absence of dependence on others for the sake of wealth. *Viṣayānatisaṅgitā* is the absence of excessive attachment to sense objects—that is, for one who has attained perfection, there is no engagement with sense objects out of passion, except for the mere maintenance of the body.

"May it be so"—this is the sense. "Not requiring long preparation" means that it does not take much time to perform; "not having a very deep nature" means that it is easy to access. Thus ends verse 75.

By the verse beginning with "vṛthā," four characteristics are stated. Among these, by the word "vṛthā" (in vain), it is expressed that [the action] is of no utility for either seen or unseen results. "With crooked minds" means with deceitful hearts. || 76 ||

By the verse beginning with *puruṣārtha*, the six characteristics are presented. Therein, the syntactical connection is as follows: the statement of the purpose of human goals (*puruṣārtha*), the composition of the inquiry into human goals, and the curiosity regarding human goals—namely, the statement of the purpose of human goals, the undertaking of the inquiry into human goals, and the curiosity concerning human goals. [The power of] non-stealing (*asteya-śakti*).

Incapacity for the act of theft; faithfulness, meaning conviction in the meanings of the scriptures; reflection on the next world, meaning contemplation of the nature and qualities of the Supreme Being, which is to say, the practice of the sacred traditions (āgama). || 77 ||

By means of this verse beginning with "devatā," five characteristics are presented. Regarding that, the construction of the text is as follows: the habit of worshipping deities, the habit of praising [them], and the habit of conversing about the majesty of the deities—namely, the habit of conversing about the worship of the deities and the habit of conversing about the majesty of the deities. [This applies to] sins...

This refers to prohibited actions and those actions arising from malevolent rites (*abhicāra*) and the like—meaning those which are harmful to oneself and others—and to the performance of merit and the performance of what is beneficial for oneself and others;
that is to say, for the sake of ending the afflictions of cyclic existence for living beings and for the sake of establishing their true nature. || 78 ||

By means of the verse beginning with "parastavana," there is a set of six characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-ṣaṭka*). Among these, "in the praising of others and in censuring others" refers to both the praising of others and the censuring of others. || 79 ||
Not concealing one's own devotees and concealing those who are not devotees;
[the practice of] the Guru, the Vidyā, the Āgamas, and right conduct; and their praise and propagation. (80)
These signs of accomplishment certainly manifest for those who possess self-mastery;
they do not appear for others, and such people even feel aversion toward them.
Listen, I shall declare that duty for one who has attained the majesty of his own self, who has cast off all the ignorance, lack of discernment, and delusion pertaining to worldly existence. (82)
Observing the customs of place, time, and family as ordained by his gurus, kings, and others,
he maintains a smiling countenance, being ever eager for both performing worship and witnessing it.

The instability of the body, as well as ignorance, and the activities that perish in an instant due to time—these are difficult for the mind of a kinsman to transcend, yet they remain situated within one's own collection [of thoughts]. (84)
One should repeatedly reflect upon the capacity of one's own senses and the actions performed by them, and thus restrain the mind that is not inclined toward the auspicious.

By the verse beginning with "agopanam" (non-concealment), seven characteristics are indicated. Among these, "agopanam" means the non-concealment of the scriptures (*āgama*) and so forth; whereas "gopanam" refers, as before, to the concealment of the scriptures and so forth. Furthermore, there is the praise of the teacher, the mantra (*vidyā*), the scriptures, and the traditional practices (*ācāra*).
The Hymn || 80 ||

These forty-seven characteristics have been declared. The word "tu" (but) is used in the sense of distinction; "eva" (indeed) is used for emphasis. "Tān" refers to those possessed of self-knowledge; "te" refers to those devoid of self-knowledge. || 81 ||

With these nine verses beginning with "That" (tat) and ending with "always" (sadā), he teaches the sequence of conduct for those possessed of self-knowledge. In this context, "that duty" refers to the duty of those possessed of self-knowledge;
[he is] one who has cast off all the ignorance and lack of discrimination that constitute the folly of saṃsāra, and who has cast off all saṃsāra.

The construction of the text is as follows: "One who has cast off all ignorance" (*nirastāśeṣamaukhyavān*), "one who has cast off all nescience" (*nirastāśeṣājñānavān*), and "one who has cast off all lack of discrimination" (*nirastāśeṣāvivekavān*). Transmigration is the cognition of something as that which it is not; ignorance is the conceit of something as that which it is not; and nescience is the absence of the cognition of that [reality] as itself.

The loss of that discernment is non-discrimination (*aviveka*). Regarding the phrase "the customs of place, time, family, and conduct": this refers to the customs of place (*deśācāra*), the customs of time (*kālācāra*), the customs appropriate to one's state (*avasthānuguṇācāra*), and the customs of family (*kulācāra*).
These are those established by the Guru, the King, and so forth. In the expression "Guru, King, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) [refers to] the Guru in the first chapter.

The subject of worship mentioned by the verse beginning with "tadagrataḥ" [is as follows]. In the phrase "rājādīn," the word "ādi" (and so forth) refers to persons of similar status. "Instability of the body by its very nature" means that one should not waste time here on gambling, women, sleep, or idle talk. (p. 736)
One should cause [the disciple] to proceed by means of the worship of deities, recitation of mantras (japa), yoga, hymns of praise, and so forth. || 86 ||
One should spend one's time incessantly through the compassionate words of the guru, discourses, hymns, and the study of the scriptures; one should not speak of the faults of others. (87)
Whether the guru is present before one's eyes or out of sight, one should praise and bow to him,
truly extolling his virtues, the excellence of his grace, and his meritorious sovereignty.
By avoiding passion, greed, intoxication, anger, evil, and slander; by constant practice of contentment and conduct; and likewise through tranquility, knowledge, and other such qualities. || 89 ||
Moderation in food, moderation in speech, dwelling in solitude, constant reflection, and purification of one's own self—these are the perpetual duties of those who possess self-mastery. 90.

The words ending in the accusative case are to be construed with the word "vimṛśet" (one should reflect upon) in the subsequent verse. "Other activities" means those that are useless for both seen and unseen purposes. "Fallen from time" means momentary;
"difficult to transgress even by the minds of kinsmen" means difficult to be disregarded by kinsmen, as well as by kings and others.

"From time," meaning from the moment they have fallen [into such states], referring to persons and so forth; "of impure nature," meaning having an impure intrinsic character. Regarding the phrase "from gambling, women, sleep, and slander," the word *dyūta* (gambling) refers to both lifeless gambling and gambling with living beings; as for the word *strī* (woman), however—
The term "except" (*vyatirikta*) refers to objects other than one's lawful wife (*dharmapatnī*). The word "sleeping" (*svāpa*) refers to instances other than those already obtained.

The word "disputation" (*vāda*) refers to subjects such as *jalpa* and *vitaṇḍā*. In the phrase "by means of praise and so forth" (*stavādinā*), the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) refers to subjects such as circumambulation and prostration. [This applies] to the guru.
By means of the compassionate speech, hymns, and study of the scriptures of the Guru; by the Guru’s compassion, the Guru’s conversations, and the Guru’s discourses;

by the hymns to the Guru and by the study of the scriptures obtained from the Guru; and by the qualities of that [Guru], that is, the qualities of the Guru—in this verse and in the following verse, these are the words ending in the instrumental case.

The connection is with the word "stuvīta" (one should praise). "Tatkṛpādhikyaiḥ" means by the excellence of his grace. Regarding the phrase "tadguṇaiḥ" and so forth, the word "guroḥ" (of the guru) should be supplied as an ellipsis for the three words ending in the instrumental case and for the two words ending in the instrumental case in the following verse. In that context, "satyataḥ" means by truth.

"By means of speech, mind, and action" means in a single form. In the phrase "by knowledge and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to giving and other such acts. "Constant reflection" (nityācintā) means reflection on the essential nature of the sixteen Nityās.
"Purification of one's own self" (svātmaśuddhi) means the purification of one's own speech, mind, and body. || 90 ||
Having placed the previously mentioned twelve [deities] in the middle according to the prescribed rite,
one should place the Yoni in the center of that, the goddess Lalitā behind it, and the Gurus behind her.
On the two sides are the eight weapons, and in the corners all around in sequence;
there, outside of that, in all twelve [spaces], are Kāmeśvarī and the others.

Or one should worship another twelve [deities] with those very Nityā-vidyās, or with the vidyās bearing their respective names; one should worship them along with the ritual preparation of the arghya offering.
One should recite the three junctions (sandhyās) sixty times with the vidyā of that day;
for him, there shall be no other duty, such as the obligatory (nitya) or occasional (naimittika) rites.

With these six verses beginning with "pūrvokta" and ending with "abhūt," he teaches the sequence of the worship of Lalitā for those who possess self-mastery, that is, the *jīvanmuktas*. In this context,
it is between the previously mentioned twelve-spoked [mandala] and the twelve-spoked [mandala] taught in the nineteenth chapter.
"Of equal measure in the middle" means that its measurement is neither less nor more than that of the circle situated in the center of all.

"The womb" (yoni) refers to the triangle whose apex faces oneself. "In the middle of that" means in the center of the womb. "Behind" means in the space between the front line and the circular line of the womb. "The gurus" means in the form of goddesses. "On both sides."

In the two spaces between the two side-lines and the circular lines, one should worship the eight weapons in reverse order from the exterior as described in the chapter on worship (pūjā-paṭala). In the corners— that is,
in the triangles starting from the tip of the central *yonis*— one should worship Kāmeśvarī and the others, surrounding them in sequence, following the clockwise order.
[Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Vajreśvarī]. "Outside of that," meaning on the twelve spokes;

"the others" refers to those distinct from Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Vajreśvarī. "By their respective Nityā-mantras" means by those taught in the third chapter. "Eva" (thus) is used for emphasis or as a particle. "Vā" (or).
Regarding the visualization: by means of those names of ignorance (*avidyā*) which were taught in the nineteenth chapter—meaning those very [names]—those [deities] are eternal. This is what is meant:
having drawn a twelve-spoked wheel according to the procedure taught in the nineteenth chapter, [one should place the deity] facing oneself in the center of the circle within that [wheel].
Having drawn an equilateral triangle, one should place Lalitā in its center; within the space between the front line of that triangle and the circular line, one should place the Lords and Śaktis;
and in the two spaces between the two circular lines on both sides of those [lines], one should likewise place them.
By proceeding counter-clockwise from the wind [direction] and so forth, one should place the weapons in the three corners starting from the front of the central *yoni*;

then, Kāmeśvarī, Bhagamālinī, and Vajreśvarī; and outside of that, on the twelve spokes, the other twelve Nityās, either with their respective *Nityā-vidyās* or by their name-mantras (*nāma-vidyās*), proceeding clockwise.

"One should sacrifice" refers to that [sacrifice] of one who possesses the Self. In the phrase "the obligatory, occasional, and so forth," the word "and so forth" (ādi) refers to optional rites (*kāmya*). In the midst of that—that is, in the center of the twelve-spoked [mandala]—one should either establish the nine-yoni [figure] in its center or [perform the rite] with the powers (*śakti*) situated therein.
One should worship, as before, through both modes by means of a single yoga. || 95 ||
This rule has been declared for the sake of perpetual accomplishment throughout one's entire life,
by means of which even all those who have attained perfection became masters of their own selves.
O Supreme Goddess, all this has been told to you in this Tantra; by the realization of which, the state of being attains the oneness of us two.
One should bestow this tantra, however, never upon one who is not a devotee,
nor upon one who is not a disciple, nor upon one who is hypocritical, nor upon one who is secretive and of ill-repute.
One should not give to an atheist, nor to a greedy person, nor to one who is arrogant;
nor to a sinner, nor to one who is wealthy, nor to one who is incompetent or divisive.

The phrase "as stated in the fifteenth chapter" is the ellipsis [to be supplied]. "Or" (*vā*) signifies an alternative. "Together with the powers residing therein" is the ellipsis. As before, by moving from the front (the tip) in a clockwise direction, according to either of the two methods, one should—within the center of the twelve-spoked [mandala]—draw either a simple *yoni* or a ninefold *yoni*; this is the meaning. For the sake of accomplishment (*siddhi*).

The word "of self-knowledge" (*ātmajñānasya*) is to be supplied [to the genitive]. "Of all" means of those who have attained self-knowledge—that is to say, those who have attained the *Śrīvidyā*. "Of those perfected in yoga" means of those perfected in the *ājñā* (the Command).
By which procedure: he is one among these four types of perfected ones; he is possessed of his own Self.
One who possesses knowledge of one's own true nature. || 96 ||

With these three verses beginning with *samastam* and ending with *bhedinaḥ*, [the author] indicates the fruit for one who knows the meaning of the Tantra, as well as the thirteen defects of the recipient to be avoided when bestowing the Tantra. In that context, *parameśvarī* is an address to the Goddess.

By reflecting upon which—referring to one who knows the meaning of the *tantra*—one attains oneness with us; that is, one becomes the very nature of the non-duality of Śiva and Śakti. By the word "that" (*tat*), the experiential power (*anubhāva*) of the *tantra* is expressed.
The particle "tu" is used for emphasis, meaning "at any time," even in times of adversity. "For hypocrisy" means for the sake of false conduct.
"To one who is secretive and of an unrighteous disposition" means to one who is both hidden and of an unrighteous character;

"to one who does not beg" means to an atheist; "for wealth" means for the sake of material gain; "to the unskilled" means to the dull-witted; "to the divisive" means to one whose nature is to cause dissension. || 99 ||
He who, having properly grasped this entire Tantra along with the sixteen Nityās by means of Śakti, worships it according to the rules, is a portion of myself. (100)
The pervasion consisting of the Śiva-principle has been correctly described;
by the constant polishing of this [pervasion] within the mind, that very principle is made one's own self. (101)
Thus ends, having been fully considered, the thirty-sixth chapter titled "The Self-Description" in the *Śrīkādimata*, the King of Tantras among the sixteen *Nityātantras*. Oṃ tatsat.
|| 36 || Om tat sat.

With the verse beginning with "He who [knows] the Tantra," he teaches the fruit for one who has obtained the meaning of the Tantra according to the prescribed rule. In that context, "according to the rule" means following the sequence taught for obligatory (*nitya*), occasional (*naimittika*), and other rites; "devoted to worship" refers to one who is intent on that practice.
"A portion of Me" means one whose nature is consciousness (*cit-svarūpa*), that is to say, the Lord (*īśvara*). || 100 ||

Thus, in the commentary named *Manoramā*, composed by Subhagānandanātha under the title *Prapañcasārasiṃharājaprakāśa*, on the complete tantra known as the venerable *Kādimata* among the sixteen *Nityātantras*.
The thirty-sixth chapter, which is dedicated to revealing the ultimate nature of the deities, the teacher, the disciple, the phenomenal world, and so forth, has been fully expounded. Oṃ tat sat.
The number of verses in this thirty-sixth chapter, which consists of the Śiva-tattva, should be known as three hundred and sixty-seven and a half explanatory verses. (267)
In this tantra called the Śrīmat Kādimata,
there are nine hundred and thirty-one chapters.
"Enjoyment, land, sweetness, fortune, fragrance, half-perfection, the assembly, and the glory of the gods"— thus, by the count of twenty-one syllables.
In that *Kādima-tantra*, the yantras are described;
there, however, is the ocean named Pariṇāmāhva, which is a mass of merit from the southern region.
Infinite mechanical devices arising from the primordial syllable have been produced together with the number of commentaries in the Śrīkādimata Tantra.
The teacher of the King of Kashmir was Śrīkaṇṭheśa, the lord of the twice-born, who was said to be twelve thousand years less fifty.
Once, having come by his own divine play to behold Rāmasetu,
he was graced by that very Lord Nṛsiṃha on the way.
Because he has studied the mantras,
he has composed this delightful commentary on the Kādimata among those eternal [texts], entitled *Manoramā*.
By the command of Śubhagānandanātha, [the author] composed the remaining chapters up to the twenty-second chapter.
The teacher Prakāśānanda, a disciple of those fourteen [masters],
previously received that commentary from the excellent king Sundara according to the traditional lineage.
And thus this commentary on the King of Tantras, the *Manoramā*, is completed. Oṃ.
